title: When and How Should Patients Be Informed About Clinicians’ or Organizations’ Sale of a Clinical Practice to a Private Equity Buyer?
case:
SB arrives for a regularly scheduled appointment with Dr W, their primary care physician for the past 25 years. While in the waiting room, SB overhears office staff members talking about Dr W’s practice being acquired by a private equity (PE) firm and what that might mean for their jobs.
When SB is taken to an examination room and Dr W enters, SB asks, “Dr W, are you planning to retire and sell your practice? If so, what does that mean for me?”
Dr W considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
SB arrived at Dr W’s office for their regularly scheduled appointment. Dr W had been SB’s primary care physician for the past 25 years, and the familiarity of the office was comforting. As SB sat in the waiting room, they couldn’t help but overhear a conversation between two office staff members nearby. The staff were quietly discussing rumors that Dr W’s practice was being acquired by a private equity (PE) firm, speculating about what such a change might mean for their own employment and the daily workings of the clinic.

After a few minutes, SB was called in and led to an examination room. A short while later, Dr W entered, greeting SB as usual. Looking concerned, SB immediately asked, “Dr W, are you planning to retire and sell your practice? If so, what does that mean for me?”

Dr W paused, considering not only how to address SB’s direct question but also how best to explain what the possible changes in ownership could mean for SB’s care, medical records, and the future of the patient-physician relationship.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians assess the impact of a private equity acquisition of their clinical practice on patients and address related ethical concerns during negotiations?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize patients’ interests when considering the sale of a clinical practice, evaluating the transaction’s impact on the quality and cost of patient care.

Physicians have an ethical obligation to address patients’ concerns during negotiations, particularly clarifying how the private equity entity will handle the storage, confidentiality, and use of patient records, as well as the management of medical records if the physician departs.

It is advisable for physicians to consult with qualified health care legal counsel prior to negotiations to obtain professional guidance and to consider alternative arrangements that may better serve the interests of patients and the community.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians inform patients about changes in practice policies and procedures under new management, as well as the impact on costs and quality of care, following a change in ownership of the clinical practice?
keypoints: Physicians should inform patients of changes in practice management through verbal or written communication and be prepared to address patients’ questions.

After the transaction is completed, physicians should provide an informational handout detailing changes in policies and procedures under the new management, including scheduling, fees, insurance coverage, and staffing.

Physicians should respond honestly to patients’ concerns regarding costs and quality of care, although they are not required to proactively disclose the impact of private equity acquisition on these aspects.
If the new management structure may jeopardize continuity of care for acute patients, physicians must disclose and address these issues immediately.

When considering changes in ownership or control of a practice, physicians must take patients’ interests into account to ensure that patients’ needs for continuity and quality of care are not compromised.
Patients should be informed that they always have the right to change their clinician, and referral assistance should be provided as needed.

ethical_issues.question: When a clinical practice is acquired by a private equity firm, how should physicians ensure that the storage, confidentiality, and use of patients’ health records comply with ethical standards and inform patients accordingly?
keypoints: Physicians should explicitly inform patients about the details of medical record management mechanisms, especially in circumstances involving planned departure or changes in practice ownership.

If the practice is acquired by a private equity firm, physicians must ensure that the storage, confidentiality, and use of patients’ health records comply with ethical standards, and obtain patient authorization for record transfer when necessary.

Physicians should disclose to patients any policy or procedural changes resulting from the private equity acquisition and explain how these changes may affect patients’ care or their continued access to services.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Clinician relations with industry
title: What Are Physicians’ Duties to Patients When They Sell Their Practices?
case: Dr W owns their community-based family practice, recently turned 65 years old, and will soon retire after 35 years of caring for patients. Dr W is approached with a lucrative buyout offer from a private equity (PE) company interested in primary care patient panel acquisition. Dr W is unfamiliar with the company and its practices and only has a few weeks to accept or decline the offer. Dr W wonders what they owe their many long-term patients as their career ends and how those patients will be affected by the change as they consider how to respond to the offer.
case_rewrite:
Dr. W has spent the past 35 years building strong, trusting relationships with patients in their community-based family practice. Now 65 and preparing for retirement, Dr. W is approached by a private equity (PE) company with a highly attractive buyout offer for the practice, focused on acquiring primary care patient panels. The PE firm is unfamiliar to Dr. W, who has limited information about its business practices and little time—just a few weeks—to decide whether to accept or decline the offer.

As Dr. W contemplates this pivotal decision, they are acutely aware of the responsibility they hold toward their many long-term patients. Dr. W wonders how the sale might affect the continuity and quality of care their patients have come to expect, especially under new ownership with clear profit-driven motives. Questions weigh heavily: What obligations do they have to ensure that patients are protected from any adverse consequences of such a transition? What steps should be taken to safeguard the clinical autonomy of the physicians who will remain after the sale? And how best to communicate the impending changes to patients, including information about Dr. W’s retirement and the procedures for managing medical records?

Faced with these ethical dilemmas, Dr. W considers whether there are ways to include protections in the sale agreement, ensuring that clinical decisions will remain in the hands of medical professionals, free from undue financial influence. Alternatives such as selling to a physician-led group or an academic medical center also cross Dr. W’s mind, as these might better uphold the standard of care their patients deserve. Regardless of the outcome, Dr. W knows they must inform patients about the ownership change, their own retirement, and how to access or transfer medical records, in full compliance with relevant legal requirements and patient rights.

As the deadline for a decision approaches, Dr. W reflects deeply on how to balance the financial and practical realities of retirement with their enduring ethical and legal responsibilities to their patients’ health and well-being.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr. W ensure that the quality of patient care is not compromised by the profit-driven motives of the private equity company when selling their practice?
keypoints: Dr W can establish protective mechanisms through contractual provisions to ensure that the clinical decision-making of remaining physicians is not influenced by the profit-driven motives of the private equity firm.
Dr W should consider alternative options, such as physician-owned medical groups or academic medical centers, to safeguard the quality of patient care.

Dr W has a legal and ethical obligation to inform patients about the change in practice ownership and the procedures for accessing or transferring medical records, thereby upholding patients’ rights to informed consent and autonomous choice.
Regardless of whether the practice is sold, physicians’ moral and legal responsibilities remain constant, with the health and well-being of patients taking precedence above all else.

ethical_issues.question: During the transition of practice ownership, how should Dr. W fulfill their ethical and legal responsibilities to patients, particularly regarding the disclosure of ownership changes and the transfer of medical records?
keypoints: Dr W has a legal and ethical obligation to inform patients about the change in practice ownership, their retirement, and the procedures for accessing or transferring medical records.
Dr W should proactively disclose information regarding the new owner in order to respect patient autonomy and assist patients in making informed decisions.
Some states require explicit patient consent for the transfer of medical records to a new treating physician; Dr W must comply with the relevant legal requirements.
Dr W’s primary responsibility is to prioritize the health and well-being of patients, regardless of any changes in practice ownership.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Dr W’s impending retirement and the potential sale of their practice to a private equity firm, how should such firms ethically balance their profit motives with respect for physicians’ clinical autonomy and the obligation to maintain high-quality patient care for Dr W’s long-term patients?
keypoints: The fundamental ethical and legal duty of physicians is to prioritize the well-being of patients above all commercial or contractual interests.

Dr. W can establish protective mechanisms through contractual provisions to ensure that the clinical decision-making of remaining physicians is not compromised by the profit-driven objectives of the private equity firm.
During sale negotiations, Dr. W may seek to secure sufficient equity stakes to retain partial operational control, thereby safeguarding the quality of patient care.

Physicians should continue to make decisions based on the individual needs of patients, resisting pressures to overprovide or underprovide care in order to meet financial targets or operational metrics.

Physicians must understand and comply with federal and state laws regarding fraud, kickbacks, and non-physician influence on clinical decision-making to ensure that patient health and welfare remain paramount.

title: How Should Surgical Care Team Members Protect Incarcerated Patients From Carceral Officers’ Surveillance or Intrusion?
case:
BB is a 40-year-old woman who presented as a high-level trauma code to the emergency department after she was assaulted in her prison. BB is shackled, naked save for limited paper drape coverage, and accompanied by Officer G, an employee of BB’s prison. Dr ED evaluates BB in the trauma bay, a large and accessible emergency department room stocked especially for acute trauma, with Officer G looking on.
BB is hypotensive and tachycardic, so Dr ED administers 2 units of packed red blood cells. BB’s vital signs return to normal in response to the blood, so she is sent for emergent CT imaging, which reveals active extravasation from a grade 4 splenic injury. While still in the CT scanner, BB becomes hypotensive and is rushed to the operating room for an exploratory laparotomy by a surgical team led by Dr S.
Dr S asks Officer G to remove BB’s handcuffs so they can utilize electrocautery and position BB properly for the procedure. Officer G responds, “I do not have clearance to remove cuffs,” so Dr S uses bone cutters to break them. As Dr S and the team perform BB’s operation, Officer G makes multiple requests for “status updates” on BB’s condition. Upon completion of the surgery, over Dr S’s objection, Officer G re-cuffs BB to her gurney rails. Officer G accompanies BB as she is transported to the surgical intensive care unit (SICU).
Dr S wonders what they should do to protect BB’s privacy and dignity, at least while she is in the SICU.
case_rewrite:
BB, a 40-year-old woman, arrives at the emergency department as a high-level trauma code after being assaulted inside her prison. She enters the trauma bay—an expansive, well-equipped room designed for acute emergencies—shackled and wearing nothing except a scant paper drape. Officer G, an employee of BB’s prison, stands by her side throughout. Dr ED immediately begins assessing BB, while Officer G observes the entire process.

BB is found to be hypotensive and tachycardic. In response, Dr ED quickly administers two units of packed red blood cells. BB’s vital signs stabilize after the transfusion, allowing her to be sent for an emergent CT scan. The imaging reveals she has a grade 4 splenic injury with active bleeding. While still inside the CT scanner, BB’s blood pressure drops again, prompting the team to rush her to the operating room for emergency surgery.

In the operating room, Dr S leads the surgical team. Preparing BB for an exploratory laparotomy, Dr S asks Officer G to remove BB’s handcuffs so the team can safely use electrocautery and position her appropriately for the procedure. Officer G refuses, stating, “I do not have clearance to remove cuffs.” Faced with this barrier, Dr S resorts to using bone cutters to break the handcuffs, ensuring the operation can proceed.

Throughout the surgery, Officer G remains nearby and repeatedly requests “status updates” on BB’s condition. Once the operation concludes, Dr S objects when Officer G insists on re-cuffing BB to the rails of her gurney, but Officer G proceeds regardless. Officer G then accompanies BB as she is transported to the surgical intensive care unit (SICU), remaining present at her side.

After the surgery, Dr S considers how best to safeguard BB’s privacy and dignity, particularly during her recovery in the SICU.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance patient privacy rights with safety requirements when correctional officers request updates on a patient’s medical condition?
keypoints: Physicians have no obligation to disclose details of the patient’s medical condition to correctional officers unless there is a threat to safety.
Patients, including those who are incarcerated, have the right to the privacy of their health information, which must not be disclosed without authorization.
Physicians should clearly articulate the patient’s needs in order to uphold their rights.
When correctional officers request health information, physicians should ask them to step out of earshot to protect the patient’s privacy.

ethical_issues.question: How should conflicts between security measures such as shackling and medical needs be managed when providing care to incarcerated patients to ensure they receive appropriate treatment?
keypoints: Physicians should recognize when shackles interfere with medical care and, based on the principle of beneficence, request that correctional officers remove handcuffs to facilitate examinations and surgical procedures, ensuring the patient receives appropriate treatment.
If physical restraints impede proper care, custody officials have the responsibility to identify alternative measures to meet the patient’s care needs.
Physicians should maintain clear communication with both the patient and correctional authorities to ensure that the patient’s rights are upheld.

tags: Informed consent/Capacity, competency for making decisions
title: How Should Physicians Manage Traumatic Injuries Sustained During Incarceration?
case:
CC is a 43-year-old patient who presented as a high-level trauma code to the emergency department after an altercation in his prison. Epidural hematoma was suspected immediately upon his arrival, and, during diagnostic imaging, CC became obtunded. A neurosurgeon, Dr N, was consulted and CC was taken emergently to the operating room for a craniotomy and transferred to the neurosurgical intensive care unit (ICU). A tracheostomy and percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube were placed for prolonged ventilatory support and enteral nutrition.
CC regains capacity to interact meaningfully with others after 2 months in the ICU. CC is weaned from the ventilator, continues to breathe room air via tracheostomy-mask; CC’s central line is removed, but a PEG tube and Foley catheter remain in place. CC is anxious and agitated and does not remember why they are in the hospital. Dr R, a surgical fellow, wonders how to respond to CC’s questions about their injuries, surgical recovery, and returning to prison.
case_rewrite:
CC, a 43-year-old incarcerated individual, arrived at the emergency department as a high-level trauma code following a violent altercation in the prison. Upon arrival, the medical team immediately suspected an epidural hematoma. While undergoing diagnostic imaging, CC became unresponsive. Dr N, the neurosurgeon on call, was consulted and promptly took CC to the operating room for a craniotomy. After surgery, CC was transferred to the neurosurgical intensive care unit (ICU), where a tracheostomy and a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube were placed to provide prolonged ventilatory support and nutrition.

Over the course of two months in the ICU, CC gradually regained the ability to interact meaningfully with others and started to show clear signs of recovering decision-making capacity. CC was successfully weaned from the ventilator and now breathes room air through a tracheostomy mask. The central line was removed, though the PEG tube and Foley catheter remain in place for ongoing medical needs. CC appears anxious and agitated, expressing confusion and repeatedly asking why they are hospitalized. CC does not recall the events leading to the injury or the hospital admission.

Dr R, a surgical fellow, is present during these interactions and considers how best to address CC's questions about the nature of the injuries, the surgical interventions performed, the recovery process, and the eventual return to the correctional facility. Dr R is mindful of the need to respect CC’s autonomy and privacy, ensuring that all necessary information is provided for CC to participate fully in medical decision-making. Dr R is also aware of the importance of maintaining a trauma-informed approach, being transparent about all procedures, and providing CC with opportunities to make choices regarding care. As the time for CC’s discharge and transition back to custody approaches, the surgical team, including Dr R, is working with hospital social workers and coordinating with prison staff to establish a comprehensive medical follow-up and to facilitate access to mental health resources to support CC’s ongoing recovery and reintegration.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians preserve patient autonomy and privacy in the medical care of incarcerated individuals?
keypoints: Patients who are incarcerated legally retain their right to make medical decisions, and physicians must ensure that the patient or their surrogate receives timely access to the information necessary to exercise medical autonomy.

Capacity assessment should be a dynamic process, wherein physicians continuously evaluate the patient’s cognitive status and preferences through empathic interviewing and open-ended questioning to uphold the patient’s dignity and autonomy.

Implied consent may be applied during emergency treatment; however, subsequent care requires involvement of a substitute decision maker to ensure respect for the patient’s medical decision-making rights.
Correctional staff must not participate in medical decision-making discussions to avoid conflicts of interest and to safeguard the patient’s autonomy.

Physicians should ensure transparency by identifying all healthcare personnel during each encounter, explaining the rationale for treatments performed or recommended, and providing patients with opportunities to make choices.

During sensitive examinations or wound assessments, physicians should inform patients of the expected procedures in advance and provide the maximum privacy possible while maintaining clinician safety, thereby protecting the patient’s right to privacy.

ethical_issues.question: How can trauma-informed care be implemented in emergency surgical management to avoid retraumatization?
keypoints: Clinicians should identify signs of trauma and avoid retraumatizing environments by implementing trauma-informed care through psychiatric screening and respecting patient boundaries.
Ensure transparency and patient autonomy by identifying all healthcare personnel during each encounter, explaining the rationale for treatments, and providing opportunities for patient choice.
For sensitive examinations or wound assessments, clinicians should notify patients of the procedural steps in advance and afford the greatest possible privacy while maintaining safety.
Establish a trusting patient-clinician relationship, with particular emphasis on rebuilding trust in the medical system for patients with prior medical trauma or mistrust.
Initiate mental health services during the emergency phase, including screening for acute and chronic stress disorders, to facilitate psychological recovery.

ethical_issues.question: How should the surgical team ensure the medical transition plan and provision of mental health resources for incarcerated patients returning to custody after surgery?
keypoints: The surgical team must ensure that all active medical problems have ongoing treatment plans and follow-up protocols that can be implemented within the prison setting.

Psychiatric evaluation should be conducted during hospitalization, and trauma-focused therapies should be provided to patients with posttraumatic stress disorder to help develop healthy coping mechanisms.
Hospital social workers and prison social workers need to collaborate in assessing patient needs for both reintegration into custody and subsequent reentry into the community.
Health care practitioners should advocate for incarcerated patients to receive stable interventions and coordinated community care upon reentry.

The surgical team should implement trauma-informed care principles within both hospital and correctional environments and advocate for enhanced mental health resource availability in carceral settings.

title: How Should Surgeons Help Formerly Incarcerated Patients With Chronic Surgical Needs Maintain Care Continuity?
case:
MM is a 24-year-old man who sustained 3-gun shots to his abdomen. MM was taken to the nearest hospital’s operating room (OR) for an emergent damage control exploratory laparotomy. MM’s planned return to the OR 3 days later resulted in bowel resection, primary gastrointestinal anastomosis, and temporary ostomy bag placement. One week after being shot, MM continues to recover. Dr S can no longer justify MM’s stay on clinical grounds and discharges MM to police custody.
MM is jailed immediately on a felony charge of illegal firearm possession. MM is convicted of this charge, imprisoned for 3 months, and then released from prison. MM has few resources, struggles to care for his ostomy, and wonders how he will get the follow-up surgical care Dr S and nurses explained to him would be so important.
Due to his conviction, MM is unable to find steady employment or sufficient insurance to cover anticipated costs of the ostomy reversal surgery Dr S plans to do. MM does his best to manage his stoma but develops abdominal pain as well as pain around the stoma. His pain finally brings him back to the hospital’s emergency department. MM is admitted with infected peristomal wounds, a peristomal hernia, and stomal prolapse.
Dr S and members of their clinical team resume MM’s care and wonder what they should do to help MM continue to have access to the staged, longitudinal surgical care plan interventions that are regarded as standard of care for patients like MM.
case_rewrite:
MM, a 24-year-old man, arrives at the emergency department after sustaining three gunshot wounds to his abdomen. He is rushed to the operating room for an emergent damage control exploratory laparotomy. Three days later, as part of his surgical management, MM undergoes a second operation that involves resection of damaged bowel, a primary gastrointestinal anastomosis, and placement of a temporary ostomy bag. Over the following week, MM’s recovery proceeds as expected.

A week after admission, Dr S, the attending surgeon, determines that MM no longer requires hospitalization from a clinical standpoint. Dr S discharges MM, who is immediately taken into police custody on a felony charge of illegal firearm possession. MM is subsequently convicted, sentenced to three months in prison, and after serving his term, is released.

Upon release, MM faces significant challenges. With limited resources, he struggles to manage his ostomy, uncertain about how to access the follow-up surgical care Dr S and the nurses had emphasized as vital. Due to his criminal record, MM finds it difficult to secure steady employment or health insurance that would cover the costs of his anticipated ostomy reversal surgery. Despite his efforts to care for his stoma, MM begins to experience worsening abdominal pain and pain around the stoma site.

Eventually, MM presents again to the hospital’s emergency department, where he is admitted for infected peristomal wounds, a peristomal hernia, and stomal prolapse. Dr S and the clinical team resume his care, now faced with the question of how best to help MM access the ongoing, staged surgical interventions that constitute the standard of care for patients in his situation.

ethical_issues.question: How can surgeons provide comprehensive patient care while addressing the unique social determinants of health affecting incarcerated or formerly incarcerated patients?
keypoints: Physicians should uphold patient privacy, trust, and dignity with empathy and respect.
Complications should be prevented through appropriate transition planning to ensure continuity of care.
Discuss all aspects of ostomy care with the patient, including its purpose, timing, supply planning, and insurance issues.
Establish direct lines of communication and provide clear discharge instructions to ensure the patient understands subsequent care steps.
Coordinate communication with correctional facility personnel to arrange follow-up and ensure the patient can attend necessary appointments.
Guide the patient to seek assistance from a social worker or care coordinator prior to release to facilitate enrollment in a health insurance plan.
Physicians should collaborate with other healthcare practitioners to reduce the frequency of patient hospital visits and minimize time burden.
Provide access to ostomy support groups and resources for obtaining free supplies to assist patients in managing their ostomy care.

ethical_issues.question: How can correctional staff ensure that incarcerated patients have adequate resources for ostomy care and promptly identify and appropriately report complications without causing harm or breaching their duty of care?
keypoints: Correctional staff should ensure that patients have adequate resources to cleanse the ostomy and change the appliance.
Correctional facilities must have trained personnel capable of early identification of complications and appropriate escalation.
A closed-loop communication system should be established between physicians and custody officials or the prison infirmary to document the patient’s ongoing medical needs.

Patients with ostomies should not be discriminated against; correctional officers should be educated to understand the patients’ limitations and needs, build and maintain trust, and encourage patient participation in their care.

title: How Should Professional Resistance Be Integrated Into Conceptions of Professional Accountability?
case: Dr A is a resident physician working with a patient, MM, in the emergency department. MM wants their nasogastric (NG) tube for feeding removed, and it is unclear to Dr A whether MM understands the risks of doing so when the NG tube is still needed from a clinical standpoint. Dr A, therefore, conducts a cognitive assessment to determine MM’s capacity to make this specific decision at this point in time to remove their NG tube against clinical indication to keep it placed. Dr A determines that MM has capacity to make an informed refusal to continue with the NG tube and then calls the on-call surgeon, Dr S. Dr S is irritated that MM, a patient frequently seen in the emergency department, wants their NG tube removed and orders Dr A to administer medication to MM to “calm them down and help them tolerate the NG tube.” Dr A is not comfortable administering medication to MM for this purpose when MM has capacity to make an informed refusal. Dr A considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Dr A, a resident physician in the emergency department, is caring for MM, a patient known to frequent the ED. MM currently has a nasogastric (NG) tube placed for feeding, but now requests its removal. Dr A is uncertain whether MM fully comprehends the risks involved in discontinuing the NG tube, especially since it remains clinically indicated. To clarify this, Dr A conducts a cognitive assessment to evaluate MM’s capacity to make this specific decision. The assessment reveals that MM does, in fact, have the capacity to make an informed refusal regarding the continued use of the NG tube. 

With this in mind, Dr A contacts Dr S, the on-call surgeon, to discuss MM’s wishes. Dr S, visibly frustrated by MM’s repeated visits and requests, instructs Dr A to administer medication to MM, with the intention of calming MM and making them more compliant with the NG tube. Dr A feels uneasy about this order, as medicating MM for the purpose of overriding a capacitated patient’s informed refusal conflicts with Dr A’s sense of ethical practice. Dr A begins to consider how best to respond to Dr S’s directive, weighing professional responsibilities and MM’s right to autonomy.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. A resist Dr. S’s directive regarding the treatment of MM?
keypoints: Given that MM possesses the capacity to make an informed refusal, Dr A should consider resisting Dr S’s order in order to uphold the patient’s autonomy.
Dr A should respect professional boundaries and clearly communicate their support for the patient’s wishes to achieve high-quality care.

Physicians have a responsibility to participate in processes of self-regulation, including remediation and discipline of members who fail to meet professional standards, thereby ensuring the maintenance of professional standards.

ethical_issues.question: If Dr. A chooses to resist Dr. S’s order, what ethical and professional standards should guide Dr. A’s decision-making, actions, and responses to potential consequences affecting the patient?
keypoints: Professional resistance should be constructive, aiming to promote transformative change in collective understanding rather than being destructive.
Acts of resistance require deliberate reflection to ensure that the intensity of the action is proportionate to the intended goals.
Resistance behaviors should be directed toward finding solutions, supporting the patient’s expressed wishes, and clearly communicating intentions.
Throughout the course of action, professional boundaries must be respected to achieve high-quality care for the patient.

title: How Should Senior Surgeons Help Junior Colleagues and Trainees Experiencing Regret?
case:
Dr R is a chief surgical resident caring for the patient, SM, who is currently admitted to the surgical intensive care unit at an academic health center. Dr R has been caring for SM for 2 weeks; 3 days ago, they decided that it was clinically appropriate to remove SM’s nasogastric tube (NGT). Speech and swallow therapists evaluated SM for dysphagia and authorized SM to consume thin liquids and minced, moist food by mouth. SM continued to make progress eating and drinking with assistance from a nurse until early this morning, when SM suddenly aspirated. SM’s blood oxygen levels dropped, even with immediate supplemental oxygen intervention. SM’s oxygen saturation percentages remained in the low 80s, at least 15% below normal, and Dr R decided to reintubate SM.
The next morning, Dr R commented to Dr A, the attending surgeon, “If only I hadn’t let SM eat.” Dr R tells Dr A that they regret letting SM eat and drink food by mouth. How should Dr A respond?
case_rewrite:
Dr R, the chief surgical resident, has been managing the care of SM, a patient currently in the surgical intensive care unit at an academic medical center. Over the past two weeks, Dr R has been closely involved in SM’s recovery. Three days ago, after careful consideration, Dr R determined that it was clinically appropriate to discontinue SM’s nasogastric tube (NGT). The speech and swallow therapy team subsequently evaluated SM for swallowing difficulties and cleared SM to have thin liquids and minced, moist foods by mouth.

SM’s progress continued steadily, with the support of nursing staff who assisted SM during meals. However, early this morning, SM experienced a sudden episode of aspiration while eating. Despite the immediate administration of supplemental oxygen, SM’s blood oxygen saturation plummeted and remained in the low 80s—about 15% below normal levels. Recognizing the gravity of the situation, Dr R made the decision to reintubate SM.

The following morning, Dr R confided in Dr A, the attending surgeon, expressing regret: “If only I hadn’t let SM eat.” Dr R shared with Dr A feelings of responsibility and remorse for allowing SM to eat and drink by mouth. How should Dr A respond?

ethical_issues.question: How Should Senior Physicians Support Junior Physicians in Coping with Regret and Self-Blame Arising from Adverse Outcomes Related to Clinical Decision-Making?
keypoints: Senior surgeons should allocate time and create a safe space to engage in open and authentic communication with junior surgeons, facilitating the expression of feelings of regret and self-blame.

Senior surgeons should collaboratively review the key facts of the case with junior surgeons, assisting them in cognitive processing and distinguishing between objective facts and subjective reactions.
Senior surgeons can normalize the junior surgeon’s emotions by sharing their own experiences and emotional responses, thereby building trust and strengthening relational bonds.

Senior surgeons should guide junior surgeons in developing coping plans, offering healthy coping strategies or access to professional mental health resources, and establishing a plan for subsequent follow-up.

ethical_issues.question: When surgeons experience emotions such as anxiety, guilt, sadness, and shame related to patient-associated complications, how should the healthcare team provide support to prevent professional burnout and “second victim” syndrome?
keypoints: Senior surgeons should proactively create a safe communication space for junior surgeons, encouraging them to express their emotional experiences.
Senior surgeons should collaboratively review the key facts of the case with junior surgeons to help them distinguish between objective facts and subjective perceptions.
Senior surgeons can normalize the junior surgeons’ experiences and emotions by sharing their own similar experiences and emotional reflections.
Senior surgeons should guide junior surgeons in developing healthy coping strategies and provide peer support or professional mental health resources when appropriate.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical practice ensure that physicians receive timely emotional support and a psychologically safe space following adverse events to facilitate their emotional processing and professional development?
keypoints: Senior surgeons should allocate time and create a safe space for communication to ensure that junior doctors receive timely emotional support following adverse events.
Senior surgeons should engage in deep listening to junior doctors’ expressions, fostering psychological safety and facilitating open and authentic dialogue.

Employ a five-step approach to assist junior doctors in managing their emotions, including reviewing facts, analyzing cognitions, recognizing reactions, normalizing experiences, and collaborative planning.
Before concluding the discussion, establish a plan for follow-up, with a check-in within one week of the initial conversation to promote the junior doctor’s professional development.

title: Which Systemic Responses Should We Evolve to Help Surgeons Navigate Their Regret Experiences?
case:
Mr P is an undocumented and uninsured immigrant in his mid-40s who currently lives in the United States. Mr P presents to a major quaternary care cancer center with a large primary chondrosarcoma localized to his right hemipelvis that is over 30 cm long and extends into his abdomen, displacing many of his abdominal organs. Chondrosarcomas typically do not respond to chemotherapy or radiation,and the surgical resection of such a massive tumor (which would require an external hemipelvectomy with amputation) would require the assistance of orthopedic, general, plastic, vascular, and urological surgeons. However, due to Mr P’s immigration status, he is unable to receive care at the cancer center and is referred to a local county health system that primarily provides care for indigent patients.
At the county hospital, Dr O, a junior attending orthopedic oncologist, and Dr G, a senior attending surgical oncologist, collaborate to manage Mr P’s care and lead discussions during tumor board meetings. Mr P’s tumor type and stage suggest a 5-year overall survival rate of 72% with surgical treatment.Without surgery, the 5-year overall survival of similar patients is 29%.Dr O and Dr G anticipate Mr P’s in-hospital intensive care unit postoperative recovery from a 2-day surgery to be nearly 40 days, with an additional 20 days in a rehabilitation space.
Dr O and Dr G meet several times to discuss Mr P’s case, both concerned that the county hospital, with its limited resources, is not sufficiently equipped to enable Mr P’s care team to meet his intraoperative and postoperative care needs. However, Dr O and Dr G meet with Mr P and explain that there is a philanthropy program at the county hospital that would enable Mr P’s transfer to the quaternary cancer center to which he first presented. Mr P considers this option for a couple of days and decides against surgery, opting to manage his cancer palliatively.
Although the regret was mainly experienced by Dr O, both surgeons felt regret regarding Mr P’s case.
case_rewrite:
Mr P is an undocumented and uninsured immigrant in his mid-40s currently residing in the United States. He arrives at a major quaternary care cancer center with a massive primary chondrosarcoma, over 30 cm in length, originating in his right hemipelvis and extending into his abdomen, pushing aside multiple abdominal organs. Standard chemotherapy and radiation offer little benefit for chondrosarcomas of this type and size; the only potentially curative option is surgical removal, which would require an external hemipelvectomy with amputation. Such a complex operation demands a coordinated effort among orthopedic, general, plastic, vascular, and urological surgeons. However, because of Mr P’s undocumented status, he is ineligible for care at the cancer center and is instead referred to a local county health system that serves mainly indigent patients.

At the county hospital, Dr O, a junior attending orthopedic oncologist, and Dr G, a senior attending surgical oncologist, work together to oversee Mr P’s case. They lead discussions during tumor board meetings to determine the best course of action. Data on Mr P’s tumor type and stage indicate that, with surgery, his 5-year overall survival rate could be as high as 72%, while without surgery, this rate drops to 29%. Dr O and Dr G estimate that Mr P’s recovery would require a roughly 40-day stay in the intensive care unit after a two-day surgery, followed by another 20 days in a rehabilitation facility.

Dr O and Dr G meet repeatedly to discuss the case, each expressing concern about whether the county hospital’s restricted resources would be sufficient to meet Mr P’s intraoperative and postoperative needs. Despite these reservations, Dr O and Dr G arrange a meeting with Mr P, during which they explain all available options, including the existence of a philanthropic program at the county hospital that could allow Mr P to be transferred back to the original quaternary cancer center for surgery. After considering his options for several days, Mr P ultimately declines surgery and chooses palliative management for his cancer.

Following his decision, Dr O experiences significant regret, a feeling shared by Dr G as well, as both surgeons reflect on the limitations imposed by systemic factors and the outcome of Mr P’s case.

ethical_issues.question: In a multidisciplinary team, how can we ensure that a patient’s informed decision-making autonomy is not compromised when physicians have differing opinions regarding the patient’s treatment plan?
keypoints: A responsible informed consent process, which includes explaining the risks and benefits of treatment options to the patient, is essential to safeguarding the patient’s autonomous decision-making by enabling them to weigh acceptable levels of risk.

Physicians within a multidisciplinary team should inform patients that their individual opinions may not fully align with the team’s final recommendation, ensuring that patients are aware of differing perspectives.

In the presence of disagreements, the team should ensure that all members have the opportunity to express their views and strive to reach consensus, thereby presenting a unified recommendation to the patient to minimize decisional conflict.

ethical_issues.question: How should hospital systems establish mechanisms to assist surgeons in managing regret experiences caused by factors beyond their control, thereby preventing moral distress and professional burnout?
keypoints: Hospitals should establish structured debriefing sessions that eliminate hierarchical differences and encourage open communication, enabling surgeons to share their feelings throughout the decision-making process and discuss how systemic factors impeded the realization of desired outcomes, thereby assisting them in processing experiences of regret.

Hospitals should proactively prevent regret arising from clinical disagreements by ensuring that every team member has the opportunity to express their perspectives and concerns, and by presenting a unified recommendation to the patient only after consensus has been reached.

Reflection on experiences of regret facilitates the identification of patient care values and the recognition of targets for systemic reform, harnessing the negative emotional experience of regret as a catalyst for change.

title: How Should IUD Placement Pain Be Described and Managed?
case:
JJ, an 18-year-old nulliparous patient, presents to discuss contraceptive options. JJ is interested in an intrauterine device (IUD) but has seen videos on social media of teenagers talking about their painful experiences with IUD insertion.Dr W is an obstetrician-gynecologist who usually deftly inserts an IUD in about 5 minutes and is aware of conflicting evidence about risks, benefits, and effectiveness of analgesia for the procedure.Dr W has reviewed both the 2009 Cochrane Reviewand its 2015 update,which call for improved availability of analgesia interventions but leave uncertainty about effective options that could constitute an analgesia “standard of care.”
Dr W has observed mentors and colleagues describe IUD placement to patients as causing some “pressure or cramping, but not sharp pain.” But Dr W has observed patients with moderate to severe pain during IUD placement and knows from the literature that discussing pain in advance may increase patients’ pain and anxiety.Dr W feels that withholding such information, even if it could increase procedural pain and anxiety, is unethical. Dr W considers how to communicate with JJ about IUD insertion and whether to administer analgesia prior to the procedure.
case_rewrite:
JJ, an 18-year-old nulliparous patient, arrives for a consultation about contraception. She expresses interest in getting an intrauterine device (IUD) but brings up concerns after watching social media videos where teenagers describe experiencing significant pain during IUD insertion. Dr W, an obstetrician-gynecologist, is accustomed to performing IUD insertions smoothly within about five minutes. Dr W is aware of the mixed evidence on the risks, benefits, and effectiveness of various pain relief methods during IUD placement. She has closely reviewed both the 2009 Cochrane Review and its 2015 update, which emphasize the need for better access to analgesia but do not clearly identify any one method as a definitive standard of care.

Dr W has observed her mentors and colleagues typically describe the IUD insertion process to patients as involving “pressure or cramping, but not sharp pain.” However, Dr W has personally witnessed patients experiencing moderate to severe pain during the procedure. She also knows from the literature that discussing the potential for pain ahead of time can sometimes heighten patients’ anxiety and even their perception of pain. Despite this, Dr W believes that withholding information about possible pain is unethical, even if disclosure could increase procedural discomfort or anxiety for the patient. As she prepares to counsel JJ, Dr W carefully considers how best to communicate about the pain associated with IUD insertion, how to address JJ’s concerns, and whether to offer any form of pain relief before proceeding with the placement.

ethical_issues.question: During intrauterine device (IUD) placement, should clinicians disclose to patients in advance the potential pain experience, even if doing so may exacerbate the patient’s anxiety and perception of pain?
keypoints: Physicians should incorporate the pain experience into the informed consent process by informing patients of the potential discomfort associated with the procedure.
Physicians should discuss the range of analgesia options according to the patient’s preferences, from no intervention to varying levels of pain management.
Physicians should conduct individualized informed consent conversations to elicit patients’ concerns, prior experiences, and expectations.
Physicians should respect patient autonomy and focus on patient-centered counseling and shared decision-making to enhance patient satisfaction.

ethical_issues.question: In the absence of effective evidence-based analgesic interventions, how should clinicians manage pain during IUD insertion to ensure patients’ informed consent and autonomous decision-making?
keypoints: Engage in patient-centered dialogue and shared decision-making to understand the patient’s medical history, concerns, and preferences, and to explore expectations regarding pain and pain management options.

Clinicians should inform patients about the potential discomfort associated with IUD insertion and discuss the spectrum of analgesia options according to the patient’s wishes, ranging from no intervention to topical anesthesia and advanced sedation techniques.

Physicians must respect patient autonomy by delegating the decision-making authority regarding analgesia to the patient, creating a supportive environment, and ensuring that patients are aware of their control over the procedure, including the right to pause or terminate it at any time, thereby enhancing patient satisfaction with both the procedure and the healthcare system.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr W ethically balance the provision of potentially costly pain management options for IUD placement with ensuring equitable access to contraception for patients like JJ in resource-limited settings, so as not to create additional barriers for low-income women or exacerbate existing healthcare inequities?
keypoints: In resource-limited settings, the use of costly and non–evidence-based pain management interventions should be avoided to prevent further barriers to intrauterine device access for low-income women.

Pain management strategies should be individualized, with clinicians engaging in shared decision-making with patients to explore pain management options, pain expectations, and procedural expectations, while eliciting patients’ values and preferences.

Clinicians should create a supportive environment that ensures patients are aware of their control over the procedure and their right to request that the procedure be paused or terminated at any time.
Through patient-centered counseling and shared decision-making, clinicians can enhance patients’ satisfaction with both the procedure and their interactions with the healthcare system.

title: How Should Physicians Manage Abortion Pain Experienced by Remote Telehealth Patients?
case: JN is a 24-year-old cis woman who has been pregnant twice and given birth vaginally both times. JN lives in a rural area, 75 miles from the nearest pharmacy or clinic. JN’s last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She had a positive home pregnancy test, and an intrauterine pregnancy was confirmed at an out-of-town urgent care clinic. She wants to terminate the pregnancy and met virtually with Dr OBGYN, who prescribed mifepristone and misoprostol. JN took mifepristone 2 days ago and misoprostol yesterday. JN is experiencing severe cramping pain, despite taking over-the-counter analgesic medication. She messages Dr OBGYN to ask for a prescription medication to help manage her pain. Dr OBGYN considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
JN, a 24-year-old cisgender woman, has been pregnant twice before and delivered both children vaginally. She resides in a rural community, approximately 75 miles from the nearest pharmacy or medical clinic. JN’s last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. After receiving a positive result on a home pregnancy test, she traveled to an urgent care clinic outside her town, where an intrauterine pregnancy was confirmed. Deciding she wanted to terminate the pregnancy, JN consulted virtually with Dr OBGYN, who prescribed mifepristone and misoprostol for a medication abortion.

Following Dr OBGYN’s instructions, JN took mifepristone two days ago and misoprostol yesterday. Since then, she has been experiencing severe cramping pain that has not improved despite taking over-the-counter pain medication. Feeling distressed by the intensity of her pain, JN reaches out to Dr OBGYN through a secure message, requesting a prescription for stronger pain medication.

As Dr OBGYN reviews JN’s message, she considers how best to respond, taking into account JN’s rural location, her current symptoms, and the ethical issues involved in remotely managing pain for a patient undergoing medication abortion.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the principle of nonmaleficence with patient autonomy in remote telemedicine, particularly in the management of pain associated with medication abortion?
keypoints: Physicians must weigh the personal, legal, and financial risks to patients associated with remote versus in-person consultations in accordance with the principle of nonmaleficence.

Informed consent is the cornerstone of ethical clinical practice; physicians must ensure that patients understand the pain experience associated with medication abortion as well as alternative options.
As pain is a significant adverse effect of medication abortion, physicians have a responsibility to counsel patients regarding pain expectations to ensure valid informed consent is obtained.
The safety of telemedicine abortion is supported by evidence, and physicians should respect patients’ autonomy to choose telemedicine abortion when fully informed.
Physicians should ensure that patients are mentally and physically prepared for pain in order to promote patient welfare.

ethical_issues.question: How can informed consent be adequately ensured for remote telehealth patients undergoing medication abortion, particularly with regard to pain management?
keypoints: Ensure that patients understand pain as a significant adverse effect prior to medication abortion and provide comprehensive counseling on pain expectations to obtain valid informed consent.
Advise patients to prepare necessary supplies and arrange for support from friends or family to assist with pain management, as well as to contact emergency services if needed.
Respect patient autonomy by ensuring that they make an informed decision to proceed with telemedicine abortion and are mentally and physically prepared for pain.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of JN’s remote telemedicine medication abortion, how should Dr OBGYN ethically adjust the dosage and quantity of prescribed analgesic medications to account for JN’s rural geographic location and limited access to healthcare?
keypoints: Considering the patient’s distance from the pharmacy, physicians may prescribe a higher dose or quantity of weak opioid analgesics than would typically be provided to patients in urban settings.
Providing a small supply of opioid medication at the initial consultation may be in the best interest of patients who must travel long distances to access care.

Decisions regarding analgesic prescriptions should be guided by clinical judgment, taking into account the patient’s proximity to healthcare services and the potential addictive properties of the medication.

title: How Should a Physician Respond to a Patient’s Unexpected Pain During a Pelvic Examination When There Is Clinical Indication of Infection?
case:
Dr B sees CC, who is 16 years old and presents with persistent, foul-smelling vaginal discharge despite finishing antibiotics prescribed by another clinician for a presumed sexually transmitted infection (STI). Dr B explains, “I need to perform a pelvic examination and get a swab sample for the lab to test. Do you understand what that means?” CC responds, “Yes,” and nods agreement. Dr B returns with a chaperone. Upon inserting and opening a lubricated speculum in CC’s vaginal canal, CC screams, “This hurts too much!” Dr B slowly withdraws the speculum and does not complete the examination.
Given CC’s recent health history, Dr B needs an accurate diagnosis to inform appropriate treatment. “Maybe I should have just quickly inserted the swab to get a sample,” Dr B wonders.
case_rewrite:
Dr B is seeing CC, a 16-year-old who arrives with a persistent, foul-smelling vaginal discharge that hasn’t improved, even after finishing a course of antibiotics previously prescribed by another provider who suspected a sexually transmitted infection (STI). Dr B sits down with CC and says, “I’ll need to perform a pelvic exam and collect a swab sample to send to the lab. Do you know what that involves?” CC replies, “Yes,” and nods. Dr B brings in a chaperone and prepares for the exam. As Dr B gently inserts and carefully opens a lubricated speculum in CC’s vaginal canal, CC suddenly cries out, “This hurts too much!” Dr B pauses and then slowly removes the speculum, stopping the examination before it is completed.

Given CC’s recent medical issues, Dr B knows that getting an accurate diagnosis is important to guide effective treatment. Dr B wonders, “Should I have just tried to quickly take the swab to get a sample?”

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician ensure that a patient fully understands the nature of a pelvic examination and obtains informed consent, especially when the patient may experience anxiety or fear?
keypoints: Physicians should explain the details of the examination in a manner tailored to the patient’s age and health literacy, and assess the patient’s true understanding through methods such as the teach-back technique to ensure informed consent.

Physicians should acknowledge the sensitive nature of the examination and the possibility of pain, as well as inquire about the patient’s prior examination experiences to open channels of communication and build trust.
Physicians should inform patients that they have the right to discontinue the examination at any time and for any reason, thereby restoring the patient’s autonomy and sense of security.
Physicians should include patients in the decision-making process, enabling them to weigh the personal risks and benefits of the examination and make autonomous decisions.

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician respond when a patient reports pain during a pelvic examination in order to ensure the patient’s comfort and autonomy?
keypoints: The physician should inquire about the specific location of the patient’s pain in order to make appropriate adjustments rather than immediately terminating the examination.
The physician should ask the patient whether they wish to continue the examination to ensure the patient’s autonomy and comfort.
The physician may consider less invasive alternatives, such as vaginal self-swabbing or urine testing, to provide the patient with greater options and control.

The physician should solicit feedback from the patient after the examination regarding ways to improve comfort, thereby involving the patient in the decision-making process and reinforcing their autonomy.

ethical_issues.question: In situations where a traditional pelvic examination cannot be performed, how should a physician select alternative approaches to ensure accurate diagnosis and treatment while respecting the patient’s autonomy and comfort?
keypoints: Physicians may opt for vaginal self-sampling or urine testing as alternative methods, which are less invasive yet effective, ensuring diagnostic and therapeutic accuracy.
Vaginal self-sampling demonstrates comparable accuracy to clinician-performed procedures, thereby enhancing patient autonomy and comfort.
Although urine samples have slightly lower accuracy, they remain preferable to no sampling and are suitable for patients unable to undergo a traditional pelvic examination.
A single-digit digital examination is better tolerated and can still effectively assess cervical motion tenderness, serving as an alternative to the conventional pelvic exam.

In cases of high clinical suspicion for infection, while other critical components of the exam cannot be assessed, patients who are informed of these limitations may choose to defer the examination and pursue infection evaluation through alternative means to tailor treatment.

title: Whom Should We Regard as Responsible for Health Record Inaccuracies That Hinder Population-Based Fact Finding?
case:
T is a 43-year-old woman who has well-controlled asthma and visits Dr A for an annual checkup from a rural part of the state. Dr A reviews T’s electronic health record (EHR), noting no documentation of COVID-19 vaccination. Dr A remembers results from a national study that rurality was associated with decreased odds for vaccination and asks T about her reasons for not getting any shots. “I did get 2 shots last year, but I didn’t get them here. That’s probably why you’re not seeing them. I plan to get a booster as soon it’s available.”
Dr A wonders why many other patients’ EHRs contain incomplete or inaccurate information and why. “Not only does this affect how I plan my time with my patients, but poor-quality data hinders epidemiological surveillance and tracking of population-level vaccine uptake. Wasn’t the harrowing transition we’ve all just made to EHRs supposed to eliminate problems like this?”
case_rewrite:
T, a 43-year-old woman with well-controlled asthma, arrives from her rural hometown for her annual checkup with Dr A. As Dr A reviews T’s electronic health record (EHR), she notices there is no record of any COVID-19 vaccinations. Recalling a recent national study linking rural residence to lower vaccination rates, Dr A decides to ask T about her vaccination status. 

T responds, “I did get two shots last year, but not at this clinic. That’s probably why you don’t see them in the record. I’m planning to get a booster as soon as it’s available.” 

Dr A reflects on the situation, noting that T’s EHR, like those of many other patients, contains gaps and inaccuracies. She wonders about the broader implications: “Incomplete or incorrect data not only affects my ability to provide the best care, but also undermines efforts to track vaccination rates and monitor public health. Wasn’t the challenging transition to EHRs supposed to solve problems like this?”

ethical_issues.question: How can the need for high-quality population health data be met while ensuring the protection of patient privacy and autonomy?
keypoints: Ensuring the simultaneous protection of patient privacy and autonomy while meeting the demand for high-quality population health data requires shared responsibility among healthcare systems, vendors, clinicians, patients, and researchers utilizing the data.
Research regulatory bodies provide foundational protections for patients by minimizing privacy risks, ensuring data security, and upholding investigator integrity.
Deidentification of integrated system-wide EHR data in accordance with privacy regulations is standard practice when used for research purposes.
Reconceptualizing patients as partners in data generation can motivate their engagement in initiatives aimed at collecting high-quality health data.
Opt-out mechanisms may partially restore patient agency over the use of their EHR data in research but have the potential to introduce bias into the data.
Data scientists and researchers bear the responsibility to ensure that high-quality EHR data are appropriately managed in population-level analyses and to safeguard against data breaches.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of inaccuracies in EHR data, how should responsibility for maintaining data accuracy be appropriately allocated?
keypoints: The responsibility for ensuring the accuracy of EHR data is shared among healthcare systems, vendors, clinicians, patients, and researchers who utilize the data.
Vendors and healthcare systems are accountable for the functionality, usability, and accuracy of the EHR.
Clinicians should actively engage with healthcare systems to ensure that data entry supports both clinical documentation and research purposes.
Patients should be regarded as partners in data generation to motivate their participation in high-quality data collection.
Data scientists and researchers must ensure that EHR data are appropriately managed in analyses and remain attentive to the five domains of data quality.

ethical_issues.question: How can the ethical issues between de-identification of EHR data and obtaining informed patient consent be balanced in research use?
keypoints: Deidentification is a standard practice in the use of EHR data for research purposes to protect patient privacy.
The use of EHR data without obtaining patient informed consent may result in patients being unaware of third-party uses of their data.
Opt-out mechanisms can partially restore patient autonomy over the use of their EHR data in research but may introduce bias into the data.
Classifying research based on deidentified EHR data as non–human subjects research may weaken regulatory oversight, thereby affecting population-level studies and inferences.

title: Which Values Should Guide Health Care Organizations’ Retrofit Expenditures on Patient-Centered and Evidence-Based Design?
case: A large health system has contracted with an architectural firm to develop plans for renovations of one of its hospitals. Originally built in the late 1960s, the building is in an urban-based community. During a planning meeting, the architect considers suggesting incorporating a white noise sound system, other sound-masking equipment, and good lighting in the design plans, since there is evidence that these features promote more peaceful inpatient environments. Despite the likelihood that these retrofits would improve patients’ experiences, the architect is concerned that they will cost far more than the contract’s budget allocates and wonders whether to suggest the retrofits.
case_rewrite: A major health system has engaged an architectural firm to draft renovation plans for one of its urban hospitals, a facility originally constructed in the late 1960s. During a planning session, the lead architect, Dr W, reflects on the possibility of recommending the integration of a white noise sound system, additional sound-masking technologies, and advanced lighting solutions. Dr W is aware that research supports the positive impact of these features, indicating that they foster more restful and healing environments for inpatients. However, Dr W is also aware that incorporating such upgrades would significantly exceed the current budget outlined in the contract. Faced with this dilemma, Dr W weighs the potential benefits to patient well-being and privacy against the financial constraints, uncertain whether to advocate for these enhancements in the renovation proposal.

ethical_issues.question: How do design decisions fulfill the obligation to align with the principles of beneficence, nonmaleficence, autonomy, and justice?
keypoints: Design decisions should adhere to the principle of nonmaleficence and be supported by an EBD business case that confirms the relationship between improved outcomes and the reduction of avoidable harm.
Design decisions should actively promote beneficence by implementing measures supported by research, such as white noise and dynamic lighting, to enhance patients’ sleep quality and overall health.
Design decisions should respect the principle of autonomy by optimizing the acoustic environment to protect patients’ speech privacy.

Design decisions must reflect the principle of justice by achieving cost savings through energy-efficient measures and health outcome improvements, with the conserved resources allocated equitably in future distributions.

title: Who Should Contribute to Decisions About Health Care Space Design?
case:
Dr A is an internist widely known for their work in evidence-based health care design. As part of a conference in design innovations in community-based health care, Dr A has been asked to lead a half-day working session for health professions students, clinicians, patient advocates, and community leaders. Dr A explains that Certificate of Need programs are means by which many states are supposed to regulate supply of health care services in their jurisdictions. Dr A then poses to audience members, “Let’s say you’re submitting a Certificate of Need application to build a new hospital. In your proposal, which features in your design drawings and descriptions will you talk about and why?”
Some audience members’ priorities focus on ventilation and waste removal streams, numbers of computer stations, and supply rooms’ proximity to patient care areas. Others suggest why features such as window sizes in patients’ rooms, access to and visibility of a garden courtyard, parking availability, sign clarity and navigability to patient care areas, locations of bathrooms and other common spaces, and easy outside access to municipal transit stops should be design priorities.
As Dr A expected, session participants identified numerous design features. The rest of the half-day, Dr A guided a discussion about how design priorities express stakeholders’ health care infrastructure needs.
case_rewrite:
Dr A, an internist recognized for expertise in evidence-based health care design, is invited to lead a half-day workshop at a conference focused on community-based health care innovations. The session brings together health professions students, clinicians, patient advocates, and community leaders. At the beginning of the session, Dr A introduces the concept of Certificate of Need programs, explaining how these state-regulated initiatives are intended to manage the supply of health care services within a region. 

Dr A then engages the group with a scenario: “Imagine you are preparing a Certificate of Need application for a new hospital. Which features would you highlight in your design plans and narratives, and for what reasons?” 

Participants respond with a variety of priorities. Some emphasize technical and operational aspects such as air ventilation systems, efficient waste disposal routes, the number of computer workstations, and the accessibility of supply rooms to patient areas. Others focus on elements aimed at patient experience and community integration, suggesting the importance of window dimensions in patient rooms, the presence and visibility of a garden courtyard, the availability of parking, clear signage and navigable routes to care areas, the locations of bathrooms and shared spaces, and convenient access to public transportation stops.

As anticipated, Dr A observes that the group’s proposals reflect a wide spectrum of design priorities, each rooted in differing stakeholder perspectives. For the remainder of the workshop, Dr A facilitates a discussion examining how these diverse priorities arise from the various health care infrastructure needs represented in the room. The conversation delves into how involving multiple stakeholders—patients, families, clinicians, administrators, architects, and community members—through shared decision-making can ensure that the final hospital design serves the broader community equitably, aligns with ethical and mission-driven standards, and allocates limited resources justly.

ethical_issues.question: In health care space design, how can the just allocation of limited public resources be achieved to prevent unjust distribution and risks of harm?
keypoints: In health care space design, incorporating representative stakeholders through a shared decision-making framework ensures fairness and diversity in the decision-making process, thereby promoting the just allocation of limited public resources.

Certificate of Need projects should represent community interests, involving value propositions and priority rankings to ensure that the project addresses the needs of the entire community rather than those of a single interest group.

During the decision-making process, stakeholders should evaluate and select options based on the hospital’s or health system’s mission, vision, and values to ensure that resource allocation aligns with ethical standards.

When multiple design options exist without strong evidence favoring one over others, a consensus mechanism involving those affected by the decisions should be employed to prevent unjust resource distribution and minimize risks of harm.

ethical_issues.question: Who should participate in the decision-making process of health care space design to ensure that the perspectives of representative stakeholders are fully incorporated and influence the final decisions?
keypoints: The decision-making process for health care space design should include experts possessing the necessary knowledge of evidence-based design, such as certified health care architects.
Patients and their family members should be directly involved in design decisions to ensure that diverse patient experiences are adequately considered.
Hospital administrators should participate in design decisions to ensure that operational, logistical, and financial realities are taken into account.
Incorporating representative stakeholders through a shared decision-making framework can promote ethically informed, evidence-based hospital design practices.

title: How Should We Respond to Spatial Injustice in Health Care Organizations?
case:
AA has lived with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) for over 10 years. During the past year, AA’s symptoms became more severe, and AA is now being hospitalized for the third time in 2 months for an acute exacerbation of COPD.
Even with the door closed, AA’s hospital room is noisy, with hallway bustle and television noise intrusion from a neighboring room. AA’s room has a single chair but no suitable furnishing to accommodate a cousin, whom AA would prefer to stay overnight. When AA feels well enough to walk the hallway, they feel anxious about having no seating on which to rest.
Given AA’s increased COPD exacerbations, a home nebulizer has been prescribed by their pulmonologist, Dr P. Before being discharged from the hospital, AA was given written instructions about how to assemble and use the nebulizer, but the nebulizer is still not working properly. “Why do they make it so hard to use this thing?” AA wonders aloud. “Medical equipment and hospital rooms are supposed to help!”
case_rewrite:
AA has managed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) for more than a decade. Over the past year, AA’s condition has worsened significantly, and this is now the third time in two months that AA has been admitted to the hospital due to an acute COPD flare-up.

Inside AA’s hospital room, the environment feels anything but restful. Despite the door being closed, the constant commotion from the hallway and the persistent sound of a neighboring television seep through, disrupting any sense of peace. The room itself is sparsely furnished—there is just one chair, and nothing suitable for AA’s cousin, who AA wishes could stay overnight for comfort and support. Whenever AA feels strong enough to take a walk in the hallway, they are unsettled by the lack of resting spots, making these short walks a source of anxiety rather than relief.

Recognizing the increasing frequency of AA’s exacerbations, Dr P, AA’s pulmonologist, has prescribed a home nebulizer to help manage symptoms. Before discharge, AA was provided written instructions on assembling and operating the nebulizer. However, despite these instructions, the device remains difficult to use and is still not functioning properly. Frustrated, AA wonders aloud, “Why do they make it so hard to use this thing? Medical equipment and hospital rooms are supposed to help!”

ethical_issues.question: How can health care organizations eliminate spatial inequities through design and implement systemic changes to enhance patient experience and community engagement?
keypoints: Identifying hostile design within healthcare spaces is a crucial starting point for eliminating health-related social disparities; healthcare institutions should critically examine their dual roles in constructing spatial hostility and actively promote spatial justice.

By positioning design as a sanctuary that ensures safety and health, healthcare institutions should guide design decisions through principles of comfort, community, and choice, thereby mitigating the institutional atmosphere of medical environments.

Healthcare institutions ought to integrate natural elements to enhance privacy, facilitate personal reflection, and support therapeutic interventions, while employing barrier-free design and flexible spaces to increase patient and visitor agency and comfort.

The development of accessible healthcare environments requires translational research that fully involves marginalized stakeholders throughout the process; medical ethicists and health professionals should collaborate with community activists, architects, and scholars to resist hostile architecture.

Healthcare personnel bear an ethical responsibility to engage in institutional consciousness-raising and collective community action addressing hostile design in healthcare spaces, enhancing awareness through training, consultation, and internal advocacy mechanisms.

Public health practitioners have a duty to advocate for community environmental changes that impact health, providing empirical evidence of the human consequences to foster environmental acceptance, inclusion, and empowerment of the most vulnerable populations.

tags: Gender, sex identity/Sexual and gender minorities
title: How Should Clinicians Share Decision Making With Patients Interested in Using Psychedelics to Feel Psychologically Safe?
case:
FG is a 33-year-old transgender man who uses the pronouns they/them and has a history of unipolar depression and alcohol use disorder. Through their employer-sponsored health insurance, FG initiates alcohol use disorder treatment. FG also reports that combined selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and psychotherapy with their psychiatrist, Dr P, have helped, but that their depression symptoms remain debilitating.
Recently, after watching a show about psychedelic mushrooms and cannabinoids and noticing sensory deprivation chambers at their local mall, FG wonders how these approaches could help them find peace of mind more often and more regularly.
At their most recent session with Dr P, FG expressed interest in trying psychedelic mushrooms. “I want more control over my ability to generate peace in my life and in my experiences,” FG says.
Dr P, a 60-year-old, cisgender woman who uses the pronouns she/her, considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
FG, a 33-year-old transgender man who uses they/them pronouns, has a history of unipolar depression and alcohol use disorder. Through their employer-sponsored health insurance, FG has recently begun treatment for alcohol use disorder. FG shares with their psychiatrist, Dr P—a 60-year-old cisgender woman who uses she/her pronouns—that while a combination of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and psychotherapy has provided some benefit, their depressive symptoms remain profoundly disruptive.

Recently, FG’s curiosity was piqued after watching a documentary about psychedelic mushrooms and cannabinoids, and noticing the presence of sensory deprivation chambers at a local mall. This exposure led FG to wonder whether these alternative approaches could help them experience a greater sense of peace and stability in their daily life.

During their most recent session, FG voices these thoughts to Dr P and expresses a specific interest in trying psychedelic mushrooms. “I want to have more control over my ability to generate peace in my life and in my experiences,” FG explains.

Dr P listens attentively, considering FG’s request and reflecting on her own perspectives about psychedelic treatments. She contemplates how best to approach this conversation, aware of her professional responsibilities and the importance of supporting FG’s autonomy and well-being as they explore treatment options.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr P, while reflecting on their own potential biases and attitudes toward psychedelic use, engage in shared decision making with FG regarding FG’s interest in exploring psychedelics as part of their mental health treatment?
keypoints: P should reflect on their own potential biases and attitudes toward psychedelic substances and their medical use to ensure FG does not feel judged or stigmatized.

P should be mindful of differences in social identity, including gender identity and lived experience, as well as the inherent power dynamics in the clinician-patient relationship, and consider how these factors may influence FG’s perception of their interactions.

P can apply harm reduction and shared decision-making principles by responding nonjudgmentally to FG’s interest in psilocybin, and by providing accurate, evidence-based information and resources to help minimize potential risks.
