P should explore with FG what “peace of mind” means to them, and use this understanding to guide a discussion of the potential risks and benefits of substances such as psilocybin in the context of FG’s mental health goals.

P should offer psychoeducation about the current evidence regarding psilocybin and other psychedelics for depression, including potential benefits, risks, and uncertainties, to foster trust and support FG’s autonomy in making informed decisions about their mental health care.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr P apply harm reduction principles and shared decision-making skills to discuss the risks and benefits of psychedelic use with FG in a nonjudgmental manner, while supporting FG’s autonomy in making an informed decision?
keypoints: Dr P should engage in self-reflection to identify and mitigate any personal biases or stigmatizing attitudes toward psychedelic therapies, ensuring an open and nonjudgmental approach to FG’s inquiry.
Dr P should explore FG’s underlying motivations, expectations, and psychological needs regarding the use of psychedelic substances, facilitating a patient-centered and empathetic dialogue.

Dr P must provide FG with balanced, evidence-based information about the potential benefits, risks, and uncertainties associated with psychedelic-assisted therapy, including current legal status and regulatory considerations.

Dr P should discuss the possible psychological and emotional effects of psychedelics, including the potential for both positive and adverse outcomes, and clarify the importance of harm reduction strategies.

Dr P may suggest alternative or adjunctive therapeutic options, such as ketamine-assisted therapy or mind-body interventions, that are supported by current clinical evidence and may address FG’s desire for improved psychological well-being.

Dr P should emphasize the importance of working with qualified and experienced practitioners if FG pursues psychedelic therapy, and explain the critical roles of preparation and integration phases in maximizing therapeutic benefit and safety.

Dr P should assess FG’s social support system and practical resources, including the ability to take time off work and access to supportive individuals, to ensure adequate support during and after psychedelic experiences.

Dr P can assist FG in identifying reputable sources of information and potential pathways for safe and ethical access to psychedelic therapies, such as participation in clinical trials, and allow FG sufficient time to consider the risks, benefits, and alternatives before making a decision.

title: Why Is Hospice One of the Few Health Care Environments Structured for Peace?
case: AC is a 68-year-old man with glioblastoma. After surgery to remove as much of his tumor as possible, he is now undergoing several rounds of radiation and chemotherapy. AC sees his oncologist, Dr M, for follow-up. While in the waiting room, he reads a brochure about hospice and the importance of a peaceful environment for end-of-life care. In his visit, AC reflects on his stressful, uncomfortable surgery and recovery experiences during his inpatient stay. “It doesn’t make sense that hospitals can’t be more supportive places for patients and their families. Why should I have to be in hospice to receive care in peace?” Dr M listens to AC and considers how to respond.
case_rewrite: AC, a 68-year-old man, is living with glioblastoma. Following a recent surgery aimed at removing as much of his tumor as possible, he is currently undergoing multiple rounds of radiation and chemotherapy. AC arrives for a follow-up appointment with his oncologist, Dr M. As he waits, he picks up a brochure in the waiting room that describes hospice and emphasizes the value of a peaceful, supportive environment for patients approaching end-of-life care. During his appointment, AC shares his thoughts with Dr M, recalling how stressful and uncomfortable his hospital stay was during and after surgery. “I just don’t understand why hospitals can’t be more comfortable and supportive for people like me and our families,” AC says. “Why is it only in hospice that patients are supposed to get care in peace?” Dr M listens carefully to AC’s concerns, reflecting on how the care environment might be improved for patients without sacrificing medical safety or urgency.

ethical_issues.question: How can patient-centered improvements to the care environment be reasonably implemented while meeting the demands of medical urgency and safety?
keypoints: Patient-centered improvements to the care environment should be implemented without compromising safety and optimized through evidence-based design to enhance the patient experience.
Hospitals can improve the comfort of inpatient areas through incremental measures, such as increasing natural light exposure or incorporating views of natural landscapes.

Health care teams should collaborate with patients to plan enhancements to comfort during hospitalization, for example, by permitting patients to bring personal belongings or adjusting the use of monitoring equipment.
The principle of beneficence should be extended to actively optimize quality of life, thereby enhancing patient peace and the overall quality of care.

title: What Might It Mean to Have a Right to Bear a Pregnancy Peacefully?
case:
Dr R is an OB/GYN caring for CC, who is 28 weeks pregnant. CC has high blood pressure and is at risk of developing preeclampsia. Dr R stresses the importance of taking the prescribed medication to help control her blood pressure, resting, and avoiding salt and stress.
CC lives in a historically disinvested, redlined community that faces infrastructural neglect and food insecurity and is downwind from a plant that processes municipal waste. CC takes 2 buses and a train to get to her appointments with Dr R, and recent closure of a critical bus route between CC’s neighborhood and affluent areas of the city means that CC must walk to catch the train and second bus to see Dr R.
When CC arrives for her next appointment, her blood pressure is 160/95 mm Hg. “I take my blood pressure medication as prescribed, but, as hard as I try, I struggle to rest and avoid stress. It took me over 2 hours to get here today.”
Dr R wonders, “How can anyone gestate peacefully under conditions in which CC lives?” and considers how to respond to CC’s concerns.
case_rewrite:
Dr. R, an OB/GYN, is providing prenatal care to CC, who is 28 weeks pregnant and managing high blood pressure, putting her at heightened risk for preeclampsia. At each visit, Dr. R emphasizes the necessity of taking her prescribed medication, getting proper rest, and minimizing salt intake and stress.

CC resides in a neighborhood that has long suffered from disinvestment and redlining. Her community faces ongoing infrastructural neglect, persistent food insecurity, and exposure to environmental hazards from a nearby municipal waste processing plant. To reach Dr. R’s clinic, CC must undertake a lengthy journey—she rides two buses and a train. The recent elimination of a key bus route connecting her neighborhood to more affluent parts of the city has made the trip even more arduous: now, CC must walk a significant distance to catch the train and her connecting bus.

At her most recent appointment, CC’s blood pressure reads 160/95 mm Hg. She tells Dr. R, “I take my blood pressure medication exactly as you told me, but, no matter how hard I try, it’s difficult for me to rest or avoid stress. It took me over two hours just to get here today.”

Dr. R finds herself reflecting, “How can anyone experience a peaceful pregnancy under the conditions in which CC lives?” As she listens to CC’s concerns, Dr. R contemplates how best to respond and support CC in the face of the social and environmental challenges that shape her pregnancy.

ethical_issues.question: How can CC’s right to a peaceful pregnancy be supported in light of the environmental and social determinants of health that she faces?
keypoints: R should recognize and respond to CC’s unique social and structural challenges, providing care that is culturally sensitive and attentive to the social determinants of health affecting her pregnancy.
R can collaborate with a multidisciplinary team, including social workers, to assess CC’s food security and connect her with nutritional support programs and other relevant community resources.
Healthcare institutions should implement innovative strategies, such as remote pregnancy monitoring and self-measured blood pressure, to help patients like CC overcome structural barriers to care.
R has an ethical responsibility to advocate for systemic changes that improve patients’ social conditions, including enhancing healthcare accessibility and reducing financial barriers to care.
Physicians must address social determinants of health by delivering culturally competent care that reduces stressors and supports CC’s right to a peaceful and healthy pregnancy.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr. R address the social determinants of health impacting CC’s pregnancy while upholding ethical principles in her medical care?
keypoints: R should provide culturally competent care by addressing relevant social determinants of health, such as transportation barriers and food insecurity, and collaborate with a multidisciplinary team—including social workers—to connect CC with targeted support resources (e.g., transportation assistance, nutritional supplementation programs).

R should advocate for systemic measures to improve CC’s social conditions, such as enhancing healthcare accessibility and reducing healthcare costs, in addition to delivering appropriate medical care.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of restricted access to abortion, how can patients’ bodily autonomy and informed consent rights be protected to achieve a peaceful pregnancy?
keypoints: The rights to contraception and abortion are essential means for individuals to exercise control over their reproductive lives and to achieve bodily autonomy.
When access to abortion is restricted, patients may be unable to truly consent to pregnancy, resulting in involuntary gestation.
Ensuring access to safe abortion should be a central issue for physician advocacy in order to optimize patient care and enable peaceful gestation.

title: How Should Clinicians Partner With Families to Promote Children’s Sleep Health?
case:
LJ is a 12-year-old arriving with their parents to an appointment with Dr Z. LJ has been more distracted and disruptive in school, their grades have dropped from a B+ average to a C, and a teacher recently mentioned seeing them dozing during class. Dr Z speaks with LJ alone and learns that LJ’s father was recently laid off from a long-time job, prompting the family to sell their home and move to an apartment. LJ’s mother has taken on 2 new jobs and is often not home until 11:00 pm, past LJ’s bedtime, which is now much harder for LJ’s parents to enforce. LJ now plays video games late into the night, delaying sleep onset, and typically wakes up a few hours later due to noise from neighbors in an adjacent apartment or on the stairs. LJ’s mother can no longer drop them off at school, so LJ must be prompt to catch the school bus at 7:00 am. Most nights, LJ gets 5 to 6 hours of sleep. LJ also tells Dr Z, “My mom and dad aren’t very happy right now. I make things worse for them when I don’t do well in school.” LJ and their family have identified LJ’s daytime sleepiness and poor grades as top problems at this visit. Dr Z considers how to address these changes in LJ’s life and LJ’s shortened sleep duration with their parents.
Dr Z wonders how to recruit LJ’s parents as allies in protecting LJ’s sleep time and quality.
case_rewrite:
LJ, a 12-year-old, arrives at a clinic appointment with their parents to see Dr Z. Recently, LJ has become noticeably more distracted and disruptive at school. Their grades, once a steady B+ average, have slipped to a C, and a teacher recently reported seeing LJ dozing off during class. When Dr Z meets privately with LJ, LJ shares that their father was laid off from a long-time job, leading the family to sell their home and move into an apartment. LJ’s mother has started working two new jobs and often doesn’t return home until after 11:00 pm—well past LJ’s bedtime, which has become much harder for the parents to enforce.

With the family’s new routine, LJ now spends late nights playing video games, delaying when they fall asleep. LJ is often awakened just a few hours later by noise from neighbors in the adjacent apartment or on the stairs. Since LJ’s mother can no longer drive them to school each morning, LJ has to catch the school bus promptly at 7:00 am. Most nights, LJ is only getting about 5 to 6 hours of sleep. During their conversation, LJ confides in Dr Z, saying, “My mom and dad aren’t very happy right now. I make things worse for them when I don’t do well in school.” At this visit, both LJ and their family agree that LJ’s daytime sleepiness and declining grades are their main concerns.

Dr Z considers how to address the recent changes in LJ’s life and the significant reduction in sleep duration with LJ’s parents. Dr Z also thinks carefully about how to involve LJ’s parents as supportive partners in protecting LJ’s sleep time and quality.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr Z promote LJ’s involvement in medical decision-making and facilitate effective communication with the family while respecting LJ’s privacy?
keypoints: Dr. Z should support LJ’s involvement in medical decision-making, ensuring their active role in the development of solutions.
Utilizing motivational interviewing techniques, Dr. Z can assist LJ in reducing nighttime video game use and promote positive lifestyle changes.

Dr. Z should engage in collaborative discussions with LJ and their parents regarding sleep issues, exploring their beliefs, goals, and perceived barriers to formulate feasible intervention strategies.
Raising awareness about the prevalence of pediatric sleep disturbances can facilitate nonjudgmental communication and help establish a family alliance to improve sleep health.
Throughout the discussion, Dr. Z must collaborate with both LJ and their caregivers to personalize recommendations and address barriers to implementation.

title: When Should Pharmacological Interventions for Insomnia Be Recommended?
case:
Dr D sees CC, a 46-year-old patient who struggles to sleep well. CC is a parent and works between 55 and 60 hours per week at 2 jobs. CC’s family lives where there is frequently noise outside of their home at night. CC has trouble falling asleep and trouble staying asleep, with sleep interrupted by periods of wakeful anxiety. In total, CC probably logs about 5 hours of sleep per night.
Over the years, CC has tried over-the-counter melatonin, a dietary supplement, and diphenhydramine (an antihistamine). CC is currently on eszopiclone, a central nervous system depressant, which Dr D prescribed, but CC would like to change, since the eszopiclone makes them feel “hung over” in the morning. CC asks Dr D, “May I get a prescription for something else? You once prescribed benzos and they worked really well.”
Dr D considers whether a benzodiazepine (eg, alprazolam, clonazepam, or diazepam) would be appropriate. Dr D also wonders, “With these drugs, I’m treating the symptom of insomnia, when they work, but not the causes of CC’s long-term life stress, worry, and environment. Do the short- and long-term side effects of these drugs balance or outweigh the risks of untreated lack of sleep?”
Dr D considers how to respond to CC’s request.
case_rewrite:
Dr D is seeing CC, a 46-year-old patient who has been struggling with chronic sleep difficulties. CC is a parent who juggles two jobs, working between 55 and 60 hours each week. CC’s family lives in a neighborhood where nighttime noise is common, making restful sleep a constant challenge. CC reports trouble both falling asleep and staying asleep, with multiple awakenings marked by anxious thoughts. Most nights, CC manages only about five hours of sleep.

Over time, CC has attempted various remedies, including over-the-counter melatonin, dietary supplements, and diphenhydramine, an antihistamine. Currently, CC is taking eszopiclone, a prescription medication from Dr D, but complains of feeling “hung over” and groggy the next morning. Seeking relief, CC asks Dr D, “Can you prescribe something different? You gave me benzos before, and they really helped.”

Dr D pauses, weighing the possibility of prescribing a benzodiazepine such as alprazolam, clonazepam, or diazepam. Dr D reflects, “If I prescribe one of these, I might help CC sleep, but I’m only addressing the symptom, not the root causes—ongoing stress, anxiety, and a disruptive living environment. Are the immediate and long-term side effects of benzodiazepines justified, or do they create more harm than the risks of unaddressed sleep deprivation?”

Considering the risks and benefits, Dr D reflects on the best way to respond to CC’s request.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of unresolved chronic life stress, anxiety, and environmental factors, should benzodiazepine medications be recommended for the treatment of insomnia?
keypoints: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBTI) should be the preferred first-line treatment for chronic insomnia, as it improves sleep by modifying sleep habits and addressing disruptive thoughts, emotions, and social pressures, and it carries no side effects.

Benzodiazepine medications are associated with multiple adverse effects, including increased risk of motor vehicle accidents, cognitive decline, and falls or fractures; long-term use carries a risk of dependence and has been linked to cognitive impairment and dementia. Therefore, in most cases, the risks of benzodiazepines for treating insomnia outweigh the benefits.
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends against the long-term use of hypnotic medications except in specific circumstances, which this patient does not meet.

For patients who are unable or unwilling to engage in CBTI, the benefits of pharmacological treatment may outweigh the potential harms associated with insomnia and sleep deprivation; however, benzodiazepines and their inherent risks should be avoided whenever possible.

ethical_issues.question: In the treatment of chronic insomnia, how should the use of pharmacological interventions be balanced with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBTI) to ensure that patients receive the safest and most effective therapeutic approach?
keypoints: In the treatment of chronic insomnia, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBTI) should be prioritized, as it improves sleep by modifying sleep habits and addressing disruptive thoughts, emotions, and social pressures, and it carries no side effects.

The risks of pharmacological treatment must be carefully evaluated, especially benzodiazepine medications, whose risks in treating insomnia generally outweigh the benefits; therefore, their use should be avoided whenever possible, particularly in elderly populations.

In specific circumstances, for patients who are unable or unwilling to engage in CBTI, pharmacotherapy may be necessary; however, shared decision-making should be employed to determine whether to use medication and to select the appropriate agent.
Clinicians should promote CBTI as the foundational treatment and avoid benzodiazepine use when possible to ensure patients receive the safest and most effective therapeutic approach.

title: How Should Clinician-Researchers Model Regard for Nonhuman Animals Bred for and Used in Human-Centered Science?
case:
Dr Q is a clinician-scientist who studies brain tumor growth. The clinical utility of Dr Q’s work has grown in importance over the decades, and Dr Q’s team has contributed to many improvements in human brain tumor diagnostics.
Over the years, Dr Q’s team has responded to many changes required by the Code of Federal Regulations (9 CFR §§1-4.11)and the Health Research Extension Act of 1985,which augments the Animal Welfare Act of 1966.Evolution in social and cultural thought, attitudes, and activism also demand Dr Q’s lab staff members’ consideration and reconsideration of their roles in creating a market for laboratory animal cultivation and in using live mice in human-centered research. Dr Q seeks advice from Dr A, a veterinarian member of their organization’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), to more carefully consider the team’s short- and long-term efforts to minimize suffering among the live mice needed to carry out Dr Q’s protocols.
Dr Q mentions to Dr A, “I’d like to model thinking carefully about whether and when our efforts to minimize our animals’ pain and suffering is enough to meet our obligations to the animals we use for human clinical science applications. I suspect that orienting ourselves to these questions and concerns will be key to the future of our lab and work.”
Dr A considers how to respond, how to continue the exchange of ideas, and how to advise Dr Q.
case_rewrite:
Dr Q, a clinician-scientist dedicated to the study of brain tumor growth, has seen their research become increasingly vital to advancements in human brain tumor diagnostics. Over the years, Dr Q’s team has adapted to various updates in federal regulations, specifically those outlined in the Code of Federal Regulations (9 CFR §§1-4.11) and the Health Research Extension Act of 1985, which both reinforce and expand upon the Animal Welfare Act of 1966. Alongside these regulatory changes, Dr Q and the laboratory staff have also faced evolving societal perspectives and activism, prompting them to regularly reconsider their responsibilities in fostering the demand for laboratory animals and using live mice in research designed to benefit human health.

Recognizing the complexity of these ethical challenges, Dr Q turns to Dr A, a veterinarian who serves on their institution’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), seeking guidance. Dr Q expresses a desire for the team to critically evaluate when and how their current efforts to reduce pain and suffering in laboratory mice are sufficient to meet their ethical obligations. “I want us to carefully reflect on whether our strategies to minimize our animals’ pain and distress are truly adequate for the responsibilities we have—both to the animals themselves and to the future of our research,” Dr Q explains. “I believe that keeping these questions at the forefront of our work is crucial as our lab moves forward.”

Dr A listens thoughtfully, considering how best to respond and continue this important conversation. Dr A reflects on how to advise Dr Q in balancing the potential clinical benefits of their brain tumor research with the moral imperative to prevent excessive suffering among the animal subjects, and how to encourage the lab to engage in ongoing ethical reflection and proactive improvements in animal care.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr Q and Dr A ethically evaluate whether the potential human benefits of their brain tumor research justify the harms caused to nonhuman animals, in accordance with current medical ethics standards?
keypoints: Assess the potential value of each study in comparison with non-alleviable harms to animals, ensuring that human benefits morally outweigh the animal harms.
Establish research parameters regarding tumor-related harms in the laboratory to exclude types of studies where the burden of animal harm is excessively great and unconscionable.
Acknowledge that certain harms inflicted on sentient beings are inherently wrong and should be avoided, even if the human benefits are significant, to prevent excessive animal pain and suffering.

ethical_issues.question: How can one, within the U.S. oversight system, go beyond regulatory requirements and public perception to proactively engage in moral justification and deeper ethical practice in order to fulfill moral obligations to the animals themselves?
keypoints: Nonhuman animals possess intrinsic moral worth, and ethical obligations are owed directly to them, not merely as means to human ends.
Regulatory compliance, while necessary for ethical research, is not sufficient in itself to justify the ethical permissibility of a project.

Researchers must rigorously evaluate the scientific and clinical value of each study in relation to the inevitable harms imposed on animal subjects, and clearly define acceptable parameters for tumor-related harms within the laboratory setting.
Research teams should strive to optimize housing, nutrition, environmental enrichment, and social groupings to meet the species-specific needs of mice to the fullest extent possible.
The adoption of innovative analgesic and palliative interventions should be prioritized to minimize suffering and promote the welfare of animal subjects, particularly in the context of tumor burden.

Dr Q’s reflection on the ethical dimensions of animal use and proactive engagement with veterinary expertise exemplify the virtues of practical wisdom and moral responsibility in clinician-researchers.

title: According to Which Criteria Should We Determine Whether and When IACUCs Are Sufficient for Protecting the Welfare of Nonhuman Animals Used in Research?
case:
Cardiologist and scientist Dr J oversees a federally funded cardiac antiarrhythmic pharmacologic research lab in a well-known academic health center. Dr J teaches in many of the health sciences programs of the university and is often invited to lecture on topics ranging from research ethics to animal research protocol design to pharmacology and cardiac pathophysiology. Dr J is especially known among students for their lecture on how mid-21st-century animal rights campaigns informed passage of the Animal Welfare Act of 1966.
Dr J’s team’s protocols have always adhered to federal animal care and use guidelines, and Dr J served for many years on the university’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Dr J’s team’s research remains a controversial point of tension, however, between animal rights activists and patient advocacy groups, whose presence is always visible to students.
Dr J’s team’s research requires induction of cardiac arrhythmias in source-bred dogs. Antiarrhythmic pharmacologic agents are then administered to the dogs, and those agents’ cardiac effects in the dogs are observed over time, sometimes until their deaths. Over the course of a typical study, many dogs experience cardiac arrest and painful gastrointestinal and pulmonary side effects of the pharmacologic agents.
Protesters, usually animal rights activists, and counter-protestors have long gathered with signs, pamphlets, and bullhorns outside the campus’s known research facilities. Counter-protesters are usually patients and patient advocates, including children and parents of children with congenital heart conditions that predispose them to cardiac arrhythmias. Protesters’ signs often show photographs of live mammals, presumably animals just like those used in research on campus, connected to invasively placed tubes and devices. Slogans like “Research is not ‘care’! IACUCs are sham federal covers for animal cruelty!” are commonly seen on signs.
Students in Dr J’s lectures sometimes ask Dr J about protesters’ messages and question whether IACUC requirements are enough protection for research animals’ welfare.
Dr J considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Dr J, a cardiologist and scientist, leads a federally funded research laboratory focused on antiarrhythmic pharmacologic agents at a prominent academic health center. In addition to overseeing the lab, Dr J is deeply involved in teaching across the university’s health sciences programs and is frequently invited to lecture on subjects such as research ethics, animal research protocol design, pharmacology, and the pathophysiology of cardiac conditions. Among students, Dr J is especially recognized for a compelling lecture detailing how animal rights movements of the mid-21st century shaped the development and eventual passage of the Animal Welfare Act of 1966.

Dr J’s research group has consistently adhered to federal guidelines on animal care and use, with Dr J having served for several years as a member of the university’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Despite this commitment to regulatory compliance, the team’s research continues to provoke sharp debate between animal rights activists and advocates for patients, a tension that is highly visible to the campus community.

The research conducted by Dr J’s team involves inducing cardiac arrhythmias in dogs bred specifically for scientific purposes. Following induction, the animals are treated with antiarrhythmic pharmacologic agents, and the effects of these agents on cardiac function are meticulously observed over time. In the course of these studies, many dogs experience cardiac arrest and endure significant gastrointestinal and pulmonary side effects, which can be painful and, in some cases, fatal.

On a regular basis, groups of protesters—primarily animal rights activists—gather outside the university’s research facilities, joined by counter-protesters who are often patients and family members of children with congenital heart conditions that predispose them to life-threatening arrhythmias. The activists’ signs display images of live animals attached to tubes and invasive devices, accompanied by slogans such as, “Research is not ‘care’! IACUCs are sham federal covers for animal cruelty!” The presence of both groups, armed with pamphlets and bullhorns, is a familiar and striking scene to students and staff alike.

During lectures, Dr J is frequently questioned by students regarding the messages presented by protesters and the sufficiency of IACUC oversight in safeguarding the welfare of research animals. Students express concern about whether compliance with existing requirements is truly enough to minimize suffering and uphold ethical standards.

Faced with these questions, Dr J carefully considers how best to address the students’ concerns about the ethical challenges and responsibilities that come with animal-based research.

ethical_issues.question: Are Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUCs) capable of identifying and minimizing avoidable suffering in nonhuman animals used in research?
keypoints: IACUCs are critical in identifying and minimizing avoidable suffering in nonhuman animals used in experiments; however, their capacity may be limited by insufficient expertise among committee members.
IACUC members must conduct impartial and unbiased reviews to ensure the adequate protection of animal welfare.
IACUCs should recruit subject matter expert researchers to review proposals in order to compensate for gaps in the members’ specialized knowledge.
There exists a fourth R, reject, which serves to constrain research when the anticipated harm to nonhuman animals clearly outweighs the potential knowledge to be gained.

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances should research protocols be rejected when the harm caused to nonhuman animals clearly outweighs the potential knowledge to be gained?
keypoints: Research proposals must be rejected if the anticipated harm to nonhuman animals clearly outweighs the potential knowledge to be gained.
The responsibilities of the IACUC include identifying and rejecting research proposals in which the knowledge gained does not justify the harm inflicted on the animals.
If the tested pharmacologic agent is demonstrably toxic in nonhuman animals, it is unsuitable for human trials, and from a scientific perspective, such research should be rejected.
The IACUC should recruit subject matter experts with relevant experience to ensure accurate assessment of animal harm and the potential benefits of the knowledge gained.

ethical_issues.question: How can we ensure that members of Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUCs) conduct impartial and unbiased reviews to protect animal welfare?
keypoints: IACUC members must conduct impartial and unbiased reviews to ensure the protection of animal welfare.
Federal regulations prohibit IACUC members from having financial, personal, or professional conflicts of interest in order to reduce bias.
Establishing a standardized system of blinded proposal review can help promote impartiality and reduce bias.
IACUCs should be able to identify and minimize avoidable suffering and reject research in which the anticipated harm clearly outweighs the potential knowledge to be gained.

title: What Should Clinicians in Organizations Without Established MLP Programs Do When Their Patients Need Lawyers to Meet Their Health Needs?
case:
In the emergency department (ED) of a large, urban academic health center near the US-Mexico border, Dr B encounters GG, who presents with severe fatigue, headache, dysuria (painful urination), and aching joints. After GG is stabilized, metabolic tests reveal that GG has kidney failure. Dr B refers GG immediately for emergency dialysis and then routine dialysis follow-up. However, due to GG’s immigration status, the state’s Medicaid program does not reimburse for routine dialysis, only for emergency dialysis.
Three weeks later, Dr B gets called back to the ED because GG is back with severe life-threatening symptoms (hyperkalemia, confusion, and hypoxia from pulmonary edema) due to lack of routine dialysis. Dr B is morally distressed and outraged that he has had to witness GG’s symptoms become life-threatening due to the state Medicaid program’s lack of coverage for optimal kidney care (eg, routine dialysis).
Dr B thinks, “My patient needs a lawyer,” and wonders what to do.
case_rewrite:
In the busy emergency department (ED) of a major academic medical center near the US-Mexico border, Dr B is on shift when GG arrives, complaining of intense fatigue, a pounding headache, painful urination, and aching joints. After stabilizing GG, Dr B runs a battery of metabolic tests, which reveal that GG is suffering from kidney failure. Recognizing the urgency, Dr B arranges for GG to receive emergency dialysis right away and instructs GG to follow up with routine dialysis sessions.

However, Dr B soon learns that because of GG’s immigration status, the state’s Medicaid program will only cover emergency dialysis but not the routine sessions needed to maintain GG’s health. Routine dialysis, which would prevent medical crises, is not reimbursed under the current policy for undocumented patients.

Three weeks later, Dr B is urgently called back to the ED. GG has returned, this time in critical condition—dangerously high potassium levels, confusion, and severe shortness of breath caused by fluid building up in the lungs. These symptoms are the direct result of missing routine dialysis treatments that GG simply could not access due to insurance barriers.

Deeply frustrated and morally distressed, Dr B finds it intolerable that GG’s life is repeatedly endangered because the state Medicaid program withholds coverage for essential kidney care from undocumented patients. Dr B thinks to himself, “My patient needs a lawyer,” and begins to consider what steps he can take in the face of this injustice.

ethical_issues.question: How can healthcare organizations and clinicians resist threats to equity-promoting immigration policies through policy advocacy and the practice of structural competency, and ensure that undocumented immigrants receive comprehensive medical care?
keypoints: Clinicians can improve care for undocumented immigrants by operationalizing structural competency to identify and resist threats to equity-enhancing immigration policies.

Health care institutions and clinicians should collaborate with community organizations and legal services to mitigate the unique barriers faced by undocumented immigrants and ensure their access to comprehensive medical care.
Clinicians and health systems should obtain information on policy advocacy and resources that promote equitable care and provide referrals to legal counsel when such policies are violated.
Clinicians and institutions should support policy reforms that expand Medicaid coverage to guarantee that undocumented immigrants receive necessary routine medical services.

Advocates and health care organizations should work to dispel the “zero-sum game” fallacy and promote multisector collaboration to address the sociopolitical barriers confronting undocumented immigrants.

title: How Should MLP Clinicians and Attorneys Help Veterans Secure Disability Benefits When Health Records Documentation Is Insufficient?
case:
AB is 55 years old, unhoused, self-employed, divorced and has no children. He is unable to work due to a back injury sustained during his job as a contractor 2 years ago that limits his functional ability. He is currently living in his van and on alternating nights at a local shelter. A staff member at the shelter advises AB to file a claim for social security disability insurance (SSDI) benefits. AB tells the staffer he tried but found the application so complicated he gave up. The staff member then remembers that AB is a veteran and connects him to a new medical-legal partnership (MLP) housed on the grounds of the local Veterans Health Administration (VHA) medical center. At the VHA MLP, AB is fortunate to meet an attorney with considerable experience in a community MLP, JD, who arranges for AB to see Dr C, a new primary care physician in the VHA MLP. JD explains to Dr C that to file an SSDI claim, AB must be able to demonstrate that he has been unable to work for the last year due to his back injury.
Preparing for her first visit with AB, Dr C learns that AB has an existing VHA electronic health record (EHR): AB served in the army as a mechanic during Operation Iraqi Freedom. AB’s health record shows that, after being discharged from the military, he was seen at a VHA medical center in another city for symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and suicidal ideation. AB attended a few appointments but then moved across the country and never reestablished care in the VHA system or in the community. After examining AB, Dr C tells JD she has “no question that AB’s back injury would likely qualify for SSDI,” and she also thought his PTSD would meet diagnostic criteria, yet she does not believe there is currently adequate evidence to support either claim. She wants to help AB get the benefits he deserves but worries about compromising her professional integrity by engaging in questionable documentation practices. JD reassures her they both have the same goal—not to manipulate the health record but to get AB the care he needs and deserves. They meet to discuss their options and consider next steps.
case_rewrite:
AB, a 55-year-old veteran, is currently unhoused, self-employed, divorced, and has no children. Two years ago, while working as a contractor, AB suffered a debilitating back injury that now severely limits his ability to work. Without stable employment or income, he lives in his van and occasionally stays at a local shelter. One evening, a shelter staff member suggests that AB apply for Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) benefits. AB explains that he previously attempted to apply, but found the process so confusing and overwhelming that he ultimately gave up. The staff member, recalling AB’s veteran status, connects him with a recently established medical-legal partnership (MLP) located at the local Veterans Health Administration (VHA) medical center.

At the VHA MLP, AB meets JD, an attorney with significant experience working in community MLPs. JD quickly arranges for AB to have a medical evaluation with Dr C, a new primary care physician in the VHA MLP. JD informs Dr C that for AB’s SSDI application to be successful, AB will need clear documentation showing he has been unable to work for at least a year due to his back injury.

As Dr C prepares for her first appointment with AB, she accesses his VHA electronic health record (EHR). She learns that AB served as a mechanic in the army during Operation Iraqi Freedom, and that after his military discharge, he had been seen at a VHA medical center in another state for symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and suicidal ideation. The record shows that AB attended a handful of appointments but, after moving across the country, did not reestablish care, either within the VHA system or in the community.

During her assessment, Dr C finds that AB’s back injury appears serious enough to meet SSDI criteria, and she suspects that his PTSD would also fulfill diagnostic requirements. However, she notes that the available documentation is insufficient to substantiate either claim at present. Dr C expresses to JD her strong desire to help AB secure the benefits he deserves, but she is concerned about maintaining her professional integrity and does not want to engage in questionable documentation practices. JD reassures her that their shared objective is to ensure AB receives the care and support he is entitled to, not to manipulate medical records. Together, they begin to discuss their available options and consider next steps.

ethical_issues.question: In assisting AB with his application for disability benefits, how should clinicians and attorneys within the MLP balance their ethical obligations to provide accurate and thorough medical documentation with their duty to advocate for AB’s best interests, particularly when existing health records are insufficient?
keypoints: The distinctiveness of VHA-MLPs enables attorneys and clinicians to address the disability diagnostic and documentation dilemma through a shared commitment to mitigating the adverse effects of social determinants of health.
VHA practitioners can utilize comprehensive, longitudinal electronic health records to bridge documentation gaps, ensuring the provision of accurate and complete medical records.
Collaborating with VHA psychologists to conduct comprehensive assessments can establish a stronger evidentiary basis to support disability benefits claims.
Clinicians and attorneys should avoid an excessive focus on the instrumental goal of securing SSDI financial benefits to prevent the emergence of ethical conflicts.

MLPs can collaboratively facilitate access to a broader range of VHA services that, in the long term, enhance veterans’ overall well-being and align with the VHA’s strategic priority to reduce suicide rates among marginalized, underserved, and unhoused veterans.

ethical_issues.question: Within the VHA-MLP framework, how can attorneys and clinicians coordinate their respective ethical obligations to avoid conflicts in diagnostic documentation?
keypoints: Attorneys and clinicians should shift the foundation of their collaboration from administrative objectives to a shared commitment centered on patient well-being in order to avoid ethical conflicts.
The distinctiveness of VHA MLPs enables attorneys and clinicians to coordinate the disability diagnostic and documentation process by addressing the adverse impact of social determinants of health.

By leveraging the VHA’s comprehensive longitudinal electronic health record, clinicians can submit medically accurate documentation, which attorneys can translate into legal language to support claims.

The VHA has implemented measures to facilitate information sharing, including requiring veterans to sign authorizations for the release of health information and mandating clinicians to complete non-VA medical and social service forms.

ethical_issues.question: How can JD, the MLP attorney, and VHA clinicians ethically utilize AB’s comprehensive electronic health record to support his disability benefits claim while maintaining professional independence and safeguarding AB’s confidentiality?
keypoints: The VHA’s comprehensive electronic health record system contains decades of longitudinal data across the entire system, which can support veterans’ benefits claims.
Veterans must sign an authorization to release health information prior to referral to ensure that information sharing complies with patient confidentiality principles.
The VHA has issued directives requiring VA clinicians to complete non-VA medical and social service forms to facilitate veterans’ benefits applications.
Through the VHA-MLP program, clinicians can submit all medically accurate existing documentation, which attorneys can then translate into legal language to support benefits claims.

title: How Is Access to Legal Resources and Advocacy Foundational to Health Justice?
case: JM is 29 years of age and presents in distress to a municipal emergency department with an acute asthma exacerbation for the third time this month. JM is admitted and seen by a hospitalist, Dr H, who learns from JM that he is living in an apartment with mold and fears being evicted after falling behind on rent. Dr H is concerned that JM will continue to experience severe asthma exacerbations and overall poor health if he remains in substandard and unstable housing.
case_rewrite: JM, a 29-year-old, arrives at the city’s emergency department in visible distress, suffering from a severe asthma attack—his third visit with the same issue this month. After being admitted, JM is evaluated by Dr H, the hospitalist on duty. During their conversation, JM discloses that he is currently living in an apartment plagued by mold. He admits he is behind on rent payments and is anxious about possibly being evicted. Dr H grows increasingly worried that unless JM’s housing situation improves, he will likely continue to face serious asthma exacerbations and persistent health problems due to the poor and unstable living conditions.

ethical_issues.question: When physicians encounter patients whose health issues stem from socioeconomic conditions, how can they effectively intervene beyond medical treatment to improve the patients’ health outcomes?
keypoints: Physicians can utilize medical-legal partnership programs to recognize patients’ housing issues as potential legal matters and refer them to attorneys.
Physicians can provide medical records or court testimony to substantiate the health harms caused by unhealthy conditions and the urgent need for remediation.
Physicians and their medical-legal partnership collaborators can offer testimony at legislative hearings to advocate for systemic reforms aimed at reducing health disparities.

Physicians can serve as resource allies by offering professional support to relevant organizations, participating in community-led research, and contributing to the development of the health justice agenda.

ethical_issues.question: How do medical-legal partnership programs identify and address patients’ legal needs through interprofessional collaboration to advance health justice?
keypoints: Medical-legal partnerships embed lawyers within healthcare settings to train healthcare partners to screen patients for social needs and refer them for legal services, thereby identifying and addressing patients’ legal needs.

Medical-legal partnerships leverage patients’ presence in healthcare settings and their trust-based relationships with healthcare providers to reduce barriers to legal assistance and promote health justice.

Lawyers can address patients’ housing issues through legal actions, such as sending letters to landlords or initiating litigation, and provide legal support to prevent eviction, ensuring patients have stable and healthy housing.

title: When Medication Treatment for Opioid Use Disorder Gets Disrupted by Extra-Clinical Variables, How Should Clinicians Respond?
case:
MJ has been in a methadone treatment program for 20 years. Moderately high doses of methadone are needed to treat MJ’s opioid cravings and are prescribed and managed by Dr D.
MJ does not use other drugs, works full-time, and spends free time with family members. After driving over the speed limit to get to a hospital where their daughter was giving birth, MJ was pulled over and arrested after violating the suspension of their driver’s license for past traffic violations. While jailed for nearly 2 days, MJ did not have access to their prescribed methadone; MJ experienced severe withdrawal symptoms and cravings, none of which were treated while they were incarcerated.
MJ’s release from jail did not incorporate follow-up appointments for MJ’s usual treatment program, and a couple of days after their release, MJ still had not returned to the clinic. Dr D worries that MJ has returned to drug use and wonders what to do.
case_rewrite:
MJ has been enrolled in a methadone maintenance program for the past 20 years, with Dr D overseeing and prescribing the moderately high doses required to control MJ’s opioid cravings. MJ does not use any illicit substances, maintains steady full-time employment, and enjoys close relationships with family members, dedicating much of their free time to them. 

One evening, MJ received a call that their daughter was in labor at a hospital across town. In a rush to be present for the birth, MJ exceeded the speed limit and was stopped by law enforcement. During the traffic stop, it was discovered that MJ’s driver’s license was suspended due to prior traffic infractions. MJ was subsequently arrested and held in jail for nearly two days.

While incarcerated, MJ did not have access to their prescribed methadone. Despite experiencing severe withdrawal symptoms and intense cravings, MJ received no medical intervention or substitute treatment during their time in custody. Upon release, there were no arrangements made to reconnect MJ with their regular methadone treatment program or to facilitate follow-up care.

Several days after release from jail, MJ had still not returned to the clinic. Dr D grows increasingly concerned that the interruption in treatment may have led MJ to relapse or resume drug use, and considers what steps should be taken to address the situation and prevent similar disruptions in the future.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians ensure continuity of medication treatment to prevent withdrawal symptoms when a patient’s treatment is disrupted by extra-clinical factors?
keypoints: Physicians should develop contingency plans to ensure the continuation of methadone treatment during patient incarceration to prevent withdrawal symptoms.

Physicians should engage in advance care planning with patients regarding potential treatment interruptions, including providing a letter for use during detention that contains a treatment summary, current medication dosage information, and emergency contact details for the prescribing physician.

Physicians should establish communication and collaboration with local jails and correctional healthcare providers to improve processes for treatment continuity and ensure that patients can maintain access to medication during incarceration.

Physicians may remind jail medical staff that federal regulations permit any physician with a Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) license to prescribe methadone for up to three days to prevent withdrawal during treatment transitions.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians and correctional institutions ensure that patients like MJ continue to receive necessary treatment for opioid use disorder during periods of incarceration, in order to prevent withdrawal, health risks, and potential overdose death?
keypoints: The provision of medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) within carceral settings can significantly reduce overdose mortality in the first month following release.
Incarcerated individuals generally retain constitutional and civil rights to receive medical care, and the Supreme Court mandates that states provide necessary healthcare to persons in custody.

Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) protects patients with substance use disorder (SUD) who are receiving MOUD; jails that fail to arrange for continued treatment may be in violation of the law.

Clinicians providing MOUD should develop contingency plans to ensure continuity of treatment during incarceration and may provide patients with signed letters summarizing their treatment to be used if detained.

Physicians and medical teams should establish communication with local jails and correctional healthcare providers and, when appropriate, remind jail physicians that federal regulations permit any Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA)-licensed physician to prescribe methadone for up to three days to facilitate treatment continuity and medication administration.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians improve treatment accessibility for patients with opioid use disorder and reduce structural inequities through legal and policy reforms?
keypoints: Clinicians can promote structural reform by reporting to the Department of Justice Civil Rights Division when jails fail to screen patients for OUD and do not provide necessary medical care.
Participating in national advocacy efforts to reform laws and policies that continue to harm people with SUD is one measure clinicians can take to improve treatment accessibility for their patients.

Advocating for policies that enhance MOUD accessibility for incarcerated populations, including reforming Medicaid exclusion policies and requiring jails to provide all three FDA-approved forms of MOUD.
Supporting legal reforms and the continuation of federal policies, such as telehealth authorization for buprenorphine, that expand access to MOUD in order to reduce structural inequities.

Clinicians should anticipate and plan for potential treatment disruptions experienced by patients, integrating strategies within treatment plans to mitigate harm caused by systemic and policy failures.

title: When Are “Paraphernalia” Critical Medical Supplies?
case: GG has opioid use disorder (OUD) with a history of multiple incidental overdoses. Part of GG’s OUD treatment plan, managed by a local clinic team, requires GG’s use of clean syringes and fentanyl test strips, a supply of which GG brings when visiting family. GG is pulled over by a state trooper just after crossing an interstate border. A search of the vehicle finds no illegal drugs, but GG’s syringes and test strips are confiscated. GG tries to explain, “Those are medical supplies I get from my clinic. I need those,” but GG is arrested and jailed for drug paraphernalia possession.
case_rewrite: GG has opioid use disorder (OUD) and a documented history of several accidental overdoses. As part of their OUD management, GG’s treatment plan—overseen by a local clinic team—includes the use of clean syringes and fentanyl test strips, which GG obtains through the clinic. When visiting family, GG brings these supplies along. On one such trip, after crossing a state border, GG is stopped by a state trooper. During a search of GG’s vehicle, officers find no illegal drugs, but do discover GG’s syringes and fentanyl test strips. Despite GG’s efforts to clarify—“Those are medical supplies from my clinic. I need them for my treatment”—the supplies are confiscated. GG is then arrested and jailed on charges of possessing drug paraphernalia.

ethical_issues.question: In jurisdictions where such supplies are legally prohibited, do physicians have an ethical obligation to provide harm reduction materials to protect the health and safety of their patients?
keypoints: Physicians face ethical dilemmas when providing harm reduction supplies in jurisdictions where such provision is legally prohibited, as compliance with the law may result in patients being denied essential medical care.

AMA Principle of Medical Ethics III states that a physician shall respect the law but also has a responsibility to seek changes in those requirements that are contrary to the best interests of the patient, implying an ethical obligation for physicians to advocate for reform to protect patient health.

AMA Principle IX (supporting access to medical care for all people), together with the principles of nonmaleficence and beneficence, forms the ethical foundation for physicians to provide harm reduction supplies even when doing so conflicts with local laws.

Clinicians should adopt a medical perspective that is more life-saving, humane, and beneficent, consistent with AMA Principle III: “A physician shall respect the law and also recognize a responsibility to seek changes in those requirements which are contrary to the best interests of the patient.”

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians balance compliance with the law and the protection of their patients’ best interests when helping patients understand the legal risks of traveling across state lines with harm reduction supplies?
keypoints: Physicians should respect the law but have an ethical obligation to advocate for modification of regulations when they conflict with the best interests of the patient.
Physicians should support patients’ access to medical care and anticipate and prevent potential legal risks that patients may encounter.
Physicians should inform patients of the legal risks associated with carrying harm reduction supplies across state lines and advise careful consideration of the risks and benefits.

Physicians may recommend that patients transport their supplies in their suitcase using the original containers, accompanied by prescription information and an official letter from the treating physician, to mitigate legal risks.

ethical_issues.question: How can patients be ensured access to necessary medical support and information to reduce health risks in jurisdictions that do not recognize harm reduction strategies as legitimate medical interventions?
keypoints: Patients are advised to carry their treatment supplies in their original containers when traveling across state lines, accompanied by prescription information and an official letter from the treating physician or treatment program to verify the legitimacy of the materials.

Physicians should respect the law while simultaneously bearing a responsibility to advocate for changes to regulations that contravene the best interests of patients, thereby ensuring access to necessary medical care.

Patients must receive comprehensive risk disclosure and informed consent, including information about the legal risks associated with carrying these supplies, to assist them in carefully weighing the benefits and risks of interstate travel.

title: How Should Risks and Benefits of Short-Acting Opioids Be Evaluated in the Care of Inpatients With OUD?
case:
KC is admitted for infective endocarditis secondary to microbes entering their bloodstream during repeated injection drug use. KC has a long history of opioid use disorder (OUD) and has intermittently been treated for it. KC’s history of using opioids started when KC exhausted a supply of oxycodone, prescribed with limited refills for postoperative pain management, which led KC to start using heroin and then fentanyl.
Members of KC’s clinical team have not come to consensus about how to manage KC’s pain or OUD. They are aware that KC has their own supply of drugs and wants to leave the hospital as soon as possible and against medical advice, if necessary. Team members consider administering short-acting opioids to keep KC comfortable and in hospital for intravenous antibiotics and evaluation for cardiac surgery, but one clinician opposes any care plan that “feeds” KC’s OUD.
case_rewrite:
KC was admitted to the hospital with infective endocarditis, a serious infection caused by bacteria entering the bloodstream through repeated injection drug use. KC has a longstanding history of opioid use disorder (OUD), for which they have received treatment intermittently. KC’s opioid use began after a postoperative prescription for oxycodone ran out and refills were limited, prompting KC to turn to heroin and later fentanyl.

The clinical team caring for KC has not reached agreement on the best approach to address both KC’s pain and OUD during hospitalization. They are aware that KC possesses their own supply of drugs and has expressed a desire to leave the hospital as soon as possible—even if that means leaving against medical advice. Some team members support administering short-acting opioids to manage KC’s pain and withdrawal symptoms, hoping this will keep KC comfortable and engaged in treatment for intravenous antibiotics and possible cardiac surgery. However, one clinician strongly opposes any care plan perceived as “feeding” KC’s opioid use disorder.

As the team discusses KC’s care, they are challenged to consider how to provide comprehensive, evidence-based, and non-stigmatizing treatment for OUD, ensure appropriate management of pain and withdrawal, and implement harm reduction strategies to address the risks associated with nonprescribed substance use while KC remains in the hospital.

ethical_issues.question: How can a full spectrum of evidence-based, non-stigmatizing treatment be provided to inpatients with opioid use disorder to maximize benefits and minimize harms?
keypoints: A full spectrum of evidence-based treatment for patients with opioid use disorder should be provided during hospitalization without stigma, in order to maximize benefits and minimize harms.
Stigmatizing language should be avoided; neutral language that recognizes patient dignity and emphasizes the medical nature of opioid use disorder should be adopted.

Patients should be guided to receive concomitant treatment that addresses both their underlying medical conditions and substance-related diagnoses, including immediate access to opioid agonist treatment and effective management of pain and withdrawal symptoms.
Short-acting opioids can be used to manage acute pain and withdrawal symptoms in patients receiving opioid agonist treatment, thereby reducing the risk of patient-initiated discharge.

In-hospital interventions such as provision of naloxone kits, access to clean injection equipment, and supervised consumption services should be offered to reduce morbidity and mortality risks during hospitalization.
Patients’ goals, values, and beliefs should guide the prioritization of clinical needs; patients must be afforded the right to choose among treatment options and have their choices respected.

ethical_issues.question: How can harm reduction strategies be implemented in the hospital setting to mitigate the risks associated with nonprescribed substance use during hospitalization and ensure that patients receive high-quality medical care?
keypoints: Implement harm reduction strategies by distributing naloxone kits and providing safer substance use education to mitigate the risks associated with nonprescribed substance use during hospitalization.
Provide new injection equipment and sharps disposal containers, and ensure patients have access to secure storage to reduce the risks of substance use within the hospital setting.
Permit hospitalized patients to use their own substances under medical supervision through supervised consumption services, thereby reducing the risks related to nonprescribed substance use.
Formalized supervised consumption services can prevent legal charges related to substance use for both patients and healthcare providers and offer immediate medical response to any adverse events.

title: When Should Patients at the End of Life Get Antimicrobials?
case: LK is a 75-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer who is admitted for pneumonia. She is administered broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics with subsequent improvement of her fever and hypoxia. Imaging of the chest reveals a tumor obstructing the right lower lobe bronchus. Due to the extent of metastatic disease, frequent infections, and generalized weakness, LK is not a candidate for additional surgery or other cancer-directed therapies. The decision is made to focus on comfort, and LK discusses her treatment preferences during transition to hospice care. While many of her preferences were previously outlined when completing her advance directive, she has not yet discussed the use of antimicrobials. LK asks if she should continue taking antibiotics when she returns home.
case_rewrite: LK, a 75-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer, is admitted to the hospital with pneumonia. She is started on broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, which lead to improvement in her fever and oxygen levels. Chest imaging reveals a tumor obstructing the right lower lobe bronchus. Given the extent of her metastatic disease, frequent infections, and marked weakness, further surgery or cancer-directed treatments are not options for LK. The medical team decides to shift the focus of her care to comfort, and LK participates in discussions about her treatment preferences as she prepares to transition to hospice care. While LK had previously documented many of her wishes in her advance directive, the use of antibiotics had not been specifically addressed. As discharge approaches, LK asks her physician, Dr. W, whether she should continue taking antibiotics when she returns home.

ethical_issues.question: In patients at the end of life, how can the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence be balanced in the use of antimicrobials to ensure patient comfort and quality of life?
keypoints: In patients at the end of life, the use of antimicrobials should be patient-centered, involving an assessment of whether a bacterial infection is present and whether it is causing distressing symptoms.
The use of antimicrobials requires weighing whether they can realistically improve symptoms and whether their effect surpasses that of non-antimicrobial medications.

When prescribing antimicrobials aligns with the principle of beneficence, clinicians should have reasonable expectations that symptom relief will occur, while also attending to the principle of nonmaleficence by considering potential harms of antimicrobial therapy.

Potential harms of antimicrobials include intolerance symptoms, allergic reactions, and indirect harms related to intravenous administration; these risks must be carefully balanced against potential benefits.

Antimicrobial prescribing must be individualized to each patient’s unique clinical context and goals of care, with clear communication to patients and families regarding realistic expectations of benefits and risks.
If antimicrobials are unlikely to achieve the patient’s known goals and may cause harm, clinicians may ethically recommend withholding or discontinuing antibiotic therapy.

ethical_issues.question: In prescribing antimicrobials for patients at the end of life, how should clinicians consider and evaluate the potential benefits of antimicrobial therapy alongside the risks of antimicrobial resistance in order to uphold the principle of justice for society?
keypoints: The use of antimicrobials at the end of life should take into account the risk of antimicrobial resistance, especially when the anticipated benefits are minimal.
Clinicians have an obligation to assess the risk of antimicrobial resistance when prescribing antimicrobials and to avoid unnecessary use of broad-spectrum agents when benefits are limited or absent.

Upholding the principle of justice requires balancing the individual needs of patients with the preservation of antimicrobial effectiveness for society in antimicrobial prescribing for patients at the end of life.
Existing microbiological data and local antimicrobial resistance patterns should be reviewed to avoid prescribing unnecessarily broad-spectrum antimicrobials.

ethical_issues.question: In advance care planning, how can the use of antimicrobials be effectively discussed to ensure patient autonomy and informed decision-making while avoiding undue psychological burden on patients or their families?
keypoints: Antimicrobial use should be discussed within advance care planning to ensure that patients make informed choices based on their own values, and clinicians have a responsibility to respect the patient’s final decisions.

Clinicians should carefully evaluate the potential benefits and risks of antimicrobials in the context of the individual goals of care and clinical circumstances of patients at the end of life, and communicate these clearly to patients and their families.
Discussing antimicrobial use facilitates better understanding of treatment implications by patients and families, providing them with additional time to make informed decisions.

title: How Should Clinicians Navigate Interprofessional Tension in Their Roles as Antimicrobial Stewards?
case:
RX is an infectious diseases (ID) pharmacist reviewing a list of antimicrobials pending prior authorization. RX calls Dr H, a hospitalist physician colleague, to discuss their prescription for meropenem, a broad-spectrum antibiotic, for JJ, an 89-year-old patient with delirium whom Dr H admitted this morning. JJ has mild hypertension and osteoporosis but is generally healthy and has not been hospitalized for several years.
During the call, Dr H explains that the order for meropenem is for empiric coverage pending further diagnostic workup, including urine cultures, to guide definitive therapy for possible sepsis from a urinary tract infection (UTI) that Dr H believes is the cause of JJ’s delirium. RX queries Dr H specifically about whether the bland urinalysis, pending urine culture, and lack of leukocytosis make UTI an unlikely cause of JJ’s delirium, particularly from a multidrug-resistant organism that would require meropenem. Dr H responds, “If JJ has an infection, a poor clinical outcome will be my professional responsibility, so I won’t change the prescription.” RX acknowledges Dr H’s perspective and responsibility for the patient’s care. But RX also shares their own assessment of the patient informed by (1) the organization’s UTI guidance, which discusses risk factors necessitating broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics (absent in this case) and (2) local susceptibility patterns (ie, hospital antibiogram) for common UTI pathogens. Dr H responds, “I agree that the information RX provided suggests that an alternative agent might work, but I remain concerned about JJ’s clinical status, so I prefer to use the broadest agent possible. I’ll switch when JJ’s urine cultures are back in a couple of days.”
RX then states that, in cases of disagreement like this one, the next step in the organization’s prescription preauthorization protocol is to consult the antimicrobial stewardship program’s medical director, Dr MD. Dr MD’s review of JJ’s record supports RX’s findings and recommendation to utilize ceftriaxone, a narrower-spectrum agent with excellent activity against common UTI pathogens based on hospital antibiogram. Dr MD calls Dr H, who now agrees to changing meropenem to ceftriaxone. Dr H adds that they do not appreciate pharmacists “acting like antibiotic police” about their empiric antimicrobial prescribing decisions. Dr MD counters, “We are all working on the same team toward the same goal to take the best care of our patients.”
After the interaction, Dr MD wonders how to improve collegiality and promote more efficient, productive interprofessional collaboration.
case_rewrite:
RX, an infectious diseases (ID) pharmacist, is reviewing the hospital’s daily list of antimicrobials that require prior authorization. As part of this stewardship role, RX contacts Dr H, a hospitalist physician, regarding a new order for meropenem—a broad-spectrum antibiotic—for JJ, an 89-year-old patient. JJ, recently admitted by Dr H, presents with acute delirium. Aside from mild hypertension and osteoporosis, JJ has remained in generally good health and has not required hospitalization for several years.

When RX calls, Dr H explains that meropenem was started empirically to cover for a possible urinary tract infection (UTI) as the cause of JJ’s delirium, pending further diagnostic workup, including a urine culture. Dr H expresses concern about missing a severe infection, stating, “If JJ does have an infection and fares poorly, it’s my responsibility. I’m not comfortable changing the prescription right now.” RX listens and acknowledges Dr H’s sense of responsibility, but also raises questions about the clinical evidence: JJ’s urinalysis is unremarkable, the urine culture is pending, and there is no leukocytosis, all of which make a UTI—especially one caused by a multidrug-resistant organism—seem unlikely.

RX shares additional perspective, referencing (1) the hospital’s UTI treatment guidelines, which outline risk factors that would require broad-spectrum antibiotics—none of which JJ has—and (2) the local antibiogram, which shows excellent coverage of common UTI pathogens with narrower-spectrum agents. Dr H responds, “I see your point, and the information you’ve provided suggests another agent might be effective, but I remain worried about JJ’s fragile condition. Until the urine culture results return in a few days, I’d prefer to use the broadest agent to be safe.”

RX explains that, according to the hospital’s preauthorization protocol, unresolved disagreements are reviewed by the antimicrobial stewardship program’s medical director, Dr MD. After reviewing JJ’s chart, Dr MD concurs with RX’s assessment and recommends switching to ceftriaxone, a narrower-spectrum antibiotic well-suited to the most likely pathogens in this case. Dr MD calls Dr H to discuss the recommendation. This time, Dr H agrees to change the prescription to ceftriaxone but voices frustration, saying, “I don’t appreciate pharmacists policing my empiric antibiotic choices.” Dr MD responds, “We’re all part of the same team, working together to provide the best care for our patients.”

After the conversation, Dr MD reflects on the exchange and wonders how to strengthen collegiality and foster more effective, collaborative relationships between healthcare professionals moving forward.

ethical_issues.question: How should antimicrobial stewards ethically balance optimizing treatment for current patients with preventing future antimicrobial resistance?
keypoints: Antimicrobial stewards must balance optimizing treatment for current patients with preventing future antimicrobial resistance, ensuring appropriate antimicrobial coverage for the present patient while safeguarding future patients from the impact of resistance.

Through the framework of virtue ethics, emphasis is placed on the importance of moral character and virtues in antimicrobial stewardship to ensure the legitimacy and fairness of clinical decision-making.

Healthcare teams should collectively pursue the goal of promoting the flourishing of patients and the broader community, with all members striving for fairness and equity in the allocation and use of limited healthcare resources.
Frontline clinicians and antimicrobial stewards should mutually encourage one another to embody the character and virtues that foster genuine flourishing for patients and the community.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians balance prescribers’ professional autonomy with pharmacists’ responsibility for medication appropriateness in antimicrobial stewardship?
keypoints: Antimicrobial stewardship should address the complex interplay of clinical decision-making and interprofessional communication through the ancient ethical framework of virtue ethics.
The healthcare team environment must cultivate virtues and corresponding actions among all members that collectively promote flourishing for patients and the broader community.
An ideal healthcare community values all members as equal contributors who share their unique expertise in service of patient care.
All members should share responsibility and commitment to the common goal of achieving the best possible outcomes for individual patients and the community at large.
Members ought to carry out their roles motivated by right intentions while interpreting the intentions of others with goodwill.
In the allocation and use of limited healthcare resources, all members should strive for fairness and justice.
Members should confidently express their perspectives and listen to others, including patients, with humility and empathy.

ethical_issues.question: How Can Antimicrobial Stewardship Teams Promote the Flourishing of Patients and Communities and Mitigate Moral Injury and Burnout Through a Virtue Ethics Framework?
keypoints: Through the framework of virtue ethics, healthcare teams should cultivate an environment in which all members collectively pursue the virtues and actions that promote flourishing for both patients and the broader community.

Members of the healthcare team should be valued as equal contributors, each bringing their unique expertise to serve patients, while sharing responsibility and commitment to the common goal of achieving the best possible outcomes for individual patients and the community.
Team members ought to carry out their roles with proper motives, interpret others’ intentions benevolently, and strive for fairness and equity when utilizing limited healthcare resources.
Healthcare team members should confidently express their perspectives and listen to others with humility and empathy to enhance the efficiency of interprofessional collaboration.

title: What Does Disability Justice Require of Antimicrobial Stewardship?
case:
Dr S is a resident physician responsible for admitting patients overnight. A patient, M, is being transferred from a nursing home (NH) for tachycardia and hypotension. The NH’s physician, Dr P, started M on a broad-spectrum antibiotic prior to M’s transfer. Dr S notices in M’s record that M has had multiple episodes of being treated with antibiotics in-hospital or in the NH, but with no specific infection diagnosis. Dr S worries about exacerbating this pattern of possible excessive antibiotic use that might expose M to unnecessary toxicity and threat of antibiotic resistance. Dr S plans to be judicious with antibiotics when treating M.
M arrives on the unit and is now under Dr S’s care. M is 57 years old with a history of cardiac arrest resulting in anoxic brain injury. M has a tracheostomy and normally breathes on her own without a ventilator; however, for transport from the NH to the hospital, she has been connected to a ventilator. M turns her head to look at Dr S when Dr S speaks to M, but M cannot speak while connected to the ventilator, appears to Dr S to be uncomfortable, and does not reliably signal “yes” or “no” in response to Dr S’s questions. Now that Dr S has met M, Dr S questions her initial instinct to limit antibiotics for M.
case_rewrite:
Dr S is a resident physician handling overnight admissions. One evening, a patient named M is transferred from a nursing home (NH) to the hospital because of tachycardia and hypotension. Before the transfer, M’s NH physician, Dr P, initiated broad-spectrum antibiotics. Reviewing M’s medical chart, Dr S finds that M has often been started on antibiotics, both during hospital stays and at the NH, yet there is rarely a clear infection diagnosis. Concerned about the risk of antibiotic overuse—such as unnecessary side effects and the development of antimicrobial resistance—Dr S resolves to be judicious with antibiotics in M’s care.

When M arrives on the unit, Dr S assumes responsibility for her treatment. M is 57 years old and has a history of cardiac arrest that resulted in an anoxic brain injury. She breathes independently through a tracheostomy under normal circumstances, but for transport from the NH, she was connected to a ventilator. Now on the unit, M is still attached to the ventilator. As Dr S greets her, M turns her head in response, making clear eye contact. However, she cannot speak while on the ventilator and appears uncomfortable.
