keypoints: Surgeons should offer and recommend therapeutic options that are most likely to achieve optimal clinical outcomes and align with the patient’s values and preferences.
Surgeons must fully disclose to patients the known information and uncertainties regarding AI-assisted robotic surgery and discuss alternative treatment options.

If a patient understands the expected outcomes of each option yet still chooses the prior standard treatment, the surgeon should respect the patient’s autonomy and proceed with the standard procedure.

If the surgeon lacks proficiency in either the standard surgical technique or the AI-assisted robotic procedure, appropriate consultation with a surgeon experienced in the relevant technique should be sought.

ethical_issues.question: How can AI-assisted technology be ensured to promote patient-centered and individualized care during the automated phases of surgery?
keypoints: During the phase of surgical automation, human monitoring or supervision is essential to ensure patient safety.
Surgeons must discuss potential risks with patients preoperatively and clearly explain when the automated portions of the surgery will occur and what their role will be during these periods.
AI-assisted technology must undergo rigorous evaluation prior to clinical application to ensure its safety and reliability.
Optimal intraoperative decision-making requires the integration of patient information, evidence-based data, and surgical experience; therefore, human oversight and intervention remain necessary.

title: Should Organizational Investment in Robotic Surgical Technology Ever Influence Surgeons’ Decisions About Surgical Approach to Patients’ Surgical Care?
case:
Dr M is a surgeon drawn to work in University Hospital, given the organization’s reputation for leadership and investment in robot-assisted surgical technology. During her job interviews, Dr M is asked how many robotic-assisted procedures she has performed, and University Hospital’s marketing director invites Dr M to discuss strategies for showcasing her robotic skills on the organization’s website and in advertising campaigns. During negotiations in her hiring process, Dr M is offered dedicated block time in University Hospital’s operating room (OR), where she could board 2 full days of surgery with access to the robot. Dr M is enthusiastic about this prospect, but she is also concerned that being hired as a minimally invasive surgeon—and, more specifically, as a robotic surgeon—could, over time, limit the scope of her professional decision making about how to approach surgical care of her patients, especially those for whom open or laparoscopic surgical techniques might be indicated.
Dr M wonders how to broach this set of concerns without appearing to extinguish University Hospital’s interest in her enthusiasm for robotic surgical innovation. Dr M also wonders how to address conflicts of interest that could emerge, especially in striving to balance University Hospital’s investment interests with appropriate exercise of her overall surgical autonomy and growing robotic surgical technique skill set. Dr M feels strongly that the professional autonomy she exercises when making decisions about her patients’ surgical care should remain uncompromised by organizational pressure to maximize profit generated from robotics use in the OR. Dr M considers how to proceed in her negotiations.
case_rewrite:
Dr M, a surgeon with a growing expertise in minimally invasive procedures, is attracted to a position at University Hospital, renowned for its commitment to cutting-edge robot-assisted surgical technology. During her interview process, Dr M is questioned about the number of robotic-assisted surgeries she has performed, and the hospital’s marketing director encourages her to consider ways she might highlight her robotic skills for the hospital’s website and promotional materials. As negotiations progress, Dr M is offered dedicated operating room block time—two full days each week—with guaranteed access to the hospital’s robotic surgical system. This opportunity excites Dr M, yet she harbors concerns that being recruited specifically as a minimally invasive and robotic surgeon could, over time, restrict her ability to choose the most appropriate surgical technique for each patient, particularly when open or laparoscopic approaches might be better suited.

As Dr M weighs how to address these concerns, she is mindful not to dampen University Hospital’s enthusiasm for her interest in robotic surgery. She also reflects on the potential conflicts of interest that could arise, especially as she seeks to balance the hospital’s significant investment in robotic systems with her own professional autonomy and evolving proficiency in robotic techniques. Dr M is adamant that her clinical decisions regarding the surgical care of her patients must remain focused on their best interests, free from organizational pressure to maximize use of the robotics platform for profitability. With these competing priorities in mind, Dr M carefully considers how best to approach further negotiations with the hospital.

ethical_issues.question: Should an Organization’s Investment in Robotic Surgical Technology Influence Surgeons’ Decision-Making Regarding the Surgical Approach to Patient Care?
keypoints: Institutional investment in robotic surgical technology should not influence surgeons’ decisions regarding the choice of surgical approach; surgeons must prioritize the best interests of the patient.
Surgeons must avoid external pressures that could affect patient care and ensure that the surgical plan aligns with the ethical principle of primacy of patient welfare.

Physicians should disclose and address any conflicts of interest that may impact medical decision-making; if such conflicts cannot be resolved, the surgeon should focus on operating for the patient rather than on the patient.
The relationship between robotic utilization and hospital profitability is not linear; surgeons should perform robotic surgery only when it aligns with the patient’s best interests.

ethical_issues.question: How can surgeons ensure the validity of informed consent and uphold ethical integrity when selecting the surgical approach?
keypoints: Surgeons must ensure that the surgical plan centers on the patient’s best interests and avoid allowing external pressures to influence patient care.
Surgeons have an obligation to obtain informed consent from patients by thoroughly explaining the risks, benefits, and alternative options of the proposed surgical approach.
Information provided during informed consent must be presented fairly, clearly, accurately, and with empathy, without exaggerating the potential benefits of the surgery.
Surgeons should honestly disclose their own experience, skills, and proficiency with various surgical techniques to enable patients to make the most informed and optimal choice.
Surgeons are required to disclose and address any conflicts of interest that may affect medical decision-making, communicating with patients in an honest and transparent manner.

ethical_issues.question: How can surgeons ensure that their choice of surgical approach aligns with the best interests of the patient while also safeguarding equitable access to robotic technology for other surgeons when facing economic pressures to utilize robotic systems?
keypoints: Surgeons should prioritize patient welfare, ensuring that surgical plans center on the patient’s best interests without being influenced by pressures to utilize robotic technology.
Surgeons must safeguard patients’ rights to make informed decisions regarding their care.
Surgeons should adhere to the ethical principle of beneficence by setting aside organizational financial considerations and recommending the surgical approach expected to yield the best outcomes.

Surgeons are obligated to disclose and address any conflicts of interest that may affect clinical decision-making; if such conflicts cannot be resolved, they should focus on operating for the patient rather than on the patient.

Minimally invasive surgeons should recognize that profitability is not directly correlated with robotic utilization and should perform robotic surgeries only when they align with the patient’s best interests, thereby ensuring equitable access to robotic systems for other surgeons.

title: How Should Risk Be Communicated to Patients When Developing Resident Surgeon Robotic Skills?
case: Dr B is a fourth-year general surgery resident physician and chief of the University Hospital minimally invasive surgery service. Dr B spends most of her time in the operating room (OR) with attending physician, Dr A, who performs laparoscopic and robot-assisted operations. Today, Dr B is instructed by Dr A to sit at the robot console. Dr B performs portions of a ventral hernia repair independently in the presence of Dr A. Dr A gives the console control to Dr B, instructing her to suture in the mesh after the primary closure of the hernia defect. Dr B is startled, as she has begun, but not yet completed, suggested robotic training console simulations for hernia repair and has only sewn in part of this particular mesh before. Dr B seizes the opportunity and wonders what the patient and family should be told, perhaps now and certainly later, about her role in the surgery.
case_rewrite: Dr B, a fourth-year general surgery resident and chief of the minimally invasive surgery service at University Hospital, spends most days in the operating room working closely with Dr A, the attending surgeon known for expertise in laparoscopic and robot-assisted procedures. On this particular day, Dr A instructs Dr B to take her place at the robotic surgery console. With Dr A supervising, Dr B is tasked with managing key parts of a ventral hernia repair. After the hernia defect is primarily closed, Dr A hands full console control to Dr B, directing her to suture the mesh into place. Dr B feels a jolt of anxiety—although she has started the recommended robotic simulation training for hernia repairs, she has not yet finished it, and her prior hands-on experience with suturing this specific mesh is limited to only a portion of the procedure. Nonetheless, Dr B embraces the challenge, aware it is a critical step in her training. As she works, Dr B begins to wonder what, if anything, should be communicated to the patient and their family about her precise involvement in the operation—both in advance and in the event of questions afterward—especially given her stage of training and the complexities of robotic surgery.

ethical_issues.question: When developing resident surgeons’ robotic skills, how should attending physicians disclose the specific roles and responsibilities of residents to patients both before and during surgery?
keypoints: Attending surgeons should disclose the roles of resident surgeons during the informed consent process to support patient autonomy.
Clarifying the distinction between the functions of the robot and the role of the surgeon to patients and their families facilitates informed surgical decision-making.
Postoperatively, surgeons should provide an overview of the surgical procedure, including whether it was more complex than anticipated, without the need for a detailed, step-by-step explanation.

ethical_issues.question: During the informed consent process for procedures involving resident participation and advanced technologies, such as in the case of Dr A and Dr B, how should surgeons communicate the risks and complexities associated with both the use of robotic surgical tools and the resident’s level of experience to ensure that patients and their families are fully informed and able to make autonomous decisions?
keypoints: Surgeons should explain the distinction between the roles of the robot and the physician during robotic surgery in the informed consent process to help patients understand the surgical procedure.
Attending physicians should disclose the specific intraoperative roles of resident surgeons during the informed consent process to support patient autonomy and informed decision-making.

Resident surgeons need to develop the ability to explain the surgical procedure and the division of responsibilities within the surgical team to ensure that patients receive comprehensive information during the informed consent process.

title: Should BMI Help Determine Gender-Affirming Surgery Candidacy?
case:
ZZ is a trans man and a patient of Dr S, a surgeon at a clinic offering gender-affirming services, including hormone therapy, chest surgeries, and genital surgeries. During 5 years of hormone treatment, ZZ’s weight increased to a point at which he now has a BMI of 35, which is clinically considered class II obesity.As a result, he does not qualify for most gender-affirming surgeries (GAS) offered by Dr S at the clinic. ZZ is distressed and asks, “What was the point of hormone therapy if all it did was make me so fat I can’t get surgery?”
Dr S considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
ZZ is a trans man who has been under the care of Dr S, a surgeon at a clinic specializing in gender-affirming care, including hormone therapy, chest reconstruction, and genital surgeries. Over the course of five years on hormone therapy, ZZ’s weight steadily increased, and he now has a BMI of 35, which falls into the category of class II obesity. Due to this, he no longer meets the eligibility criteria for most gender-affirming surgeries offered by Dr S at the clinic. Distressed by this development, ZZ voices his frustration: “What was the point of hormone therapy if all it did was make me so fat I can’t get surgery?”

As Dr S listens to ZZ’s concerns, they reflect on how best to respond and support ZZ, considering the implications of using BMI as a rigid barrier to surgery.

ethical_issues.question: Should BMI be used as the sole criterion for determining candidacy for gender-affirming surgery, or should it be considered in conjunction with factors such as weight stigma, type of procedure, and body composition?
keypoints: BMI should not be used as the sole criterion for determining candidacy for gender-affirming surgery; a comprehensive assessment must incorporate factors such as weight stigma, type of procedure, and body composition.

In the absence of definitive evidence establishing a direct causal relationship between elevated BMI and adverse surgical outcomes, a more holistic approach should be adopted when evaluating surgical candidacy.
Body composition may offer greater clinical relevance than BMI, as BMI does not account for the impact of body composition on surgical outcomes.
Surgical candidacy assessments must balance the risks associated with high BMI against the life-changing and potentially lifesaving benefits of gender-affirming surgery.

ethical_issues.question: How can a more comprehensive surgical candidacy assessment framework be developed to achieve equitable treatment in the absence of definitive evidence establishing a direct causal relationship between high BMI and poor surgical outcomes?
keypoints: Employ a shared decision-making model that avoids using BMI as the sole criterion for surgical eligibility, instead considering weight stigma, procedure type, body composition, and other relevant factors in a comprehensive manner.
When assessing surgical candidacy, weigh the risks associated with elevated BMI against the life-changing and potentially lifesaving benefits of gender-affirming surgery.
In the context of limited data, achieve fully informed consent through patient education and involve patients in the final decision-making process.
When evaluating surgical risks, body composition may provide more informative value than BMI, as BMI does not account for the impact of body composition on surgical outcomes.
Acknowledge that body size diversity will persist, and seek solutions that enable surgeons to safely operate on individuals of all body sizes, including fat patients.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of increased risk of surgical complications, how can shared decision-making promote patient autonomy and strengthen the patient–provider relationship to ensure equitable access to surgery?
keypoints: Achieve comprehensive informed consent through patient education and involve patients in the final decision-making process to promote patient autonomy.
Establish a more equitable division of responsibility between clinicians and patients to alleviate surgeons’ concerns about surgical safety and patients’ fears of adverse outcomes.
When assessing surgical candidacy, it is necessary to weigh the risks associated with high BMI against the life-changing and potentially lifesaving benefits of gender-affirming surgery.
Strengthening informed consent and collaborative decision-making models can consolidate the patient-surgeon relationship and ensure equitable access to surgery.

title: Why We Need to Stop Labeling Behaviors Influencing a Person’s WeightIdealorHealthy
case:
X is a large employer looking to reduce number of employee sick days, optimize productivity, encourage adherence to its wellness program activities, and promote “ideal health behaviors.” Employees who engage in such behaviors, document them, and maintain a body mass index (BMI) at or below 25 will be eligible for reduced insurance premiums.
CR is an X employee with a BMI of 29 and learns after a “weigh in” at a wellness day event that this means she is “nearly obese.” CR has never considered herself unhealthy, maintains an overall diet that is about 90% plant-based, and participates in many recommended “ideal health behaviors.” CR sees the offer for reduced insurance premiums, views those savings as significant, but feels they are out of reach. CR feels demoralized about being asked by her employer to “weigh in,” about being described as “nearly obese,” and about her health being  deemed not good enough for her employers’ insurance premium reductions.
Many employees have complained that 25 as the BMI cutoff is discriminatory, encourages body negativity, and expresses views of wellness that are fundamentally racist, sexist, and ableist and that might not be “healthy” at all for many of X’s employees. Others have submitted formal written complaints arguing that protected health information should never be used to financially incentivize any company’s vision of employee health and wellness.
case_rewrite:
X is a major employer intent on decreasing employee sick days, boosting productivity, and promoting participation in its wellness program by encouraging what it defines as “ideal health behaviors.” As part of this initiative, employees who document engagement in these behaviors and maintain a body mass index (BMI) of 25 or below become eligible for reduced insurance premiums.

CR, who works for X, has a BMI of 29. At a company “wellness day” event, she participates in a required “weigh-in” and is told that, by company standards, she is “nearly obese.” This comes as a shock to CR, who has always viewed herself as healthy. Her diet is approximately 90% plant-based, and she regularly practices many of the “ideal health behaviors” recommended by the program. When CR learns about the insurance premium reductions, she recognizes the considerable savings but feels they are unattainable for her under the current rules. The experience of being weighed by her employer, labeled as “nearly obese,” and deemed ineligible for the incentive leaves CR feeling demoralized and stigmatized.

Numerous other employees have voiced concerns that the use of a BMI cutoff of 25 is discriminatory, encourages negative body image, and reflects standards of wellness that are inherently racist, sexist, and ableist. They argue that such measures may not be truly “healthy” or appropriate for many employees at X. Formal written complaints have also been submitted, asserting that protected health information should not be used as a basis for financially incentivizing adherence to any corporate definition of health and wellness.

ethical_issues.question: Should corporate wellness programs avoid using BMI as a health metric?
keypoints: BMI as a health metric has significant limitations; it may serve as a reference but should not be used as the sole indicator.
Using a BMI cutoff of 25 is discriminatory, fosters body negativity, and reflects conceptions of health that are fundamentally racist, sexist, and ableist.

If corporate wellness programs aim to reduce healthcare costs and the incidence of BMI-related comorbidities, they should focus on behaviors such as consuming whole foods and engaging in physical activity without referencing BMI itself.

ethical_issues.question: Should company wellness programs avoid labeling behaviors with normative terms such as "ideal" or "healthy" in order to prevent reinforcing healthism ideology and perpetuating social inequities?
keypoints: The use of terms such as "ideal" or "healthy" may reinforce the ideology of healthism by neglecting the social factors that constrain individual choices.
Financial incentives within wellness programs may entrench and exacerbate social inequities by attributing health responsibility solely to the individual.
Labeling behaviors can contribute to body negativity, resulting in stigma and the reinforcement of social hierarchies.

tags: Access to care/Gender or gender transition barriers
title: How Should Surgeons Approach Gender-Affirming Surgery Revisions When Patients Were Not, Perhaps, Well Informed in Prior Counseling?
case:
T is a 32-year-old transgender man who presented to Dr D, a reconstructive urologist. Five years ago, he underwent an abdominal phalloplasty and scrotoplasty, along with partial colpocleisis and hysterectomy, in a different state, and now he wishes to pursue urethral lengthening to the tip of the penis, which was previously constructed without a urethra. Dr D recognizes urethroplasty in abdominal phalloplasty (UAP) as a revision procedure with high risk for complications, which is why a radial forearm flap phalloplasty (RFFP) is the typical recommendation for patients desiring urethral lengthening.
On further discussion with T, T clarifies that he was never told about the relative advantages of RFFP or the broad consensus that abdominal phalloplasty was incompatible with urethral lengthening. T tells Dr D that he has always wanted urethral lengthening as a goal but that he does not recall discussing this with the surgeon prior to the first phalloplasty. T is dismayed by the information from Dr D, but after contemplation of the risks and burdens of treatment presented still wishes to proceed with urethral lengthening while avoiding any additional donor sites, such as would be required for RFFP. Dr D mentions that other phalloplasty patients have had skin grafting procedures to reconstruct the urethra after phalloplasty. On examination, Dr D believes that the revision surgery would be unsafe for T and would fail to reach his expectations. Considering T’s unfortunate past experiences, Dr D knows that he must approach his recommendations both sensitively and scientifically, providing continued care with multidisciplinary support.
case_rewrite:
T, a 32-year-old transgender man, has come to see Dr D, a reconstructive urologist, about further surgical options. Five years ago, T underwent an abdominal phalloplasty and scrotoplasty, along with partial colpocleisis and hysterectomy, in another state. At that time, the phalloplasty was performed without creating a urethra. Now, T wishes to pursue urethral lengthening to the tip of his penis.

Dr D is aware that urethroplasty following abdominal phalloplasty (UAP) is considered a revision procedure with a high risk of complications, which is why the standard recommendation for patients seeking urethral lengthening is a radial forearm flap phalloplasty (RFFP). During their conversation, T shares that he was never informed about the advantages of RFFP or the widely recognized view that abdominal phalloplasty is not compatible with urethral lengthening. T explains that urethral lengthening has always been his goal, but that he does not recall discussing this with his previous surgeon prior to his initial phalloplasty. He expresses distress at learning this information from Dr D.

After weighing the risks and challenges explained by Dr D, T remains determined to pursue urethral lengthening, but he is adamant about avoiding further donor sites, as would be required for RFFP. Dr D notes that some phalloplasty patients have undergone skin grafting procedures to reconstruct the urethra after phalloplasty. However, upon examination, Dr D believes that proceeding with revision surgery would be unsafe for T and is unlikely to achieve the results T hopes for.

Given T’s difficult prior experiences, Dr D recognizes the need to approach his recommendations with both sensitivity and scientific rigor. He is mindful of the importance of supporting T through a collaborative, multidisciplinary care process. Dr D considers how best to provide T with clear, realistic information about what is possible, to validate T’s goals, and to ensure that T’s consent is fully informed and centered on his values as they discuss the path forward.

ethical_issues.question: How Should Surgeons Ensure Patient Autonomy and Informed Consent When Patients May Not Have Been Fully Informed?
keypoints: Surgeons should acknowledge the possibility that patients may have been insufficiently informed during prior counseling and establish a therapeutic alliance without presuming ill intent or negligence on the part of the original surgeon.
Physicians must clarify the surgical treatment goals with the patient and communicate realistic expectations regarding treatment outcomes.

Utilizing the Best Case/Worst Case framework, surgeons should detail the best possible, worst possible, and most likely outcomes for each treatment option to facilitate patient understanding of potential consequences.
A shared decision-making process should be initiated to ensure that the patient’s consent is autonomous and maximally informed.
Informed consent should be centered on the patient’s core values and regarded as an ongoing, iterative process rather than a rigid, terminal checklist item.
Physicians should offer opportunities for follow-up consultations to reach a mutually agreed final decision and openly address the inherent disappointment involved in necessary compromises.

If the surgeon believes that the patient’s surgical goals are unachievable, the patient should be encouraged to seek consultation with other surgeons who may have differing clinical experience or risk tolerance.

Physicians may assist patients in connecting with others who have undergone similar revision surgeries and recommend consultation with mental health professionals to provide continued care through multidisciplinary support.

ethical_issues.question: How should surgeons balance the principle of nonmaleficence with the patient’s surgical goals when confronted with high-risk procedures?
keypoints: Surgeons should guide clinical decision-making by providing their professional knowledge and experience to evaluate the risks and benefits of surgery.
Patient autonomy is an important ethical principle, but surgeons are not obligated to comply with all patient wishes, especially when the surgery is deemed unsafe.

Surgeons bear responsibility for all necessary clinical steps to achieve the patient’s surgical goals and should recommend that patients seek consultation with other surgeons who may have differing clinical experience or risk tolerance when those goals are unattainable.

ethical_issues.question: How can surgeons establish realistic expectations and address patients’ feelings of disappointment when communicating surgical risks?
keypoints: When communicating surgical risks to the patient, the physician should acknowledge the potential for prior medical trauma experienced by the patient and convey risks with sensitivity.

The physician should recognize that the patient’s current outcome might have been preventable with more thorough counseling, without assuming ill intent or negligence on the part of the original surgeon, in order to establish a therapeutic alliance.
The physician should employ the Best Case/Worst Case framework, using case-based narratives to detail the best possible, worst possible, and most likely outcomes for each treatment option.

The physician must explain that the patient’s requested method carries an unacceptably high risk of adverse outcomes and clarify that, with currently available techniques, urethroplasty cannot be performed on the patient’s existing phallus.
The physician should consistently validate the legitimacy of the patient’s current treatment priorities and express that, if it were safe and feasible, they would offer the requested surgery.
The physician must directly address the inherent disappointment involved in the necessary compromises to optimally support the patient in proceeding with care.

title: How Should Food Offered by Health Care Organizations Meet Individual, Community, and Ecological Needs?
case:
NN is hospitalized due to pneumonia and eats only plant-based foods. Vegan food options are few, and NN’s nutrition has been limited to sides of vegetables, plain toast, fruit juices, and fruit salads for a few days. NN has requested more nutritionally dense foods that are easy to prepare (ie, quinoa, oatmeal, whole vegetables, whole fruits, nuts).
The organization’s dietetics administrator has apologized and explained that their food offerings are limited by their suppliers. An order has been placed for some of the items NN requested yesterday, but the supplier has reiterated that demand for meat and dairy alternatives is just too low to warrant their regular availability and delivery without the organization’s food supply costs increasing.
NN does not have anyone at the time who could bring her prepared, or even raw, plant-based foods from outside the hospital. NN’s caloric intake has been substantially reduced, despite high caloric demands of illness recovery; NN is losing weight, feels hungry, and is worried. NN asks, “I’ve requested simple items that are easy to prepare. I’d even eat some items raw. Why is this organization not able to meet my basic health nutritional needs?”
Members of NN’s clinical team wonder how to respond.
case_rewrite:
NN has been admitted to the hospital for treatment of pneumonia. NN follows a strict plant-based diet, but the hospital’s vegan meal options are extremely limited. For several days, NN’s meals have consisted almost entirely of side servings of vegetables, plain toast, fruit juices, and fruit salads. Concerned about the lack of variety and nutritional value, NN has asked for more substantial plant-based foods that are also easy to prepare, such as quinoa, oatmeal, whole vegetables, whole fruits, and nuts.

The hospital’s dietetics administrator spoke with NN, expressing regret for the situation and clarifying that their food offerings are constrained by what their suppliers can provide. Although an order for some of NN’s requested foods was placed the day before, the supplier responded that there is insufficient demand for meat and dairy alternatives to justify regular stocking or delivery without driving up the organization’s food supply costs.

At present, NN does not have anyone available to bring prepared or even raw plant-based foods from outside the hospital. NN’s caloric intake has dropped considerably at a time when her body’s energy needs are elevated due to illness; as a result, NN has been losing weight, feels persistent hunger, and is growing increasingly anxious. NN voices her worry to the care team: “I’ve asked for simple foods that don’t take much to prepare. I would even eat some things raw. Why can’t this organization meet my basic nutritional needs for my health?”

Members of NN’s clinical team are now discussing how best to respond to her concerns.

ethical_issues.question: How can hospitals accommodate patients’ cultural, religious, and moral beliefs in meal provision to ensure nutrition is appropriate and acceptable to patients?
keypoints: Hospitals should provide food that aligns with patients’ cultural, religious, and moral acceptability to ensure the effectiveness and inclusivity of health care services.

Upon non-emergency admission, hospitals should collect information on patients’ dietary habits and religious or cultural dietary restrictions, and offer inclusive menus that accommodate patients’ preferences.
Hospitals should adopt a coordinated multidisciplinary approach to improve nutrition care in order to optimize patients’ short-term and long-term outcomes.

Education and training should be provided to food preparers, staff, and clinical personnel to enable them to offer individualized, culturally sensitive, and health-promoting dietary options for diverse populations.
Collaborating with local suppliers to procure ingredients that reflect different cultural traditions is essential to provide more culturally inclusive meals.

ethical_issues.question: How should health care organizations balance economic incentives and ethical responsibilities in their food services to promote public health and disease prevention?
keypoints: Health care organizations have an ethical responsibility to prioritize health promotion and disease prevention in their dietary services, rather than focusing solely on economic incentives.
Providing plant-based food options can not only meet patients’ individualized nutritional needs but also potentially reduce dietary costs, aligning with the principle of fiscal responsibility.
Neglecting patients’ nutritional needs may result in poorer clinical outcomes and increased health care costs; therefore, ensuring adequate nutrition is a core obligation of health care institutions.
Health care organizations have a duty to procure high-quality food to promote public health and fulfill their mission of disease prevention and health promotion.

ethical_issues.question: How can hospitals fulfill their ethical responsibilities to the community and the global environment through the procurement and provision of sustainably grown plant-based foods?
keypoints: Hospitals have an ethical obligation to procure sustainably grown plant-based foods to promote public health and reduce environmental impact.
By collaborating with local suppliers, hospitals can support the community economy and provide culturally inclusive meal options.
Offering appropriate plant-based dietary options not only benefits patient health but also reflects respect for patient dignity and the principles of person-centered care.

title: Which Concerns Deserve Consideration in Dietary Counseling of Patients Earning Low Incomes?
case:
At an American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) conference, Dr M learned about the AAFP’s environmental health initiatives and attended a presentation about meat’s contributions to pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and climate change and the importance of physicians’ clinical and public health roles in counseling patients to reduce industrial meat production and consumption.
One of Dr M’s patients is JT, who washes dishes in a local restaurant known for its “cheap and delicious” barbeque. JT eats there regularly since a meal is free with each shift. Dr M, who eats animal protein only when it’s locally sourced and organic, wonders about the nature and scope of their responsibility as a health professional to promote environmental health patient education through dietary counseling to JT, whose cardiovascular risk is currently low.
case_rewrite:
At an American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) conference, Dr M attended a session highlighting the organization’s environmental health initiatives. One presentation focused on how meat production contributes to pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and climate change, and emphasized the critical role physicians play in guiding patients to reduce industrial meat intake for both health and environmental reasons.

Back at their community clinic, Dr M thinks about JT, a patient who works as a dishwasher in a local restaurant famous for serving “cheap and delicious” barbeque. JT regularly eats meals provided by the restaurant as part of his job benefits, relying on these free meals to help make ends meet. Currently, JT’s cardiovascular risk is low, but his diet is heavily meat-based due to his work circumstances and limited resources. Dr M personally chooses to eat animal protein only when it is locally sourced and organic.

Dr M now reflects on the extent of their responsibility to incorporate environmental health education into dietary counseling with JT. They consider how best to approach JT’s eating habits, given his socioeconomic challenges and the cultural importance of barbeque in the local community, while respecting JT’s autonomy and maintaining the trust at the core of their physician-patient relationship. Dr M wonders how to offer practical, attainable advice without disregarding JT’s lived realities and considers the potential of working with local partners—including community organizations and restaurants—to help expand healthy, affordable food options. Dr M also thinks about collaborating with nutritionists and community members to find ways to make dietary recommendations relevant for patients like JT, possibly through initiatives such as fresh produce prescription programs, while ensuring that any advocacy or educational efforts are grounded in respect for JT’s individual needs and circumstances.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ensure that dietary counseling does not undermine the trust relationship with patients while taking into account patients’ socioeconomic backgrounds and cultural factors?
keypoints: Physicians should consider patients’ socioeconomic backgrounds and cultural factors when providing dietary advice to ensure that the recommendations are realistically achievable for the patient.
Physicians must ensure that their advice aligns with the patient’s best interests in order to maintain the trust inherent in the physician-patient relationship.

Physicians should utilize a long-standing physician-patient relationship to gain comprehensive understanding of the patient’s dietary patterns and access to food, thereby enabling the provision of practical and tailored guidance.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance public health recommendations to reduce meat consumption for climate change mitigation with the specific health needs and living conditions of individual patients?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize the specific health needs and living conditions of individual patients when providing health advice in order to maintain their trustworthiness.

When advising patients to reduce meat consumption, physicians should assess the patient’s willingness and capacity to respond to such advice, ensuring that recommendations are realistic and feasible to preserve trust.

Physicians must consider the social determinants that influence patients’ health choices and ensure that advocacy for dietary change does not undermine their responsibility to prioritize individual patient interests.
Physicians may collaborate with local community groups and restaurants to offer more diverse menus that support patients’ healthy dietary choices.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Dr M’s dietary counseling of JT, how can physicians ethically balance their responsibilities to promote environmental health with respect for patient autonomy and social justice, and how might interprofessional collaboration and community engagement enhance the feasibility and relevance of their recommendations for patients in low-income, resource-limited settings?
keypoints: Physicians should regard public health advocacy as an interprofessional effort, integrating the expertise of various health professionals such as nutritionists and dietitians to ensure the feasibility and relevance of their recommendations.
Interprofessional advocacy should seek community endorsement and involve close collaboration with community members to ensure that their needs are met and their voices are heard.
Physicians can collaborate with local community groups and restaurants to provide a more diverse menu that accommodates the needs of low-income and resource-limited communities.
Initiating fresh fruit and vegetable prescribing programs can help address local food insecurity, with the involvement of trusted community members to ensure the effectiveness of such initiatives.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Clinician relations with industry
title: How Should the US Federal Government Oversee Clinicians’ Relationships With Industry?
case:
Suppose Dr M is a renowned endocrinologist with a long, distinguished record of national clinical and research service and the chair of the National Clinical Care Commission (NCCC), a committee charged with helping review improvements to US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) diabetes-related care programs. Dr M also consults and serves on speaker panels for companies developing diabetes interventions. Frequently for international conference presentations, Dr M receives honoraria and travel expenses (ie, transportation, meals, accommodations, document-processing fees) from diabetes therapeutics industry sponsors. Most recently, for example, Dr M spoke about the efficacy and safety profile of a drug that only recently received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration. Company A researched and developed this drug using federal funds. Medicare and Medicaid also cover several million US patients’ prescriptions for this drug, so conferences like this one are also often attended by clinician members of watchdog organizations and advocacy groups, such as Public Citizen.
Public Citizen recently issued a press release describing Dr M’s blatant conflicts of interest (COIs) and misappropriation of federal funds for personal gain due to Dr M’s acceptance of honoraria and travel expense reimbursement from Company A. Public Citizen urged HHS to take action.
Dr M subsequently receives a letter from HHS outlining its concern with Dr M’s acceptance of payment from Company A. HHS stated its intent to investigate and take action.
Dr M offers to return all monies received from Company A and issues a rebuttal to the complaint and a press release, saying: “First, I spoke only as a physician and scientist; I did not speak as a representative of the US NCCC. Second, my remarks did not constitute an endorsement of Company A’s drug. Third, I disclosed my relationship with Company A at the conference. Finally, the remuneration I received from Company A is insufficient to constitute a conflict of interest so substantial as to warrant such a complaint.”
HHS considers how these explanations should inform a decision on whether to take action against Dr M.
case_rewrite:
Dr M is a prominent endocrinologist, widely recognized for a distinguished career in both clinical practice and research, and serves as the current chair of the National Clinical Care Commission (NCCC), a committee tasked with advising the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on enhancing diabetes care programs nationwide. Alongside these public responsibilities, Dr M regularly consults and participates in speaker panels for companies that are actively developing new diabetes interventions. For international conferences, Dr M often accepts honoraria and reimbursement for travel expenses—including airfare, meals, hotel accommodations, and document-processing fees—from sponsors within the diabetes therapeutics industry.

At a recent international conference, Dr M delivered a presentation on the efficacy and safety of a newly FDA-approved diabetes medication. This drug, developed by Company A with the support of federal research funding, is now prescribed to millions of patients covered by Medicare and Medicaid. Such conferences commonly attract healthcare professionals as well as members of oversight and advocacy organizations, such as Public Citizen. 

Following Dr M’s appearance, Public Citizen released a public statement accusing Dr M of clear conflicts of interest and of inappropriately benefiting from federal funds by accepting honoraria and travel reimbursements from Company A. The organization called upon HHS to respond and take appropriate action.

Shortly thereafter, Dr M received a formal notice from HHS expressing concern regarding the acceptance of payments from Company A. The letter stated that HHS intended to open an investigation and consider further actions.

In response, Dr M offered to return all compensation received from Company A and issued both a rebuttal to the complaint and a public statement, asserting: “First, I participated solely in my capacity as a physician and scientist—not as a representative of the US NCCC. Second, my comments did not amount to an endorsement of Company A’s drug. Third, I fully disclosed my relationship with Company A during the conference. Lastly, the payments I received from Company A were not substantial enough to create a conflict of interest serious enough to justify these allegations.”

HHS is now reviewing Dr M’s explanations as it determines whether to take disciplinary measures or other action in this case.

ethical_issues.question: How should the government regulate the financial relationships between clinicians and industry to prevent conflicts of interest from influencing patient care recommendations?
keypoints: The government should establish clear procedures to eliminate or mitigate conflicts of interest when physicians hold public office, such as prohibiting financial relationships with industry.
Clinicians serving in public roles must adhere to standards higher than those for ordinary physicians and receive ongoing education in deep professionalism.

Disclosure of clinician-industry relationships does not resolve the biasing influence of conflicts of interest; policymakers should be cautious that disclosure measures do not supplant more effective conflict management strategies.

Eliminating or reducing conflicts of interest improves the quality of patient care recommendations more effectively than disclosure policies; the only effective approach to managing conflicts of interest is their sincere elimination.

ethical_issues.question: Is disclosure of conflicts of interest sufficient to address potential bias in physicians’ clinical decision-making?
keypoints: Disclosure of conflicts of interest (COIs) is insufficient to resolve potential biases in physicians’ clinical decision-making, as disclosure does not eliminate the biasing influence of COIs.
Disclosure of COIs may undermine public trust in medicine, even though it is ethically essential from a transparency standpoint.
The purpose of disclosure is to identify conflicts so that institutions can implement measures such as elimination of the conflict, rather than merely managing it.
COI disclosure can place recipients in a difficult position, leading to either increased or decreased trust in the physician, which in turn affects adherence to the physician’s recommendations.
Mere disclosure of relationships is far from adequate; the only effective approach to managing COIs is the genuine elimination of such conflicts.

title: How Should Clinicians and Researchers in Government Respond to Threats to Their Offices?
case:
As the US Surgeon General, Dr SG is also vice admiral of the US Public Health Service (USPHS) Commissioned Corps, overseeing thousands of uniformed public health professionals in federal health service clinical and governance roles, each of whom are widely regarded as top clinicians and researchers in their fields. Dr SG recently testified before a congressional committee looking to restrict USPHS personnel members’ discussion, in the course of their duties, of politically contentious topics (eg, gun violence, needle-exchange programs, contraception), regardless of these topics’ evidence base or relevance to public health and safety.
Legislators cite a recent poll revealing that 56% of Americans disapprove of the US Department of Health and Human Services Office of the Surgeon General (OSG) and another poll indicating that 43% of Americans distrust science and health information released by the OSG. OSG press agents have also been struggling to manage confusion about science and health recommendations published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that don’t fully accord information on the OSG website. Atop those frustrations, OSG press agents have also tried to manage some media channels’ portrayal of Dr SG as “part of a science elite on a mission to instill enough fear to justify curtailing Americans’ civil liberties.” Since becoming the US Surgeon General, Dr SG and family members have frequently received threatening correspondence and now retain security personnel for public and even some personal events.
Dr SG’s testimony to the congressional committee reiterates that the OSG’s accountability is to best available science, not to public opinion, and not to extremist distortions of facts. Nominated by the US President and confirmed by the US Senate, Dr SG underscores that the OSG has always been an important expression of government balance of powers. Dr SG also emphasizes that OSG independence and credibility are compromised by politically motivated congressional restrictions of OSG staff members’ speech, actions, and other standard means of engaging stakeholders—including the public—on critical health and safety matters.
After a grueling day of testimony, Dr SG confesses to a colleague, “I’m nearing the end of my 4-year term, but the stress gets to me. I wonder whether I should resign.” This colleague urges Dr SG to remain in office and fulfill the term, emphasizing that resignation could mean that the OSG would be at risk of crumbling under less skilled leadership. Dr SG continues, “I expected to confront doubters and skeptics in my many roles as a public servant, but good health and science communication in this age of apathy about facts makes this impossible. My skills might be put to better use if I start a media company.”
Dr SG considers what to do.
case_rewrite:
As the US Surgeon General, Dr SG also serves as vice admiral of the US Public Health Service (USPHS) Commissioned Corps, overseeing thousands of uniformed public health professionals who hold key federal clinical and leadership positions and are widely recognized as leading experts in their fields. Recently, Dr SG was called to testify before a congressional committee considering legislation to restrict USPHS personnel from discussing politically charged topics—such as gun violence, needle-exchange programs, and contraception—in the course of their official duties, regardless of the scientific evidence or their relevance to public health and safety.

Lawmakers pointed to a recent poll showing that 56% of Americans disapprove of the US Department of Health and Human Services Office of the Surgeon General (OSG), as well as another poll indicating that 43% of Americans distrust scientific and health information disseminated by the OSG. Meanwhile, OSG press agents have found themselves struggling to address public confusion over discrepancies between recommendations published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the information on the OSG website. Adding to these difficulties, certain media outlets have portrayed Dr SG as “part of a science elite aiming to stoke public fear and justify restrictions on civil liberties.” Since taking office, Dr SG and family members have received frequent threats, prompting them to retain security personnel not only at public events but even at some private gatherings.

During testimony, Dr SG firmly reiterated that the OSG’s primary accountability is to the best available scientific evidence—not to shifting public opinion or to distorted narratives. Dr SG reminded the committee that, as an official nominated by the US President and confirmed by the Senate, the Surgeon General is tasked with maintaining an independent and credible voice in public health, embodying the government’s system of checks and balances. Dr SG argued that attempts to impose politically motivated restrictions on the speech and activities of OSG staff compromise the office’s independence and erode its ability to engage stakeholders—including the public—on matters of critical health and safety.

After an exhausting day before the committee, Dr SG confided in a close colleague, “My four-year term is almost up, but the ongoing stress is overwhelming. Sometimes I wonder if I should just step down.” The colleague encouraged Dr SG to remain in office and see the term through, warning that a premature resignation could leave the OSG vulnerable to less experienced leadership. Dr SG mused, “I knew I’d face skepticism and opposition as a public servant, but it feels nearly impossible to communicate the importance of health and science in an era when people seem indifferent to facts. Maybe my efforts would have more impact if I started a media company instead.”

Now, Dr SG weighs the future—torn between the duty to public health and the pressures of political scrutiny and public mistrust.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinician policy makers uphold the independence and credibility of public health while adhering to scientific evidence in the face of public skepticism toward scientific information and political pressure?
keypoints: Clinician policy makers must present unbiased data, research, and evidence, and remain candid about areas of uncertainty in order to uphold the independence and credibility of public health.

When communicating with the public, clinician policy makers should guide understanding of the dynamic nature of knowledge and the inevitability of emerging new conclusions, ensuring that medical information provided is accurate and based on valid scientific evidence.

Clinician policy makers ought to recognize successful examples of bipartisan collaboration, avoid being influenced by the political views of superiors, and refrain from selectively highlighting evidence that supports predetermined political positions.

To formulate more feasible recommendations, clinician policy makers need to integrate perspectives from diverse population groups and other governmental agencies, acknowledge the consequences of public actions, and focus on common goals both within and across government entities.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of political polarization and the widespread proliferation of misinformation, how can clinician policy makers effectively communicate scientific information and earn public trust?
keypoints: Clinician policy makers should uphold the values, norms, and integrity of the medical profession, ensuring that the information they provide is accurate and based on valid scientific evidence.
Clinician policy makers need to acknowledge the current limitations of knowledge and emphasize the iterative and rapidly evolving nature of scientific information in order to gain public trust.
Clinician policy makers should promote education about the scientific process to guide the public in understanding the dynamic nature of knowledge and the inevitability of new conclusions.
Clinician policy makers must transcend partisan positions, adhere to ethical guidelines, and remain uninfluenced by the political views of their superiors.

title: What Should Be Roles of Federal Clinician Governors in Motivating Equity in Locally Coordinated Triage Protocols?
case:
Dr D is an infectious disease specialist, an epidemiologist, and the medical director of a state department of health. Following a flu season that was socially and fiscally devastating, Dr D administers budget for essential personnel, surge planning, tertiary triage strategy, and critical care inventory (eg, ventilators, dialysis machines, medications, personal protective equipment). Dr D assembles a central committee of regional triage officers from around the state, which forges consensus about communication plans that activate the triage strategy across the state in response to an emergency (ie, epidemic, multi-locale mass casualty events, natural disaster) and how to train teams to implement protocols efficiently and equitably.
State epidemiological data reveal that low-income communities and communities of color were inequitably burdened (in terms of higher morbidity, more complications, higher mortality) by the most recent flu outbreak. Age-adjusted flu hospitalizations were highest among Black persons, second highest among American Indian and Alaska Native persons, and third highest among Latinx persons.
Dr D is contacted by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) officials, who offer specific clinical recommendations to amend the state’s triage protocol to avoid replicating inequity demonstrated during the past flu season. The CDC officials specifically expressed concern that inequity stems prominently from states’ triage protocols’ reliance on Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores, which are routinely used to prioritize critical care resource allocation to patients with the lowest SOFA scores, often by one of 2 approaches. One triage strategy Dr D and committee members created uses just patients’ SOFA scores to inform critical care resource allocation to patients. A second strategy sorts patients more granularly (ie, by preexisting comorbidities, age, and other factors, including equity, which inform prognosis and survivability), with “ties” among scores being broken by clinicians’ on-site assessments about how to best identify, interpret, and apply these and possibly other factors.
Dr D is unsure about the legal nature and scope of any federal authority in defining, developing, implementing, and overseeing equitable on-site triage practices in organizations and locales across the state. Triage plans normally vary by state, so Dr D wonders how best to separate the state department of health’s ethical from its legal obligations in overseeing local implementation of triage protocols and responding to persistent inequity. Dr D considers how to respond to the CDC’s inquiry.
case_rewrite:
Dr D, an infectious disease specialist and epidemiologist, serves as the medical director for the state department of health. In the wake of a flu season that left both the community and state finances severely strained, Dr D is responsible for allocating the budget to support essential personnel, surge planning, tertiary triage strategies, and maintaining an inventory of critical care resources such as ventilators, dialysis machines, medications, and personal protective equipment. Recognizing the need for coordinated action during emergencies—whether epidemics, multi-site mass casualty incidents, or natural disasters—Dr D convenes a central committee of regional triage officers from across the state. Together, they build consensus on communication plans that would trigger the triage strategy statewide and design training for teams to implement these protocols efficiently and equitably.

As the latest epidemiological data is analyzed, Dr D learns that the most recent flu outbreak disproportionately burdened low-income communities and communities of color. Hospitalization rates, adjusted for age, were highest among Black individuals, followed by American Indian and Alaska Native persons, with Latinx individuals closely behind. These groups also suffered higher rates of complications and mortality.

Amid these troubling findings, officials from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reach out to Dr D. They urge revisions to the state’s triage protocol to prevent a repeat of the inequities observed during the prior flu season. The CDC officials specifically highlight concerns that reliance on the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score in triage protocols may contribute to inequitable outcomes. Typically, the state’s triage strategies—developed by Dr D’s committee—either allocate resources strictly according to patients’ SOFA scores or use a more nuanced approach that considers preexisting comorbidities, age, and additional factors, sometimes including equity considerations. In cases where patients’ scores are tied, clinicians on site make judgment calls about how best to interpret these criteria.

The CDC points out that the SOFA score, while standard, can overestimate mortality for Black patients, leading to their systematic deprioritization for critical resources. They recommend that Dr D and the committee consider alternatives: modifying the SOFA score (such as removing the creatinine component, which disproportionately affects Black patients), or compensating for inequities by awarding additional points to Black patients or residents from resource-deprived areas. The CDC also suggests adopting a reserve system, setting aside a portion of scarce resources for populations with high chronic disease burden or those living in low socioeconomic status zip codes. Incorporating the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) into triage decision-making, they argue, can help prioritize patients based on social determinants and context. Expanding the diversity of triage decision-making teams is also encouraged as a procedural safeguard to ensure more equitable processes.

As Dr D contemplates these recommendations, questions arise regarding the extent of federal authority to define, shape, and enforce equitable triage practices across states. Given that triage protocols traditionally vary by state, Dr D is uncertain about how to distinguish the state department’s ethical responsibilities from its legal obligations, especially in overseeing local implementation and addressing persistent inequities. Dr D considers how best to respond to the CDC’s inquiry and whether to advocate for binding federal guidelines—such as a unified Crisis Standards of Care (CSC) framework—to protect minority populations and reduce clinicians’ moral distress in the face of structural inequities. Dr D reflects on precedents such as the use of the SVI in federal vaccine allocation protocols, and weighs the role that national organizations and agencies might play in advancing equitable standards at both state and federal levels.

ethical_issues.question: How can equitable allocation of resources be ensured in triage protocols, particularly for patients from low-income communities and communities of color?
keypoints: Adopt alternative approaches to the SOFA score to avoid overestimating mortality among Black patients and thereby prevent inequitable allocation of resources.

Implement a reserve system that allocates scarce resources to specific population subsets, prioritizing areas with high chronic disease burdens and low socioeconomic status zip codes, thus benefiting historically marginalized groups.
Incorporate the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) into triage decision-making to prioritize patients based on social determinants and contextual factors.
Modify the SOFA score, such as by removing the creatinine component or providing compensatory points to Black patients to alleviate their triage burden.
Enhance the diversity of decision-making teams as a procedural safeguard to promote equity.

ethical_issues.question: When using the SOFA score for triage, how should the scoring system be adjusted to prevent the occurrence of racial inequities?
keypoints: Remove the creatinine component from the SOFA score, as elevated creatinine levels are common in Black populations and may lead to unfair scoring.
Amend the SOFA score by allocating additional points to Black American patients to compensate for their burden in triage and by assigning extra points to residents of resource-deprived areas.
Integrate socioeconomic and geographic markers with disease-related biomarkers to enhance the accuracy of predictive models and reduce racial inequities.

Implement a reserve system that allocates scarce resources specifically for certain populations (e.g., patients with chronic conditions, residents of low socioeconomic status zip codes) to benefit Black and other historically marginalized groups.
Utilize the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) as a tiebreaker among patients with equal priority to ensure equitable resource allocation.

ethical_issues.question: What roles should federal agencies play in overseeing and revising state triage protocols to reduce racial inequities, and how should binding federal guidelines be developed to protect minority populations?
keypoints: The absence of federal guidelines permits states to determine whether and how to address the harms of racially inequitable triage protocols; as members of federally protected classes, minority groups should be safeguarded under a unified federal Crisis Standards of Care (CSC) framework.

D and federal clinician leaders should advocate for the revision of CSC guidelines at the national level to promote equitable allocation of scarce resources and to mitigate the effects of structural inequities on the health of Black and other historically marginalized populations.

D may encourage federal agencies, such as the CDC, to develop and implement binding federal guidance through established mechanisms, thereby reducing the moral distress experienced by clinicians who are committed to social justice in clinical decision-making.

National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine into vaccine allocation protocols provides a precedent; the SVI, which ranks census tracts based on social determinants of health, can inform the development of equitable federal triage guidelines.

title: How Should Clinicians Minimize Bias When Responding to Suspicions About Child Abuse?
case: A 9-month-old boy is brought to an emergency department (ED) by his mother. The baby’s mother reports that she slipped in an icy parking lot while lifting the baby from the car seat. She reports that, as she fell to the ground, the baby slipped out of her hands, hitting his head on the icy concrete. Physical examination of the baby reveals right-sided scalp swelling and multiple bruises on the torso and extremities. When asked about the bruises, the mother panicked, stating, “I didn’t think to check under my baby’s clothes. It was too cold. I just drove right here.” The ED physician and nurse caring for the baby are distressed by the severity of the baby’s injuries. The physician reviews the baby’s electronic health record (EHR). Notes from an ED visit 6 months ago include photographic and narrative documentation of 2 bruises on the then-3-month-old baby’s right arm. The physician and nurse confer quietly about what they observed, what they know, and how to respond.
case_rewrite:
A 9-month-old boy arrives at the emergency department (ED) accompanied by his mother. She explains that an accident occurred in a slippery parking lot: while she was lifting her son from his car seat, she slipped on the ice, causing him to fall from her grasp and strike his head on the frozen concrete. During the physical exam, the physician notes swelling on the right side of the infant’s scalp and observes multiple bruises scattered across his torso and limbs. When questioned about these additional bruises, the mother becomes visibly anxious and says, “I didn’t think to check under my baby’s clothes. It was too cold. I just drove straight here.”

Both the ED physician and the nurse are troubled by the extent of the child’s injuries. The physician reviews the child’s electronic health record and finds documented evidence—both narrative and photographic—of two bruises on the boy’s right arm from an ED visit six months earlier, when he was three months old. The physician and nurse quietly discuss their observations, the mother’s account, and the information from the medical record, as they contemplate the appropriate next steps.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians minimize bias arising from social risk factors when responding to suspicions of child abuse?
keypoints: Clinicians should focus on the specific, objective details provided by caregivers and the identified injuries, minimizing attention to subjective information or potential risk factors in order to avoid bias.
Clinical decision-making should not be influenced by the mother’s race, ethnicity, marital status, income, or educational attainment.
The use of patient safety tools, such as STAR, can assist clinicians in reflecting on cases and help prevent reliance on risk factors like socioeconomic status.
Establishing a multidisciplinary team with heterogeneous backgrounds can help mitigate bias in medical decision-making.
Hospital child protection teams can support clinicians in reviewing clinical information and assessing the level of concern for physical abuse.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians fulfill their mandatory reporting obligations in cases of suspected child abuse without undermining the trust in the clinician-patient relationship?
keypoints: Clinicians have a responsibility to communicate concerns about physical abuse and subsequent steps to caregivers using clear, nonjudgmental language.
Fulfilling mandated reporting is the clinician’s primary legal and ethical obligation.
Although it may be difficult to directly mention the term “abuse” to caregivers, family-centered care remains a priority principle that facilitates trust and partnership with families.

Social workers play a critical role in ensuring that clinicians fulfill mandated reporting obligations promptly and accurately, as well as supporting clinicians’ communication with families and community agencies.

title: How Should Academic Health Centers Desegregate Health Professions Education?
case:
PR is a community organizer who lives in a historically Black neighborhood in a large city near a prominent academic health center (AHC). Despite PR’s community’s proximity to this AHC, PR and other community members do not seek care there if they can avoid doing so, since they do not generally feel it is “meant for us.” PR and others in the community know that world-class clinicians practice at this AHC and that wealthy people from all over the world come to see them. Neither PR nor PR’s neighbors have ever seen a physician in this AHC, but they have received care at the AHC’s clinics that are staffed by trainees and students who are “volunteering” and doing “service learning.”
When PR and other local community leaders were invited to participate in a symposium hosted by the AHC, many referred to their health and health care experiences as segregated, or “2-tiered,” and felt condescended to by office staff and clinicians who knew they were insured by Medicaid. In the wake of social, cultural, and institutional responses not only to inequity laid bare by the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, but also to anti-Black racism and state-sanctioned violence, the AHC is trying to learn how to respond more justly to health needs of its community members.
The AHC considers how to redesign and desegregate its health professions education structures to motivate health equity in communities in which the center and its clinics reside.
case_rewrite:
PR is a dedicated community organizer living in a historically Black neighborhood just blocks from a major academic health center (AHC) in a large city. Despite the AHC’s close proximity, PR and most neighbors avoid seeking care there whenever possible, feeling that the institution is not truly intended for people like them. They are well aware that the AHC boasts world-renowned clinicians and that wealthy patients from across the globe travel to be treated there. Yet, neither PR nor any of their neighbors have ever seen a physician at the AHC itself. Instead, their medical experiences are limited to visits at AHC-affiliated clinics, which are predominantly staffed by medical students and trainees participating in “volunteer” or “service learning” programs.

Recently, PR and other prominent community leaders were invited to participate in a symposium hosted by the AHC. During the event, many voiced their perspectives, describing their health care encounters as distinctly segregated or “2-tiered.” They recalled feeling patronized by office staff and clinicians, especially when it became clear that they were insured by Medicaid. These sentiments have only sharpened in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and in light of ongoing social and institutional reckonings with anti-Black racism and state-sanctioned violence. The AHC, recognizing these realities, has begun to explore how it might more justly address the health needs of its surrounding communities.

In response, the AHC is actively considering how to redesign its health professions education and desegregate its structures, aiming to inspire and sustain health equity in the very neighborhoods it serves.

ethical_issues.question: How Should Academic Health Centers Restructure Health Professions Education to Eliminate Racial Segregation and Promote Health Equity?
keypoints: Academic health centers should integrate community perspectives and wisdom through reforms in education and research to cultivate clinicians and design equitable health care systems.

In the training of health professionals, community leaders should be involved in selection and training processes, with a focus on public health needs, including the incorporation of community members and leaders on admissions committees.

Trainees should learn, under the guidance of community leaders, about the impact of medical racism on the community and the shared responsibility of academic health centers in perpetuating these issues.

Trainees must receive education on ethical concepts such as dual loyalty, analyzing the conflicts arising from allegiance to the academic health center’s interests within a segregated health care system.

Academic health centers should encourage students to dedicate time typically reserved for academic research to working with community organizations, even if this does not yield conventional research outputs.
Residency programs and other employers should recognize and value students’ experiences in community organizing during their selection processes.
Contributions to community activism and social justice should be incorporated into criteria for faculty promotion and leadership appointments.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of PR’s community and their experiences with the academic health center (AHC), how can academic health centers ethically ensure equitable access to high-quality medical care for historically marginalized populations, such as minority, uninsured, and Medicaid patients, comparable to that received by more affluent White communities?
keypoints: Change agents should step beyond the walls of hospitals to learn from and follow the leadership of grassroots organizers within the communities they serve, in order to dismantle medical segregation and racism.
Academic medicine must acknowledge its own limitations as part of the existing system and adopt a supportive rather than a leading role in driving transformative change.
Academic Health Centers (AHCs) should more fully integrate community perspectives, energy, and wisdom through reforms targeting their two core historical legacies: education and research.
AHCs can include community members and leaders on admissions committees to recruit students from diverse backgrounds who originate from the communities they aim to serve.

In research, AHCs should adhere to the principles of participatory community-based research, establishing equitable partnerships with community collaborators and ensuring dissemination of results to promote meaningful change.
To ensure the effectiveness of reforms, contributions to community activism and social justice should be incorporated into criteria for faculty promotion and leadership appointments.

ethical_issues.question: How should academic health centers integrate community perspectives, energy, and wisdom into the training of clinicians and the design of equitable health care systems to reduce racism and segregation?
keypoints: In health professions education, academic health centers should incorporate community leaders to ensure that selection and training focus on public health needs.
Trainees should learn, under the guidance of community leaders, about the impact of medical racism on surrounding communities and the shared responsibility of their academic health center.
Academic health centers should adhere to participatory community research principles by establishing equitable partnerships and ensuring dissemination of findings to promote systemic change.
Academic health centers should encourage students to dedicate time typically reserved for academic research to community organization work, even if it does not yield traditional scholarly outputs.
Contributions to community activism and social justice should be incorporated into criteria for faculty promotion and leadership appointments.
The academic medical community should acknowledge its limitations as part of the existing system and adopt a supportive rather than a leading role in driving transformative change.

title: How Should Health Professions Educators and Organizations Desegregate Teaching and Learning Environments?
case:
Dr W is a well-respected, well-liked physician of some status in the Department of Medicine at University Health (UH), an academic health center in the middle of a campaign to recoup “charity care” losses incurred when patients with insufficient insurance or no insurance can’t pay or when care of Medicaid patients is reimbursed at a low rate. The campaign continues with the UH network opening SwankCare, which will be staffed exclusively by UH faculty subspecialists. Patients eligible to receive SwankCare inpatient, outpatient, or expedited laboratory services must be sufficiently resourced to pay out of pocket, as neither Medicare nor patients’ insurance of any kind will be accepted.
Even now, resident physicians and fellows typically see patients insured by Medicaid or Medicare in UH outpatient clinics, while patients with generous insurance coverage and Medicare supplemental insurance are funneled into attending faculty practices. This trend is a source of ongoing concern among a growing number of community activists, as well as students, trainees, and faculty in medicine, nursing, pharmacy, and physical therapy programs, who have voiced concern about these practices’ roots in race- and class-based patterns of oppression in US health care and about their perpetuation and growth in UH network campaigns like SwankCare.
Dr W hopes to join colleagues speaking out to promote health equity but isn’t sure how to be part of the solution. Specifically, Dr W wonders how UH services should be delivered to promote revenue sharing that would enable more efficient, network-wide coordination of care and service integration and wonders how to gain needed support from colleagues of status who don’t share the view of equity as a goal of health care.
case_rewrite:
Dr W is a highly regarded and popular physician with significant standing in the Department of Medicine at University Health (UH), an academic health center currently focused on recovering losses from “charity care”—the uncompensated costs accrued when patients lacking sufficient insurance, or holding only Medicaid, are unable to pay or when reimbursement rates are low. As part of this effort, UH has launched SwankCare, a new facility staffed solely by UH faculty subspecialists.
