SwankCare offers inpatient, outpatient, and expedited laboratory services exclusively to patients who can afford to pay out of pocket; it accepts no Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurance.

At present, the UH outpatient clinics tend to be staffed by resident physicians and fellows, who primarily see patients insured through Medicaid or Medicare. Meanwhile, patients with robust insurance plans or comprehensive supplemental Medicare coverage are directed to the faculty practices of attending physicians. This pattern of segregating patient care based on insurance status has become a growing concern for community activists, as well as for students, trainees, and faculty across medicine, nursing, pharmacy, and physical therapy programs. Many have expressed alarm about the deep roots of these practices in race- and class-based inequalities in the US health system, and about how initiatives like SwankCare may further entrench and expand such inequities within the UH network.

Dr W aspires to stand with colleagues who are advocating for health equity but feels uncertain about how best to contribute to meaningful change. Dr W is particularly interested in how UH’s services might be restructured to promote fairer revenue sharing, support more integrated care, and break down barriers to coordination across the network. Additionally, Dr W is seeking ways to engage influential colleagues who may not view equity as a central goal of health care, hoping to build broader support for systemic reforms aimed at advancing health equity.

ethical_issues.question: What specific actions should Dr W and leaders at University Health take to dismantle structural and institutional segregation in clinical teaching and learning environments, in order to promote health equity and uphold ethical standards in medical education?
keypoints: Implement stratified analysis of segregated care data and establish systems for the collection, maintenance, and analysis of patient data stratified by race, ethnicity, and other key demographic factors.
Eliminate bias in clinical practice and discrimination and racism within the health care environment.
End the separation of clinical services between trainees and faculty, and dismantle barriers related to insurance contracting and referral networks.
Review and rectify discriminatory policies as well as interpersonal acts of discrimination.
Provide protected time and dedicated funding for the development, implementation, and evaluation of desegregation initiatives.
Ensure meaningful involvement of patients and community members throughout the entire process with appropriate compensation, conduct regular data analyses, and establish clear metrics and timelines.
Well-respected academic health care institutions and clinicians should leverage their influence to advocate for policy and regulatory changes at the national level.

title: Is It Reasonable to Expect Students and Trainees to Internalize Equity as a Core Professional Value When Teaching and Learning Occurs in Segregated Settings?
case: AB is a student who often hears patients referred to as “clinic patients” when they are insured by Medicaid and as “private patients” when they have more generous insurance coverage. Now rotating in an obstetrics and gynecology unit, AB talks with fellow students about having also observed a norm of asking a laboring patient with private insurance whether they will permit a student to participate in their delivery and a norm ofnotasking a laboring patient insured by Medicaid—often a person of color or fluent in languages other than English—whether they will permit a student to participate in their delivery. Several students agree that they observe differences in how patients are treated and that they are invited, if not de facto required, to participate in routine, long-standing patterns of inequitable care of patients, which makes them feel complicit, morally distressed, and outraged. Some students express fear of reprisals if they question the unit’s practices and their teachers’ perpetuation of inequity and suggest it’s not “worth it” to speak up. Some students, however—even some among those who fear reprisals—also state that they feel terrible about not speaking up. The students exchange ideas and consider how to respond.
case_rewrite:
AB is a medical student who has repeatedly noticed that patients are labeled as “clinic patients” if they are insured by Medicaid, while those with more comprehensive insurance are referred to as “private patients.” Now on rotation in the obstetrics and gynecology unit, AB observes another troubling pattern: when a laboring patient has private insurance, staff routinely ask whether the patient consents to a student participating in their delivery. In contrast, when the patient is insured by Medicaid—often someone who is a person of color or communicates primarily in a language other than English—no such permission is sought. Instead, it is simply assumed that students will participate, and these patients are rarely given the opportunity to voice their preferences.

AB discusses these observations with fellow students, many of whom have noticed the same disparities in patient treatment. The students agree that they are often invited, or even expected, to take part in longstanding practices that result in inequitable care. This makes them feel complicit in a system that treats patients differently based on insurance status, race, and language, causing them significant moral distress and outrage. Some students express fear of negative repercussions if they challenge the unit’s practices or question the ways their supervisors perpetuate these inequities, and suggest that it may not be “worth it” to speak up. Nonetheless, even those who are most concerned about potential reprisals admit that they feel deeply uncomfortable remaining silent.

As the conversation continues, the group exchanges ideas about how best to respond to the situation. They grapple with their sense of responsibility to their patients and their desire to advocate for equitable treatment, while also worrying about the risks involved in challenging entrenched norms. The students consider possible actions they might take together, and reflect on the need for a system that supports trainees in reporting and resisting inequitable practices without fear of retaliation.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of AB’s observations during medical training, how can educators and trainees uphold the ethical principle of equity by ensuring that all patients—regardless of race, language, or insurance status—are treated with equal respect and afforded the same opportunities for informed consent and participation in the educational process?
keypoints: Medical schools and their affiliated academic medical centers must prioritize the creation of a more equitable healthcare system to ensure that all patients receive equal respect and treatment during the educational process.

Implementing healthcare desegregation is essential to achieving equity in both medical care and training environments, guaranteeing that patients with the same needs or conditions are seen at the same location by the same clinicians, with equal wait times for appointments.

Medical schools have a responsibility to support, protect, and train students who advocate for healthcare desegregation by establishing systems free from fear of retaliation, thereby encouraging students to report inequities encountered during their training.

Evaluation criteria should emphasize dedication to building an equitable healthcare system throughout medical school, residency, and career advancement, in order to resist racism and bias inherent in segregated healthcare systems.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical schools and academic medical centers create an environment in which students like AB can report observed inequities—such as differential treatment of patients based on insurance status—without fear of retaliation, and in which clinicians are empowered and expected to actively oppose practices that perpetuate segregation?
keypoints: Medical schools and academic medical centers should establish systems free from fear of retaliation to support students in reporting inequities encountered during their training.
Medical schools ought to cultivate students as active advocates for equitable health care systems, providing them with protection and support.
Creating a more equitable health care system must be a core mission of medical schools and their affiliated academic medical centers.
Evaluation criteria should emphasize dedication to building an equitable health care system, thereby assisting students in balancing career advancement with adherence to their values.

ethical_issues.question: How can structural racism and insurance-based segregation be resisted and eliminated in medical training to create a truly equitable healthcare and educational environment?
keypoints: Medical schools and their affiliated academic medical centers must prioritize the creation of a more equitable healthcare system as a core mission.
Medical schools have a responsibility to support, protect, and train students who advocate for desegregated healthcare by establishing a system free from fear of retaliation.
Evaluation criteria should emphasize dedication to building an equitable healthcare system, spanning from medical school through residency and career advancement.
Students should initiate petitions, organize social media campaigns, and lobby government officials to promote healthcare desegregation.
A desegregated system must ensure that patients with the same needs or conditions are seen at the same location, by the same clinician, with equal wait times for appointments.

title: Decision Aids, Doorknob Moments, and Physician-Patient Solidarity in EDs
case:
Something does not sit right about this emergency department (ED) patient. His asthma flare-ups have brought him to the ED multiple times for shortness of breath, despite escalating asthma medication interventions by his pulmonologist. The emergency medicine intern, who is a few months into her training, listens to his lungs. He’s wheezing, but mildly. His symptoms could fit an asthma exacerbation, but he appears comfortable. Does asthma explain his visit to the ED? Could it be a pulmonary embolism (PE)? What about risk factors for heart disease?
The intern knows a senior resident physician will ask for her differential diagnosis. The patient’s heart rate is over 100, so a common decision tool validated for use with patients at low risk will not rule out PE.She considers ordering a d-dimer to further stratify his risk for PE. He could have underlying pneumonia, so she orders a chest x-ray. There’s also a clinical decision rule for assessing the 6-week likelihood that a patient like this one (eg, with symptoms suggesting an acute cardiac syndrome) will experience an adverse cardiac event.
The intern finishes examining the patient. Now about to leave, with her hand on the doorknob, she asks, “Sir, what do you think is causing your shortness of breath?”
He responds, “My neighbors have been trying to kill me with poisonous vapors in the air conditioning vents.”
case_rewrite:
Something unsettles Dr. W, the emergency medicine intern, about this patient in the emergency department. He’s a frequent visitor, often presenting with shortness of breath from asthma flare-ups, even though his pulmonologist has already escalated his asthma medications. Dr. W, just a few months into her training, carefully listens to his lungs. There’s a mild wheeze, but nothing severe. While his symptoms could be attributed to an asthma exacerbation, he seems at ease—almost too comfortable for someone in distress.

Dr. W starts assembling her differential diagnosis. Is asthma truly the cause of his current symptoms, or is there something more? Could a pulmonary embolism be at play? She wonders about his risk factors for heart disease as well. She knows her senior resident will soon expect her to justify her diagnostic reasoning.

Noting his elevated heart rate—over 100 beats per minute—Dr. W recalls that a commonly used decision tool won’t rule out a pulmonary embolism in a patient with tachycardia. She considers ordering a d-dimer test to further assess his risk. Since underlying pneumonia is another possibility, she orders a chest x-ray. Dr. W also remembers a clinical rule designed to gauge the likelihood that someone with these symptoms might experience an acute cardiac event in the next six weeks.

After completing the physical exam, Dr. W prepares to leave the room. With her hand resting on the doorknob, she turns and gently asks, “Sir, what do you think is causing your shortness of breath?”

The patient looks at her and replies, “My neighbors have been trying to kill me with poisonous vapors in the air conditioning vents.”

ethical_issues.question: How can decision aids be appropriately utilized in the emergency department to ensure optimal patient care without neglecting patients’ subjective data and genuine concerns?
keypoints: Decision aids should be used appropriately to avoid misapplication that may lead to deviation from the correct diagnostic and therapeutic pathways.
Clinicians should lead the diagnostic process, employing technological aids judiciously and not allowing these tools to define the clinical questions themselves.
In emergency decision-making, technology should augment rather than replace clinical reasoning, assisting in data processing and supporting decisions made under conditions of uncertainty.
Attention must be given to patients’ subjective data and genuine concerns, avoiding overreliance on objective data that may overlook what matters most to the patient.
Ideally, decision aids should alleviate cognitive burdens, thereby creating the temporal and spatial conditions necessary for meaningful physician-patient interactions.

ethical_issues.question: How can the integration of technological decision aids and the humanities be balanced in the clinical decision-making process to promote physician-patient solidarity and accommodate uncertainty and complexity?
keypoints: Clinical decision aids should alleviate cognitive burdens and create space and time for physician-patient interactions, rather than replace critical thinking.
The humanities and arts in medicine challenge us to embrace uncertainty, attend to what is unsaid, and recognize how emotions influence our thinking.
In emergency medicine, the humanities and arts foster moments of stillness and solidarity with patients through the use of technology, cultivating humility and adaptability to uncertainty.

Establishing solidarity with patients requires first achieving solidarity with technology; the humanities and arts help discern when technological assistance is needed and when the human mind and heart suffice.

title: How Should Clinicians Own Their Roles as Past and Present Exacerbators of Health Inequity and as Present and Future Contributors to Health Equity?
case:
You are a cardiologist and researcher investigating outcomes after coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention at a large academic health center (AHC) as part of a multisite, longitudinal study. Among patients who are part of a regional cohort of patients who came to the AHC’s emergency department with chest pain, many were confirmed to have elevated troponin levels, indicating myocardial infarction (MI). Several years of data consistently reveal, and now definitively confirm, that Black patients living close to the AHC are more likely than White patients to experience poorer outcomes (ie, increased mortality and hospital readmission).
You suspected your AHC’s data would express racial and ethnic inequity patterns similar to those revealed throughout the country, so you are not surprised by what the final data reveal. The data’s conclusiveness seems now to have new urgency for you, however, given widespread racial and ethnic health inequity throughout the country during the COVID-19 pandemic and those years’ social, cultural, and political upheaval. Your impulse is to share these data with colleagues, despite your fear that a recently launched public relations campaign by your AHC could spur reprisals. You feel urgency about responding justly to your many individual patients of color; you wonder whether responding justly means sharing with those patients and the community what you know about inequitable cardiac care where you practice. You also wonder how your own cardiology practice has contributed to and continues to contribute to inequity.
You are aware of the need to act quickly, as you expect to see some of your patients during what remains of the week. You are also aware of the need to act thoughtfully and deliberately, to try to be part of a long-term solution to a long-term problem. You consider what to do next.
case_rewrite:
As a cardiologist and researcher at a large academic health center (AHC), you are leading a multisite, longitudinal study on outcomes following coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention. Your research focuses on a regional cohort of patients who arrived at the AHC’s emergency department presenting with chest pain. Many of these patients were found to have elevated troponin levels, confirming diagnoses of myocardial infarction (MI). Over the course of several years, your data have consistently shown—and now irrefutably confirm—that Black patients living in the immediate vicinity of the AHC experience significantly poorer outcomes compared to White patients. These disparities manifest as higher rates of mortality and more frequent hospital readmissions.

You had anticipated that your institution’s data might mirror the racial and ethnic inequities documented at the national level, so the findings themselves do not surprise you. However, the clarity and finality of these results hit differently now, especially in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic and the accompanying nationwide reckoning with racial injustice in healthcare and beyond. The urgency of the moment weighs on you, and you feel compelled to share these findings with your colleagues. Yet, you are also wary—your institution has just launched a major public relations campaign, and you worry that bringing such inequities to light could provoke backlash from the administration.

Amid this tension, you reflect on your duty to your patients of color. You ask yourself whether justice requires that you inform these patients—and the broader community—about the inequitable cardiac care they are receiving at your institution. You also grapple with the uncomfortable question of how your own clinical practice may have contributed to, and may still be perpetuating, these disparities.

Time is of the essence; you are scheduled to see several patients before the week ends. At the same time, you recognize the importance of moving thoughtfully, engaging in meaningful reflection, and considering how your actions might contribute to longer-term solutions for systemic problems. You find yourself at a crossroads, weighing the need for a swift, just response against the necessity of deliberate planning and collaboration. As you consider your next steps, you reflect deeply on your responsibilities—to your patients, your colleagues, your institution, and the wider community.

ethical_issues.question: Do clinicians have a moral obligation to disclose to patients and the community the existence of local inequities in cardiac care?
keypoints: Clinicians have a moral responsibility to share research findings with the communities who have contributed their time and effort to the study, thereby embodying a sense of solidarity.
Withholding research results contravenes scientists’ social responsibility to promote human flourishing; clinicians should disclose data to address racial health inequities.
Knowledge obtained through public funding carries an ethical obligation of sharing; clinicians ought to disclose research outcomes to the public to advance the public good.

Participation of community members in research generates a reciprocal obligation; clinicians should disclose findings to patients who have assumed research risks in accordance with principles of reciprocity and respect.
Research findings should benefit all who stand to gain; clinicians bear the responsibility to release data to dismantle structural factors that perpetuate health inequities.

ethical_issues.question: When confronting racial health inequities, how should clinicians ethically balance the demands for prompt action with those for prudent restraint?
keypoints: Clinicians confronting racial health inequities should respond swiftly to new information to improve health outcomes while maintaining prudent restraint, focusing on empathy, and forging a pathway from empathy to solidarity.

Prudent restraint is a state of intentional stillness and deep reflection that facilitates contemplation, self-awareness, consultation, and planning, thereby enabling clinicians to gain a fuller understanding of the circumstances of patients whose lived experiences differ markedly from their own.

Critical reflection cultivates empathy, which in turn drives ethical practice and structural change, helping to build bridges of solidarity between groups with power and privilege and those experiencing health inequities.

ethical_issues.question: Do the medical and scientific communities have a responsibility to dismantle the systems and structures that perpetuate health inequities and crises of trust, and if so, how should this be achieved?
keypoints: The medical and scientific community holds a responsibility to dismantle the systems and structures that perpetuate health inequities and crises of trust.
Clinicians should step away from the demands of daily busyness and remain open to reflecting on the entrenched structures of oppression within the healthcare system and their role in health inequity.
Critical reflexivity, through examining power dynamics and embedded social structures, deepens understanding of others’ experiences and cultivates empathy.
Empathy serves as the foundation for structural change and can guide the medical profession toward solidarity and equity.
Solidarity is a necessary force for advancing health equity, arising from a humanitarian commitment across groups and collective action.
Achieving racial equity in healthcare requires active collaboration among stakeholders and intentional antidiscrimination practices.

title: What Should Clinicians Do When Health Services Are Improperly Billed in Their Names?
case:
Dr L completed residency training 4 years ago and continues to pay down a balance of over $300 000 in loans used to finance college and medical education. Dr L practices medicine as an employee of Urban Health Care (UHC). Upon hire, Dr L was required to agree to grant UHC exclusive rights to bill for, collect, and retain reimbursement payments for Dr L’s professional services. The agreement does not indemnify Dr L for erroneous or fraudulent billing by UHC on Dr L’s behalf but does specify that UHC report speed and efficiency productivity targets calledwork relative value units(wRVUs) to Dr L, which inform Dr L’s performance reviews, incentives, and compensation.
Dr L recently noticed that salary deposits during the last few months do not seem to track with wRVU productivity reported by UHC. Dr L has also been asked by UHC billing staff, with increasing frequency during these months, to revise documentation of some services to some patients. Dr L asks other physician colleagues about their experiences with UHC’s billing practices and finds that several suspect that UHC is upcoding services they have provided to patients. Dr L learns that a few who have questioned UHC about this apparent irregularity have been terminated or had their hours reduced. One colleague expressed frustration, “We’re personally and professionally liable for the accuracy of bills sent in our names, yet we can’t question UHC without reprisal.” The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Medical Learning Network posts instructions for reporting suspected fraudulent or erroneous billing,but none of Dr L’s colleagues have yet done so.
Dr L wonders whether to contact CMS.
case_rewrite:
Dr L, who finished residency training four years ago, is still working to pay off more than $300,000 in student loans accumulated from college and medical school. Dr L is employed as a physician by Urban Health Care (UHC). When joining UHC, Dr L signed an employment agreement granting UHC exclusive authority to bill for, collect, and retain all reimbursement for Dr L’s professional services. The contract makes clear that Dr L is not protected—indemnified—if UHC submits erroneous or fraudulent bills on Dr L’s behalf. However, it does specify that UHC will regularly provide Dr L with reports on work relative value units (wRVUs), which are used to evaluate Dr L’s productivity, performance reviews, bonuses, and overall compensation.

Over the past few months, Dr L has noticed that salary deposits have not matched up with the wRVU productivity reports provided by UHC. At the same time, UHC’s billing department has increasingly requested that Dr L revise documentation for certain patient encounters. Curious and concerned, Dr L talks with several physician colleagues at UHC, only to discover that many also suspect UHC is upcoding—submitting billing codes for more complex or costly services than were actually provided. Some colleagues share that when they raised concerns about these irregularities, UHC either terminated their employment or reduced their clinical hours. One frustrated physician remarks, “We’re both personally and professionally responsible for the bills submitted in our names, but we can’t question UHC’s billing practices without risking our jobs.” Dr L is aware that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Medical Learning Network offers guidance for reporting potentially fraudulent or erroneous billing, but none of Dr L’s colleagues have taken the step to contact CMS.

Faced with growing uncertainty, Dr L is now considering whether to reach out to CMS to report these concerns.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr L ethically ensure the accuracy of bills and claims submitted in their name when lacking transparency, decision-making authority, and control over the billing process?
keypoints: Clinicians should have unrestricted access to review billing and claims data submitted in their names to identify potential errors or fraudulent activities.

If access to billing and claims information is denied, clinicians may notify the Office of Inspector General (OIG) or the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to address suspected billing fraud or errors.
Employers ought to indemnify clinicians against liability arising from erroneous, fraudulent, or inaccurate billing or claims submissions when clinicians are not at fault.

Federal, state, and organizational policies should promote billing transparency and incentivize organizations either to share relevant proprietary information with clinician-employees who require access to billing and claims data submitted in their names or to assume full accountability for billing accuracy.

ethical_issues.question: How Can Clinicians Protect Themselves from Legal Liability and Professional Reprisal When Faced with Nontransparent Billing and Claims Practices by Their Employers?
keypoints: Clinicians should have unrestricted access to billing and claims data submitted in their names in order to protect themselves from legal liability.
Clinicians may notify the Office of Inspector General (OIG) or the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to report denial of access to billing and claims information.

The American Medical Association (AMA) recommends legislation or regulation to eliminate contractual provisions that prohibit or restrict physicians’ access to their billing records and associated medical records.
Employers should indemnify clinicians against liability arising from erroneous, fraudulent, or inaccurate billing or claims submissions when the clinicians are not at fault.

Federal, state, and organizational policies should promote billing transparency and incentivize organizations either to share relevant proprietary information with clinician-employees who require access to billing and claims data submitted in their names or to assume full accountability for billing and claims accuracy.

title: How Might Patients and Physicians Use Transparent Health Care Prices to Guide Decisions and Improve Health Care Affordability?
case: NN is a 54-year-old woman with congestive heart failure, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease who is enrolled in a marketplace health insurance plan with a $6000 annual deductible. Last year, NN was hospitalized for decompensated heart failure. Her out-of-pocket (OOP) expenses for this hospitalization were high, which led to increased credit card debt and required her to spend less on food. Thus, even when NN experiences shortness of breath and leg swelling, she is reluctant to refill her prescribed diuretic. Furthermore, because of her concerns about the costs of her care, she often does not attend follow-up appointments with her physicians and only occasionally completes the laboratory testing they recommend. In her local newspaper, NN reads that hospitals are now required to publicly report to patients their negotiated prices for health care services. She is curious about this information and wonders if it could help with her financial concerns, but she isn’t sure where to find this information or how to use it.
case_rewrite:
NN is a 54-year-old woman living with congestive heart failure, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease. She is insured through a marketplace health plan that carries a $6000 annual deductible. The previous year, NN was admitted to the hospital due to worsening heart failure. The hospitalization resulted in substantial out-of-pocket expenses, forcing her to accumulate credit card debt and reduce her spending on essentials like food. As a consequence, NN has become hesitant to refill her prescribed diuretic, even when she notices symptoms such as shortness of breath and swelling in her legs. Her financial worries also make her reluctant to attend follow-up appointments and she only sporadically completes the recommended laboratory tests.

Recently, NN read in her local newspaper that hospitals are now mandated to make their negotiated prices for healthcare services available to patients. While she is intrigued by the possibility that this information might help her address her financial challenges, NN feels uncertain about where to locate these details or how to interpret them to make better choices about her care.

ethical_issues.question: In medical decision-making, how can patients’ financial circumstances and the potential financial consequences of treatment options be incorporated to prevent financial harm as a form of iatrogenic injury?
keypoints: Physicians should incorporate patients’ financial circumstances into health decision making to prevent adverse outcomes resulting from unrecognized financial consequences.
Physicians and patients should discuss insurance deductibles, confirm the indications and necessity of recommended services, and compare the quality and prices of these services.
Clinicians have a responsibility to support patients in accessing and interpreting price and quality information of health care services to facilitate informed treatment decisions.
Cost discussions and the use of price comparison tools should be integrated routinely into clinical workflows to assist patients in managing out-of-pocket expenditures.
By controlling out-of-pocket spending, chronic conditions can be more effectively managed, thereby delaying or avoiding the need for costly interventions or hospitalizations.

ethical_issues.question: What measures should health care organizations and clinicians take to support patients in accessing and interpreting price and quality information in order to promote equity and improve patient-centered outcomes?
keypoints: Health care institutions and clinicians should discuss patients’ insurance deductibles, confirm the indications and necessity of recommended services, and identify which services require comparison of quality and price.
Health care institutions should inform patients of the price and quality information of services prior to obtaining their consent, to facilitate informed decision-making.

Clinicians should collaborate with business units responsible for billing and insurance contracts to investigate the prices of laboratory tests and interventions, and integrate relevant cost information into shared decision-making with patients.
Electronic health record systems should be enhanced to incorporate publicly available price information and insurance plan data, generating personalized out-of-pocket cost estimates.
Price information should be accompanied by quality metrics and interpretive guides to assist patients and clinicians in evaluating the cost-effectiveness of services.
Cost discussions and the use of price comparison tools should be incorporated into routine clinical workflows to encourage patients to compare prices for nonurgent medical care.
Clinicians have a responsibility to support patients in accessing and interpreting price and quality information to assist them in obtaining necessary services.

title: How Should Cost-Informed Goals of Care Decisions Be Facilitated at Life’s End?
case:
DD is the designated durable power of attorney for health care, who has served well in this capacity by prioritizing her mother’s previously expressed wishes to the best of her ability. DD has also, to this point, represented all DD’s siblings as they discuss with care teams the care of their elderly parent in hospital and nearing death. DD and the health care team have discussed initiation of life-sustaining interventions (eg, mechanical ventilation, intubation, artificial nutrition and hydration), as well as a hospice care referral, given the patient’s diagnosis and impending death.
DD explains to the health care team that her mother had previously indicated she wanted all lifesaving therapies but that she values quality of life over extended life. The patient had also expressed a desire not to become a family burden. While sharing this sentiment, DD expresses, “For long hospital stays, no one needs to know the price of services to know it’s expensive and that it will leave us bankrupt—$100 a day, $1000 a day out of our pockets. That is too much for most American families and it’s too much for us. Our kids won’t be able to go to college, and we won’t have enough to pay for my father’s medicines.”
case_rewrite:
DD serves as the designated durable power of attorney for health care for her elderly mother, a role she has fulfilled with dedication by consistently prioritizing her mother’s previously stated wishes. DD has also acted as the spokesperson for all her siblings during discussions with the hospital care team regarding their mother’s care as she nears the end of her life. Together with the health care team, DD has reviewed the possibility of initiating life-sustaining treatments such as mechanical ventilation, intubation, and artificial nutrition and hydration, as well as the option of transitioning to hospice care, in light of her mother’s diagnosis and imminent passing.

In these conversations, DD shares that her mother had clearly stated a desire to receive all lifesaving therapies available, yet also emphasized her preference for quality of life over mere prolongation of life. Her mother further expressed that she did not want to become a burden to the family. As DD relays this to the team, she adds, “For long hospital stays, the cost is obvious to everyone—it’s expensive, and it could leave us bankrupt. We’re talking $100 a day, $1000 a day coming out of our pockets. That’s more than most American families can handle, and it’s too much for us. If we keep paying, our kids might not be able to go to college, and we may not have enough left for my father’s medicines.”

ethical_issues.question: In end-of-life care, how should the ethical considerations between life extension and quality of life be balanced?
keypoints: In end-of-life care, the trade-offs among life extension, quality of life, and cost considerations should be balanced and aligned with patient preferences.
Life-saving treatments should not be regarded as the sole or primary criterion for decision making, especially at the end of life.
The impact of treatments on quality of life should constitute a critical component of medical decision making and physician-patient communication at the end of life.
Patients, family members, and healthcare professionals need to reflect on the patient’s goals and values, using these as a guide for medical decisions.
Concordance between patient preferences and the care actually received is a hallmark of high-quality end-of-life care.

ethical_issues.question: How can the financial burden on patients’ families be effectively incorporated as an ethical consideration in end-of-life care decision-making?
keypoints: End-of-life care decisions should balance life prolongation, quality of life, and cost considerations, ensuring alignment with patient preferences.

Physicians should discuss the overall expensiveness of treatments with patients and their families, inquire about their financial circumstances and insurance coverage, to facilitate informed decision-making.
Physicians can guide patients or their health care proxies to apply for financial assistance programs or utilize price transparency platforms to alleviate economic burdens.
Social workers and case managers play a critical role in helping patients understand the financial implications of treatments and in connecting them to appropriate resources.

Advance care planning should encompass information on prognosis, the clinical benefits and harms of treatments, and treatment costs to ensure that health care proxies accurately comprehend patient preferences.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of DD acting as the durable power of attorney for her mother’s end-of-life care, how can clinicians ensure that DD fully understands prognostic information, the clinical benefits and burdens of proposed interventions, and the associated treatment costs, so that she can make ethically informed decisions consistent with her mother’s previously expressed values and wishes?
keypoints: Ensure that surrogates, such as DD, fully understand the patient’s prognosis to facilitate informed evaluation of care options; clinicians should explicitly communicate life expectancy and likely outcomes at the end of life.

When discussing treatment options with surrogates, emphasis should be placed on the anticipated impact of interventions on the patient’s quality of life, rather than focusing solely on life extension; clinicians should ensure that surrogates comprehend the potential benefits, burdens, and side effects of proposed treatments.

Transparent discussion of treatment costs is essential for informed decision making; clinicians should address the potential financial burden of interventions, inquire about the family’s financial circumstances as appropriate, and provide guidance regarding available financial assistance resources.

Advance Care Planning (ACP) is critical to ensure that surrogates like DD are aware of the patient’s prognosis, the clinical benefits and harms of proposed treatments, and associated costs; ACP enables patients to document their medical preferences and formally designate a surrogate decision maker.

title: How Should We Respond to Health Sector Emissions That Exacerbate Climate Change and Inequity?
case: City Y has ambient levels of particulate matter (PM) of 2.5, a rate 25% higher than most American cities. The American Lung Association had flagged Y as 1 of 2 cities that fail State of the Air evaluationsin ozone and PM pollution. Y’s air pollution is due to wood burning, which is common in nearby rural communities; its geographical location downwind from plants that power and process solid waste for 4 larger metropolitan regions in nearby neighboring states; and 3 major academic health centers. Thirty percent of contemporary illnesses (eg, diabetes, asthma, cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and lung cancer) in Y are attributable to poor air quality. In the United States, communities of lower socioeconomic status are at risk of exposure to higher levels of air pollution than those of higher socioeconomic status,and, worldwide, low- and middle- income countries are most at risk.Moreover, diseases caused by pollution were estimated to be responsible for 16% of global mortality and 268 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) worldwide in 2015.
case_rewrite:
City Y is notable for its persistently elevated levels of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), with concentrations averaging 25% higher than those found in most American cities. The American Lung Association has identified Y as one of only two cities in the state that fail to meet State of the Air standards for both ozone and particulate pollution. Multiple factors contribute to Y’s poor air quality: widespread wood burning in surrounding rural communities, its geographic position downwind from several solid waste power and processing plants that serve four major metropolitan areas in neighboring states, and the presence of three major academic health centers within the city. 

Approximately 30% of current illnesses in City Y—including diabetes, asthma, cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and lung cancer—are attributable to the city’s poor air quality. In the United States, lower socioeconomic status communities are disproportionately exposed to higher levels of air pollution in comparison to wealthier areas. This trend is mirrored globally, where low- and middle-income countries face the greatest risks. In 2015, diseases linked to pollution were estimated to account for 16% of deaths worldwide and 268 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs).

Within this context, the healthcare sector in City Y faces a significant ethical challenge: how to provide high-quality care while also minimizing environmental harm. Hospitals and clinics in the city generate substantial medical waste, both from necessary patient care and from unnecessary tests and treatments. The location of medical waste processing facilities—often sited in or near vulnerable neighborhoods—raises additional concerns about fairness and the distribution of environmental risks. 

Dr. W, a physician at one of Y’s large academic health centers, is increasingly aware of the ways the hospital’s practices contribute to the city’s pollution burden. Dr. W has noticed that unnecessary diagnostic tests and treatments—many of which could be avoided by adopting best practices, such as those advocated by the Choosing Wisely campaign—result in avoidable waste and emissions. Meanwhile, even necessary care produces waste that, if not properly managed, can end up disproportionately affecting the very communities already burdened by poor air quality.

Administrative leaders at the hospital, including SB from the purchasing department, are discussing strategies to reduce waste at the source. They are exploring supplier contracts designed to minimize packaging and single-use items, and are also considering conducting waste audits to identify hotspots for improvement. Collaboration with the hospital’s electronic medical record team is underway to implement alerts that help curb unnecessary orders. Furthermore, Dr. W and colleagues are leading educational sessions for staff on regulated medical waste and the correct use of waste receptacles, aiming to prevent misuse and lower overall emissions.

At the institutional level, there is a growing recognition of the need to track and report on both the methods and locations of medical waste disposal, to ensure that waste processing does not unfairly burden certain neighborhoods. Hospital administrators are advocating for national reimbursement policies that account for the environmental impacts of excessive and unnecessary care, and that incentivize equitable, sustainable health care delivery.

In this environment, Dr. W and SB are working together to ensure that the hospital upholds its ethical responsibility: minimizing environmental harm while delivering the highest standard of care, and ensuring that all patients—regardless of socioeconomic status—have a fair opportunity to achieve health and avoid disease and injury.

ethical_issues.question: How should the health care sector fulfill its ethical responsibility to minimize environmental harm while delivering high-quality care?
keypoints: The health care sector has an ethical obligation to seek solutions that reduce environmental harm while delivering high-quality care.
Clinicians should reduce common unnecessary testing and treatments by implementing best practices from the Choosing Wisely campaign to minimize waste from non-indicated clinical activities.
Waste generated from appropriately indicated care should be reduced through waste audits of clinical spaces and optimization of waste receptacle placement to prevent misuse.

Health care institutions should collaborate with administrative and purchasing teams to establish supplier contracts that promote waste reduction at the source, thereby minimizing waste associated with necessary care.

The siting of medical waste disposal facilities must consider the impact on neighboring communities, and metrics tracking both the methods and locations of waste disposal should be implemented to inform equitable emission reduction policies.

National reimbursement policies should reflect the negative consequences of excessive unnecessary care and incorporate a sustainability perspective to measure and incentivize equity in health care delivery.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians and hospitals minimize unnecessary health care waste to ensure that all patients have an equitable opportunity to achieve health and be free from disease and injury?
keypoints: Physicians and hospitals should reduce health care waste by streamlining unnecessary care and delivering necessary services in the most sustainable manner to uphold the principles of justice and equity.
Clinicians can reduce waste generated by unnecessary clinical activities through the implementation of best practices from the Choosing Wisely campaign.
Within institutions, collaboration with electronic medical record teams to establish alert systems for potentially unindicated care can help mitigate overutilization.
National-level reimbursement policies should reflect the impact of excessive unnecessary care on quality, costs, and health inequities.
For waste associated with appropriate and indicated care, institutions can conduct waste audits of clinical spaces to identify priority areas for emission reduction.
Clinicians can lead educational initiatives on regulated medical waste and optimize the placement of waste receptacles to reduce misuse.
At the institutional level, collaboration with administrative and purchasing teams is essential to develop supplier contracts that promote waste reduction at the source.
Ensuring equity in health care waste disposal requires tracking metrics on both the methods and locations of waste processing, which is critical for formulating equitable waste mitigation policies.
Utilizing tracking methods such as ICD-10 Z codes to document social determinants of health can identify institutions in need of support for implementing waste reduction strategies.

title: What Would It Mean for Health Care Organizations to Justly Manage Their Waste?
case:
Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, US hospitals produced 29 pounds of waste per bed per day—over 14 000 tons of waste per day.Increasing numbers of clinicians, trainees, and students in a regional university academic health center have anonymously reported (via a hotline maintained by the organization’s risk managers) inappropriate disposal of recyclable items, common refuse items, and red bag items (ie, medical waste, hazardous waste). Many students have also noted that applying disinfectant, donning personal protective equipment (eg, masks, gloves, gowns), and using high-volumes of water to thoroughly wash their hands and arms (colloquially known as “scrubbing in”) is wasteful when they are seeming sufficiently distant from a sterile field protecting a surgical patient in an operating theater.
Health care organizations pay to decontaminate red bag waste to make it safe for disposal (ie, by microwave or steam sterilization, chemical disinfection, or other processes) and must comply with federal, state, and local regulations about how disposal is done.Some hotline reporters have noted that incorrect placement of recyclable or municipal waste in red bags incurs unnecessary costs to organizations and that processing (primary) red waste generates (secondary) air- and waterborne emissions that inequitably influence health outcomes in minoritized communities; nationally, people of color are exposed to 38% higher levels of outdoor nitrogen dioxide than White people.
Two risk managers who field hotline concerns and inquiries also regularly apprise the organization’s senior managers about these concerns and offer recommendations on how to respond. They wonder which recommendations to offer senior managers to help protect the short- and long-term interests of the organization.
case_rewrite:
Before the COVID-19 pandemic, hospitals across the United States generated a staggering 29 pounds of waste per hospital bed each day—totaling more than 14,000 tons daily. At a regional university academic health center, a growing number of clinicians, residents, and students have begun to anonymously voice concerns, using a hotline managed by the facility’s risk managers, about improper handling of various types of waste: recyclable items, ordinary refuse, and red bag materials (which include medical and hazardous waste). Many students have also remarked that the routine use of disinfectant, repeated donning of personal protective equipment—such as masks, gloves, and gowns—and the practice of washing hands and arms extensively (“scrubbing in”) seem unnecessarily wasteful, especially when they remain at a safe distance from the surgical sterile field in the operating room.

Health care organizations are required to pay for the decontamination of red bag waste, making it safe for disposal through processes such as microwave or steam sterilization, chemical disinfection, or other approved methods, all while adhering to federal, state, and local regulations governing waste disposal. Some individuals calling the hotline have pointed out that mistakenly discarding recyclables or regular trash in red bags not only drives up costs for the institution but also leads to additional processing. This primary red waste processing results in secondary emissions—airborne and waterborne—that have a disproportionate effect on the health of minoritized communities. Nationwide, people of color experience 38% greater exposure to outdoor nitrogen dioxide than their White counterparts.

Among those monitoring these reports, the two risk managers who handle the hotline’s incoming concerns regularly brief the organization’s senior management. In their discussions, they weigh which recommendations to present that would safeguard both the immediate and future interests of the institution. They recognize that policies must not only address the financial and regulatory aspects of waste management, but also acknowledge the broader ethical responsibility to minimize environmental harm, particularly where it unjustly burdens vulnerable populations.

In considering their guidance, the risk managers understand the importance of transparency in waste management practices, including clear policy development and open sharing of data, to demonstrate and uphold the organization’s commitment to environmental stewardship. They also contemplate how the health center might use its purchasing power and standing in the community to influence suppliers and advocate for industry-wide changes that would promote both environmental sustainability and health equity.

At the same time, the risk managers are aware that the implementation of medical waste management directly affects the safety and workload of those tasked with handling waste—often low-paid cleaning staff who were not responsible for generating the waste in the first place. There is concern that these workers may face undue exposure to hazardous materials during the sorting process. To address this, the managers consider advocating for a restructured workflow that incorporates input from these frontline workers, ensuring their perspectives are central to the decision-making process.

They also contemplate forming a multidisciplinary committee that would bring together staff from all levels and departments. This committee would collaborate on tasks such as sorting and weighing waste, thereby fostering a more equitable distribution of labor and encouraging shared ownership of both the challenges and solutions. By involving a diverse group of stakeholders, the risk managers hope to elevate the importance of waste analysis, deepen department-wide engagement, and prompt all health care personnel to reflect on how their daily practices contribute to the broader impact of hospital waste—on both the environment and the communities the institution serves.

ethical_issues.question: How can health care organizations ethically manage their waste to ensure that they do not cause unjust health impacts on minoritized communities?
keypoints: Health care organizations should center justice by minimizing the quantity of waste generated and implementing sustainable disposal methods for unavoidable waste to reduce health impacts on minoritized communities.

Enhancing transparency in waste management through policy development and data sharing is essential to ensure that organizations’ commitments to environmental sustainability are both recognized and held accountable.

Health care systems should leverage their purchasing power and community influence to drive more equitable and sustainable transformations within related industries and advocate for policies that reduce health care–associated waste emissions.

Successful waste management requires the engagement and buy-in of all stakeholders within the health care system and the incorporation of diverse perspectives during implementation to ensure that sustainable practices benefit all patient populations.

ethical_issues.question: In the implementation of medical waste management, how can the health and safety of key workers handling medical waste be ensured, and how can labor tasks be distributed fairly?
keypoints: To ensure the health and safety of workers handling medical waste, workflows must be restructured to incorporate their perspectives.
The burden should not fall solely on low-paid cleaning staff who are not involved in waste generation; exposure to hazardous materials during sorting must be avoided.

A multidisciplinary committee should be established, involving staff at all levels within departments to collaboratively participate in waste sorting and weighing, thereby achieving an ethical distribution of labor.

Multidisciplinary engagement enhances the significance of waste analysis, increases intradepartmental involvement, and encourages all personnel to reflect on their respective responsibilities and the potential impacts of their practices.

title: How Should Clinicians and Health Care Organizations Respond When Civic Planning Concentrates Waste Processing in Minoritized Communities?
case:
Primary care physician Dr G sees long-term patient Ms T (57 years old) for follow up to a radical nephrectomy performed 2 weeks ago. Ms T has seen several family members, friends, and neighbors—mostly people of color—in her rural community succumb to cancer and experience chronic illnesses during their lifetimes. High rates of morbidity, mortality, adverse birth outcomes, and diminished life expectancy relative to residents in other areas of the state have long been suspected to be linked to airborne emission and runoff exposures from a landfill that accepts solid waste from communities throughout half the state and from a facility that processes medical and chemical waste. Both are within a few miles of Ms T’s neighborhood.
Dr G and her colleagues have long considered how to best support patients like Ms T, who live and die in communities where toxic waste exposures are higher than in communities where they live.
case_rewrite:
Dr G, a primary care physician, meets with her long-standing patient, Ms T, who is 57 years old and recovering from a radical nephrectomy performed two weeks earlier. Ms T’s life in her rural community has been shaped by witnessing many loved ones—family, friends, and neighbors, most of whom are people of color—struggle with cancer and chronic illnesses. She has mourned the loss of several members of her community to these conditions over the years. The neighborhood where Ms T resides has long been burdened by elevated rates of disease, poor birth outcomes, and shorter life expectancies compared to other parts of the state. These persistent health disparities are widely believed to be connected to two facilities situated just a few miles from Ms T’s home: a landfill that receives solid waste from half the state’s communities and a separate site that processes both medical and chemical waste.

Within the clinic, Dr G and her colleagues have engaged in ongoing discussions about how best to care for patients like Ms T, who are exposed to higher levels of environmental toxins than residents of other areas. They reflect on the challenges of practicing medicine in a community where environmental hazards are an everyday reality, and where their patients’ health has been shaped by these long-standing exposures. Dr G is mindful of the broader context of environmental injustice that affects Ms T’s life and health, and she and her colleagues continue to grapple with how to support their patients in the face of these entrenched and inequitable risks.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr G and her colleagues ethically respond to the environmental racism and health inequities affecting Ms T and other members of their community?
keypoints: Clinicians must recognize historical environmental racism and their own unconscious biases, and improve professional practice guided by ethical principles.
In the workplace, clinicians should speak candidly during interdisciplinary rounds to ensure treatment plans are based on patients’ authentic narratives rather than biases.
Clinicians should empower patients to understand the health risks of toxic waste in their communities and reduce material, pharmaceutical, and chemical waste during clinical shifts.
Clinicians should participate in developing monitoring and care protocols for patients at risk of environmental exposures to mitigate the environmental impact of clinical care.
At the community level, clinicians should advocate at the legislative level for policies that protect the right to health for all, serving as strong advocates for patient health and planetary ethics.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr G and her health care organization develop protocols, training programs, and advocacy initiatives to ethically address the environmental injustices affecting patients like Ms T and her community?
keypoints: Health care organizations should provide antiracism educational programs for employees to eliminate racial bias and educate clinicians about the impact of medical waste dumping on minoritized communities.

Monitoring and care protocols should be established for patients at risk of environmental exposures, including screening for toxic waste-related cancers, kidney diseases, and prenatal harm, as well as providing preventive care to affected communities.

Health care institutions should progressively phase out toxic chemicals, adopt green cleaning agents, and invest health care funds into minority-owned businesses and local economies through engagement with diverse suppliers.
Environmental justice task forces should be established and maintained within hospitals and clinics to advocate for public policy reforms addressing environmental injustice.

title: How Should Clinicians of Status Express Solidarity With Workers Earning Low Wages in Health Care?
case:
Several health systems’ house staff members have unionized in recent years to address working conditions during residency program and fellowship training. Dr T, a third-year resident physician, has suggested that they have obligations to help other workers in the organization to unionize, too. Dr T convinced several other resident physicians, nurses, and other clinicians of status in the organization to join a rally outside a hospital entrance to draw attention to environmental services workers having not been paid overtime or hazard pay during the worst of the 2020-2021 COVID-19 pandemic. In response, some clinicians and organizational senior managers have suggested that rallies are not helpful to employees with lower incomes, that bad press is costly overall to the organization and community, and that those attending the rally should gather somewhere other than the hospital entrance.
Dr T and others respond by inviting them, other organizational senior managers, attending physicians, and members of the organization’s Office of General Counsel to join the rallies scheduled at the hospital entrance during times when they’re off duty. Rally speakers remind those listening about high-exposure risks of infection and injuries that environmental services employees endured and suffered during the pandemic. Those within earshot of Dr T’s and other rally speakers’ calls consider whether to join the rally.
case_rewrite:
In recent years, house staff members across several health systems have unionized to advocate for improved working conditions during residency and fellowship training. Dr T, a third-year resident physician, has argued that their ethical responsibilities extend beyond their own group and include supporting other workers within the organization who may also benefit from unionization. Motivated by this conviction, Dr T rallied a group of resident physicians, nurses, and other clinicians of status to organize a demonstration outside the hospital entrance. Their aim was to highlight the plight of environmental services workers who had not received overtime or hazard pay during the most severe months of the 2020-2021 COVID-19 pandemic.

This action drew mixed reactions from within the institution. Some clinicians and senior managers expressed skepticism, contending that such rallies might not truly aid low-income employees. They voiced concerns that negative media attention could ultimately harm both the organization and the surrounding community, and recommended that the demonstrators relocate their gathering away from the hospital entrance.

In response, Dr T and the other organizers extended an open invitation to these senior managers, attending physicians, and representatives from the organization’s Office of General Counsel to participate in the scheduled rallies at the hospital entrance during off-duty hours. Rally speakers, including Dr T, made a point of reminding attendees and passersby of the significant risks of infection and injury faced by environmental services workers throughout the pandemic. As these calls for solidarity echoed across the hospital entrance, those within hearing distance—including clinicians of status—found themselves weighing whether to join the demonstration.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians of status express solidarity with low-wage workers in health care settings, while taking into account the influences of politics, power, and economics?
keypoints: Clinicians of status should recognize that solidarity with low-wage workers during the pandemic is far more urgent than in normal times.

Clinicians ought to adhere to the Hippocratic Oath’s principle of “first, do no harm” and the American Medical Association’s injunction to participate in activities that contribute to the improvement of the community and the betterment of public health.
Clinicians need to understand Bernard Williams’ concept of “thick contexts,” situating professional judgments of right and wrong within broader, more complex frameworks.

Given the current context, clinicians’ cautious yet determined concern for the circumstances of low-wage coworkers and support for unionization is insufficient; clinicians must engage in more direct and large-scale actions to express solidarity with low-wage colleagues.

title: What Do Organizations and Clinicians of Status Owe Their Patients’ Home Health Aides?
case:
Mr G, who is 77 years old and lives alone, has mild cognitive impairment, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease and currently has a suprapubic catheter due to urinary incontinence. His 2 adult children hire Ms S through a home care agency to help bathe Mr G, prepare his meals, clean as needed, organize (and often administer) his medications, and spend time with Mr G.
Ms S sought asylum in the United States 10 years ago and first began working for a cleaning service and then also for the home care agency as a home health aide. Ms S is 46 years old and most proud of her role in health care, which she considers her primary job and for which she received no formal training. The agency hires its employees as independent contractors and does not sponsor benefits (ie, health or dental insurance, paid leave, retirement contributions, or employee assistance counseling services). Ms S works full time at minimum wage, and, though she pays federal and state income taxes, her annual income falls below the federal poverty level and has been and remains insufficient for her to accrue savings. Ms S and her children currently qualify for Medicaid, are currently enrolled in their state’s supplemental nutrition program, and visit a food pantry for groceries.
Mr G is currently Ms S’s sole patient. Ms S is grieving the loss of a patient for whom she cared for 3 years until his transfer to home hospice and subsequent death. Ms S hopes her agency will assign another patient to her soon, as she needs the income, and is considering taking on a third job. To make her typical morning arrival time of 6:30AM, Ms S makes 3 bus transfers from her apartment in the city to Mr G’s suburban home. When Ms S arrives, Mr G is in his bathroom. She checks on him there, verifies that he is safe, and then returns to the kitchen to clean up milk on the floor that appears to have been spilled after she left yesterday. She then prepares Mr G’s breakfast and medications. Mr G has spent more time with Ms S than any other person during the past 2 years and regularly calls her at home for companionship, comfort, and reassurance.
Ms S prepares a Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services Home Health Certification and Plan of Care (CMS-485) form online, which must be signed by Dr P, Mr G’s physician. She was also asked to document prescription medication modifications ordered by Dr P, following Mr G’s primary care appointment earlier this week. Ms S makes the changes but is unsure about how to implement a change to Mr G’s insulin and is unsure whether one of Mr G’s new prescriptions, just received by mail, contains the correct number and kind of pills, as the shapes and colors of and numbers on the capsules do not match those in a photograph she references online. Ms S calls Dr P’s office to confirm; a member of Dr P’s staff returns her call the next day but confirms only the name and dose of the medication. Ms S remains unsure what to do, so she also contacts Mr G’s son. He is unfamiliar with the prescription changes and advises, “Just fill the boxes in the pill container for each day of the month as best you can. Dad will know which ones to take.”
Still unsure what to do, Ms S leaves out the capsules that don’t look right to her as she fills Mr G’s pill box slots. She attaches an electronic sticky note in the online CMS-485 form, hoping Dr P will see it and clarify the prescription. Dr P does not see the electronic sticky note, signs the CMS-485 form, and moves to the next electronic health record document requiring review and sign off.
case_rewrite:
Mr G, age 77, lives alone and manages several chronic health conditions, including mild cognitive impairment, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease. He currently relies on a suprapubic catheter to manage urinary incontinence. To help support him at home, Mr G’s two adult children have arranged for Ms S, a home health aide from an agency, to assist with his daily needs. Ms S’s responsibilities include helping Mr G bathe, preparing his meals, cleaning the house as necessary, organizing—and often administering—his medications, and providing companionship.

Ms S, now 46, sought asylum in the United States a decade ago. Her first job was with a cleaning service, but she soon began working as a home health aide through an agency. Ms S is deeply proud of her role in health care, which she considers her main profession, even though she has received no formal training. The agency classifies its aides as independent contractors, offering no health or dental insurance, paid leave, retirement benefits, or employee assistance programs. Ms S works full time earning minimum wage. Despite paying both federal and state income taxes, her annual income remains below the federal poverty threshold, making it impossible for her to save money. Ms S and her children are enrolled in Medicaid and their state’s supplemental nutrition program, and they regularly visit a food pantry for groceries.

Currently, Mr G is Ms S’s only client. She is still mourning the loss of a previous patient, whom she cared for over three years until his transfer to home hospice and subsequent death. The loss has been emotionally significant for her, and she is anxious for the agency to assign her another patient soon, as she depends on the income. She is even considering taking on a third job to make ends meet. To arrive at Mr G’s suburban home by 6:30 in the morning, Ms S commutes by bus, making three transfers from her city apartment. On a typical morning, she finds Mr G in his bathroom and checks in to ensure his safety, then heads to the kitchen to clean up spilled milk she notices on the floor—remnants from the previous day. She proceeds to prepare his breakfast and set out his medications. Over the past two years, Ms S has become the person Mr G interacts with most frequently, and he often calls her at home for comfort, reassurance, and companionship.

Ms S routinely completes the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services Home Health Certification and Plan of Care (CMS-485) form online, which requires Dr P, Mr G’s physician, to sign. Following Mr G’s recent primary care visit, Ms S is also tasked with documenting new medication orders from Dr P. While she updates the records, Ms S finds herself uncertain about how to implement a change to Mr G’s insulin regimen. She also receives a new prescription by mail and is unsure if it’s correct—the pills’ shapes, colors, and markings don’t match the online reference photo she uses. Ms S calls Dr P’s office for clarification. The next day, a staff member returns her call and confirms only the name and dose of the medication, leaving other questions unanswered. Still unsure, Ms S contacts Mr G’s son, who is unfamiliar with the recent prescription changes and advises, “Just fill the boxes in the pill container for each day of the month as best you can. Dad will know which ones to take.”

Faced with ongoing uncertainty, Ms S decides not to include the capsules that don’t match her reference as she fills Mr G’s pill organizer. She attaches an electronic sticky note in the CMS-485 form online, hoping Dr P will notice and clarify the prescription. However, Dr P does not see the note, signs the form, and moves on to the next electronic health record awaiting review and approval.

ethical_issues.question: How can the labor value and professional dignity of home health aides be fully recognized and protected within the home care system?
keypoints: Acknowledge the labor value of home health aides and emphasize that their work constitutes a profession rather than uncompensated care provided among family members.
Provide infrastructure and funding through public policy to create quality jobs that afford workers a voice in the labor they perform.
Address discrimination based on race, gender, and immigration status, as well as the resulting low wages, in order to enhance the professional dignity of home health aides.
Offer competency-based training and living wages to home health aides to improve client outcomes and recognize the importance of aides’ observational knowledge.
Recognize the critical role of home health aides in identifying patient changes and difficulties on site, ensuring they receive the dignity and security they rightfully deserve.

ethical_issues.question: In home care, how can the observational knowledge of home health aides be effectively integrated to improve continuity of care and patient outcomes?
keypoints: The observational knowledge of home health aides is essential in patient care but is frequently excluded from the medical team, thereby undermining continuity of care.
Recognizing the practical experience and emotional support provided by home health aides can supply physicians with critical information, ultimately improving patient outcomes.
Providing competency-based training and living wages to home health aides can enhance patient prognosis, contingent upon valuing their observational knowledge.

Although electronic monitoring and documentation are efficient, they cannot replace interpersonal communication and coordination; acknowledging the value of home health aides constitutes the most ethical response.

title: How Should Health Care Organizations Protect Personnel in Environmental Services and Related Fields?
case:
Ms A is a hospital administrator at RR Hospital in the United States. RR Hospital is a 150-bed community hospital in an urban environment. Dr V, an infectious disease physician, oversees RR’s Department of Hospital Epidemiology and Infection Control, which includes developing infection prevention and control (IPC) protocols and planning for pandemics. A novel strain of influenza that is airborne transmissible has emerged and is beginning to impact the entire United States and RR Hospital.
Effective IPC plans must include hospital personnel in environmental services and related fields ESRF)—who enter, maintain, repair, and clean all areas of the hospital, including patient’s rooms—and waste management staff in protocol development, but Dr V realizes the IPC plans were not created in consultation with the waste management firm with which RR Hospital contracts. The contract stipulates that waste management workers will enter hospital rooms and empty biohazardous containers and that RR Hospital must provide gloves. For an airborne transmissible pathogen, however, gloves are insufficient personal protective equipment (PPE); N95 respirators are also needed.
RR Hospital does not have enough N95 respirators for the waste management firm’s workers, however, due to national shortages. The waste management firm does not have an N95 supplier, as respirators were previously not needed, and they cannot secure one. Ms A and Dr V are concerned about the safety of waste management workers, who, in addition to not having N95s, have little training in IPC. Ms A has neither extra staff nor available supplies but recognizes the importance of protecting all workers, especially RR’s lowest paid workers from historically marginalized communities. Ms A and Dr V wonder what to do.
case_rewrite:
Ms A serves as the hospital administrator at RR Hospital, a 150-bed community facility located in an urban area in the United States. Dr V, an infectious disease specialist, leads RR Hospital’s Department of Hospital Epidemiology and Infection Control. Among Dr V’s responsibilities are the development of infection prevention and control (IPC) protocols and overseeing the hospital’s preparedness for pandemics. A new, airborne-transmissible strain of influenza has begun to spread rapidly across the country, and RR Hospital is already feeling its effects.

An effective IPC strategy at RR Hospital must extend beyond clinical staff to include personnel in environmental services and related fields (ESRF)—those who enter, maintain, repair, and clean every area of the hospital, including patient rooms—as well as the staff responsible for waste management. Dr V soon realizes, however, that the IPC protocols were developed without direct consultation with the contracted waste management company. According to the existing contract, waste management workers are required to enter patient rooms to remove biohazardous waste containers, and RR Hospital is obligated to provide them with gloves. Yet, with the arrival of this novel airborne pathogen, Dr V recognizes that gloves alone are insufficient; N95 respirators are now necessary to properly safeguard these workers.

Due to a nationwide shortage, RR Hospital’s supply of N95 respirators is inadequate to meet the needs of the waste management company’s employees. The waste management firm, having never before needed such equipment, lacks an existing supplier and is unable to procure N95s on their own. Ms A and Dr V are deeply concerned about the vulnerability of these waste management staff, who not only lack proper respirators but also have received minimal training in infection prevention and control. Ms A faces a difficult situation: she has neither additional staff nor surplus supplies to draw from, yet she recognizes the ethical imperative to protect all hospital workers—especially those who are among the lowest paid and come from historically marginalized communities.

Confronted with these challenges, Ms A and Dr V deliberate over how best to ensure the safety and equitable treatment of all personnel, including contracted workers, in the midst of this escalating public health crisis.

ethical_issues.question: How Should Health Care Organizations Ensure the Health, Safety, and Equitable Treatment of Personnel in Environmental Services and Related Fields During Infectious Disease Outbreaks?
keypoints: Health care organizations must ensure the health and safety of all personnel involved in infection prevention and control, including workers in environmental services and related fields.

During infectious disease outbreaks, health care organizations should equitably address the risks faced by all workers, regardless of whether they are frontline clinical staff or contracted personnel.

Health care organizations should engage in consultation with workers in environmental services and related fields prior to the emergence of novel infectious disease threats to ensure the adequacy of personal protective equipment as well as administrative and engineering controls.
