Procedural health justice requires health care organizations to maintain transparency and accountability during infectious disease outbreaks to foster trust among those bearing additional exposure risks.

Distributive health justice mandates that health care organizations consider the disproportionate burdens that emerging infectious diseases may impose on specific groups and ensure the equitable allocation of resources and responsibilities.

ethical_issues.question: During an infectious disease outbreak, how should health care organizations equitably allocate personal protective equipment and training resources to protect all personnel, including contracted workers?
keypoints: Health care organizations should ensure that all personnel involved in infection prevention and control, including contracted workers, receive equitable access to personal protective equipment and training resources during infectious disease outbreaks.

Health equity encompasses both procedural and distributive dimensions, requiring transparency and accountability to foster trust, and the fair allocation of resources and responsibilities based on the recognition that emerging infectious diseases may disproportionately burden certain groups.

Hospitals should engage in consultation with environmental services and related field workers prior to the emergence of infectious disease threats to identify and address issues such as shortages of personal protective equipment and lack of fit testing before these problems arise.

Health care administrators must reevaluate contracts and protocols to accommodate environmental changes and increased risks posed by highly infectious diseases, ensuring the safety of all workers, including contracted personnel.

Hospitals can conserve N95 respirators and better protect the health of waste management workers by having health care workers pass waste containers to waste management personnel stationed outside patient rooms.

title: What Do We Owe Health Workers Earning Low Wages Who Are at Risk of Harm?
case:
After high school graduation, HH hopes someday to go to college and become a health professional. For now, HH takes care of their mother, as they have for the last 3 years, and takes a 40-hour course to become a psychiatric aide. HH now works full time in an inpatient psychiatry unit, earning just above minimum wage during an overnight 8-hour shift in which they monitor a patient, who is involuntarily committed.
HH’s patient is ZZ, who is 58 years old and has a history of bipolar I disorder. ZZ’s symptoms were well controlled with risperidone and lamotrigine until a right rotator cuff repair surgery 5 days ago. Since then, ZZ has been demonstrating acute psychosis and hyperverbalism (inability to stop talking). Dr P’s and nurses’ efforts to redirect, interrupt, or calm ZZ have not succeeded, and ZZ’s agitation has now increased to aggression toward anyone who tries to administer medication.
None of the psychiatric aides wants to monitor ZZ, whose hyperverbalism is exhausting and whose aggression, when not well controlled, is unpredictable and generally feared. HH is assigned to monitor ZZ for the third night in a row. Last night was particularly stressful, as ZZ asked HH to help her use the bathroom and then pressed HH to a wall before others intervened.
In the morning, during rounds, ZZ points to a bruise on her right shoulder and shouts, “That dyke man-handled me!” Dr P, the lead psychiatrist, asks HH about the incident. Dr P looks to HH and says, “Don’t worry, we know nothing happened.”
“Nothing happened to ZZ,” HH thought, recalling yesterday when a fellow overnight psychiatric aide stated to Dr P during morning rounds that a patient had threatened her overnight. HH observed that Dr P ignored her, so HH decided not to say anything this morning about being pressed to a wall.
case_rewrite:
After graduating high school, HH dreams of one day attending college and pursuing a career in healthcare. For the past three years, however, HH has been the primary caregiver for their mother. Recently, HH completed a 40-hour course to become a psychiatric aide and has begun working full time on an inpatient psychiatric unit. HH works the overnight 8-hour shift, earning just above minimum wage, and is responsible for monitoring patients who are involuntarily admitted.

HH’s current patient is ZZ, a 58-year-old with a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder. ZZ’s symptoms had been well managed with risperidone and lamotrigine, but five days ago, she underwent right rotator cuff repair surgery. Since the operation, ZZ has manifested acute psychosis and relentless hyperverbalism—she is unable to stop talking. Efforts by Dr P, the attending psychiatrist, and the nursing staff to redirect or calm ZZ have failed, and in recent days, her agitation has escalated into aggression, especially toward anyone attempting to administer medication.

Among the psychiatric aides, none wants to be assigned to ZZ. Her non-stop talking is draining, and her unpredictable aggression is a source of widespread anxiety. For the third consecutive night, HH is tasked with monitoring ZZ. The previous shift was especially difficult: when ZZ asked HH for help to use the bathroom, she suddenly pushed HH against the wall, and it took other staff intervening to de-escalate the situation.

During morning rounds, ZZ points to a bruise on her right shoulder and loudly accuses, “That dyke man-handled me!” Dr P, leading the team, turns to HH for an explanation of what happened. Without waiting for HH’s response, Dr P reassures, “Don’t worry, we know nothing happened.”

“Nothing happened to ZZ,” HH thinks, remembering how, just the day before, another overnight psychiatric aide reported to Dr P during rounds that a patient had threatened her overnight. Dr P had ignored her comment entirely. Seeing this, HH decides to stay silent about being pressed against the wall by ZZ.

ethical_issues.question: What are the ethical responsibilities of healthcare institutions regarding the safety of direct care personnel?
keypoints: Healthcare organizations have an obligation to provide a safe working environment for their employees, including appropriate training and adequate staffing, to ensure the physical and psychological safety of staff.
Organizations should establish mechanisms for reporting and addressing incidents of violence, ensuring that employees can report safety concerns or adverse events without fear of retaliation.

Organizations bear the responsibility to treat all employees fairly, support psychiatric aides in reporting safety issues, and promote their professional development through training and educational opportunities.

Organizations should eliminate disparities between groups of differing prestige within the institution, convey respect for frontline psychiatric care workers, and thereby foster a safer work environment.

ethical_issues.question: What ethical responsibilities do psychiatrists have as team leaders in managing workplace violence incidents?
keypoints: Psychiatrists, as team leaders, bear the responsibility to create and maintain a physically and psychologically safe workplace environment for both patients and care staff.
Psychiatrists have the duty to provide strong leadership that fosters a culture of cohesiveness and effective communication, particularly in the management of violent incidents.
Psychiatrists must respond robustly to violent events by acknowledging the experiences of staff and implementing consistent procedures to provide comfort and support.
Psychiatrists are responsible for advocating for dignified compensation and benefits for direct care employees, ensuring their equitable treatment and safe working conditions.

ethical_issues.question: Do healthcare organizations have an ethical obligation to provide career development opportunities and equitable treatment for low-wage workers in order to improve their working conditions and quality of life?
keypoints: Healthcare organizations have an obligation to treat all employees justly and to provide living wages, health insurance, educational opportunities, and pathways for career advancement in order to improve working conditions and quality of life.

Organizations bear an ethical responsibility to facilitate career development by offering training, educational opportunities, and tuition assistance, thereby enhancing productivity and improving staff morale.

Both organizations and team leaders are responsible for creating and maintaining a physically and psychologically safe work environment, eliminating disparities between groups of differing prestige, and conveying respect for frontline psychiatric care workers.
The current compensation paradigm reflects systemic discrimination, and inadequate remuneration undermines the cohesion of the treatment team.

title: How Should Clinicians Respond to Race-Based Algorithms as Sources of Iatrogenic Harm?
case:
Dr OB is a resident physician in a high-volume obstetrics unit at a county hospital serving predominantly Black and urban Indigenous community members. Like other resident physicians, Dr OB often uses a mobile phone application to calculate, via algorithm, vaginal birth risk for birthing people who have delivered a prior child via cesarean section (C-section).This vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC) calculator has 2 race-based correction factors.Scores yielded by the calculator are used to inform clinical management decisions—specifically, about which delivery options to offer patients in the unit—and to motivate standard of care. For individuals who have delivered by C-section before, the score is clinically and ethically important, since vaginal delivery complication risk for a person who has had a C-section is lower than C-section delivery complication risk for a person who has had a C-section. Strangely, though, Dr OB notices that most patients in the unit who have had a C-section are not offered an option to attempt labor and vaginal delivery.
Dr OB enters a patient’s race as White instead of Black a few times and notices score changes substantial enough to influence whether a patient who has had a C-section will be offered an option to try labor and vaginal delivery. Dr OB wonders about the validity of the VBAC calculator’s “correction” factors in light of such starkly different results based on how a clinician perceives and enters a patient’s race.
Given C-sections’ higher risk of morbidity and mortality and of longer stay in the intensive care unit,Dr OB worries that patients of color in the unit are more frequently exposed to higher-risk deliveries than White patients. Structural determinants of health, such as systemic racism, which are independent risk factors in maternal mortality and morbiditywhen other factors such as socioeconomic statusare controlled for, are widely documented as exacerbating racial health inequity. In light of long-standing high rates of maternal mortality in the United Statescompared to other high-income countries, and in light of Black patients suffering stark inequity in childbirth-related mortality within the United States,Dr OB wonders what to do.
case_rewrite:
Dr OB is a resident physician working in a busy obstetrics unit at a county hospital that primarily serves Black and urban Indigenous community members. Like many of their colleagues, Dr OB relies on a mobile phone app that calculates, through an algorithm, the likelihood that a patient who previously delivered by cesarean section (C-section) will have a successful vaginal birth in a subsequent pregnancy. This VBAC (vaginal birth after cesarean) calculator uses two race-based correction factors. The numerical scores it generates play a direct role in clinical decisions—specifically, in determining which delivery options are presented to patients on the unit—and drive the standard of care. For people with a history of C-section, the calculated score carries significant clinical and ethical weight, as the risk of complications from a vaginal delivery following a C-section is actually lower than the risk associated with a repeat C-section. Yet, Dr OB finds it troubling that, in practice, most patients on the unit who have previously had a C-section are not given the choice to attempt labor and vaginal delivery.

Curious about this pattern, Dr OB experiments by entering a patient’s race as White instead of Black in the calculator for several cases, and notices that the resulting scores change markedly—often enough to affect whether a patient will be offered the opportunity to try labor and vaginal delivery. This raises serious doubts for Dr OB about the validity of the calculator’s race-based “correction” factors, especially given the dramatic differences that arise based solely on how a clinician records a patient’s race.

Given that C-sections carry a higher risk of morbidity, mortality, and longer intensive care unit stays, Dr OB becomes increasingly concerned that patients of color in the unit are being exposed to higher-risk deliveries more often than White patients. Dr OB is acutely aware that structural factors—such as systemic racism—are independent risk contributors to maternal mortality and morbidity, even when other variables like socioeconomic status are accounted for. These factors are well documented as exacerbating racial health inequities. Considering the persistently high rates of maternal mortality in the United States compared to other high-income countries, and the especially stark disparities in childbirth-related deaths among Black patients, Dr OB is left questioning what steps to take next.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians ensure patients’ informed consent and autonomy when using race-based algorithms?
keypoints: Clinicians must inform patients about the risks, benefits, and reasonable alternatives to support autonomous decision-making.
When using race-based algorithms, clinicians should ensure that patients are aware of how race is determined and applied, and that they participate in or consent to related decisions.
Patient-centered dialogues should be conducted to emphasize the impact of racism and to facilitate transparent discussions within the context of structural racism.
Transparency should be established by clarifying how and why racial and ethnic data are collected and utilized in research and clinical tool development.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians prevent structural racism and iatrogenic harm caused by race-based algorithms in clinical decision-making?
keypoints: Clinicians should abandon race-based corrections and instead identify racism as the marker of health inequities.
Prioritize respect for patient autonomy and shared decision making by implementing race-conscious medicine that emphasizes racism.
Facilitate transparent discussions of patient values and preferences regarding TOLAC within the context of structural racism’s impact.
Acknowledge the harms of race-based medicine and continuously engage in critical reflection on tools that essentialize identity.
Recognize patients as the foremost experts on their illnesses, histories, and lives to strengthen shared decision making and patient autonomy.
Structurally just algorithms should prioritize upstream social determinants of inequity that can be clearly defined, measured, and addressed.
Measure specific and modifiable markers of risk, such as insurance coverage and incarceration history.
Professional organizations must reform race-based guidelines, and interdisciplinary researchers should innovate and implement measures of structural harm.
Clinicians should advocate professionally for structural interventions that advance health equity, including living wages, universal health insurance, affordable housing, and quality education.
Continuing education on race, racism, and race-based medicine is indispensable.

ethical_issues.question: How should healthcare institutions prioritize upstream social determinants of inequity in algorithm design to promote health equity?
keypoints: Healthcare institutions should prioritize addressing upstream social determinants of inequity that can be clearly defined, measured, and remedied to promote health equity.
Race should not be used as a proxy for intersecting factors, as it is an overly crude measure unsuitable for nuanced clinical decision-making.
Specific and modifiable risk markers, such as insurance coverage and incarceration history, should be measured, alongside assessments of structural vulnerability.
These measurements should be dynamic and fluid, reflecting the mutable nature of social forces, to more accurately correct inequities.
Social determinants of inequity should be explored during prenatal care or family planning to improve rates of successful VBAC.
Transparency should be established by clearly specifying how and why racial and ethnic data are collected and utilized in research and clinical tool development.

title: When Experiencing Inequitable Health Care Is a Patient’s Norm, How Should Iatrogenic Harm Be Considered?
case:
ST is a 45-year-old woman with a long-standing history of schizophrenia and violence. Occasionally, ST can respond appropriately to clinicians’ questions. But she has been hospitalized in several organizations in the city several times for swallowing sharp objects, which require surgical removal, to which ST typically objects with fear and anxiety so great that she must be forcibly anesthetized. She has experienced several episodes of physical, chemical, and legal uses of restraints during her encounters with clinicians. She has not kept posthospitalization follow-up appointments and cannot adhere to prescribed medications without close supervision.
Most recently, ST swallowed a pen, underwent an initial surgery to extract the pen, and began recovering steadily until she noticed Dr L, a second-year surgery resident physician, to whom she said, trying to yell, “I never want any more surgery, ever!” Dr L approaches ST and sits with her, explaining that she will need at least one more surgery to check for bowel perforation. ST despairs, “No one cares about what I want. My decisions don’t matter and have never mattered.”
case_rewrite:
ST is a 45-year-old woman with a long-standing history of schizophrenia and episodes of violence. At times, ST is able to respond appropriately to clinicians’ questions. However, she has been admitted to several different hospitals in the city on multiple occasions for swallowing sharp objects, which require surgical removal. Each time, ST reacts with intense fear and anxiety to the prospect of surgery, consistently refusing the procedure and requiring forcible anesthesia. Throughout her medical encounters, ST has been subjected to physical, chemical, and legal forms of restraint. After discharge, she rarely attends follow-up appointments and is unable to take prescribed medications unless closely supervised.

Most recently, ST swallowed a pen and required surgery to have it removed. She began to recover after the operation until she noticed Dr L, a second-year surgical resident, entering her room. ST, attempting to raise her voice, declared, “I never want any more surgery, ever!” Dr L approached her and sat at her bedside, explaining gently that at least one more surgery would be needed to check for possible bowel perforation. Listening, ST became despondent and said, “No one cares about what I want. My decisions don’t matter and have never mattered.”

ethical_issues.question: How can the ethical principle of “first, do no harm” be prioritized in the diagnosis and treatment of patients with mental illness, particularly when physical restraints, chemical restraints, and legal coercion are involved?
keypoints: In the diagnosis and treatment of patients with mental illness, the ethical principle of "first, do no harm" should be prioritized, with careful consideration given to the risks of iatrogenic harm associated with physical restraint, chemical restraint, and legal coercion.

Healthcare professionals managing emergencies involving patients with mental illness should strive to balance patient autonomy and safety, and following crisis intervention, reflect on strategies to prevent future crises that violate patient autonomy.

Interdisciplinary care teams should adopt a trauma-informed approach to build trust with patients, treat underlying mental illness, identify drivers of intentional ingestion of foreign objects, and maximize patient voice and choice in care decisions to avoid further harm and repair existing harm.

To achieve health equity for patients with mental illness, both physical and psychological iatrogenic harms must be addressed, particularly for the most vulnerable patients with serious mental illness who have historically experienced inequitable treatment.

ethical_issues.question: When patients with mental illness face emergency medical interventions, how can a balance be sought between patient autonomy and safety, and how can their autonomy be restored following crisis management?
keypoints: In emergency medical interventions, healthcare professionals must seek a balance between patient autonomy and safety, particularly when the patient’s behavior poses an immediate threat to themselves or others.
Following crisis management, the clinical team should reflect on how to prevent future crises that violate patient autonomy and work to restore the patient’s autonomy during the recovery period.

Healthcare providers should adopt a trauma-informed approach to build trust with the patient, treat underlying mental illness, identify drivers of intentional ingestion of foreign objects, and empower the patient with voice and choice in their care.

Shared decision making is a process of reaching consensus based on the patient’s informed preferences regarding treatment options, wherein the clinician’s perspective should not override that of the patient.

Utilizing an interprofessional team-based model that integrates collaboration among physicians, nurses, social workers, and family members is essential to address the patient’s complex needs and reduce the likelihood of future emergencies.

ethical_issues.question: How can healthcare institutions eliminate stigma experienced by patients with mental illness through systems, clinical care processes, and policies in order to reduce iatrogenic harm and improve the quality of care and patient outcomes?
keypoints: Healthcare institutions should implement clinician bias training to identify and eliminate stigma against mental illness, thereby reducing iatrogenic harm.
Patient advocacy programs should be established to ensure that the wishes and decisions of individuals with mental illness are respected throughout the healthcare process.
The promotion of team-based care models is essential to facilitate interprofessional collaboration, improve quality of care, and enhance patient outcomes.

Shared decision-making processes must be developed to guarantee that interactions between clinicians and patients are equitable, respectful, and dynamic, with the clinician’s perspective not overriding that of the patient.
Healthcare teams should proactively challenge their own unconscious biases and stigmatizing attitudes by practicing mindfulness, fostering empathy, and maintaining a nonjudgmental approach.
Iatrogenic harm should be identified and repaired, and measures should be taken to prevent its recurrence, thereby reducing systemic healthcare inequities experienced by patients with mental illness.

tags: Gender, sex identity/Sexual and gender minorities
title: When Is Iatrogenic Harm Negligent?
case:
MJ is a 33-year-old transgender man who transitioned with hormone therapy during college. His parents immigrated from Mexico in their early 20s, settled in suburban Texas, and retain views about gender identity that MJ has, for many years, experienced as oppressive.
Recently diagnosed with advanced colorectal cancer, MJ has been hospitalized several times during the past year. His physicians recently conveyed to MJ that no curative options remain. MJ’s family members are distraught, blame MJ for bringing this upon himself and his family through his “lifestyle choices,” and insist that MJ denounce his gender identity. MJ expresses to Dr R, the hospitalist attending physician directing MJ’s inpatient hospice care, and Dr S, the resident physician, that he fears he will die alone, without anyone at his side, if he does not do as his family members ask.
Dr R reiterates the importance of family visits while MJ goes through the dying process and suggests that his gender identity, at this point in his life, should probably be regarded as less significant than his comfort and sense of family belonging. When alone with MJ, Dr S, who disagrees with Dr R, considers telling MJ,There is no need to compromise your identity. Be who you are to the end. We will be here with you, and you will not be alone when you die. Dr S considers whether to speak these words.
case_rewrite:
MJ, a 33-year-old transgender man, began hormone therapy during his college years as part of his gender transition. His parents, who immigrated from Mexico to suburban Texas in their twenties, have long-held beliefs about gender identity that MJ has experienced as restrictive and burdensome throughout his life.

Recently, MJ received a diagnosis of advanced colorectal cancer. Over the past year, his illness has required multiple hospital admissions. Now, his medical team has informed him that there are no curative treatments remaining. MJ’s family is devastated by his prognosis, but rather than offering unconditional support, they blame MJ’s “lifestyle choices” for his illness and urge him to renounce his gender identity. They insist that MJ must reject his identity in order to be with them as he nears death.

In conversations with Dr R, the hospitalist overseeing MJ’s inpatient hospice care, and Dr S, the resident physician, MJ confides that he is terrified of dying alone. He fears that unless he complies with his family’s demands, he will have no one at his side during his final days.

Dr R emphasizes to MJ the importance of family presence during this stage and suggests that, given the circumstances, his gender identity might now be less important than his comfort and sense of belonging with his family. Privately, Dr S feels differently. Alone with MJ, Dr S contemplates saying, “There is no need to compromise your identity. Be who you are to the end. We will be here with you, and you will not be alone when you die.” Dr S wrestles with whether to voice this reassurance to MJ.

ethical_issues.question: How can a balance be ensured between patient autonomy and family involvement in end-of-life care?
keypoints: Upholding patient autonomy is central to resolving ethical dilemmas, ensuring that patients can weigh the values and courses of action most important to them.

Respect for patient autonomy requires placing the patient’s perspective at the core of decision-making; physicians should engage in open, collaborative communication to thoroughly understand the patient’s genuine wishes and specific preferences regarding family involvement.

The concept of relational autonomy emphasizes that although individuals exist within complex interpersonal networks, ultimate decision-making authority resides with the person most affected, while also encouraging consideration of their responsibilities and care for connected others, thereby reconciling conflicts between autonomy and relationality.

Best practice guidelines for end-of-life care indicate that whether patients reconcile with their families of origin should follow the patient’s wishes, and that patients have the legal right to include chosen family members in medical decision-making and the end-of-life process.

The determination of iatrogenic harm should be based on respect for the patient’s preferences regarding family involvement; if a patient refuses participation by their family of origin, the absence of those family members does not constitute iatrogenic harm.

ethical_issues.question: How can affirming communication be used to meet the end-of-life care needs of LGBTQ patients and reduce the risk of negligent iatrogenic harm?
keypoints: Affirming communication should allow patients to freely express their personal history, identity, preferences, and end-of-life goals in order to meet the care needs of LGBTQ patients during the terminal phase.
Respect for patient autonomy requires that the patient’s perspectives be central in medical decision-making, particularly regarding preferences for involvement of biological family or chosen family.
According to best practice guidelines in palliative care, patients have the right to decide whether to reconcile with their biological family and to include chosen family in medical decision-making.

Failure to employ affirming communication to ascertain the patient’s authentic wishes may constitute negligent iatrogenic harm; physicians should prioritize communication quality to mitigate this risk.

title: Underrecognition of Dysmenorrhea Is an Iatrogenic Harm
case:
While taking a contraceptive history in clinic, Dr G’s 55-year-old patient, JJ, remarks, “I wish I could have had an IUD when I menstruated.” Dr G then uncovers a long history of JJ’s painful menses with severe nausea, crippling cramps, and occasional fainting. JJ regularly missed at least a day of school or work each month.
“Did you see a physician when you had pain?” asks Dr G.
“No,” said JJ. “Women didn’t see physicians for that. I thought every woman had pain like me.”
case_rewrite:
During a routine clinic visit, Dr G is taking a contraceptive history from JJ, a 55-year-old patient. As they talk, JJ remarks wistfully, “I wish I could have had an IUD back when I was still menstruating.” This prompts Dr G to ask more about JJ’s past experiences. JJ describes a longstanding history of excruciating periods marked by severe nausea, debilitating cramps, and occasional episodes of fainting. JJ recalls regularly missing at least a full day of school or work every month due to the intensity of the pain.

Dr G asks gently, “Did you ever see a physician about your pain at the time?”

JJ shakes her head. “No,” she replies. “Women didn’t go to the doctor for that sort of thing. I just assumed every woman went through what I did.”

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ensure the timely recognition and effective treatment of dysmenorrhea symptoms in female patients to prevent hermeneutic injustice–related iatrogenic harm?
keypoints: Physicians should proactively inquire about the presence of dysmenorrhea to help overcome patients’ reluctance to report symptoms due to sociocultural factors, and to clarify that their distressing symptoms constitute a legitimate medical issue warranting attention and treatment.

A thorough assessment of dysmenorrhea severity should be conducted, including characterization of pain quality, onset timing, and its impact on work, education, and daily activities; pain intensity should be quantified using a 1-to-10 scale to guide therapeutic decision-making and monitor treatment response.

Patients should be informed about effective nonpharmacological and pharmacological treatment options, and empowered through the provision of clear diagnostic terminology to understand their condition, thereby facilitating expression and sharing of their experiences, promoting timely care for others with similar symptoms, and reducing iatrogenic harm caused by hermeneutic injustice.

ethical_issues.question: How can the healthcare system enhance awareness of dysmenorrhea and its treatment options through education and advocacy to promote hermeneutic justice?
keypoints: Enhance awareness of severe dysmenorrhea and its treatment options through public health campaigns and educational curricula, particularly targeting adolescents in school settings, as this population exhibits high prevalence rates and relies heavily on peer-to-peer knowledge sharing; early recognition and management of dysmenorrhea can reduce the risk of future suffering.

Develop standardized terminology for severe dysmenorrhea to assist patients in more accurately describing and understanding their condition, potentially by introducing the term “severe dysmenorrhea” or creating a more accessible alternative phrase, thereby promoting societal recognition and acceptance of the disorder.

Inform patients about available nonpharmacological and pharmacological treatment options, which not only directly improve patient health outcomes but also empower them to share their experiences and encourage others to seek medical care proactively.

The act of diagnosis itself provides patients with socially recognized terminology to articulate their experiences, enabling them to share this information with friends and relatives who may be silently suffering, thereby expanding access to interpretive resources within marginalized groups and advancing hermeneutic justice.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians incorporate patients’ self-interpretations of their experiences during the diagnostic and treatment process to achieve testimonial justice and support patients’ epistemic empowerment?
keypoints: Clinicians should respect and validate the authenticity and significance of patients’ pain, clearly informing them that their symptoms represent a medical issue that remains underrecognized, for which effective treatment options exist.

Healthcare professionals must acknowledge patients’ self-interpretations to achieve testimonial justice, while also providing the conceptual knowledge necessary for understanding and communicating their experiences to realize hermeneutic justice, thereby promoting patients’ epistemic empowerment.
The diagnostic process should furnish patients with socially recognized terminology to describe their symptoms and treatments, enhancing their capacity for expression and communication.

Physicians ought to encourage and support patients in sharing their experiences, thereby expanding access to hermeneutic resources for both patients and their communities and helping to alleviate suffering exacerbated by silence.

title: Is a Video Worth a Thousand Words?
case:
Ms K is an 80-year-old woman initially hospitalized with sepsis. Multiple hospital setbacks include kidney injury, aspiration, and heart failure. She has been hospitalized for a month, with evidence of deconditioning, malnourishment, pressure injuries, anasarca, and delirium.
While previously cognitively unimpaired, she now fluctuates between agitation and somnolence. According to her family, she never discussed her critical illness or end-of-life care preferences. They consider her a “fighter” and therefore feel uncomfortable pursuing a palliative approach. Because of COVID-related visitor restrictions, they have not seen her in person. Her clinicians think she is unlikely to survive hospitalization. If she declines further, next steps could include a percutaneous endoscopicgastrostomytube, hemodialysis, and intensive care unit (ICU) transfer. Thinking it best for the patient, her clinicians believe that Ms K’s family should opt to stop aggressive treatments and focus on comfort, although family meetings have not produced this change.
Ms K’s attending physician, Dr B, has told the team that one way to “change her family’s mind” would be to increase video calls to the family during times when Ms K appears uncomfortable or distressed and during activities such as wound care, so that the family “gets it” that Ms K is “in horrible shape.” Dr B advises against video calling the family when Ms K is asleep or relaxed, since “it paints too rosy a picture,” and “they’ll just cling to unreasonable hope.”
A resident feels uncomfortable but also thinks that knowledge is power and that providing this information can’t be wrong if it results in less suffering for the patient.
case_rewrite:
Ms K is an 80-year-old woman who was admitted to the hospital for sepsis. Over the course of her month-long hospitalization, she has experienced multiple complications, including acute kidney injury, episodes of aspiration, and worsening heart failure. Her physical condition has steadily declined, and she now shows signs of severe deconditioning, malnutrition, pressure ulcers, generalized edema, and intermittent delirium. While Ms K was previously mentally sharp, she now alternates between periods of agitation and deep sleep. Her family reports that Ms K never spoke about her wishes in the event of serious illness or her preferences for end-of-life care, but they describe her as a “fighter” and feel uneasy about adopting a palliative approach. Due to COVID-related visitor restrictions, the family has not been able to visit her in person. Ms K’s healthcare team believes that her chance of surviving this hospital admission is very low. If her condition worsens further, the next interventions might include placing a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube, starting hemodialysis, or transferring her to the intensive care unit (ICU) for escalated care. The clinicians feel that it would be in Ms K’s best interest for her family to agree to forgo aggressive treatments and instead focus on comfort measures, but despite several family meetings, the family remains unconvinced.

Ms K’s attending physician, Dr B, suggests to the clinical team that one way to “change her family’s mind” is to increase the frequency of video calls with the family at times when Ms K appears uncomfortable or in distress—particularly during procedures like wound care—so that the family “gets it” and sees that Ms K is “in horrible shape.” Dr B specifically advises against arranging video calls when Ms K is sleeping or appears peaceful, warning that such images “paint too rosy a picture” and might cause the family to “cling to unreasonable hope.” 

A resident on the team feels uneasy about this approach but also considers that providing more information could be beneficial if it ultimately leads to less suffering for Ms K.

ethical_issues.question: Does the selective presentation of a patient’s bodily images by clinicians during video calls constitute manipulation?
keypoints: Manipulation in medical ethics refers to the intentional use of deception, undue influence, or similar tactics to undermine a surrogate’s or patient’s rational decision-making capacity in order to achieve the clinician’s preferred outcome.

Video calls may introduce the potential for manipulation, as clinicians can influence surrogates’ emotions and decisions through selective presentation of the patient’s physical condition and environment.

Selectively sharing images or video footage of Ms K that support a particular clinical recommendation, while withholding images that might prompt alternative decisions, constitutes a form of deception and undermines informed surrogate decision-making.

Timing video calls to coincide with moments when Ms K appears particularly unwell, or framing the visual narrative to elicit specific emotional responses from the family, may reflect an intent to exert undue influence on surrogate decision-makers.

Unlike in-person bedside visits, video calls afford clinicians greater control over what is seen, when it is seen, and how it is contextualized, thereby increasing the risk of manipulation and compromising the transparency of the decision-making process.

In Ms K’s case, a video call strategy that is selectively curated and outcome-oriented—using the patient’s appearance as a tool to steer the family toward the clinical team’s preferred decision—raises significant ethical concerns regarding respect for surrogate autonomy and the integrity of shared decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: How can surrogate decision makers be supported to make informed decisions during video calls without being subject to affective manipulation?
keypoints: Clinicians should primarily use video calls to inform about the patient’s condition, focusing on supporting surrogates in a comprehensive and rational informed decision-making process rather than attempting to influence or manipulate the decisional outcome.

Clinicians should be transparent about the specific purpose of displaying bodily features, clearly explaining how viewing the patient’s body aids surrogates in understanding the severity of the condition and promotes substituted judgment consistent with the patient’s preferences.

Clinicians should proactively inform family members about the potential for strong emotional impact when viewing images of their loved one’s suffering, helping them to integrate this experience into a holistic decision-making process rather than treating it as the sole or decisive basis for decisions.

Clinicians should reflect on and carefully manage the selectivity and framing of information presented during video calls, including narrative details and the composition of bodily imagery, to avoid eliciting emotional manipulation through deliberate arrangement.

Whenever possible, clinicians should respect the patient’s wishes by obtaining patient assent prior to video calls, especially when these involve displaying the patient’s body or wounds, thereby safeguarding patient dignity and privacy.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians transparently communicate the purpose and potential emotional impact when using video calls to show a patient’s body?
keypoints: Clinicians should clearly and honestly articulate the specific purpose of displaying particular features of the patient’s body, thereby assisting family members in understanding the severity of the condition and the associated care needs.
Clinicians should explain how viewing the patient’s physical condition supports surrogates in making substituted medical decisions that align with the patient’s values and preferences.

Clinicians should proactively inform family members about the potential for strong emotional responses triggered by viewing images of the patient’s body, emphasizing the healthcare team’s intermediary role in conveying information and providing emotional support, to ensure that surrogates participate in decision making in a comprehensive and informed manner.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Clinicians as agents of the state
title: How Should Access to Military Health Care Facilities Be Controlled in Conflict?
case:
MM commands a military field hospital, physically based on a semi-trailer truck convoy that follows combat troops into disputed territory as part of a United Nations (UN) peacekeeping and security mission to implement and maintain a fragile truce between local government forces and opposition forces. In the disputed territory, the humanitarian crisis is escalating; the number of casualties from armed conflict and the number of displaced persons from affected ethnic groups are increasing. When the convoy arrives and the field hospital setup is complete, MM expects large numbers of injured and ill patients to arrive and seeks resources to meet their basic needs for food, water, shelter, medicines, and other kinds of clinical intervention.
Guards will protect the field hospital’s perimeter and determine who will be allowed to enter the hospital. MM is asked to provide guidance to these guards about admission criteria and whether patients’ ethnic or village origins will be included among those criteria. MM considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
MM commands a military field hospital that operates from a convoy of semi-trailer trucks, closely following combat troops as part of a United Nations (UN) peacekeeping and security mission. Their goal is to enforce and maintain a tense ceasefire between local government and opposition forces in a disputed region. The situation on the ground is worsening, with armed conflict leading to a surge in casualties and a growing number of displaced persons among several ethnic communities. Once the convoy arrives and the field hospital is fully set up, MM anticipates a large influx of wounded and sick individuals and begins coordinating efforts to secure enough supplies—food, water, shelter, medications, and other clinical necessities—to address their basic and medical needs.

The hospital’s perimeter is to be guarded, with security personnel assigned the task of controlling access and deciding who is permitted to enter. MM is asked to provide these guards with clear guidance regarding the criteria for admitting patients, specifically whether a patient’s ethnicity or village of origin should influence their eligibility for care. As the humanitarian emergency intensifies outside the hospital gates, MM must consider how to advise the guards, weighing the imperative to allocate limited resources effectively while ensuring that admission decisions are consistent with medical ethics and international humanitarian law.

ethical_issues.question: In a military field hospital operating in a conflict zone, how can it be ensured that patient admission criteria are based on clinical need and resource availability rather than ethnic or village origin?
keypoints: Patient admission criteria should be strictly based on clinical need and resource availability, with no discrimination based on ethnicity or village of origin.
Military medical units must adhere to the principles of the International Committee of the Red Cross, providing immediate attention and requisite care to emergency patients.
The Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols explicitly prohibit discrimination against patients based on status, covering enemy combatants, prisoners of war, civilians, and the shipwrecked.
Medical Rules of Eligibility (MRoE) should be established and implemented to reasonably define the population at risk, balancing bed capacity allocation with urgent humanitarian needs.
A clinical assessment system should be established at the hospital entrance to verify whether patients meet the MRoE, ensuring security and prioritizing emergency medical needs.

Clinical healthcare personnel must be guaranteed the lawful and independent exercise of medical judgment and ethical duties, ensuring that medical services are provided solely based on clinical need and individualized care.

ethical_issues.question: How should the dual objectives of reserving resources for the designated population at risk and addressing the urgent humanitarian needs of all patients be balanced within military medical facilities?
keypoints: Medical facilities should provide individualized care based on clinical need, ensuring that patients are not discriminated against on the basis of ethnicity or village origin.

Clear Medical Rules of Eligibility (MRoE) should be established to define the scope of eligible populations and the emergency circumstances under which civilians may receive treatment (such as conditions threatening life, limb, or eyesight), thereby balancing the dual objectives of reserving resources for the designated population at risk and addressing the urgent humanitarian needs of all patients.
In the absence of other clinically suitable alternatives and under emergency conditions, military medical units should provide direct or indirect health assistance to civilians only as a last resort.
Non-urgent patients should be advised to seek care through civilian health systems to prioritize medical resources for patients with conditions that threaten life, limb, or eyesight.

Admission policies for patients outside the designated population at risk must be developed with a comprehensive assessment of the entire health system’s capacity, including local public and private medical facilities and support from non-governmental organizations, to ensure patients receive continuous and appropriate medical care.

title: How Should Relief Organizations Fund Care of Patient-Asylees Who Have Cancer?
case:
MQ is a 63-year-old man of Syrian origin who fled the town of Daraa and sought asylum in Beirut, Lebanon, in 2015. That year, he registered for and received official refugee status with the government of Lebanon and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Lebanon. MQ was unable to find work in Beirut, but he still had money in his possession from his life in Syria.
In early 2016, MQ experienced his first tonic-clonic seizure, in which he fell to the floor, his body stiffening and jerking. No factors were recognized as provoking this seizure. MQ previously smoked cigarettes (30 pack-years), but he had no history of prior malignancy. He had no symptoms of weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. At first, he did not seek medical advice for his seizure. In fact, he had not visited a clinic since he sought asylum in Lebanon. But when MQ experienced a second seizure several weeks later, family members took him to a hospital in Beirut.
MQ’s blood test results were normal. Computed tomography (CT) imaging of his head, however, demonstrated a single 5 x 7 x 2 cm space-occupying lesion within the right frontal lobe of his brain, extending into the corpus callosum. The mass lesion had hemorrhagic components (blood) and surrounding edema (swelling). To further investigate and treat MQ’s mass lesion, physicians recommended that he be admitted to the hospital for urgent steroid treatment; CT imaging of his chest, abdomen, and pelvis; and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of his brain. The UNHCR, through its partners, paid the hospital for MQ’s CT imaging but could not cover the costs of his brain MRI. Realizing he urgently needed the MRI, MQ paid with some of his own and borrowed money.
MQ’s images suggested his disease was limited to his brain. MQ’s care team recommended biopsy and excision of the mass lesion with adjuvant chemotherapy. The surgery alone cost the equivalent of about 6500 US dollars. Aware of MQ’s (and most patients’) inability to pay or even borrow such an amount, his care team helped him request funds from the Exceptional Care Committee (ECC) of the UNHCR in Lebanon.
The ECC is a group of physicians and others convened by the UNHCR to adjudicate payment amounts for medical cases that exceed a prespecified amount of money and that a refugee cannot pay. ECC reviewers agreed to pay 90% of the cost of MQ’s surgery, which occurred 2 months after his first seizure. In Lebanon, the UNHCR’s ECC does not pay for chemotherapy, as it is deemed too expensive. MQ saw no other option than to forego chemotherapy, given that he was already indebted to family and friends and barely able to finance his 10% of the surgery cost.
MQ’s tumor was partially resected during his surgery. He recovered and was discharged from the hospital. Nine months later, MQ had another generalized seizure, and his family members brought him back to the hospital, where tumor extension was noted on imaging. Dr T attends MQ, who was visibly distressed, crying while he explained what he has been through and despairing about his illness, symptoms, and poverty. Dr T evaluated him and expects that, without adjuvant chemotherapy, MQ will probably die within the year. Dr T and members of MQ’s care team wonder how to respond.
case_rewrite:
MQ, a 63-year-old man from Syria, fled his hometown of Daraa and arrived in Beirut, Lebanon, in 2015, seeking asylum. He registered with the Lebanese government and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), obtaining official refugee status that same year. Despite his efforts, MQ was unable to secure employment in Beirut, though he managed to support himself for a time with savings he had brought from Syria.

In early 2016, MQ suffered a sudden tonic-clonic seizure—collapsing to the ground as his body stiffened and convulsed violently. There were no obvious triggers for this episode. MQ had a history of heavy cigarette smoking (30 pack-years) but no previous diagnosis of cancer, nor had he experienced unexplained weight loss, fever, or night sweats. Initially, he chose not to seek medical attention, having not visited a clinic since arriving in Lebanon. However, when a second seizure occurred several weeks later, his family insisted he be taken to a hospital in Beirut.

At the hospital, MQ’s blood tests returned normal results, but a head CT scan revealed a single 5 x 7 x 2 cm mass in the right frontal lobe of his brain, infiltrating the corpus callosum. The lesion showed signs of bleeding and surrounding swelling. The medical team urgently recommended hospital admission for steroid therapy, further CT scans of his chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and an MRI of his brain to better characterize the mass. While the UNHCR, through its partner organizations, covered the costs of the CT scans, it was unable to fund the brain MRI. Recognizing the importance of this test, MQ paid for the MRI himself, using a mix of his remaining money and funds borrowed from family and friends.

The imaging suggested the disease was confined to the brain. MQ’s care team advised him to undergo a biopsy and surgical excision of the mass, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. The surgery alone was estimated to cost the equivalent of $6,500 USD, a sum MQ and most refugees could not afford. His doctors assisted him in applying for financial assistance from the Exceptional Care Committee (ECC) of the UNHCR in Lebanon.

The ECC, composed of physicians and other experts, reviews requests for cases that exceed a certain financial threshold and are unaffordable for refugees. After reviewing MQ’s case, the ECC agreed to cover 90% of the surgery cost. The operation was scheduled two months after his initial seizure. However, in Lebanon, the ECC does not fund chemotherapy, considering it prohibitively expensive. Already deeply in debt and struggling to pay even his portion of the surgery, MQ felt he had no choice but to forgo chemotherapy.

During surgery, the team was able to partially remove the tumor. MQ recovered and was eventually discharged. Nine months later, he suffered another generalized seizure. His family rushed him back to the hospital, where imaging revealed that the tumor had progressed. Dr T, who was now part of MQ’s care team, found MQ in visible distress, weeping as he described his worsening illness and the financial hardship he faced. After evaluating him, Dr T concluded that without chemotherapy, MQ’s prognosis was poor, with likely less than a year to live. Dr T and the rest of the care team were left grappling with how to respond to MQ’s situation.

ethical_issues.question: Should funding for refugee medical care be allocated as a fixed amount per individual, or restricted to specific interventions?
keypoints: Allocating funds by setting a maximum per capita limit may result in some patients receiving only partial treatment or no treatment at all, thereby compromising both treatment outcomes and equity.

Prioritizing full curative treatment for a limited number of patients can improve individual survival rates but may diminish financial support for other patients requiring rehabilitation or palliative care, leading to inequitable resource distribution.

Grounded in the principle of justice, prioritizing the health improvement of the most vulnerable groups through a dynamically adjusted minimum level of medical support—without fixed caps or full funding of curative interventions—balances patient needs with the capacities of the host country or institution.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Clinicians as agents of the state
title: How Should Military Health Care Workers Respond When Conflict Reaches the Hospital?
case:
Dr M is an active-duty internist in a military medical center in Eastern Europe. The hospital treats active-duty and retired military service members and their families. The hospital also treats civilians in the emergency department and transfers them once they are stable. Recently, her country’s military has been in conflict with an aggressive militant group.
Today, the cell phones of the staff and patients buzz with a text alert sent from the country’s emergency warning system, stating there are ballistic missiles coming toward their area and to seek shelter immediately. Dr M notices several of her colleagues rushing out of the hospital in attempts to reach their loved ones. She instead works to rally her floor staff to keep their focus trained on their patients to keep them stable and protect them from any impending blasts.
Meanwhile, the hospital responds in different ways simultaneously. There is a sturdy basement level where many of the laboring mothers, neonatal intensive care unit (ICU) babies, and pediatric ICU children are being transported. Arguments erupt in the emergency department regarding the prioritization of active-duty personnel over families and civilians. Becoming increasingly agitated, the patients on Dr M’s floor question the decision that leaves them on the upper floors.
One hour passes, and nothing happens. Authorities later clarify that the text alert was a false alarm and was never meant to be sent. Dr M feels guilty for not trying to reach her husband and children.
case_rewrite:
Dr M serves as an internist at a military medical center situated in Eastern Europe. The facility provides care for active-duty and retired service members alongside their families, while also handling civilians in the emergency department—transferring them to outside hospitals once stabilized. Recently, Dr M’s country has become embroiled in an escalating conflict with an aggressive militant group, intensifying the atmosphere throughout the hospital.

On this particular day, a sudden text alert blares on the cell phones of staff and patients alike. The country’s emergency warning system announces incoming ballistic missiles in their vicinity, instructing everyone to seek immediate shelter. Dr M watches as several colleagues hastily leave the hospital, desperate to reach their families. In contrast, she gathers her floor staff, urging them to remain focused on their patients—to keep them stable and protect them as best as possible from any potential explosions.

Across the hospital, responses are varied and tense. A secure basement level becomes a shelter for many: laboring mothers, newborns in the neonatal intensive care unit, and critically ill children from the pediatric ICU are all rushed downstairs. In the emergency department, heated arguments break out over whether to give priority to active-duty service members rather than their families or civilian patients. On Dr M’s floor, anxiety intensifies as patients demand to know why they are being kept on the upper floors rather than moved to safety below.

An hour drags by without incident. Eventually, authorities announce that the missile warning was a false alarm, mistakenly issued in error. As relief settles over the hospital, Dr M is left grappling with guilt for having chosen her duty to her patients over checking on her own husband and children.

ethical_issues.question: In conflict zones, how should military health care workers make decisions between prioritizing active-duty service members and civilians with more urgent medical needs?
keypoints: In conflict zones, military medical facilities typically prioritize the treatment of active-duty service members to ensure their rapid recovery and return to duty, thereby maintaining force readiness and national security.

Priority decisions within military medical environments are based not only on the medical urgency and likelihood of survival of patients but also take into account operational readiness, mission requirements, and national defense interests.
During emergencies, resource allocation may be directed by the President or Secretary of Defense to prioritize operational and national security needs rather than solely medical necessity.

This practice of prioritizing active-duty service members can create moral distress for clinicians, particularly when it results in other critically injured patients being unable to receive timely care.

ethical_issues.question: In cases like Dr M’s, how should military medical institutions ethically allocate resources during emergencies to balance patient care obligations with national security imperatives?
keypoints: Military medical facilities in emergency situations should adhere to a utilitarian principle, prioritizing the treatment of those most likely to survive with intervention in order to maximize the number of lives saved.

In urgent conflict scenarios, prioritizing active-duty service members aims to ensure their rapid return to duty, maintain military order, and safeguard national security; this priority may supersede that of other eligible patients.

Resource allocation decisions should be based not only on medical necessity and patient risk assessment but also take into account national security requirements and strategic directives from superior commanders, such as the President or Secretary of Defense.

Military medical institutions must balance medical ethics with military missions, ensuring that while protecting patient rights, they also support overall combat readiness and national defense objectives.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Dual roles as clinicians and researchers
title: Should Children Be Enrolled in Clinical Research in Conflict Zones?
case:
Dr P is a physician and researcher from an East African country that has been immersed in violence and civil conflict for years. He and his colleagues work in the region with an international nonprofit organization that both provides health care services and aims to strengthen the evidence available to guide practitioners during humanitarian crises. Dr P and colleagues care for many adults and children injured by violence and are concerned about availability of interventions for diseases endemic to the region. Many children hospitalized for war injuries also have infectious diseases, such as HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. Dr P and colleagues consider researching these diseases’ prevalence among children in the region and whether and to what extent current policies address their needs. Some enthusiastically support these research ideas, but others question whether clinical research during conflict would be the best use of clinicians’ time and skills.
Dr P and colleagues form a team to collectively consider practical and ethical issues they could face when conducting research. One plan that emerges during their meetings includes enrolling children arriving at the hospital and sampling their blood, monitoring children who test positive for an infectious disease, and evaluating how well current policies support clinicians’ capacity to offer evidence-based interventions and psychosocial care.
Since children often arrive at the hospital accompanied not by their parents but by other relatives or adults, parental informed consent might not be possible. Although consent from an adult relative accompanying a child is standard for medical interventions in the region, some team members wonder whether a child’s assent to participate in research or an adult relative’s consent to enroll a child in research would be ethically sufficient. Assuming consent can somehow be appropriately secured, some team members worry that it’s not ethical to even attempt research that might not even be feasible because participants’ blood samples can deteriorate and expire while being transported to the capital city for analysis. Long transportation delays are not easily averted in the region due to security incidents, roadblocks, and ambushes. Even assuming good blood sample preservation and analysis, test results (normally available 14 days after collection) will need to be conveyed to children’s parents by research team members who travel to their villages. If the children’s parents have been killed and no guardian is present, it’s unclear whether keeping newly orphaned children in a research protocol is ethically appropriate.
Dr P and colleagues remain neutral about the region’s conflict, but the government has authority over the hospital, and nearby villages are controlled by antigovernment rebel forces. Rebel groups have not objected to villagers seeking care at the hospital, but if researchers are viewed as government collaborators or agents reporting on rebel activities, everyone in the hospital could be at risk of violence. Another complexity is that the government’s Ministry of Health, which would have to approve a research protocol, might oppose any project it sees as beneficial to the interests of people living in rebel-held regions.
Although convinced that children with infectious diseases are not adequately cared for under existing policies, Dr P and colleagues believe that the capacity to respond to need can’t be improved without a good evidence base that research would likely establish. They are also convinced that it is ethically problematic to wait until conflict ends to conduct research that could lead to improvements, and so Dr P and colleagues continue to deliberate about what they should do.
case_rewrite:
Dr P is a physician and researcher from an East African country that has endured years of violence and civil unrest. He and his colleagues work in the region with an international nonprofit organization that both provides direct health care and seeks to strengthen the evidence base available to guide practitioners during humanitarian emergencies. Dr P and his team regularly care for adults and children wounded by conflict and are deeply concerned about the limited availability of interventions for diseases endemic to the area. Many of the children hospitalized for war injuries are also suffering from infectious diseases such as HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis.

Dr P and his colleagues begin discussing the possibility of researching the prevalence of these infectious diseases among children in their region, and assessing how well existing policies address the needs of these vulnerable patients. Some team members are enthusiastic about these research ideas, seeing the potential to improve care, while others question whether undertaking clinical research during ongoing conflict is the best use of clinicians’ time and energy.

To address these concerns, Dr P and his colleagues form a team to carefully consider both the practical and ethical challenges they might face if they pursue this research. One proposal that emerges involves enrolling children as they arrive at the hospital, collecting blood samples, monitoring those who test positive for infectious diseases, and evaluating the extent to which current policies enable clinicians to provide evidence-based interventions and psychosocial support.

However, in this setting, children often reach the hospital accompanied by relatives or unrelated adults rather than their parents, making parental informed consent difficult or impossible to obtain. While consent from an accompanying adult relative is standard for medical interventions in the region, some members of the team question whether a child’s assent or a non-parental adult's consent is ethically sufficient for research participation. Even if appropriate consent can be secured, others worry that conducting research may not be practical or ethical if participants’ blood samples are likely to deteriorate during transportation to the capital for analysis. Security risks, frequent roadblocks, and the threat of ambushes often cause significant delays, and the integrity of samples can be compromised. Assuming samples can be preserved and analyzed, test results—typically available two weeks after collection—would then need to be communicated to children’s parents by research staff traveling to remote villages. If a child’s parents have been killed and there is no guardian present, the ethical appropriateness of continuing to include newly orphaned children in the study becomes even more uncertain.

Throughout their deliberations, Dr P and his team remain neutral regarding the ongoing conflict. However, the hospital is under government control, while surrounding villages are controlled by anti-government rebel groups. Although rebel forces have not prevented villagers from seeking care at the hospital, there remains a significant risk: if researchers are perceived as collaborators with the government or as informants, everyone in the hospital could face violent reprisals. Further complicating matters, the government’s Ministry of Health—which must approve any research protocol—might oppose projects perceived as benefiting people living in areas under rebel control.

Despite these obstacles, Dr P and his colleagues are convinced that children with infectious diseases are not adequately cared for under current policies. They believe that without solid research evidence, it is impossible to improve the capacity to meet these urgent needs. They also recognize that waiting until the conflict ends to conduct research would be ethically problematic, as it would delay necessary improvements in care. As a result, Dr P and his team continue to deliberate, seeking a path forward that responsibly balances their dual commitments to urgent clinical care and the advancement of research that could benefit both current and future pediatric patients.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr P and colleagues ethically balance their dual responsibilities of providing clinical care to injured children and conducting research on endemic diseases in conflict zones?
keypoints: Clinical practitioners should avoid viewing the treatment of injured patients and the conduct of research as mutually exclusive options; instead, they should actively seek alternative approaches that integrate both, thereby promoting the synergistic advancement of clinical care and scientific investigation.

When balancing the urgent clinical needs of children with war-related injuries against the long-term benefits of research aimed at improving the health of future pediatric populations, it is important to recognize that focusing solely on trauma care may overlook potentially fatal risks such as infectious diseases, thereby limiting the overall medical benefit.

In contexts where medical services are already being provided, research evaluating the effectiveness and safety of these interventions is not only feasible but also ethically justified, as it contributes to the optimization of therapeutic strategies.

The research team can achieve a balance in time and resource allocation by implementing reasonable division of labor, assigning certain members to focus on clinical duties while others concentrate on research activities, thus ensuring the simultaneous fulfillment of both treatment and research objectives.

ethical_issues.question: How can ethical standards for informed consent be ensured when enrolling children in research in conflict settings, especially in situations where parents are not present?
keypoints: Informed consent is an internationally recognized ethical requirement for research participation; researchers should engage deeply with participant communities to ensure understanding and respect for community values and cultural contexts.

Employing participatory research methods helps to identify consent or assent processes acceptable to the community, and innovative adaptations of ethical guidelines—such as permitting relatives to provide consent on behalf of children—are reasonable when accepted locally.

In the absence of parents, careful consideration should be given to allowing caregivers outside the nuclear family to make decisions based on the best interests of the child, avoiding simplistic assumptions.

Children’s capacity to provide consent is complex and contested; trauma may affect their ability to express genuine wishes, yet exceptional circumstances may also accelerate their maturity. Assessment should be holistic, taking into account the child’s age, cultural background, and level of risk, with respect for the child’s views and, where appropriate, seeking their consent or assent.

Researchers should balance ethical risks with practical needs, ensuring that children’s participation in research both meets ethical standards and effectively safeguards their interests, with particular caution exercised in consent procedures within conflict settings.

title: How Should Clinicians Respond to Patient Interest in Dietary Supplements to Treat Serious Chronic Illness?
case: Mr R visits Dr G to follow up on his type 2 diabetes after initiating basal insulin, mealtime insulin, empagliflozin, and metformin. Mr R explains that his metformin prescription expired, so he’s only taking empagliflozin, and that he prefers not to restart insulin because it gives him “brain fog.” Due to past pancreatitis, Mr R is not a candidate for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist treatment. Mr R states that he’d like to control his diabetes by modifying his diet, and he also expresses interest in taking a blood sugar control product he found at a nutrition store, which is labeled as containing cinnamon, chromium, bitter melon extract, gymnema, zinc, and a B-complex. Mr R’s most recent hemoglobin A1C is 8.6% (diabetic range) and his renal and liver function test results are normal. Dr G wonders how to respond to Mr R.
case_rewrite:
Mr R arrives at Dr G’s office for a follow-up appointment regarding his type 2 diabetes management. He had previously been prescribed a regimen that included basal insulin, mealtime insulin, empagliflozin, and metformin. During the visit, Mr R explains that he has not refilled his metformin prescription since it expired, and therefore is currently only taking empagliflozin. He also shares that he would prefer not to resume insulin therapy, citing that it causes him to experience “brain fog.” Due to a history of pancreatitis, Mr R is not eligible for treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists.

Mr R expresses a desire to manage his diabetes primarily by making dietary changes. Additionally, he mentions his interest in starting a blood sugar control supplement he recently discovered at a nutrition store. The product’s label lists ingredients such as cinnamon, chromium, bitter melon extract, gymnema, zinc, and a B-complex vitamin. Mr R’s latest hemoglobin A1C is 8.6%, which remains in the diabetic range, though his renal and liver function tests are within normal limits. Dr G considers how best to respond to Mr R’s preferences and questions regarding the new supplement.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians ethically balance respect for patient autonomy with their responsibilities to ensure medical safety and efficacy when patients choose to use dietary supplements instead of conventional medications for the treatment of chronic illness?
keypoints: Clinicians should adhere to the principle of shared decision making, respecting patient autonomy while ensuring the safety and efficacy of the treatment plan.
Physicians should thoroughly inquire about the patient’s past, current, and intended use of dietary supplements, and comprehensively assess their potential impact on the patient’s health.

When patients consider substituting dietary supplements for prescription medications, clinicians must evaluate the safety and efficacy of such supplements based on scientific evidence, and collaborate with pharmacists for expert information when necessary.

If a dietary supplement is assessed to be safe and to have some glucose-lowering potential, clinicians may support the patient in trialing the supplement for a specified period, but should clearly communicate that it is unlikely to fully replace conventional pharmacotherapy.
Physicians should continuously monitor changes in the patient’s condition and treatment outcomes, and promptly adjust therapeutic strategies to ensure optimal medical care.

For dietary supplements with unclear safety or efficacy, clinicians should engage in open discussions with patients regarding associated risks and concerns, and explore whether more appropriate alternatives exist.

If a patient insists on using ineffective or high-risk dietary supplements, clinicians should emphasize the importance of conventional pharmacological treatment and discuss the necessity of resuming or adjusting medication regimens.

title: Should Clinicians Ever Recommend Supplements to Patients Trying to Lose Weight?
case:
Ms S is a 42-year-old Latina woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 30.2 kg/mand a long history of dieting for weight loss. She gained weight with her 2 pregnancies and is now heavier by 56 pounds, 10 of which she gained during the COVID-19 pandemic. As an administrative assistant, she sits most of the day and has no planned physical activity. Her mother, who has a BMI of 37 kg/m, was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at age 50 and has experienced a mild stroke. Ms S takes no prescription medications but has risk factors for chronic disease: fasting blood glucose (110 mg/dL), lipids (total cholesterol of 220 mg/dL and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 100 mg/dL), and blood pressure (138/89 mmHg). Ms S has made an appointment to address her weight gain and ways to improve her health without taking medications. Her overall goal is not to have the same health issues as her mother. A friend has recommended that Ms S consider taking a fat-burning weight loss supplement.
Ms S has tried many diets over the years, but they have not worked with her family’s lifestyle; she has 2 active teenage boys who play sports and a husband who is a construction manager. She loves to cook and prepares many traditional dishes learned from her mother, who emigrated from Mexico. When she does not have time to cook, the family orders takeout food (3 to 4 times per week). Coming to see a physician for weight loss help has been difficult, since she is not sure a physician will understand her weight struggles.
case_rewrite:
Ms S, a 42-year-old Latina woman, arrives for her appointment feeling both hopeful and apprehensive. Her body mass index (BMI) is 30.2 kg/m², and she has struggled with dieting for many years, particularly since the birth of her two sons. After each pregnancy, she gained weight, and now she is 56 pounds heavier than she was before having children, with 10 of those pounds gained during the COVID-19 pandemic. As an administrative assistant, her job requires her to remain seated for most of the day, and she does not have a routine for physical activity.

Family health is a concern for Ms S. Her mother, who emigrated from Mexico, has a BMI of 37 kg/m² and was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at the age of 50. She has also suffered a mild stroke. Ms S is determined to avoid her mother’s health issues and wants to take preventive steps, especially since her own fasting blood glucose is 110 mg/dL, her total cholesterol is 220 mg/dL, her LDL cholesterol is 100 mg/dL, and her blood pressure measures at 138/89 mmHg. Although she currently takes no prescription medications, she recognizes her risk factors for chronic disease.

Ms S’s lifestyle is busy and centered around her family. She has two energetic teenage sons who play sports and a husband who works as a construction manager. She enjoys cooking and often prepares traditional Mexican dishes taught to her by her mother. However, when time is limited, the family relies on takeout meals three to four times a week. Over the years, Ms S has tried multiple diets, but none have fit well with her family’s preferences or their hectic routines.

Recently, a close friend suggested she try a fat-burning weight loss supplement. Unsure, Ms S has come to Dr W seeking guidance on how to address her weight gain and improve her health without resorting to medications.
