title: How Should Clinicians Help Homeless Trauma Survivors Make Irreversible Surgical Care Decisions?
case:
M is a 32-year-old transgender woman who is unsheltered. She has an extensive history of physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, which began when she was 5 years old. M has had many encounters with the health care system and, when admitted as an inpatient, frequently left against medical advice. During her last hospital admission, a surgical team recommended that M undergo an amputation. M left against medical advice but was readmitted 4 days later with tachycardia, hypertension, and a fever. A surgical team again emphasized that amputation was very likely needed to save M’s life. Despite many conversations, M remained frightened and refused surgery, but the surgical team had no good reason to doubt her capacity to make health decisions.
When M spoke with the team’s social worker, SW, she explained that she felt rushed to consent to amputation and that she neither trusted her physicians’ desire to help her nor understood why she needed an amputation to live. She expressed frustration with clinicians “who use big words to make me feel stupid and force me to do what they want.” M continued, “They have no idea what my life on the streets is going to be like when I don’t have this limb anymore.” M also shared with SW that she often does not understand what she is told, is scared, and needs more time to think and ask questions.
Altered cognition does not necessarily imply that trauma survivors have compromised decision-making capacity.
Based on these conversations with M, SW suggests to her fellow team members that slower speech, short sentences, writing down key points, and making more time for questions could help clinicians feel less frustrated about M refusing indicated and much-needed surgery. It would also help M consider what such surgery would mean for her now and when she leaves the hospital.
case_rewrite:
M is a 32-year-old transgender woman experiencing homelessness. Since the age of five, she has endured repeated physical, emotional, and sexual abuse. M is no stranger to the health care system; her medical record includes frequent hospitalizations, but she often leaves the hospital against medical advice. During her most recent admission, the surgical team advised that she needed an amputation. M, feeling overwhelmed, left the hospital on her own terms. Just four days later, she was readmitted, now presenting with tachycardia, hypertension, and a high fever. Once again, the surgical team strongly recommended amputation, emphasizing that it was almost certainly necessary to save her life. Despite multiple discussions, M remained terrified and refused the operation. The surgical team, however, had no substantial reasons to doubt her ability to make informed decisions about her care.

During a conversation with the team’s social worker, SW, M confided that she felt pressured to consent to the amputation and did not trust the intentions of her doctors. She admitted she did not fully understand why the surgery was essential for her survival. M voiced her frustration with clinicians who, in her words, “use big words to make me feel stupid and force me to do what they want.” She added, “They have no idea what my life on the streets is going to be like when I don’t have this limb anymore.” M further explained to SW that she often fails to comprehend medical explanations, feels frightened, and wishes she had more time to think and ask questions before making a decision.

It is important to recognize that trauma survivors, like M, may exhibit altered cognition without necessarily lacking decision-making capacity.

After hearing M’s concerns, SW proposed to the clinical team that they adjust their approach when speaking with her: slow down their speech, use shorter sentences, write down the most important points, and allow extra time for M to ask questions and process information. SW suggested that these strategies could ease clinicians’ frustration over M’s refusal of critical surgery, while also helping M more thoroughly consider what the amputation would mean for her both now and after she leaves the hospital.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians respect the autonomy of homeless patients and avoid retraumatization during the informed consent process?
keypoints: Clinicians should adopt a trauma-informed approach to deepen their understanding of patients’ neurobiological makeup and psychosocial histories, with particular attention to the cognitive and emotional impacts of trauma during discussions of interventions and the informed consent process.

When communicating the prospective risks and benefits of interventions, clinicians should create a safe and supportive environment that minimizes triggers, avoids retraumatization, promotes patients’ emotional well-being, and respects their autonomy.

A sensitive informed consent process that enhances communication, builds trust, and demonstrates respect helps patients gain greater control and agency in both medical decision-making and their broader lives.

Using clear and accessible language, slowing speech, employing short sentences, writing down key points, and allowing ample time for patients to ask questions and reflect can improve patients’ comprehension and capacity to give informed consent or refusal, while also reducing frustration among clinical team members.

Assessments of patients’ decision-making capacity should be conducted under the most favorable conditions and, when necessary, supplemented with cognitive supports such as visual aids, repeated conversations, and corrective feedback to responsibly facilitate patients’ self-determination.

ethical_issues.question: When assessing the decision-making capacity of trauma survivors, how should clinicians take into account the neurobiological effects and psychosocial background of these patients?
keypoints: Clinicians should adopt a trauma-informed approach to deepen their understanding of trauma survivors’ neurobiological foundations and psychosocial backgrounds, demonstrating sensitivity and respect especially when discussing interventions and during the informed consent process.

Prolonged childhood trauma can lead to abnormal development of memory systems (such as the hippocampus, amygdala, and frontal cortex) and brain regions related to executive functioning (such as the orbitofrontal cortex, cingulate gyrus, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex), affecting language comprehension and information processing speed; therefore, patients should be given more time for decision making.

Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) often causes patients to have a heightened perception of threat and negative interpretative bias in ambiguous situations; clinicians should consider the emotional and cognitive impacts of PTSD during clinical assessment.

Altered cognitive function does not necessarily equate to impaired decision-making capacity; clinicians should assess patients’ capacity under the most favorable conditions and avoid prematurely denying their autonomy due to trauma histories.

The use of cognitive support strategies—such as plain language, visual aids, repeated communication, corrective feedback, and sufficient time for questions—can enhance trauma survivors’ comprehension and engagement, thereby promoting effective informed consent or refusal.

A thorough understanding of patients’ sociocultural backgrounds, trauma histories, lived experiences, and values is essential for building trust, facilitating effective communication, and enabling responsible assessment of decision-making capacity and the exercise of autonomy.

title: Holding Curative and Palliative Intentions
case:
Mr H, a 75-year-old former carpenter, was diagnosed with advanced cancer just above his esophagus. He had spent a long time in a rehab facility recovering from chemotherapy and radiation treatments. After 2 months, he could swallow soft foods again and recovered enough to move home. But 3 weeks later, he experienced pain, weight loss, and couldn’t swallow his own saliva. A biopsy confirmed that the persistent cancer above his esophagus had now spread to a lymph node in his neck. It was unclear from imaging studies whether or to what extent the cancer was safely resectable from either site. Mr H was clear with his radiation oncologist, medical oncologist, and surgeon, Dr L, that he wanted everything done to try to remove the cancer.
Dr L explained, “We’d do a major surgery called a salvage laryngopharyngectomy,in which we’d try to remove all of the cancer. We’d remove your voice box and pharynx, so you might never swallow again. We’d also try to remove cancer in the neck lymph node. Due to chemotherapy and radiation, your tissues are less likely to heal after surgery, so here is higher risk for complications with this surgery, but salvage surgery, after primary chemotherapy and radiation, is your best hope for a cure.” Mr H consented to surgery.
Dr L presented Mr H’s case at a multidisciplinary tumor board meeting that week. Dr L’s colleague, Dr M, pointed out, “There’s a good chance you’ll find out intraoperatively that the cancer encases the carotid artery or has spread to the spine fascia. Then you’ll have to abort the case, and he will be worse. Either way, rates of successful salvage for hypopharyngeal recurrence go as low as 15%.At the very least, I wouldn’t call this surgery ‘curative.’”
“He wants surgery,” replied Dr L. “I agree that we could find unresectable disease, but we’ll go in with intention to cure his cancer. So, surgery should be presented to him as curative.”
Colleagues in the meeting considered how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Mr H, a 75-year-old retired carpenter, had been diagnosed with advanced cancer located just above his esophagus. Following a prolonged stay in a rehabilitation facility to recover from chemotherapy and radiation therapy, he gradually regained the ability to swallow soft foods and was able to return home after two months. However, only three weeks later, Mr H developed severe pain, experienced significant weight loss, and lost the ability to swallow even his own saliva. A subsequent biopsy revealed that the persistent cancer above his esophagus had now metastasized to a lymph node in his neck. Imaging studies could not clearly determine the extent to which the cancer might be safely resected from either site.

Throughout discussions with his radiation oncologist, medical oncologist, and his surgeon, Dr L, Mr H was adamant that he wanted every possible measure taken to remove the cancer. Dr L explained, “The operation we’re considering is a major one called a salvage laryngopharyngectomy. Our goal would be to remove all of the cancer, but this would mean removing your voice box and pharynx, so you might never be able to swallow again. We would also attempt to take out the cancerous lymph node in your neck. Because your tissues have already been affected by chemotherapy and radiation, your risk of complications is much higher, and your tissues might not heal well after surgery. Nonetheless, salvage surgery following chemotherapy and radiation is your best hope for a cure.” Mr H agreed to proceed with the surgery.

Later that week, Dr L presented Mr H’s case at a multidisciplinary tumor board meeting. Dr M, a colleague, voiced concern: “There’s a real chance that, once you’re in the operating room, you’ll discover the cancer is wrapped around the carotid artery or has invaded the fascia of the spine. In that case, you’d have to stop the operation, and he could end up worse off than before. Even if you proceed, the chances of successful salvage surgery for a recurrence in the hypopharynx can be as low as 15%. At a minimum, I wouldn’t describe this procedure as ‘curative.’”

Dr L responded, “He wants surgery. I recognize we may find unresectable disease, but our intent going in is to cure his cancer. So, I believe the surgery should be presented to him as curative.”

The team at the tumor board began to deliberate on how to address these issues.

ethical_issues.question: Can surgeons simultaneously hold both curative and palliative intentions during surgery, and how should they understand patients’ expectations and wishes during the informed consent process?
keypoints: Surgeons can concurrently pursue both curative and palliative objectives within a single operation; curative surgeries may also achieve palliative outcomes such as pain relief, mitigation of disfigurement, and functional improvement. These goals are not mutually exclusive and should be considered comprehensively and clearly communicated to the patient.

During the informed consent process, clinicians must thoroughly understand the patient’s expectations and priorities. Utilizing open-ended questions, eliciting patient preferences (e.g., “least bad” options), and anticipating best- and worst-case scenarios can assist patients in clarifying their values, managing expectations realistically, and facilitating prudent decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: When faced with a significant new diagnosis or decisions regarding cancer treatment, how can clinicians effectively guide patients to consider the potential consequences of both pursuing and refusing treatment in order to minimize decisional regret?
keypoints: At the time of a significant new diagnosis or cancer treatment decision, patients often focus on whether to take action rather than on the specific action to be taken; therefore, clinicians need to guide patients to consider the potential consequences of different treatment options as well as of treatment refusal.

Physicians should anticipate potential clinical thresholds during disease progression at which surgery may become infeasible or require intraoperative abandonment, and proactively discuss these uncertainties and risks with patients to demonstrate forward-looking and transparent communication.

Utilizing open-ended questions to assist patients and their surrogates in reflecting on the consequences of various choices—for example, asking how they would wish to spend their time if they were to die from the disease by the end of the year, how they might feel if surgery fails to cure or alleviate symptoms, and their attitudes toward foregoing surgery in favor of symptom management—facilitates a comprehensive weighing of benefits and burdens.

Effective shared decision-making requires eliciting patients’ values and preferences (such as identifying “least bad” options or “least acceptable” outcomes) and integrating clear communication about potential outcomes—including both health-related and experiential endpoints—to help patients manage expectations, clarify priorities, and reduce future decisional regret.

ethical_issues.question: In the physician-patient relationship, how can curative and palliative intentions be concurrently embraced to achieve multiple therapeutic goals while ensuring that the patient’s priorities are thoroughly discussed and understood?
keypoints: Curative and palliative treatments can be implemented concurrently within the physician-patient relationship; clinicians should avoid framing these approaches as mutually exclusive and instead offer patients an integrated care plan that addresses disease eradication, holistic treatment, symptom relief, and quality of life enhancement.

During the informed consent process, clinicians must thoroughly understand patients’ expectations and values, managing their anticipations through clear and honest communication to ensure that patients’ priorities are fully discussed and respected, thereby minimizing future decisional regret.

Utilizing open-ended questions to guide patients and their surrogates in exploring the potential consequences of accepting or refusing treatment facilitates comprehensive understanding of the best-case, worst-case, and most acceptable outcomes associated with different choices.

Early integration of palliative care principles throughout the oncologic treatment trajectory—particularly when surgical interventions involve multiple therapeutic goals—supports deeper physician-patient communication, fosters consensus, and enhances the quality of treatment decision-making.

title: When Should Neuroendovascular Care for Patients With Acute Stroke Be Palliative?
case:
Mr J is a 64-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), who, while eating, abruptly developed right hemiplegia and aphasia. He had been diagnosed 10 months earlier with NSCLC; his estimated life expectancy was approximately 1 year. After a course of chemotherapy with pemetrexed and carboplatin, Mr J started pembrolizumab, an antiprogrammed death-1 immune checkpoint inhibitor offered possibly to extend his life but not as a cure for his cancer.Since diagnosis, Mr J has suffered multiple hematologic complications, including thrombosis and hemorrhage. When brought to an emergency department, he was confirmed as full code and intubated on arrival due to poor mental status and aspiration risk. Computed tomography (CT) imaging of his head and neck revealed normal brain parenchyma and occlusion of the proximal left middle cerebral artery (MCA), which supplies blood to most of the brain’s left hemisphere, including areas critical for language and right-side sensorimotor function.The mechanism of Mr J’s left MCA occlusion was presumed to be thromboembolism, to which he was predisposed by hypercoagulability of malignancy, pembrolizumab,and intracardiac hemostasis, given his known low left ventricular ejection fraction.
After discussion of acute stroke as a likely a complication of Mr J’s cancer, Mr J’s health care proxy, GG, consented to Mr J undergoing an emergent thrombectomy. This neuroendovascular procedure is a minimally invasive alternative to more invasive interventions and is the standard method for thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke with large-vessel occlusion using an endovascular approach. Emergent thrombectomy utilizes femoral artery access to position an intracranial catheter system that permits intracerebral thrombus removal, with the goals of reestablishing blood flow to vascular territory downstream from an occlusion and enabling salvage of the ischemic penumbra to restore neurological function and prevent further impairment.If thrombectomy is not performed, a large proximal-vessel stroke typically occurs, potentially leading to extended brain tissue infarction, cerebral edema, and other symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure (eg, nausea, vomiting, headache, visual changes, and cranial neuropathies) that can exacerbate a patient’s impairment and suffering.
Mr J’s thrombectomy was uncomplicated and resulted in rapid and successful left MCA territory reperfusion. A subsequent brain magnetic resonance (MR) image, however, revealed multifocal infarcts affecting the left and the right hemisphere of Mr J’s brain and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, consistent with his presumed cardioembolic etiology. Mr J was unable to communicate or meaningfully interact. After neurological examination, Dr N informed GG of key findings, including bilateral infarcts expected to produce long-term bilateral weakness, disordered speech, and cognitive impairment. Dr N also explained to GG that Mr J would likely need life support, including tracheostomy, gastrostomy, and rehabilitation if he survived much longer. GG expressed understanding and asked the team to prioritize Mr J’s comfort.
case_rewrite:
Mr J, a 64-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), suddenly developed right-sided paralysis and lost his ability to speak while eating. Ten months earlier, he had been diagnosed with NSCLC and given a life expectancy of about one year. Following initial chemotherapy with pemetrexed and carboplatin, Mr J began pembrolizumab, an anti-programmed death-1 immune checkpoint inhibitor, which was offered not as a cure but with the hope of extending his life. Throughout his illness, he had experienced multiple blood-related complications, including both clotting and bleeding events.

When Mr J was brought to the emergency department, he was confirmed as full code and was intubated immediately because of his diminished mental status and the risk of aspiration. A CT scan of his head and neck showed that the brain tissue appeared normal, but there was an occlusion in the proximal left middle cerebral artery (MCA), responsible for supplying much of the left hemisphere, including areas vital for language and right-sided movement. The presumed cause of this occlusion was thromboembolism, given Mr J’s cancer-related hypercoagulability, recent pembrolizumab treatment, and a background of impaired heart function with a known low left ventricular ejection fraction.

After the clinical team discussed the likelihood that Mr J’s acute stroke was a complication of his underlying cancer, they spoke with his health care proxy, GG. GG gave consent for Mr J to undergo an emergent thrombectomy—a minimally invasive neuroendovascular procedure that is the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke caused by large vessel occlusion. Thrombectomy involves accessing the femoral artery and threading an intracranial catheter to remove the clot, aiming to restore blood flow to the affected brain region, salvage threatened brain tissue, and prevent further neurological impairment. Without this intervention, Mr J was at risk for a large stroke with significant brain infarction, swelling, increased intracranial pressure, and symptoms such as headache, visual disturbances, cranial nerve deficits, and further decline.

The thrombectomy proceeded without complication and resulted in prompt reperfusion of the left MCA territory. However, subsequent MRI of the brain revealed multifocal infarcts in both the left and right hemispheres and in both cerebellar hemispheres, consistent with an underlying cardioembolic process. Following the procedure, Mr J remained unable to communicate or meaningfully interact with others. After a thorough neurological evaluation, Dr N met with GG to review the findings: bilateral brain infarcts were expected to result in long-term bilateral weakness, severely impaired speech, and significant cognitive deficits. Dr N also explained that, should Mr J survive, ongoing life support would likely be necessary—including tracheostomy, gastrostomy, and intensive rehabilitation. After hearing this prognosis, GG expressed understanding and requested that the medical team focus on Mr J’s comfort above all else.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of end-of-life care, should clinicians seek to prevent or reverse neurological dysfunction in order to improve the patient’s quality of life?
keypoints: Clinicians have an ethical responsibility to actively identify and manage neurological symptoms throughout the patient’s illness trajectory in order to improve quality of life.

Minimally invasive neuroendovascular interventions can be considered palliative measures aimed at preventing disabling neurological injury and alleviating end-of-life suffering, and should not be withheld solely on the basis of a patient’s terminal status or incurable comorbidities.

Clinicians should respect the rights of patients and their surrogates to accept or decline interventions, ensuring that medical decision-making aligns with the patient’s values, preferences, and best interests.

ethical_issues.question: For patients at the end of life, when, to what extent, and according to whose judgment should thrombectomy be considered palliative care?
keypoints: Whether thrombectomy serves as palliative care in patients with terminal illness should be based on a patient-centered shared decision-making process that comprehensively assesses the patient’s baseline functional status, values, preferences, and goals for quality of life; the ethical justification of the procedure lies in its alignment with the wishes and goals of the patient and their surrogate decision-maker.

During shared decision-making and informed consent, clinicians should explicitly communicate the limitations and uncertainties regarding the applicability of existing evidence to the individual patient, ensuring that the patient or surrogate fully understands the potential benefits and risks of the procedure.

Minimally invasive neuroendovascular interventions can reasonably be considered palliative treatment modalities for patients with limited life expectancy and should not be categorically excluded solely due to terminal comorbidities; evaluation must be conducted on a case-by-case basis considering the stroke location and the extent of salvageable ischemic penumbra.

The core goal of palliative thrombectomy is to alleviate or prevent neurological dysfunction caused by stroke, thereby maximizing preservation of the patient’s quality of life and avoiding additional suffering and functional loss attributable to stroke progression.

Clinicians should proactively identify and manage stroke-related neurological symptoms (such as weakness, aphasia, delirium, etc.) to ensure the comprehensiveness of palliative care, recognizing it as an integral component of holistic patient management.

ethical_issues.question: How can the stroke treatment decision-making process be ensured to sensitively reflect the patient’s preferences, values, and goals, while enabling rapid decisions in emergency situations?
keypoints: Stroke treatment decisions must be made rapidly due to the urgency of acute stroke and its impact on the patient’s capacity to participate in decision making.

Advance care planning should include designation of a health care proxy and discussion of preferences regarding minimally invasive interventions to ensure subsequent decisions align with the patient’s values and goals.
Patient-centered care requires assessment of the patient’s baseline functional status, preferences, values, goals, and prospects for recovery, with surrogate input as needed.

Clinicians should clearly communicate to the patient or surrogate the intended aims, potential benefits, possible risks of neuroendovascular interventions, the likely outcomes of foregoing intervention or pursuing alternative treatments, and explain the range of possible postprocedural outcomes to promote transparency.
During shared decision making and informed consent, clinicians must explicitly convey the limitations and uncertainties regarding the applicability of existing evidence to the individual patient.
The decision-making process and outcomes should be clearly documented and effectively communicated to the entire care team to ensure consistency in subsequent treatment and care.

title: How to Support Patients Near the End of Life Whose Pain Is Best Treated With Surgery?
case:
Mr F is 80 years old and has peripheral vascular disease with arterial insufficiency in his left leg. He has excruciating pain in his foot that wakes him up at night and is relieved by hanging his foot over the side of the bed. He also has a small ulcer on his left big toe. Some nights, he sleeps in his recliner with his foot down to mitigate the pain (gravity increases blood flow). He also has emphysema and diabetes and has suffered a major heart attack and several small strokes. He and his primary care physician, Dr K, agree that because of his multiple medical problems, he is “wearing out.” Mr F thinks of himself as a “tough cookie,” but he understands his remaining life is limited and agrees to an out of hospital do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order.
However, the pain in Mr F’s foot is making his life unbearable. Dr K refers him to a vascular surgeon, Dr T, to discuss treatment to improve blood flow and relieve his pain. After noting that endovascular intervention is not an option for Mr F because of his severe common femoral disease, Dr T notes, “We can offer you major surgery to address your symptoms, but it won’t prolong your life. And if you have complications, it could shorten your life.” “I’ll take the risk of surgery,” Mr F responds. “Life with this much pain isn’t worth it. Maybe I’ll die during the surgery, and that’s OK.”
Mr F undergoes a left common femoral endarterectomy and lower extremity bypass graft. The long operation and significant blood loss generate major complications, including postoperative myocardial infarction and aspiration pneumonia requiring intubation. When Mr F is weaned from the ventilator after an extensive intensive care unit (ICU) stay, he has lost weight, is severely deconditioned, and has a decubitus pressure ulcer. Throughout Mr F’s decline, Dr T says, “I’ll get you through this.” Dr T feels guilty and sad about Mr F’s decline and difficult postoperative course. Dr T visits Mr F again after another bout of aspiration pneumonia requiring Mr F’s urgent transfer to the ICU for respiratory distress. “I’m so sorry to see you so sick, Mr F,” says Dr T. “If I’d known it would be like this,” says Mr F, “I never would have let you operate on me. You shouldn’t have offered me surgery if there was even a chance for things to turn out this way. You’re the expert, but I didn’t know any better.” Subsequently, Mr F declines intubation, transitions to comfort measures, and dies several hours later.
At the surgical morbidity and mortality (M and M) conference, Dr T presents Mr F’s case. “I feel terrible about how things turned out,” says Dr T, speaking in front of a room of surgeons. “From an operative standpoint, I’m not sure what I could have done better. Surgery was risky, but he was adamant he wanted to try. Complications of surgery unquestionably shortened and worsened his remaining lifetime. But how could I not have offered him surgery when I thought it could help him? What would you have done?” M and M conference attendees consider how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Mr F, an 80-year-old man, suffers from peripheral vascular disease with severe arterial insufficiency in his left leg. The pain in his foot is intense, often waking him at night, only subsiding when he dangles his foot over the edge of the bed. He has developed a small ulcer on his left big toe and sometimes resorts to sleeping in his recliner with his foot hanging down, using gravity to ease the discomfort. Alongside this, Mr F lives with emphysema and diabetes, and his medical history includes a major heart attack and several minor strokes. Aware of his declining health, both he and his primary care physician, Dr K, agree that he is “wearing out.” Mr F, who considers himself a “tough cookie,” recognizes his life expectancy is limited and consents to an out-of-hospital do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order.

Despite his stoicism, the pain in Mr F’s foot has become intolerable. Dr K refers him to Dr T, a vascular surgeon, to explore possible interventions for improving blood flow and relieving the pain. After evaluation, Dr T explains that less invasive endovascular procedures are not feasible due to Mr F’s extensive common femoral disease. Dr T tells him, “We can offer you major surgery to try to address your symptoms, but it won’t extend your life. If there are complications, it could even shorten it.” Mr F replies, “I’ll take the risk of surgery. Life isn’t worth living with this much pain. If I die during surgery, that’s okay.”

Mr F undergoes a left common femoral endarterectomy with lower extremity bypass grafting. The operation is lengthy and complicated by significant blood loss, leading to major postoperative challenges: a myocardial infarction and aspiration pneumonia, which require intubation and a stay in the intensive care unit (ICU). When Mr F is finally weaned off the ventilator after a prolonged ICU course, he is frail, has lost weight, is severely deconditioned, and now suffers from a pressure ulcer. Throughout his decline, Dr T offers reassurance, saying, “I’ll get you through this.” However, Dr T is troubled by guilt and sadness over Mr F’s difficult recovery and setbacks.

After another episode of aspiration pneumonia, Mr F is urgently transferred back to the ICU with respiratory distress. Dr T visits him and says, “I’m so sorry to see you so sick, Mr F.” Mr F responds, “If I’d known it would be like this, I never would have let you operate on me. You shouldn’t have offered me surgery if there was even a chance it would end up this way. You’re the expert—I didn’t know any better.” Mr F decides against further intubation, choosing instead to focus on comfort measures, and dies several hours later.

At the surgical morbidity and mortality (M and M) conference, Dr T presents Mr F’s case. Speaking before the assembled surgeons, Dr T confesses, “I feel terrible about how things turned out. From a surgical perspective, I’m not sure what I could have done better. The surgery was risky, but he was adamant about wanting to try. There’s no doubt that the complications shortened and worsened his remaining life. But how could I not have offered surgery when I thought it might help? What would you have done?” The M and M conference attendees reflect on how they might respond.

ethical_issues.question: When evaluating surgical interventions, how can clinicians ensure that the patient’s treatment goals are fully understood and aligned with the proposed surgical plan?
keypoints: Utilize communication tools such as the “best case/worst case” framework to thoroughly discuss the patient’s treatment goals, preferences regarding life-sustaining treatments, and acceptable treatment burdens preoperatively, ensuring that surgical decisions are closely aligned with the patient’s values and wishes.

Clearly define plans for managing potential adverse events before surgery, especially for patients with life-limiting illness, by understanding their preferences in the event of disability or severe complications, thereby helping to avoid unwanted invasive interventions.

Integrate palliative care early to enhance patients’ understanding of their illness and treatment risks, optimize symptom management, alleviate psychological and spiritual distress, align treatment goals with patient preferences, and support complex medical decision-making.

Surgeons should respect patient autonomy and redefine surgical success as achieving outcomes consistent with the patient’s health goals and quality of life expectations, rather than solely focusing on prolongation of survival.

ethical_issues.question: Before high-risk surgery, how should physicians discuss patients’ preferences for postoperative life-sustaining treatments and possible prognostic outcomes?
keypoints: Physicians should utilize the “best case/worst case” communication tool to engage in detailed discussions with patients regarding possible postoperative prognoses and preferences for life-sustaining treatments.

Through scenario planning, patients can be assisted in anticipating adverse outcomes (such as prolonged intubation or functional decline), moving beyond a binary “alive/dead” framework to articulate their acceptance of varying qualities of life and the underlying personal values.

Discussing postoperative rescue measures and potential treatment limitations encourages patients to clarify which interventions they are willing to accept or refuse, aligning these decisions with their treatment goals and expectations for quality of life.

Preoperatively, it is essential to thoroughly understand and document the patient’s preferences concerning postoperative life-sustaining treatments, explicitly defining plans for managing severe complications or excessive treatment burdens to guide subsequent medical decisions and avoid unwanted interventions.

ethical_issues.question: How can palliative care be effectively integrated into the surgical management of patients like Mr F to support complex medical decision-making and ensure that treatment goals remain aligned with the patient’s values and preferences?
keypoints: Early identification of surgical patients requiring palliative care support through screening for frailty, serious chronic illnesses, and refractory symptoms.

Early integration of palliative care facilitates enhanced patient understanding of their disease and treatment risks, optimizes symptom management, alleviates psychological distress, and promotes alignment of treatment goals with patient preferences.

Utilization of communication tools such as the “best case/worst case” framework assists patients in anticipating possible surgical and recovery outcomes, clarifying interventions and treatment results they find unacceptable.

Palliative care support within a range of invasive treatment options helps coordinate expectations among the medical team, patients, and families, thereby optimizing complex medical decision-making processes.

Understanding patients’ treatment preferences in the context of disability or severe complications guides clinicians in making decisions that balance treatment burdens and benefits consistent with the patient’s values.

title: How Should Surgeons Communicate About Palliative and Curative Intentions, Purposes, and Outcomes?
case:
LL is a 66-year-old patient with a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. In consultation, Dr B recommended that LL undergo a Whipple pancreaticoduodenectomy and indicated that his “intention in doing this procedure is to cure your cancer.” There were no postoperative complications, and LL completed adjuvant chemotherapy. But 18 months later, surveillance computed tomography imaging revealed a 3 cm mass in LL’s right liver. Metastatic pancreatic cancer was confirmed by biopsy.
LL returned to see Dr B and asked why her operation wasn’t curative. Dr B explained that most often pancreatic cancer recurs and that the operation was palliative.
case_rewrite:
LL, a 66-year-old patient, was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head. During consultation, Dr B discussed the option of a Whipple pancreaticoduodenectomy. Dr B told LL, “My intention in recommending this surgery is to cure your cancer.” Following the operation, LL’s recovery was uncomplicated, and she completed a course of adjuvant chemotherapy. However, 18 months after the procedure, surveillance CT scans detected a 3 cm lesion in her right liver. Biopsy confirmed that the mass was metastatic pancreatic cancer.

LL returned to see Dr B and asked why the surgery had not cured her. Dr B explained that pancreatic cancer commonly recurs and stated that, in fact, the operation had been palliative in nature.

ethical_issues.question: How should surgeons avoid using ambiguous and misleading terminology when communicating the intentions and prognosis of pancreaticoduodenectomy to ensure informed consent?
keypoints: Physicians should avoid using ambiguous and potentially misleading terms such as "curative" and "palliative" when communicating about pancreaticoduodenectomy, ensuring that language accurately reflects the actual prognosis and objectives of the surgery.

Surgeons should emphasize informing patients about the predictable outcomes and specific therapeutic goals of the procedure, rather than focusing solely on the surgeon’s intention, to facilitate genuine informed consent.

Utilizing precision medicine and multiomic tumor data to assist in assessing individualized surgical benefits enables clinicians to provide more scientifically grounded and personalized prognostic information, supporting patients in making decisions aligned with their own values.

Optimizing the terminology and content used in informed consent discussions enhances the integrity and transparency of physician-patient communication, strengthens patient autonomy, and promotes patient-centered clinical practice.

ethical_issues.question: How can terminology be used to ensure that patients have an accurate understanding of the prognosis of pancreaticoduodenectomy in order to uphold the shared decision-making process?
keypoints: Physicians should avoid using ambiguous or potentially misleading terms such as “curative” and “palliative” when describing pancreaticoduodenectomy to ensure that patients have an accurate and realistic understanding of the surgical prognosis.

Physicians should adopt a patient-centered approach by clearly communicating the predictable outcomes and realistic therapeutic goals of pancreaticoduodenectomy, avoiding emphasis on the surgeon’s intention, so as to prevent terminological ambiguity from undermining patient autonomy and to safeguard informed consent or refusal by patients and their surrogates based on truthful information.

Utilizing precision medicine tools, including clinical and multiomic tumor data, can assist physicians in more accurately assessing the individualized benefits of surgery, thereby facilitating transparent and personalized communication with patients and enhancing the integrity of communication and the quality of informed consent.

ethical_issues.question: How should surgeons balance truthfulness and optimism when describing pancreaticoduodenectomy to enhance the integrity of communication and the quality of informed consent?
keypoints: Physicians should avoid using ambiguous and potentially misleading terms such as “curative” and “palliative” when describing pancreaticoduodenectomy to ensure that patients receive accurate and clear information.

Physicians should emphasize informing patients about the predictable outcomes and realistic therapeutic goals of the surgery, rather than focusing solely on the surgeon’s intention, thereby enhancing the quality of informed consent and supporting patient decisional autonomy.

By utilizing clinical and multiomic tumor data, physicians can more precisely assess the individualized benefits of surgery and communicate with patients based on prognosis, facilitating evidence-based and personalized informed decision-making.

The core value of adjusting communicative terminology lies in improving the integrity of communication and trust between physicians and patients, rather than altering the underlying poor prognosis of the disease, thereby clarifying the ethical boundaries and objectives of communication.

title: How Should Surgical Palliative Success Be Defined?
case:
“All I want from life is the opportunity to have sex with my wife, and without this,” said Mr J, tearful and despondent, pointing to an ostomy appliance attached to his abdominal wall. Following initial diagnosis of rectal cancer several years ago, Mr J underwent chemoradiation followed by proctectomy and ileorectal anastomosis, with a “protective” diverting ileostomy to reduce risk of anastomotic leak. Mr J felt initially led to believe that the ileostomy was temporary. Despite assistance from enterostomal therapists, Mr J was extremely distressed about ostomy leakage during sex and felt dismissed when someone told him he needed to learn to live with it.
After developing bilateral pulmonary metastases, Mr J chose to undergo palliative systemic chemotherapy. During that time, his disease remained stable, and he felt frustrated by not being able to convince his 2 prior surgeons to reverse his ileostomy. The first surgeon, Dr S, performed the protectomy and ileostomy and told Mr J that temporary suspension of chemotherapy to treat metastatic disease for the sake of reversing his ileostomy was not a good idea. After much discussion with Mr J, Dr S sympathized and sought to help Mr J adapt to life with the ileostomy but could not agree to reverse it. The second surgeon, Dr T, agreed with Dr S that there was no clinical indication to reverse his ileostomy, given that he was adequately hydrated and had no electrolyte imbalances, and agreed with Dr S that reversal would not be a good decision.
Mr J sought the opinion of a third surgeon, Dr Q, to whom he was referred by his primary care clinician. Dr Q and Mr J had a lengthy conversation. Dr Q saw no reason to question Mr J’s capacity to make health decisions for himself; felt Mr J had a solid understanding of an ileostomy takedown procedure’s prospective benefits and risks for complications and how possible complications could compromise his survival; and felt that ileostomy reversal expressed Mr J’s values and quality-of-life (QOL) priorities. Dr Q is aware of Dr T’s and Dr S’s refusals to reverse Mr J’s ileostomy and considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
“All I really want is to be able to be intimate with my wife again, but I can’t do that with this,” Mr J said, his voice trembling as he gestured to the ostomy appliance fastened to his abdomen. Years earlier, after being diagnosed with rectal cancer, Mr J had undergone chemoradiation followed by a proctectomy and ileorectal anastomosis, with a so-called “protective” diverting ileostomy created to reduce the risk of an anastomotic leak. At the time, Mr J was left with the strong impression that this ileostomy would be temporary. Despite working closely with enterostomal therapists, he continued to struggle with profound distress about the possibility of ostomy leakage during sexual activity. He felt especially disregarded when a caregiver told him he simply needed to learn to live with it.

After the cancer later spread to both of his lungs, Mr J opted to pursue palliative systemic chemotherapy. His disease stabilized, but frustration mounted as he failed to persuade two different surgeons to consider reversing his ileostomy. Dr S, the surgeon who performed his original operation, explained that pausing chemotherapy to address the metastatic disease in order to reverse the ileostomy would not be advisable. Dr S, after many conversations with Mr J, expressed empathy and tried to help him adjust to life with the ostomy, but ultimately could not agree to reversal. Dr T, a second surgical consultant, concurred with Dr S’s opinion—there was no clinical indication for reversal, since Mr J was well hydrated and did not have electrolyte disturbances, and Dr T also felt that reversal would not be in Mr J’s best interest.

Unwilling to give up, Mr J sought out a third opinion from Dr Q, after being referred by his primary care clinician. Mr J and Dr Q engaged in a lengthy, thoughtful discussion. Dr Q saw no grounds to question Mr J’s capacity for making his own healthcare decisions, and believed that Mr J had a clear understanding of both the potential benefits and the risks of complications associated with ileostomy takedown, including how these complications might impact his survival. Dr Q recognized that seeking reversal was consistent with Mr J’s values and his personal priorities for quality of life. Aware of Dr S’s and Dr T’s previous refusals to reverse the ileostomy, Dr Q carefully considered how best to respond to Mr J’s request.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient’s quality of life priorities conflict with the clinician’s determination of optimal therapeutic efficacy, how should the core concerns of the patient be balanced with clinical rationality in medical decision-making?
keypoints: Medical decision-making should shift from paternalistic authority to shared decision-making, respecting patient autonomy and practicing patient-centered care.
Surgical palliative care should be guided by the primary goals from the patient’s perspective, prioritizing the patient’s quality of life and values.

Through discussion of expectations during the informed consent process, clinicians should deeply explore the patient’s underlying motivations and anticipated outcomes, using the patient’s self-assessment of quality of life as the central basis for goal setting and defining success.

ethical_issues.question: In surgical palliative care, how can patients’ psychosocial and spiritual needs be adequately recognized and addressed?
keypoints: Surgeons should abandon paternalistic authority, practice shared decision making, respect and uphold patient autonomy, and give full attention to patients’ psychosocial and spiritual needs.
Patient-centered care should be responsive to individual patient preferences, needs, and values, with surgical treatment goals guided by the patient’s perspective and quality-of-life priorities.

In palliative care, clinicians should proactively explore the patient’s definition of surgical success, clarify the primary goals of palliation, and address the complexity of decision making through communication about expectations.
The effectiveness of palliative surgery should be evaluated primarily based on patient-reported improvements in quality of life and symptom relief, rather than solely on traditional surgical metrics.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient requests a specific surgical intervention to improve quality of life, how can the informed consent process ensure that the patient comprehends the potential risks and benefits of the surgery and actively participates in shared decision-making?
keypoints: Surgeons should respect patient autonomy and ensure through a shared decision-making process that patients fully understand the potential risks, benefits, and impacts on quality of life associated with surgery.

During the informed consent process, clinicians should thoroughly explore how patients define surgical success, centering decision making on patients’ self-assessments of quality of life and their values, thereby ensuring that the treatment plan aligns with the patient’s priorities and expectations.

Physicians should employ discussions of expectations, integrating the palliative triangle model, to systematically review the short- and long-term effects of surgery, potential complications, and therapeutic trade-offs, thereby assisting patients in rationally confronting the complexity of the decision.

Both patients and clinicians should engage in multidimensional communication and emotional support grounded in the patient’s quality-of-life goals and palliative care principles, fostering collaborative decision making among the patient, family members, and the healthcare team.

title: How Should Clinicians and Organizations Assess Risks and Benefits of First-in-Human Implantation of Investigational Devices?
case:
A hospital purchasing committee is considering contracting with a company that produces an artificial lumbar spinal disc. The literature cited within the disc manufacturer’s proposal claims that, compared to lumbar fusion, the benefits of the disc include earlier hospital discharge, a quicker return to work, and fewer opioids to manage postoperative pain. Several members of the committee, however, raise the concern that the disc could collapse and migrate, which would require further surgeries.
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the disc via the 510(k) pathway, which does not require clinical testing data. Instead, clearance is based on “substantial equivalence” to a predicate device on the assumption that the benefit-risk profile of the new device will be similar to the predicate device’s profile. A new device is substantially equivalent to the predicate device if the new device has the same intended use as the predicate device and either (1) has the same technological characteristics as the predicate or (2) has different technological characteristics but does not raise different questions of safety and effectiveness and the information submitted for clearance demonstrates comparable safety and effectiveness.
Several members of the committee disagree about whether the 510(k) process provides sufficient assurance of device effectiveness and safety and, on that basis, disagree about entering into a purchasing contract with the device manufacturer. It should be noted, however, that in the presentation of the hypothetical case, no information is provided on the predicate or differences between the predicate and the current product (although it might be reasonable for the committee to seek out that information before making its decision).
case_rewrite:
Dr. W sits at the head of the hospital’s purchasing committee as they review a proposal from a company manufacturing a new artificial lumbar spinal disc. The manufacturer’s presentation touts advantages over traditional lumbar fusion surgery, referencing published literature that claims their disc enables patients to leave the hospital sooner, return to work faster, and reduce their need for opioid pain medications after surgery. However, SB, another committee member, expresses concern about the device’s potential drawbacks. SB points out that the artificial disc could collapse or migrate after implantation, possibly necessitating additional surgeries—complications that could put patients at further risk.

The committee pays close attention to the regulatory history of the device. The disc was cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) through the 510(k) pathway, a process that does not require new clinical trial data but instead relies on the concept of “substantial equivalence” to an existing predicate device. This means the disc was approved based on its intended use and technological similarities—or, if different, a lack of new safety or effectiveness concerns—compared to a prior device. Yet, the committee notes that the manufacturer’s proposal does not specify what the predicate device is or how similar this new disc is to its predecessor, information that Dr. W and others believe is essential for making an informed purchasing decision.

Committee members debate whether the 510(k) pathway provides a sufficient guarantee of the disc’s safety and effectiveness. While some argue that FDA clearance should be enough to justify a contract, others, like SB, worry about the lack of clinical trial data and the associated uncertainties. Dr. W suggests that, rather than entering a bulk purchasing agreement, the hospital should consider making the device available only on a case-by-case basis. In this approach, the device would be procured when an attending physician can demonstrate that a specific patient is likely to benefit and that the potential risks are manageable.

The discussion turns to how these uncertainties should be communicated to patients. Dr. W emphasizes the ethical obligation to ensure that patients are fully informed about the nature of the device’s approval process—including the absence of robust clinical trial data and the unknowns this creates regarding long-term safety and effectiveness. The committee agrees that clinicians must engage patients in shared decision making, clearly outlining the risks, benefits, and limitations of the artificial disc compared to established treatments. Patients’ individual risk tolerance, preferences, and understanding of the device’s uncertainties should guide the final treatment decision, thereby respecting patient autonomy and avoiding paternalistic judgments.

SB raises concerns about equitable access, noting that patients in rural or under-resourced settings should not be denied potential benefits of the device, but also cautions against its disproportionate use among vulnerable populations—such as patients of color—without thorough informed consent. The committee discusses the importance of ensuring that all patients, regardless of background or financial capacity, have access to the same information and safeguards. They agree that special caution is warranted for patients who might struggle to afford additional treatments if complications arise, and that the hospital must remain vigilant against conflicts of interest and ensure close follow-up after implantation to monitor for adverse events and report them promptly to regulatory authorities.

As the meeting concludes, Dr. W and SB agree that the committee must balance innovation with patient safety and justice. They resolve that any future use of the artificial disc must be grounded in transparent communication, case-by-case evaluation, and an unwavering commitment to informed patient choice.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians and healthcare organizations weigh the risks and benefits of investigational devices to ensure patient safety and effective treatment?
keypoints: Hospitals should avoid bulk purchasing of 510(k) medical devices that lack key clinical data, adopting a case-by-case decision-making approach and procuring the device only when the attending physician can demonstrate that the patient is likely to benefit and that the risks are manageable.

Physicians should clearly communicate to patients the nature and relevant details of the clinical testing underlying the device’s market clearance, emphasizing the uncertainty regarding the device’s safety and effectiveness; this uncertainty itself constitutes a risk that patients must be fully informed of and voluntarily accept.

Clinicians should engage in shared decision making to understand the patient’s individual risk tolerance and comprehension of the limitations of the device, thereby respecting and upholding patient autonomy and avoiding unilateral subjective judgments about the patient’s best interests.

When uncertainties exist regarding device use, clinicians and healthcare organizations should proactively disclose these uncertainties to patients, restrict financial relationships that may give rise to conflicts of interest, and conduct close post-implantation follow-up to promptly report safety information to regulatory authorities.

ethical_issues.question: How can equitable access to 510(k)-cleared devices be ensured for patients while preventing overuse and potential harm to vulnerable populations, thereby upholding the ethical principle of justice?
keypoints: Ensure equitable access to 510(k)-cleared devices for patients in rural and resource-limited settings, thereby promoting balanced distribution of healthcare resources.

Prevent the disproportionate use of 510(k)-cleared devices in potentially vulnerable populations, such as patients of color, without adequate informed consent, safeguarding the authenticity and sufficiency of the consent process.
Uphold the ethical principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence by ensuring that equitable access to new devices does not expose patients to unnecessary risks or harm.

Clinicians should carefully evaluate the potential benefits and risks of 510(k)-cleared devices compared to established alternatives based on individual patient risk profiles, with particular attention to circumstances that may increase the risk of device-related harm.

Exercise heightened caution when considering the use of 510(k)-cleared devices in patients with limited financial capacity who may be unable to afford subsequent treatment costs in the event of serious adverse events, in order to prevent exacerbating patient burden and harm.

ethical_issues.question: When using 510(k)-cleared devices, how should clinicians ensure that patients provide adequate informed consent and understand the risks of the device as well as alternative treatment options?
keypoints: Clinicians should engage in shared decision making, respect patient autonomy, and understand patients’ risk tolerance and cognitive capacity.
Clinicians should ensure that patients have a comprehensive understanding of the known risks and benefits of the proposed device and its alternatives, thereby facilitating informed patient choice.

Patients need to understand the limitations of the 510(k) clearance process, recognizing that this pathway does not require clinical trial data and may entail insufficient evidence regarding safety and effectiveness.
The initial uncertainty regarding some risks and benefits of the device constitutes a risk in itself, which patients must be fully informed of and voluntarily accept.

Physicians should clearly communicate to patients the nature of any clinical testing (if any) underlying the device’s market approval and provide relevant safety and effectiveness information, so as to avoid patients being unable to accurately assess their treatment options due to insufficient information.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Clinician relations with industry
title: What Should Patients Be Told About Device Representatives’ Roles at the Point of Surgical Care?
case:
Rep, a medical device representative for an orthopedic company, received a call from Dr N asking Rep to bring a specialized primary hip system and instrumentation for a patient with congenital dysplasia of the hip. Rep knew that Dr N had not previously worked with this implant, scheduled a time to meet Dr N and other resident physicians, and planned to perform a practice case using plastic foam pelvis and femur replicas. Upon arriving for the practice case, Dr N informed Rep that he did not need to perform the practice case. When Rep approached resident physicians working with Dr N and asked whether they would like to perform a practice case, they declined. Rep then tried to share with Dr N a training video illustrating the surgical technique, suggesting that Dr N review it over the weekend. Dr N declined and Rep agreed to be present for the case.
On the day of the case, Rep arrived in the operating room suite to find that the resident physicians had started the case. Dr N arrived and took over. Due to the unique shape of the acetabular cup Dr N wished to use, a specially designed reamer was needed for the cup. Dr N struggled with this reamer’s assembly and use and the seating of the cup; Dr N requested fluoroscopy to visualize the cup’s placement. After reviewing the fluoroscopy images, Dr N secured the cup. Dr N also encountered difficulty seating the liner and asked Rep to verify that the liner was properly seated. Positioned beyond the sterile field, Rep was unable to see the liner. After struggling for 15 minutes to properly secure the acetabular liner, Dr N started the process of implanting the femoral prosthesis. The femoral component’s unique design required Dr N to use special instruments to prepare the proximal femur for the prosthesis. Dr N struggled with the specialized instrumentation; to complete implantation of the femoral component, Rep held an illustration of the surgical technique and talked Dr N through each step. A trial reduction was completed, and the trial component was then replaced with the permanent femoral prosthesis.
case_rewrite:
Rep, a medical device representative for an orthopedic company, received a request from Dr N to bring a specialized primary hip system and the necessary instrumentation for a patient diagnosed with congenital hip dysplasia. Aware that Dr N had no prior experience with this particular implant, Rep arranged to meet with Dr N and several resident physicians for a hands-on practice session, planning to use plastic foam models of the pelvis and femur to simulate the procedure.

When Rep arrived for the scheduled practice, Dr N informed Rep that he did not feel the practice session was necessary. Attempting to ensure adequate preparation, Rep approached the resident physicians assisting Dr N and offered to conduct the practice case with them, but they also declined. Rep then suggested that Dr N review a training video demonstrating the surgical technique and recommended watching it over the upcoming weekend. Dr N declined this offer as well, but confirmed that Rep would be present during the actual surgery.

On the day of surgery, Rep arrived in the operating room to find that the resident physicians had already begun the procedure. Dr N entered shortly thereafter and assumed control of the case. The procedure involved the use of an acetabular cup with an unusual design, requiring a specially engineered reamer. Dr N encountered difficulty both assembling and using the reamer, as well as seating the cup properly. To address these challenges, Dr N requested intraoperative fluoroscopy to check the position of the cup. After reviewing the images, Dr N managed to secure the cup in place.

Dr N then struggled to seat the liner and asked Rep to confirm whether the liner was properly positioned. However, because Rep was situated outside the sterile field, he could not visually confirm the liner’s placement. After about 15 minutes of effort to secure the acetabular liner, Dr N proceeded to the next stage: implanting the femoral component. This component, having a unique design, required the use of specialized instruments to prepare the proximal femur. Again, Dr N found the instrumentation challenging. To assist, Rep stood at the edge of the operating room holding an illustration of the surgical technique and provided step-by-step verbal guidance to Dr N throughout the process. After a successful trial reduction, the team proceeded to replace the trial femoral component with the permanent prosthesis.

ethical_issues.question: How should the role of device representatives in the operating room be defined to ensure that it does not substitute for surgeons’ professional training and competence?
keypoints: The core responsibility of a device representative is to provide training resources and opportunities to surgeons and the surgical team, assisting with preoperative preparation, but not substituting for the surgical team’s preoperative training and development of technical competence.

The surgical team has the responsibility to undergo adequate preoperative training and demonstrate competence in the safe application of relevant instrumentation and techniques, thereby ensuring professionalism and safety in surgical procedures.

The presence of a device representative in the operating room must adhere to ethical duties of patient care, serving a technical support role without participating in clinical decision-making or substituting for the physician’s professional judgment.

Learning on the spot and relying on a device representative for real-time surgical guidance contravenes medical ethics; postponing training until the actual surgical procedure undermines the patient-clinician relationship and patient safety, and must be avoided.

ethical_issues.question: How can mechanisms be established to enable device representatives to raise concerns when they identify inadequate physician training and to receive support from both manufacturers and healthcare institutions?
keypoints: Establish collaboratively developed training requirements and standards that enable device representatives to promptly identify and raise concerns regarding surgeons’ inadequate training, ensuring that both manufacturers and healthcare organizations jointly support and assume corresponding responsibilities.

Clarify and promote diverse channels for reporting violations (including anonymous reporting) to guarantee that device representatives can freely and effectively express concerns when patient safety is at risk.

Strengthen communication and coordination mechanisms between manufacturers and healthcare organizations to address disconnects in the content, processes, and dissemination of training for new devices, ensuring that training information is conveyed accurately and in a timely manner.

Healthcare organizations should establish and continuously improve rigorous training and continuing education systems to ensure that all clinicians possess the necessary technical proficiency and operational competence, thereby enhancing clinical safety and outcomes for patients receiving new materials or devices.

title: What Do Clinicians and Organizations Owe Patients With Recalled Implanted Devices or Materials?
case:
As of January 2020, 733 cases of breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) had been reported to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), with a large majority of those cases involving textured breast implants manufactured by one company.In response, the FDA requested that the company voluntarily withdraw its textured breast implants and tissue expanders from the market.The company sent Urgent Medical Device Recall letters to US customer surgeons, instructing them to return all unused products to a third-party recall provider, and sent notification letters to patients.
Dr W is a plastic surgeon who has implanted textured breast implants in patients, but not those manufactured by the company in question. Dr W’s retired practice partner and friend, Dr X, did implant this company’s textured breast implants in patients, many of whom still live locally. Stimulated by local news coverage of the textured breast implant recall, hundreds of her own and Dr X’s patients have been calling to request appointments to discuss the risks and benefits of implant removal and replacement and whether they require increased monitoring.
case_rewrite:
By January 2020, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had received 733 reports of breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), the vast majority of which were linked to textured breast implants produced by a specific manufacturer. In response to these findings, the FDA requested that the manufacturer voluntarily withdraw its textured breast implants and tissue expanders from the market. The company subsequently issued Urgent Medical Device Recall letters to surgeons across the United States, instructing them to return all unused products to a designated third-party recall provider, and also sent notification letters directly to affected patients.

Dr W is a plastic surgeon who has placed textured breast implants in patients, but none sourced from the implicated manufacturer. However, Dr W’s close friend and former practice partner, Dr X—now retired—did utilize the recalled textured implants in a number of patients, many of whom still reside in the local area. Following widespread news coverage of the textured breast implant recall, Dr W’s office has been inundated with calls from both her own patients and those previously under Dr X’s care. Hundreds of women are now requesting appointments to discuss the implications of the recall, seeking guidance on the risks and benefits of removing or replacing their implants, and asking whether they should undergo increased medical monitoring. The situation has compelled Dr W to navigate complex conversations with concerned patients, balancing the need to provide clear, up-to-date information with an understanding of the personal and financial ramifications they face, all while helping them make informed decisions about their health in the wake of the recall.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of breast implant recalls, how should clinicians balance patient education and financial considerations to assist patients in making informed decisions?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize providing accurate information, clearly explaining the nature of the recall and its clinical implications, emphasizing that proactive removal of already implanted devices is not currently required, thereby helping patients develop a rational understanding of the risks.

Physicians need to thoroughly describe the risks of breast implant explantation, potential postexplantation aesthetic changes, and alternative options, while integrating current knowledge limitations and the latest literature to assist patients in comprehensively weighing benefits, risks, and uncertainties.

Physicians should proactively communicate the impact of financial considerations on patient decision making, clarify insurance coverage and potential economic burdens, and offer reasonable plastic surgical care recommendations to support patients in making choices aligned with their individual circumstances.

Through respecting patients, enhancing education, and promoting shared decision making, physicians can strengthen patients’ autonomy and sense of control, thereby providing psychological support and actionable plans amid the recall event.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr W and other clinicians apply principles of shared decision making and multidisciplinary collaboration to uphold patient autonomy and trust when managing patients affected by breast implant recall events?
keypoints: Physicians should engage in shared decision making to acknowledge and understand patients’ health concerns, comprehensively consider individual patient circumstances and preferences, thereby strengthening the physician-patient relationship, optimizing quality of care, and enhancing patient satisfaction and trust.

Patient education should demonstrate physicians’ concern and professional expertise, transparently communicate the limitations and uncertainties of current knowledge, assist patients in understanding the clinical implications of the recall event, support informed decision making, and enhance patient autonomy and empowerment.

Multidisciplinary management and ongoing care, including routine breast cancer surveillance and health management beyond the perioperative period, contribute to comprehensively addressing patient needs and improving overall quality of care and patient trust.

Physicians should assist patients in developing concrete action plans to address the risks and complications associated with explantation surgery, thereby reinforcing patients’ sense of control and security in an uncertain environment.
