title: What Should Physician-Researchers Tell Patient-Subjects About Their Relationships With Industry?
case:
Dr M is a senior resident physician conducting research on a vagal nerve stimulator (VNS) with supervision from the attending physician and principal investigator, Dr A. The VNS was initially approved as a device for a specific indication and application by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) following clinical trials. Anecdotal reports from subjects in those clinical trials suggest that VNS might also be helpful for another indication, so the device’s manufacturer, Company K, suggested that a novel off-label application of the VNS be investigated by Drs M and A. This new clinical trial is federally funded and also supported financially by Company K. Dr A has received numerous research grants, dinners, and speakers’ fees from Company K.
Dr M asks Dr A about the nature and scope of what they need to disclose to subjects during informed consent in order to comply with the Physician Payments Sunshine Act. This law requires manufacturers to report all payments to physicians and for physicians to either confirm or dispute and correct the data within 60 days of it being posted.
“Nothing,” responds Dr A to Dr M. “That law applies to manufacturers, not to physicians and patients.”
“Well, that’s true, but if you were going to enroll in our study, wouldn’t you want to know?” Dr M continues.
“I guess I’m not sure what exactly you think patients should be told,” says Dr A. “I mean, how much detail is necessary? In the VNS world, there are a limited number of experts, folks like us, to research new technologies like this device. We have financial ties to these companies because if we don’t, we help these companies for free. So, of course, we have financial ties to these companies. And, of course, we can’t recuse ourselves from decisions affected by ties to these companies because we are the ones best positioned to try to help these subjects, and we are the ones with the expertise needed to take good care of patients who can benefit from new VNS devices. So, Dr M, I do see your concern. I see what you’re saying about disclosure. But when you have limited time with patients, it’s hard to clarify everyone’s interests. I try just to keep things simple when I talk with patients, and I try to keep the focus on what’s at stake for them. If you can think of a better, clearer way for us to be as transparent as we can with our patient-subjects, we can talk about your ideas, but I’ve been doing this for a long time, and this is the best I’ve come up with. Does that help, Dr M?”
“Yes,” says Dr M. Dr M still wonders, however, what their patient-subjects should be told about Dr A’s relationships with Company K before enrolling them in the VNS trial.
case_rewrite:
Dr M, a senior resident physician, is working on a research study involving a vagal nerve stimulator (VNS) under the supervision of Dr A, who is both the attending physician and principal investigator. The VNS device originally received FDA approval for a particular medical indication following a series of clinical trials. However, during those trials, some participants shared anecdotal experiences suggesting the VNS might benefit another condition. Encouraged by these reports, Company K, the device’s manufacturer, recommended that Drs M and A investigate this novel, off-label use of the device. The new clinical trial is funded by federal grants and also receives financial support from Company K. Dr A has a history of accepting research grants, sponsored dinners, and speaker honoraria from Company K.

As they prepare to recruit participants, Dr M approaches Dr A with a question about what needs to be disclosed to potential subjects regarding their financial relationships, especially in light of the Physician Payments Sunshine Act. This law requires manufacturers to publicly report all payments made to physicians, and allows physicians sixty days to review and correct these disclosures.

Dr A responds, “We don’t need to tell patients anything about that. The Sunshine Act is about manufacturers reporting to the government, not about what we have to say to patients.”

Dr M hesitates. “That may be so, but if you were a patient signing up for this study, wouldn’t you want to know about any financial ties your doctors had to the company funding it?”

Dr A considers this. “I understand what you’re getting at, Dr M. But how much detail do you think is necessary? In the VNS research community, there are only a handful of experts with the know-how to move these new technologies forward. Of course, we have relationships with these companies—if we didn’t, we’d be providing expertise for free. We can’t just recuse ourselves from studies like this; we’re the ones best equipped to look after these patients and advance the field. I get your concern about disclosure, but with limited time to spend with each patient, it’s not always practical to get into the weeds about everyone’s interests. I try to keep things straightforward for patients and focus on what’s most relevant to their care. If you have ideas for making our process clearer or more transparent, I’m open to them. But I’ve been doing this for years, and this is how I’ve handled it. Does that answer your question, Dr M?”

“It does, in a way,” Dr M replies. Still, Dr M is left wondering what, exactly, they owe their patient-subjects when it comes to informing them about Dr A’s—and by extension their own—financial connections with Company K before enrolling participants in the VNS study.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians disclose their financial relationships with industry to patient-subjects during the informed consent process?
keypoints: Investigators should disclose to patient-subjects during the informed consent process any significant financial relationships with industry to ensure that subjects can make autonomous decisions about participation based on adequate information.

Financial interest disclosure should be an integral part of the informed consent process and included in all written consent materials, with the specific wording determined by the Institutional Review Board (IRB).

The disclosure should clearly state that the relevant financial interests have been reviewed and managed by the Conflict of Interest Committee and the IRB, and have been determined not to pose any additional significant risk to the welfare of subjects or to the integrity of the research.

Transparent disclosure of financial relationships helps promote research transparency and enhances subjects’ trust in investigators and the research process, consistent with the ethical standards of medicine.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of financial relationships between investigators and industry, how can the trust and informed consent rights of research subjects be ensured?
keypoints: Investigators should comprehensively disclose their financial interests with industry to patient-subjects during the informed consent process to safeguard subjects’ right to know and their autonomous decision-making.
Disclosure of financial interests helps promote research transparency, enhances and maintains subjects’ trust in investigators, and reflects ethical responsibility.

Informed consent documents should explicitly include the specifics of financial interest disclosures, with the wording determined by the Institutional Review Board (IRB), and should state that the relevant interests have been reviewed and overseen by the conflict of interest committee to ensure no additional significant risk to subjects’ welfare or research integrity.

Transparent disclosure aligns with medical ethical standards; although the actual effectiveness of disclosure in reducing bias remains uncertain, this uncertainty should not justify foregoing disclosure.

Beyond disclosure, reducing or eliminating investigators’ financial ties to industry constitutes a more fundamental and effective strategy to mitigate the risk of bias arising from conflicts of interest and to ensure research integrity.

ethical_issues.question: How should investigators manage or eliminate conflicts of interest with industry when conducting clinical trials in order to ensure research integrity?
keypoints: Researchers should disclose significant financial interests to their institutions so that the institution can identify, manage, or eliminate conflicts of interest and ensure research integrity.

Conflicts of interest are typically addressed by institutional committees, such as the IRB; common management strategies include disclosure of conflicts of interest in publications or requiring data analysis to be conducted by investigators without conflicts of interest.

Disclosure of conflicts of interest to subjects helps promote transparency and respect for informed consent, but reducing or eliminating conflicts of interest themselves is a more effective way to minimize the risk of research bias. When disclosing, both transparency and communication efficiency should be balanced to ensure that subjects understand the financial relationships and their potential impact.

title: How Should Willingness-to-Pay Values of Quality-Adjusted Life-Years Be Updated and According to Whom?
case:
A willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), is a value used to represent “an estimate of what a consumer of health care might be prepared to pay for the health benefit” and is often based on a country’s per capita gross domestic product.In the United States, a WTP threshold of $50 000 to $100 000 is still referenced and used today by public and private policymakers, insurers, and researchers, for example, despite having been established in 1982.
One health care organization’s executive, Dr CXO, has suggested, “Given how insurers and other third-party payers in the US health care system rely on population-based WTP thresholds to guide decisions, we should probably be leerier of using estimates that are so old.”
Dr CXO continued, “If a patient or that patient’s physician, for example, asked me why we’ve been using decades-old value estimates to determine, say, what a patient’s additional quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) might be worth, I don’t think I’d be able to come up with a very convincing answer.”
Dr CXO then assembled a long-term task force charged with updating the WTPs the organization uses, particularly as they relate to QALYs. How the WTPs should be updated is, however, unclear to task force members as they begin to deliberate.
case_rewrite:
A willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold, as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO), estimates what a health care consumer might be willing to pay for a particular health benefit, and is commonly based on a country’s per capita gross domestic product. In the United States, a WTP threshold of $50,000 to $100,000 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) continues to be used by policymakers, insurers, and researchers, despite being set in 1982.

Within one major health care organization, Dr CXO, an executive, has raised concerns. “Given that insurers and other third-party payers in the US health care system rely on population-based WTP thresholds to make important decisions, shouldn’t we be cautious about using estimates that are decades old?” Dr CXO noted further, “If a patient or a physician were to ask me why we’re relying on these outdated estimates to determine, for instance, the dollar value of a patient’s additional QALY, I don’t think I could give a very satisfactory answer.”

Recognizing the importance of this issue, Dr CXO formed a long-term task force to review and update the WTP thresholds the organization uses, with particular attention to their application to QALYs. As the task force began its work, however, members realized that it was not at all clear how these WTP values should be revised or what ethical and methodological issues should guide their deliberations.

As discussions unfolded, some task force members questioned whether the QALY, as a unified measure, truly captures the dual value individuals with impaired health-related quality of life place both on extending life and on improving quality of life. There was concern that, by combining life extension and quality-of-life improvement into a single score capped at 1.0, the QALY framework risks undervaluing the distinct and significant importance patients assign to both aspects, especially for those living with chronic or severe health impairments.

The group debated whether, to address these ethical shortcomings, WTP values for life-years and for quality-of-life improvements should be separated—rather than merged—so the unique value of each could be properly recognized. Some argued that the value of a life-year should not be constrained by the quality adjustment factor, which can diminish the prioritization of life extension in certain health states, and that the theoretical and ethical underpinnings of the QALY itself deserved careful reexamination, not just the numerical threshold.

Throughout these deliberations, several task force members emphasized that updating the WTP threshold should not be a purely technical exercise. Dr CXO and others insisted that patients’ real preferences and experiences must be at the center of any reform, as patients are the ones who actually live with the consequences of health states. They stressed that core data should reflect patient-reported values, and that the structure of the QALY, by restricting the combined value of life extension and quality-of-life improvement, risks misrepresenting these values. The phenomenon of adaptation—patients’ ability to find meaning and value in life even in states others might rate as low quality—was cited as further evidence that the intrinsic value of life should not be diminished by quality-of-life adjustments.

As the task force moved forward, it became clear to Dr CXO and the team that simply updating the dollar value of the WTP threshold would be insufficient. The whole WTP/QALY assessment framework required critical review and ethical improvement to ensure that it truly reflected patient values and met modern standards for fairness and transparency. Dr CXO was determined that the organization should be open with patients and physicians about the limitations of the current system, and that their process for updating WTP and QALY methodology should prioritize both threshold adjustment and deeper reform, so that future health care resource allocation would better align with patient interests and ethical imperatives.

ethical_issues.question: How should the ethical flaw be addressed that the QALY, as a unified measure of health benefit, fails to accurately reflect the dual value that individuals with impaired health-related quality of life place on both life extension and quality-of-life improvement?
keypoints: As a unified unit of health benefit, the fundamental structure of the QALY fails to adequately reflect the dual value trade-offs that individuals with impaired health-related quality of life assign to both life extension and quality-of-life improvement.

To address the ethical shortcomings of the QALY, willingness-to-pay (WTP) values for life-years and for health-related quality-of-life improvements should be established separately, thereby avoiding the conflation of these distinct values into a single scale.

The value of a life-year should not be jointly constrained with the value of quality-of-life improvement by a maximum limit of 1.0, as this risks diminishing the priority of life extension in certain health states due to the quality adjustment factor.

The long-term task force should not only update the WTP thresholds but also undertake a systematic reexamination and revision of the theoretical foundations and ethical limitations inherent in the QALY.

ethical_issues.question: How should patients’ preferences and values be prioritized when updating the willingness-to-pay threshold for quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs)?
keypoints: Health care should prioritize the preferences of patients, as they are the actual experiencers of health states; core data must be based on patients’ real experiences and value judgments.

As a unified metric for measuring both quality of life and life extension, the structure of the QALY is flawed: by constraining the combined value of life extension and quality-of-life improvement to a maximum of 1.0, it fails to adequately reflect patients’ true preferences and the dual value they assign to both life extension and quality-of-life improvement.

The phenomenon of adaptation and patients’ perceptions of the value of life across different health states indicate that the intrinsic value of life itself should be regarded as relatively constant, and the priority of life extension should not be diminished due to lower quality-of-life adjustment values.

Therefore, when updating the willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold, it is necessary not only to adjust the numerical value of the threshold, but also to re-examine and improve the entire WTP/QALY assessment framework to ensure its ethical soundness and authentic reflection of patient values.

Dr. CXO and the task force should clearly communicate to patients and physicians that the current WTP/QALY system has fundamental problems; the updating process should address both threshold adjustment and methodological reform of the QALY, in order to promote health care resource allocation decisions that better align with patient interests and ethical standards.

title: How Should Economic Value Be Considered in Treatment Decisions for Individual Patients?
case:
Dr M is giving a lecture on biological therapies for ulcerative colitis (UC), an inflammatory disorder of the colon and rectum known for being expensive to treat and intrusive in the everyday lives of patients. Dr M explains that, for patients with moderate-to-severe disease, UC can be managed medically, since numerous drugs are available. Dr M emphasizes that, although newer biologic drugs seem to be more effective than older drugs, their costs are generally prohibitive. Moreover, newer biologics are not considered cost-effective, although there is wide variation in results of cost-effectiveness analyses for UC drugs, presented in the form of incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs).
A student in Dr M’s lecture asks, “What role should ICERs have in informing decisions about what to prescribe for a patient with UC? I’m trying to reconcile our obligation to recommend evidence-based care while avoiding unnecessary costs to our patients. If the evidence points to a drug that patients can’t afford, then how should we think about value-based care for these patients? It seems like most UC patients don’t really have access to value-based care.” Fellow students consider this comment and Dr M prepares to respond.
case_rewrite:
Dr M stands at the front of the lecture hall, discussing the complex landscape of biological therapies for ulcerative colitis (UC), a chronic inflammatory disease of the colon and rectum. She describes to her attentive audience how UC, especially in moderate-to-severe cases, can often be managed with an expanding array of medications. Dr M draws attention to the newer biologic drugs, noting their promising efficacy compared to older treatments but also emphasizing their substantial price tags. She points out that, despite their clinical advantages, these biologics are often considered not to be cost-effective, as demonstrated by the wide-ranging results of cost-effectiveness analyses, typically presented as incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs).

As Dr M pauses, a student raises a hand and asks, “What role should ICERs play in deciding which medication to prescribe for a patient with UC? I’m struggling to reconcile our duty to provide evidence-based care with our responsibility to shield patients from unnecessary financial burden. If the most effective drug isn’t affordable for the patient, how do we interpret ‘value-based care’ in this context? It seems like many patients with UC can’t really access value-based care if they can’t afford the most effective treatments.”

The question lingers in the room as fellow students exchange thoughtful looks. Dr M gathers her thoughts, preparing to address the challenge of integrating economic considerations, patient well-being, and the ethical imperatives inherent in clinical decision making.

ethical_issues.question: In treatment decisions for individual patients, how should economic value be integrated into the clinical and ethical assessments of evidence-based medicine and value-based care?
keypoints: Physicians’ primary ethical obligation is to promote the well-being of individual patients while simultaneously serving as responsible stewards of healthcare resources.
Cost-effectiveness represents an important form of evidence within evidence-based medicine and value-based care, and its application should ultimately aim to improve outcomes for individual patients.

ICERs provide information on the efficiency of treatment strategies at the population level, aligning with the ethical principle of maximizing health outcomes, but they should not be directly used to guide treatment decisions for individual patients.

When conflicts arise between the interests of individual patients and societal obligations regarding resource allocation, physicians’ primary responsibility is to prioritize the welfare of the patient before them.
Physicians should engage in open and transparent discussions with patients about treatment goals, preferences, and the risks of cost-related nonadherence to facilitate shared decision making.

Cost conversations should integrate patients’ actual financial burden and the overall economic value of treatment to assist patients in weighing therapeutic options and to prevent adverse medical outcomes related to economic hardship.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the economic burden on individual patients with cost-effectiveness considerations at the societal level in prescribing decisions?
keypoints: Physicians’ primary ethical obligation is to promote the well-being of individual patients, prioritizing the patient’s treatment needs rather than using societal-level cost-effectiveness as a direct basis for clinical decision making.
ICER analyses are based on average data from patient populations and are not intended to directly guide treatment choices for individual patients.

The process of shared decision making constitutes the ethical core of evidence-based medicine and value-based care; physicians should engage in transparent discussions with patients regarding treatment goals, preferences, and the risk of nonadherence related to cost.

The purpose of cost discussions is to assist patients in understanding the economic value of different treatment options, thereby supporting them in making choices that best align with their individual circumstances after weighing benefits and risks, ultimately improving individual patient outcomes rather than simply applying societal-level cost-effectiveness analyses.

title: A Womanist Approach to Caring for Patients With Empirically Unverifiable Symptoms
case: LL is 27 years old and has been experiencing fatigue, joint paint, insomnia, and muscle soreness since she was 19. She has visited many physicians during those 8 years but has not found symptom relief. Despite a family history of autoimmune disease, LL’s autoimmune serological panels have always been negative. She reports that, since onset of her symptoms as a teenager, different physicians have suggested she is “malingering” and has “conversion disorder,”diagnoses that have followed her for years in her health record. LL’s last physician added fibromyalgiato her list of diagnoses and prescribed amitriptyline, duloxetine, and psychological therapy for 8 weeks. Despite LL’s having diligently executed interventions as directed, her symptoms persist. LL decided not to return to her last physician, who accused LL of not taking her medications.Most recently, severe exhaustion, muscle tenderness, and spasms have kept LL home for 5 consecutive days, so LL now visits Dr E, a rheumatologist, for the first time in hopes that Dr E will see LL as a credible patient and help her find symptom relief.
case_rewrite:
LL, a 27-year-old Black woman, has endured persistent fatigue, joint pain, insomnia, and muscle soreness since she was 19. Over the past eight years, she has consulted numerous physicians but has yet to find lasting relief for her symptoms. Despite a significant family history of autoimmune disease, LL’s serological tests for autoimmune disorders have always returned negative. Throughout her journey, LL recounts that several doctors have suggested she is “malingering” or suffering from “conversion disorder,” and these labels have remained in her medical records for years.

Most recently, her previous physician added fibromyalgia to her diagnoses and prescribed a regimen including amitriptyline, duloxetine, and an eight-week course of psychological therapy. LL followed these recommendations meticulously, yet her symptoms continued unabated. When she returned for follow-up, this physician accused LL of non-adherence, asserting she must not be taking her medications as instructed. Feeling dismissed and misunderstood, LL chose not to return to that physician.

Now, after five consecutive days confined to her home by severe exhaustion, muscle tenderness, and spasms, LL seeks out Dr E, a rheumatologist, for the first time. She arrives at Dr E’s office hoping that, at last, she will be recognized as a credible patient and that her lived experience will be taken seriously. Above all, LL wishes for relief from her ongoing symptoms and for a physician who will listen to her narrative with respect and without bias.

ethical_issues.question: How can implicit racial bias and affinity bias be overcome in medical practice to achieve patient-centered care?
keypoints: Clinicians must identify and overcome implicit racial bias and affinity bias to ensure patient-centered care grounded in equality and respect.

A womanist ethic of care emphasizes centering patients’ subjective symptom experiences in clinical diagnosis and treatment, with particular attention to symptoms that are difficult to verify through traditional empirical methods, thereby reducing medical bias.

Health care professionals should unconditionally acknowledge the veracity of patients’ narratives, respect the existence of symptoms that are unmeasurable or invisible, and regard patients’ accounts as essential evidence for diagnosis and alleviation of invisible illness.

Practicing a womanist ethic of care requires going beyond empathy to actively engage in self-questioning and reflection, examining whether diagnostic and treatment decisions are influenced by bias, and ensuring equitable treatment of patients from diverse backgrounds.

Medical students and clinicians have an obligation to cultivate cultural humility and self-awareness, continuously reflecting on and correcting their own biases to prevent the marginalization or misunderstanding of illness experiences among Black women and other marginalized groups.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians acknowledge and respect the illness experiences of Black women and women of color as credible epistemic agents in clinical care to mitigate medical bias?
keypoints: In clinical diagnosis and treatment, applying a womanist ethic of care centers the patient’s lived experience within the clinical encounter to mitigate medical bias.

Black women and women of color should be recognized as credible knowers of their lived experiences and physical, mental, and spiritual health; acknowledging the veracity of their symptom narratives and incorporating these accounts into evidence considerations—especially in the absence of objective evidence—promotes equity in health outcomes.
Health care professionals must abandon condescending skepticism and thoughtfully consider the patient’s experience, even when symptoms are neither measurable nor visible.

Practicing a womanist ethic of care requires going beyond empathy to take concrete actions that challenge one’s own biases, including reflecting on whether the same diagnostic or treatment decisions would be made if the patient were oneself or a close family member.
Clinicians and medical students have an obligation to cultivate self-reflective awareness to overcome implicit racial and affinity biases, thereby achieving truly patient-centered care.

title: When Imaging Data Contradict a Patient’s Self-report, How Should Clinicians Proceed?
case:
JM is a 46-year-old woman who has lived with primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS) for over 20 years. She visits her neurologist, Dr N, regularly to review symptoms (mainly chronic fatigue, intermittent pain, right-side weakness, difficulty with word finding and recall, and spasticity) and revisit therapeutic options. She gets a magnetic resonance image (MRI) every year when she visits her neurologist and had her most recent MRI one month ago. JM has been taking glatiramer acetate injections as directed for the last 7 years, during which time her symptoms have not worsened and fewer than 5 new plaques have been visible on imaging during this therapy.
JM has been ambulating without gait disturbances and states that she’s been feeling better. JM attributes feeling better to a now 3-month-old regimen of daily exercise and eating a Mediterranean diet. “After a month of my new exercise and diet routine, I stopped the glatiramer acetate injections, and I feel so freed from having to do that to myself. And I feel terrific.”
“I’m so glad you’re feeling better,” Dr N says. On physical exam, JM’s symptoms have not worsened, and Dr N notices that JM certainly looks energized and content. Upon reviewing her MRI, however, Dr N noticed 2 new plaque lesions in her motor cortex, and she wonders what to say next.
case_rewrite:
JM, a 46-year-old woman, has been living with primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS) for over two decades. She has long been under the care of her neurologist, Dr N, whom she visits annually to monitor her symptoms—which include chronic fatigue, intermittent pain, right-sided weakness, difficulties with word finding and recall, and spasticity—as well as to discuss ongoing and potential treatments. Each visit includes a routine MRI scan to evaluate her disease progression, with her most recent MRI performed just a month ago.

For the past seven years, JM has adhered to a regimen of glatiramer acetate injections, during which her symptoms remained stable and fewer than five new plaque lesions appeared on her MRI scans. Recently, however, JM reports feeling noticeably better: she has been walking without any gait disturbances and attributes her improvement to a daily exercise routine and adherence to a Mediterranean diet, both of which she adopted three months ago. “After a month on my new exercise and diet plan, I stopped the glatiramer acetate injections,” she tells Dr N. “I feel so liberated not having to give myself those injections, and I feel terrific.”

Dr N listens attentively and responds, “I’m so glad you’re feeling better.” During her physical examination, Dr N observes that JM’s neurological symptoms have not worsened, and JM appears noticeably more energetic and content. However, when Dr N reviews the results of JM’s most recent MRI, she notes the appearance of two new plaques in JM’s motor cortex. With these findings in mind, Dr N pauses, uncertain about how best to address the discrepancy between JM’s positive self-report and the objective imaging evidence.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient’s self-report contradicts imaging data, how should clinicians balance patient autonomy and medical recommendations within the framework of shared decision making?
keypoints: Clinicians should integrate the patient’s subjective report with objective imaging data, comprehensively document both, and use them as the basis for formulating clinical recommendations.

When clinical data contradict the patient’s self-report, physicians should allocate time for a detailed explanation of the data and, when necessary, present the abnormal imaging findings to assist the patient in understanding the clinician’s concerns and the necessity of treatment during asymptomatic periods.
Physicians need to proactively explore the patient’s values and treatment goals related to clinical care, gaining in-depth insight into their preferences, expectations, and concerns.

Clinicians should empower patients to make informed and autonomous treatment decisions by explaining the risks and benefits of treatment options, utilizing patient decision aids, and having patients “teach back” their understanding of these risks and benefits.

In cases where the patient’s disease is novel or understudied and therapeutic benefits are uncertain, greater weight should be given to respecting patient autonomy, allowing the patient’s self-report to take precedence over empirical data.

When a patient refuses treatment in the absence of clinical symptoms, and when the therapeutic benefit is limited and associated with risks, foregoing treatment is reasonable; clinicians should support the patient’s rational choice and maintain a positive patient-physician relationship.

ethical_issues.question: In the absence of clinical symptoms but with imaging evidence of disease activity, how should clinicians explain the necessity of treatment to patients to ensure informed consent?
keypoints: Clinicians should integrate the patient’s subjective experience with objective imaging data, providing a detailed explanation of the presence of disease activity and the necessity of treatment during asymptomatic phases.
By presenting abnormal imaging findings and comparing test results with normal values, clinicians can help patients gain a visual and intuitive understanding of disease progression.
Actively eliciting the patient’s treatment preferences, personal values, expectations, and concerns through targeted questioning fosters patient-centered, bidirectional communication.
Communication with the patient should focus on the potential benefits of treatment and how these benefits may help achieve the patient’s core therapeutic goals.

Utilizing written, video, or online interactive patient decision aids promotes shared decision making and assists patients in comprehensively understanding the risks and benefits of various treatment options.

Ensuring patient comprehension of treatment risks and benefits by having the patient “teach back” their understanding allows clinicians to assess health literacy, promptly correct misunderstandings, and address any residual knowledge gaps.

ethical_issues.question: How can patient decision aids be effectively utilized in medical decision-making to enhance patients’ health literacy and autonomy?
keypoints: Utilize written, video, or interactive patient decision aids that are concise and easily readable (e.g., at an eighth-grade reading level), clearly presenting care options, risks, side effects, and potential benefits to promote patient education and enhance health literacy.

Clinicians should proactively provide patients with appropriate decision aids as a foundation for personalized care discussions grounded in the patient’s values and preferences, thereby supporting shared participation in medical decision making.

Integrate patient decision aids with the shared decision-making process to strengthen patients’ informed empowerment and autonomy, assisting them in making treatment choices that align with their individual wishes.

Clinicians must dedicate sufficient time and employ effective communication skills to ensure patient comprehension of the information provided, thereby facilitating improvements in health literacy and active engagement in healthcare decisions.

title: When Symptoms Aren’t Visible or Measurable, How Should Disability Be Assessed?
case:
CR is a 52-year-old woman who suffered a concussion in a car accident. CR struck the left side of her frontal bone against the car’s dashboard and was transported by ambulance to a hospital. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging ruled out hemorrhage, and imaging studies were negative. CR was scheduled for an outpatient visit with a local neurologist, Dr N, and was sent home with symptoms of headache, photophobia, nausea, and fatigue, which persisted. CR reported to Dr N about 1 week after the accident that she felt “hazy” and was crying a lot. Dr N encouraged CR to try to avoid stress, screens, and sensory overstimulation. CR used up her 2 weeks of vacation time to recover.
Now 1 year after the accident, CR’s postconcussive symptomsare ongoing. She reports to Dr T, her primary care physician, that she’s frustrated about not feeling able to return to work full time and to daily activities with family. She reports feeling guilty for resting, but sounds and light still frequently trigger disabling nausea and headaches. CRknows she needs time toheal, but she is concerned about losing her job, falling short on mortgage payments, and providing for her family. One problem is that CR’s job requires nearly constant screen interaction, which also triggers debilitating symptoms. CR states that her manager has asked her to “step it up” and adds, “I look fine, so people don’t understand what I am going through and are frustrated when it takes me so long to do things I used to do quickly.”
CR presents disability benefits forms to Dr T and asks for help completing these forms. Without reliable serological tests or imaging studies to quantify CR’s symptoms’ severity or help determine her prognosis, Dr T consults Dr N. Both physicians are unsure about whether postconcussive syndromeis a qualifying disability. They wonder how to respond to CR’s request for help with the forms.
case_rewrite:
CR, a 52-year-old woman, sustained a concussion when her car was involved in an accident, causing her to hit the left side of her forehead against the dashboard. Emergency responders brought her to the hospital, where both CT and MRI scans excluded hemorrhage or other acute brain injuries; the imaging results were unremarkable. CR was discharged home with persistent symptoms of headache, sensitivity to light, nausea, and fatigue, and was referred for an outpatient consultation with Dr N, a neurologist in her community.

About a week after the accident, CR saw Dr N and described feeling “hazy” and emotionally fragile, often crying without clear reason. Dr N recommended minimizing stress, avoiding screens, and limiting sensory overload. CR took two weeks of her available vacation time to rest and recover, but her symptoms persisted beyond this period.

A full year after the accident, CR continues to struggle with ongoing postconcussive symptoms. During a visit with Dr T, her primary care provider, she expresses frustration at not being able to resume her full work responsibilities or engage in normal family life. She voices feelings of guilt about needing to rest, while exposure to light and sounds frequently provokes severe headaches and nausea. CR is aware that her recovery requires patience, but she is increasingly anxious about job security, keeping up with mortgage payments, and supporting her family. Her job involves almost continuous use of screens, which intensifies her symptoms and makes work nearly impossible.

CR shares with Dr T that her manager has pressured her to “step it up,” remarking that because she appears outwardly healthy, colleagues have difficulty understanding her struggles and become impatient with her slower pace. She presents Dr T with disability benefits paperwork, requesting assistance in completing it. Lacking objective laboratory or imaging evidence to measure the severity of CR’s symptoms or predict her recovery, Dr T consults Dr N for guidance. Both physicians are uncertain whether postconcussive syndrome qualifies as a disability and are unsure how best to respond to CR’s request for help with the forms.

ethical_issues.question: When assessing the nature of disability in chronic illnesses, how should physicians consider issues of gender and racial inequity to ensure fair diagnosis and evaluation?
keypoints: Lack of diversity in research samples leads to gender and racial inequities, increasing the complexity and uncertainty of disability assessment for chronic illnesses.
Gender, race, and cultural background influence how patients express and manage pain and symptoms; physicians must take these differences into account to achieve equitable diagnosis.

Patients may conceal their disabilities due to concerns about discrimination, unemployment, or social marginalization, which can affect clinical judgment and disability determination in chronic illnesses.

Physicians should proactively identify and address systemic biases, integrate psychosocial factors, and adopt individualized, sensitive, and equitable assessment strategies to ensure fairness in disability evaluation.

title: How Should Clinicians Minimize Harms and Maximize Benefits When Diagnosing and Treating Disorders Without Biomarkers?
case:
J sobbed in frustration in Dr R’s office. After 4 years of unsuccessful treatment with an array of anti-tremor medications from her primary care physician and then a general neurologist, J had been referred to Dr R, a movement disorder specialist, for further evaluation. Based on a history and physical examination, Dr R diagnosed J with a functional movement disorder, a form of functional neurological disorder or conversion disorder. Initial referrals for treatment—to a psychotherapist for cognitive behavioral therapy and to a physical therapist for a motor reprogramming treatment protocol—had not gone well.
J felt like her caregivers had given up, and Dr R recognized J’s feelings of abandonment. J stated, “I’ve been having this shaking for 5 years now. I lost my job, and nobody wants to hire me once they see me shaking. The judge took my kids away. My last 2 doctors gave up on me and think I just make this up, and now you’re telling me to go see a psychotherapist and a physical therapist. The psychotherapist I saw before took one look at me shaking and kicked me out, and my insurance company won’t pay for physical therapy.”
Dr R responded, “Your tremor is having a terrible impact on your life, and it feels like people who are supposed to be helping you are turning their backs on you.” Dr R sat and continued, “I’m sorry that you’ve faced stigma and poor care on top of your illness. I’m not going to give up on you. I know you’re not making up these symptoms and that the suffering you’re experiencing is real. I want to work with you, so you can get your life back on track. How does that sound?”
J replied, “I’d like that.”
case_rewrite:
J wept in frustration in Dr R’s office. After four years of trying a variety of anti-tremor medications prescribed first by her primary care physician and then by a general neurologist, J had finally been referred to Dr R, a specialist in movement disorders, for a more thorough evaluation. After taking a careful history and performing a physical exam, Dr R concluded that J had a functional movement disorder, a type of functional neurological disorder—also known as conversion disorder. However, the initial treatment referrals—for cognitive behavioral therapy with a psychotherapist and for a motor retraining program with a physical therapist—had not yielded positive experiences.

J felt abandoned by her medical team, and Dr R was keenly aware of her sense of isolation. J expressed her distress: “I’ve been dealing with this shaking for five years. I lost my job because of it, and now no one will hire me once they see my hands. The judge took my kids away. My last two doctors gave up on me and think I’m faking it, and now you’re telling me to see a psychotherapist and a physical therapist. The psychotherapist I went to before took one look at my tremor and told me to leave, and my insurance won’t approve physical therapy.”

Dr R listened closely and replied, “Your tremor has had a devastating impact on your life, and it must feel like the people who are supposed to help are turning away from you.” Dr R continued, “I’m truly sorry that, on top of your illness, you’ve had to deal with stigma and inadequate care. I won’t give up on you. I understand that what you’re experiencing is real, and I know you’re not inventing these symptoms. I want to partner with you and help you reclaim your life. Would you be willing to work together?”

J wiped her tears and said, “I’d like that.”

ethical_issues.question: In the diagnosis and treatment of disorders without biomarkers, how can clinicians avoid stigmatization and minimize harm to patients?
keypoints: Describe symptoms and diagnoses transparently and respectfully with a focus on promoting patient engagement and autonomy, thereby enhancing patient trust and treatment adherence.
Respect patients’ experiences and preferences through empathic, nonjudgmental communication and person-centered language, deepening understanding of the individual patient’s perspective.

Rely on expert history taking and physical examination during the diagnostic process, take patient-reported symptoms seriously, and avoid unnecessary and potentially harmful tests and treatments to minimize patient harm.

Proactively seek interdisciplinary professional support, such as consult-liaison psychiatry and neurology, in complex clinical judgments to improve the quality and scientific rigor of diagnosis and treatment decisions.

Clinicians should assume an active advocacy role by facilitating patients’ access to social workers, patient organizations, and relevant support resources to mitigate the negative effects of systemic barriers and stigma.

Recognize and address the risks of stigma faced by patients with functional disorders, seriously engage with the associated ethical challenges, uphold the principle of nonmaleficence, and safeguard patient dignity and rights.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians provide effective diagnostic and treatment recommendations for patients with difficult-to-measure disorders while avoiding unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis?
keypoints: Clinicians should conduct comprehensive assessments of patients’ symptoms and concerns through professional history taking and physical examination, and, guided by rigorous clinical judgment, avoid unnecessary and potentially harmful tests and treatments in order to achieve a difficult balance.

Clinicians need to sincerely attend to patients’ perspectives and, drawing upon clinical experience and evidence-based medicine, establish a patient-centered therapeutic relationship, provide clear and strong diagnostic and treatment recommendations, and collaboratively interpret the nature and impact of symptoms in accordance with ethical principles.

When faced with complex clinical judgments, clinicians should actively seek interdisciplinary expertise, such as consult-liaison psychiatry and neurology, to optimize diagnostic and therapeutic strategies and patient care.

Diagnosis should facilitate evidence-based treatment or timely referral to specialists, employ best practices, educate other health care professionals, and alleviate patients’ sense of isolation through peer support and community resources.

title: Pharmacist and Prescriber Responsibilities for Avoiding Prescription Drug Misuse
case:
Ms D is one of 2 pharmacists at an Indian Health Service (IHS) unit in Oklahoma. Familiarity with community members who recently died by prescription medication overdose has prompted Ms D to focus more on preventing misuse and abuse of prescription medications. She has, for example, recently reviewed the Indian Health Manual’s pharmacy section, which outlines standards of practice and the mission to “ensure efficacious, safe, and cost-effective drug therapy.”Since her license to practice pharmacy is from the state of Ohio, Ms D also reviewed the Ohio Administrative Code’s State Board of Pharmacy section about prescribers’ and dispensing pharmacists’ “corresponding responsibility”to properly issue prescriptions to patients.
Ms D is processing a loperamide refill for Mr T, a 32-year-old Cherokee patient with chronic intermittent diarrhea. When viewing Mr T’s electronic health record, Ms D notices his history of opioid use disorder. She also sees that Mr T’s clinician, Dr O, has refilled the loperamide prescription 4 times over the last 3 months, and there was no documentation of symptom exacerbations during that time. Ms D wonders whether Mr T could be misusing loperamide to try to mimic effects of opioids.Ms D calls Dr O to discuss this possibility.
According to Dr O, Mr T’s history of substance use disorder is in the distant past. Dr O notes that it is also important for Mr T to have loperamide to manage his symptoms. Ms D is unconvinced, however, and states that dispensing loperamide could contravene Mr T’s best interests and violate her duties to this patient as explicated in the Indian Health Manual and Ohio Administrative Code. Exasperated, Dr O reminds Ms D that Mr T has no supplemental insurance, that Mr T does not have access to a hospital or other clinic within 2 hours of his home, and that the IHS pharmacy is his only source for obtaining loperamide.
Ms D and Dr O remain on the telephone line and wonder how to resolve their disagreement about whether it is appropriate to refill Mr T’s prescription.
case_rewrite:
Ms D serves as one of two pharmacists at an Indian Health Service (IHS) unit in Oklahoma. Recently, after learning about several community members who died from prescription medication overdoses, Ms D has become increasingly vigilant about preventing misuse and abuse of prescription drugs. She has proactively reviewed the pharmacy section of the Indian Health Manual, which defines the mission as ensuring “efficacious, safe, and cost-effective drug therapy” for patients. Additionally, since her pharmacy license is issued by the state of Ohio, Ms D has also examined the relevant section of the Ohio Administrative Code, which details the “corresponding responsibility” of both prescribers and pharmacists to ensure prescriptions are properly and appropriately issued.

One afternoon, Ms D is preparing to process a refill request for loperamide for Mr T, a 32-year-old Cherokee man with a history of chronic intermittent diarrhea. As she reviews Mr T’s electronic health record, she notes that he has a documented history of opioid use disorder. She also observes that Dr O, Mr T’s clinician, has approved four refills of loperamide for him over the past three months, despite there being no notes of worsening symptoms or flare-ups during this period. This discrepancy causes Ms D to question whether Mr T might be misusing loperamide to replicate the effects of opioids. Concerned, she contacts Dr O by phone to discuss her suspicions.

During their conversation, Dr O explains that Mr T’s substance use disorder is in the distant past, and that maintaining access to loperamide is crucial for managing his ongoing symptoms. Despite this, Ms D remains unconvinced. She raises her concern that dispensing loperamide under these circumstances could conflict with Mr T’s best interests and might violate her professional and ethical responsibilities as articulated in both the Indian Health Manual and the Ohio Administrative Code.

Sensing the tension, Dr O responds with some frustration, pointing out that Mr T lacks supplemental insurance and that the nearest alternative clinic or hospital is over two hours away from his home. The IHS pharmacy, Dr O reminds Ms D, is Mr T’s sole source for obtaining loperamide.

With both parties still on the phone, Ms D and Dr O face a dilemma: how best to resolve their disagreement regarding whether it is appropriate to refill Mr T’s prescription, striving to balance patient safety, access to care, and their respective professional obligations.

ethical_issues.question: How should pharmacists balance legal and ethical responsibilities when they suspect a patient may be misusing prescription medications in order to ensure the patient’s best interests?
keypoints: Pharmacists bear a corresponding responsibility to ensure the medical appropriateness of dispensed medications when potential prescription drug misuse is identified, including a comprehensive review of the patient’s medical history, prescription records, and relevant information to assess the safety and rationality of dispensing.

Pharmacists should engage in thorough communication with prescribers to express concerns regarding misuse risks, while also seizing the opportunity to advocate for reassessment of the patient’s underlying conditions (such as chronic diarrhea) to promote a more comprehensive and optimized treatment plan.

Both pharmacists and prescribers have ethical obligations to act compassionately and cost-effectively, with all decisions centered on the patient’s best interests, balancing medical safety and the patient’s actual access to care.

If the prescriber can provide reasonable responses to the pharmacist’s inquiries, the pharmacist should recognize that the refill aligns with a legitimate medical purpose within the usual course of professional practice; if reasonable explanations are lacking, the pharmacist is entitled to refuse dispensing based on professional judgment.

Both parties should document their communications thoroughly to serve as evidence that medical and pharmaceutical decisions were made prudently, prioritizing patient welfare and adhering to accepted standards of medical and pharmacy care.

ethical_issues.question: When pharmacists and prescribers disagree about the appropriateness of a prescription refill, how can a culture of collaborative communication be employed to mitigate cognitive biases and ensure the patient’s best interests?
keypoints: Pharmacists and prescribers must reach a consensus: pharmacists bear a corresponding responsibility to ensure the medical appropriateness of medications; all healthcare professionals are committed to the patient’s best interests; and clinical judgment inherently involves uncertainty.

By cultivating a workplace culture characterized by mutual respect, transparency, and nonpunitive learning, defensive attitudes and cognitive biases can be mitigated, thereby facilitating the identification of systemic issues and continuous quality improvement.

Within a safety culture environment, standardized pharmacy processes and evidence-based tools should be implemented to ensure practice consistency, alongside proactive exploration of alternative therapies with no potential for misuse.

Both parties should center their actions on the patient’s best interests; the final decision to approve or deny a prescription refill depends on the prescriber’s ability to provide satisfactory responses to the pharmacist’s reasonable inquiries, with the entire process documented transparently and supported by evidence, reflecting the principles of prudence and professional ethics.

ethical_issues.question: How should Ms D, as the dispensing pharmacist, ethically balance economic considerations—such as Mr T’s limited insurance coverage and barriers to healthcare access—with her professional responsibility to ensure the appropriateness and safety of prescription medications in the best interests of the patient?
keypoints: Medical decision-making should center on the patient’s best interests, ensuring the appropriateness and safety of medication use.

Clinical indications for intervention should be established as a priority; economic considerations and healthcare accessibility factors should only be incorporated after clinical appropriateness has been confirmed.
Both prescribers and pharmacists bear legal and ethical responsibilities to collaborate in preventing prescription drug misuse and safeguarding the patient’s overall health interests.

When managing limitations in healthcare resources, caution must be exercised to avoid allowing economic factors to overshadow the substance of clinical indications; if a medication is not the optimal choice, related economic or accessibility considerations are irrelevant.

title: How Should Clinicians Help Patients Navigate “Model Minority” Demands?
case:
JJ is a student doing a rotation in a university clinic. JJ’s patient introduces himself as “Todd” and is an 18-year-old Chinese American student who states that he hasn’t been feeling well. As JJ talks with Todd, JJ learns that Todd studies electrical engineering and that his parents, brother, and sister run a restaurant in a neighboring state. JJ notices Todd’s flat affect and difficulty maintaining eye contactand asks Todd about his courses, part of a curriculum widely known for its rigor and intensity. As JJ leafs through Todd’s health record, a clinic note from 3 months ago suggests Todd experienced suicidal ideation.
JJ continues to try to engage Todd, who says, “Classes are fine. My engineering project group goes out for drinks without me, though, typically leaving me with group problem sets to do alone. I hate that.”
JJ responds, “I see why you hate it: that’s a lot of pressure.”
Todd denies that this is the case. “Sorry,” he says, “I shouldn’t have brought it up. It doesn’t matter. I just have to get this degree so I can help my family and make my parents happy we came to this country.”
JJ wonders what to say next.
case_rewrite:
JJ, a medical student on rotation at a university clinic, welcomes his new patient, who introduces himself as “Todd.” Todd is an 18-year-old Chinese American student who complains of not feeling well. As JJ begins the visit, he learns that Todd is studying electrical engineering—a major known for its demanding workload—and that Todd’s parents, brother, and sister operate a restaurant in a nearby state.

During their conversation, JJ observes that Todd appears withdrawn and has difficulty making eye contact. Wanting to learn more, JJ gently asks about Todd’s classes. While reviewing Todd’s chart, JJ comes across a clinic note from three months earlier indicating that Todd had previously reported suicidal thoughts.

Trying to connect, JJ listens as Todd says, “Classes are okay. But my engineering project group usually goes out for drinks without me, and they leave me with the group problem sets to finish on my own. I hate that.” JJ responds, “I can understand why that would be difficult—there’s a lot of pressure on you.” However, Todd shakes his head and replies, “It’s not really like that. Sorry, I shouldn’t have brought it up. It doesn’t matter. I just need to get this degree so I can help my family and make my parents proud—they sacrificed a lot to come to this country.”

JJ finds himself pausing, uncertain what to say next.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians identify and avoid racial biases and stereotypes arising from the Model Minority Myth (MMM) during the clinical encounter?
keypoints: Clinicians must recognize that the model minority myth (MMM) may influence their perceptions of Asian American patients, symptom assessment, and medical decision-making, and should proactively acknowledge their own racial identity and potential biases.
Through self-reflection, clinicians can reduce the risk of projecting their unexamined personal issues onto patients and adjust their behaviors to eliminate discriminatory actions.

Assessing the extent to which patients have internalized the model minority myth is a critical dimension for understanding racial dynamics within the therapeutic relationship and aids in accurately addressing patients’ cultural identities and psychological needs.

Clinicians should tailor their interventions according to the specific needs of the patient, balancing efforts to help patients understand the historical context of race in the United States and the existence of the MMM, while fostering the patient’s agency to resist its adverse effects.

For patients with limited awareness of societal oppression, clinicians should avoid exclusively emphasizing internal regulation to prevent inadvertently implying patient deficiency, and instead promote cultural awareness, empathic understanding, and a balanced approach to addressing both internal and external factors.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians effectively address patients’ mistrust in the therapeutic relationship during cross-racial interactions and enhance trust between clinician and patient?
keypoints: Clinicians should proactively recognize their own racial identity and potential biases to mitigate patients’ mistrust in the therapeutic relationship.
Clinicians should attend to patients’ perceptions of the clinician’s race, anticipate possible mistrust scenarios, and respond to them actively.

Understanding Asian American patients’ self-identity and cultural background, alongside integrating traditional healing practices with Western medicine, can strengthen the patient-clinician trust alliance.

Balancing the introduction of U.S. racial history and racialized power structures with fostering patients’ agency to resist related impacts contributes to establishing a more equitable therapeutic relationship.

title: How Should Clinicians Address a Patient’s Experience of Transgenerational Trauma?
case:
A retired veteran, Mr S enlisted in the US Army with hopes of giving his family a better life. He is an active Black elderly man with no significant illnesses or injuries before being brought to an emergency department (ED) after collapsing at home. Clinicians learn that, for about 3 months, Mr S has experienced early satiety (feeling full after consuming only a few bites of food), weight loss, and persistent fatigue. Following hospital admission, an endoscopic biopsy reveals localized gastric adenocarcinoma, and a surgical team, led by Dr D, evaluates Mr S for gastric resection.
Mr S’s wife, children, and several grandchildren are present with him in the hospital. Dr D explains gastric resection to Mr S and his family, and Mr S clarifies that he does not want surgery because he is “unsure whether I would make it.” Dr D asks him to say more about not wanting surgery. Mr S explains that, when he was young, his father had an operation for an infected foot ulcer. His father was discharged home the morning after his operation with minimal instruction on how to care for the wound and without any home resources to facilitate ongoing wound care. Despite the operation, the foot infection did not get better. Instead, the infection got much worse. His father’s leg became rapidly necrotic after discharge home. The involved skin, fat, and muscles of his foot began to die as the infection spread rapidly up his father’s leg. His father sought care from multiple surgeons, and no one agreed to care for him. Mr S remembers waiting for hours and hours in numerous emergency rooms with his father as they sought treatment. He remembers his father being accused by one nurse in an examination room of “not taking care of himself.” Unfortunately, by the time his father was appropriately evaluated and able to be admitted to a hospital, the infection had spread all the way up to his thigh and hip. He was admitted to an intensive care unit and died the following day. Mr S explains that he worries this could happen to him, although times have changed. “Some things haven’t changed. It’s nothing personal against you, Doc. I just don’t want this surgery.” Dr D wonders how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Mr S, a retired Black veteran who once enlisted in the US Army in hopes of securing a better future for his family, is known for his active lifestyle and has no significant prior illnesses or injuries. One afternoon, he suddenly collapses at home and is rushed to the emergency department (ED). Upon evaluation, the clinicians discover that over the past three months, Mr S has been experiencing early satiety—feeling full after just a few bites of food—alongside noticeable weight loss and unrelenting fatigue. After his hospital admission, an endoscopic biopsy uncovers a localized gastric adenocarcinoma. A surgical team led by Dr D assesses Mr S as a candidate for gastric resection.

Surrounded by his wife, children, and several grandchildren at the hospital, Mr S listens as Dr D explains the nature of gastric resection and what the surgery would entail. When the conversation shifts to Mr S’s wishes, he expresses his reluctance: “I’m not sure I would make it,” he admits, voicing his decision to decline surgery. Dr D encourages him to elaborate on his hesitation. Mr S recounts a painful memory from his youth—his father underwent surgery for an infected foot ulcer. The day after the operation, his father was discharged with little guidance on wound care and no resources at home to manage his recovery. The infection failed to improve, and his father's condition rapidly deteriorated as the infection spread up his leg. Mr S vividly recalls accompanying his father through countless emergency rooms, waiting for hours in search of help, only to be turned away by surgeons. He remembers a nurse accusing his father of “not taking care of himself,” a moment that left a lasting scar. By the time his father received appropriate attention and was admitted to the hospital, the infection had advanced up to his thigh and hip. He was placed in the ICU but died the following day.

Mr S confides in Dr D that he fears history could repeat itself, even if he recognizes that some things have changed over the years. “Some things haven’t changed. It’s nothing personal against you, Doc. I just don’t want this surgery.” Dr D finds himself reflecting on how best to respond to Mr S’s concerns and support him in making an informed decision.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians effectively address patients’ mistrust arising from transgenerational trauma during clinical interactions?
keypoints: Clinicians should actively respond to and listen to patients, understanding the cultural and historical contexts underlying their experiences of transgenerational trauma, in order to establish trust and acknowledge patient vulnerability.

Clinicians must examine their own biases and awareness of professional privilege, recognizing and assuming responsibility for addressing the impacts of structural racism and related historical trauma on patient health.

Engage in respectful and honest communication with patients and their families, support shared decision-making, allow sufficient time for independent deliberation, and provide diverse supportive resources including pastoral care, social assistance, and psychological consultation.

Through ongoing understanding of patients’ intersecting identities and experiences of social injustice, combined with self-reflection, promote the rebuilding of trust and the healing process within the patient-clinician relationship.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians examine their own biases and awareness of professional privilege when patients refuse recommended treatment in order to uphold patient rights?
keypoints: Clinicians should identify the origins of their own biases toward patients, including differences in gender roles, race and culture, educational background, disease understanding, and medical experience, in order to gain a profound understanding of the foundations of professional privilege.

Clinicians must recognize that professional privilege equates to power; neglecting to acknowledge one’s own privilege may inadvertently lead to the misuse of power, thereby undermining patient-clinician trust and compromising patient rights.

Clinicians should proactively listen to the concerns of patients and their families, respect the worries arising from historical trauma and familial experiences, and avoid denying or minimizing their feelings.

Clinicians ought to reflect on their own behaviors within the frameworks of social justice and cultural sensitivity, striving to prevent patients from experiencing in the healthcare setting the same social injustices and discrimination they face in broader society.

Communicating with patients and their families in a manner that is respectful, honest, and empathetic, and fostering shared decision-making, are essential to establishing and maintaining patient-clinician trust and safeguarding patient rights.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians, such as Dr D, ensure that patients like Mr S—whose experiences may be shaped by transgenerational trauma and historical racial discrimination—fully comprehend proposed diagnostic and treatment options and are able to make truly informed decisions?
keypoints: Clinicians should proactively inquire about patients’ and their families’ histories of trauma, with particular attention to adverse medical experiences related to racial discrimination, in order to understand patients’ concerns and the context of their decision-making.

Clinicians must ensure that patients have a comprehensive understanding of their disease and the scientific rationale behind proposed treatments, utilizing diverse communication tools such as diagrams and videos to enhance clarity and acceptability of information.

Clinicians should respect patient autonomy by allowing patients and their families sufficient time for independent deliberation and by providing multifaceted support resources, including pastoral care, social assistance, and psychological counseling.
Clinicians ought to listen to patients and their families with respect, empathy, and honesty, fostering open dialogue, facilitating shared decision-making, and upholding patients’ rights and dignity.

Clinicians need to reflect upon and actively identify their own implicit biases and professional privilege that may affect the patient-clinician relationship, striving to eliminate systemic barriers and rebuild trust damaged by transgenerational trauma.

title: How Should Clinicians Respond to Children in Transgenerationally Traumatized Families?
case:
Dr A practices primary care in a US plains state that is home to many recent Honduran refugees. HH is an 11-year-old patient brought to the free clinic by their mother for a routine check-up. Dr A greets HH and HH’s mother and interviews HH, who does not make eye contact. Dr A confirms that HH doesn’t hurt anywhere, is eating well, and attends school. “Are you sleeping all right?”
HH shrugs. HH’s mother states, “It has been hard on my children,” and explains why the family recently fled Honduras. HH’s ancestors lived on land now known as Honduras for centuries until recent political upheaval made life there intolerable. HH’s father was murdered near their home. This necessitated that the remaining family members leave Honduras on foot and seek asylum by crossing through Mexico and entering the United States. At the US border, they were separated and detained for several weeks. HH’s family members were each granted asylum and have been staying with cousins.
HH’s mother begins to cry after saying, “I don’t know what would’ve happened to us if we didn’t have any cousins here.”
HH begins to cry, too, but does not want to speak with a counselor. Dr A wonders how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Dr A works as a primary care physician in a US plains state that has recently become home to many Honduran refugees. One afternoon, HH, an 11-year-old child, arrives at the community free clinic accompanied by their mother for a routine check-up. As Dr A welcomes them, HH avoids making eye contact and sits quietly while Dr A conducts the interview. Dr A checks in: “Are you having any pain? How’s your appetite? Are you going to school?” HH answers quietly that there’s no pain, eats well, and attends classes. Dr A then asks, “How have you been sleeping?”

HH merely shrugs in response. At this, HH’s mother gently interjects, her voice unsteady: “It’s been very hard on my children.” She recounts the family’s recent journey—how their ancestors had lived in Honduras for generations, but recent political turmoil made it impossible to stay. HH’s father was killed near their home, forcing the rest of the family to flee on foot, seeking safety. They traveled through Mexico and reached the US border, where they were separated and held for several weeks in detention. Eventually, each family member was granted asylum, and they have since been living with cousins in the area.

As she tells their story, HH’s mother’s composure falters and tears begin to fall. “I don’t know what would’ve happened to us if we didn’t have cousins here,” she says, her voice breaking. Sitting beside her, HH also starts to cry, but when asked if they would like to talk to a counselor, HH quietly declines. Dr A feels the weight of the moment and carefully considers how best to support both HH and HH’s mother.

ethical_issues.question: When caring for children and their families who have experienced trauma, how should clinicians identify and address the impact of trauma while providing appropriate psychological support and resource referrals?
keypoints: Clinicians should routinely screen children for trauma exposure and related symptoms, with particular attention to specific indicators such as sleep patterns, appetite, and academic performance, in order to identify multiple mental health issues including trauma, anxiety, depression, and PTSD.
Clinicians should concurrently attend to and assess the trauma history and psychological state of the child’s mother, reflecting the principle of holistic, family-centered care.

Clinicians should provide psychosocial support to both the child and their mother, employing evidence-based and culturally sensitive assessment and treatment tools that respect linguistic and cultural differences to facilitate effective communication.

Clinicians should refer the child and their mother to appropriate psychotherapists and compile a directory of local mental health services offering pro bono or sliding-scale fees, ensuring the availability of language support and cultural adaptation.

Clinicians should consider establishing an interdisciplinary team—including behavioral therapists, social workers, mental health specialists, school counselors, and immigration legal aid—to comprehensively address the multidimensional needs of the child and mother and promote their overall health and well-being.

ethical_issues.question: When managing cases that might involve child abuse, how should clinicians identify warning signs and fulfill their reporting obligations to protect the rights and well-being of children?
keypoints: Clinicians should be attentive to potential risks of abuse in the child’s environment, including influences from family members and other individuals with whom the child has contact.

Identification of warning signs includes the discovery of injuries during physical examination, reports of physical or psychological abuse by the child or guardian, and the presence of unusual behaviors in the child (such as emotional withdrawal, avoidance of eye contact, or excessive anxiety and other psychological manifestations).
All 50 states in the United States have laws requiring clinicians to report suspected cases of child abuse, and failure to report may result in criminal liability in most states.
Clinicians should respect the child’s wishes and provide timely psychological support or referrals to mental health services to help the child cope with traumatic experiences.
