Specifically, he is concerned about colleagues who underprescribe clinically indicated opioids, and he is equally concerned about other colleagues who overprescribe opioids and do not manage patients’ pain care skillfully or responsibly. Dr O’s patients typically require opioid pain relief for more than 7 days after a surgery, so he and other physicians resent being legally required to offer inadequate pain care to many patients.
Dr O and many of his physician colleagues realize, however, that questioning the appropriateness of this new law as public health policy is not enough. He and fellow physicians wonder whether and when they should try to become engaged as a socially and culturally influential group to shape and influence policy decisions that affect their practices and patients.
case_rewrite:
Dr O, an orthopedic surgeon in private practice, is working to adjust to a new state law that restricts opioid prescriptions. The law now limits physicians to prescribing no more than five days’ worth of opioids for acute pain—defined as pain expected to last three months or less—after an initial consultation, unless the prescription is for postoperative pain, in which case a seven-day supply is permitted. 

Dr O is acutely aware of the medical community’s responsibility in addressing the state’s opioid crisis. He is troubled by colleagues who, on one hand, underprescribe opioids even when clinically indicated, potentially leaving patients to suffer needlessly, and on the other hand, by those who overprescribe opioids without careful, responsible management of their patients’ pain. Most of Dr O’s patients require opioid pain relief for longer than seven days following surgery, so he and his peers are frustrated by legal limitations they feel force them to provide insufficient pain management for many of their patients.

Despite their reservations about the law, Dr O and many of his colleagues recognize that simply questioning its merits as public health policy is insufficient. They find themselves debating not only how to navigate the tension between their obligations to individual patients and to public health, but also when and how they should unite as a professional group to influence policy decisions that directly affect their medical practice and the welfare of their patients.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance their obligations to individual patients with their obligations to improve public health?
keypoints: Physicians bear dual ethical responsibilities to individual patients and public health, and must seek a balance between these obligations.

At the individual level, physicians should base their pain management recommendations and prescribing decisions on evidence-based practice by integrating the best available evidence, clinical expertise, and patient preferences, while upholding compassion and respect and attending to the patient’s overall well-being.
Physicians should actively participate in the development and updating of clinical practice guidelines to promote evidence-based and ethically grounded standards of care.

When individual obligations conflict with public health policies, physicians ought to collectively advocate through professional organizations for policy reforms that align with evidence-based and ethical principles.
Physicians must acknowledge and appropriately manage conflicts of interest that may influence professional behavior to ensure fairness and integrity in medical decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: What collective action strategies should physicians adopt to improve public health in responding to the opioid crisis?
keypoints: Physicians should stay current with updates in opioid-related knowledge and actively participate in emergency planning and harm reduction efforts.

Physicians should collectively advocate through professional organizations, such as associations and societies, for regulatory and policy reforms that are evidence-based and ethically sound to promote public health improvement.
Physicians have an obligation to advance public education and enhance the accessibility and utilization of medication-assisted treatment (MAT), naloxone, and harm-reduction strategies.

Physicians should critically appraise existing clinical evidence and actively engage in the development and revision of clinical practice guidelines to ensure that medical practice is scientific, ethical, and effective.

Physicians should participate in establishing and refining standards for education and training across the continuum of learning to improve healthcare professionals’ expertise in pain management and opioid use.

At the state and local levels, physicians should advocate through lobbying state medical societies, engaging in hospital credentialing and privileging processes, and participating in community initiatives to promote improved pain management, risk assessment, and quality of patient care.

tags: Disparities in health and health care/Social determinants
title: Should the Location of a Patient’s Home Inform Physicians’ Opioid Prescription Practices?
case:
Mr W is a 51-year-old man who had a successful partial colectomy 5 days ago for severe diverticulitis. He is tolerating by-mouth intake and is passing stools, and his pain levels are becoming more manageable. Dr M, Mr W’s surgeon, gives the “go ahead” for Mr W to go home. Ms K, a nurse, instructs Mr W about how to take care of his surgical wound, and he is discharged to his home with oxycodone and acetaminophen for pain and docusate sodium and polyethylene glycol for constipation. A clinic follow-up appointment is scheduled for one week.
During the follow-up appointment, Mr W reports, “I’m feeling better. I used all the pain meds. May I get a refill?” Dr M authorizes a 5-day refill of the oxycodone and refers Mr W to his primary care physician for follow-up.
Dr M later wonders, however, whether she should have authorized a refill for a patient living in an area of the city struggling desperately with regular deaths by opioid overdose.
case_rewrite:
Mr W, a 51-year-old man, underwent a successful partial colectomy five days ago due to severe diverticulitis. Since surgery, he has been able to eat by mouth, pass stools, and his pain is gradually improving. Dr M, Mr W’s surgeon, assesses his recovery and determines that he is ready to be discharged. Before leaving the hospital, Ms K, the nurse, carefully explains to Mr W how to care for his surgical wound at home. Upon discharge, Mr W is provided with prescriptions for oxycodone and acetaminophen to manage his pain, as well as docusate sodium and polyethylene glycol to prevent constipation. He is scheduled for a follow-up visit at the clinic in one week.

At his follow-up appointment, Mr W tells Dr M, “I’m feeling better. I used all the pain meds. May I get a refill?” After considering his request, Dr M authorizes a five-day refill of oxycodone and advises Mr W to see his primary care physician for further follow-up.

Afterward, Dr M finds herself reflecting on her decision to grant a refill. She is aware that Mr W lives in a part of the city where opioid overdose deaths are a frequent and serious problem, and she questions whether she should have prescribed additional opioids given this context.

ethical_issues.question: Should a Patient’s Place of Residence Influence Physicians’ Opioid Prescription Decisions?
keypoints: Physicians’ opioid prescribing should be based on medical assessment, the patient’s specific needs, and reasonable expectations of effectiveness, rather than the patient’s place of residence.
Basing prescribing decisions solely on geographic location may lead to bias and discrimination, thereby contributing to health inequities, and should be avoided.

Although opioid overdose mortality rates in a patient’s residential area constitute important contextual information, physicians should critically appraise the actual clinical relevance of this data for individual patient care.

Physicians should adopt a comprehensive evaluation of the patient’s overall condition, respect patient autonomy, and implement prudent, individualized prescribing management through risk assessment and interdisciplinary team collaboration.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians avoid bias and discrimination based on geographic location when prescribing opioids, thereby ensuring equity in treatment?
keypoints: Physicians should base opioid prescribing on the patient’s specific medical needs and reasonable expectations of effectiveness, avoiding reliance solely on epidemiological data related to the patient’s place of residence.

Prescribing decisions must guard against biases and discrimination related to race, gender, age, ethnicity, or other factors that may arise from geographic considerations, thereby ensuring equity in healthcare.
Respecting patient autonomy, clinicians should implement individualized and safe pain management plans through comprehensive clinical assessment and the use of risk mitigation tools.
With the support of interdisciplinary healthcare teams, opioid prescriptions should be made judiciously, balancing the patient’s best interests with broader community public health responsibilities.

title: Does Using Humor to Cope With Stress Justify Making Fun of Patients?
case:
Having heard 2 fellow students, JR and CC, joking about a patient’s looks and demeanor, MK asks CC, “Don’t you think it’s unprofessional and inappropriate for JR to be making fun of a patient like that?”
“He’s just venting because the patient has been so frustrating to deal with,” responded CC. “Now that he’s got that off his chest, he’ll be less stressed the next time he sees that patient.”
“Yes, I’ve heard that line of thought before, but I don’t think you can just make jokes like that about patients without it affecting the way you interact with them.” MK continues, “Aren’t there better ways to deal with stress without making patients the butts of jokes?”
case_rewrite:
While walking through the hospital corridor, MK overhears two classmates, JR and CC, laughing about a patient. JR is making sarcastic remarks about the patient’s appearance and behavior, prompting CC to chuckle along. Troubled by what she hears, MK turns to CC and asks, “Do you really think it’s okay for JR to make fun of a patient like that? Isn’t that unprofessional and inappropriate?”

CC shrugs and replies, “He’s just blowing off steam. That patient has been really difficult to handle. JR needed to let it out somehow. Now that he’s joked about it, he’ll probably feel less stressed next time he has to see that patient.”

MK frowns and responds, “I’ve heard people say that before, but I don’t think joking at a patient’s expense is harmless. It might actually affect how you treat them. Aren’t there healthier ways to deal with stress that don’t involve making fun of patients?”

ethical_issues.question: Does Using Humor to Cope with Stress Justify Making Fun of Patients?
keypoints: Derogatory and cynical humor directed at patients is both unprofessional and unethical, with the potential to harm relationships with patients and colleagues.
Even in challenging clinical environments, the use of derogatory humor as a coping mechanism is not ethically justifiable.
Derogatory humor can damage patients’ emotional well-being and trust, while also negatively impacting the emotional health of healthcare professionals.
Clinicians should develop alternative coping strategies that effectively alleviate stress while preserving the therapeutic relationship.

ethical_issues.question: Does derogatory humor have a negative impact on the therapeutic relationship between healthcare professionals and patients?
keypoints: Derogatory humor directed at patients is neither professional nor ethical; it not only undermines the patient-provider relationship but may also exacerbate negative emotions and stress among healthcare professionals, thereby hindering effective emotional coping.
Even when patients are unaware, derogatory humor damages trust and collaboration among healthcare professionals, colleagues, and patients.
If patients overhear derogatory jokes made at their expense, they may experience emotional harm and a loss of trust, which can adversely affect treatment adherence and continuity of care.
Derogatory humor can reinforce inherent biases among healthcare professionals, impairing objective judgment and clinical decision-making, ultimately compromising the quality of care.
Clinicians should adopt more respectful and dignified strategies to manage stress, thereby preserving the therapeutic relationship and upholding professional ethics.

ethical_issues.question: How can healthcare professionals ensure that the use of humor as a coping strategy does not undermine the patient-provider relationship and remains consistent with professional ethical standards?
keypoints: Healthcare professionals should enhance their awareness of different types of humor and their respective benefits and drawbacks, with particular emphasis on the negative impact of derogatory humor on patients, colleagues, and their own professional image.

Safe spaces and dedicated time should be provided for healthcare professionals to discuss the stresses and challenges encountered during clinical rotations, to clarify acceptable boundaries of humor within the healthcare team, and to firmly oppose the use of derogatory humor.

The adoption of constructive coping strategies, such as positive humor (e.g., self-deprecation, light-hearted commentary on general situations) and appreciative inquiry, should be advocated to alleviate stress without resorting to humor that disparages patients.
Healthcare professionals should learn from role models and actively practice professional humor and communication skills that help maintain and promote therapeutic relationships with patients.

Methods such as appreciative inquiry should be employed to guide healthcare professionals in focusing on patients’ strengths and progress, deepening the understanding of patients’ narratives and clinical challenges, and fostering the development of collaborative therapeutic relationships.

title: Are “Other Doctors Are Stupid” Jokes Appropriate?
case:
LC and JJ are third-year resident physicians in obstetrics and gynecology on their way to grand rounds. “Guess what I got called for yesterday?” asks LC. “There was a pregnant woman in the emergency department suspected of having meningitis, and the intern called to ask if a lumbar puncture would pose any risk to her baby.”
JJ rolls her eyes. “Did you tell them that when pregnant women get lumbar punctures, their fetuses instantly liquify?”
LC responds, laughing, “I should have. That’s definitely a new one for the bulletin board tally sheet of stupid consultation questions.”
case_rewrite:
LC and JJ, both third-year resident physicians specializing in obstetrics and gynecology, were making their way to grand rounds together. On the walk, LC turned to JJ and said, “You won’t believe the consult I got yesterday. There was a pregnant woman in the emergency department, and they suspected she might have meningitis. The intern called me to ask whether doing a lumbar puncture would be risky for the baby.”

JJ raised her eyebrows and, with a wry smile, replied, “So, did you reassure them that a lumbar puncture doesn’t magically liquefy the fetus?”

LC chuckled and shook her head. “Maybe I should have said that. That kind of question is definitely going on our running list of memorable consults!”

The two laughed together as they continued down the hallway, their camaraderie evident as they prepared for the busy day ahead.

ethical_issues.question: In clinical settings, should humor be employed to avoid fostering dysfunctional tribalism?
keypoints: In clinical settings, humor should not reinforce dysfunctional tribalism, as this undermines teamwork and trust.
Disparagement humor may foster illusions of superiority among colleagues, weakening mutual respect and ultimately impairing patient care.
Humor ought to serve as a tool to promote team cohesion and well-being by sharing rather than weaponizing it, thereby breaking down “us versus them” barriers.
Appropriate and positive humor can alleviate emotional stress in clinical work and enhance communication, collaboration, and empathy among individuals from diverse backgrounds.

ethical_issues.question: How can humor be used in medical settings to promote teamwork rather than undermine interpersonal relationships?
keypoints: Humor in clinical workplaces can alleviate stress and foster interpersonal connection and emotional support.
Humor should be used to share laughter with colleagues rather than weaponize it by ridiculing them, thereby breaking down the barriers of “us versus them” and promoting team collaboration.
Through shared laughter, team members can unify their goals, enhance empathy, and improve overall well-being and quality of patient care.

ethical_issues.question: In medical teams, how can disparaging humor toward colleagues be avoided to prevent negative impacts on patient care quality?
keypoints: Humor should be shared to break down tribal barriers and promote teamwork, rather than weaponized to disparage colleagues.
Mocking colleagues may hinder effective collaboration, whereas laughing together can unify goals, enhance team well-being, and improve the quality of patient care.
Humor ought to facilitate communication, cooperation, and empathy among individuals from diverse backgrounds, while avoiding the reinforcement of dysfunctional group divisions.
It is essential to recognize the fragile boundary between humor and humiliation and to refrain from using disparagement humor in order to preserve team relationships and ensure patient safety.

title: How Should the Recovery Process Be Shared Between Patients and Clinicians?
case:
Ms M is a 32-year-old, right-hand-dominant engineer who developed weakness, numbness, and shooting pain through her right shoulder and arm 3 months ago, following a fall from a bicycle during a recent vacation. She cannot raise her arm overhead and cannot flex her elbow. Her symptoms are consistent with an injury to the brachial plexus (the network of nerves that connect the spinal cord to the muscles and skin of the shoulder, arm, and hand), which can manifest as weakness or absence of muscle function, loss of sensation, or shooting pain. Nerve regeneration is a lengthy process and many patients experience emotional distress, financial strain, and increased reliance on others during the prolonged recovery.
Due to concern for a brachial plexus injury (BPI), Ms M’s primary care physician referred her to a peripheral nerve surgeon, Dr D, whom she has been seeing in follow-up for her diagnosis of BPI (attributed to a stretch injury to the nerves sustained in the fall). As is standard of care, Ms M did not receive immediate posttraumatic intervention but has had close monitoring of her motor function, which has unfortunately demonstrated only modest return of function. Dr D counseled her that many patients with her injury (an upper trunk BPI) recover nearly full strength with observation,and those who do so typically start to see signs of muscle reinnervation by 3 to 6 months.However, some patients do not have recovery of muscle innervation and may benefit from reconstructive surgery (eg, nerve transfer). At this point in her recovery (3 months from her injury), early intervention with surgery is a viable option, although it remains unknown whether Ms M would spontaneously regain further function over the coming months. Dr D and Ms M begin a discussion about the choice for early surgery vs continued monitoring, given the considerations involved.
case_rewrite:
Ms M, a 32-year-old engineer who is right-hand dominant, began experiencing weakness, numbness, and intense shooting pain in her right shoulder and arm three months ago, following a fall from her bicycle during a recent vacation. Since the accident, she has been unable to lift her arm above her head or flex her elbow. Her symptoms are consistent with a brachial plexus injury, which affects the network of nerves connecting the spinal cord to the muscles and skin of the shoulder, arm, and hand. This type of injury can lead to significant muscle weakness or paralysis, loss of sensation, and ongoing pain. Recovery from nerve injuries is often slow, and patients like Ms M frequently face not only emotional distress and financial difficulties, but also increased dependence on others during the extended healing process.

Concerned about her persistent symptoms, Ms M’s primary care physician referred her to Dr D, a peripheral nerve surgeon. Dr D has managed Ms M’s care since her diagnosis of an upper trunk brachial plexus injury, believed to be the result of a stretch injury from her fall. In keeping with standard medical practice, Ms M did not undergo immediate surgical intervention after her injury, but instead has been closely monitored for signs of returning motor function. Unfortunately, her progress over the past three months has shown only modest improvement.

Dr D explained that many patients with similar injuries recover nearly full strength over time with observation alone, and that initial signs of muscle reinnervation usually appear within three to six months. However, Dr D also noted that some patients do not regain muscle function spontaneously and may benefit from reconstructive procedures such as nerve transfer surgery. Now at the three-month mark, Ms M faces a decision: she could choose to proceed with early surgical intervention, or continue with ongoing observation in hopes that further recovery might occur naturally.

As they discuss her options, Dr D and Ms M begin a thorough conversation about her personal recovery goals, the potential outcomes of each approach, and the uncertainties involved. Dr D encourages Ms M to share her values, expectations, and priorities—both in terms of her professional life as an engineer and her daily independence. Together, they explore the risks and benefits of surgery versus continued monitoring, openly addressing the uncertainty surrounding her prognosis and the possible impact on her quality of life. Through this collaborative process, Dr D supports Ms M in reflecting on her values, articulating her preferences, and actively participating in the decision-making process, ensuring that the chosen care pathway aligns with both her personal goals and the best available clinical evidence.

ethical_issues.question: How can a balance be achieved between patients’ personal recovery goals and possible clinical outcomes during the recovery process to select the optimal path forward?
keypoints: Patients and clinicians should collaboratively select the optimal recovery pathway based on a shared decision-making (SDM) model that integrates the patient’s personal recovery goals with possible clinical outcomes.

In the SDM process, patients contribute their individual values and preferences, while clinicians provide professional expertise and communication support; together, they identify and prioritize recovery goals.

Recovery goals should be clarified through open-ended questioning, the applicability and potential outcomes of treatment options assessed, and patient preferences reconciled with clinical evidence to achieve consensus.

Prognoses and patient expectations may evolve over time, necessitating regular reevaluation of recovery goals to ensure that patients and clinicians continue to co-construct a recovery concept that optimizes clinical outcomes while reflecting patient preferences.

ethical_issues.question: In the shared decision-making process, how can patients’ subjective experiences and values be adequately considered and respected in clinical decision-making?
keypoints: Acknowledge that patients are experts in their own experience, integrating patients’ personal recovery goals with possible clinical outcomes to select the optimal care pathway.
Understand the socio-emotional context of health impacts, with attention to core values such as patient independence, confidence, and social and family roles.

Clinicians should facilitate patients’ clarification of value judgments and prioritization of recovery goals through specific inquiry, thereby promoting patients’ recognition of the relative importance of treatment options.

Encourage patients to actively reflect upon and articulate their values and recovery expectations, and to proactively raise questions about the information provided by clinicians, fostering transparency and bidirectional communication.

Shared decision making is a collaborative process in which clinicians and patients jointly explore care options based on medical evidence and patient preferences, reaching consensus that ensures patients’ subjective experiences and values are central to the decision-making process.

ethical_issues.question: How can risks and uncertainties be effectively communicated to assist patients in making informed choices when faced with uncertain prognoses and multiple treatment options?
keypoints: Clinicians should assist patients in clarifying and prioritizing their recovery goals, thereby facilitating informed decision-making grounded in the patients’ own values.

Physicians must be proficient in understanding and communicating prognostic information, evaluating the applicability of population-based data to the individual patient, and ensuring that information provided is comprehensive, accurate, and personalized.

Clinicians should openly acknowledge the inherent uncertainty in prognostication, helping patients to comprehend and accept the unknown, thereby supporting psychological adaptation and confidence in decision-making.

Risk communication ought to employ formats that enhance comprehension, such as absolute risks, risk differences, and natural frequencies, supplemented by visual aids to improve the effectiveness of information delivery.

Clinicians need to understand psychological factors influencing patient decision-making—such as anticipatory regret and affective forecasting errors—and promote rational judgment by exploring patients’ reasoning and guiding reflective deliberation.

title: Sliding-Scale Shared Decision Making for Patients With Reduced Capacity
case:
Dr Q is an academic hepatologist meeting a new patient, Mr R, for newly diagnosed cirrhosis. The patient has clear signs of liver dysfunction and has already been admitted to the hospital previously for a gastrointestinal bleed related to esophageal varices. He also has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obesity, and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Dr Q and her student, Ms G, interview and examine Mr R together. They learn that Mr R did not complete high school and lives on what he calls “the wrong side of the tracks.” He lives alone and drinks 4 beers daily. He thinks his brother might have had “liver problems,” too.
As the conversation unfolds, it becomes clear that Mr R does not know why he’s in clinic today. “My doc said it was something about my liver, but…” He shrugs.
Ms G and Dr Q teach Mr R about cirrhosis. They emphasize the importance of alcohol abstinence and start to explain that further workup is necessary—including, potentially, a liver biopsy. Their goal is to enter into shared decision making with Mr R about liver biopsy.
Mr R holds up his hand midway through their explanation and says, “I’m not a detail guy, Doc. I trust you. You tell me what to do, and I’ll do it.”
They talk more, and, ultimately, Dr Q asks, “Do you have any questions for me?” Mr R pauses for a second, starts to ask a question, and then tapers off.Finally, he says, “Whatever you say, Doc. I’m in your hands.”
In the hallway, after Mr R has left to reschedule a follow-up visit, Ms G asks, “Did he really understand what we were talking about?” “Great question!” says Dr Q. “I have no idea. How can we be patient centered if the patient can’t or won’t tell us what he wants?”
case_rewrite:
Dr Q, an academic hepatologist, is meeting Mr R for the first time in the hepatology clinic. Mr R has recently been diagnosed with cirrhosis and exhibits unmistakable signs of liver dysfunction. His medical history includes a previous hospitalization for a gastrointestinal bleed caused by esophageal varices. Complicating his health further, he suffers from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obesity, and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Accompanying Dr Q is her medical student, Ms G. Together, they interview and examine Mr R. As they speak, they learn that Mr R did not finish high school and lives alone in what he describes as “the wrong side of the tracks.” He drinks four beers every day and mentions, somewhat uncertainly, that his brother might have had “liver problems” as well.

As the encounter progresses, Dr Q and Ms G realize that Mr R seems unsure about the reason for his visit. “My doc said it was something about my liver, but…” he says, shrugging with a puzzled look.

Dr Q and Ms G begin to explain the diagnosis of cirrhosis to Mr R, stressing the significance of abstaining from alcohol. They start to outline the need for further evaluation, which may include a liver biopsy. Their intention is to involve Mr R in shared decision making regarding the biopsy and next steps.

However, midway through their explanation, Mr R holds up his hand. “I’m not a detail guy, Doc. I trust you. You just tell me what to do, and I’ll do it,” he says.

They continue to discuss his condition and possible interventions, but when Dr Q finally asks, “Do you have any questions for me?” Mr R hesitates, begins to ask something, then trails off. After a quiet moment, he concludes, “Whatever you say, Doc. I’m in your hands.”

After Mr R leaves to arrange his follow-up appointment, Ms G turns to Dr Q in the hallway. “Did he really understand what we were talking about?” she asks. Dr Q smiles thoughtfully and replies, “That’s a great question. Honestly, I’m not sure. How do we stay patient centered when the patient can’t—or doesn’t want to—tell us what he wants?”

ethical_issues.question: How can patient-centered shared decision making be achieved in the context of impaired patient decision-making capacity?
keypoints: Patient decision-making capacity is dynamic and stratified, requiring individualized assessment specific to the decision at hand and the timing, thereby avoiding simplistic binary judgments.

Employ a capacity-adjusted sliding-scale shared decision-making approach that tailors the depth of communication, presentation of information, and degree of patient involvement according to the patient’s decision-making capacity.

When patient decision-making capacity is impaired, clinicians should adopt a more directive and supportive communication style while actively involving surrogate decision makers to ensure the decision-making process remains patient-centered.

The essence of shared decision making lies in flexibly adapting the clinician-patient interaction model to respect the patient’s capacity and preferences; even when a parentalistic approach is employed, the patient’s wishes must be thoroughly considered and honored.

Through a multi-stage communication process—comprising team talk, option talk, and decision talk—clinicians can dynamically assess patient capacity and willingness, thereby facilitating personalized decision support and effective patient engagement.

Extending the shared decision-making paradigm to patients with impaired decision-making capacity enhances the inclusivity and ethical soundness of medical decisions, preventing the unjust deprivation of patient autonomy due to diminished capacity.

ethical_issues.question: How can surrogate decision makers be ensured to accurately reflect the patient’s preferences and wishes when the patient is unable to make decisions independently?
keypoints: Surrogate decision makers are the preferred option when patients are unable to make decisions independently; however, their accuracy in representing patient preferences is approximately 68%, necessitating the use of advance directives and decision support tools to enhance this accuracy.

Clinicians should ensure that surrogate decision makers can accurately convey the patient’s wishes and pay close attention to how these preferences are expressed as well as the transparency of the communication process.

The role of surrogate decision makers should be flexibly tailored according to the patient’s decision-making capacity: when patients can make simple decisions but struggle with complex choices, surrogates assist with nuanced decisions, reflecting the principle of capacity-adjusted sliding-scale shared decision making; in cases of mild impairment, surrogates predominantly act as “preference advocates,” whereas with further decline in capacity, they assume more of a “clinical facilitator” role.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians adjust shared decision-making strategies to accommodate patients’ decision-making capacity and preferences while respecting patient autonomy?
keypoints: Physicians should assess patients’ decision-making capacity and preferences, and flexibly adjust shared decision-making strategies accordingly, as such adaptability constitutes a genuine respect for patient autonomy.

Capacity-adjusted sliding-scale shared decision making involves evaluating patient decision-making capacity and openness to shared decision making through three stages—team talk, option talk, and decision talk—and tailoring subsequent communication and decision-making approaches based on these assessments.

When patient decision-making capacity is impaired or expression of preferences is limited, clinicians should adopt a more directive approach while actively engaging surrogate decision makers to safeguard the patient’s interests.

Shared decision-making models are diverse (e.g., parental, directive), and clinicians should flexibly select the approach best suited to the individual patient’s circumstances, avoiding rigid application of any single model to achieve truly patient-centered medical decision making.

tags: Clinical research/Dual roles as clinicians and researchers
title: Can Consent to Participate in Clinical Research Involve Shared Decision Making?
case:
Dr T is a rheumatologist and principal investigator in several clinical trials on biologic agents. One of her patients, Mr X, has rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded well to standard treatment. Dr T approaches Mr X about enrolling in a phase II trial, the purpose of which is to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and dose specifications of a new monoclonal antibody. Dr T explains the trial’s design to Mr X, emphasizing the possibility that he would not receive the antibody if he is randomized to the placebo arm of the study. Dr T also explains that, if he does receive the antibody, Mr X could experience negative side effects and complications. Mr X agrees to participate in the trial.
About 2 weeks into the trial, during a follow-up visit, Dr T asks Mr X about his responses to the experimental agent. Mr X says, “Thank you, Dr T, for letting me try this treatment.” Dr T explains that the antibody is neither a treatment nor (even anywhere near being) an approved clinical intervention. Dr T reminds Mr X of the trial’s goals. Mr X responds, “I’m so lucky I have a doctor like you who can use research to help patients in ways other doctors can’t. This new medicine is great.”
Dr T wonders how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Dr T, a rheumatologist actively involved as the principal investigator in multiple clinical trials of biologic agents, is treating Mr X, a patient suffering from rheumatoid arthritis that has proven resistant to conventional therapies. Recognizing Mr X’s limited options, Dr T discusses with him the possibility of joining a phase II clinical trial, designed to assess the efficacy, safety, and optimal dosing of a novel monoclonal antibody. During their conversation, Dr T carefully outlines the structure of the study, making it clear to Mr X that participation involves randomization and that he could be assigned to either the group receiving the experimental antibody or the placebo group. She stresses that, should he receive the antibody, there are both unknown benefits and the risk of adverse side effects or complications.

After considering these points, Mr X consents to enroll in the trial. Approximately two weeks later, at a scheduled follow-up visit, Dr T inquires about Mr X’s experience thus far with the investigational agent. Mr X expresses his gratitude, saying, “Thank you, Dr T, for letting me try this treatment.” Sensing a misunderstanding, Dr T responds by clarifying that the antibody is not an established treatment, nor is it an approved clinical intervention at this stage; instead, it is still under investigation as part of the research. She reiterates the primary purpose and objectives of the clinical trial. Mr X replies, “I’m so lucky I have a doctor like you who can use research to help patients in ways other doctors can’t. This new medicine is great.”

Dr T pauses, reflecting on how best to address Mr X’s perception and ensure he fully understands his role as a research participant.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Dr T’s clinical trial, how can the informed consent process be structured to ensure that Mr X fully understands his role as a research participant and the purpose of the study?
keypoints: Assess the patient’s health literacy and use language that the patient can understand to clearly communicate research options, risks, and potential benefits.

Explicitly explain the nature of clinical research, emphasizing the significant uncertainty regarding the efficacy of experimental interventions, and correct any therapeutic misconception the patient may have.

Engage in open and honest communication with the patient to clarify major misunderstandings, resolve potential conflicts of interest, and ensure transparency of motivations and interests on both sides.
Evaluate the patient’s level of understanding by having them restate, in their own words, their comprehension of their role and the purpose of the research, and promptly correct any inaccuracies.

If the patient remains unable to understand the inherent risks and benefits of participation in the experimental study despite multiple clarifications, recommend withdrawal from the study to ensure the authenticity and validity of informed consent.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr T, as a clinical investigator, balance her professional interests in conducting research with her ethical obligation to prioritize Mr X’s welfare during the clinical trial?
keypoints: Investigators recruiting research subjects must rationally balance the public interest in scientific advancement with their own interests, preventing personal gains from overriding the ethically central value of subject-centeredness.

Clinical researchers should proactively disclose personal interests related to the study, including financial incentives, career advancement goals, and ownership of shares in the study sponsor, to ensure transparency and build trust.

Investigators ought to candidly explore potential subjects’ motivations and expectations during the shared decision-making process, clarify misconceptions, and comprehensively explain the reasons for both participation and refusal, thereby facilitating subjects’ rational judgment and high-quality informed consent.

ethical_issues.question: How can shared decision making be effectively implemented in clinical research to respect patient autonomy and avoid therapeutic misconception?
keypoints: Assess the patient’s health and research literacy to ensure that information about study options, risks, and benefits is communicated in language the patient can understand.
Clinical investigators should disclose their personal interests, including whether they receive compensation for recruiting subjects or hold equity in the company funding the research.
Confirm the patient’s understanding of the research purpose, procedures, and their own role—using methods such as teach-back—to ensure genuine comprehension.
Engage in transparent communication about the true aims of the trial and the inherent uncertainties, clarifying therapeutic misconceptions and potential conflicts of interest.
Accurately convey all known information about the experimental intervention, emphasizing that there remains significant uncertainty regarding its efficacy and safety.
Assist the patient in envisioning the potential impact of participating or not participating in the research on their lifestyle, supporting autonomous decision making aligned with their values.

title: When a Patient Regrets Having Undergone a Carefully and Jointly Considered Treatment Plan, How Should Her Physician Respond?
case:
Ms S is a 60-year-old woman with stage I breast cancer. After diagnosis, she was referred to a surgical oncologist, Dr J. Over the course of several visits, Dr J and Ms S considered risks and benefits of 2 primary treatment options: breast-conserving surgery with follow-up radiation and total mastectomy, which generally does not require radiation. The patient and surgeon agreed that a left total mastectomy would be best.
The mastectomy went well, and, during a follow-up visit, Dr J reported good news: there was no evidence to suggest that Ms S’s cancer had spread beyond her breast. Ms S was pleased to hear this news. She also seemed worried, however. “So, I was reading that there is no difference in survival between breast-conserving surgery and mastectomy.”
“Yes, you’re right. But as we discussed before your surgery, mastectomy patients are less likely to need radiation.You didn’t want radiation,” Dr J responded.
Ms S resumed, “Well, that was what I thought at the time.But now I wish I’d had the breast-conserving therapy with the radiation. Maybe I didn’t need the more disfiguring surgery.”
Dr J listened. “I think I understand your concerns, yet I think we had a good discussion about the decision we made together. We talked through all the relevant details, and you seemed to understand them thoroughly at the time. That was important to both of us. I think this decision was well made and had a good outcome. That said, I understand that postsurgical hindsight can make us think differently about what the details mean at different times in our reflections. Why don’t we talk more during your next follow-up visit?”
Ms S agreed, wiping a tear from her face. Dr J wondered if she could have done or said more to help Ms S with her feelings of postsurgery regret.
case_rewrite:
Ms S, a 60-year-old woman, was recently diagnosed with stage I breast cancer. Following her diagnosis, she was referred to Dr J, a surgical oncologist. Over several appointments, Ms S and Dr J engaged in careful discussions about the two main treatment approaches available to her: breast-conserving surgery followed by radiation therapy, or a total mastectomy, which typically does not require radiation. Together, they weighed the risks and benefits of each option. After thoughtful consideration and discussion, both Ms S and Dr J agreed that proceeding with a left total mastectomy aligned best with Ms S’s preferences and concerns at the time.

The surgery was successful, and at a follow-up visit, Dr J shared encouraging news—there was no indication that Ms S’s cancer had spread beyond her breast. Ms S expressed relief, but her demeanor shifted as she voiced a lingering concern. “I was reading that survival rates are the same whether you have breast-conserving surgery or a mastectomy,” she said quietly.

Dr J nodded. “That’s correct. But as we discussed before your surgery, patients who have a mastectomy are much less likely to need radiation afterward. I remember you were especially keen to avoid radiation.”

Ms S hesitated, then admitted, “That’s what I thought at the time. But now I wish I’d chosen the breast-conserving surgery with radiation. Maybe I didn’t need to go through a more disfiguring operation.”

Dr J listened attentively. “I understand where you’re coming from. I do think we had a thorough discussion and considered all the relevant information together. It was very important to me that you understood all your options, and you seemed comfortable with the choice we made. We both wanted to make sure the decision was right for you. Sometimes, after surgery, it’s natural to look back and see things differently. Why don’t we talk more about your feelings and any questions you have during your next visit?”

Ms S agreed, dabbing at a tear. As she left, Dr J reflected on the situation, wondering if there was anything more she could have done or said to help Ms S cope with her post-surgical regrets.

ethical_issues.question: Did the physician adequately respect the patient’s autonomy and ensure that the patient understood the risks and benefits of all treatment options during the shared decision-making process?
keypoints: The shared decision-making process should respect patient autonomy and ensure that the patient fully understands the risks and benefits of all treatment options.
Both the physician and the patient must mutually recognize that a treatment decision needs to be made and understand the advantages and disadvantages of each option through thorough communication.
Decisions should integrate the physician’s professional guidance with the patient’s personal preferences and values, reflecting the principle of individualized care.
The physician should conduct the decision-making process with beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, and respect for patient autonomy to ensure ethical compliance.

Even if the patient experiences decisional regret postoperatively, the process can still be considered ethically appropriate provided it adheres to the above principles and the information was conveyed clearly and comprehensively.

ethical_issues.question: When multiple treatment options with equivalent efficacy but different clinical implications exist, did the physician thoroughly discuss the differences among all options and take into account the patient’s individual preferences and values?
keypoints: Both the physician and the patient must mutually recognize the need to make a treatment decision and fully understand the risks and benefits of each treatment option.

Treatment decisions must integrate the physician’s professional guidance with the patient’s personal preferences and values; this principle is especially applicable to preference-sensitive decisions where multiple medically reasonable options exist.

ethical_issues.question: Did the physician act according to the principles of beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice during the decision-making process, and did the physician discuss the possibility of decisional regret and its implications for future treatment with the patient?
keypoints: Physicians should adhere to the principles of beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, and respect for patient autonomy, ensuring that patients fully understand the information provided and actively participate in the decision-making process.

Physicians should act in the best interests of the patient, communicate necessary information in a manner that is easily understood by the patient, and safeguard the patient’s rights to informed consent and autonomy.

When multiple treatment options with equivalent efficacy but differing clinical characteristics are available, physicians should comprehensively and objectively discuss the risks, benefits, and potential impacts on quality of life for each option to assist patients in making a well-considered choice.

Physicians should proactively discuss the possibility of decisional regret with patients, including its potential impact on future treatment and psychological well-being, to help patients form realistic expectations and prepare psychologically.

Even if a patient experiences decisional regret postoperatively, physicians should reflect on the communication and support process, continue to attend to the patient’s emotional state, ensure that the principles of medical ethics are upheld, and provide necessary psychological support.

title: What Constitutes Effective Team Communication After an Error?
case: After taking over an all-day abdominal perineal resection in which a patient experienced “some blood loss,” the patient’s surgical team was informed about the anesthesiology team’s plan to transfuse the patient with a third unit of packed red blood cells. The team members looked up in acknowledgement and continued surgery. A blood gas was drawn, revealing the patient’s hemoglobin (Hgb) level as 6.6 g/dL, compared to 14.8 g/dL at the start of the surgery. When the surgeons were informed of the Hgb, they indicated that more bleeding should be expected but didn’t say why. On 3 separate occasions, the attending anesthesiologist asked the surgeons for updates on the patient’s current surgical situation because the anesthesiology team was not able to keep up with the patient’s blood, fluid, and resuscitation demands. Specifically, the amount and source of blood loss (eg, arterial vs venous vs oozing) and the surgical team’s plan to continue dissection despite continued bleeding was not clearly communicated to the anesthesia team. The patient’s hemodynamics continued to worsen. A massive transfusion protocol, transesophageal electrocardiogram, and rapid infuser were initiated, and additional anesthesia personnel were called. The surgeons finally disclosed to the anesthesiology team that the patient’s iliac vein was nicked earlier in the surgery. The extent of injury to the patient now became evident, as did one consequence of the absence of real-time communication from the surgeons: the anesthesia team had dramatically underestimated how much blood loss the patient would suffer during the earlier intraoperative resuscitation. Fortunately, hemostasis was achieved, and the patient stabilized. The surgeons recommended additional blood resuscitation to the anesthesia team before completing the surgery and leaving the operating room. At the end of the surgery, the patient was not extubated as usual, and, based on the update provided by the surgeon, the patient’s family members understood that the anesthesia team was responsible for the patient’s unplanned postsurgical stay in the intensive care unit (ICU).
case_rewrite:
After taking over an extensive abdominal perineal resection, during which the patient had experienced “some blood loss,” the surgical team was made aware that the anesthesiology team planned to administer a third unit of packed red blood cells. The surgeons briefly acknowledged this update and proceeded with the operation. A subsequent blood gas analysis revealed that the patient’s hemoglobin had dropped to 6.6 g/dL from 14.8 g/dL at the beginning of surgery. When this critical lab value was reported to the surgeons, they noted that further bleeding was likely, though they did not elaborate on the underlying cause. Throughout the procedure, the attending anesthesiologist requested updates from the surgeons on three separate occasions, seeking clarification on the current surgical situation. The anesthesia team was struggling to match the patient’s escalating blood and fluid resuscitation needs, but they received no clear information regarding the volume or source of the blood loss—whether arterial, venous, or diffuse oozing—nor did the surgical team communicate their plan to proceed with dissection in the setting of ongoing hemorrhage.

As the patient’s hemodynamic status continued to deteriorate, the anesthesia team initiated a massive transfusion protocol, performed transesophageal echocardiography, employed a rapid infuser, and called for additional anesthesia staff. Only at this point did the surgeons inform the anesthesia team that the patient’s iliac vein had been nicked earlier in the operation. This disclosure made the true extent of the patient’s injury apparent, as well as the consequences of the lack of real-time communication: the anesthesia team had underestimated the anticipated blood loss during previous resuscitative efforts.

Fortunately, bleeding was eventually controlled and the patient’s condition stabilized. Before concluding the operation and leaving the operating room, the surgeons advised the anesthesia team to continue aggressive blood resuscitation. At the end of the case, the patient was not extubated as would typically be expected. When the surgeon updated the patient’s family, the family was left with the impression that the anesthesia team was responsible for the patient’s unexpected postoperative stay in the intensive care unit (ICU).

ethical_issues.question: How can effective communication be ensured among medical teams with different professional backgrounds during surgery to safeguard patient safety?
keypoints: Establish an egalitarian model of team collaboration that replaces the traditional paternalistic and authoritative decision-making approach, ensuring that patients, family members, and all relevant clinical professionals participate in the discussion and decision-making of the treatment plan.

Ensure that critical information—such as the volume and source of blood loss and the surgical plan in the context of ongoing intraoperative bleeding—is communicated to the anesthesia team in a timely, comprehensive, and accurate manner.
Use clear and comprehensible language accessible to all parties involved to avoid confusion and misunderstanding caused by specialized medical terminology.
Avoid blame and finger-pointing, focusing instead on an objective description of the sequence of events and the subsequent response and action plans.
Promote interdisciplinary collaboration through open, respectful, and cooperative team communication to safeguard patient safety and maintain the overall integrity of the healthcare system.

ethical_issues.question: When a medical error or adverse outcome occurs, how should the clinical team communicate transparently with the patient and their family in order to maintain trust and professional relationships?
keypoints: The medical team should jointly participate in postoperative communication with the patient and family members to promote improvement in medical quality and system refinement.
The key clinicians involved should collaboratively review the case, reach consensus on the details of the event, and ensure consistency of information.
Communication should take place in an appropriate setting, focus on the patient’s best interests, clearly identify a lead communicator, and ensure the effectiveness of the exchange.
The goal of communication is full and transparent disclosure of the course of events, with an emphasis on constructive dialogue and avoidance of blame or shifting of responsibility.
Language used should be clear, accessible, and accurate, avoiding confusion caused by medical jargon, and should reflect empathy and concern.
The medical team should collaboratively explain the sequence of events, the remedial measures taken, and future plans for prevention.

Family members’ questions should be actively addressed, with emotional support and sincere apologies provided, updates on the investigation and improvement measures communicated, and efforts made to rebuild trust and maintain ongoing communication.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with a medical error, how should the medical team avoid mutual blame and instead share responsibility to promote optimal patient outcomes?
keypoints: The medical teams should jointly review the case, reach a consensus on the details of the event, avoid mutual blame, and promote internal trust and collaboration within the team.

Both parties should participate together in postoperative communication with the patient and family, providing a transparent account of the events, the remedial measures taken, and future strategies for error prevention.
The teams should offer a collective apology and demonstrate sincerity, reinforcing collaborative problem-solving and enhancing trust in the patient-clinician relationship.
Emphasize the importance of team-based collaboration, focus on achieving the best possible patient outcomes, and uphold the integrity and continuous improvement of the health care system.

title: Who Should Manage a Patient’s Airway?
case:
Ms C is a 52-year-old woman with a hoarse voice and trouble swallowing. She has a history of obesity and obstructive sleep apnea and cannot lay flat without getting short of breath, due to a large (8 x 8 cm) benign thyroid mass that deviates her trachea and narrows its oral opening. Ms C has elected to have a total thyroidectomy with Dr E, a senior ear, nose, and throat surgeon and Dr A, a junior anesthesiologist new to the practice group.
Being able to breathe for a patient after suppressing (via administration of anesthetics and paralytics) the natural drive to breathe is an anesthesiologist’s primary focus during surgery. Developing an airway plan is how anesthesiologists and surgeons work together to map out how they will intubate the patient and manage risk that a patient’s airway could collapse during general anesthesia induction. A Mallampati score is used topredicthow likely a patient can be intubated without complication. Ms C’s Mallampati score is 3, indicating her intubation will probably be difficult.
When discussing the airway plan for Ms C’s procedure, Dr A recommends fiberoptic intubation, emphasizing the importance of a more conservative, less risky approach to securing Ms C’s airway. That is, Dr A’s preferred airway plan involves keeping Ms C awake and breathing on her own while they place and secure her breathing tube prior to general anesthesia induction.
Dr E asserts that fiberoptic intubation is not necessary. Although preserving Ms C’s drive to breathe longer is less risky, being awake can also make a patient anxious. Dr E is concerned that Ms C will feel terrified and panic during fiberoptic intubation and thus prefers an airway plan that rapidly secures her airway via rigid bronchoscope.
Dr A reluctantly defers to Dr E’s seniority and experience and agrees to implement Dr E’s airway plan. Ms C is brought to the operating room, monitors are applied, and she is placed in a 45-degree, head-up position to help her feel more comfortable breathing. Dr A administers anesthetics and paralytics and places an oral airway, but he has trouble securing it. Dr A uses a 2-handed technique to mask ventilate Ms C, but not much oxygen moves into her lungs and her oxygen saturation falls to 88%. Dr A then performs direct laryngoscopy but cannot visualize Ms C’s vocal cords and thus cannot intubate her. The team again attempts to mask ventilate Ms C but without success. (After amending the initial fiberoptic intubation plan, Dr A apparently has no back-up plans for failed direct laryngoscopy.) Dr E then attempts several times to place the airway via rigid bronchoscope, but Ms C’s oxygen saturation, blood pressure, and heart rate fall, indicating looming cardiac arrest. Finally, Dr E secures Ms C’s airway, she slowly stabilizes, and her surgery proceeds.
Drs A and E are relieved. They wonder about how they weighed potential risks and benefits in planning and implementing Ms C’s airway plan.
case_rewrite:
Ms C, a 52-year-old woman, presents with a persistently hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing. She has a background of obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, and she is unable to lie flat without experiencing shortness of breath. This is due to a large, benign thyroid mass measuring 8 x 8 cm, which has shifted her trachea and narrowed its upper opening. After discussing her options, Ms C chooses to undergo a total thyroidectomy with Dr E, an experienced ear, nose, and throat surgeon. Dr A, a junior anesthesiologist who is new to the practice, will manage her anesthesia.

A central responsibility for anesthesiologists during surgery is maintaining the patient’s ability to breathe, especially after administering anesthetics and paralytics that suppress this natural drive. To prepare, anesthesiologists and surgeons jointly develop an airway plan—a strategy for safely intubating the patient and minimizing the risk of airway collapse during induction of general anesthesia. The Mallampati score, which predicts the likelihood of a straightforward intubation, is a key tool in this planning. Ms C’s Mallampati score is 3, suggesting her airway will likely be difficult to manage.

As they prepare for surgery, Dr A proposes a fiberoptic intubation approach, stressing the advantages of a more cautious and less risky technique. His plan would involve keeping Ms C awake and breathing independently as her breathing tube is placed and secured, only then proceeding with general anesthesia. Dr E, however, disagrees, arguing that fiberoptic intubation is unnecessary. He acknowledges that preserving Ms C’s spontaneous breathing is safer but raises concerns about the anxiety and fear a patient might experience while awake for this process. Dr E prefers a faster method: securing the airway with a rigid bronchoscope after induction.

Despite his reservations, Dr A defers to Dr E’s seniority and agrees to use the rigid bronchoscope approach. On the day of surgery, Ms C is brought to the operating room, where monitors are applied and she is positioned at a 45-degree angle to ease her breathing. Dr A administers the anesthetic agents and paralytics, then attempts to place an oral airway, but encounters difficulty. He tries a two-handed technique to mask ventilate her, yet only minimal oxygen reaches her lungs and her oxygen saturation drops to 88%. Turning to direct laryngoscopy, Dr A is unable to visualize the vocal cords, making intubation impossible. The team tries again to mask ventilate, but without success. (After abandoning the initial fiberoptic plan, Dr A has no further backup strategies for failed direct laryngoscopy.) Dr E steps in and attempts several times to secure the airway using the rigid bronchoscope, but Ms C’s oxygen saturation, blood pressure, and heart rate fall—signs of impending cardiac arrest. At last, Dr E manages to secure her airway, and Ms C gradually stabilizes, allowing the surgery to proceed.

Afterward, both Dr A and Dr E are relieved but find themselves reflecting on the process. They question how they balanced the risks and benefits in planning and carrying out Ms C’s airway management.

ethical_issues.question: In the decision-making process regarding a patient’s airway management, how can informed consent be ensured and shared decision-making facilitated so that the patient understands the surgical goals and potential challenges?
keypoints: Patients should be fully informed of the surgical objectives, potential risks, and challenges, and actively involved in shared decision-making whenever possible to ensure that their preferences and values are respected.

Anesthesiologists and surgeons should engage collaboratively in communication, employing a professional and empathetic approach to ensure that the patient comprehends the details of the treatment plan and that informed consent is confirmed.

Any difficulties, adverse events, or unexpected occurrences during the intraoperative and postoperative periods should be disclosed truthfully to the patient or their surrogate, maintaining transparency and openness.

The airway management process and associated risks should be thoroughly documented postoperatively in written form (e.g., a letter to the patient) to provide a basis for subsequent care and facilitate ongoing patient-provider communication.

title: What Should an Anesthesiologist and Surgeon Do When They Disagree About Terms of Perioperative DNR Suspension?
case:
A 76-year-old woman with dementia, Ms B, is brought to the emergency department after she fell at her nursing home. An X-ray reveals a left femoral neck fracture, and she is seen by an orthopedic consultant, Dr S, who recommends surgical repair.
Ms B has numerous comorbidities, including aortic stenosis and chronic atrial fibrillation (severe heart disorders that affect the heart’s rhythm and overall function). To treat these conditions, she takes a blood thinner. Ms B also uses supplemental oxygen to treat her chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder. For the past 3 years, her husband took care of her at home and was her surrogate decision maker. Since her husband’s recent death, Ms B’s son, who lives abroad, placed her in a skilled nursing facility. Last year, Ms B’s husband agreed with clinicians’ recommendation that Ms B’s code status should be do not resuscitate (DNR). Ms B’s son, who is her current surrogate decision maker, continues to agree with this recommendation.
That night, an orthopedic surgeon, Dr O, explains via telephone to Ms B’s son that surgery should be done within 24 hours to achieve the best possible outcome and that the goals of surgery are to restore Ms B’s hip mobility and help palliate her pain. Ms B’s son gives consent for his mother to undergo surgery in the morning.
In the morning, with surgery scheduled to begin in 30 minutes, the anesthesiologist, Dr A, meets Ms B in the preoperative holding area; she is agitated and disoriented. Dr A calls Ms B’s son to confirm her past medical history and explains that, based on her comorbidities, she is at a high risk for complications and adverse outcomes. Dr A also explains that, in many cases, a patient’s DNR order is suspended during and immediately after surgery. Ms B’s son seems surprised. “This is the first time I’m hearing about her being high risk. And, well, the DNR…. She’s been DNR for years. Why would I suspend it now? I just talked with the surgeon yesterday about this. I thought this procedure would help reduce her pain.” After a pause, Ms B’s son rescinds consent for his mother’s surgery.
Dr S is surprised and frustrated to learn this news. “Ms B needed this operation and delaying it will only increase her risk of mortality and other complications.”
Dr A replies, “I agree that the surgical goals make sense overall. But Ms B is a sick, frail, elderly person for whom a DNR order has been appropriately in place for many years. She could die during surgery, or she could make it through but then require ventilator support and intensive care. Her son was surprised when I mentioned suspending her DNR order.”
They stood together, concerned about what to do next for Ms B.
case_rewrite:
Ms B, a 76-year-old woman with dementia, arrives at the emergency department after suffering a fall at her nursing home. An X-ray reveals that she has fractured her left femoral neck. Dr S, the orthopedic consultant, assesses her and recommends surgical repair.

Ms B’s medical history is significant for several serious comorbidities, including aortic stenosis and chronic atrial fibrillation—both severe heart conditions for which she takes a blood thinner. She also relies on supplemental oxygen to manage her chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Over the past three years, Ms B’s husband cared for her at home and acted as her surrogate decision maker. Following his recent death, Ms B’s son, who lives overseas, arranged for her to be placed in a skilled nursing facility and became her new surrogate. Last year, Ms B’s husband, in agreement with her clinicians, established a “do not resuscitate” (DNR) order for her. Ms B’s son, now responsible for her decisions, continues to support this status.

That evening, Dr O, the orthopedic surgeon who will perform the procedure, phones Ms B’s son. Dr O explains that operating within 24 hours will give Ms B the best chance of recovery and that the primary goals are to restore her hip mobility and alleviate her pain. Ms B’s son gives his consent for the surgery to proceed the following morning.

On the morning of the scheduled surgery, with the procedure set to begin in half an hour, Dr A, the anesthesiologist, meets Ms B in the preoperative holding area. Ms B is noticeably agitated and confused. Dr A contacts Ms B’s son to verify her medical background and discusses the significant risks posed by her multiple health issues, emphasizing that she is at high risk for complications and adverse outcomes. Dr A also brings up a critical point: in many hospitals, a patient’s DNR order is typically suspended during and shortly after surgery. This surprises Ms B’s son. “No one has told me she was such a high risk before. And as for the DNR… She’s had that in place for years. Why would we change it now? I just spoke with the surgeon yesterday and thought this was mainly to help with her pain.” After a moment’s reflection, Ms B’s son decides to withdraw his consent for the surgery.

Dr S is startled and dismayed by this sudden change. “Ms B really needs this operation. Delaying it will only make things worse, increasing her risk of death or other complications.”

Dr A responds, “I understand the surgical objectives, but Ms B is a frail, elderly patient with longstanding, appropriate DNR orders. There’s a real possibility she could die during surgery, or she may survive but end up needing a ventilator and intensive care. Her son was clearly caught off guard when I mentioned suspending the DNR.”

The two physicians stand together, worried and uncertain about the best course of action for Ms B.

ethical_issues.question: Should a Patient’s DNR Order Be Automatically Suspended Perioperatively to Allow for Surgical Resuscitation?
keypoints: Policies that automatically suspend DNR orders may inadequately protect patient autonomy and should be reviewed and revised.

Decisions regarding suspension of DNR orders should be made on a case-by-case basis through preoperative discussion, ensuring respect for patient autonomy and allowing for dynamic adjustment according to the patient’s health status and clinical context.

If there is disagreement among the patient (or surrogate), anesthesiologist, and surgeon regarding perioperative DNR suspension, surgery should be postponed until effective communication establishes consensus or at least a basic agreement.

Discussions about perioperative DNR orders should be initiated as early as possible, ideally during the surgical planning phase, to prevent last-minute conflicts and to facilitate informed shared decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: How should conflicts between patient autonomy and clinical expertise be managed in the perioperative period?
keypoints: When managing conflicts between patient autonomy and clinical expertise in the perioperative period, automatic suspension of DNR orders should be avoided to prevent undermining patient autonomy.

Preoperative decisions regarding temporary informed suspension of DNR orders should be made on a case-by-case basis through detailed discussion, respecting the autonomous choices of the patient and their surrogate.

Perioperative discussions about DNR orders should involve the patient (or surrogate), surgeon, and anesthesiologist to ensure informed shared decision-making and to maintain trust in the physician-patient relationship.

Ideally, perioperative DNR discussions should be initiated during the surgical planning phase, clarifying the patient’s values and treatment goals, and thoroughly communicating the specific surgical risks, expected benefits, and anesthesia options.
If disagreements arise regarding the terms of perioperative DNR suspension, surgery should be postponed until effective communication facilitates consensus or at least a basic agreement.

title: How Should a Surgeon and Anesthesiologist Cooperate During Intraoperative Cardiac Arrest?
case:
Ms D is a 43-year-old woman who consents to undergo an elective laparoscopic left nephrectomy to remove a renal cell carcinoma. The surgery team, led by Dr S, and the anesthesiology team, led by Dr A, agree that Ms D’s risk for perioperative complications is low. Her surgery proceeds routinely, and she wakes from anesthesia in stable condition.
A few hours later, however, Ms D develops a tense, distended abdomen; her heart rate is elevated; and her blood pressure is low. Dr S evaluates Ms D and believes that she has internal bleeding and needs to be taken back to the operating room.
Back in the operating room, massive transfusion of blood products is begun. After induction of anesthesia, Ms D’s blood pressure drops significantly. Dr A’s team administers medications to try to raise her blood pressure. Dr S’s team opens Ms D’s abdomen, and it is clear that there is significant internal bleeding. Dr V, the on-call vascular surgeon, is paged to the room, and everyone works together to try to control of Ms D’s bleeding. Dr A continues to deliver blood products and escalates doses of blood pressure-augmenting medications, but Ms D’s condition declines, with ST elevations on her electrocardiogram indicating cardiac compromise. Dr A communicates this information to surgical team members, who continue to try to identify the source of bleeding. After 15 minutes, however, Dr A asks the surgical team to pause to allow the anesthesiology team to resuscitate the patient.
The surgery team stops, but only after applying packing and pressure to what they’ve now finally identified as the source of the bleeding, Ms D’s inferior vena cava (IVC). Dr A administers more blood products.
The surgery team resumes operating, and Ms D sustains cardiac arrest. The surgical team stops operating and applies pressure to Ms D’s IVC during resuscitation, led by Dr A for 10 minutes—and after administration of more than 100 units of blood products.
Spontaneous circulation is achieved, and Dr S’s team resumes operating. Dr A now worries about Ms D’s neurological status, as anesthetics have not been administered for several minutes, suggesting Ms D has had brain injury as a result of low blood pressure.
Ms D sustains a second cardiac arrest. Dr A’s team resumes resuscitation, then requests resuscitation be stopped, believing Ms D is moribund. Dr S’s team requests resuscitation be continued while they attempt to control the IVC bleeding.
Dr A wonders whether to insist on ceasing resuscitation.
case_rewrite:
Ms D, a 43-year-old woman, consents to undergo an elective laparoscopic left nephrectomy for removal of a renal cell carcinoma. Dr S leads the surgical team, and Dr A heads the anesthesiology team. Both teams agree that Ms D is at low risk for perioperative complications. The surgery proceeds without incident, and Ms D awakens from anesthesia in stable condition.

Several hours later, Ms D develops a tense, distended abdomen, her heart rate accelerates, and her blood pressure drops. Dr S evaluates her and suspects internal bleeding, recommending immediate return to the operating room.

In the OR, a massive transfusion of blood products is initiated. After anesthesia induction, Ms D’s blood pressure plummets. Dr A’s team administers medications in an attempt to stabilize her hemodynamics. As Dr S’s team reopens her abdomen, they encounter substantial internal bleeding. Dr V, the on-call vascular surgeon, is urgently paged. All teams work together to control the hemorrhage. Dr A continues to deliver blood products and increases the doses of blood pressure-supporting medications, but Ms D’s condition continues to deteriorate. ST elevations appear on her electrocardiogram, signaling cardiac compromise. Dr A informs the surgical team of these findings, but the search for the bleeding source continues.

After about 15 minutes, Dr A requests a pause in surgery so the anesthesiology team can focus on resuscitating Ms D. The surgical team temporarily halts, but only after packing and applying pressure to the source of the bleeding—her inferior vena cava (IVC), now identified. Dr A administers additional blood products.

Once resuscitation efforts stabilize Ms D’s circulation somewhat, the surgical team resumes their work. Suddenly, Ms D suffers a cardiac arrest. The surgical team stops operating and maintains pressure on the IVC while Dr A leads a 10-minute resuscitation, during which over 100 units of blood products have been administered.

Spontaneous circulation returns, and Dr S’s team resumes operating. Meanwhile, Dr A grows concerned about Ms D’s neurological status, as she has received no anesthetics for several minutes, suggesting possible brain injury from prolonged low blood pressure.

Soon after, Ms D experiences a second cardiac arrest. Dr A’s team initiates another round of resuscitation, but this time Dr A requests that resuscitative efforts be stopped, believing Ms D’s condition to be moribund. However, Dr S’s team asks that resuscitation continue as they attempt to control the IVC bleeding.

Dr A is left to consider whether to press for cessation of resuscitation.

ethical_issues.question: In the event of intraoperative cardiac arrest, should resuscitative efforts be terminated, and how should the futility of resuscitation be determined?
keypoints: The decision to cease resuscitation during intraoperative cardiac arrest should be based on a comprehensive assessment of the patient’s comorbidities, functional status, cause of arrest, and the perioperative context.

When all reversible causes have been corrected without success and there is a possibility of neurological injury, the utilitarian implications of continuing resuscitation must be carefully weighed, including the patient’s prognosis and the prudent use of limited medical resources.

The decision to terminate resuscitative efforts should be made collectively by the entire perioperative team, with respect and thorough consideration given to the opinions of all professional members, reflecting a multidisciplinary collaborative approach.

The decision-making process must be open and transparent, with a clear expression of the intent to cease resuscitation; if any team member disagrees, resuscitative efforts should be immediately resumed to ensure that patient interests are maximized through communication and cooperation.

Currently, there is a lack of high-quality evidence and definitive guidelines to direct the cessation of resuscitation during intraoperative cardiac arrest; decisions must therefore rely on existing data and clinical judgment.

ethical_issues.question: How should the utilitarian implications of continuing resuscitation be balanced against the consumption of limited resources following intraoperative cardiac arrest?
keypoints: When all efforts to correct underlying causes have failed, the utilitarian implications of continued resuscitation and the consumption of limited resources such as blood products must be carefully weighed.
Although there is currently a lack of high-quality evidence to determine the futility of resuscitation, existing data trends can be used to make prognostic predictions that assist in decision-making.
Initial resuscitation decisions should be made based on a rational assessment that integrates the patient’s comorbidities, functional status, cause of cardiac arrest, and contextual factors.

Evidence indicates that patients with multiple comorbidities or those who experience hypotension, asystole, or pulseless electrical activity prior to arrest have a lower likelihood of survival with favorable neurological outcomes.

Decisions to cease resuscitative efforts during intraoperative cardiac arrest must be made collaboratively by all members of the perioperative team, openly communicated in the room, and all opinions respected; if disagreement arises, resuscitation should continue.

Team members should collaborate from their respective professional perspectives, maintaining open communication and mutual trust to ensure patient welfare and the scientific integrity of decision-making.
