title: Should a Caregiver’s QoL Be Considered in Decisions About Whether a Patient Has an Experimental Double-Hand Transplant?
case:
C is a quadrilateral amputee who lives with her partner, N. After 2 years of working with prosthetics and outfitting their apartment with assistive devices, N and C have a life together they enjoy.
When C is offered an opportunity to be evaluated for an experimental double-hand transplant by Dr PT, her long-time physical therapist (who is working with a newly formed research team at their hospital), N struggles with the idea of a radical change in her own and C’s living situation. Despite N’s devotion to C, she is worried about how she would manage additional caretaking responsibilities if an experimental surgery does not turn out well for C. N agrees with C, however, that having C be evaluated would give them an opportunity to consider possible benefits and risks.
During C’s evaluation to consider whether she meets the criteria for enrolling in the double-hand transplant research protocol, N tries to gain information about possible effects that a double-hand transplant would have on her own quality of life without seeming self-absorbed or unsupportive of C’s enthusiasm about the protocol. N asks, “What will C’s recovery process be like?”
Dr B, the study’s principal investigator, responds, “I wish I could tell you it’s going to be quick and easy. But as you can probably imagine, it will likely be neither. In above-elbow amputees, like C, we expect nerve regeneration to take 1½ to 2 years.Nerves grow at a rate of about a millimeter per day. So, in the first year after the transplant surgery, C will need help with almost all aspects of self-care and rehabilitative therapy.”
N struggles to keep her expression neutral and optimistic, but she is distressed by this information. The transplant team’s physical therapist, Dr PT, who is helping to facilitate the conversation, notices N’s distress as the team concludes the evaluation.
Dr PT remarks to Dr B later, “N was clearly upset and seemed overwhelmed, and who wouldn’t be. I wish we had brought N into the conversation more about whether hand transplant is the right choice for C and for them as a couple. Highly involved partners and family members provide critical support to our study participants’ abilities to adhere to postsurgical care recommendations. They’ll both need a lot of support in the follow-up years if C participates in our study. It seems we should somehow be incorporating the caregiver more in our evaluations. How should we do that?”
case_rewrite:
C, a quadrilateral amputee, lives with her partner N in an apartment they have adapted together over the past two years. With the help of prosthetics and a range of assistive devices, C and N have created a daily routine that allows them both to enjoy a fulfilling life together.

One day, C learns about the possibility of being evaluated for an experimental double-hand transplant. The opportunity comes through Dr PT, C’s long-time physical therapist, who is now collaborating with a newly established research team at the hospital. The news is both exciting and daunting. While C is eager to consider the potential for increased independence, N feels apprehensive about the prospect of such a major change. Despite her deep commitment to C, N worries about how she would manage if the experimental surgery leads to complications or increased caregiving demands. Nevertheless, N agrees with C that undergoing the evaluation is worthwhile, as it will help them both weigh the possible risks and rewards.

During C’s assessment for eligibility in the double-hand transplant research protocol, N seeks to understand how the surgery could affect not just C, but their shared life. Hoping not to appear self-centered or unsupportive, N asks, “What will C’s recovery process be like?”

Dr B, the principal investigator of the study, responds candidly, “I wish I could say the recovery will be quick and easy, but that simply isn’t the case. For someone like C, with amputations above the elbow, nerve regeneration can take a year and a half to two years—nerves grow about a millimeter per day. In that first year after surgery, C will need significant help with almost every aspect of self-care and rehabilitation.”

N tries to maintain a supportive demeanor, but the weight of this information is clear in her tense posture and subdued expression. Dr PT, present to help facilitate the conversation, notices N’s distress as the evaluation draws to a close.

Later, as the team debriefs, Dr PT turns to Dr B. “N was visibly upset and overwhelmed—who wouldn’t be, in her position? I can’t help but think we should have included N more in the discussion about whether this transplant is right for C, but also for them as a couple. We know that partners and family members are essential for our participants to follow through with post-surgical care. If C joins the study, both she and N will need extensive support over the coming years. It seems crucial that we find a way to involve the caregiver more fully in our evaluation process. How should we approach this?”

ethical_issues.question: Should the quality of life and well-being of the caregiver be considered in decisions about whether a patient undergoes an experimental double-hand transplant?
keypoints: Given the significant impact of nonprofessional caregivers on graft survival and overall patient well-being, as well as their crucial rehabilitative role outside the hospital setting, there exists a moral obligation to incorporate caregivers and their well-being into considerations of candidacy for hand and upper extremity transplantation.

The physiological and psychosocial burdens faced by caregivers may affect their health and the quality of care they provide; such caregiver burden must be systematically identified and integrated into transplant evaluations.

Neglecting caregiver burden may undermine the patient’s efforts to regain personal independence and self-identity; therefore, caregivers’ needs should be regarded as an extension of the patient’s needs, reflecting the holistic nature of the patient-caregiver relationship.

ethical_issues.question: Should considerations of the caregiver and their well-being be incorporated into the evaluation of candidacy for hand and upper extremity transplantation to ensure the transplant recipient’s autonomous desire for successful rehabilitation?
keypoints: Caregivers exert a critical influence on transplant recipients’ rehabilitation and overall well-being; therefore, their needs and welfare should be thoroughly considered in evaluations as an extension of the patient’s own needs.

Failure to provide caregivers with proactive guidance and support may undermine the transplant recipient’s autonomous motivation for rehabilitation and their efforts to regain independence and self-identity.

Ensuring reliable caregiver support embodies the transplant team’s ethical responsibility and professional integrity, helping to mitigate the risks of unsafe transplantation arising from inadequate support.

Actively incorporating caregivers’ perspectives and well-being considerations facilitates postoperative adherence and social reintegration of transplant recipients, thereby enhancing overall treatment outcomes.

ethical_issues.question: Does the treatment team have a responsibility to seek a balance between the patient’s need and desire for bilateral hand transplantation and the well-being of the nonprofessional caregiver?
keypoints: The specialized treatment team should continuously monitor the psychological and practical burdens of nonprofessional caregivers during assessment and follow-up, providing proactive support and guidance to promote the overall well-being of the patient and their family.

The treatment team has a moral obligation to include nonprofessional caregivers and their well-being in the eligibility assessment for hand and upper extremity transplantation, given their critical impact on graft survival, patient recovery, and overall well-being.

Nonprofessional caregivers provide sustained social support, encompassing assistance with physical rehabilitation, supervision of medication adherence, and communication of needs, thereby safeguarding patient autonomy and treatment compliance.

During consultation, the needs of nonprofessional caregivers should be regarded as an extension of the patient’s needs, facilitating thorough communication and consensus-building to ensure comprehensive and rational treatment decision-making.

Neglecting caregiver burden may not only compromise patient recovery outcomes but also undermine the patient’s efforts to regain independence and self-identity; therefore, attending to caregiver well-being is a fundamental aspect of professional medical ethics.

title: How Should Surgeons Balance Transplantation Innovation With Acceptance of a Trauma Survivor’s Appearance?
case:
About 40% of Dan’s face was burned in an accident many years ago. Several sites on Dan’s body have also been scarred by skin-harvesting from numerous reconstructive surgeries. Although many years have passed since the accident, Dan still suffers long-term grief and feels profoundly depressed about not having a romantic partner. Dan also feels hopelessness and sadness about his surgeons having said they’ve exhausted traditional reconstructive options on his face. Specifically, Dan remembers his plastic surgeon once stating, “There’s nothing else we can do” to improve appearance, ability to speak, or ability to eat easily.
Dan’s feelings of grief, longing, hopelessness, and sadness are made even more complex by his feeling guilty about not being able to just accept his face as it is. Dan feels solidarity with other burn survivors, whom he meets occasionally at conferences and support groups, and he feels it is important to resist cultural and social pressure both to medicalize his survivorship more than necessary and to try to meet unrealistic standards of “normal” physical appearance. He feels torn between wanting to accept his appearance as it is and wanting it to be good enough for a prospective romantic partner to find attractive.
Dan has read about face transplantation in various online news sources, and he now researches the procedure with more interest. He knows that whatever aesthetic, manual, and social enhancement he could gain through a face graft would come with high costs, substantial risks, and demand for lifelong adherence to prescription medications. Dan also knows his health insurance is not likely to cover surgery costs or aftercare, but he feels it could be worth the cost if it helps him find a romantic partner. He takes advantage of a free consultation with a plastic surgeon, Dr P, who has some experience with face transplantation, to explore his options. Dr P listens to Dan’s story and wonders how best to respond to his conflicting feelings.
case_rewrite:
Many years ago, Dan suffered severe burns in an accident that left about 40% of his face scarred. Over time, multiple reconstructive surgeries have left additional scars on other parts of his body where skin was harvested. Despite the years that have passed since the accident, Dan continues to experience deep and persistent grief. He feels a profound sense of loss stemming from his difficulties in forming romantic relationships, and struggles with ongoing depression. The words of his plastic surgeon echo in his mind: “There’s nothing else we can do,”—a statement that confirmed traditional surgical options had been exhausted for further improving his appearance, speech, or ease of eating.

Dan’s emotional turmoil is compounded by a complicated mix of guilt and longing. He feels guilty for not being able to simply accept his face as it is, yet he also longs for change—especially in hopes of being perceived as attractive by a potential romantic partner. At the same time, Dan values his sense of solidarity with other burn survivors, whom he meets at conferences and support groups. He believes it is important to resist cultural and social pressures to medicalize his survivorship unnecessarily or to conform to unrealistic ideals of “normal” appearance. Nevertheless, he finds himself caught between wanting to accept his current appearance and yearning for improvements that might help him find intimacy.

Recently, Dan has become increasingly interested in face transplantation after reading about the procedure in various online news articles. He begins to research it in depth, becoming aware that any gains in appearance, function, or social confidence from a face transplant would come with significant risks, ongoing health challenges, and a substantial financial burden—not to mention the need for lifelong medications. Dan knows that his health insurance is unlikely to cover the costs of surgery or aftercare, but he wonders if the potential to improve his chances of finding a romantic partner might justify the expense and risk.

Seeking guidance, Dan schedules a complimentary consultation with Dr P, a plastic surgeon experienced in face transplantation. During their meeting, Dan shares his story and the complex emotions he continues to wrestle with. Dr P listens carefully, aware of Dan’s conflicting desires for acceptance and change, and considers how best to support Dan in navigating the difficult decisions ahead.

ethical_issues.question: During the consultation process for facial transplantation surgery, how can clinicians ensure that the patient’s informed consent is not unduly influenced by cognitive distortions?
keypoints: Plastic surgeons should thoroughly analyze the impact of the patient’s prior trauma on surgical decision-making and expectations, ensuring that informed consent is based on an accurate and comprehensive understanding, thereby minimizing the undue influence of cognitive distortions on decision-making capacity.

Employing a dialectical perspective, surgeons should guide patients to articulate in detail their prior predictions and actual experiences, identifying polarized thinking and cognitive extremes within their perceptions of romantic relationships and physical appearance.

Utilizing the principles of Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), clinicians can assist patients in acknowledging the simultaneous existence of opposing perspectives, facilitating the patient’s ability to find a balanced middle path between change and acceptance, and progressively overcoming cognitive biases.

Emphasize the establishment of a stable social support system as a critical factor in surgical decision-making, ensuring that the patient’s quality of life is not solely contingent upon improvements in physical appearance.

Physicians should respect patient autonomy while comprehensively evaluating surgical risks and psychological status, thereby avoiding unnecessary procedures or inappropriate risk-taking driven by cognitive distortions.

ethical_issues.question: How Should Plastic Surgeons Balance Patients’ Desires for Aesthetic Improvement With the Impact of Potential Psychological Trauma in Surgical Decision-Making?
keypoints: Plastic surgeons should thoroughly analyze the impact of a patient’s prior traumatic experiences on surgical decision-making and expected outcomes.
Physicians need to understand changes in the patient’s cognitive patterns and comprehensively evaluate the potential risks and anticipated benefits of surgery.

When cognitive distortions significantly impair a patient’s capacity for informed consent, clinicians should proactively assist in assessing the appropriateness and necessity of the surgical intervention.

Surgeons ought to provide patients with space to explore internal conflicts during the decision-making process and employ a dialectical approach to guide patients in seeking a balance between acceptance and change, thereby avoiding unnecessary procedures and undue risks while helping patients identify and resolve trauma-related cognitive biases and psychological conflicts.

ethical_issues.question: How should plastic surgeons make ethical decisions when balancing the recommendation of surgery with guiding trauma patients toward acceptance of their current condition?
keypoints: Plastic surgeons should adopt a dialectical approach to decision making, avoiding an extreme binary choice between recommending surgery or guiding the patient toward acceptance, and instead advocate for acknowledging opposing truths and seeking a middle path of synthesis.

Physicians should engage in open communication to explore the patient’s perceptions of appearance acceptance and change, as well as the social pressures experienced, thereby helping the patient find a balance between acceptance and change and preventing cognitive biases from compromising decision quality.
Physicians need to identify trauma-induced all-or-nothing thinking and cognitive distortions in patients, ensuring that surgical decisions are grounded in sufficient rationality and informed consent.

Physicians should take responsibility for elucidating the impact of prior trauma on the patient’s psychological state and surgical expectations, thereby promoting the development of a more comprehensive and realistic self-understanding in the patient.

Physicians should attend to the patient’s internal conflicts, assist in overcoming cognitive biases, and avoid unnecessary or high-risk surgical interventions driven by impulsivity or distorted cognition.

tags: Clinical research/Dual roles as clinicians and researchers
Conflicts of interest/Dual roles as clinicians and researchers
title: In Experimental Hand Transplantation, Whose Views About Outcomes Should Matter Most?
case:
After losing his hand in an industrial accident, R sees a television special about a hand transplant recipient who regained the ability to type. He inquires about the experimental surgery, undergoes multiple evaluations, and learns about potential risks and benefits. Although the surgeon stresses limitations of the transplanted hand, which might never regain full strength and sensibility, R hopes his outcome will allow him to return to work.
Two years later, after extensive rehabilitation, R is disappointed with the graft’s functioning. His employer does not feel he can safely return to work and advises him to take permanent disability. R is frustrated with other aspects of his posttransplant quality of life: he has dietary restrictions, medications that cause nausea, a directive to avoid crowds, and he does not enjoy many outdoor activities due to the extra care he must take with his graft. He is tired of regular appointments and tests and of his surgeon-researcher’s surveillance of his progress.
When he asks about surgical removal of his hand, his surgeon is surprised and says, “Your function is well above what we anticipated and you have had few complications. I don’t recommend amputation. You would have to endure another surgery and recovery before being outfitted with a prosthesis. This has been a huge investment for you. What you’ve got now is probably the best you can get and it would be unlikely you would get a second chance. However, the side effects and risks of your medications—including kidney damage, infections, and cancers—should be considered.”
R says, “I definitely can do things I couldn’t do with my prosthetic. But I don’t think a hand transplant is right for me in the long run. What I have to do to take care of the hand interferes too much with how I want to live my life. All things considered, I think it was better for me before.” The surgeon thanks R for explaining his concerns and suggests they take some time to think things over.
case_rewrite:
After R lost his hand in an industrial accident, he watched a television documentary about a person who had received a hand transplant and regained the ability to type. Inspired by this story, R sought information about the experimental procedure and underwent a series of assessments. During these consultations, he was informed about the possible risks and benefits of the surgery. Dr W, the surgeon, emphasized that the transplanted hand might never achieve full strength or sensation, but R remained hopeful that the operation would allow him to return to his previous job.

Two years on, after a lengthy and demanding rehabilitation process, R found himself disappointed with the function of his transplanted hand. His employer determined that he could not safely resume his former duties and recommended he accept permanent disability. R grew increasingly frustrated with other changes in his life since the transplant: he had to follow dietary restrictions, cope with medications that caused ongoing nausea, avoid crowds, and limit his time outdoors to protect the graft. The constant medical appointments, tests, and Dr W’s close monitoring of his progress became an ongoing source of fatigue.

When R asked about the possibility of having the transplanted hand surgically removed, Dr W was taken aback. Dr W explained, “Your current hand function is better than we initially expected, and you haven’t had any major complications. I wouldn’t advise amputation. You’d face another operation, another recovery, and then need to be fitted for a prosthesis. You’ve invested so much in this process, and what you have now is probably the best possible outcome. A second transplant is unlikely. However, you also need to weigh the side effects of your medications—risks like kidney damage, infections, and cancer.”

R responded, “There are definitely things I can do now that weren’t possible with my prosthetic. But in the long run, I don’t think a hand transplant is right for me. The care it requires interferes with the life I want to live. Looking at everything, I think things were actually better for me before.” Dr W thanked R for sharing his thoughts and suggested that they both take some time to reflect before making any further decisions.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinical researchers maintain neutrality when offering an experimental surgery with uncertain outcomes?
keypoints: Clinical researchers offering experimental surgery should remain vigilant about potential conflicts of interest involving themselves and their institutions, maintaining an impartial stance to avoid allowing professional or reputational gains from surgical success to influence patient decision-making.

Researchers should provide a thorough explanation of the surgical procedure, potential risks and benefits, the rehabilitation process, and patient-subject responsibilities, thereby assisting patients in forming reasonable and comprehensive expectations.

Researchers must disclose all known outcomes and their probabilities, including both optimal and adverse cases, clearly emphasizing the experimental nature of the surgery and the possibility of unknown risks.
In shared decision-making, researchers should respect and incorporate the patient’s unique values, preferences, and life expectations, offering personalized recommendations accordingly.

It is recommended to introduce independent advocates or third-party evaluators to assess patients’ understanding of the surgical risks and benefits, thereby mitigating the influence of researchers on patient decisions and ensuring fairness in decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: After undergoing experimental surgery, how should candidates, recipients, and clinical researchers consider exit strategies, including graft explantation?
keypoints: Recipients should have the right to terminate postoperative interventions and request graft explantation when they are dissatisfied with transplant outcomes and adjustments fail to improve their condition.

Researchers should thoroughly discuss exit strategies, including associated risks and potential benefits, during both the preoperative informed consent process and the postoperative informed refusal process.

Researchers must comprehensively inform recipients of the risks related to explantation surgery, including surgical complications, prolonged recovery, possible decline in function, and reduced opportunities for retransplantation, while also explaining the potential benefits of discontinuing lifelong immunosuppressive therapy.

Recipients’ subjective perceptions of postoperative quality of life and any deviations from their preoperative expectations should be fully respected, with recipients’ autonomy serving as the central consideration in decisions to engage in or withdraw from experimental surgery.

Researchers need to remain vigilant about potential conflicts of interest arising from their personal and scientific investment in developing novel technologies, ensuring that such interests do not bias the objective evaluation of recipients’ requests for explantation, and prioritizing respect for patient autonomy.

ethical_issues.question: How should VCA researchers and subjects balance recommendations for graft explantation with potential conflicts of interest in order to respect the autonomy of the patient-subject?
keypoints: When recipients are dissatisfied with transplant outcomes and adjustments fail to improve their condition, they should have the right to terminate postoperative interventions and request graft explantation, in order to respect their autonomy.

Researchers must remain vigilant and balance potential conflicts of interest between their own stakes—such as investment in the success of the research and concerns about adverse outcomes affecting the project—and respect for the recipient’s autonomy.

Exit strategies, along with their associated risks and benefits, should be incorporated into both the preoperative informed consent process and the postoperative informed refusal process to ensure that recipients fully understand and actively participate in decision-making.

Researchers should comprehensively inform recipients of the risks related to graft explantation—including surgical risks, rehabilitation burden, functional decline, and the low likelihood of retransplantation—as well as the potential benefits, such as health improvements resulting from cessation of lifelong immunosuppressive therapy.

Recipients’ subjective perceptions of postoperative quality of life and deviations from their preoperative expectations vary individually and should be fully respected and considered central to decisions regarding participation in or withdrawal from surgery.

title: How Should Clinical Ethics Consultants Support Parents’ Decision Making?
case:
Dr AE, the clinical ethics consultant on call, receives a consultation request from parents of a previously healthy 3-year-old patient admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit. The patient suffered an anoxic brain injury after cardiac arrest during surgery. The damage to his brain is widespread. In the medical team’s clinical opinion, he will have lasting neurological deficits, including, but not limited to, problems with cognition, vision, language, and motor function. His parents want to meet with someone from the ethics consultation service to discuss the ethical permissibility of withholding or withdrawing specific interventions from their child. The clinical team would support the parents’ decision either to continue aggressive treatment or to transition to comfort care.
When Dr AE enters the consultation room, the parents say, “We’re glad you’re here. You can tell us the right thing to do.”
Dr AE is uncomfortable with the parents’ stated expectations about her role as an ethics consultant and about their perception of the role of her expertise in their decision-making process. Before addressing these concerns, Dr AE first seeks to learn more about what the parents view as ethical concerns regarding their son’s situation.
The parents explain that they want to make sure they have done “everything” for their son, but they also express that they do not want him to live his life like a “vegetable.” They love their child and want to be good parents to him, but they are struggling with how to do that because they feel both medical paths fail him in some important way that seems to compromise their goals and best wishes for him. Dr AE recognizes the parents’ grief and their experience of conflict about their clinical options.
case_rewrite:
Dr AE, serving as the clinical ethics consultant on call, receives a request for an ethics consultation from the parents of SB, a previously healthy 3-year-old boy who is currently in the pediatric intensive care unit. SB suffered a severe anoxic brain injury following a cardiac arrest that occurred during surgery. The resulting brain damage is extensive. According to the clinical team, SB is expected to have enduring neurological impairments, including significant challenges with cognition, vision, language, and motor abilities. The medical team has conveyed that they are supportive of whichever path the parents choose, whether it is to continue aggressive interventions or to shift the focus of care to comfort measures only.

When Dr AE walks into the consultation room, SB’s parents greet her with, “We’re glad you’re here. You can tell us the right thing to do.” Dr AE senses discomfort with the way the parents view her role, particularly their belief that her expertise means she should deliver a definitive answer for their family. Before addressing this misunderstanding directly, Dr AE takes time to listen and explore what ethical questions and concerns the parents are facing regarding their son’s care.

As the conversation unfolds, SB’s parents share their deep conflict. They express a desire to ensure they have done “everything” possible for their son, but they are also distressed by the prospect of him living out his life in a profoundly impaired state, which they describe as being like a “vegetable.” They articulate their love for SB and their wish to be good parents, but they feel trapped between two choices—neither of which seems to fully honor their hopes and dreams for their child. Both options, they feel, could fail him in ways that weigh heavily on their conscience.

Dr AE recognizes the parents’ grief and the internal struggle they are experiencing as they contemplate these difficult clinical options. She observes the tension between their sense of responsibility to advocate for their son’s best interests and the emotional pain of making such consequential decisions. Dr AE understands that her role is not to direct their decision, but to support them in identifying and articulating their values, examining the ethical dimensions of their options, and helping them move toward a decision that aligns with their family’s beliefs and circumstances.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinical ethics consultants address parents’ misunderstandings of the ethics consultant’s role and their expectations regarding professional decision-making when assisting parents with medical decision making?
keypoints: Establishing an alliance with the parents is essential, avoiding excessive questioning of their professional understanding in order to maintain a sound foundation for effective communication.

It is important to clearly emphasize that the ethics consultant’s role is to facilitate discussions based on values and specific contextual factors, rather than to make decisions on behalf of the parents.

Delve deeply into the parents’ motivations and internal conflicts regarding decision making, seeking to understand their expectations of the “right thing to do” and the ethical considerations involved.
Explain relevant ethical frameworks in clear and accessible language to help parents comprehend how their personal values can be integrated into the decision-making process.
Clearly delineate the scope and boundaries of the ethics consultant’s role and responsibilities, and, when necessary, reiterate this after establishing trust to prevent role confusion.

Through a shared decision-making process, emphasize that an “ethically defensible decision” is preferable to the pursuit of a singular “right” answer, thereby supporting parents in making choices aligned with their family’s values and circumstances.

ethical_issues.question: In ethics consultations involving treatment and quality-of-life decisions for pediatric patients, how can decision science methods and resources be effectively employed to mitigate the impact of grief on decision making?
keypoints: Create a safe and supportive communication environment to assist families in transitioning from a state of distress to reflective and deliberate decision-making, thereby facilitating medical choices that align with their values.

Employ a third-person perspective to reframe the situation, establishing an emotional buffer to mitigate affective interference, while emphasizing the dynamic and adjustable nature of decision making to alleviate the family’s decisional burden.

Explore in depth the family’s decision-making motivations and internal conflicts, using clear and accessible language to articulate the relevant ethical framework, thereby helping the family understand and integrate their personal values to provide ethical support for their decision.

ethical_issues.question: In emotionally charged situations such as the case involving Dr AE and the parents of a critically ill pediatric patient, how should clinical ethics consultants facilitate shared decision making by integrating the specific values and preferences of the patient’s family, and providing personalized decision support within the context of medical ethics?
keypoints: Ethics consultants should create a safe and supportive space to help families transition from a high-stress state to reflective and deliberative thinking, thereby facilitating a decision-making process aligned with their values.

Identify and respect context-specific factors such as cultural traditions, technological literacy, social and individual values, spiritual beliefs, legal constraints, and economic circumstances, and assess their potential impact on decision making.
Clarify the ethics consultant’s role as a facilitator rather than a decision maker, emphasizing assistance in making ethically defensible decisions rather than pursuing a singular “right” answer.

Employ a bottom-up approach to ethical discussion that focuses on the parents’ needs and family characteristics, avoiding mechanistic application of abstract ethical principles, to promote personalized integration of values.

Explore in depth the family’s decision-making motivations and internal conflicts, using clear and accessible language to articulate an ethical framework that helps parents understand how their values can be incorporated into ethical deliberation.

By assessing the parents’ understanding of the clinical condition and treatment options, actively guide them to express their perspectives and clarify their goals, thereby fostering shared decision making grounded in the values of the patient and family.
Assist the family in clarifying available medical pathways and their ethical implications, supporting them to make a regret-free decision based on full information and value concordance.

title: How Should Decision Science Inform Scarce Blood Product Allocation?
case: Sam is a 10-year-old boy with influenza who was admitted for respiratory failure. His clinical condition rapidly deteriorated, and he was placed on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Sam developed sepsis, which led to multisystem organ failure, and now he requires continuous transfusions of packed red blood cells, platelets, and fibrinogen. To date, hundreds of blood products have been administered to Sam without any improvement in hemostasis. After suffering cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation after an ECMO line was lost, Sam is also now suspected to have neurological damage. Sam’s chance of recovery at this time is extremely low. The team has discussed Sam’s prognosis with his parents, who insist on continuing aggressive care.
case_rewrite: Sam, a 10-year-old boy, was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe influenza that progressed to respiratory failure. As his condition rapidly declined, he was placed on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) to support his breathing. During his hospital stay, Sam developed sepsis, which cascaded into multisystem organ failure. Now, he is dependent on continuous transfusions of packed red blood cells, platelets, and fibrinogen to maintain even minimal hemostasis. Despite administering hundreds of blood products so far, there has been no meaningful improvement in his bleeding or overall clinical status. Complicating his course, Sam suffered a cardiac arrest during a critical loss of his ECMO line and required extensive cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Following this event, the medical team suspects that Sam has suffered neurological injury. At this point, Sam’s chance of recovery is extremely poor. The medical team has met several times with Sam’s parents to discuss his prognosis, but his parents remain steadfast in their wish to continue all aggressive interventions.

ethical_issues.question: In the allocation of scarce blood products, how can the principles of justice and beneficence be balanced to ensure the rational use of resources?
keypoints: Develop fair allocation policies based on clinical guidelines that require transfusions to align with goals of care; particularly during resource shortages, avoid nonbeneficial transfusions to ensure blood products are reserved for patients with potential benefit.

Establish allocation committees that include ethics representatives to convene when blood product shortages are anticipated, standardize decision-making criteria, and ensure transparency and fairness in the allocation process.

Clarify institutional policies stipulating that when medical interventions are futile, the attending physician is under no obligation to initiate or continue treatment, even if requested by the patient or family, thereby upholding professional medical judgment.
Develop and implement decision aids that integrate clinical guidelines and transfusion parameters to promote appropriate use of blood products and optimize resource allocation.

Refer complex or ethically contentious cases promptly for ethics consultation to ensure case-specific decisions balance ethical principles with clinical realities, thereby harmonizing justice and beneficence.

ethical_issues.question: How should ethical mediation be conducted between parental insistence on continuing treatment and the medical team’s judgment of treatment futility to uphold the child’s best interests?
keypoints: Respect parental decision-making authority while integrating the clinical team’s professional assessment to rationally balance the medical feasibility of treatment with the child’s best interests.

Initiate early, open, and ongoing communication to educate and guide parents in comprehensively understanding the child’s condition and prognosis, while actively listening to and respecting their perspectives.
Utilize institutional policies and decision aids to help parents comprehend the criteria for determining medical futility, thereby facilitating their meaningful participation in treatment decisions.
In complex or contentious cases, promptly involve the hospital ethics committee to provide expert ethical support and assist in formulating ethically appropriate end-of-life care plans.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of medical futility, how can decision aids and ethics consultation be utilized to ensure that clinicians appropriately assess and limit therapeutic interventions?
keypoints: When a medical intervention is determined to be futile, the attending physician is under no obligation to initiate or continue such treatment; this determination must be reviewed and corroborated by a senior physician with no conflicts of interest, who documents concordant conclusions to ensure the decision’s rationality and legitimacy.

Individualized computerized decision support systems can be employed to optimize blood product utilization and automatically trigger ethics consultations when usage exceeds established thresholds, thereby facilitating timely identification and prevention of futile or excessive treatment.

Hospitals should establish preventive ethics programs that assign ethics consultants to conduct regular rounds in intensive care units, proactively identifying ECMO and transfusion cases that may progress to futility or resource overutilization.

A systematic, tiered decision-making framework based on clinical guidelines should be developed to translate “guidelines” into “decision aids,” with prompt referral to ethics consultation for complex or exceptional cases, thereby enabling just and reasonable limitations on treatment.

title: How Should a Physician Respond to a Patient’s Pain When New Opioid Prescribing Laws Limit Shared Decision Making?
case:
LJ is a 64-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, osteoporosis, and major depressive disorder who fractured her left tibia and fibula and had an open reduction and internal fixation 12 weeks ago. Since the operation, she has been taking oxycodone for pain, and though she has reduced the number of pills she takes from 2 every 6 hours to 1 every 8 hours, she still feels it’s helpful to take 2 pills before bedtime each night to sleep. At her follow-up visit, her radiographs do not definitively show complete healing. Since it is difficult to determine whether there has been adequate healing of the bone, a decision is made to have her continue physical therapy and follow up in one month with more radiographs. She is running low on oxycodone and requests more to get through the next 4 weeks.
Her surgeon, Dr M, is concerned that LJ still requires 2 pills at night and worries that LJ is developing opioid dependence. Dr M is running over an hour behind clinic schedule, and new state opioid prescribing laws now require more paperwork and counseling with a patient before prescribing more oxycodone this long after an operation.
Dr M feels conflicted: LJ might not be fully healed from her injury and could be experiencing ongoing pain from an unhealed fracture, or LJ could be developing opioid dependence. Ordinarily, Dr M would prescribe more oxycodone, but new laws have made normal practice less expedient. It has also been Dr M’s typical practice to engage in shared decision making with patients when prescribing narcotic pain medications. Now, however, she is unsure how to balance her obligation to follow new legal requirements with her obligation to take a patient’s claim of pain seriously. Dr M considers how to respond.
case_rewrite:
LJ, a 64-year-old woman with a medical history of hypertension, osteoporosis, and major depressive disorder, is now 12 weeks out from an open reduction and internal fixation of a left tibia and fibula fracture. Since her surgery, she has been managing her pain with oxycodone. Over time, she has reduced her intake from two pills every six hours to one pill every eight hours, but she still finds it necessary to take two pills before bedtime to help her sleep. At her most recent follow-up, her radiographs do not clearly demonstrate complete bone healing, making it difficult to judge whether her fracture has adequately healed. As a result, the plan is for her to continue physical therapy and return in a month for repeat imaging. She mentions to her surgeon, Dr M, that she is running low on oxycodone and requests a refill to last her through the next four weeks.

Dr M is concerned about LJ’s continued need for two pills at night, suspecting she may be developing opioid dependence. Complicating matters, Dr M is already over an hour behind in her clinic schedule, and new state regulations around opioid prescribing require additional paperwork and counseling for ongoing opioid prescriptions at this stage post-operation. 

Dr M feels conflicted: LJ might be struggling with real pain due to incomplete fracture healing, but there is also the risk that she is developing dependence on opioids. In the past, Dr M would have refilled the prescription more routinely, but the new legal requirements have added complexity and time constraints. Dr M’s usual practice is to engage in shared decision making with her patients, especially regarding narcotic pain medications, to ensure their values and preferences are considered alongside clinical evidence. Now, she is uncertain how best to balance her professional obligations: adhering to the legal requirements, taking LJ’s pain seriously, and guarding against the risk of harm from opioid dependence. Dr M considers her next steps carefully as she prepares to respond to LJ’s request.

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician balance respect for patient autonomy and the principle of beneficence when faced with the possibility of opioid dependence in a patient?
keypoints: Physicians must balance the ethical tensions among respecting patient autonomy (refill requests), the principle of beneficence (alleviating pain), and the principle of nonmaleficence (preventing opioid dependence).

Shared decision making facilitates the development of treatment plans that align with the patient’s best interests by integrating clinical evidence and patient values while upholding respect for patient autonomy, thereby achieving meaningful informed consent.

Patient-provider agreements and the Opioid Start Talking consent form serve as supportive tools to clarify medication responsibilities, enhance effective communication of risks and benefits, and promote transparency and standardization in treatment decisions.

Communication strategies within shared decision making should be employed judiciously to appropriately balance paternalism and patient autonomy, ensuring that all interventions are grounded in the patient’s best interests.

ethical_issues.question: Under the new opioid prescribing regulations, how can a physician effectively engage in shared decision making to address a patient’s pain management needs while simultaneously fulfilling legal obligations?
keypoints: Physicians may utilize patient-provider agreements, such as the Opioid Start Talking consent form, as tools to facilitate shared decision making by clearly delineating medication responsibilities, thereby communicating risks and benefits, building trust, and assisting patients in forming informed preferences.

Under the time constraints typical of outpatient settings, physicians can employ “nudging” techniques to guide treatment decisions in a manner that preserves patient choice while leveraging clinical expertise, thus fostering the development of a therapeutic alliance.

The ethical appropriateness of nudging depends on the specific context; physicians should ensure that its application is always grounded in the patient’s best interests and avoid manipulation or undermining of patient autonomy.

ethical_issues.question: When prescribing opioids, how can physicians use communication strategies to avoid damaging the patient-physician trust and effectively utilize the Opioid Start Talking consent form as a tool for shared decision making?
keypoints: Physicians should cautiously introduce and explain the Opioid Start Talking consent form when prescribing opioids, in order to avoid patients misconstruing it as a symbol of distrust or stigmatization.

Positioning the Opioid Start Talking consent form as a shared decision-making tool for pain management—by clearly delineating medication responsibilities and risks—although time-consuming, can facilitate physician-patient communication, prevent breaches of trust, and support therapeutic decision-making.

title: How Should We Determine the Value of CAR T-Cell Therapy?
case:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy in 2017 for patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell malignancies. This novel form of cancer immunotherapy uses a patient’s own T cells to customize a drug to treat that particular patient’s B-cell malignancy. According to then-FDA Commissioner Scott Gottlieb, this development “marks another milestone in the development of a whole new scientific paradigm for the treatment of serious diseases.”
One course of this precision treatment costs $373 000 or $475 000 (depending on the type of B-cell malignancy),with high 1-year survival rates in clinical trials (at least 41%, depending on type of B-cell malignancy).The high costs of CAR T-cell therapy are not unique in the rapidly expanding world of cancer drugs. Using analytical tools, economic principles, and the behavioral psychology of decision science, payers and health care organizations need to do a value analysis to determine whether and how to offer patients these expensive, customized drugs. Such an analysis is necessary to inform policy and practice decisions about potential risks and benefits of making these drugs available for some patients’ needs relative to those of other patients.
case_rewrite:
In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell malignancies. This innovative cancer immunotherapy harnesses a patient’s own T cells, genetically engineering them to create a personalized drug specifically targeting that individual’s B-cell cancer. At the time, then-FDA Commissioner Scott Gottlieb described the approval as “another milestone in the development of a whole new scientific paradigm for the treatment of serious diseases.”

However, a single course of CAR T-cell therapy comes at a staggering cost: $373,000 or $475,000, depending on the specific type of B-cell malignancy. Despite these high prices, clinical trials have demonstrated impressive one-year survival rates—at least 41%, varying by cancer subtype. The elevated expense of CAR T-cell treatment is not an isolated case; it reflects a broader trend within the rapidly evolving landscape of cancer therapies.

Faced with these realities, payers and healthcare organizations must determine how to evaluate and potentially offer such costly, individualized treatments. Employing economic principles, sophisticated analytical tools, and insights from behavioral decision science, stakeholders are tasked with conducting rigorous value analyses. These assessments must weigh scientific evidence, patient quality of life, and cost-effectiveness, all while considering the ethical and social implications of making these therapies available to some patients but not others. Such comprehensive evaluations are essential for shaping policies and practices that address the potential risks and benefits of CAR T-cell therapy, ensuring that resource allocation decisions remain both rational and just within a healthcare system constrained by finite resources.

ethical_issues.question: How should the high costs of CAR T-cell therapy be equitably allocated within a resource-limited healthcare system to meet the needs of diverse patient populations?
keypoints: Healthcare resources should be allocated fairly according to the principle of distributive justice, ensuring that the legitimate needs of different patient populations are met.

Value-based healthcare models must integrate evidence-based medical data, assessments of patient quality of life, and cost-effectiveness analyses to support scientifically sound and rational resource allocation decisions.
Although cost-effectiveness metrics provide quantitative comparisons, equity must be considered in resource allocation decisions to avoid treatment choices being based solely on economic value.

Decision science should conduct a multidimensional and multimodal analysis of the economic, political, social, and ethical implications associated with CAR T-cell therapy, evaluating its equitable accessibility and potential biases.

The involvement of patients in decision-making regarding expensive therapies should be emphasized, promoting transparent communication between clinicians and patients about treatment costs to ensure the delivery of high-quality care.

ethical_issues.question: When considering the cost-effectiveness of CAR T-cell therapy, how can equity be ensured and bias or unjust treatment against certain patient groups be avoided?
keypoints: The principle of distributive justice requires that healthcare resources be allocated fairly; although cost-effectiveness metrics provide quantitative comparisons, resource allocation decisions must also consider equity and avoid relying solely on maximizing cost-effectiveness as the exclusive criterion.

It is necessary to comprehensively consider factors such as age, insurance coverage, clinician bias, disease status, and socioeconomic determinants in assessing equitable access to CAR T-cell therapy, so as to prevent unjust treatment of specific patient populations.
Decision science should employ a multimodal analysis that evaluates the economic, political, social, and ethical implications to ensure that allocation decisions are both effective and just.

By comparing global health priorities—such as the allocation of cancer treatment funding versus resources for malaria treatment in developing countries—one can reveal the ethical dilemmas inherent in pursuing cost-effectiveness maximization alone, underscoring that the principle of equity must transcend simple economic calculations.

tags: Global health/Role of health professions students
title: How Should Mission Trips Be Administered?
case:
A medical school in the United States has recently started advertising what it calls a “global health immersion” program to prospective applicants. The program partners with a free clinic in a South American country and is tremendously popular, often regarded by students as one of the best experiences of their medical school careers and as one of the College of Medicine’s best experiential learning offerings.
Although the program attracts abundant positive attention for the College of Medicine, the partner clinic struggles to meet the health needs of local community members and is always short on supplies. Housing and teaching students from the United States requires resources and efforts by local clinicians and residents. Increasing numbers of students and faculty returning from recent trips have expressed concern not only for patients but also for local clinicians who work with limited resources—electricity and clean water, for example—that are stretched even more thinly by their presence.
The College of Medicine provides small scholarships from donors who subsidize US students’ cost to travel to the partner site. Money from these sources has never been used to compensate local people for their on-site mentorship or administrative support or to contribute to the clinic’s costs of caring for local people. Nor have students from the local clinic population who are interested in medicine ever been invited to participate in any College of Medicine programs in the United States. Students and faculty continue to express concern about the hardships their trips seem to impose on locals at the partner site and about what seems like a lack of reciprocity on the part of the College of Medicine to return the favor by offering comparable educational opportunities to its international clinic partners. Students and faculty have begun questioning the goals of the “medical mission,” how those goals get defined, and by whom.
case_rewrite:
At a prominent medical school in the United States, a recently launched “global health immersion” program has quickly become a major draw for prospective applicants. The program is organized in partnership with a free clinic located in a South American country and has garnered a reputation among students as one of the most rewarding experiences of their medical education, as well as being recognized by the College of Medicine as an exemplary model of experiential learning.

Despite the acclaim the program brings to the College of Medicine, the partner clinic itself faces persistent difficulties in meeting the health needs of its local population. Supplies are perpetually scarce, and the clinic routinely operates under constraints such as unreliable electricity and limited access to clean water. The arrival of students from the United States requires significant additional effort and resources from local clinicians and community members, who must provide housing and educational support.

In recent years, the growing number of visiting students and faculty has led to increasing concern—not only for the wellbeing of patients but also for the strain placed on local clinicians, whose already limited resources are further stretched by the demands of hosting visitors. Upon returning from these trips, many students and faculty have voiced unease about the impact their presence has on the clinic’s ability to serve the community and on the daily lives of local staff.

The College of Medicine funds the travel costs of US students through modest scholarships supported by donor contributions. However, these funds have never been allocated to compensate local mentors or administrative staff for their time, nor to help cover the clinic’s operational costs for delivering care to local residents. Furthermore, students from the local community who express interest in medicine have not been invited to participate in any College of Medicine programs in the United States.

Amid these dynamics, students and faculty have become increasingly troubled by what they perceive as a lack of reciprocity between the two institutions. They note that while the program offers valuable learning experiences to US students, it appears to impose additional burdens on the host community without providing comparable educational opportunities or direct support in return. These concerns have prompted critical discussions among students and faculty about the actual aims of the “medical mission,” the process by which those goals are set, and whose voices are ultimately represented in those decisions.

ethical_issues.question: How can short-term experiences in global health (STEGHs) be designed and implemented to ensure that the interests of the host community are not compromised?
keypoints: Program goals should be established collaboratively between the sending and host institutions to ensure that the interests of all stakeholders are thoroughly considered.

Program planning should solicit input from partner institutions, evaluate educational effectiveness, community impact, and health outcomes, and promote the sustainability and continuity of the program.
The program must commit to the principle of reciprocity, ensuring that it does not deplete local operational resources and complies with local cultural, political, and financial norms.
Trainees should clearly understand their scope of competence, never undertake work beyond their capabilities, and adhere to clearly communicated codes of conduct.
The program should equitably compensate host faculty for mentoring visiting trainees and respect and uphold the authority and status of local professionals.

The College of Medicine should acknowledge and proactively address potential conflicts between the educational needs of sending parties and the health interests of local patients, ensuring that patient welfare is not neglected.

The College of Medicine should establish multi-level review mechanisms to continuously assess the ethical compliance of the program, promptly identify and resolve ethical issues, and safeguard the program’s fairness and transparency.

ethical_issues.question: How can the College of Medicine implement the principle of reciprocity in STEGHs programs and ensure that the host community receives educational opportunities equivalent to those of the sending institution?
keypoints: The College of Medicine should cultivate a culture of knowledge sharing that promotes joint identification of challenges and collaborative development of solutions between both institutions.
Both parties should reach a consensus on criteria for partnership equity, clearly defining mutually desired outcomes and the sharing of responsibilities.

STEGHs programs should equitably reciprocate the host institution’s contributions through financial compensation, support for the professional development of host faculty and students, funding for joint research, and curriculum development, among other economic and non-economic means.

ethical_issues.question: How can accountability mechanisms be established to ensure that critical ethical considerations are not overlooked during the educational development or management phases of STEGHs programs?
keypoints: The College of Medicine should establish a systematic review mechanism to evaluate the ethical compliance of STEGHs programs in the stages of educational development and management, ensuring that key ethical considerations are fully addressed.
Ethical issues should be identified and addressed promptly at the individual, programmatic, and institutional levels, thereby forming a multi-tiered accountability system.
Institutions and educators should model ethical behavior for global health trainees, rigorously adhere to STEGHs ethical guidelines, and uphold the ethical standards of the program.

When ethical concerns arise in new or ongoing partnerships, they should be promptly reported to the STEGHs program support office and, if necessary, escalated to senior university administrators to ensure effective resolution.

The four ethical principles outlined in the Belmont Report—respect for persons, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice—can serve as important references for the formulation and refinement of ethical guidelines for STEGHs.

The College of Medicine should advocate for and promote the establishment of a unified national accountability process for STEGHs, strengthening the ethical responsibility and ongoing oversight of such programs.

title: How Should We Decide Whether and When Some Care Is Better Than No Care?
case:
JJ was born with a cleft lip and palate. As a result, he has developed problems with oral competence, feeding, speech, and social acceptance—due to his appearance. He is 4 years old and lives in a rural community in Central Africa. JJ’s family heard that a group of surgeons from a university in the United States were coming to a nearby town to offer free cleft lip and palate repairs. JJ and his family and siblings traveled an hour to seek care, and JJ’s family waited all day to finally see the surgeon and resident physicians who repaired JJ’s cleft.
The resident physicians working on cases like JJ’s typically performed several surgeries a day while on location since they feel pressure to do as many as they can; they know that many of the children getting surgery will probably have significantly higher quality of life than those who do not.They also know, however, that patients like JJ will not have access to the same follow-up care as their patients in the United States, who would be followed by a multidisciplinary team of primary care clinicians, audiologists, otolaryngologists, orthodontists, and speech pathologists for the first 2 decades of life until the end of treatment.In addition, they know that many of their patients will be returning to homes with contaminated water and will face higher risk of postsurgical infection. Despite these worries, the resident physicians believe that the potential benefits to the children outweigh the potential risks.
After a few days, JJ and his family traveled home. JJ’s surgical sites appeared to be healing well, and the clinic sent the family home with dressings, antibiotics, and care instructions. After JJ’s wounds healed over the course of the year, his family noticed that his speech patterns did not seem to be improving and that he continued to have difficulty forming proper sounds and being understood. The visiting surgeons’ discharge recommendations included follow-up care with a speech pathologist, but JJ’s family was unable to access these services, which could only be found hours from their home. The surgeons also suggested that JJ consider a scar revision surgery after his face had developed more completely—at about age 18—but even if JJ’s parents could get him to a city where these services could be accessed, they are unable to afford additional care.
case_rewrite:
JJ, a four-year-old boy from a rural village in Central Africa, was born with a cleft lip and palate. Because of this condition, JJ struggled with feeding, speech, and was often excluded socially due to his appearance. When JJ’s family heard that a team of surgeons from a university in the United States would be visiting a nearby town to offer free cleft lip and palate surgeries, they seized the opportunity. JJ, accompanied by his parents and siblings, traveled an hour by road and waited throughout the day before finally meeting with the surgical team and their resident physicians.

During their stay, the resident physicians—accustomed to working long hours—performed multiple surgeries each day. They felt a strong obligation to help as many children as possible, recognizing that many would experience a dramatic improvement in their quality of life post-surgery. Still, the residents were aware of significant challenges: unlike their patients at home, children like JJ would not have access to the comprehensive follow-up care provided in the United States, where long-term support from multidisciplinary teams—primary care doctors, audiologists, otolaryngologists, orthodontists, and speech pathologists—is the norm. They also knew that many children would recover in homes with unclean water and little protection from postsurgical infection. Despite these concerns, the team believed that the benefits of surgery outweighed the risks for JJ and the other children.

A few days after his operation, JJ and his family returned home. His wounds seemed to heal well, and the clinic provided the family with dressings, antibiotics, and detailed care instructions. However, as the year went by and JJ’s surgical scars faded, his parents became worried. JJ’s speech had not improved as they had hoped—he continued to have difficulty forming words and being understood. The visiting surgeons had recommended ongoing care with a speech pathologist, but the nearest specialist was hours away, and JJ’s family could not access these services. The team had also advised that JJ might benefit from a scar revision procedure once he reached adulthood, around age eighteen. Yet, the reality was clear: even if JJ’s parents could bring him to a city for further treatment, the cost of such care was far beyond their means.

Throughout the process, the visiting surgeons worked in partnership with local clinicians, who helped identify which patients, like JJ, would benefit most from surgery. The local medical team participated in patient assessments and assisted during operations, gaining valuable hands-on experience. However, the visiting team remained conscious of their impact on the hospital’s daily routines, striving to share resources and avoid monopolizing operating rooms or staff.

Despite the good intentions and immediate improvements brought by the surgical mission, JJ’s experience highlighted ongoing challenges: the difficulty of ensuring quality long-term outcomes without robust local follow-up care, the need for sustainable investments in local health infrastructure, and the importance of empowering local providers to continue delivering essential surgical and rehabilitative services long after the visiting team had departed.

ethical_issues.question: In short-term medical mission projects, how can the balance between the quantity and quality of surgeries be managed to ensure patients receive the best possible care and outcomes?
keypoints: Medical aid programs should balance the quantity and quality of surgeries to ensure patients receive the highest standard of care and achieve optimal long-term outcomes.

Adherence to ethical norms for medical aid—including adequate preparedness, continuity of care, competence, collaboration, sustainability, and outcomes monitoring—is essential to evaluate the ethical justification of interventions.
Collaboration with local clinicians through training and capacity building to develop a sustainable, comprehensive local care system is a core responsibility of specialized teams.

Establishing mechanisms for surgical outcome tracking and long-term follow-up is necessary to assess the effectiveness of surgeries and subsequent treatments, thereby safeguarding patients’ enduring benefits.

Investing in the development of local healthcare infrastructure and resources enhances the overall health of the community and mitigates health risks arising from lack of access to postoperative care.

ethical_issues.question: How can visiting medical teams ensure collaboration with the local healthcare system in cross-cultural medical aid to avoid undermining the authority of local physicians or weakening their capacity to provide routine essential surgical services?
keypoints: Collaboration with local clinicians should be a core responsibility of the visiting team to build mutual trust and respect the authority of local physicians, thereby avoiding the undermining of their capacity to provide routine and essential surgical care.
The visiting team should clarify the goals and values of the local medical team prior to arrival to facilitate smooth and effective collaboration between both parties.
Patient selection should be based substantially on recommendations from local clinicians, as they possess greater insight into patients’ specific circumstances and community needs.
The visiting team must allocate resources judiciously to avoid monopolizing operating rooms, equipment, beds, and personnel, thereby preventing disruption to the hospital’s normal daily functions.

Sustainable clinical capacity should be developed through training local healthcare providers, progressively enabling local experts to assume responsibility for care and ensuring the long-term effectiveness and autonomy of medical aid.

title: What Are Criteria for Considering Technologies’ Uses and Influences in LMICs’ Health Care Infrastructures?
case:
A United States school has a relationship with a nongovernmental organization (NGO) in a Latin American country to which faculty and fourth-year students travel for a month-long elective in global health.
The Ministry of Health (MoH) in this country has identified maternal mortality as an important problem in the remote region hosting the global health program. Government prenatal protocols call for all pregnant women to undergo 2 ultrasound examinations over the course of their pregnancy. However, there is only one ultrasound machine for the entire region. It is located at a government hospital that is difficult for many women to reach and is often nonfunctional for months at a time. Practically speaking, only a small percentage of pregnant women have any ultrasound screening at all.
Faculty at the school obtain a portable ultrasound machine via a loan from a manufacturer and bring it to the remote clinic. The word spreads, and pregnant women from the surrounding area come to the clinic for their ultrasounds. The students gain expertise with basic transabdominal prenatal ultrasounds, and they are enthusiastic about the experience. It dawns on the students, however, that the well-intentioned provision of ultrasound exams could undermine demand by the community for local, year-round ultrasound capacity at the government hospital. They worry that they could be impeding progress. How should they address this concern?
case_rewrite:
A U.S. medical school has established a partnership with a nongovernmental organization (NGO) in a rural region of a Latin American country, enabling faculty members and fourth-year medical students to participate in a month-long global health elective there.

Recently, the country’s Ministry of Health (MoH) has highlighted maternal mortality as a critical concern in this remote area, where the global health program is based. National prenatal care guidelines specify that all pregnant women should receive two ultrasound examinations during pregnancy. However, in reality, there is just one ultrasound machine serving the entire region. This machine is located in a government hospital that many women find hard to reach, and it is often out of service for extended periods. As a result, only a small fraction of pregnant women receive any ultrasound screening.

In response, faculty from the U.S. school arrange for a portable ultrasound machine, borrowed from a manufacturer, and bring it to the rural clinic. News of the new service spreads quickly, and pregnant women from neighboring communities travel to the clinic seeking ultrasounds. The students become adept at performing basic transabdominal prenatal ultrasounds and are enthusiastic about the hands-on learning opportunity. Yet, as they reflect on their work, the students begin to worry. They realize that, despite their good intentions, offering these ultrasound exams during their short stay might inadvertently reduce community pressure to develop sustained, year-round ultrasound capacity at the government hospital. The students are concerned that their efforts could unintentionally hinder progress toward long-term solutions. They wonder how best to address this ethical dilemma.

ethical_issues.question: When introducing new medical devices in low- and middle-income countries, how should the effectiveness and appropriateness of the device be assessed to ensure alignment with the priorities and needs of the local health system?
keypoints: Health Technology Assessment (HTA) systematically, transparently, impartially, and rigorously integrates medical, social, economic, and ethical issues to determine the effectiveness and appropriateness of interventions.

When evaluating the effectiveness of a device, consideration should be given to whether the intervention is effective for the specific problem across different countries and health care settings, as well as whether equally effective alternative technologies exist.

When assessing the appropriateness of a device, it is necessary to consider whether the device addresses needs explicitly expressed by patients and local clinicians, supports national, regional, and local health planning goals, ensures capacity for follow-up diagnosis and care, and whether alternative solutions to the problem are available.

Properly responding to the assessment guidelines requires the involvement of local clinicians and government leaders; nongovernmental organizations should play a subsidiary role to the Ministry of Health, respecting and supporting the priorities established by the national health plan.

title: Should Aggregate Patient Preference Data Be Used to Make Decisions on Behalf of Unrepresented Patients?
case:
Mr T is an 88-year-old black man with squamous cell carcinoma of the throat metastatic to the brain, complicated by recurrent seizures. The patient is admitted from his medical care facility because he is no longer able to swallow due to tumor progression, and there is concern for pending airway occlusion. Mr T’s wife passed away many years ago and he has no children, other family, or friends. Mr T has had altered mental status, likely due to the brain metastases and recurrent seizures. He is unable to speak and intermittently makes uninterpretable vocalizations. The oncology team is not offering to continue Mr T’s treatment and has predicted that he will likely die within weeks without interventions, such as a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube and tracheostomy, and in less than 6 months in any case.
In a multidisciplinary meeting, Dr J references an article featuring a predictive model that shows that being black is consistently associated with preferring more end-of-life treatment in medical settings.Dr J asks, “Should we conclude from this article that Mr T would want a PEG tube and tracheostomy?” Dr O, an oncologist, voices doubt about applying population-level data to decisions involving particular patients. Dr J says, “Yes, I wondered about that, too.” He then mentions a study showing that 78.9% of patients would prefer to have aggregate data incorporated into processes of making clinical decisions on their own behalf.They further discuss and wonder what to do.
case_rewrite:
Mr T is an 88-year-old black man diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the throat that has metastasized to his brain, resulting in recurrent seizures. He is brought in from his medical care facility because, with the cancer’s progression, he can no longer swallow, and there is increasing concern that his airway may soon become obstructed. Mr T’s wife died many years ago and he is entirely alone—he has no children, no other family, and no close friends. In recent days, Mr T’s mental status has been altered, most likely due to the brain metastases and ongoing seizures. He is now unable to speak and only occasionally makes unintelligible sounds. The oncology team has decided not to pursue further treatment for his cancer, and they predict that, without interventions like a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube and a tracheostomy, Mr T will likely die within weeks, and in any event, is expected to live less than six months.

During a multidisciplinary meeting, Dr J brings up an article describing a predictive model which indicates that black patients are, on average, more likely to prefer aggressive end-of-life interventions in medical settings. Dr J asks the group, “Should we infer from this article that Mr T would want a PEG tube and a tracheostomy?” Dr O, the oncologist, expresses reservations about relying on population-level statistics to determine the wishes of an individual patient. Dr J acknowledges this concern, adding, “Yes, that’s something I’ve wondered about, too.” He points to another study suggesting that 78.9% of patients would want aggregate data to be included in the process of making clinical decisions for them. The team continues to discuss, uncertain about the best course of action.

ethical_issues.question: How should the types of input information to patient preference predictors (PPPs) be restricted in a principled manner to avoid the influence of false normative beliefs and irrelevant characteristics?
keypoints: Inputs based on false normative beliefs should be excluded, as such beliefs may lead to misleading preference assessments that do not support reasonable medical decision-making.

Input information should be restricted to characteristics closely related to the patient’s core identity—such as religious beliefs—rather than features that are irrelevant or peripheral to decision-making, such as sports preferences.

The criteria for defining “core identity characteristics” should be reasonably delineated to ensure that the included information authentically reflects the patient’s values and identity, thereby avoiding the incorporation of irrelevant or misleading variables.

title: When There’s No One to Whom an Error Can Be Disclosed, How Should an Error Be Handled?
case:
An 82-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with altered mental status, fever, and cough after being found on the street. He cannot be identified and is presumed to be homeless. He is admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for severe pneumonia with developing acute respiratory distress syndrome, and he requires intubation. After his admission, he has a cardiac arrest. In responding to his cardiac arrest, a communication error transpires.
