title: How Should Health Care Professionals Address Social Determinants of Refugee Health?
case:
Dr G is a physician who follows up with RJ, a 17-year-old resettled refugee, about his feelings of isolation and depression revealed in an earlier visit in which RJ needed a physical exam to get a work permit. RJ was subjected to psychological trauma during his early childhood and, from 2009 to 2013, lived in a refugee camp, where he learned English. After reviewing RJ’s blood work from his last visit, Dr G explains to RJ that he is anemic and has a vitamin B12deficiency, probably due to poor nutrition. Dr G inquires about RJ’s daily life, school, and work. RJ spends most of his free time working to help support his grandparents, mother, and sister. Job opportunities are scarce, and RJ is currently the only member of the household earning an income. After further conversation, RJ reveals that he still feels depressed and isolated. “I have to work, so I don’t have time to go to the outreach programs you recommended. Besides, my family and I just don’t seem to fit in. We don’t belong here.” He describes how his family members have similar feelings and how he is worried about their health.
Dr G and RJ discuss RJ’s concerns and therapeutic options. RJ is not willing to take medication and says, “Why would I spend money on a drug just for me? It won’t help. We are all so alone here.”
Dr G hears similar concerns expressed by her other refugee patients and has described these patients as melancholy, fatigued, and malnourished. There are over 1000 refugees living in her city; roughly 60 receive care at Dr G’s clinic. She knows that there are higher-than-average rates of mental illness and suicide among this local population. She does her best to serve these patients, but it doesn’t seem to generate improved health outcomes in the community. Dr G wonders what to do.
case_rewrite:
Dr G, a dedicated physician, is meeting with RJ, a 17-year-old refugee she has been following since his initial visit for a physical examination needed to obtain a work permit. During that earlier encounter, RJ disclosed feeling isolated and depressed. RJ’s background is marked by significant psychological trauma in early childhood and several years, from 2009 to 2013, spent in a refugee camp, where he learned English.

At this follow-up appointment, Dr G reviews the results of RJ’s recent blood work and informs him that he is anemic with a significant vitamin B12 deficiency, most likely stemming from inadequate nutrition. Dr G gently inquires about RJ’s everyday routine, school life, and work commitments. RJ explains that he spends nearly all of his free time working to help support his grandparents, mother, and sister. With job opportunities being scarce, RJ is currently the sole wage earner in his household.

As their conversation deepens, RJ admits that his feelings of depression and isolation have not improved. “I have to work, so I don’t have time to go to the outreach programs you suggested. Besides, my family and I just don’t fit in here. We don’t belong.” He shares that his family members face similar struggles and that he worries constantly about their wellbeing.

Dr G and RJ explore possible ways to address his concerns and discuss therapeutic options. However, RJ is reluctant to consider medication. He says, “Why would I spend money on a drug just for me? It won’t help. We are all so alone here.” His words reflect deep doubts about the value of treatment for himself, especially when weighed against his family’s needs.

Dr G recognizes that RJ’s situation is not unique. Many of her refugee patients express similar concerns—describing themselves as melancholy, fatigued, and malnourished. In her city, there are over 1,000 refugees; about 60 of them receive care at Dr G’s clinic. She is keenly aware of the elevated rates of mental illness and suicide within this local refugee community. Despite her efforts to provide attentive care, Dr G is troubled by the persistent poor health outcomes among her refugee patients and wonders what more she can do to make a meaningful difference.

ethical_issues.question: How should health care professionals reconcile the relationship between a refugee patient’s family financial circumstances and the patient’s own health needs when the patient refuses pharmacological treatment?
keypoints: Health care professionals must thoroughly understand the patient’s experiences, current circumstances, and life aspirations, particularly recognizing that patients may perceive their own health and prescribed medications as a “luxury” due to financial pressures; only then can appropriate support plans tailored to the patient’s specific needs be developed.

Engage in open and honest discussions with the patient to help them realize how valuing their own health can align with other values and interests, such as supporting their family, and assist the patient in understanding the potential negative impact of their health status on their work capacity and ability to provide for their family.

Through an integrated and coordinated team approach—including social workers, case managers, and others—assist the patient and their family in securing long-term health benefits, nutritional support, and community resources to alleviate financial burdens and promote effective health management.

ethical_issues.question: How should health care professionals identify and address the mental health issues of refugee patients while taking into account the impact of cultural differences and language barriers on the diagnostic and treatment process?
keypoints: Health care professionals should identify symptoms of mental health disorders commonly exhibited by refugee patients, such as major depressive disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder, and provide timely professional treatment or referrals for specialized interventions.

Persistent social isolation is a significant risk factor for suicidal ideation and behaviors; clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion and actively assess the patient’s social support network.

Stigma surrounding mental illness, lack of awareness or understanding of mental health concepts, language barriers, and cultural differences collectively constitute major obstacles to help-seeking among refugee patients; health care providers must possess cross-cultural communication skills and demonstrate cultural sensitivity to patients’ backgrounds and belief systems.

Attention to and integration of social determinants of health—such as economic hardship, social integration, and family responsibilities—facilitate deeper mutual understanding between clinicians and patients and enhance the adaptability and effectiveness of mental health services.

Employing specific communication strategies, such as explaining psychiatric symptoms in terms of physiological and neurochemical abnormalities while avoiding stigmatizing terminology, and constructing explanatory models aligned with the patient’s cultural framework, can improve patients’ willingness to accept treatment and adherence to therapeutic recommendations.

ethical_issues.question: How can healthcare institutions and practitioners enhance the health and well-being of refugee populations and support their realization of full human capabilities through community engagement and clinical practice?
keypoints: Health care institutions and professionals have an ethical responsibility to promote community health improvement and public health, ensuring accessibility and equity of medical services for refugee populations.

Practitioners should attend to the social determinants of health (SDH) and, by respecting patients’ values and cultural backgrounds, facilitate effective communication to deliver mental health services that are responsive to the needs of refugee patients.

Clinical practice should develop disease management plans grounded in patients’ cognitive frameworks and value systems, balancing health objectives with core values such as familial responsibilities, thereby enhancing treatment adherence.

A multidisciplinary team collaboration mechanism should be established to integrate resources such as social workers and case managers, assisting refugee families in securing long-term medical support, nutritional provision, and community services.

Through comprehensive medical record management, quality improvement initiatives, and ongoing communication with refugee communities, health care providers should identify and monitor unique physical and mental health trends and high-risk factors within refugee populations.

Active advocacy is required to eliminate structural barriers to health care access—including transportation difficulties, limited health literacy, financial burdens, and restrictive work schedules—to improve health care utilization among refugees.

Efforts should be made to enhance public and community awareness of social determinants of health and refugee health issues, advancing social justice and inclusion, and fostering community engagement to support refugee social integration and restoration of human capabilities.

Health care professionals ought to regard each refugee patient as a whole person with unique needs, gaining a deep understanding of their social environment and health status to provide personalized health promotion and rights advocacy.

title: How Should AI Be Developed, Validated, and Implemented in Patient Care?
case:
Dr A is a pathologist who has been working at the Community Hospital for several years. She begins her day by evaluating biopsy specimens from Ms J, a 53-year-old woman who underwent a lumpectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy for breast cancer (a procedure to determine whether a primary malignancy has spread). The surgeon removed 4 lymph nodes that were submitted for biopsy. The lymph node samples were processed and several large (multiple gigabytes), high-resolution images were uploaded to the patient’s health record for Dr A’s evaluation and review.
While searching an image for abnormal-appearing cells, Dr A recalled reading about a new artificial intelligence (AI) computer program published by the Google Brain project. This computer program is based on an AI algorithm that is able to scan images at a fraction of a second and find possible cancerous cells. The authors reported that this program’s sensitivity for detecting breast cancer was 92.4%, better than the human eye’s 73.2% sensitivity.As the program is based on a neural network algorithm that is able to learn from its mistakes, it is designed to have the ability to improve its scan sensitivity over time with continued use.
Dr A hopes her team can use this algorithm as a screening tool to help patients like Ms J. This algorithm could help by facilitating the pathology team’s capacity to (1) identify potentially cancerous cells—or positive “hits”—in biopsied tissue images and (2) further evaluate those hits to see whether they truly are metastatic cancer cells. Dr A’s colleagues agree that this technology could increase their power to identify abnormalities in patients’ samples, but some hesitate to advise Community Hospital labs to invest in this technology due to the algorithm’s yet unknown risk for generating false-positive or false-negative hits. Some are also concerned aboutautomation bias, or overreliance on output from a clinical decision support system after users become accustomed to easier workflow facilitated by the program.Automation bias could result in a human user overlooking potential cancerous cells in an image. The team plans to consider these items at their next pathology department meeting.
case_rewrite:
Dr A, a seasoned pathologist at Community Hospital, starts her morning by reviewing biopsy samples from Ms J, a 53-year-old patient who recently underwent a lumpectomy combined with a sentinel lymph node biopsy to assess the spread of her breast cancer. Four lymph nodes were excised by the surgeon and submitted for pathological analysis. The tissue samples were processed, and several high-resolution, multi-gigabyte images were uploaded to Ms J’s electronic health record for Dr A’s careful examination.

As Dr A meticulously scans the images for suspicious or abnormal cells, she recalls reading a recent publication from the Google Brain project about an innovative artificial intelligence (AI) program. This AI tool uses a neural network algorithm designed to analyze pathology images in a fraction of a second, highlighting cells that may be cancerous. The developers reported a sensitivity rate of 92.4% for breast cancer detection, notably higher than the 73.2% sensitivity associated with human evaluation. Because the algorithm is structured to learn from its errors, its diagnostic abilities are expected to improve over time with ongoing use.

Inspired by the potential of this technology, Dr A envisions her pathology team employing the AI tool as an initial screening mechanism to assist in the analysis of cases like Ms J’s. The program could help the team quickly pinpoint possible cancerous regions in biopsy images and allow for more focused evaluation to determine if those findings indeed represent metastatic cancer. While several of Dr A’s colleagues are optimistic that such a system could strengthen their capacity to detect abnormalities in patient samples, some express reservations. They worry about the possibility of the AI producing false positives or false negatives, given that the algorithm’s real-world performance is not yet fully established.

Additionally, certain team members raise concerns about automation bias—the risk that pathologists might become overly reliant on the AI’s assessments once they become accustomed to the streamlined workflow the tool provides. Such overdependence could lead to complacency, causing pathologists to miss cancerous cells that the AI fails to identify. Recognizing both the promise and the potential pitfalls of adopting this technology, Dr A and her team agree to discuss these issues thoroughly at their upcoming pathology department meeting.

ethical_issues.question: How does automation bias affect the diagnostic accuracy of pathologists when using AI-assisted programs?
keypoints: Automation bias refers to a complacency that arises among healthcare professionals when part of the diagnostic work is delegated to an AI program, leading to an overreliance on the AI’s output.
This bias may cause pathologists to depend excessively on the AI program’s results, potentially overlooking cancerous cells present in the images and thereby compromising diagnostic accuracy.
Since AI and human diagnosticians may make different types of errors, integrating the expertise of pathologists with AI-assisted diagnosis can contribute to achieving higher diagnostic accuracy.

ethical_issues.question: How does the black-box problem of artificial intelligence programs in cancer cell detection affect the trust of pathologists and patients in their use?
keypoints: The black-box problem of the AI program refers to its basis in neural network algorithms, which renders it unable to explain the specific mechanisms by which it identifies cancer cells; this affects the level of trust that pathologists and patients have in the technology.
Pathologists and patients generally hope to understand the basis for the AI program’s decisions before its use, in order to enhance the transparency of the technology and foster greater trust.
Achieving transparency by elucidating the rationale behind the AI program’s determinations can help increase pathologists’ and patients’ sense of reassurance and acceptance of the technology.
Some perspectives hold that when the AI program’s accuracy in cancer detection is extremely high, the ethical and clinical significance of the black-box problem may be relatively diminished.

title: How Should Clinicians Communicate With Patients About the Roles of Artificially Intelligent Team Members?
case:
Mr K is a 54-year-old man referred to Dr L’s outpatient spine neurosurgery clinic because he has a 6-week history of left-sided lower back pain, left leg weakness, and shooting pain. Prior to Mr K’s appointment, Dr L reviewed the MRI of Mr K’s lumbar spine, noting herniation of disc between the fifth lumbar vertebra and the first sacral vertebra (L5-S1), which is compressing Mr K’s sacral (S1) nerve root.
“What a classic case,” Dr L murmurs to herself. She grabs her reflex hammer and walks down the hall to exam room 3. After performing a brief evaluation and reviewing Mr K’s MRI with him, Dr L recommends surgery to relieve compression of the S1 nerve.
“Isn’t that a dangerous procedure? Could I end up paralyzed?” Mr K asks.
“There are certain risks, but with the help of theMazor RoboticsRenaissanceGuidance System technology, the procedure is relatively safe.” Dr L explains the surgical planning using the Mazor system: “It employs artificially intelligent software to analyze your images and plan placement of my surgical tools. I’ve been using this technology for about a year now, and I’ve done over 30 surgeries—just like the one I’m recommending for you—with this technology.”
Mr K looks uncomfortable. “I don’t want a robot doing my surgery. I want you to do it all.”
Dr L wonders how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Mr K, a 54-year-old man, was referred to Dr L’s outpatient spine neurosurgery clinic with a six-week history of left-sided lower back pain, accompanied by weakness in his left leg and episodes of sharp, shooting pain. Before meeting Mr K, Dr L carefully reviewed his lumbar spine MRI and identified a herniated disc at the L5-S1 level, visibly compressing the S1 nerve root.

“This is a textbook presentation,” Dr L thought quietly, reaching for her reflex hammer before making her way to exam room 3. After conducting a focused physical examination and discussing the MRI results with Mr K, Dr L recommended a surgical procedure designed to relieve the pressure on his S1 nerve root.

Mr K hesitated. “Isn’t that kind of surgery risky? Could something go wrong, like paralysis?” he asked anxiously.

Dr L acknowledged the inherent risks but continued, “There are some risks, but with the Mazor Robotics Renaissance Guidance System, the operation is generally quite safe.” She went on to describe how the Mazor system employs advanced artificial intelligence software to process patient images and assist in planning the precise placement of surgical instruments. “I’ve been using this technology for about a year, and I’ve completed more than 30 procedures just like the one I’m suggesting, all with the assistance of this system,” she assured him.

Mr K appeared uneasy. “I really don’t like the idea of a robot operating on me. I want to be sure that you’re the one actually doing everything,” he said.

Dr L paused, considering how best to address Mr K’s concerns.

ethical_issues.question: Are physicians able to understand the mechanisms by which AI predictions or decisions that lead to errors occur?
keypoints: The opacity of AI systems (the black-box problem) makes it difficult for physicians to trace and understand the basis of AI decisions and the root causes of errors, thereby limiting comprehensive knowledge of AI prediction or decision-making mechanisms.

Physicians’ insufficient understanding of the internal mechanisms of AI systems may lead to inadequate disclosure of information during the informed consent process, thereby undermining the realization of patient autonomy.
This knowledge deficit not only compromises the quality of informed consent but may also negatively impact medical quality and safety, increasing the complexity of risk management in healthcare.

title: Should Watson Be Consulted for a Second Opinion?
case:
Ms L is a 63-year-old woman who visits her primary care physician, Dr R, with new-onset fatigue and gum bleeding. After a thorough history and physical examination, Dr R orders a complete blood count, the results of which show anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis. Dr R urgently refers Ms L to Dr O in hematology-oncology. Following more testing, Dr O concludes that Ms L has acute myeloid leukemia, admits her to the hospital, and schedules her for induction chemotherapy.
After several weeks of therapy, Ms L seems to be benefitting little from treatment and her condition has worsened since admission. Stumped by what once seemed like a routine case, Dr O recommends to Ms L genetic testing of her cancerous cells, which could offer additional information that could potentially lead to a different diagnosis or treatment plan. Dr O also considers consulting colleagues at the University of Tokyo, who recently used the IBM Watsonartificial intelligence (AI) system to correctly diagnose a rare form of leukemia in a very similar case.Dr O recalls Watson being able to sift through millions of pages of clinical literature as well as being able to incorporate a patient’s genetic background and clinical history to come up with a diagnosis and treatment plan, all in a fraction of the time that it would take a physician to do.
Dr O wonders:Perhaps Watson would come to the same conclusion I did. Or maybe Watson would find something I missed and help save Ms L’s life. Or maybe Watson would be totally unhelpful and waste my and Ms L’s time. Dr O also wonders whether to explain Watson to Ms L and invite her to consider these questions.
case_rewrite:
Ms L, a 63-year-old woman, arrives at her primary care physician Dr R’s office, complaining of recent fatigue and episodes of gum bleeding. Dr R conducts a thorough history and physical examination before ordering a complete blood count. The results reveal anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis. Recognizing the urgency, Dr R refers Ms L to Dr O, a hematology-oncology specialist. After further diagnostic workup, Dr O diagnoses Ms L with acute myeloid leukemia, admits her to the hospital, and initiates induction chemotherapy.

After several weeks in the hospital, it becomes clear that Ms L is responding poorly to treatment; her health continues to deteriorate. What initially seemed a straightforward case now leaves Dr O puzzled. Hoping for more insight, Dr O proposes genetic testing of Ms L’s leukemic cells, suggesting that it might clarify the diagnosis or reveal alternative treatment options. As Dr O contemplates next steps, she recalls the recent work of her colleagues at the University of Tokyo, who had successfully used the IBM Watson artificial intelligence (AI) system to diagnose a rare leukemia variant in a patient with a remarkably similar presentation.

Dr O reflects on Watson’s capabilities: its ability to analyze millions of pages of clinical literature, process a patient’s genetic and clinical background, and synthesize this data to generate diagnostic and treatment recommendations at speeds no human could match. Dr O considers whether consulting Watson might confirm her own conclusions, uncover something she might have missed, or perhaps yield no useful information at all—thereby consuming valuable time for both herself and Ms L.

As Dr O weighs her options, she also considers whether she should explain the Watson system to Ms L, discuss its potential benefits and limitations, and invite her input regarding the use of this AI resource in her ongoing care.

ethical_issues.question: What liability risks do physicians face when using the Watson system?
keypoints: The use of the Watson system may lead to diagnostic and treatment errors; physicians who rely blindly on the system’s recommendations without adequate verification may face malpractice litigation risks.
The application of the Watson system may elevate the standard of medical duty of care, requiring physicians to exercise a higher level of clinical caution, failing which they may be found negligent.

Given that Watson’s diagnostic and treatment recommendations currently lack comprehensive clinical trial validation, physicians may bear corresponding liability if patient harm results from following its advice.

Should Watson be proven effective in the future and become an industry standard, failure to consult the system for a second opinion could be regarded as a breach of ethical duty and give rise to legal liability.

ethical_issues.question: What are the limitations of the Watson system and their ethical implications?
keypoints: Due to the lack of comprehensive clinical trial data covering all diagnostic and treatment options, as well as issues related to the completeness and consistency of patient medical records, the accuracy and reliability of the diagnostic and therapeutic recommendations provided by the Watson system may be limited.

The Watson system exhibits a “black-box” problem, wherein its decision-making processes and reasoning mechanisms are difficult for both developers and users to fully explain, potentially resulting in conclusions that are inconsistent with physicians’ judgments and thereby affecting the transparency of clinical decision-making.

The use of AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment may increase liability risks for healthcare professionals and institutions, and could raise the standard of medical care, exposing practitioners to heightened legal and ethical risks.

Watson may generate unrealistic patient expectations regarding treatment outcomes; therefore, healthcare professionals should thoroughly inform patients about the assistive nature and limitations of AI tools to ensure transparency and maintain trust in the patient-physician relationship.

As the clinical effectiveness of AI systems becomes increasingly established, failure to utilize such decision support tools in the future may be regarded as a breach of ethical duty and could give rise to legal liability; healthcare professionals must stay informed about technological advancements and apply these tools judiciously.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr O consult an artificial intelligence system, such as IBM Watson, for a second opinion in Ms L’s case, and to what extent should such AI input influence or potentially replace physicians’ clinical judgment?
keypoints: The Watson system is designed to assist physicians’ clinical judgment, enhancing confidence and efficiency in diagnostic and therapeutic decision making, rather than replacing physicians’ professional judgment.

As an augmented intelligence tool, Watson expands physicians’ cognitive capacities by integrating vast amounts of clinical data and patient information, thereby helping them to accomplish diagnostic and therapeutic tasks with greater precision.

Clinical decision making should be centered on the physician’s professional judgment; physicians must evaluate the scientific validity and applicability of Watson’s recommendations, weigh potential clinical and legal risks before deciding whether to adopt them, and be able to justify their decisions.

Physicians should transparently explain to patients the purpose, advantages, and limitations of using artificial intelligence–assisted tools, respecting patients’ rights to be informed and to participate in decision making.

Intelligent systems such as Watson will not replace health care professionals, but they are expected to advance patient care and clinical research beyond current limitations, promoting improvements in health care quality and the development of personalized treatment.

title: Are Clinicians Obliged to Disclose Their Immigration Status to Patients?
case:
Dr T has a busy morning ahead of her in the cardiology clinic. Her first patient is Mr B, a 67-year-old man, for whom she has been caring since he suffered a heart attack 3 years ago. Dr T always enjoys seeing Mr B, and they have developed a good relationship over the years. Dr T walks into the exam room, greets Mr B, and notices that he isn’t his usual jovial self. “What’s wrong, John?”
Mr B responds, “I saw you in the newspaper the other day, Doc. The article mentioned that you were an illegal immigrant and were one of those ‘Dreamers.’ I’ve told you some pretty personal things about my life, and I feel like that was something you should have told me.” Dr T has recently become active in advocating for immigrants’ rights and, as a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient herself, she has been vocal about her own status as undocumented. Until now, she had not considered how her immigration status might affect her relationships with her patients. She wonders if she should have disclosed her immigration status to Mr B earlier and how to address his concerns now.
case_rewrite:
Dr T faces a packed schedule in the cardiology clinic this morning. Her first appointment is with Mr B, a 67-year-old man she has managed since his heart attack three years ago. Dr T looks forward to these visits; over the years, she and Mr B have built a strong rapport. Entering the exam room, Dr T greets Mr B warmly, but immediately senses that something is amiss—he seems unusually subdued. “What’s wrong, John?” she asks gently.

Mr B hesitates before replying, “I saw your name in the newspaper, Doc. The article said you were an undocumented immigrant and one of those ‘Dreamers.’ I’ve shared a lot of personal things with you over the years, and I feel like that’s something you should have told me.” 

Recently, Dr T has been outspoken in advocating for immigrant rights. As a DACA recipient, she has publicly shared her own undocumented status, believing it important for her activism. Until this moment, she hadn’t considered how her immigration status might impact her patient relationships. Now, she wonders whether she should have disclosed this information to Mr B earlier, and she’s uncertain how best to respond to his feelings and concerns.

ethical_issues.question: To what extent, if any, is Dr T ethically obligated to disclose her immigration status or personal political views to Mr B during their clinical encounter?
keypoints: Physicians should exercise caution when disclosing their personal political views; according to the American Medical Association Code of Medical Ethics, such disclosure should be guided by careful consideration of the specific clinical context, patient preferences, and emotional state, with the aim of preserving the therapeutic physician-patient relationship.

Physicians ought to be prepared to respond to patients’ inquiries regarding their political views, provided that such discussions do not undermine trust or the effectiveness of care within the physician-patient relationship.

Physicians, as citizens, have a responsibility to advocate for improved access to healthcare and for the amelioration of socioeconomic conditions that affect patient health; engagement in related political activities is ethically justifiable and necessary.

title: Should Immigration Status Information Be Considered Protected Health Information?
case: ABC Hospital prided itself on providing comprehensive care to the community, which included a sizeable population of undocumented immigrants. Dr A, a neurosurgeon, was first on the agenda to speak at ABC’s monthly meeting. Everyone on the board had heard of the case about which Dr A was to speak, since it attracted local media attention. Dr A described a case in which MJ, an undocumented patient admitted to evaluate causes of his headaches and balance issues, was found to have a brain tumor, for which Dr A had secured charity funds to perform surgery. Immigration authorities had been searching for MJ, on whom a deportation order had been issued, and requested information from ABC. An ABC employee revealed MJ’s room number, clinical condition, surgery date, and date of expected discharge. Upon discharge, just outside the hospital, MJ was apprehended by immigration officials and taken to a local detention center. As it was Dr A’s view that disclosure of MJ’s information compromised MJ’s care and recovery, Dr A questioned whether members of the care team and the organization were obligated under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule to protect MJ’s privacy and the confidentiality of MJ’s information, despite requests for information about MJ from immigration officials.
case_rewrite:
At ABC Hospital, known for its commitment to comprehensive care for all members of its diverse community—including a large number of undocumented immigrants—the monthly board meeting was underway. Dr A, a respected neurosurgeon, was scheduled to present first. The board members were already familiar with the case Dr A was about to discuss, as it had recently drawn considerable attention from the local press.

Dr A began by recounting the story of MJ, an undocumented patient who had been admitted to ABC Hospital for evaluation of persistent headaches and problems with balance. After a thorough assessment, Dr A diagnosed MJ with a brain tumor. Recognizing the urgency and seriousness of MJ's condition, Dr A proactively secured charity funding to ensure MJ could undergo the necessary surgery, despite MJ’s lack of insurance and documentation.

During MJ’s hospitalization, it became known that immigration authorities were actively searching for him, as he was subject to a deportation order. The authorities formally approached ABC Hospital, requesting information about MJ. In response, an employee at ABC disclosed MJ’s room number, details about his clinical status, the scheduled date for his surgery, and the anticipated date of his discharge.

Shortly after MJ was discharged, and just steps outside the hospital doors, immigration officials apprehended him and transported him to a local detention center. Dr A, deeply troubled by the impact this disclosure had on MJ’s immediate care and ongoing recovery, raised concerns at the meeting. Dr A questioned whether the care team and ABC Hospital were bound, under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule, to protect MJ’s privacy and the confidentiality of information related to his immigration status and health, even in the face of direct requests from immigration authorities.

ethical_issues.question: Should Immigration Status Information Be Considered Protected Health Information (PHI) and Protected Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule?
keypoints: The determination of whether immigration status information constitutes protected health information (PHI) hinges on whether such information is related to the individual’s past, present, or future physical or mental health condition.

Immigration status information has a clear relationship with health, particularly considering that undocumented immigrants face multiple stressors that may impact mental health; therefore, it meets the definition of “individually identifiable health information” under PHI.

As PHI, a patient’s immigration status is protected under the HIPAA Privacy Rule and may not be disclosed for purposes other than treatment, payment, or health care operations without the patient’s authorization.

Health care organizations and clinicians bear legal and ethical obligations to safeguard patients’ immigration status information, preventing unauthorized disclosure and thereby protecting the patient’s rights to treatment and recovery.

ethical_issues.question: Are healthcare institutions obligated to disclose a patient’s immigration status to immigration authorities without the patient’s authorization?
keypoints: Health care organizations have no obligation to disclose a patient’s immigration status to immigration authorities, as such status is related to the patient’s health condition and constitutes protected health information (PHI) under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, which may not be disclosed without the patient’s authorization.

Clinicians and health care organizations must not disclose a patient’s immigration status to any authority, or they risk penalties under HIPAA, except in the presence of applicable and valid exceptions.

ethical_issues.question: In the current political climate, how should clinicians and health care organizations balance patient privacy with legal obligations in the context of immigration enforcement policies and practices?
keypoints: A patient’s immigration status, due to its substantial relationship with the patient’s health condition, meets the definition of protected health information (PHI) under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule and should therefore be afforded equivalent protections.

Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, a patient’s immigration status, as PHI, may not be disclosed without the patient’s authorization; clinicians and health care organizations are prohibited from releasing such information to any authority, including immigration enforcement agencies, unless a valid legal exception mandates disclosure.

Clinicians and health care organizations must thoroughly understand and comply with the HIPAA Privacy Rule, exercising caution in evaluating requests for disclosure related to immigration enforcement, to prevent unauthorized release of patients’ immigration status and mitigate associated legal risks.

title: Is Organ Retransplantation Among Undocumented Immigrants in the United States Just?
case:
Anna was 2 years old when she was diagnosed with polycystic kidney disease, a life-threatening illness. Her family was told that Anna would need a kidney transplant to live. Although Anna was an undocumented immigrant, the hospital had a pool of funding for charity kidney transplants, and the state would provide Medicaid to cover additional costs. Anna received a kidney transplant at the age of 2½.
At age 18, Anna’s family was notified that Medicaid funding would no longer be available to cover her transplant-related medical care. She would now be responsible for purchasing the immunosuppressive drugs required to maintain her kidney transplant as well as costs of regular follow-up appointments. After high school, Anna found work as a waitress making below minimum wage, mostly working double shifts on an unpredictable schedule, with no health insurance. She stopped taking her immunosuppressive medications because she could not afford them and could not follow up with her nephrologist due to her demanding schedule. Two years passed, and Anna now presents to the county hospital emergency department. Her kidney transplant has failed. She needs a new kidney or faces a lifetime of dialysis. In addition to her undocumented status, she has no health insurance. What should be done?
case_rewrite:
Anna was just two years old when she was diagnosed with polycystic kidney disease, a severe and life-threatening condition. Her family learned that a kidney transplant was the only way to save her life. Although Anna was an undocumented immigrant, the hospital had a special fund for charity kidney transplants, and the state provided Medicaid to cover additional expenses. At age two and a half, Anna received her kidney transplant.

When Anna turned eighteen, her family was informed that Medicaid would no longer cover the ongoing medical care related to her transplant. Anna now had to pay out of pocket for the immunosuppressive medications essential for keeping her transplanted kidney healthy, as well as for her regular follow-up appointments. After finishing high school, Anna found work as a waitress. She earned less than minimum wage, mainly working double shifts with unpredictable hours, and had no health insurance. Unable to afford her immunosuppressive drugs and unable to schedule regular visits with her nephrologist due to her demanding job, Anna stopped taking her medications.

Two years later, Anna arrives at the county hospital emergency department. Her transplanted kidney has failed. Without another kidney transplant, she will require dialysis for the rest of her life. Anna remains undocumented and still has no health insurance. What should be done?

ethical_issues.question: Should retransplantation be offered to undocumented immigrants who fail to adhere to immunosuppressive therapy after their initial organ transplant due to lack of resources?
keypoints: Nonadherence to immunosuppressive therapy due to resource limitations following the initial kidney transplant is commonly regarded as a contraindication to retransplantation and serves as a justification for transplant centers to deny a second transplant.

Access to medical care is a fundamental human right; denying retransplantation to undocumented immigrants contravenes physicians’ ethical responsibility to safeguard the medical well-being of their patients.

The cumulative cost of emergent dialysis exceeds that of transplantation, and retransplantation significantly reduces patient mortality compared to ongoing dialysis, representing the medically optimal long-term treatment following graft failure.

Most states lack funding mechanisms to ensure undocumented immigrants receive immunosuppressive medications and follow-up care after reaching adulthood, highlighting an urgent need for policy development to guarantee sustained posttransplant medical support.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of limited organ supply, should deceased donor organs be prioritized or exclusively allocated to U.S. citizens and legal residents rather than undocumented immigrants?
keypoints: Opponents argue that U.S. citizens and legal residents should be prioritized or exclusively allocated deceased donor organs, citing limited public healthcare resources and the potential for undocumented immigrants to be deported or lose access to follow-up care, which increases transplant risks and the likelihood of resource wastage.

Denying transplantation to undocumented immigrants may be unjust, given that noncitizens contribute to the deceased donor organ pool, and undocumented immigrants serve both as organ donors and recipients; their net contribution to the organ pool warrants consideration.

Proponents contend that organ allocation should be based on medical need and principles of equity rather than citizenship status, emphasizing that citizenship should not be a criterion for inclusion on the transplant waiting list.

title: How Should Clinicians Respond When Different Standards of Care Are Applied to Undocumented Patients?
case:
Dr K is an internal medicine resident starting his community-based rotation at Salud Completa, a clinic that provides health care primarily to undocumented immigrants. He is eager to apply his clinical skills to providing care to this underserved population. After an afternoon so busy that some patients had to be turned away, Dr K’s last patient is Mr L, who presents with persistent epigastric pain and nausea. He has visited the clinic twice over the past 5 months with similar symptoms and was prescribed a proton-pump inhibitor. Since his symptoms have not resolved, Dr K wants to order an upper endoscopy. Upon discussing Mr L’s case with his attending physician, he learns that the gastroenterologist, who had been performing upper endoscopies free of charge for Salud Completa patients, has moved. Since there is nowhere else to refer Mr L, who cannot afford to pay for an endoscopy himself, the attending physician told Dr K to increase Mr L’s medication dose and follow up with him at the clinic in a few months.
Dr K considers this recommendation, worried that he is providing substandard care to Mr L. Although there are often no other options for undocumented patients like Mr L, Dr K still wonders about his role in providing care that’s different in quality from care he provides patients in the university teaching hospital setting. He wonders whether and how he should respond to his attending physician’s recommendation. He also wonders how he should respond to Mr L, who is still waiting for him in the exam room.
case_rewrite:
Dr K, an internal medicine resident, begins his community-based rotation at Salud Completa, a clinic devoted primarily to caring for undocumented immigrants. Eager to put his clinical expertise to work for this underserved group, Dr K finds his afternoon quickly overwhelmed—so much so that some patients must be turned away. As the clinic quiets, his final patient, Mr L, arrives complaining of persistent epigastric pain and nausea. Mr L has visited the clinic twice in the past five months for similar symptoms, each time receiving a prescription for a proton-pump inhibitor. With little improvement, Dr K now believes an upper endoscopy is necessary to further evaluate Mr L’s condition.

Dr K consults with his attending physician about arranging the endoscopy. He learns, however, that the gastroenterologist who previously provided free upper endoscopies for Salud Completa’s patients has recently left. There are no other specialists available, and Mr L cannot afford to pay for the procedure out of pocket. The attending advises Dr K to increase Mr L’s medication dose and have him return for follow-up in several months.

As Dr K considers this plan, he feels uneasy, concerned that he is offering Mr L a lower standard of care than he would provide to patients in the university teaching hospital. He is troubled by the limitations imposed by the clinic’s resources and worries about the implications of offering care that differs in quality from what he believes is optimal. Dr K questions how he should respond to his attending’s recommendation and wonders what to tell Mr L, who is still waiting in the exam room for answers.

ethical_issues.question: In resource-limited settings, how should physicians provide the best attainable medical care to patients when standard treatments are not available?
keypoints: Physicians should provide the best possible diagnostic and treatment options based on professional judgment within resource-limited settings, even if such care falls below accepted standards.

Physicians should maintain maximal transparency by thoroughly explaining to patients the diagnostic and treatment options as well as their limitations—including state-of-the-art therapies that may be unaffordable or unavailable—while promoting full patient informedness and respecting patient autonomy.

Physicians should vigorously advocate on behalf of their patients by articulating and actively seeking superior alternative options (such as referral to other safety-net clinics or identifying specialists willing to provide pro bono care) to improve the patient’s medical condition.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr K balance transparency with Mr L’s expectations when discussing the limitations in accessing necessary treatments due to Mr L’s financial and immigration status?
keypoints: Physicians should maintain maximal transparency by informing patients of all treatment options, including the optimal choices that may be unavailable, and actively advocate for improved medical care conditions on behalf of the patient.

Communication should embody humanistic care, encompassing more affordable and feasible prioritized diagnostic and therapeutic options, thereby assisting patients in understanding their medical choices and limitations.

Although concealing treatment options that patients cannot afford may be well-intentioned, it risks damaging the patient-physician relationship and undermining patient trust in the healthcare system; transparency is essential for preserving this trust.

Fully informed patients are empowered to make autonomous decisions; physicians must respect patient autonomy by comprehensively explaining the disease status, treatment plans, prognosis, and alternative options.

Physicians should acknowledge and candidly communicate that the patient is currently receiving suboptimal care, while striving to secure the best possible medical resources and support within existing constraints.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr K balance his ethical responsibilities to advocate for Mr L’s individual care needs with his obligations to promote systemic health care reform for undocumented patients?
keypoints: Physicians should simultaneously engage in both agency—advocating for the interests of individual patients—and activism—promoting reform of the health care system; these two approaches are complementary and indispensable.

Physicians have an ethical responsibility to practice both agency and activism, thereby meeting the specific medical needs of patients while also advancing social and systemic changes to improve population health.

In real-world clinical settings, physicians should strive to provide ethically appropriate medical care while actively participating in efforts to improve the social determinants that impact patient health.

title: Should Immigration Status Information Be Included in a Patient’s Health Record?
case:
Dr Lopez’s next visit is a well-child check with Anna, an 8-year-old Korean American who is new to his county-affiliated clinic. Her intake form indicates a history of asthma with one prior hospitalization and no current medications. He makes a mental note to explore this issue and walks into the patient room to see Anna playing with her mother, Ms P.
After introducing himself, Dr Lopez asks Ms P about her concerns. “Anna used to love school, but her grades have been slipping lately. Sometimes she asks to stay home or asks me not to go to work because her stomach hurts. I don’t know what’s going on.” After validating Ms P’s concerns, Dr Lopez asks if there have been any major changes or stressors in Anna’s life. She sighs, “I don’t get paid much at the nail salon, and it’s just the two of us at home. But that’s not new.”
She continues hesitantly, avoiding eye contact, “Actually, Anna once said she’s afraid I’m going to be taken away. I think she’s heard scary things in the news about what could happen to someone without papers.”
Dr Lopez realizes Anna is likely experiencing anxiety about her mother’s tenuous immigration status and possible deportation. He wonders how or even whether to document her mother’s immigration status in Anna’s health records. Documenting Ms P’s immigration status could help facilitate referrals, such as medical-legal referrals, and alert other clinicians to this significant life stressor. However, it could also impair the patient-physician relationship if he documents this detail without knowing potential risks or discussing them with Ms P. In a time of rapidly changing immigration policies, fear, and uncertainty, could he be exposing her family to discrimination or deportation risk?
case_rewrite:
Dr Lopez’s next patient is Anna, an 8-year-old Korean American girl who is visiting his county-affiliated clinic for a well-child check. Anna is new to the clinic, and her intake form notes a history of asthma, including a previous hospitalization, but lists no current medications. Dr Lopez makes a mental note to ask about her asthma management and steps into the exam room, where Anna is quietly playing a game with her mother, Ms P.

After a warm introduction, Dr Lopez turns to Ms P and asks if she has any particular worries about Anna’s health. Ms P hesitates, then shares, “Anna used to be excited about school, but her grades have gone down. Lately, she keeps saying her stomach hurts, asks to stay home, or begs me not to leave for work. I’m really concerned, but I can’t figure out what’s wrong.” Dr Lopez listens empathetically and asks whether there have been any recent changes or stressful events in their lives. Ms P sighs, “I still work at the nail salon. It’s tough, and it’s just the two of us, but that hasn’t changed.”

After a pause, Ms P glances away and lowers her voice. “Actually, Anna mentioned once that she’s scared I’ll be taken away. I think she’s picked up on things from the news about people getting in trouble if they don’t have the right papers.” 

As Dr Lopez considers Ms P’s words, he becomes aware that Anna’s anxiety may be tied to fears about her mother’s uncertain immigration situation and potential separation. He wonders whether, and how, to record this context in Anna’s medical file. On one hand, documenting the family’s situation could help other care providers understand Anna’s stressors and make appropriate referrals, such as connecting them with legal or social services. On the other hand, Dr Lopez recognizes that explicitly noting Ms P’s immigration status could jeopardize the trust between him and the family and potentially expose them to risks, especially in a climate of shifting policies and heightened fears.

He weighs whether to use indirect language to describe Anna’s situation or to refrain from documenting details that could put the family at risk of discrimination or worse. Dr Lopez reflects on his responsibility to protect his patient’s safety and privacy, knowing that information in the health record can be difficult to control or remove once entered, and wonders how best to proceed to support Anna and her mother without inadvertently causing harm.

ethical_issues.question: Should Healthcare Providers Document Immigration Status Information in a Patient’s Health Record to Help Identify Stressors and Provide Comprehensive Care?
keypoints: Avoid explicit documentation of patients’ and their family members’ immigration status in health records to minimize potential risks and emotional distress.

Identifying stressors and modifiable social determinants of health facilitates comprehensive care but should be conducted through indirect inquiry rather than direct questioning about immigration status.

Referral services can be coordinated through verbal communication between clinicians and patients or via indirect language in the health record (e.g., “immigration-related stressors” or “ineligible for insurance”) without explicitly recording immigration status.

Prioritizing the ethical principle of “first, do no harm,” clinicians should avoid exposing patients to risks of discrimination, disrespect, or deportation resulting from disclosure of immigration status, thereby safeguarding patient safety and trust.
Given that recorded information is difficult to completely remove, potentially exposing patients to long-term risks, the necessity of documenting immigration status should be carefully evaluated.
Healthcare systems should develop and implement policies and guidelines aimed at reducing stigma and discrimination for all patients, ensuring an equitable and dignified care environment.

ethical_issues.question: In situations where documenting immigration status may lead to discrimination or legal risks, how can healthcare professionals protect patient privacy and adhere to the principle of confidentiality?
keypoints: Healthcare providers should first explicitly commit to protecting the privacy of patients and their families, inform them of relevant privacy regulations, and invite them to express any concerns, thereby establishing a foundation of trust and open communication.

In situations where immigration status may lead to discrimination or legal risks, explicit documentation of the patient’s and their family members’ immigration status in the health record should be avoided, especially when the risks outweigh the potential benefits.

If knowledge of immigration status is necessary to assist patients in accessing services or resources, priority should be given to verbal communication between clinician and patient, or indirect language describing social context (e.g., “immigration-related stressors” or “ineligible for insurance”) should be used in the health record to avoid explicit notation of immigration status.

Under HIPAA regulations, patients’ personally identifiable information may only be shared under limited circumstances such as treatment, payment, public safety, or legal requirements (e.g., court orders). Healthcare providers must strictly adhere to confidentiality principles and refrain from disclosing such information to law enforcement or immigration authorities unless legally compelled to do so.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians respect patient autonomy and ensure informed consent when documenting immigration status information?
keypoints: Clinicians should approach the documentation of immigration status information within an informed consent framework, fully explaining the associated risks and benefits, and respecting the patient’s autonomy in deciding whether to include this information in the health record.

Given the rapidly changing and complex nature of immigration policies, clinicians may face practical challenges in explaining the risks and benefits, and should be transparent with patients about this uncertainty.

Clinicians should inform patients of their privacy rights under HIPAA and the limitations on data sharing with external agencies, ensure the confidentiality of patient information, and invite patients to discuss their concerns; protecting patient privacy is a key prerequisite for establishing and maintaining trust in the patient-clinician relationship.

title: How Should Physicians Use Their Authority to Name a Stigmatizing Diagnosis and Respond to a Patient’s Experience?
case:
Ms M presents to Dr P’s family medicine clinic for assessment of severe pruritus (itch) that she has been experiencing for the past 4 years. She first noted the itch in association with small bumps on her ankles and wrists. She was diagnosed with bed bugs and had her apartment cleaned and fumigated. The bumps went away, but the itching persisted. She became concerned that the infestation had returned and ultimately moved out of her apartment and into a new building. She sold all her belongings, including her bed and books, gave away her cat, and bought new furniture 3 years ago. She continues to note severe itching of her arms, legs, and back since that time. She had her new apartment fumigated 3 more times. She discusses with Dr P that, recently, she thinks she has been able to see the bugs—they are hatching eggs and she can pull them out. She brings the “eggs” with her in plastic bags for Dr P to review. She has found topical permethrin to be helpful in the past.
Dr P examines her skin and notes scabbed-over bumps from repeated manipulation of the skin. He sees no signs of an infestation. He reviews the contents of her bag and notes that it is consistent with simple keratin. Dr P suspects the source of Ms M’s symptoms and experiences to be delusional infestation, and he wonders how he should respond in a way that is respectful and truthful.
case_rewrite:
Ms M comes to Dr P’s family medicine clinic, seeking help for severe itching that has troubled her for the past four years. She recalls that the itch started along with small bumps on her ankles and wrists. At that time, she was told she had bed bugs, so she arranged for her apartment to be cleaned and fumigated. The bumps disappeared, but the relentless itching remained. Worried that the bed bugs had returned, Ms M ultimately made the difficult decision to move out of her apartment altogether. She sold all her possessions—including her bed and books—gave away her beloved cat, and purchased new furniture when she moved into a new building three years ago.

Despite these drastic steps, Ms M continues to experience intense itching on her arms, legs, and back. She has since had her new apartment fumigated three additional times, hoping to rid herself of the problem. During her conversation with Dr P, Ms M shares that recently she believes she has actually seen the bugs. She describes how she thinks they are laying eggs, and she claims she can pull them out herself. She even brings what she believes are the “eggs,” carefully stored in plastic bags, and asks Dr P to examine them. Ms M mentions that she has found topical permethrin creams somewhat helpful in the past.

On examination, Dr P notices scabbed-over bumps on Ms M’s skin, most likely the result of her repeatedly scratching and manipulating the areas. He finds no evidence of any current or past infestation. When he inspects the items Ms M brought, he recognizes them as simple keratin, not insect eggs. Given the chronicity of symptoms, the lack of physical findings, and Ms M’s firm beliefs about being infested despite evidence to the contrary, Dr P suspects that Ms M is experiencing delusional infestation. He is now faced with the challenge of how to proceed in a manner that is both honest and respectful, while also considering the potential impact of how he communicates his assessment and recommendations to Ms M.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians withhold the name of the diagnosis when diagnosing delusional infestation in order to avoid the patient feeling invalidated and refusing treatment?
keypoints: Prematurely labeling a patient’s symptoms as delusional infestation may cause the patient to feel invalidated, potentially leading to refusal of further treatment and disengagement from medical care.
Withholding a diagnosis constitutes deception and is ethically unacceptable without sufficient and justifiable reasons.
Delusional infestation represents a rare exception in which physicians may temporarily withhold a diagnosis, but such concealment should only be implemented when strict criteria are met.

The conditions under which physicians may temporarily withhold a diagnosis include: the patient’s incapacity for informed decision-making due to delusions and lack of insight; the patient’s inability to understand or weigh key information relevant to treatment despite adequate decision-making support; the likelihood of harm if left untreated; the patient’s probable refusal of medication due to lack of insight; and the unavailability or inappropriateness of conventional coercive treatment measures due to the severity of harm or legal constraints.

When temporarily withholding the diagnosis and the nature of the medication, physicians should truthfully communicate that the treatment’s goal is symptom relief, thereby upholding the patient’s right to information and respecting their dignity.

After the patient has recovered and regained decision-making capacity, physicians have an obligation to disclose the diagnosis, the rationale for the chosen treatment, and the reasons for the initial nondisclosure, in order to promote patient understanding and trust.

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances, if any, may Dr P ethically employ temporary therapeutic deception with Ms M to facilitate her treatment, without violating core principles of medical ethics such as respect for patient autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice?
keypoints: Physicians may consider temporary deception only when the patient’s delusions and lack of insight result in an incapacity for informed decision-making, such that even with adequate decision-making support, the patient is unable to understand or weigh information relevant to consent.

If failure to provide timely treatment is likely to cause harm to the patient, and the patient, due to lack of insight, is likely to refuse necessary medication, physicians may regard this as a prerequisite condition for considering deception.

When conventional means of compulsory treatment are not feasible, specifically including (a) the harm requiring prevention is not sufficiently severe or immediate, or (b) the legally sanctioned coercive measures themselves would cause greater harm than withholding information, physicians may contemplate temporary deception.

Only when all the above conditions are simultaneously satisfied is it ethically justifiable for physicians to consider temporarily deceiving the patient in order to facilitate treatment without violating medical ethical principles.

ethical_issues.question: Are physicians obligated to disclose the diagnosis and the reasons for initially withholding full explanation after a patient’s recovery, and how can they avoid exacerbating stigmatization?
keypoints: Physicians have an obligation to disclose the diagnosis, the rationale for treatment, and the reasons for the initial withholding of information once the patient’s psychotic symptoms have remitted and decision-making capacity has been restored, accompanied by an appropriate apology and an explanation of the diagnostic reasoning process.

When revealing the diagnosis, physicians should thoroughly assess the patient’s understanding and beliefs about the illness, proactively provide scientifically accurate and comprehensible information, and assist in dispelling misconceptions and prejudices.
Physicians must attend to any self-stigmatizing beliefs held by the patient, addressing them with a gentle yet firm approach, and refer for psychological therapy support when necessary.

The process of disclosing the diagnosis should be conducted with caution and skill, avoiding stigmatizing language, respecting the patient’s feelings, and preventing exacerbation of stigma or damage to the therapeutic relationship.
Physicians should continuously monitor the patient’s psychological state and treatment adherence, support autonomous decision-making, and promote recovery and restoration of social functioning.

title: When Should Iatrogenic Polypharmacy Be Considered a Disease?
case:
Ms M and her daughter, Ms J, present to Dr R’s neurology office for an initial evaluation. Ms J is concerned that her 83-year-old mother might be developing Parkinson’s or another neurodegenerative disease and has sought out Dr R’s expertise.
Ms J has noticed that her mother has been moving much more slowly recently, has had numerous falls, and looks depressed. Her mother, who had always been full of energy, now spends the day watching TV and sleeping. Her mother has been slurring some of her words lately and has even developed a tremor. Dr R reviews Ms M’s exam. She has no cogwheel rigidity, but her gait is wide based and she wobbles as she turns. She has mild ataxia and an intention tremor. Her concentration is poor, as is her 3-object recall. She agrees that she is not herself and is worried she is developing Parkinson’s disease, a condition from which her uncle suffered before his death.
Dr R reviews her history and notes that her symptoms have worsened in the setting of a few recent hospitalizations for heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations, and a gastrointestinal bleed. During her most recent hospitalization, she was initiated on amiodarone and a beta blocker, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and trazodone for sleep, as well as albuterol nebulizers every 4 to 6 hours. During a previous hospitalization, she was placed on 2 new medications for gastroparesis and initiated on a more intensive, insulin-based diabetes regimen. Prior to that, she was placed on 2 diuretics for severe volume overload. In discussing her regimen with Ms J, Dr R notes that Ms M is currently taking 17 medications for her numerous medical conditions including heart failure, atrial fibrillation, COPD, diabetes complicated by gastroparesis, and hypertension. While Ms M has difficulty remembering which medications she takes, her daughter has been very diligent about ensuring that she takes her medications as prescribed.
Dr R reviews Ms M’s illness history. Ms M was hospitalized 10 times last year for heart failure or COPD exacerbations, but, looking at her long medication list, she realizes she is not sure what is making her sick—her illnesses or the medications to treat them.
case_rewrite:
Ms M and her daughter, Ms J, arrive at Dr R’s neurology clinic for an initial consultation. Ms J is worried that her 83-year-old mother might be developing Parkinson’s disease or another neurodegenerative disorder and has sought Dr R’s evaluation. 

Ms J explains that her mother, once lively and energetic, has become noticeably slower in her movements, has experienced frequent falls, and appears withdrawn and depressed. Ms M, who used to be active, now spends most of her days sleeping or watching television. Ms J mentions that her mother’s speech has become slurred, and recently, she has developed a tremor. 

During the examination, Dr R observes that Ms M does not have cogwheel rigidity, but her gait is broad and unsteady, especially when she turns. She displays mild ataxia and an intention tremor. Her concentration is impaired, and she has difficulty recalling three objects. Ms M herself acknowledges that she doesn’t feel like her usual self and confides her worry that she might be developing Parkinson’s, as her uncle did before passing away.

Dr R reviews Ms M’s recent medical history and notes that her symptoms have worsened following several hospitalizations for heart failure, COPD exacerbations, and a gastrointestinal bleed. Most recently, during a hospital stay, Ms M was started on amiodarone and a beta blocker, as well as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and trazodone for sleep. She is also receiving albuterol nebulizers every four to six hours. In a prior hospitalization, two new medications were added for gastroparesis, and her diabetes management became more intensive with the addition of insulin. Before that, she was started on two diuretics for severe fluid overload.

As Dr R speaks with Ms J, it becomes clear that Ms M is now taking 17 different medications to manage her multiple chronic conditions, including heart failure, atrial fibrillation, COPD, diabetes complicated by gastroparesis, and hypertension. While Ms M struggles to remember all her medications, Ms J has been conscientious about ensuring her mother takes them as prescribed.

Reviewing the events of the past year, Dr R notes that Ms M was hospitalized ten times for heart failure or COPD exacerbations. Staring at the extensive medication list, Dr R finds it difficult to determine whether Ms M’s decline is due to her underlying illnesses or the many medications prescribed for them.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with iatrogenic harm potentially resulting from polypharmacy, should Dr. R ethically intervene to deprescribe non-essential medications in Ms M’s treatment plan?
keypoints: When the diagnosis remains unclear and may involve the effects of polypharmacy, priority should be given to avoiding the addition of new medications to prevent exacerbation of iatrogenic harm, thereby upholding the principle of non-maleficence.

Dr. R should collaborate with relevant specialists, including the primary care physician, to systematically evaluate the necessity and benefits of Ms. M’s current medications and gradually discontinue those that are non-essential.
By reducing the use of non-essential medications, the risk of drug interactions and adverse effects can be minimized, which in turn may alleviate Ms. M’s symptoms.
Deprescribing facilitates more accurate diagnosis by preventing the misattribution of medication side effects to neurodegenerative diseases, thereby optimizing the overall treatment plan.
This approach reflects respect for patient safety and the principle of maximizing benefit within medical ethics, contributing to the restoration of Ms. M’s function and quality of life.
