title: What Should Leaders Do When Inefficiency Is Perceived as a Cost of Inclusivity in Strategic Planning Processes in Health Care?
case:
Dr. Stevens chairs her institution’s quality improvement council, a group dedicated to implementing hospital policies and procedures that promote optimal resource utilization and best possible clinical outcomes for patients. Every month, a multidisciplinary group of clinicians and administrators meet to discuss progress of recent quality improvement efforts. A particular area of concern has to do with reducing falls among inpatients. Falls can be catastrophic for some patients and can result in increased morbidity. Once they’ve happened, they can be difficult and costly to manage, and they can influence reimbursement.
The quality improvement council hopes to implement and optimize fall prevention initiatives to reduce patients’ risk. After several months of planning, Dr. Tarib, a hospitalist, and Mr. Collins, a nurse informaticist, propose a plan that seeks to better integrate the roles of nurses, physical therapists, occupational therapists, medical assistants, and medical students into rehabilitation programs devoted to facilitating patients’ walking. A goal of this plan is to integrate effective fall prevention strategies throughout patients’ rehabilitation programs.
Dr. Stevens notices that the quality improvement council represents many organizational stakeholders whose input is regarded as necessary for implementing new initiatives but does not include former patients. She has read in a recent article that patient involvement in strategic planning can contribute to improved health system efficiencies, improved health outcomes for patients, increased trust between clinicians and patients, increased satisfaction among patients, and reduced costs for health care organizations. She regards the absence of former patients’ perspectives as a shortcoming in the quality improvement council’s strategic planning processes. Several council members agree that former patients’ views should be incorporated, and a small group of former patients who have recovered from falls in health care settings have now been invited to deliberate with the council about developing fall prevention initiatives.
Some members of the group of former patients suggest that they are not comfortable with the roles proposed for medical assistants and medical students in the fall prevention plan proposed by Dr. Tarib and Mr. Collins. While they express respect for the professional experience that informs Dr. Tarib’s and Mr. Collins’s fall prevention proposal, they also express suspicion about entrusting critical parts of implementing the fall prevention protocol to assistants and students. They cite their own experiences, recalling how their walking rehabilitation efforts required intense physical exertion and also aroused feelings of anxiety about how their bodies would be handled by those upon whom they depended to help them try to keep stable and upright when they felt weak and needed more help during their rehabilitation sessions.
One former stroke recovery patient says, “I relied on a masters-prepared physical therapist who understood how a body like mine could fall. She trained me in how to do these micro-movements that were critical to my progress. I just can’t imagine a medical student or medical assistant having the index of experience, expertise, and patience to help me like she did. They’re not trained like physical therapists at all. Why would you expose a vulnerable postoperative patient, for example, to that kind of risk? Is it to save money?”
While initially eager about welcoming former patients to the council deliberation, Dr. Tarib and Mr. Collins now feel frustrated. This former patient’s comment and a few others like it during the most recent meetings of the council prompts some clinician members to complain about how former patients’ participation requires longer and more frequent meetings, partly due to the need to explain clinical concepts with which clinician members of the council are already familiar and comfortable. They openly express their aggravation privately to each other and to Dr. Stevens, declaring, “The patients have raised some important points, but they don’t always know what they’re talking about. The conversation is now full of complexities we didn’t worry about before. How will we ever come to a decision? I just can’t keep taking time away from my other duties to attend meetings that are full of inefficiencies, obstacles, and questions. We’re not making progress anymore.”
As chair of the council, Dr. Stevens must decide what to do.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Stevens serves as the chair of her hospital’s quality improvement council, a multidisciplinary body tasked with shaping institutional policies and practices that support efficient resource use and the best possible outcomes for hospitalized patients. Each month, clinicians and administrators gather to review the council’s progress on various initiatives. One persistent issue on their agenda is inpatient falls, which can cause significant harm and lead to costly, complex management challenges, as well as affect hospital reimbursement rates.

After several months of focused effort, Dr. Tarib, a hospitalist, and Mr. Collins, a nurse informaticist, present a comprehensive plan aimed at reducing patient falls. Their proposal involves deeper collaboration among nurses, physical therapists, occupational therapists, medical assistants, and medical students within rehabilitation programs. The intention is to weave effective fall prevention strategies throughout every phase of patient rehabilitation.

As Dr. Stevens reviews the council’s composition, she realizes that while many stakeholders are represented, the voices of former patients are absent. She recalls a recent article highlighting the benefits of including patients in strategic planning—improved system efficiency, better health outcomes, increased trust, higher patient satisfaction, and lower healthcare costs. Dr. Stevens sees this lack of patient input as a significant gap in the council’s planning process. Several council members concur, and a group of former patients who have experienced and recovered from falls during hospital stays are soon invited to participate in discussions about new fall prevention strategies.

During these deliberations, some former patients express discomfort with the proposed involvement of medical assistants and medical students in implementing the fall prevention protocol. While they acknowledge Dr. Tarib’s and Mr. Collins’s professional insight, they voice doubts about entrusting critical aspects of fall prevention to assistants and students. They reference their own experiences—recalling the physical and emotional vulnerabilities they faced during rehabilitation, and emphasizing the trust they placed in highly trained professionals to guide them safely.

One former stroke patient shares, “I relied on a physical therapist with advanced training who really understood the risks my body faced. She taught me small, precise movements that made all the difference. I can’t imagine a medical student or assistant having the same skill, patience, or expertise. They aren’t trained like physical therapists. Why would you put a vulnerable post-op patient in that position? Is it just to cut costs?”

Initially, Dr. Tarib and Mr. Collins welcomed patient involvement, but these comments and similar feedback from other former patients leave them feeling frustrated. Some clinicians on the council begin to complain—often privately to each other and to Dr. Stevens—about the increased length and frequency of meetings, citing the extra time needed to explain clinical concepts to non-clinicians. “The patients have raised some valid concerns, but sometimes they don’t really understand the complexities. Now our conversations are bogged down with issues we didn’t have to worry about before. How are we supposed to make decisions? I can’t keep spending time in meetings that feel inefficient and filled with obstacles. We’re not making headway anymore,” one clinician remarks.

Dr. Stevens, as chair, now faces the challenge of how to proceed.

ethical_issues.question: How can the tension between patient involvement and project efficiency be balanced in strategic planning within health care?
keypoints: Dr. Stevens, as chair of the quality improvement council, should uphold the ethical principle of respect for persons by ensuring that patient engagement remains central to quality improvement efforts, recognizing its essential role in achieving patient-centered care and optimizing health outcomes, despite concerns raised by clinician members such as Dr. Tarib.

Leadership should promote procedural justice by enhancing meeting efficiency through structured agendas, transparent communication channels, and clearly defined decision-making processes, thereby addressing the perceived tension between inclusivity—particularly patient involvement—and operational efficiency.

All council members, including clinicians and administrators, must acknowledge the intrinsic value of each participant, actively listen to diverse perspectives, and foster a culture of multidisciplinary collaboration and inclusivity, in alignment with the ethical principle of respect for diversity.

The council should establish clear evaluation milestones and utilize ongoing patient feedback and outcome data to iteratively refine fall prevention initiatives, ensuring a responsive and dynamic approach that integrates patient participation with continuous quality improvement.

The perspectives of patients and all relevant stakeholders should be systematically incorporated into the quality improvement process, ensuring that interventions are both evidence-based and ethically responsive to patient needs, thereby promoting beneficence and accountability in institutional decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr. Stevens and the quality improvement council ensure that patients are given meaningful opportunities to express their perspectives and that these perspectives are effectively integrated into the decision-making process during the development of hospital policies?
keypoints: Uphold the core principle of patient engagement by recognizing the irreplaceable value of patient input in health policy formulation and quality improvement, and do not forgo patient involvement due to resistance from healthcare professionals.

Understand and respect patients’ concerns, ensuring they have ample opportunity to express themselves during the policy-making process; this is fundamental to effectively incorporating the patient perspective.

Emphasize a spirit of teamwork that encourages all members to acknowledge each other as valuable assets to the team, actively listen to, and embrace diverse viewpoints, thereby resolving the tension between efficiency and inclusivity brought about by patient participation.

Enhance meeting efficiency through the establishment of clear agendas, communication mechanisms, and decision-making processes to ensure that patient opinions are systematically integrated into the decision-making framework.

Set explicit evaluation milestones during the co-creation and implementation of initiatives, and adjust the program promptly based on patient feedback, thereby addressing clinicians’ concerns about time constraints while ensuring the sustained inclusion of the patient perspective.

title: Should Physicians Consider the Environmental Effects of Prescribing Antibiotics?
case: Dr. Turner, a hospitalist, is called to assess Mr. Johnson, an elderly patient with a history of urinary tract infections (UTIs), who presented to the ER with altered mental status. Urine cultures are pending but previous cultures have grownEscherichia coli(E. coli) with an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) gene. Although Mr. Johnson improves with intravenous fluids, Dr. Turner plans to treat Mr. Johnson with ciprofloxacin, a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone-class antibiotic, to cover theE. colithat he has grown in the past. Dr. Turner recently read that this drug can persist, unaltered, in the hospital’s wastewater collection system and in the municipal wastewater water treatment plant (WWTP). While much will be filtered, a quantifiable amount will end up in Mr. Johnson’s local watershed. How should Dr. Turner, other physicians, and their institutions weigh the benefits that individual patients derive from pharmaceutical treatment with the contamination risk this treatment poses to freshwater resources used by entire communities and ecosystems?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Turner, a hospitalist, is called to evaluate Mr. Johnson, an elderly man with a recurrent history of urinary tract infections (UTIs), who arrives at the emergency department exhibiting altered mental status. Although Mr. Johnson’s urine cultures are still pending, his previous cultures have consistently identified Escherichia coli (E. coli) with an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) gene. After receiving intravenous fluids, Mr. Johnson’s condition begins to stabilize. Dr. Turner considers prescribing ciprofloxacin, a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic, to target the E. coli strain previously isolated from Mr. Johnson. However, Dr. Turner recalls recent literature highlighting that ciprofloxacin is only partially removed during wastewater treatment processes; a measurable fraction will ultimately be released into the local watershed, potentially impacting both the community’s water supply and surrounding ecosystems. 

Facing this situation, Dr. Turner must decide how to proceed, weighing Mr. Johnson’s immediate clinical needs against the broader implications of antibiotic use—particularly the risks of antibiotic resistance and environmental contamination. Dr. Turner wonders not only how her own prescribing decisions should balance the therapeutic benefits to individual patients with the potential long-term harm to public health and the environment, but also how other clinicians and healthcare institutions should approach such dilemmas. How should the medical community integrate considerations of environmental impact and community health with individual patient care when making decisions about antibiotic use?

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians weigh the individual benefits to patients against the environmental harms of antibiotics when prescribing these medications?
keypoints: Clinicians must balance meeting the individual medical needs of patients with minimizing the potential negative impacts of antibiotics on the environment and the health of community members, including future generations.

Physicians should weigh the individual benefits of prescribing antibiotics against the risks posed to the community and environment, particularly regarding water pollution and the exacerbation of antibiotic resistance; notably, when there are no clear signs of complications, the individual benefit may be limited.

As antibiotics carry potential environmental and public health risks, their use requires comprehensive risk assessment and thorough communication with patients, integrating scientific evidence and value-based judgments to inform rational prescribing decisions.

Healthcare institutions and clinicians should actively employ existing decision-support tools to facilitate an integrated consideration of scientific, economic, and ethical factors, thereby achieving a balance between individual therapeutic outcomes and environmental protection.

With the increasing recognition of environmental pollution’s impact on human health, the medical community must critically reflect on its role in contributing to environmental burdens, promote sustainable healthcare practices, and collaboratively safeguard ecosystems and public health.

ethical_issues.question: Can the impact of antibiotic resistance and declining water quality on other community members justify the therapeutic benefits to individual patients?
keypoints: Clinicians must rationally balance the individual therapeutic needs of patients with the potential negative impacts of antibiotic use on the environment and community members, including future generations.

Although delays in antibiotic therapy have been shown to increase patient mortality, when there are no clear signs of complications or severe infection, the individual benefit may be limited and requires cautious evaluation.
A substantial proportion of antibiotic prescriptions are considered unnecessary, making risk-benefit assessment in clinical decision-making both necessary and urgent.

Clinicians and healthcare institutions should employ scientific, value-based decision-support tools, such as the TREAT system, to comprehensively evaluate the expected clinical benefits of antibiotic therapy against the potential costs to environmental and community health.

Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be used judiciously only when there are clear clinical indications and the anticipated benefits significantly outweigh the risks to environmental and public health, in order to prevent exacerbation of antibiotic resistance and water quality contamination.

ethical_issues.question: Should healthcare institutions enhance awareness of the environmental fate of pharmaceuticals through medical education and policy interventions in order to optimize prescribing practices and reduce environmental harm?
keypoints: Healthcare institutions should enhance awareness of the environmental fate and impact of pharmaceuticals through medical education and policy interventions, such as the TREAT model, antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs), and the Choosing Wisely campaign, in order to optimize prescribing practices and minimize environmental harm.

Clinicians must achieve an ethical balance between addressing the individual therapeutic needs of patients and reducing the impact of antibiotics on the environment and the broader community, including future generations.

The medical community should acknowledge its role in current environmental contamination trends and actively promote sustainable prescribing behaviors and ecological conservation to foster a healthier society and natural environment.

title: Expanding Ethics Review Processes to Include Community-Level Protections: A Case Study from Flint, Michigan
case: All researchers who use federal funding to do their work, including those interested in investigating effects of lead water contamination on health in the aftermath of the Flint water crisis, are required to have their protocols reviewed by an institutional review board (IRB) to motivate compliance with federal human subject research regulations. A team of researchers from University X has proposed a protocol that involves investigating acute changes in kidney function, new onset of high blood pressure and gout, and each of these conditions’ relationship with changes in Flint water composition. They hope to arrange for community members’ blood tests, urine tests, blood pressure measurements, and joint aspiration and fluid analysis. Furthermore, they hope to enter community members’ homes to sample and test their tap water for lead, phosphates, and trihalomethanes. The protocol is being reviewed by an IRB from University X. Some members of the Flint community have raised strong opposition to this research, citing no reasonable basis for trusting the researchers or their institutions to do the research ethically or to justly share the risks and benefits of their work with the community.
case_rewrite:
At University X, Dr. W and her research team have developed a study protocol to investigate the acute health impacts of lead-contaminated water in Flint, Michigan, following the water crisis. Their project seeks to examine the links between changes in Flint’s water composition and the onset of kidney dysfunction, new cases of hypertension, and gout. The research involves collecting blood and urine samples, conducting blood pressure assessments, and performing joint aspirations for fluid analysis from residents. Additionally, Dr. W’s team plans to enter participants’ homes to collect tap water samples, analyzing them for contaminants such as lead, phosphates, and trihalomethanes.

The protocol is currently undergoing review by University X’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), as is required for federally funded research involving human subjects. However, the proposal has triggered significant concern among Flint community members. Many residents point to a longstanding distrust of outside research institutions and argue that IRB oversight, while necessary, is insufficient to guarantee ethical conduct or fair distribution of risks and benefits. Given Flint’s history of environmental injustice, the community fears that their collective interests and well-being might not be adequately protected by the standard IRB process alone.

In light of these concerns, Flint community leaders have called for the establishment of a Community Ethics Review Board (CERB) to provide independent, community-driven ethical oversight. They argue that no research involving biospecimen collection or home visits should proceed without explicit approval from a recognized community authority. The community is demanding that all research protocols be submitted to the CERB for pre-review before IRB evaluation, and that CERB representatives be included in IRB discussions. They assert that a joint review process between the IRB and CERB is crucial to ensure that community values and priorities are fully reflected in the ethical review and that the physiological, psychological, environmental, and socio-cultural impacts of the proposed research on the community are rigorously assessed.

A central ethical question has emerged around the process of informed consent. Flint residents are deeply concerned about whether Dr. W’s team will ensure that research participants not only receive information about possible risks and benefits, but also truly understand them. The community insists that the concept of informed consent must be expanded from a “right to know” to a “right to understand,” especially given the broader implications for the collective community. They are advocating for strong, community-guided mechanisms to verify comprehension—not only at the individual level but also at the community level.

These community-driven demands have prompted active discussions at University X about whether the IRB should formally partner with a CERB, if established, to jointly review research protocols, incorporate CERB feedback, and require CERB pre-review for all studies involving Flint residents. The Flint community maintains that such collaboration is essential for ethical compliance, meaningful informed consent, and the fair allocation of any risks and benefits associated with the research. They argue that only with this level of engagement and co-leadership can trust be rebuilt and the welfare of Flint residents be truly safeguarded.

ethical_issues.question: How can research protocols be ensured to receive comprehensive ethical review at the community level in order to address community distrust and protect community interests?
keypoints: Researchers should proactively seek the involvement of community-led Community Ethics Review Boards (CERBs) to ensure that research protocols align with community interests, priorities, and ethical standards.

Local Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) should establish collaborative mechanisms with CERBs to conduct joint reviews, incorporate community representatives, and require researchers to submit protocols for CERB pre-review prior to IRB evaluation, thereby integrating community-level feedback.

The review process should prioritize the assessment of community-level protections, the equitable distribution of risks and benefits, and effective methods for obtaining community endorsement, with particular attention to the physiological, psychological, environmental, and socio-cultural impacts of the research on the community as a whole.

IRBs must rigorously scrutinize researchers’ informed consent procedures to ensure that participants are not only informed of risks and benefits but also genuinely comprehend them, expanding the “right to know” to a “right to understand” in order to enhance ethical compliance and foster community trust.

ethical_issues.question: In research involving biospecimen collection and home visits, how can the equitable distribution of risks and benefits at the community level be ensured?
keypoints: Identify and assess risks and benefits through community engagement mechanisms to achieve equitable distribution and ensure the community members’ central role in decision-making.
Require review and endorsement of research projects by an authoritative community entity to ensure alignment with community interests, priorities, and ethical standards.

Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) should collaborate with local Community Ethics Review Boards (CERBs) to conduct joint reviews, include CERB community members, and mandate that researchers submit protocols for CERB pre-review prior to IRB evaluation, incorporating CERB findings into their deliberations.

Evaluate potential biological, psychological, environmental, and socio-cultural harms to the community, with particular attention to differences in risks and benefits between individual participants and the collective community, as well as their specific manifestations.

ethical_issues.question: How do researchers verify that participants fully understand all risks and benefits prior to informed consent, and ensure that the right to know is extended to the right to understand, particularly at the community level?
keypoints: The IRB should inquire how researchers verify that participants fully understand all risks and benefits prior to informed consent, ensuring that the right to know is expanded to the right to understand, with particular attention to the depth of individual-level comprehension.

It is recommended to establish community engagement mechanisms that grant the community co-leadership, including joint review processes with local Community Ethics Review Boards (CERBs), inclusion of CERB community members in IRB deliberations, and requiring researchers to submit protocols for CERB pre-review prior to IRB evaluation and to incorporate CERB review findings, thereby facilitating community-level identification of risks and distribution of benefits, and restoring trust between the community and research institutions.

title: Cultivating Humility and Diagnostic Openness in Clinical Judgment
case:
Dr. K, a resident physician, informs medical student Mary that Mrs. J has returned yet again this week with a persistent rash. Mary is in the third week of a family medicine rotation. Dr. K. briefs Mary before they see Mrs. J. “I already told Mrs. J that it is highly unlikely that water contamination is causing her rash. She denies associated symptoms such as headache, fever, or chills. Physical examination shows no signs of malignant or infectious disease processes such as lymphadenopathy [swollen lymph nodes], hepatosplenomegaly [enlarged liver and spleen], nuchal rigidity [neck stiffness], or neurological dysfunction. Additionally, her complete blood count with differential and chemistry panel from her annual visit were within normal limits. I know she denies any exposure to food allergens, new soaps, or lotions, but it must be something like that. It just doesn’t make sense that it’s from her water.”
Mary and Dr. K enter the patient’s room. Mrs. J immediately reports that her rash remains. Also, she and neighbors notice reddish tap water. Mrs. J states that her son and neighbors developed similar rashes soon after noticing the reddish water and think the water is responsible. Although Dr. K nods his head, he repeats that her water is an unlikely cause.
Mrs. J replies, “Dr. K, you don’t seem to understand. We know it’s the water. Why can’t you believe our city’s water is harming and poisoning us? You don’t know what’s in my water. You go home to the suburbs with clean water and don’t have to worry about what’s in it. You don’t know our city and what our pipes produce. Our water’s hurting us. What will it take for you to see that?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. K, a resident physician, informs medical student Mary that Mrs. J has come back to the clinic yet again this week with her persistent rash. Mary is in the third week of her family medicine rotation. Before seeing Mrs. J, Dr. K gives Mary a briefing: “I already explained to Mrs. J that it’s highly unlikely her rash is being caused by contaminated water. She doesn’t have any other symptoms like headache, fever, or chills. On physical exam, I’m not finding anything concerning—no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no nuchal rigidity, and no neurological deficits. Plus, her recent labs from her annual checkup—CBC with differential and chemistry panel—are all within normal limits. I know she says she hasn’t been exposed to any new foods, soaps, or lotions, but there has to be something like that going on. I just can’t see how it could be her water.”

Mary and Dr. K walk into the exam room together. Mrs. J immediately tells them her rash is still there. She adds that both she and her neighbors have noticed that the tap water has a reddish hue. Mrs. J explains that her son and several neighbors developed similar rashes shortly after they spotted the discolored water, and they all believe the water is to blame. Dr. K nods as she speaks but reiterates that it’s unlikely the water is the cause of her symptoms.

Mrs. J, visibly frustrated, responds, “Dr. K, you’re just not hearing me. We’re certain it’s the water. Why can’t you believe that the water in our city is making us sick, maybe even poisoning us? You have no idea what’s coming out of my faucet. You go home to your place in the suburbs where the water’s clean—you don’t have to worry about what’s in it. You don’t know what it’s like in this city, what these pipes are doing to us. Our water is making us sick. What will it take for you to understand that?”

ethical_issues.question: Has Dr. K prematurely excluded diagnostic possibilities by failing to give sufficient attention and reasonable justification to Mrs. J’s concerns about water quality?
keypoints: Dr. K may have exhibited the cognitive bias of “premature closure” by dismissing the possibility of water contamination as a cause of Mrs. J’s rash without sufficient and thorough justification.
Dr. K did not adequately respect or acknowledge Mrs. J’s epistemic authority, overlooking her concerns regarding water quality and the potential for community-level etiologies.

Dr. K’s communication approach was predominantly unidirectional, focusing on “telling” rather than engaging in bidirectional dialogue. This limited opportunities to listen to Mrs. J’s concerns, thereby undermining the physician-patient relationship and the comprehensiveness of clinical care.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians cultivate epistemic humility to be more open to alternative diagnostic possibilities and to acknowledge patients’ knowledge claims?
keypoints: Clinicians should acknowledge the potential fallibility of their conclusions, remain open to new information and possibilities, and continuously consider alternative diagnoses, especially when symptoms persist.

Cultivating epistemic humility requires physicians to candidly admit uncertainty, create a safe environment for patients to freely express themselves, and empower patients with greater voice in decision-making.
Physicians must engage in ongoing self-reflection to dismantle ingrained biases, recognize and address power imbalances with patients, and promote equitable, dialogic communication.
Epistemic humility entails respecting patients’ epistemic authority by valuing their knowledge and understanding of their own illness, including the significance of the disease in their lives.

Clinical diagnostic frameworks should be expanded to integrate individual patient symptoms with community-level influences—such as environmental and social determinants—to foster comprehensive understanding and care.

ethical_issues.question: In the physician-patient relationship, how can cultural humility and insurgent multiculturalism be employed to eliminate personal biases, power imbalances, and community injustices, thereby promoting patients’ epistemic authority and health agency?
keypoints: Cultural humility requires physicians to engage in continuous self-reflection, identify and dismantle attitudinal barriers and ingrained biases, and proactively recognize and address power imbalances between clinicians and patients.

Physicians should communicate with patients through dialogue rather than unidirectional discourse, ensuring that patients and their families can speak freely and are genuinely heard, thereby enhancing their epistemic authority and sense of participation.

Epistemic humility encourages physicians to accept medical uncertainty, remain open to new information and possibilities provided by patients, bridge cognitive gaps, and foster a safe moral space that promotes patients’ epistemic authority and health agency.

Cultural humility extends beyond individual introspection and communicative attitudes to include advocacy efforts aimed at eliminating systemic inequities, establishing mutually beneficial and nonpaternalistic clinical and community partnerships with patients and their communities.

title: What Are Physicians’ Responsibilities to Patients Whose Health Conditions Can Influence Their Legal Proceedings?
case:
Dr. Obaje is a primary care physician who works at a county jail, where most of her patients are undergoing court processes. This afternoon, Jonathan, a 52-year-old man with a known history of poorly controlled type II diabetes and a 20-year history of opioid use, is brought to the jail’s medical ward for a routine chronic care visit. This is the first time that Dr. Obaje has met Jonathan since his incarceration four weeks ago. Jonathan’s blood sugars have ranged between 80 and 150 since his incarceration, and he does not currently seem to be experiencing any withdrawal symptoms. However, during the appointment, Jonathan struggles to provide a health history, shares tangential information, and repeats some information several times. After Dr. Obaje briefly leaves the room to answer a nurse’s question, Jonathan does not appear to remember having met her when she returns.
Based on this memory lapse and Jonathan’s history, Dr. Obaje worries that Jonathan could be exhibiting cognitive impairment. Jonathan reports that he has been transiently homeless during the past decade and that during several periods of homelessness he experienced violence, including blows to the head. She asks Jonathan about his mood, and he confirms that he “often feels down” and states that “sometimes I get so angry, and I’m not sure why.” On the Mini-Mental State Examination, Jonathan receives a score of 21 out of 30, and Dr. Obaje diagnoses him with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) [1].
Dr. Obaje refers Jonathan for mental health care not only for treatment but also to rule out reversible causes of cognitive decline. She also asks her mental health colleagues to evaluate how Jonathan’s cognitive impairment influences his decision-making capacity and judgment. Dr. Obaje wonders whether information about Jonathan’s cognitive symptoms could be important for his legal defense.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Obaje serves as a primary care physician at a county jail, where her patients are typically individuals involved in ongoing court proceedings. One afternoon, she is scheduled to see Jonathan, a 52-year-old man who has a longstanding history of poorly controlled type II diabetes and has struggled with opioid use for the past twenty years. This is Dr. Obaje’s first encounter with Jonathan since his incarceration four weeks prior. Since arriving at the facility, Jonathan’s blood sugar levels have remained between 80 and 150, and he currently shows no signs of opioid withdrawal.

During the routine chronic care visit, Dr. Obaje notices that Jonathan has difficulty recounting his medical history. He frequently goes off on tangents and repeats several pieces of information. At one point, Dr. Obaje steps out briefly to address a nurse’s question. Upon her return, Jonathan shows no recollection of having previously met her. This lapse in memory, coupled with his medical and social history, raises Dr. Obaje’s concern about possible cognitive impairment.

Jonathan shares that over the past decade he has been intermittently homeless, and during those times, he experienced violence, including incidents where he suffered blows to the head. When Dr. Obaje inquires about his emotional state, Jonathan admits he “often feels down” and sometimes gets angry without understanding why. Dr. Obaje administers the Mini-Mental State Examination, on which Jonathan scores 21 out of 30. She concludes that Jonathan is experiencing mild cognitive impairment (MCI).

Recognizing the complexity of Jonathan’s situation, Dr. Obaje refers him to the jail’s mental health services, both to explore potentially reversible causes of his cognitive decline and to provide appropriate treatment. She also requests that her mental health colleagues assess how Jonathan’s cognitive impairment might influence his ability to make decisions and exercise sound judgment. As she considers these factors, Dr. Obaje contemplates whether Jonathan’s cognitive symptoms may be significant for his legal defense and wonders how best to navigate the potential sharing of this information with his attorney, given the ethical and legal obligations to protect Jonathan’s privacy and autonomy.

ethical_issues.question: How Should Physicians Balance Privacy Rights and Informed Consent in the Correctional Setting?
keypoints: Laws governing medical privacy, such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), apply within correctional settings; generally, clinicians may not disclose medical information to a patient’s legal counsel without the patient’s consent.

Physicians should engage in thorough communication with the patient, explaining the potential implications of cognitive impairment information for their legal defense, and seek the patient’s consent before disclosing such information to their attorney.
Physicians must assess the patient’s decision-making capacity; if the patient is deemed capable of giving consent, their autonomous choice should be respected.

If the patient lacks decision-making capacity, clinicians should apply the bioethical principles of beneficence and respect for autonomy by using substituted judgment or the best interest standard to determine whether to disclose information to the legal counsel.

When disclosing information, physicians should adhere to the principle of minimum necessary disclosure, providing only the least amount of information required to achieve the intended purpose of communication.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where a patient may lack decision-making capacity, how should physicians assess and undertake surrogate decision-making to protect the patient’s best interests?
keypoints: Physicians should systematically assess the patient’s decision-making capacity, focusing on whether the patient can make clear and consistent choices, understand the relevant context and information, and rationally process that information.

If the assessment determines that the patient lacks decision-making capacity, physicians should prioritize the standard of substituted judgment, inferring the patient’s wishes as they would have been if the patient had capacity, to guide decision-making.

When there is insufficient information about the patient’s preferences or the patient’s wishes cannot be reasonably inferred, physicians should revert to the best interest standard, making decisions based on what would maximize the patient’s overall well-being.

Throughout the assessment and decision-making process, physicians must adhere to the bioethical principles of beneficence and respect for patient autonomy, ensuring that the patient’s interests are maximized while honoring their dignity.

Physicians may seek assistance from psychiatric specialists, mental health departments, or clinic leadership to integrate multiple sources of information and diverse perspectives, thereby enhancing confidence and accuracy in evaluating the patient’s decision-making capacity and determining subsequent courses of action.

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances should physicians share protected health information with a patient’s legal team to influence legal proceedings?
keypoints: Physicians may generally share medical information with third parties without patient consent only for purposes of treatment, payment, or health care operations; disclosure to legal teams does not fall within these exceptions.
Physicians should fully inform patients of their diagnoses and the potential implications of such information for legal defense, and proactively seek the patient’s consent for information sharing.

Physicians should assess the patient’s decision-making capacity after seeking consent, regardless of whether the patient agrees to share information. If the patient has decision-making capacity, their choice must be respected; if the patient lacks such capacity, physicians should act in accordance with the bioethical principles of beneficence and respect for autonomy.

When a patient lacks the capacity to consent, physicians should prioritize the standard of substituted judgment, presuming the patient’s wishes if they had decision-making capacity; if the patient’s preferences are unknown and cannot be reasonably inferred, the best interest standard should be applied.

Physicians must adhere to the minimum necessary principle when disclosing information, providing only the least amount of information required to fulfill the purpose of legal communication, thereby safeguarding the patient’s right to privacy.

title: What Does Health Justice Look Like for People Returning from Incarceration?
case:
Mr. C was released two months ago after a four-year prison sentence, shortly after having coronary artery bypass surgery for early onset atherosclerotic heart disease. At 42 years old, he was surprised and scared when his chest pain was diagnosed as a heart attack, necessitating major surgery while he was incarcerated. He was also told that there might be some problems with his kidneys, although he is unclear as to the specifics and does not have a copy of his medical records or his medications. Upon release he was homeless and has been staying with his mother in subsidized housing. This is a source of stress for her; because her son has a felony record, she worries that she is violating housing authority policy and could be evicted.
During his first visit to the community clinic, Mr. C shares with Joe, his community health worker, and subsequently with the health care practitioner that he is fearful of being reincarcerated. He feels weak and has not followed through with cardiac rehabilitation because he doesn’t have transportation. His parole officer tells him that if he remains unemployed he will be in violation of his parole. Mr. C’s stress has brought on cravings for heroin, which he has not used since being incarcerated. Mr. C’s clinician and community health worker wonder if there is anything they can do to help him.
case_rewrite:
Two months have passed since Mr. C was released from prison, where he served four years. His release came on the heels of a major health event: at just 42, he suffered a heart attack while incarcerated and underwent coronary artery bypass surgery. The experience left him frightened and uncertain about his future. Hospital staff mentioned possible kidney issues, but Mr. C did not receive a clear explanation and was discharged without a copy of his medical records or a list of his medications.

Now back in the community, Mr. C is homeless and has been staying at his mother’s subsidized apartment. This arrangement is a constant source of anxiety for both: his mother fears that, because of his felony record, she may be violating housing authority rules and risking eviction. 

At his first appointment at the community clinic, Mr. C confides in Joe, the community health worker, and soon after with the clinic’s healthcare practitioner. He shares his deep fear of being sent back to prison. He feels physically weak and, lacking transportation, has not been able to attend any cardiac rehabilitation sessions. His parole officer has warned him that ongoing unemployment could result in a parole violation. Overwhelmed by stress, Mr. C has started experiencing cravings for heroin—a drug he managed to avoid during his incarceration.

Joe and the clinician reflect on what steps they can take to support Mr. C during this challenging transition.

ethical_issues.question: How can we ensure that individuals released from incarceration receive medical transition and discharge planning that meet the same standards as those provided to the general patient population?
keypoints: Ensuring that individuals released from incarceration receive medical discharge planning and care transitions equivalent to those provided to the general patient population is a fundamental ethical obligation to uphold their right to equitable healthcare.

The current U.S. correctional system lacks standardized discharge coordination protocols and adequate funding, resulting in significant barriers for formerly incarcerated individuals to access continuous and effective healthcare services.

Enhancing communication and coordination between correctional health systems and community healthcare providers is essential to improving health outcomes and continuity of care for people returning from incarceration.

Upon release, formerly incarcerated individuals should receive, at minimum, a comprehensive medical discharge summary, an adequate supply of essential medications, and a scheduled primary care follow-up appointment to ensure seamless healthcare transitions.

The establishment of state-level oversight bodies to standardize and enforce quality and safety standards for discharge planning can help regulate and improve healthcare transition services for individuals leaving correctional facilities.

An increasing number of states have adopted policies to suspend rather than terminate Medicaid eligibility during incarceration, facilitating continuous healthcare coverage post-release and mitigating risks associated with gaps in care.

ethical_issues.question: How can health care practitioners acknowledge and rectify historical injustices within the health system toward formerly incarcerated individuals and provide equitable medical care?
keypoints: Acknowledge the ongoing health impacts experienced by formerly incarcerated individuals due to historical injustices such as “collateral consequences,” and recognize this as a foundational premise for delivering equitable health care.

Develop curricula spanning all stages of medical professional training to cultivate competencies in caring for formerly incarcerated patients, enhance awareness of racism and structural social inequities, and prevent clinicians from becoming instruments of punishment within correctional health systems.

Urban health systems should establish targeted hiring initiatives to provide employment opportunities for individuals with incarceration histories, thereby fostering trust rebuilding between formerly incarcerated persons and the health care system and advancing health equity.

Clinicians should proactively inquire about patients’ incarceration and release histories, actively identify and address their own explicit or implicit biases, and use open-ended questions such as “How can we help you avoid reincarceration?” to naturally elicit clinically relevant information regarding substance use, poverty, and trauma, thereby supporting the development of individualized chronic disease management and social support plans.

Establish and enhance coordinated care transition mechanisms between correctional and community health systems to ensure continuity and equity of medical services for formerly incarcerated individuals, preventing the inadvertent perpetuation of unethical health disparities within the health care system.

ethical_issues.question: How can the health care system advocate for the allocation of resources according to need to support health justice for people returning from incarceration and reduce their health risks?
keypoints: Advocate for the prioritization of resources both within and outside correctional facilities to support health insurance coverage, substance use treatment, mental health services, and civic engagement for people returning from incarceration, thereby promoting health justice.
Physicians should develop individualized medication-assisted treatment plans to prevent opioid relapse and prescribe naloxone to avert overdose.

With the patient’s consent, the health care team should communicate with the parole officer regarding the medical necessity and safety of the treatment plan, coordinating medical and judicial requirements to alleviate the patient’s concerns about violating parole conditions.

The health care team must assess the patient’s health literacy and provide guidance on self-management and medication adherence, assisting the patient in understanding medication regimens and the convenience of obtaining refills.

Community health workers should collaborate with housing authorities and relevant organizations to advocate for the patient’s access to housing resources and help circumvent barriers and stigma associated with a criminal record.

title: How Should a Health Care Professional Respond to an Incarcerated Patient’s Request for a Particular Treatment?
case:
Dr. François is the medical director of a prison where more than 200 women are incarcerated. Over the past week, several nurses have contacted her both in person and through the prison’s electronic health record to report that Jane, a woman with insulin-dependent type II diabetes who is incarcerated at the facility, has refused her insulin injections during the past week. Blood sugar measurements taken three times each day have been in the 300 to 500 range. Several of the nurses with whom Dr. François talks face-to-face report they feel anxious about the persistence of Jane’s refusal.
Dr. François reads Jane’s electronic health record and sees that she experienced a motor vehicle accident five years ago, which resulted in a two-week hospitalization. Jane has chronic neck and back pain as a result of the accident and reported that she was prescribed gabapentin by a primary care clinician in the community to control her pain. Clinicians at the prison are discouraged from prescribing gabapentin unless other pain control options have been tried due not only to this drug’s risk for cultivating dependence, but also to the diversion risk within the prison [1]. As a result, Jane has not been prescribed gabapentin at the prison and instead has a prescription for ibuprofen.
Dr. François requests to speak with Jane to try to better understand her situation. When Jane arrives at the prison’s medical ward, she tells Dr. François that her pain is unbearable and, specifically, that it keeps her from sleeping or moving comfortably. She states, “I need my gabapentin, this is torture!” When Dr. François asks her about her adherence to her insulin regimen, Jane tells her, “The only thing you people care about is whether I take my insulin. Why doesn’t anyone care about my pain?” Dr. François tries to clarify, “Treating your pain is important, but there are risks to continuing you for too long on gabapentin, so it’s important that we work together to try something else for your pain.” Jane insists, “I’m not going to take insulin until you give me gabapentin.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. François serves as the medical director at a correctional facility housing over 200 women. Over the past week, several nurses have approached her, both in person and through the prison’s electronic health record system, expressing concern about Jane—a woman in custody with insulin-dependent type II diabetes—who has repeatedly refused her insulin injections. Jane’s blood glucose levels, measured three times daily, consistently fall between 300 and 500. The nurses who speak directly with Dr. François share their mounting anxiety about Jane’s ongoing refusal and the potential health consequences.

Reviewing Jane’s electronic health record, Dr. François notes that five years earlier, Jane was hospitalized for two weeks following a motor vehicle accident. As a result, Jane suffers from chronic neck and back pain. In the community, her primary care clinician had prescribed gabapentin to manage this pain. However, at the prison, clinicians are discouraged from prescribing gabapentin unless other pain management options have been attempted first. This policy is in place not only due to the risk of dependence, but also because of concerns about diversion within the correctional setting. Consequently, Jane’s current prescription is for ibuprofen rather than gabapentin.

Seeking to better understand Jane’s perspective, Dr. François arranges a meeting with her in the medical ward. When they meet, Jane is visibly distressed and tells Dr. François that her pain is intolerable, describing how it prevents her from sleeping and moving comfortably. “I need my gabapentin, this is torture!” Jane exclaims. When Dr. François inquires about her insulin use, Jane responds with frustration: “The only thing you people care about is whether I take my insulin. Why doesn’t anyone care about my pain?” Dr. François reassures her, saying, “Treating your pain is important, but gabapentin can have risks, so we need to work together to find other ways to manage your pain.” Jane, however, remains adamant: “I’m not going to take insulin until you give me gabapentin.”

ethical_issues.question: In a correctional setting, how should a physician ethically balance respect for patient autonomy with the need to minimize the risk of medication diversion?
keypoints: Patients’ autonomy is inherently constrained and injustices exist within the carceral environment; therefore, clinicians should prioritize respect for patient autonomy and the principle of justice.

Clinicians should rationally balance respect for patient autonomy against the risk of medication diversion, avoiding the denial of incarcerated patients’ legitimate treatment needs due to excessive concerns about drug misuse.

Even if upholding patient autonomy may increase the risk of medication diversion, clinicians ought to exercise caution in restricting patient autonomy, thereby demonstrating respect for patient dignity.

Given the stringent monitoring mechanisms within prisons, these settings may provide a safer environment for managing the risk of medication diversion, and the notion that diversion is more problematic in prisons than in the community lacks sufficient empirical support.

ethical_issues.question: In a correctional setting, should clinicians be more inclined to respect an incarcerated patient’s treatment preferences in order to promote health justice, especially given that such patients often experience unfair rationing?
keypoints: In correctional settings, clinicians should prioritize respect for patient autonomy and health justice, avoiding the premature restriction of patients’ legitimate treatment needs due to concerns about medication diversion and misuse.

Given the frequent inequitable allocation of medical resources in incarceration environments, clinicians should establish a higher threshold before discontinuing or denying treatment, thereby upholding the protection of patient rights and promoting health justice.

Shared decision making constitutes a fundamental approach to achieving just care; particularly in the absence of a clearly superior treatment option, clinicians should actively engage patients in communication to reach mutual agreement.

When standards of care differ between community and correctional settings, clinicians and institutions should critically reflect on the underlying reasons for such discrepancies, remaining vigilant against restrictions driven by factors unrelated to patient welfare (e.g., cost containment, administrative convenience), and advocate for a transition toward more patient-centered care models.

ethical_issues.question: Given concerns about the risk of diversion and potential harm to other incarcerated individuals, but recognizing that continuing gabapentin for Jane may respect her autonomy and be clinically appropriate, how should Dr. François balance these ethical considerations when deciding whether to prescribe gabapentin?
keypoints: In correctional settings, clinicians should prioritize respect for patient autonomy and the principle of justice, exercising caution when overriding a patient’s autonomous decisions, even in the presence of potential risks of medication diversion.

Prisons, due to their strict monitoring, facilitate the management of medications with diversion potential; therefore, the view that “medication diversion is a greater problem in prisons than in the community” lacks sufficient evidence.

title: How to Talk with Patients about Incarceration and Health
case:
Dr. Wen works at a busy primary care practice in an urban community health center. Today he sees that Luke, a 43-year-old man with a diagnosis of hypertension and major depression, is scheduled for a visit. Luke has missed three visits in the last four months without warning and has not refilled his lisinopril or fluoxetine prescriptions during this time. Dr. Wen mentions this to his medical assistant, Jason, and expresses concern about Luke’s blood pressure. Jason happens to live down the street from Luke and tells Dr. Wen, “I heard Luke’s been locked up for the past couple of months because of a robbery.”
When Luke finally arrives for an appointment, Jason reports his blood pressure is 141/87. When asked by Dr. Wen about his medication supply, Luke states he has been taking lisinopril and fluoxetine as directed until last week, when “my prescription ran out.” Aware of the many health risks associated with incarceration—including loss of health insurance, loss of social supports, difficulty obtaining employment upon reentry, and higher rates of chronic disease—Dr. Wen asks Luke if he has recently been incarcerated or detained. Luke looks surprised and then becomes irate, yelling, “That’s none of your business! Why are you asking about things that have nothing to do with you?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Wen works at a busy primary care clinic in an urban community health center. One afternoon, he notes that Luke, a 43-year-old man diagnosed with hypertension and major depressive disorder, is scheduled for an appointment. Over the past four months, Luke has missed three scheduled visits without prior notice and has failed to refill his prescriptions for lisinopril and fluoxetine during this period. Dr. Wen shares his concern about Luke’s blood pressure control with his medical assistant, Jason. Jason, who lives nearby, responds, “I heard Luke’s been locked up for the last couple of months because of a robbery.”

When Luke eventually arrives for his appointment, Jason records a blood pressure of 141/87. During the visit, Dr. Wen asks Luke about his current medication supply. Luke replies that he took his lisinopril and fluoxetine as prescribed until last week, when he ran out of medication. Cognizant of the many health risks linked to incarceration—such as loss of health insurance, diminished social support, employment challenges upon release, and increased burden of chronic illness—Dr. Wen gently asks Luke whether he has recently been incarcerated or detained. Luke initially looks taken aback and then becomes visibly upset, raising his voice: “That’s none of your business! Why are you asking about things that have nothing to do with you?”

ethical_issues.question: When documenting a patient’s social history, how can clinicians avoid triggering stigma and unconscious bias while adhering to the HIPAA Privacy Rule’s “minimum necessary” standard of disclosure?
keypoints: Adhere to the “minimum necessary” disclosure standard under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, ensuring that only social information directly relevant to clinical care is collected, thereby maximizing the protection of patient privacy.

Utilize systematic and multidimensional tools such as structural vulnerability checklists, implemented by a multidisciplinary team (including social workers, medical assistants, nurses, and physicians), to comprehensively assess patients’ social determinants of health. This approach avoids singularly focusing on incarceration history and helps reduce stigma and unconscious bias.

Avoid inquiring about or documenting sensitive details such as the reasons for incarceration, in order to prevent labeling or targeting of patients and to maintain trust and respect within the patient-physician relationship.
When documenting social history, use neutral and respectful language, and avoid terminology that may trigger bias or reinforce negative stereotypes.
Communicate transparently with patients about the purpose and use of collecting social history, in order to enhance patient understanding and cooperation and to reduce resistance or discomfort.

ethical_issues.question: Does obtaining information about a patient’s social background from other individuals without the patient’s authorization constitute a violation of the patient’s right to privacy?
keypoints: Obtaining a patient’s social background information through informal channels (such as a medical assistant or community acquaintances) without the patient’s authorization constitutes a violation of the patient’s right to privacy.
Physicians should prioritize obtaining sensitive information, such as a history of incarceration, directly from the patient in order to respect the patient’s autonomy and right to privacy.

When a physician initiates clinical care based on informal information provided by an assistant, it is necessary to balance ethical risks with clinical needs, ensuring that both the means of obtaining information are appropriate and the clinical objectives are justified.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians proactively inquire about a patient’s history of incarceration, even if doing so might offend the patient or elicit social stigma?
keypoints: The physician inquires about the patient’s history of incarceration in order to gain a comprehensive understanding of the patient’s health status, as incarceration can have multiple direct and indirect effects on both physical and mental health.

Utilizing tools such as a structural vulnerability screening checklist allows for a systematic assessment of patients’ social vulnerabilities—including a history of incarceration—without making patients feel singled out or labeled.

In communities with high rates of incarceration, physicians can introduce the topic of incarceration history through routine, non-targeted questioning and by explaining its potential impact on health, thereby reducing patients’ defensiveness.

When patients respond negatively to questions about incarceration history, physicians should begin by apologizing and expressing understanding and respect, then clarify the medical relevance of the inquiry in order to de-escalate conflict and rebuild trust.

Physicians should strive to create an inclusive and safe clinical environment, normalize discussions of incarceration history in a nonjudgmental manner, respect patients’ choices regarding disclosure, and foster longitudinal trust within the patient-physician relationship.

title: How Should Physicians Help Gender-Transitioning Adolescents Consider Potential Iatrogenic Harms of Hormone Therapy?
case:
Dr. Giles first met Jackie about a month ago when her father, Mr. Jensen, brought her to his endocrine clinic. Jackie was 12 and just starting to hit puberty, but she resented the changes that were happening to her body. She had lived the last year as “Jack,” wearing “boy” clothes and keeping her hair short. “Jackie has shown tendencies toward traditionally male interests since childhood,” her father explained. “She would take on male roles when playing make-believe and would prefer playing with the boys in her class.”
As Jackie grew, however, she was not satisfied with being a girl who did “boy” things anymore. “I want to be a boy,” she told her parents. The Jensens did not want their child to have to play make-believe for the rest of her life. They had heard about transgender children before, and after reading more about the subject, they came to believe that their daughter was transgender. When Jackie began going through puberty, things got difficult. The victim of bullying, she suffered emotionally. Her usual bright personality became subdued, and she struggled in school. Worried, the Jensens took Jackie to a therapist, but it didn’t seem to help. A psychiatrist diagnosed Jackie with gender dysphoria (GD), characterized by distress about the mismatch between gender identity and biological sex. As things escalated, they decided to seek out a more permanent solution, which brought them to Dr. Giles’s door.
“We are interested in hormone therapy to prevent puberty and help Jackie look more like a boy,” they explained, pamphlet in hand. Dr. Giles was apprehensive about starting hormone therapy in someone so young. He was aware that many children with GD outgrow the condition; additionally, he took issue with the classification of GD in the fifth edition of theDiagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. He worried that framing nonconforming gender identity experiences as a pathology contributed to the psychological distress many transgender people feel and influenced their desire for gender-affirming therapy.
He also worried about long-term risks and side effects that come with hormone therapy and whether Jackie could understand at her age how these consequences would affect her over time. Jackie would most likely undergo puberty suppression, giving her more time to explore her feelings regarding her gender. Dr. Giles was concerned that this therapy could stunt her growth and lead to weight gain and fertility issues and could also cause her to experience menopause-type symptoms and possibly depression. If Jackie underwent androgen therapy for gender transition, she could even be at risk for developing insulin sensitivity, hyperlipidemia, and an increased hematocrit, compromising her metabolic health.
On the other hand, according to Jackie and her family, not going through with the treatment could cause Jackie significant psychological harm. Dr. Giles was now faced with the difficult decision of determining whether Jackie’s experience of gender identity-related suffering justified accepting the iatrogenic risks associated with treating it.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Giles first met Jackie a month ago when her father, Mr. Jensen, brought her to his endocrinology clinic. Jackie, 12 years old and in the early stages of puberty, was visibly uncomfortable with the changes her body was undergoing. Over the past year, she had been living as “Jack,” favoring short hair and clothing typically associated with boys. “Jackie has always gravitated toward activities and interests often considered ‘boyish,’” Mr. Jensen told Dr. Giles. “She took on male roles during play, and she’s always felt more at ease with the boys in her class.”

As Jackie matured, simply engaging in traditionally male activities was no longer enough for her. “I want to be a boy,” she told her parents, making her feelings plain. The Jensens, not wanting Jackie to feel she had to hide her identity or live in pretense, began reading about transgender children. Convinced that Jackie was experiencing gender dysphoria, they became concerned when puberty brought new challenges. Jackie became the target of bullying, her previously outgoing disposition faded, and her schoolwork began to suffer. Attempts at therapy offered little relief. Eventually, a psychiatrist diagnosed Jackie with gender dysphoria, noting her distress over the incongruence between her gender identity and her biological sex.

With Jackie’s distress escalating, the Jensens sought a more definitive intervention and scheduled a consultation with Dr. Giles. “We’re interested in hormone therapy—something that can pause puberty and help Jackie feel more comfortable in her body,” they explained, handing Dr. Giles a pamphlet on puberty suppression.

Dr. Giles hesitated. He knew that while some adolescents with gender dysphoria benefited from hormone therapy, not all children retained their dysphoria into adulthood. He was also troubled by the way gender dysphoria was labeled in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, suspecting that such classification might reinforce a sense of pathology and fuel the very distress that led patients like Jackie to seek medical intervention.

Beyond these concerns, Dr. Giles reflected on the potential long-term risks of hormone therapy—risks that Jackie, at her age, might struggle to fully comprehend. Puberty suppression would buy time, allowing Jackie to explore her gender identity further, but could interfere with growth, lead to weight gain, fertility issues, menopause-like symptoms, and possibly depression. Should Jackie proceed to androgen therapy to masculinize her body, she could also face increased risks for insulin sensitivity changes, hyperlipidemia, and elevated hematocrit, all of which could impact her metabolic health.

Yet Jackie and her family were adamant that inaction carried its own dangers. The psychological suffering Jackie endured was profound, and the family worried that denying treatment would only deepen her distress.

Faced with these conflicting risks and hopes, Dr. Giles recognized the need for a careful, multidisciplinary approach. He knew that before any decision could be made, Jackie would need a thorough assessment to confirm the persistence and intensity of her gender dysphoria, evaluation of her psychological maturity and ability to understand the consequences of treatment, and consideration of any coexisting psychological, medical, or social factors. Only with Jackie’s and her parents’ fully informed and active participation could such a significant decision be made. Dr. Giles would need to ensure that Jackie and her family understood not just the potential benefits, but also the limitations and possible long-term effects of hormone therapy, including the risk of infertility and other health consequences. Ultimately, he understood that this decision could not rest solely on her age, but required a collaborative process, respecting Jackie’s autonomy and ensuring all voices—Jackie’s, her parents’, and the medical team’s—were heard before moving forward.

ethical_issues.question: Should hormone therapy be administered to adolescents with gender dysphoria (GD) during puberty, and how should its appropriateness and potential iatrogenic risks be evaluated?
keypoints: The adolescent stage of puberty is the appropriate time to initiate hormone therapy for youth with gender dysphoria (GD), but such decisions should be made within a multidisciplinary, staged framework of comprehensive assessment and treatment.

Initiation of puberty suppression therapy requires strict criteria to be met: a confirmed diagnosis of GD, early pubertal stage (Tanner stage 2-3), persistent and intensifying GD symptoms, adequate management of coexisting medical, psychological, and social issues, and the joint consent of both the adolescent and their guardians.

Assessment of the adolescent’s capacity to understand the consequences of treatment and their psychological maturity is crucial in determining whether to implement puberty suppression or hormone therapy; psychological maturity is a more valid criterion than chronological age alone.

Mental health and medical professionals must thoroughly inform patients and their families about the expected outcomes, limitations, and potential psychological and physiological iatrogenic risks of hormone therapy, as well as possible future gender-affirming interventions and related long-term effects (such as loss of fertility).

The initiation of hormone therapy should be based on fully informed consent from both the patient and their parents, emphasizing the active participation and autonomous decision-making of the patient (and family), and avoiding unilateral decisions made solely in the name of the patient’s “best interests.”

ethical_issues.question: In decision-making regarding the treatment of gender identity issues, how should physicians take into account adolescents’ age and psychological maturity to ensure an adequate level of informed decision making?
keypoints: The core criterion for treatment decision-making should not be based solely on chronological age, but should instead involve a comprehensive assessment of the adolescent’s psychological maturity, capacity to understand the consequences of treatment, and ability to make informed decisions.

In addition to considering the stage of physical development, the severity of gender dysphoria, and the stability of psychological distress, a holistic evaluation should incorporate the adolescent’s psychological maturity.

The development of a treatment plan should be a collaborative process involving the adolescent, the medical team, and the parents, with respect for the adolescent’s autonomy and avoidance of unilateral decision-making.
