title: Should Clinicians Medicate against Structural Violence? Potential Iatrogenic Risks and the Need for Social Interventions
case:
Jordan threw himself down on Dr. Eitel’s couch. He stared into the distance with a scowl on his face. Anger and frustration emanated from him—he was in no mood to talk. Jordan had once again gotten into a fight at school resulting in a five-day expulsion. Although the police had been called, thanks to the school’s misconduct policy, an official arrest had not been made with the understanding that the school would handle the situation. Nevertheless, this was no victory for Jordan. “He knew exactly how to piss me off!” Jordan yelled at Dr. Eitel, “He did it on purpose. He wastryingto push me over the edge because he knew this was my last shot!” A string of muttered expletives followed. The principal had warned him that one more misdemeanor would meet criteria for permanent expulsion from the school. Following his five-day expulsion, Jordan would have to attend a committee meeting to determine whether he would be allowed to remain at St. Joseph’s Academy. Dr. Eitel felt bad for Jordan—she knew that he had been trying hard to stay out of trouble. He was making an effort, but it just was not good enough. Jordan’s demeanor changed to one of resignation and defeat. “Whatever, I heard the alternative school makes you wear jumpsuits. It’d be nice, like wearing pajamas all day,” he joked.
Jordan had not been dealt an easy hand in life. At the age of eight he had been placed in the foster care system and was presently in his third foster home. His current foster family seemed to take a greater interest in Jordan than his prior placements, but Dr. Eitel could sense that even their patience was running thin. They had worked hard to get Jordan placed in this school and Jordan knew that his poor behavior had disappointed them.
Jordan was now a junior in high school, and his more recent activity worried Dr. Eitel and his foster parents. His violent actions were escalating, and the possibility of his being incarcerated seemed increasingly likely. He would soon be considered an adult by the state and his behavior would have a permanent impact on his future.
Dr. Eitel shared Jordan’s frustration. She was tired of the failing systems that let kids like Jordan down, and she wondered if there was a way to help “level the playing field” for him via an “off-label” prescription for the antipsychotic risperidone. In Dr. Eitel’s professional opinion, Jordan did not meet standard criteria for psychosis, yet she wondered if placing him on an antipsychotic such as risperidone could help him control his outbursts and keep him out of the penal system, possibly even affording him opportunities in the future. However, she was also aware of the substantial side-effect profile of risperidone and other atypical antipsychotics. These drugs were known to increase young patients’ risk for weight gain and metabolic syndrome, which could predispose them to developing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Dr. Eitel wasn’t sure which was worse for Jordan: possibly living out the rest of his days behind bars or, assuming risperidone would be helpful for him, living with its iatrogenic consequences. “Maybe there’s still something I can do for this kid,” she thought as she considered her blank prescription pad.
case_rewrite:
Jordan flung himself down on Dr. Eitel’s office couch, his gaze fixed on a far corner of the room, a deep scowl carved into his face. Every gesture radiated frustration and barely contained anger—he was in no mood to open up. Once again, Jordan had gotten into a fight at school, this time earning a five-day suspension. The police had been called to the scene, but, under the school’s misconduct policy, no official arrest was made, with the understanding that the school would handle disciplinary measures internally. Still, Jordan felt no relief. “He knew exactly how to get under my skin!” Jordan shouted at Dr. Eitel. “He did it on purpose, trying to push me over the edge because he knew this was my last chance!” His words trailed off into a string of curses under his breath. The principal’s warning echoed in his mind: one more incident, and he’d meet the criteria for permanent expulsion from St. Joseph’s Academy. After serving his suspension, Jordan would have to appear before a committee to decide if he could stay at the school.

Dr. Eitel watched him with concern. She knew Jordan had been fighting hard to avoid trouble, making a real effort to stay on track, but somehow it was never enough. The anger in his voice slowly faded, replaced by a look of weary resignation. “Whatever,” he sighed, “I heard the alternative school makes you wear jumpsuits. Could be nice, like wearing pajamas all day,” he joked, trying to mask his disappointment.

Jordan’s life had never been simple. At eight years old, he was placed in foster care, and now, as a junior in high school, he was living with his third foster family. His current foster parents cared more than the previous families, but Dr. Eitel sensed that their patience was being stretched thin. They had worked hard to get Jordan admitted to St. Joseph’s, and he knew he had let them down with his recent behavior.

More troubling still, Jordan’s episodes of aggression seemed to be increasing in both frequency and intensity. Dr. Eitel and his foster parents worried about where this path might lead—he was nearly old enough to be tried as an adult, and his actions could soon have lifelong consequences.

Dr. Eitel felt a familiar sense of helplessness and anger at a system that seemed to fail kids like Jordan. She wondered if there was a way she could help “level the playing field.” One idea tugged at her: an “off-label” prescription for the antipsychotic risperidone. Clinically, she knew Jordan didn’t meet criteria for psychosis, but she couldn’t help but wonder if risperidone might help him manage his outbursts, keep him in school, and perhaps prevent him from ending up incarcerated. At the same time, she was acutely aware of the serious side effects that came with risperidone and similar antipsychotic medications—weight gain, metabolic syndrome, and increased risks for chronic diseases like type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular problems. Dr. Eitel weighed her options: would it be worse for Jordan to risk a lifetime in the criminal justice system, or, if the medication did prove helpful, to live with the burden of its side effects? She stared at her blank prescription pad, thinking, “Maybe there’s still something I can do for this kid.”

ethical_issues.question: When addressing the mental health needs of adolescents in foster care, how can clinicians balance pharmacological treatment with multimodal interventions to avoid iatrogenic harm and promote the development of long-term social adaptability?
keypoints: Pharmacotherapy should be integrated as part of a multimodal intervention, in combination with psychotherapy and social support, to address the social injustices and maladaptive behaviors experienced by foster youth, thereby avoiding the limitations and iatrogenic risks associated with sole reliance on medication.

Psychotherapy should be prioritized to help foster youth identify and address the underlying causes of impulsive and aggressive behaviors, promote emotional regulation and conflict resolution skills, and reduce the risk of future behavioral dysregulation.

Multimodal treatment should provide a stable, supportive environment and opportunities for long-term mentoring relationships, enabling foster youth to remodel behavioral patterns, develop prosocial skills, and enhance social adaptability, thereby laying the foundation for meeting challenges in adulthood.

title: Should Long-Term Consequences of NICU Care Be Discussed in Terms of Prognostic Uncertainty or Possible Harm?
case:
Dr. Mattingly met Miriam and Thomas when Miriam arrived a week ago in preterm labor, which was successfully stopped with tocolytics. Suspecting that Miriam would again have preterm labor, that the baby would be born extremely prematurely, needing NICU care to survive, and that the baby’s prognosis might be poor, he has met with the couple over the last few days to determine which NICU interventions they might want.
Miriam and Thomas wanted to know what sort of life their baby would have if they committed to doing everything NICU staff could to help him live. Dr. Mattingly explained that there had been significant advancements in the care of premature infants, but that the future of their child was still uncertain. He discussed various risks premature infants might face including breathing difficulty related to immature lungs, which might necessitate a breathing tube and could result in long-term problems, and injury to the developing brain and eyes that could result in lifelong sensory, cognitive, and motor impairments. He discussed surgery their child might need for his heart, and the risk of intestinal injury and infections while in the NICU. He told the couple that their child might die early or late in his NICU course. “Of course,” Dr. Mattingly had said, “decisions about when and how much to intervene are up to you.” He also explained the option of comfort care, which would focus on keeping the infant comfortable after birth, without attempts at resuscitation; in this case, the focus would not be on survival, but on making sure the time he had would be as peaceful as possible.
Miriam and Thomas wanted more than anything for their child to live and to give their child the best chance possible, but they also wanted his life, however long or short, to be a happy one. They also wondered how having a child with severe disabilities would affect their four other children. They felt they could not truly grasp what awaited their child in terms of potential complications or disabilities, should they opt for full resuscitation. “Dr. Mattingly,” Thomas began, “You see the sorts of futures these children have and the joy and pain the parents go through in either option. What would you counsel us to do?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Mattingly first met Miriam and Thomas when Miriam was admitted to the hospital a week ago in preterm labor. Through prompt administration of tocolytics, the labor was halted, but Dr. Mattingly remained concerned that Miriam might go into labor again soon. He anticipated that their baby would likely be born extremely prematurely, would require intensive NICU support to survive, and that the outlook for the child might be uncertain or even poor. Over the past several days, Dr. Mattingly has spent time with Miriam and Thomas, discussing which interventions in the NICU they might consider for their baby should he be born prematurely.

During these conversations, Miriam and Thomas expressed a deep desire to give their child every possible chance at life. At the same time, they wanted to understand what kind of life their baby might have if the medical team did everything possible to sustain him. Dr. Mattingly explained that while the care of premature infants has advanced greatly, many challenges remain. He described the possible complications: the baby’s lungs might be too immature to breathe on their own, requiring a breathing tube and possibly leading to long-term respiratory problems; there was a risk of injury to the developing brain and eyes, which could cause lifelong sensory, cognitive, and motor disabilities; and surgeries might be needed for heart issues, while intestinal injury and infections were also potential risks during the NICU stay. Dr. Mattingly was frank that, even with the best available care, the baby might die at any point in the NICU—either early on, or after a prolonged course.

He told Miriam and Thomas, “Ultimately, decisions about how much and when to intervene are yours to make.” Dr. Mattingly also presented the alternative of comfort care, in which the focus would be on keeping the baby comfortable after birth, without attempting resuscitation or intensive interventions. He explained that, in such a scenario, the emphasis would shift from survival to ensuring that whatever time the baby had would be as peaceful and free of suffering as possible.

Miriam and Thomas were torn. They longed for their baby to live and wanted to do everything possible for him, but they also wished for whatever life he might have—no matter how short—to be a happy one. They worried about how raising a child with potentially severe disabilities might affect not only the baby himself but also their four other children at home. Faced with uncertainty about what the future could hold, they struggled to comprehend the range and severity of possible complications or disabilities that might result from full resuscitation and intensive care.

Sitting together in the hospital room, Thomas turned to Dr. Mattingly and said, “You see what happens to these children, and what families go through—both the happiness and the heartbreak, whichever way things go. What would you advise us to do?”

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance medical knowledge with parental family values when providing recommendations about resuscitation, in order to ensure that decisions are made in the best interests of the child?
keypoints: Physicians should assist parents in rationally evaluating their own values, family circumstances, and medical information to make a comprehensive judgment about whether resuscitation is in the best interest of the child.

Physicians need to develop a deep understanding of the parents’ values, emotional concerns, and specific circumstances—including financial status, occupation, religious beliefs, and the presence of other children—to ensure that communication is targeted and empathetic.

When parents have difficulty making a decision or actively seek advice, physicians should, while respecting parental autonomy and avoiding paternalism, provide individualized and clear guidance that integrates the family’s values, situational understanding, and medical expertise, in order to alleviate the emotional burden on parents and help them make decisions that align with the child’s best interests.

When the burdens of treatment clearly outweigh the potential benefits, physicians should proactively offer directive counseling and explicitly present the option of comfort care, thereby reducing parental decisional stress and the infant’s physical suffering, and upholding the ethical principle of prioritizing the child’s welfare.

ethical_issues.question: In the process of shared decision making during the perinatal period, how can physicians avoid unintentionally influencing parental decisions through the framing of information, and ensure that parents fully understand the significance of statistical data?
keypoints: Physicians should balance the presentation of multidimensional statistical information, such as mortality and survival rates, to avoid framing effects caused by exclusively positive or negative descriptions, thereby preventing their own emotional biases from inadvertently influencing parental decision making.

Physicians need to assess and confirm parents’ understanding of statistical data, utilizing visual aids and communication methods tailored to the parents’ cognitive characteristics, in order to facilitate comprehensive understanding and rational deliberation, thereby supporting an informed and autonomous decision-making process.

title: Should Dementia Be Accepted as a Disability to Help Restore Hope during Cognitive Decline?
case:
As a fourth-year psychiatry resident, Dr. Daniel is spending elective time with a geriatric psychiatrist, Dr. Woods, while rotating through a memory diagnostic clinic within the department of psychiatry at the hospital. The first evaluation in which Dr. Daniel participated was for an 82-year-old man, Mr. Farnal, with a history of coronary artery disease. He had a myocardial infarction about five years ago and several transient ischemic attacks over the past several years, although he has no appreciable residual deficits. He was referred to the memory clinic by his primary care physician for further evaluation due to his concerns about worsening memory over the past two to three years.
Mr. Farnal has lived by himself since his wife passed away about five years ago due to metastatic breast cancer. They had no children. He retired from his position as a professor eight years ago and many of his connections to friends at the university have lapsed, particularly over the last couple of years. On the initial evaluation, he denied any previous psychiatric history and scored a 1 out of 15 on the geriatric depression scale (scoring a point only for indicating that he didn’t feel like he had much energy). He scored 18 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA), for which a score of at least 26 indicates normal cognition [1]. Based on the initial assessment done by Drs. Woods and Daniel, dementia signs seemed to justify referral for further evaluation with behavioral neurology, formal neuropsychology testing, and MRI. These test results corroborated that dementia was probable, most likely due to vascular dementia as well as a comorbid Alzheimer dementia. Drs. Daniel and Woods communicated to Mr. Farnal that his symptoms, though mild, were likely to progress and that it would likely become increasingly difficult for him to function independently.
Although not surprised by the diagnosis, Mr. Farnal was devastated. He reported that he took care of his father, who had lived with dementia many years before his death, and he also reported that this experience suggested to him that life with dementia becomes less and less worth living. As a fiercely independent individual, Mr. Farnal expressed that he did not see himself living in a nursing home or having an aide to help him. He again denied symptoms of depression and denied any active thoughts or plans of killing himself, but he strongly indicated that a life of worsening dementia was not one that he wanted to live. Drs. Woods and Daniels wondered how to respond to him.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Daniel, a fourth-year psychiatry resident, is spending part of his elective rotation with Dr. Woods, a geriatric psychiatrist, at the hospital’s memory diagnostic clinic within the psychiatry department. On his first day, Dr. Daniel assists Dr. Woods in evaluating Mr. Farnal, an 82-year-old man referred by his primary care physician due to concerns about progressive memory problems over the past two to three years. Mr. Farnal’s medical history is notable for coronary artery disease; he suffered a myocardial infarction five years ago and has experienced several transient ischemic attacks, but he does not have any significant lingering deficits.

Mr. Farnal has lived alone since his wife died of metastatic breast cancer five years ago. The couple had no children. Since retiring from his professorship eight years earlier, Mr. Farnal’s connections with his former university colleagues have gradually faded, a trend that has accelerated over the last couple of years. During the initial assessment, Mr. Farnal denies any prior psychiatric history and scores 1 out of 15 on the geriatric depression scale, noting only a lack of energy. His score on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) is 18 out of 30, well below the normal cutoff of 26.

After conducting their evaluation, Dr. Daniel and Dr. Woods determine that Mr. Farnal’s presentation warrants further investigation and refer him for a behavioral neurology consult, formal neuropsychological testing, and an MRI. The additional assessments confirm probable dementia, most consistent with a combination of vascular dementia and comorbid Alzheimer disease. Drs. Daniel and Woods explain to Mr. Farnal that his cognitive symptoms, though currently mild, are likely to worsen over time, and that maintaining independent living will probably become increasingly difficult.

While Mr. Farnal is not surprised by the diagnosis, he is profoundly disheartened. He shares that he previously cared for his father, who suffered from dementia for many years before his death, and that this experience convinced him that life with dementia gradually becomes less worthwhile. Fiercely independent by nature, Mr. Farnal expresses a strong aversion to the idea of living in a nursing home or relying on at-home assistance. He repeatedly denies feeling depressed or having any active thoughts or plans to end his life, but he makes it clear that he does not wish to live through the progression of dementia. Drs. Woods and Daniel find themselves grappling with how best to respond to his feelings and needs.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians respect the autonomy of patients with dementia who are experiencing hopelessness, while providing sufficient support to help restore meaning and hope in their lives?
keypoints: Physicians should rationally assess the patient’s sense of hopelessness, recognizing that such decisions may be based on personal experience and a considered judgment about the meaning of life with dementia, rather than impulsivity or depression.
Physicians need to reflect upon and correct their own biases regarding dementia and its care, avoiding stereotypes that may affect their support for and communication with patients.
Physicians should assist patients in exploring and discovering sources of meaning and hope in their future lives, facilitating a positive reappraisal of their quality of life.
Physicians can guide patients to utilize community support organizations and peer groups to alleviate feelings of loneliness and enhance their sense of social belonging.
Physicians should help patients identify and strengthen elements of life that can continue to bring pleasure and satisfaction despite cognitive decline, thereby improving quality of life.

While respecting patient autonomy, physicians should listen attentively and engage in discussions regarding the patient’s wishes about end-of-life issues, clarifying the relevant rights and options for lawful refusal of treatment and dignified dying.
Through ongoing support and resource integration, physicians can help patients gradually accept the progression of their illness and find psychological comfort and life value in their remaining days.

ethical_issues.question: How should the need to provide high-quality care for patients with dementia be balanced against the care needs of other groups in society when resources are limited?
keypoints: High-quality dementia care embodies the principle of beneficence, emphasizing compassion and support for patients.

Providing high-quality dementia care aligns with the principle of justice, as elderly individuals have contributed to society and society has a responsibility to support them during their period of dependency.
High-quality dementia care is costly, necessitating a balance of resources between the care needs of patients with dementia and those of other groups in society.

A utilitarian perspective may oppose allocating substantial resources to dementia care, advocating instead for prioritizing resources toward younger and more productive populations to maximize overall happiness or utility.

tags: Informed consent/Capacity, competency for making decisions
title: Ethics and Intimate Sexual Activity in Long-Term Care
case:
As a second-year psychiatry resident, Dr. Brian is working in a long-term care facility during his geriatric psychiatry rotation. The facility is structured to accommodate residents’ escalating needs with various levels of care, ranging from independent living to assisted living to nursing home. Dr. Brian is working with a geriatric psychiatrist, Dr. Anderson, whose main role in the long-term care facility is to provide psychiatric consultation.
One afternoon, Drs. Brian and Anderson receive a consultation request regarding Mrs. Shera, an 80-year-old woman living in the nursing home section who has dementia. When reviewing her record, Dr. Brian sees that she was admitted to the long-term care facility about six months ago, after living independently with her husband of 55 years. Over time, it became more difficult for him to manage some of her behavioral issues at home. For instance, when she would take walks through the woods near their house, she would get lost on the paths. Sometimes, the police were called to search for her and take her home. When Mr. Shera tried to limit her excursions, she would become severely irritable, yelling at him and ultimately swinging at him when he tried to keep her from leaving the house. These episodes would last about 5-10 minutes, at which point Mrs. Shera would shut down and then forget what had just happened.
In the nursing home, Mr. Shera visited her as much as he could and she was always happy to see him. Once, a nurse walked into Mrs. Shera’s room and found her and her husband in bed together with some of their clothes removed. After Mr. Shera left, the nurse returned to talk further with Mrs. Shera about what had happened. Mrs. Shera indicated that she loved her husband and that he was a good man, but she wasn’t able to answer questions about whether she felt comfortable engaging sexually with him. Troubled that Mrs. Shera’s illness compromises her decision-making capacity, the nurse discussed her concerns with Drs. Brian and Anderson. After talking with Mrs. Shera, the nurse and the two physicians still were not clear whether and how it was appropriate for Mr. Shera to engage sexually with Mrs. Shera. They wondered what to do.
case_rewrite:
During his second year of psychiatry residency, Dr. Brian is completing his geriatric psychiatry rotation at a long-term care facility designed to meet the evolving needs of its residents, ranging from independent living to assisted living and, finally, to a nursing home section. Dr. Brian works alongside Dr. Anderson, an experienced geriatric psychiatrist whose primary responsibility is to provide psychiatric consultations to the residents.

One afternoon, Dr. Brian and Dr. Anderson receive a consult regarding Mrs. Shera, an 80-year-old woman residing in the nursing home section who has a diagnosis of dementia. As Dr. Brian reviews her chart, he notes that Mrs. Shera moved into the facility about six months prior, following a long period of independent living with her husband of fifty-five years. Over the years, Mr. Shera had found it increasingly challenging to manage his wife’s behavioral changes at home. For example, when Mrs. Shera would go for walks in the wooded area near their house, she would at times become disoriented and unable to find her way back, necessitating police involvement to locate and return her safely. Attempts by Mr. Shera to restrict her outings would often result in Mrs. Shera becoming acutely irritable—yelling and, on occasion, physically lashing out at him. These agitated episodes were typically brief, lasting five to ten minutes, after which Mrs. Shera would become quiet and unable to recall what had just occurred.

Since her admission to the nursing home, Mr. Shera visits as frequently as possible, and Mrs. Shera is always visibly pleased to see him. On one occasion, a nurse entered Mrs. Shera’s room and found her and Mr. Shera in bed together, with some of their clothing removed. After Mr. Shera left, the nurse returned to speak privately with Mrs. Shera to better understand the encounter. Mrs. Shera stated that she loved her husband and described him as a good man, but she was unable to answer questions regarding whether she felt comfortable engaging in sexual activity with him.

Concerned that Mrs. Shera’s dementia might compromise her ability to consent to sexual activity, the nurse brought her concerns to Drs. Brian and Anderson. Despite further discussion with Mrs. Shera, the nurse and the two physicians remained uncertain about Mrs. Shera’s capacity to consent to intimacy with her husband, and questioned how best to proceed in this ethically complex situation.

ethical_issues.question: How can capacity to consent to sexual activity be assessed in long-term care facilities to ensure that residents’ autonomy and safety are respected and protected?
keypoints: Assessment of sexual consent capacity should be decision-specific; incapacity cannot be presumed solely on the basis of a diagnosis of dementia or other cognitive impairment, and capacity in different decision-making domains should not be simply equated.

The assessment should encompass rationality (the ability to weigh risks and benefits and make an informed decision), sexual knowledge (understanding the nature of the sexual activity and the right to accept or refuse it), voluntariness (awareness of and ability to exercise the right to choose), and specific functional abilities (awareness of the identity and relationship of the sexual partner, ability to articulate acceptable forms of intimacy, consistency of behavior with previously expressed beliefs and preferences, ability to refuse unwanted sexual activity, and ability to anticipate one’s reaction if the activity is terminated).

The assessment process should be conducted by a multidisciplinary team through interviews and capacity testing, supplemented by environmental observation to verify the consistency between the resident’s behavior and interview responses, thereby ensuring objectivity and comprehensiveness of the evaluation.

The standard for assessment should be flexible, with the stringency adjusted according to the nature and risk of the specific sexual activity; for example, the capacity standard for consenting to kissing should differ from that for sexual intercourse.

The assessment should include a thorough understanding of the nature of the activity and the relationship between the participants, with open communication involving the resident and trusted relevant parties (such as a spouse) to clarify the behavioral context and prior sexual patterns.

Safety considerations should influence not only the decision of whether to permit sexual activity, but also guide how to minimize potential risks of harm, ensuring the resident’s physical and psychological safety while respecting their autonomy.

It is recommended that the capacity assessment be conducted by an assessor who is of the same gender as the resident and whom the resident is likely to trust, in order to facilitate genuine expression and reduce assessment bias.

ethical_issues.question: How should nursing homes balance respect for residents’ autonomy with the need to protect them from harm in cases involving intimate sexual activity?
keypoints: Long-term care facilities should conduct assessments of residents’ capacity to consent to sexual activity, with particular attention to whether the resident understands the identity and relationship of the sexual partner, can express and sustain a voluntary desire for intimate behavior, whether their actions are consistent with their prior values and preferences, their ability to refuse non-voluntary activity, and their capacity to anticipate the consequences of the behavior and articulate their response to its termination.

Long-term care facilities need to engage in open communication with residents, their families, and the healthcare team to clarify the specific nature of intimate behaviors and potential physical and psychological risks, develop individualized safety measures, and, while respecting privacy, arrange for appropriate supervision and support, such as periodic check-ins and provision of private spaces.

Long-term care facilities should establish and refine institutional safeguards, including the development of guidelines and policies for the management of residents’ intimate activities, training staff in ethical sensitivity, and promoting the concept of “preventive ethics.” Through proactive planning and multidisciplinary collaboration, facilities can reduce the risk of ethical conflicts and achieve a dynamic balance between respecting resident autonomy and preventing harm.

title: Strategies for Building Trust with the Caregiver of a Patient with End-Stage Dementia
case:
As part of a geriatric medicine elective in his fourth year of medical school, Thomas spends a couple of afternoons a week at a local nursing home seeing patients with the attending geriatrician, Dr. Smith. One of the patients that Thomas sees with Dr. Smith is Mindt, a 78-year-old man with a history of advanced dementia who is recovering from pneumonia. He was diagnosed approximately ten years ago and moved into the nursing home about five years ago when he experienced greater functional and cognitive decline. His wife, Nila, who is in her early 70s, lives in the community and visits him frequently. They had one son who died of a myocardial infarction about 13 years ago. Nila is the health care proxy, but since Mindt didn’t clarify his preferences for end-of-life care while he had decision-making capacity, she and his other caregivers are unsure about how to respond when Mindt’s dementia progresses to the point at which he has trouble eating. Now that he either won’t open his mouth or appears to be choking when she has been trying to feed him, it seems that the time has arrived for a critical end-of-life conversation and decision.
Nila requests a meeting with Dr. Smith to discuss her concerns about her husband’s eating. A family meeting is arranged among Nila, Dr. Smith, Thomas, and a nurse and speech-language therapist who both work closely with Mindt. During this meeting, Nila expresses that if Mindt is not eating, he won’t be able to keep up his strength, and if he can’t keep up his strength, she worries that he won’t continue to recover from pneumonia. Dr. Smith explains to Nila that appetite loss and difficulties in eating are part of the natural progression of end-stage dementia. She further explains how hospice works and suggests hospice as an approach for keeping him as comfortable as possible.
Nila expresses her disagreement with Dr. Smith and clarifies that she wants everything done to prolong Mindt’s life. She repeats that she wants to know what can be done to get him to eat more.
Dr. Smith is aware that though some patients with advanced dementia receive a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) so that nutrition can be provided by a tube, this treatment is not recommended for patients with advanced dementia according to guidelines from the American Geriatrics Society because, among other reasons, it is thought that the benefits do not outweigh the burdens of a patient’s discomfort, aspiration, risk of infection, increased oral secretions, tube malfunction, and possible use of restraints [1]. Dr. Smith strives to focus the conversation on preparing for Mindt’s death and keeping him comfortable; she feels that bringing up the possibility of tube feeding could lead to his prolonged discomfort. Nila is steadfast, however, about learning more about improving his nutrition. Dr. Smith and Thomas wonder whether to pose the PEG tube as an option.
case_rewrite:
During his fourth year of medical school, Thomas is participating in a geriatric medicine elective, spending several afternoons each week at a local nursing home alongside the attending geriatrician, Dr. Smith. One of their patients is Mindt, a 78-year-old man who has lived with advanced dementia for many years. Mindt was diagnosed about a decade ago and, after a steady decline in both cognitive and functional abilities, he moved into the nursing home five years ago. Recently, he has been recovering from pneumonia. Mindt’s wife, Nila, in her early seventies, lives nearby and visits him regularly. The couple lost their only son to a heart attack thirteen years ago. Nila is Mindt’s health care proxy, but because Mindt never expressed his wishes for end-of-life care when he was still able to make decisions, Nila and his caregivers now face uncertainty about how to proceed as his condition worsens.

Lately, Mindt has been struggling to eat; he often refuses to open his mouth or seems to choke when Nila tries to feed him. Recognizing the gravity of the situation, Nila requests a meeting with Dr. Smith to discuss her growing concerns about Mindt’s ability to eat and regain strength. In response, a family meeting is arranged with Nila, Dr. Smith, Thomas, and both a nurse and speech-language therapist who are closely involved in Mindt’s care.

During the meeting, Nila voices her deep worry: if Mindt is unable to eat, she fears he will lose the strength necessary to recover from pneumonia. Dr. Smith listens attentively, acknowledging Nila’s devotion and the care she has provided. She carefully explains that loss of appetite and difficulty swallowing are common and expected in the later stages of dementia. Dr. Smith goes on to describe hospice care, emphasizing its focus on comfort, dignity, and quality of life as patients approach the end of life.

Despite this, Nila becomes distressed and firmly insists that everything possible be done to keep Mindt alive. She repeatedly asks what can be done to help him eat more. Dr. Smith is aware that although some patients with advanced dementia are given percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tubes for nutrition, current guidelines from the American Geriatrics Society advise against PEG tubes in such cases. The risks—discomfort, aspiration, infection, excess oral secretions, tube malfunction, and potential need for restraints—are believed to outweigh any benefits. Dr. Smith tries to steer the conversation toward preparing for Mindt’s final days and ensuring his comfort, concerned that introducing the idea of tube feeding may ultimately prolong Mindt’s suffering.

Nevertheless, Nila remains resolute, wanting to know about any options to improve Mindt’s nutrition. As the conversation continues, Dr. Smith and Thomas find themselves uncertain: should they mention the possibility of a PEG tube, knowing it may not serve Mindt’s best interests, or continue focusing on comfort and quality of life? They reflect on how best to communicate with Nila, hoping to foster trust, validate her caregiving journey, and help her navigate the difficult transition from pursuing life prolongation to embracing meaningful moments with her husband in his remaining time.

ethical_issues.question: When discussing end-of-life care with the family caregiver, how can effective communication strategies be employed to rebuild trust and help the caregiver come to terms with the reality of the situation?
keypoints: The healthcare team should seek to understand the caregiver’s perspective, reconstruct their narrative about the caregiver, and create a safe, nonjudgmental environment that enables the caregiver to openly share her experiences and feelings.

The team should express recognition and respect for the caregiver’s exemplary care, employ empathic listening, and invite the caregiver to speak more deeply, thereby encouraging her to articulate the meaning of her caregiving journey and the shared goals for both parties.

The team should guide the caregiver to shift her expectations for the patient from life-prolongation to short-term, concrete, and achievable goals, and facilitate the expression of care through meaningful interactions such as hand or foot massage, looking through family photographs together, and sharing music.
Repairing damaged trust is a central goal of communication, as it helps to reduce misunderstandings and fosters effective future collaboration and ongoing dialogue.

title: How Should Clinicians Counsel a Woman with a Strong Family History of Early-Onset Alzheimer’s Disease about Her Pregnancy?
case:
During his third-year OB-GYN clerkship in medical school, Samuel is working with Dr. Bowers seeing patients both in the hospital (on the labor and delivery service) and in the outpatient clinic for routine prenatal visits. For the outpatient visits, he sees patients who present for initial appointments to confirm pregnancy and for appointments just prior to delivery.
About halfway through his clerkship, Samuel and Dr. Bowers see Mrs. Castle and her husband for an initial visit to confirm a pregnancy. Mrs. Castle is a healthy 41-year-old woman with a strong family history for early-onset Alzheimer’s dementia. Her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s dementia at age 45 and died about five years later. Mrs. Castle’s older sister, who is in her late 40s, has also been diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s dementia and is currently living in long-term care due to complications of the disease.
Mrs. Castle and her husband had tried to conceive for more than a year without success. They had met with a specialist and briefly considered assisted reproductive technology when they put their plans on hold due to Mrs. Castle’s sister’s illness. The couple thought carefully about what a pregnancy would mean for Mrs. Castle and her family; they chose not to pursue genetic counseling related to Mrs. Castle’s family history of early-onset Alzheimer’s dementia. Recently, Mrs. Castle has been more concerned about her own worsening short-term memory. Her husband has also noticed that she seems to have become more irritable and anxious over the last couple of years. They question whether they should continue with the pregnancy.
Dr. Bowers wondered how best to provide support for the patient not only in prenatal care but also in addressing the couple’s concerns about parenting in the setting of a strong family history of early-onset Alzheimer’s dementia.
case_rewrite:
During his third-year OB-GYN clerkship, Samuel is assigned to work with Dr. Bowers, caring for patients on both the labor and delivery unit and in the outpatient clinic during routine prenatal appointments. Together, they meet patients at their first prenatal visits to confirm pregnancies and again during late-stage check-ups leading up to delivery.

Midway through the rotation, Samuel and Dr. Bowers are joined by Mrs. Castle and her husband for their first prenatal appointment. Mrs. Castle is a 41-year-old woman in good general health, but her family history is notable for early-onset Alzheimer’s disease. Her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s at age 45 and died five years later. Her older sister, now in her late 40s, also has early-onset Alzheimer’s and currently resides in a long-term care facility due to the disease’s progression.

Mrs. Castle and her husband had struggled with infertility, trying to conceive for more than a year. They consulted a specialist and briefly considered assisted reproductive technology, but these plans were paused as her sister’s illness advanced. The couple spent considerable time deliberating what a pregnancy would mean for their family, especially in light of Mrs. Castle’s family history, ultimately deciding not to pursue genetic counseling about Alzheimer’s risk at that time. Recently, however, Mrs. Castle has grown increasingly worried about her own short-term memory, which she feels has been declining. Her husband, too, has noticed changes—she has become more irritable and anxious over the past couple of years. Now, they are uncertain about whether to proceed with the pregnancy.

Dr. Bowers recognizes the complexity of their situation and contemplates how best to support Mrs. Castle and her husband—not only by providing standard prenatal care but also by addressing their concerns about parenting in the face of a significant familial risk for early-onset Alzheimer’s disease.

ethical_issues.question: Should Mrs. Castle undergo genetic testing during the course of genetic counseling to determine her own and her fetus’s genetic risk, and how can her autonomy be preserved throughout this process?
keypoints: Mrs. Castle should fully understand the potential downstream consequences of each step in the genetic counseling process to ensure the effective exercise of her autonomy.

Genetic counseling is a neutral process of education and psychological support, intended to help patients weigh the risks of genetic testing against their personal values, and does not mandate genetic testing.

Mrs. Castle’s right to decline genetic testing should be respected, even if her motivation is to avoid the psychological burden of knowing her disease status; this is an important expression of her autonomy.

While Mrs. Castle meets the criteria for genetic testing, priority should be given to testing living affected family members for pathogenic mutations in order to increase the interpretive value of the results.

If information about the genetic status of family members is unavailable, Mrs. Castle’s autonomous choice regarding whether to undergo genetic testing herself to inform reproductive decision-making should be respected and supported.

Mrs. Castle needs to make phased decisions regarding whether to pursue genetic testing for herself and for the fetus, and should rationally assess the actual impact and significance of each test result on her pregnancy-related decisions.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Mrs. Castle’s strong family history of early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, should genetic testing be performed early in pregnancy to inform the decision about whether to continue the pregnancy?
keypoints: Decisions regarding genetic testing should ideally be made prior to conception, as a thorough understanding of genetic risk and the ethical implications of reproductive choices is fundamental to informed decision making.

It is recommended to first perform testing for known pathogenic mutations in living affected family members (such as Mrs. Castle’s sister) to clarify the familial disease-causing gene; without this information, a negative genetic test result for Mrs. Castle herself has limited value for risk assessment.

In the absence of familial genetic information, Mrs. Castle should be supported in weighing whether to undergo genetic testing herself to inform her pregnancy decision, with careful attention to the complex psychological and ethical considerations involved.

If Mrs. Castle tests positive for a causative mutation and wishes to know the genetic status of the fetus, prenatal diagnostic procedures such as amniocentesis are required during the second trimester.

Mrs. Castle must confront and carefully consider the complex ethical question of whether she has the moral authority to judge her child’s quality of life and right to be born based on the risk of early-onset Alzheimer’s disease.

ethical_issues.question: In the case where Mrs. Castle is considering amniocentesis to determine whether the fetus carries a gene for early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, how should the procedural risks be weighed against the potential informational benefits?
keypoints: Mrs. Castle must be fully informed of the miscarriage risk associated with amniocentesis, which is approximately 0.1%, and incorporate this risk into her decision-making process.

If the results of amniocentesis indicate that the fetus carries a gene associated with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, Mrs. Castle should anticipate how she would respond to this information, including its potential impact on her decision to continue the pregnancy.

This decision raises fundamental ethical questions: Do parents have the authority to determine, based on a predicted disease, that their future child’s quality of life would be so diminished as to justify termination of the pregnancy? Such a judgment may exceed the proper scope of parental ethical decision-making, especially when the future child’s own subjective experience of quality of life remains unknown.

The ethical justification for amniocentesis depends on whether its results will influence Mrs. Castle’s decision regarding the pregnancy: if the outcome will serve as the basis for decision-making, then the pursuit of key information may warrant the associated risk; conversely, if the result will not affect her decision to continue the pregnancy, then exposing the fetus to this risk lacks ethical justification.

The clinician’s primary responsibility is to provide accurate and comprehensive information about the risks and potential benefits of amniocentesis, to respect patient autonomy, and to support Mrs. Castle in making a choice that aligns with her own values and those of her family.

title: How Should Physicians Respond When the Best Treatment for an Individual Patient Conflicts with Practice Guidelines about the Use of a Limited Resource?
case:
Dr. Ellis is an urologist at a community hospital. He treats several patients with bladder cancer who require treatment with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy. However, there is a current worldwide shortage of BCG due to manufacturing problems. There are no national policies in the United States governing the dispensation of BCG in the setting of a shortage, so a multidisciplinary task force was recently convened at Dr. Ellis’s hospital in order to decide how the hospital should respond.
The hospital task force, of which Dr. Ellis is a member, voted unanimously to adopt guidelines similar to those adopted by other hospitals, namely, to offer a one-third dose of BCG for induction and maintenance courses up to one year. These guidelines are based on a randomized trial by the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer that showed no difference in toxicity between one-third dose BCG and full-dose BCG [1]. Notably, however, the lower dosage resulted in higher recurrence rates. Dr. Ellis and many of his colleagues also recently attended a urology conference where a study of patients eligible for treatment with BCG during the shortage was presented: 87 percent of patients had treatment regimens that did not follow the standard of care, but the recurrence rate was highest among those who required induction BCG therapy and those who received an alternative to BCG [2]. The presenters recommended prioritizing patients who need induction BCG therapy.
When Dr. Ellis returned from the conference, he saw a patient named Jaan that he has had a long relationship with due to his history of prostate problems. Jaan is a fairly healthy 61-year-old man who has just been diagnosed with bladder cancer requiring BCG therapy. Dr. Ellis is aware that from a population and organizational perspective, he should not recommend the full dose of BCG treatment for Jaan but believes that he might be at higher risk for recurrence of his bladder cancer if the alternative regimen is used.
Talking to a colleague about Jaan’s clinic visit, he says, “I voted to implement the BCG guideline, but I believe this patient should get the full dose.” His colleague advises, “Give him the full dose of BCG. The guidelines aren’t mandatory; guidelines have legitimate exceptions. You have to do what is best for the patient in front of you.” Dr. Ellis considers this advice, but later he thinks, “Making an exception for Jaan means other patients might not receive BCG at all. How do I know that, down the road, another patient might be as worthy of being granted an exception to the guideline as Jaan? If I grant too many exceptions, the guidelines I helped implement won’t mean much.” Dr. Ellis continues to consider what to do.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Ellis, a urologist at a community hospital, regularly manages patients with bladder cancer who need Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy. Recently, a worldwide shortage of BCG has arisen due to manufacturing issues, and there are no national policies in the United States to guide hospitals on rationing BCG during such shortages. In response, Dr. Ellis’s hospital convened a multidisciplinary task force, including Dr. Ellis himself, to determine how best to allocate BCG among their patients.

After thorough discussion, the hospital task force unanimously agreed to implement guidelines mirroring those of other institutions: patients would receive a one-third dose of BCG for both induction and maintenance courses for up to one year. This decision was grounded in evidence from a European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer randomized trial, which showed comparable toxicity between the reduced and full doses, though it was noted that patients receiving the lower dose experienced higher rates of cancer recurrence. Furthermore, Dr. Ellis and his colleagues had just returned from a urology conference where new data were presented: among patients treated during the BCG shortage, 87 percent received regimens deviating from standard care, and recurrence rates were highest in those needing induction BCG or who received BCG alternatives. The conference presenters advised prioritizing full-dose BCG for those requiring induction therapy.

Shortly after returning, Dr. Ellis saw Jaan, a 61-year-old man in generally good health, with whom he has had a longstanding relationship due to Jaan’s previous prostate issues. Jaan has now been diagnosed with bladder cancer, and BCG therapy is indicated. Dr. Ellis recognizes, from both an institutional and broader community perspective, that he should adhere to the new guideline and not recommend a full dose of BCG for Jaan. Yet, he worries that the reduced regimen may increase Jaan’s risk of recurrence.

Dr. Ellis confides in a colleague about his dilemma regarding Jaan’s care. “I voted in favor of the BCG guideline, but I feel Jaan should really get the full dose,” he admits. His colleague responds, “Go ahead and give him the full dose. Guidelines aren’t binding—they allow for justified exceptions. Your responsibility is to do what’s right for the patient in front of you.” Dr. Ellis contemplates this advice, but later reflects, “If I make an exception for Jaan, that could mean another patient may not get BCG at all. What if, in the future, I have another patient just as deserving of an exception as Jaan? If I allow too many exceptions, the guidelines we put in place lose their meaning and fairness.”

With these concerns weighing on him, Dr. Ellis continues to deliberate over the best course of action for Jaan, wrestling with the challenge of balancing his duty to the individual patient with his responsibility to the wider patient community.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the individual interests of their patients with the principle of utility for the greater good when the best treatment for an individual patient conflicts with guidelines for the use of a limited resource?
keypoints: Physicians should clearly recognize the ethical conflict between providing the best treatment for individual patients and adhering to the principle of community utility in the allocation of limited resources, which involves a tension between the principles of beneficence and justice.

When ethical analysis cannot definitively determine the morally superior option, the question of who should make the decision becomes paramount; physicians should prioritize incorporating decision-making into multidisciplinary or institutional processes to minimize the impact of personal bias on patient care.

Clinical decision-making by physicians should be grounded in rigorous ethical reasoning, with careful reflection on and correction for their own emotional inclinations, in order to avoid allowing affective motivations to undermine the principles of fair and reasonable resource allocation.

In the context of resource scarcity, physicians should balance individual and collective interests by actively participating in the development and adherence to transparent and just allocation guidelines, while maintaining a cautious approach to reasonable exceptions in special cases, but avoiding excessive exceptions that would undermine overall fairness.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of limited medical resources, should physicians be transparent with patients about their ethical dilemmas in order to preserve the patient-physician relationship and alleviate their own moral distress?
keypoints: Physicians should discuss ethical dilemmas with patients to achieve shared responsibility, thereby preserving the patient-physician relationship and alleviating their own moral distress.

Physicians should be candid with patients about the reality of resource shortages, but should avoid asking patients to participate in weighing resource allocation decisions, so as to prevent placing them in the painful position of sacrificing their own interests for others.

Physicians should maintain transparency in the decision-making process, openly acknowledging concerns about undue favoritism or excessive restraint, in order to foster mutual trust and reduce feelings of isolation for both parties.

title: How Should Resident Physicians Respond to Patients’ Discomfort and Students’ Moral Distress When Learning Procedures in Academic Medical Settings?
case:
Lauren is a medical student who is doing her clinical year rotation in neurology. She has never performed a lumbar puncture (LP), also known as a spinal tap, but a patient on the neurology inpatient service requires one for diagnosis. Her resident physician, Adam, suggests that she attempt to perform one.
Lauren is initially excited about this prospect, and Adam demonstrates to her the steps involved in this procedure. When Adam tells her, “It might cause some pain, but you have to make sure the patient is perfectly still,” she begins to feel apprehensive.
Lauren and Adam go to see the patient, Mrs. Jones, together. Adam tells the patient that they will need to do an LP. The patient looks warily at Lauren and says, “Well, I don’t want you practicing on me.” Adam responds, “Don’t worry. You’re in good hands.”
Lauren feels extremely conflicted. On the one hand, she feels as though she is practicing on the patient and could cause pain or a more serious consequence, since it is her first time ever performing the procedure. On the other, she knows that she needs to learn this important skill and that “practicing” in this manner is the only way to do so. She wonders whether to tell the resident physician that she doesn’t want to do the LP on this patient, given this particular patient’s statement, but she is also concerned that opting out might prompt a negative response from the resident physician, who evaluates her.
case_rewrite:
Lauren, a medical student in her neurology clinical rotation, faces a pivotal moment in her training. She has never performed a lumbar puncture (LP), a procedure necessary for one of the patients on the neurology inpatient service. Her resident physician, Adam, encourages her to perform the LP, suggesting, “This is a good opportunity for you to learn.” 

At first, Lauren is eager, watching attentively as Adam demonstrates each step of the procedure on a model and explains the process. “There might be some discomfort for the patient,” Adam cautions, “and it’s essential that the patient remains completely still. If you’re unsure at any point, I’ll be right here.” Hearing this, Lauren’s initial excitement turns to anxiety; she worries about causing the patient unnecessary pain or complications, especially since this would be her first time attempting the procedure on a real person.

Together, Lauren and Adam enter the hospital room of Mrs. Jones, the patient requiring the LP. Adam explains to Mrs. Jones, “We need to perform a spinal tap to help with your diagnosis.” Mrs. Jones glances at Lauren, her apprehension clear. She says, “I would prefer not to have someone practice on me.” 

Adam responds with reassurance: “I understand your concern. Lauren is a medical student learning this procedure, and I will be supervising her very closely. You’re in good hands.” He does not elaborate further on Lauren’s experience level or discuss the risks or benefits of student involvement.

Lauren is deeply conflicted. She feels uneasy about performing a procedure, for the first time, on a patient who has expressed reservations. She recognizes the importance of developing these clinical skills and knows that supervised practice is often the only way to learn. Yet, Mrs. Jones’s hesitance weighs on her conscience. Lauren considers telling Adam that she is uncomfortable proceeding given the patient’s explicit concerns, but she fears that refusing might negatively affect Adam’s perception of her and her evaluation.

As she stands at the bedside, Lauren struggles to balance her responsibility to respect the patient’s wishes and autonomy with her own need for clinical training. She quietly debates whether to suggest observing the procedure first or ask for alternative training, such as additional practice in the simulation lab. At the same time, she worries about speaking up and how this might be viewed in the hierarchy of the medical team.

ethical_issues.question: How should resident physicians communicate effectively to address patients’ concerns about medical students performing procedures while also meeting educational needs?
keypoints: Resident physicians should respect patient autonomy through skillful communication, assisting patients in rationally weighing procedural risks against educational value, thereby demonstrating respect for the patient’s moral agency.

Resident physicians should provide full disclosure to patients regarding the increased risk of pain or the possibility of a second attempt associated with medical student involvement, and explicitly return the final decision-making authority to the patient.

Resident physicians should commit to closely supervising the medical student throughout the procedure and promptly intervening in the event of excessive pain or other risks, thereby ensuring patient safety.

Resident physicians should explain that patient participation in teaching not only contributes to the development of medical students’ skills but may also benefit future patients, helping patients understand the altruistic significance of their involvement.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical students acquire the necessary clinical skills training while respecting patient autonomy in academic medical settings?
keypoints: Academic medical centers should clearly inform patients of their educational mission and its implications for clinical care, and respect patients’ rights to informed consent and autonomous decision-making.

Resident physicians should coordinate patients’ autonomy and educational needs through effective communication, respect patients’ moral agency, and ensure that patients fully understand and independently decide whether to allow medical students to perform procedures.

Medical students should proactively express their ethical concerns and technical apprehensions, and, when necessary, propose alternative approaches (such as observing first), in order to safeguard patient interests and ensure the quality of their own learning.

Medical students should make full use of alternative resources such as simulation laboratories for skills training, thereby reducing the risks associated with first-time procedures on real patients and enhancing their technical preparedness and confidence.

Academic medical centers should foster a culture of safety that encourages medical students to express concerns without being insubordinate, viewing speaking up as an important action to protect patient welfare and promote educational quality.

ethical_issues.question: How can academic medical centers achieve an ethical balance between training a highly competent physician workforce and respecting patient autonomy?
keypoints: Academic medical centers should clearly inform patients of their educational mission and its potential impact on the care process, ensuring that patients are fully informed and involved in decision making.
Respect for patient autonomy is a fundamental ethical requirement; patients have the right to refuse to be the subject of trainee procedures, and their decisions must be respected.
Adequate and ongoing clinical supervision should be provided to ensure that medical students receive professional guidance during procedures, thereby minimizing risks to patients.

The development and utilization of alternative training resources, such as simulation laboratories, should be promoted to reduce the potential harm to patients from students’ first clinical procedures.

An open and safe cultural environment should be fostered, encouraging medical students and staff to voice concerns as a legitimate action in the best interest of patients, supported by faculty training, leadership endorsement, and strict enforcement of anti-retaliation policies.

title: What Should Physicians Do When They Disagree, Clinically and Ethically, with a Surrogate’s Wishes?
case:
Charlie is a resident in the intensive care unit (ICU). He meets a patient, a man who has a medical history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, mitral valve repair, chronic kidney disease, and two failed kidney transplants. He developed kidney failure and subsequently progressed to shock and heart failure, requiring continuous dialysis and ICU care. He began to show signs of intensive care unit delirium very early on and refused surgical interventions.
The patient’s wife, who was present in the ICU, was informed as he became increasingly delirious that her husband likely had limited time left, but she left the room during the discussion and refused to participate. Her husband rapidly decompensated. Nevertheless, she insisted on the continuation of intensive medical care. “Why does everyone keep talking about the negative?” she said. She refused palliative care involvement.
As the patient’s ICU stay continued, he developed multiple ulcers all over his body and was unresponsive. He also developed gangrene of the leg and genitals and required a tracheostomy and percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube. Multiple conversations were held with the patient’s wife about the futility of medical care at this point, but she said, “I believe in miracles, and everyone in the church is praying for him,” and continued to push for aggressive care.
Charlie feels extremely conflicted. He believes that the patient is suffering greatly from continued intensive medical care, and that despite this approach’s promise to prolong his life, the patient’s prognosis and quality of life (and possibly his experience of death) will not improve. He has the impulse to stop care, despite the wishes of the patient’s wife. He wonders whether to stop writing orders for blood transfusions and antibiotics.
case_rewrite:
Charlie, a resident in the intensive care unit (ICU), is caring for a patient with a complex medical history: hypertension, atrial fibrillation, mitral valve repair, chronic kidney disease, and two unsuccessful kidney transplants. The patient has entered kidney failure, which has led to shock and worsening heart failure, necessitating continuous dialysis and intensive ICU support. Early in his ICU course, the patient developed pronounced delirium and began refusing any further surgical interventions.

Throughout his stay, the patient’s wife has remained at his bedside. When Charlie and the medical team explained that her husband’s condition was deteriorating and that his time was likely limited, she abruptly left the conversation and declined to engage further. Even as her husband’s condition rapidly worsened, she insisted on continued aggressive medical care. “Why does everyone keep talking about the negative?” she asked, firmly rejecting any involvement from the palliative care team.

As the days passed, the patient's situation declined further. He developed multiple ulcers across his body and became completely unresponsive. Gangrene set in, affecting both his leg and genitals, and he required a tracheostomy and the placement of a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube. Despite numerous discussions with the patient’s wife about the futility of ongoing intensive care, she remained resolute. “I believe in miracles, and everyone in the church is praying for him,” she insisted, continuing to demand all possible interventions.

Charlie finds himself deeply conflicted. He sees firsthand the suffering caused by continued intensive care, and believes that further treatment, while possibly extending the patient’s life, will not improve his prognosis, quality of life, or dying experience. The urge to halt interventions—such as discontinuing blood transfusions and antibiotics—grows stronger, even though this would be contrary to the wishes of the patient’s wife. Charlie is left wrestling with the ethical dilemma of whether to honor the family's requests or to act in what he believes is the patient’s true best interest.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the wishes of a patient’s family with their own medical judgment in clinical decision making when they believe that continued treatment is futile and only prolongs the patient’s suffering?
keypoints: Physicians should begin by establishing trust, narrowing the power differential with the patient’s family through the demonstration of empathy and humility.

Physicians need to guide the patient’s family to understand that the most appropriate goal of care at this stage is to shift from aggressive treatment to a focus on alleviating suffering and ensuring a good death.

Physicians should employ effective communication strategies, including building rapport, preparing for conversations, skillful questioning, active listening, providing reflective feedback, clear expression, and knowing when to remain silent.

Even if it is not possible to change the family’s position, physicians should acknowledge the potential tragedy of providing treatment that prolongs the patient’s suffering, maintain empathy, forgive themselves for unmet care goals, and continue to fulfill their professional duties.

ethical_issues.question: When physicians and a patient’s family members disagree about the goals of care, what communication strategies should physicians employ to promote understanding and potentially facilitate a change in the family’s position?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize the core virtues of empathy and humility in order to establish a relationship of trust with the patient’s family members.
Physicians need to guide family members to understand the necessity of shifting from aggressive treatment to end-of-life care, with a focus on the patient’s quality of life and dignity.

Physicians should possess and flexibly employ a comprehensive set of communication skills, including establishing rapport, preparing for conversations, asking questions, active listening, providing reflective feedback, clearly conveying medical facts, and knowing when to remain silent.

Communication is not merely the transmission of information, but a moral practice that expresses empathy and humility through both verbal and nonverbal means, thereby facilitating emotional understanding and psychological support for family members.

title: How Should Integrity Preservation and Professional Growth Be Balanced during Trainees’ Professionalization?
case: Reema is a medical student with strong beliefs about preservation of human life as a primary purpose of medicine. One of her patients is a 65-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer. The attending physician, Dr. Alnin, decides to have a conversation with the patient about hospice care. The patient asks about a new and expensive chemotherapy that he had seen advertised. Dr. Alnin recommends against this option, citing the patient’s low likelihood of a positive response and minimal extension of the patient’s life even with an optimal response. Hearing this, the patient decides to pursue hospice. Reema is distressed by this decision because she feels that the team is giving up on this patient. She does not tell anyone that she feels this way, however, because she is concerned about being evaluated poorly by Dr. Alnin if she expresses disagreement with her advice to the patient and his family.
case_rewrite:
Reema, a medical student who firmly believes that preserving human life is the central mission of medicine, finds herself involved in the care of a 65-year-old man recently diagnosed with metastatic lung cancer. The attending physician, Dr. Alnin, schedules a meeting with the patient to discuss the possibility of enrolling in hospice care. During their conversation, the patient mentions having seen advertisements for a new, expensive chemotherapy drug and asks whether it could be a viable option for him. Dr. Alnin listens attentively, then explains that, given the advanced stage of the cancer, the likelihood of meaningful benefit from this chemotherapy is extremely low, and even under the best circumstances, it would prolong life only minimally. After hearing Dr. Alnin’s explanation, the patient ultimately chooses to begin hospice care.

Observing this interaction, Reema feels unsettled. She perceives the decision to forgo further active treatment as a form of abandonment and is deeply troubled by what she sees as the medical team stepping away from the fight to preserve life. Despite her strong feelings, Reema remains silent. She worries that if she were to voice her disagreement with Dr. Alnin’s recommendation in front of the team or the patient’s family, it might reflect negatively on her or affect her evaluation from Dr. Alnin. As a result, Reema keeps her concerns to herself, struggling internally with her discomfort and uncertainty about her responsibilities and role as she continues her journey to becoming a physician.

ethical_issues.question: How can ethics education programs help medical students resolve moral distress arising from an underdeveloped professional identity?
keypoints: Case-based ethics education programs facilitated by ethicists provide medical students with opportunities to explore and develop their personal professional identity and ethical perspectives in medicine.
Case-based ethical discussions promote peer support and the sharing of experiences, enhancing medical students’ sense of belonging and mutual assistance.
Such programs offer a safe space for expressing ethical viewpoints, ensuring that medical students can engage in open communication and reflection when facing ethical dilemmas.
These initiatives deepen medical students’ understanding of medical ethics, including the purpose of medicine, physician virtues, and the complexity of ethical decision-making.
Integrating case-based ethics education into medical training is an important approach to promoting medical students’ professional growth, particularly in the ethical dimension.

ethical_issues.question: How can Reema, as a medical student, balance her personal beliefs about the purpose of medicine with ethical principles such as patient autonomy and beneficence during clinical decision-making as she develops her professional identity?
keypoints: Medical students should, under the guidance of mentors, develop a comprehensive and pluralistic understanding of the purpose of medicine, which can help them clarify their conception of the goals of medicine and alleviate moral distress related to professional identity.

Medical students should be encouraged to reflect on and critically examine traditional assumptions regarding life preservation and quality of life, thereby fostering a deeper understanding of the complexities of medical ethics.

In-depth exploration of physicians’ responsibilities and roles in end-of-life treatment decisions should be undertaken to help medical students move beyond the singular view that only maximally aggressive care is laudable.

Case-based ethics education should be systematically incorporated into medical training programs to create an environment—through peer learning and expert guidance—in which ethical perspectives can be safely expressed, thus promoting professional growth and the development of ethical competence among medical students.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical students express dissenting opinions regarding attending physicians’ clinical decisions without violating professional ethics?
keypoints: It should be recognized that it is reasonable and common for medical students to have concerns about questioning attending physicians due to power differentials; this understanding is an important premise for interpreting their behavior.

Medical students should cultivate physician virtues such as courage, academic integrity, and truthfulness during their medical training, as these qualities enable them to appropriately express differing opinions when faced with the clinical decisions of attending physicians.

Case-based ethics education should be incorporated into medical training programs to provide medical students with a safe space to express ethical viewpoints through peer support and expert guidance, thereby helping them to develop their personal professional identity and ethical perspectives in medicine.
