title: Do Pediatric Patients Have a Right to Know?
case:
Jenny is a medical student following the care of Adam, a 13-year-old boy who has just been diagnosed with Ewing’s sarcoma of the left distal femur. The attending physician, Dr. K, explains to Adam and his parents that the treatment has a very high cure rate and should be started immediately. Dr. K also explains to Adam’s parents that Adam will likely be infertile after treatment and that he might not have time to bank sperm. Adam’s parents say that they are not interested in sperm banking and request that Dr. K not mention the possibility of infertility to Adam. Adam’s father states, “He’s too young to understand.” Later, Jenny is talking with Adam about his hobbies and aspirations and Adam says, “I can’t wait to have a big family one day.” Jenny relates this to Dr. K, and he and Jenny discuss Adam’s future views about family at length with no mention of the infertility risk posed by Adam’s treatment. They also discuss Adam’s anger, which often stems from his feeling a lack of control over his life, commonly seen in adolescents with cancer.
Later, Jenny asks Dr. K about whether to inform Adam about the virtual certainty of his infertility due to the chemotherapy he needs. Dr. K says, “His parents understand that Adam needs to be treated immediately and they’ve clearly stated that they don’t want him to know about the infertility risk. We must respect their wishes.” Jenny wonders whether Adam could suffer psychologically if he survives his cancer and later realizes he was uninformed about the treatment’s infertility risk. She also wonders whether Adam, who clearly is interested in his future with respect to being a father, has a right to know about this side effect. What, if anything, should Jenny do?
case_rewrite:
Jenny, a medical student, is closely following the care of Adam, a 13-year-old boy who has recently been diagnosed with Ewing’s sarcoma affecting his left distal femur. The attending physician, Dr. K, meets with Adam and his parents to explain the situation. Dr. K informs them that the treatment regimen for Ewing’s sarcoma offers a very high chance of cure and emphasizes the need to begin therapy without delay. During the discussion, Dr. K also privately tells Adam’s parents that the necessary treatment will almost certainly result in Adam becoming infertile and mentions that, given the urgency, sperm banking might not be feasible.

Adam’s parents respond firmly, telling Dr. K that they are not interested in pursuing sperm banking for Adam. Furthermore, they explicitly request that Dr. K not mention to Adam the possibility of infertility arising from the treatment. Adam’s father states, “He’s too young to understand.”

Later, while Jenny is spending time with Adam, he shares his interests and dreams, saying, “I can’t wait to have a big family one day.” Jenny takes note of this and reports it to Dr. K. Together, Jenny and Dr. K talk at length about Adam’s hopes for his future family, but at no point do they address the risk of infertility that treatment poses. They also discuss Adam’s frequent expressions of anger, which they recognize as a common reaction among adolescents with cancer who often feel a lack of control over their circumstances.

Afterwards, Jenny approaches Dr. K with her concerns, asking whether Adam should be informed about the near certainty that his chemotherapy will leave him infertile. Dr. K replies, “Adam’s parents understand how urgent it is to start treatment, and they have made it clear they don’t want him to know about the possibility of infertility. We need to respect their wishes.”

Jenny finds herself troubled, wondering whether Adam could experience psychological harm if he survives cancer and later discovers he was never told about the risk of infertility. She also questions whether Adam, given his strong desire to have a family someday, has a right to be informed about this significant side effect. Jenny is left uncertain about what, if anything, she should do next.

ethical_issues.question: When parents refuse to inform a minor patient about the side effects of treatment, do physicians have a responsibility to oppose this decision and disclose the potential iatrogenic harms to the patient?
keypoints: Physicians have a moral obligation and legal responsibility to question and, when necessary, to oppose the decisions of surrogate decision-makers or patients when such decisions may place the patient at significant and imminent risk of harm.

Traditionally, pediatric clinicians and other caregivers for patients lacking decision-making capacity have afforded great deference to the expressed wishes of surrogates, unless there is sufficient reason to believe that their decisions could place the patient at imminent and serious risk of harm.

“Harm” is typically narrowly construed as imminent physical harm; in this case, the infertility and potential psychological harm resulting from treatment lack sufficient certainty and severity to constitute a significant risk of harm that would justify overriding the parents’ decision.
Legally, minors such as Adam do not possess the authority to provide consent or the right to be informed; physicians are required to comply with the decisions of parents as the legal surrogates.

Future iatrogenic harms resulting from treatment toxicity are inherently uncertain and speculative; physicians should respect parental wishes and, unless there is an imminent and serious risk of harm, should not contravene parental authority by disclosing related information to the patient.

In this case, the medical student Jenny and the attending physician Dr. K face an ethical dilemma; Jenny’s concerns regarding the patient’s right to know and potential future psychological harm reflect the moral struggle healthcare professionals experience in balancing respect for surrogate authority with the obligation to protect the patient’s interests.

This case highlights the need for physicians to balance legal requirements, ethical principles, and the individual needs of the patient in major medical decisions involving minors, and, when necessary, to seek support from an ethics committee or legal counsel.

ethical_issues.question: Is the physician obligated to unconditionally comply with the parents’ wishes regarding disclosure of information to a minor patient?
keypoints: Pediatric clinicians generally defer to the wishes of surrogates (parents) unless there is sufficient reason to believe that their decisions could place the patient at risk of imminent harm.
When a surrogate’s medical decision may result in significant harm to the patient, physicians have a moral obligation and legal responsibility to question and, if necessary, oppose that decision.
The rationale for medical decisions that could lead to significant harm must be sufficiently rational and not reasonably subject to objection in order to be considered acceptable.

title: Influence of Psychiatric Symptoms on Decisional Capacity in Treatment Refusal
case:
Dr. A is the oncologist for Catherine, a 55-year-old woman with newly diagnosed stage II breast cancer. When Dr. A asks about Catherine’s past medical history during her initial consultation, Catherine mentions that she has often felt so tired over the past two years that she could barely get out of bed. “It just didn’t seem worth it to wake up,” she explains. “So I’d just sleep all day because I didn’t want to do anything. It’s not like anyone would really miss me, anyway.” Dr. A asks if Catherine feels that way now, and she shrugs, “Sometimes. It comes and goes. It was bad after my husband died two years ago, but I guess I feel okay now.” Dr. A also notices in Catherine’s health record that her weight has fluctuated up to thirty pounds in both directions. When asked about this, Catherine says, “I don’t really remember why—probably different diets.” Catherine reports that she has never talked about her mood with a clinician. She adds, “Everybody used to say I was just moody.”
During treatment, Catherine experiences side effects so severe that she cannot go to work and reports difficulty with activities of daily living, as she lives alone and lacks immediate family or close friends. As Dr. A evaluates her initial response to treatment, he sees that her tumor burden has actually increased slightly, and he informs Catherine that she might have to undergo more aggressive therapy. At this, Catherine shakes her head and says, “I won’t do it.” When pressed further, Catherine says, “It isn’t worth it to me. I’ve thought a lot about my life over the past weeks, and there just isn’t any reason to keep going, especially since my husband died.” Dr. A asks Catherine to consider people or activities she still enjoys, to which Catherine retorts, “That’s exactly what I did. I couldn’t think of any.” Dr. A then asks about her struggling to come to terms with her cancer and suffering during treatment. Catherine says sarcastically, “Well, it’s no picnic. But honestly, Dr. A, I’m okay with things ending here. I’ve lived my life, and, at this point, I’m tired of suffering. I just want to be with my husband. I miss him all the time.”
Uncertain about Catherine’s mental health, particularly given her history, Dr. A consults Catherine’s primary care physician, Dr. B. Dr. B recalls, “There were times over the years when she seemed a little withdrawn, but nothing ever jumped out at me.” He confirms that her husband, who was her main social support, died two years ago and says that he has not seen her since then. “She and I had a pretty good relationship, though,” Dr. B adds. “I’m sure I can convince her to consent to further treatment. I can’t imagine havingnothingto live for.”
Wanting additional and more up-to-date information, Dr. A refers Catherine to a psychiatrist, Dr. C, who diagnoses Catherine with complicated grief and prescribes antidepressants. However, Catherine does not fill the prescription. When Dr. A calls to ask her about this, Catherine says, “Look, I understand what’s at stake here, and I’ve made up my mind. Please don’t make this harder for me.” She expresses understanding of the risks and benefits of refusing further treatment for her cancer.
Dr. A wonders if Catherine’s grief has compromised her capacity to give an informed refusal. He also wonders just how far her current feelings are from her baseline mood, how much distress her cancer experience has caused her, and the degree to which this could be influencing her decision making. Lastly, Dr. A considers Dr. B’s offer to try to “convince” her and wonders whether further attempts at persuading her might not be respectful of her decision and values. What should Dr. A do?
case_rewrite:
Dr. A, an oncologist, is caring for Catherine, a 55-year-old woman recently diagnosed with stage II breast cancer. At their first meeting, Dr. A takes a thorough medical history. Catherine reveals that for the past two years, she has often felt so exhausted that getting out of bed seemed impossible. “It just didn’t seem worth it to wake up,” she says. “So I’d sleep all day because I didn’t want to do anything. It’s not like anyone would really miss me, anyway.” Dr. A asks if she still feels this way. Catherine shrugs, “Sometimes. It’s not as bad as it was after my husband died two years ago, but it still comes and goes. I guess I’m okay now.” Dr. A notes in her chart that her weight has swung by as much as thirty pounds in either direction. When he brings this up, Catherine responds, “I don’t really remember why—probably just different diets.” She adds that she has never spoken with a clinician about her mood. “People always just said I was moody,” she explains.

As treatment progresses, Catherine develops severe side effects, leaving her unable to work and struggling with daily activities. She lives alone and has no close friends or immediate family. When Dr. A assesses her response to initial therapy, he finds that her tumor burden has actually increased slightly. He explains to Catherine that more aggressive treatment may be necessary. At this, Catherine shakes her head emphatically, saying, “I won’t do it.” When Dr. A presses for her reasons, Catherine replies, “It isn’t worth it to me. I’ve thought a lot about my life these past weeks, and there’s just no reason to keep going, especially since my husband died.” Dr. A encourages her to consider people or activities she still enjoys, but Catherine retorts, “That’s exactly what I did. I couldn’t think of any.” He asks whether her difficulty accepting her cancer and the suffering from treatment are influencing her. Catherine responds with a touch of sarcasm, “Well, it’s no picnic. But honestly, Dr. A, I’m okay with things ending here. I’ve lived my life, and at this point, I’m tired of suffering. I just want to be with my husband. I miss him all the time.”

Unsure about Catherine’s mental health and its impact on her decision-making, Dr. A contacts her primary care physician, Dr. B. Dr. B recalls, “Over the years, she sometimes seemed withdrawn, but nothing ever really stood out to me.” He confirms that Catherine’s husband, her main support, died two years ago, and admits he hasn’t seen her since then. “She and I had a good rapport, though,” Dr. B adds. “I’m sure I can convince her to agree to more treatment. I can’t imagine having nothing to live for.”

Seeking more current insight, Dr. A refers Catherine to a psychiatrist, Dr. C, who diagnoses her with complicated grief and prescribes antidepressants. However, Catherine does not pick up the medication. When Dr. A calls to follow up, Catherine says, “Look, I understand what’s at stake here, and I’ve made up my mind. Please don’t make this harder for me.” She demonstrates understanding of the risks and benefits involved in refusing further treatment.

Dr. A is left questioning whether Catherine’s grief and depression undermine her ability to make an informed refusal. He wonders how much her current mood differs from her baseline, how much her cancer experience is affecting her, and how these factors influence her capacity for medical decision making. He also considers Dr. B’s suggestion to “convince” her and whether further efforts to persuade Catherine would disrespect her autonomy and values. Dr. A must now decide on the most ethical and appropriate course of action.

ethical_issues.question: Do psychiatric symptoms affect a patient’s decisional capacity to refuse treatment?
keypoints: The capacity for informed consent in patients with psychiatric disorders may be diminished, particularly in those with severe depression, as their abilities in information processing and reasoning can be impaired, significantly affecting their medical decision-making capacity.

A psychiatric diagnosis in itself does not equate to a lack of decisional capacity; assessment must be individualized, and it is essential to avoid making determinations of incapacity based solely on diagnostic labels.

Catherine’s severe depression, significant functional impairment, and possible passive suicidality suggest that her capacity for medical decision making may be compromised, warranting particular attention to the authenticity and rationality of her decision-making process.
If a patient is experiencing a mood disorder or is at potential risk for suicide, prompt referral to psychiatry for a formal assessment is necessary to clarify the patient’s decisional capacity.

By diagnosing and treating reversible psychiatric conditions (such as complicated grief), it may be possible to restore or optimize the patient’s decisional capacity; this is a key ethical and clinical objective of psychiatric consultation and intervention.

ethical_issues.question: Who is best positioned to assess the patient’s decisional capacity and best interest?
keypoints: Psychiatrists are commonly involved in the assessment of a patient’s decisional capacity, but any licensed physician is qualified to perform this evaluation.

The assessment of a patient’s decisional capacity is not only a clinical judgment but also an ethical one; it should not rely solely on objective measures but should integrate considerations of the patient’s cognition, emotional state, and values.

Discussions with family members and the multidisciplinary team—including the primary physician and the hospital ethics committee—are valuable for comprehensively understanding the patient’s values and background relevant to medical decision making.
Consistency between a patient’s prior medical decisions and the current decision can serve as important evidence supporting the presence of decisional capacity.

Information provided by family members and other healthcare professionals not only supports the assessment of capacity but also offers critical reference for surrogate decision making, especially when the patient is deemed to lack decisional capacity.

When a patient is determined to lack decisional capacity, surrogate decision makers should make decisions based on the patient’s values, beliefs, and previously expressed wishes, adhering to the principle of best interest.
Formal ethics consultation is an effective approach for managing complex or uncertain cases, helping to balance respect for patient autonomy with the duty of protection.

ethical_issues.question: Is it appropriate for a physician to attempt to influence a patient’s decision?
keypoints: The core element of informed consent is the absence of coercion, with the prerequisite that the patient possesses independent decision-making capacity.
Physicians may assist patients in making decisions in an unbiased manner, provided that the patient’s autonomy is respected.

Physicians should evaluate the serious consequences that may result from a patient’s refusal of critical treatment, while remaining vigilant against the risk of paternalism and avoiding excessive intervention.
By treating reversible psychiatric conditions such as depression, physicians can optimize the process of assessing the patient’s decision-making capacity.
For patients with impaired decisional capacity, physicians should simplify information and employ alternative communication methods to facilitate understanding and participation in decision making.

title: Ethical Management of Patients with Cancer and Mental Illness
case:
TM, a 56-year-old man with schizophrenia, presented to his primary care physician with intermittent difficulty swallowing. He did not elaborate on exacerbating or alleviating features or associated symptoms. His review of systems was negative.
TM lived locally in an adult home. He was unwilling to consistently perform activities of daily living, such as bathing and dressing. The nursing staff of the adult home provided his medications. TM’s younger sister was his next of kin and had health care power of attorney. She attended appointments with him and assisted him in making decisions regarding his health care. Specifically, she aided in explaining clinical information to him in a manner that he seemed to better understand. She would not consent to procedures or therapies to which he was opposed.
Physical exam revealed a thin and disheveled man. He was alert and oriented. He had no outward signs of perceptual disturbances such as delusions or hallucinations. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable. A chest radiograph revealed a 3.8-cm lung mass. The patient was referred for a CT-guided biopsy of the lesion. Although he was initially reluctant, he ultimately agreed to the procedure after further counseling and discussion, and his sister supported his decision and provided consent. The biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma. Further staging did not reveal locally extensive or metastatic disease. Therefore the cancer was considered to be Stage Ib (T2aN0M0). He was referred to the surgical oncology service for possible resection of the mass.
During the initial surgical consultation, the patient stated that he did not believe he had cancer and would not consent to any surgical procedures. However, during a subsequent visit, the patient acknowledged the diagnosis and stated that he would consider surgery. After lengthy deliberation about the case, the members of the surgical oncology team opted against surgical intervention based on their feeling that the patient did not reliably demonstrate a good understanding of the diagnosis and might therefore have a higher risk of complications postoperatively. They stated that they did not feel it was safe to operate but offered no further explanation. TM completed radiation therapy, and a six-week post-treatment CT scan revealed stable disease, although with possible residual tumor.
case_rewrite:
TM is a 56-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia who presented to his primary care physician with intermittent difficulty swallowing. He was unable to specify what made his symptoms better or worse, nor did he report any related complaints. A comprehensive review of systems was otherwise negative.

TM resides nearby in an adult home, where he receives assistance from the nursing staff with his medications. He is often resistant to performing basic activities of daily living, such as bathing and getting dressed. TM’s younger sister serves as his next of kin and holds his health care power of attorney. She regularly accompanies him to medical appointments and helps him understand his health care decisions, often explaining medical information in ways that TM finds easier to grasp. She is careful not to consent to any procedures or treatments that TM personally opposes.

On physical examination, TM appeared thin and disheveled but was alert and oriented. There were no outward signs of delusions or hallucinations. The rest of his examination was unremarkable. A chest X-ray revealed a 3.8-cm lung mass. TM was referred for a CT-guided biopsy of this lesion. Though initially hesitant, after further counseling and discussion, he ultimately agreed to the procedure with his sister’s support and consent. The biopsy results showed squamous cell carcinoma. Further staging studies revealed no evidence of locally advanced or metastatic disease, categorizing the cancer as Stage Ib (T2aN0M0). He was then referred to the surgical oncology service to discuss possible surgical removal of the mass.

At the initial surgical consultation, TM stated that he did not believe he had cancer and refused to consent to any surgery. However, at a subsequent visit, he acknowledged the diagnosis and said he would consider undergoing surgery. After extensive discussion, the surgical oncology team decided against pursuing surgical intervention. Their reasoning was that TM did not consistently show a full understanding of his diagnosis, and they were concerned this could increase his risk of complications after surgery. The team stated they did not believe it was safe to operate but did not offer a more detailed explanation. TM subsequently received radiation therapy, and a CT scan six weeks after treatment showed stable disease, though possible residual tumor remained.

ethical_issues.question: Should patients with mental illness be presumed to have decision-making capacity unless there is evidence to the contrary that warrants further assessment?
keypoints: The assessment of medical decision-making capacity must be contextualized to the specific moment and the particular medical decision at hand, as capacity is a clinical standard that applies to a specific issue.

Patients with mental illness should be presumed to have decision-making capacity; a psychiatric diagnosis alone does not equate to incapacity unless there is clear evidence to the contrary that warrants further evaluation.

Many individuals with mental illness retain the ability to understand information, communicate choices, appreciate the situation and its consequences, and rationally process information to make reasonable medical decisions.

Determining whether a patient with mental illness possesses the mental capacity to participate in medical decision making requires a specific capacity assessment, rather than relying solely on diagnostic labels.

ethical_issues.question: How can we ensure that patients with mental illness receive a standard of cancer care equivalent to that provided to other patients?
keypoints: Cancer care for patients with mental illness should be grounded in their individual values, providing the highest quality, patient-centered diagnosis and treatment.

Patients with mental illness should be presumed to have decision-making capacity unless there is clear evidence to the contrary requiring further assessment; their autonomy should be supported by providing information in an accessible manner and carefully evaluating the appropriateness of treatment.

When a patient’s autonomy is compromised, a surrogate decision maker should act based on the patient’s known values (substituted judgment) or the best interest standard, with substituted judgment prioritizing the patient’s personal wishes.

The care team should include mental health professionals to optimize the management of psychiatric illness and ensure effective communication and collaboration between psychiatry and oncology clinicians.
Clinicians should demonstrate empathy, imagination, and a nonjudgmental attitude, respect patient dignity, and strive to provide care that is just and compassionate.
The principle of equivalence should be followed to ensure that patients with mental illness receive cancer care of the same quality as that provided to other patients.

The health care system and society should provide additional resources and support to reduce disparities in cancer care between patients with mental illness and those who are not part of vulnerable populations.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians assess the capacity of patients with mental illness to understand cancer treatment options, and how can information be provided to ensure it is communicated in a manner that is more comprehensible to them?
keypoints: Patients with mental illness should be presumed to have decision-making capacity unless there is clear evidence to the contrary requiring further professional assessment, and they should not be deemed to lack capacity without formal evaluation.

Assessment of decision-making capacity should be based on the patient’s current mental status and the specific clinical decision at hand, with particular attention to the patient’s ability to understand information, evaluate risks and benefits, and make autonomous choices.

Psychiatrists and oncologists should collaborate actively to jointly assess the patient’s decision-making capacity and comprehensively determine the safety and appropriateness of proposed treatment plans.

For patients with limited comprehension, information should be conveyed in a simplified, concrete manner tailored to their cognitive level, with an emphasis on empathy and health literacy to ensure the patient fully understands the treatment.

Family members and caregivers should be encouraged to participate deeply in the decision-making process, utilizing their knowledge of and empathy for the patient to help explain information and support the patient in expressing their true preferences.

title: How Should Clinicians Respond to Transference Reactions with Cancer Patients?
case:
Amy is a 25-year-old woman who has recently been diagnosed with lymphoma, but her prognosis seems to be good. She has a history of drug use and abusive relationships. Amy’s father abandoned her mother when she was a child, and Amy spent most of her adolescence caring for her mother, who was also addicted to drugs, before having an argument and moving away. She has weekly meetings with the cancer center’s psychiatrist, Dr. T, to discuss her well-being and her adjustment to cancer and cancer treatment.
Over the course of treatment, Amy opens up to Dr. T and begins to confide in him. She admits that her last boyfriend recently cheated on her and that she has not told any of her friends about her illness because she is afraid that they might desert her. “Everybody always leaves me,” she says on multiple occasions. “I’ve never been able to open up to someone without them running away.”
Dr. T notices that Amy seems to put a lot of effort into her personal appearance when she comes to appointments, sometimes asking him what he thinks of a particular outfit. She also asks him about his personal life despite his efforts to keep the conversation focused on her and wonders if she is his favorite patient. Dr. T remembers his psychodynamic training and worries that Amy is developing an eroticized transference, unconsciously transposing her past and ongoing feelings of abandonment onto him and experiencing them now as a fantasy that he might be the attachment figure she longs for and have similar feelings for her. He is uncertain whether he should comment on this or try to focus on the more immediate concerns of the cancer treatment.
Amy becomes agitated as her treatment progresses. She confesses that she is afraid of losing her relationship with Dr. T if she gets better and that she has grown deeply attached to him. She asks to see him outside the hospital. “You’re the only one who understands me,” Amy says. Dr. T explains that he must maintain professional boundaries and that it is his job to be understanding. At this point, Amy accuses him of only pretending to care about her. She leaves angrily and does not answer any of Dr. T’s subsequent phone calls.
Amy does not come in for her subsequent oncology appointment. When the oncologist, Dr. Y, finally reaches her, she says that she doesn’t need more treatment and that he cannot force her to come in. Dr. Y discusses this exchange with the rest of the care team, including Dr. T, who explains what happened during his last meeting with Amy. Dr. Y groans in frustration, “Say whatever you need to say to her to get her back here for treatment.” What should Dr. T do?
case_rewrite:
Amy, a 25-year-old woman, has recently been diagnosed with lymphoma, though her outlook appears favorable. Her background includes a history of drug use and abusive relationships. Amy’s father left her mother when she was a child, and much of her teenage years were spent caring for her mother, who struggled with addiction, until a heated argument led Amy to move out. Currently, Amy meets weekly with Dr. T, the cancer center’s psychiatrist, to talk about her mental health and how she is coping with her illness and its treatment.

As the weeks pass, Amy begins to trust Dr. T and shares increasingly personal details with him. She confides that her most recent boyfriend was unfaithful, and she hasn’t told her friends about her cancer, fearing they might abandon her. “Everybody always leaves me,” she repeats in their sessions. “I’ve never been able to open up to someone without them running away.”

Dr. T notices that Amy puts significant effort into her appearance before their appointments, sometimes seeking his opinion on what she’s wearing. She asks questions about his personal life, despite his attempts to keep the conversation centered on her, and wonders aloud if she is his favorite patient. Drawing on his psychodynamic training, Dr. T becomes concerned that Amy is developing an eroticized transference, unconsciously redirecting her longstanding fears of abandonment onto him and imagining him as the caring figure she has always sought. He is unsure whether to bring up these emerging feelings or to focus instead on her immediate medical needs.

As Amy’s treatment continues, she becomes increasingly anxious. She confesses to Dr. T that she fears losing their connection if she recovers, explaining that she feels profoundly attached to him. Amy then asks if she can see him outside of the hospital. “You’re the only one who understands me,” she insists. Dr. T gently tells her that he must keep their relationship professional and that his role is to be supportive within those boundaries. At this, Amy accuses him of only pretending to care and storms out, ignoring all of Dr. T’s follow-up phone calls.

Amy subsequently misses her next oncology appointment. When Dr. Y, her oncologist, eventually reaches her by phone, Amy states she doesn’t want further treatment and insists that Dr. Y cannot force her to return. Dr. Y discusses this development with the team, including Dr. T, who explains the events of his last session with Amy. Frustrated, Dr. Y says, “Say whatever you need to say to her to get her back here for treatment.” Now, Dr. T must decide how best to respond.

ethical_issues.question: After recognizing a patient’s transference reaction, how should a clinician determine when and how to interpret these feelings in a manner that best promotes the patient’s well-being and treatment goals?
keypoints: Clinicians should continuously assess the patient’s psychological state, their own emotional responses, and the dynamics of the patient-clinician relationship, in order to determine when and how to interpret transference in a manner that best serves the patient’s well-being and treatment goals.

A stable and trusting collaborative relationship between patient and clinician forms the foundation for exploring and managing transference; the strength and nature of the therapeutic alliance determine the timing and depth of transference interpretation, as premature or inappropriate interpretation may lead to patient misunderstanding, resistance, or treatment disruption.

Clinicians should encourage patients to freely express their emotional responses toward the clinician with a nonjudgmental, open, and empathic attitude, helping patients understand that these feelings reflect their interpersonal patterns and thereby reducing feelings of shame and guilt.

Clinicians need to clearly explain to patients the necessity and specifics of professional boundaries, emphasizing that boundaries are essential for ensuring safe and effective treatment, and should strive to avoid patients experiencing boundary-setting as rejection or abandonment, thus balancing empathic responses with therapeutic standards.

In addressing transference, clinicians should flexibly manage the timing and manner of interpretation, ensuring that the existence of transference is neither avoided nor explored too deeply so as to provoke patient defensiveness or treatment resistance, thereby promoting a stable therapeutic alliance and the achievement of treatment objectives.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians effectively respond to patients’ emotional needs while maintaining professional boundaries when managing eroticized transference?
keypoints: Clinicians must first recognize and manage their own countertransference, ensuring that their personal emotions and attitudes do not interfere with an objective understanding and response to the patient’s transference.

Clinicians should identify and acknowledge the patient’s eroticized transference, maintain an open and empathic attitude, and strictly uphold therapeutic boundaries to prevent the patient from feeling rejected or abandoned.

Clinicians should encourage patients to openly express and discuss their feelings toward the clinician, helping them to gain deeper insight into their interpersonal relationship patterns and to dispel any sense of shame or taboo associated with these feelings.

Clinicians should clearly explain the boundaries and professional responsibilities inherent in the psychotherapeutic relationship, emphasizing that these boundaries are essential for ensuring safe and effective treatment and supporting the patient in better coping with cancer therapy and its associated challenges.

ethical_issues.question: What measures should clinicians take to salvage treatment and ensure that patients continue to receive necessary medical care when treatment is interrupted due to transference reactions?
keypoints: Understanding the phenomenon of transference and its impact on the patient-clinician relationship and treatment adherence is a crucial prerequisite for addressing patient discontinuation of treatment.

Clinicians should attend to the patient’s holistic needs, particularly psychological and emotional aspects, and remain sensitive and vigilant to psychological responses such as transference, even when these do not appear to be the immediate focus of treatment, in order to promote continuity of care.

When a patient refuses telephone communication, it may be appropriate to attempt contact through written correspondence, explaining the importance of treatment and expressing willingness to continue providing support or to arrange for referral if needed.

If the patient remains unresponsive, other members of the healthcare team should actively attempt to reach out, coordinating multidisciplinary collaboration to ensure the patient receives necessary medical care.

title: How Should Clinicians Respond to Medical Requests from Clinician Family Members of Patients?
case:
Dr. Rose, a family medicine practitioner, is seeing patients at her outpatient clinic. The nurse, Jack, hands her the chart saying, “Room two is ready. It’s Dr. Little; she brought in her son, Andrew.” Not having had time to look at the chart, Dr. Rose asks, “What was the chief complaint?” Jack responds, “Andrew has back pain.” After taking a few minutes to glance through the rest of the chart, Dr. Rose exits her office, walks down the hall to room two, knocks, pauses, and enters.
Dr. Little—a vascular surgeon at a nearby hospital whose family is part of Dr. Rose’s practice—greets Dr. Rose, “How’s clinic today?” Dr. Rose replies, “Not too bad.” Dr. Rose then turns to Andrew and asks, “What brought you in today?” Andrew says, “I’ve been having back problems for the last several weeks, particularly after wrestling practice.” Dr. Rose locates Andrew’s pain in the lower back and then performs a thorough neurological exam. Finding no evidence of any neurological deficiencies, Dr. Rose states, “This is likely musculoskeletal in nature, I would recommend rest and perhaps some pain killers. If it doesn’t go away in 4-6 weeks, then come back.”
Dr. Little responds, “Would you mind imaging it? An MRI or even a CT would do.”
Dr. Rose replies, “None of the guidelines suggest imaging for this clinical presentation—study after study has shown that it’s not beneficial.”
Dr. Little responds, “I know imaging might not be helpful for the average patient, but it would be helpful just for our peace of mind to know that there’s nothing rare going on.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Rose, a family medicine physician, is seeing patients at her outpatient clinic. The nurse, Jack, approaches her with a chart and says, “Room two is ready. It’s Dr. Little; she’s brought her son, Andrew.” Without having reviewed the chart yet, Dr. Rose asks, “What’s the chief complaint?” Jack replies, “Andrew is experiencing back pain.” Dr. Rose takes a few moments to skim through the chart, then leaves her office, makes her way down the hall, knocks on the door of room two, waits briefly, and enters.

Inside, Dr. Little—a vascular surgeon from a nearby hospital whose family is under Dr. Rose’s care—greets her warmly. “How’s clinic going today?” Dr. Little asks. Dr. Rose answers, “Not too bad.” Turning to Andrew, Dr. Rose inquires, “What brings you in today?” Andrew responds, “I’ve been having back pain for the past several weeks, especially after wrestling practice.” Dr. Rose carefully identifies the pain as being located in Andrew’s lower back and proceeds with a thorough neurological examination. Finding no signs of neurological deficits, Dr. Rose says, “This seems most likely to be a musculoskeletal issue. I’d recommend rest and possibly some pain relievers. If you’re not feeling better in four to six weeks, please come back so we can reassess.”

Dr. Little interjects, “Would you mind ordering some imaging? An MRI or even a CT scan would be great.”

Dr. Rose replies, “Current guidelines don’t recommend imaging for this type of case—there’s a lot of evidence that it doesn’t provide any benefit in situations like this.”

Dr. Little persists, “I understand it might not be necessary for most patients, but it would give us peace of mind to know we’re not missing something rare.”

ethical_issues.question: Should a physician order additional tests in the absence of clinical indications in response to a family member’s anxiety and concerns?
keypoints: Clinicians should respond to the emotional concerns of patients and their families with empathy, engaging in patient and thorough communication to explain clinical judgment and treatment plans, thereby fostering understanding and trust.

Clinicians should provide professional recommendations based on clinical assessment and evidence-based guidelines, and avoid arranging additional investigations solely in response to the anxiety of patients or their family members.

Ordering non-indicated tests in the absence of clinical indications may not serve the patient’s best interests and can lead to unnecessary medical risks, potential adverse effects, and waste of healthcare resources.

Arranging investigations solely due to the concerns or emotional distress of patients or their families may undermine the scientific rigor and standardization of medical decision-making, set a negative precedent, and should be avoided.

Conservative management should be maintained, with a clear follow-up plan; if symptoms persist or worsen, appropriate imaging studies may then be considered, thus balancing clinical judgment with patient needs.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians manage potential conflicts of interest and the impact on professional relationships when providing care to colleagues or their family members?
keypoints: Providing medical care to colleagues or their family members requires particular caution, as potential referral interests may create conflicts of interest that could influence clinical decision-making and professional relationships.
Physicians should offer professional recommendations based on objective clinical assessment, respecting patient autonomy, but should not order non-indicated tests due to relational pressures.

A negotiated compromise may be considered, such as initiating conservative management and only considering imaging studies if symptoms persist or worsen, thereby balancing clinical guidelines with patient concerns.

If the patient or clinician-colleague continues to have doubts, the option of a second opinion should be offered, with a commitment to ongoing follow-up of the patient’s condition and test results, maintaining professional and patient-centered communication.

Physicians should proactively uphold transparency and trust in the patient-physician relationship, avoid allowing professional relationships to affect the quality of care, and ensure that the patient’s best interests remain the priority.

title: Do Physicians Have an Ethical Duty to Repair Relationships with So-Called “Difficult” Patients?
case:
John is a third-year medical student on his first day with a new service during his surgery rotation. On this particular morning, John is going on rounds with the chief resident, Dr. M, and an intern, Dr. S. As the team walks down the hall to the next room, John quickly glances over his rounding sheet for a 48-year-old man, Mr. C. Mr. C had a toe amputation three days ago and suffers from chronic pain and diabetes mellitus type I. He also has a history of using opioids, and his pain medications are being carefully controlled in the hospital.
Before they enter the room, the intern Dr. S softly says to Dr. M, “Hey, just as a heads up, I heard this one was feisty last night. Apparently, the attending physician came down hard on his request for more analgesia. The patient was not happy with the refusal and gave the nursing staff a lot of trouble.” Dr. M responded, “I heard about that. But he’s always been difficult; I saw him in clinic last month.” The team then enters the room.
As Dr. M begins questioning Mr. C, “How are you doing this morning?” Mr. C starts to moan in pain and offers short responses. Dr. M concludes his questions, “Now we’re going to take a look at the toe.” Mr. C begins shouting in pain as John and Dr. S remove the bandages. “Please stop!” he moans. Dr. M tries to soothe him, “I promise we’ll give you more for the pain; I’ll talk to your nurse when we leave. But right now, we need to get this off and take a look at the surgical site.” Mr. C retorts, “You’ve never taken care of my pain! I’ve been asking for help every day, but you don’t listen!”
When John rips open the packet of gauze to apply a new dressing, Mr. C angrily states, “I don’t want to be touched, poked, or prodded anymore.” John and Dr. S pause, bandage in hand, waiting for instructions from Dr. M.
Dr. M responds, “We’re trying to help you, but we need you to work with us.” Mr. C flatly refuses and shouts, “Nobody cares about my pain—you have no idea what I’ve been through.”
Dr. M silently stares for a few seconds at Mr. C who whimpers quietly. Dr. M turns his gaze from Mr. C to Dr. S, mutters “Let’s go—don’t worry about the bandage,” and walks out of the room. John wonders what to do with the bandage he’s holding and how to respond to Mr. C.
case_rewrite:
John, a third-year medical student, was beginning his first day on a new surgical service. Early that morning, he joined the team for rounds: the chief resident, Dr. M, led the group, accompanied by the intern, Dr. S. As they made their way down the hospital corridor toward the next patient, John quickly reviewed his notes for Mr. C, a 48-year-old man who had undergone a toe amputation three days prior. Mr. C suffered from chronic pain and type I diabetes, and his opioid use history meant his analgesia was being closely monitored during his stay.

Just before entering the room, Dr. S leaned over to Dr. M and spoke in a low voice, “Just so you know, he gave the staff a tough time last night. The attending was strict about not giving him extra pain meds, and after being denied, he became really upset with the nurses.” Dr. M nodded, replying, “I heard something about that. He’s always been a handful—I saw him last month in clinic.” With that, the team stepped inside.

Dr. M addressed Mr. C, “How are you feeling this morning?” Mr. C responded with a groan, his words short and strained by pain. After a few questions, Dr. M said, “We’re going to check your toe now.” As John and Dr. S began to remove the bandages, Mr. C cried out, “Please stop!” Dr. M tried to reassure him, “I know it hurts. I’ll talk to your nurse after this and make sure you get something more for the pain. But right now, it’s important for us to see how your surgical site is healing.” Mr. C shot back, “You keep saying that, but you never manage my pain! I’ve asked for help over and over, but no one listens!”

With the new gauze packet in hand, John prepared to redress the wound. Suddenly, Mr. C snapped, “Don’t touch me anymore. I’m done being poked and prodded.” John and Dr. S froze, uncertain, still holding the bandage and waiting for Dr. M’s direction.

Dr. M responded, “We’re here to help you, but we need your cooperation.” Mr. C, visibly frustrated and hurt, shouted, “None of you care about my pain! You can’t possibly understand what I’m going through.”

For a moment, Dr. M silently regarded Mr. C, who now whimpered softly, curled up on the bed. Then, turning to Dr. S, Dr. M muttered, “Let’s go—leave the bandage,” and led the team out of the room. Left standing in the doorway, John hesitated, unsure what to do with the gauze still in his hand, and uncertain how to respond to Mr. C’s distress.

ethical_issues.question: Do physicians have an ethical obligation to repair a fractured relationship with a patient, even if the patient is, in some sense, responsible for the breakdown?
keypoints: Physicians have an ethical responsibility to treat patients, which arises both from their professional obligations and from patients’ fundamental right to receive medical care.

The ethical duty to treat should be understood as including the obligation to repair patient-physician relationships that threaten patient health, and this obligation is as important as providing any other necessary medical intervention.
Even when patients are in some sense “responsible” for their illness or for the breakdown of the relationship, physicians still have a continuing duty to treat and to repair the relationship.

The weight of responsibility for repairing the patient-physician relationship depends on each party’s capacity to do so; since physicians generally possess greater power and resources by virtue of their professional status, they bear greater responsibility for repair.
Physicians should avoid allowing moral judgment or personal bias to undermine their compassion and care for patients, thereby upholding the essence of medicine—compassion and respect for the patient.

ethical_issues.question: In pain management, how can physicians ensure that their own biases and cognitive errors do not undermine the therapeutic alliance, especially when patients’ reports of pain are called into question?
keypoints: Physicians should recognize that their own biases and cognitive distortions may influence their assessment of patients’ subjective experiences such as pain, and should avoid allowing these biases to undermine the therapeutic alliance.

Clinicians should adopt the default position that patients’ subjective reports of pain are genuine and credible, actively listen, and take responsibility for gathering evidence to rule out alternative motives for patient behavior.

A patient’s history of substance use or certain behavioral expressions alone are insufficient to discount the legitimacy of their pain experience; physicians should avoid using negatively charged labels such as “difficult” or “drug-seeking.”

Physicians should respond to patients’ expressions of pain with empathy, communicate clinical challenges transparently, and actively collaborate with patients to develop individualized pain management plans.

The medical team should remain vigilant about the impact of language and attitudes on patients’ sense of empowerment and the patient-physician relationship, and avoid treatment errors and relational breakdowns caused by bias.

title: When and How Should Clinicians Share Details from a Health Record with Patients with Mental Illness?
case:
Dr. Kelly, a psychiatrist, has been seeing Maya, a 36-year-old woman, for management of a personality disorder for several years. Based on her symptom profile, Dr. Kelly has diagnosed her with borderline personality disorder. He has noted her fragile self-image, volatility, and frequent displays of anger, intense paranoia, unstable relationships, substance abuse, and serious threats of self-injury as well as suicidal ideation. Despite the difficulties in caring for a patient with a personality disorder, Dr. Kelly has managed to develop a working relationship with Maya using psychodynamic psychotherapy.
One day after a session that was a bit awkward, Maya—who had recently met with a friend who had suffered a medical error in an emergency department—became suspicious of Dr. Kelly and requested access to her health record in order to see what had been written about her.
Dr. Kelly worries that if Maya sees her record, it will disrupt all the progress she has made so far in identifying perceptual distortions and developing healthier modes of perception and response. In the past, he has written in his notes about how Maya can be “manipulative,” is an “addict,” and has several “failed relationships.” He worries that Maya’s already fragile self-image could be further damaged after reviewing her record and wonders what to do.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Kelly, a psychiatrist, has been working with Maya, a 36-year-old woman, for several years in the management of her personality disorder. After careful assessment of her symptoms—including a fragile sense of self, emotional volatility, frequent expressions of anger, episodes of intense paranoia, unstable interpersonal relationships, substance misuse, and recurrent threats of self-harm and suicidal thoughts—Dr. Kelly has diagnosed Maya with borderline personality disorder. Treating Maya has presented significant challenges, but through ongoing psychodynamic psychotherapy, Dr. Kelly has succeeded in building a functional therapeutic alliance with her.

During a recent session, which felt somewhat tense, Maya appeared noticeably unsettled. She had recently met with a friend who had suffered harm due to a medical error in an emergency department, which led Maya to become wary and distrustful of Dr. Kelly’s intentions. Following the session, Maya approached Dr. Kelly and requested access to her health record, expressing a desire to see exactly what had been documented about her.

Dr. Kelly now faces a dilemma. He is concerned that allowing Maya to review her record could undermine the progress she has made in recognizing and modifying her perceptual distortions and in developing healthier interpersonal responses. In his notes, Dr. Kelly has described Maya at times as “manipulative,” referred to her as an “addict,” and commented on her “failed relationships.” He worries that encountering these terms could further erode Maya’s already delicate self-image, potentially leading to a setback in her treatment. With these concerns in mind, Dr. Kelly must consider how best to proceed.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians use neutral language in the health records of patients with mental illness to avoid stigmatizing effects?
keypoints: Clinicians should employ nonjudgmental, fact-based, and objective descriptive language while maintaining diagnostic accuracy, avoiding subjective judgments or pejorative labels in order to minimize negative impacts on patients’ self-perception.

Descriptive language should serve as objective substantiation for the diagnosis, which itself must be clearly documented using authoritative and current standard terminology such as that of the DSM, thereby ensuring the professionalism and accuracy of the medical record.

The use of neutral and sensitive language not only helps protect patients’ rights and interests, but also reduces clinician bias arising from clinical buzzwords, prevents premature diagnostic conclusions, and ultimately enhances the overall quality of care.

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances should psychiatrists allow patients with mental illness to access their own health records in order to avoid causing harm to the patient?
keypoints: Clinicians should rationally assess the patient’s motivation for accessing their health record, including what information the patient hopes to obtain and any concerns they may have about the potential content.

The patient’s clinical status and therapeutic alliance should be evaluated; patients who are clinically stable and have established a strong therapeutic relationship with their clinician are at lower risk of adverse effects from reviewing their records.

The timing of disclosure should be chosen with caution; patients experiencing acute psychotic episodes should not access their records, and it is advisable to wait until clinical stability has been achieved.

The method of record review should be determined collaboratively by both clinician and patient, weighing whether independent review or review in the presence of the clinician would be more therapeutic and conducive to understanding.

The scope of information shared should be reasonably limited according to the patient’s specific objectives for accessing the record, avoiding disclosure of sensitive information that could exacerbate negative cognitions.
Timely sharing and discussion of record content during the course of treatment should be encouraged to facilitate immediate clarification and strengthen the therapeutic alliance.

ethical_issues.question: In the process of increasing transparency of psychiatric health records, how should clinicians assess the patient’s motivation, timing, context, and scope for accessing their records in order to ensure the quality of care and respect for patient autonomy?
keypoints: Clinicians should rationally assess the patient’s motivation for reviewing their health record, including what information the patient hopes to obtain and any concerns they may have about the potential content.
The timing of disclosure should be based on the patient’s psychiatric stability, avoiding record review during acute episodes or periods of extreme emotional fluctuation.

The patient and clinician should jointly determine the context and manner of record review (for example, reviewing the record together during a clinical encounter) in order to maximize therapeutic value and facilitate immediate communication and clarification.

Based on the patient’s specific goals for accessing the record, the clinician should appropriately delineate the scope of information shared; for instance, if the patient seeks only to understand the basis for a diagnosis, a case summary or selected portions of the record may be provided.

Allowing patients to participate in real-time review and collaborative creation of their health record—by discussing and correcting inaccuracies or misunderstandings—can promote patient autonomy, informed decision-making, and therapeutic collaboration.

title: Why It’s Unjust to Expect Location-Specific, Language-Specific, or Population-Specific Service from Students with Underrepresented Minority or Low-Income Backgrounds
case:
Amanda is a second-year medical student at a private Midwestern medical school, which she is able to attend thanks to an institutional scholarship and federal financial aid. She has been seriously engaged with campaigns on campus for health equity and social justice in the community and in the country at large. Amanda grew up in a family with mixed Native American and Latin American roots and was a first-generation college graduate in her family; thus, issues of access to education and health care are very important to her.
Amanda grew up speaking Spanish fluently and studied medical Chinese in her first year of medical school. She has used her language skills in a medical student-run clinic that provides free basic clinical services to those with limited English proficiency (LEP), which includes Spanish and Chinese speakers. As a second-year medical student, she has begun thinking about clinical years and plans for a successful residency match. During her recent visit with her family over Christmas, her parents and maternal grandmother expressed their pride in her accomplishments and their desire that she match into a competitive specialty and residency program.
At school, she is having a discussion with friends about their current career interests. When she expresses her anxieties about what it takes to match into a competitive specialty in an elite residency program, her friends express surprise. “I thought since you were so passionate about social justice, you’d be more interested in working with minority populations back home.” Others concur and express the opinion that, as someone with the cultural competencies and language skills to work with immigrants in her home state, she has a responsibility to utilize her skills for LEP populations. She wonders what to say.
case_rewrite:
Amanda, a second-year medical student at a private medical school in the Midwest, attends on the strength of both an institutional scholarship and federal financial aid. Deeply committed to health equity and social justice, Amanda has become an active voice in campus movements for accessible healthcare and education, both locally and nationally. Her personal history—growing up in a family with mixed Native American and Latin American heritage and being the first in her family to graduate from college—has made these issues profoundly important to her.

Fluent in Spanish from childhood, Amanda also began learning medical Chinese during her first year of medical school. She often puts these language skills to use at a student-run clinic that offers free basic healthcare to individuals with limited English proficiency, serving both Spanish- and Chinese-speaking patients. Now, as she looks ahead to her clinical years and starts considering her options for residency, Amanda feels the weight of future decisions. During a recent holiday visit, her parents and maternal grandmother expressed their pride in her progress and their strong hope that she will match into a highly competitive specialty and residency program.

Back at school, Amanda finds herself engaged in a conversation with friends about their career plans and aspirations. She shares her anxiety about the challenges of matching into a top-tier specialty at a prestigious residency. Her friends express surprise, with one remarking, “Given how passionate you are about social justice, I thought you’d want to work with minority communities back home.” Others agree, suggesting that, because of her cultural background and language abilities, Amanda has a responsibility to use her skills for the benefit of immigrant and LEP populations in her home state. As Amanda listens, she is left wondering how to respond to these expectations.

ethical_issues.question: What criteria should be used to assess the fairness of expecting students or graduates from underrepresented minority or low-income backgrounds to provide location-specific, language-specific, or population-specific service?
keypoints: It is unjust to require students from underrepresented minority (URM) backgrounds to serve specific regions or populations, as this is based on differential expectations arising from their disadvantaged status.
Presuming that minority students are better suited for particular career paths due to their ethnic, cultural, or language abilities—and thereby restricting their autonomy—constitutes an unfair bias.
This bias-driven burden of expectation can become institutionalized, systematically limiting URM students’ career development and capacity to envision diverse professional futures.
All medical professionals share a responsibility to serve diverse patient populations; this obligation should not be uniquely imposed on minority students.
When assessing the fairness of service expectations for medical students, institutions should universally ask, “If not me, then who?” to prevent inequitable distribution of responsibility.

ethical_issues.question: Should students from underrepresented minority backgrounds be expected to follow specific career paths based on their ethnicity, culture, or language abilities?
keypoints: It is unjust to require students from underrepresented minority (URM) backgrounds to follow specific career pathways based on their ethnicity, culture, or language abilities, as such expectations are grounded in stereotypical assumptions about their suitability for certain service domains.

The concept of the “burden of expectation” highlights the responsibilities imposed on URM students regarding specialty choice, type of practice, patient population, and practice location—responsibilities that both reflect and reinforce implicit biases.

Implicit biases are subtly formed through medical education and socialization processes, resulting in constraints on URM students’ professional development and diminishing their capacity for self-determination and upward mobility.

Medical professional ethics emphasize that all healthcare practitioners have a responsibility to serve diverse patient populations, and it is unjust to unfairly place the responsibility of serving specific groups solely on URM students.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical schools challenge and change the disproportionate burden of expectation placed on students from underrepresented minority groups in order to promote equity in career development?
keypoints: Discussions of ethical dilemmas often overlook the profound impact of structural conditions on the career choices and expectations of students from underrepresented minority groups.

Scholarship and financial aid systems not only support the enrollment of underrepresented minority students, but are also leveraged to enhance institutional diversity metrics and the image of social responsibility, reflecting institutional interests.
Imposing differentiated service expectations on students based on their ethnic or linguistic backgrounds effectively increases the unfair burden of expectation on underrepresented minority students.

The presumption that underrepresented minority students are better suited for certain specialties or career paths due to cultural or language advantages neglects individual diversity and constitutes a form of structural bias in professional development.
Such biases and burdens of expectation constrain the professional imagination and upward mobility of underrepresented minority students, impeding their pursuit of diverse career goals.

The core ethical principle of the medical profession is to serve diverse patient populations; expectations of service to any single ethnic group or community should not become a compulsory obligation for underrepresented minority students.

Medical schools should promote institutional and cultural change to challenge and eliminate disproportionate service expectations placed on underrepresented minority students, thereby fostering fairness and autonomy in professional development.

When assessing the fairness of service expectations for medical students, all members should be encouraged to ask themselves, “If not me, then who?” so as to strengthen a sense of shared responsibility and avoid unjustly concentrating obligations on underrepresented minority students.

title: Clinicians’ Obligations to Use Qualified Medical Interpreters When Caring for Patients with Limited English Proficiency
case: Shiv is a fourth-year medical student hoping to match into dermatology. He knows what program he wants to rank as his top choice and is currently doing a month-long, hospital-based dermatology rotation. He is excited to get additional exposure to a field he genuinely enjoys, and naturally he also feels pressure to do well. One morning while Shiv is rotating with a couple of residents, the attending physician wants to demonstrate some skin findings on a patient, a Haitian woman with an immunologic condition who has limited English proficiency. The attending physician briefly explains, in English, to her and the residents what they will be looking for. As she is giving a hesitant nod to his request, he abruptly pulls down her hospital gown exposing her breasts. She seems to be acutely uncomfortable, her eyes widen, and her arms remain paralyzed at her sides. She doesn’t say anything. Having spent a year working on tuberculosis (TB) in Haiti, Shiv happens to speak Haitian Creole and, sensing her discomfort, asks her in Creole if she is OK and explains that it is a teaching session. This seems to calm her somewhat. The attending physician chides Shiv for carrying on a conversation with the patient that the rest of the group can’t understand and accuses him of detracting attention from his teaching time. Shiv wonders how to respond.
case_rewrite:
Shiv, a fourth-year medical student with ambitions to match into dermatology, is currently completing a month-long dermatology rotation at a hospital. Deeply passionate about the field and eager to make a strong impression on the faculty of his preferred residency program, Shiv approaches each day with enthusiasm. One morning, Shiv joins two residents to round with Dr. W, the attending physician overseeing their rotation. Dr. W announces his intention to demonstrate certain dermatologic findings to the group, selecting as his subject a Haitian woman admitted with an immunologic disorder. The patient speaks little English and appears somewhat anxious as the team enters her room.

Dr. W addresses both the patient and the residents in English, briefly explaining his plan for the examination. The patient, not seeming to fully understand, offers a hesitant nod in response. Without seeking further clarification or pause, Dr. W proceeds to pull down the patient’s hospital gown, exposing her breasts to those present. The woman’s body tenses; her eyes widen with visible discomfort, and her arms remain stiffly at her sides. She does not utter a word.

Shiv, who previously spent a year in Haiti working on tuberculosis projects and is attentive to cultural and language barriers, observes the interaction closely.

ethical_issues.question: Is it necessary to obtain informed consent from patients with limited English proficiency through a qualified medical interpreter prior to performing an invasive examination?
keypoints: Invasive examinations require obtaining the patient’s informed consent, even if a formal written process is not used.

The attending physician must obtain valid informed consent from patients with limited English proficiency (LEP) through a qualified medical interpreter; failure to do so seriously undermines patient autonomy and poses significant risks of error.
Patients with LEP have a legal right to access health care services in their preferred language, ensuring the accuracy and effectiveness of medical communication.

ethical_issues.question: Do clinicians have an obligation to use qualified medical interpreters to ensure effective communication when providing care to patients with limited English proficiency?
keypoints: Clinicians have legal and ethical obligations to ensure effective communication and quality of care for patients with limited English proficiency by utilizing qualified medical interpreters.

According to Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, patients with limited English proficiency have the right to access language services; clinicians must not discriminate on the basis of language barriers and are required to use qualified interpreters to safeguard patients’ rights.

The absence of qualified medical interpreters can result in ineffective informed consent, increased risk of medical errors, and potential tort liability, thereby exposing health care professionals to civil responsibility.

The use of ad hoc interpreters—such as patients’ friends or family members, or untrained bilingual staff—should be avoided, as they lack professional training and significantly increase the risk of communication errors and adverse medical outcomes.

The use of professional, qualified interpreters enhances comprehension, health care utilization, clinical outcomes, and patient satisfaction for individuals with limited English proficiency, and is an essential requirement for providing appropriate medical care.
