title: Who Should Ration?
case: Mr. J is a 58-year-old black man who has been mostly homeless for the past eight years. He has a number of chronic medical conditions of which end-stage renal failure is his most critical. He has been receiving hemodialysis for six years. Because he does not have health insurance and is not eligible for Medicaid in the state in which he resides, Medicare covers many of the costs associated with care for his kidney disease under the end-stage renal disease benefit. Mr. J is not a known substance abuser but does have significant mental health issues and has preferred to live on the streets rather than in the shelters and the halfway houses to which he has been assigned. He has also proved to be unable to maintain a relationship with outpatient dialysis centers, despite multiple attempts and interventions by social services. He is an ultra-frequent visitor to the university hospital emergency department (ED), with up to ten visits a week in the cold winter months. Most of his dialysis is administered there or at the hospital’s inpatient dialysis facility. Not surprisingly, his erratic care and his lifestyle have contributed to a slow deterioration in his overall condition. The physicians who see him most often—ED physicians and hospitalists—believe that further provision of dialysis is a waste of hospital and national resources (and their time); they believe that Mr. J is incorrigible and is “using” them and the system for his own purposes. They wish to unilaterally stop treatment and switch him to hospice care, even though Mr. J retains decision-making capacity and expresses a desire to continue living as he has been doing. Should the physicians be able to limit his access to specific kinds of care by appeals to his excess consumption of resources they believe to be in short supply?
case_rewrite:
Mr. J is a 58-year-old Black man who has spent most of the past eight years without stable housing. He suffers from several chronic medical conditions, the most severe of which is end-stage renal failure. For the past six years, he has been dependent on hemodialysis. Because he lacks health insurance and does not qualify for Medicaid in his state, Medicare covers a significant portion of the expenses related to his kidney disease through the end-stage renal disease benefit. Mr. J is not known to use substances, but he does have major mental health challenges, and he prefers living on the streets over staying in shelters or halfway houses assigned to him. Despite repeated interventions and support from social services, he has not been able to sustain a relationship with outpatient dialysis centers.

During the winter, Mr. J is a frequent presence in the university hospital emergency department (ED), sometimes presenting as often as ten times a week. Most of his dialysis treatments are carried out either in the ED or in the hospital’s inpatient dialysis facility. His irregular access to care and his lifestyle have contributed to a gradual decline in his overall health. The physicians who interact with him most often—ED doctors and hospitalists—have grown increasingly frustrated, feeling that continuing his dialysis is a misuse of hospital and national resources, as well as their time. They believe Mr. J is intentionally manipulating the system to serve his own needs. Some of these physicians are now advocating to discontinue his dialysis and transition him to hospice care, even though Mr. J remains mentally capable of making decisions about his own treatment and clearly states his wish to continue living as he has.

This situation raises the ethical question: should physicians have the authority to restrict Mr. J’s access to specific medical services based on their perception that he is consuming an excessive share of scarce resources?

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians be permitted to limit a patient’s access to specific medical services on the grounds of excessive resource consumption?
keypoints: Physicians should not restrict patients’ access to medical services on the grounds of resource consumption, as individualized bedside rationing is susceptible to bias and arbitrary judgments, thereby undermining patient interests and violating professional ethics.

Refusing to provide dialysis for Mr. J does not guarantee that the resources saved will be more effectively allocated to others; micro-level resource rationing does not benefit others and may in fact harm individual patients.

The allocation of public resources should be determined through public deliberation and institutionalized mechanisms, rather than by unilateral decisions made privately by hospitals or physicians, in order to ensure fairness and reasonableness in resource distribution.

ethical_issues.question: Is it possible to establish a systematic mechanism to ensure that conserved resources are utilized more effectively, in order to prevent or minimize unauthorized bedside rationing?
keypoints: Unless a systemic mechanism is established to ensure that conserved resources are utilized more effectively, granting physicians unilateral discretionary authority to restrict patients’ access to medical services on the grounds of resource overutilization lacks proper justification.

The fundamental flaw of bedside rationing lies in its inability to guarantee that resources saved from one patient will be better allocated to others; therefore, a fair distribution framework based on individual and group medical needs must be established.
Allocation schemes for public medical resources should be developed through democratic processes and public deliberation, rather than being determined privately by hospitals or individual clinicians.

Regulatory mechanisms such as the MELD score in the national organ transplantation system—which are based on objective clinical indicators and exclude subjective biases and discriminatory factors—should be emulated to construct a transparent and equitable resource allocation system.

Only by excluding personal characteristics irrelevant to clinical outcomes (such as race, gender identity, immigration status, etc.) can limited resources be effectively utilized to provide patients with genuinely beneficial medical options.

Physicians play a critical role in formulating resource allocation policies at the population level, but should not implement unregulated bedside rationing for individual patients on the grounds of resource scarcity.

title: How Should Therapeutic Decisions about Expensive Drugs Be Made in Imperfect Environments?
case:
Dr. C sits on a committee as part of his tertiary care center’s accountable care organization (ACO) that is considering whether a new biologic, Expensivimab, should be included in the organization’s bundled treatment plan for its patients. Expensivimab is a new humanized antibody that targets an apoptotic receptor. One study suggests that it increases tumor-free survival in late stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) by a median of six months relative to a drug approved several years ago. Another suggests that it increases overall survival by a month-and-a half relative to the same drug. Yet no research on the comparative effectiveness of Expensivimab relative to other interventions for NSCLC exists, and even data on the risks of Expensivimab relative to the older drug is scant.
Furthermore, assessing Expensivimab’s cost-benefit ratio is difficult. Although Expensivimab costs $750,000 per patient, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) did not request any data on trial participants’ perceptions of their quality of life. Hence, no assessment of quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) is available to assess the cost-benefit ratio of Expensivimab—either on its own or relative to other interventions.
Dr. C has grown worried about the increasing costs of drug coverage—especially relative to the potential benefits. Containing such costs is especially difficult because the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), which determine whether Medicare will cover a drug and whose decisions many other insurers follow, are legally prohibited from negotiating the prices of such drugs. He worries that unless providers and insurers start to demand evidence regarding quality of life and benefits relative to other available drugs, pharmaceutical companies will have no incentive to investigate Expensivimab. In consequence, assessments of benefit will be only informed by standard clinical parameters such as time-to-mortality and tumor-free survival.
A similar committee at a nearby tertiary center’s ACO decided that the drug was not part of its coverage. Dr. C fears that this only makes his ACO’s decision more politically controversial. A decision to cover the drug would be seen as a disagreement with fellow experts, a message that may be particularly problematic when the precedent for covering oncologic agents has been to cover agents with similar benefits.
While considering how to vote, Dr. C’s thoughts turn to two patients that he recently met. Ms. G is a 68-year-old woman who was just diagnosed with NSCLC. She could benefit from Expensivimab. Mr. J is 71-year-old patient with colorectal cancer who recently started a similar agent that has recently been approved for colorectal cancer and has a benefit profile similar to that of Expensivimab. Mr. J’s drug is very expensive but costs slightly less than Expensivimab. Dr. C worries how he might feel the next time he sees Ms. G or Mr. J, knowing how his vote might affect patients like them. Dr. C considers what to say and how to vote at the upcoming meeting.
case_rewrite:
Dr. C serves on a committee within his tertiary care center’s accountable care organization (ACO, a group responsible for managing both clinical and financial aspects of patient care) that is currently deliberating whether to include a new biologic agent, Expensivimab, in the organization’s bundled treatment plan. Expensivimab is a recently developed humanized antibody targeting an apoptotic receptor. One published study reports that Expensivimab increases tumor-free survival for patients with late-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) by a median of six months compared to a drug approved several years prior. Another study shows an increase in overall survival by about a month and a half over the same comparator. However, no studies have directly compared the effectiveness of Expensivimab with other available NSCLC interventions, and there is little reliable data about the risks of Expensivimab in comparison to the older drug.

Evaluating the cost-benefit profile of Expensivimab is also challenging. The drug is priced at $750,000 per patient, yet the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) did not require data on trial participants’ quality of life. As a result, there is no assessment of quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) available to objectively determine the cost-effectiveness of Expensivimab, either as a standalone treatment or relative to alternatives.

Dr. C is increasingly concerned about rising drug costs, particularly since the clinical benefit of such expensive therapies often appears limited. Efforts to contain these costs are complicated by the fact that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)—which sets the standard for whether Medicare will cover a drug, and whose decisions are often followed by private insurers—are legally prohibited from negotiating drug prices. Dr. C worries that unless providers and insurers begin to demand higher standards of evidence, including measures of quality of life and comparative effectiveness, pharmaceutical companies will have little incentive to pursue such research. Consequently, decisions will continue to rely primarily on traditional clinical outcomes, such as time-to-mortality and tumor-free survival, without a full understanding of the real-world value of these drugs.

Recently, a neighboring tertiary care center's ACO committee decided against covering Expensivimab, which makes Dr. C’s committee’s upcoming decision even more politically sensitive. Approving coverage could be interpreted as a disagreement with peer institutions, especially since the prevailing practice has generally been to approve oncology drugs offering similar benefits.

While weighing his options, Dr. C recalls two patients he has recently treated. Ms. G, a 68-year-old woman newly diagnosed with NSCLC, could potentially benefit from Expensivimab if it were covered. Mr. J, a 71-year-old man with colorectal cancer, has just started on a newly approved, similarly expensive agent for colorectal cancer—one that costs slightly less than Expensivimab and offers a comparable benefit profile. Dr. C is troubled by the thought of how his committee vote will directly impact patients like Ms. G and Mr. J, and he contemplates how he will explain these decisions to them in the future. As the committee meeting approaches, Dr. C reflects on his responsibilities to his patients and to the broader community, considering both what stance to take and what message to convey during the discussion.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr. C and the committee ethically allocate limited healthcare resources to ensure fair and just access to optimal treatment options for patients, given budget constraints and incomplete evidence regarding the benefits and risks of Expensivimab?
keypoints: Physicians must balance the best interests of patients with the constraints of limited social resources, taking into account both fairness and individualized medical decision-making.

Under budgetary constraints, considerations of fairness and justice require reasonable limitations on patients’ expectations for high-cost cancer treatments, while also respecting patients’ values and individual differences.

The ACO committee should evaluate the cost-effectiveness of drugs based on sufficient and transparent scientific evidence, and establish clear coverage criteria to ensure the rational allocation of resources.

Value-based pricing and performance-linked reimbursement mechanisms should be promoted to dynamically align drug prices with actual clinical effectiveness, partially shifting financial risk to pharmaceutical companies.

Physicians have a moral obligation to protect patients from both medical and financial burdens associated with high-cost drugs, and should exercise particular caution when the therapeutic benefit is limited.
Physicians should actively participate in professional organizations to advocate for policy reforms, establish patient protection mechanisms, and promote a more just allocation of social resources.

Physicians should engage in thorough communication with patients to help them understand the social and personal value of medical choices, supporting patients in making informed decisions that align with their own interests.
As both advocates for patient interests and stewards of social resources, physicians bear the dual responsibility of balancing individual welfare with the public good.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the best interests of their patients with the responsible stewardship of social resources when confronted with high-cost, low-benefit drugs?
keypoints: Physicians must safeguard the best interests of cancer patients while prudently managing limited social resources, ensuring that medical expenditures reflect principles of fairness, justice, and cost-effectiveness.

Physicians have a moral obligation to protect patients from the potential medical risks and financial burdens associated with high-cost, low-benefit drugs, and should exercise particular caution when the therapeutic benefits are limited.

Physicians should actively participate in professional organizations to promote policy reforms that establish more robust patient protection mechanisms and rational systems for the allocation of social resources.

Physicians need to engage in open cost-related conversations with patients, assisting them in making informed medical decisions that align with their personal values and consider the broader context of social resource allocation.

Physicians should not passively acquiesce to policy constraints, but rather proactively communicate with policymakers to advocate for reasonable exceptions in specific cases and to challenge guidelines that are unreasonable or inapplicable.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. C and the committee advocate, through their professional organizations, for policy changes that protect patients’ financial interests and promote the cost-effectiveness of cancer treatments such as Expensivimab?
keypoints: Physicians have a moral obligation to protect patients from unnecessary medical and financial harms associated with expensive drugs, especially when such drugs are likely to provide minimal benefit.

Physicians should engage in sensitive conversations with patients to help them understand the potential benefits and financial burdens of treatment, thereby supporting patients in making more prudent financial and therapeutic choices.

Advancing policy change through professional organizations can establish more robust mechanisms for protecting patients’ financial interests, promote cost-effectiveness evaluation in cancer care, and facilitate the just allocation of resources.

Individual physicians have limited capacity to effect policy change, but physician professional organizations, by mustering sufficient political courage, have the potential to achieve positive systemic reforms.

Physicians have a professional duty to communicate with policymakers, to question and provide feedback on the applicability of guidelines in specific cases, and to ensure that therapeutic decisions uphold the principles of fairness, just allocation, and the maximization of patient welfare.

title: Polarities in Clinical Thinking and Practice
case:
Dr. Jones sees a new patient, Mr. Thompson, a 68-year-old man in her outpatient, primary care clinic today. In reviewing his intake forms, Dr. Jones sees that Mr. Thompson scored 18 points on the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), suggesting “moderately severe depression.” When she asks Mr. Thompson about how he is feeling, he tells her that his wife died three weeks ago but that he did not want to tell Dr. Jones about this because he did not want to trouble her.
In further talking to Mr. Thompson, Dr. Jones discovers that he has lost appetite, interest in his activities, and the ability to concentrate at work. He feels tired yet has had trouble falling and staying asleep. Finally, family and friends tell him that he seems a little “distracted” or slower lately. Dr. Jones asks whether Mr. Thompson has thought of hurting himself, and Mr. Thompson says no. She also asks if he owns a gun, and he says no.
Dr. Jones begins to consider how to diagnose and treat Mr. Thompson. She knows that recent changes to theDiagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders(DSM) regarding bereavement have caused significant debate among her psychiatric colleagues. She often refers psychiatric patients to either Dr. Taylor or Dr. Martinez, who seem to have very different stances on the issue as she learned on discussions during recent consults. Dr. Taylor worries that theDSM-5is medicalizing normal grief even more than previous editions had: “Researchers find that grieving people typically yearn for their loved ones roughly every other day at one year after losing them, but the newDSMwill lead many to label such people diseased.” He prefers to attentively watch such patients to see how their symptoms progress over time. Dr. Martinez shares Dr. Taylor’s worry about overmedicalization and “false positive” diagnoses but believes that, generally, clinicians should initiate treatment of possible depression if the symptoms are severe enough: “It’s entirely normal for one’s connective tissue to sever under blunt force trauma and for one’s body to react with fever and other symptoms to a viral invasion. It is easier to distinguish such dysfunction with ‘normal compensation’ in physical medicine from ‘normal function.’ Yet, in psychiatry, it is difficult to distinguish dysfunction with normal compensation from a ‘problem of living.’”
On the one hand, Dr. Jones feels that if she refers to Dr. Taylor, Mr. Thompson will receive watchful waiting, but she is concerned that his insurer will fight against reimbursement without a diagnosis. On the other hand, she is worried that a referral to Dr. Martinez will result in treatment with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) that is unnecessary and that Mr. Thompson may come to see himself as diseased rather than normal. Hence, she feels that her choice will ultimately determine Mr. Thompson’s diagnosis and treatment. She is unsure of what to do.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Jones is seeing a new patient in her outpatient primary care clinic today: Mr. Thompson, a 68-year-old man. As she reviews his intake paperwork, Dr. Jones notes that Mr. Thompson has scored 18 on the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), which points to “moderately severe depression.” During their conversation, Dr. Jones asks Mr. Thompson how he has been feeling lately. He hesitates before sharing that his wife passed away three weeks ago. He admits that he originally didn’t want to mention it, not wanting to burden Dr. Jones.

As their discussion continues, Dr. Jones learns more about Mr. Thompson’s struggles. He describes a loss of appetite, a diminished interest in his usual activities, and difficulty concentrating at work. He feels persistently tired, but nonetheless has trouble both falling asleep and staying asleep. Family and friends have told him he seems more distracted and slower than usual. When Dr. Jones asks directly if Mr. Thompson has considered harming himself, he responds no. She inquires about gun ownership, and he says he does not own any firearms.

Faced with these symptoms, Dr. Jones starts to consider how best to diagnose and treat Mr. Thompson. She is mindful of recent changes in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) regarding bereavement, which have sparked considerable debate among her psychiatric colleagues. When she refers patients for psychiatric input, she often chooses between Dr. Taylor and Dr. Martinez, both of whom have expressed markedly different views on the subject in recent consults.

Dr. Taylor is concerned that the DSM-5 is pathologizing normal grief to an even greater extent than before. He often remarks, “Researchers have found that it’s typical for people to yearn for their loved ones every other day, even a year after the loss, but the new DSM criteria risk labeling many such people as diseased.” Dr. Taylor prefers to observe bereaved patients carefully, monitoring how their symptoms evolve over time before making a formal diagnosis.

Dr. Martinez, while sharing Dr. Taylor’s concerns about overmedicalization and the risk of “false positive” diagnoses, generally believes that clinicians should start treatment when depressive symptoms are severe. As she puts it, “It’s entirely normal for connective tissue to tear under trauma, or for the body to react with a fever to a virus. In physical medicine, it’s easier to distinguish normal compensation from dysfunction. In psychiatry, though, it’s much harder to separate dysfunction with normal compensation from a simple ‘problem of living.’”

Dr. Jones now faces a dilemma. If she refers Mr. Thompson to Dr. Taylor, he is likely to be placed under watchful waiting, but Dr. Jones is concerned that the lack of a formal diagnosis might create challenges with his insurance coverage. Conversely, if she refers him to Dr. Martinez, Mr. Thompson may be started on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and come to view himself as having a disease when perhaps he is experiencing a normal grief reaction. Dr. Jones realizes that her referral decision could significantly influence both Mr. Thompson’s diagnosis and his treatment course. She finds herself uncertain about the best path forward.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with the boundary between normal bereavement and pathological depression in patients, how should clinicians balance diagnostic accuracy with their ethical responsibility to avoid overmedicalization?
keypoints: Clinicians should avoid framing the distinction between normal grief and pathological depression as a false dichotomy; diagnosis is merely the starting point for exploring the patient’s condition.

Even if the patient meets DSM-5 criteria for a major depressive episode, physicians must critically assess the clinical utility of the diagnosis, integrating the patient’s individual presentation and specific context.

In the process of diagnosis and treatment, physicians should give full consideration to the patient’s personal values, sociocultural background, and means of healthcare payment, thereby avoiding hasty decision-making.

Physicians should engage in open communication and shared decision making with the patient, discussing possible diagnoses and treatment options, and iteratively testing and revising initial assessments through a series of outpatient follow-ups.

ethical_issues.question: How should a primary care physician make an ethical decision between respecting the patient’s preferences and ensuring that the patient receives appropriate treatment when considering whether to refer a patient to a psychiatric specialist?
keypoints: The primary care physician’s foremost responsibility is to ensure that the patient receives appropriate care, which should take precedence over external considerations such as insurance reimbursement.

Physicians should avoid reductionist “either/or” thinking and, through shared decision making with the patient, respect the patient’s role as an “expert by experience” regarding their own health, exploring a range of therapeutic options.
Physicians should engage in thorough communication with the patient, soliciting and understanding the patient’s preferences and values in order to facilitate consensus between both parties.

Physicians are not required to make an immediate referral decision at the initial consultation; instead, they should reserve time to discuss available options with the patient and arrange timely follow-up visits for ongoing assessment.

Regardless of whether a referral is made, the primary care physician should continue to personally monitor the patient’s condition, thereby preventing potential over-intervention or neglect in psychiatric consultation and embodying the core values of primary care.

title: What to Do When There Aren’t Enough Beds in the PICU
case:
Dr. A, the attending physician on the pediatric surgical team, calls the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) to schedule a patient with mitral valve stenosis for admission to the pediatric intensive care unit for monitoring during the surgical stay. The director of the PICU, Dr. L, tells Dr. A that she will have to get back to him about availability because beds are fully occupied.
Dr. L and Dr. A admit to each other being greatly frustrated that this problem has arisen multiple times in the past few years. Dr. L tells Dr. A that a number of patients have been in PICU beds for exceptionally long periods with little chance of recovery and that this has meant that a number of surgeries have been delayed and that a number of nonsurgical cases have been transferred to other facilities. They agree to request an ethics consultation.
At the time of the request, Dr. L expressed her concerns to an ethics consultant that care being provided to long-time PICU patients was often futile, constituted inappropriate uses of clinical resources, and violated clinicians’ professional autonomy. The ethics consultant wondered what constitutes futility and how many PICU patients’ care was futile, and suggested that some of these cases were ones in which “bedside rationing” might be appropriate. At this point, Dr. L became concerned that if long-term care was not futile—if some patients might still benefit from intensive care—then if the hospital and its staff did not provide such care they would be failing to do their best for the patients and might be failing in their professional obligations. However, Dr. L was not sure she felt comfortable creating a rule that forced her PICU staff to withhold potential benefits from particular patients—even if those benefits were slight. Although she thought this was generally sensible, she was not sure that her role was to make other clinicians act this way in all cases.
The consultant suggested that deliberation upon these cases could be helpful and suggested that a larger group of stakeholders from the hospital be convened with the full ethics committee to draft a PICU policy that would address two elements: (1) guidelines regarding PICU admissions decision making and for establishing a PICU care discontinuation protocol; and (2) guidelines for how such decisions would be made and implemented, who would be involved in such decisions, and how those affected by the decisions—including caregivers, patients, and their families—would be notified. A time for deliberation on these two issues was scheduled.
Dr. A now plans to call his patient and family to deliver the news that they will have to wait until a bed is available. She worries about how she can justify the delay to them and wonders what to say.
case_rewrite:
Dr. A, the attending physician on the pediatric surgical team, contacts the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) to arrange for admission of a patient with mitral valve stenosis, needing close monitoring throughout the surgical stay. The director of the PICU, Dr. L, responds that she will need some time to check on bed availability, as all beds are currently occupied.

Both Dr. L and Dr. A acknowledge their shared frustration with this recurring problem, noting that they have grappled with similar situations several times over the past few years. Dr. L confides in Dr. A that a significant number of patients have been occupying PICU beds for extended periods, with little realistic chance of recovery. As a consequence, several surgeries have been postponed, and some nonsurgical cases have required transfer to other institutions. Together, they decide to seek an ethics consultation.

When the ethics consultant arrives, Dr. L expresses her deep concern that the ongoing care of long-term PICU patients often seems futile, represents an inappropriate use of limited clinical resources, and undermines the professional autonomy of clinicians. The ethics consultant raises the question of what precisely constitutes futility and wonders how many current PICU patients are actually receiving futile care. He suggests that, in such situations, “bedside rationing” might sometimes be justified. This suggestion gives Dr. L pause; she worries that if even minimal benefits from intensive care remain possible, then withholding such care might mean failing the patients and falling short of professional responsibilities. Dr. L is uncertain about implementing a policy that would compel her PICU staff to deny possible benefits to certain patients, even if those benefits are minor. While she sees the rationale, she is unsure whether it is her role to require other clinicians to act this way in every scenario.

The ethics consultant recommends that these complex cases be discussed more broadly. He proposes convening a larger group of hospital stakeholders and the full ethics committee to develop a comprehensive PICU policy. This policy would address two main elements: (1) clear guidelines for PICU admissions and protocols for discontinuing PICU care; and (2) structured processes for making and implementing these decisions, specifying who would be involved and how those affected—including caregivers, patients, and families—would be informed. A meeting is scheduled to deliberate these issues.

Meanwhile, Dr. A prepares to call her patient and family to explain that there will be a delay in their admission until a PICU bed becomes available. She is anxious about how best to justify the postponement and what exactly she should say to help them understand the situation.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of limited PICU bed availability, how should futile treatments be appropriately defined and managed in order to free up bed resources?
keypoints: Futile treatment should be strictly limited to the physiological domain, that is, when a treatment cannot achieve its intended biological goal; withholding or withdrawing such treatment has a strong foundation in bioethics.

For treatments that are not physiologically futile but potentially inappropriate, a multistep dispute resolution process should be employed, involving clinicians, patients and their families, and ethics consultants to collaboratively resolve disagreements between the medical team and the patient.

A systematic PICU policy should be developed to clearly define admission decision-making criteria, protocols for discontinuation of treatment, decision-making processes, the parties involved, and mechanisms for communication and notification of affected stakeholders.

ethical_issues.question: How can resources be allocated fairly under conditions of scarcity to ensure the best interests of patients?
keypoints: Rationing decisions under conditions of limited resources should be as objective as possible, adhering to recognized principles of allocation in order to maximize medical benefit.

Criteria for rationing should be based not only on medical facts, but also on a comprehensive consideration of societal consensus regarding the allocation of health care resources, financial investment, and rules for patient prioritization, among other multidimensional factors.

Rationing decisions should be made by those capable of objective judgment; emergent bedside rationing may be determined by nurses or physicians, while the development of broader policies should involve representatives from the medical profession as well as relevant stakeholders who reflect the will of society.

To ensure fairness and objectivity in decision making, patients themselves should not directly participate in resource allocation decisions, as this process requires weighing and comparing the needs of multiple patients who may potentially benefit.

title: Taking Up the Mantle of Human Trafficking Education: Who Should Be Responsible?
case:
It’s a busy summer night in the emergency department. You have seen 15 patients so far, and the fourth-year acting intern is approaching you with the sixteenth. He describes the patient as a young woman complaining of dysuria and increased urinary frequency whose history of present illness and physical exam are suggestive of cystitis. After discussing appropriate antibiotic and follow-up plans with the acting intern, you make your way to the bedside to confirm the student’s findings. But before you can open the door the student stops you with additional concerns.
“She seems younger than eighteen,” he says, “and I get the feeling she wasn’t telling me the truth about her social situation. I also noticed a few poor-quality tattoos that look homemade on physical exam. This made me suspicious, so I searched through her medical history. It looks like she’s been here at least three times in the last several months for other complaints. She had a sexually transmitted infection (STI), a broken finger, and an eyebrow laceration. When I asked her about the injuries she was evasive and said she was clumsy. She seems sober now, but other physicians have noted that she was high on previous presentations. I may be way off base here, but I’m worried that she’s being exploited. We learned about human trafficking last year, and this patient is showing several red flags.”
The student shows you some information online about the prevalence of human trafficking and its associated symptoms, and you decide to call the National Human Trafficking Resource Center (NHTRC) hotline. What seemed like a cut-and-dried case has now become much more complex. This new information has made you wonder if you have missed these signs in the past with similar patients.
case_rewrite:
It’s a hectic summer evening in the emergency department. You’ve already evaluated fifteen patients, and now the fourth-year acting intern approaches with details about your sixteenth. He reports that the patient is a young woman presenting with dysuria and increased urinary frequency; her history and exam are consistent with cystitis. After discussing the appropriate antibiotics and follow-up plan with the intern, you prepare to confirm his findings at the bedside. However, just as you reach for the door, the intern quietly pulls you aside.

“She seems younger than eighteen,” he confides, “and I had the impression she wasn’t being completely honest about her social situation. On exam, I noticed a few tattoos that looked homemade and poorly done. That raised some red flags for me, so I looked over her medical records. She’s visited here at least three times in the past several months for other issues—once for a sexually transmitted infection, another time for a broken finger, and once for an eyebrow laceration. When I asked about these injuries, she avoided my questions and just said she was clumsy. She’s sober now, but previous notes mention she was high during earlier visits. Maybe I’m reading too much into this, but I’m genuinely concerned she might be a victim of exploitation. Last year we learned about human trafficking, and this patient seems to fit several warning signs.”

The intern pulls up some online resources detailing the prevalence and warning signs of human trafficking. With this new context, you decide to call the National Human Trafficking Resource Center (NHTRC) hotline for guidance. What started as a straightforward case of cystitis now feels far more complicated. This experience leaves you questioning whether, in the rush of your busy shifts, you might have missed these critical signs in other patients before.

ethical_issues.question: When encountering a potential victim of human trafficking, how should health care professionals provide trauma-informed care while ensuring that they do not judge the patient or cause further harm?
keypoints: Medical professionals should use nonjudgmental language and uphold principles of privacy and confidentiality to establish trust and a sense of safety for patients.
It is essential to understand the profound impact of traumatic events on patients’ overall health and to integrate both social cues and physical symptoms when identifying potential victims.
Clinicians should be aware that victims often experience intense fear, shame, or defensiveness as a result of abuse, and may withhold disclosure even when the trafficker is not present.
In clinical practice, human trafficking should be actively considered in the differential diagnosis, with attention to relevant red flag symptoms to avoid missing potential victims.
The application of trauma-informed communication strategies in the doctor-patient relationship should be emphasized to foster a safe and supportive environment for interaction.

ethical_issues.question: Does the medical school have an ethical responsibility to incorporate the identification of and response to human trafficking into the core medical curriculum to ensure that future physicians are able to effectively assist victims?
keypoints: Medical schools have a responsibility to incorporate the identification of and response to human trafficking into the core curriculum to ensure that future physicians possess the necessary knowledge and skills to effectively recognize and assist victims.
Future physicians should be proficient in screening for human trafficking and should actively consider relevant risk factors in their clinical differential diagnoses.

Enhancing awareness of human trafficking will encourage future physicians to more actively participate in community advocacy, victim support, and related research, thereby contributing to the eradication of this global human rights violation.

title: Human Trafficking, Mental Illness, and Addiction: Avoiding Diagnostic Overshadowing
case:
Dr. Shah, an emergency department (ED) resident in New York City, entered the room of a young pregnant patient who was bleeding and visibly frightened. The patient, who only spoke Spanish, was accompanied by her brother, who translated. He explained that the patient suffered from schizophrenia and had been refusing her medications for the last couple of weeks. He added that she’d had a few episodes of aggressive behavior, directed at others and herself. While the patient’s brother was talking, Dr. Shah noticed a few bruises and puncture marks with associated ecchymosis (subcutaneous bleeding similar to a bruise) on the patient’s arm. The brother saw that Dr. Shah had noticed these marks and explained that the patient sells herself for drugs.
Dr. Shah began to suspect that the patient’s brother might not be trustworthy, so she requested a certified clinical interpreter. Through the interpreter, the patient conveyed that she was miscarrying and asserted that she does not have schizophrenia, although she admitted feeling depressed sometimes. The patient’s tone became increasingly desperate and she explained, through the interpreter, that the man claiming to be her brother was holding her captive. She stated she was brought to the US as his fiancée, and, upon arrival, he confiscated her passport, forced her to have sex with him, and introduced her to drugs.
At this point, the man explained that his sister had long had delusions of persecution. He also disclosed that she had required temporary restraints the day before after threatening family members while she was high. He suggested that perhaps this episode had fueled the current delusion.
Dr. Shah had recently read about a case in which a 14-year-old girl had been to the emergency department for treatment and had told the staff she was being sex trafficked. The man accompanying the girl had also claimed she had schizophrenia. The clinicians believed the man and discharged the girl to his care; he was later found to be trafficking girls into commercial sex. The girl was not rescued until police found her bound in a closet during a drug raid weeks later.
Dr. Shah wondered what to do.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Shah, an emergency department (ED) resident in New York City, stepped into the exam room where a visibly distressed young pregnant woman sat, blood staining her clothing. The patient spoke only Spanish and was accompanied by a man who introduced himself as her brother and acted as her translator. He explained to Dr. Shah that his sister had schizophrenia and had recently stopped taking her medications, which, he said, had led to several episodes of aggression, both towards others and herself. 

As Dr. Shah listened, she noticed several bruises and puncture marks with ecchymosis on the woman’s arm. The brother caught Dr. Shah’s glance and immediately offered an explanation: his sister, he said, sold herself for drugs. 

Dr. Shah began to question the reliability of the brother’s account. Wanting to ensure clear communication and privacy, she requested a certified clinical interpreter. With the interpreter present and the brother asked to step outside, Dr. Shah spoke to the patient alone. Through tears and in a trembling voice, the patient said she believed she was miscarrying. She denied having schizophrenia, though she admitted she sometimes felt very sad. As the conversation continued, the patient’s desperation grew. She revealed that the man claiming to be her brother was actually holding her captive. She explained that she had been brought to the United States as his fiancée, and soon after her arrival, he had taken her passport, forced her into sex, and introduced her to drugs.

Meanwhile, outside the room, the man insisted to staff that his “sister” suffered from paranoid delusions, citing a recent episode in which she had supposedly threatened family members while intoxicated, necessitating temporary restraints the day before. He suggested her current accusations were further evidence of her mental illness.

Dr. Shah could not shake a troubling memory from her recent reading: she recalled a case of a 14-year-old girl who had come to the ED reporting she was being trafficked. The man with her claimed she had schizophrenia, and staff had believed him, discharging the girl to his care. Weeks later, police discovered she had been trafficked and was only rescued during a drug raid.

Now, faced with a similar situation, Dr. Shah weighed her responsibilities, wondering how best to support her patient’s health and safety.

ethical_issues.question: When caring for a potentially trafficked patient, how can clinicians ensure the provision of trauma-informed care to improve the patient’s health and safety, rather than simply attempting to rescue them?
keypoints: When caring for a potentially trafficked patient, the primary objective of the clinical encounter is to improve the patient’s health and safety, rather than simply attempting rescue or making decisions on the patient’s behalf.

Respect the patient’s own assessment of her situation and safety risks, and adopt a trauma-informed care perspective to create a safe and supportive clinical environment that helps the patient regain a sense of autonomy and control.

Use a certified interpreter to interview the patient alone, ensuring that interviews and examinations are conducted in a private, warm, quiet, and comfortable setting to avoid threats or undue pressure on the patient.

Allow the patient to lead or set the pace of the examination, ensure that the patient maintains control over physical contact, and obtain explicit permission before each touch in order to uphold the patient’s dignity and sense of safety.

Obtain the patient’s informed consent before sharing information, initiating diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, or making referrals; respect her right to independent decision-making and personal choice, and avoid coercion or surrogate decision-making.

Collaborate closely with a multidisciplinary health care team, including patient advocates and social workers, to coordinate the care plan and avoid repeated interviews or unnecessary retraumatization.

Remain sensitive to power dynamics, be vigilant for potential manipulation and abuse, ensure that the patient’s voice is heard, and prevent secondary harm that may result from misplaced trust in accompanying individuals.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians avoid diagnostic overshadowing when confronted with co-occurring mental illness and addiction, and ensure that each health concern expressed by the patient is carefully evaluated?
keypoints: Clinicians must remain vigilant regarding their own biases and diagnostic overshadowing, avoiding the misattribution of legitimate health concerns to mental illness.
Maintain a high index of suspicion for interpersonal violence or exploitation by carefully evaluating each concern expressed by the patient, listening to and respecting the patient’s self-assessment.
Even when a patient has known delusions, clinicians should not assume that the patient’s other concerns are invalid or unworthy of attention.
Adopt a trauma-informed care perspective to ensure a safe clinical environment and help patients regain a sense of agency and control.

title: Saving the Starfish: Physicians’ Roles in Responding to Human Rights Abuses in Global Health Practice
case:
Kathy, a medical student, traveled to Kathmandu, Nepal, during her fourth year for a global health elective. While in the clinic, the attending physician, a local Nepalese doctor, instructed her to examine a female patient while he spoke with her chaperone.
Through an interpreter, Kathy interviewed a 12-year-old girl named Laxmi who was holding her forearm wrapped in a shawl. The girl said her injury occurred when her “mistress” hit her with a stick as punishment for not cleaning the pots thoroughly enough. On examination of the wrist, Kathy noted bruising over the back of the wrist associated with significant point tenderness. She suspected a wrist fracture due to blunt force trauma.
Kathy asked the interpreter about the consequences to child abusers. He explained that nothing could be done, because Laxmi was owned by the person who abused her. He went on to tell Kathy about the local custom of kamlaris. In the 1950s, when migrants occupied their land and filed ownership papers, the Tharu people lost their ancestral farms. In exchange for allowing the Tharu people to keep their farms, the new owners demanded the Tharu families’ young daughters as house servants. These indentured daughters are called kamlaris and those who own them are referred to as “masters” and “mistresses.”
Laxmi told Kathy and the interpreter that she missed her parents and wanted to go home. She was fed only scraps from her owners’ plates. And she was concerned for her safety because a girl from her village had been repeatedly raped by the junior master and then sent home in shame when she became pregnant. Laxmi had also seen a news story about a kamlari named Srijana who had been burned to death.
Kathy asked the interpreter if kamlaris were able to leave the owners’ homes. The interpreter explained that the distance from Kathmandu to the country farms was too great for the girls to travel on their own. He also explained that, although the kamlaris system had been outlawed in 2006, the laws were not enforced for wealthy landowners. Unless Laxmi willingly left her owners, there was nothing they could do to stop the abuse. Kathy wondered what more physicians could do about these kinds of situations.
case_rewrite:
Kathy, a medical student in her fourth year, traveled to Kathmandu, Nepal, for a global health elective. At a local clinic, the attending physician, a Nepalese doctor, directed Kathy to examine a young female patient while he conversed with the patient’s chaperone. With the help of an interpreter, Kathy began to interview a 12-year-old girl named Laxmi, who kept her forearm wrapped tightly in a shawl. Laxmi explained, through the interpreter, that her injury resulted when her “mistress” struck her with a stick as punishment for not cleaning the pots thoroughly.

During the examination, Kathy observed bruising on the back of Laxmi’s wrist, along with pronounced point tenderness, leading her to suspect a possible wrist fracture from blunt force trauma. Concerned, Kathy asked the interpreter about the legal consequences for child abusers in Nepal. The interpreter replied that nothing could be done, since Laxmi was considered the property of the woman who hurt her. He described the local practice of kamlaris, explaining that after the Tharu people lost their ancestral lands in the 1950s, the new landowners demanded young Tharu daughters as house servants in exchange for allowing the families to remain on their farms. These indentured girls are called kamlaris, and those who control them are known as “masters” and “mistresses.”

Laxmi confided to Kathy and the interpreter that she missed her parents and longed to return home. She revealed that she was only given scraps from her owners’ plates to eat and felt unsafe, recalling how another girl from her village had been repeatedly raped by the junior master and then sent home in disgrace when she became pregnant. Laxmi also mentioned seeing news about a kamlari named Srijana who was burned to death.

Kathy inquired if it was possible for kamlaris to leave their owners’ homes. The interpreter explained that the journey from Kathmandu to the rural farms was far too long and dangerous for the girls to attempt alone. He added that although the kamlari system had been officially outlawed in 2006, the law was not enforced for wealthy landowners. Unless Laxmi chose to leave on her own accord, there was little anyone could do to intervene. This left Kathy deeply troubled, as she wondered what more physicians could do to address such entrenched abuse and injustice.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance patients’ social, cultural, economic, and political vulnerabilities with their immediate clinical needs when confronted with culturally complex and sensitive situations?
keypoints: Physicians must first assess the patient’s injuries and provide necessary medical care to ensure that immediate clinical needs are met.

Physicians should actively assume responsibility for safeguarding the health and well-being of their patients and oppose the injustice and suffering experienced by patients, particularly when patients’ social, cultural, economic, and political vulnerabilities overshadow their clinical needs.

Physicians should adopt a multilevel approach and seek support from multiple sources, such as consulting with the attending physician, collaborating with the patient’s family, and working with local nongovernmental organizations, in order to jointly address the patient’s medical and social challenges.
Physicians should advocate for structural, political, and educational changes to promote the long-term health and social well-being of patients and their communities.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians take action to safeguard patients’ health and well-being when confronted with structural violence and social inequalities affecting their patients?
keypoints: Physicians have professional and ethical responsibilities to actively advocate for patients’ health care, attend to the impact of their socioeconomic conditions on health, and oppose the injustice and suffering experienced by their patients, especially in culturally complex and sensitive contexts.

Physicians should comprehensively assess the patient’s injuries and provide necessary medical care, while respecting the patient’s wishes by inquiring whether she is willing to leave the abusive environment and supporting her autonomous decision.

Physicians should seek multidisciplinary collaboration, including with the attending physician, hospital administration, the patient’s family, and local nongovernmental organizations, leveraging their social influence to connect patients with resources, coordinate support, and publicly condemn abusive systems.

Physicians should promote structural, political, and educational changes aimed at alleviating the systemic violence and social inequalities faced by patients and their communities, thereby fulfilling the social responsibilities of the medical profession.

ethical_issues.question: Should medical schools incorporate advocacy and activism training into their curricula to prepare students to address structural inequalities and cross-cultural complexities in global and international health?
keypoints: Medical schools should incorporate knowledge and skills that promote health equity and social justice into their training, enabling students to identify and address structural inequalities in global health.

Training should teach students to denounce and intervene in everyday violence, inequality, and injustice, and to take proactive measures to reduce health care disparities, particularly by advocating for impoverished and vulnerable populations.

Students need to understand in their clinical practice that their professional responsibilities extend beyond medical expertise to include protecting patients from social and structural harms, especially when patients’ medical issues are intertwined with social suffering.
Medical schools should motivate students to commit to social justice and cultivate them as active advocates for social change and health equity.

These educational objectives should be achieved through diverse approaches such as curriculum development, case analysis, community engagement, critical reflection, problem-solving training, volunteer service, and cross-cultural experiential learning.

Training should place particular emphasis on cross-cultural sensitivity and the complexities of international health contexts, strengthening students’ ability to intervene effectively within different cultural and social structures.

title: Physician Encounters with Human Trafficking: Legal Consequences and Ethical Considerations
case:
Dr. W is an obstetrician working at a women’s health clinic in a state that has a high prevalence of human trafficking. A couple arrives at her office, requests a private consultation, and asks whether she keeps information confidential. She assures them that she follows all state and federal laws and regulations regarding the management of protected health information.
The couple informs Dr. W that they “employ and manage” several young women as sex workers. They ask if the clinic would be able to screen their employees for sexually transmitted infections (STIs). They clarify that all services will be compensated; however, they request that no health records be kept for the women. They state that this is necessary to assure the women that they will not be at risk of being arrested because of the nature of their work.
Dr. W feels wary about providing STI testing and managing care for this small group of patients outside of her clinic’s standard operating procedure. Dr. W understands that, legally, she is required to maintain health records for all patients, but she is also concerned that this particular underserved and vulnerable group of young women would never receive appropriate gynecological care if their employers find out she keeps records for them. The couple promise to facilitate the patients’ compliance with STI treatments, if necessary. Dr. W feels torn: she wants to give the women the best care possible while also protecting the community from the possible spread of STIs. But she also worries that, by agreeing to terms set by the couple who employs and manages these women (who might be trafficked and some of whom might be minors), she might be complicit in their exploitation.
case_rewrite:
Dr. W is an obstetrician at a women’s health clinic in a state known for its high rates of human trafficking. One afternoon, a couple arrives at her office and requests a private consultation. They begin by inquiring whether Dr. W keeps patient information confidential. Dr. W explains that she adheres strictly to all state and federal laws and regulations regarding the protection and management of patient health information.

During the consultation, the couple discloses that they “employ and manage” several young women who work as sex workers. They ask if Dr. W’s clinic can provide screening for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) for these women. They emphasize that they will pay in full for all services, but specifically request that no health records be maintained for the women. According to them, the absence of records would reassure the women that their work will not put them at risk of arrest.

Dr. W is uneasy about providing STI screening and follow-up care for this small group under conditions that fall outside her clinic’s established procedures. She is aware that she is legally required to keep health records for every patient, yet she is also concerned that these vulnerable young women—who may never otherwise seek gynecological care—will not be seen if their employers learn that records are kept. The couple assures Dr. W they will ensure the women comply with any necessary STI treatments.

Torn between her desire to deliver appropriate care to the women and her obligation to prevent the community spread of STIs, Dr. W also worries that by agreeing to the terms set by the couple, she could become complicit in their exploitation—especially since she suspects some of the women may be minors and could be victims of trafficking. As Dr. W weighs her options, she recognizes both her legal obligations to report suspected abuse and her ethical duty to avoid endorsing or enabling acts that may violate the rights and dignity of these young women.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians provide medical care when they are aware that patients may be victims of human trafficking, and how can they avoid becoming complicit in acts of exploitation?
keypoints: The physician’s provision of care may, objectively, facilitate exploitation; therefore, it is necessary to carefully assess the legal and ethical consequences of such actions to avoid inadvertently becoming complicit in criminal activity.

The physician has a statutory duty to report, especially when minors may be among the women under the couple’s control; suspected cases of child abuse or human trafficking must be reported to child protective services or law enforcement agencies to protect victims from further harm.

The physician should refuse the couple’s unlawful requests (such as not maintaining health records) and proactively report the couple to law enforcement authorities to prompt investigation and intervention.

The ethical and legal responsibilities of medical professionals are to safeguard the rights and interests of patients and to avoid participating in any acts that violate human rights; regardless of how well-intentioned the motives may be, physicians must not assist or condone exploitative practices.

ethical_issues.question: Does a physician have a duty, under mandatory reporting laws, to report to the relevant authorities when confronted with a situation that may involve the sexual exploitation of minors?
keypoints: If minors are among the women controlled by the couple, Dr. W may have a legal duty to report, as all states in the U.S. have enacted mandatory reporting laws for child abuse.
Health care professionals are typically designated as mandatory reporters and must report suspected cases of child abuse or neglect, including sexual abuse and sexual exploitation.

Even if the state does not explicitly include sex trafficking within the scope of mandatory reporting, sexual abuse and sexual exploitation are still reportable acts, making it difficult for a physician to argue that a patient exhibits only signs of sex trafficking without other indicators of victimization.

Once a physician identifies symptoms of sexual abuse or similar harms that may result from sex trafficking, the reporting process should be initiated immediately; failure to do so may constitute a violation of the law.

The physician’s obligation to report suspected sexual abuse or sex trafficking of minors is intended to facilitate timely intervention and prevent further harm to children, in accordance with the legislative purpose of mandatory reporting laws.

The ethical goal of reporting is to seek help and protection for victims, not to return them to their abusers, reflecting the physician’s ethical responsibility and the principle of prioritizing the patient’s best interests.

title: Neuroethics and Disorders of Consciousness: Discerning Brain States in Clinical Practice and Research
case:
Sam had been driving his SUV when his car skidded on ice as he crossed the bridge around the corner from his apartment. The car tumbled over the guardrail and landed in the icy river below, causing Sam to lose consciousness. The first responders estimated that Sam had spent at least ten minutes underwater before two civilians were able to remove him from the car and pull him to the riverbank. The civilians immediately began CPR, but Sam never regained consciousness after the incident.
Sam’s parents refused to give up hope and decided to send him to a rehabilitation center. One day while searching online for studies on persistent vegetative state (PVS) patients, Sam’s mother came across a study that examined new ways to communicate with patients. The researchers had discovered that some PVS patients were actually in a minimally conscious state (MCS) and could communicate with the researchers with the right technology.
Molly was a bright neurology resident who had decided to take a research year while preparing her application for a fellowship. She had chosen to work on the MCS project after seeing families struggle with end-of-life decisions for PVS and brain-dead patients. When she witnessed her mentor use the team’s technology to interact with a patient who had been considered to be in PVS for the past five years, she was hooked.
Despite the breathtaking nature of their technology, however, the team members didn’t pretend to be miracle workers. They realized their technology was still in its infancy and would require thorough testing before it could be implemented across the country. Until then, use of the technology adhered to strict rules. It could only be used to elicit yes or no answers from the patients to questions that were limited to a specific list:Is the sky blue? Is the grass purple?The researchers didn’t want to ask anything serious that could potentially upset the study’s participants.
Molly’s mentor thought that Sam would be an ideal participant for the study. He had been a young healthy adult in his prime at the time of the accident, which had also occurred less than a year ago. The entire team was optimistic going into the testing session.
As Sam was wheeled into the testing room, his mother pulled Molly aside. “I know you’re only supposed to ask him specific questions, but can you ask him if he wants all of this?” she asked. “Can you ask if he’s in pain? Does he want us to keep providing care?”
case_rewrite:
Sam was driving his SUV back to his apartment when his vehicle suddenly skidded on a patch of ice as he crossed the bridge near his building. The SUV crashed through the guardrail and plunged into the freezing river below. Sam lost consciousness as his car filled with water. According to the first responders, Sam was submerged for at least ten minutes before two bystanders managed to pull him from the wreckage and drag him to the shore. The civilians immediately began CPR, but Sam never regained consciousness after the accident.

Despite Sam’s unresponsive state, his parents clung to hope and transferred him to a rehabilitation facility. Determined to find any chance for recovery, Sam’s mother began searching online for research related to patients in persistent vegetative states (PVS). During her search, she discovered a recent study exploring new technologies for communicating with patients diagnosed with PVS. The study revealed that some individuals presumed to be in PVS were actually in a minimally conscious state (MCS), and that, with specialized equipment, researchers could establish basic communication with them.

Molly, an ambitious neurology resident taking a research year before applying for fellowship, had joined the MCS communication project after witnessing firsthand the painful uncertainty families faced when making end-of-life choices for patients diagnosed with PVS or brain death. She was deeply moved after observing her mentor use the team’s technology to communicate with a patient believed to have been in a PVS for five years. The possibility of giving a voice to such patients inspired her commitment to the project.

Despite the remarkable progress of their technology, Molly and her team remained realistic about its limitations. The system was still experimental and required rigorous validation before it could become standard practice. For now, its use was governed by strict protocols: researchers could only pose yes-or-no questions from a predetermined list, such as “Is the sky blue?” or “Is the grass purple?” They purposefully avoided questions that might cause distress or confusion for the participants.

When Molly’s mentor suggested Sam as a candidate for the study, the team agreed he was an excellent fit—he had been a healthy young adult before his accident, and less than a year had passed since his injury. The team entered the testing session with cautious optimism.

As Sam was brought into the research suite, his mother approached Molly privately. “I know you’re only supposed to ask him certain questions,” she whispered. “But could you please ask if he wants all of this? Can you find out if he’s in pain? Does he want us to continue his care?”

ethical_issues.question: Is it necessary to distinguish between patients in the vegetative state and those in the minimally conscious state when providing care or withdrawing life support?
keypoints: Ethical decision-making should be based on an accurate assessment of the patient’s brain state, with a clear distinction between the vegetative state (PVS) and the minimally conscious state (MCS) to guide the continuation or withdrawal of treatment and life support.
Clinically, it is essential to precisely differentiate between PVS and MCS, as there are fundamental differences in the level of consciousness between these two conditions.

Patients in MCS possess a certain degree of consciousness and perceptual capacity and may experience pain; therefore, there is an ethical obligation to address their needs for analgesia and palliative care.

Patients in PVS typically lack consciousness and perceptual abilities, resulting in a lower need for pain management; however, their dignity must still be respected, and basic care should be provided.

Ethical decision-making should integrate accurate clinical diagnosis and the latest scientific evidence to ensure appropriate assessment of the patient’s condition and corresponding medical interventions.

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethical for patients with disorders of consciousness who are unable to provide informed consent to participate in research?
keypoints: Patients with disorders of consciousness may be enrolled in appropriate clinical research provided there is a reasonable scientific hypothesis and surrogate authorization.
It is necessary to distinguish between “informed consent” and the core ethical principle of “respect for persons” as articulated in the Belmont Report.

Requiring consent from patients who are unable to provide informed consent is complex and challenging; however, in research aimed at restoring patients’ communicative abilities and facilitating their participation in subsequent decision-making, this limitation may be appropriately adjusted.

Restoration of functional communication is an important goal in both clinical practice and research, as it enhances patient autonomy and quality of life; enabling suitable patients to achieve this goal through research is ethically appropriate.

title: Who Should Assess the Needs of and Care for a Dementia Patient’s Caregiver?
case:
It was subtle at first. A missed exit on the turnpike. A puzzled look when running into an old neighbor. A set of car keys in the fridge. Sally attributed it to normal aging at first, but after Hank called to say he was lost trying to drive to his sister’s house, she knew something was wrong. During several appointments, other diagnoses were ruled out and the doctor diagnosed Hank with Alzheimer’s disease. Sally’s and Hank’s lives quickly became filled with endless doctor’s appointments, which meant less and less time for grandchildren and friends. By the time Sally had Hank dressed, fed, and set up in his chair each morning she was exhausted. She barely had time or energy to shower and curl her hair, something she would never have left the house without doing prior to Hank’s diagnosis.
“Who knew our ‘golden years’ would be over so quickly?” Sally wondered as she organized the prescription bottles that now occupied their kitchen counter. “His and my blood pressure medication. His Alzheimer’s medicine. My arthritis medicine. His heartburn medicine. Or was it his arthritis medicine and my heartburn medicine?” It was all becoming so complicated.
At Hank’s latest neurologist appointment, Dr. Smith tested Hank’s memory and reported that his mini-mental status exam (MMSE) results were similar to those from his previous appointment. Dr. Smith was pleased and convinced they had found the right dosage for Hank’s medications, but he felt Sally just didn’t look herself. Sally attended all of Hank’s appointments, so Dr. Smith felt he knew Sally almost as well as he knew Hank. Over the past year, the impeccably matched outfits and perfectly coifed hair had disappeared. She looked exhausted and jittery, like someone who was constantly on edge. Dr. Smith wanted to ask if she was doing okay, but he didn’t want to offend her. “She’s not actually my patient,” he told himself, but seeing her look so radically different from the first time they met was nagging at him.
As Dr. Smith finished his examination, Sally squirmed uncomfortably in her seat, mentally preparing herself for another exhausting evening of cooking dinner and then cutting it into bite-size pieces for Hank, bathing Hank, and spending the night with a stranger she felt she barely knew anymore.
Dr. Smith thought to ask, “Before you go, Sally, how are you holding up?” and wondered whether he should.
case_rewrite:
The changes crept in gradually. Missing an exit on the highway. A confused pause when greeting a familiar neighbor. Car keys turning up in the refrigerator. At first, Sally brushed these off as simple signs of getting older, but when Hank called one afternoon, lost on his way to his sister’s house—a route he’d driven for years—her concern deepened. After several doctor visits ruled out other conditions, the diagnosis was clear: Alzheimer’s disease. From that moment, Sally and Hank’s world shifted. Their days began to fill with back-to-back medical appointments, leaving little time for visits from grandchildren or catching up with friends. Each morning, after Sally managed to dress Hank, help him eat breakfast, and settle him comfortably in his chair, she was already spent. She barely found the energy to shower, let alone style her hair, something she would never have skipped before Hank’s illness.

Sally often found herself staring at the kitchen counter, now cluttered with prescription bottles. “My blood pressure pills. Hank’s Alzheimer’s medicine. My arthritis prescription. His heartburn tablets. Or wait—was that his arthritis medicine and my heartburn pills?” It was all starting to blur together, and the routine that once kept her grounded now felt overwhelming.

At Hank’s latest appointment with his neurologist, Dr. Smith, the routine memory tests showed that Hank’s cognitive scores on the mini-mental status exam hadn’t changed since the last visit. Dr. Smith was encouraged and believed the medication regimen was working, but something about Sally caught his attention. Over the past year, Sally had become a familiar face—she never missed a visit—but the energetic woman with perfectly styled hair and carefully chosen outfits seemed transformed. Now, she looked weary, her movements tense and restless, as if she were constantly bracing herself for the next demand. Dr. Smith hesitated. Although Sally wasn’t his patient, it was hard to ignore how much she had changed since he first met her. He wondered if he should ask how she was coping, but worried it might seem intrusive.

Finishing up the examination, Dr. Smith watched as Sally shifted uneasily, already thinking ahead to another long evening: preparing dinner, cutting it into small pieces for Hank, helping him bathe, and then settling in for the night beside a man who, in many ways, felt like a stranger now.

As they prepared to leave, Dr. Smith considered saying, “Sally, how are you holding up?” He wondered if he should voice his concern, knowing how much depended on her well-being.

ethical_issues.question: Does Dr. Smith have an ethical obligation to assess Sally’s well-being and provide appropriate support to her as Hank’s primary caregiver during the clinical encounter?
keypoints: From a family-centered perspective, clinicians should understand the patient within the context of their life environment and support systems; proactively inquiring about and attending to the caregiver’s health status is a fundamental ethical responsibility.

According to the deontological framework, Dr. Smith, based on his specific duty to the patient and from a humanitarian standpoint, has a moral obligation to reach out to and inquire about Sally’s well-being.

Clinical practice should proactively assess and support the health and caregiving capacity of family caregivers, providing necessary education, psychological support, and referral resources in order to minimize harm to both the patient and the caregiver.

The caregiver’s health status directly affects the quality and overall well-being of ongoing patient care; ensuring the health and well-being of family members deeply involved in dementia care is consistent with the principle of justice and constitutes an unshirkable moral obligation for clinicians.

ethical_issues.question: How can the health care system be transformed to provide comprehensive, family-centered dementia care that supports the needs of both patients and their family caregivers?
keypoints: The health care system should establish a comprehensive, family-centered model for dementia management that holistically addresses the multidimensional challenges faced by patients and their families, including medical, social, emotional, physical, behavioral, financial, and familial relationship domains.

At the policy level, reimbursement mechanisms should be reformed to support billing for services provided to the family unit, and legislative efforts should be advanced to eliminate institutional barriers to family member involvement in care decision-making, thereby strengthening recognition of and support for the role of family caregivers.

Clinicians should actively participate in policy development and public discourse, advocate for the comprehensive needs of patients with dementia and their family caregivers, and promote systemic changes in medical organizational practices and policies.

Health care institutions should integrate family caregiver education and support into routine clinical care, develop clear protocols to facilitate caregiver participation in the clinical encounter, and enhance both the quality of care and family satisfaction.

Medical education and clinical research should be restructured to strengthen attention to the needs of family caregivers, effectively integrating caregiver resources and support systems while respecting patient autonomy and dignity.
