title: Should Mental Health Screening and Psychotherapy Be Required Prior to Body Modification for Gender Expression?
case:
Among her patients, Dr. Leonard, a family medicine practitioner, has developed a reputation as a physician especially welcoming to lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ) patients. Over the years, Dr. Leonard has noticed—with much happiness—that her LGBTQ patients are coming out at younger ages and embracing identities that span an increasingly diverse spectrum of gender and sexuality—an indication, she thinks, that important social and cultural progress has been made.
Today, Dr. Leonard’s nineteen-year-old patient, Tyler, is coming to see her. Tyler was female-sex assigned at birth; however, four years ago, Tyler came out to friends and family as a transgender male. In recent visits, Tyler has begun discussing with Dr. Leonard the possibility of pursuing medical assistance with gender transitioning, including gender-transitioning hormone therapy and gender reassignment surgery, which might involve “top” surgery—breast removal, in this case—or “lower” (also called gender affirmation, gender confirmation, or genital reassignment) surgery, a procedure to change genitalia. On his last visit, Dr. Leonard sent Tyler home with some readings relevant to the next steps of his transition to try to help him decide whether and when—if ever—to pursue gender transitioning with medical interventions.
“Dr. Leonard, I read what you gave me about the next steps of possible treatments, and I wanted to ask you about something,” Tyler said during his appointment. “While I do want to begin transitioning with top surgery, I read that I’ll have to get clearance from a mental health counselor first. But I don’t think my transition should require mental health counseling or approval.”
Dr. Leonard conceded that current guidelines from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health do recommend that patients receive at least an assessment and one documented referral for gender-transitioning surgery from a mental health professional before undergoing a procedure. She suggested to Tyler that he might view mental health counseling as a way to learn about and prepare for the potentially long lasting and irreversible effects of surgical body modification.
Tyler was still resistant. “Dr. Leonard, I don’t think I should have to prove to someone that I am who I am. Who else has to do that?” Tyler added that he had seen counselors in the past—for instance, to help him cope with his parents’ divorce. When it came to gender identity, however, he explained, “It’s the one thing about me I struggle with least. I’m really being pressed to do the counseling to make others comfortable with my decision, so it bothers me that this is pitched as being ‘for my own good.’”
Dr. Leonard had never been prompted to question the process of mental health assessment and counseling for transgender patients in the past. And while her medical judgment still sided with the idea that patients probably benefit from mental health counseling for gender-transitioning HRT or surgery, she also sympathized with Tyler. Dr. Leonard wondered if, in some cases, it could be harmful to ask a patient for identity affirmation through such institutionalized, formal channels. She wondered what to do next.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Leonard, a family medicine physician, is known in her community for fostering a welcoming environment for LGBTQ patients. Over time, she has observed with satisfaction that her LGBTQ patients are coming out at younger ages and are embracing a broad spectrum of gender and sexual identities, which she sees as a testament to positive social change.

One afternoon, Dr. Leonard meets with her nineteen-year-old patient, Tyler. Assigned female at birth, Tyler came out as a transgender male to his friends and family four years prior. During several recent appointments, Tyler has expressed interest in pursuing medical steps for gender transition, specifically hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries. He is considering “top” surgery—mastectomy—as well as the possibility of “lower” surgery, procedures intended to align his physical body with his gender identity. At Tyler’s last visit, Dr. Leonard provided him with educational materials about the potential treatments, hoping to help him make an informed decision about whether and when to proceed with medical interventions.

Now, seated in Dr. Leonard’s office, Tyler brings up a concern. “Dr. Leonard, I went through the information you gave me about the next steps, and I have a question,” he begins. “I want to start transitioning with top surgery, but I read that I’ll need to get clearance from a mental health counselor first. I don’t think it’s right that my transition should require mental health counseling or approval.”

Dr. Leonard acknowledges that current standards set by the World Professional Association for Transgender Health recommend at least an assessment and a documented referral from a mental health professional before undergoing gender-affirming surgery. She suggests to Tyler that this process might be seen as an opportunity to prepare for the potentially permanent changes and to more fully understand what the procedures entail.

Tyler remains unconvinced. “I don’t see why I should have to prove who I am to anyone,” he replies. “Who else has to do that?” He mentions that he has seen counselors before, such as when he dealt with his parents’ divorce, but explains, “When it comes to my gender identity, it’s honestly the thing I’m most sure about. It feels like I’m being asked to do this counseling just to make other people comfortable, not for my own benefit. That bothers me, especially when it’s described as being ‘for my own good.’”

Dr. Leonard realizes she has never before truly questioned the process of requiring mental health assessments for transgender patients. While she still believes that counseling can help patients prepare for the lasting effects of hormone therapy or surgery, she empathizes with Tyler’s perspective. She wonders whether, in some cases, the requirement for formal identity affirmation through institutional channels could actually be more harmful than helpful. Faced with Tyler’s concerns, Dr. Leonard finds herself questioning how best to proceed.

ethical_issues.question: Should mandatory mental health screening and psychotherapy be required prior to body modification for gender expression in order to ensure patients’ commitment to and understanding of irreversible surgical interventions?
keypoints: The World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH) recommends mental health assessment prior to body modification for gender expression, in order to help patients understand the irreversibility and potential impacts of surgical interventions.

Psychological assessment and counseling can clarify patients’ motivations and goals for gender transition, identify personal capacities and psychological preparedness that facilitate successful transition, and explore possible physical and psychological effects as well as issues of social adaptation.

Mandatory psychological assessment may be regarded as a form of paternalistic intervention toward transgender individuals, especially given the ethical concern of a double standard, since comparable irreversible body modifications (such as cosmetic surgery) typically do not require similar assessments.

Given that WPATH guidelines allow for flexibility in clinical practice, psychological assessment and counseling should serve as optional supports to facilitate successful gender transition, rather than as mandatory barriers; however, clinicians must exercise caution to ensure the psychological and ethical integrity of patients’ decisions.

Clinicians must ensure that patients provide fully informed consent prior to body modification, understanding the nature of the intervention, anticipated outcomes, risks and benefits, and available alternatives, thereby safeguarding patient autonomy and the quality of decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: Is there a double standard between body modifications for transgender individuals and similar modifications for non-transgender individuals, particularly regarding the mandatory nature of mental health assessment?
keypoints: Non-transgender individuals seeking equally irreversible body modifications (such as cosmetic surgical procedures) are generally not required to undergo mandatory mental health assessments.

Mandating mental health assessments for transgender individuals may constitute paternalistic intervention and warrants scrutiny as to whether it genuinely respects patient autonomy and best interests.
Clinical approval processes for body modification in transgender adult patients involve not only medical risk management but are also influenced by sociocultural norms of gender binarism.

The primary purpose of mental health assessment is to support patients in fully understanding the long-term implications and potential risks of medical interventions, rather than serving as a “gatekeeping” mechanism or proof of identity authenticity.

While ensuring patient safety, it is essential to respect individuals’ self-identity and decision-making authority, and to avoid institutionalized procedures becoming additional barriers or sources of discrimination for transgender persons.

title: How Should Physicians Refer When Referral Options Are Limited for Transgender Patients?
case:
As a fourth-year medical student, Jasmine volunteers at a women’s health clinic affiliated with her medical school. During her shifts at the clinic, Jasmine helps conduct initial patient interviews and physical exams and works with attending physicians—one of whom is Dr. Fan—to create care plans for her patients. On this afternoon, Jasmine sat down with a 29-year-old patient named Brianna.
Brianna told Jasmine that she had experienced recent episodes of nausea, which Brianna thought might be related to her hormone therapy. Brianna, who identifies as female but was birth-assigned male, began feminizing hormones five years ago. Brianna’s hormone regimen is currently being managed by Dr. Maize, a specialist not affiliated with the clinic but known to the community.
“I’ve never had these symptoms before,” Brianna said. Jasmine asked Brianna if she had told Dr. Maize about these recent symptoms. Brianna replied, “To be honest, I don’t like spending much time at her office. I just try to show up for my check-ups, get my prescriptions, and leave.” Brianna explained that, while at her appointments with Dr. Maize, she often catches the inconsiderate lingering stares of her staff. And on multiple occasions, Dr. Maize has said impolite things to her. During one visit, for example, Dr. Maize said to her, “Now that you’ve been doing well on hormones for a while, feminizing facial surgery could really help you complete ‘the full look,’” which hurt Brianna and convinced her that Dr. Maize wasn’t adept at making transgender patients feel comfortable.
At the conclusion of Brianna’s patient interview, Jasmine went to Dr. Fan, explained Brianna’s discomfort with Dr. Maize, and asked if there were another specialist to whom they might refer Brianna for hormone therapy.
“I’ve heard similar complaints about Dr. Maize from other trans patients,” Dr. Fan said, “but she’s the only gender-transitioning hormone specialist in the area.” Dr. Fan explained that there were specialists in a big city nearby who had better reputations for trans-friendliness, but they tended to be younger and less experienced with hormone therapy for gender transitions than Dr. Maize. “Since Brianna has her own share of pre-existing health complications, from a strictly medical point of view, Dr. Maize could be the most qualified to care for her—but given Brianna’s discomfort with her … I’m not so sure.”
“So, what should we recommend to Brianna as her best referral option?” Jasmine asked Dr. Fan.
case_rewrite:
Jasmine, a fourth-year medical student, volunteers at a women’s health clinic affiliated with her medical school. During her shifts, she assists with initial patient interviews, physical examinations, and collaborates with attending physicians—Dr. Fan among them—to develop care plans for patients. One afternoon, Jasmine meets with Brianna, a 29-year-old patient.

Brianna shares that she’s been experiencing episodes of nausea, which she suspects might be linked to her hormone therapy. Brianna identifies as female, though she was assigned male at birth, and has been on feminizing hormones for five years. Her hormone regimen is overseen by Dr. Maize, a specialist outside of the clinic but well-known in the local community.

“I haven’t had these symptoms before,” Brianna tells Jasmine. Jasmine asks if Brianna has discussed these new symptoms with Dr. Maize. Brianna hesitates, then admits, “Honestly, I don’t like spending much time at her office. I try to get in for my check-ups, pick up my prescriptions, and leave as quickly as possible.” She explains that Dr. Maize’s staff often give her uncomfortable, lingering stares during visits, and that Dr. Maize herself has made several hurtful remarks. For example, at one appointment, Dr. Maize commented, “Now that you’ve been on hormones for a while, feminizing facial surgery could really help you complete ‘the full look.’” The remark stung, leaving Brianna feeling misunderstood and unwelcome, and convinced her that Dr. Maize lacked sensitivity toward transgender patients.

After finishing the interview, Jasmine approaches Dr. Fan, recounting Brianna’s discomfort with Dr. Maize and asking if there is another specialist to whom Brianna could be referred for hormone therapy. 

Dr. Fan responds, “I’ve actually heard similar complaints about Dr. Maize from other transgender patients. Unfortunately, she’s the only gender-transitioning hormone specialist in the area.” Dr. Fan adds that while there are specialists in a nearby large city known for being more trans-friendly, they tend to be younger and less experienced in managing gender-affirming hormone therapy compared to Dr. Maize. “Given Brianna’s complex health history, from a purely medical perspective, Dr. Maize might be the most qualified. But, since Brianna feels so uncomfortable with her… I’m not so certain anymore.”

Jasmine considers this and asks, “So, what should we recommend to Brianna as her best referral option?”

ethical_issues.question: When medically qualified specialists lack the knowledge or interpersonal skills necessary to care for transgender patients, how should physicians select referral options to ensure patient trust and continuity of care?
keypoints: The core principle of transgender health care should be guided by the patient’s self-identification, with the process of medical assistance directed by informed consent that ensures patient autonomy.

Referral decisions should be grounded in the ethical imperative to minimize both physical and emotional harm to the patient, with particular attention to preventing emotional harm and safeguarding the patient’s dignity and sense of trust.

Physicians should prioritize referring patients to clinicians whom they trust and who are either experienced in or willing to learn about transgender health care, thereby ensuring individualized and culturally competent care.

Any physician with basic medical qualifications can manage hormone therapy for transgender patients by utilizing authoritative tools and guidelines; it is both feasible and appropriate for primary care physicians to assume responsibility for hormone management.

A primary care-centered model of hormone management facilitates continuity of care, addresses the comprehensive health needs of transgender patients, and reduces both gaps in medical care and emotional barriers.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr. Fan and Jasmine apply the principle of harm reduction to minimize emotional and physical harm when transgender patients like Brianna avoid seeking care due to prior negative medical experiences?
keypoints: Physicians should avoid referring transgender patients back to health care providers with whom they feel uncomfortable, in order to reduce emotional harm and maintain patient-provider trust.

Referral and care management decisions should be guided by the principle of minimizing both physical and emotional harm to the patient, taking into account the cultural competence of clinicians, the importance of continuity of care, and the feasibility of primary care physicians managing hormone therapy.
Transgender patients require safe and continuous access to comprehensive health care to ensure that both their physical and psychological needs are met.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Brianna’s case at the women’s health clinic, how should Dr. Fan and Jasmine balance respect for Brianna’s self-identified gender with prevailing clinical interpretations of gender norms to ensure informed consent and the development of an individualized care plan?
keypoints: As there is no unified “ideal” standard for gender transition, physicians should be guided by the patient’s self-identity, respect their gender identity, and ensure that patients retain autonomy throughout the medical process.

Medical assistance should be centered on informed consent, ensuring that patients are fully informed about the risks, benefits, alternatives, unknowns, and limitations of treatment, thereby enabling autonomous decision-making.

When evaluating referral options, clinicians must comprehensively consider both the potential specialist’s experience in transgender care and their willingness and ability to develop individualized care plans.

The majority of transgender health-related medical care can be provided by any physician who is willing to learn best practices, respect patient needs, and develop individualized care plans; referral is not the only option.

title: Should Psychiatrists Prescribe Gender-Affirming Hormone Therapy to Transgender Adolescents?
case:
In the medium-sized city where he practices psychiatry, Dr. Lao has developed expertise in treating and counseling transgender adolescents. This afternoon, Dr. Lao is scheduled to meet with Jessie, a 15-year-old high school student with autism spectrum disorder. Jessie has been Dr. Lao’s patient since elementary school. Within the last two years, Jessie, who was birth-assigned male, began opening up to her family and Dr. Lao about her identity as a transgender female.
In the waiting room, Jessie’s parents pulled Dr. Lao aside. “Is it true that you will soon start administering hormone therapy yourself?” Jessie’s father asked Dr. Lao. “Because it would be great if we didn’t have to find another physician when Jessie starts hormone treatment. Jessie said she would much rather have you perform the treatments.”
It was true that Dr. Lao was considering becoming trained to administer hormone therapy. Many of Dr. Lao’s transgender patients and families have complained about the lack of physicians in their rural community who are trained in hormone therapy administration. Dr. Lao thought he might play a role in reducing this resource disparity for his patients by becoming trained himself.
Their previous session ended just as Jessie began to describe some of her anxieties to Dr. Lao about transitioning from male to female. Jessie worried about what her classmates might think about her transition, and, while her immediate family was very supportive, Jessie worried about the opinions of members of her extended family, who tended to be less progressive on issues of gender and sexuality.
In their session today, Dr. Lao wanted to follow up with Jessie about these concerns. “Jessie, when we last met, you mentioned concerns regarding how your classmates and family members might react to your transition—would you like to keep discussing that?” With that question, Dr. Lao noticed that Jessie seemed somewhat withdrawn and uncharacteristically uncomfortable in front of him. “No,” she replied, “I thought it over, and I’m not as worried anymore about what they’ll think.” Dr. Lao tried a couple more times in their discussion—with little success—to veer the conversation back to Jessie’s formerly expressed worries about her transition. At the end of their session, Jessie said to Dr. Lao before leaving his office, “I’m feeling very ready to begin hormones—and it would make me so happy if you were the one managing my treatments, Dr. Lao.”
As Dr. Lao waved goodbye to Jessie and her family, he couldn’t help but wonder if Jessie’s refusal to discuss her anxieties about her transition were related to her wish to pursue hormone therapy under his care. Could it be that Jessie feared Dr. Lao would be hesitant to treat her or might delay the process if Jessie disclosed her anxieties about transitioning with him? Dr. Lao wondered: If he developed expertise in hormone therapy, would his patients then perceive him as a kind of gatekeeper in the process of their transition? Will his role in offering hormone therapy sacrifice important elements in his therapeutic relationships with his patients like Jessie?
case_rewrite:
In the mid-sized city where he practices, Dr. Lao has become known for his expertise in counseling and caring for transgender adolescents. This afternoon, Dr. Lao is scheduled to meet Jessie, a 15-year-old high school student with autism spectrum disorder. Jessie has been under Dr. Lao’s care since elementary school. Over the past two years, Jessie, who was assigned male at birth, has gradually come out to her family and Dr. Lao as a transgender girl.

Before the appointment, Jessie’s parents approach Dr. Lao in the waiting room. Jessie’s father asks, “Is it true you’re planning to start providing hormone therapy yourself? It would really help us if we didn’t have to look for another doctor when Jessie begins hormone treatment. Jessie told us she would feel much more comfortable if you handled the treatments.”

Dr. Lao confirms that he is indeed considering specialized training to administer hormone therapy. Many of his transgender patients and their families have expressed frustration about the shortage of local doctors trained in hormone therapy, especially in their rural community. Dr. Lao feels he could help address this gap by becoming qualified himself.

At Jessie’s last session, she had begun to share anxieties about transitioning from male to female. Jessie expressed fears about how her classmates would react and, while her immediate family had been supportive, she was uneasy about the attitudes of her extended family, who tended to be less accepting of gender and sexuality differences.

Today, Dr. Lao plans to follow up on these concerns. “Jessie, last time you mentioned feeling anxious about how your classmates and family might respond to your transition. Would you like to talk more about that today?” he asks. Jessie appears withdrawn and less open than usual. “No,” she responds, “I’ve thought about it, and I’m not as worried about what they’ll think anymore.” Dr. Lao gently tries a few more times to revisit Jessie’s concerns, but she remains reluctant to discuss them.

At the end of the session, as Jessie prepares to leave, she turns to Dr. Lao and says, “I really feel ready to start hormones—and I’d be so happy if you were the one to manage my treatment.”

Watching Jessie and her family leave, Dr. Lao finds himself reflecting. He wonders whether Jessie’s sudden reluctance to discuss her worries is connected to her desire to begin hormone therapy with him. Is Jessie worried that sharing her anxieties might make Dr. Lao hesitate or delay her treatment? Dr. Lao also questions whether, if he becomes trained in hormone therapy, his patients might see him as a gatekeeper to their transition. Would taking on this new role compromise the openness and trust in his therapeutic relationships with patients like Jessie?

ethical_issues.question: Should psychiatrists provide gender-affirming hormone therapy to transgender adolescents in order to support patient autonomy and the principle of beneficence?
keypoints: The principles of patient autonomy and beneficence jointly support psychiatrists in providing gender-affirming hormone therapy to transgender adolescents, in order to promote the patients’ physical and mental health and well-being.
Effective hormone therapy has a positive impact on the psychological health and quality of life of transgender adolescents, especially during the critical developmental period of puberty.

Delaying hormone therapy can result in irreversible physiological changes (such as facial masculinization, deepening of the voice, and male-pattern hair growth), highlighting the urgency of timely medical intervention and the obligation of beneficence.

Physicians should respect the right of transgender patients to express their gender identity through medically indicated interventions in accordance with standards of care, thereby safeguarding their medical autonomy.
In the absence of other qualified physicians able to provide treatment, Dr. Lao has an ethical obligation, based on the principle of beneficence, to provide hormone therapy to his patients.

ethical_issues.question: How can psychiatrists uphold the principle of nonmaleficence when providing hormone therapy, particularly in addressing potential iatrogenic harms and monitoring for medication side effects?
keypoints: Psychiatrists must carefully assess potential iatrogenic harms when providing late-adolescent estrogen therapy, including increased risk of deep vein thrombosis, prolactinoma, and loss of fertility in patients who have not undergone sperm cryopreservation.
Psychiatric residency training programs typically do not cover hormone therapy and pubertal suppression techniques, which constitutes an important ethical and clinical challenge for physicians.

Physicians must possess, or establish through multidisciplinary collaboration, the ability to monitor and manage adverse effects of hormone therapy medications, thereby ensuring adherence to the principle of nonmaleficence.

In the absence of support from transgender health specialists and when geographic and cultural factors limit access to care, physicians have a responsibility to proactively seek relevant training to meet patient needs if the benefits of treatment outweigh the risks.

Multidisciplinary collaboration is the preferred approach for gender-affirming care in adolescents; physicians should exercise due diligence in identifying and involving experienced specialists to ensure the safety and efficacy of treatment.

ethical_issues.question: In resource-limited rural areas, does Dr. Lao have an ethical obligation, based on the principle of justice, to expand his scope of practice and provide gender-affirming hormone therapy to patients like Jessie, given the pressing need for both mental health and gender-affirming care?
keypoints: Psychiatrists practicing in resource-limited rural areas have an obligation to ensure that transgender patients receive all medically indicated gender-affirming care, particularly when geographic and cultural barriers restrict access and when the benefits of treatment outweigh the risks.

According to the principle of distributive justice, physicians must weigh the impact of pursuing training in hormone therapy and providing related services on existing mental health resources (such as increased wait times for high-acuity patients), to ensure the fair allocation of scarce resources and the balance of competing needs.

Dr. Lao should carefully consider his own professional competence, time resources, and patient needs, and rationally assess the clinical appropriateness and ethical necessity of expanding his scope of practice, in order to avoid compromising the quality of care for other patients with urgent mental health needs due to overextension.

title: Requests for VIP Treatment in Pathology: Implications for Social Justice and Systems-Based Practice
case: Javier, the surgical pathology resident on duty, gets a call about a biopsy performed for a “VIP” patient who is an important hospital donor. A handwritten note from the department chair accompanies the specimen: “Take good care of Mr. Armstrong and make sure his biopsy gets read immediately.” The laboratory technician has already gone home, and Javier wonders why this biopsy should be handled more quickly than others. “All of the patients whose samples are in this lab want their results as soon as possible,” Javier reasons. “They’re all worried about their results. Why should I prioritize Mr. Armstrong’s sample?” He is, however, concerned about the personal and professional consequences of defying orders from the chair of his department. He feels pressured, and he wonders what to do.
case_rewrite:
Javier, the on-call surgical pathology resident, receives a late-evening call regarding a biopsy specimen taken from Mr. Armstrong, a “VIP” patient known for being a major hospital donor. Attached to the specimen is a handwritten note from the department chair: “Please give Mr. Armstrong’s case your immediate attention and ensure his biopsy is read as soon as possible.” The laboratory technician has already left for the day, and Javier is left alone in the quiet lab, surrounded by other biopsy samples awaiting review.

As Javier looks over the backlog of specimens, he reflects on the situation. Every patient whose sample is pending is anxiously awaiting their results; each one hopes for news as soon as possible. Javier questions why Mr. Armstrong’s biopsy should be singled out for expedited processing simply because of his VIP status. “All these patients have loved ones and anxieties,” Javier thinks. “What makes Mr. Armstrong’s case more urgent than the rest?”

Despite his reservations, Javier feels uneasy. The note from the department chair carries significant weight, and he is acutely aware of the possible consequences—both personal and professional—if he chooses not to comply. Pressure mounts as he considers whether to break protocol and prioritize Mr. Armstrong’s biopsy over others or to adhere to the established workflow that treats every patient equally. Javier remains uncertain about the right course of action and is caught between a sense of ethical responsibility and the expectation to fulfill his superior’s request.

ethical_issues.question: How should the healthcare system address requests for preferential treatment of VIP patients, such as Mr. Armstrong, while upholding principles of social justice and ensuring equitable access to care for all patients?
keypoints: Medical institutions should prohibit any VIP prioritization mechanisms based on social status, ensuring that all patients have equitable access to diagnosis and treatment.

Surgical and diagnostic prioritization should be strictly determined by the urgency of the medical condition and clinical need, rather than patient identity, in order to avoid delaying care for patients with acute conditions.
Development offices and non-clinical departments should not interfere with patient scheduling policies and procedures, thereby safeguarding fairness in care delivery and professional autonomy.
Healthcare professionals and institutions should firmly resist favoritism and avoid deviating from standard workflows in response to special requests from VIP patients or their representatives.

Patient education should be strengthened to correct misconceptions held by VIP patients and their families regarding access to care and quality of treatment, thereby promoting reasonable expectations for medical services.

If systemic issues exist with waiting times or processes for diagnosis and treatment, efforts should be made to optimize and improve these for all patients, rather than creating exceptions for VIP patients.

ethical_issues.question: How should medical institutions prevent deviations from standard clinical workflows and potential patient harm resulting from preferential treatment of VIP patients?
keypoints: Medical institutions should firmly prevent any systematic prioritization mechanisms for VIP patients, ensuring that clinical workflows remain fair, just, and consistent with established protocols.

Development offices and similar administrative departments must not interfere with patient scheduling policies, in order to avoid process adjustments based on special status that could lead to potential patient harm.

Hospital administrators and professionals should collectively resist pressures to deviate from standard workflows in favor of VIP patients, uphold medical quality and professional ethics, and reduce risks to patients.

Patient education should be strengthened to clarify clinical processes and standards, correct misconceptions held by VIP patients and their families regarding access and quality of care, and prevent unrealistic expectations from influencing medical decision-making.

Medical institutions should systematically identify and address process bottlenecks commonly faced by all patients (such as laboratory turnaround times), improving overall service quality rather than making exceptions for VIP patients, thereby safeguarding fairness and safety.

title: How Should Colleagues Respond to Diminishing Capacities of an Aging Surgeon?
case:
Dr. Roberts is a revered 70-year-old general surgeon at a major university-affiliated hospital, where he has been practicing surgery for almost four decades. He has mentored many generations of surgeons, including his junior colleague Dr. Patel, a 39-year-old surgeon who completed his residency four years ago. Because Dr. Roberts trained and advised him throughout medical school and residency, Dr. Patel holds his long-term mentor in high esteem.
In the last few months, Dr. Patel has realized that more of Dr. Roberts’s patients have been experiencing postsurgical complications than in the past and that his laparoscopic surgeries have resulted in patients bleeding more than usual, which has in turn led to those patients’ need for transfusions. Furthermore, Dr. Roberts has been losing dexterity and endurance during long procedures and has relied increasingly on Dr. Patel and other junior colleagues to step in to finish operations. Recently, Dr. Roberts even started falling asleep near the end of a long procedure, and Dr. Patel and a resident had to quickly step in to keep the patient safe. Numerous colleagues of Dr. Roberts have also noticed decline in his performance, but they are reluctant to discuss their concerns due to their regard for their long-term mentor.
While Dr. Patel feels that he is obligated to address his and his colleagues’ concerns, he is not sure whom to approach or what to do.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Roberts, a highly respected 70-year-old general surgeon, has been a fixture at a prominent university-affiliated hospital for nearly forty years. His reputation as a master surgeon and gifted teacher has shaped the careers of many, including Dr. Patel, a 39-year-old surgeon who finished his residency four years ago. Dr. Patel, who benefited from Dr. Roberts’s mentorship throughout his training, deeply admires his senior colleague.

Recently, however, Dr. Patel has noticed troubling changes in Dr. Roberts’s performance in the operating room. Several of Dr. Roberts’s patients have experienced more postoperative complications than usual, particularly after laparoscopic surgeries, with an increased incidence of bleeding that has necessitated additional transfusions. During lengthy procedures, Dr. Roberts has struggled with diminished dexterity and stamina, frequently leaning on Dr. Patel and other junior surgeons to step in and finish operations. The situation escalated when, during an especially long case, Dr. Roberts began to doze off near the end of the surgery, forcing Dr. Patel and a resident to intervene quickly to ensure the patient’s safety.

It is not just Dr. Patel who is concerned—other colleagues, too, have observed Dr. Roberts’s declining abilities. Yet, out of deference to their mentor’s years of service and stature, they have hesitated to voice their worries openly.

Now, Dr. Patel finds himself wrestling with a difficult dilemma. He feels a growing ethical responsibility to address the risks posed by Dr. Roberts’s declining skills, both for the sake of patient safety and the integrity of their profession. Despite his respect for Dr. Roberts, Dr. Patel is uncertain about the best course of action or whom to approach for guidance.

ethical_issues.question: When a surgeon’s physical capacities decline to the point of potentially endangering patient safety, when and how should colleagues intervene to ensure patient safety?
keypoints: Colleagues have an ethical responsibility to take immediate and necessary protective measures upon discovering that a surgeon’s physical decline is placing patients at risk, in order to ensure the safe completion of surgical procedures.

Colleagues should engage in honest and transparent communication with the surgeon in question, providing objective evidence—such as increased complication rates and other specific indicators—to help the surgeon understand the decline in capacity and the necessity of intervention, thereby facilitating self-adjustment.
The responsibility to ensure patient safety must take precedence over loyalty to, or emotional considerations regarding, senior colleagues.
Colleagues are obligated to report suspected impairment or diminished capacity of a physician to the appropriate authority; such reporting is an independent and mandatory professional duty.

If the surgeon in question refuses to voluntarily modify their practice to avoid placing patients at risk, departmental leadership should intervene and, when necessary, enforce limitations on the surgeon’s scope of practice.

ethical_issues.question: How can patient safety be protected while avoiding the unnecessary removal of clinical privileges from aging surgeons?
keypoints: If Dr. Roberts is unable to maintain the standards of surgical safety, he should discontinue performing independent surgeries. However, he can continue to make valuable contributions through teaching, surgical assisting, research, or administrative roles within the department.

Discussions with Dr. Roberts should be conducted with respect for his seniority and longstanding contributions, emphasizing that declining technical skills and physical endurance may compromise patient safety, while affirming his ongoing value in non-operative capacities.
Dr. Roberts should be encouraged to recognize changes in his clinical abilities and to participate in a constructive, evidence-based process for assessing and addressing these changes.

Dr. Roberts should prioritize shorter, less technically demanding procedures and refer complex or high-risk cases to colleagues with greater current capacity, thereby upholding the ethical principle of nonmaleficence and ensuring patient safety.

A systematic competency assessment process should be established, employing objective tools to regularly evaluate manual dexterity, physical stamina, and clinical decision-making, with longitudinal tracking and timely feedback provided to the surgeon.

Interventions should be proactive, occurring before a physician’s abilities fall below the minimum safety threshold, in order to maximize patient safety and preserve the physician’s dignity and professional legacy.

Departments should foster an open and supportive culture that reduces stigma around discussing age-related decline in clinical abilities, encourages honest communication, and promotes collective responsibility for maintaining high standards of medical care.

ethical_issues.question: When a surgeon’s capacities have declined but they have not voluntarily adjusted their practice, how should the department chair intervene based on objective evidence to ensure patient safety?
keypoints: Department chairs have a responsibility to promptly identify, assess, and intervene in cases of physician competency decline based on objective evidence, ensuring that all team members practice safely and that patient safety is protected.

Interventions and communications should respect the physician’s professional dignity, clearly articulate the specific risks to patients posed by declines in skill, dexterity, and endurance, and affirm the physician’s valuable contributions to the department in other roles.

When a physician does not voluntarily adjust their practice and declining abilities may endanger patient safety, the department chair should take appropriate measures, including restricting surgical privileges, to ensure clinical safety.

If a physician refuses to voluntarily modify their practice, colleagues have an obligation to report to the department chair or hospital administration to prompt necessary interventions, such as limiting surgical privileges, with the primary aim of safeguarding patient safety.

The intervention process should adhere to principles of fairness, transparency, and professionalism, balancing the rights of the physician with the interests of patients, and maintaining the overall professional integrity and trust within the medical team.

title: How Should Medical Schools Respond to Students with Dyslexia?
case:
Dr. Miller is a senior physician and an influential administrator at a medical school. She is meeting with James, an incoming first-year medical student. James has dyslexia and requested to meet with Dr. Miller when he heard of her past efforts to try to help students with disabilities. James informs Dr. Miller that he was diagnosed with dyslexia after his fourth grade teacher noted his difficulty with reading and his parents arranged for him to be assessed by an educational psychologist. In grade school, he attended special reading programs to improve his reading and spelling skills. He studied twice as hard as his peers, received accommodations for extra testing time from grade school through college, and performed well in school exams.
By his junior year of college, James had maintained a GPA of 3.8 and excelled in clinical research in the Department of Radiology at his school’s affiliated medical school, fueling his ambition to become a radiologist. He took the Medical College Admissions Test (MCAT) with accommodations and was accepted to his college’s affiliated medical school, where he enrolled. Now a first-year medical student, James is struggling with the fear that his dyslexia will negatively impact his education, performance, and reputation among faculty and fellow students. He explains to Dr. Miller that he is worried that requesting accommodations could lead faculty and classmates to perceive him as less capable of becoming a qualified physician. However, he knows that he would struggle to perform well in medical school without accommodations.
Dr. Miller realizes that James will likely suffer either way that she advises him. That is, either James must “out” himself to faculty and administrators if he is to use accommodations and thus risk being stigmatized, or he must remain silent about his disability and take his exams without accommodations to which he is legally entitled and risk performing poorly in his medical school coursework. Dr. Miller feels dismayed about this dilemma and wonders how her medical school’s policies and culture can be reformed to advocate for students like James. Specifically, she has wanted to make her medical school’s environment more accepting of students with disabilities for a few years now, but she’s also aware that this might upset some influential faculty who are not supportive of this goal. Dr. Miller wonders what to do next.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Miller, a respected senior physician and prominent administrator at her medical school, sits in her office awaiting a meeting with James, an incoming first-year medical student. James, recently accepted into the program, specifically requested to speak with Dr. Miller after learning about her longstanding commitment to supporting students with disabilities.

As they sit down, James shares his story: he was diagnosed with dyslexia in elementary school after his fourth grade teacher noticed persistent struggles with reading. Following an evaluation by an educational psychologist arranged by his parents, James began attending specialized reading programs. Throughout his education, he devoted twice as much time to studying as his classmates and, from grade school through college, relied on accommodations such as extended time on exams. These supports enabled him to excel academically, consistently achieving high marks on school assessments.

By his junior year in college, James had maintained an impressive 3.8 GPA and stood out in clinical research within the Department of Radiology at the university’s affiliated medical school. This experience cemented his aspiration to become a radiologist. When it came time for the MCAT, James received testing accommodations and, with his strong performance, earned acceptance to the very medical school where Dr. Miller works. Now, as he embarks on his first year, James confides in Dr. Miller about apprehensions that have begun to overshadow his excitement.

James explains that he is deeply concerned his dyslexia will hinder his progress in medical school, not only academically but also in terms of how he is perceived by faculty and fellow students. He tells Dr. Miller that while he knows he needs accommodations to succeed, he fears that disclosing his disability will cause others to doubt his abilities or question his fitness for a medical career. Yet, the alternative—foregoing accommodations—would likely lead him to struggle with coursework and assessments, undermining his potential.

Listening to James, Dr. Miller recognizes the complexity of his predicament. She realizes that no matter her advice, James faces a difficult choice: if he requests the accommodations to which he is legally entitled, he risks exposing his disability and possibly being stigmatized; if he remains silent, he jeopardizes his academic performance. This ethical tension leaves Dr. Miller troubled.

Reflecting on James’s situation, Dr. Miller thinks about her ongoing efforts to make the medical school a more welcoming and supportive environment for students with disabilities. She knows that meaningful change would require not only institutional reforms—such as privacy protections, proactive support for accommodations, and faculty training on the specific challenges of dyslexia—but also a shift in campus culture. However, she is also aware that advocating for these measures could provoke resistance from certain influential faculty members who have been skeptical of such initiatives in the past.

Confronted with James’s dilemma and the broader issues it raises, Dr. Miller wonders what steps she should take next to ensure that her school upholds fairness, respects student privacy, and truly supports students like James.

ethical_issues.question: How should medical schools provide necessary reasonable accommodations for students with dyslexia without compromising fairness in competition?
keypoints: According to the law, students who have been diagnosed with dyslexia are entitled to reasonable accommodations to ensure that examinations and learning environments reflect their true abilities, rather than being limited by their disability.

Medical schools should respect students’ right to privacy, allowing students to decide for themselves whether to disclose information about their disability, and should proactively inquire about the need for reasonable accommodations after admission.

Faculty and staff should receive relevant training to understand the specific impacts of dyslexia and actively support and implement reasonable accommodations such as separate testing rooms and extended testing time.

Medical schools should promote institution-wide education and training to increase awareness of dyslexia and related disabilities, thereby fostering a culture of inclusion, understanding, and support for students with disabilities.

In accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and its amendments, it is prohibited to indicate the use of accommodations in student records or examination reports, in order to prevent bias and discrimination and to safeguard the right of students with disabilities to compete fairly.

title: Prioritizing Cross-Disciplinary Teaching and Learning and Patient Safety in Hospital-Based Environments
case:
Darvid is a third-year medical student starting his first inpatient hospital-based clerkship, in internal medicine. He is following Mr. S, an 81-year-old man with diabetes who was admitted to the hospital for pneumonia. Darvid is expected to visit Mr. S each morning before 8 a.m. rounds to see how he is feeling and to perform a physical exam, which gives him opportunities to practice his patient interview and exam skills and to learn more about pneumonia and diabetes. He is expected to report his findings to the team during morning rounds. The internal medicine first-year resident physician, Dr. Alexa, also visits Mr. S each morning and is responsible for prescribing his medications and ordering tests.
One morning when Darvid arrives at Mr. S’s room, a nurse, Jemma, is at the bedside, getting ready to measure Mr. S’s morning glucose after a finger stick and then to help him to the bathroom. Darvid doesn’t want to interrupt her work, but there are only a few minutes before morning rounds. He decides to wait outside the room until Jemma is finished with her tasks but has to leave for rounds before getting to see Mr. S. As he’s waiting outside the room in the hallway, Dr. Alexa asks him what he’s doing. He explains that Jemma was in the room and he didn’t want to interrupt. She responds that he’s here to learn how to be a physician and needs be more assertive so that he can see the patient before rounds; she adds that Jemma can come back to Mr. S later.
The next day, Darvid finds himself in the same situation. He needs to be prepared for rounds shortly and wants to respect Dr. Alexa’s instructions, but he also thinks the care Jemma provides is more important to Mr. S’s health than being seen by a medical student seeking practice opportunities. He’s not sure whether he should interrupt Jemma’s work or come back later and risk being underprepared for rounds again and receiving a poor evaluation from Dr. Alexa. Darvid wonders whether a practical scheduling solution could be found; he also wonders whether he should talk with Jemma, but he’s not quite sure what to say.
case_rewrite:
Darvid, a third-year medical student, has just begun his first inpatient internal medicine clerkship at the hospital. He has been assigned to follow Mr. S, an 81-year-old man with diabetes who was admitted for pneumonia. Each morning before 8 a.m. rounds, Darvid is expected to visit Mr. S to check on how he is feeling and perform a physical examination. These visits are intended to help Darvid develop his clinical interviewing and examination skills, as well as deepen his understanding of pneumonia and diabetes. Darvid is to present his findings to the medical team during morning rounds. Dr. Alexa, the first-year internal medicine resident, is also responsible for seeing Mr. S each morning, managing his medications, and ordering necessary tests.

One morning, as Darvid approaches Mr. S’s room, he sees Jemma, the nurse, already at the bedside. Jemma is preparing to check Mr. S’s blood glucose with a finger stick and assist him to the bathroom. Not wanting to disrupt her care, Darvid waits in the hallway, glancing at his watch as the minutes tick closer to the start of rounds. He ultimately has to leave for rounds without seeing Mr. S. While waiting outside, Dr. Alexa notices him and asks what he’s doing. Darvid explains that Jemma was with Mr. S and he didn’t want to interrupt. Dr. Alexa reminds him that he is there to learn and needs to be more assertive so that he can see the patient before rounds, adding that Jemma can return to Mr. S afterwards if necessary.

The following morning, Darvid finds himself facing the same dilemma: Jemma is once again attending to Mr. S, and time before rounds is short. He wants to follow Dr. Alexa’s advice and be prepared for rounds, but he feels that Jemma’s care—like monitoring Mr. S’s blood glucose and helping with toileting—directly impacts Mr. S’s health and comfort, and that his own need for practice is less urgent. Darvid worries that if he waits again, he will have to go to rounds unprepared and risk a negative evaluation from Dr. Alexa. He begins to consider whether a better scheduling arrangement could be made and wonders if he should talk to Jemma, though he’s uncertain how to start the conversation or what to propose.

ethical_issues.question: How can patient needs be prioritized over medical students’ learning opportunities in hospital-based environments?
keypoints: Patient needs and safety must be the foremost principle guiding medical decision making, and when there is a conflict between nursing care and medical education, the patient’s interests should take priority.

Mr. S’s nursing needs—such as privacy during toileting and blood glucose monitoring—take precedence over the medical student’s learning opportunities, especially considering the potential urgency of care related to his diabetes.

Hospitalized patients, due to their physical and psychological vulnerability, have the right to timely and appropriate clinical care, which should not be delayed or neglected because of the training needs of medical students.

Medical students should respect nursing workflows and proactively communicate to coordinate scheduling, balancing their educational needs with patient care to ensure that patient safety and quality of care are not compromised.

The health care team should coordinate to safeguard patient safety and quality of care while also creating an environment conducive to learning, thereby promoting the harmonious integration of education and clinical care.

ethical_issues.question: How can effective communication be achieved within interprofessional teams to avoid communication barriers caused by hierarchical structures?
keypoints: Interventions to improve team communication must address barriers arising from hierarchical structures at the individual, group, and organizational levels, systematically overcoming communication obstacles caused by power differentials.

By teaching effective communication strategies, conducting joint team training, and utilizing team-based simulation exercises, team members’ communication skills and collaborative abilities can be enhanced.

Establishing a democratic and inclusive team environment, developing an organizational culture that supports interprofessional equality, and fostering an atmosphere in which all voices are encouraged promote the free flow of information.
Empowering all team members, regardless of their position or seniority, to speak up and raise safety concerns ensures that a culture of open communication is implemented in practice.

Interprofessional education (IPE) emphasizes communication, mutual respect, and shared decision making, facilitating collaboration and understanding among clinicians from different professions and improving the quality of patient care.

ethical_issues.question: How can nursing care in a health care team be protected from being disrupted by physicians’ priorities, in order to safeguard patient safety and dignity?
keypoints: The needs, goals, and values of the patient must always take precedence over the learning needs of medical students or other trainees, in order to safeguard the patient’s safety, dignity, and right to timely and appropriate care.

The nursing responsibilities carried out by nurses are central to clinical care and patient safety; they must not be regarded as ancillary or secondary tasks, nor should they be disrupted by the perceived priorities of other professions.

Members of the health care team should engage in open, respectful, and effective interprofessional communication based on the patient’s immediate needs, avoiding professional antagonism and the devaluation of nursing contributions, and collaboratively develop and implement shared plans of action.

Improving communication within health care teams requires interventions at the individual, team, and organizational levels, including the promotion of interprofessional joint training, simulation exercises, and the cultivation of a democratic and inclusive team culture, in order to establish standardized systems of collaboration.

All team members, regardless of rank or position, should be empowered to speak up and halt procedures when potential risks or deviations from patient needs are identified, thereby fostering a culture of safety and patient-centered clinical practice.

title: Interprofessional Training: Not Optional in Good Medical Education
case:
As director of an obstetrics and gynecology rotation, one of Dr. Chan’s goals is to emphasize interprofessional collaboration so that her students will be prepared for the cross-disciplinary practice environments into which they will be graduating. In particular, she wants students to learn from nurse midwives, whom she admires as experts in normal deliveries, as role models and leaders in patient-centered care, and as fellow professionals who offer safe labor and delivery options for women with low-risk pregnancies. To achieve these goals, Dr. Chan divides each student’s time on this rotation into two parts, one with an ob-gyn physician and one with a nurse midwife.
After the student assignments have been distributed, Dr. Chan receives an email from a student that says, “I recognize that many women want midwives for their deliveries, but I came to medical school to learn what physicians do. I will soon have to make a decision about which residency to do, and I want as much time as possible to work with physicians. I would like my schedule to be changed so I can spend my time in medical school learning from physicians, not nurses or midwives.”
Dr. Chan has received a few emails like this in the past. She is concerned that accommodating this student’s request will send a message to other students that learning what nurse midwives do is optional and unimportant. How ought Dr. Chan to address students with the kinds of concerns raised in the email?
case_rewrite:
As the director of the obstetrics and gynecology rotation, Dr. Chan is deeply committed to preparing her students for the realities of modern, team-based clinical practice. She believes that interprofessional collaboration is essential, and she particularly values the expertise and patient-centered approach of nurse midwives. Dr. Chan views nurse midwives not only as experts in normal deliveries but also as exemplary leaders in providing holistic care and as essential partners in ensuring safe outcomes for women with low-risk pregnancies. With these principles in mind, Dr. Chan has structured the rotation so that each student spends half of their time working alongside an ob-gyn physician and the other half learning from a certified nurse midwife.

After distributing the assignment schedules, Dr. Chan receives an email from a student named SB. The message reads, “I understand that many women prefer midwives for their deliveries, but my main reason for coming to medical school was to learn what physicians do. Since I’ll soon need to decide on a residency, I want to maximize my exposure to physician practice. I would like my schedule adjusted so that I spend my time learning from physicians, not from nurses or midwives.”

This is not the first time Dr. Chan has received such a request. She is concerned that granting SB’s wish would signal to the rest of the students that learning from nurse midwives is optional or less important, undermining the goals of the rotation and the model of collaborative care she seeks to promote. Dr. Chan now faces the task of responding to SB’s concerns in a way that upholds the educational standards of the program and reinforces the significance of interprofessional learning.

ethical_issues.question: Should medical students have the option, during interprofessional training, to choose to learn only from physicians and not from nurse midwives?
keypoints: Medical students do not have the right to opt out of interprofessional training; interprofessional team collaboration is fundamental to contemporary medical practice, and students must develop collaborative skills and an understanding of multidisciplinary roles.

Certified nurse midwives are highly specialized health professionals; by learning from midwives in the management of normal pregnancy and childbirth, medical students receive an ideal introduction to obstetrics and gynecology that aligns with the educational progression from the normal to the pathological.

Receiving training exclusively from physicians leads to a lack of understanding of the skills and terminology of other key health professionals, impairs comprehension of multidisciplinary team collaboration, and hinders effective cooperation within future healthcare teams.

Dr. Chan should refuse the student’s request to work only with physicians, fulfill her educational responsibility to correct the student’s misconceptions about medicine as a whole and the physician’s role specifically, and emphasize the importance of interprofessional training in cultivating competent practitioners and adapting to the modern healthcare environment.

ethical_issues.question: Should medical education emphasize interprofessional collaboration to prepare students for future team-based practice environments?
keypoints: Medical education must emphasize interprofessional collaboration, enabling students to learn within clinical teams and preparing them to adapt to team-based medical practice after graduation.

Interprofessional education helps students understand the roles and value of each professional team member, fosters mutual respect and effective communication, and thereby enhances the comprehensiveness and quality of patient care.

Students who are trained solely from the physician’s perspective may struggle to function effectively in future multidisciplinary teams and may have significant gaps in their understanding of the skills and terminology of other health professionals.

The current healthcare environment prioritizes multidisciplinary collaboration, and integrating the expertise of non-physician clinicians is a key strategy for meeting the complex needs of patients and achieving high-quality care.

Clinical clerkships should authentically reflect the operational model of modern healthcare teams; educational arrangements that separate students from shared interprofessional responsibility for patients lack justification and practical relevance.

ethical_issues.question: Does the medical school have a responsibility to correct students’ misconceptions about the nature of medicine as a whole and the role of physicians, particularly in the context of interprofessional collaboration?
keypoints: Medical schools have a responsibility to correct students’ misconceptions about the nature of medicine as a whole and the role of physicians, particularly in the context of interprofessional collaboration, ensuring that students understand the contemporary meaning of the physician’s role.

Interprofessional collaboration reflects the team-based nature and practice model of modern medicine; medical schools should introduce this model to cultivate students’ ability and attitude to learn from all members of the health care team.

Medical students must participate in interprofessional team-based care in order to understand and respect the professional value of each team member, thereby becoming competent for the complex collaborative clinical environments of the future.

title: Resisting Outdated Models of Pedagogical Domination and Subordination in Health Professions Education
case:
LaBecca is a fourth-year medical student working in a primary care clinic. Her medical school has recently changed its curriculum to provide medical students with opportunities to learn and work collaboratively with nursing students. LaBecca is paired with a nursing student, Brooke, in the office of Dr. Wilson, a senior internist on the faculty. Dr. Wilson has never before had a nursing student in the clinic. When LaBecca and Brooke arrive for the first day at the clinic, Dr. Wilson greets them warmly and then tells them, “As you both know, while nurses are a vital part of the team, physicians ultimately run the show. LaBecca, this is an opportunity for you to develop your leadership skills. Brooke, I’m going to have LaBecca delegate tasks to you; please follow her instructions.”
Gemma, the nurse who typically works with Dr. Wilson, is busy with a patient and is not included in this orientation. Brooke is disappointed to hear Dr. Wilson’s message, especially without Gemma present. LaBecca notices Brooke’s disappointment; she feels awkward and isn’t sure how to respond. She admires Dr. Wilson and wants to forge a good relationship with him, and it seems to her that questioning his ideas about team members’ roles might cause unnecessary conflict at the outset of the rotation. She’s not sure how to work with Dr. Wilson and Brooke in the upcoming clinic sessions.
case_rewrite:
LaBecca, a fourth-year medical student, has just started a new rotation in a primary care clinic. Her medical school recently updated its curriculum to promote interprofessional education by pairing medical students with nursing students for collaborative learning. LaBecca is partnered with Brooke, a nursing student, and together they report to Dr. Wilson, a senior internist and long-standing faculty member. Dr. Wilson has never supervised a nursing student in the clinic before.

On their first morning, Dr. Wilson greets both students with a friendly smile and quickly begins the orientation. “As you both are aware, nurses are essential to our work,” he says, “but ultimately, it’s the physicians who direct patient care. LaBecca, I see this as your chance to build your leadership abilities. Brooke, I’d like you to follow LaBecca’s instructions as she delegates tasks to you.”

Gemma, the clinic nurse who usually works alongside Dr. Wilson, is busy attending to a patient and misses this initial orientation. Brooke listens to Dr. Wilson’s remarks with visible disappointment, particularly since Gemma—her potential mentor and advocate—is absent. LaBecca immediately notices Brooke’s downcast expression and feels unease settle in. She deeply respects Dr. Wilson and is eager to establish a positive working relationship with him. At the same time, she senses that the rigid hierarchy being introduced goes against the spirit of the new curriculum and might undermine team cohesion.

Conflicted, LaBecca hesitates. She wonders whether she should address her concerns about Dr. Wilson’s hierarchical approach, but worries that doing so might provoke tension or jeopardize her standing at the very start of her rotation. She is uncertain how best to move forward in fostering an effective and respectful working relationship with both Dr. Wilson and Brooke in the clinic’s team-based environment.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of interprofessional collaboration, should LaBecca, as a medical student, challenge Dr. Wilson’s hierarchical approach in order to promote team equality and uphold the principles of collaborative practice?
keypoints: Medical students should rationally weigh the dilemma between challenging the authority of senior physicians and conforming to hierarchical structures, seeking a middle ground that prioritizes the shared goal of patient-centered care.

In interprofessional collaboration, medical students should communicate with senior physicians in a respectful and non-confrontational manner, using an exploratory approach to express conflicts regarding team models and to promote constructive dialogue.
By assuming informal leadership roles, medical students can help drive a cultural shift toward inclusivity and foster equality and collaboration among team members.

Achieving a patient-centered interprofessional care model requires a collective effort by all health care professionals to promote cultural transformation, dismantle traditional hierarchical barriers, and create an environment of equal collaboration.

ethical_issues.question: How can effective communication be achieved within a health care team to address and resolve potential conflicts arising from traditional professional hierarchies?
keypoints: Maintain a respectful and non-confrontational attitude, using inquiry-based communication to engage authority figures constructively and avoid eliciting defensive reactions.
Choose a private and appropriate setting for discussions to prevent placing authority figures in awkward or passive positions.
Balance listening and expression during communication, allowing the other party to fully articulate their views and demonstrating active listening by summarizing key points.

Acknowledge the authority figure’s perspective, explain the benefits of collaborative approaches and the potential discomfort caused by traditional models, and propose a trial of clearly defined roles and egalitarian collaboration.
Actively seek the perspectives of nursing colleagues, promote open dialogue, focus on shared goals of patient care, and establish mutually respectful and trusting team relationships.

Utilize structured communication mechanisms such as huddles to guide team members in introducing their roles, goals, and care plans for patients, thereby ensuring professional equality and the right to speak.

Recognize that the realization of interprofessional care models depends on a collective cultural transformation among all health care professionals, emphasizing the importance of systemic change that goes beyond individual communication skills and process optimization.

ethical_issues.question: How can the roles and contributions of nursing students be fully recognized and respected within interprofessional health care teams?
keypoints: Question traditional professional hierarchies, advocate for shared leadership and team equality, and ensure that the roles and contributions of nursing students are fully recognized and respected.
Faculty preceptors should serve as role models in clinical settings by demonstrating interprofessional collaboration and equality, and actively teaching and promoting the principles of teamwork.

Establish and implement open communication mechanisms (such as huddles) to facilitate clarity of roles, responsibilities, and goals among all professional team members, enhance mutual understanding and collaboration, and maintain a focus on patient-centered care.

Fully acknowledge the unique value of the nursing profession in patient care, avoid excluding or devaluing the participation of nursing students and nurses, and prevent the reinforcement of professional bias and historical interprofessional conflict.

title: Is Consent to Autopsy Necessary? Cartesian Dualism in Medicine and Its Limitations
case:
Dr. Zinker, a cardiac surgeon, is surprised by the rapid and unexpected death of his patient, Ms. Foster, whose postsurgery recovery had appeared complication-free. Prior to her death, she complained of shortness of breath and was found to have a pleural effusion, an abnormal volume of fluid around one of her lungs. The pleural effusion was drained, but she developed unstable blood pressure, which required increasing administration of vasopressors. Despite these supports, Ms. Foster died. Dr. Zinker wants to order an autopsy to determine the exact cause of Ms. Foster’s death. Specifically, he wants to discover whether something he did during the surgery contributed to her unexpected death.
Dr. Zinker meets with Ms. Foster’s husband, Jim, and adult daughter, Alta, to obtain consent for an autopsy. He explains to them what’s involved in an autopsy and how long it might take. The normal protocol for autopsy includes examining both the head and the body, but Dr. Zinker explains that the family may limit autopsy to the body if so desired. He also explains that the autopsy should take a few hours and that preliminary results would be available shortly after the procedure was complete. He tells the family that final results might not be available for several weeks because academic autopsies often involve microscopic evaluation of tissues, which requires additional histologic processing. Jim and Alta are reluctant to consent to the autopsy of Ms. Foster, stating, “She’s already suffered so much. I can’t imagine putting her body through that.” They are also concerned about delaying her funeral. Finally, they ask, “Why do you want to do an autopsy, anyway? Why does it matter now?”
Dr. Zinker wonders what to say next. Is understanding what happened to Ms. Foster worth further upsetting her grieving family? How should he counsel them about the autopsy process? Should he admit that there might have been a surgical error? He contacts the hospital’s pathologist for advice.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Zinker, a cardiac surgeon, is deeply troubled by the sudden and unanticipated death of his patient, Ms. Foster. Her recovery following surgery appeared to be going well, and there were no indications of postoperative complications. However, shortly before her death, Ms. Foster reported feeling short of breath. Further assessment revealed a pleural effusion—an abnormal collection of fluid surrounding one of her lungs. The clinical team acted quickly to drain the fluid, but soon after, Ms. Foster’s blood pressure dropped to dangerous levels, requiring escalating doses of vasopressors. Despite all interventions, she died unexpectedly.

In his search for clarity, Dr. Zinker feels compelled to request an autopsy to determine the exact cause of Ms. Foster’s death, particularly to discern whether any intraoperative factors may have contributed. He is guided by a sense of responsibility to both Ms. Foster’s family and future patients, and he wants to be open about any possibility that a surgical issue played a part.

Dr. Zinker arranges a meeting with Ms. Foster’s husband, Jim, and her adult daughter, Alta, to discuss the prospect of an autopsy and to seek their consent. He carefully explains what an autopsy entails, noting that a standard procedure involves examination of both the head and the rest of the body, but also reassures them that the family has the right to request certain limitations if they so desire. He emphasizes that the autopsy usually takes only a few hours, with preliminary findings available soon after, while final results may take several weeks as tissues are examined in detail.

Jim and Alta listen quietly, taking in the information as Dr. Zinker patiently answers their questions about the process, what it might reveal, and how it could impact their understanding of Ms. Foster’s final hours.

ethical_issues.question: Is consent from the deceased patient’s family required prior to performing an autopsy?
keypoints: Autopsy generally requires the consent of the deceased’s family, as the body holds unique value in a pluralistic society, encompassing sociocultural and spiritual traditions, and reflecting respect and commemoration for the deceased.

Physicians should communicate thoroughly with the family, clearly explaining the purpose, process, and significance of the autopsy, guiding them with patience to foster understanding, balancing the medical value of investigation with the emotional needs of the family, and upholding the autonomy of both the deceased and their family.

Forensic cases represent a primary exception, in which autopsy may be performed without family consent in accordance with the law, for the purposes of determining cause of death, collecting criminal evidence, or meeting judicial requirements.

In non-forensic cases, if the family continues to refuse autopsy after receiving a full explanation, their decision should be respected, analogous to honoring a living patient’s right to refuse treatment, so as to avoid exacerbating the family’s psychological distress.

Physicians should adhere to the principle of beneficence, weighing the potential benefits of medical investigation against the family’s emotional capacity, and strive to facilitate mutual understanding and consensus between both parties.

ethical_issues.question: How can an autopsy be conducted to obtain medically relevant information while respecting the sociocultural beliefs and values of Ms. Foster and her family?
keypoints: Physicians should respect the sociocultural beliefs of the deceased and their family members, communicating with next-of-kin to convey the wishes of the deceased and thereby uphold the autonomy and dignity of the deceased.

Physicians should communicate proactively, honestly, and empathetically, exploring the values of the patient and family, and clearly explaining the purpose, necessity, potential benefits, and risks of autopsy to help the family understand the significance of autopsy for medical knowledge and determination of cause of death.

Physicians should appropriately disclose any potential medical errors according to the circumstances, avoiding both overpromising and evasion, thereby demonstrating honesty and a sense of responsibility, while emphasizing that autopsy can facilitate learning from mistakes and improving the quality of care.

Physicians may seek the assistance of bereavement counselors or mental health professionals to enhance communication with the family, alleviate their emotional distress, and promote rational decision-making.

If, after thorough explanation and communication, the family continues to refuse the autopsy, their decision should be respected, analogous to respecting a living patient’s right to refuse treatment, and coercive measures should be avoided in order to honor the family’s emotional and cultural needs.

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances can the public interest in performing an autopsy take precedence over the autonomy and beliefs of the deceased and their family?
keypoints: In forensic cases, autopsy can provide critical evidence for crime investigation or conviction, and the pursuit of justice allows the public interest to take precedence over the autonomy and beliefs of the deceased and their family members.

When a physician suspects that a medical error poses a systematic risk that may endanger the safety of future patients, the protection of public interest and future patients can justifiably override the autonomy and beliefs of the deceased and their family members.

title: Ordering Stains That Aren’t Indicated
case: Dr. B is in the process of executing a retroperitoneal soft tissue mass biopsy. Midway through, she gets a call from Dr. M, who asks her to apply additional stains to this specimen, which Dr. M believes will identify the possible cause of a patient’s infection. Based on her original assessment of the sample, however, Dr. B believes that the so-called “bug stains” will not help diagnose the cause of this patient’s illness, that they are not indicated in this case, and that ordering them would require resources that would probably be wasted. If any additional testing is performed, Dr. B thinks that tissue cultures would be more likely to identify the cause of the infection. At the same time, she wants to maintain a good professional relationship with Dr. M, so she wonders if she should just apply the additional stains to avoid disagreement.
case_rewrite:
Dr. B is performing a biopsy of a retroperitoneal soft tissue mass.
