ethical_issues.question: When considering the decision for hysterectomy, how can the wishes of a patient with intellectual disabilities be respected while ensuring that she understands the implications and risks of the surgery?
keypoints: Patients with intellectual disabilities should be presumed to have decision-making capacity unless there is clear evidence demonstrating a lack of such capacity.

When assessing decision-making capacity, it is essential to confirm that the patient understands the nature and consequences of the specific medical decision, particularly regarding key concepts such as contraception, pregnancy, fertility, and parenting responsibilities.

The decision-making process should follow a shared decision-making model that prioritizes the patient’s personal values and preferences, ensuring they have a substantive voice in their medical care and future life planning.

Even if the patient cannot fully comprehend or evaluate all consequences, their clearly expressed wishes should remain a significant factor in decision-making; proxy decision-makers must not base decisions solely on their own values or interests but must adhere to the principle of the patient’s best interests.

Hysterectomy should not be performed unless the patient explicitly consents after fully understanding the implications and risks of the surgery, thereby avoiding involuntary sterilization and ensuring compliance with medical ethical standards.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr. Jones and Amy’s mother ensure that Amy receives appropriate sexual counseling and education that supports her understanding of the potential consequences of sexual activity and promotes healthy sexual behavior, while respecting her autonomy and decision-making capacity as a young adult with intellectual disabilities?
keypoints: Formal education on sexual behavior and sexual health is essential for adolescents and young adults with intellectual disabilities, and the curriculum should be tailored to the individual’s level of health literacy and comprehension.
The use of plain yet accurate anatomical terminology, supplemented by visual materials and models, is particularly effective for individuals with limited verbal communication skills.
Sexual education should not be confined to school settings but must be continuously reinforced and supported by parents and professional caregivers within the home environment.

Parents and caregivers should acknowledge the capacity of individuals with intellectual disabilities to form intimate social relationships, including friendships, romantic relationships, and sexual relationships, and avoid evading these topics.
Training and support for parents and caregivers are equally important to help them overcome concerns about sexual education and to enhance their communication skills and knowledge in this area.

ethical_issues.question: How should caregiver convenience be balanced with patient benefit in the menstrual suppression treatment of patients with intellectual disabilities?
keypoints: Distinguish the primary motivation behind the caregiver’s request for treatment—whether it is to reduce caregiver burden or to improve the patient’s quality of life—and ensure that decision making is centered on the patient’s best interests.

Weigh the potential benefits and risks of menstrual suppression therapy for the patient, ensuring that the treatment plan aligns with the patient’s best interests rather than serving solely for caregiver convenience.

Adhere to a shared decision-making model, respect the patient’s ability to express preferences, and promote her participation in medical decisions, avoiding situations in which the proxy substitutes her own values for those of the patient.

Conduct a comprehensive assessment of the patient’s quality of life, physical health, psychological well-being, and social support, emphasizing a balanced consideration of risks and benefits, and avoiding decisions based solely on fertility or caregiving challenges.

Even if the patient has limited capacity to assess consequences, her clearly expressed needs and preferences should remain a key reference in decision making, ensuring that the patient retains a central voice in her medical planning.

title: Managing Care of an Intrapartum Patient with Agitation and Psychosis: Ethical and Legal Implications
case:
Ms. S arrived, unaccompanied, at the emergency department of an urban academic hospital in the early evening. She was disheveled and delusional, exclaiming that she had been invaded by an alien force. Because she was obviously pregnant and apparently in labor, she was seen by the obstetrician on call. No useful history could be obtained, and Ms. S did not cooperate with attempts to evaluate the status of her pregnancy.
Review of the limited electronic health record at the hospital indicates that Ms. S, 27 years of age, was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder six years earlier and has been relatively stable on haloperidol in the intervening period. She was hospitalized once during this period for a week, during which time her medication regimen was adjusted and she was discharged. At that time, Ms. S lived alone and worked part-time as an archivist at a local museum. She took her medication regularly and kept her regular appointments with her psychiatrist. The electronic health record’s last entry was a year ago; it contains reports of four unsuccessful attempts over a period of three months to contact her through her family and her job.
The obstetrician considers how to fulfill his professional responsibility with respect to both the patient’s mental health needs and her pregnancy. In particular, he wonders how best to gain her trust to enable fuller and more comprehensive examination for the sake of the developing child, too.
case_rewrite:
Ms. S arrived alone at the emergency department of a large urban teaching hospital as dusk settled in. Her clothes were rumpled, and her hair was unkempt; she appeared confused, loudly insisting that an alien entity had taken over her body. It was immediately apparent that Ms. S was pregnant and, judging by her physical signs, likely in active labor. The obstetrician on call, Dr. W, was summoned to evaluate her. Attempts to obtain a medical history proved futile, as Ms. S was unable or unwilling to answer questions, and she resisted efforts to assess the progress of her pregnancy.

A brief review of the hospital’s electronic health record revealed that Ms. S is 27 years old and was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder six years ago. Since then, she had been maintained on haloperidol and, until recently, had remained relatively stable. One prior hospitalization was documented: she was admitted for a week, her medications were adjusted, and she was discharged in improved condition. At that time, Ms. S lived alone and was employed part-time as an archivist at a local museum. She was noted to be medication-adherent and attended her scheduled psychiatric appointments. However, the last entry in her health record, from a year earlier, indicated that four unsuccessful attempts had been made over three months to reach her through family and her workplace.

Now, facing Ms. S’s acute distress and psychosis in the context of imminent childbirth, Dr. W reflected on his dual responsibilities: to address her psychiatric needs while ensuring the safety of both Ms. S and her unborn child. He wondered how best to gain her trust so that a thorough and respectful evaluation—essential for both her well-being and that of her baby—could be performed.

ethical_issues.question: How should decision-making capacity be assessed and respect for autonomy be ensured in a pregnant patient exhibiting psychotic symptoms during labor?
keypoints: The assessment of a patient’s decision-making capacity should be premised on respect for her autonomy; clinicians ought to presume that adult patients possess decision-making capacity unless there is clear evidence warranting further evaluation.
Psychotic symptoms may impair a patient’s decision-making capacity, and the obstetrician should promptly seek assistance from psychiatric colleagues to assess the patient’s capacity.

During labor, when a patient refuses intervention, the guiding principles should be respectful persuasion and beneficence-based clinical judgment, balancing respect for patient autonomy with the obligation to protect the health of both the pregnant woman and the fetus.

The healthcare team’s shared objective is to identify and address specific impairments to the patient’s decision-making capacity and to restore it as fully as possible, enabling the patient to participate in medical decisions in accordance with her longstanding values and beliefs.

Throughout the process of assessing decision-making capacity or when capacity is impaired, physicians must continue to respect the patient’s autonomy in practice by seeking permission for specific interventions such as physical examinations, ultrasound, and fetal monitoring.

ethical_issues.question: In the absence of decision-making capacity, how should an appropriate surrogate decision maker be identified and prioritized for medical decision making?
keypoints: When the patient lacks decision-making capacity and both assisted decision making and respectful persuasion have failed, hospital records should be reviewed in accordance with hospital policy and applicable law to identify and prioritize potential surrogate decision makers.
The typical priority order for surrogate decision makers is the adult patient’s spouse, adult children, parents, or other family members.

When the usual surrogate decision makers are unavailable or do not exist, a “surrogate of last resort,” such as a clergy member or other designated surrogate as specified by law, should be considered.

If there is any doubt regarding the selection of a surrogate decision maker, hospital legal counsel should be consulted promptly to ensure that the decision complies with relevant legal and ethical standards.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians and the medical team respond when a patient refuses to authorize treatment, in order to ensure the health and well-being of both the pregnant woman and the fetal or neonatal patient?
keypoints: When the patient refuses authorized treatment, physicians should interact with the patient with respect and empathy, balancing the pregnant woman’s personal dignity with the health interests of both mother and fetus.

Once the patient expresses an impaired refusal, legal counsel should be notified promptly and, in accordance with institutional policy, a court order should be sought to ensure legal support and procedural compliance.

It is essential to assess whether there are evidence-based maternal or fetal complications (such as indications for cesarean delivery) to determine the necessity and potential benefit of clinical intervention.

If there are indications for cesarean delivery and a surrogate decision maker has authorized the procedure, preparations for surgery should begin, while simultaneously promoting patient engagement through psychological support and assisted decision making.

Physicians should explain the indications for cesarean delivery and their evidentiary basis to the patient in clear and concise language, in order to gain her cooperation and reduce psychological resistance.

If the patient lacks decision-making capacity and her physical resistance cannot be safely overcome, necessary measures should be taken in accordance with legal and regulatory requirements to safeguard the safety of both mother and infant and to prevent serious perinatal or neonatal adverse outcomes.

Throughout the entire process, priority should be given to respecting the patient’s dignity and rights, striving through communication and support to achieve the best possible clinical and ethical outcomes.

title: How Should Clinicians Treat Patients Who Might Be Undocumented?
case:
Dr. Connelly, who recently finished her residency program, has now worked as a partner in a private primary care practice for a year. She shares the practice with an older physician who is considering retirement, taking on fewer responsibilities, and reducing his hours. The practice is part of a large hospital network and serves a diverse community in a large city. Dr. Connelly loves the prospect of owning the practice but is unsure whether she wants to assume sole responsibility for managing the business when her partner retires. She acknowledges that her training was medical and her business-oriented expertise is limited.
One day, the clerk at the front desk of the practice is welcoming one of the new patients, Ms. Nunez, and notices that the identification (ID) she presents lacks the holograms and graphics on IDs typically issued in the state. Unsure what to do, the clerk instructs Ms. Nunez to complete the usual forms and shows her ID to the fellow clinic staff members, some of whom suspect it to be false. One of the nurses, Kim, holds strong beliefs about illegal immigration and, based on Ms. Nunez’s ethnicity and language preferences marked on her forms, assumes that she is an undocumented immigrant.
Kim approaches Dr. Connelly and demands that someone from their office report Ms. Nunez to the appropriate federal authorities. Taken by surprise and pressed for time, Dr. Connelly asks Kim to wait to discuss the matter as she enters another patient’s room to try not to get further behind in her appointment schedule. By the time Dr. Connelly invites Kim to talk more about Ms. Nunez’s ID, she learns that Kim has mobilized other members of the office and nursing staff, who agree upon their responsibility to report Ms. Nunez.
Dr. Connelly is reluctant to join them, as she is not convinced that a patient’s immigration or political status should be a factor in determining who receives care. She considers seeking legal advice and wonders whether she does indeed have a legal obligation to report a patient suspected of not being a legal resident. But she also wonders whether Ms. Nunez, who may have presented a false ID, would give accurate clinically relevant information, given that she might not feel comfortable telling the whole truth.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Connelly, having recently finished her residency, has spent the past year as a partner in a private primary care clinic. She works alongside Dr. Martin, an older physician who is gradually reducing his hours and handing off more responsibilities as he prepares for retirement. Their clinic, which is affiliated with a large hospital network, serves a diverse and multicultural patient base in a bustling metropolitan area. Although Dr. Connelly is interested in the possibility of one day owning the practice, she hesitates at the thought of managing the full range of business operations, aware that her skills are almost exclusively clinical rather than administrative or financial.

One particularly busy afternoon, the front desk clerk greets a new patient, Ms. Nunez. As Ms. Nunez presents her identification, the clerk notices that the card lacks the standard holographic features and design elements typical of state-issued IDs. Unsure of how to proceed, the clerk asks Ms. Nunez to complete the usual paperwork and quietly brings the questionable ID to the attention of the clinic staff. Some staff members voice concern that the identification might be counterfeit. Among them is Nurse Kim, who holds strong opinions regarding undocumented immigration. Kim immediately makes the assumption—based on Ms. Nunez’s ethnicity and her preference for Spanish on the forms—that Ms. Nunez could be an undocumented immigrant.

Without delay, Kim approaches Dr. Connelly and asserts that the clinic has a duty to alert federal authorities about Ms. Nunez. Caught off guard and pressed for time amid a packed schedule, Dr. Connelly asks Kim to refrain from taking any action until they can discuss the situation further, then hurries into her next patient’s exam room to avoid falling behind. In the meantime, Kim discusses the matter with other staff and nurses, and together they decide that reporting Ms. Nunez is the right thing to do.

When Dr. Connelly is finally able to revisit the situation, she discovers that the staff has reached a strong consensus in favor of notifying the authorities. However, Dr. Connelly is deeply uneasy with this decision. She questions whether a patient’s immigration status—or the authenticity of their identification—should have any impact on her commitment to provide appropriate care. She contemplates seeking legal advice to clarify whether she is legally obligated to report a patient suspected of being undocumented, as she is uncertain about the relevant laws. Simultaneously, she worries that if Ms. Nunez feels threatened or unwelcome because of her perceived status, she may withhold crucial health information, ultimately compromising her own care.

Dr. Connelly now finds herself at a pivotal crossroads, weighing her ethical duty to treat every patient with compassion and to safeguard their privacy, against mounting pressure from her staff and her own uncertainty about the legal implications of the situation.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians refuse to provide medical care based on a patient’s immigration status?
keypoints: Healthcare professionals must not refuse medical services to patients based on their immigration status, as explicitly stipulated by the American Medical Association’s Code of Medical Ethics.
The physician’s oath requires healthcare providers to promote the well-being of all patients, regardless of their social attributes or status.

The physician’s duty to provide care embodies the principle of beneficence, which emphasizes mercy, kindness, altruism, and the promotion of others’ welfare, serving as a fundamental theoretical foundation in medical ethics.

ethical_issues.question: Do physicians have a moral obligation to protect the privacy rights of patients who may be undocumented?
keypoints: Protecting patient privacy is not only a legal requirement under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) but also a fundamental ethical responsibility of physicians grounded in the principle of beneficence. All clinic staff members, including nurses, are bound by this obligation and must not disclose patient information to immigration or law enforcement authorities.

Physicians have a moral duty to provide necessary treatment when a patient’s condition is critical and must offer care equitably regardless of the patient’s background or nationality, respecting their fundamental right to medical care.

Even if legal mandates exist requiring mandatory reporting, physicians may, on ethical grounds informed by beneficence and the trust inherent in the doctor-patient relationship, morally refuse to report, prioritizing the protection of patient confidentiality and clinical safety.

title: Ethical Challenges for the Medical Expert Witness
case:
Dr. Lopez is a well-respected, board-certified academic behavioral neurologist who primarily treats patients with cognitive dysfunction and has a special interest in traumatic brain injury (TBI). On rare occasions she has served as an expert witness but, as a rule, does not testify against physicians in her community in malpractice cases. Now a plaintiff’s attorney, Mr. Sewell, has contacted her to engage her services in a case brought against a cross-country trucking company. One year ago the plaintiff, Ms. Dewey, was pulling out of a parking lot when her car was hit by a truck from the defendant’s fleet. She alleged a variety of injuries sustained as a result of the accident, including chronic headaches and residual cognitive dysfunction from a mild traumatic brain injury (TBI). The mild TBI category, which is the most prevalent type of TBI, includes concussions and other brain trauma that have initial symptoms such as loss of consciousness and/or “a state of being dazed, confused or disoriented” [1].
Mr. Sewell told Dr. Lopez that she would be given an opportunity to review the documents and would then be asked whether she could testify that it was more likely than not that the mild traumatic brain injury sustained during the motor vehicle accident was the proximate cause of Ms. Dewey’s cognitive dysfunction. Intrigued by the facts and interested in serving as an expert witness for a case not involving malpractice, Dr. Lopez agreed to review the documents once Mr. Sewell agreed to the terms of her fee schedule and she received her retainer fee for document review.
Upon reviewing the documents—including the plaintiff’s and defendant’s depositions; the police report from the accident; and Ms. Dewey’s medical records from the emergency medical services, the emergency center, and the treating neurologist—a number of facts struck Dr. Lopez as potentially problematic. In both the police report and the EMS documents, there was no mention of Ms. Dewey’s being confused or disoriented, and it was unclear whether she actually lost consciousness. The EC records were vague and contradictory, although the neurologist’s evaluation did seem to meet the standard of care. After her document review, Dr. Lopez remained interested in helping Ms. Dewey receive just compensation, but she also knew that, at some point, she would be asked to reveal that Ms. Dewey’s records did not definitively document a loss of consciousness, a fact that would likely put the severity of her injuries in question and possibly substantially undermine her claims to compensation. The evidentiary standard in civil litigation is “the preponderance of the evidence,” which essentially requires 51 percent certainty that the facts are as the plaintiff claims them to be [2]. Dr. Lopez is undecided about whether she believes the evidence meets this evidentiary threshold.
Accordingly, Dr. Lopez is faced with deciding whether to continue to work on Ms. Dewey’s behalf in the role of expert witness or to decline further engagement with her case. She wonders whether she has an obligation to tell Ms. Dewey’s attorney about her impressions of the records she reviewed.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Lopez is a respected, board-certified academic behavioral neurologist recognized for her expertise in cognitive dysfunction, with a particular focus on traumatic brain injury (TBI). Although she has occasionally served as an expert witness, Dr. Lopez generally avoids testifying against physicians in her local community in malpractice lawsuits. Recently, she was contacted by Mr. Sewell, a plaintiff’s attorney, who sought her expertise in a case against a national trucking company. The plaintiff, Ms. Dewey, was involved in a collision a year earlier when her vehicle was struck by a truck belonging to the defendant’s fleet as she exited a parking lot. Following the accident, Ms. Dewey alleged multiple injuries, including persistent headaches and ongoing cognitive difficulties that she attributed to a mild traumatic brain injury. This category of TBI—which includes concussions and similar injuries—is the most common and is typically characterized by initial symptoms such as loss of consciousness or experiencing confusion, disorientation, or a state of being dazed.

Mr. Sewell explained to Dr. Lopez that she would be asked to review all relevant records and determine whether she could testify that Ms. Dewey’s cognitive dysfunction was, more likely than not, directly caused by the mild TBI sustained during the accident. Interested in participating in a legal case unrelated to malpractice, Dr. Lopez agreed to conduct a review once her fee schedule was accepted and her retainer for document review was received.

Dr. Lopez meticulously examined the materials provided: depositions from both parties, the police report from the day of the accident, and Ms. Dewey’s medical records from emergency services, the emergency center, and her treating neurologist. Several details gave Dr. Lopez pause. Neither the police report nor the records from emergency medical services documented any evidence of Ms. Dewey being confused, disoriented, or losing consciousness at the scene. The emergency center’s notes were ambiguous and at times contradictory, although the neurologist’s assessment appeared to be thorough and consistent with the standard of care. After completing her review, Dr. Lopez remained sympathetic to Ms. Dewey’s situation and wanted to help her secure appropriate compensation. However, she also recognized that the absence of clear, definitive evidence of loss of consciousness or confusion would be a significant weakness in linking the accident conclusively to Ms. Dewey’s ongoing cognitive issues. This gap in documentation could undermine the credibility of her injury claims.

Dr. Lopez understood that, as an expert witness, her testimony would need to meet the civil litigation standard of “preponderance of the evidence”—meaning she would have to be at least 51 percent certain that the facts support the plaintiff’s claims. Yet she remained uncertain whether the current evidence rose to that level. Now, Dr. Lopez finds herself at a crossroads: she must decide whether to continue working as an expert witness for Ms. Dewey or to withdraw from further involvement in the case. At the same time, Dr. Lopez considers whether she is ethically obliged to share her reservations about the strength of the evidence with Mr. Sewell, candidly explaining her concerns about the documentation and the potential impact on the case.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr. Lopez balance the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence when providing expert testimony in this case?
keypoints: Lopez must ensure that her testimony is truthful, objective, and reliable, thereby avoiding potential harm to the plaintiff, the attorney, the judicial process, and her own professional integrity that could result from false or misleading statements.

Lopez has reservations about whether the available evidence adequately supports the plaintiff’s claim of mild traumatic brain injury (TBI), she has an ethical obligation to communicate these concerns transparently to the attorney. She should assist in evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of the case, which may involve recommending further evidence or reconsidering her involvement as an expert witness.

Lopez should uphold her ethical and legal responsibilities by refraining from providing testimony that does not meet the standard of a preponderance of the evidence, regardless of personal sympathy for the plaintiff. Her expert opinion must be based on objective medical facts, sound clinical judgment, and adherence to professional standards.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Lopez continue to serve as an expert witness on behalf of Ms. Dewey if she does not believe that the preponderance of the evidence supports the theory that the plaintiff suffered a mild TBI?
keypoints: If Dr. Lopez does not believe that the preponderance of the evidence supports the theory that the plaintiff suffered a mild TBI, she has an obligation to promptly inform the plaintiff’s attorney of the key weaknesses in the case and is obligated to withdraw from her role as an expert witness.
Dr. Lopez must adhere to professional guidelines and fulfill her fiduciary duty to the plaintiff by ensuring that her testimony is based on objective, truthful, and sufficient evidence.
Even if she feels sympathy for the plaintiff, Dr. Lopez must not allow her emotions to compromise her objective judgment, as all parties involved have the right to testimony that is grounded in fact.

title: Should Physicians Attempt to Persuade a Patient to Accept a Compromised Organ for Transplant?
case:
While in an administrative meeting, Dr. Calvin, chief of transplant surgery at a major academic hospital in California, receives a phone call from a regional organ procurement organization. A liver has become available for the hospital’s sickest patient, Mr. Lawrence, who was recently admitted with severe complications from advanced alcoholic liver disease and encephalopathy. Knowing how severe Mr. Lawrence’s condition has suddenly become, Dr. Calvin excitedly breaks away from his meeting to page other attending physicians on the transplant service and review the donor information.
They find that the available liver is not without concern: it comes from an older donor with multiple comorbidities, including obesity with a degree of fatty liver, and, most importantly, the patient passed away from cardiac failure, which results in considerable hypoxemia and free-radical damage. The risk of graft failure is significant enough for the center to classify the organ as an “extended criteria donation (ECD).” Nevertheless, the team is confident and enthusiastic about the potential for transplantation, having had extensive experience successfully transplanting similar organs. So, the team rushes upstairs to the patient’s room to relay the news about an available liver.
“Mr. Lawrence!” Dr. Calvin exclaims, “We’re going to save your life today! An organ has become available!”
Waking from a foggy state, exhausted, exasperated, and fearful, Mr. Lawrence tries to process everything the team is telling him about the organ and the prospective transplant surgery. “So you’re saying you want to give me a damaged liver?”
His daughter, who had been sitting in a chair on the side of her father’s bed, stands up to take in what is being said. “Maybe we should just wait until a better one comes along,” she suggests.
Dr. Calvin reminds them that they’ve discussed ECD organs before, and all the risk factors in their previous conversations are present in this one. He then explains the list of additional risk factors present and what they mean, eventually concluding that this is a calculated risk, but one they have to take.
Mr. Lawrence says, “Doc, I don’t understand what you are saying,” while squinting at the dense text on the consent form they just handed him with a pen, “but I trust you and want to do whatever you tell me. I’m just so overwhelmed and tired. I don’t have the energy to get through something like this now—I’m so exhausted. All I want to do is cry.”
The team listens patiently and intently, and Dr. Calvin tells Mr. Lawrence sternly but compassionately, “Mr. Lawrence, there is no better time to do this than now. Without this liver, you will die. This organ is a blessing.”
His daughter says to Mr. Lawrence, “Well, I understand what the doctors are saying. There’s no way to really know what the outcome with this organ will be, or whether a better organ will come along in time. But I’m not the one who has to go through surgery, Dad. You do. And no one can make this decision for you.”
Mr. Lawrence requests more time to think about the decision.
“Mr. Lawrence,” another caregiver speaks up, “The longer we wait, the worse the organ quality gets. If you don’t take this liver right now, it’s gone.”
case_rewrite:
During an administrative meeting, Dr. Calvin, chief of transplant surgery at a prominent academic hospital in California, is interrupted by a phone call from the regional organ procurement organization. A liver has become available for the hospital’s most critically ill patient, Mr. Lawrence, who was recently admitted with serious complications from advanced alcoholic liver disease and worsening encephalopathy. Recognizing the gravity of Mr. Lawrence’s deteriorating condition, Dr. Calvin excused himself from the meeting, eager to alert the other attending physicians on the transplant team and review the donor’s medical information.

As the team examines the details, they note that the liver in question poses several concerns: the donor was older, struggled with obesity and had a degree of fatty liver, and, crucially, died from cardiac failure—leading to significant hypoxemia and potential free-radical injury to the organ. The risk of graft failure is notable enough for the center to classify the liver as an “extended criteria donation (ECD).” Still, the team remains optimistic, drawing on their considerable experience with similar transplants. With a sense of urgency, they head to Mr. Lawrence’s hospital room to share the news.

“Mr. Lawrence!” Dr. Calvin announces, his voice filled with hope, “We have a chance to save your life today! An organ has become available for you.”

Rousing from a confused and fatigued state, Mr. Lawrence tries to comprehend the flurry of information about the donor liver and the proposed surgery. “So you’re telling me you want to give me a damaged liver?” he asks, his voice tinged with anxiety.

His daughter, seated beside his bed, stands up, digesting the conversation. “Maybe we should just wait for a better one,” she suggests, her concern evident.

Dr. Calvin gently reminds them that they have previously discussed ECD organs, and that all the risk factors they talked about before are present in this offer. He systematically explains the additional risks associated with this particular liver, emphasizing the calculated nature of the decision but also the necessity of acting now.

Mr. Lawrence, struggling to focus on the dense consent form now handed to him along with a pen, admits, “Doc, I don’t really understand what you’re saying,” his eyes straining, “but I trust you and want to do whatever you say. I’m just overwhelmed and so tired. I don’t have the strength to go through with this right now—I feel like I could just cry.”

The team listens closely and respectfully. Dr. Calvin, firm yet compassionate, tells him, “Mr. Lawrence, this is the best opportunity we have. Without this transplant, you will not survive. This organ is a real chance for you.”

His daughter turns to her father, saying, “I get what the doctors are saying. There’s no way to guarantee what will happen with this liver, or if a better one will come along soon enough. But, Dad, you’re the one who has to go through the surgery. No one else can make this choice for you.”

Mr. Lawrence, clearly overwhelmed, asks for more time to consider his decision.

Another member of the care team gently interjects, “Mr. Lawrence, the longer we wait, the more the organ’s quality declines. If you don’t accept this liver now, it will have to be offered to someone else.”

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians urge a patient to make a decision to consent or refuse while respecting the patient’s autonomy?
keypoints: Physicians should reasonably urge patients to make timely decisions to consent or refuse transplantation within an ethical framework grounded in the principles of nonmaleficence, justice, respect for autonomy, and beneficence.

Patients who possess decision-making capacity have the right to autonomously consent to or refuse transplantation; however, they must be clearly informed that hesitation is time-limited and that the organ may be allocated to another recipient.

Delayed decision-making may result in clinical deterioration (e.g., worsening encephalopathy), thereby diminishing the patient’s future autonomy—this constitutes a significant ethical rationale for encouraging prompt decision-making.

Physicians have the responsibility to provide an accurate and comprehensive risk assessment and to establish trust through transparent, patient, and ongoing education and communication, thereby facilitating fully informed patient decisions.

The medical team should consider the patient’s specific clinical circumstances and family support, respect the patient’s emotional and psychological state, assist in overcoming doubts, and promote the realization of optimal autonomous decision-making.

title: How to Communicate Clearly about Brain Death and First-Person Consent to Donate
case:
Michael is a healthy 21-year-old man who is brought by ambulance to an emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. His family is devastated when he falls into a coma, is put on a ventilator, and, three days later, is declared brain-dead by two physicians. Dr. Allen, the attending trauma physician on service in the intensive care unit that week, explains to Michael’s parents the unlikelihood of his recovering and initiates a discussion about whether and for how long the family would like to continue life-sustaining care. Michael’s parents are distraught over the idea of stopping it. His mother says, “How can you even suggest discontinuing care? His heart is still beating, he still has life energy inside of him, and you want us to kill him?”
Later that afternoon, a nurse taking care of Michael, Rhana, learns that he had registered to be an organ donor on the state’s donor registry and lets Dr. Allen know. She asks whether he would like her to inform the local organ bank so it can send an organ procurement representative to speak with the family, as is expected of hospitals when a patient has either died or is in critical conditionandis a potential organ donor [1]. Rhana and Dr. Allen know that such involvement of organ procurement organizations (OPOs) is standard practice in the US, in order to ensure that all potential donors’ families are eventually approached by someone trained to speak to them in a thoughtful manner. However, although OPOs must be notified, organ procurement coordinators may not directly speak with families until death is declared. Although Dr. Allen could follow the regulations strictly and contact the local OPO, he thanks Rhana but says that he will revisit the issue in the next day or so after the family has had more time to process what’s happening to Michael.
After several days with no change in Michael’s reflexes or vital signs, Dr. Allen again brings up the issue of continuing life-sustaining care, this time to a slightly more amenable, and extended, family. He also tells the family that Michael has listed himself as an organ donor on the state’s registry. The family is shocked by this news and questions Dr. Allen about the procedures by which organs are actually taken from a donor. Some family members respond with agitation when they learn the answers: Michael would be left on a ventilator until being taken to surgery for organ retrieval and would die after the organs are removed from his body and the ventilator is turned off. Michael’s father is the first to speak. “Wait. We had no idea that the retrieval procedures would interfere with Michael’s dying process so much. That’s not what we’ve envisioned for him. We’re not comfortable with that.”
Afterward, Rhana asks Dr. Allen whether she should still call the organ bank. He explains that the state’s first-person consent law—as established in Illinois, for example, in 2006—prohibits one’s next of kin from overriding a documented decision to donate [2]. Every state in the country has such a law [3]. Rhana asks, “Can the patient’s family override Michael’s decision if he would have declined to be an organ donor?” He nods and starts to emphasize the extent of the organ shortage crisis, but she says, “I don’t understand. How can respect for patients’ autonomy apply only if they made the ‘right’ decision according to the state and the OPO? Especially in a case like this one, when the state’s and the OPO’s priorities are really different from the family’s?”
case_rewrite:
Michael, a healthy 21-year-old man, is rushed by ambulance to the emergency department after being involved in a severe motor vehicle accident. His family is overwhelmed with distress when he slips into a coma, is placed on a ventilator, and, three days later, is declared brain-dead by two physicians. Dr. Allen, the attending trauma physician in the intensive care unit that week, sits down with Michael’s parents. He gently explains the gravity of Michael’s condition, emphasizing the extremely remote chance of recovery, and initiates a conversation about whether and for how long the family wishes to continue life-sustaining interventions. Michael’s parents, devastated, struggle with the possibility of discontinuing support. His mother, distraught, exclaims, “How can you even suggest discontinuing care? His heart is still beating, he still has life energy inside of him, and you want us to kill him?”

Later that same afternoon, Rhana, the nurse caring for Michael, discovers that he had registered as an organ donor in the state’s donor registry and promptly informs Dr. Allen. She asks whether he would like her to notify the local organ bank so they can send an organ procurement representative to speak with Michael’s family, as is standard practice when a patient has died or is in critical condition and is a potential donor. Rhana and Dr. Allen both know that involving organ procurement organizations (OPOs) is routine in the U.S. to ensure that all potential donor families are approached by trained professionals in a sensitive manner. However, while OPOs must be informed, procurement coordinators are only permitted to engage directly with families after death has been formally declared. Dr. Allen, mindful of the family’s distress, thanks Rhana for bringing this to his attention and says he will revisit the issue in a day or two, allowing the family more time to come to terms with Michael’s situation.

Several days pass with no change in Michael’s neurological status or vital signs. Dr. Allen once again approaches the family—now joined by extended relatives—and revisits the discussion about continuing life-sustaining care. He also shares with them that Michael had registered himself as an organ donor. The family is taken aback by this revelation and begins to question Dr. Allen about the processes involved in organ donation. As Dr. Allen answers their questions, explaining that Michael would remain on a ventilator until surgery for organ retrieval, and that death would follow the removal of organs and discontinuation of support, some family members react with visible agitation. Michael’s father voices the family’s concerns: “Wait. We had no idea that the retrieval procedures would interfere with Michael’s dying process so much. That’s not what we’ve envisioned for him. We’re not comfortable with that.”

After the conversation, Rhana asks Dr. Allen whether she should proceed with notifying the organ bank. Dr. Allen explains that the state’s first-person consent law, like that established in Illinois in 2006, prevents next of kin from overturning a documented decision to donate organs. He notes that every state has such a law. Rhana then asks, “Can the patient’s family override Michael’s decision if he had chosen not to be an organ donor?” Dr. Allen nods, beginning to discuss the severity of the organ shortage, but Rhana interrupts: “I don’t understand. How can respect for patients’ autonomy apply only if they made the ‘right’ decision according to the state and the OPO? Especially in a case like this, when the state’s and the OPO’s priorities seem so different from the family’s?”

ethical_issues.question: In cases of brain death, how can clinicians communicate effectively and ethically with family members about the definition of death and information related to organ donation?
keypoints: When declaring brain death, the physician should clearly inform the family that, according to state law, the patient has been pronounced dead.
The physician should empathetically explain that the patient’s signs of life merely indicate that his body is being artificially sustained, but that the patient himself is gone.
The physician should clarify that brain death is a completely reliable diagnosis, with no cases of recovery ever documented, distinguishing it from other forms of brain injury.
It is reasonable and necessary to give the family time and space to process their cognitive dissonance and emotional responses.
When raising the issue of organ donation, it should be emphasized that the declaration of death occurs prior to organ procurement, and that the patient is legally dead before any organs are removed.

The physician should avoid proactively engaging the family in philosophical debates about the definition of brain death, unless the family themselves raise such questions, in order to minimize unnecessary conflict and confusion.

title: What’s the Role of Autonomy in Patient- and Family-Centered Care When Patients and Family Members Don’t Agree?
case:
Dave’s health is on the decline. Despite surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and hormonal treatments, his prostate cancer has metastasized to his bones. When he’s been in and out of the hospital for four months or visiting clinic for lab tests and treatments, he’s often accompanied by his wife Jessica and one or both of his two children, Christine and Alex. Dave’s family has remained optimistic, confident, and encouraging; they fully expected him to pursue aggressive treatment. Dave’s physicians, however, now want to transition his care and incorporate hospice and palliative approaches to managing his illness.
The palliative care physician, Dr. Barelle, sits down alone with Dave to discuss his end-of-life wishes. Dave insists on pursuing aggressive acute care for his prostate cancer, but he also seems exhausted. As Dr. Barelle continues to describe what aggressive acute care would entail over the next months and begins to probe deeper into Dave’s goals of care, Dave slowly confesses that he worries about aggressive treatment, states that it isn’t what he wants, and also says, “I’m not the hero type.” He goes on to express that he particularly values his independence and that he fears pain, suffering, impending loss of functioning, and loss of his autonomy. He finally admits that aggressive acute care seems to him to be excessive and futile at this point but that he doesn’t want to let his family down by not “fighting.” He fears that his family thinks of hospice and palliative care as capitulating and “giving up.”
Dr. Barelle has suspected that Dave’s wishes were diverging from his family’s, and she wonders how to acknowledge this and how to advocate on Dave’s behalf in ways that won’t be divisive. What should she do? Should she downplay the potential of aggressive care to better persuade the family to respect the patient’s wishes?
case_rewrite:
Dave’s health has been steadily deteriorating. His prostate cancer, despite surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and hormonal therapies, has now spread to his bones. Over the past four months, Dave has been in and out of the hospital or visiting the clinic for tests and treatments, almost always accompanied by his devoted wife Jessica and sometimes one or both of his children, Christine and Alex. Throughout this difficult period, Dave’s family has remained upbeat and supportive, urging him to continue fighting and fully expecting him to pursue every available aggressive treatment. However, Dave’s medical team now believes it is time to shift the focus of his care, suggesting that hospice and palliative care should be integrated into his treatment plan.

One afternoon, Dr. Barelle, the palliative care physician, sits privately with Dave to discuss his preferences regarding end-of-life care. Dave initially insists that he wants to keep pursuing aggressive, acute interventions for his cancer. Yet, Dr. Barelle notices signs of fatigue in Dave’s demeanor. As she gently explains what aggressive treatment would involve in the coming months and asks about his hopes and concerns, Dave gradually opens up. He confesses that the prospect of more intense treatment worries him and, in truth, it isn’t what he wants. “I’m not the hero type,” he admits quietly. Dave reveals that he deeply values his independence and is afraid of pain, prolonged suffering, and losing his ability to make decisions for himself. Ultimately, he acknowledges that aggressive care now feels excessive and futile, but he is reluctant to stop because he doesn’t want to disappoint his family or be seen as giving up. He worries his family views hospice and palliative care as surrender rather than a meaningful choice.

Dr. Barelle has long suspected that Dave’s true wishes may not align with the expectations of his family. She now faces the challenge of how to support Dave and advocate for his preferences in a way that will not create division within his family. She considers how best to approach the conversation with Dave and his loved ones—how to respect his autonomy, recognize the family’s good intentions, and ensure honest, transparent communication without minimizing any treatment options or bypassing Dave’s explicit wishes. Dr. Barelle wonders how to balance her role in upholding Dave’s independence, maintaining confidentiality, and helping the family navigate these difficult choices together.

ethical_issues.question: When patients and family members disagree, how should physicians respect patient autonomy while also acknowledging the well-intentioned and caring role of the family?
keypoints: Respecting patient autonomy includes not only respecting the patient’s final decision but also respecting the manner in which the decision is made, that is, the patient’s right to autonomously choose to prioritize the family’s wishes over their own.

Physicians must, on the basis of respecting patient autonomy, also take into account the well-intentioned and caring role of family members in the patient’s care, establishing a trusting relationship to facilitate treatment recommendations.

Physicians should clearly define with the patient the scope of information that may be disclosed to family members, strictly adhere to confidentiality principles, and protect the patient’s right to privacy.

Physicians should collaborate with the patient to plan the optimal manner of presenting medical information and values, so that effective communication regarding risks, benefits, and value-based goals can be conducted during discussions involving family members.

If family members exert undue influence on the patient, the physician has the responsibility to promptly identify its unacceptability and communicate with the patient to safeguard the patient’s interests.

When familial disagreements lead to relational tension, the timely involvement of third parties such as social workers and chaplains to mediate family dynamics can help alleviate conflicts and protect the interests of all parties.

Physicians must not downplay or withhold any treatment options to persuade family members without the patient’s explicit permission; they should uphold transparency of information and respect for the patient’s wishes.

ethical_issues.question: When physicians face conflicts between patient autonomy and family influence, how can they ensure that the patient’s decision is free from coercion, persuasion, or manipulation?
keypoints: Physicians should first clarify with the patient the scope of information that may be disclosed to family members, strictly adhere to confidentiality principles, and safeguard the patient’s right to privacy and the foundation of trust.

Physicians have an obligation to respect patient autonomy, remain vigilant to and intervene against any coercion, persuasion, or manipulation exerted by family members, ensuring that the patient’s decision is authentic and voluntary.

Upon identifying undue influence from family members, physicians should promptly communicate with the patient to confirm their true wishes and, after discussing with the family, persist in honoring the patient’s autonomous decision.

Physicians should sensitively recognize and address the patient’s internal conflict arising from family pressure, support the patient in expressing their genuine wishes, and prevent the patient from acting against their own will due to concerns about family members’ feelings.

The involvement of social workers, chaplains, or other professionals to assist in mediating family dynamics and alleviating tension can help protect the patient’s interests and promote mutual understanding and support among family members.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient’s end-of-life wishes differ from those of their family members, how should the physician communicate with the patient and family to reach consensus or accept disagreement, while upholding the principle of confidentiality?
keypoints: The physician’s primary responsibility is to guide the patient in exploring his core values, clarifying his treatment goals, and identifying his true preferences.

The physician should work with the patient to explicitly define the scope of information that may be disclosed to family members, ensuring respect for patient privacy and strict adherence to confidentiality principles.
The physician should collaborate with the patient to plan the optimal way to present medical information and values, in order to be fully prepared for communication with the family.

On the premise of respecting patient autonomy and obtaining explicit consent, the physician may organize meetings involving family members to jointly establish care goals based on the values and expectations of both parties.
The physician should maintain consensus with other relevant healthcare professionals to ensure that a unified and clear treatment plan is communicated to the patient and his family.

Even if the patient and family are unable to reach complete agreement, the physician should continue to promote mutual understanding, alleviate conflict, and maintain a harmonious therapeutic relationship.

When persistent family disagreement and relational tension arise, professionals such as social workers or chaplains may be involved to help mediate family dynamics, facilitate communication, and safeguard the interests of all parties.

Without the patient’s explicit permission, the physician must not downplay, exaggerate, or conceal any treatment options in order to influence the family’s decision-making, and must faithfully represent the patient’s true wishes.

title: Should Children be Asked to be Bone Marrow Donors for Siblings?
case:
Fifteen-year-old Mandy has acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and needs a bone marrow transplant. Mandy’s parents and younger sister Jessica all undergo testing to determine whether any of them is a prospective donor. Jessica, who is eight, is found to be a match, and Mandy and her family are overjoyed that she will be able to have the transplant.
Jessica’s parents explain to her that she is able to help her sister by having an operation to take part of the marrow inside her bones and give it to her sister, who, as Jessica knows, is critically ill. Jessica seems excited about the possibility of helping her older sister, so the parents provide initial consent for her to do so.
Jessica’s enthusiasm remains when she and her parents meet with Dr. Malone, the bone marrow transplant physician, and his team. Jessica asks some questions, and Dr. Malone assures her that her bones and blood will make more marrow to replace what is removed. Then Dr. Malone asks Jessica to stay to talk with him by herself. During this conversation, it becomes clear to him that she has not fully understood what the donation would entail. She seems concerned and anxious as she asks him whether it will hurt and about what could happen to her if she has the procedure, and she is visibly frightened about having to be put to sleep.
Dr. Malone is concerned that Jessica may be unduly influenced by her parents’ and sister’s expectations that she will donate. When he talks with her parents, however, they say they know Jessica well and that her sister’s health is more important to her than the immediate pain of the procedure. They explain that they, along with Mandy, will give Jessica much support and attention, and they insist that she will feel privileged and glad to have been able to help her sister for the rest of her life.
case_rewrite:
Fifteen-year-old Mandy has been diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and her only hope for recovery is a bone marrow transplant. To find a suitable donor, Mandy’s parents and her eight-year-old sister, Jessica, all undergo compatibility testing. The family is elated when it turns out that Jessica is a match, raising everyone’s hopes that Mandy will receive the lifesaving transplant she urgently needs.

Jessica’s parents sit down with her and explain that she can help Mandy by undergoing an operation to remove some of the marrow from her bones, which will then be given to her sister. Jessica knows that Mandy is very ill, and she initially appears enthusiastic about the idea of helping her. Encouraged by Jessica’s positive response, her parents provide their initial consent for her to proceed as the donor.

When Jessica and her parents meet with Dr. Malone, the bone marrow transplant specialist, and his team, Jessica remains cheerful and asks several questions. Dr. Malone reassures her that her body will regenerate the bone marrow that is taken. Afterward, Dr. Malone invites Jessica to speak with him privately. During this one-on-one conversation, it becomes apparent that Jessica does not fully grasp what the donation process will involve. She grows anxious and apprehensive, asking Dr. Malone if the procedure will hurt, what could happen to her during and after the operation, and expressing visible fear about being put to sleep for the surgery.

Dr. Malone becomes concerned that Jessica may be feeling pressure from her parents and Mandy to go through with the donation, rather than making the decision freely. When he discusses his concerns with Jessica’s parents, they maintain that they know Jessica very well and are confident that her desire to help her sister outweighs any worries she has about pain or the procedure. They assure Dr. Malone that both they and Mandy will offer Jessica plenty of support and attention, and they believe that, in time, Jessica will feel proud and grateful for having helped save her sister’s life.

ethical_issues.question: In cases of pediatric bone marrow donation, how should the donor child's assent, dissent, or refusal be weighed in ethical decision-making?
keypoints: The opinions of child donors should be carefully considered, especially in cases where there is no direct medical benefit to the child; respecting the child’s autonomy and expressed wishes holds paramount ethical significance.

Given the limited cognitive and comprehension capacities of children, they should not have sole authority over the decision-making process between physicians and parents regarding donation; however, their reasonable concerns and objections must be seriously heard and respected.

Direct attention should be given to actively addressing the child’s fears related to pain, anesthesia, and surgical risks. It is recommended to appoint an independent adult advocate to communicate privately with the child, explore their anxieties, and represent their voice, thereby avoiding conflicts of interest and undue pressure.

The fundamental basis of ethical decision-making should be the maximal protection of the physical and psychological well-being of the child donor, minimizing harm from the procedure and related processes, rather than relying solely on the child’s limited cognitive understanding or emotional responses.

ethical_issues.question: How can we ensure that a child donor’s assent is truly voluntary and not merely a result of acquiescence to parental authority or expectations?
keypoints: Appoint an independent adult advocate to communicate with Jessica alone, assisting her in fully understanding the process and risks of bone marrow donation, exploring her genuine feelings and concerns, and ensuring that her assent is voluntary rather than a result of submission to parental authority or expectations.

The involvement of an independent advocate not only helps to balance appropriate attention to Jessica’s pain and fears—avoiding both neglect and overemphasis of her concerns—but also embodies respect for and protection of the child donor’s personhood, preventing undue influence from authority figures on her decision-making.

The ethical legitimacy of donor assent is rooted in respect for the donor’s personal dignity; ensuring that the child donor makes an autonomous decision under conditions of informed understanding and absence of coercion is a core principle for safeguarding the rights and interests of pediatric donors.

ethical_issues.question: How should the risk-benefit ratio of pediatric donor procedures be evaluated to ensure that the medical, emotional, and psychological risks to the child donor are proportionate to the benefits gained by both the donor and the recipient?
keypoints: In assessing the risk-benefit ratio of pediatric donor procedures, it is essential to ensure that the medical, emotional, and psychological risks to the child donor are minimal and reasonable, and that these risks are proportionate to the benefits gained by both the donor and the recipient.

Bone marrow harvesting is generally safe for children and carries a low risk; however, general anesthesia and the harvesting procedure itself may cause adverse effects, and a small number of donors are at risk for nerve, bone, or tissue injury.

Pediatric donors may face psychological risks such as fear, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress; these potential psychological sequelae are difficult to quantify and must be taken seriously and addressed with empathy.
Bone marrow transplantation should confer a reasonable and clear benefit to the recipient; in this case, the transplant is a necessary condition for Mandy’s survival.

The benefits to the donor include maintaining and deepening the sibling bond, avoiding long-term psychological trauma associated with the loss of a sibling, and potentially gaining a sense of personal accomplishment and self-worth.

The core of protecting pediatric donors lies in minimizing physical and psychological harm from the procedure and related processes, respecting their fears and anxieties, and ensuring their overall well-being.

Respecting the autonomy of pediatric donors requires making every effort to obtain their informed assent and giving due consideration to their concerns and objections, which is of particular ethical importance when there is no direct medical benefit to the child.

title: Could Good Care Mean Withholding Information from Patients?
case:
Every morning for three weeks, Isalita has sat at her patient Janet’s bedside. As a third-year medical student on an oncology rotation, Isalita has the most time of anyone on the health care team to get to know her patients. Janet has talked to Isalita about her past medical experiences, both good and bad, saying that she appreciates physicians’ being open and honest with her about her medical condition. She wants the chance to understand what is going on, she tells Isalita, even if in the end she asks for and takes the physician’s recommendation.
Janet’s oncologist, Dr. Haveford, has been seeing Janet since her initial diagnosis and treatment for breast cancer. They have a trusting and comfortable relationship with one another. Dr. Haveford pays particular attention to each of his patient’s preferences and values. In Dr. Haveford’s experience, Janet, when presented with a number of choices, has appeared uncertain and ultimately asked him what he thinks would be best for her.
Janet’s cancer has now metastasized. Other than some clinical trials for which she might be eligible, Dr. Haveford does not think that more treatment will slow her cancer’s progress, even though some available drugs might extend her life, and he believes that going through any of the available trials would likely diminish Janet’s remaining quality of life. Moreover, he does not want to overwhelm her with details about clinical trial options, risks, and potential benefits. Knowledgeable and responsive patient-centered care in this instance, he thinks, means not telling her about clinical trials.
When Dr. Haveford discusses Janet’s treatment options with her, Isalita is dismayed that he only presents Janet with a recommendation to pursue conventional options in combination with palliative treatment. She is uncomfortable with the idea of not sharing the clinical trial options with Janet, but she does not want to appear to be trying to undermine Dr. Haveford’s authority or question his judgment.
case_rewrite:
For the past three weeks, Isalita, a third-year medical student on her oncology rotation, has made a point of sitting with her patient Janet each morning. With more time than the rest of the busy medical team, Isalita has come to know Janet well—listening as Janet shares stories about her previous medical experiences, her hopes, and her fears. Janet has repeatedly told Isalita how much she values openness and honesty from her physicians. “I need to understand what’s happening,” Janet says, “even if, in the end, I ask the doctor for their recommendation.”

Janet’s oncologist, Dr. Haveford, has cared for her since her initial breast cancer diagnosis. Over the years, they have developed a warm rapport built on mutual trust. Dr. Haveford prides himself on being attentive to each patient’s individual preferences and values. In his experience, Janet often seems uncertain when faced with multiple choices, and she has tended to ask Dr. Haveford directly for his opinion about what course she should take.

Now, Janet’s cancer has metastasized. With most standard treatments exhausted, Dr. Haveford knows that the only remaining options are a handful of clinical trials. He suspects, however, that none of these trials are likely to slow the cancer’s progression, and the drugs involved might only marginally extend Janet’s life—potentially at the cost of significant side effects and a diminished quality of life. Dr. Haveford worries that discussing the complexities, risks, and uncertain benefits of these trials might overwhelm Janet. In his view, respecting her need for clarity and comfort means not burdening her with details about clinical trials. Instead, he believes that the most compassionate and patient-centered care is to recommend a combination of conventional management and palliative care, omitting mention of the clinical trials altogether.

When Dr. Haveford meets with Janet to discuss her options, he presents only his recommendation for conventional and palliative treatment. Isalita, who is present during the conversation, feels deeply uneasy. She knows from her conversations with Janet that honesty and the opportunity to understand her situation matter greatly to her. Isalita is troubled by the idea of withholding information about the clinical trial options, but she hesitates to speak up, uncertain how to express her concerns without seeming to challenge Dr. Haveford’s authority or judgment.

ethical_issues.question: At the end of a patient’s life, how should physicians balance information disclosure with the patient’s emotional burden within the shared decision-making process?
keypoints: Physicians engaged in end-of-life care should possess excellent communication skills and high emotional intelligence, dynamically adjusting the extent of information disclosure based on a deep understanding of the patient’s values, goals of care, and emotional state, thereby guiding the patient to identify the most appropriate level of participation along the “physician-driven” to “patient-driven” shared decision-making continuum.

Physicians ought to respect patients’ preferences regarding information disclosure, ensuring that the information provided meets the patient’s need to understand their condition without unduly increasing emotional burden, and when necessary, inviting patients to collaboratively assess the relevance and utility of the information.

Under exceptional circumstances, physicians may invoke the principle of therapeutic privilege (therapeutic exception) to cautiously withhold certain information when they are convinced that disclosure would cause acute emotional distress or other substantive harm, while maintaining respect for the patient and striving for transparency.

In the shared decision-making process, physicians should assume appropriate decision-making responsibility to help alleviate the emotional burden patients may experience from foregoing aggressive treatment, facilitating patients’ acceptance of end-of-life medical decisions and preventing the transfer of the entire decisional responsibility onto patients or their families.

ethical_issues.question: How should a medical student handle disagreements with a supervising physician’s decisions to ensure the patient’s best interests are upheld?
keypoints: Medical students, due to their extended contact with patients, are able to gain a deeper understanding of patients’ values and should, based on their role as learners, proactively raise questions and express concerns regarding patient care to the attending physician.
Medical students and all members of the healthcare team have an obligation to advocate for patients with respect and candor, even in the presence of disagreements with senior physicians.

Through communication and discussion with supervising physicians, medical students not only promote the best interests of patients but also deepen their own understanding of medical ethics and patient-centered care.
When necessary, medical students should possess the moral courage to transcend hierarchical structures in order to uphold the best interests of the patient.
The paramount interest of the patient always supersedes seniority and position; medical students should consistently prioritize patient welfare and confidently voice justified concerns.
