title: Assessing Information from Pharmaceutical Company Representatives
case:
“Just five minutes of your time, doc!”
Dr. Herman turns to see a brilliantly white, winning smile aimed her way. This is the third drug company detail rep who’s come looking for her this week.
Newly finished with her residency training, Dr. Herman has joined an outpatient practice group. Her residency program had a policy requiring that interactions with pharmaceutical representatives be pre-approved by the program director, that no gifts or freebies be accepted, and that the scheduled time be used only for the group of residents to discuss peer-reviewed publications and indications for FDA-approved uses with the rep; the guidelines for the interactions were very clear. Not so now.
Dr. Herman actually does have a few minutes before her next appointment, but she turned away the last pharmaceutical rep because she was busy when he came by.I need an actual plan for this, she thinks to herself. Should she make a habit of talking to these representatives? Just accept their samples—every doctor she knows seems to do that, but is it a good idea? Send them away? In her new position, she is realizing, it’s up to her to set the rules, the times, and the tone for these interactions.
case_rewrite:
“Just five minutes of your time, doc!”

Dr. Herman turns to see a dazzlingly bright smile directed at her—another pharmaceutical company representative, the third one to approach her this week alone. Since finishing her residency, Dr. Herman has started working at an outpatient practice group, where things operate quite differently from what she was used to. During her residency, there were strict rules for meeting with pharmaceutical reps: any interaction had to be pre-approved by the program director, gifts or freebies were strictly off-limits, and whenever reps visited, the discussion was limited to peer-reviewed articles and FDA-approved indications. The process was transparent and controlled.

Now, in her new practice, there are no such clear guidelines. Dr. Herman actually has a brief window before her next patient, but she remembers that she already turned away the previous rep earlier this week when she was too busy to talk. As she watches the current rep waiting expectantly, she realizes she needs a strategy for handling these situations. Should she routinely meet with pharmaceutical reps, as many of her colleagues seem to do? Just accept the free samples that nearly every doctor she knows takes? Or should she turn them away entirely?

Dr. Herman is aware that, unlike in residency, the responsibility now lies with her. It's up to her to decide if, when, and how these interactions will happen. She considers whether accepting gifts or forming friendly relationships with reps could influence her decisions, and wonders if she should instead focus her limited non-clinical time on reviewing independent research and critically appraising new information herself. As she contemplates what kind of boundaries to set, she realizes the importance of determining the rules, the timing, and the nature of her relationships with pharmaceutical representatives going forward.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians avoid conflicts of interest and maintain professional judgment in their interactions with pharmaceutical company representatives?
keypoints: Physicians should keep acceptable gifts and financial incentives to a minimum in order to avoid conflicts of interest.

Physicians need to be aware that information provided by pharmaceutical representatives may be biased toward promotion and should avoid forming personal relationships with representatives, maintaining a professional distance.

Physicians should dedicate non-clinical time to reviewing more reliable sources of information, such as scholarly journals, critically appraising all information, and developing competencies to evaluate the validity of research design, identify bias, and understand scientific data, thereby enhancing critical appraisal skills and numeracy.

The duration of meetings with pharmaceutical representatives should be minimized, and such interactions should serve as a starting point for exploring new drugs or new indications rather than as definitive conclusions.

title: Close-Call Screening and Shared Decision Making
case:
Dr. Samuelson is an internist employed by a large hospital system. As she walks into the office, a colleague greets her.
“Hey, Dr. Sam! You’re looking a lot better than the last time I saw you!” Dr. Martin had seen Dr. Samuelson’s last couple of patients for her one night the previous week, when she’d suddenly been laid low by what was probably the flu.
“Thanks for covering for me.”
“No problem! Just don’t make it a habit,” Dr. Martin jokes. “By the way, while I was seeing Mr. Johnson and entering his visit info into the record, the little flag lit up reminding me that he met the criteria for lung cancer screening, so I went ahead and gave him a script to get the CT scan done. You saw the policy memo about the new core quality measures, right? They’ve really been pushing for 100 percent adherence to the USPSTF lung cancer screening guidelines in the EMR.”
“Oh, OK. Well, I should get caught up on my work. Thanks again for seeing my patients.”
As she walks to her office, Dr. Samuelson wishes she had told her colleague not to order any routine testing for her patients—only tests that were indicated by their present concerns. She did not automatically order even the recommended scans for her patients because of the unintended consequences of false-positive and false-negative results, incidental findings, and radiation exposure. She had seen it time and time again with mammography and worried that the USPSTF recommendations ended up causing trouble and pain for more patients than were helped.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Samuelson, an internist at a major hospital, arrived at work just as her colleague, Dr. Martin, greeted her with a friendly smile.  
“Hey, Dr. Sam! You look much better than when I last saw you!” Dr. Martin had taken over Dr. Samuelson’s last couple of appointments the previous week when she had to leave suddenly, likely due to a bout of the flu.  
“Thanks for covering for me,” Dr. Samuelson replied, grateful for the help.  
“No problem! Just try not to make it a regular thing,” Dr. Martin joked. “By the way, while I was seeing Mr. Johnson and updating his chart, the alert popped up in the EMR saying he was eligible for lung cancer screening, so I went ahead and gave him an order for a CT scan. You saw the memo about the new core quality measures, right? They’re really pushing for 100 percent compliance with the USPSTF lung cancer screening guidelines in the system.”  
“Oh, I see. Well, I should get caught up on everything. Thanks again for seeing my patients,” Dr. Samuelson said, heading toward her office.

Walking down the hallway, Dr. Samuelson found herself wishing she’d told Dr. Martin not to order routine tests for her patients unless they were directly related to the patient’s current concerns. She preferred not to automatically order recommended screenings, even those backed by guidelines, because she was acutely aware of the unintended consequences—false positives, false negatives, incidental findings, and cumulative radiation exposure. Having witnessed the distress and harm that sometimes arose from mammography, she worried that even well-intentioned USPSTF recommendations could end up causing more harm than benefit for some patients.

ethical_issues.question: When implementing lung cancer screening, how can clinicians respect patient autonomy and uphold the principle of nonmaleficence while adhering to hospital guidelines and USPSTF quality measures?
keypoints: Address the ethical dilemma between hospital guidelines and patient autonomy through shared decision making (SDM), ensuring that patients’ choices and values are respected throughout the screening process.

The shared decision making process enables clinicians to balance adherence to evidence-based guidelines with clinical judgment in patient care, particularly when screening involves weighing potential benefits against harms.

The USPSTF guidelines and hospital system explicitly endorse shared decision making, emphasizing that clinicians and patients should thoroughly discuss the potential benefits, harms, and uncertainties of screening to facilitate informed choices.

Clinicians should clearly explain to patients the purpose of LDCT screening, its potential benefits and risks (including radiation exposure, false positives, and the burden of follow-up), scientific uncertainties, and subsequent procedures, thereby supporting patients in making decisions aligned with their personal values.

Adherence to guidelines should be understood as implementing the shared decision making process rather than mechanically ordering screening tests, thereby genuinely respecting patient autonomy and upholding the principle of nonmaleficence.

ethical_issues.question: When faced with screening programs that may involve false-positive results and radiation exposure, how can clinicians balance potential benefits and harms through shared decision making?
keypoints: Clinicians should balance the potential benefits and harms of screening through shared decision making (SDM), respecting patient autonomy while adhering to the principle of nonmaleficence.

Physicians ought to provide patients with comprehensive information regarding the purpose of screening, its potential benefits and harms, including radiation exposure, the risk of false-positive results, and the scientific uncertainties related to follow-up and diagnostic costs.
The provision of decision aids facilitates the enhancement of patients’ knowledge and risk perception, thereby encouraging their active participation in the decision-making process.

“Adherence to guidelines” should be understood as the implementation of the shared decision-making process rather than the mechanical ordering of screening tests, emphasizing individualized clinical judgment and the integration of patient preferences.

ethical_issues.question: When implementing evidence-based recommendations on an individual level, how can clinicians ensure that patients fully understand the potential harms of screening and actively participate in the decision-making process, thereby avoiding the mechanical ordering of screening tests?
keypoints: When applying evidence-based recommendations at the individual level, it is essential to balance guideline adherence with clinical judgment through shared decision making (SDM) to ensure that medical decisions align with the patient’s specific circumstances and values.

The shared decision making process involves discussing with patients the potential benefits, harms (such as radiation exposure and false-positive results), and uncertainties of screening, thereby ensuring that patients are fully informed and understand the possible risks and benefits associated with screening.

Clinicians may utilize decision aids to enhance patients’ knowledge and risk perception, promote active patient engagement in the decision-making process, and improve the quality and satisfaction of decisions made.

True adherence to guidelines means implementing a shared decision making process that acknowledges patient preferences and values, rather than mechanically ordering screening tests; this approach helps avoid overlooking individual differences and potential risks due to blind compliance with quality measures.

title: Utility of Physician Report Cards in Patient Referral
case:
A large hospital system, wanting to improve outcomes on coronary artery bypass surgeries (CABG), has decided to implement a public surgery report card for cardiothoracic surgeons based on morbidity and mortality outcomes on these procedures. While sitting in the doctors’ lounge, Dr. Smith, a cardiologist, overhears her colleagues discussing the report card system.
“You have to refer your patients to the best possible cardiothoracic surgeon. If I know that a surgeon has high complication rates, why would I risk the health of my patient?” explains Dr. Cummings.
Dr. Thomas looks skeptical. “So you think those reports will be accurate? Do you really think the cases will be risk adjusted so that the surgeons who take the most difficult cases don’t end up getting the worst ‘grades,’ so to speak? And what happens when one of your patients needs an emergency CABG and the best surgeon is unavailable? Are you going to advise him or her to refuse the surgery?”
Dr. Smith hears her pager and gets up to return the page. The call center connects her with the hospitalist on service to notify her that Mr. Green—a long-time patient—has just been admitted and is on his way to the catheterization lab. The hospitalist notes that he is planning to consult cardiothoracic surgery if Mr. Green’s catheterization report reveals clogged arteries and the need for CABG surgery. Ordinarily, Dr. Smith would have referred the patient to Dr. Anderson, who has performed CABG surgery for most of her patients. But now she considers what she overheard in the lounge and replies, “Let me call you back with a specific surgeon to consult. I need to look something up.”
case_rewrite:
At a prominent hospital system aiming to enhance outcomes for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgeries, leadership has introduced a public report card system that rates cardiothoracic surgeons based on their morbidity and mortality statistics for these procedures. One afternoon in the doctors’ lounge, Dr. Smith, a cardiologist, listens as her colleagues debate the implications of the new report cards.

Dr. Cummings asserts, “You have to make sure your patients are referred to the very best cardiothoracic surgeon. If I’m aware that a surgeon has a pattern of complications, why would I jeopardize my patient’s health by sending them there?”

Dr. Thomas, however, raises concerns. “You really trust those reports are accurate? Are they truly adjusting for the complexity of cases? I worry that surgeons who take on the toughest patients will end up with the lowest scores. And what about emergencies—if the top-rated surgeon isn’t available when your patient needs a CABG right away, are you going to tell them to wait or refuse the surgery?”

Just then, Dr. Smith’s pager goes off. She steps out to return the call, and the hospital’s call center connects her to the hospitalist on duty. The hospitalist informs Dr. Smith that Mr. Green—a patient she has cared for over many years—has just been admitted and is being sent to the catheterization lab. The hospitalist mentions that if Mr. Green’s cath reveals severe blockages and CABG is indicated, he plans to consult cardiothoracic surgery.

Ordinarily, Dr. Smith would have no hesitation in recommending Dr. Anderson, who has successfully handled CABG surgeries for many of her previous patients. But now, recalling the heated discussion about the report cards and their potential influence on referrals, she hesitates. “Let me get back to you with a specific surgeon to consult,” Dr. Smith says. “I need to check something first.”

ethical_issues.question: In the absence of physician report cards as a standard of care, how can the principle of justice—that is, the fair distribution of societal resources—be ensured?
keypoints: Be vigilant against biases in report cards arising from physicians’ avoidance of high-risk patients—particularly those from specific socioeconomic or ethnic groups—which may lead to inflated scores and inequitable allocation of resources, thereby undermining the principle of justice in the fair distribution of societal resources.

Physicians should rationally and comprehensively consider report card data alongside their own, colleagues’, and patients’ evaluations of the referred physician, avoiding overreliance on a single metric to ensure referral decisions are fair and well-founded.

During the referral process, patients should be adequately informed about how and why report cards are utilized, thereby demonstrating respect for patients’ rights to informed consent and autonomous decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ensure respect for patient autonomy and provide informed consent when using physician report cards to make referral decisions?
keypoints: Physicians should objectively assess and fully understand the anticipated risks and benefits associated with a particular physician’s care, thereby fulfilling their professional responsibility to both benefit the patient and avoid harm.

Physicians should provide patients with adequate information regarding the specific use and rationale of report cards in referral decision-making, thereby ensuring informed consent and respecting patient autonomy.
Patients have the right, based on sufficient information, to independently accept or refuse referral recommendations made by physicians on the basis of report card evaluations.

title: Patient Satisfaction Reporting and Its Implications for Patient Care
case:
A hospital’s Committee on Patient Quality meets monthly to discuss a strategic plan to address deficiencies in scores on its Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (HCAHPS) survey results. Dr. Anderson begins the meeting by proposing a new pain management protocol to the group. He references the plateau in pain management scores in the HCAHPS report, warning that the organization will sustain substantial financial penalties by failing to improve in the “patient experience of care” domain. As Dr. Anderson begins to explain the new protocol for pain management and how it will bring about an upward trend in scores, Dr. Parker interjects.
“Can we take a step back for a moment? I understand that patient satisfaction surveys can provide a lot of useful information to our hospital system. But a low rating on—let’s say pain control—doesn’t mean the patient received low-quality care.”
“I agree with what you’re saying, but this is the reality of pay for performance. Plus, there is value in considering patient satisfaction—happier patients are more likely to adhere to our recommendations and return in the future. As you mentioned, we can learn a lot from these surveys—like how helpful it was to have extra volunteer greeters in the lobby to assist patients with finding their way in the hospital,” explains Dr. Anderson.
“I still don’t think it makes sense for Medicare to tie the survey results to our reimbursement,” Dr. Parker counters. “Financial penalties for hospital-acquired infections and preventable readmissions make sense. Public reporting of morbidity and mortality encourages systemic improvements and patient empowerment. But all of these are objective measures. Patient satisfaction just isn’t an objective measure of care quality.”
case_rewrite:
The hospital’s Committee on Patient Quality gathers for its monthly meeting to review strategic initiatives aimed at improving performance on the Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (HCAHPS) survey. As the meeting begins, Dr. Anderson introduces a proposal for a revised pain management protocol. He points to the recent stagnation in the hospital’s pain management scores on the HCAHPS report, cautioning the group that continued underperformance in the “patient experience of care” category could result in significant financial penalties for the organization. As Dr. Anderson lays out the details of the new pain management approach and the potential for raising the hospital’s survey scores, Dr. Parker raises a hand to interject.

“Before we move forward, can we pause for a moment?” Dr. Parker asks. “I recognize that patient satisfaction surveys offer valuable insights into our hospital’s functioning. But just because a patient rates us poorly on something like pain control, it doesn’t automatically mean they received substandard care.”

Dr. Anderson nods. “I understand your point, but under the current pay-for-performance system, these scores directly affect our reimbursement. And there’s merit in listening to patient feedback—patients who feel well cared for are more likely to follow our advice and return for future care. We’ve seen positive changes from these surveys before, like when we added extra volunteer greeters in the lobby to help patients navigate the hospital—it made a real difference.”

Still unconvinced, Dr. Parker replies, “I’m not sure it’s right for Medicare to tie our payments to how we score on these surveys. It makes sense to penalize hospitals for preventable readmissions or infections—those are clear, objective metrics. Publicly reporting morbidity and mortality rates drives real improvement and empowers patients. But patient satisfaction is subjective; it reflects personal expectations and perceptions, not necessarily the technical quality of the care we provide.”

ethical_issues.question: How might Dr. Anderson’s emphasis on improving patient satisfaction scores, as measured by the HCAHPS survey, influence the ethical delivery of quality care, and to what extent do such scores accurately reflect the true quality of care provided within the healthcare system?
keypoints: Patient satisfaction scores demonstrate a certain positive correlation with quality of care; hospitals with higher patient experience scores generally perform better on objective quality measures such as acute myocardial infarction and surgical care, reflecting stronger teamwork and organizational improvement capabilities.

Patient satisfaction scores are not objective measures of care quality, as they are based on patients’ subjective expectations and perceptions, which may not correlate with technical quality; a low pain control score does not necessarily indicate poor quality of care.

Linking patient satisfaction to financial incentives carries risks, as it may lead physicians to acquiesce to patients’ unreasonable demands in pursuit of higher satisfaction scores, thereby potentially compromising the delivery of high-value care.
Incentive programs may adversely affect institutions serving a greater proportion of vulnerable populations, exacerbating inequities in healthcare resource allocation and health disparities.

Improving patient experience is a critical goal for healthcare systems; however, satisfaction measurement and incentive mechanisms must be carefully designed to avoid unintended negative consequences, with ongoing evaluation of their validity and impact.

title: Safety and Ethical Considerations in Discharging Patients to Suboptimal Living Situations
case:
Dr. Wayne, a physiatrist, is part of an interdisciplinary team that provides comprehensive services for people with conditions that result in long-term cognitive and physical limitations, such as stroke, spinal cord injury, amputation, major trauma, and brain injury. Dr. Wayne and the rehabilitation team are meeting with Martha, a 45-year-old woman who has spent the last six weeks in an acute inpatient rehabilitation unit. Martha sustained a T12 complete spinal cord injury and a moderate traumatic brain injury as the result of a car accident.
Dr. Wayne is pleased with Martha’s rehabilitation course and overall adjustment to her injuries. Martha is able to use a manual wheelchair without assistance for mobility and is independent with her bowel and bladder management. She has also made excellent progress from hertraumatic brain injuryand has been evaluated to make sure she is competent to make her own decisions. Based on her functional and medical status, Martha is ready for discharge, and she wants to go home with her 22-year-old son, Brett, who lived with her prior to her accident. The social work team has secured disability status for Martha, and her social security disability payments—which Martha hopes will be enough to cover her bills—will begin in a month. Dr. Wayne hopes to discuss some of the issues related to the current discharge plan with Martha and Brett.
A physical therapist has performed a home evaluation and noted that the apartment is not optimal for Martha. The bathroom is too narrow to maneuver her wheelchair, and there are no handrails near the toilet and shower to help with her transfers. Her apartment unit also lacks an appropriate ramp to allow Martha to enter and exit the apartment without assistance. While the initial discharge planning identified these concerns, Brett has refused to find more appropriate housing for his mother, stating that he prefers to stay in the same apartment. The social work team members who have interviewed Brett say that his only employment is doing odd jobs for others in the apartment building. Without Martha’s income in the last four months, the electricity in the apartment had been turned off once. The nursing staff has also raised some concerns about Brett’s behavior with his mother and report that he smells of alcohol when he visits her on the rehabilitation unit. Many of his visits with his mother end in his becoming angry and raising his voice at her before he stomps out of the hospital. Despite these concerns, both Martha and Brett insist that she will be safe at home.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Wayne, a physiatrist, is a member of an interdisciplinary team dedicated to providing comprehensive care for individuals with long-term cognitive and physical disabilities stemming from conditions such as stroke, spinal cord injury, amputation, major trauma, and brain injury. Currently, Dr. Wayne and the rehabilitation team are meeting with Martha, a 45-year-old woman who has spent the past six weeks as an inpatient in the rehabilitation unit. Martha’s injuries—a complete spinal cord injury at the T12 level and a moderate traumatic brain injury—were sustained in a car accident.

Throughout her rehabilitation, Dr. Wayne has been impressed by Martha’s progress and her adjustment to her injuries. Martha now navigates independently using a manual wheelchair and manages her bowel and bladder care without assistance. She has also made significant strides in her recovery from her brain injury, and assessments confirm that she retains the capacity to make her own decisions. With her current functional and medical status, Martha is considered ready for discharge, and she has expressed her wish to return to the apartment she previously shared with her 22-year-old son, Brett. The social work team has secured disability status for Martha, with her social security disability payments set to begin in a month—funds she hopes will be sufficient to pay her bills. Dr. Wayne wants to discuss several important aspects of the discharge plan with both Martha and Brett.

A physical therapist has conducted a home evaluation and found notable shortcomings in Martha’s apartment. The bathroom is too narrow for her wheelchair, and there are no handrails by the toilet or shower to assist her with transfers. Additionally, the apartment lacks a ramp, making independent entry and exit impossible for Martha. These concerns were raised early in discharge planning, but Brett has refused to seek alternate housing for his mother, insisting that they remain in their current apartment. According to the social work team, Brett’s only source of income is doing odd jobs around the apartment complex. During the past four months, when Martha had no income, the apartment’s electricity was shut off once due to nonpayment. Nursing staff have also voiced concerns about Brett’s interactions with his mother, noting that he often smells of alcohol during visits and that many of his visits end with him raising his voice and storming out angrily. Despite these issues, both Martha and Brett maintain that she will be safe at home.

ethical_issues.question: In light of Martha’s demonstrated decisional capacity, should Dr. Wayne respect her autonomy in choosing to return to a suboptimal living environment?
keypoints: Respect the autonomy and preferences of patients with decisional capacity, especially when they clearly express a desire to return home.
Physicians must objectively assess whether the patient’s decision is subject to coercion or undue influence by family members, ensuring that the decision is genuinely autonomous.
Physicians have an ethical and legal obligation to promptly report any suspected physical, psychological, or financial abuse to safeguard the patient’s safety.
A comprehensive discharge plan must thoroughly evaluate the patient’s social support and environmental risks to promote safe and sustained rehabilitation.

title: Physician Paternalism and Severe Disability: Strengthening Autonomy through Therapeutic Engagement
case:
Dr. Gill’s rehab inpatient, Joel, is a decorated former Navy Seal. By age 35, he had served around the globe for a decade. His military career ended two years later, when he suffered a spinal cord injury from two gunshot wounds to his neck. The injuries left him an incomplete quadriplegic—Joel can eat and swallow and move his arms somewhat, but he cannot use his hands; he has nerve pain and spasticity in his extremities. Three months ago, following his initial surgery and monthlong hospitalization, Joel was sent to Dr. Gill’s unit.
During these months, Dr. Gill has kept a close watch on Joel’s depression and adaptation to his medical condition. In general, Joel’s depression is in line with what any formerly able-bodied—indeed athletic—person would experience in a like situation. Joel has rejected antidepressant medication, however, and has been determined competent to do so. He is not married and did not have a romantic relationship at the time of his injury. On the occasions when some of his friends from the Seals or from college have visited, Dr. Gill has watched Joel enjoy their company and even laugh.
Nevertheless, Joel has said and shown that he does not want to live in his current condition. Lamenting that he is unable to take his own life, he ribbed Dr. Gill, “And I’m sure you’re not gonna help me, doc, are you? Even if I did keep your country safe and all that other hero stuff. Right?” Joel has had hospital staff pull up information about spinal cord injuries on the computer that he keeps in his room and has decided that his physical condition is not going to improve. Dr. Gill and the team have shown Joel an Internet support group for people with spinal cord injuries and have told him that, like many of those in the support group, Joel could be discharged from the unit to a handicap-adapted home and could live independently with round-the-clock caregivers to feed him and tend to his other activities of daily living. But Joel does not want to put any friend or family member into that role, so active discharge planning is on hold.
Now Joel has developed acute renal failure from antibiotics he was taking for infected pressure sores. Dr. Gill tells Joel that he must undergo temporary hemodialysis and that he (Dr. Gill) expects that Joel’s kidney function will return to normal.
In response, Joel says, “This is the gift I’ve been waiting for. This kidney failure will kill me, right, doc? I’m going to refuse the hemo-whatever, so send the shrinks in to interview me again. I’m as sane as you are, and I don’t want to live like this.”
case_rewrite:
Joel, a decorated former Navy SEAL, is now an inpatient under Dr. Gill’s care in the rehabilitation unit. By age 35, Joel had spent a decade serving in combat zones around the world. His military career came to a sudden halt two years ago when he sustained a spinal cord injury from two gunshot wounds to his neck. As a result, Joel became an incomplete quadriplegic—he can move his arms to some extent and can feed himself and swallow, but he is unable to use his hands. He also suffers from nerve pain and spasticity throughout his limbs. After his initial surgery and a month-long hospital stay, Joel was transferred to Dr. Gill’s unit three months ago.

Since his arrival, Dr. Gill has closely monitored Joel’s adjustment and mental health, especially his depression. Joel’s mood and outlook largely mirror what one might expect from someone who was previously athletic and fully able-bodied, suddenly faced with such a life-altering injury. Despite this, Joel has declined all offers of antidepressant medication, and his decision-making capacity has been formally assessed and found to be intact. At the time of his injury, Joel was single and not involved in any romantic relationship. When friends from his SEAL days or from college come to visit, Dr. Gill has noticed Joel genuinely enjoying their company and even laughing at times.

Yet Joel remains adamant that he cannot accept life in his current state. He has expressed, both in words and actions, that he does not wish to go on living like this. Joking darkly with Dr. Gill, Joel once said, “And I’m sure you’re not gonna help me, doc, are you? Even if I did keep your country safe and all that other hero stuff. Right?” Joel has asked staff to help him research spinal cord injuries on the computer he keeps in his room, and he has concluded that his physical condition is unlikely to improve. Dr. Gill and the team have introduced Joel to an online support group for people with spinal cord injuries, and they have explained that, like many in that group, he could be discharged to a handicap-adapted home and live independently with 24-hour caregivers to assist with feeding and daily needs. However, Joel is unwilling to burden any friends or family members with caregiving responsibilities, so his discharge planning has stalled.

Recently, Joel developed acute renal failure as a complication from antibiotics prescribed to treat infected pressure sores. Dr. Gill informs Joel that he will need temporary hemodialysis, and reassures him that his kidney function is expected to return to normal. Hearing this, Joel responds, “This is the gift I’ve been waiting for. This kidney failure will kill me, right, doc? I’m going to refuse the hemo-whatever, so send the shrinks in to interview me again. I’m as sane as you are, and I don’t want to live like this.”

ethical_issues.question: How can patients make clear and definitive medical decisions in the face of sudden major tragedies, especially when information is incomplete?
keypoints: In the face of sudden major tragedies, patients often find it difficult to accurately forecast their own capacity for adaptation to loss and adversity, making it exceptionally challenging to make clear and definitive medical decisions.

Cognitive biases in affective forecasting, including focalism, immune neglect, and the inability to anticipate substantive adaptation, significantly influence patients’ judgments and choices in critical medical decision-making.

The core responsibility of the rehabilitation physician is to assist patients in constructing possible narratives for a new chapter of life, particularly by facilitating interactions with experienced individuals living with disabilities (“experts by experience”), thereby enabling patients to gain insight and hope from real-life experiences and to make more informed medical decisions amid incomplete information and complex emotions.

ethical_issues.question: Does a patient have the right to refuse medical interventions, including life-sustaining treatment, particularly when they possess decision-making capacity?
keypoints: Competent patients have the right to refuse medical interventions, including life-sustaining treatment; this is a core expression of respect for patient autonomy.

Dr. Gill should first assess the impact of Joel’s depressive symptoms on his decision-making capacity; unless the depression is severe enough to impair rational judgment, Joel should be considered to possess decision-making capacity.
Joel essentially meets the criteria for decision-making capacity, as he is able to understand his own condition, the treatment options, and the consequences of refusing dialysis.

Once it is confirmed that Joel has adequate decision-making capacity, his decision to refuse medical intervention should be respected, while continuing to provide psychological support and necessary medical information.
The medical team should maintain open communication, monitor changes in the patient’s psychological state, and ensure that his decisions are made with full information and without coercion.

title: Athlete Return-to-Play Decisions in Sports Medicine
case:
Jordan is a 17-year-old senior in high school who has been his football team’s star quarterback, led his team to two state championships, and has a real possibility of receiving a full scholarship to a top college sports program next year.
In his last session of summer training camp, Jordan took a fierce hit, a tackle that knocked him to the ground. He landed on his right arm and shoulder and instantly felt sharp pain and then lost some sensation. Jordan was taken to the hospital. An MRI was taken, which showed that Jordan had a torn labrum in his right shoulder that would require surgery and months-long recovery, meaning that he would miss the rest of his final season. A week later, Jordan underwent surgery and soon thereafter began seeing physiatrist Dr. Brown for further treatment and follow-up.
Two months after his surgery and continued treatment with Dr. Brown, Jordan felt that his recovery was lagging. He was worried that his slow recovery process coincided with the recruitment period for college programs. Top programs were increasingly inquisitive about his recovering shoulder, so he scheduled an urgent appointment with Dr. Brown.
Dr. Brown had known instances in which this particular type of injury ended a quarterback’s athletic career. She had also read about a few cases in which athletes recovered fully from the injury. Since so much of recovery depends on the injured person’s following the rehabilitation and physical therapy plans, Dr. Brown wanted Jordan to approach his injury with the optimism that adherence to the plan would enable him to return to athletics. At the same time, she did not want to hold out false hope that might keep Jordan focused exclusively on football when, in the long term, that might not be the best use of his senior year.
case_rewrite:
Jordan, a 17-year-old high school senior, has earned a reputation as his football team’s star quarterback, leading them to two state championships. With his impressive record, he stands a real chance of securing a full scholarship to a leading college sports program in the coming year. 

During the final session of summer training camp, Jordan suffered a hard tackle that sent him crashing to the ground. He landed heavily on his right arm and shoulder, immediately experiencing sharp pain and a loss of sensation. He was swiftly transported to the hospital, where an MRI revealed a torn labrum in his right shoulder. The severity of the injury required surgery and would mean a recovery period spanning several months, effectively ruling Jordan out for the entirety of his last high school football season. A week later, the surgical repair was completed, and soon after, Jordan began seeing Dr. Brown, a physiatrist, for ongoing care and follow-up.

Two months into his rehabilitation and regular appointments with Dr. Brown, Jordan grew increasingly concerned that his recovery was not progressing as hoped. The slow pace of improvement weighed on him, especially as it coincided with the crucial college recruitment window. With college programs pressing for updates on the status of his shoulder, Jordan scheduled an urgent consultation with Dr. Brown to discuss his prospects.

Dr. Brown was aware that this type of injury had, in some cases, ended the careers of promising quarterbacks. However, she also knew of rare instances where athletes made a full recovery and returned to high-level play. Dr. Brown recognized that a significant portion of the rehabilitation outcome depended on Jordan’s commitment to his prescribed physical therapy regimen. She wanted to encourage him to stay positive and committed to his recovery plan, instilling hope that he could possibly return to competitive sports. At the same time, Dr. Brown was cautious not to give unrealistic assurances that might cause Jordan to focus solely on football, potentially at the expense of broader opportunities in his senior year and his long-term well-being.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of an athlete’s eagerness to return to play, how can a physiatrist balance respect for the athlete’s autonomy with ensuring their safety?
keypoints: The physiatrist should provide appropriate medical guidance to ensure the athlete’s safe return to play, prioritizing the athlete’s long-term health as the primary basis for medical decision-making.

The physician should engage the athlete in discussing the dual goals of safe return to sports participation and prevention of future long-term health complications through optimized management of the current injury.

Implementing a staged return-to-play plan with progressive goals shifts the basis of return decisions from the physician’s subjective judgment to the athlete’s achievement of objective milestones, thereby enhancing adherence and empowering athlete autonomy.

Establishing effective communication mechanisms among the physician, athlete, and relevant parties promotes transparency and consensus-building, thereby optimizing the ethical balance in the management of sports injuries.

ethical_issues.question: How can ethical issues in the management of Jordan’s sports injury be effectively addressed through the establishment of a strong patient-physician relationship and multidisciplinary collaboration among healthcare professionals?
keypoints: Establishing a strong patient-physician relationship is essential for effective communication regarding rehabilitation expectations and phased planning, directly influencing decision-making and implementation of the athlete’s safe return to play.
Multidisciplinary collaboration, through a staged return-to-play plan, optimizes injury management and ethical decision-making, thereby enhancing treatment adherence and rehabilitation outcomes.

Physicians should work together with the athlete to discuss the dual goals of ensuring a safe return to sports participation and preventing long-term health risks by optimizing management of the current injury.

A phased return-to-play plan sets progressive goals, helping the athlete understand the appropriate timing for returning to sport, and promotes rational decision-making and active engagement in treatment.

The treatment of sports injuries must address both physiological impairments and their psychosocial impact, ensuring that the rehabilitation plan comprehensively supports the athlete’s overall health and quality of life.
For minor athletes, appropriate family communication should be incorporated to strengthen the support system, enhance treatment adherence, and promote ethical transparency.

Establishing effective communication mechanisms among the physician, athlete, and relevant treatment team members (such as athletic trainers and physical therapists) is key to resolving ethical issues in the management of sports injuries.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical decision-making be guided primarily by the athlete’s long-term health when the athlete faces multiple incentives to return to play prematurely?
keypoints: Medical decision-making should prioritize the athlete’s long-term health, ensuring a safe and evidence-based return to play.
The physician should communicate clearly with the athlete regarding the dual goals of facilitating a safe return to sports participation and preventing or managing long-term health risks.
A staged return-to-play plan should be developed, with progressive goals to help the athlete understand and accept the appropriate timing for resuming participation.
Treatment of sports injuries must address both physiological recovery and the impact on other aspects of the athlete’s life, with attention to overall well-being.

Through multidisciplinary collaboration and effective communication, a safe return-to-play pathway can be scientifically planned, and ethical issues in sports injury medical decision-making can be appropriately managed.

title: Does Helping a Patient Find a Job Violate Professional Boundaries?
case:
Dr. Manning had been Mr. Hayden’s primary care physician for two decades. Previously in general good health, at 51 Mr. Hayden experienced severe chest pain and shortness of breath. His wife drove him to the local emergency room. After receiving a work-up for his symptoms, Mr. Hayden was diagnosed with an arrhythmia and transferred to the cardiology unit. He received a pacemaker and was prescribed medication to help manage his condition. He was also advised to take things easy and cautioned that, even after his recovery, he could not return to his job as a metalworker in a machine fabrication shop.
Some months after the pacemaker surgery, Mr. Hayden visited Dr. Manning for follow-up. He told Dr. Manning that, because he could not return to his job, he would lose his employer-sponsored insurance at the end of the month when he had exhausted his sick time and vacation. He said he had been unsuccessful in finding less strenuous work that fit his skills and knowledge. Even with the provisions provided by the Affordable Care Act, maintaining basic payments and covering his necessary medications would be difficult.
The following day, a friend of Dr. Manning who owned a small business told him that she was hiring for a position that seemed to fit Mr. Hayden’s education and skills and would not, it seemed to Dr. Manning, jeopardize Mr. Hayden’s health. The position came with benefits, including health insurance coverage. Dr. Manning wondered whether he should tell Mr. Haydon about the position.
case_rewrite:
For over twenty years, Dr. Manning had served as Mr. Hayden’s primary care physician. Throughout that time, Mr. Hayden had enjoyed generally good health. However, at age 51, he was suddenly struck by intense chest pain and shortness of breath. His wife immediately drove him to the local emergency department. There, after a thorough evaluation, Mr. Hayden was diagnosed with an arrhythmia and admitted to the cardiology unit. He underwent pacemaker implantation and was started on medications to manage his heart condition. The cardiology team instructed him to avoid strenuous activity, and made it clear that—even after recovery—he could not safely return to his job as a metalworker in a machine fabrication shop.

Several months after his pacemaker surgery, Mr. Hayden came in for a follow-up appointment with Dr. Manning. During their conversation, Mr. Hayden explained that his inability to resume work at the fabrication shop meant he would lose his employer-sponsored health insurance at the end of the month, once his sick leave and vacation time ran out. He shared his frustration at being unable to find less physically demanding work that matched his skills and experience. Even with options available under the Affordable Care Act, he admitted that keeping up with essential payments and affording his medications would be a real struggle.

The next day, Dr. Manning spoke with a friend who owned a small business. The friend mentioned she was looking to hire someone for a position that, to Dr. Manning, seemed well-suited to Mr. Hayden’s background and abilities. Importantly, the job appeared unlikely to endanger Mr. Hayden’s health and came with benefits, including health insurance coverage. Dr. Manning found himself wondering whether he ought to let Mr. Hayden know about this opportunity.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians assist patients in addressing life challenges, or should their support be limited strictly to medical issues?
keypoints: The physician’s responsibilities encompass both medical and psychosocial dimensions, aiming to promote patient autonomy and assist in addressing all issues that cause dysfunction in the patient’s life, while avoiding the fostering of dependency.
Physicians must adhere to professional ethics by rigorously safeguarding patient confidentiality and respecting the patient’s right to informed consent.

Effective patient-physician communication is a prerequisite; the physician should fully inform the patient of relevant circumstances and obtain the patient’s consent before initiating further assistance.

Utilizing personal resources or networks to help a patient find suitable employment constitutes a reasonable and feasible form of concrete assistance, provided that professional boundaries and ethical standards are maintained.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians delineate professional distance and boundaries when forming emotional connections with patients in order to maintain professionalism?
keypoints: Physicians should strictly maintain professional boundaries, appropriately manage relationships with patients, and avoid exploiting patients for personal gain or creating conflicts of interest.
Physicians must respect and protect patient confidentiality while demonstrating genuine humanistic care and a spirit of helpfulness.
Establishing an appropriate emotional connection with patients can facilitate recovery, but the scope and limits of assistance should be rationally delineated.
The physician’s assistance should aim to promote patient autonomy and encourage positive coping with life’s challenges, rather than fostering patient dependence.

In complex relationships, physicians should possess ethical sensitivity, balance professional responsibilities with interpersonal emotions, and ensure objectivity and fairness in medical decision-making.

title: Balancing Practice Policies with Patient Needs
case:
Dr. Rekai is a psychiatrist who has been working in a private practice with several other physicians for quite some time. The practice recently went through a difficult legal action in which allegations were made about a psychiatrist’s conduct during a house call. The action resulted in an out-of-court settlement, and the practice put a temporary suspension on house calls while the system and processes were reviewed. In the interim, the clinic psychiatrists were advised to see patients in the office or link them to emergency services if an office visit was not possible. All of the practice’s clients received notices, and verbal and written consent were obtained to ensure that they understood the temporary change in the policy. Psychiatrists who continued to make house calls would risk suspension from the practice.
One day, the practice receptionist received a phone call from a patient who was frantic and repeatedly asked to speak with Dr. Rekai. Dr. Rekai took the call. It was Rebecca, a usually stable patient, who was having a crisis. Dr. Rekai believed that Rebecca should be seen immediately and suggested that she go to the emergency room (ER) or call an ambulance to take her there, but Rebecca adamantly refused.
Dr. Rekai and the receptionist attempted to reach the managing partner (who had overseen the change in policy), but she was out of the office and unavailable. Dr. Rekai had no patients scheduled for the next few hours and contemplated going to Rebecca’s house despite the clinic’s prohibition on house calls.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Rekai, a psychiatrist, has long worked alongside several colleagues in a private group practice. Recently, the clinic became embroiled in a challenging legal dispute arising from allegations about a psychiatrist’s behavior during a home visit. After the matter was settled out of court, the practice leadership decided to halt all house calls temporarily while they reviewed their protocols and safeguards. In this period, psychiatrists were instructed to either see their patients in the office or, if that wasn’t feasible, direct them to emergency services. Every patient was notified of this change, and the clinic sought both verbal and written consent to ensure everyone was aware and understood the revised policy. The message was clear: any psychiatrist who chose to continue providing house calls risked immediate suspension from the practice.

One afternoon, the receptionist answered a call from a visibly distressed patient who persistently insisted on speaking with Dr. Rekai. Dr. Rekai came to the phone and found it was Rebecca—a patient who was typically stable, but now in the midst of a crisis. After listening to Rebecca, Dr. Rekai judged that she needed urgent attention. He advised her to either visit the emergency room or call an ambulance, but Rebecca resolutely refused both suggestions.

Attempting to seek guidance, Dr. Rekai and the receptionist tried to contact the managing partner who had overseen the policy change, but she was unavailable and out of the office. With no other patients scheduled for several hours, Dr. Rekai found himself weighing the possibility of visiting Rebecca at her home, despite the clinic’s explicit ban on house calls.

ethical_issues.question: Is the clinic’s policy of suspending home visits reasonable, and does it adequately consider patients’ decision-making capacity as well as the potential harm to the patient-doctor relationship?
keypoints: Although the clinic’s policy to suspend home visits aims to reduce legal risk, it is overly conservative and neglects the reliance of certain patients on home-based care, potentially resulting in actual harm to these patients.

The policy insufficiently accounts for the decision-making capacity of psychiatric patients, who may be unable to fully understand or effectively consent to the policy changes during periods of symptom fluctuation; thus, verbal or written consent does not necessarily indicate that they possess adequate autonomy in making such choices.

The practice of prohibiting physicians from conducting home visits under threat of suspension is unreasonable, placing clinicians in an ethical dilemma between adhering to institutional regulations and advocating for their patients’ best interests, and may undermine the foundational trust in the patient-physician relationship.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr. Rekai ensure that her patient receives necessary psychiatric care while adhering to the clinic’s policy, given that the patient refuses to go to the emergency room?
keypoints: Dr. Rekai should first conduct a remote psychiatric assessment by telephone, focusing on evaluating the patient’s risk of suicide and harm to others, and implement appropriate interventions, such as inquiring about access to lethal means and advising the removal of dangerous items.

If the telephone assessment cannot effectively confirm the patient’s safety, Dr. Rekai should make a concerted effort to persuade the patient to come to the office for an in-person evaluation, clearly explaining the necessity of an office visit and that this measure may help prevent the need for a more coercive emergency assessment.

In the event that the patient refuses to come to the office and the telephone assessment still cannot confirm safety, Dr. Rekai should recognize that the patient’s risk level has increased and should reassess whether the current situation meets the threshold for initiating involuntary hospitalization.

As a last resort, and only after confirming the presence of imminent and serious risk through assessment, Dr. Rekai should consider initiating involuntary hospitalization procedures to protect the safety of the patient and others, while avoiding misuse of this intervention.

title: A Friend’s Request for Treatment
case:
Peter and Tom have been best friends for more than a dozen years. Peter, a surgeon, is reputedly the best gastroenterological surgeon in the region. He is known for polyp resections, colectomies, and related surgical procedures of the gut. Tom teaches math at the county community college. They have been meeting to play golf at Peter’s golf club on the first Saturday of the month for many years. One Saturday, Tom approaches Peter with a look of concern, telling him that his last colonoscopy revealed a tumor and that he has to have surgery to resect part of his ascending colon. Peter listens intently. Then Tom says, “You’re the best colorectal surgeon around.”
Peter nods his head. “So they say.”
“Well, I know you don’t usually operate on your friends, but can’t you make an exception for me?”
Peter is slightly taken aback but remains silent. Tom continues, “It doesn’t seem to make sense for me to go to a ‘runner-up’ surgeon just because we happen to be friends.”
case_rewrite:
Peter and Tom have shared a close friendship for over twelve years. Peter, a highly regarded surgeon, is renowned throughout the region for his expertise in gastrointestinal surgery, particularly in performing polyp resections and colectomies. His reputation as the leading specialist in gut surgeries is well established. Tom, meanwhile, teaches mathematics at the county community college. The two have a longstanding tradition of meeting to play golf at Peter’s club on the first Saturday of each month.

One crisp Saturday morning, as they finish the sixth hole, Tom approaches Peter with a serious expression. “Peter, I need to talk to you about something important,” Tom begins, his voice tinged with anxiety. He explains that after his recent colonoscopy, a tumor was discovered, and his doctor has recommended surgery to remove a section of his ascending colon. Peter listens carefully, his demeanor shifting to one of concern.

Tom glances at Peter and says, “You know, everyone says you’re the best colorectal surgeon in the area.”

Peter gives a modest nod. “That’s what people say,” he replies.

Tom continues, “I realize you usually don’t operate on friends, but would you make an exception for me? I trust you, and it just doesn’t seem right to settle for a second-best surgeon simply because we’re friends.”

Peter is caught off guard by Tom’s request. He hesitates, weighing his response, as silence hangs between them. Tom adds quietly, “I just want the best care I can get.”

ethical_issues.question: How can Peter, as Tom’s close friend and surgeon, maintain objectivity and uphold professional ethical standards in diagnosing and treating Tom, given their longstanding personal relationship?
keypoints: When a physician has an emotional involvement with a patient, the objectivity and professionalism of diagnosis and treatment may be compromised; therefore, careful evaluation is required before personally assuming treatment responsibility.
Patients have the right to receive fair and objective medical care; physicians should prioritize the patient’s best interests and generally avoid performing surgery on friends or relatives.
Physicians may serve in an advisory capacity to assist patients in selecting appropriate specialists and guide them through the healthcare process and decision-making.

In emergencies or when no other qualified physicians are available, exceptions may be made for treating friends, provided that such care aligns with the patient’s best interests and adheres to ethical standards.
Physicians should communicate openly with patients about potential conflicts of interest and risks, thereby maintaining transparency and trust in the physician-patient relationship.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians provide medical care to close friends, especially when other qualified physicians are available?
keypoints: When a physician has an emotional involvement with a patient, it may compromise the objectivity and professional judgment in diagnosis and treatment, as well as give rise to issues of confidentiality and trust; therefore, providing medical care to individuals with close personal relationships should be avoided.

Multiple authoritative medical organizations, such as the American College of Physicians, the General Medical Council of Great Britain, and the Medical Council of New Zealand, recommend that physicians refrain from treating relatives and close acquaintances to ensure the objectivity and quality of care.

Friendship may hinder a physician’s ability to comprehensively inquire about medical history and perform necessary examinations, thereby affecting the accurate assessment of the condition and the quality of diagnosis and treatment.

Surgical procedures carry the risk of serious complications; when a physician operates on a friend, it may not only impair professional judgment but also increase emotional burden, potentially damaging the relationship and the physician’s psychological well-being.

Based on the patient’s best interests and professional responsibility, it is prudent and responsible for a physician to politely decline to perform surgery on a friend; this should be communicated with respect and empathy, and the physician may offer to act as an advocate during the treatment process, assisting the friend in finding a qualified surgeon and navigating the healthcare system.

tags: Decision making/Patient and family centered care
title: Conflicts in Family-Centered Pediatric Care for Patients with Autism
case:
Dr. Woods entered the patient exam room to meet with 6-year-old Kari and her mother. In her hand, she held the report from Dr. Hoffman, the developmental pediatrician Kari had seen two months ago, which confirmed a diagnosis of moderate to severe autism. After greeting Kari and her mother, Dr. Woods began, “I see Dr. Hoffman started Kari on guanfacine for some of her symptoms and had some recommendations for therapy.”
“Yes,” Kari’s mother said, her voice unsteady. “She wanted us to start going to these therapists for speech and behavior and all kinds of things. And we saw a social worker, and she’s going to help us with the paperwork to get it all paid for. And Kari has started the guanfacine.”
“This all sounds good,” Dr. Woods said gently. She knew guanfacine was the first-line treatment for irritability associated with autism, often prescribed for young children because of its low profile of side effects.
“It’s just—” Kari’s mother began to cry. “The guanfacine doesn’t seem to be helping. In fact, I think she’s getting worse. She’s angry all the time, and she has these temper tantrums…I don’t know what to do.”
“What about the behavioral therapy?” Dr. Woods asked.
“I can’t manage all these appointments. I just can’t. I’m a single mom, I have two other kids, I work—there’s no way I can go to all of these. I don’t have anyone in town here to help me, and I can’t be missing work to drive Kari to appointments every day and doing all this therapy. I know she said it’s the best option for Kari, but I have to tell you, it just isn’t going to happen.” Looking at Dr. Woods, she added, “Don’t get me wrong, I love my daughter and I would do anything for her. But to take care of all my kids, I have to work. Look. I read the pamphlets. I know there are other medications that could help. Couldn’t we just try one of the stronger medications—the antipsychotics, maybe, they’re supposed to help, or an antidepressant—just something that would help her calm down and make her life more manageable…” She trailed off.
Dr. Woods hesitated. While guanfacine was relatively benign, there were significant side effects associated with atypical antipsychotics, and she wasn’t sure how comfortable she was prescribing a strong psychiatric medication when behavioral therapy hadn’t been attempted.
“I know it’s not ideal,” Kari’s mother said. “But isn’t it better than nothing?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Woods stepped quietly into the exam room where six-year-old Kari sat beside her mother, her small hands fidgeting with a toy. In Dr. Woods’s hand was the report from Dr. Hoffman, the developmental pediatrician Kari had seen two months prior. The diagnosis was clear: moderate to severe autism. Dr. Hoffman had started Kari on guanfacine and recommended a regimen of speech and behavioral therapies.

Dr. Woods greeted them both gently. “I see Dr. Hoffman started guanfacine for Kari and made some recommendations for therapy as well.”

Kari’s mother gave a tired nod, her voice trembling as she spoke. “Yes. She wanted us to get Kari into all these therapies—speech, behavioral, everything. We met with a social worker, who’s helping us figure out payment, and Kari’s taking the guanfacine now.”

“That’s a good start,” Dr. Woods said, her tone encouraging. She knew guanfacine was considered a first-line treatment for irritability in children with autism, chosen for its comparatively mild side effect profile.

But Kari’s mother’s composure faltered. Tears welled in her eyes. “The guanfacine…it doesn’t seem to be making anything better. If anything, Kari’s angrier. She’s having more tantrums. I’m at a loss.”

Dr. Woods leaned forward slightly. “Have you been able to start the behavioral therapy sessions?”

Kari’s mother shook her head, wiping her eyes. “I can’t. I’m a single mom, I have two other kids, and I work full-time. There’s just no way for me to make all these appointments. I don’t have family nearby, and I can’t keep missing work to shuttle Kari around every day for therapy. I know Dr. Hoffman said this is what’s best for Kari, but it’s just not possible for us.” She looked pleadingly at Dr. Woods. “Please understand, I love my daughter and I want what’s best for her. But I have to be able to take care of all my kids. I read about other medications—antipsychotics, antidepressants. Couldn’t we try something stronger, just something to help her calm down so our lives are a little more manageable?”

Dr. Woods hesitated, weighing the options. She knew the possible side effects of antipsychotic medications could be significant, especially in children, and they were not usually prescribed without first attempting behavioral therapies.

Kari’s mother’s voice was barely above a whisper. “I know it’s not the way it’s supposed to be done, but isn’t it better than nothing?”

ethical_issues.question: In situations where the recommended first-line treatment for Kari has not yet been implemented, should physicians honor the family's request to initiate a more potent medication, or should they prioritize adherence to established treatment protocols?
keypoints: Physicians should understand the family’s perspective, listen to their difficulties and requests, and guide the discussion back to the treatment goals, collaborating to achieve the shared objective of improving the patient’s symptoms.

Physicians retain the professional authority to determine clinically appropriate interventions and are not obligated to fulfill medication requests that lack scientific evidence or do not conform to best practice, even when respecting patient autonomy.

When first-line treatments have not been implemented and the patient’s condition warrants it, physicians may consider the short-term use of more potent medications as a compromise, provided that the potential side effects and risks are fully disclosed.

Refusing reasonable medication requests from the patient’s family also carries risks, potentially resulting in symptom worsening that adversely affects learning, social interactions, and family functioning; physicians must carefully weigh these benefits and harms.
Physicians should respect the family’s ultimate decision, as they bear the long-term responsibility for treatment and are best positioned to balance the risks and benefits and make informed choices.

ethical_issues.question: How can a balance be achieved between family-centered care and evidence-based medicine to ensure that pediatric patients receive the scientifically recommended optimal treatment?
keypoints: Physicians should recognize and regulate their own emotions, maintain professional composure, and employ effective communication skills to facilitate rational discussion, thereby avoiding emotional interference in the decision-making process.

Physicians should understand and respect the patient’s mother’s perspective and real-life challenges, guiding the discussion to focus on shared treatment goals and expressing a willingness to collaborate in order to achieve the best possible plan.

Physicians need to clearly and comprehensively explain to the patient’s mother the scientific rationale, risks, and benefits of each treatment option—including the advantages and disadvantages of behavioral interventions and pharmacotherapy, as well as alternative choices—to support informed decision-making.

Physicians may propose a compromise approach, such as augmenting behavioral therapy support (e.g., arranging for in-home guidance) while cautiously employing short-term pharmacologic treatment, balancing the risks of medication side effects with the family’s practical needs.

Provided that safety and scientific appropriateness are ensured, physicians should respect the family’s final decision, continue to offer support and follow-up, and monitor changes in the patient’s symptoms as well as the family’s capacity to cope.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians effectively manage their own emotions and communicate with patients’ families to collaboratively develop the best plan for improving the child’s symptoms and behavior?
keypoints: Revised Key Points:

Physicians should recognize their own emotions and employ techniques such as mindfulness to focus on problem-solving, acknowledge the emotional dimensions of medical practice, and avoid allowing emotions to interfere with professional judgment.

Physicians need to acknowledge the perspectives of patients’ families, demonstrate empathy, redirect discussions toward treatment goals, and commit to collaboratively developing practical plans to improve the patient’s symptoms and behavior.

Physicians should clearly explain the risks, benefits, and alternative options of various treatment approaches, assist families in understanding the potential impacts on the patient and family, and facilitate informed decision-making.

Physicians ought to provide practical support such as referrals to social work and coordination of home-based therapies to alleviate the multiple burdens on families, helping them balance caregiving responsibilities with life stresses.

Physicians may adopt a flexible, compromise approach grounded in scientific evidence and safety principles, integrating short-term pharmacologic treatment with behavioral interventions to balance medication side effects and therapeutic benefits while addressing the family’s real-world needs.
