title: Autonomy and Autism: Who Speaks for the Adolescent Patient?
case:
Jake was diagnosed with autism at the age of four. His symptoms were treated with behavioral therapy until the age of 14, when he began having frequent angry outbursts. He often shouted at his parents and had fits of screaming, occasionally at school. At the time, his mother noticed that he was very irritable and often seemed depressed. He was prescribed an SSRI and an atypical antipsychotic for his outbursts and mood symptoms.
Now 17, Jake has cognitive abilities in the low-normal range, but his ability to perform daily activities is more substantially impaired, and his mother is heavily involved in his care. He needs reminders and supervision to care for himself, including taking his medication and doing his homework, and refuses to brush his teeth or hair unless his mother insists. He experiences sensory overload. He attends an alternative high school because of his repeated angry outbursts at school and difficulties paying attention.
His physician, Dr. Mullins, greets Jake and his mother cheerfully at Jake’s check-up. “How have things been going?” she asks.
Jake resentfully stares at the wall behind her. “I’m not going to take this stupid medicine anymore,” he says. “I hate it. I hate taking it every day.”
His mother adds to the conversation. “He does,” she confesses. “But it really does make a difference. When we tried to go off the meds a year ago, Jake was out of control. He screamed at his little sisters whenever they spoke to him, he got in trouble at school; he was just difficult. When he takes his meds—and I make sure he takes them every day—he just seems less irritated and annoyed. He doesn’t have these outbursts; he does better in school. I hate making him take medication, but I just can’t imagine trying to take care of all my kids when Jake is as volatile as he was last year.”
Dr. Mullins turns to Jake. “What do you think about that, Jake? Do you think the medications make a difference in how you feel?”
Jake doesn’t answer right away. Staring at the floor, he says sullenly, “I don’t care. It’s just for everyone else that I take this medicine. I don’t like the way it makes me feel. I don’t care if everyone else doesn’t want to be around me. I’m sick of it. I’m almost an adult. Why does everyone else get to decide what I do, and I don’t get to have any say?”
case_rewrite:
Jake was diagnosed with autism at age four. For years, he responded to behavioral therapy, but by fourteen he began having frequent, angry outbursts—shouting at his parents, and sometimes screaming at school. Around this time, his mother noticed that he seemed increasingly irritable and often showed signs of sadness. In response to these changes, Jake’s physician prescribed him an SSRI along with an atypical antipsychotic to manage his mood symptoms and outbursts.

Now seventeen, Jake’s cognitive abilities remain in the low-normal range, yet he struggles more significantly with everyday tasks. His mother remains deeply involved in his daily care, reminding and supervising him to ensure he takes his medication and completes his homework. Unless his mother insists, Jake refuses to brush his teeth or hair. He experiences frequent sensory overload and, because of persistent angry outbursts and trouble focusing, he attends an alternative high school.

At a routine check-up, Dr. Mullins greets both Jake and his mother with a warm smile. “How have things been going?” she asks.

Jake glares at the wall, his voice edged with frustration. “I’m not going to take this stupid medicine anymore. I hate it. I hate taking it every day.”

His mother glances at Dr. Mullins and sighs. “He really does hate it. But honestly, it makes a big difference. When we tried stopping the medication last year, Jake was out of control. He yelled at his little sisters whenever they spoke, constantly had trouble at school—it was just so hard. With the medication, and with me making sure he takes it every day, he’s less irritated and doesn’t have those explosive outbursts. He does better in school, too. I hate forcing him to take medicine, but I just don’t know how I could manage everyone if Jake was as volatile as he was last year.”

Dr. Mullins turns to Jake, her tone gentle. “Jake, what do you think about what your mom just said? Do you feel the medicine makes any difference to you?”

Jake doesn’t reply immediately. He drops his gaze to the floor and mutters, “I don’t care. The only reason I take this medicine is for everyone else. I don’t like how it makes me feel. I don’t care if people don’t want me around. I’m tired of it. I’m almost an adult. Why does everyone else get to decide what I do, and I don’t get any say?”

ethical_issues.question: In medical decision-making for adolescent patients with autism, how should the patient’s autonomy be balanced with parental decision-making authority?
keypoints: In medical decision-making for adolescent patients with autism, parents or guardians are typically the ultimate decision-makers, but the scope of the patient’s autonomy should be assessed based on their maturity and functional capacity.

The patient’s functional limitations should be acknowledged while maximizing their autonomy by promoting participation in medical decisions through a formal shared decision-making model, which specifically includes listening to the patient’s preferences, addressing their concerns, and offering reasonable treatment options.

While protecting the patient from making choices that may harm their health and well-being, parents should prioritize the patient’s academic success and maintenance of positive interpersonal relationships, simultaneously supporting the gradual development of the patient’s autonomous decision-making abilities.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with an autistic patient’s resistance to pharmacological treatment, how should physicians manage the situation to ensure the patient’s best interests are upheld?
keypoints: Physicians should acknowledge and respect the patient’s resistance to medication, actively listen to their expressions, and facilitate the patient’s engagement in the shared decision-making process.
Physicians should assess and explore the possibility of adjusting the medication regimen, seeking alternatives with fewer side effects that are more acceptable to the patient.
Clinicians, family members, and relevant support agencies should prioritize the patient’s needs and treatment goals, collaborating to ensure the patient’s best interests are upheld.
The adoption of a formal shared decision-making (SDM) model can enhance the patient’s autonomy and promote maturity and independence within the patient’s capacity.

While safeguarding the patient’s safety and well-being, efforts should be made to progressively support the development of the patient’s autonomous medical decision-making abilities, providing necessary support and supervision.

title: Communicating Concern about Early Signs of Autism to Parents
case:
Dr. Peterson smiled at Elizabeth, a 15-month-old who was in his office for her well-child check. He made small talk with Elizabeth’s mother for a few minutes while Elizabeth played with a doll from the exam room’s toy chest.
“Do you have any concerns today?” he asked the mother.
Elizabeth’s mother smiled. “Not really,” she said. “She’s been a little slow to talk—her brothers were both talking much more at this age—but I think she’s catching up.”
Dr. Peterson noticed that Elizabeth was flapping her hands slightly. “Does she do that often?” he asked the mother.
“Oh, once in a while.”
He continued to observe Elizabeth play as he asked her mother a series of questions. Elizabeth continued to flap her hands throughout the interview. To Dr. Peterson, it looked like “stimming,” or self-stimulation, behavior that is frequently associated with autism. Elizabeth had poor eye contact, although she did respond to her name and come to her mother’s side when called. She also rocked back and forth on her knees, singing to herself lightly. The hand-flapping, rocking behavior, and poor eye contact gave Dr. Peterson reason to consider autism.
He hesitated. According to Elizabeth’s mother, Elizabeth had met all of her developmental milestones, although recently it seemed that her speech development was not on track. There were plenty of signs that she could be developing normally: she played with the doll attentively and demonstrated affection toward it, she responded to her name, and was well-behaved. Her mother—who had two older children—hadn’t noticed anything out of the ordinary.
Dr. Peterson considered his course of action. He knew that Elizabeth would undergo routine screening for autism at her 18-month visit and didn’t feel that he saw anything severe enough to warrant an extensive evaluation at the moment. However, he wondered if Elizabeth’s mother had a right to know that he was concerned. He was apprehensive that conveying his concern to the mother involved a certain degree of unnecessary risk: it would mostly likely cause increased anxiety for the family and possibly spur Elizabeth’s parents to perceive normal behavior as pathology. But did he have an ethical obligation to share his concerns with her mother?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Peterson greeted Elizabeth, a lively 15-month-old, as she toddled into his exam room for her regular well-child visit. While Elizabeth’s mother settled into a chair, Dr. Peterson chatted with her, observing as Elizabeth became engrossed with a doll from the room’s toy chest.

“Are there any concerns you’d like to discuss today?” he asked.

Elizabeth’s mother smiled reassuringly. “No big worries. She’s been slower to talk than her brothers were at this age, but I think she’s getting there.”

Dr. Peterson watched Elizabeth and noticed a subtle fluttering of her hands. “Does she flap her hands like that often?” he inquired gently.

“Every now and then,” her mother replied.

Throughout their conversation, Elizabeth continued flapping her hands. Dr. Peterson recognized this as possible “stimming”—a repetitive movement sometimes seen in children on the autism spectrum. He also noticed that Elizabeth seemed to avoid eye contact, though she did respond when her mother called her and came over promptly. As she played, she rocked on her knees and hummed softly to herself. The combination of hand-flapping, rocking, and limited eye contact made Dr. Peterson consider the possibility of early autism signs.

He paused, weighing his impressions. According to her mother, Elizabeth had reached all her developmental milestones so far, but her speech seemed to have slowed in recent months. Still, there was much that seemed typical: Elizabeth played attentively with the doll, showed affection, responded to her name, and behaved calmly. Her mother, experienced with two older children, hadn’t noticed anything unusual.

Dr. Peterson considered his next steps. He knew that routine autism screening was scheduled for Elizabeth’s 18-month visit, and nothing he observed urgently warranted an immediate, extensive evaluation. Yet, he wondered whether he owed it to Elizabeth’s mother to share his concerns. He worried that mentioning autism might unnecessarily alarm the family or lead them to interpret normal behaviors as problematic. Still, he questioned whether he had an ethical responsibility to be transparent with his observations and to involve Elizabeth’s mother in ongoing monitoring and decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: Does Dr. Peterson have an ethical obligation to inform Elizabeth’s mother about his concerns that Elizabeth may be exhibiting early signs of autism?
keypoints: Peterson has an ethical responsibility to act in the best interests of his pediatric patients by ensuring timely recognition and appropriate communication regarding potential neurodevelopmental concerns, such as early signs of autism spectrum disorder.

Peterson should communicate his clinical observations and concerns to Elizabeth’s mother in a sensitive, non-stigmatizing manner, aiming to minimize unnecessary anxiety while recommending appropriate follow-up and ongoing developmental monitoring.

Peterson to establish a trusting, collaborative relationship with the family, facilitating shared decision-making and access to suitable medical and educational resources, thereby fostering a sustained therapeutic alliance.

ethical_issues.question: How can unnecessary family anxiety and the pathologization of a child’s behavior be avoided when communicating the possibility of autism?
keypoints: Peterson should communicate his preliminary concerns regarding possible early signs of autism using sensitive, non-stigmatizing language, framing autism as a form of neurodevelopmental diversity. This approach helps parents understand their child’s unique characteristics and avoids pathologizing normal or mild behavioral variations.

Peterson can foster trust and establish a strong therapeutic alliance with Elizabeth’s parents, which is essential for promoting parental acceptance, reducing anxiety, and alleviating potential feelings of guilt.
This helps prevent unnecessary medicalization and reduces the risk of emotional and financial strain on the family.

Peterson should arrange timely follow-up assessments to monitor Elizabeth’s developmental progress, applying the “test of time” principle to guide the need for intervention. Throughout this process, he should provide ongoing psychological support and clear, evidence-based information to the family.
This individualized approach ensures ethically sound and patient-centered care.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of limited resources, how can equity in autism treatment and the maximization of cost-effectiveness be ensured to meet the needs of a greater number of individuals?
keypoints: Ensuring equity in autism treatment requires legal and policy measures to guarantee insurance coverage, thereby securing equal access to care for all patients.

Physicians and parents should prioritize safe and effective interventions supported by robust evidence, allocate limited resources judiciously, and avoid waste on ineffective or unnecessary treatments.

Prioritizing cost-effective intervention programs helps free up resources to meet the treatment needs of a broader patient population and promotes equitable distribution of overall healthcare resources.

title: Abusive and Disruptive Behavior in the Surgical Team
case:
With six years of experience under his belt, Dr. Richards was hired as an anesthesiologist at a small private hospital. His first patient, Mr. Jarvis, was scheduled to undergo surgical resection of an abdominal tumor. Dr. Richards interviewed Mr. Jarvis and went over his record with him, discovering that his patient was 64 years old and had chronic hypertension. The attending surgeon, Dr. Palmatti, was a well-respected general and endocrine surgeon with over 30 years’ experience and the chief executive officer of the largest surgical group in the city. About an hour into the case, Dr. Palmatti instructed Dr. Richards to administer a fluid bolus and electrolytes.
Dr. Richards politely explained that the patient’s urine output, intraoperative fluid management, blood loss, and arterial blood gas measurement all suggested that his fluids and electrolytes were in balance, so he recommended not administering fluid and electrolytes at this time.
Dr. Palmatti remarked that, in his experience as a surgeon, he had “never had an anesthesiologist display such blatant disregard for authority.”
A nervous Dr. Richards responded, “While fluid administration in this patient would not likely have any significant negative consequence, Mr. Jarvis’s numbers clearly suggest that fluids are not necessary. I feel as though there is slightly more room for harm than good.”
Clearly irritated, Dr. Palmatti turned to Dr. Richards and asks, “Oh, you ‘feel as though,’ do you? And what exactly entitles you to question my 35 years of experience?”
Dr. Richards reassessed the patient’s volume status and intraoperative fluid loss and considered what effect his refusal might have on his and the hospital’s other anesthesiologists’ standing with the surgeon and whether the risk of adverse effects was sufficiently minimal to permit administering unnecessary fluids.
case_rewrite:
After six years of practicing anesthesiology, Dr. Richards began his new role at a small private hospital. His first assignment was with Mr. Jarvis, a 64-year-old man with chronic hypertension, who was scheduled for the surgical removal of an abdominal tumor. Prior to surgery, Dr. Richards met with Mr. Jarvis, carefully reviewed his medical history, and discussed the anesthetic plan. The attending surgeon, Dr. Palmatti, was known throughout the city as a highly respected general and endocrine surgeon, boasting more than three decades of experience and serving as the chief executive officer of the city’s largest surgical group.

About an hour into the operation, Dr. Palmatti directed Dr. Richards to give a fluid bolus and administer electrolytes. Dr. Richards reviewed the intraoperative data, including urine output, blood loss, fluid balance, and arterial blood gas results. He calmly explained to Dr. Palmatti, "Based on Mr. Jarvis’s current measurements, his fluids and electrolytes are well balanced. I don’t recommend additional fluids or electrolytes at this moment."

Dr. Palmatti, visibly displeased, retorted, "In all my years as a surgeon, I have never had an anesthesiologist show such blatant disregard for authority."

Feeling anxious but maintaining his composure, Dr. Richards replied, "While giving fluids now might not cause significant harm, the numbers suggest they’re unnecessary. I believe there’s actually a slightly greater potential for harm than benefit."

Dr. Palmatti, now openly irritated, turned to Dr. Richards and said, "Oh, you ‘believe,’ do you? And what exactly gives you the right to challenge my 35 years of experience?"

Dr. Richards reassessed Mr. Jarvis’s volume status and intraoperative fluid loss, weighing the potential consequences of refusing Dr. Palmatti’s order—not just for his own relationship with the surgeon but for the standing of the entire anesthesiology team. He considered whether the risk of any adverse effect was truly minimal, and whether it was ethically permissible to comply with an unnecessary intervention, even temporarily, or if he should stand firm to protect the patient’s best interest.

ethical_issues.question: How can abusive and disruptive behavior be effectively addressed within the medical team to ensure patient safety and promote team collaboration?
keypoints: Malicious, abusive, and disruptive behaviors among healthcare professionals impede team collaboration and communication, directly endangering patient safety.

Effective management of disruptive behavior requires coordinated efforts at multiple levels, including individuals, departments, hospitals, and healthcare systems, to safeguard patient safety and promote teamwork.

During critical tasks in the operating room, patient safety and team dynamics must be carefully balanced to avoid unnecessary conflict; however, if an order clearly jeopardizes patient safety, refusal to comply is ethically mandated.

Postoperatively, unprofessional behavior should be addressed through professional dialogue with the involved physician regarding its negative impact on the team; if this proves ineffective, the matter should be reported and managed according to institutional policies and procedures.

Healthcare systems must establish comprehensive policies and procedures that ensure the investigation and resolution of disruptive behavior are straightforward, protect whistleblowers from retaliation, and are conducted promptly by neutral parties.
Once abusive or disruptive behavior is confirmed, corrective measures should initially be implemented at the departmental level, with escalation to institutional medical leadership as necessary.

If disruptive behavior cannot be effectively controlled, patient safety considerations require the implementation of ultimate measures, including removal of the offending physician from clinical duties.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with unreasonable orders from a senior physician, how should a junior doctor ethically balance the responsibilities of patient safety and maintaining team relationships?
keypoints: Junior physicians should prioritize patient care and safety, conducting a rational assessment of whether the instructions from senior physicians may lead to adverse patient outcomes.

If the risk of harm from complying with the instructions is minimal and the likelihood of patient injury is negligible, junior physicians may consider temporarily following the directive while planning to discuss any disagreements with the senior physician at an appropriate time postoperatively.

If the junior physician determines that executing the instructions would jeopardize patient safety, they must firmly refuse and may seek support from other colleagues in the operating room to reinforce their position and protect the patient’s interests.

Members of the medical team should treat each other with mutual respect and collaboration, avoiding mean, abusive, and disruptive behaviors, as such conduct undermines teamwork and effective communication essential to prioritizing patient welfare. Regulating professional behavior is fundamental to achieving the ethical goals of medical practice, and when necessary, measures should be taken to ensure patient safety, including restricting clinical duties of individuals who engage in severe disruptive conduct.

ethical_issues.question: How should healthcare institutions establish policies and procedures to investigate and address abusive and disruptive behavior among physicians, while ensuring that those who report such behavior are protected from the threat of retaliation?
keypoints: Medical institutions should develop and implement systematic policies and procedures specifically for the investigation and management of abusive and disruptive (MAD) behavior among physicians, ensuring that these processes are standardized, practical, and enforceable.
Ongoing education should be provided to enhance all staff members’ awareness of the dangers posed by abusive and disruptive behavior, fostering a culture of zero tolerance.
Simple, anonymous, and secure reporting channels should be established to protect whistleblowers from any form of retaliation or adverse consequences.

Investigations should be conducted promptly by an independent and neutral third party, strictly adhering to established policies and procedures to ensure fairness, transparency, and the protection of all parties’ legal rights.

Once abusive or disruptive behavior is confirmed, corrective and containment mechanisms should first be initiated at the departmental level, with escalation to senior institutional leadership as necessary.

Clear codes of conduct and professional standards should be established, with substantive disciplinary measures for violations; when necessary, restrictions or suspension of the involved physician’s clinical duties should be imposed, while safeguarding the individual’s right to due process.

Upholding appropriate professional conduct among medical staff is fundamental to ensuring patient safety and achieving the ethical goals of medical care, and should be regarded as an essential component of healthcare quality management.

title: Withholding Information from an Anxiety-Prone Patient?
case:
Ms. Chen is in general good health. The only medication she takes is duloxetine, a serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that her psychiatrist prescribed for generalized anxiety disorder. After experiencing increased pain for three months when straining and lifting objects, Ms. Chen made an appointment with her primary care physician, who took a history, examined Ms. Chen, and referred her to a general surgeon for further evaluation. The surgeon performed a physical exam and diagnostic workup that confirmed that Ms. Chen had an inguinal hernia and scheduled her for elective hernia repair the following week.
On the morning of the scheduled operation, Ms. Chen was greeted by Dr. Billings, a third-year resident in anesthesiology. The surgeon had informed Ms. Chen about the risks of the surgical procedure and had obtained her informed consent. But the nurse told Dr. Billings that Ms. Chen was “very worried about dying” and “barely made it through the surgery consent.” On interviewing her, Dr. Billings noted that she was a highly anxious woman who was unable to remain still. After speaking with Ms. Chen, Dr. Billings reviewed her medical history and medications and confirmed that she was a good candidate for general anesthesia.
Given Ms. Chen’s good health, low risk of adverse effects from general anesthetic, and current level of anxiety, Dr. Billings considered whether to inform Ms. Chen fully about all possible risks associated with general anesthesia, including the risk of death. She recalled an ethics grand rounds lecture in which an anesthesiologist invoked therapeutic privilege when choosing not to disclose full risk information to a psychiatric patient. Dr. Billings stepped out of the holding area to gather her thoughts. Unable to locate the attending physician, she considered whether withholding the risks of anesthesia from Ms. Chen would be a failure to obtain truly informed consent.
case_rewrite:
Ms. Chen is generally in good health. The only medication she takes is duloxetine, which her psychiatrist prescribed for her generalized anxiety disorder. Over the past three months, Ms. Chen has noticed increasing pain when straining or lifting objects, prompting her to schedule an appointment with her primary care physician. After taking a thorough history and performing a physical examination, her physician referred her to a general surgeon. The surgeon’s assessment, including a physical exam and diagnostic testing, confirmed that Ms. Chen had an inguinal hernia. Elective hernia repair was scheduled for the following week.

On the morning of surgery, Ms. Chen arrived at the hospital and was greeted by Dr. Billings, a third-year anesthesiology resident. The surgeon had already discussed the surgical procedure’s risks and obtained Ms. Chen’s informed consent. However, the preoperative nurse privately informed Dr. Billings that Ms. Chen appeared “very worried about dying” and had “barely made it through the surgery consent.” When Dr. Billings interviewed Ms. Chen, she found her extremely anxious and unable to sit still. After their conversation, Dr. Billings reviewed Ms. Chen’s medical history and medications, confirming that she was an appropriate candidate for general anesthesia.

Given Ms. Chen’s good overall health, low risk of complications from general anesthesia, and her current heightened anxiety, Dr. Billings pondered whether she should disclose all possible anesthesia risks, including the rare risk of death. She recalled an ethics grand rounds lecture where an anesthesiologist had cited therapeutic privilege as a reason for not fully disclosing risks to a psychiatric patient. Dr. Billings stepped out of the holding area to collect her thoughts. Unable to locate the attending physician for guidance, she questioned whether withholding some anesthesia risks from Ms. Chen would undermine the validity of informed consent.

ethical_issues.question: When caring for a highly anxious patient, should all anesthesia risks be disclosed to ensure the completeness of informed consent?
keypoints: All patients with decision-making capacity should provide informed consent prior to undergoing invasive procedures, except in emergency situations where delaying the process would cause harm.
The depth and breadth of information disclosed should be flexibly tailored to the patient’s preferences, needs, and capacity for understanding given their current mental state.

Patients have the right to refuse to receive some or all risk information; if a patient explicitly expresses this preference, the physician should respect it, and this does not constitute a failure to obtain informed consent.
Withholding information without the patient’s knowledge or consent is ethically unacceptable.
Invoking therapeutic privilege to withhold risk information is not ethically justified when the patient is in good health and not experiencing suicidal ideation.

title: Balancing Supervision and Independence in Residency Training
case:
Chad is in his first year of residency in emergency medicine. He is working a night shift when a woman brings in her four-year-old daughter suffering from a high fever and ear pain. Chad decides to give the girl ibuprofen, start her on a course of antibiotics, and keep her under observation. Over the next couple of hours the toddler’s condition seems to worsen, and Chad worries that she might have something more serious than a middle ear infection, such as meningitis, which would require a spinal tap to rule out. He considers phoning the physician on call, Dr. Gardner, but hesitates as he picks up the phone. It’s late at night and he doesn’t want to wake the doctor for what could be a trivial matter. “And I don’t want to come across as incapable of making my own decisions,” he thinks to himself.
A while later, he still feels unsure about what to do, so he calls Dr. Gardner. After hearing a summary of the situation, she tells him, “It’s most likely a typical ear infection; sometimes they just take time to clear up. I would just wait and watch her.”
After putting down the phone Chad feels more conflicted than before. His young patient looks worse than other patients he has seen with ear infections, and he has a strong suspicion she may have something more serious; however, doing a spinal tap now would be ignoring Dr. Gardner’s advice. An hour later he decides to perform the spinal tap anyway, reasoning that, after all, this child is his patient and, ultimately, his responsibility. After reviewing the procedure briefly, he performs the tap with the help of a nurse and without complications. The results of the test come back negative, ruling out meningitis. Chad knows that he ought to feel relieved that the child is all right, but he is also disappointed to find that his instinct was wrong. He took a risk by going against Dr. Gardner’s advice, and the results now indicate that it might have been better to have followed it.
When Dr. Gardner arrives in the morning she looks over the girl’s chart and takes note of the negative spinal tap. She is aggravated that Chad chose to perform an invasive procedure, with its own set of risks, against her advice. “These young doctors always jump to rare and dire diagnoses, when most cases turn out to be as obvious and simple as they seem,” she mutters to herself, wondering why, if Chad was still worried after their conversation, he didn’t call again or ask for a consult from a doctor working last night. After the initial wave of annoyance passes, she considers another point: Chad needs to develop his own professional identity and she wants to encourage him to have confidence in his own clinical knowledge. She wonders how her reaction would have been different if the spinal tap had come back positive.
case_rewrite:
Chad, a first-year emergency medicine resident, is working a night shift in the emergency department. Late into the night, a concerned mother brings in her four-year-old daughter, who has a high fever and is complaining of severe ear pain. After examining the child, Chad prescribes ibuprofen to reduce her fever, begins a course of antibiotics for a presumed ear infection, and decides to keep her under observation. 

As the hours pass, Chad notices that the girl's condition appears to be deteriorating. She seems more lethargic and unwell than other children he has treated for ear infections. Growing uneasy, Chad starts to wonder whether something more serious could be happening—perhaps meningitis, which would require a spinal tap to rule out. He thinks about calling Dr. Gardner, the attending physician on call that night, but he hesitates. It's the middle of the night, and he worries about disturbing her for what might turn out to be a routine case. Chad also feels anxious about appearing overly dependent or unable to make decisions for himself.

Eventually, still uncertain, Chad decides to call Dr. Gardner and explains the situation. After listening to his summary, Dr. Gardner reassures him, “It sounds like a typical ear infection. Sometimes it just takes time for symptoms to improve. I think you should wait and continue to observe her.” 

After hanging up, Chad remains unsettled. The child’s condition is not improving, and he is troubled by how much sicker she seems compared to other similar cases. He feels a strong suspicion that something more serious might be at play, but he also knows that performing a spinal tap would mean disregarding Dr. Gardner’s advice. An hour later, unable to shake his concerns, Chad decides to proceed with the spinal tap. He reasons that, ultimately, the child is his responsibility as her physician. He quickly reviews the procedure, then performs the spinal tap with a nurse’s assistance. The procedure goes smoothly, and the results come back negative—there is no evidence of meningitis.

Relieved that the child does not have a life-threatening illness, Chad nonetheless feels disappointed that his clinical suspicion was not confirmed. He is keenly aware that he took a risk by going against Dr. Gardner’s recommendation, and now questions whether he should have simply followed her guidance.

When Dr. Gardner arrives in the morning and reviews the chart, she notices the negative spinal tap result and is frustrated to see that Chad proceeded with an invasive test despite her advice. “These new doctors always assume the worst-case scenario, when most cases are straightforward,” she mutters, wondering why Chad didn’t call her again or seek a consult from another doctor on duty if he remained concerned. As her initial irritation fades, Dr. Gardner reflects that Chad is in the process of developing his professional judgment and that she wants to support his confidence as he grows in his clinical abilities. She also finds herself wondering how she might have felt if the spinal tap had revealed a serious diagnosis.

ethical_issues.question: How can supervision and independence be balanced in residency training to ensure patient safety and the professional development of residents?
keypoints: Residency training requires a phased and gradual increase in residents’ autonomy, with patient safety as the foremost priority.
Trust and open communication are essential to balancing supervision and independence, fostering a constructive interaction between residents and supervising physicians.
Interns (first-year residents) require the highest level of supervision, typically necessitating direct oversight by faculty physically present on site.
When residents have mastered key skills and demonstrated responsible judgment, they should be granted appropriate increases in independence.
In the event of errors, resident autonomy should be temporarily restricted, accompanied by timely feedback and remediation to ensure patient safety and support professional development.

ethical_issues.question: How can effective communication and mutual trust be fostered between Chad and Dr. Gardner to support appropriate supervision and resident autonomy, particularly in situations where they may disagree about patient management?
keypoints: Residents must recognize their own limitations, respect the extensive experience of attending physicians, and promptly consult their supervisors when making significant clinical decisions.
Residents should trust that attending physicians will provide effective guidance and feedback, and that they will be granted increasing autonomy as their competence develops.

Attending physicians should foster an open communication environment, encourage teamwork, explicitly welcome residents to call at any time if the patient’s condition changes or if doubts arise, and proactively provide in-person support when necessary, thereby building trust through concrete actions.

Both parties should maintain timely and honest communication based on mutual trust and respect, avoiding barriers to information exchange caused by anticipated negative reactions, to ensure patient safety and quality of care.

ethical_issues.question: How can resident physicians ensure that they recognize their own limitations and respect the expertise of attending physicians in order to safeguard patient safety when performing invasive procedures?
keypoints: Intern physicians must maintain a clear awareness of the limitations of their own clinical experience and abilities, and respect the extensive experience and guidance of the attending physician.
Residents must promptly consult and obtain explicit instructions from supervising physicians when making significant clinical decisions or performing invasive procedures.
According to ACGME guidelines, interns should receive the highest level of direct, on-site supervision from faculty when performing invasive procedures to ensure patient safety.
Undertaking invasive procedures in defiance of medical directives not only endangers patient safety, but also undermines trust and teamwork among physicians, thereby compromising the quality of care.

title: Professionalism and Appropriate Expression of Empathy When Breaking Bad News
case:
Kelsey is a third-year medical student doing rounds in internal medicine. Yesterday, she met Ms. Foster, a quiet woman who was admitted due to a bad case of bronchitis. Kelsey was asked to help prep Ms. Foster for an x-ray. At first, Ms. Foster was a little standoffish and their interactions were awkward. Kelsey decided to try and make some small talk. Noticing a picture of a Great Dane as the backdrop on Ms. Foster’s phone, she asked if it was a photo of her dog.
Ms. Foster smiled. “Yes. His name is Stormy,” she said.
“I have a dog too—a pit mix named Finny,” replied Kelsey.
With the ice broken, they began to talk more, and soon Ms. Foster mentioned that she had two sons, Andrew and Stu. Stu, the older, was nervous about starting high school. “I just hope I’m better by the end of the week so that I can be there when he comes home from his first day,” Ms. Foster admitted nervously.
“We’ll do all we can to help make that happen,” Kelsey assured her. By the time Ms. Foster was ready for radiology, she seemed to be in a better mood, and she thanked Kelsey for talking with her.
The next day, Dr. Baum, the attending physician for Kelsey’s internal medicine unit, approached Kelsey as she was prepping for rounds. “The x-ray of the 48-year-old woman with bronchitis showed some suspicious masses, so I sent the images to radiology for a second opinion, and they confirmed what I feared. There is a 5-centimeter mass in her right lung and two smaller masses in her left lung.” Kelsey’s heart dropped. She knew what this meant: late-stage lung cancer. “Of course, I will want to confirm with a CT scan and biopsy, but today we have the difficult task of informing Ms. Foster of what we suspect we have found and what the next steps are.”
Feeling five times heavier than she had that morning, Kelsey followed Dr. Baum into Ms. Foster’s room. There were fresh flowers on her nightstand with a note signed, “Your favorite boys.” Ms. Foster lit up at the sight of a familiar face, and Kelsey felt that her heart might burst.
Dr. Baum took a seat beside the bed, and Kelsey followed. After the preliminary greeting, Dr. Baum gently cleared her throat and began, “I saw some suspicious masses on your x-ray yesterday that could be cancerous.” She paused a while before continuing, “I’d like to order a CT scan so that we can learn more.”
Ms. Foster sat for a while in stunned silence and then began to cry. Tears ran down Kelsey’s face as well, and, overcome with sympathy, she reached for Ms. Foster’s hand and began to rub it gently with both of hers.
After answering Ms. Foster’s questions, Dr. Baum and Kelsey left the room. As they walked down the hall together, Dr. Baum turned to Kelsey. “Kelsey, it’s all right to feel sympathy for patients, but you crossed a line there. Crying can detract attention from the patient, and some patients do not like to be touched. It’s natural to want to help patients, but you need to learn to channel that energy into being a good practitioner and leave the more personal comforting to family and friends.” Then, more gently, she added, “It will get easier over time. As you see more and more, you won’t feel the emotions as much.”

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians prevent emotional exhaustion and professional burnout while managing the emotional trauma encountered during clinical care, and simultaneously maintain empathy and compassion for their patients?
keypoints: Physicians must acknowledge that emotions are an inseparable part of the profession and understand their own emotional response patterns to prevent emotional exhaustion and professional burnout.

Establishing effective channels to manage emotional fluctuations arising from clinical care, such as communicating with the healthcare team to confirm the emotional states of both patients and oneself, helps maintain empathy and compassion toward patients.

Regulating emotions through self-reflection, confiding in family or friends, and engaging in hobbies or leisure activities can prevent desensitization in the patient-physician relationship and sustain professional enthusiasm.

ethical_issues.question: When breaking bad news to patients, how can physicians express empathy while maintaining professional boundaries, in order to avoid the potential negative impact of excessive emotional disclosure on the patient?
keypoints: When delivering bad news to patients, physicians should be attentive to the patient’s emotional responses and demonstrate empathy through sincere verbal and nonverbal communication, while avoiding excessive displays of their own emotions.

Crying or exhibiting marked emotional fluctuations in front of patients may be interpreted by patients as a sign of medical hopelessness, unprofessionalism, or emotional instability, thereby increasing the patient’s psychological burden; such behaviors should be avoided.

Physicians can convey understanding and support for the patient’s emotions through non-intrusive gestures such as adjusting their seating position, maintaining an appropriate physical distance, or offering tissues, while respecting the patient’s comfort level with physical contact.

The desire to help should be translated into professional clinical care; emotional comfort should be provided in moderation and primarily by the patient’s family, with physicians maintaining professional boundaries to ensure that emotional support does not interfere with clinical judgment or the treatment process.

Physicians should acknowledge and manage their own emotions, recognizing that empathy and emotional responses are integral to the medical profession, and maintain emotional stability through self-regulation in order to respond to patients’ emotional needs in a more professional and effective manner.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians recognize and adapt to patients’ varying levels of receptiveness to emotional expression and physical touch during interactions, in order to ensure effective and professional communication?
keypoints: When delivering bad news, physicians should demonstrate empathy by keenly observing the patient’s emotional state and responses, recognizing their receptiveness to emotional expression and physical contact, in order to guide appropriate adjustments in communication strategies.

Physicians should flexibly adapt their communication style based on the patient’s personality, emotional state, and cultural background, choosing between a direct or more gentle approach to ensure effective information delivery and support the patient’s psychological resilience.
Physical contact should be strictly limited to what is clinically necessary, avoiding overly intimate gestures of comfort, in order to maintain the patient’s trust and uphold professional boundaries.

Physicians should convey care and understanding through sincere verbal expressions—such as offering tissues at appropriate moments or affirming the patient’s emotions—as alternatives to physical touch for providing support.

Physicians need to manage their own emotions professionally, avoiding loss of emotional control, and channel empathy into rational and steady supportive actions to ensure the professionalism and effectiveness of communication.

Physicians should continually accumulate experience to enhance their sensitivity to patients’ emotional cues and their ability to respond, gradually achieving a balance between emotional regulation and professional communication.

title: Risk Perception, Bias, and the Role of the Patient-Doctor Relationship in Decision Making about Cerebral Aneurysm Surgery
case:
Dr. Swan, a young neurosurgeon, felt a nearly palpable anxiety in the air as he entered the examination room to see Mrs. Jones.
Mrs. Jones had been diagnosed with an unruptured cerebral aneurysm and referred to Dr. Swan. Her primary care physician had ordered an MRI scan of her head to work up her recurrent headaches, which were, ultimately, diagnosed as tension headaches. However, her workup incidentally revealed a moderate-sized aneurysm of the right posterior communicating artery.
In her initial visit, Dr. Swan had counseled Mrs. Jones that her aneurysm carried a roughly 1 percent annual risk of rupture and that a rupture carried a roughly two-thirds chance of neurologic disability or death. After conferring with his partners in interventional neuroradiology, Dr. Swan and his team recommended craniotomy on the basis of the characteristics of her aneurysm. In response to Mrs. Jones’s questions about the danger of the surgery, he said, “If everything goes well, you could be out of the hospital three days after your craniotomy and the aneurysm will be gone. However, all surgeries have risk and this one is a complicated, delicate procedure. In my experience, you would have a roughly 15 percent risk of suffering a stroke or neurological deficit from surgery. The risk of wound infection, which could potentially result in a washout surgery, is about 5-8 percent. The surgery could also result in death, although this is rare, less than 1 percent of the time. Of course, every patient is different and no one has ever done a study on you, but this is what our experience tells us.” Momentarily overwhelmed, Mrs. Jones asked to postpone treatment and think it over.
Dr. Swan reassured Mrs. Jones that, although hers was not an emergency, delaying treatment would result in no benefit and would yet expose her to a continued risk of neurologic catastrophe.
Several weeks later, Mrs. Jones returned to Dr. Swan’s clinic for a followup visit. Dr. Swan scrutinized the new angiogram study he had ordered as part of her preoperative workup. To his concern, the aneurysm appeared to have subtly increased in size. Mrs. Jones, however, was not ready to provide consent for a craniotomy. She told Dr. Swan: “I have been thinking about all those risks you mentioned, like disability from stroke, and I wouldn’t want my children to see me like that. I’m a gambler. At my age, I might just take my chances with a tiny annual risk rather than the known risks of going under the knife.”
Dr. Swan was taken aback. Although he had recommended surgery, he was determined to respect his patient’s wishes. Mrs. Jones appeared to understand the details of her medical condition and the risks and benefits of Dr. Swan’s treatment recommendation. However, she decided not to pursue treatment because of her age and her own self-described “gambler” disposition in the face of personal risk.
Dr. Swan was reminded of a popular magazine article he had seen, describing the follies and errors of human risk perception in behavioral economics, especially those risks that are rare, unfamiliar, or emotionally clouded. He wondered how informed consent could be preserved amidst these confounding factors and biases.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Swan, a young neurosurgeon, could feel the tension in the room as he stepped in to meet Mrs. Jones. Mrs. Jones had recently been referred to him after her primary care physician ordered an MRI for recurrent headaches, which, after evaluation, turned out to be tension headaches. However, the imaging had incidentally uncovered a moderate-sized aneurysm on the right posterior communicating artery. 

During their first consultation, Dr. Swan explained to Mrs. Jones that her aneurysm carried about a 1 percent chance each year of rupturing, and that should a rupture occur, there was a two-thirds likelihood of either severe neurological disability or death. After discussing her case with his colleagues in interventional neuroradiology, Dr. Swan and his team recommended a craniotomy, citing the aneurysm’s characteristics. When Mrs. Jones inquired about the risks of surgery, Dr. Swan responded, “If everything goes well, you could be discharged three days after the craniotomy, with the aneurysm eliminated. However, like all surgeries, this one carries substantial risks. In my experience, there’s about a 15 percent risk of stroke or neurologic complication, and a 5 to 8 percent risk of wound infection, which could mean another surgery. The chance of death is rare—less than 1 percent. Of course, every patient is unique, and these numbers reflect our collective experience, not a study on you personally.” 

Overwhelmed by the complexity and weight of these risks, Mrs. Jones asked for time to consider her options. Dr. Swan reassured her that, while her situation was not emergent, delaying surgery would not reduce her risk and would leave her exposed to the ongoing threat of a catastrophic neurological event.

A few weeks later, Mrs. Jones returned for a follow-up appointment. Dr. Swan carefully reviewed her new angiogram, which showed a slight increase in the size of the aneurysm. Despite this finding, Mrs. Jones was still hesitant to consent to surgery. She told Dr. Swan, “I keep thinking about the risk of being left disabled from a stroke. I don’t want my children to see me that way. I’m something of a gambler. At my age, I might rather take my chances each year with a small risk than face the known risks of surgery.”

Dr. Swan was surprised by her response. Although he continued to believe that surgery was the best option, he was committed to honoring Mrs. Jones’s wishes. She demonstrated a clear understanding of her diagnosis and the potential outcomes of both surgery and observation, but ultimately decided against surgery, citing her age and her self-described gambler’s approach to risk.

Reflecting on this, Dr. Swan recalled an article he had read about how people often misjudge rare or emotionally charged risks—a phenomenon well-known in behavioral economics. He wondered how physicians could best ensure that consent is truly informed when patients’ perceptions of risk are shaped by such cognitive biases.

ethical_issues.question: How can genuine informed consent be ensured in the presence of cognitive biases?
keypoints: Informed consent must fully consider the impact of cognitive biases on rational judgment, recognizing that the expectation of completely autonomous and rational decision making may be unrealistic.

High-risk treatment decisions should be achieved through dynamic interaction between physician and patient, wherein patient preferences and professional recommendations are integrated equally to form an individualized treatment plan.

Physicians should disclose the geographic and individual biases inherent in their recommendations and employ both positive and negative framing, using visual aids such as bar charts, pie charts, or icon-based pictographs to present risk information objectively and intuitively, thereby assisting patients in understanding abstract medical risks.

Physicians must candidly express their concerns, respect patient autonomy, avoid coercion, and encourage patients to attend regular follow-up visits for ongoing discussion of treatment options and goals of care.

Ensuring the informed and autonomous nature of patient decision making is the ultimate goal, guaranteeing that patients make choices aligned with their own values based on a comprehensive understanding of risks and benefits.

ethical_issues.question: In the informed consent process, how can patient autonomy be preserved by ensuring that the patient fully understands the relevant risks, benefits, and alternative treatment options?
keypoints: Ensure that the patient fully comprehends the relevant risks, benefits, and alternative options of the treatment recommendation in order to uphold patient autonomy.

The informed consent process should address the impact of cognitive biases on the patient’s risk perception and decision making, going beyond mere information transmission to promote rational judgment.

A dynamic and interactive communication framework between physician and patient is necessary to facilitate shared decision making, ensuring that patient preferences and physician recommendations carry equal weight in the decision-making process.

Physicians should employ various communication strategies, including visual aids (such as bar charts, pie charts, and icon-based pictographs), balanced framing of risks and benefits, and transparent disclosure of potential biases in their recommendations, to help patients gain a more comprehensive understanding of abstract medical risks.

Physicians must respect the patient’s autonomous decisions, openly express their concerns regarding the patient’s refusal of treatment, recommend regular follow-up visits for ongoing discussion of treatment options, and avoid any form of coercion or undue pressure.

ethical_issues.question: In high-risk decision making, how can a dynamic interaction between the patient and physician be promoted to form a final treatment plan that ensures the patient’s decision is both informed and autonomous?
keypoints: The patient and physician should maintain a dynamic interaction to ensure that patient preferences and physician recommendations carry equal weight in the treatment decision-making process, thereby achieving a shared decision-making model.

Physicians should present risk information using a balanced framing approach that includes both positive and negative aspects, supplemented by visual aids such as bar charts, pie charts, or icon-based pictographs to assist patients in comprehending abstract and complex medical risks.

When faced with a patient’s initial refusal of treatment, physicians should candidly express their concerns, recommend a timely follow-up visit, and engage in ongoing communication and discussion through continued monitoring, avoiding treating the initial decision as final.

Physicians must respect the patient’s autonomous decision-making, refraining from exerting pressure or coercion, thereby ensuring that the patient’s choice is made in an informed and voluntary manner.

If the risk of non-intervention is higher, physicians should anticipate that regular follow-up and communication regarding changes in the patient’s condition may encourage the patient to reassess and potentially revise their treatment decision in the future.

title: Telepsychiatry as Part of a Comprehensive Care Plan
case:
Dr. Lincoln, a young psychiatrist with a successful telepsychiatry practice, received a call from Dr. Adams, a hospital psychiatrist who had referred a patient to him a few months earlier.
Dr. Adams explained that he had Dr. Lincoln in mind for a patient named Justin whom he had been seeing recently. Justin had served in the military and completed a tour of combat Afghanistan, where he sustained a severe injury to his leg that ended his military career. He had been suffering from posttraumatic stress disorder and severe depression since his return home. After several months’ unsuccessful struggle to find a job, Justin moved in with his parents and, frustrated with his physical condition, attempted suicide by drug overdose. Dr. Adams had been seeing Justin daily for four weeks and had started him on medication that appeared to be having some positive effect. Justin was ready to be discharged home to the care of his parents and thrice-weekly outpatient treatment, but, Dr. Adams explained, the hospital’s psychiatrists couldn’t take on additional outpatients at the moment, and Justin lived 200 miles from the nearest VA clinic.
Dr. Lincoln agreed to take Justin on. Their first telesession took place the following afternoon, and Justin kept all of his appointments for the first two weeks. But Dr. Lincoln noticed that, by the third week of their psychotherapy sessions, Justin seemed to be losing his enthusiasm. Justin also reported feeling that his medication was not helping him as much as it had initially done. Dr. Lincoln encouraged Justin to give the treatments a chance to fully exert their effects. In closing the session, he asked Justin—as he had in each of the prior sessions—if he had plans to hurt or kill himself. “No,” Justin mumbled, and then, at a fainter volume not picked up by the webcam, he added, “not today.”
Two days later, Dr. Lincoln logged on to his computer for his scheduled session with Justin. When the appointment time arrived, Justin’s username failed to show up on the screen. Later that afternoon, Dr. Lincoln was contacted by Justin’s parents, who informed him that Justin had committed suicide that morning.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Lincoln, a young psychiatrist who had established a successful telepsychiatry practice, was starting his day when he received a call from Dr. Adams, a hospital psychiatrist with whom he had previously exchanged referrals. Dr. Adams wanted to discuss one of his current patients, Justin, a young man who had recently completed military service. While deployed in Afghanistan, Justin had sustained a serious leg injury that brought his service to an abrupt end. Since returning home, Justin’s life had been marked by relentless depression and symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder. Despite months of searching, he had been unable to find work and eventually returned to live with his parents. The combination of his physical disability and psychological anguish became overwhelming, culminating in a suicide attempt through an overdose of medication.

For the past four weeks, Justin had been under Dr. Adams’s care in the hospital, where daily visits and a new medication regimen had brought some gradual improvement. Justin was now deemed ready for discharge, with a plan for him to move back in with his parents and participate in three outpatient therapy sessions each week. However, Dr. Adams explained that the hospital psychiatrists were unable to accept additional outpatients due to caseload constraints, and the closest VA clinic was more than 200 miles away from Justin’s home.

Dr. Lincoln agreed to assume responsibility for Justin’s continuing care via telepsychiatry. Aware of the importance of coordinated care, Dr. Lincoln reached out to Justin’s primary care physician to discuss the details of Justin’s recent hospitalization, his ongoing psychiatric needs, and the need for regular communication about his treatment and risk factors. Dr. Lincoln also asked the primary care physician about local mental health resources that might be available for Justin’s support, and recommended that, when possible, Justin attend his telepsychiatry sessions at his primary care clinic to encourage collaboration and offer in-person support as needed.

Their first virtual session took place the following afternoon. Over the next two weeks, Justin was prompt and engaged at every appointment. However, by the third week, Dr. Lincoln noticed a decline in Justin’s participation. Justin confided that his medications no longer seemed as effective as before. Dr. Lincoln encouraged him to stay the course, explaining that improvement sometimes required more time, and immediately updated Justin’s primary care physician, urging the care team to keep a close watch on Justin between virtual visits. As was his custom at the conclusion of each session, Dr. Lincoln asked Justin if he was having any thoughts of self-harm or suicide. “No,” Justin answered softly. Then, almost under his breath and barely caught by the webcam microphone, he added, “not today.”

Two days later, Dr. Lincoln logged on for their scheduled session, but Justin’s username never appeared. Later that day, Justin’s parents reached out to Dr. Lincoln to share the devastating news that Justin had died by suicide earlier that morning.

ethical_issues.question: Do telepsychiatrists have an ethical responsibility to ensure that patients receive a standard of care equivalent to that of in-person treatment?
keypoints: Telepsychiatrists must ensure that the standard of care delivered via telemedicine is equivalent to that of in-person treatment, thereby guaranteeing patients receive clinically equivalent services.

Telepsychiatrists should be thoroughly familiar with the local, in-person mental health resources available to the patient to facilitate timely referrals or coordination of additional support when clinically indicated.

Telepsychiatry practice should adhere to relevant professional guidelines, such as those established by the American Telemedicine Association (ATA), to standardize clinical conduct and safeguard patient rights.

ethical_issues.question: Should telepsychiatry professionals collaborate closely with patients’ primary care physicians to reduce the risk of suicide?
keypoints: Telepsychiatry should be conducted in close collaboration with the patient’s primary care physician to effectively reduce the risk of suicide.

Primary care physicians play a crucial role in identifying and intervening with patients at high risk of suicide, as a significant proportion of individuals who die by suicide have previously consulted primary care providers.
Primary care physicians are able to coordinate between remote mental health professionals and local healthcare resources, addressing patients’ physical health needs and reducing barriers to care.

Familiarity of primary care physicians with the specific services and resources available in the patient’s locality compensates for the telepsychiatrist’s limited knowledge of the local context, which is particularly important for enhancing patient safety.
It is recommended that patients attend videoconference appointments at their primary care clinics to facilitate effective collaboration between telepsychiatrists and primary care physicians.

title: The Tele-ICU
case:
Dr. Gray, a critical care specialist in a rural emergency room, was evaluating Mrs. Mason. The 80-year-old wife and grandmother, accompanied by her daughter Sarah, had been brought in by ambulance after body aches, fever, and persistent coughing of a day’s duration turned into extreme shortness of breath and shaking chills. She was febrile and had tachycardia, low blood pressure, and dangerously low oxygen saturation. A chest x-ray demonstrated a significant, severe pneumonia. In keeping with a desire previously expressed to her husband and children to “do everything,” she was intubated and transferred to the hospital’s four-bed intensive care unit where she received IV fluids and antibiotics. Her vital signs returned to normal on the higher level of support.
Dr. Gray began preparing to sign out for the evening at 7 o’clock. Mrs. Mason remained intubated but appeared clinically stable. Dr. Gray anticipated that she might have the breathing tube removed in the morning.
Overnight, the intensive care unit was staffed remotely by Dr. Reed, a teleintensivist—an off-site critical care specialist with real-time access to patient monitors, test results, and audiovisual information from several hospital ICUs. The rural hospital, unable to find a specialist physician to staff the intensive care units, had established the teleintensivist care model the previous year. When Sarah asked Dr. Gray who would be taking his place, he explained that all of the patients were closely watched by a remote physician on a monitor and that nurses—and additional physicians, although they were not directly involved in Mrs. Mason’s case—were available in the unit at all times in case a patient’s condition became unstable.
Sarah asked, “Couldn’t we arrange for her to go somewhere where there’s a doctor actually on duty in-person at night?”
Dr. Gray paused before replying. The nearest hospital was several hours away, arranging a transfer would take several hours and might be dangerous due to the distance and the severity of Mrs. Mason’s illness.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Gray, a critical care specialist in a rural emergency department, was assessing Mrs. Mason, an 80-year-old grandmother and wife, who had arrived by ambulance accompanied by her daughter, Sarah. Mrs. Mason’s symptoms—a day of body aches, fever, and relentless coughing—had escalated into severe shortness of breath and intense chills. On arrival, she was febrile, tachycardic, hypotensive, and her oxygen levels were critically low. A chest x-ray revealed a severe pneumonia. Respecting her previously stated wish to her husband and children to “do everything,” Dr. Gray proceeded with intubation and transferred her to the hospital’s small, four-bed intensive care unit, where intravenous fluids and antibiotics were promptly started. Thanks to aggressive treatment and the higher level of support, Mrs. Mason’s vital signs stabilized.

As the evening approached and his shift neared its end, Dr. Gray prepared to hand off care. It was now 7 p.m. Mrs. Mason remained intubated but was clinically stable, and Dr. Gray was hopeful she could be extubated the following morning.

Overnight, the ICU would be overseen not by an in-person physician, but by Dr. Reed, a teleintensivist. Dr. Reed, working remotely, had real-time access to patient monitors, laboratory data, and audiovisual feeds from several regional ICUs. The rural hospital, unable to recruit a full-time on-site critical care physician, had adopted the teleintensivist model the previous year. When Sarah asked Dr. Gray who would be responsible for her mother’s care during the night, he explained that Dr. Reed would be continuously monitoring all ICU patients remotely, and that nurses—as well as other physicians, though not directly caring for Mrs. Mason—would be physically present in the unit at all times to respond if her condition changed.

Concerned, Sarah asked, “Isn’t there a way to have her somewhere with a doctor actually present in person at night?”

Dr. Gray paused, understanding her worry. The nearest hospital with overnight, on-site critical care staff was several hours away. Arranging a transfer would require significant time and posed risks given both the distance and the severity of Mrs. Mason’s current illness.

ethical_issues.question: How can the impact of tele-ICUs on the patient-physician relationship be addressed, particularly in the critical care setting, to maintain trust among patients, their families, and the healthcare team?
keypoints: Maintaining trust among patients, their families, and the healthcare team is a fundamental responsibility of the intensivist and serves as the foundation for addressing the ethical challenges posed by telemedicine.

Telemedicine may risk reducing patients to mere “collections of data points,” thereby impeding compassionate care; this can be mitigated by direct audiovisual communication between the patient, the bedside care team, and remote clinicians via in-room monitoring screens to strengthen interpersonal interaction and empathy.

Patients or their surrogates should be specifically informed about the nature of telemedicine and its associated privacy risks, and their informed consent must be obtained to preserve the trust inherent in the patient-physician relationship.

Patients or their authorized representatives have the right to refuse remote monitoring or to request transfer to another facility after being fully informed of the available treatment options and their respective risks and benefits; this right should be afforded the same respect as any other refusal of medical treatment.
Telemedicine itself possesses no intrinsic ethical qualities; its ethical value depends on whether core medical principles are upheld in clinical practice and whether inadvertent harm is avoided.

title: A Request for “Conversion Therapy”
case:
Michael is visiting his pediatrician, Dr. Smith, with his parents. After Dr. Smith performs a well-child exam, Michael’s mother asks whether she and her husband can talk with Dr. Smith alone. They leave Michael in the exam room to dress and go into Dr. Smith’s office.
Michael’s mother, Mary, is concerned because Michael mentioned having a “crush” on his school friend Steven. Both boys are 12 years old and in the seventh grade. “We’re a religious family,” Mary explains, “and we want to do what’s right for Michael now and in the future. We want to save him from this sinful lifestyle before it’s too late, and we have heard there has been some success with the One Choice Conversion Therapy Camp. We are ready to make him work hard at this.”
Dr. Smith is also concerned. He, too, wants what’s best for Michael, but his knowledge of behavioral therapies that attempt to change sexual orientation does not accord with Mary’s. “I share your concern for Michael’s well-being and future. He’s a great kid. He’s healthy and seems to be happy, which is what parents hope and pray for. We don’t know much about his sexuality at the present, but if it is different than yours, we still want him to be able to choose the life that makes him healthiest and happiest. Do you agree?”
“Not if that means being homosexual,” Michael’s dad replies. “It’s a sin. It’s our job to protect him and keep him on the right path.”
Dr. Smith offers what he has read about conversion therapies. “They have been shown to be ineffective and even psychologically damaging. One of the originators of the method later renounced it. I can give you some literature on the therapy, if you’d like.”
“Well, we must do something to prevent Michael from being gay,” Mary interjects, as her husband nods, “and we were hoping that you, as Michael’s doctor, would help us.”
Dr. Smith’s suggestion that the family see a therapist who specializes in children’s developing sexuality is rebuffed by Michael’s parents. “We don’t need counseling,” they say. “We know what the right path is here.”
case_rewrite:
Michael arrives at Dr. Smith’s pediatric office for his routine checkup, accompanied by his parents, Mary and John. After completing Michael’s well-child examination, Dr. Smith is approached by Mary, who asks if she and her husband might speak with him privately. They leave Michael in the exam room to dress while the three adults step into Dr. Smith’s office.

Mary begins, her voice filled with concern. “Michael told me recently that he has a ‘crush’ on his friend Steven from school. They’re both twelve and in seventh grade. We’re a religious family, Dr. Smith, and we want to do what’s right for Michael—now and in the future. We want to save him from this sinful lifestyle before it’s too late. We’ve heard about the One Choice Conversion Therapy Camp and that there have been cases where it helped. We’re ready to see this through for Michael’s sake.”

Dr. Smith listens carefully, his own concern for Michael evident. He values Michael’s well-being and future and speaks gently. “I understand that you care deeply about Michael and want what’s best for him. He’s a wonderful boy—healthy and, from what I can see, happy. That’s every parent’s hope. Right now, we don’t know much about his sexuality, but no matter what, our goal should be for Michael to live a life that’s healthiest and happiest for him. Would you agree with that?”

John shakes his head. “That doesn’t include being homosexual, Dr. Smith. It’s a sin. As his parents, it’s our responsibility to protect him and keep him on the right path.”

Dr. Smith remains composed as he shares what he knows. “I want to be honest with you. Conversion therapies like the one you mentioned have been extensively studied and have been found not only to be ineffective, but also potentially harmful. In fact, some of the earliest supporters of these methods have since renounced them. I can provide you with some literature about what experts in the field have found, if you’re interested.”

Mary interrupts, her determination clear. “We have to do something to stop Michael from being gay,” she insists, with John nodding in agreement. “We were hoping you, as his doctor, would help us.”

Dr. Smith suggests thoughtfully, “It may be helpful for the family to speak with a therapist experienced in guiding children and families through questions about sexuality and development.”

But Michael’s parents reject the idea firmly. “We don’t need counseling,” John says. “We know what’s right for our son, and that’s what we intend to do.”

Dr. Smith recognizes the challenge before him, committed both to evidence-based care and to maintaining open lines of communication with Michael’s family during this important period in his patient’s development.

ethical_issues.question: Is Dr. Smith adhering to the principles of evidence-based medicine in responding to Michael’s parents’ request for conversion therapy?
keypoints: Dr. Smith adheres to the principles of evidence-based medicine and rejects the request for conversion therapy made by Michael’s parents. This stance is grounded in extensive evidence-based data and the unanimous condemnation of sexual orientation change efforts (SOCE) by leading medical organizations such as the Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine (SAHM), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American Psychiatric Association (APA), and the American Medical Association (AMA), which highlight that such therapies are not only ineffective but may also cause serious psychological harms including depression, anxiety, and self-destructive behaviors.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr. Smith, while respecting Michael’s parents’ religious beliefs, encourage them to support their son during the critical period of sexual identity development in accordance with medical ethics?
keypoints: Smith should maintain a careful balance between supporting Michael’s sexual identity development and avoiding actions that could intensify parent-child conflict, refraining from confrontational opposition that might alienate Michael’s parents.
Smith should affirm Michael’s trust in his parents and his willingness to share personal feelings, highlighting the importance of open family communication and a supportive environment.
Smith should emphasize the priority of Michael’s physical and mental health, underscoring the need for unconditional support from family and other significant individuals.

Smith may guide Michael’s parents toward evidence-based resources, such as inclusive religious organizations and parent support groups (e.g., PFLAG), to address their moral concerns and provide ongoing support.

Smith should arrange for follow-up visits to continue engaging with the family, respecting the parents’ beliefs while gradually encouraging acceptance and support for Michael during this critical stage of sexual identity development.

ethical_issues.question: What are Dr. Smith’s ethical obligations to his patient, Michael, when parental requests or decisions—such as seeking conversion therapy—may place the child at risk?
keypoints: Dr. Smith has an ethical obligation of nonmaleficence and must firmly oppose conversion therapy, which is ineffective and may cause psychological harm.
Dr. Smith should adhere to the principle of beneficence, safeguarding Michael’s best interests by supporting his healthy and happy development, beyond parental biases rooted in religious beliefs.

Dr. Smith should respect the family’s cultural and religious background, balancing support for Michael’s sexual development with effective communication with the family, and strive to facilitate collaboration among all parties to ensure Michael’s physical and mental well-being.

Dr. Smith should establish a trusting relationship with Michael through confidential interviews, assess his mental health risks (such as suicidal ideation and bullying), and proactively provide appropriate psychological support and LGBT youth resources.

Dr. Smith should maintain ongoing communication with the family, advocate for referral to a specialist in pediatric sexual development, and promote family understanding and cooperation to jointly safeguard Michael’s welfare.

title: Medicine's Authority to Advocate: Responsibilities and Limitations
case:
Dr. Molleur is a family doctor in a state that accepts federal funding for abstinence-only sex education in its public schools. She believes that abstinence-only sex education is harmful to adolescents and to society because it results in unplanned pregnancies, the spread of STDs, psychological harm to those who don’t conform to the norms of the curriculum, and reversal of decades of progress in the social status of women and gay people.
Dr. Molleur submits a resolution for consideration at her state medical society’s annual meeting entreating the society to adopt a position urging the state’s governor to reject federal funding for abstinence-only education programs and to replace them with comprehensive sex ed, which would include abstinence but also cover such topics as correct use of condoms. Her resolution discusses not only what she views as problems with the factual information in the abstinence-only curriculum (for example, the assertion that HIV can get through pores in condoms) but also her objections to the sexual mores promulgated in the abstinence-only curriculum (for example, that nonmarital, nonheterosexual sexual activity is likely to have harmful psychological and physical effects and that abstaining from sexual activity outside of marriage is the expected standard). “This,” her proposal concludes, “is misinformation, and, as highly educated professionals devoted to promoting the health and welfare of the public, we have a responsibility to combat the teaching of inaccurate and problematic beliefs.”
Getting a cup of coffee before the meeting begins, she runs into her friend Dr. Baxter in line and asks him, “Did you see the resolution I submitted?”
Dr. Baxter hesitates. Eventually he says, “I did see it. But I’m not sure I’m with you on this. Is it appropriate for a physician group to be making judgments about what constitutes healthy or normal—or moral—sexual behavior? Who are we to prescribe sexual norms for society?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Molleur, a family physician, practices in a state that receives federal funding specifically allocated for abstinence-only sex education in public schools. She holds strong convictions that abstinence-only education harms adolescents and society at large by leading to increased rates of unplanned pregnancies, the spread of sexually transmitted diseases, psychological distress among those who do not fit the curriculum’s prescribed norms, and a regression in the progress made toward equality for women and LGBTQ+ individuals.

Determined to address these issues, Dr. Molleur drafts a resolution to be considered at the upcoming annual meeting of her state medical society.
