In her proposal, she urges the society to adopt a stance encouraging the state’s governor to reject federal funding for abstinence-only programs and instead support comprehensive sex education—programs that would still address abstinence, but would also include essential topics like correct condom usage. Her resolution not only critiques the factual inaccuracies in the abstinence-only curriculum—such as the misleading assertion that HIV can pass through pores in condoms—but also raises concerns about the sexual norms the curriculum promotes, for example, that nonmarital or nonheterosexual sexual activity is likely to cause psychological or physical harm and that sexual abstinence outside of marriage should be the standard expectation. “This,” she concludes in her proposal, “constitutes misinformation, and as highly trained professionals committed to safeguarding the public’s health and well-being, we are obligated to challenge the teaching of inaccurate and problematic beliefs.”

Before the meeting begins, Dr. Molleur stops for a cup of coffee and encounters her colleague and friend, Dr. Baxter, waiting in the line ahead of her. She greets him and asks, “Did you happen to see the resolution I put forward?”

Dr. Baxter pauses before responding. After a moment, he says, “I did see it. But I’m not entirely sure I agree with you. Should a group of physicians be the ones deciding what counts as healthy, normal—or moral—sexual behavior? Are we really in a position to dictate sexual norms to society?”

ethical_issues.question: Do physicians have a duty to oppose scientifically inaccurate information presented in curricula in order to protect public health and welfare?
keypoints: By virtue of their professional training and clinical experience, physicians are equipped to identify and challenge improper and deceptive medical information, thereby promoting public health and welfare.

If physicians choose to remain silent or fail to refute scientifically erroneous information they are aware of, this may result in harm to public health and undermine society’s trust in the medical profession.

Physicians have an obligation to oppose scientifically inaccurate information promoted in curricula (such as the erroneous claim that HIV can penetrate condoms); this is not only a professional duty but also an ethical responsibility aimed at upholding scientific accuracy and protecting public health.

title: Interviewing a Patient about Intimate Partner Violence
case:
Melinda is visiting with Dr. Sherman, her internist, for a well-woman check-up. After the exam, Dr. Sherman asks Melinda whether she has any concerns about her health or well-being that she wants to discuss. Melinda nervously and hesitatingly says that her husband of many years has begun “demanding more and more of me,” as she puts it.
“How do you mean?” Dr. Sherman asks.
“He is a good father,” Melinda says first. Then she says, “But he is more and more aggressive in bed. He didn’t used to be like this. If I say I’m scared or that I don’t want to have sex, he doesn’t stop. He just keeps going. I don’t want to make him mad. I don’t want to ruin things between us.”
Dr. Sherman says, “I’m concerned for you, Melinda. No one should be frightened into having sex when she doesn’t want to. Do you feel unsafe? Do you think your husband might get abusive if you refused?”
Melinda withdraws at these questions and says dismissively, “Guess it’s just how men are. I’ll figure it out.”
case_rewrite:
Melinda arrives for her annual check-up with Dr. Sherman, her long-time internist. After the routine examination, Dr. Sherman sits down across from Melinda and gently asks, “Is there anything on your mind about your health or well-being that you’d like to talk about today?” 

Melinda shifts in her seat, her hands fidgeting in her lap. After a moment of hesitation, she says softly, “Lately, my husband has been… well, he’s been demanding more and more from me.” 

Dr. Sherman leans forward, keeping her tone open and nonjudgmental. “Can you tell me a bit more about what you mean?” 

Melinda glances down before responding. “He’s a good father, and he’s always provided for us. But recently, he’s become much more aggressive in bed. He never used to act this way. If I say I’m scared or that I don’t want to have sex, he doesn’t stop. He just keeps going. I don’t want to upset him. I’m afraid of making things worse between us.” 

Dr. Sherman listens carefully, using Melinda’s own words in her response. “I’m really concerned to hear that you’re feeling scared, Melinda. No one should be pressured or frightened into having sex when they don’t want to. Do you feel unsafe at home? Do you worry that your husband might become abusive if you tried to refuse?” 

As Dr. Sherman asks these questions, Melinda’s posture shifts—she crosses her arms and looks away. “I guess it’s just how men are,” she says quietly, her tone dismissive. “I’ll figure it out on my own.”

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians effectively take a patient’s history and establish a trusting relationship without judgment when addressing cases involving intimate partner violence?
keypoints: Physicians should obtain the patient history prior to the physical examination and before the patient disrobes, in order to identify concerns requiring attention and to be sensitive to the patient’s vulnerability, thereby laying the foundation for building trust in subsequent interactions.
Physicians should collect the history in a nonjudgmental manner, respecting the patient’s feelings and avoiding eliciting defensive or withdrawn responses.
Physicians should use the patient’s own language and expressions to demonstrate active listening and understanding, thereby enhancing the patient’s sense of safety and trust.

Physicians should proactively inquire about the patient’s desired form of assistance, fostering the patient’s active engagement and empowering her to be a central participant in the problem-solving process.
Physicians should offer multiple options for the patient to explore, avoiding a “savior” posture, and respecting the patient’s autonomy and individual pace.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ensure that, both in practice and ethically, they do not cause harm or discomfort to patients when discussing sexual concerns?
keypoints: Physicians should adopt a nonjudgmental attitude, use the patient’s own language and pace when taking the history, build a trusting relationship, and facilitate effective communication so that the patient feels respected and heard.
Physicians should discuss sexuality-related concerns prior to the patient disrobing and before the physical examination, in order to avoid causing discomfort or compromising the patient’s privacy.
Physicians should consciously reflect on their own biases, convey an open and inclusive attitude, and avoid making provocative or misleading statements based on personal beliefs or ignorance.
Physicians should explore the patient’s needs and goals, promote active patient participation, and empower the patient to be the primary agent in developing solutions.

title: Teen Pregnancy and Confidentiality
case:
Jennifer, 15, is a sophomore at Middlefield High School who has made an office appointment with Dr. Wilson, an ob-gyn, for the first time. During the new patient history, Dr. Wilson asks, “Are you sexually active now, or do you plan to be?”
Jennifer hesitates to answer. Instead, she tells Dr. Wilson that the visit will be charged to her parents’ insurance and asks whether what she says will be confidential.
Dr. Wilson replies, “Conversations that teens have with their physicians about matters of sexuality and drug use are kept confidential. We want you to be able to discuss things that are of concern to you and your health without fearing that we will ‘tell on you’ to you parents or anyone else.”
“Whew,” Jennifer says. She then tells Dr. Wilson that she recently entered a pact with her friends. Each girl promised the others she would get pregnant within the next year. “And I want you to be my doctor,” she concludes.
“My goodness, Jennifer. That is quite a serious pact. We must talk some more about this. We must think about how having a child will influence the rest of your life, and how profound and difficult the consequences of this decision can be, especially at your age. How many of your friends are in this pact?”
Jennifer responds, “Four of them. Our families will help us take care of the kids. We all know that. We just want to go through this together, before we separate and go to college or something.”
case_rewrite:
Jennifer, age 15, is a sophomore at Middlefield High School. She arrives alone for her first appointment with Dr. Wilson, an obstetrician-gynecologist. As Dr. Wilson begins taking her medical history, she asks Jennifer, “Are you currently sexually active, or do you anticipate becoming sexually active soon?”

Jennifer pauses before responding, her expression uncertain. She then asks Dr. Wilson if their conversation will be kept confidential, especially since the visit will be billed to her parents’ insurance.

Dr. Wilson reassures her, “The things teenagers discuss with their doctors—particularly about sexuality or substance use—are generally confidential. My goal is to make sure you feel safe sharing what’s on your mind, without worrying that I’ll report everything to your parents or anyone else.”

Jennifer exhales in relief. She then confides, “I recently made a pact with a group of my friends. Each of us promised that we’d get pregnant within the next year. And I’d like you to be my doctor through this.”

Dr. Wilson is taken aback. “That’s a very serious commitment, Jennifer. We need to talk more about this decision. Becoming a parent at your age can have far-reaching and difficult consequences, both for you and your child. Can you tell me how many friends are in this pact?”

Jennifer replies, “There are four of us. We’ve talked about it a lot, and we know our families will help us raise the babies. We just want to experience this together, before we all go off to college or whatever comes next.”

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances may a physician breach an adolescent’s confidentiality in order to protect the adolescent’s best interests?
keypoints: Physicians have an obligation to breach adolescent confidentiality when there is a legal duty to report, such as in cases of suspected child abuse.

When a patient poses a serious threat to themselves, for example, exhibiting suicidal ideation or significant psychiatric disturbance, physicians should breach confidentiality to ensure the patient’s safety.
If a patient poses a clear danger to others, such as expressing homicidal intent or tendencies to harm others, physicians are ethically required to breach confidentiality to mitigate risk.

For sexually active adolescents, clinicians must assess for immediate and serious threats—such as partner coercion or involvement in sex trafficking—and breach confidentiality when necessary to protect the patient.

An adolescent’s expression of a desire to become pregnant or disclosure of unprotected sexual activity does not, in itself, meet the threshold of harm that mandates breaching confidentiality; physicians should respect the adolescent’s emerging autonomy and provide appropriate health counseling.

Physicians should carefully weigh the benefits and harms of breaching confidentiality and exercise clinical judgment in determining when to involve parents or relevant authorities, with the goal of maximizing protection for both the patient and others.

ethical_issues.question: How can necessary medical support and counseling be provided to adolescents while respecting their autonomy?
keypoints: Providing confidential medical care to adolescents is a fundamental principle respecting their autonomy, particularly in the realm of reproductive health, and it facilitates the establishment of trust and promotes open communication.

Physicians should conduct a thorough sexual and reproductive history, employing techniques such as motivational interviewing to explore the social context of the patient’s pregnancy plans, including the specifics of any “pact,” in order to identify modifiable factors influencing her intentions.

Counseling should be provided to help the patient develop a more comprehensive understanding of the risks, benefits, and consequences associated with her pregnancy plans, thereby supporting informed and rational decision-making.

Physicians may recommend that the patient delay her pregnancy plans until a more appropriate time point (e.g., high school graduation or reaching legal adulthood) and offer long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) as supportive measures.

Patients should be encouraged to utilize diverse resources and consider disclosing their pregnancy intentions to parents or other trusted adults, or to engage with professional support such as counselors or social workers.

On the foundation of respecting confidentiality, a therapeutic alliance should be established to continuously monitor the patient’s physical and mental health as well as any changes in decision-making, providing necessary medical support and guidance.

title: The Challenge of Physician Civic Engagement: Promoting Health While Preserving Public Trust
case:
Dr. Molleur is a family doctor in a state that accepts federal funding for abstinence-only sex education in its public schools. She believes that abstinence-only sex education is harmful to adolescents and to society because it results in unplanned pregnancies, the spread of STDs, psychological harm to those who don’t conform to the norms of the curriculum, and reversal of decades of progress in the social status of women and gay people.
Dr. Molleur submits a resolution for consideration at her state medical society’s annual meeting entreating the society to adopt a position urging the state’s governor to reject federal funding for abstinence-only education programs and to replace them with comprehensive sex ed, which would include abstinence but also cover such topics as correct use of condoms. Her resolution discusses not only what she views as problems with the factual information in the abstinence-only curriculum (for example, the assertion that HIV can get through pores in condoms) but also her objections to the sexual mores promulgated in the abstinence-only curriculum (for example, that nonmarital, nonheterosexual sexual activity is likely to have harmful psychological and physical effects and that abstaining from sexual activity outside of marriage is the expected standard). “This,” her proposal concludes, “is misinformation, and, as highly educated professionals devoted to promoting the health and welfare of the public, we have a responsibility to combat the teaching of inaccurate and problematic beliefs.”
Getting a cup of coffee before the meeting begins, she runs into her friend Dr. Baxter in line and asks him, “Did you see the resolution I submitted?”
Dr. Baxter hesitates. Eventually he says, “I did see it. But I’m not sure I’m with you on this. Is it appropriate for a physician group to be making judgments about what constitutes healthy or normal—or moral—sexual behavior? Who are we to prescribe sexual norms for society?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Molleur practices family medicine in a state where public schools receive federal funding for abstinence-only sex education. She is firmly convinced that abstinence-only programs are detrimental to adolescents and society at large, citing increased rates of unplanned pregnancies, the spread of sexually transmitted diseases, psychological harm to students who do not fit the program’s norms, and a reversal of longstanding advances in the social standing of women and LGBTQ individuals.

Motivated by these concerns, Dr. Molleur drafts a resolution for the state medical society’s upcoming annual meeting. Her proposal urges the society to take an official stance, calling on the governor to decline federal funding for abstinence-only programs and instead implement comprehensive sex education—including abstinence, but also information on condom use and other aspects of sexual health. In her resolution, Dr. Molleur highlights her objections to the abstinence-only curriculum’s factual inaccuracies, such as the claim that HIV can pass through condom pores, as well as her concerns about the values the curriculum promotes, including the idea that nonmarital or nonheterosexual sexual activity results in negative psychological and physical outcomes, and that abstinence outside of marriage should be the universal standard. She concludes, “This is misinformation, and as highly trained professionals committed to safeguarding the health and welfare of the public, we are obligated to challenge the propagation of inaccurate and problematic beliefs.”

Before the meeting, while waiting in line for coffee, Dr. Molleur greets her friend Dr. Baxter and asks, “Did you see the resolution I submitted?”

Dr. Baxter pauses before responding. Finally, he says, “Yes, I did. But I have some reservations. Is it really the place of a physician group to decide what is healthy or normal—or even moral—sexual behavior? What gives us the authority to set sexual norms for society?”

ethical_issues.question: Do physician groups have the authority to determine what constitutes healthy, normal, or moral sexual behavior?
keypoints: Physician groups may exceed their professional responsibilities by engaging in complex and pluralistic social moral issues when making judgments about the healthiness, normality, or morality of sexual behavior.

Sex education pertains not only to public health but is also deeply influenced by sociocultural and moral divergences, making it difficult for a single professional group to comprehensively define and decide upon.

Supporting or formulating sex education policies requires a multidimensional consideration of health, economic, cultural, and moral factors, relying on a broad democratic societal decision-making process.

Physician groups should focus on providing scientifically evidence-based health information and objectively elucidate the health implications of policy choices, while avoiding direct advocacy for policies that embody specific moral positions.

Circumventing broad societal dialogue by invoking medical professional authority risks provoking social polarization and political backlash, thereby undermining the medical profession’s public credibility and the effectiveness of future public health education efforts.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance their duty of stewardship of medical knowledge with the neutral presentation of public health information when engaging in the formulation of public health policy?
keypoints: Physicians should ensure the integrity of medical knowledge, candidly acknowledge its limitations, and proactively disseminate it when appropriate to preserve its public value.

The medical community should focus on providing objective and comprehensive information about the consequences of policies to the public and public officials, thereby facilitating fact-based democratic decision-making.

When engaging in discussions on public health policy, physicians should avoid directly advocating for specific restrictive policies based on professional authority, respecting societal pluralism and public dialogue.
Physician groups should educate legislators and the public about the factual inaccuracies and informational gaps in current policies that may negatively impact public health.
Legislative bodies have the authority to consider the medical information conveyed by physicians, weigh health issues against other social concerns, and ultimately determine public policy.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians avoid coercion or manipulation when advocating for healthy choices while respecting the autonomy of patients and the public?
keypoints: Physicians should engage in forthright, scientifically informed conversations that respect patients’ values and goals when advocating for healthy choices, avoiding coercion or manipulation, and fully honoring patient autonomy.
Physicians have a duty to provide complete and accurate information to support patient autonomous decision-making and to uphold their therapeutic responsibilities regardless of the patient’s choices.

The medical community’s role in public policy discussions should focus on delivering objective, scientific information about the health consequences of policies to facilitate democratic decision-making, while refraining from advocating for specific or proscriptive policies in order to respect the plurality of societal dialogue.

title: Sex Selection for Family Balancing
case:
Dr. Shah is the medical director of a busy fertility practice. In the middle of office hours, she sees a couple scheduled for an in vitro fertilization (IVF) consultation. The Warrens are longstanding patients who have already had three boys via IVF. They had trouble conceiving naturally due to Mrs. Warren’s blocked Fallopian tubes, presumably related to extensive scarring due to complications from a childhood appendectomy. Dr. Shah is surprised to see this couple again because, at the time of the last pregnancy, they had mentioned that finances would preclude them from having a fourth child. Now they tell her that, having reconsidered all the options since their youngest son was born, they have concluded that, despite the financial struggles IVF entails, they would like to have a daughter. If they can select only female embryos for transfer, they tell her, they would go through it again.
Dr. Shah is unsure what to think of this request. Having another child will require IVF, but she cautions them that there is extra cost and risk associated with the embryo manipulation required to determine sex. Additionally, there is always the possibility that all the embryos in the cycle will be male. The couple states that, in that case, they would not have any of the male embryos transferred, since they do not want another son. They say that they are willing to undertake the cost and invasive procedures even with the knowledge that they might not get any healthy female embryos. Dr. Shah tells them that she will have to discuss this request with the rest of the practice, including the embryologists, to see if all parties involved are comfortable with proceeding.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Shah, the medical director of a bustling fertility clinic, is midway through a packed clinic day when she greets the Warrens, a couple she has known for years. The Warrens have already welcomed three sons into their family, each conceived through IVF under Dr. Shah’s care, due to Mrs. Warren’s blocked Fallopian tubes—a complication likely stemming from significant scarring after a childhood appendectomy. Dr. Shah recalls their last visit, when the Warrens had spoken candidly about the financial challenges of pursuing another round of IVF, stating that a fourth child was out of reach for them.

Now, seated across from her in the consultation room, the Warrens explain that their feelings have shifted since their youngest son’s birth. Despite lingering financial worries, they have reconsidered their priorities and are resolved to try for a daughter. Their request is explicit: they would only attempt another IVF cycle if Dr. Shah’s team can select exclusively female embryos for transfer.

Dr. Shah listens carefully, weighing the implications. She explains to the Warrens that identifying the sex of embryos involves additional procedures—preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD)—which adds both cost and medical risk. She reminds them there is no guarantee; all viable embryos in a cycle could be male. The Warrens are undeterred. If only male embryos are available, they state, they would not transfer any, as they do not wish to have another son. They fully accept the financial burden and physical demands, even with the understanding that they might not achieve a pregnancy if no healthy female embryos are found.

Unsettled by the ethical complexity of the request, Dr. Shah tells the Warrens that she must consult with the clinic’s team, including embryologists, to ensure that everyone is comfortable with proceeding. She also notes that cases like theirs are often reviewed by the clinic’s ethics committee before a final decision is made. Dr. Shah promises to discuss their request in detail with her colleagues and inform the Warrens once an agreement has been reached.

ethical_issues.question: Do physicians or professional societies have the authority to restrict the use of technology, particularly in cases of nonmedical sex selection?
keypoints: Physicians or professional societies have the authority to restrict the use of assisted reproductive technologies, particularly in cases of nonmedical sex selection, in order to uphold ethical standards and societal values.

The slippery slope argument is frequently cited against nonmedical sex selection, expressing concern that once the threshold for applying the technology is crossed, it may lead to selection of other non–health-related embryonic traits, thereby posing ethical risks.

The American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) Ethics Committee explicitly does not encourage the use of preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) for nonmedical sex selection, even for couples with existing IVF indications; furthermore, it opposes initiating IVF/PGD solely for sex selection in patients without medical indications.

Many academic institutions and fertility clinics routinely submit ethically challenging cases such as nonmedical sex selection to medical school ethics committees for review, serving as an important reference and safeguard in clinical decision-making.

There are international regulatory differences regarding nonmedical sex selection; some European countries explicitly prohibit the use of PGD for elective sex selection, whereas the United States currently lacks unified regulation or indication restrictions for PGD.

ethical_issues.question: Should preconception sex selection for family balancing be permitted, and under what conditions might such selection be implemented?
keypoints: Preconception sex selection for family balancing may be conducted within a framework of data collection and ethical review, provided that the family already has at least one or more children of the non-requested sex.
Additional requests for sex selection after PGD/PGS may be permitted when embryos of both sexes are available and the choice between them is not fully determined by medical criteria.

The American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) Ethics Committee does not encourage the use of PGD for nonmedical sex selection and particularly opposes initiating IVF/PGD solely for sex selection in fertile individuals, reflecting the ethical controversy of this issue and the divergence among authoritative bodies.
All requests for nonmedical sex selection should be submitted to the medical school’s ethics committee for review to ensure ethical compliance and balance of multiple interests.

ethical_issues.question: Should non-medical sex selection be permitted, particularly in cases where there is no medical indication for IVF?
keypoints: Non-medical sex selection carries a slippery slope risk, potentially leading to the extension of technology from sex selection to screening for other non-health-related embryonic traits, thereby presenting ethical challenges.

Requests for sex selection without a medical indication for IVF may utilize limited healthcare resources, and, as such procedures are not covered by insurance, may raise concerns regarding social equity and resource allocation.

The Ethics Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine does not encourage the use of PGD for non-medical sex selection, and is particularly opposed to initiating IVF/PGD solely for sex selection in fertile individuals; however, the committee has not reached a consensus on this issue.

The European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology recommends that preconception sex selection for family balancing may be permitted under strict conditions and for data collection purposes, with requirements such as the family already having one or more children of the non-desired sex.

title: The Professional Responsibility Model and Patient Requests for Nonindicated Early Delivery
case:
Jane, at 37 weeks and 3 days gestation in her second pregnancy, is meeting with her obstetrician, Dr. Stevens, for a routine prenatal visit. As the visit is wrapping up, Jane mentions that, due to her work schedule, a week from now would be the best time for her to deliver, and she requests a labor induction during that week. Seeing the curiosity on Dr. Stevens’ face, she says plaintively, “The baby is already full-term, right? Waiting longer is only going to make it harder for me to keep up with my job!”
Dr. Stevens agrees. “Yup, 37 weeks and beyond is considered full-term. You had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery last time, let’s do it. We’ll call once we get you on the schedule.” At the end of office hours, he sits down to submit the scheduling request, but when he logs into his email, he sees a reminder email from the head of the quality improvement (QI) committee of the OB/GYN department at his hospital. The message reiterates the hospital’s adoption of a policy that will bring the department in line with the recommendation by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) against elective deliveries prior to 39 weeks.
Dr. Stevens realizes that scheduling this induction may become an uphill battle. In his low-risk practice at a community hospital, he has been offering labor induction for low-risk patients for nearly 30 years, and, when the QI committee first approached him about this initiative, he went so far as to complete a retrospective audit confirming that his outcomes have been comparable to those of other obstetricians working at that hospital. He feels strongly that the mother’s request should be honored, and wonders what will be the best way to achieve this.
case_rewrite:
Jane, now 37 weeks and 3 days into her second pregnancy, sits across from her obstetrician, Dr. Stevens, during a routine prenatal checkup. As their conversation winds down, Jane hesitates, then remarks, “Next week would really be the best time for me to have the baby, with my work schedule and everything. Is there any way we could plan to induce labor then?” She glances at Dr. Stevens, her voice tinged with hope. “The baby’s full-term now, isn’t it? If we wait any longer, it’ll just be harder for me to manage things at work.”

Dr. Stevens nods reassuringly. “Yes, 37 weeks is considered full-term. Your last delivery was straightforward, so I don’t see a problem. Let’s get you on the schedule for an induction next week—I’ll have someone call you with the details.” 

Later that evening, as he prepares to send the induction request, Dr. Stevens opens his email and notices a message from the head of the hospital’s OB/GYN quality improvement (QI) committee. The email reminds staff of the hospital’s updated policy, aligning with the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommendation against elective deliveries before 39 weeks.

Dr. Stevens pauses, realizing the induction he just agreed to may not be easily approved. For almost thirty years at this community hospital, he has offered elective inductions to low-risk patients and, when the QI committee recently raised concerns, he even completed a retrospective review that showed his outcomes were on par with his colleagues. He feels strongly that honoring Jane’s wishes is important, but now wonders how best to proceed in light of the hospital’s policy and professional guidelines.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where a patient requests a nonindicated early delivery, should the physician comply with the patient’s request despite the recommendations of evidence-based clinical guidelines?
keypoints: Physicians should not comply with patient requests for nonindicated early delivery, as elective induction prior to 39 weeks is not medically reasonable and increases the risk of iatrogenic neonatal prematurity and unnecessary cesarean delivery.

Physicians should adhere to evidence-based clinical guidelines (such as the ACOG guideline) and hospital policies based on these guidelines, appropriately limiting patient requests for treatments that are not medically reasonable.

When patients request forms of clinical management that are not medically reasonable, the obstetrician should patiently explain why such options are not considered reasonable alternatives, thereby enhancing respect for and understanding of the pregnant woman’s autonomy.

title: Informing Patients about Declining Fertility
case:
Niki, a 37-year-old single woman, has been seeing her gynecologist, Dr. Goldstein, for the past 15 years. A busy attorney trying to make partner at a high-powered firm, Niki has focused on her career during that time. She wants to marry and have a family, but is surrounded by women who have waited until their late 30s and early 40s to have children and envisions doing the same. From what Niki sees around her, this timeframe has become the norm for professional women. When she calls to schedule her annual visit, the receptionist tells her that Dr. Goldstein is on an extended leave, but that one of her partners, Dr. Chang, can see Niki instead.
Everything proceeds as usual during the visit. When Dr. Chang asks whether Niki plans on having children, she says that she plans on having at least one child. Dr. Chang explains briefly that a woman’s fertility naturally begins declining in the mid-30s, and she offers Niki a serum anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) test to evaluate her ovarian reserve [1]. She suggests that Niki might find this information useful in deciding how to balance her career and reproductive future. As a lifelong planner, Niki agrees to the test and thanks Dr. Chang for telling her about it. As she is leaving, Dr. Chang tells her that Dr. Goldstein is reviewing her patients’ test results remotely and will be the one to call her with them.
A week later, Dr. Chang is just coming out of another patient visit when her assistant tells her that Dr. Goldstein is on the phone, waiting to speak to her about “a very urgent issue.” When she picks up the call, Dr. Goldstein says in a very agitated manner, “Why would you check AMH levels on Niki? They came back nearly undetectable. What am I supposed to tell her? She doesn’t even have a partner! She’s going to freak out, and all of this could have been prevented!”
Dr. Chang replies that she provides fertility counseling and AMH testing to all her patients because she believes patients deserve access to this information. Dr. Goldstein counters that this approach creates unnecessary fear among career women who should not face additional pressure from their physicians to think about children when they can use reproductive technologies to achieve pregnancy on their own timeline.
case_rewrite:
Niki, a 37-year-old single woman, has been a patient of her gynecologist, Dr. Goldstein, for the past 15 years. As a dedicated attorney striving to make partner at a prominent law firm, Niki has spent much of her adult life focused on advancing her career. She hopes to marry and have children in the future, and she’s surrounded by colleagues and friends who have postponed motherhood until their late 30s or early 40s. Observing this trend, Niki has come to view it as typical among professional women and expects to follow a similar path herself. 

When Niki calls to arrange her annual exam, the receptionist explains that Dr. Goldstein is on an extended leave but offers her an appointment with Dr. Chang, one of Dr. Goldstein’s partners. Niki agrees.

During the appointment, everything seems routine. Dr. Chang inquires about Niki’s plans regarding children, and Niki shares that she intends to have at least one child. Dr. Chang takes the opportunity to explain that female fertility naturally declines in the mid-30s and discusses the option of checking Niki’s ovarian reserve with a serum anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) test. She mentions that having this information could help Niki as she considers how to navigate her career and reproductive goals. As someone who values planning, Niki agrees to the test and thanks Dr. Chang for raising the topic. Before Niki leaves, Dr. Chang informs her that Dr. Goldstein will be reviewing patient test results remotely and will contact her with the results.

A week later, Dr. Chang has just finished seeing another patient when her assistant informs her that Dr. Goldstein is on the line with an urgent matter. Picking up the call, Dr. Chang hears Dr. Goldstein’s anxious voice: “Why did you order an AMH test for Niki? The results are almost undetectable. What am I supposed to tell her? She isn’t even in a relationship—she’s going to be devastated, and all of this could have been avoided!”

Dr. Chang calmly explains that she routinely offers fertility counseling and AMH testing to patients because she believes they are entitled to this information. Dr. Goldstein, however, argues that such testing can cause unnecessary alarm for career-driven women, who shouldn’t feel pressured by their doctors to rush family planning when reproductive technologies are available to help them conceive later if needed.

ethical_issues.question: Do physicians have a duty to inform patients about declining fertility, even if doing so may cause the patient anxiety or distress?
keypoints: Physicians have a responsibility to provide patients who express a desire for fertility with professional information regarding their reproductive capacity, thereby respecting and safeguarding the patient’s reproductive autonomy.

Concealing or avoiding disclosure of declining fertility may undermine the patient’s right to informed consent and decision-making ability; physicians should support patients in making informed choices aligned with their values and life plans through comprehensive and objective information.

The patient is the ultimate decision-maker in her life planning; physicians should avoid substituting their own value judgments for the patient’s preferences, instead offering scientific evidence and reasonable guidance to assist the patient in weighing benefits and risks within the context of her life framework to make the optimal decision.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where a patient expresses a desire to have children, should physicians proactively recommend fertility assessment tests, such as anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) testing?
keypoints: Physicians should proactively recommend fertility assessment testing based on the patient’s clearly expressed reproductive intentions, in order to support informed decision-making that aligns with the patient’s personal goals.

Providing patients with information related to fertility assessment constitutes an important respect for their reproductive autonomy and assists patients in reasonably balancing career development with family planning.

Physicians must thoroughly explain the principles, accuracy, and limitations of the testing, helping patients understand potential results and their implications, guiding them to consider possible responses, and ensuring that patients autonomously decide whether to undergo testing.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians balance respecting patient autonomy with avoiding excessive paternalism when providing fertility-related information?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize respecting patient autonomy and avoid withholding information or manipulating patient decisions under the pretext of acting in the patient’s “best interests,” thereby preventing excessive paternalism.

Physicians ought to serve as consultants who assist patients in making reasoned reproductive health decisions based on comprehensive and relevant information within the framework of the patient’s individual life goals and values.

Physicians must thoroughly explain the principles, accuracy, and potential outcomes of testing to help patients anticipate and manage different scenarios, ensuring that patients achieve truly informed autonomous decision-making grounded in professional knowledge.

Fully informing patients about declining fertility and related reproductive options reflects respect for the individual and supports patients in making optimal choices aligned with their personal life plans.

title: Advocate as a Doctor or Advocate as a Citizen?
case:
Dr. Gonzales, an orthopedic surgeon, enjoys mentoring medical students who are contemplating a career in his specialty. He is also involved in trying to get more students from minority backgrounds interested in becoming physicians and is frequently invited to speak at the local high school near the academic center where he is on staff.
On a recent “Doctors Back to School” event at Riverside High, Dr. Gonzales learned from several teachers that the school board was contemplating closing the school at the end of the academic year because of poor student performance on statewide tests.
“I can’t believe the school board thinks closing down this school is a good thing for our students,” said Mrs. Winters, a science teacher. “You’ve been coming here for several years now, Dr. Gonzales. You know how challenging it’s been for us to build a safe learning environment for these kids. We’re just starting to turn the corner, and we may have the rug pulled out from under us. Look—many of us think of you as one of us. There’s going to be a school board meeting in a few weeks, and many of the teachers are planning to attend. Given your position as a respected physician in this community, I think it would be extremely helpful if you came to this meeting and spoke on our behalf.” Dr. Gonzales gave a slight nod, but said nothing, not quite sure how to respond to Mrs. Winters’s invitation.
By the time Dr. Gonzales was telling his wife about the invitation that evening, he had come pretty close to a decision. “At first, I wasn’t sure if I should attend this school board meeting,” he said. “But the more I think about what those teachers are doing… Many of the students come from families whose primary language is Spanish, and it’s important that many of the teachers there are bilingual. Those state test grades can’t be the most important part of school, and it can’t be good for these kids to be bused to another school and a neighborhood that is unfamiliar to them.”
His wife was concerned. “Honey,” she said, “You should think twice about attending this meeting. I know that you have a positive impression of the school, but you’re not an education expert.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Gonzales, an orthopedic surgeon, takes great satisfaction in mentoring medical students who are considering a future in his field. He is also deeply committed to encouraging students from minority backgrounds to pursue careers in medicine and is regularly invited to speak at the local high school near the academic hospital where he works.

During a recent “Doctors Back to School” event at Riverside High, Dr. Gonzales was approached by several teachers who shared troubling news: the school board was considering shutting down the school at the end of the year due to low statewide test scores.

“I can’t believe the school board thinks closing down this school is a good thing for our students,” Mrs. Winters, a science teacher, confided in him. “You’ve spent years coming here, Dr. Gonzales. You know firsthand how hard we’ve worked to create a safe and supportive environment for these students. We’re finally starting to make real progress, and now it feels like everything could be taken away. Honestly, a lot of us see you as part of our community. There’s a school board meeting coming up in a few weeks, and many teachers are planning to speak out. Given your standing as a respected physician here, it would mean a lot if you could attend and share your perspective on our behalf.” Dr. Gonzales nodded slightly, unsure how to respond to Mrs. Winters’s request.

That evening, as Dr. Gonzales recounted the conversation to his wife, he felt himself leaning toward a decision. “At first, I wasn’t sure if I should go to the school board meeting,” he admitted. “But the more I think about the situation… So many of these students come from families where Spanish is the main language, and it really matters that the teachers at Riverside are bilingual. I just can’t see how test scores alone should determine a school’s fate. And I worry about what it would mean for these kids to be sent to a different, unfamiliar neighborhood.”

His wife listened with concern. “I understand how strongly you feel,” she said gently. “But maybe you should think carefully before attending. You know the school in a positive light, but remember—you’re not an expert in education.”

ethical_issues.question: When physicians engage in public advocacy, is the issue directly relevant to their medical training and experience?
keypoints: When physicians engage in public advocacy, they should first assess whether the issue is highly relevant to their medical training and the direct experience accumulated in their professional practice.

In evaluating the medical relevance of an issue, physicians should consider specific dimensions, including the direct practical experience gained through sustained professional interactions within the affected community or specific populations. When such experience serves as the basis for advocacy, statements should be strictly limited to objective descriptions of these experiences and their potential impact on health.

If the issue is unrelated to the physician’s medical expertise or relevant direct experience, the physician should speak as an ordinary citizen and avoid leveraging medical credentials to endorse personal positions.

If the issue does pertain to the physician’s area of medical expertise or relevant direct experience, the physician has a responsibility to provide professional information or fact-based observations with deliberation, honesty, and rigor.

In all circumstances, physicians should strictly limit their public advocacy statements to their professional authority, verified facts, and relevant experience, avoiding commentary beyond their scope of expertise or the use of professional prestige to advance non-expert opinions.

title: Medical Students and Rights Campaigns
case:
Bill, a third-year medical student, had just started his internal medicine clerkship rotation. Seriously considering a career in primary care medicine, Bill was eager to be exposed to as many clinical scenarios as possible during this two-month rotation.
The first patient he was assigned to care for was Mr. Wolfe, who came to the emergency room with shortness of breath and was subsequently admitted for congestive heart failure (CHF). Mr. Wolfe responded well to medical treatment, and Bill was able to learn firsthand how to care for CHF patients. Because Mr. Wolfe was 68 and this was his second hospitalization in the last 9 months for CHF exacerbation, the resident physician in charge wanted Bill to make sure that Mr. Wolfe understood the importance of taking his medications and limiting his sodium intake. As a result of their many conversations, Bill developed a good rapport with Mr. Wolfe.
On the day that Mr. Wolfe was being discharged, Bill visited to see if he had any questions and to wish him well. Mr. Wolfe thanked Bill for his attention and care and before parting ways said, “I’ve been meaning to ask you about that button you’ve been wearing.”
Bill explained, “It’s a Human Rights Campaign pin. The HRC works to ensure that gay and lesbian Americans have equal basic rights, including the right to marriage.”
Mr. Wolfe paused before muttering “Uh, OK. Thanks for stopping by.”
Later that day, Bill told his classmate Anna about his conversation with Mr. Wolfe, saying, “It was so disappointing. I really like Mr. Wolfe and felt like we had a great relationship. Then he asked about my pin and acted weird when I said what it was.” Bill added that he thought HRC’s mission was an important one for doctors to support because social stigmatization of gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people could have detrimental health effects.
Anna said, “But if it makes some patients uncomfortable, maybe it’s better if you just stop wearing the pin at work.”
case_rewrite:
Bill, a third-year medical student, had just begun his internal medicine clerkship rotation. With a strong interest in primary care, Bill was eager to gain exposure to as many clinical scenarios as possible during his two-month rotation. 

His first assigned patient was Mr. Wolfe, a 68-year-old man who arrived in the emergency department with shortness of breath and was subsequently admitted for congestive heart failure (CHF). Mr. Wolfe responded well to medical management, and Bill took the opportunity to learn firsthand about the care of patients with CHF. Noting that this was Mr. Wolfe’s second hospitalization in nine months for CHF exacerbation, the resident supervising Bill asked him to ensure that Mr. Wolfe understood the importance of adhering to his medications and following a low-sodium diet. Through their repeated conversations, Bill developed a strong rapport with Mr. Wolfe.

On the day of Mr. Wolfe’s discharge, Bill stopped by his room to see if he had any remaining questions and to wish him well. Mr. Wolfe thanked Bill for his care and, before they parted, said, “I’ve been meaning to ask you about that pin you’re wearing.”

Bill replied, “It’s a Human Rights Campaign pin. The HRC is an organization that advocates for equal rights for gay and lesbian Americans, including the right to marry.”

Mr. Wolfe paused, then muttered, “Uh, OK. Thanks for stopping by.” The atmosphere shifted, and Bill sensed a change in Mr. Wolfe’s demeanor.

Later that day, Bill recounted the conversation to his classmate Anna. “It was disappointing,” he said. “I really liked Mr. Wolfe and felt we had built a great relationship. But when he asked about my pin and I explained what it was, he acted differently.”

Bill added that he believed supporting the HRC’s mission was important for physicians, since the social stigmatization of gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people can have serious negative health consequences. He felt that advocating for equal rights was part of improving health equity.

Anna responded, “But if it makes some patients uncomfortable, maybe it’s better if you just don’t wear the pin at work.”

ethical_issues.question: Should medical students wear badges expressing personal viewpoints in the clinical setting, especially when these badges pertain to controversial political issues?
keypoints: The core ethical conflict in this case lies in balancing the responsibilities of medical students and physicians as individuals providing patient care with their duties as members of a professional community to advocate for public health.

It is important for medical students and physicians to support human rights campaigns because social stigmatization of gay, bisexual, and transgender individuals adversely affects their health; advocating for equal rights contributes to improving health equity.

Wearing badges that express personal viewpoints in the clinical setting may cause discomfort or misunderstanding among some patients, potentially undermining the physician-patient relationship and treatment outcomes; therefore, refraining from wearing such badges at work may be more appropriate.

It is reasonable and necessary for healthcare institutions and medical schools to implement strict policies prohibiting the expression of personal political views on white coats or within clinical environments to avoid potential misunderstandings and harm.

Medical schools and teaching hospitals should cultivate medical students’ capacity for health advocacy through institutional frameworks and education—for example, by permitting coordinated public information campaigns initiated by accredited student organizations or professional societies, subject to policy review and institutional approval, to ensure that such expressions align with institutional values and are appropriately presented.

The medical profession must utilize its expertise and influence to promote public policies that benefit societal health; abandoning advocacy efforts that advance the health and well-being of the public would undermine its professional status and social responsibility.

title: A Call to Service: Social Justice Is a Public Health Issue
case:
Dr. Gregory has been in family practice in Allentown, Pennsylvania, for more than 30 years, during which time he has cared for three generations of local residents and earned a place as a respected leader in the community.
Over the past couple of years, Dr. Gregory has grown increasingly concerned about the impact that human activity through the burning of fossil fuels has had on the climate and environment and, in turn, on the health of the public. After reading in the peer-reviewed literature and studying the science behind global climate change, Dr. Gregory decided to pen a letter to the local newspaper advocating for policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions, including the installation of carbon-capture technologies in coal-fired power plants.
Mr. Peterson, a longtime patient of Dr. Gregory, mentions this letter during a routine visit. After they have discussed how Mr. Peterson is doing—taking all of his medication as prescribed, but admitting that he could do better with what he eats—Mr. Peterson says, “I read the letter to the editor you wrote in theMorning Calllast week, Doc.” Mr. Peterson is not employed in the mines, but he has several family members and friends who work in the coal industry. “I’m concerned that all this talk about global warming will result in less coal being used and that will mean fewer jobs for us,” Mr. Peterson says. “And letters like yours, especially from a doc, don’t help matters.”
Dr. Gregory replies, “I realize that there might be financial hardships for some, but it will cost all of us more, economically and healthwise, in the long run if we ignore the problem and do nothing.” But after Mr. Peterson leaves, Dr. Gregory wonders if he should have prioritized his patients’ livelihoods above more general public health concerns.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Gregory has practiced family medicine in Allentown, Pennsylvania, for over three decades, caring for three generations of families and establishing himself as a trusted figure in the community. Throughout his career, he has developed long-standing relationships with his patients, earning their respect and confidence.

In recent years, Dr. Gregory has become increasingly troubled by the effects of human activities—particularly the burning of fossil fuels—on the environment and public health. After delving into peer-reviewed studies and the scientific literature on global climate change, he decided to take a public stance. Dr. Gregory wrote a letter to the local newspaper, advocating for policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as implementing carbon-capture technology at coal-fired power plants.

During a routine office visit, Mr. Peterson, one of Dr. Gregory’s long-term patients, brings up the letter. Their appointment begins as usual, with Dr. Gregory reviewing Mr. Peterson’s medication adherence and encouraging improvements in his diet. Afterward, Mr. Peterson remarks, “I saw your letter to the editor in the Morning Call last week, Doc.” Although Mr. Peterson himself does not work in the mines, many of his relatives and friends are employed in the coal industry. He adds, “I’m worried that all this talk about global warming is going to mean less coal being used, and that could put jobs like ours at risk. Letters like yours, especially coming from a doctor, don’t make it any easier.”

Dr. Gregory responds, “I understand that there’s a real possibility of financial hardships for some people. But I believe that if we ignore these environmental issues, it could cost all of us more—in our wallets and in our health—down the line.” After Mr. Peterson leaves, Dr. Gregory finds himself reflecting on the conversation, questioning whether, in his advocacy, he should have given more weight to the livelihoods of his patients compared to broader public health concerns.

ethical_issues.question: When physicians and patients disagree about social issues, can the therapeutic alliance withstand the test?
keypoints: Divergent viewpoints are a natural occurrence in the clinical setting; physicians should engage in open and respectful dialogue, avoiding the avoidance of sensitive topics.

Physicians’ responses should be grounded in reliable scientific evidence and conducted in a conversational rather than didactic manner, reflecting concern for the patient, the community, and future generations.

Physicians must remain vigilant regarding power dynamics and maintain nonjudgmental respect and tolerance for diverse perspectives, expressing their own positions while remaining open to patients’ experiences and viewpoints, always mindful of their responsibility to address the conditions patients face.

Physicians should explicitly reaffirm their core professional commitment—that regardless of differing views, they will consistently provide the highest standard of care to their patients—serving as the foundation of the therapeutic alliance.
Managing discussions on controversial topics with a respectful and nonjudgmental “agreeing to disagree” approach can facilitate, rather than undermine, the physician-patient relationship.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians express their views on social change while avoiding negative impacts on patient care and the doctor-patient relationship?
keypoints: Physicians should respond based on sound scientific evidence, employing a conversational rather than a didactic approach, reflecting concern and responsibility for their patients, the community, and future generations.

Physicians must maintain nonjudgmental respect and tolerance for diverse viewpoints, remain vigilant to power dynamics and social inequalities affecting the doctor-patient relationship, and avoid exploiting this relationship to coerce patients or impose personal views.
Transparent and respectful dialogue is more constructive than avoiding disagreements; skillful engagement with controversial topics can enhance, rather than undermine, the therapeutic alliance.

Physicians should ensure that, regardless of differences in opinion, they consistently provide the best possible care to their patients while simultaneously advocating—on the basis of respect for their patients—for the well-being of patient populations and a more just society.

ethical_issues.question: Beyond caring for their patients, can and should physicians also serve as advocates for broader social change?
keypoints: Physicians’ responsibilities are not limited to treating individual patients; they should also attend to the environments in which their patients live, as many health problems have their roots in public health, environmental, economic, and social policies.

Physicians should leverage their professional influence and the public’s trust to actively participate in advocating for social change, seeking to improve the health challenges faced by patients and communities through a public health approach.
Physicians have a duty to speak up for vulnerable and marginalized groups, advocating for social, economic, educational, and political changes that alleviate suffering and promote well-being.
Collective advocacy for social change and the protection of individual patient interests are mutually reinforcing, creating a virtuous cycle that advances overall health and well-being.

title: Fostering Student Engagement in Medical Humanities Courses
case: It’s a Tuesday afternoon, and Daniel, a first-year medical student, sits down with his classmates in a sunlit conference room to discuss a documentary they have all just watched about the daily lives of wheelchair-bound patients and the challenges of the complex medical system those patients have to navigate. The course in which the documentary was shown is not graded because of the difficulties in assessing what a student learns from the study of the humanities in the medical context. As Daniel sees his classmates logging onto social networking sites on their laptops and only peripherally participating in the discussion, he wonders if the course should be graded, even though it differs from most medical school courses by trying to foster unquantifiable attitudes such as empathy, patience, and comfort with complexity. What is the best way to demonstrate to medical students that the administration believes that studying the humanities is important to the education of a physician?
case_rewrite: On a bright Tuesday afternoon, Daniel, a first-year medical student, joins his classmates in a sunlit conference room. The group has just finished watching a documentary that intimately portrays the everyday experiences of patients who use wheelchairs and the multifaceted obstacles they face within the medical system. The course that features this documentary stands apart from their usual curriculum—it is ungraded, reflecting the inherent challenges of measuring how students internalize lessons from the humanities in a medical setting. As the discussion begins, Daniel notices that many of his classmates are only half-engaged. Some are quietly browsing social networking sites on their laptops, their attention drifting away from the conversation. This scene prompts Daniel to question the current approach: should this course be graded, even though it aims to nurture qualities like empathy, patience, and comfort with ambiguity—attributes less tangible than the technical skills emphasized elsewhere in their training? Daniel wonders what would be the most effective way for the administration to show that it truly values the role of the humanities in shaping the education and character of future physicians.

ethical_issues.question: Can medical humanities education promote ethical behavior and tolerance of uncertainty among medical students?
keypoints: Preliminary research suggests that medical humanities can promote ethical behavior and tolerance of uncertainty among medical students; however, the empirical literature on this topic remains limited.
Fundamental skepticism regarding whether core humanistic qualities such as empathy are “teachable” constitutes a central challenge in the field of medical humanities education.

Writing training, as a core practice within medical humanities, fosters the intellectual and personal development of medical students, enhances reflective capacity, facilitates coping with uncertainty, and deepens understanding of the plurality of patients’ experiences.

The cultivation of medical humanities should be integrated with medical knowledge and technical competencies, while also emphasizing the development of intellectual and emotional flexibility in future physicians to avoid a solely technical orientation in medical education.

title: Joey Knows Best? Balancing Conflicts and Defending a Child's Best Interest in Difficult Clinical Decisions
case:
After experiencing morning headaches, vomiting, and increasing lethargy for about 3 months, Joey, 12 years of age, was found to have a medulloblastoma. He had surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Joey had a postoperative MRI that showed no focal metastatic sites. His treatment plan called for radiation immediately following the surgery and then chemotherapy.
Joey’s oncologist, Dr. Burnet, told his mother that an ongoing study was investigating the use of lower-than-standard doses of craniospinal radiation in a subset of children like Joey. The study was testing the hypothesis that the lower radiation dose followed by high-dose chemotherapy would produce the same survival rates as the standard high radiation dosage while reducing the neurocognitive side effects of the radiation.
When Joey and his mom met with Dr. Burnet, his mom told Dr. Burnet that she did not want Joey to participate in the experimental treatment regimen. Joey didn’t say anything during the meeting, but on the way home he told his mother that he wanted to be a part of the experimental treatment study. She asked him why. Joey, who had always been a curious kid, loved school, and was proud of his ability to excel at his studies, said, “Mom, they think this is going to be better than what they’re doing now. I don’t want to be a cancer-free dummy…”
Joey’s mother and father were separated, and, although Joey lived with his mom, his father remained close to both of them and involved in his son’s life. When Joey’s mother told him about the treatment decision they were being asked to make, Joey’s dad said, “I think we should let Joey decide. He’s old enough to understand what the risks and possible benefits are. It’s his life.” The mother and father were alone, and Joey’s mom was fighting back tears. “I can’t say yes to this experiment; I just want our son to live,” she said.
The three of them went to Dr. Burnet together so that they all could hear what Dr. Burnet had to say. In the meantime, they learned as much as they could from the Internet, and what they were able to find just confirmed what Dr. Burnet had said. This time Joey spoke up in the office, telling Dr. Burnet that he wanted to participate in the lower-dose radiation study.
“Because this regimen is experimental,” Dr. Burnet told Joey’s folks, “Joey’s assent is really important, but it’s best for everyone if all of you to agree to the treatment. I’m sure you can see why it’s critical that everyone be on board when you’re facing a possibly life-changing decision. We have a physician-ethicist on staff,” Dr. Burnet continued, “who might be able to help you sort out some of the questions you have. The key one, as I see it, is who gets to decide what is in Joey’s best interest. Would you like to meet with our physician-ethicist, Dr. Klein?”
case_rewrite:
For the past three months, 12-year-old Joey had been struggling with persistent morning headaches, frequent vomiting, and growing fatigue. After a series of tests, doctors discovered he had a medulloblastoma. Joey underwent surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible, and a subsequent MRI revealed no focal metastatic lesions. The proposed treatment plan for Joey included immediate craniospinal radiation followed by chemotherapy.

During a consultation, Joey’s oncologist, Dr. Burnet, explained to his mother that there was an ongoing research study exploring the use of lower-than-standard doses of craniospinal radiation in children like Joey. The study aimed to determine whether a reduced radiation dose, followed by high-dose chemotherapy, could achieve survival rates equivalent to those of standard higher-dose radiation, but with a lower risk of neurocognitive side effects.

When Joey and his mother met with Dr. Burnet to discuss the options, his mother quickly voiced her reluctance to have Joey participate in the experimental protocol. Joey remained silent during the meeting. However, on their way home, Joey confided in his mother that he wanted to join the research study. When she asked him why, Joey—always an inquisitive student who enjoyed school and took pride in his academic achievements—replied, “Mom, they think this could be better than what they do now. I don’t want to survive cancer and not be able to think clearly anymore…”

Joey’s parents were separated, but his father remained involved and supportive, maintaining a close relationship with both Joey and his mother. After Joey’s mother told his father about the treatment dilemma, his father responded, “I think Joey should have a say in this. He’s old enough to understand the risks and what might help him. It’s his life.” Alone together, Joey’s mother, on the verge of tears, said, “I just can’t agree to have him in an experiment. I want our son to live.”

Seeking clarity, the three of them visited Dr. Burnet together. In the days leading up to the appointment, they scoured the Internet for information, which largely echoed what Dr. Burnet had explained. This time, Joey spoke for himself at the appointment, telling Dr. Burnet he wanted to participate in the study involving lower-dose radiation.

Dr. Burnet addressed the family: “Because this regimen is experimental, Joey’s agreement is very important, but the best situation is when everyone is on the same page. You can see why it’s crucial that you all agree when faced with a decision that could change Joey’s life. We have a physician-ethicist on our team—Dr. Klein—who can help you work through your questions. The central issue, as I see it, is who should decide what’s in Joey’s best interest. Would you like to meet with Dr. Klein to talk things through?”

ethical_issues.question: How should a child’s treatment preferences be balanced against parental preferences when a minor is facing a life-threatening illness?
keypoints: Medical decision-making for minors is complex and requires individualized assessment of their cognitive maturity and decisional capacity, recognizing that decisional capacity develops along a continuum and varies among individuals.

Parents, as primary caregivers, are generally regarded as the best surrogate decision-makers; however, parental permission does not equate to definitive consent. The core ethical consideration lies in determining whether overriding or respecting the child’s preferences better serves the child’s best interests.

When clinical outcomes are comparable and no clearly superior treatment option exists, disregarding the child’s treatment preferences may lead to adverse psychosocial consequences. Therefore, the child’s treatment preferences and their understanding of associated risks and benefits must be given substantial weight.

Final decisions should be grounded in a comprehensive and systematic analysis of harms and benefits, encompassing physiological, psychological, social, and economic dimensions, while precisely weighing these factors in light of the family’s unique circumstances to strive for consensus among all parties.

ethical_issues.question: In treatment options involving clinical research, how can healthcare providers ensure that the patient and their family understand the fundamental distinction between treatment and research in order to avoid therapeutic misconception?
keypoints: Clearly distinguish the fundamental purposes of clinical treatment and clinical research: treatment aims to provide the patient with the best individualized medical care, whereas research seeks to generate generalizable scientific knowledge by comparing different approaches, with the superiority of the current regimen remaining undetermined.

Explicitly define the concept of the "therapeutic misconception," whereby patients and their families may mistakenly believe that research-based treatments will necessarily confer direct benefit, emphasizing the risks of this cognitive bias and its impact on decision-making.

Provide a detailed explanation of the potential risks associated with the research protocol, including the possibility that reduced-dose radiation may lead to increased mortality or fail to reduce side effects as anticipated, thereby cautioning patients and families to carefully weigh the benefits and harms.

Emphasize the autonomy of the patient and family within the informed consent process by clearly informing them of their right to withdraw from the study at any time, thereby safeguarding the flexibility and voluntariness of their decision-making.

Recommend the provision of comprehensive informational support through multidisciplinary communication—including clinicians and physician-ethicists—to assist patients and families in rationally understanding the nature and uncertainties of the research, thereby preventing misunderstandings arising from information asymmetry.

ethical_issues.question: In the case of parental disagreement, who has the authority to determine the child’s best interests, and how can consensus be achieved among family members to uphold the child’s best interests?
keypoints: The ethical limitation of parental permission lies in the fact that the identity of the decision-maker should be secondary to choosing the option that best serves the child’s best interests; achieving family consensus and maintaining the integrity of family relationships most closely aligns with Joey’s best interests.

When there is disagreement between parents, Joey’s treatment preferences should be fully respected, and, based on his level of maturity, emphasis should be placed on his decisional capacity and understanding of the treatment options.
Dr. Klein’s central task is to assess whether overriding or respecting Joey’s treatment preference better serves his best interests and to assist in clarifying the ethical controversy.

The family should be guided to systematically evaluate the potential benefits and harms of each treatment option, weighing the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence to promote rational decision-making.

Ethical analysis must incorporate the unique circumstances of the family, allowing for a precise weighing of risks and benefits to arrive at the most appropriate treatment decision for this specific family.
Through multidisciplinary communication and professional ethical support, consensus between parents and the child should be promoted, thereby safeguarding Joey’s best interests and family harmony.

title: A Night at the Museum: Helping Residents “See” Their Patients
case:
Katherine is a third-year medical student on her internal medicine rotation at an academic medical center that serves as a busy tertiary-care hospital for its region. The residents she works with are swamped with work; when they are not actively admitting and caring for patients, they are inundated with paperwork, submitting online orders, and completing health record notes. Katherine knows that the residents are kind and generous people who have been selected twice—for medical school and then for residency—on the basis of test scores, academic performance, and character recommendations. She cannot help but note, however, their frustration with patients who demand so much of their time, their irritation with nurses who page them about questions the residents think have obvious answers, and their eagerness to “turf” patients to another service or practice center to lighten their case loads. She can understand the origins of these behaviors while feeling that the residents are in danger of burning out and becoming more cynical than would be healthy for a long-term career.
One evening, Katherine’s entire team is asked to stop working at 4 p.m. and take a trip to the Museum of Fine Arts. The residency program director is an advocate for innovative approaches to encouraging self-reflection among the residents and helping them see patients as people rather than diagnoses. He has asked the internal medicine teams to take turns going to the museum to look at and frame discussion around artwork as a way of generating conversation about medicine, patients, and life as a trainee. Katherine hears the residents complain that this outing is intended to force-feed them empathy and humanism; they consider it a waste of time that could be better spent on patient care and leaving the hospital at a decent time.
case_rewrite:
Katherine, a third-year medical student, is completing her internal medicine rotation at a large academic medical center that acts as a bustling tertiary-care hospital for the region. The residents she works alongside are perpetually overwhelmed: when not actively managing patient admissions and care, they are buried under a mountain of paperwork, entering orders online, and racing to finish electronic health record notes. Katherine sees that these residents are genuinely compassionate and well-intentioned individuals, carefully chosen for both medical school and residency based on their academic achievements, exam scores, and personal recommendations. Yet, she observes their mounting frustration—patients frequently demand significant time and attention, nurses page them with questions the residents feel should have obvious answers, and there is a palpable eagerness to transfer patients to other services or facilities to ease their own caseloads. Katherine empathizes with the residents’ exhaustion, recognizing how easily these pressures could push them toward burnout and a cynical outlook, threatening their well-being and long-term commitment to medicine.

One afternoon, the entire team receives an unexpected directive: at 4 p.m., they are to set aside their clinical work and visit the Museum of Fine Arts. This initiative comes from the residency program director, who passionately believes in creative strategies to foster self-reflection and to remind residents to see their patients as unique individuals—not merely diagnoses. Each internal medicine team is scheduled for such an outing, with the intention that viewing and discussing artwork together will spark conversation about the nature of medicine, patient care, and the lived experience of being a medical trainee. As they prepare to leave, Katherine overhears several residents expressing their dissatisfaction. They grumble that the outing is a misguided attempt to force empathy and humanism upon them, arguing that their time would be better spent caring for patients or simply finishing their work so they can go home at a reasonable hour.

ethical_issues.question: How can residents’ empathy and curiosity toward patients be effectively promoted in the context of their resistance, in order to alleviate professional burnout?
keypoints: Engage in respectful and open dialogue with residents to acknowledge and address their objections to educational activities, avoiding top-down imposition of learning.

Critically examine biases within the culture of medical education regarding forms of learning, emphasizing that the museum visit is not a departure from clinical duties but holds significant clinical and professional relevance.

Clarify that the purpose of the museum visit is to stimulate residents’ empathy and curiosity toward patients, citing research that supports emotional connection as a means to alleviate professional burnout.

Through skilled facilitation, employ methods such as attentive seeing, nonjudgmental curiosity, and multiple perspectives to help residents move beyond their cognitive comfort zones, fostering perspective-taking and critical thinking, thereby deepening their understanding of patients and promoting patient-centered care.
