title: Evaluating the Risks and Benefits of Participation in High-School Football
case:
Dr. Gupta is a private practice pediatrician in a small, rural town. As a primary care physician, he is often asked to evaluate children and teenagers for participation in youth sports programs. This means much of his work is dedicated to high school football, one of the mainstays of youth athletics in the region. Dr. Gupta is often happy to serve in this capacity; he has spent much of his career working to prevent child obesity and believes strongly that community sports and fitness are crucial components of healthy lifestyles.
He is asked to evaluate 15-year-old Jesse in preparation for the boy’s first season on a junior varsity high school football team. Jesse is accompanied by both of his parents. As Dr. Gupta walks into the examination room, he senses that the atmosphere is tense. After a brief history and pre-participation physical exam, he asks Jesse’s mother and father if they have any questions.
Jesse’s mother speaks up. “I’ve read that they’ve started placing sensors in players’ helmets, and they show that a lot of these boys are taking pretty hard hits. They say that concussions are actually more harmful than we knew about back in our day, and that over time all these head injuries could really cause damage to the brain. I’m worried, because Jesse’s already had one or two concussions in the past. Should we really let Jesse play football?”
Jesse’s father shakes his head and interjects: “Jesse’s brothers played high school football, and they got banged up pretty bad, but they’re fine. One of them has a scholarship to a good university, and he’s still playing football. I played the game myself when I was in school and it taught me a lot of important life skills—skills that served me as a unit leader in the Army and that I still use in running my business. I want Jesse to have the chance to play on a team and learn the value of sportsmanship. More important, I don’t want him hanging around after school with these other kids who are doing drugs and getting into trouble.”
Dr. Gupta listens carefully to each parent’s arguments. He says that he understands Jesse’s mother’s concerns about the risks of the sport, and he makes a point of acknowledging them. However, he also agrees with Jesse’s father that youth sports play an important part in teaching children and teens teamwork, leadership, and healthy lifestyles. He asks the parents to discuss their concerns with each other further, as well as with Jesse, and in the end to decide as a family how they want to proceed. The parents thank Dr. Gupta for his time, but as they get up to leave the office, he feels they wanted something more from him.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Gupta is a pediatrician with a private practice in a small rural town. In his role as a primary care physician, he frequently conducts evaluations for local children and teenagers seeking to join community sports teams—a responsibility that often centers on high school football, which is a cornerstone of youth athletics in the area. Dr. Gupta takes pride in this aspect of his work, as he has dedicated much of his career to combating childhood obesity and strongly believes that organized sports and regular fitness are vital to children’s health.

One afternoon, Dr. Gupta is scheduled to see 15-year-old Jesse, who is preparing for his very first season on the junior varsity high school football team. Jesse arrives at the clinic with both of his parents. As Dr. Gupta enters the exam room, he immediately senses an undercurrent of tension between the family members. After completing a thorough history and a standard pre-participation physical examination, Dr. Gupta turns to Jesse’s mother and father and invites them to share any questions or concerns they might have.

Jesse’s mother is the first to speak. “I’ve been reading about the new helmet sensors they’re using, and it seems like a lot of kids are getting hit pretty hard out there. I’ve learned that concussions are even more dangerous than we realized when we were young, and that repeated head injuries can really affect the brain in the long run. I’m nervous because Jesse has already had one, maybe even two concussions in the past. Should we really let Jesse play football?”

Before Dr. Gupta can respond, Jesse’s father weighs in. “Jesse’s brothers played football in high school. Sure, they got their share of bumps and bruises, but they turned out fine. One even earned a scholarship and is still playing at college. I played football, too, and it taught me a lot—leadership, discipline, working as a team. Those are skills I used as a unit leader in the Army, and I rely on them every day running my business. I want Jesse to have those same opportunities, and honestly, I’d rather see him practicing with his team after school than hanging around with kids who might be getting into trouble or using drugs.”

Dr. Gupta listens closely to both parents, carefully considering the mother’s worries about the dangers of football and the father’s emphasis on the positive life lessons and structure sports can provide. He acknowledges the validity of Jesse’s mother’s concerns, noting the real risks of concussion and the uncertainty surrounding their long-term effects. At the same time, he recognizes the importance Jesse’s father places on teamwork, leadership, and the health benefits of organized sports.

Dr. Gupta explains that while evidence about the risks of concussions, especially repeated ones, is growing, there are still many unanswered questions about the likelihood and severity of long-term consequences. He shares the current scientific understanding, including what is and isn’t known about brain injury risks in youth football, and candidly discusses the limitations of existing research. He emphasizes that the decision about Jesse’s participation should be made after thoughtful family discussion, weighing both the potential risks and the benefits that football may offer.

He encourages Jesse and his parents to continue the conversation among themselves, taking into account Jesse’s own perspective and wishes, and to reach a decision together based on the full information provided. As the family prepares to leave, they thank Dr. Gupta for his guidance. However, as Dr. Gupta watches them go, he senses that they were hoping for even more direct advice from him.

ethical_issues.question: When evaluating adolescent participation in American football, how should physicians balance respect for family autonomy with the principle of beneficence?
keypoints: When evaluating adolescent participation in American football, physicians should balance respect for family autonomy with the principle of beneficence; respect for autonomy acknowledges the right of patients and families to make decisions based on their own values, while beneficence requires physicians to take reasonable actions in the best interest of the patient’s health.

Given that the risks of concussion and its long-term effects related to American football are not yet fully understood, physicians cannot accurately predict an athlete’s future risk of injury or sequelae, and therefore, it remains uncertain whether prohibiting participation yields a net health benefit.

Physicians should present the existing scientific evidence comprehensively to the patient and family, candidly acknowledge clinical uncertainties, and thereby facilitate an autonomous and rational risk-benefit analysis and decision-making process based on full information.

If the patient exhibits clear risk factors or vulnerabilities—such as a lowered threshold for concussion or abnormal recovery patterns—the physician has a duty, grounded in the principle of beneficence, to intervene by recommending or prohibiting participation in high-risk contact sports.

ethical_issues.question: When faced with an athlete’s history of concussion, how can physicians ensure that the athlete’s family makes an informed and autonomous decision regarding continued participation in sports?
keypoints: Physicians should attentively listen to the differing perspectives of family members, appreciating both concerns regarding the risks of sports participation and the value of sportsmanship.
Physicians should enhance their medical recommendations through a comprehensive evaluation of the patient’s health status and potential injury risks.
Physicians should provide balanced information regarding the risks of concussion, including evidence on cumulative effects as well as the current limitations and uncertainties of the research.
Physicians should assist families in conducting a thorough risk-benefit analysis to facilitate autonomous decision-making based on informed consent.
Physicians should recommend that the patient and family engage in in-depth discussions and arrive at a joint decision, thereby respecting the family’s autonomy.

ethical_issues.question: In the field of sports medicine, how can physicians provide guidance under conditions of uncertainty to balance the conflict between the risks of athletic participation and the benefits to health?
keypoints: Physicians should balance the principles of respect for autonomy and beneficence by respecting the patient’s and family’s autonomy while making decisions supported by a comprehensive evaluation of the athlete’s health status and relevant medical evidence.

Physicians need to systematically assess the athlete’s physical readiness for participation in collision sports and the potential risk of brain injury, incorporating comparative analyses of concussion incidence in football versus other team sports.

Physicians should clearly articulate the existing evidence and limitations regarding chronic traumatic encephalopathy and sport-related concussions, honestly addressing clinical uncertainties to facilitate the patient’s and family’s rational understanding of the risks involved.

Through a shared decision-making process, physicians should encourage the athlete and family to engage in in-depth discussions of risks and benefits, thereby forming an informed and value-congruent consensus decision.

If the athlete presents with clear special risks or vulnerabilities (such as a lowered concussion threshold, prolonged or incomplete recovery), the physician has a responsibility to proactively intervene and recommend suspension or prohibition from high-risk sports participation.

title: Nonmaleficence in Sports Medicine
case:
Dr. Robles is a sports medicine specialist in a group practice in a major urban area. While some of her patients compete in professional sports, she also serves many younger athletes. She is an active member of several local professional societies, and she often attends conferences with her colleagues in sports medicine around the country.
Today, she is asked to see 18-year-old Alison, a high school senior and a promising soccer player. Alison has an impressive record as a center forward, and her team is poised to enter a national championship. Alison feels her performance in this competition may also influence the scholarships she hopes to be offered when she enters college in the next academic year.
As Dr. Robles enters the room, she sees that Alison is obviously uncomfortable, holding an ice pack to her knee. After a brief history and physical exam, Dr. Robles concludes that Alison has injured her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). She says that Alison cannot play a cutting and pivoting sport like soccer with an ACL-deficient knee because it could risk further, irreversible damage to the articular cartilage and menisci.
Alison leans forward. “I understand what you’re saying, but the championships are on the line. I have to play in this game. The school won’t let me play without a doctor’s note.”
Dr. Robles shakes her head and says, “I cannot recommend that you return to play with your knee injury.”
Alison thinks for a moment, and then asks, “Well, what if you write a note to the school saying that, although you don’t recommend that I play, I’m legally an adult now, and I accept the risks you’ve explained to me. Then I can just play with a knee brace—and all of the liability falls on me.”
Dr. Robles is taken aback, but quickly regains composure and reemphasizes her conservative recommendations. Alison repeats her suggestion—that Dr. Robles should write a note explaining that it’s okay for Alison to decide whether to play or not, so long as she assumes liability for playing on the injured knee. Dr. Robles wonders if Alison understands the long-term implications of further damage to her knee.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Robles, a sports medicine specialist practicing in a large metropolitan group, cares for athletes ranging from professionals to high school students. She is well connected in her field, regularly attending national conferences and actively participating in local professional societies.

On this day, Dr. Robles is scheduled to see Alison, an 18-year-old high school senior and standout soccer player. Alison, who has been instrumental as her team’s center forward, now faces a pivotal moment: her team is about to compete in the national championships, and her performance could determine whether she receives the college scholarships she’s been working toward.

As Dr. Robles enters the exam room, she finds Alison seated on the edge of the table, an ice pack pressed firmly against her knee, her discomfort evident. After taking a thorough history and conducting a physical examination, Dr. Robles diagnoses Alison with an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. She explains to Alison that playing soccer, with its demands for quick cuts and pivots, is unsafe with an ACL-deficient knee. Dr. Robles cautions that returning to play could cause irreversible harm to the knee’s cartilage and menisci, potentially jeopardizing Alison’s long-term mobility.

Alison listens intently, then leans forward with determination. “I understand what you’re telling me, but this championship means everything. I need to play in this game. The school won’t let me unless I have a doctor’s note.”

Dr. Robles meets Alison’s gaze and responds firmly, “I cannot recommend that you return to play with this injury. It’s not safe.”

Alison hesitates, then continues, “What if you write a note to the school—not saying you recommend it, but that I’m legally an adult and I accept all the risks you’ve explained? If I wear a brace, and make it clear the liability is mine, then I can play.”

Dr. Robles is momentarily taken aback by Alison’s proposal, but quickly reaffirms her position. “My recommendation remains the same. I cannot support your return to play under these circumstances.”

Alison persists, suggesting again that Dr. Robles could simply acknowledge in a letter that Alison is informed of the risks and is choosing to play at her own discretion. Dr. Robles is left wondering whether Alison fully comprehends the long-term consequences of further knee damage. She knows the stakes are high for Alison, but remains firm in her professional and ethical obligations.

ethical_issues.question: In a situation where the patient explicitly expresses willingness to assume the risks, should the physician respect the patient’s autonomy and permit participation in the competition despite the injury?
keypoints: Physicians should uphold the principle of nonmaleficence by refusing to endorse or support a patient’s participation in sports while injured, even if the patient explicitly consents to assume the risks.
The physician’s fundamental duty is to fully inform the patient of the serious risks associated with an ACL injury and to clearly advise against engaging in high-risk athletic activities.

Physicians must not issue clearance or certification permitting the patient to participate in sports while injured, so as to avoid professional misconduct and to preserve honesty and societal trust within the physician-patient relationship.

ethical_issues.question: When a physician faces a situation that may cause further harm to the patient, should the principle of nonmaleficence take precedence, leading the physician to refuse the patient’s request?
keypoints: The core ethical conflict in this case lies in the tension between the patient’s autonomy and the physician’s duty of nonmaleficence.

The principle of nonmaleficence requires physicians to avoid causing further harm to the patient; therefore, when a course of action may lead to deterioration of the patient’s health, nonmaleficence should take precedence.
Even if the patient is a legal adult who voluntarily assumes the risks, the physician should not facilitate or endorse actions that may result in serious harm.

The physician’s responsibility is to fully inform the patient of the risks associated with participating in sports with an ACL-deficient knee and to clearly advise against participation, rather than issuing clearance or waiving liability.

If the patient insists on participating, the decision and negotiations should be managed by the patient and the relevant athletic authorities; the physician must maintain a professional stance and avoid becoming a facilitator of potential harm.

ethical_issues.question: When Alison requests that Dr. Robles provide documentation that may involve professional deception, should Dr. Robles refuse in order to uphold the principles of honesty and nonmaleficence, thereby maintaining the trust of both society and her patients in the medical profession?
keypoints: The honesty of the physician is fundamental to maintaining the trust of society and patients; any form of deception would seriously undermine this foundation of trust.

Physicians should refuse to participate in professional misconduct requested by patients; if the patient insists on competing against medical advice, she should assume the risks herself and negotiate with the athletic department independently.

Physicians should adhere to their professional judgment, clearly informing the patient of potential health risks and long-term consequences, and avoid issuing misleading certifications that could result in further harm to the patient.

Physicians should respect patient autonomy on the basis of professional judgment, fulfill their duty of full disclosure and professional responsibility, and uphold medical ethics and professional integrity.

title: Mention of a Patient’s “Race” in Clinical Presentations
case:
It is a big day for Michaela. A fourth-year medical student, she is just beginning a sub-internship in internal medicine at City Hospital, her top choice for residency. She took her first call yesterday and is about to present on rounds for the first time the patients she admitted. Knowing how important a letter of recommendation from her attending Dr. Ross will be for her residency application, she is eager to make a good impression. Although she is a bit nervous, she is well prepared and confident.
When it comes her turn to present her first patient, Michaela takes a deep breath and begins, “Ms. Adler is a 76-year-old woman, with a history—”
Before she can finish her sentence, Dr. Ross interrupts her: “76-year-old black woman, right?”
“Uh, yes,” Michaela answers, after a brief hesitation. “As I was saying, she has a history of coronary artery disease and presented to the ED after a fall and a brief loss of consciousness.”
Although she is a bit unsettled by the interruption, the remainder of the presentation goes well and she gets positive feedback from Dr. Ross on her management plan for Ms. Adler. With this confidence boost, Michaela begins presenting her next patient. “Mr. Rocha is a 26-year-old man with recently diagnosed Crohn’s disease presenting—”
To her surprise, Dr. Ross interrupts her again. “White?”
“Well, I… I didn’t ask…” Michaela stutters, as she sees Dr. Ross raise an eyebrow briefly.
“OK,” he responds with a wave of his hand, “Go on.” Although she is worried that she is not making the impression she was aiming for, Michaela gets through the rest of her presentation uneventfully.
Later that day, as Dr. Ross is about to leave, Michaela approaches him to get some feedback on her presentations. “I’m sorry I didn’t ask the patient’s ethnicity. It’s just that it wasn’t relevant to the case.”
“Well, I can’t decide what’s relevant if you don’t tell me, can I?” Dr. Ross responds. “Listen, you’re doing a great job for a beginner in managing these patients, but you have to make sure that your presentations are complete: name, age, race, chief complaint, same old script every time. I’ll give you a pass for today but just don’t forget next time, OK? See you tomorrow, bright and early!”
case_rewrite:
Michaela’s anticipation is palpable as she steps onto the internal medicine ward at City Hospital. As a fourth-year medical student just starting her sub-internship, she knows how much rides on her performance. City Hospital is her top choice for residency, and she’s keenly aware that a strong letter of recommendation from Dr. Ross, her attending, could make all the difference. Though a bit on edge, Michaela has prepared thoroughly for her first day of rounds after her initial call shift, ready to present the patients she admitted.

As the team gathers, Michaela steadies herself and begins her first case presentation. “Ms. Adler is a 76-year-old woman, with a history—”

Dr. Ross interjects before she can continue. “76-year-old black woman, right?”

Michaela pauses, slightly thrown off. “Uh, yes,” she replies, collecting herself. “As I was saying, she has a history of coronary artery disease and came to the ED after a fall with brief loss of consciousness.”

Despite the interruption, Michaela completes the rest of her presentation smoothly and receives encouraging feedback from Dr. Ross about her management approach for Ms. Adler. Buoyed by his comments, she moves on to her next patient. “Mr. Rocha is a 26-year-old man with recently diagnosed Crohn’s disease, presenting—”

Once again, Dr. Ross interrupts. “White?”

Michaela hesitates. “Well, I… I didn’t ask…” She notices Dr. Ross give her a fleeting look of disapproval.

“OK,” he says with a dismissive gesture, “Go on.” Michaela pushes through, uneasy that she may not be meeting his expectations, but manages to finish her presentations without further issue.

Later that afternoon, as Dr. Ross is about to leave, Michaela approaches him for feedback. “I’m sorry I didn’t mention the patient’s ethnicity. I just didn’t think it was relevant to their cases.”

Dr. Ross replies, “Well, I can’t decide what’s relevant if you don’t tell me, can I? Look, you’re doing a solid job for someone just starting out, but your presentations need to be complete: name, age, race, chief complaint—always the same structure. I’ll let it slide today, but don’t forget next time, all right? See you first thing in the morning!”

ethical_issues.question: Should a Patient’s Race Be Mentioned in Clinical Case Presentations?
keypoints: The impact of patient race information on clinical decision-making is extremely limited and is generally insufficient to serve as a central basis for optimizing diagnosis and treatment.

Emphasizing race prominently in case presentations may distract attention and is prone to eliciting stereotypes and implicit biases, thereby affecting the doctor-patient relationship and fairness in care.

Race should only be mentioned during the physical examination or social history sections when it is clearly relevant to the specific clinical condition, ensuring both the clinical pertinence of the information and the completeness of the report.

title: Incorporating Genetic Testing Ancestry Results into Medical Decisions
case:
Ms. Stewart was eagerly awaiting her upcoming trip to Boston to celebrate her parents’ fiftieth wedding anniversary. She had grown up in a large Irish family, with two brothers and two sisters, but she rarely got to see them since moving to Oregon for her job. She was especially looking forward to seeing her sister Anna, who was recovering from a mastectomy after receiving a diagnosis of breast cancer several months earlier.
As a gift to her parents, Ms. Stewart had decided to create a book tracing the family’s genealogy. Growing up, her mother told her stories about how her great-grandfather had arrived at Ellis Island with hardly anything besides the clothes on his back, and she had always been curious about the family’s roots in Ireland. As she was searching the Internet for genealogy records websites, an advertisement on the side of her screen caught her eye. “Find out where your genes come from!” Her curiosity piqued, Ms. Stewart clicked on the link to geneheritage.com, an online service for genetic testing of ancestry and ethnicity. She had heard of these online genetic testing services before and even read in a magazine that one of her favorite actresses had gotten one, but she had never before thought of doing it herself. “I could put it in the book,” she thought, as she perused the website. She decided to order a kit and, a few days later, she sent off a cheek swab for the DNA tests.
Two weeks later, Ms. Stewart got her eagerly awaited results. To her surprise, the results indicated that she carried several polymorphisms that are known to be more common among Ashkenazi Jews than in the general population. According to the test, she had 23 percent Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in her genetic panel.
Later that week, Ms. Stewart went to see her primary care physician, Dr. Lowe, for her annual physical. During the review of systems when Dr. Lowe asked her whether she had had any lumps or pain in her breasts, Ms. Stewart hesitated a bit. “Well I haven’t had any problems, but I was thinking…I want to get tested for the breast cancer gene.”
Somewhat surprised, Dr. Lowe explained that the BRCA is not a routine test and is recommended for women who are at increased risk of breast cancer due to their family history and ancestry.
“Well that’s just it,” Ms. Stewart responded. “You know my sister had breast cancer recently, and now I just took this test and it turns out that I’m part Jewish. I think I need the test.”
case_rewrite:
Ms. Stewart was looking forward to her upcoming trip to Boston, where her family would gather to celebrate her parents’ fiftieth wedding anniversary. Having grown up in a lively Irish household with two brothers and two sisters, she cherished these rare occasions to reconnect, especially since her move to Oregon for work meant she seldom saw her siblings. She was particularly eager to spend time with her sister Anna, who was in recovery following a mastectomy after being diagnosed with breast cancer several months before.

As a special present for her parents, Ms. Stewart had embarked on creating a family genealogy book. She had always been fascinated by the stories her mother shared of their great-grandfather’s arrival at Ellis Island with nothing but his clothes, and she wanted to weave these tales into a record of their Irish heritage. While researching online for genealogy resources, a colorful advertisement caught her attention: “Find out where your genes come from!” Intrigued, Ms. Stewart clicked on the link for geneheritage.com, a website offering direct-to-consumer genetic testing focused on ancestry and ethnicity. She recalled reading about such services and even remembered an article about a favorite actress who had tried it. The idea of including her own genetic ancestry in the book seemed appealing, so she ordered a test kit and, after it arrived in the mail, sent off her cheek swab for analysis.

Two weeks later, Ms. Stewart received her results. She was surprised to learn that her genetic profile included several polymorphisms often found in people of Ashkenazi Jewish descent, and the report suggested she had 23 percent Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.

Later that week, at her annual physical with Dr. Lowe, her primary care physician, Ms. Stewart’s thoughts turned to her sister’s illness. When Dr. Lowe inquired about any breast lumps or pain during the review of systems, Ms. Stewart paused before saying, “I haven’t noticed any problems, but…I was thinking I’d like to be tested for the breast cancer gene.”

Dr. Lowe, a bit taken aback, explained that BRCA testing is not part of routine screening and is generally recommended only when there’s an increased risk based on family history or ancestry.

“That’s why I’m asking,” Ms. Stewart replied. “You know my sister had breast cancer this year, and now this genetic test says I’m part Jewish. I think that means I should have the test.”

ethical_issues.question: In the absence of professional genetic counseling, how should information from direct-to-consumer (DTC) genetic testing be interpreted and applied in clinical decision-making?
keypoints: Due to limitations in the selection of genetic markers, the definition of reference populations, and data analysis methods, DTC genetic testing results may not accurately reflect an individual’s ancestral background, posing risks of misclassification or omission.

Clinical risk assessment should be based on a comprehensive family history; in the absence of professional interpretation and supporting evidence, information from DTC ancestry testing generally does not significantly influence decisions regarding genetic counseling and subsequent testing.

Individuals concerned about hereditary disease risk should be promptly referred for genetic counseling to ensure that genetic testing is conducted with adequate pre- and post-test counseling support, enabling a thorough understanding of the personal and medical implications of the test results.

title: The Prejudiced Patient
case:
Dr. Simms is a new physician at Harbor Clinic, a primary care practice in a small town. He does not yet have a full panel of patients so he has agreed to fill in for his colleague Dr. Chen while he is on vacation. Things are finally starting to wind down after a busy day, when he welcomes his next patient. Ms. Smith, a 53-year-old woman, has been a patient of Dr. Chen’s for the past five years. She is here because of her diabetes, which she has been controlling with diet and metformin. As he steps into the room, Ms. Smith exclaims “Oh, are you the new doctor? It’s so nice to see a black doctor here! When did you start?” Dr. Simms hesitates for a second before responding, “Uh, yes, I just started a month ago and I’m filling in for Dr. Chen today. So I see you are coming in for your regular diabetes check-up?” Dr. Simms introduces himself to Ms. Smith and explains that he is replacing Dr. Chen for the week.
Ms. Smith seems to be doing well with her diabetes control. Her A1c is well within her goal range, and she has been able to keep to her diet and exercise regimen on most days. As the visit is about to end, Dr. Simms asks whether there is anything he can do for Ms. Smith. “Well, actually, I have this mole, I don’t know I’m a bit worried about it.”
“OK, let’s take a look,” Dr. Smith responds. After asking a few questions and examining the mole Dr. Simms reassures Ms. Smith that it is actually a benign skin tag.
Ms. Smith smiles, relieved. “Thank you so much! I was so worried about that!”
As she is walking towards the door, she turns back towards Dr. Smith: “You know, I really like you. I mean, Dr. Chen is good, but sometimes I can barely even understand what he’s saying. You know? The accent? I mean, everywhere you go now, it’s immigrants. Sometimes you just want someone who looks like you, you know?” Dr. Simms is slightly taken aback and does not know how to respond. Before he can say anything, Ms. Smith adds: “Can you be my doctor from now on?”

ethical_issues.question: Do patients have the right to choose their physician based on race, and is such a choice consistent with medical ethical principles?
keypoints: Patients have the right to choose their physicians, including choices based on race, which is a core principle of patient-centered care and respect for patient autonomy.
Accommodating a patient’s preference for a physician of a particular race is consistent with medical ethical principles such as informed consent and respect for autonomy.
Existing civil rights legislation does not prohibit the practice of patients selecting physicians based on race.
The discomfort surrounding such choices stems from the underlying potential biases, racism, and xenophobic attitudes, rather than from the patient’s request itself.

Physicians and the medical profession have a responsibility to respect patient autonomy while actively working to address and transform both patient and provider biases, thereby promoting an equitable and inclusive healthcare environment.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians address potential racial biases in patients while respecting their preferences?
keypoints: Respect patient autonomy by allowing patients to choose physicians according to their preferences.
Physicians should rationally assess whether a patient’s prejudices may affect the patient-physician relationship and the quality of care provided.
If a physician determines that a patient’s prejudices could impair the quality of care, they have the right to express their concerns and seek open communication.
Through candid and respectful dialogue, physicians and patients should strive to reach clinical decisions that align with the values of both parties.
While acknowledging patient choice, physicians and the medical profession bear the responsibility to gradually challenge and change patients’ and society’s prejudices through education and guidance.

ethical_issues.question: Should health care systems establish policies to accommodate or deny patients’ requests for race-concordant physicians?
keypoints: Patients have the right to choose their clinicians, and both medical ethical principles and the AMA Code of Medical Ethics support respect for patients’ individual preferences and autonomy.

Existing civil rights legislation does not prohibit patients from selecting physicians based on racial preferences; however, healthcare institutions must guard against discrimination and inequity arising from such preferences.

The healthcare system lacks sufficient resources and mechanisms to systematically assess the motivations underlying patients’ choices of physicians, making it difficult to establish uniform policies that fully accommodate or deny all requests for race-concordant care.

When formulating relevant policies, it is important to balance respect for patient autonomy with anti-discrimination principles, and to avoid reinforcing racial stereotypes or exacerbating inequities in the allocation of healthcare resources.

title: Is Parental Smoking Neglect of an Asthmatic Child?
case:
A mother carrying a coughing child walks into the emergency room. She hysterically flags down a triage nurse and tells her that her daughter, Rose, is having trouble breathing. The nurse directs mother and child to a bed in the emergency room cordoned off by a light blue curtain. Less than five minutes later, Tricia, a third-year medical student on her pediatrics rotation, shows up to do a thorough history and physical of the patient. The first thing Tricia notices is that both mother and daughter are saturated in the scent of cigarettes. Upon questioning, the mother admits to smoking two packs a day in the house.
“Have you tried quitting?” Tricia asks.
The mother scowls. “The smoking’s not a problem. I keep all the windows open.” At that moment, her daughter has a severe coughing fit. She scoops Rose into her arms, and rubs soothing circles on her back. “My daughter has asthma. That’s why we’re here,” she tells the student.
Tricia jots a note in the patient’s record and sees Rose has been admitted multiple times in the past for asthma. After flipping through these notes, Tricia sees that the mother has been counseled repeatedly about the need to stop smoking for the sake of Rose’s health. Tricia goes to find her attending and presents Rose’s case, highlighting signs of neglect. She then asks whether or not this would be grounds to notify child protective services.
case_rewrite:
A mother carrying her coughing daughter hurries into the emergency department. She anxiously waves down the triage nurse, her voice trembling as she explains that her daughter, Rose, is struggling to breathe. The nurse quickly ushers them to a bed in the emergency area, separated from the rest of the unit by a light blue curtain. Within minutes, Tricia, a third-year medical student on her pediatrics rotation, arrives to conduct a full history and physical exam.

The heavy scent of cigarette smoke immediately strikes Tricia as she approaches; both mother and daughter’s clothes are saturated with it. During the interview, Tricia gently asks the mother about smoking in the home. The mother admits, “I smoke about two packs a day, but only in the house.”

Tricia asks, “Have you considered trying to quit, or maybe smoking outside instead?”

The mother stiffens, her expression defensive. “I don’t think the smoking’s the problem. I always keep the windows open.” Just then, Rose is racked by a fierce coughing spell. The mother scoops her up, rubbing soothing circles on her back. “She has asthma. That’s why we’re here again,” she says, casting a worried glance at her daughter.

Tricia makes a note in Rose’s chart and reviews her medical history. She notes that Rose has been admitted numerous times before for asthma exacerbations. The records indicate that previous providers have repeatedly counseled the mother about the dangers of smoking around Rose and the urgent need to protect her from secondhand smoke. Despite these conversations, the notes suggest little change in the mother’s behavior.

Tricia seeks out her attending, Dr. W, and presents Rose’s case, emphasizing the repeated hospitalizations and persistent exposure to secondhand smoke at home. She voices her growing concern about whether this ongoing pattern amounts to medical neglect and asks Dr. W if these circumstances might require notifying child protective services.

ethical_issues.question: How can children’s exposure to secondhand smoke be effectively reduced when parents are not ready to quit smoking?
keypoints: Implement gradual measures to reduce children’s exposure to secondhand smoke, respecting parents’ readiness to change and avoiding coercive demands for smoking cessation.
Establish a partnership with smoking parents to enhance communication and trust, thereby facilitating incremental improvements in the home environment.
Advise parents to smoke outdoors whenever possible to minimize the direct impact of indoor smoke on the child.
Emphasize the importance of prohibiting smoking inside vehicles to prevent children’s exposure to secondhand smoke in enclosed spaces.
Encourage smokers to use a designated smoking jacket kept outdoors and to wash their hands after smoking to reduce smoke odor and residue exposure to the child.

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances should physicians report parental neglect to child protective services in order to safeguard the child’s safety?
keypoints: If, after comprehensive interventions, the child continues to be harmed by secondhand smoke, physicians have an ethical and legal obligation to report neglect in order to ensure the child’s safety.

When the actions or omissions of parents or caregivers result in serious physical or emotional harm to the child, or present an imminent risk of such harm, physicians are required by law to report to child welfare authorities.

It is necessary to assess whether there is a persistent pattern of neglect, such as repeated noncompliance with medical advice, missed medical appointments, or failure to fill the child’s prescriptions, as this constitutes an important criterion for reporting.

Physicians must weigh the benefits and risks of reporting, with particular emphasis on evaluating the relative harm of secondhand smoke exposure versus the potential adverse effects of removing the child from the family environment on the child’s safety and well-being.

ethical_issues.question: Does parental smoking constitute neglect of a child with asthma?
keypoints: Neglect includes the failure to meet a child’s basic needs and to protect the child from health hazards such as exposure to secondhand smoke.
Exposure to secondhand smoke can trigger or exacerbate asthma in children, seriously compromising their health and safety.
The US Department of Health and Human Services classifies asthmatic children exposed to secondhand smoke as cases of hazard exposure, which may constitute inadequate supervision and neglect.
In some states, parental failure to follow medical advice—such as recommendations to quit smoking—is considered medical neglect.

The Children and Families Safe Act of 2003 defines child maltreatment as any act or failure to act by a parent or caregiver, including medical neglect, that results in serious physical or emotional harm or presents an imminent risk of serious harm.

A mother’s persistent smoking and failure to take effective measures to quit, despite being aware of the harm of secondhand smoke to a child with asthma, constitutes neglect of the child’s health and safety.

title: Drug Samples: Why Not?
case:
Dr. Williams, the medical director of a large clinic, announces to her staff, “As of next month, we will no longer be offering free drug samples to patients here.” Over the immediate dissent of the doctors, she continues, “I am concerned that, with our limited supply, we are often starting patients on drug regimens that we know we cannot continue to provide for free and that they will not be able to afford once their samples run out.”
“This is the only way some of our patients can get their medication!” protests one physician.
Dr. Williams explains that the office has stopped accepting gifts such as dinners from pharmaceutical companies and says she thinks that this is really just in keeping with those policies.
Dr. Silverstein points out that, under the new Physician Payments Sunshine Act, drug samples are exempt from mandatory reporting, unlike material goods, stock options, grants, consulting fees, travel, and other perks. He insists that this is clear evidence that drug samples are unlike these other things the clinic has stopped accepting and that Dr. Williams ought to reconsider her position. In turn, she asks him, are drug samples really helping their patients if they can’t receive the full regimen without financial hardship?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Williams, medical director of a bustling urban clinic, gathers her team for a staff meeting. “Starting next month,” she announces, “we will discontinue the practice of giving out free drug samples to patients.” A wave of protest ripples through the room. One physician objects, “But for some of our patients, these samples are the only way they can get their medications!”

Dr. Williams holds her ground. “With the limited supply we receive, we’re often initiating treatments that we know we can’t sustain—once the samples run out, our patients are left unable to afford the full regimen. I worry that we’re setting them up for hardship or treatment interruptions.” She reminds the group that the clinic has already stopped accepting other incentives, such as complimentary dinners from pharmaceutical representatives, and asserts, “I see this as consistent with those changes in our policies.”

Dr. Silverstein raises his hand. “But under the Physician Payments Sunshine Act, drug samples are specifically exempt from mandatory reporting—unlike material gifts, consulting fees, or travel perks. That distinction shows drug samples aren’t the same as the other items we’ve stopped accepting. Maybe we should reconsider this decision, Dr. Williams.”

Dr. Williams turns to him. “But are we truly helping our patients when we start them on medications they won’t be able to continue without significant financial strain? Are free samples actually improving their long-term care, or are we just offering a temporary fix that leads to more problems later?”

The room falls silent as the staff weighs the dilemma: for some patients, free samples are the only opportunity to begin essential therapy and see if the medication works for them without risking money they don’t have. Yet, the samples often introduce patients to expensive brand-name drugs, which become unaffordable once the samples end, sometimes resulting in interrupted care and increased stress. The team is left to consider whether the use of samples—while providing short-term relief—may ultimately do more harm than good, and whether their distribution influences not only patient health, but also the physicians’ own prescribing habits and the clinic’s ethical standards.

ethical_issues.question: Are drug samples truly beneficial to patients who cannot afford the full treatment regimen?
keypoints: Drug samples constitute the sole means by which some patients can access medications, thereby helping to alleviate short-term financial burdens associated with medical treatment.
Free samples enable patients to evaluate a drug’s efficacy, tolerability, and personal preference prior to incurring the high costs of full treatment, thus reducing resource wastage.

The use of drug samples is particularly important among high-risk patient populations who experience poor medication adherence and deteriorating health status due to economic constraints; restricting sample distribution may consequently diminish their access to necessary medications.

The appropriate use of drug samples requires implementation of adequate safeguards and reliance on physicians’ professional judgment to ensure that the benefits outweigh the risks, thereby genuinely assisting patients unable to afford complete therapeutic regimens.

ethical_issues.question: Does the provision of drug samples influence physicians’ prescribing behavior and lead to increased medication costs for patients?
keypoints: Drug samples influence physicians’ prescribing habits, making them more likely to prescribe higher-cost brand-name drugs rather than equivalent generic medications.

The use of free samples may lead patients to continue using brand-name drugs after the samples are exhausted, resulting in treatment interruptions due to inability to afford the full course, thereby increasing patients’ financial burden.

As a marketing tool of pharmaceutical companies, the costs associated with drug samples are ultimately passed on to society through higher drug prices, contributing to the escalation of overall healthcare expenditures.

title: Professionalism versus Antiharassment in Student Evaluation
case:
You look up to see Dr. Syed walk into the attending physician lounge, throwing her long white coat on the table while collapsing onto the couch in one fluid, practiced movement. You haven’t seen her looking this beat since you were emergency medicine residents together, and certainly not since you were both hired as tenure-track attending physicians.
“What’s up?” you ask her.
“It’s these students,” she says, exasperated.
“What happened?” you ask.
She bolts upright on the couch, fists clenched at her sides. “I have students being rude to nurses, not preparing for rounds, being cavalier about the practice of emergency medicine,” she barks. “People’s lives are at stake! I absolutely cannot have that kind of behavior in the ER.”
“So, write them up,” you say nonchalantly. “This isn’t the first time you’ve had bad students. The ER seems to attract them.”
“That’s the problem,” she said, slumping back against the cushion. “I know I need to be pretty critical of these students, but after that student harassment workshop last month, it seems we can’t say anything negative about them.”
“But you just said patients were at stake,” you interject. “They’re just going to keep doing it if you don’t say something.”
“I know, I know,” she admits, “but you saw what happened to Abena, yeah? A few legitimate critical comments about a student’s performance—trust me; I worked with him before—and all of a sudden, off the tenure track. You think that’s a coincidence?”
You doubt it was a coincidence. “So, what are you going to do? Using negative language in evals is unavoidable, especially with this batch of students.”
“I don’t know,” she mutters. “This ‘antiharassment’ movement,” she says, making air quotes with her fingers, “is getting out of hand. I feel like I’ve been muzzled. How am I supposed to teach if I’m worried I’ll lose my job or a promotion if I criticize my students?”

“Rough day?” you ask.

Dr. Syed sits upright, fists pressing into the cushion at her sides. “They’re being disrespectful to the nurses, coming to rounds unprepared, acting flippant about emergency medicine,” she snaps. “This isn’t just about grades—people’s lives are on the line. I can’t tolerate that kind of behavior in the ER.”

“If they’re that bad, just write them up,” you suggest, not unkindly. “You’ve dealt with problem students before. The ER always seems to draw them.”

She shakes her head, slumping back. “That’s just it. I know I have to call them out, but after that student harassment workshop last month, it feels like we can’t say anything critical anymore.”

You raise an eyebrow. “But you just said patient safety is at risk. If you don’t address it, nothing will change.”

She nods, looking conflicted. “You remember what happened to Abena, right? She made a few legitimate, critical comments on a student’s evaluation—someone I’d worked with, so I know it was warranted—and suddenly she’s off the tenure track. You think that was a coincidence?”

You’re fairly certain it wasn’t. “So what’s your plan? With students like this, negative feedback in their evaluations is unavoidable.”

“I honestly don’t know,” she admits, her tone low. “This so-called ‘antiharassment’ movement,” she says, making exaggerated air quotes, “has gone too far. I feel like I can’t say anything without risking my job or a promotion. How am I supposed to teach if I’m afraid to criticize students, even when it’s necessary?”

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with students whose professional behavior falls seriously short of the required standards, how should faculty fulfill their duties of reporting and remediation?
keypoints: Faculty have a nonnegotiable duty to report and remediate students whose professional behavior falls seriously short of the required standards, and this obligation must be steadfastly upheld.

Prior to formally documenting evaluations, faculty should engage in candid communication with students to ascertain whether temporary stressors or other factors may have contributed to the unprofessional behavior, thereby providing an opportunity for correction.
Faculty ought to treat students with attentiveness, respect, and empathy, avoiding treating them in ways they would not want the students to treat patients, thereby serving as positive role models.
In cases of repeated and serious breaches of professionalism, faculty must take decisive and timely corrective actions to safeguard patient safety and maintain quality of care.

If institutional policies or administrative practices impede faculty from fulfilling their duties to report and remediate, faculty should proactively raise these concerns with the administration and advocate for systemic improvements to uphold professional standards.
Faculty bear the responsibility to ensure that graduates possess at least the minimal level of professional competence necessary to practice safely in the public healthcare domain.

ethical_issues.question: How should faculty balance the conflict between providing negative evaluations of students’ professionalism and adhering to antiharassment policies?
keypoints: Faculty have a responsibility to ensure that students possess at least the minimal standard of professional conduct and are duty-bound to report and remediate serious deficiencies in professionalism.

Before submitting a negative evaluation, faculty should engage in frank communication with the student to explore whether the inappropriate behavior stems from temporary stressors or misunderstandings.
Repeated and serious breaches of professionalism require firm and appropriate corrective action.
Faculty should treat students in the manner they would expect students to treat patients—demonstrating attentiveness, respect, and empathy.

If institutional policies or antiharassment mechanisms impede faculty from providing reasonable evaluations of students, faculty should proactively engage with the administration to advocate for policy improvements.

Faculty must seek a balance between safeguarding students’ rights and upholding professional oversight; ideally, policies should support faculty in guiding students professionally and protect those acting in good faith from undue restriction or retaliation.

title: Pimping: Report or Do Nothing?
case:
Mark shuffled behind Dr. Powell, furiously writing out the LaFarge equation for estimating oxygen consumption on his clipboard. As usual, he had embarrassed himself while presenting the previous patient after forgetting to do the basic cardiac calculations before rounds. He promised himself he wouldn’t forget it again.
Mark’s pediatric cardiology clerkship, now only in its second week, had been the worst of his clinical years. Cardiology had never been his strong suit. During the first week, Mark’s struggle with interpreting blood gas results and repeated confusion of VSD with ASD had made it apparent that he was the weakest of the five clerkship students.
Today, however, none of his peers were having luck with Dr. Powell’s relentless pimping. Dr. Powell was a decent teacher, though his reliance on that particular teaching tool made every morning miserable.
“Mark, maybe you can do better than your colleague.” Mark snapped to attention. Dr. Powell had begun questioning the group about the next patient. Mark was standing second in the line of students outside the room. His colleague to the left of him looked distraught, fumbling in his notes for the answer to the question he just missed. “Based on the echocardiogram, what kind of congenital defect should we be looking for?”
“Uh,” Mark stuttered. He had viewed the imaging study for this patient before rounds this morning, but he was always terrible at septal defects. “Is it an ASD?” Mark answered tenuously.
“Jesus, Mark, have you learned anything in school?” Dr. Powell barked at the top of his lungs. “I can’t believe you’re even in the same class as these guys! At this rate, the only good thing I’ll be able to do is fail you from this clerkship. Go the library and do not come back until you know what you’re talking about.”
Mark was stunned. Hadn’t the other guy missed the same question? Out of the corner of his eye, Mark saw his colleague’s shocked expression turn into steeled discomfort as he suddenly faced forward. Dr. Powell stared at Mark expectantly. Taking the hint, Mark turned away and started towards the end of the hall as the pimping continued behind him.
Nurses at the charge station at the end of the hallway looked at him sympathetically; they had heard the tirade all the way at the end of the ward. Staring dejectedly at his feet and hating every stupid neuron in his head, Mark literally ran into his colleague Jarna on her pediatrics rotation, tripping over her neon orange clogs.
She put her hand on his shoulder, looked at him straight in the eye, and said, “Suck it up, dude. This is medical school.”
case_rewrite:

He still cringed at how he had floundered during rounds, forgetting basic cardiac calculations and earning a pointed glare from Dr. Powell. This pediatric cardiology clerkship, now in his second week, felt like the hardest stretch of his clinical training. Cardiology had always been his weak spot. In the first week alone, Mark had muddled through blood gas interpretations and mixed up VSDs with ASDs so often that it was clear to everyone—himself included—that he was struggling more than any other student in the group.

But today, Mark wasn’t alone in feeling under siege. None of the five clerks seemed able to handle Dr. Powell’s barrage of rapid-fire questions. Dr. Powell was known for his tough teaching style, and while he was a decent educator, his relentless use of “pimping” made every morning feel like a trial by fire.

“Mark, maybe you can do better than your colleague,” Dr. Powell suddenly called out, his voice slicing through the awkward silence. Mark’s attention snapped back to the group. He stood second in line outside the patient’s room, a step behind his classmate, who was fumbling through his notes after missing a question. “Based on the echocardiogram, what congenital defect are we looking for?” Dr. Powell pressed.

Mark hesitated. He had reviewed the patient’s imaging earlier that morning, but septal defects always tangled him up. “Um, is it an ASD?” he offered, voice uncertain.

Dr. Powell’s reaction was swift and loud. “Jesus, Mark, have you learned anything in school?” he shouted, his tone echoing down the hall. “I can’t believe you’re even in the same class as these guys! At this rate, the only good thing I’ll do is fail you from this clerkship. Go to the library and don’t come back until you know what you’re talking about.”

Mark stood frozen in disbelief. Hadn’t his classmate just missed the same question? He caught a glimpse of his colleague’s face—shocked, then quickly hardening into a mask of discomfort as he turned forward. Dr. Powell stared at Mark, making it clear he expected him to leave. Defeated, Mark turned away and trudged down the hallway, the sound of Dr. Powell’s questioning resuming behind him.

Near the nurses’ station, Mark could feel sympathetic eyes following him—the nurses had heard every word of Dr. Powell’s tirade. Staring at the floor, feeling every bit a failure, he rounded the corner and nearly collided with his friend Jarna, who was on her own pediatrics rotation, her neon orange clogs impossible to miss.

Jarna steadied him with a hand on his shoulder, looked him straight in the eye, and said, “Suck it up, dude. This is medical school.”

ethical_issues.question: Should Mark report Dr. Powell’s persistent questioning style (“pimping”) if he believes it undermines student well-being and human dignity?
keypoints: Reporting Dr. Powell’s inappropriate verbal abuse contributes to upholding the human dignity of medical students and promotes accountability of attending physicians for their teaching conduct.

From the perspective of practical consequences, Mark’s report may not necessarily result in a worse grade; rather, it could prompt the academic administration to revoke Dr. Powell’s evaluation privileges, thereby alleviating Mark’s concerns about grade impairment.

If Dr. Powell’s behavior stems solely from neglecting evidence-based teaching methods, reporting him may facilitate improvements in his instructional approach, benefiting both future students and the physician himself.

If Dr. Powell acts with malicious intent or exhibits character flaws, early reporting and removal from his teaching position is more conducive to protecting student rights and maintaining a healthy educational environment.
Mark should weigh his personal short-term interests against long-term values and choose actions that contribute to fostering a respectful and just teaching environment.

title: Advising the “Gunner”: The Student with Noncognitive Learning Difficulties
case:
You’re barely one sip into your first cup of coffee of the day when the administrative assistant drops it on the desk with a thud: the looming stack of clerkship evaluations. It is going to be a very long day. When you became clerkship director of surgery, you expected the worst part of your job to be dealing with arrogant attending physicians. Little did you know that reviewing resident notes about medical students would be the bane of every rotation. The first file in the stack is flagged with a bright red sticky note. You grumble to yourself, knowing exactly what that means. You open the file.
Melanie, a third-year medical student, is currently in the middle of her surgery clerkship. You recall the chief resident saying she was “brilliantly talented” in a department meeting last week, a “future pioneering vascular surgeon, for sure.” Perusing the scribbled notes, you see that one resident reports that Melanie is an “anatomy expert” in the operating room during every procedure and “knows exactly how long to cut sutures.” An attending note states: “the most efficient presenter of patients I have ever known.” There is even a note from a patient: “Melanie was considerate, compassionate, and went out of her way to make sure all of our questions were answered, even when other students and doctors couldn’t answer them for us.”
Puzzled, you wonder why this file had the infamous red note.
As you thumb through the file, you find one note from a resident: “intense, rubs me the wrong way, doesn’t seem to know when to stop asking questions.” Another resident note calls Melanie a “gunner” with the “typical gunner problem of being almost unprofessional.” You start to find more negative notes, including one from an attending who was approached by Melanie’s clerkmates, saying that Melanie’s competitiveness made him and other students uncomfortable. According to that anecdotal report, Melanie subtly interrupts her peers to answer pimp questions and aggressively asks questions in front of studentsandresidents to demonstrate her knowledge. Even in front of patients, she is continually competing with others to be the best. Another student reported that Melanie clearly treated the others as inferior students with her condescending demeanor and her hypercompetitive attitude. She was a gunner and her behavior was unprofessional, the student concludes.
As you spread all the notes out on your desk, you cannot find a description of a specific incident in which Melanie clearly stepped out of line to mistreat her fellow students. The opinions on Melanie vary widely. On one hand, some of her colleagues feel attacked and mistreated by her. On the other, she is an excellent student with keen bedside manner and a promising career in surgery.

One resident describes Melanie as “intense, rubs me the wrong way, doesn’t seem to know when to stop asking questions.” Another labels her a “gunner” who is “almost unprofessional.” As you read on, negative comments accumulate. An attending notes that Melanie’s clerkship peers approached him, expressing discomfort with her competitiveness. According to their account, Melanie regularly interrupts classmates to answer questions directed at the group, and aggressively asks questions herself in front of both students and residents, seemingly to showcase her knowledge. Even in front of patients, she appears to be in constant competition to stand out. A fellow student reports that Melanie acts as though her peers are inferior, citing her condescending manner and relentless drive to outshine others, ultimately concluding that her “gunner” behavior crosses into unprofessionalism.

You spread the evaluations across your desk, looking for any documentation of a clear, concrete incident where Melanie mistreated her peers. There are none—just a collection of subjective impressions and conflicting perspectives. On the one hand, Melanie’s patients and some faculty praise her clinical skills, efficiency, and bedside manner. On the other, her colleagues describe feeling undermined and uncomfortable in her presence.

You’re left with a dilemma: Melanie is undoubtedly a gifted and compassionate student, but the discord among her peers and instructors raises significant concerns about her professionalism and the learning environment she helps to shape.

ethical_issues.question: How should unprofessional behaviors exhibited by medical students during clinical clerkships be addressed to ensure the upholding of professional ethics?
keypoints: The clerkship director should comprehensively gather information and engage in thorough communication with faculty and students who have raised concerns, ensuring firsthand data is obtained before directly interviewing the student, and conduct a rational assessment of the nature and severity of the issue.

Interventions should focus on specific behavioral manifestations, clearly communicating the potential evaluative and professional consequences of failing to correct such behaviors, while avoiding excessive speculation regarding underlying motivations.

A systematic approach to investigating and directly addressing student behavior should be implemented as early as possible, utilizing the SOAP teaching framework (Subjective impression, Objective facts, Assessment, Plan) to provide concrete feedback and develop a behavioral remediation plan.

Formative feedback should be delivered in a timely manner, ideally at the midpoint of the clerkship, to ensure the student has sufficient opportunity to understand the concerns and modify their behavior accordingly.

The clerkship director should incorporate professionalism into the formal learning objectives, explicitly defining its meaning, assessment criteria, and the consequences of failing to meet these standards, thereby emphasizing to students that clinical knowledge and professionalism are equally important.

Documentation of all advisement and interventions must be maintained and reported to the appropriate academic administration in accordance with institutional policies to ensure systematic educational and managerial oversight.

Medical students should be cultivated to accept feedback of all types, valuing positive evaluations while also embracing constructive criticism, thereby promoting the ongoing development of their professional competence.

title: Is More Screening Always Better?
case:
Andrew, a fourth-year medical student, applied for a residency in family medicine. While on a rotation at his top-choice program, he noticed something interesting. During the family medicine rotation at his medical school, residents and attending physicians had recommended biopsy if a patient’s prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels were above 4 nanograms per milliliter (ng/mL). In the program that Andrew hoped to become part of, however, residents and attending physicians often recommended biopsies if the patient’s PSA levels were above 2.5 ng/mL, a practice Andrew had not seen before.
When Andrew asked the resident about this, he was told that this lower PSA threshold for biopsy allowed doctors not only to catch more cases of prostate cancer but to catch those cancers earlier, when they were more treatable. This made sense to Andrew, and he wondered why the family medicine department at his medical school did not do the same.
He approached the chair of family medicine at his school, who told him there was not enough evidence that biopsies at lower thresholds actually improved patient outcomes and, in fact, they could lead to overuse of resources and overdiagnosis of prostate cancer.
Andrew was confused. Both approaches seemed reasonable to him, and, given his lack of experience and his respect for both institutions, he was unsure which was better. He decided to talk to the dean of curriculum at his medical school about his dilemma. After their discussion, the dean wondered how many of his students encountered similar variations in care on rotations at other hospitals and how those variations should be discussed in the medical school curriculum.
case_rewrite:
Andrew, a fourth-year medical student, was in the midst of applying for a residency in family medicine. Eager to impress at his top-choice program, he paid close attention to the clinical practices during his rotation there. As he observed patient care, Andrew noticed something that stood out to him. At his own medical school, the family medicine residents and attending physicians had consistently recommended a prostate biopsy only when a patient’s prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level exceeded 4 nanograms per milliliter (ng/mL). However, at this new program, he saw that residents and attendings frequently advised biopsies for patients whose PSA levels were above 2.5 ng/mL—a threshold significantly lower than what he was used to.

Perplexed by this difference, Andrew asked one of the residents why they used a lower cutoff. The resident explained that by recommending biopsies at a PSA level above 2.5 ng/mL, they could identify more cases of prostate cancer, and do so at an earlier stage, increasing the chances of effective treatment. The explanation seemed logical to Andrew, and he began to question why his own institution did not adopt this approach.

Seeking clarity, Andrew decided to consult the chair of family medicine at his medical school. The chair explained that there was insufficient evidence that initiating biopsies at lower PSA thresholds actually led to better patient outcomes. In fact, he cautioned, lowering the threshold could result in more unnecessary procedures, overuse of healthcare resources, and a higher risk of overdiagnosing prostate cancer—finding cancers that might never have caused harm if left undetected.

Andrew found himself genuinely confused. Both rationales appeared reasonable, and given his respect for both institutions and his limited clinical experience, he felt uncertain about which practice was best. Wanting to make sense of the conflicting approaches, he arranged a meeting with the dean of curriculum at his school to discuss his observations and concerns. After their conversation, the dean reflected on how often students might encounter such variations in care during their rotations at different hospitals and pondered how best to address these discrepancies and the ethical issues they raise in the medical school curriculum.

ethical_issues.question: If services with unclear evidence are indeed offered, how should we ensure that patients’ rights to make informed decisions are protected?
keypoints: Respect patient autonomy by ensuring that patients fully understand the potential benefits, risks, and scientific evidence underlying PSA screening before making a decision about whether to undergo the test.

Clearly inform patients that PSA testing may trigger a cascade of subsequent diagnostic and therapeutic procedures, emphasizing that the benefits of early prostate cancer detection are limited and that there is a significant risk of overdiagnosis and overtreatment.

Provide an impartial explanation of the variations in PSA biopsy thresholds used by different institutions, highlighting that the additional benefits of a lower threshold lack conclusive evidence, while associated harms and resource utilization are nearly inevitable.

Encourage patients to make autonomous decisions regarding screening by integrating their personal values and weighing the risks of prostate cancer mortality against the harms of overdiagnosis and overtreatment, thereby avoiding healthcare providers making decisions on their behalf.
