title: The Importance of Quality of Life to Patient Decision Making in Breast Cancer Care
case:
When Marsha was diagnosed with stage I breast cancer, her gynecologist referred her to Dr. Martin, a highly respected surgeon, to discuss removal of the mass. Dr. Martin recommended a mastectomy, explaining that he had long-term experience and success with the procedure, with very low complication rates and few cancer recurrences in his patients. Marsha was comforted by Dr. Martin’s confidence and success rate, but left the appointment greatly concerned about undergoing such extensive surgery.
After some online research, Marsha found that, for women her age (38) diagnosed with early-stage breast cancers, a lumpectomy was an equally effective tumor-removal alternative to mastectomy. She read that, while the latter may provide more peace of mind by removing the entire breast, it was a more invasive procedure, often followed by reconstructive surgery and a significant recovery period. The lumpectomy would preserve most of the shape and sensation in her breast. And, as an avid runner who raced frequently and had an active lifestyle overall, Marsha considered the shorter recovery time and avoidance of reconstruction added benefits. Of course, her health and curing the cancer were her foremost concern, but, after careful consideration and many conversations with her family, Marsha decided to ask Dr. Martin to perform a lumpectomy instead of a mastectomy.
Marsha was surprised by Dr. Martin’s reaction. Although studies had shown no statistically significant difference in survival rates in patients with stage I breast cancer who underwent lumpectomies versus mastectomies, Dr. Martin said that, based on his own training and experience, a mastectomy was a much better way of preventing recurrence. He said he did not want Marsha to have to face the possibility of a second surgery should the postoperative pathology report show positive lymph nodes or unclear margins. Dr. Martin urged Marsha to rethink her decision.
She left his office confused and overwhelmed. While her limited research had led her to believe that a lumpectomy was the better choice for her, she respected Dr. Martin’s experienced clinical judgment and his concern for his patients’ well-being. “When it comes to breast cancer in a woman your age,” he told Marsha, “there is no such thing as being too cautious.” Marsha would have to travel to a nearby city to find a surgeon to perform the lumpectomy if Dr. Martin refused. Since both forms of treatment had comparable outcomes, Marsha wondered whether she should put aside her own preferences and follow Dr. Martin’s recommendation.
case_rewrite:
When Marsha received a diagnosis of stage I breast cancer, her gynecologist referred her to Dr. Martin, a highly regarded and experienced surgeon, to discuss surgical options for removing the tumor. During their appointment, Dr. Martin recommended a mastectomy, emphasizing his extensive experience with the procedure and highlighting his record of low complication rates and rare cancer recurrence among his patients. Marsha found reassurance in Dr. Martin’s confidence and expertise, yet she left the consultation feeling deeply unsettled about the prospect of such an extensive operation.

Determined to understand her options, Marsha turned to online resources and discovered that, for women her age—38—with early-stage breast cancer, a lumpectomy could be just as effective as a mastectomy for removing the tumor. She learned that while a mastectomy might provide a greater sense of security by removing the entire breast, it was notably more invasive, often entailing complex reconstructive surgery and a lengthy recovery. In contrast, a lumpectomy would allow her to preserve most of the breast’s appearance and sensation. Given Marsha’s passion for running and her highly active lifestyle, the benefits of a quicker recovery and avoiding reconstruction were particularly appealing. Above all, Marsha’s top priority was her health and the effective treatment of her cancer. After many thoughtful discussions with her family, she decided to ask Dr. Martin if he would perform a lumpectomy instead of a mastectomy.

Marsha was taken aback by Dr. Martin’s response. Despite evidence from clinical studies indicating no significant difference in survival rates between lumpectomy and mastectomy for stage I breast cancer, Dr. Martin insisted that, based on his training and personal experience, mastectomy was the superior option for preventing recurrence. He expressed concern about the possibility that the pathology report after a lumpectomy might reveal positive lymph nodes or unclear margins, potentially necessitating a second surgery. Dr. Martin urged Marsha to reconsider her decision.

Marsha left his office feeling confused and overwhelmed. Her research had convinced her that a lumpectomy was more suitable for her needs, but she also respected Dr. Martin’s clinical judgment and clear concern for her well-being. “With breast cancer in someone your age,” Dr. Martin told her, “there’s no such thing as being too careful.” If Dr. Martin declined to perform the lumpectomy, Marsha would need to seek out a surgeon in a neighboring city. With both treatment options offering comparable outcomes, Marsha now wondered whether she should defer to Dr. Martin’s recommendation or stand by her own preferences.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the principle of nonmaleficence with respect for patient autonomy when recommending treatment options?
keypoints: Physicians should adhere to the ethical principles of nonmaleficence, beneficence, and respect for patient autonomy when recommending treatment plans.

Within a shared decision-making model, physicians ought to integrate their professional expertise with the patient’s values, comprehensively presenting the medical evidence, risks, and benefits of all treatment options to facilitate a consensus decision that is both medically sound and aligned with the patient’s expectations.
Physicians must avoid offering treatments they consider ineffective or harmful and must not sacrifice the principle of nonmaleficence under the pretext of respecting patient autonomy.

When consensus on a treatment plan cannot be reached between physician and patient, the physician should respect the patient’s wishes while appropriately recommending referral to another healthcare provider to ensure the patient receives suitable medical care.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient is faced with two treatment options of comparable efficacy, how can physicians ensure that the patient’s personal values and quality of life are incorporated into the decision-making process?
keypoints: Physicians should adopt a shared decision-making model that integrates their professional expertise with the patient’s values and life expectations to reach a consensus on treatment decisions.

Physicians should actively explore and assist patients in articulating their values, fears, and treatment goals through effective questioning, ensuring that the treatment plan is both medically appropriate and aligned with the patient’s quality of life and personal preferences.

When the patient faces no immediate life-threatening risk and treatment outcomes are comparable, physicians should move beyond discussions focused solely on survival rates to address the patient’s multidimensional concerns—including treatment process, recovery time, appearance, and lifestyle—to facilitate comprehensive and individualized treatment decisions.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient’s treatment choice conflicts with the physician’s professional judgment, how should the physician manage the situation to maintain trust and a collaborative decision-making relationship?
keypoints: Physicians should respect patients’ values and treatment goals, advocate for, and practice shared decision making, avoiding unilateral treatment decisions.

Physicians have the responsibility to comprehensively and objectively present the medical evidence, risks, and benefits of different treatment options to ensure that patients can make fully informed choices.
By inquiring about patients’ treatment goals and concerns, physicians can more accurately understand patients’ value orientations and priorities.

Shared decision making must be founded on mutual trust, respect, and open communication, aiming to reach a treatment plan that is both medically appropriate and aligned with the patient’s personal life expectations and psychological needs.

title: Are IVF Risk-Sharing Programs Ethical?
case:
Dr. Rearden, the head of a fertility clinic in Philadelphia, called a meeting with his staff to discuss budgeting for the coming year. During the meeting, Dr. Rearden proposed implementing a “risk-sharing” program. Patients selected for such programs would initially pay a higher fee to the clinic. If a patient had a successful pregnancy, then the clinic would keep her entire fee. If the patient did not become pregnant, a previously specified proportion of the fee would be returned to her.
In his presentation to the staff, Dr. Rearden explained that the program would be beneficial to both the clinic and patients. The program represents a safety net for patients who pay for IVF out of pocket by leaving them money to pursue other options should their treatment fail. Moreover, the higher fee paid by patients who become pregnant ensures that the clinic will have money to reimburse the patients for whom treatment is unsuccessful.
At the conclusion of Dr. Rearden’s presentation, Dr. Whipple, a long-time ob-gyn physician in the clinic, asked to speak. “I can appreciate wanting to offer a safety net for patients, especially given that IVF is not covered by insurance,” Dr. Whipple began. “But I have some serious reservations about implementing such a program. First, it seems that those who would be selected as candidates for the program are also those most likely to become pregnant, so we would be taking advantage of patients in a moment of substantial emotional stress by essentially overcharging them. Second, and more importantly, if medical payment is based on outcome, our focus will inevitably shift from doing what is best for our patients to trying to get the desired outcome, in this case pregnancy, regardless of what that means for the people we’re treating. I just don’t think we should go down this road.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Rearden, the director of a fertility clinic in Philadelphia, convened his staff for an annual budget meeting. As everyone settled in, Dr. Rearden introduced a new proposal: the implementation of a “risk-sharing” program for their IVF patients. Under this arrangement, patients who enrolled would pay an elevated fee upfront. If a patient achieved a successful pregnancy, the clinic would retain the entire amount. However, if the patient did not become pregnant, a predetermined portion of her payment would be refunded.

Presenting the concept, Dr. Rearden emphasized the benefits for both the clinic and their patients. He explained that this model could serve as a financial safety net for patients forced to pay out of pocket for IVF, potentially easing the blow of an unsuccessful cycle by providing funds to pursue alternative options. Additionally, he noted, the increased fees from successful pregnancies would supply the clinic with adequate resources to reimburse those whose treatments failed.

As Dr. Rearden wrapped up his presentation, Dr. Whipple—a veteran ob-gyn at the clinic—raised her hand to speak. “I understand the desire to support our patients, especially since insurance rarely covers IVF,” Dr. Whipple began thoughtfully. “But I have significant concerns about this program. First, it appears that candidates selected for the risk-sharing option would likely be those with the highest chance of becoming pregnant. That could mean we’re targeting emotionally vulnerable patients and charging them extra at a difficult time in their lives. Second, and perhaps more troubling, if our reimbursement depends on patients getting pregnant, our priorities might shift. We could end up focusing on achieving a pregnancy at any cost, rather than truly acting in the patient’s best interest. That could lead us, even unintentionally, to recommend aggressive or unnecessary treatments just to avoid refunding fees. I’m not sure this is the direction we want to take.”

ethical_issues.question: Do risk-sharing programs cause physicians to shift their focus from the best interests of the patient to pursuing pregnancy outcomes, thereby neglecting the impact of treatment on the patient?
keypoints: Risk-sharing programs may shift physicians’ focus from the best interests of the patient to achieving pregnancy outcomes, as medical remuneration is contingent upon results, thereby creating conflicts of interest.

Conflicts of interest may incentivize physicians to engage in inappropriate high-risk practices—such as multiple embryo transfers or excessive ovarian stimulation—to avoid issuing refunds, which can compromise patient welfare and overlook the comprehensive impact of treatment on patients.

Physicians should adhere to evidence-based medical principles and avoid recommending ancillary procedures that lack clear indications and incur substantial costs, in order to prevent economic motivations from unduly influencing clinical decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: In risk-sharing programs, how can it be ensured that patients fully understand the risks and alternatives of the program during the informed consent process and are able to make rational decisions?
keypoints: Given patients’ emotional vulnerability and susceptibility to cognitive biases (such as overestimation of success rates, anchoring effects, and confirmation bias), clinicians must convey accurate information in a clear, objective manner that actively counteracts these biases to assist patients in rationally assessing risks.
The program design should incorporate mechanisms that protect patient interests, ensuring that patients have sufficient time and space to evaluate the risk-sharing program and alternative options.

Detailed explanations should be provided regarding patients’ probability of achieving pregnancy, the fee structure of the program, the definition of success (pregnancy versus live birth), the proportion of refunds in the event of unsuccessful outcomes, and any potential additional costs, thereby guaranteeing transparency and completeness of information.

Clinicians should proactively identify and avoid reinforcing patients’ cognitive biases, particularly excessive optimism regarding success rates, to safeguard patients’ ability to make informed and rational decisions based on comprehensive information.

ethical_issues.question: Is the pricing mechanism of risk-sharing programs reasonable, or might it lead patients to question whether the program is primarily intended to generate profit rather than to share risks fairly?
keypoints: The pricing mechanism of risk-sharing programs, which charges fees contingent on outcomes, may be challenged as illicit or contingent fees, raising ethical concerns.

Patients selected for these programs are often those with higher probabilities of achieving pregnancy, which may be perceived as overcharging vulnerable patients during emotionally stressful periods, thereby affecting fairness.

Patients who achieve successful pregnancy pay higher fees than they would at clinics without risk-sharing programs, potentially prompting concerns about the fairness and underlying motives of the program.

If the refund proportion for patients who do not conceive does not adequately reflect their objectively low likelihood of success, patients may perceive the program as primarily profit-driven rather than a fair risk-sharing arrangement.

Key factors in evaluating whether a program genuinely embodies risk sharing—pooling patient risks and allowing the clinic a modest return—include the fee increase, refund percentage, ancillary costs, and scope of services; rational design of these elements enhances the program’s ethical justification and patient trust.

title: Physician Responsibility When a Surrogate Mother Breaks Her Contract
case:
Dr. Kerr greets Stacy, who is in her first trimester of pregnancy, for her second prenatal visit. Stacy’s situation is still relatively rare in Dr. Kerr’s obstetric practice: after extensive counseling, Stacy decided to become a surrogate mother for a gay couple. During her first visit, Stacy told Dr. Kerr about the surrogacy contract she had entered into, which detailed the compensation she would receive for her time and medical bills and stipulated that she would report for all prenatal visits, refrain from risky behavior such as smoking or alcohol consumption, and keep an open medical record, so the couple could know directly how the pregnancy was progressing.
Stacy tells Dr. Kerr that, apart from a little morning sickness, she has no complaints. Dr. Kerr goes through her examination as usual. “Everything looks great,” she tells Stacy. “Do you have any questions for me?”
Stacy hesitates for a moment, but after an encouraging look from Dr. Kerr, she begins to speak. “When I signed the surrogacy contract,” Stacy says, “I didn’t think I’d have any trouble not drinking alcohol. But I’m finding it really hard to give it up. I did some research online and read a little alcohol won’t hurt the baby, so I’ve started drinking a glass or two of wine a week. I know I said I wouldn’t, so please don’t put anything in my record, but what I’m doing is OK, right?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Kerr welcomes Stacy into the exam room for her second prenatal appointment. Stacy, now in her first trimester, presents a situation that is still uncommon in Dr. Kerr’s obstetric practice: following thorough counseling, Stacy chose to act as a surrogate for a gay couple. At her initial visit, Stacy had explained to Dr. Kerr that she had signed a surrogacy contract. The agreement specified the compensation Stacy would receive for her time and medical expenses and required her to attend all prenatal appointments, avoid high-risk behaviors such as smoking or drinking alcohol, and allow her medical records to remain accessible so the couple could directly follow the progress of the pregnancy.

During today’s visit, Stacy reports that, aside from some mild morning sickness, she feels well. Dr. Kerr completes the routine examination and reassures Stacy, “Everything looks excellent.” She then asks if Stacy has any concerns or questions.

Stacy hesitates, glancing at Dr. Kerr before speaking. Encouraged by Dr. Kerr’s attentive demeanor, Stacy admits, “When I agreed to the surrogacy contract, I honestly thought it would be easy to give up alcohol. But I’m realizing it’s harder than I expected. I did some reading online, and it seems like a little alcohol isn’t supposed to be harmful, so lately I’ve been having a glass or two of wine each week. I know I promised not to drink, so please don’t include this in my chart, but is what I’m doing really a problem?”

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician balance maintaining patient confidentiality with the obligation to ensure the accuracy of the medical record when a surrogate mother requests concealment of her alcohol consumption?
keypoints: The physician must ensure the accuracy and completeness of the medical record, strictly prohibiting any concealment or alteration of medical information.
The physician should clearly prioritize Stacy’s and her child’s health, committing to provide professional protection and support.
Open and honest communication by Stacy should be encouraged to foster trust and facilitate risk assessment between the patient, the physician, and the intended parents.
The physician should assist Stacy and the intended parents in jointly evaluating the potential effects of alcohol consumption on the fetus based on scientific evidence.
The physician should support Stacy and, when necessary, recommend behavioral interventions or counseling to safeguard the health of both mother and child.

ethical_issues.question: In surrogacy arrangements, how can physicians ensure that the welfare of the unborn child is adequately prioritized and foreseeable risks are effectively mitigated?
keypoints: Revised Key Points:

Physicians bear responsibility for the unborn child and must provide both the surrogate mother and the intended parents with information regarding the avoidance of risks to the child’s life, assisting them in making informed decisions that align with the child’s best interests.

Physicians should proactively communicate with the surrogate mother to assess her understanding of the potential risks associated with assisted reproduction and pregnancy, promptly addressing any gaps in knowledge and responding to her questions.

Physicians must clearly inform the surrogate mother that, despite thorough planning and preventive measures, unforeseeable risks may still arise; however, foreseeable risks related to surrogacy, assisted reproduction, and behaviors such as alcohol consumption should be minimized through appropriate planning.

All parties involved share the responsibility to collectively avoid foreseeable risks that could compromise the health and welfare of the child; when necessary, physicians should arrange for professional counseling to guide the surrogate mother in adopting responsible behaviors for her own health and that of the fetus.

ethical_issues.question: In the case of a surrogate mother breaching her contract, should the physician prioritize the terms of the surrogacy agreement or the health and welfare of the surrogate mother and fetus?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize the health and well-being of the surrogate mother and the fetus; their professional ethical obligations are not constrained by the terms of the surrogacy contract.
The obstetrician must provide professional and evidence-based medical advice and care based on the best interests of the pregnant woman and the fetus.
Physicians should respect the pregnant woman’s autonomy, communicate potential risks honestly, and support her in making informed and responsible decisions.
Physicians should maintain the accuracy and completeness of medical records, while promoting maternal and fetal safety and protecting patient confidentiality.

title: Shared Decision Making about IVF for Savior Siblings
case:
When Joe and Dana brought home their son Carl from the hospital, they were overjoyed. He quickly became their everything. Together, they lovingly captured Carl’s “firsts”—his first bite of solid food, his first steps, the first time he put on his Thomas the Tank Engine backpack to head off to preschool. When Carl began to fall asleep earlier and earlier, they attributed it to all the activity of preschool. They thought his pallor was due to a wintertime lack of sun. They became concerned though, when they noticed swelling in his abdomen and face. Not long afterward, bruises began blooming over his skin, especially on his trunk and abdomen, and they knew that something was wrong.
They were devastated when, at just five years old, Carl was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). They vowed to do everything they could to save their son. And when it became clear that a stem cell transplant was the best option, and no one they knew was a match, they decided to have another child to supply stem cells for Carl. They went to see Dr. Preed, a reproductive endocrinologist, and began the process of in vitro fertilization (IVF) with preimplantation human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing in earnest.
After a series of hormone injections, ova were taken from Dana and fertilized in vitro with Joe’s sperm. Resulting embryos were biopsied and tested for aneuploidy and they were HLA-typed. Only euploid embryos that were HLA matches for Carl were transferred, but they were few, and, after three cycles and $40,000 spent, Joe and Dana had not conceived. The hormones and appointments, on top of caring for a child who was quite sick, began to take a toll on the whole family. The course had also started to take its toll on Dr. Preed. Dana and Joe were impatient and frustrated. They called Dr. Preed many times each week, and he returned the calls, though he had nothing new to tell them. When Dana failed to conceive after a fourth cycle, Dr. Preed decided it was time to raise his concerns with the family.
When he started to do so, Joe stopped him. “We’re not going to give up,” he said, his eyes flashing, whether with anger or sadness Dr. Preed could not tell. Dana grasped her husband’s hand and nodded her assent. “If Carl were your child, you’d do anything you could to save him too. If you won’t continue to help us, we’ll find someone else who will.”
case_rewrite:
Joe and Dana were ecstatic when they brought their newborn son, Carl, home from the hospital. He immediately became the center of their world, and together they delighted in every milestone: capturing photos of Carl’s first taste of solid food, cheering when he toddled his first steps, and taking proud pictures as he donned his Thomas the Tank Engine backpack for his first day of preschool. As Carl started falling asleep earlier than usual, Joe and Dana chalked it up to the busy days at preschool. They dismissed his pale complexion as just a consequence of the gray winter months. But when swelling appeared in Carl’s abdomen and face, their concerns grew. Soon after, they noticed unusual bruises—dark patches blooming across his trunk and abdomen—and it became clear that something was terribly wrong.

Their world was turned upside down when, at only five years old, Carl was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Determined to do whatever it might take to save their son, Joe and Dana began searching for the best treatment. When doctors explained that a stem cell transplant offered Carl the best chance but that no suitable donor could be found, the couple decided to try to have another child who might serve as a stem cell donor for Carl. They sought out Dr. Preed, a reproductive endocrinologist, and started in vitro fertilization (IVF) with preimplantation HLA typing.

Dana underwent rounds of hormone injections, and eggs were retrieved and fertilized in the lab with Joe’s sperm. The resulting embryos were carefully tested for aneuploidy and HLA-typed. Only embryos that were both chromosomally normal and a tissue match for Carl were considered for transfer. However, such embryos were rare. Despite three cycles of IVF and $40,000 spent, there was still no pregnancy. The relentless cycle of medical appointments, hormone treatments, and the stress of caring for a seriously ill child began to weigh heavily on the family. The emotional strain also began to affect Dr. Preed. Joe and Dana, anxious and increasingly desperate, called Dr. Preed multiple times each week, hoping for updates and reassurance. Dr. Preed always returned their calls, even when there was no new information to offer.

After a fourth unsuccessful IVF cycle, Dr. Preed felt it was necessary to talk openly with Joe and Dana about his concerns. As he began, Joe cut him off, eyes bright with a mix of anger and grief that Dr. Preed couldn’t quite decipher. “We’re not going to give up,” Joe insisted. Dana squeezed his hand, silently agreeing. “If Carl were your son, you’d do everything too. If you won’t keep helping us, we’ll find someone else who will.”

ethical_issues.question: During the course of IVF-PGD treatment, how can patients’ psychological support needs be adequately met, especially when these needs exceed the physician’s professional expertise?
keypoints: A multidisciplinary approach should be adopted, with a core emphasis on referring patients to mental health professionals who possess specialized qualifications in reproductive counseling and infertility, while integrating psychological support.
Fertility treatment centers typically have mental health professionals on staff or should establish effective referral mechanisms to ensure patients receive specialized psychological support.

Maintaining open communication with the medical team caring for the affected child facilitates a comprehensive understanding of the patient’s family circumstances and supports the psychological health needs of the patients.

ethical_issues.question: When the prognosis for IVF treatment is very poor in Joe and Dana’s case, should the physician continue to provide treatment, or would it be more ethically appropriate to refer them to another clinic with a higher success rate?
keypoints: Decisions regarding treatment or refusal of treatment should always be patient-centered; physicians should communicate and collaborate fully with patients and their families to develop treatment plans jointly.

Clinicians have the authority to refuse to initiate treatments they regard as futile or having a very poor prognosis, but such decisions should be based on thorough medical assessment and ethical considerations.

When the prognosis for treatment is very poor or the intervention is deemed futile, physicians should fully inform patients and their families of the situation and proactively provide referral information, especially if other clinics have demonstrated higher success rates for similar medical indications.

Physicians should be attentive to the psychological burden and treatment-related stress experienced by patients and their families, and should provide support or recommendations as appropriate to promote the overall well-being of the patient.

title: Assisted Reproduction for Postmenopausal Women
case:
Dr. Deans, a fertility specialist, is meeting Lily and her husband Bill for the first time. As Dr. Deans gets to know her, he learns that Lily has wanted to have children since she was a little girl, but work—she lists her occupation as a corporate CEO—always seemed to get in the way. Now, at 53, she and her husband have decided to have a child before it is too late. Lily, who has undergone menopause, realizes that she no longer is able to have a child that will be genetically related to her, but she is willing to use donor eggs and her husband’s sperm to carry the child to term herself.
Dr. Deans carefully takes a complete history and does a thorough workup and physical exam. As he finishes, Lily looks up at him hopefully. “So,” she says, “can you help me to become a mother?”
Under Lily’s expectant gaze, Dr. Deans realizes he has conflicting responses to her request. Pregnancy is always riskier the older a woman is, but, if he’s being honest with himself, there’s really no medical reason why he shouldn’t help Lily get pregnant. Lily is 2 years younger than the age at which the American Society for Reproductive Medicine’s guidelines say IVF should be “discouraged” [1], and she has no comorbidities, such as hypertension or diabetes, that would make her a poor candidate for IVF. Indeed, Lily is in excellent health.
What’s making Dr. Deans uncomfortable doesn’t have much to do with the clinical situation at all—it’s the image of a 63-year-old mother cheering on her 10-year-old during school plays and soccer matches, or a 68-year-old telling her 15-year-old that she’s been diagnosed with cancer, or a devastated 17-year-old sitting on a hard wooden pew at his or her mother’s funeral.
Dr. Deans knows that the future is unpredictable regardless of a parent’s age, and, had Lily become pregnant without ART, he recognizes that he would not have the same hesitation. Still, he can’t help feeling that using ART resources in this case is not quite right, and he finds himself wanting to advise Lily against a procedure.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Deans, a fertility specialist, greets Lily and her husband, Bill, as they settle into his office for their first consultation. Throughout their conversation, Dr. Deans learns that Lily has dreamed of motherhood since childhood, but her demanding career as a corporate CEO repeatedly delayed her plans. Now, at 53, Lily and Bill have decided to pursue having a child before the window closes entirely. Lily, who has gone through menopause, understands that a child genetically related to her is no longer possible. Undeterred, she expresses her willingness to use donor eggs and Bill’s sperm, hoping to carry the pregnancy herself.

Dr. Deans conducts a thorough medical history, assessment, and physical examination. As he concludes, Lily gazes at him with eager anticipation. “So,” she asks, “can you help me become a mother?”

Caught by Lily’s hopeful expression, Dr. Deans feels torn. He knows that advanced maternal age brings increased risks with pregnancy; yet, clinically, there are no clear contraindications in Lily’s case. She is two years younger than the age at which the American Society for Reproductive Medicine suggests discouraging IVF, and she has no health conditions like hypertension or diabetes that would make the procedure inadvisable. In fact, Lily is in excellent health.

However, Dr. Deans realizes his discomfort is not rooted in Lily’s medical suitability, but rather in the broader implications. He pictures a 63-year-old mother cheering at a ten-year-old’s school performance, or a 68-year-old explaining a cancer diagnosis to her teenage child, or a 17-year-old coping with the loss of a parent. The unpredictability of life weighs on him, and he acknowledges that had Lily conceived naturally, these concerns might not trouble him as much.

Despite knowing that age alone should not be a barrier—especially when society values autonomy, equality, and non-discrimination—Dr. Deans finds himself questioning whether it is right to use assisted reproductive technology in this situation. He contemplates advising Lily against pursuing the procedure, even as he recognizes the need to balance her reproductive wishes, the welfare of any future child, and his ethical responsibilities as a physician.

ethical_issues.question: Should Postmenopausal Women Be Permitted to Fulfill Their Reproductive Desires Through Assisted Reproductive Technologies?
keypoints: The core ethical issue in assisted reproduction for postmenopausal women lies in balancing the patient’s reproductive autonomy with the welfare of the children born.

Arguments in favor of providing assisted reproductive technologies (ART) to postmenopausal women assert that denying donor-egg IVF contradicts societal values of equality and personal freedom, and that restricting reproductive rights based solely on age constitutes gender discrimination.

Opposing views emphasize that, from the perspective of the child’s welfare, postmenopausal pregnancy may increase the risk of obstetrical and neonatal complications for both mother and child, as well as the potential harm caused by early parental loss.

Physicians should, based on comprehensive medical screening, assessment of social support, and thorough counseling regarding the risks of advanced maternal age pregnancy and potential impacts on offspring, adhere to the principles of respect for patient autonomy and beneficence/nonmaleficence, providing assisted reproductive services in accordance with established professional guidelines.

ethical_issues.question: How do the parenting capacities of older parents and the potential harm to their children influence the ethical decision-making regarding postmenopausal reproduction?
keypoints: Reproductive matters should prioritize the best interests of the child, especially when medical interventions may contravene social and biological norms, warranting careful ethical consideration.
Parenting requires substantial emotional and physical investment, and some older parents may face risks related to insufficient capacity.

Children of older parents face an increased risk of early parental loss, which may lead to psychological harms such as depression and substance abuse, representing a potential harm that demands ethical attention.

Given that society generally accepts grandparents raising children—and that grandparents often contribute economic stability and parental maturity to the family unit—it follows that healthy older adults raising their own biological children should also be reasonably accepted.

The ethical evaluation of advanced-age reproduction centers on balancing the patient’s reproductive autonomy with the welfare of the child, taking into account the interests of both parties as well as the practical support systems available.

title: When Physicians and Surrogates Disagree about Futility
case:
Mrs. Smith was 46 when she suffered a cardiac arrest at home. Her 20-year-old daughter was with her at the time and called 911. Mrs. Smith was resuscitated by the paramedics and rushed to the nearest hospital, but had suffered severe loss of oxygen to the brain during the episode. She was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and required intubation and mechanical ventilation. An EKG revealed that Mrs. Smith had long QT syndrome, which her daughter said had never been diagnosed. Her daughter insisted that “everything be done” for her mother.
After 2 months in the ICU, Mrs. Smith’s brain functioning had not returned or shown improvement; she had not awakened or been conscious of where she was or who was in the room. Mrs. Smith’s care had been complicated by infections from the intravenous lines into and from her body, kidney failure and the need for dialysis, and worsening heart function that required an intra-aortic balloon pump. Her physicians judged that further treatment would be futile; it was highly unlikely that Mrs. Smith would leave the hospital alive, or, if she did, it was likely that she would return within days or weeks. Mrs. Smith was too sick to be placed in an outpatient center and remained in the medical ICU.
The medical team, treating complication upon complication, believed they were not helping Mrs. Smith heal in any way. They felt that continuing aggressive treatment violated medicine’s fundamental “first-do-no-harm” precept. When end-of-life care measures such as comfort care, withdrawing treatments, or assigning do-not-resuscitate status to Mrs. Smith were suggested, her daughter became extremely upset, saying “My mom gave me life, how can I take hers away?” At one point her daughter broke down and said, “I would rather visit my mom in the hospital than in the graveyard.”
case_rewrite:
At age 46, Mrs. Smith suffered a sudden cardiac arrest at home. Her 20-year-old daughter, who was present, immediately called 911. Paramedics arrived swiftly, resuscitated Mrs. Smith, and transported her to the nearest hospital. However, during the event, Mrs. Smith’s brain was deprived of oxygen for a significant period. Upon arrival, she was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), where she required intubation and mechanical ventilation. An EKG revealed Mrs. Smith had long QT syndrome—a condition her daughter insisted had never been diagnosed before. Distressed and anxious, her daughter demanded that “everything be done” to save her mother.

After two months in the ICU, there had been no improvement in Mrs. Smith’s brain function. She remained unresponsive and unconscious, showing no awareness of her surroundings or the people at her bedside. Over this period, her medical condition grew increasingly complicated: she suffered repeated infections from her intravenous lines, developed kidney failure requiring dialysis, and her heart function deteriorated to the point that she needed an intra-aortic balloon pump. The medical team concluded that further aggressive interventions were futile. They believed there was little chance that Mrs. Smith would ever leave the hospital alive; even if she did, she would likely return within days or weeks. Because of her fragile condition, she was not a candidate for transfer to a rehabilitation or outpatient center and continued to remain in the medical ICU.

As the team addressed one complication after another, they became convinced that their interventions were no longer contributing to Mrs. Smith’s healing. They worried that persisting with invasive treatment contradicted the core medical principle of “first, do no harm.” When the physicians recommended shifting to end-of-life care, such as focusing on comfort measures, withdrawing aggressive interventions, or assigning Mrs. Smith do-not-resuscitate status, her daughter became overwhelmed with emotion. She protested, “My mom gave me life, how can I take hers away?” In a moment of anguish, she broke down and said, “I would rather visit my mom in the hospital than in the graveyard.”

ethical_issues.question: In cases where the patient’s brain function has not recovered and treatment is deemed futile, should aggressive interventions be continued to prolong life?
keypoints: The evaluation of treatment efficacy depends on clearly defined therapeutic goals; if the goal is to restore consciousness and improve the patient’s condition, aggressive treatment may be deemed futile; however, if the goal is to prolong life, aggressive treatment should not be categorically considered futile.

Physicians must balance the principle of “first, do no harm” with respect for patient autonomy when deciding whether to continue aggressive treatment, recognizing that honoring the religious, cultural, and personal values of patients and their families is a crucial component of ethical decision-making.

Due to differences in values and expectations between physicians and patients or surrogates, the definitions of “reasonable” and “futile” treatment are inherently subjective and complex; conflicts and misunderstandings should be mitigated through empathy, expert clinical judgment, and effective communication.

There are no simple answers to medical ethical dilemmas; the key lies in how physicians convey their professional judgments with patience and wisdom to foster mutual understanding and consensus between medical staff and families, rather than focusing solely on the “appropriateness” of treatment.

ethical_issues.question: When patients or their surrogates request treatments that appear to be futile, should physicians respect patient autonomy and provide such treatment?
keypoints: Patient autonomy should be respected, regardless of whether the patient or surrogate chooses to accept or refuse end-of-life care, provided that the decision is based on adequate informed consent and clearly defined treatment goals.

Informed consent is fundamental to respecting patient autonomy; physicians should ensure that the patient or surrogate fully understands the medical condition, treatment options, expected outcomes, and potential risks and limitations.

The definition of “medical futility” is relative and depends on the treatment goals of different stakeholders: physicians tend to focus on recovery and clinical improvement, while patients or family members may prioritize prolonging life or maintaining vital signs.

If a particular intervention is judged to be medically inappropriate or futile in the clinical context, physicians are not obligated to provide such treatment, but should thoroughly explain the rationale and engage in patient, empathetic communication with the patient or surrogate.

The medical team should employ professional judgment, empathy, and effective communication skills to actively engage with the patient’s surrogate, helping them understand the clinical situation, the limits of treatment, and the basis for medical recommendations, thereby promoting consensus.

It is generally not ethically acceptable for physicians to unilaterally withdraw or modify treatment, especially in cases of terminal illness, without the knowledge and consent of the patient or surrogate; such actions should be avoided.

title: Integrating Palliative Care with Disease-Modifying Therapy
case:
Mr. James had been a heavy smoker most of his life. At 76, he had moderately severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and coronary artery disease, and he had been feeling weak and coughing for several months. When he began to cough up blood his son took him to the emergency room, where a chest x-ray showed a speculated 3-centimeter right upper lobe mass and enlarged mediastinal nodes. Mr. James was admitted to the hospital. A positron emission tomography (PET) scan showed both the mass and the nodes to be highly reactive. A needle biopsy of the mass showed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma (non-small cell cancer) that was stage III-B.
Mr. James’s tumor did not have any of the mutations that would have enabled him to be treated with targeted therapy, so he was offered standard chemotherapy with cisplatin and paclitaxel. After two rounds of chemotherapy he began to feel slightly better. He had more energy and was no longer coughing up blood. His three children and their families had been a constant source of support; everyone tried to be optimistic, hoping that a remission would last for many years. But within 2 months, Mr. James began to notice back pain.
His first follow-up computed tomography (CT) scan revealed that, despite the chemotherapy, the tumor mass in his right lung was larger and the cancer had metastasized to his ribs and spine. The oncology resident on Mr. James’s care team, Dr. George, had the responsibility of delivering this news to Mr. James and his family. Dr. George was aware of studies that had found associations between early referral to palliative care services and improved quality of life.
So, when he met with Mr. James and his family, Dr. George explained that the cancer had metastasized to Mr. James’s ribs and spine. He said that, if chemotherapy were to continue, different agents would be needed and that radiation was indicated for the areas of Mr. James’s spine that showed evidence of cancer. Dr. George introduced palliative care by saying, “I would also like you to talk to the staff in our palliative care service.”
“Wait, what?” exclaimed Mr. James’s daughter. “We’ve barely started fighting this thing and you want us to give up? You want us to just let him die? To help him die faster?” Murmurs and exclamations from the family followed. “No. No way. We’re not going to let them pull the plug, Pops. We’re going to fight this, and we’re going to win.”
Dr. George was unsure of how to proceed. He believed the sooner palliative care measures were started, the better off Mr. James would be. At the same time he wanted to assure the family that he wasn’t “giving up” on Mr. James.
case_rewrite:
Mr. James had spent most of his life as a heavy smoker. Now 76, he suffered from moderately severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and coronary artery disease. Over the past several months, he had grown increasingly weak and struggled with a persistent cough. When he began coughing up blood, his son brought him to the emergency room. There, a chest x-ray revealed a spiculated 3-centimeter mass in the right upper lobe of his lung, along with enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. Mr. James was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation. A PET scan showed that both the lung mass and the lymph nodes were highly active. A needle biopsy confirmed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma—non-small cell lung cancer—at stage III-B.

Genetic testing did not reveal any mutations that would make Mr. James eligible for targeted therapies. As a result, he was started on standard chemotherapy with cisplatin and paclitaxel. After completing two cycles, Mr. James noticed a slight improvement. He had more energy and the bleeding had stopped. Throughout this time, his three children and their families remained steadfast, surrounding him with support and optimism. They all hoped that the current remission might last for years. However, within two months, Mr. James began experiencing persistent back pain.

A follow-up CT scan delivered unwelcome news: despite chemotherapy, the lung mass had grown, and the cancer had now spread to his ribs and spine. Dr. George, the oncology resident on Mr. James’s team, was tasked with discussing these developments with Mr. James and his family. Dr. George was mindful of evidence showing that early involvement of palliative care could significantly improve quality of life for patients facing advanced illness.

When Dr. George met with Mr. James and his family, he explained that the cancer had metastasized to the bones in his ribs and spine. He discussed possible changes to Mr. James’s treatment plan, including switching to different chemotherapy agents and adding radiation for the areas of cancer in the spine. Dr. George also introduced the idea of involving the palliative care team, saying, “I think it would be very helpful for you to meet with our palliative care staff, who can offer additional support.”

Mr. James’s daughter reacted immediately. “Wait, what?” she exclaimed. “We’ve just started fighting, and now you want us to give up? You’re talking about helping him die faster?” The rest of the family erupted in anxious murmurs and objections. “No, no way. We’re not giving up on Pops. We’re going to keep fighting and we’re going to beat this.”

Dr. George hesitated, uncertain of how best to proceed. He knew that early palliative care could ease Mr. James’s symptoms and support the family through the challenges ahead. Yet he also wanted to reassure them that suggesting palliative care was not an act of surrender, but rather an added layer of care focused on Mr. James’s comfort and well-being, working alongside ongoing treatment.

ethical_issues.question: How can palliative care be effectively integrated with disease-modifying therapy to avoid family members misunderstanding it as giving up treatment or hastening death?
keypoints: Correct the erroneous perception that disease-modifying therapy and palliative care are mutually exclusive, emphasizing that both can be concurrently integrated to jointly promote the overall well-being of the patient.

Reframe palliative care as an additional layer of support alongside disease-modifying treatment, clarifying that its core objectives are symptom relief, alleviation of suffering, and enhancement of quality of life for both patients and their families; it is appropriate at any age and stage of illness and is delivered by a multidisciplinary team of specialists providing expert and comprehensive care, thereby dispelling the misconception that palliative care signifies “giving up” on treatment.

Establish clear referral criteria recommending timely referral to palliative care teams when patients experience increased symptom burden or difficulty coping with diagnosis and treatment decisions; employ empathetic, transparent, and respectful communication strategies that emphasize the compatibility and concurrent nature of palliative care with disease-modifying therapies.

Integrate palliative care interventions early in the disease trajectory to mitigate the physical and psychological distress experienced by patients and their families, thereby embodying the ethical principles of beneficence, respect, and patient-centered care.

title: Medical Students and Dying Patients
case:
Kelsey is a first-year medical student in her second semester. One of her classes focuses on bedside manner. The purpose of the course is to give students time to speak with patients and understand their perspectives—their knowledge, hopes, and fears. Kelsey and a few of her classmates are assigned to a hospice, where each spends time talking in a nonmedical capacity with a patient.
In the previous semester, the students heard lectures on how to take histories from different types of patients (e.g., children, the elderly) and on special topics (e.g., cultural sensitivity and end-of-life care). Kelsey had had one lecture about talking with the elderly and one lecture about end-of-life issues and options before her first visit to the hospice.
On one trip, Kelsey was assigned to spend time with Mrs. Walsh, an amiable 70-year-old woman who had entered hospice care 2 days earlier. Mrs. Walsh’s chart said that she and her family members had elected to discontinue chemotherapy, which was making her feel terrible and not having any effect on her cancer, which had metastasized to her spine and lungs. Mrs. Walsh had a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order in place. The visit was going well: Mrs. Walsh was talking happily about her husband, her children, and her grandchildren. Then Mrs. Walsh related her struggles with cancer and the decision to enter hospice care. Next Mrs. Walsh began to talk about facing mortality and said she was frightened about how she would die. She was not sure what the end would be like for her and questioned whether hospice was the right choice, though she was not really sure what would have been a better choice.
Throughout this time, Kelsey remained quiet. She wanted to empathize with Mrs. Walsh, to encourage her to continue thinking about these tough topics, and to ask questions that would help Mrs. Walsh flesh out her own ideas. She wanted to talk about the other options (not having a DNR order, receiving aggressive treatment, dying in an ICU on a ventilator) in ways that might remind Mrs. Walsh why she and her family had chosen hospice care in the first place. But Kelsey didn’t know whether she was allowed to enter into this type of conversation with a patient—she’d barely begun her medical training, after all.
case_rewrite:
Kelsey, a first-year medical student now in her second semester, is enrolled in a class devoted to bedside manner. The course is designed to give students the opportunity to interact with patients and appreciate their perspectives—their knowledge, aspirations, and anxieties. Kelsey and several classmates have been assigned to a local hospice, where each student spends time with a patient, not in a medical role, but simply conversing.

During the previous semester, Kelsey attended lectures on taking histories from various patient populations (like children and the elderly), as well as sessions on topics such as cultural sensitivity and end-of-life care. Before her initial hospice visit, she had participated in a lecture on communicating with elderly patients and another on end-of-life decisions and options.

On one of her hospice visits, Kelsey was paired with Mrs. Walsh, a warm and friendly 70-year-old woman who had arrived at the hospice two days prior. Mrs. Walsh’s chart indicated that she and her family had chosen to stop chemotherapy, as it had been causing her significant discomfort without any positive impact on her cancer, which had now spread to her spine and lungs. Mrs. Walsh also had a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order in place.

The visit began pleasantly, with Mrs. Walsh reminiscing about her husband, children, and grandchildren. Gradually, the conversation shifted, and Mrs. Walsh opened up about her experience with cancer and the difficult decision to enter hospice care. She went on to express her fears about facing mortality, admitting that she was frightened about how she would die. Mrs. Walsh confessed uncertainty about what the end would be like for her, and questioned whether choosing hospice had truly been the right path, even though she could not identify a preferable alternative.

Throughout their conversation, Kelsey listened quietly. She wanted to show empathy, to encourage Mrs. Walsh to explore her thoughts and feelings openly, and to ask questions that might help Mrs. Walsh articulate her own ideas. Kelsey also wished she could gently discuss the alternatives—what it might mean not to have a DNR, to pursue aggressive interventions, or to die in an intensive care unit on a ventilator—in a way that could remind Mrs. Walsh of the reasons she and her family had chosen hospice care. Yet, Kelsey hesitated, uncertain if it was appropriate for her, as a student just beginning her medical training, to engage in such a conversation with a patient.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians overcome their own death anxiety when caring for dying patients in order to provide optimal care?
keypoints: Physicians must acknowledge and accept their own death anxiety and confront their internal discomfort in order to communicate honestly and provide optimal care.

Supporting patients at the end of life begins with entering the appropriate emotional and psychological state, creating a safe space through silent presence and other means, guiding patients to explore their fears and concerns (exploratory dimension), and assisting them in finding meaning in death while deepening emotional connections.

Providing directive support involves commitments not to abandon the patient or their family, objectively informing them of the benefits and drawbacks of aggressive treatments, discussing advance directives, and addressing palliative care options including pain and symptom management, all delivered with sustained empathy.

Mentorship and multidisciplinary team collaboration are critically important; physicians should continuously enhance their communication skills and deepen their understanding and practice of end-of-life care through observation, direct feedback, and debriefing.
