title: Primary Care Practice Response to Retail Clinics
case:
You are chief of pediatrics at a New York City community health center. Your center has a particularly high census and is fully booked for appointments for the next 3 weeks.
One day, Dr. Colbert, a recent addition to the staff, walks into your office looking concerned. “Chief, what are we going to do about all of these CareNow patients?”
Confused, you ask for clarification. Dr. Colbert explains that because the clinic has been fully booked and has had unusually long wait times for urgent appointments, several patients on the panel have been getting checkups and care at the local CareNow, a retail clinic located in a pharmacy that is staffed by nurse practitioners. The CareNow providers are able to see patients sooner than the community health center can and write prescriptions to treat common illnesses such as strep throat and ear, eye, sinus, bladder, and bronchial infections. Minor wounds, abrasions, and joint sprains are treated, and vaccinations for common viral infections such as influenza, tetanus, pneumonia, and hepatitis A and B are also available.
“I just had a patient come in with a severe case of strep throat who had been prescribed a course of antibiotics, and I never even knew about it,” Dr. Colbert says. “What if he’d been allergic to the medication, or what if the nurse didn’t fully examine him? I had to spend an extra 20 minutes just getting the details of a medical problem I didn’t even know about, and I’m the kid’s pediatrician! What’s our policy for patients going to these clinics?”
As a seasoned physician, you are sympathetic to Dr. Colbert’s concerns about the quality of care at retail clinics. Furthermore, you realize that, since your practice’s electronic medical records are not synced with those of CareNow, there is no way to know what treatments patients actually receive. Most importantly, you want your clinic to be your patients’ “medical home,” and that means keeping tabs on all of your patients’ health interventions. At the same time, you realize that the CareNow clinic can usually treat patients faster than they can be seen in a doctor’s office, and some problems just don’t need to be dealt with by a physician. You struggle to come up with formal policy concerning the CareNow clinics.
case_rewrite:
You serve as the chief of pediatrics at a busy community health center in New York City. The center is currently at maximum capacity, with all appointment slots filled for the next three weeks.

One afternoon, Dr. Colbert, a new member of your medical team, enters your office with a troubled expression. “Chief, what are we supposed to do about all these CareNow patients?”

Perplexed, you ask Dr. Colbert to elaborate. He explains that, due to the clinic’s packed schedule and the unusually long wait for urgent visits, several of your patients have turned to CareNow—a local retail clinic inside a pharmacy. Staffed by nurse practitioners, CareNow offers quicker access for patients needing checkups or care. The clinic provides prompt treatment for common illnesses like strep throat, as well as ear, eye, sinus, bladder, and bronchial infections. They also manage minor wounds, abrasions, and joint sprains, and administer vaccines against infections such as influenza, tetanus, pneumonia, and hepatitis A and B.

Dr. Colbert shares his recent experience: “I just saw a patient with a pretty serious case of strep throat—he’d already been given antibiotics at CareNow, and I had no idea. What if he’d had a medication allergy, or if the nurse practitioner missed something during the exam? I spent an extra 20 minutes just piecing together what happened, and I’m supposed to be his pediatrician! What’s our stance on patients using these clinics?”

As an experienced physician, you understand Dr. Colbert’s concerns about the consistency and quality of care at retail clinics. You are also aware that your clinic’s electronic health records do not interface with those of CareNow, leaving you in the dark about treatments your patients receive elsewhere. Most of all, you’re committed to making the health center a true “medical home” for your patients, with oversight of all their health interventions. At the same time, you recognize that CareNow can usually see patients far more quickly than your clinic, and that some acute issues may not require a physician’s attention. You begin to grapple with how to develop an official policy regarding patient use of CareNow retail clinics.

ethical_issues.question: How can the need for patient access to care be balanced with physicians’ vision of establishing a patient-centered medical home to achieve high-quality primary care?
keypoints: Promote efficient exchange of information between primary care providers (PCPs), retail clinics, and other community-based providers by establishing a standardized process for sharing visit summaries to improve informational continuity of care.

PCPs should proactively acknowledge the reality of collaborative, multidisciplinary care, assume a central role in care coordination, and educate patients on the importance of, as well as encourage, inter-institutional information sharing.

Adopt advantageous features of retail clinics, such as walk-in availability and extended hours, to enhance access to acute care within primary care clinics and strengthen the capacity of the medical home.

Understand the reasons patients choose retail clinics for simple acute conditions, respect patient autonomy in healthcare-seeking behavior, and optimize care delivery models in alignment with patient needs and preferences.

title: Responding to Patients’ Requests for Nontraditional or Unproven Treatments
case:
Dr. Jeffries is a neurologist in private practice in a Virginia suburb. One day Ms. Ballard, a patient with a history of recurrent migraines, comes to his office in the midst of another splitting, pulsing headache centered on her right forehead and typical of her previous migraines. This is her third episode in the past month.
Ms. Ballard is frustrated and discouraged that her migraine regimen has been so ineffective. While reasonably well controlled for the past 3 years with beta blockers, her migraines have increased in frequency and severity over the past 6 months. They have been somewhat relieved but not eliminated with a variety of pain-relieving medications including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories and triptans.
On this visit, Ms. Ballard brings up “feverfew,” a supplement from the sunflower family that she says has been shown to be effective in preventing migraines. She first found out about feverfew fromThe Dr. Oz Show, a popular daytime television show whose host is a surgeon. “Dr. Jeffries,” she explains, “I saw onDr. Ozthat feverfew has been tested in clinical trials and helps prevent migraines. And you can get it online for $12!”
Dr. Jeffries has no idea what feverfew is. After quickly stepping out to conduct a quick online search, he finds one published clinical trial that suggests that feverfew compares reasonably well with beta blockers as preventive therapy. However, its side effects include allergic reaction and painful rebound headaches, and it is not known whether it interacts with the antihypertensive and oral hypoglycemic that Ms. Ballard is currently taking.
Ms. Ballard is desperate to try the new medication. Furthermore, she has not had any history of medication abuse, and she and Dr. Jeffries have enjoyed a good relationship over the past 3 years.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Jeffries, a neurologist with a private practice in a Virginia suburb, was midway through his clinic schedule when Ms. Ballard arrived, clutching her temple and wincing in pain. She had been his patient for over three years, initially responding well to beta blockers for her recurrent migraines. But over the past six months, her headaches had grown both more frequent and more severe, often disrupting her work and home life. Today marked her third migraine this month alone, and she looked weary and discouraged.

As Dr. Jeffries reviewed her records, Ms. Ballard voiced her frustration. “I’m so tired of this. The beta blockers worked for a while, but now it’s like nothing touches the pain. I’ve tried ibuprofen, naproxen, triptans—everything you’ve prescribed, but I still end up here, miserable.”

After taking a few deep breaths, she shared something new. “I was watching The Dr. Oz Show, and they were talking about this supplement called feverfew. Apparently, it’s from the sunflower family and has been tested in clinical trials for migraines. Dr. Jeffries, they said it could really help, and you can just order it online for twelve dollars. Do you think I can try it?”

The name “feverfew” was unfamiliar to Dr. Jeffries. Wanting to give her question the consideration it deserved, he excused himself for a moment and quickly searched reputable medical sources. He found one published clinical trial indicating that feverfew might compare reasonably well with beta blockers as a preventive therapy for migraines. However, he also noted potential side effects: allergic reactions, the possibility of painful rebound headaches, and, importantly, a lack of information about interactions with other medications—specifically, Ms. Ballard’s antihypertensive and her oral hypoglycemic.

Returning to the exam room, Dr. Jeffries found Ms. Ballard waiting expectantly. She reiterated her desire to try feverfew, her desperation clear, but he also remembered that she had never shown signs of medication misuse and that their longstanding relationship had always been open and trusting.

Now, Dr. Jeffries faced a dilemma: how to support her autonomy and honor her initiative, while ensuring her safety in the face of uncertain evidence and possible risks.

ethical_issues.question: How should patient autonomy be balanced with physician professional judgment when a patient requests unproven treatments?
keypoints: Physicians should respect patient autonomy by acknowledging the patient’s right to make decisions regarding their own treatment and, on this basis, facilitate informed decision making.

Physicians should actively empathize with the patient’s situation, express understanding and support, and demonstrate a willingness to collaborate in problem-solving to strengthen the patient-physician trust.

Physicians should avoid outright dismissal of the patient’s chosen therapy and instead focus on explaining specific concerns related to the patient’s individual circumstances, thereby preventing escalation of conflict.

Physicians should clearly communicate the potential risks, uncertainties, and evaluation process associated with the therapy to help the patient gain a comprehensive understanding of side effects and alternative options.

When the patient is fully informed of the risks and insists on proceeding, the physician may consider a trial under formal informed consent or recommend referral to a migraine specialist for a second opinion.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians effectively communicate to maintain the patient-physician trust relationship when patients request treatments based on incomplete or biased medical information?
keypoints: Physicians should empathize with patients’ frustration arising from inadequate therapeutic effects and affirm their proactive efforts to seek information and consultation in order to strengthen trust.

Physicians should candidly acknowledge the need to further evaluate the safety and suitability of new treatments in the context of the patient’s specific medication history and health status, avoiding criticism of the patient’s information sources to prevent adversarial dynamics in the patient-physician relationship.

Physicians should educate patients by clearly explaining the process of drug evaluation and potential risks, fostering a scientific understanding of supplement safety and the importance of individualized medication management.

Physicians should maintain a professional and objective stance, respect patient autonomy, and, when appropriate, recommend referral to a specialist for a second opinion, thereby embodying the principles of beneficence and respect for persons.

title: Physician-Rating Websites
case:
Dr. Jones is a family practitioner in a suburban Chicago group practice. At a staff meeting, he recently learned from a colleague that some patients of their practice have been rating their physicians on a popular doctor-rater website. Several of the physicians are concerned about the low ratings they received.
The next day during his lunch break, Dr. Jones decides to look to see if he has been rated. He is shocked to find that he has only been rated only 2 out of 5 stars. Specifically, he has received the lowest possible scores in “Time spent with patient” and “Helps patient understand his/her condition.” He realizes this score is based on the ratings of only 2 patients. Dr. Jones is disappointed because he strives to provide the best care possible for his patients, and he thought he had great relationships with all of them.
Exploring the site further, Dr. Jones thinks,these ratings are subjective and largely based on measures not directly in the doctor’s control, anyway!For example, patients are asked to rate doctors on mostly nonclinical criteria such as waiting time, rapport, and patient satisfaction. The site rating system also seems to prioritize treating diseases over watchful waiting.
He stops his Internet search when his next patient, Mr. Jenkins, comes in for a regular checkup. Dr. Jones asks him whether he has heard of the rating website. Mr. Jenkins replies, “Sure I’ve heard of it—haven’t you seen the commercials?”
Mr. Jenkins has had a cough for the past 2 days and asks for antibiotics. Dr. Jones, in a hurry because he is quite overbooked that afternoon, believes Mr. Jenkins has a simple viral infection. He thinks,I never prescribe antibiotics in this situation, even though some doctors might, and they don’t seem indicated this time. But Mr. Jenkins already knows about the website, and might be upset that I’m not dealing with his symptoms. What if this guy rates me poorly for not following his request? Could stuff like this drive future patients away from my practice?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Jones is a family physician working in a group practice in suburban Chicago. At a recent staff meeting, he heard from a colleague that some patients had been posting reviews of their doctors on a widely used physician-rating website. Several doctors in the group expressed concern about the low scores they had received on the site.

The following afternoon, during lunch, Dr. Jones grew curious and decided to see if he had been rated online. To his dismay, he discovered he had been given an overall score of just 2 out of 5 stars. He noticed he had received the lowest marks in the categories “Time spent with patient” and “Helps patient understand his/her condition.” Dr. Jones saw that these ratings came from only two patients. He felt disappointed and troubled, since he has always prided himself on providing attentive care and building strong relationships with his patients.

As he browsed the website further, Dr. Jones found himself questioning the fairness of the system. He thought, these ratings seem subjective and depend on factors that aren’t entirely under my control. The categories focus mainly on nonclinical aspects like wait times, rapport, and patient satisfaction. He also noticed that the site appeared to reward more aggressive treatment, rather than considering the merits of watchful waiting when appropriate.

Dr. Jones’s contemplation was interrupted when his next patient, Mr. Jenkins, arrived for a routine checkup. During the visit, Dr. Jones asked Mr. Jenkins if he was familiar with the physician-rating website. Mr. Jenkins replied, “Oh yes, I know about it—haven’t you seen the commercials?”

Mr. Jenkins mentioned he’d had a cough for two days and asked Dr. Jones to prescribe antibiotics. Feeling rushed due to a tightly packed afternoon schedule, Dr. Jones quickly assessed that Mr. Jenkins likely had a mild viral infection. He thought to himself, I never prescribe antibiotics for uncomplicated viral coughs, even though some other doctors might—and there’s no clinical reason to do so now. But Mr. Jenkins already knows about the website, and if he’s dissatisfied, he could leave me a bad review. Could negative ratings like this end up driving patients away from my practice?

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians alter their medical judgment due to concerns about online ratings, such as prescribing antibiotics unnecessarily?
keypoints: Physicians should not alter their medical judgment due to concerns about online ratings, and in particular, should not prescribe antibiotics without clinical indication.
Dr. Jones needs to recognize and manage his anxiety and vulnerability arising from the ratings, so as to prevent emotional responses from adversely affecting professional decision-making.

Physicians ought to foster understanding and trust by patiently explaining the rationale for diagnosis and treatment and addressing patients’ concerns, rather than acquiescing to unreasonable demands for the sake of expediency.
Online ratings may provoke defensive medical practices, resulting in unnecessary treatments that compromise quality of care and increase healthcare costs.
The ideal physician-patient relationship should be founded on collaboration and shared decision-making, avoiding unilateral accommodation or coercion.

ethical_issues.question: Should online physician-rating websites refrain from publishing individual physicians’ ratings until a sufficient number of reviews have been received, in order to prevent inaccurate evaluations from adversely affecting the physicians’ reputations?
keypoints: Physician-rating websites should establish a minimum threshold for the number of ratings—such as 5 to 10—before publicly displaying individual physicians’ scores, in order to reduce evaluation bias caused by insufficient sample sizes and to prevent unfair impacts on physicians’ reputations.

These websites should implement effective measures to prevent malicious rating behaviors, including safeguarding against competitors impersonating patients to post false negative reviews, thereby ensuring the authenticity and fairness of the ratings.

Medical professional organizations, such as the American Medical Association, should actively advocate for and participate in the development of standards and governance frameworks for physician-rating websites, promoting transparency, fairness, and responsible management of rating systems.

title: Speculating on a Public Figure’s Mental Health
case:
Dr. Garcia was a pediatrician in private practice specializing in adolescent patients. Her hobby was writing, which she hoped to make a larger part of her career. To that end, she had been keeping a blog on medical issues and local politics. More recently, she had been invited to contribute commentary to the local public radio station.
Tragedy struck in the suburb where she practices. In a scenario that has become all too familiar, a 16-year-old tenth grader named John went to school with a gun, killed two classmates, and injured several others before surrendering to the police. One of Dr. Garcia’s own patients had been shot. In the days following the violence, a few details emerged about John in the media. He was the only child of divorced parents. His father was a drug addict who had cut off contact with his son. Now John lived with his mother. Though he was a good student, he didn’t seem to have many friends at school and had been the brunt of teasing. Classmates were quoted as saying he was “weird” and “a loner.” An English teacher recalled a disturbingly violent short story he had written in a creative writing class the year before. A neighbor described seeing John through the window of his bedroom playing video games at all hours of the day and night. In video footage as he was led to the courthouse, John looked disheveled and was muttering to himself.
Like everyone else in town, Dr. Garcia was shocked and riveted. She was devastated by the shooting and longed to understand what had motivated John to act in this way. Moreover, she had long thought that there was insufficient mental health counseling at the local high school. She followed the media coverage intently and talked of little else with colleagues and friends.
Dr. Garcia believed that video games could desensitize some players to violence. By piecing bits of information together, she had begun to develop a theory about what had led John to such a desperate act. She surmised that he had had a troubled childhood and little support at home or school and was struggling with an emerging mental illness.
A reporter from the local radio station called to ask Dr. Garcia for an on-air interview about the shooting. As an expert on adolescence, Dr. Garcia could add insight into John’s motivations, he said. Dr. Garcia eagerly agreed.
On air, Dr. Garcia said that information coming to light about John from his teachers’ and classmates’ descriptions unfortunately suggested a picture much like that of several other young school shooters in the past few years. She said she suspected that most of them had clinical psychiatric problems that, if the schools had put enough resources into mental health services, could have been identified. It seemed possible, she said, that John had a severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia, and that he carried out the crime while he was psychotic. She went on to say that she had noticed in her pediatric practice that teens who felt ostracized and friendless often turned to videogames in their free time and that their playing only isolated them further. And, yes, she believed that violent videogames could desensitize some habitual players to real violence. The sad case of John illustrated why action needs to be taken on these fronts, Dr. Garcia argued.
The next day at work a senior doctor in her practice, Dr. Humphrey, mentioned that he had heard her on the radio. Dr. Garcia smiled and asked him what he thought.
“To be honest, I was pretty shocked. How could you make such suggestions about a young man you haven’t even met? He’ll be tried in this town. Your opinion carries weight because you’re a doctor. Did you ever think you’d be influencing a jury?”
Dr. Garcia was chastened. When she went home, she read through comments on the online version of her story. Some people endorsed her opinion and others disagreed. But it was true, she realized, that none of them knew what was going on with John. A lot of people disagreed with the policy changes she recommended. A few accused her of using the town’s tragedy to promote her own social agenda.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Garcia was a pediatrician with a private practice, focusing on adolescent patients. Beyond her clinical work, she enjoyed writing and aspired to make it a larger part of her professional life. She maintained a blog discussing medical topics and local politics, and recently, she had begun providing commentary for the local public radio station.

A devastating event shook the suburban community where Dr. Garcia practiced. In a tragic and all-too-familiar scenario, a 16-year-old tenth grader named John brought a firearm to school, fatally shooting two classmates and injuring several others before surrendering to law enforcement. One of the wounded students was a patient of Dr. Garcia’s. In the aftermath, a few details about John began to surface in news reports. John was the sole child of divorced parents. His father, struggling with addiction, had ceased all contact with him. Now, John lived with his mother. Despite being a competent student, he was described as having few friends and was often teased by peers. Some classmates labeled him “weird” and “a loner.” An English teacher recalled a short story John had written the previous year that was notably violent. A neighbor mentioned seeing John through his bedroom window, playing video games at all hours. When cameras captured John being led to the courthouse, he appeared disheveled and was muttering under his breath.

Like many in the town, Dr. Garcia was deeply affected by the shooting and felt compelled to understand what drove John to such violence. She had previously been concerned about the lack of mental health resources at the local high school, and now followed every news update closely, discussing the case frequently with her colleagues and friends.

Dr. Garcia believed that video games might desensitize some young people to violence. By piecing together what she read and heard, she began to form a theory about John’s actions: she speculated that John’s difficult upbringing, lack of support at home and school, and social isolation could have contributed to the tragedy, possibly in the context of an emerging mental illness.

Soon, a reporter from the local radio station contacted Dr. Garcia, inviting her to participate in a live interview about the incident. The reporter said that, as someone with expertise in adolescent health, she could offer valuable insight into what might have motivated John. Dr. Garcia readily agreed.

During the broadcast, Dr. Garcia discussed the emerging details about John, noting that his background and behaviors resembled those of other young perpetrators in recent school shootings. She commented that, in her view, many such individuals appeared to struggle with psychiatric conditions that might have been identified had schools invested more in mental health services. Dr. Garcia speculated that John could be suffering from a severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia, and might have been psychotic at the time of the crime. She further remarked that, in her practice, she had observed socially isolated teens often turning to video games, which she felt could deepen their isolation, and that, in her opinion, repeated exposure to violent games might desensitize some youth to real-life violence. Dr. Garcia used John’s case as an example to argue for changes in mental health support and video game regulation.

The following day, at her office, Dr. Garcia was approached by Dr. Humphrey, a senior colleague. He mentioned hearing her interview on the radio. Dr. Garcia smiled and asked his impression.

“To be honest, I was quite surprised. How could you make such assertions about a young man you’ve never even met? Remember, he’ll be tried here in town. People listen to you because you’re a doctor. Did it occur to you that your words might influence the jury?”

Dr. Garcia felt unsettled by his remarks. That evening, she read through the comments on the online version of the interview. Some readers supported her perspective; others disagreed. It struck her that, like herself, none of them truly knew what John was experiencing. There was also considerable debate over the changes she had recommended. A few commenters accused her of using the tragedy to advance her own viewpoints.

Reflecting on the day, Dr. Garcia realized the complexity and responsibility involved in sharing professional opinions about individuals she had never evaluated, especially in such a public and sensitive context.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Garcia explicitly disclose that her commentary on the mental health of the public figure reflects her personal opinions, and clarify that her professional qualifications and lack of direct involvement in the case do not confer additional authority or credibility to these views?
keypoints: Garcia should explicitly state that her views are personal opinions and that her professional qualifications or proximity to the case do not confer additional authority or legal weight to her statements.

Garcia’s speculations regarding the suspect’s motives or mental state must be accompanied by a clear and emphatic disclaimer, clarifying that psychiatric diagnosis and assessment are beyond her professional scope of practice.

Garcia should adhere to the ethical principles reflected in the American Psychiatric Association’s “Goldwater Rule” by refraining from making public statements about the mental health of individuals she has not personally evaluated.

Garcia has an ethical obligation to uphold medical professionalism and social responsibility by avoiding conjecture that could be misinterpreted or unduly relied upon by the public or legal authorities, even if her opinions are informed by professional knowledge or personal observation.

ethical_issues.question: Is it appropriate for Dr. Garcia to express her personal beliefs through mass media in the absence of direct evidence, and how can she ensure that the impartiality of the jury is not compromised?
keypoints: When physicians publicly speculate on the mental state or motivations of undiagnosed individuals through mass media in the absence of direct evidence, this constitutes a serious breach of professional ethics, an abuse of professional status and influence, and a violation of industry standards such as the “Goldwater Rule.”

Such public conjecture may inappropriately influence judicial proceedings, particularly by potentially biasing the objectivity of the jury and undermining the presumption of innocence, thereby compromising the fairness of the legal process.

Physicians should refrain from making diagnostic or inferential comments about individuals they have not personally evaluated based on hearsay or personal opinion, and must clearly state that their views are personal, specify their professional qualifications and limitations, and emphasize that no formal assessment has been conducted, in order to prevent the public from misconstruing their statements as carrying professional authority.

Medical professionals should balance freedom of expression with professional responsibility, exercise caution when handling sensitive information related to specific cases, safeguard patient privacy and public trust, and ensure that contributions to public policy discussions are grounded in scientific evidence and ethical principles.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr. Garcia appropriately balance her civic responsibilities and professional duties as a physician, while maintaining professionalism and adhering to ethical standards when commenting on public events?
keypoints: Garcia comments publicly on events of public concern, she should clearly state her professional qualifications and limitations, explicitly emphasizing that psychiatric assessment falls outside the scope of her pediatric expertise, in order to avoid misleading the public.

Garcia should refrain from making professional diagnoses or judgments about the suspect’s psychological state based on hearsay or speculation; when commenting, she must include a clear and explicit disclaimer to prevent her views from being overinterpreted or misused by the public or media.

Garcia must fully recognize that her statements may impact the fairness of judicial proceedings, particularly by potentially undermining the presumption of innocence, and should exercise caution to avoid misuse of professional authority or improper influence on the legal process.

Garcia should uphold professional standards and ethical principles when speaking to the media, and avoid using community tragedies to advance personal agendas or make unsubstantiated policy recommendations.

Garcia should balance her right as a citizen to express concern with her professional responsibilities as a physician, ensuring that her statements are scientifically grounded, respectful of patient confidentiality, and consistent with the principles of social justice and medical ethics.

title: The Treating Psychiatrist and Worker’s Compensation Reporting
case:
Stanley Crumb was a train conductor. Starting long before sunrise, he took passengers from distant suburbs into a bustling downtown. One morning, on his first run of the day, he saw a figure flash before the train. He pulled on the brakes, but it was too late. The train had killed a young woman. Mr. Crumb later learned that the woman had been severely depressed and had left a suicide note, but he could not help blaming himself.
Mr. Crumb was shattered by the event. Several weeks after the incident, he still could not sleep because of horrible nightmares. He kept having flashbacks, and in a disturbing variation he imagined jumping in front of a train himself. At the urging of his wife and his supervisor, he went to the employee assistance program and was referred for evaluation for psychiatric hospitalization. It was determined that Mr. Crumb needed to be hospitalized.
Dr. Young was his psychiatrist at the hospital. She diagnosed Mr. Crumb with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). She started him on medication for depression and nightmares and on cognitive behavioral trauma therapy. After discharge, Mr. Crumb continued to see Dr. Young on a weekly basis.
Mr. Crumb was benefitting from psychiatric care, but it became clear to Dr. Young that PTSD was not his only problem. Mr. Crumb had a strong family history of mental illness, and several episodes in his past suggested to her that Mr. Crumb might have bipolar disorder. Dr. Young encouraged Mr. Crumb to continue treatment to better understand the nature of his illness.
One afternoon, Mr. Crumb arrived at her office in great distress. His insurance company was challenging the necessity of his continuing with therapy through his worker’s compensation. Worse still, they were disputing payment of Mr. Crumb’s hospitalization. Mr. Crumb hired an attorney and asked Dr. Young to provide a written statement about his current mental state and need for hospitalization.
A few days after submitting her statement, Dr. Young received a call from Mr. Crumb’s lawyer. He asked her to remove certain sections of the written statement. Specifically, he wanted her to redact the section about her suspicions of preexisting bipolar disorder. It would destroy Mr. Crumb’s chances of getting compensation, the lawyer warned.
Dr. Young believed her primary duty was to be an advocate for her patients. But if this went to a hearing, she would be sworn to tell the “whole truth” and that truth was complicated. She believed that Mr. Crumb may well have had a psychiatric illness before the accident, though the woman’s suicide was the defining trauma prior to hospitalization.
case_rewrite:
Stanley Crumb worked as a train conductor, guiding early-morning commuters from far-flung suburbs into the heart of the city. On a quiet morning, during his first run, Stanley’s routine was shattered when a figure darted onto the tracks. He slammed on the brakes, but the train struck a young woman. Later, Stanley learned that she had suffered from severe depression and left behind a suicide note, but despite this knowledge, he could not shake the feeling of personal responsibility.

The tragedy left Stanley deeply traumatized. Weeks passed, but his anguish only deepened—he was haunted by nightmares and plagued by vivid flashbacks. Sometimes, in his mind’s eye, he saw himself leaping in front of a train. At the urging of his wife and supervisor, Stanley reached out to the employee assistance program and was soon referred for a psychiatric evaluation. The conclusion was clear: Stanley required hospitalization.

During his stay at the hospital, Dr. Young became his psychiatrist. She diagnosed Stanley with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and initiated treatment, prescribing medication for his depression and nightmares, and beginning cognitive behavioral therapy focused on trauma. After Stanley left the hospital, he continued weekly sessions with Dr. Young.

Stanley made progress in therapy, but Dr. Young began to suspect that his struggles went beyond PTSD. A strong family history of mental illness, along with episodes from Stanley’s past, led her to consider that he might have bipolar disorder. She encouraged him to stick with treatment so they could better understand the nature of his illness together.

One afternoon, Stanley arrived at Dr. Young’s office looking distraught. His insurance company was challenging the need for ongoing therapy under his worker’s compensation claim. Even worse, they were disputing his hospitalization costs. Stanley hired an attorney and asked Dr. Young to provide a written statement detailing his mental health status and the necessity of his hospitalization.

After Dr. Young submitted her report, she received a call from Stanley’s lawyer. The attorney requested that she remove certain sections, specifically her remarks about the possibility of a preexisting bipolar disorder. Including that information, the lawyer warned, would ruin Stanley’s chances of receiving compensation.

Dr. Young found herself torn. She saw her foremost duty as advocating for Stanley’s well-being. Yet if the matter went before a hearing, she would be required to testify under oath and provide the complete truth—a truth that was nuanced and complicated. Dr. Young recognized that Stanley may have had a psychiatric illness before the accident, although his most recent trauma was undeniably the event that precipitated his hospitalization.

ethical_issues.question: In legal or quasi-legal contexts, how can psychiatrists maintain a delicate balance among their triple responsibilities to the patient, to third parties, and to their profession?
keypoints: Psychiatrists in legal or quasi-legal contexts should adhere to ethical principles including respect for persons, honesty, justice, and social responsibility.
Psychiatrists must uphold the principle of presenting the whole truth, ensuring that the content of their reports is objectively accurate and professionally precise.

Psychiatrists should remain vigilant to the risks of role conflict when preparing reports, avoiding unprincipled endorsement of patients’ compensation claims as well as outright rejection of their requests.

Physicians should prioritize the best interests of their patients and respect patient rights, while retaining core content and conclusions related to their professional judgment, even if these conflict with the wishes of the patient or their legal representative; only factual inaccuracies provided by the patient or third parties may be corrected.

ethical_issues.question: Should psychiatrists avoid evaluating their own patients for legal purposes in order to prevent role conflicts and the risk of bias?
keypoints: Psychiatrists should generally avoid conducting evaluations of their own patients for legal purposes in order to prevent role conflicts and unconscious bias, thereby safeguarding the objectivity and fairness of the assessment.

In legal or quasi-legal contexts, psychiatrists must maintain a delicate balance among their duties to the patient, third parties, and their professional responsibilities, ensuring both the protection of patient interests and the truthful reflection of clinical facts.

In certain circumstances—such as workers’ compensation claims, disability evaluations, and civil commitment hearings—the treating psychiatrist may still be required to provide a psychiatric evaluation report, representing a significant exception to the general avoidance principle and illustrating the complexity of ethical dilemmas in such cases.

title: Pedophilia: Is There a Duty to Report?
case:
Dr. Gregory is a third-year psychiatry resident at a large academic medical center. Several months ago, Mr. Green was assigned to his care. A taciturn, overweight, 59-year-old janitor, Mr. Green was admitted to the emergency room with acute alcohol poisoning. He arrived at the hospital after having made a scene at a bar. When he sobered up, Mr. Green explained that he wasn’t a regular drinker, but had tried getting drunk because he was so miserable.
Dr. Gregory had a particular interest in dynamic psychotherapy and had been hoping for patients open to that approach. Before discharge, Mr. Green agreed to return to Dr. Gregory’s outpatient clinic for help.
Mr. Green was a responsive patient. He pledged never to touch alcohol again and readily admitted that he needed help for depression. In addition to prescribing medication, Dr. Gregory began weekly counseling sessions with Mr. Green. As Dr. Gregory began to earn his trust, Mr. Green shared some intimate details of his past. He had grown up with alcoholic, neglectful parents and had been molested by a family friend when he was a young boy. As an adult, he had no friends and had not had an intimate relationship for more than 2 decades. Dr. Gregory encouraged Mr. Green to be open and trusting. “This is a safe space,” he assured him.
Several months into treatment, Mr. Green admitted that he was sexually attracted to little girls. He quickly added that he had never acted on these fantasies. Dr. Gregory reminded him that it was illegal to download pornographic images of children from the Internet. They both acknowledged that it would be catastrophic to act on the fantasies.
Dr. Gregory’s acceptance seemed to embolden Mr. Green. Week after week, the conversation was dominated by descriptions of his pedophilic fantasies. More disturbing still, the fantasies all began to revolve around a little girl Mr. Green called “A.” Though he spoke about her if she were a real girl, he insisted that she was purely a figment of his imagination.
Despite Mr. Green’s insistence that this was fantasy, the specificity of the descriptions and explicit nature of his fantasies caused Dr. Gregory concern that “A” was not a fantasy but a real little girl whom Mr. Green had been watching. But if “A “were indeed an actual child, Dr. Gregory had no idea who she was. A relative? A neighbor? A co-worker’s daughter?
Dr. Gregory was unsure what to do about Mr. Green. On the one hand, he had encouraged Mr. Green to be open about his feelings and private thoughts. He had assured him that he was safe. And, as far as Dr. Gregory knew, Mr. Green had never hurt a child. Everyone is entitled to a private fantasy life, Dr. Gregory thought. On the other hand, Dr. Gregory worried that Mr. Green might be a current or potential child molester. Mr. Green was starting to seem obsessed with the idea of “A.” If she were a real little girl, she could be in imminent danger.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Gregory, a third-year psychiatry resident at a large academic medical center, had been treating Mr. Green, a reserved and overweight 59-year-old janitor, for several months. Their therapeutic relationship began after Mr. Green was admitted to the emergency room for acute alcohol poisoning, following a disruptive incident at a local bar. Once sober, Mr. Green confided to Dr. Gregory that he was not typically a heavy drinker, but had become intoxicated due to overwhelming misery.

With a keen interest in dynamic psychotherapy, Dr. Gregory recognized a chance to help Mr. Green through in-depth talk therapy. Before discharging Mr. Green from the hospital, Dr. Gregory met with him to outline the proposed treatment plan. As part of a thorough informed consent process, Dr. Gregory spoke frankly about the nature and boundaries of psychotherapy, making sure to detail the limits of confidentiality. He clearly explained that, while most conversations would remain private, there were key exceptions: if Mr. Green ever revealed intentions or actions suggesting harm to himself or others, or disclosed involvement in child abuse or exploitation, Dr. Gregory would be legally required to report such information to authorities. Dr. Gregory encouraged questions and took care to confirm that Mr. Green understood these limitations before agreeing to begin outpatient treatment.

Mr. Green responded positively to the initial course of therapy, pledging abstinence from alcohol and being candid about his struggles with depression. Dr. Gregory prescribed medication and initiated weekly counseling sessions. As their rapport deepened, Mr. Green began to share more intimate aspects of his life: his upbringing by alcoholic, neglectful parents; being molested as a child by a family friend; and his persistent social isolation and absence of intimate relationships as an adult. Throughout their work, Dr. Gregory supported Mr. Green’s openness, periodically reiterating that confidentiality had clear limits, especially regarding threats of harm or abuse.

After several months, Mr. Green disclosed a deeply troubling aspect of his inner life: he was sexually attracted to young girls, though he insisted he had never acted on these urges. Dr. Gregory responded by again outlining the legal and ethical boundaries of therapy. He reminded Mr. Green that possessing child pornography or acting on such fantasies would be illegal and profoundly harmful to others, and stressed his own obligation to report any information suggesting a credible risk. They discussed the gravity of these issues, with Dr. Gregory emphasizing that, while their sessions were confidential, he was required to act if there was a threat to others’ safety.

Over time, Mr. Green’s sessions grew increasingly preoccupied with explicit descriptions of his fantasies, especially those involving a little girl he called “A.” Mr. Green described “A” in vivid and detailed terms, though he insisted she was purely a figment of his imagination. The specificity and frequency of these accounts, however, unsettled Dr. Gregory, who began to suspect that “A” might not be imaginary after all. Dr. Gregory had no concrete information about “A’s” identity or whether she was someone Mr. Green actually observed—perhaps a relative, neighbor, or someone else entirely.

Now, Dr. Gregory found himself facing a profound ethical dilemma. He had worked to foster trust by encouraging Mr. Green’s honesty and by assuring him of safety within the boundaries of therapy, while always clearly explaining the legal limits of confidentiality. To Dr. Gregory’s knowledge, Mr. Green had not harmed a child, and the sanctity of private thoughts remained an important ethical consideration. Yet, as Mr. Green’s fixation on “A” intensified and the possibility grew that she was a real child, Dr. Gregory became increasingly concerned about his duty to protect a potentially at-risk individual. He was forced to weigh his commitment to confidentiality and therapeutic trust against his ethical and legal responsibility to intervene if there was credible risk of harm to a reasonably identifiable person.

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician clearly inform the patient of the limits of confidentiality in the psychotherapeutic relationship and the potential duty to report during the course of treatment?
keypoints: Physicians should explicitly clarify the limits of confidentiality during the comprehensive informed consent process in psychotherapy, including their duty to protect against credible threats of harm and the mandatory reporting obligations related to suspected child abuse.
Informed consent must ensure that patients understand the risks of disclosure arising from confidentiality limitations, thereby safeguarding patients’ right to know and maintaining therapeutic trust.
When the duty of confidentiality conflicts with a serious danger to a reasonably identifiable person, the principle of protection should take precedence over the privilege of confidentiality.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where a patient discloses possible pedophilic fantasies, does the physician have a duty to report this to law enforcement or child welfare authorities?
keypoints: When a patient discloses pedophilic fantasies, the physician must balance the duty of confidentiality with the ethical responsibility to protect children from potential harm.
The Tarasoff precedent does not apply in this case, as its mandatory reporting criteria—namely, a serious threat of violence toward a reasonably identifiable victim—are not met here.

Although most state laws require physicians to report upon reasonable suspicion of child abuse, in the absence of an identifiable victim, Dr. Gregory is generally under no immediate ethical or legal obligation to report to law enforcement or child welfare agencies.

The physician should continue to assess the patient’s risk; if the patient’s work environment involves contact with children and symptoms worsen, this may constitute an actual risk of harm and thereby trigger a mandatory reporting obligation.

title: Civil Commitment for Substance Abuse
case:
Mr. Robinson arrived at the emergency room in the middle of the night after crashing a car through a glass storefront. Luckily for him, he hadn’t been going very fast, but had a large cut on his hand. He was not an easy patient; he swung at a nurse who was cleaning his wound, yelled obscenities at the doctor who was trying to get a history, and urinated in his cubicle. His hand required 20 stitches. His blood alcohol level was 400.
When Mr. Robinson’s daughter Margaret arrived at the hospital, she was frantic with worry, not only about the health of her father but also about her own family. The car was hers and she needed it to get to work. She was the single mother of two young children, whom she’d had to leave with a neighbor. Her father had come to live with them in the Boston suburbs a year earlier after going through a messy divorce. He’d struggled with alcohol throughout his life, but had started drinking heavily again soon after moving in with Margaret. This was his third visit to the emergency department for an alcohol-related crisis. Margaret was at her wit’s end. She asked to see Dr. Diallo, a psychiatrist who had been called in to interview Mr. Robinson during a previous hospitalization.
“We’ve tried everything—individual therapy, group therapy, AA, outpatient full-day programs. It just isn’t enough for him. He’s wonderful when he’s sober, but drunk is another story.” Dr. Diallo agreed that Mr. Robinson needed more intensive care to achieve sobriety. He decided to admit Mr. Robinson to the hospital for detoxification and to broach the subject of longer-term inpatient treatment with him that afternoon when he had sobered up and Margaret got out of work.
Mr. Robinson was a completely different person in the afternoon. He gave Margaret a hug when she came in and asked about his grandchildren, but he was less pleased to see Dr. Diallo. “I just got a little too drunk last night,” he said impatiently.
Margaret reminded him that they had been through similar episodes three other times. “You’re an alcoholic, Dad. You scare me when you’re drunk.”
Dr. Diallo told him about the advantages of ongoing hospitalization for substance-abuse treatment, but Mr. Robinson shook his head. He wasn’t interested. Margaret begged Dr. Diallo to intervene. “He got into a car in that state! He’s a menace to himself, my family, and the whole community,” she argued.
Unlike many states, Massachusetts allows for involuntary civil commitment for patients with substance use issues if they are at risk of “serious harm” to themselves or others as a result of their use of substances. Though a judge ultimately determines whether or not a patient can be involuntarily committed for substance-abuse treatment, the psychiatrist must make the decision whether or not to petition the court for such an order.
The decision weighed heavily upon Dr. Diallo. On the one hand, Mr. Robinson had come into the ED three times with dangerously high levels of alcohol. On the other hand, infringing someone’s freedom demanded strong justification, especially when that person had, so far, not harmed anyone or been accused of harming anyone. Dr. Diallo wondered if mandating inpatient treatment for substance abuse was in his patient’s best interest.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Robinson was brought to the emergency department in the early hours after he drove a car through the front window of a local shop. Fortunately, his speed had been low, sparing him from more severe injuries, but he suffered a deep laceration on his hand. He proved to be a challenging patient—he lashed out at a nurse tending to his wound, hurled profanities at the attending physician, and urinated in his treatment area. His hand needed twenty stitches. When his blood was drawn, his alcohol level read an astonishing 400.

Margaret, his daughter, arrived at the hospital visibly distraught. She worried not only about her father’s physical condition but also about the ripple effects on her own life. The car Mr. Robinson had crashed belonged to her, and she relied on it to commute to her job. As a single mother with two young children, she’d had to leave them with a neighbor in her rush to the hospital. Mr. Robinson had moved in with Margaret a year earlier, seeking refuge after a bitter divorce. His lifelong battle with alcohol had intensified following his relocation to the Boston suburbs. This was now the third time Margaret had found herself in the emergency department because of her father’s alcohol-fueled crisis. At her wit’s end, she asked to speak to Dr. Diallo, the psychiatrist who had interviewed Mr. Robinson during a previous hospital stay.

“We’ve tried everything—individual counseling, group sessions, Alcoholics Anonymous, even intensive outpatient programs,” Margaret explained desperately. “It just isn’t enough. He’s a wonderful father and grandfather when he’s sober, but when he drinks, he becomes someone else.” Dr. Diallo agreed that Mr. Robinson required more robust intervention to reach sobriety. He admitted Mr. Robinson for detoxification and planned to discuss the possibility of a longer-term inpatient treatment program with him and Margaret later that day, once Mr. Robinson had sobered up and Margaret could return after work.

By the afternoon, Mr. Robinson appeared transformed. He embraced Margaret warmly and asked after his grandchildren, but his demeanor cooled when Dr. Diallo entered. “I just drank too much last night, that’s all,” he said, dismissively.

Margaret reminded him, her voice strained, that this had happened before—three times now. “Dad, you’re an alcoholic. I’m terrified for you, and for us, when you drink.”

Dr. Diallo gently outlined the benefits of sustained inpatient care for substance abuse, but Mr. Robinson quickly rejected the idea. Margaret, visibly upset, pleaded with Dr. Diallo. “He got behind the wheel in that condition! He’s a danger to himself, to my kids, to everyone,” she insisted.

Unlike in many other states, Massachusetts law allows for involuntary civil commitment when substance use puts someone at “serious risk” of harm to themselves or others. Ultimately, whether Mr. Robinson could be involuntarily committed would be decided by a judge, but it fell to Dr. Diallo to determine whether or not to initiate the legal process by petitioning the court.

The weight of this decision pressed heavily on Dr. Diallo. Mr. Robinson’s repeated emergency visits, each fueled by dangerously high levels of alcohol, suggested a pattern of escalating risk. Yet Dr. Diallo knew that restricting a patient’s liberty was a profound step, particularly when the patient had not yet directly harmed anyone. He also considered the formidable hurdles ahead: the paperwork, court proceedings, and coordination required for mandated treatment, all of which could divert valuable time and resources from other patients and families.

Dr. Diallo reflected on the uncertain effectiveness of compulsory treatment—studies had yet to show that mandated care led to better outcomes than voluntary participation. He grappled with the ethical dilemma: Should he move to curtail Mr. Robinson’s autonomy for the sake of his safety and the community’s welfare, even though Mr. Robinson remained adamant in his refusal and had not yet caused irreversible harm? The answer was far from clear, and the responsibility rested on his shoulders.

ethical_issues.question: Is civil commitment appropriate for patients with substance abuse disorders, especially when considering the complexity of the commitment process and the uncertainties surrounding its efficacy and ethical implications?
keypoints: Massachusetts law permits involuntary civil commitment for patients who pose a “serious risk” of harm to themselves or others due to substance abuse; however, determining appropriate candidates involves legal and clinical controversies and complexities.

The process of petitioning for mandated treatment is cumbersome, requiring written documentation, court testimony, and coordination of patient transfer, imposing significant procedural and time burdens on physicians and family members, which may impact the allocation of other medical resources.

Existing research on the efficacy of coerced treatment is inconclusive, with most studies showing no significant difference in sobriety retention rates or overall outcomes between mandated and nonmandated treatment, leaving the effectiveness unresolved.

Involuntary commitment raises critical ethical considerations, necessitating a balance between restricting patient autonomy and protecting the patient’s life and the welfare of the broader community, especially when the patient has not yet caused actual harm but presents a potential risk.

ethical_issues.question: Is there a legal mechanism that permits involuntary treatment against the patient’s will to address the serious risk of self-harm and harm to others caused by substance dependence?
keypoints: Massachusetts permits involuntary civil commitment for patients who pose a “serious risk” of harm to themselves or others as a result of substance abuse.

Under Chapter 123, Section 35 of the Massachusetts General Laws, spouses, blood relatives, guardians, physicians, and police officers may petition the court to involuntarily commit substance-dependent patients to a locked facility for up to 90 days of treatment.
The majority of states nationwide (approximately 38) have similar laws permitting civil commitment for substance abuse, although the specific eligibility criteria and procedures vary.
A minority of states do not have laws authorizing involuntary treatment for substance dependence but generally allow for short-term involuntary hospitalization in emergency situations.

title: Induced Lactation for the Nongestating Mother in a Lesbian Couple
case:
Ms. Forte is 6 months pregnant with her second child, a daughter. She was impregnated via insemination by an anonymous donor and comes to her prenatal care visits with her wife, Ms. Smith. Ms. Forte’s obstetrician, Dr. Bustamante, begins to discuss Ms. Forte’s plans for breastfeeding after the birth, which Ms. Forte did successfully with their first child. Ms. Forte explains that she plans to breastfeed the second child as well but would like her wife, Ms. Smith to also breastfeed their newest child. Ms. Smith, who is also Dr. Bustamante’s patient, asks Dr. Bustamante if she can help induce her lactation.
Dr. Bustamante has known both women for several years. She was extremely happy for them when they got married and helped them to find a pediatrician for their first child who would be supportive of same-sex parents. However, this request for induced lactation strikes her as medically unnecessary. The baby will already have one mother who can breastfeed her, and the process of inducing lactation may carry some risks for Ms. Smith.
case_rewrite:
Ms. Forte is six months pregnant with her second child, a daughter, conceived through insemination with an anonymous donor. She attends her regular prenatal appointments accompanied by her wife, Ms. Smith. During one such visit, Dr. Bustamante, their long-standing obstetrician, raises the topic of feeding plans for the new baby. Ms. Forte shares that she intends to breastfeed, just as she did successfully with their first child. However, she adds that this time, she hopes Ms. Smith can also participate in breastfeeding their newborn.

Ms. Smith, who is also under Dr. Bustamante’s care, expresses her interest in sharing the breastfeeding experience and asks if Dr. Bustamante can assist her in inducing lactation. The couple explains that they want their child to have the opportunity to bond closely with both mothers from the earliest moments.

Dr. Bustamante has known Ms. Forte and Ms. Smith for several years, having supported them through their marriage and even helping them find a pediatrician who would welcome same-sex parents when their first child was born. Despite her strong rapport with the couple, Dr. Bustamante hesitates at Ms. Smith’s request. She considers induced lactation to be medically unnecessary in this situation, since Ms. Forte is already able and willing to breastfeed. Dr. Bustamante is also aware that inducing lactation for Ms. Smith, though generally safe, may involve some mild risks and side effects.

As she reflects on the request, Dr. Bustamante recognizes that, for Ms. Smith, the desire to breastfeed goes beyond nutritional concerns; it represents an important way to forge a deep emotional bond with her child and actively participate in caregiving from the start. Nevertheless, Dr. Bustamante questions whether it is appropriate to proceed with induced lactation in a case where the infant already has a source of breast milk, and wonders if declining the service could be viewed as treating Ms. Smith differently from other nonbiological mothers, such as adoptive mothers, for whom induced lactation is often supported. The ethical dilemma centers on whether her reluctance to provide induced lactation arises from genuine medical concern or reflects a potential bias regarding the needs and rights of LGBTQ families.

ethical_issues.question: Does a physician’s refusal to provide induced lactation services to the nongestating mother in a lesbian couple, when the gestational mother is able to breastfeed, constitute discrimination?
keypoints: The primary benefit of induced lactation lies in fostering the emotional bond between the nongestating mother and the infant, rather than solely providing nutritional value; therefore, denying induced lactation services overlooks this fundamental significance.

In the context of widespread medical consensus supporting induced lactation for other nonbiological mothers (such as adoptive mothers), refusing to provide induced lactation services to Ms. Smith may reflect potential discrimination against LGBTQ patients.

Even when the infant already has a source of breast milk, induced lactation remains an important means for the nongestating mother to participate in the breastfeeding process and establish a parent-child relationship, and thus should be treated and supported equally.

ethical_issues.question: Are the emotional bonding benefits of induced lactation sufficient to outweigh the potential health risks, thereby constituting an ethical justification for physicians to provide this service?
keypoints: The health risks associated with induced lactation in nongestating mothers are extremely low, while its emotional bonding benefits—particularly in establishing mother-infant intimacy—are significant and far outweigh the potential risks.

The relevant pharmacologic agents (such as chlorpromazine and metoclopramide) pose minimal or negligible risk to the infant, and the side effects experienced by breastfeeding mothers are generally short-term and overall low risk.
The medical consensus holds that the primary value of induced lactation lies in promoting the emotional bond between mother and infant, rather than solely providing nutritional benefits.

The American Academy of Family Physicians and the American Academy of Pediatrics endorse induced lactation in contexts involving adoptive and nongestating mothers, considering the risks to mother and infant minimal and the benefits clear.

Given the health status of Ms. Forte and the newborn in this case, ethical concerns regarding induced lactation lack sufficient justification, and physicians should respect the patients’ emotional and caregiving needs.
