title: Minors’ Right to Know and Therapeutic Privilege
case:
“Why do I feel so bad, doctor?”
Dr. Marion’s heart broke as she looked at the adorable 9-year-old girl who asked the question. Jill had been diagnosed with acute lymphocytic leukemia almost 5 months earlier, and Dr. Marion had quickly grown attached to the young girl. When Dr. Marion first started caring for Jill, it appeared that she was responding to treatment quite well. But over the past several weeks, Jill was in the hospital more often—the combined result of frequent infection and the toxic agents needed to treat her leukemia.
Throughout Jill’s treatment course, her parents had insisted she not be told about her diagnosis. A friend at school had died from cancer, and the loss had affected Jill profoundly. For months afterward, Jill had not wanted to go back to school and refused to sleep in her own room, preferring to be close to her parents. Not long after Jill seemed to be recovering from the most intense effects of her schoolmate’s death, she was diagnosed with leukemia. Her parents feared that telling her she had leukemia would compromise her emotional health and well-being. They asked Dr. Marion and others involved in Jill’s care to refrain from disclosing her diagnosis to her.
Dr. Marion—and the rest of the medical staff—had thus far respected their wish, but felt strongly that Jill was mature enough to understand her condition and that she deserved to know what was going on, given that her leukemia might be life-limiting. Once, when her parents were not around, Jill asked what was wrong with her, and Dr. Marion offered an explanation that did not mention cancer but focused on side effects of medications. Now, Jill was asking again.
case_rewrite:
“Why do I feel so bad, doctor?”

Dr. Marion felt a deep ache as she met the wide, searching eyes of nine-year-old Jill, who sat curled on the hospital bed. Nearly five months had passed since Jill was diagnosed with acute lymphocytic leukemia, and over that time, Dr. Marion had developed a close, protective bond with the gentle, inquisitive child. Early in Jill’s treatment, there had been hope—she seemed to be responding well, and her bright spirit persisted despite the long days at the hospital. But recently, Jill’s hospital stays had become more frequent, the result of repeated infections and the severe side effects of the treatments meant to help her.

From the beginning, Jill’s parents had been adamant that she must not be told about her diagnosis. Not long before her own illness, a classmate of Jill’s had died from cancer—a loss that left her withdrawn and anxious. For months, Jill clung to her parents, refusing to sleep in her own room and dreading the return to school. By the time she was starting to recover emotionally from her friend’s death, Jill herself received the devastating diagnosis of leukemia. Her parents, fearing the emotional turmoil the truth might cause, asked Dr. Marion and the rest of the care team never to mention “leukemia” or “cancer” to Jill.

Dr. Marion, along with the other staff members, had respected the parents’ wishes thus far, but she found herself increasingly troubled by the situation. She believed Jill was perceptive and mature enough to understand her illness at an age-appropriate level, and that she deserved to know the truth about her health—especially because her condition could be life-limiting. Once, when Jill’s parents had stepped out of the room, Jill had quietly asked Dr. Marion what was wrong with her. Struggling with her obligations, Dr. Marion answered in vague terms, describing the side effects of the medications but carefully avoiding any mention of cancer.

Now, sitting beside Jill’s bed as the child asked again—her small voice tinged with confusion and worry—Dr. Marion felt the weight of the dilemma. Jill’s searching gaze made it clear that she sensed something more was being hidden from her. Dr. Marion knew she needed to consider not only her responsibility to Jill’s parents, but also her duty to Jill herself: to provide honest, compassionate answers, and to support Jill’s understanding and participation in what lay ahead.

ethical_issues.question: In medical decision making for minor patients, how should the balance be struck between parental authority and the physician’s obligation to be honest with the patient?
keypoints: In medical decision making involving minor patients, a child-centered collaborative model should be upheld, balancing the child’s emerging autonomy, the physician’s therapeutic obligations, and the parents’ legal authority.

Physicians should facilitate the young patient’s participation in medical decision making according to the child’s cognitive and emotional developmental level, providing information about the illness and treatment in a developmentally appropriate manner.

The physician’s obligation to be honest with the patient is a fundamental ethical requirement; when directly questioned by the child, physicians should respond truthfully and appropriately, while clearly communicating this obligation to the parents.

In communication with parents, physicians should avoid framing diagnostic disclosure as merely seeking parental permission; instead, they should clearly inform parents that the diagnosis will be disclosed to the child within a reasonable timeframe and invite parental involvement in designing a staged disclosure plan to respect the parent-child relationship and facilitate parental acceptance.

Concealment or deception regarding diagnostic information from the child must be firmly avoided to protect the child’s developing autonomy and right to know, ensuring that medical decisions align with the child’s best interests.

ethical_issues.question: Does a physician have an obligation to disclose diagnostic information to a minor patient in an age-appropriate manner when the parents request nondisclosure?
keypoints: Physicians have an obligation to disclose diagnostic information to minor patients in an age-appropriate and comprehensible manner, respecting their emerging right to know and developing autonomy, even when parents request nondisclosure.

Disclosure of information not only facilitates the cultivation of the patient’s decision-making capacity and psychological adjustment but also promotes trust and collaboration between the physician and patient.

Physicians should comprehensively assess the patient’s age, cognitive developmental level, emotional state, willingness to be informed, and the potential impact of the information on the patient’s physical and mental health, thereby appropriately determining the timing and manner of disclosure.

The patient’s autonomy and the physician’s professional ethical obligations should take precedence over parental protective wishes; prolonged concealment or deception of the patient is ethically impermissible.
In the absence of parents or when the patient actively inquires, physicians must respond honestly, avoiding evasion or misleading answers, thereby demonstrating respect and care for the patient.

ethical_issues.question: When a minor patient inquires about their own health condition, how should the physician respond in order to avoid potential harm to the patient’s psychological well-being?
keypoints: Physicians have an obligation to respond to inquiries from minor patients about their health status in an age-appropriate, honest, and sensitive manner, avoiding deception and evasion.
Concealment of the diagnosis may lead to unrealistic fears and misunderstandings in the child, adversely affecting their psychological well-being and treatment adherence.

Physicians should proactively communicate with the patient’s parents to clarify the necessity and timing of diagnostic disclosure, emphasizing that this is a professional responsibility aimed at protecting the patient’s best interests rather than merely seeking parental permission.

Parental involvement in designing the manner of disclosure should be encouraged by offering multiple options, thereby respecting the parent-child relationship and enhancing parental acceptance and cooperation.

Diagnostic disclosure should be conducted in a phased and gradual manner, taking into comprehensive consideration the patient’s age, cognitive development, emotional capacity, and the potential impact of information on their physical and mental health.

Open and transparent communication facilitates the patient’s long-term psychological adjustment and treatment cooperation, reducing the negative psychological consequences associated with nondisclosure.

title: Pay for Performance: What We Measure Matters
case:
Mr. Ozonoff arrived at Dr. Mehta’s office for his annual checkup. His blood pressure had been in the normal range until a few months ago, when it had started to creep up, according to the blood pressure machine he sometimes used outside his workplace cafeteria. At Dr. Mehta’s office, it registered 145/90—just into the hypertensive range.
Dr. Mehta wanted to get Mr. Ozonoff’s blood pressure back into the normal range and thought the goal could be achieved by changes in his eating and exercising habits. At the same time she recognized that her practice received a financial bonus every quarter from several of the health plans they contracted with when a certain percentage of the patient panel maintained blood pressures within the normal range, and medication was the surest and simplest way to accomplish the goal quickly.
Because Mr. Ozonoff’s blood pressure was only slightly above the 140/90 cutoff for hypertension, Dr. Mehta began to discuss lifestyle changes—such as regular exercise and eating a healthier, lower-salt diet— with him, changes that would help not only with his blood pressure but with other health problems; his weight, for example, had been edging upward over the past few years.
Mr. Ozonoff seemed uninterested in Dr. Mehta’s suggestions that he alter his lifestyle in any way. “I’m too busy right now to change anything,” he said. “But I know I can’t continue with my blood pressure going up and up. Just write me a prescription and we’ll see how that works.”
Writing a prescription is a quick fix that’ll leave him dependent on medication and not change his poor eating habits for the better, Dr. Mehta reasoned to herself. Moreover, she thought, does having a certain percentage of blood pressures under 140/90 really indicate that we’re doing a good job clinically?
case_rewrite:
Mr. Ozonoff arrived at Dr. Mehta’s office for his annual physical. Over the past several years, his blood pressure readings had always been within normal limits, but recently, he’d noticed higher numbers on the blood pressure machine he occasionally used near the cafeteria at his workplace. Today, in Dr. Mehta’s office, his blood pressure measured 145/90—just over the threshold for hypertension.

Dr. Mehta was eager to help Mr. Ozonoff bring his blood pressure back into the healthy range. She believed that modifying his diet and increasing his physical activity could be effective, especially since she’d observed that his weight had gradually increased in recent years. At the same time, she was aware that her clinic received quarterly financial bonuses from several health plans when a certain proportion of their patients maintained blood pressures within the normal range. Prescribing medication would be the fastest and most reliable way to meet this target.

Given that Mr. Ozonoff’s blood pressure was only slightly above the 140/90 cutoff, Dr. Mehta began by discussing non-pharmacological options—encouraging regular exercise and a diet lower in salt, both of which would benefit his overall health, including his rising weight. However, Mr. Ozonoff showed little interest in adopting these changes. “Life is just too hectic right now for me to change my habits,” he told her. “But I realize my blood pressure can’t keep getting higher. Why don’t you just give me a prescription and let’s see how that goes.”

Dr. Mehta hesitated. She knew that prescribing medication would quickly lower his blood pressure and help the clinic achieve its financial benchmarks, but it wouldn’t address the underlying issues with his diet and activity, and could leave him dependent on medication instead of encouraging healthier habits. She also questioned whether simply having enough patients under the 140/90 mark genuinely reflected good clinical care.

As Dr. Mehta weighed her options, she considered her responsibility to provide care centered on Mr. Ozonoff’s needs and preferences, rather than being swayed by the clinic’s potential financial gains.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Dr. Mehta’s care for Mr. Ozonoff, how can a pay-for-performance healthcare system ensure that financial incentives do not undermine physicians’ ethical obligation to prioritize patient well-being over the financial interests of themselves or their practice?
keypoints: Professionalism should compel physicians to prioritize patient well-being and avoid placing personal or practice financial interests above those of the patient.
The design of performance incentives should aim to ignite physicians’ intrinsic motivation rather than coerce or suppress their professionalism.

Incentive mechanisms ought to reward physicians for performing the “right clinical actions,” including respecting patient preferences, providing thorough lifestyle counseling, and making individualized treatment decisions, rather than solely evaluating whether patients achieve specific health targets.

Physician involvement in the design and implementation of performance-based compensation programs helps ensure that incentive structures uphold professionalism and patient welfare, thereby promoting high-quality medical care.

title: Ethical Concierge Medicine?
case:
Dr. Lamb opened her e-mail inbox on Monday to find a message from her group practice manager—the third one that month—explaining more upcoming changes in how to code for what government and private insurers call E&M (evaluation and management services). The physician groaned and rolled her eyes. As members of a medium-sized group (40 members) that cared for many patients on Medicare, Dr. Lamb and her colleagues had been notified that the Affordable Care Act required them to phase in a value-based payment modifier (VPM) starting in 2015. The details of VPM and the measurement data participating groups had to provide if they did not want to accept an automatic reduction in payments seemed overwhelming to many group members whose primary goal was patient care.
Before the VPM reporting business started, it had been a new electronic records system. The original electronic records system the practice acquired just a few years before did not talk properly to other systems or report certain performance measures, and now Dr. Lamb and others had to learn the new system, apologizing to each patient as they searched for the right boxes and codes on the screen.
Then there was the upcoming switch from the current ICD-9 diagnosis coding system to the ICD-10 coding system, the latter containing 68,000 codes—a fivefold increase from the current number. In addition to these government requirements, physicians had the usual insurance filing to keep up with.
Dr. Lamb knocked on the office door of her co-worker, Dr. Tau, a pediatrician.
“Did you get the latest e-mail about the value-based payment modifier?” she asked.
“Sure did,” Dr. Tau answered with a groan. “You know, for the first time, I’m thinking about ‘going off the grid’ and starting my own concierge practice just to escape all of this paperwork. Sure, my patients will have to pay me directly, but instead of spending my time trying to understand the next government scheme and filling out forms, I’ll be able to spend my time helping them—which is why I went into medicine in the first place.”
Back in her office, Dr. Lamb thought about what Dr. Tau had said. She’d never even considered concierge medicine and knew that many, probably most, of her patients couldn’t afford it. Still, the idea of getting back to simply and purely practicing medicine was tantalizing.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Lamb opened her e-mail inbox on Monday morning and sighed as she saw yet another message from her group practice manager—the third this month—about upcoming changes in coding requirements for government and private insurers regarding E&M (evaluation and management) services. She rolled her eyes, feeling the familiar frustration bubble up. As part of a 40-member group practice that cared for a substantial number of Medicare patients, Dr. Lamb and her colleagues had recently been informed that, under the Affordable Care Act, they were required to phase in a value-based payment modifier (VPM) starting in 2015. The VPM’s complex details and the extensive measurement data they would have to submit to avoid an automatic reduction in payments overwhelmed many in the group, whose primary focus remained patient care.

This was just the latest in a series of administrative hurdles. Not long before, the practice had struggled through the implementation of a new electronic records system. The previous system, installed only a few years earlier, had been incompatible with other platforms and couldn’t report certain performance metrics. Now, Dr. Lamb and her colleagues found themselves apologizing to patients as they hunted for the correct boxes and codes on the unfamiliar screens, trying to learn the new system on the fly.

Looming ahead was yet another challenge: the transition from the ICD-9 to the ICD-10 diagnosis coding system, which would require them to navigate a bewildering 68,000 codes—a fivefold increase. These mounting government mandates came on top of the usual insurance paperwork that already consumed much of their time.

Seeking a moment of commiseration, Dr. Lamb knocked on the door of her colleague, Dr. Tau, a pediatrician down the hall.

“Did you see the latest e-mail about the value-based payment modifier?” Dr. Lamb asked.

Dr. Tau groaned in response. “Yes, I did. Honestly, for the first time, I’m thinking about just leaving all this behind and starting a concierge practice. If I go that route, my patients would pay me directly—not through insurance—and I could finally get back to actually helping people instead of drowning in bureaucracy. That’s why I became a doctor in the first place.”

Back at her desk, Dr. Lamb mulled over Dr. Tau’s words. She had never seriously considered concierge medicine before, acutely aware that most of her patients probably couldn’t afford such a model. Still, the idea of returning to the core of patient care, free from endless forms and coding changes, was deeply appealing.

ethical_issues.question: Does concierge medicine lead to discontinuity of care for existing patients and shift the burden onto other physicians?
keypoints: Transitioning to a retainer (concierge) medical practice may result in discontinuity of care for the majority of patients, as physicians who switch retain only about 12% of their original patient panel, necessitating that displaced patients find new providers.
Given the existing shortage in the primary care workforce, the reduced patient panel size of retainer physicians may shift the care burden onto other physicians who are already overextended.

Other professional changes, such as physician relocation or reduction in working hours, similarly cause patient care discontinuity and increased workload for colleagues; however, these are generally not regarded as ethical concerns, providing an important comparative framework for evaluating the ethical implications of transitioning to retainer medicine.

ethical_issues.question: Before deciding to transition to concierge medicine, how should a physician weigh its advantages against the ethical concerns raised by the unique fiduciary nature of the medical profession?
keypoints: The medical profession holds a special status and bears societal responsibilities, with physicians carrying fiduciary duties that go beyond those of ordinary commercial transactions.

Physicians should carefully weigh the advantages of concierge medicine against the ethical concerns arising from the fiduciary nature of medical practice, ensuring that the interests of patients remain paramount.

Transitioning to a retainer practice may result in some patients facing restricted access to medical resources due to their inability or unwillingness to pay additional fees; physicians should attend to issues of equity in order to fulfill their ethical obligations.
In making practice decisions, physicians should fully consider the fairness of resource allocation and the diversity of patient populations, striving to avoid exacerbating health care disparities.

Ethical decision-making requires physicians to evaluate all reasonable alternatives and choose the course that maximizes overall patient benefit and minimizes harm, thereby embodying professional responsibility and altruism.

ethical_issues.question: Does concierge medicine restrict patients’ access to necessary medical care due to their inability to pay additional service fees, thereby impacting health care accessibility and equity?
keypoints: Concierge medicine poses a core ethical risk by restricting patients’ access to basic medical care through additional service fees, thereby challenging physicians’ fiduciary responsibilities and the principle of healthcare equity.
Transitioning to a concierge practice typically results in discontinuity of care for the majority of former patients, increasing care fragmentation and the burden of patient reassignment.

The proportion of African American, Hispanic, Medicaid, and chronically ill patients is significantly reduced in concierge practices, reflecting a negative impact on healthcare access for vulnerable populations.

The medical profession bears an ethical responsibility to ensure equitable access to resources; if practitioners neglect this obligation, the profession’s overall capacity to fulfill its social responsibility is undermined.

title: Team Response to Internal Disagreement about Professional Conduct
case:
Mr. Berkley is a physical therapist on a home-based primary care (HBPC) team. The HBPC team is multidisciplinary, with independent practitioners who visit patients in their homes. The team meets weekly, and is composed of physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, physical therapists, respiratory therapists, social workers, dieticians, and nondenominational members of the clergy. The team’s leader, Dr. Miller, is a specialist in geriatric medicine.
When the team learned that one of their patients, Mr. Noland, was not adhering to his prescribed regimen of antipsychotic medication, the team members worked diligently with him, explaining the medication’s importance and encouraging him to take it, but his adherence remained spotty.
At a recent team meeting, Mr. Berkley, a physical therapist, cheerfully reported that Mr. Noland had become much more consistent with taking his antipsychotic medication. However, other team members did not seem pleased by this news. A few of them had seen Mr. Berkley taking small gifts, meals, and groceries to Mr. Noland’s house. They believed this violated professional boundaries. Other team members noted that Mr. Berkley and Mr. Noland shared the same religion and surmised this might be motivating Mr. Berkley to give special attention to Mr. Noland. The team members discussed their concerns, with most concluding that Mr. Berkley’s conduct was inappropriate and set the wrong example for patient care. They recommended that Mr. Berkley be removed from Mr. Noland’s case. Mr. Berkley responded that his care had led to Mr. Noland’s improved adherence to his medication regimen.
After the meeting, Dr. Miller decided to investigate by making a visit to Mr. Noland’s house. Dr. Miller confirmed the allegations discussed at the team meeting. She mentioned to Mr. Noland that Mr. Berkley might be assigned to another client. Mr. Noland was upset by this and threatened to stop taking his medication if Mr. Berkley stopped visiting.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Berkley serves as a physical therapist on a home-based primary care (HBPC) team, which is comprised of independent practitioners who conduct home visits to patients. The HBPC team meets weekly and includes physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, physical therapists, respiratory therapists, social workers, dieticians, and nondenominational clergy members. The team is led by Dr. Miller, a geriatric medicine specialist.

The team recently confronted a challenge: Mr. Noland, one of their patients, was not reliably taking his prescribed antipsychotic medication. Team members made considerable efforts to educate Mr. Noland on the importance of his medication and encouraged him to comply, but his adherence remained inconsistent.

During a recent team meeting, Mr. Berkley shared, in a positive tone, that Mr. Noland was now taking his antipsychotic medication much more regularly. Contrary to his expectations, several colleagues responded with concern rather than approval. Some had noticed Mr. Berkley bringing small gifts, prepared meals, and groceries to Mr. Noland’s home. These actions, in their view, overstepped professional boundaries. Others pointed out that Mr. Berkley and Mr. Noland shared the same religious background and speculated that this may have influenced Mr. Berkley to give Mr. Noland extra attention. The team discussed these issues, with the majority concluding that Mr. Berkley’s conduct was inappropriate and set a problematic precedent for patient care. They recommended that Mr. Berkley be reassigned away from Mr. Noland’s case. In response, Mr. Berkley argued that his involvement was responsible for Mr. Noland’s improved medication adherence.

After the meeting, Dr. Miller decided to look into the situation further by visiting Mr. Noland’s home. During her visit, she confirmed the concerns raised by the team: Mr. Berkley had indeed been providing gifts, meals, and groceries. Dr. Miller informed Mr. Noland that Mr. Berkley might soon be assigned to another patient. Distressed by this possibility, Mr. Noland became upset and threatened to discontinue his medication if Mr. Berkley stopped his visits.

ethical_issues.question: Does Mr. Berkley’s behavior reflect a permissible difference in professional practice style, or does it constitute a violation of professional boundaries?
keypoints: Mr. Berkley provided special attention to the patient by giving gifts, meals, and groceries, thereby crossing professional boundaries.
Mr. Berkley’s actions bypassed established team collaboration protocols, violated the multidisciplinary team’s regulations, and undermined the foundation of team cooperation.
Professional ethics require practitioners to limit their conduct to direct clinical care and to maintain their professional role; Mr. Berkley’s behavior contravened this principle.
While a personable practice style can facilitate the development of therapeutic relationships, it does not justify crossing professional boundaries or disregarding team protocols.

title: Common Misconceptions about Opioid Use for Pain Management at the End of Life
case:
Dr. Cohen practices internal medicine at a small community hospital in Nebraska. He recently admitted Mr. Lopez for rib and back pain, found, upon x-ray, to be due to pathological fractures. Mr. Lopez, 72, had a history of metastatic squamous cell lung cancer that had progressed despite two cycles of chemotherapy. Prior to admission, he had been on palliative chemotherapy and oxycodone, which provided imperfect relief of his day-to-day cancer-related pain.
When Dr. Cohen entered the room, he found Mr. Lopez wincing in pain. Though he was on high dose opiates, he continued to ask for more. Seeing Mr. Lopez’s intense pain, Dr. Cohen wrote an order to increase the amount of his medication.
Later in the day, Mr. Lopez’s nurse told Dr. Cohen that Mr. Lopez had started to get increasingly drowsy. Dr. Cohen went to check and found Mr. Lopez somnolent but arousable and oriented to time, place, and location. Looking at the cardiac monitor, he saw that Mr. Lopez’s respiratory rate had decreased and wrote a new order to return to the previous dose of pain medication.
Within the next 4 hours, Mr. Lopez was breathing well, but once more in extreme discomfort. Dr. Cohen went to the bedside to talk with Mr. Lopez about why he had reduced the pain medication to the current level. When Mr. Lopez responded, his speech was labored. He said the pain was intolerable and that he couldn’t “take any more.”
Dr. Cohen explained again the danger of lowering Mr. Lopez’s respiration, but Mr. Lopez said, “You don’t understand this, this…I can’t take it. I would rather be dead.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Cohen is an internist at a small community hospital in Nebraska. He recently admitted Mr. Lopez, a 72-year-old man, for severe rib and back pain. Imaging revealed that the pain was due to pathological fractures. Mr. Lopez had a known history of metastatic squamous cell lung cancer, which had continued to progress despite two rounds of chemotherapy. Before coming to the hospital, he had been managed with palliative chemotherapy and oxycodone, though this regimen had never fully controlled his daily cancer pain.

When Dr. Cohen first entered Mr. Lopez’s hospital room, he found him visibly grimacing and struggling with intense pain. Despite being on high doses of opioids, Mr. Lopez repeatedly asked for more medication. Witnessing the extent of his patient’s suffering, Dr. Cohen decided to increase the opioid dosage to try to bring Mr. Lopez some relief.

Later that day, Mr. Lopez’s nurse approached Dr. Cohen to report that Mr. Lopez had become increasingly lethargic. Dr. Cohen went to review the situation and found Mr. Lopez somnolent, though he could still be awakened and remained oriented to time, place, and situation. Noticing on the cardiac monitor that Mr. Lopez’s respiratory rate had dropped, Dr. Cohen wrote a new order to return the pain medication to its previous, lower dose.

Within the next four hours, Mr. Lopez’s breathing stabilized, but he was again wracked with severe pain. Dr. Cohen returned to the bedside to speak with Mr. Lopez about the decision to decrease his pain medication. When Mr. Lopez tried to answer, his breathing was labored, and he spoke slowly, saying that the pain was unbearable and that he could not “take any more.”

Dr. Cohen carefully explained the risks associated with higher opioid doses, particularly the danger of suppressing Mr. Lopez’s breathing. Still, Mr. Lopez insisted, “You don’t understand this, this… I can’t take it. I would rather be dead.”

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically acceptable to reduce consciousness or shorten life when alleviating pain in terminally ill patients?
keypoints: The principle of double effect permits the acceptance of harm in certain circumstances to do good; therefore, the use of necessary doses of opioids to relieve pain, even if it may compromise consciousness or shorten life, is morally justifiable.

The intention of the caregiver is central to ethical judgment; there is a clear moral distinction between administering potentially lethal medication to alleviate suffering and intentionally administering poison to cause death.

Patients or their surrogates should be fully informed of all treatment options and their potential consequences, and physicians must respect patient autonomy by obtaining informed consent prior to initiating therapy.

Clinicians should not withhold necessary analgesics from terminally ill patients out of fear of hastening death, provided that the primary intent of treatment is pain relief rather than causing death.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians refuse to administer necessary analgesics to terminally ill patients out of concern for hastening death?
keypoints: According to the principle of double effect, the use of necessary doses of opioids to relieve pain, even if it may potentially hasten death, is ethically and professionally justified.
Official U.S. guidelines explicitly state that undertreatment of pain in terminally ill patients constitutes a deviation from the standard of medical practice.

Studies have demonstrated no significant difference in survival between patients receiving escalating doses of opioids and those on stable doses, indicating that high-dose opioid use does not necessarily shorten life.
The legitimacy of treatment is contingent upon informed consent from the patient, whose autonomous wishes serve as the critical basis for clinical decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: Are There Legal Restrictions on the Use of High-Dose Opioids for Pain Management at the End of Life?
keypoints: The Federal Controlled Substances Act does not interfere with physicians’ decisions regarding drug selection and dosage; physicians may prescribe high-dose opioids to alleviate pain based on legitimate medical need.

The U.S. Supreme Court has explicitly required states to ensure that their laws do not obstruct the provision of adequate palliative care for terminally ill patients, particularly effective relief of pain and other physical symptoms.

Provided that the intent of treatment is to relieve pain rather than to hasten death, the administration of high-dose analgesics is widely recognized as ethically and professionally acceptable, even in the presence of potential risks.

Authoritative guidelines consider undertreatment of pain itself as a deviation from acceptable medical practice standards, emphasizing the physician’s responsibility to adequately manage pain at the end of life.
In end-of-life cancer pain management, physicians generally need not fear legal liability arising from opioid prescriptions, including claims related to harm or addiction.

title: Drug Seeking or Pain Crisis? Responsible Prescribing of Opioids in the Emergency Department
case:
Dr. Jones is an emergency room physician in Baltimore. Late one afternoon, he sees a young woman named Marie who has come to the ER because of extreme abdominal and knee pain over the past 12 hours. Marie says that she is in great distress and rates her pain at a 10 out of 10. She says that the pain resembles that of her previous sickle cell crises and that only Dilaudid helped. She points to her abdomen and both of her knees as the sites of pain and refuses to allow Dr. Jones to touch them. Dr. Jones observes no overt swelling or redness.
Looking at her chart, Dr. Jones sees a long list of emergency department visits and admissions over the past 2 years. Marie, 25, has a diagnosis of sickle cell disease. On most ER visits, the peripheral blood smear reports were inconclusive for vaso-occlusive crisis. Notes from her hematologist comment that she is habitually noncompliant and that they have considered consulting psychiatry to help address her persistent chronic pain.
As he is leafing through the file, Dr. Jones is interrupted by his colleague, Dr. Kapoor, who recognizes the patient’s name and quips, “Good luck with her—she’s a pro at getting drugs.”
When Dr. Jones reenters the room, Marie is tearfully pleading for pain relief.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Jones, an emergency room physician in Baltimore, is nearing the end of a long shift when a young woman named Marie arrives, visibly distressed. She reports severe abdominal and knee pain that began twelve hours ago, describing it as a “ten out of ten.” Between quiet sobs, Marie tells Dr. Jones that her pain is identical to her prior sickle cell crises and insists that only Dilaudid has ever provided relief. When Dr. Jones approaches to examine her, Marie gestures protectively to her abdomen and knees, refusing any physical contact. Dr. Jones notes that there is no visible swelling or erythema on the areas she indicates.

Reviewing Marie’s electronic chart, Dr. Jones sees a history spanning two years of frequent emergency department visits and hospital admissions. Marie is twenty-five and carries a diagnosis of sickle cell disease. However, on most visits, peripheral blood smears have been inconclusive for vaso-occlusive crisis. Her hematologist’s notes mention Marie’s habitual noncompliance with treatment, and document consideration of a psychiatry referral to help address her ongoing chronic pain.

As Dr. Jones continues to review the record, his colleague Dr. Kapoor steps in, glancing at the patient list. Recognizing Marie’s name, Dr. Kapoor comments, “Good luck with her—she’s a pro at getting drugs.” Dr. Jones, a bit unsettled, returns to Marie’s room, where she is now tearfully pleading for pain medication.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians ethically balance the needs of patients with genuine pain against the risk of contributing to opioid addiction when confronted with potential drug-seeking behavior?
keypoints: Physicians should utilize existing safety nets, uphold the principle of patients as partners in their care, and firmly refuse to prescribe opioids when the potential harm to the patient and the community outweighs the benefit to the patient.
Pain assessment should be based on the patient’s functional status rather than solely on numerical pain scores, with emphasis on overall clinical presentation and impact on daily living.

Prior to prescribing opioids when clinical indications are unclear, physicians should conduct a thorough review of the patient’s medical history, consult state Prescription Monitoring Program (PMP) databases, and communicate with the patient’s primary care provider and pharmacist to verify medication use.

Physicians should be proactive in accurately documenting terms such as “addiction,” “substance abuse,” “dependence,” and “doctor shopping” in the electronic medical record (EMR) problem list, providing detailed descriptions of relevant patient behaviors to ensure transparency and ease of identification.

A psychosocial assessment—including evaluation for anxiety, depression, and life stressors—should be conducted, even in the emergency department setting, to comprehensively understand the psychosocial context underlying the patient’s pain.

For patients with a history of drug-seeking behavior and questionable reliability, refusal to undergo a full physical examination or necessary diagnostic tests should be regarded as refusal of care, warranting cautious consideration before prescribing opioids.

When test results do not support a diagnosis of vaso-occlusive crisis, physicians should consult hematology colleagues to review the diagnosis, and in the interim, manage pain with acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as alternative therapies.

ethical_issues.question: In the emergency department, should physicians refuse to prescribe opioids without conducting a comprehensive physical examination or blood tests?
keypoints: A patient’s refusal to undergo necessary comprehensive physical examination or blood tests should be regarded as a refusal of care, thereby providing the physician with reasonable grounds to decline prescribing opioids.

For patients exhibiting drug-seeking behavior and questionable reliability, physicians must conduct due diligence prior to prescribing opioids, including reviewing medical records and test results from other providers, consulting state Prescription Monitoring Program (PMP) databases, and contacting the patient’s primary care physician and pharmacist.
In Ms. Marie’s case, physicians should review test results that do not support a vaso-occlusive crisis with hematology colleagues before administering opioids.
During the period awaiting review and further evaluation, acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be employed as alternative analgesic strategies.

Physicians should adhere to clinical evidence and patient safety in their decision-making; at times, the refusal to prescribe opioids represents the ethically appropriate course of action to protect patient welfare.

ethical_issues.question: When prescribing opioid medications, do physicians have a responsibility to utilize prescription monitoring programs (PMPs) to assess patients’ medication histories in order to protect both patient and public safety?
keypoints: Physicians have an ethical responsibility to utilize Prescription Monitoring Programs (PMPs) to assess patients’ medication histories; although the process may be time-consuming, it is a critical duty to ensure the safety of both patients and the public.

Upon identifying aberrant behavioral patterns through PMP data—such as frequent emergency department visits or doctor-shopping—physicians should engage in appropriate communication with other healthcare providers and pharmacists, respecting patient confidentiality, to collaboratively manage high-risk patients.

When clinical indications are unclear, physicians must review records from other practitioners, consult PMP databases, and contact the patient’s primary care provider and pharmacist to ensure that prescribing decisions are safe, justified, and evidence-based.

title: Use of Narcotics Contracts
case:
Brad was a 53-year-old postal worker who moved from Lansing, Michigan, to Tucson, Arizona. He had been relatively healthy since quitting drinking at 48. Due to his prior alcohol abuse, however, he had developed chronic pancreatitis, which caused him debilitating abdominal pain. He had modified his diet and had been taking pancreatic enzyme supplements faithfully for some time but needed long-acting daily morphine to carry on his normal work activities at the post office.
To continue his care in Tucson, Brad went to a primary care clinic, where he was seen by Dr. Lee. Dr. Lee had long experience in prescribing opioid medications and required all his patients to sign opioid treatment contracts, which explicitly state the risks and benefits of treatment, prohibited behaviors, and criteria for termination of treatment.
A resident physician in Dr. Lee’s clinic approached Brad to discuss the terms by which he could continue to receive his prescriptions for long-acting morphine from Dr. Lee. As the resident explained the contract, Brad got increasingly upset. Finally he said, “Stop. Why are you treating me like a criminal when I have a legitimate medical condition?”
The resident physician saw his point. She wondered whether this contract had been offered in good faith and whether it was Dr. Lee’s way of managing legal risks or discouraging patients he didn’t want to treat. If the latter, it seemed to manage risk at the expense of the patient-physician relationship. The resident didn’t know what to say to Brad.
case_rewrite:
Brad, a 53-year-old postal worker, had recently relocated from Lansing, Michigan, to Tucson, Arizona. After stopping drinking at age 48, he had remained generally healthy, but the years of prior alcohol use had left him with chronic pancreatitis. The condition caused him severe, persistent abdominal pain. To manage this, Brad had carefully adjusted his diet and consistently taken pancreatic enzyme supplements, yet he still relied on daily long-acting morphine to maintain his ability to work at the post office.

Seeking to continue his treatment in Tucson, Brad visited a local primary care clinic and was assigned to Dr. Lee, an experienced physician well-versed in prescribing opioid medications. Dr. Lee had a longstanding policy: every patient receiving opioid prescriptions was required to sign an opioid treatment contract. These contracts detailed both the risks and benefits of opioid therapy, outlined prohibited behaviors, and spelled out the circumstances that could lead to discontinuation of treatment.

During Brad’s initial visit, a resident physician working under Dr. Lee sat down with him to go over the requirements for continuing his morphine prescriptions. As she explained the terms of the treatment contract, Brad’s demeanor shifted from attentive to visibly agitated. After a few moments, he interrupted her, saying, “Stop. Why are you treating me like a criminal when I have a legitimate medical condition?”

The resident paused, recognizing Brad’s frustration. She began to wonder whether the contract was truly being offered in the spirit of partnership and good faith, or if it was Dr. Lee’s way of managing legal risks or subtly deterring certain patients from seeking care. If the latter, she thought, the approach might protect the clinic but could do so at the cost of damaging the trust at the core of the patient-physician relationship. Unsure how to respond to Brad’s concerns, the resident found herself at a loss for words.

ethical_issues.question: Do the potential benefits of narcotics contracts outweigh their potential burdens to the patient or the patient-physician relationship?
keypoints: Narcotics contracts may convey a message of mistrust, thereby undermining the foundational trust in the patient-physician relationship.
Existing research evidence indicates that narcotics contracts have limited effectiveness in reducing drug misuse and the strength of this evidence is weak.
The widespread implementation of narcotics contracts for all patients may place those at low risk of abuse at increased risk of undertreated pain.

The use of narcotics contracts for patients at high risk of abuse or diversion is justified, as it aids in risk management and helps avoid the extreme consequences of prescribing without safeguards or refusing treatment altogether.
Physicians should employ evidence-based risk assessment tools to individualize patient risk evaluation and require contracts only for high-risk patients, thereby avoiding mechanistic application.

title: Lifestyle is Medicine
case:
Dr. McDaniel is a cardiologist who is preparing to see a new patient, Mrs. Huber. As she looks through Mrs. Huber’s paperwork prior to her visit, she sees that the patient is 42 years old and has a family history of diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and heart disease. Her pre-visit blood work reveals mildly elevated LDL cholesterol and borderline low HDL cholesterol.
Dr. McDaniel sits down to speak with Mrs. Huber. She introduces herself and begins to review Mrs. Huber’s medical history. While Mrs. Huber says that she currently has none of the symptoms that would suggest cardiac problems to Dr. McDaniel, no past hospitalizations or surgeries, and no history of personal medical issues, she is very concerned about her family history of cardiac disease. She keeps stating her worry that she will die of a heart attack like her father did when he was 67 years old.
Dr. McDaniel acknowledges her concerns, completes a physical exam, and discusses the laboratory findings. “While we did find mildly elevated cholesterol values on your blood work, Mrs. Huber, I am reassured by your personal medical history, lack of current or past health problems, and normal physical exam. I find that many of my patients are able to successfully improve their risk factors like elevated ‘bad’ cholesterol or low ‘good’ cholesterol by making some different choices in how they live their daily lives and incorporating healthy nutrition and physical activity. Often patients can improve their risk factors through such behavioral changes and avoid the development of further disease without having to take drugs.”
Mrs. Huber appears anxious and expresses some concerns to Dr. McDaniel that her health risks must be dealt with immediately. “Doctor, I don’t think I can afford to try some fruit and vegetables for the next 6 months. I don’t know if I can wait any longer when my arteries are clogging up as we speak! Isn’t there something you can give me to take care of this now so I don’t have to keep worrying so much about dying of a heart attack?”
Dr. McDaniel appreciates Mrs. Huber’s concerns and understands her anxiety, but she has seen that, in many cases, lifestyle interventions including dietary changes are very effective for improving patients’ cholesterol levels and other cardiac risk factors. She also believes that teaching Mrs. Huber about dietary changes would have fewer potential adverse side effects than a medication at this time, and that, unlike a pill, educating her about nutrition and lifestyle behaviors will have benefits on many aspects of her life, building skills she can use to make positive behavioral choices for a long time to come.
case_rewrite:
Dr. McDaniel, a cardiologist, is preparing to meet her new patient, Mrs. Huber. As she reviews Mrs. Huber’s intake forms, Dr. McDaniel notes that Mrs. Huber is 42 years old and has a striking family history: diabetes, high cholesterol, and heart disease run in her family. The results from Mrs. Huber’s recent blood tests show her LDL cholesterol is mildly elevated, and her HDL cholesterol is just at the lower edge of normal.

When Dr. McDaniel meets Mrs. Huber, she introduces herself and begins to go through Mrs. Huber’s medical background. Mrs. Huber reports no current symptoms that would raise cardiac concerns, has never been hospitalized or needed surgery, and has no prior personal health issues. Despite this reassuring history, Mrs. Huber is visibly anxious. She repeats her fears about her family’s cardiac history, especially her father’s fatal heart attack at age 67. “I just can’t stop thinking that I’m going to end up like my dad,” she confides.

Dr. McDaniel listens carefully, acknowledges Mrs. Huber’s concerns, and performs a thorough physical examination. After reviewing the lab findings together, Dr. McDaniel says, “Mrs. Huber, your cholesterol numbers are a little elevated, but considering your overall health, lack of symptoms, and normal exam, I feel reassured. Many patients in your situation have had great success lowering their cardiac risks by making changes in their daily habits—things like nutrition and exercise. With these lifestyle modifications, it’s often possible to improve cholesterol levels and reduce the likelihood of heart disease without starting medication right away.”

Mrs. Huber, however, remains tense. She leans forward and voices her distress: “Doctor, I don’t think I can just wait and try eating more fruits and vegetables for half a year. I’m terrified that every day I’m getting closer to a heart attack—my arteries could be clogging up even now! Isn’t there something you can prescribe to help me right away so I don’t have to live with this constant fear?”

Dr. McDaniel recognizes the depth of Mrs. Huber’s anxiety and the urgency she feels. Although Dr. McDaniel knows from experience that lifestyle changes can be highly effective for improving cholesterol and lowering cardiac risk—and that these changes carry fewer side effects and lasting benefits compared to medication—she also understands the importance of acknowledging Mrs. Huber’s worries. Dr. McDaniel considers how best to help Mrs. Huber understand the potential advantages and disadvantages of each option, and how Mrs. Huber’s emotional state might be shaping her decision-making about her health. Dr. McDaniel is mindful of balancing evidence-based recommendations with respect for Mrs. Huber’s autonomy and values, while also striving to build trust and provide support that addresses both her physical and emotional well-being.

ethical_issues.question: In situations like Dr. McDaniel’s consultation with Mrs. Huber, where there is a divergence in understanding between physician and patient regarding the definition of treatment, how can Dr. McDaniel provide recommendations grounded in evidence-based practice while upholding Mrs. Huber’s autonomy and respecting her values and concerns?
keypoints: Physicians should respect patient autonomy, recognizing that the patient is the ultimate decision-maker.
Physicians have the responsibility to provide professional recommendations based on the best available evidence-based practices, clearly articulating their perspectives and rationale.

When patients exhibit hesitation or anxiety, physicians should employ communication techniques such as motivational interviewing to assist patients in understanding the benefits and risks of different treatment options.
If a patient insists on pharmacotherapy, physicians should incorporate the patient’s preferences into a comprehensive risk-benefit assessment to ensure individualized decision-making.

Establishing a strong therapeutic alliance is essential; lack of trust may lead to failure of lifestyle interventions, and appropriate short-term pharmacologic treatment can serve as a bridge to facilitate subsequent implementation of lifestyle changes.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient, such as Mrs. Huber, expresses significant anxiety or concern about her family history of cardiac disease despite having no current symptoms, what ethical responsibilities does Dr. McDaniel have to assess and address the patient’s mental health in order to ensure that her decision-making regarding prevention and treatment is not unduly influenced by emotional factors?
keypoints: The physician’s primary ethical responsibility is to screen for the presence of acute grief, anxiety, or other mental health conditions in the patient and to assess their impact on cognitive judgment and decision-making capacity, thereby ensuring care that is responsive to the individual needs of the patient.

If the severity of the patient’s anxiety suggests a possible anxiety disorder, the physician should further attend to the psychological state’s interference with health management decisions and coordinate mental health support as necessary.

Ethical practice requires the physician to balance medical evidence with the patient’s psychological state while respecting the patient’s emotional experience, thereby avoiding inappropriate medical decisions influenced by emotional distress.

ethical_issues.question: When faced with a choice between lifestyle interventions and pharmacotherapy, how should physicians balance the principle of nonmaleficence with the patient’s treatment preferences to ensure the provision of the most appropriate care for the patient?
keypoints: Physicians should adhere to the principle of non-maleficence and, based on the best available evidence-based guidelines, prioritize lifestyle interventions as the first-line treatment for mild dyslipidemia.

The patient is the primary decision-maker in treatment choices; physicians must respect the patient’s treatment preferences and employ communication techniques such as motivational interviewing to help the patient understand the importance of lifestyle interventions and to encourage active engagement.

If the patient insists on pharmacotherapy, the physician should conduct a comprehensive risk-benefit assessment, incorporating the patient’s preferences into the decision-making process, thereby establishing a therapeutic alliance that facilitates subsequent lifestyle interventions.

title: Meeting Patients Where They Are
case:
Mr. Kresser was on his way to see his primary care physician, Dr. Patterson, when his wife phoned to say that she had to work late and he needed to pick up the children from their afterschool activities. Mr. Kresser knew he could not leave his children at their activities but was concerned since he had been late for his last appointment with Dr. Patterson a month before when he was stuck at a job interview. The month before that, he cancelled his appointment because he was out of work and could not pay for the visit. Mr. Kresser also worried that Dr. Patterson would be upset with him because, with all the stress in his life, he had not stopped smoking, a behavior that Dr. Patterson had been telling him for years to stop. Even worse, he had not lost any of that extra weight Dr. Patterson was always on his case about. Mr. Kresser knew that his eating habits were not helping with his weight, but, frankly, his weight and smoking were not the aspects of his life that he was most worried about.
Mr. Kresser picked up his kids, dropped them at home, and then rushed to get to Dr. Patterson’s office, arriving more than an hour and a half late. The receptionist told him to wait while she asked whether Dr. Patterson could see him. Dr. Patterson had had a busy day and was running behind his schedule also.
The receptionist told Dr. Patterson that Mr. Kresser had arrived for his appointment an hour and a half late and asked whether Dr. Patterson could see him. Dr. Patterson said “sure.” He wanted to find out whether Mr. Kessler was making any progress on his weight control and smoking. As Dr. Patterson closed the exam room door, he said, “You just caught me. I was about to leave. What’s going on?"
Mr. Kresser felt ashamed at his inability to make better choices for his health. He said, “I have been so busy, and I was on my way on time for my appointment, but I had to pick up the kids at the last minute.” Dr. Patterson took a deep breath and said, “Well you made it. Now how are you doing on the changes to diet and smoking that we talked about?”
Mr. Kresser looked down at the floor. He believed that Dr. Patterson wanted the best for his health, but didn’t think the doctor appreciated all that was going on in his life that was making it difficult for him to change his eating and smoking habits. He felt like he was doing the best he could with everything he had to worry about.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Kresser was on his way to see his primary care physician, Dr. Patterson, when his phone rang. It was his wife, calling to let him know that she would have to work late and that he needed to pick up their children from afterschool activities. Mr. Kresser realized he could not leave the kids waiting, but the thought of missing or being late to his appointment worried him. Only a month earlier, he had been late to see Dr. Patterson after a job interview ran long. The month before that, he had canceled his visit altogether, unable to afford the cost after losing his job. Now, he was anxious that Dr. Patterson would be frustrated with him—not only for his unreliable attendance but also because he hadn't managed to quit smoking, despite years of encouragement from Dr. Patterson. Worse still, his weight hadn’t changed, and he was well aware that his eating habits were far from ideal. But with everything else on his plate, his weight and smoking felt like less pressing concerns compared to the stresses of daily life.

After picking up his children and dropping them off at home, Mr. Kresser hurried to Dr. Patterson’s office, arriving over ninety minutes past his scheduled time. The receptionist greeted him and asked him to wait while she checked if Dr. Patterson could still see him. Meanwhile, Dr. Patterson, already behind schedule after a demanding day, paused when the receptionist relayed Mr. Kresser’s late arrival and inquired if he would like to proceed. After a moment’s consideration, Dr. Patterson agreed—he wanted to check in on Mr. Kresser’s progress with weight management and smoking cessation.

When Dr. Patterson entered the exam room and closed the door, he remarked, “You just caught me. I was about to leave. What’s going on?” Mr. Kresser shifted uncomfortably, feeling a wave of shame over his health choices. “I’ve just been so busy,” he admitted. “I was on my way here on time, but at the last minute, I had to pick up the kids.”

Dr. Patterson took a moment, drew a deep breath, and responded, “Well, you made it. Now, how are you doing with the changes to your diet and the smoking we talked about?” Mr. Kresser dropped his gaze to the floor. He trusted that Dr. Patterson cared about his health, but he didn’t think the doctor truly understood the pressures and challenges he faced. With so much going on in his life, he felt he was doing the best he could, even if his eating and smoking hadn’t changed.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the best interests of the patient with the demands of time management when faced with a patient’s late arrival?
keypoints: Appointment adherence is a shared responsibility between physician and patient; when either party anticipates an inability to meet the scheduled time, proactive communication and negotiation should be undertaken to identify a mutually acceptable resolution.
In cases of patient tardiness, physicians should rationally balance the patient’s best interests with their own time management needs, prioritizing the patient’s access to necessary medical care.

Physicians should employ open-ended questioning to explore the patient’s life circumstances and stressors, respecting the patient’s narrative pace, thereby embodying the principle of patient-centeredness and avoiding an immediate focus on progress toward expected health goals.

When patients face significant life stressors, physicians ought to adjust the clinical focus to address current sources of stress and practical difficulties rather than insisting on immediate behavioral health changes.

Physicians should demonstrate empathy by understanding the patient’s life challenges, fostering a supportive environment that promotes trust and effective communication within the therapeutic relationship.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians balance respect for patient autonomy with the promotion of the patient’s best interests when assisting patients with lifestyle changes?
keypoints: Physicians must strike a balance between respecting patient autonomy and promoting beneficence, avoiding both the permissiveness that may result from unqualified respect for autonomy leading to the tolerance of unhealthy behaviors, and the paternalism that arises from overemphasizing physician-centered goals.

Physicians should assume the role of a guide or coach, grounded in an understanding of the patient’s life circumstances, assessing the patient’s readiness to change, providing personalized advice and factual education, while simultaneously respecting the patient’s agency and leadership in the process.

Physicians ought to base their approach on the patient’s current reality, collaboratively negotiating achievable and mutually agreed-upon health improvement goals, and dynamically adjusting strategies according to the patient’s stage of change to facilitate autonomous and sustained behavioral modification.

title: The Ethics of Hospital Cafeteria Food
case:
Dr. Ashby, Dr. Bennett, and Dr. Morgan all serve on their hospital board, which met to discuss a proposed new policy to revamp the cafeteria and inpatient dietary offerings. The board members expressed many opinions about this issue, and the physicians debated the issue hotly.
Standing to address the board, Dr. Ashby said, half jokingly, “Esteemed colleagues, I believe that it is simply unethical to be serving patients’ families and visitors and our staff members the unhealthy food that is currently being sold in this institution. It is our responsibility as a health-promoting organization to foster all aspects of health. The hospital is a role model for our visitors and staff, and we must set high-quality standards when it comes to our nutritional offerings.”
Next to the podium was Dr. Bennett. “While I agree with Dr. Ashby that we want to promote health,” states Dr. Bennett, “When it comes down to it, it’s every person’s responsibility to make his or her own food choices. Our main responsibility as the hospital’s representatives is not to change individual behavior but to serve the low-income population in our community—and to do that we must ensure the fiscal future of our institution. Our current food vendor is the only option that makes that possible. In order to uphold both our fiscal responsibility and our duty to educate the public about health issues, we could post the ingredients, calories, and nutritional content such as the amount of fat, cholesterol, and sodium in the cafeteria offerings and then leave it up to the visitors and staff to make their own choices.”
Dr. Morgan piped up, “While I think that Dr. Ashby and Dr. Bennett both bring up valid points and have some solutions that we might want to consider, we should not forget that, as a large hospital, decisions we make about the food served in our cafeteria affect not only the health of the patients, their visitors, and employees, but also the broader community, society, and the environment.”

Rising to address her colleagues, Dr. Ashby remarked, partly in jest but with clear conviction, “Colleagues, I honestly believe it is unethical for us to continue serving the kind of unhealthy food that currently fills our cafeteria. As a hospital, our core mission is to promote health in every dimension. We are not just treating illness, but also setting an example for our staff, patients’ families, and visitors. We ought to lead by providing nutritious, high-quality food—anything less undermines our credibility as a health-promoting institution.”

Dr. Bennett took the floor next. “I share Dr. Ashby’s commitment to health,” he began, “but at the end of the day, people must be free to make their own dietary choices. We need to consider all these factors as we decide how to move forward.”

ethical_issues.question: How can a hospital avoid achieving profitability through the sale of unhealthy foods while ensuring its financial sustainability, and does such a practice align with the hospital’s broader mission?
keypoints: The overarching mission of hospitals is to promote community health and public health, with disease prevention and health promotion becoming central priorities of their work.

Ensuring the hospital’s financial sustainability is a fundamental prerequisite; cafeteria services should achieve a reasonable balance between revenue and costs to support the institution’s overall operations.
Generating profit through the sale of clearly unhealthful foods that harm health fundamentally conflicts with the hospital’s health-oriented overarching mission and lacks ethical justification.

Hospitals should proactively assume responsibility for health promotion by avoiding the provision of unhealthful foods to patients, visitors, and staff, and by actively conveying scientifically sound and accurate nutritional information.

Decisions regarding cafeteria food services should comprehensively consider the overall well-being of patients, employees, visitors, and the community, reflecting the hospital’s social responsibility as a health-promoting organization.

ethical_issues.question: Does a hospital have a responsibility to consider the overall impact of its food offerings on the community, society, and the environment, and to select ethically sourced ingredients and supply methods accordingly?
keypoints: Decisions regarding hospital cafeteria food not only affect the health of patients, visitors, and staff but also bear on the overall well-being of the community, society, and the environment.

Hospitals should practice comprehensive ethical decision-making, with their menus and ingredient selections reflecting an integrated consideration of human health, animal welfare, environmental protection, and the local economy.
By choosing ethically sourced ingredients and supply methods, hospitals not only disseminate messages that promote health but also support community sustainability and public health objectives.

ethical_issues.question: Does a hospital have an ethical responsibility to provide health-promoting food to patients, staff, and visitors, rather than offering unhealthful food?
keypoints: Food service is an extension of the hospital’s relationship with the community, and hospitals should assume responsibility for promoting the overall health of the community; the foods provided should be consistent with the dietary advice of clinical physicians.

Hospitals have an ethical responsibility to provide health-promoting foods and to avoid offering unhealthful foods, as disease prevention is a core mission of hospitals, and providing healthy meals helps to fulfill this goal.
Providing healthy foods not only conveys appropriate nutritional messages but also aids in disease prevention and nourishes patients, staff, and visitors, thereby promoting overall health.
As health-promoting organizations, hospitals should set high standards for nutritional offerings and avoid providing unhealthful foods to prevent ethical conflicts with their broader mission.
Hospitals should make the healthy choice the easy choice by implementing sound dietary policies that support behavior change, thereby advancing chronic disease prevention and health promotion.

title: Invoking Shared Beliefs in End-of-Life Decision Making
case:
Mr. Getty’s polycythemia vera had progressed dramatically over the last few months, even as he slowly regained function from his recent stroke. Mr. Getty had expressed more than once—emphatically—that he didn’t want to do hospice at home. This meant that, when the time came, Dr. Burks, his longtime physician, would oversee his care in the several-hundred bed hospital a few miles away. The doctor had been able to persuade Mr. Getty to allow him to visit him at home every month or so, a rare concession on the part of the old cattle rancher.
Mr. Getty’s wife stood at the door and swung it open as the doctor approached. He smiled. “Where’s the young man?”
“None here!” came a voice from the other room. Dr. Burks and Mrs. Getty moved from the kitchen into the room in back, where Mr. Getty sat in an armchair in front of the television. He reached across for the remote and turned off the set. Dr. Burks reached down and shook his hand, then pressed his shoulder. For a moment the two men held each other in silent regard.
“How are your sores?”
“They hurt.”
Dr. Burks listened to his heart, looked closely at his fingernails and hands for signs of bruising. He sat on the chair Mrs. Getty had set for him and crossed his legs. “Looking all right, Mr. Getty,” he said, opening his briefcase.
“Jan, grab those papers, will you?” said Mr. Getty. When she returned, the doctor took them into his hands and flipped through them. “Great, OK, advance directives…”
On the last page was a brief checklist. Suddenly the doctor was conscious of the print his wet finger was making on the page.
“Everything OK, Doc?” Mr. Getty looked at him.
“Uh, yes. Fine.” But really he felt cold. Dr. Burks looked again. “Are you sure about this part?” he asked, pointing to the middle of the page.
Mr. Getty waved his hand in dismissal, or absolution. “Ah, I’m an old man, doc. I don’t want to be a burden on anyone. If it’s my time, it’s my time.”
The doctor stole a look over to his patient’s wife. She sat in the chair listening, then met his gaze. For a flash Dr. Burks was back at the bedside of his dying grandfather, feeding him ice cubes. Dr. Burks had been much younger then; his family had decided to withdraw his grandfather’s feeding tube for reasons he’d long since forgotten. Even in his obtunded state, far past coherence, his grandfather had lunged for the cubes, sucked on them desperately with noisy gulps. Dr. Burks looked down again and read through the conditions listed on the page: “…or (c) a minimally conscious condition in which I am permanently unable to make decisions or express my wishes….” His eyes lingered on the blue check mark next to the option, in that clinical language to which he had never grown accustomed: I do not want artificial nutrition and hydration.
Almost automatically, he finished the exam, shook Mr. Getty’s hand, and exchanged a few more kind words. He slipped the copy of the document into his briefcase. Mrs. Getty walked him to the door. “You know, Dr. Burks, you have been such a blessing for us,” she said. “I don’t know what we would do without you. And even if he doesn’t say it—” she glanced with a kind smile to the other room, then pressed closer, “it means so much to Dan that you’ll be the one there for him if anything happens.”
As he drove, the radio low, his mind lingered over the documents in his briefcase. He became more and more certain that it was a directive with which he could not comply.
