ethical_issues.question: In end-of-life decision making, does the designation of a health care proxy more accurately reflect the patient’s true wishes than advance directives, especially when the patient may face a variety of clinical scenarios?
keypoints: Advance directives are generally broad statements that are difficult to encompass the diverse clinical scenarios a patient may encounter, and therefore may not accurately reflect the patient’s true wishes.

Designating a health care proxy who is familiar with the patient’s values and preferences facilitates a flexible interpretation and application of advance directives according to the specific clinical situation, enabling end-of-life decisions that better align with the patient’s authentic intentions.

In this case, Mr. Getty ultimately agreed to reconsider the clause in his advance directive regarding refusal of artificial nutrition and hydration in a minimally conscious state and to appoint his wife as his health care proxy, illustrating the pivotal role of a health care proxy in end-of-life decision making.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient’s wishes conflict with the physician’s moral convictions, how should the physician address this situation to ensure that he or she does not act against his or her conscience?
keypoints: Physicians should regard themselves as advisors providing the best medical recommendations rather than decision-makers, and should proactively initiate in-depth discussions with patients regarding their end-of-life care preferences.

Physicians and patients should jointly explore their fears concerning suffering and loss of function at the end of life, share their understandings of advance directives, nutritional support, and the role of physician conscience in clinical care, thereby fostering mutual understanding.

When significant moral disagreements arise between physician and patient, both parties should seek an ethical consensus that transcends individual preferences, balancing the interests of the patient with the physician’s conscience.

Physicians should clearly inform patients that, for reasons of conscience, they may not be able to fully comply with the patient’s wishes, and should actively seek solutions through enhanced communication and clarification of mutual obligations.

If such conflicts cannot be reconciled, the physician should consider discontinuing the specific physician-patient relationship to ensure that the rights and ethical principles of both parties are respected.

title: Positive Claims of Conscience and Objections to Immigration Law
case:
Dr. Prado flipped the hallway flags outward and pushed his shoulder into the door. Inside the room a man and woman sat, the woman manifestly pregnant. They bowed their heads shyly as he entered and then looked up at him expectantly.
Dr. Prado sat. “Senora, buenas tardes. Senor.”
The woman smiled at his articulation, clumsy but sincere.
“Todo parece bien. Su bebe esta…creciendo bueno. Er, bien.”
All three laughed. The couple pleased, as they should be; they awaited good news with all the anxiety of first-time parents.
They proceeded through the visit without incident, and Dr. Prado assured them that he would be there when she finally went into labor. When they rose to leave, the man hesitated for a moment and looked at the doctor. He was on the verge of a question.
“Yes?” Dr. Prado asked. The man explained something quickly, in Spanish. Dr. Prado frowned for a moment, struggling to translate. “Papeles,” the man said, shaking his head and gesturing to his wallet.
“Ah. No.” Dr. Prado shook his head. “I don’t report. No reporto.” He wasn’t concerned that patients like these seemed to find him more or less regularly, and he considered it part of his duty to treat them regardless of their immigration status. Often they would find a way to pay, sometimes not. He had never asked for documentation, and preferred not to cast his relationship with his patients in an atmosphere of suspicion. It was somewhat unclear whether his actions were legal; state law prohibited him only from providing sanctuary for the immigrants, without requiring him to report them.
As Dr. Prado was returning to his desk, another physician in the practice, Dr. Hartz, intercepted him. “Listen,” he said, “I don’t want you endangering this practice.”
Dr. Prado sat back from his computer, but remained silent. Dr. Hartz glared. This wasn’t the first time he had confronted Dr. Prado about some of the patients he took, but the intensity of his criticism had grown in recent months.
“Be a doctor, not a zealot,” he said evenly.
Dr. Hartz turned and walked away. Dr. Prado watched him go, then turned back to the open chart on his desk.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Prado flipped the hallway flags outward and leaned his shoulder against the exam room door. Inside, a man and woman sat together—she was visibly pregnant. As Dr. Prado entered, they both lowered their heads shyly before looking up with hopeful eyes.

Dr. Prado took a seat. “Senora, buenas tardes. Senor.”

The woman’s smile reflected her appreciation for his Spanish, imperfect but heartfelt.

“Todo parece bien. Su bebe está… creciendo bueno. Er, bien.”

All three laughed, the couple reassured. The tension of awaiting news as first-time parents seemed to ease. The appointment proceeded smoothly, and Dr. Prado assured them he would be present when labor began. As they stood to leave, the man paused, uncertainty flickering across his face. He glanced at Dr. Prado, gathering the courage to speak.

“Yes?” Dr. Prado prompted. The man spoke quickly in Spanish, his words tumbling out. Dr. Prado concentrated, parsing the meaning. “Papeles,” the man said, shaking his head and patting his wallet.

“Ah. No,” Dr. Prado replied, shaking his own head. “I don’t report. No reporto.” He had grown accustomed to patients like these coming to him, and he saw it as his responsibility to care for them, regardless of immigration status. Sometimes they managed to pay, sometimes not. He never asked for documentation, preferring not to create an atmosphere of mistrust. Legally, his position was ambiguous; state law barred him from offering sanctuary, but did not require him to report undocumented patients.

Heading back to his desk, Dr. Prado was intercepted by Dr. Hartz, another physician in the practice. “Listen,” Dr. Hartz said, his tone tense, “I don’t want you putting this practice at risk.”

Dr. Prado leaned back from his computer, choosing to stay silent. Dr. Hartz’s gaze was stern. This wasn’t the first time he had confronted Dr. Prado about his patient choices, but his objections had grown sharper.

“Be a doctor, not a zealot,” Dr. Hartz said, voice level but firm.

Without waiting for a response, Dr. Hartz turned and walked away. Dr. Prado watched him disappear down the hallway, then turned his attention back to the patient chart open on his desk.

ethical_issues.question: Should the law protect physicians’ positive claims of conscience, allowing them to violate prohibitions against treating undocumented patients without facing penalties?
keypoints: The law should protect physicians’ positive claims of conscience to preserve their moral integrity and prevent moral harm resulting from acting against their core ethical beliefs.
Positive conscience claims are of equal moral weight and protective value as negative conscience claims and should receive equivalent legal recognition.
Recognizing and protecting positive conscience claims does not amount to condoning illegal conduct; the law can legitimize such exercise of conscience through the establishment of exemption clauses.
In the context of treating undocumented patients, safeguarding physicians’ positive conscience claims contributes to the respect of patient rights and the promotion of equitable access to healthcare.

ethical_issues.question: Should immigration laws exempt health care professionals so that physicians do not have to fear prosecution when providing medical services to undocumented patients?
keypoints: Health care is of paramount importance, and any obstacles that may hinder patients’ access to medical services are unjustified, especially in the context of emergency and basic health needs, where unimpeded access should be ensured.

Relevant laws prohibit providing sanctuary to undocumented immigrants but do not explicitly mandate that medical institutions report them, leaving room for legal interpretation and exposing physicians to legal risks when treating undocumented patients.

Physicians’ positive claims of conscience, grounded in ethical obligations to actively provide care, differ from negative claims of conscience, which involve only refusing to participate in actions deemed unethical or illegal; the latter do not exempt physicians from legal penalties in this context.

Protecting physicians’ positive claims of conscience based on ethical obligations helps promote respect for patients’ rights and prevents legal sanctions from undermining the ethical integrity of medical care.

Therefore, immigration laws should at least provide exemptions for health care professionals who, on the basis of ethical obligations, cannot in good conscience comply with relevant legal requirements, in order to safeguard the ethical integrity of medical services and the rights of patients.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians refuse to provide medical care to undocumented patients on the basis of their immigration status?
keypoints: Dr. Prado’s provision of care regardless of immigration status demonstrates respect for patients’ basic rights and upholds the ethical duties of the medical profession.
Positive conscience claims are of equal moral significance to negative conscience claims (refusing to act against one’s ethical convictions).
Protecting physicians’ positive claims of conscience not only preserves their moral integrity but also promotes respect for and protection of patients’ rights and interests.

Tensions may arise between legal requirements and ethical obligations; physicians should, while remaining mindful of the law, carefully weigh their ethical responsibilities and seek a reasonable balance between legal compliance and ethical practice.

title: Medical School Accommodations for Religious and Cultural Practices
case:
Joni had looked forward to her second-look medical school visit with excitement; this school had been her top choice throughout the application process. The first in her family to finish college, Joni felt as if she was carrying enough hopes and expectations for ten people. She was pushing through her last courses with characteristic tenacity. And every day this week, she had worn the silver and turquoise squash blossom necklace that her grandmother gave her before she left for school.
Now, she stood with her fellow accepted students in a cold room with tiled floors, necklace stashed away and her long black hair tied back. The students were passing around a prosection that one of the teaching assistants had given them. It was small and firm, a dusky red—as it got closer, Joni could see that it was a heart. When it got to her, she felt her gloved hands leave her side almost automatically. Then she stopped, quickly shook her head and motioned to the student next in line. Her classmate hesitated for a moment and stood holding the heart, but after a moment passed it in front of Joni to the next student at the tank.
Later that day Joni walked into the lab director’s office. She shook his hand and introduced herself.
“Welcome. Hope you’ve had a good day so far. What is it you would like to talk to me about?” he asked.
Joni was quiet, then gathered her courage. “I’m Navajo. Our cultural beliefs do not allow us to touch dead bodies,” she said gently.
The lab director seemed genuinely puzzled. “Well, I don’t think that this is something that we have encountered before. We have had one or two students find out that they were bothered by the lab, but we always worked through that discomfort…it was an important learning experience.”
case_rewrite:
Joni had been eagerly anticipating her second-look visit to the medical school she’d dreamed about since the start of her application process. As the first in her family to graduate from college, she felt the weight of her family’s hopes on her shoulders, propelling her through the final stretch of her undergraduate studies with her usual determination. All week, she wore the silver and turquoise squash blossom necklace her grandmother had pressed into her hands before she left home, a quiet anchor to her heritage.

Now, standing among other accepted students in a chilly, echoing room with tiled floors, Joni had tucked her necklace safely away and tied her long black hair back. The group was gathered around a prosection prepared by a teaching assistant. It was small, compact, and a deep red. As the object made its way closer, Joni realized it was a human heart. When it was passed to her, her gloved hands instinctively began to reach out, but she paused, pulled back, and shook her head, signaling to the next student. Her classmate hesitated briefly, standing with the heart in hand, then moved past Joni and handed it to the next person at the tank.

Later that afternoon, Joni found herself outside the lab director’s office. She entered, greeted him, and shook his hand, introducing herself.

“Welcome. I hope your visit’s been going well. What would you like to discuss?” he asked.

Joni hesitated, then drew a steady breath. “I’m Navajo,” she began softly. “According to our cultural beliefs, we are not permitted to have contact with dead bodies.”

The lab director looked at her, clearly surprised. “I don’t think we’ve come across this before,” he replied. “We’ve had a couple of students in the past who felt uneasy around the cadaver lab, but we always managed to help them work through that discomfort—it’s an important part of the learning experience.”

ethical_issues.question: Should medical schools provide reasonable accommodations based on cultural beliefs to Navajo students to avoid contact with cadavers?
keypoints: Navajo cultural and religious beliefs prohibit contact with cadavers; medical schools should respect students’ cultural and religious convictions and recognize such objections as reasonable conscience-based refusals.

Denying students’ requests for accommodations grounded in cultural beliefs undermines their moral integrity and forces them to make a difficult choice between their professional aspirations and their personal ethical standards.

Failure of medical schools to provide reasonable accommodations effectively creates barriers for Navajo students entering the medical profession, thereby impeding the advancement of diversity and inclusion within the institution and the medical field.

Contemporary medical education has seen the adoption of non-cadaveric methods for teaching anatomy in some medical schools, demonstrating that cadavers are neither the sole nor indispensable means for anatomical instruction.

Institutions such as the University of Arizona have implemented effective educational practices that respect cultural beliefs by minimizing Navajo students’ exposure to cadavers and arranging cultural purification ceremonies.

ethical_issues.question: Does a medical school’s refusal to accommodate a Navajo student’s conscientious objection undermine the student’s moral integrity and sense of self-identity?
keypoints: Denying Navajo students’ requests based on conscientious objection undermines their moral integrity, as it requires them to violate core ethical beliefs that form the foundation of their self-identity; such violation can result in self-betrayal and diminished self-respect.

Refusal of this request forces the student to choose between relinquishing her professional aspirations and contravening her guiding principles, potentially causing significant psychological distress that may adversely affect her academic performance and overall well-being.

ethical_issues.question: Should medical schools explore and adopt non-cadaveric methods of anatomy instruction to accommodate the needs of students from diverse cultural backgrounds?
keypoints: The use of cadavers for anatomical instruction directly conflicts with the Navajo cultural prohibition against touching dead bodies. Medical schools should respect cultural diversity by exploring and adopting non-cadaveric teaching methods to accommodate the needs of students from diverse cultural backgrounds.

Refusing to provide culturally adaptive educational support for Navajo students forces them to make a difficult choice between their professional aspirations and cultural beliefs, undermining their moral integrity and hindering the advancement of diversity within both the institution and the medical profession.

Recent experience from several medical schools has demonstrated that anatomy education can be effectively conducted without reliance on cadavers, indicating that cadavers are not an indispensable resource for anatomical teaching. Medical schools should actively explore and promote alternative instructional approaches.

Institutions such as the University of Arizona have successfully supported the cultural needs of Navajo students by minimizing exposure to cadavers and arranging culturally significant ceremonies, exemplifying how medical schools can foster cultural inclusion and diversity through flexible curricular adaptations.

title: Profiling Patients to Identify Prospective Donors
case:
As Dr. McGrath entered Mr. Drew’s hospital room, he bumped into a pleasant-looking woman in a suit walking out. “I beg your pardon. I’m Dr. McGrath, Mr. Drew’s physician. Are you his wife?” he asked.
“No,” she replied, “I’m Dana, I’m with the hospital’s foundation. I was just paying Mr. Drew a visit to see how he is enjoying his stay, and if there’s anything we can do to make him more comfortable.”
“Oh,” said Dr. McGrath, surprised. “Is he a hospital donor?”
“Not yet,” she smiled. “We do daily wealth-screening of the patient census—it’s just software that checks what ZIP code they’re from—and then we visit patients from traditionally wealthier ZIP codes, trying to ensure that they have a pleasant hospital stay. If they want, we arrange for a newspaper to be delivered daily, and we send a welcome basket with snacks and flowers. We rely on grateful patients for a lot of the donations we receive, so this is a way to identify and impress potential donors early.”
Dr. McGrath was nonplussed. “So if it looks like he could possibly donate, he gets special treatment? That doesn’t seem right to me.”
“He’s not getting better medical treatment, Dr. McGrath,” said Dana. “And if we impress him and he donates money to the foundation, we can use that money to cover the costs of indigent patients, or to improve the hospital. Just last year, a donor we identified through wealth screening gave a daVinci Robot for the surgical floor.”
In the physician’s lounge, Dr. McGrath brought up his concerns with Dr. Frosch, a highly respected cardiologist.
“Oh sure,” said Dr. Frosch, “It’s no different than the ‘VIP floors’ that a lot of top-tier hospitals have for their super wealthy patients—you know, with famous chefs and marble floors and what-not. Dana actually has me keep one or two appointment slots open every week for donors: if we can keep them happy with our hospital, they’re much more likely to donate to the foundation, and that translates to better care for everyone.”
case_rewrite:
As Dr. McGrath stepped into Mr. Drew’s hospital room, he nearly collided with a well-dressed woman in a suit who was just leaving. “Excuse me,” he said politely. “I’m Dr. McGrath, Mr. Drew’s physician. Are you family?”

The woman smiled. “No, I’m Dana. I work with the hospital’s foundation. I was just dropping by to see how Mr. Drew is finding his stay here, and whether there’s anything we can do to make him more comfortable.”

Dr. McGrath raised his eyebrows in surprise. “Oh, I see. Is Mr. Drew a donor to the hospital?”

“Not at this point,” Dana replied, her smile widening. “We actually perform daily wealth-screening of the patient list. It’s just a software program that checks which ZIP code patients come from. We then visit patients from ZIP codes that are considered more affluent, trying to make their stay as pleasant as possible. If they’re interested, we can arrange for a daily newspaper delivery, and we send a welcome basket with snacks and flowers. Our hospital relies heavily on grateful patient donations, so this helps us identify and engage potential donors early on.”

Dr. McGrath looked uneasy. “So, he receives special attention just because he might be able to donate? That doesn’t quite sit right with me.”

Dana replied smoothly, “He’s not receiving superior medical care, Dr. McGrath. But if we make a good impression and he decides to contribute to the foundation, those funds can help us cover costs for patients who can’t pay, or improve hospital facilities for everyone. For example, last year we received a daVinci Robot for surgery, thanks to a donor discovered through wealth screening.”

Still troubled, Dr. McGrath later shared his concerns with Dr. Frosch, a distinguished cardiologist, in the physician’s lounge.

Dr. Frosch nodded knowingly. “Yes, I’m familiar with the process. It’s really not so different from the ‘VIP floors’ that many prestigious hospitals have for their wealthiest patients—with gourmet chefs, luxurious decor, and such. Dana often asks me to keep an appointment slot or two open each week for donors. If we keep those patients happy with their experience at our hospital, they’re more likely to donate, and those contributions can enhance care for everyone.”

ethical_issues.question: Does the integration of wealth screening with patient care constitute exploitation of patients, and how can the integrity of professional ethics be maintained?
keypoints: The core of medical professionalism includes respect for patients, the principle of honesty, protection of individual privacy, and the refusal to exploit patients’ vulnerability for profit; these are the ethical foundations for evaluating the practice of wealth screening.
The conflation of patient care with fundraising activities may constitute exploitation of patients and represents unprofessional and unethical conduct.

The integration of wealth screening with patient care may undermine the trust relationship between physicians, patients, and the hospital, compromising the fairness, transparency, and protection of patient rights in medical services.

The ethics committee should take the lead in formulating explicit wealth screening policies, incorporating input from the hospital foundation, medical professionals, and ethics committee members to ensure that such activities comply with professional ethical standards.

If wealth screening must be combined with patient care, practitioner involvement in the development of guidelines and oversight mechanisms is essential to safeguard patient rights and the integrity of professional ethics.

title: Secret Shoppers and Conflicts of Interest
case:
Delta Health was one of three large health insurers that shared a Midwest multistate market. Recently all individual and group practices and clinics that were among Delta’s preferred provider organizations (PPOs) received letters from the company informing them that Delta was about to perform a quality audit on some providers, in the hope that the objectively acquired and reported information would help the physicians maintain or improve the quality of care. Delta employees would be calling to schedule appointments and reporting on the ease of getting a timely appointment, the helpfulness of the telephone and office staff, the physician’s attentiveness and response to their reasons for the visit, and the treatment recommendations. The results concerning a physician or clinic would be shared with that physician or clinic only.
Reaction to the Delta Health letter at one PPO, Mid-West Internal Medicine Clinic, was typical. At a specially called meeting, 12 of the clinic’s 15 physicians met to discuss what steps they should take to prepare for Delta audits if, indeed, they were among the “providers” visited.
“This is a secret shopper attack,” said the first speaker, “and we’re not Wal-Mart, and our patients aren’t customers. We have difficulty seeing everyone who really needs care in a timely manner. Now that patient is going to have to wait while we see a secret shopper who’s not even sick. It makes no sense.”
“I’m not worried in the least,” said a second physician. “It’s a one-time thing. They’re not going to send these fake patients in week after week. And we could get some observations that would really help. I don’t have a clue what patients expect when they first walk into the waiting room.”
But others feared that what Delta Health called “information to help maintain or improve quality care” was really going to be economic profiling. A physician whose husband had been getting treated at the faculty practice organization associated with an academic health center in a neighboring state said that Delta had recently dropped that organization as one of its PPOs.
case_rewrite:
Delta Health, one of three dominant health insurers in a multistate Midwest region, recently sent letters to all the individual and group practices and clinics included in its preferred provider organizations (PPOs). The letter announced that Delta would soon be conducting a quality audit on selected providers, explaining that the data gathered would be used to help physicians maintain or raise the standard of care. According to the letter, Delta employees would be calling to set up appointments, and would later report on the ease of scheduling, the helpfulness of both telephone and office staff, the attentiveness of the physician, how well the physician addressed the stated reason for the visit, and the nature of the treatment recommendations. Delta assured the providers that the findings relevant to a particular physician or clinic would be shared only with that physician or clinic.

At Mid-West Internal Medicine Clinic, one of Delta’s PPOs, the response to this letter was typical. The clinic’s 12 out of 15 physicians promptly convened a special meeting to discuss how they should prepare for the possibility of being included in Delta’s upcoming audits.

“This is nothing but a secret shopper ploy,” the first physician declared. “We’re not Wal-Mart, and our patients aren’t retail customers. We already struggle to see everyone who genuinely needs medical attention in a timely way. Now, an actual patient might get delayed because we’re seeing a fake patient who isn’t even sick. It just doesn’t add up.”

Another physician voiced a different opinion: “Honestly, I’m not concerned at all. It sounds like a one-off thing to me. They’re not going to keep sending these fake patients in week after week. We might even get feedback that’s useful. Frankly, I have no idea what patients expect when they first step into our waiting room.”

Still, several colleagues expressed concern that what Delta termed “information to help maintain or improve quality care” was actually a guise for economic profiling. One physician, whose husband had received care at the faculty practice of an academic health center in a nearby state, offered a cautionary example: Delta had recently removed that organization from its roster of PPOs.

The group weighed the implications, debating whether Delta’s secret shopper audit would genuinely assist in improving patient care, or if it was just another layer of scrutiny that could threaten their practice’s status with the insurer.

ethical_issues.question: Is the Use of Secret Shopper Patients Ethical?
keypoints: The use of secret shopper patients may divert medical resources from genuine patients; however, in a busy primary care clinic, a small number of secret shoppers would not materially affect the quality or timeliness of care.

The secret shopper evaluation method introduces deception into the patient-physician relationship, but such concealment has precedents in medical research and clinical quality assessments, and its primary aim of improving quality provides ethical justification for the method.

The secret shopper approach may involve oversight and privacy concerns regarding the clinic, yet physician evaluation and supervision are standard practices in medical care and do not constitute ethical violations.
Taken together, the secret shopper evaluation method can be an ethical, valid, and potentially valuable means of assessing patient experience in healthcare under certain circumstances.

title: Is the Standard of Care Always Worth the Cost?
case:
Mrs. Howard was writhing in pain on the paper-covered bed in the emergency room. She clutched her abdomen. “Yes, I’ve had this pain in the past,” she said to Dr. Murphy, the resident taking her history. “I know I have gallstones. My right side usually aches after I eat greasy foods, but it’s never been this bad before.”
“Okay,” said Dr. Murphy, after performing the physical exam. “I’m almost certain that you have cholecystitis, but we’ll order an ultrasound just to confirm. Most likely, we’ll start you on some antibiotics and fluids until the inflammation goes down, and then we’ll take the gallbladder out with surgery.”
“Wait a minute,” said Mrs. Howard, sitting up in bed. “I’m on a health savings account, and I haven’t spent my deductible yet. Can we just go ahead with the antibiotics and fluids and skip the ultrasound? We already know I have gallstones, so this test is just taking money out of my pocket.”
When Dr. Murphy went to discuss Mrs. Howard’s case with his attending, he asked whether they could skip the ultrasound due to Mrs. Howard’s finances.
His attending wasn’t pleased. “The standard of care in this hospital is to get a confirmatory ultrasound,” she said, “regardless of the patient’s preference to not spend $200 out of her HSA. If you start changing the way you treat patients based on their payment preferences, you’re in dangerous territory.”
“We’re not denying her care or skipping a crucial step because she’s unable to pay, or because we’re trying to cut costs for the emergency room,” Dr. Murphy argued. “We’re just trying to save her money. We could see it as part of acting her best interests.”
The attending fired back, “You know, failing to meet the standard of care feels better when it’s to directly benefit a patient, but the bottom line is, you need to be consistent about the way you practice medicine. The cost of a test shouldn’t enter into your thinking when you’re trying to diagnose a patient—especially not when there’s a standard of care to be followed. You’re a doctor, not her accountant.”
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Howard lay doubled over in pain on the crinkling paper of the emergency room bed, her hands pressed tightly against her abdomen. “Yes, this pain has happened before,” she told Dr. Murphy, the resident carefully taking her history. “I’ve been told I have gallstones. Usually, I get a dull ache on my right side after I eat something greasy, but it’s never hurt this much.”

Dr. Murphy completed his physical exam and spoke reassuringly. “Given your symptoms and history, I’m almost certain you have cholecystitis. We’ll order an ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis. In the meantime, we’ll probably start you on antibiotics and fluids to get the inflammation under control, and then we’ll look at surgery to remove your gallbladder.”

Mrs. Howard sat up slightly, wincing. “Hold on,” she said. “I have a health savings account, and I haven’t met the deductible yet this year. Is the ultrasound really necessary? We already know I have gallstones—this test is just going to cost me more money. Can’t we just do the antibiotics and fluids without it?”

Dr. Murphy paused, then stepped away to discuss the situation with his attending physician. “Mrs. Howard is concerned about the cost of the ultrasound,” he explained. “She’s hoping we can skip it and proceed with treatment since she already has a known history of gallstones.”

The attending’s expression tightened. “Our standard of care requires that we get an ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis,” she responded. “That doesn’t change because a patient doesn’t want to spend $200 from her HSA. If you start making clinical decisions based on who wants to save money, you’re treading into dangerous territory.”

Dr. Murphy replied, “But we’re not withholding care or skipping a test because she can’t pay, and we’re not doing it to save money for the ER. We’re just trying to help her avoid unnecessary expenses. Isn’t that part of acting in her best interest?”

The attending shook her head. “It might feel more justifiable to deviate from the standard when it seems to help your patient, but the reality is that you have to practice medicine consistently. The cost of a test shouldn’t override the need to make a clear diagnosis, especially when there’s a standard protocol in place. Remember, you’re her doctor—not her financial advisor.”

ethical_issues.question: In medical decision-making, should physicians consider a patient’s financial situation and adjust the diagnostic and treatment plan to reduce the patient’s expenses?
keypoints: The physician’s primary ethical obligation is to protect and promote the individual well-being of the patient; clinical decisions should integrate the patient’s medical history, individual characteristics, and economic circumstances.

Medical decision-making ought to be grounded in a rational assessment of the patient’s needs and anticipated benefits, with cost considerations incorporated as part of the overall evaluation of patient needs.

Respecting patients’ non-medical preferences—such as out-of-pocket expenses, timing, and location of treatment—helps strengthen the patient-physician relationship and reflects recognition of patients as autonomous individuals.

Physicians should adhere to established standards of care but remain flexible within the permissible scope of those standards, engaging in thorough communication with patients when necessary to balance medical benefits against financial burdens.

Situations involving clear and irreplaceable standards of care are relatively rare; physicians must avoid omitting essential diagnostic or therapeutic steps solely due to cost concerns, thereby ensuring patient safety and quality of care.

ethical_issues.question: When treating individual patients, should physicians tailor diagnostic and treatment plans based on the patient’s unique medical history, individual characteristics, and financial circumstances, rather than strictly adhering to a uniform standard of care?
keypoints: The physician’s primary ethical obligation is to protect and promote the well-being of the individual patient. In clinical decision-making, physicians should tailor diagnostic and treatment plans by integrating the patient’s unique medical history (such as known gallstones and typical symptoms), individual characteristics, and economic circumstances, thereby allowing for reasonable deviations from the conventional standard of care.

In this case, the patient’s specific clinical background provides an important basis for physician judgment, permitting appropriate adjustments to the diagnostic and treatment process, provided that safety and efficacy are maintained.

Giving due consideration to patients’ nonmedical preferences (such as financial circumstances) helps to strengthen the patient-physician relationship and demonstrates the physician’s respect for the patient as an autonomous individual, rather than merely as a bearer of disease.

Although individualized adjustments may be justified, physicians must still adhere to scientific evidence and principles of medical safety, avoiding the omission of critical diagnostic steps solely due to economic factors, in order to ensure the quality and consistency of care.

title: Communicating Evidence in Shared Decision Making
case:
Dr. Garrison is a third-year resident in internal medicine who takes pride in helping patients make educated decisions regarding their health care, informing them of recent research and answering their questions.
One afternoon in the outpatient medicine clinic, Dr. Garrison spoke with Mr. Mendez, a 62-year-old man who had come in for a yearly physical. In reviewing Mr. Mendez’s chart, Dr. Garrison noted that his total cholesterol was high at 242 mg/dL, while his HDL cholesterol was low at 35 mg/dL. He was otherwise healthy, having normal blood pressure, no other symptoms or signs of cardiovascular disease, no family history of cardiovascular disease, and no history of smoking. According to the Framingham 10-year risk calculator, this picture corresponded to a 15 percent risk of a myocardial infarction in the next 10 years (“moderate risk”).
After discussing the findings of the physical exam with Mr. Mendez, Dr. Garrison entered into a discussion of the lab results. “Mr. Mendez, your lab results indicate that you have high cholesterol. Based upon your current state of health and lab results, you have about a 15 percent risk of experiencing a heart attack in the next 10 years. For patients in your situation, we typically recommend treatment with a drug known as a statin, which helps to lower your bad cholesterol.” Dr. Garrison proceeded to explain the benefits and side effects of statin therapy to Mr. Mendez, who stated that he was willing to try whatever the doctor thought was best.
Dr. Garrison added, “You should also know that, for the average person with your medical history and state of health, the number needed to treat—that is, the number of individuals who must be treated with a statin to prevent one death from a cardiovascular event such as a heart attack or stroke—is generally between 60 and 100, which means that if I treated 60 people in your situation, 1 would benefit and 59 would not. As these numbers show, it is important for you to know that most of the people who take a statin will not benefit from doing so and, moreover, that statins can have side effects, such as muscle pain, liver damage, and upset stomach, even in people who do not benefit from the medication. I am giving you this information so that you can weigh the risks and benefits and then make an informed decision.”
Mr. Mendez looked surprised. He said that he felt fine and, having heard the statistics, did not wish to start statin therapy at this time.
Later that day, Dr. Garrison met a fellow third-year internal medicine resident, Dr. Parra, for coffee in the hospital cafeteria. Discussing some of their cases from the day, Dr. Garrison remarked that several of her patients had elected to try lifestyle modifications rather than initiate drug therapy for hyperlipidemia and some other conditions. “That’s remarkable,” Dr. Parra observed, thinking that most of her patients elected pharmacologic treatment despite her encouragement to consider behavioral changes. Dr. Garrison continued, “I’ve found that providing patients more evidence regarding the effectiveness of drugs, and giving them information such as the number needed to treat, encourages them to think more realistically about the benefits and risks of pharmacologic treatment.”
Dr. Parra wondered about this and responded with concern: “Really? I don’t think our patients can make sense of all this information. They’re not trained in statistics and don’t know how to interpret scientific data. That’s our job.” Dr. Garrison asserted that it is an ethical obligation for physicians to provide information such as the number needed to treat and asked Dr. Parra, “How can our patients make informed decisions regarding their health care if they don’t know the evidence?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Garrison, a third-year internal medicine resident, takes great pride in helping her patients make informed decisions about their health care. She makes it a point to keep up with the latest research and is always ready to answer her patients’ questions in detail.

One afternoon at the outpatient medicine clinic, Dr. Garrison met with Mr. Mendez, a 62-year-old man who had come in for his annual physical examination. As she reviewed his chart, Dr. Garrison saw that Mr. Mendez’s total cholesterol measured 242 mg/dL, which is considered high, and his HDL cholesterol was low at 35 mg/dL. Otherwise, his blood pressure was normal, he had no symptoms or signs of cardiovascular disease, no family history of heart problems, and he had never smoked. Using the Framingham 10-year risk calculator, Dr. Garrison determined that Mr. Mendez had a 15 percent chance of experiencing a heart attack in the next decade—a risk categorized as “moderate.”

After completing the physical exam and discussing those findings, Dr. Garrison turned to the laboratory results. “Mr. Mendez, your lab work shows that your cholesterol is elevated. Based on your overall health and these results, your chance of having a heart attack in the next ten years is about 15 percent. For someone in your situation, we usually recommend starting treatment with a medication called a statin, which can help lower your bad cholesterol.” Dr. Garrison carefully described the potential benefits and possible side effects of statin therapy. Mr. Mendez responded that he trusted Dr. Garrison’s judgment and was willing to do whatever she thought was best.

Dr. Garrison continued, “I also want you to know that, for people with your health profile, the ‘number needed to treat’—which means the number of people who would need to take a statin to prevent one death from a heart attack or stroke—is usually between 60 and 100. That means if we treated 60 people like you, only one would benefit from the medication, while the other 59 would not. Most people who start statins won’t directly benefit, and, just as importantly, these drugs can have side effects like muscle pain, liver issues, and stomach upset—even for people who don’t ultimately see a benefit. I’m sharing all this so you can weigh both the risks and the benefits and make the decision that feels right for you.”

Mr. Mendez appeared taken aback. He said he felt well and, after hearing the statistics, decided that he did not want to begin statin therapy at this time.

Later that day, Dr. Garrison met her colleague, Dr. Parra, another third-year internal medicine resident, for coffee in the hospital cafeteria. As they chatted about their day, Dr. Garrison mentioned that several of her patients had chosen to pursue lifestyle changes instead of starting medication for high cholesterol and some other conditions. “That’s interesting,” Dr. Parra remarked, noting that most of her own patients usually opted for medication, even when she encouraged them to consider non-pharmacologic approaches. Dr. Garrison explained, “I’ve found that when I share more evidence about how effective these drugs really are—like explaining the number needed to treat—it helps patients think more realistically about what medications can and can’t do.”

Dr. Parra, however, expressed some concern. “Really? I’m not sure our patients can make sense of all that. Most people don’t have training in statistics or interpreting scientific studies. Isn’t that our job as physicians?” Dr. Garrison replied that she believes it’s an ethical responsibility to provide patients with information such as the number needed to treat. She asked, “How can our patients make truly informed choices about their care if they don’t know what the evidence actually shows?”

ethical_issues.question: How much evidence should physicians communicate when supporting patients in making informed decisions?
keypoints: Physicians have an obligation to communicate research evidence relevant to specific clinical decisions to patients in order to support informed medical choices.
The communication of evidence is a clinical cornerstone of respecting patient autonomy and an indispensable core element of the shared decision-making model.

The amount of information to be provided should be individualized, representing a comprehensive judgment by the physician that balances respect for autonomy, the principle of beneficence, and the principle of justice, while integrating patient preferences, the clinical context, and the uncertainty inherent in the evidence.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance respect for patient autonomy with the principles of beneficence and justice in the context of shared decision making?
keypoints: Physicians in shared decision making must respect patient autonomy while simultaneously safeguarding the patient’s best interests based on professional judgment, thereby embodying the principle of beneficence.

When providing information, physicians need to consider their social responsibility and the principle of distributive justice, recognizing and balancing the potential tension between individual well-being and the conservation of societal resources.

The information shared by physicians reflects their ethical values and interpretation of evidence, assisting patients in understanding the uncertainties inherent in medical choices and promoting informed decision making through effective communication.

Patient autonomy is relational and partly shaped by the information provided by physicians; therefore, physicians should guide patients in weighing the risks and benefits to facilitate rational decision making.

The ethical balance in shared decision making requires physicians to acknowledge and reconcile their multiple responsibilities to the patient, to their own professional judgment, and to society, reflecting the ethical complexity and dynamic adjustments inherent in clinical practice.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians consider the potential conflict between societal benefit and individual well-being when communicating treatment options?
keypoints: Physicians should carefully balance the potential conflicts between individual well-being and societal benefits when communicating treatment options, respecting patient autonomy while safeguarding the patient’s best interests.

Physicians have an ethical responsibility to provide comprehensive, transparent, and comprehensible evidence and information during the shared decision-making process to assist patients in making informed choices, while also reflecting a commitment to social accountability.

Physicians should acknowledge the inherent uncertainty of evidence and, within specific clinical contexts, balance the ethical principles of respect for autonomy, beneficence, and distributive justice to guide patient-physician communication and the formulation of treatment plans.

title: Authority, Health Advocacy Organizations, and Scientific Evidence
case:
Dr. Sanders, a second-year oncology fellow, arrived for work carrying a sheath of bright pink pamphlets. He set them down on a table in the staff room and proclaimed to his colleagues: “It’s that time of year again—the annual charity walk is coming up! The sign-up sheet is on the table here for anyone who wants to participate. The work this group does is so important in the fight against breast cancer!”
A new oncology fellow, Dr. Wang, walked over to the table and picked up one of the pamphlets. “These guys want to increase access to mammography for all women under 50. That’s the opposite of the new U.S. Public Health Task Force recommendations.” The evidence was pretty good, he thought, for their guideline that mammography for women under 50 be limited to high-risk groups because of the risks associated with false positive results—unnecessary biopsies, anxiety, and so on.
Dr. Sanders replied, “Well, I think that the work the group does to help vulnerable women avoid and treat breast cancer is really important. I have a lot of respect for what they do.”
“But,” Dr. Wang interjected, “isn’t it problematic for you, a physician, to support a group that promotes health care activities that go against the evidence? This seems like bad medicine. Plus, doesn’t this group just encourage even more people to think of evidence-based medicine as rationing? You are supposed to be a steward of our profession and of the best evidence-supported medicine. I don’t think it’s right for someone in your profession to support a group like this—it seems bad for medicine and bad for patients.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Sanders, a second-year oncology fellow, strode into the staff lounge one morning, balancing a stack of vivid pink pamphlets. Placing them on the corner table, he addressed his colleagues with enthusiasm: “It’s that time of year—the annual charity walk is on the horizon! If anyone’s interested, the sign-up sheet is right here. The organization behind this event does outstanding work supporting women in the fight against breast cancer!”

Nearby, Dr. Wang, a new fellow on the oncology team, approached and picked up one of the pamphlets. He scanned its contents and remarked, “This group is pushing for increased mammography access for all women under 50. That’s not in line with the latest U.S. Public Health Task Force guidelines. The data actually supports limiting screening in women under 50 to those at high risk, mainly because of the harms from false positives—unnecessary biopsies, anxiety, all those things.”

Dr. Sanders nodded, but replied, “I really believe in the organization’s mission to help vulnerable women get the care they need for breast cancer. I respect the advocacy work they do, especially for people who might otherwise fall through the cracks.”

Dr. Wang frowned slightly. “But as a physician, isn’t it problematic to support a group whose agenda goes against what the evidence tells us? Promoting widespread screening could be seen as encouraging bad medical practice. And by supporting them, aren’t we reinforcing the misconception that evidence-based recommendations are just rationing care? Our primary duty is to uphold the best evidence-based medicine for our patients. Supporting a group like this doesn’t seem right—it could be misleading for both our profession and for patients.”

ethical_issues.question: How should the prioritization between supporting patient advocacy organizations and upholding scientific integrity be balanced under the principles of professionalism?
keypoints: Physicians have a responsibility to serve patient welfare and respect patient autonomy; evidence-based medicine is an important tool to achieve this goal rather than an end in itself.

Physicians do not occupy the role of social planners; their ethical positioning should prioritize patient interests and avoid extending their responsibilities to the formulation of public health policy.

Physicians may ethically support patient health advocacy organizations while maintaining a rational attitude toward scientific evidence, avoiding uncritical acceptance of all the organization’s claims.

When supporting patient organizations, physicians should provide individualized information about the associated benefits and risks to help patients understand rationally and make autonomous decisions, thereby embodying truly patient-centered care.

Good clinical practice requires integrating clinical research evidence, professional experience, and knowledge of the individual patient’s circumstances, achieving an organic synthesis of science and humanism.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians provide social support while avoiding misleading patients about mammography?
keypoints: Physicians may ethically support health advocacy organizations but should critically evaluate their claims and avoid unconditionally endorsing them.

It is recommended that pamphlets be placed in staff break rooms rather than distributed in patient waiting areas to prevent patients from misconstruing the organization’s views as official or professional endorsements.

Dr. Sanders should individualize discussions with patients regarding the organization’s benefits and drawbacks, assisting patients in rationally understanding the risks and benefits of mammography while emphasizing the positive value of social support.

In the absence of more appropriate support resources, Dr. Wang should candidly inform patients that the organization may serve as a potential source of support while clearly expressing his concerns about certain aspects of its recommendations.

Both physicians should actively engage in promoting and supporting health advocacy organizations that align more closely with evidence-based medicine principles, advancing professional development and public awareness through education, speaking engagements, or scholarly writing.

title: Personality Testing in Resident Selection, Commentary 2
case:
Brent, a fourth-year medical student applying to residencies in internal medicine, has worked diligently during medical school, achieving high grades, garnering commendations for empathic bedside care, assuming leadership positions in several organizations, and volunteering in underserved care programs. He is a competitive applicant for the specialty and has already received a number of interview requests. His first interview is at a small, exclusive, but well-known program, and Brent is feeling nervous but excited after having achieved what he had thought was his best.
After the program director introduces himself and the program, a personality test is administered to all of the applicants. Brent begins to feel apprehensive; why is this test being administered? He is worried that his chance of matching at such a program could be ruined if he doesn’t give the “right” answers to these questions that, as far as he can tell, aren’t even pertinent to medicine. Brent’s discomfort about the personality test rattles him to the point that it affects his mood and candor during the interview.
Upon returning home, Brent and his classmates discuss what they have encountered on the interview trail, from colorful interviewers to student faux pas. He tells them about the personality test: “I don’t see the importance of this personality test. Shouldn’t my application speak for itself? It makes me so mad that I might not match there because of how I did on some ridiculous personality test. Seriously, were they interviewing me to see if I’d make a good doctor, or to see if they wanted to date me?”
case_rewrite:
Brent, a fourth-year medical student with his sights set on internal medicine residencies, has invested countless hours in his education. He has consistently earned top marks, received praise for his compassionate bedside manner, held leadership roles in various student organizations, and dedicated time to volunteering in underserved communities. With a strong application, Brent has already received several invitations to interview and is feeling a mix of nerves and excitement as he heads to his first interview at a small, prestigious, and highly selective program.

After a warm welcome and introduction to the program by the director, Brent and the other applicants are informed that they will be taking a personality test as part of the interview process. Brent is caught off guard—he feels uneasy and starts to question the relevance of such a test in evaluating his qualifications for residency. He worries that his responses, which seem unrelated to his medical skills or experience, could jeopardize his chances of matching with the program. The uncertainty about how the test will be used and what it means for his candidacy leaves Brent unsettled, and this anxiety lingers throughout his interview, affecting his confidence and the openness of his responses.

Once back home, Brent reconnects with his classmates, and together they share stories from their interviews—ranging from quirky interviewers to awkward applicant moments. Brent recounts his experience with the personality test: “I just don’t get why they’re making us take it. Shouldn’t my track record in med school and all the work I’ve put in be enough? It’s frustrating to think my chances could be hurt by this personality quiz that doesn’t even seem to relate to medicine. Honestly, were they interviewing me to see if I’d make a good doctor or to see if I’d be fun to hang out with?”

Brent’s comments spark a lively discussion among his peers about what residency programs are really looking for, how much weight is given to different parts of the application, and whether such testing is fair or transparent. The group debates the role of personality assessments in the selection process and whether applicants should be informed in advance about their purpose and impact, all while reflecting on their hopes for a fair and meaningful evaluation of their future as physicians.

ethical_issues.question: How should the interests of the different stakeholders (applicants, medical schools/residency programs, and society) be identified, weighed, and integrated?
keypoints: Applicants expect the selection process to be fair and transparent, focusing on their actual achievements and controllable variables, avoiding the influence of inherent traits on admission opportunities, while also desiring a thorough understanding of the admission criteria and procedures.

The core interest of medical schools and residency programs is to select applicants who can successfully complete training, obtain licensure, and continuously keep pace with developments in medicine and clinical practice.
Society expects the admissions process to select future physicians who can provide high-quality medical care, promote medical advancements, and meet diverse healthcare needs.

The admissions process must balance applicants’ expectations for fair evaluation based on past achievements with the institutional and societal need to predict future physician characteristics and potential, thereby avoiding conflicts and misunderstandings between these interests.

To ensure fairness and transparency, the purpose, potential risks, and scientific validity of personality testing should be fully disclosed to applicants in advance, thereby reducing unnecessary anxiety and misconceptions.

Interviews and selection should primarily focus on applicants’ actual achievements and capabilities, clearly articulating the institution’s expectations for future physicians to ensure applicants understand and endorse the educational objectives.

Personality assessments may serve as auxiliary tools to evaluate applicants’ fit with the institutional culture and environment, or as references for professional development and support, rather than as decisive screening criteria.
Respecting personality diversity contributes to fulfilling society’s pluralistic values and enhances the comprehensive capabilities and innovative potential of healthcare teams.

ethical_issues.question: Is it fair to select medical students based on uncontrollable variables such as personality traits?
keypoints: Requiring applicants to undergo personality testing may create unfair disadvantages in the absence of justifiable reasons or transparent disclosure.

Judging candidates based on uncontrollable variables such as personality traits may constitute discrimination, as these factors are unrelated to job qualifications and undermine the principle of equal opportunity.

Ethicists contend that the introduction of personality tests into the admissions process must be approached with caution, with a clear demonstration of their relevance and justification for predicting success in the physician role.

Personality tests assess aptitude rather than actual achievement; therefore, selection should primarily focus on verifiable accomplishments and demonstrated abilities to ensure fairness and reasonableness.

The effectiveness of assessment tools should be central to residency selection, and personality testing should only be incorporated as a selection criterion when it demonstrably outperforms achievement-based evaluations.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Clinicians as agents of the state
title: Incentives for Medical School Students to Practice Primary Care through the Lens of John Rawls
case:
State University Medical School’s explicit, community-based mission is to educate primary care physicians for its home state, which comprises mainly small towns and rural areas.
As its fortieth anniversary approached, State U. Medical School administration reviewed alumni data and realized that the school had not come close to fulfilling its mission. The school required those who received financial aid to complete residency in a primary care specialty within the state. If they did so—and most did—their loans were forgiven. But the alumni data showed that, over the years, an average of 60 percent of residents had gone on to fellowships in subspecialties immediately after residency, and many of those had moved out of state to practice.
As a corrective to this “mission slippage,” a new policy for state-funded loans and privately funded scholarships was proposed such that students who declared their interest in practicing primary care in the state and received full tuition from state or private sources had to practice primary care in the state for 10 years after completion of their residencies to repay the cost of their medical education. There was a sliding repayment scale based on service increments of 1 year for those who practiced primary care in-state but did not fulfill their 10-year service agreement.
Several of the school’s private funders objected to the proposed policy; at least one was outraged.
“I’ve always supported our mission,” he said, “but this new policy is coercive. It’s social engineering, is what it is. Flies in the face of everything this country and this state stand for. When my grandfather came to this state in the early part of the last century, a man could make his living any way he wanted to, long as he didn’t break the law.”
“What’s worse,” the funder continued, “is that this policy hurts the middle- and low-income kids. The rich kids don’t need our support, so they can practice anything they want, anywhere they want.”
case_rewrite:
State University Medical School was founded with a clear, community-oriented mission: to train primary care physicians to serve its home state, a region largely made up of small towns and rural communities. As the institution neared its fortieth anniversary, the administration undertook a thorough review of alumni outcomes. They were dismayed to discover that the school had fallen far short of its intended mission. Although students who received financial aid were required to complete a primary care residency within the state—fulfilling this obligation resulted in their loans being forgiven—alumni records revealed a troubling trend. Over the years, about 60 percent of these residents proceeded directly to subspecialty fellowships after residency, often leaving the state to practice elsewhere.

To address this “mission drift,” the administration developed a new policy governing both state-funded loans and privately sponsored scholarships. Under this proposal, students who accepted full tuition support from state or private sources—and declared an intention to practice primary care in the state—would be required to work as primary care physicians within the state for 10 years following the completion of their residencies, thereby repaying the cost of their medical education through service. For those who practiced primary care in-state but did not complete the full 10-year commitment, there was a sliding scale for repayment, based on how many years they served.

This proposal sparked fierce opposition among several private funders of the school. One, in particular, was incensed. “I’ve always stood behind our mission,” he protested, “but what you’re proposing now is coercion, plain and simple. It’s nothing short of social engineering. That goes against everything this state and country represent. When my grandfather settled here nearly a hundred years ago, he could make his way however he chose, as long as he stayed within the law.”

He went on, voice rising with indignation, “And the real losers here are the kids from families without money. The wealthy students don’t need our loans or scholarships—they can choose whatever specialty they want and go wherever they please. But our policy would trap the less fortunate, taking away their freedom to decide their own futures.”

ethical_issues.question: Does the policy requiring students to practice primary care in the state for 10 years comply with Rawls’s principles of justice, particularly regarding compensating benefits for the least advantaged members of society?
keypoints: According to Rawls’s principles of justice, inequalities can be considered just if they benefit the least advantaged members of society.

This policy aims to improve primary care services in medically underserved areas such as small towns and rural regions within the state, where residents have greater medical needs and poorer health status, representing the most disadvantaged groups in society.

Although the policy may impose an economic burden on some physicians and restrict their freedom to choose their practice location or specialty, it aligns with Rawls’s principles of justice due to its significant benefits in enhancing healthcare services for vulnerable communities and should therefore be implemented.

title: National Resident Matching Program Violations
case:
Violet, a medical student from a top-tier medical school who hopes to match into a residency in dermatology, is currently on the interview trail. She goes to her third interview at a program near her school, feeling confident and satisfied with her performance so far. The program director, a nationally renowned figure in the specialty, tells her that she is “ranked to match” by the program and asks what her rank list is. Violet responds that, while she had a great experience at the program that day, it was too early in the season to tell what her actual rank list would be, but that she would keep in close correspondence with the program.
When discussing this situation in an online forum with some fellow students interested in matching in the same specialty, Violet hears of some students being accepted to NRMP programs outside of the proper match protocol. She tells the next program she interviews with that she is ranking them first despite the interviews she still has coming up, reasoning that this is the only way to optimize her chances of matching in the specialty if the interviewees insist on asking about her rank list.
case_rewrite:
Violet, a medical student at a prestigious medical school with aspirations to secure a dermatology residency, is currently navigating the interview circuit. At her third interview, held at a program close to her home institution, Violet feels self-assured and pleased with her performance up to that point. During her interview, the program director—a figure well-known on the national stage within dermatology—tells Violet that she is “ranked to match” at their program. The director then asks Violet to share her own rank list. Violet replies that, while she thoroughly enjoyed her interview experience at their program, it is still early in the interview season and she has not yet finalized her rank list, but she assures the director that she will stay in close touch.

Later, in conversation with peers on an online forum dedicated to medical students pursuing dermatology, Violet learns that some applicants have accepted positions at NRMP-affiliated programs through channels that circumvent the official match process. Influenced by these stories, Violet decides to tell the director at her next interview that she is planning to rank their program first, even though she still has several interviews scheduled. She justifies this decision to herself by reasoning that, if interviewers continue to press her about her rank intentions, claiming a program as her top choice is the best strategy to maximize her chances of matching in dermatology.

ethical_issues.question: Does the program director’s inquiry about the applicant’s intended rank violate the core rules of the NRMP?
keypoints: The program director’s inquiry into the applicant’s intended rank order constitutes a violation of the NRMP’s cardinal rule.

The NRMP permits applicants and programs to express mutual interest; however, it explicitly prohibits soliciting verbal or written statements that imply a commitment, including questions regarding intended rank order.

Faced with improper inquiries, the applicant engaged in deceptive conduct by misrepresenting her ranking intentions to subsequent programs out of concern for optimizing her chances of matching, illustrating the detrimental impact of rule violations on applicant decision-making.

Violations of NRMP regulations may result in sanctions against the involved programs or applicants, including suspension from participation in the match, thereby safeguarding the fairness and integrity of the matching process.

title: The Purpose of a Medical School
case:
State University Medical School’s explicit, community-based mission is to educate primary care physicians for its home state, which comprises mainly small towns and rural areas.
As its fortieth anniversary approached, State U. Medical School administration reviewed alumni data and realized that the school had not come close to fulfilling its mission. The school required those who received financial aid to complete residency in a primary care specialty within the state. If they did so—and most did—their loans were forgiven. But the alumni data showed that, over the years, an average of 60 percent of residents had gone on to fellowships in subspecialties immediately after residency, and many of those had moved out of state to practice.
As a corrective to this “mission slippage,” a new policy for state-funded loans and privately funded scholarships was proposed such that students who declared their interest in practicing primary care in the state and received full tuition from state or private sources had to practice primary care in the state for 10 years after completion of their residencies to repay the cost of their medical education. There was a sliding repayment scale based on service increments of 1 year for those who practiced primary care in-state but did not fulfill their 10-year service agreement.
Several of the school’s private funders objected to the proposed policy; at least one was outraged.
“I’ve always supported our mission,” he said, “but this new policy is coercive. It’s social engineering, is what it is. Flies in the face of everything this country and this state stand for. When my grandfather came to this state in the early part of the last century, a man could make his living any way he wanted to, long as he didn’t break the law.”
“What’s worse,” the funder continued, “is that this policy hurts the middle- and low-income kids. The rich kids don’t need our support, so they can practice anything they want, anywhere they want.”
case_rewrite:
State University Medical School was founded with a clear, community-oriented mission: to train primary care physicians who would serve the small towns and rural populations of its home state. As the school neared its fortieth anniversary, the administration undertook a comprehensive review of alumni outcomes and was confronted with a troubling revelation: the institution was not living up to its mission. The existing policy required students who accepted financial aid to complete residencies in a primary care specialty within the state. Upon fulfilling this obligation, their loans were forgiven—a provision most aid recipients had taken advantage of. Yet, the alumni records revealed that, over time, about 60 percent of these residents immediately pursued subspecialty fellowships after residency, and a significant portion eventually left the state to practice elsewhere.

To address this drift from its founding purpose, the administration proposed a new policy regarding state-funded loans and privately funded scholarships. Under this proposal, students who declared an intention to practice primary care in-state and who received full tuition support from state or private funds would be required to practice primary care within the state for 10 years after completing their residencies. This service would serve as repayment for the cost of their medical education. For those who practiced primary care in-state but did not fulfill the full 10-year commitment, a sliding repayment scale based on the number of service years was put forward.

The policy immediately met resistance from some of the school’s private donors. One particularly vocal funder expressed outrage: “I’ve always stood behind our mission,” he said, “but this is going too far. This policy feels coercive—it’s social engineering, plain and simple. It goes against everything our state and country are supposed to represent. When my grandfather came here in the last century, a man could make his living however he chose, as long as he stayed within the law.”

The funder went on to voice a further concern: “What really bothers me is that this policy ends up punishing kids from low- and middle-income families. The wealthy students don’t need our help, so they can do whatever they want, wherever they want. But the ones who count on our support are the ones whose options get limited the most.”

ethical_issues.question: Is it just to preferentially allocate scarce resources (financial aid) to students who are willing to provide primary care services to the rural residents of the state?
keypoints: The core ethical conflict in this case lies in the tension between the public interest in ensuring an adequate supply of primary care physicians for the rural areas of Home State and the individual interests of students in pursuing financial autonomy and freedom of career choice.

Prioritizing the allocation of scarce financial aid resources to students who are willing to provide primary care services in the rural regions of Home State constitutes a reasonable and justifiable policy decision grounded in the public interest.

As a public medical school, SUMS bears an obligation of accountability to the taxpayers of its state; thus, adjusting financial aid policies to ensure that students fulfill their commitments to primary care service aligns with principles of public responsibility and the legitimate use of resources.

Although the new policy may restrict the career choice freedom of low- and middle-income students who rely on loans—specifically by removing their option to pursue subspecialty fellowships while qualifying for loan forgiveness—students do not have an entitlement to have taxpayers bear the full cost of their training. This model of service in exchange for financial support has established precedents in programs such as the Health Professions Scholarship Program and the National Health Service Corps.

Applicants who are unwilling to engage in primary care still have access to other private medical schools without service obligations, thereby preserving educational diversity and professional freedom.

title: "Social Engineering" versus "Medical Patriotism": What Flexner Can Teach Us about Solving the Primary Care Crisis
