title: Informed Consent for Biobank-Dependent Research
case:
Dr. Hundt is a physician at a major research hospital. He is visiting a new patient, Mr. Clifton, who was recently admitted to the hospital for right upper quadrant pain suggestive of gallstones and cholecystitis. Dr. Hundt checks in with the patient to examine him and to explain what the course of hospitalization will be. The patient appears ill, but is alert and oriented. “We will have to draw blood to check some basic labs and to see if you have any possibility of infection,” Dr. Hundt explains. Mr. Clifton nods in understanding.
“I do want to mention to you a program of ours that has been approved by our IRB, which oversees human subjects research,” Dr. Hundt continues. “When obtaining blood samples for labs, we often have leftover blood and tissue. Because we have many researchers studying and developing therapies for genetic diseases, we are attempting to build up our database of genetic material to study population trends and genetic variations of disease. We have therefore established a program for banking leftover blood in our DNA database, in conjunction with basic demographics and medical information obtained from your medical record. We extract the DNA and make the information available to our researchers. Your name and identifying information are removed, and our researchers sign a confidentiality form promising that they will not try to reidentify the source of any genetic specimen.”
“Can you tell me more about what kinds of research the samples are used for?” Mr. Clifton asks.
“The spectrum of research varies across disciplines and disease systems, and the specimens will be used for as-yet-undetermined projects.”
Dr. Hundt gives Mr. Clifton a brochure. As Dr. Hundt is leaving, Mr. Clifton asks if he has to sign anything before the lab comes. “No need, Mr. Clifton. The specimen will be automatically entered into our database without any further action from you,” Dr. Hundt explains. “If you choose not to participate, there is a form at the end of that brochure. Please give that to the phlebotomist and that will let us know not to send your blood to the biobank.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Hundt, a physician at a prominent research hospital, steps into the hospital room of Mr. Clifton, a newly admitted patient suffering from right upper quadrant pain consistent with gallstones and possible cholecystitis. Mr. Clifton looks unwell but remains alert and fully oriented as Dr. Hundt greets him and begins the examination.

“We’ll need to draw some blood to run basic laboratory tests, and to check for signs of infection,” Dr. Hundt explains, his tone calm and reassuring. Mr. Clifton listens and nods his understanding.

Dr. Hundt continues, “I’d also like to tell you about a program we have here that’s been reviewed and approved by our Institutional Review Board, which oversees research involving human subjects. Often, when we draw blood for clinical reasons, there’s a small amount left over. Because many of our researchers are working on therapies for genetic diseases, we’re building a database of genetic material to help us better understand how these diseases affect different populations.”

He moves a step closer and elaborates, “The leftover blood is stored in our DNA biobank, along with basic demographic and medical information taken from your record. We extract DNA from these samples, and the data is made available to approved researchers. Importantly, your name and any identifying details are stripped away, and all researchers must sign a confidentiality agreement promising not to attempt to identify anyone from the samples.”

Mr. Clifton, thoughtful, asks, “What kinds of research will my samples be used for?”

“The research spans a wide range of disciplines and disease areas,” Dr. Hundt replies. “Right now, many of the specific projects are yet to be determined.”

He hands Mr. Clifton a brochure, saying, “This explains the program in more detail. Please take a look when you have a moment.”

As Dr. Hundt prepares to leave the room, Mr. Clifton inquires, “Do I need to sign something before the lab comes in?”

Dr. Hundt shakes his head gently. “No, Mr. Clifton. Unless you tell us otherwise, your leftover blood will automatically be included in our biobank program. If you would prefer not to participate, there’s a form at the end of the brochure. Just give that form to the phlebotomist when your blood is drawn, and your sample will not be sent to the biobank.”

ethical_issues.question: Should patients be required to contribute their data and residual tissues for research?
keypoints: Public surveys indicate that the majority of individuals desire some degree of choice regarding the research use of their tissues and data; this expectation forms the ethical foundation that patients should be informed and be able to exercise their choices without undue burden.

Patients should be explicitly informed of the options concerning the use of their residual clinical tissues and associated data for research purposes, and be able to easily express consent or refusal, thereby safeguarding their autonomy and right to informed consent.

There exists a gap between current ethical and regulatory standards concerning waiver of consent or the use of de-identified specimens and public expectations; innovative mechanisms need to be explored to balance the protection of patient rights with the efficiency demands of large-scale research.

Maintaining and enhancing public trust is essential for advancing high-quality biobank research, with transparent disclosure of information and respect for patient choice being core elements to achieve this goal.

ethical_issues.question: In biobank-dependent research, how can patients be ensured informed rights and the ability to make choices regarding the research use of their tissue samples?
keypoints: Ensure that patients are fully informed about the research uses of their tissue samples and related information, and explicitly communicate their right to choose whether to participate, thereby safeguarding informed consent and patient autonomy.
Provide a convenient and non-burdensome opt-out mechanism that allows patients to freely decide whether to include their residual samples in the biobank, reflecting respect for patient choice.

Under the premise of ethical review approval, adopting an “opt-out” model combined with comprehensive disclosure can achieve a high ethical standard, balancing research efficiency with the protection of patient rights.

title: Genetic Testing: Clinical and Personal Utility
case:
Dr. Orson is a family practice physician who has been treating Michael since he was born. He knows Michael’s parents and siblings, having been their family doctor for nearly 30 years. He is also intimately familiar with Michael’s family history: 3 members of his family in their 30s and 40s have suffered sudden cardiac death. Michael is now 22 years old, 10 years younger than his uncle was when he died of this cause. Michael is therefore vigilant about clinical surveillance of his overall health, but tends to avoid the subject of his family history altogether. He has, however, happily shared with Dr. Orson news of his recent marriage and his desire to start a family.
In preparation for Michael’s first office visit since his marriage, Dr. Orson has done some research and found a genetic testing kit that examines a 5-gene profile of known inherited mutations that can lead to arrhythmias or death. Dr. Orson believes that the testing will either alleviate Michael’s anxiety or allow him and his wife to prepare for possible cardiac complications.
Dr. Orson enters the exam room to find Michael accompanied by his wife Susan, who announces that they are expecting their first child. Dr. Orson congratulates them and inquires after the course of the pregnancy. Then he turns to Michael to continue the annual check-up. After giving Michael a clean bill of health, he brings up the topic of genetic testing and encourages Michael to submit a sample to test for the known channelopathies. Michael’s mood changes; he becomes upset and angry about the suggestion.
“I’m about to become a father and you’re telling me to take a test that might announce a death sentence?” Michael eventually says.
“I think it would be valuable information to know so we could initiate treatment or, at worst, prepare your family to anticipate…complications. We have ways of better predicting likelihoods of serious diseases now; why not use that information to prepare yourself appropriately?” Dr. Orson retorts.
“Why would I want to know that I might die soon? Can’t I just live my life like everybody else, without thinking about my own mortality?” Michael responds.
Dr. Orson insists, “But the test could also provide reassurance, and think of your family and how they should prepare. I’m confident that if this testing had been available for others in your family, they would have gotten it. I really think you should consider it, for your good and the good of your family.”
Michael curtly thanks Dr. Orson for his time and the check-up and leaves the appointment. As Susan prepares to follow, Dr. Orson asks her to see if she can talk with him at home about the testing.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Orson, a seasoned family physician, has cared for Michael since infancy and has developed a close rapport with his entire family over nearly three decades. He is acutely aware of Michael’s family history: three relatives—each in their 30s or 40s—have died suddenly from cardiac events. Now 22, Michael is a full decade younger than his uncle was at the time of his untimely death. Michael, vigilant about his health, regularly attends appointments but consistently avoids discussing his family’s cardiac history. Recently, he shared with Dr. Orson the joyful news of his marriage and his hopes of becoming a parent.

Before Michael’s first check-up since his wedding, Dr. Orson researches a genetic testing kit that analyzes five genes commonly linked to inherited arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. He believes that such testing could either help ease Michael’s underlying anxieties or enable Michael and his wife to plan for any potential health challenges.

When Dr. Orson walks into the exam room, he finds Michael accompanied by his wife, Susan, who excitedly announces that they are expecting their first child. Dr. Orson congratulates them and inquires about the pregnancy, then proceeds with Michael’s annual examination. After confirming that Michael is in good health, Dr. Orson shifts the conversation to genetic testing. He recommends that Michael consider submitting a sample for analysis of known channelopathies, highlighting the value of the information.

Michael’s demeanor abruptly changes—his mood darkens, and frustration surfaces. “You’re telling me, right as I’m about to become a father, that I should take a test that could tell me I’m living with a ticking time bomb?” Michael says, visibly distressed.

Dr. Orson replies, “It’s important information, Michael. If we know your risk, we can take early steps to treat or, at the very least, help your family anticipate any complications. With the advances we have, it seems wise to use this knowledge to your advantage.”

Michael pushes back, “But why should I want to know if I might die young? Why can’t I just live my life without that hanging over me, like everyone else?”

Dr. Orson persists, “The results could reassure you, and it’s also about your family’s future. I’m certain that if this testing had been available to your relatives, they would have wanted to know. I really think it’s worth considering, for your sake and theirs.”

Clearly unsettled, Michael tersely thanks Dr. Orson for the check-up and leaves the office. As Susan prepares to follow him out, Dr. Orson quietly asks her if she might speak with Michael at home about the possibility of testing.

ethical_issues.question: In genetic testing, how can the conflict between the duties of beneficence and nonmaleficence and the respect for patient autonomy be balanced?
keypoints: Dr. Orson must balance the ethical principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence with respect for Michael’s autonomy, ensuring that both physician and patient collaboratively consider the clinical and personal utility of genetic testing while fully acknowledging Michael’s values, preferences, and emotional responses.

While genetic testing may offer significant clinical and personal benefits, the ultimate decision rests with Michael; Dr. Orson should respect Michael’s right not to know his genetic risk and must avoid exerting coercion or undue influence.

Referral to a genetic counselor or genetics specialist can provide Michael with professional, nondirective support, helping him to thoroughly understand the potential benefits and risks of genetic testing and facilitating truly autonomous, informed decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Orson have discussed genetic testing at an earlier time point to enable the patient to make a more informed decision?
keypoints: As Michael’s long-term physician with comprehensive knowledge of the family history of sudden cardiac death, Dr. Orson should proactively and sensitively introduce the discussion of genetic testing at an appropriate time.

Early discussion of genetic testing facilitates Michael’s psychological and practical preparedness, especially during the significant life stage of planning to start a family, thereby supporting him in making more comprehensive and informed health decisions.

Physicians should respect the patient’s receptiveness to genetic testing information and emotional responses, employing a gradual and empathetic communication approach to avoid eliciting fear and resistance.
Early communication not only reflects the physician’s professional responsibility but also helps build patient trust and promotes active patient engagement in health management and risk prevention.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of limited clinical utility of genetic testing, how should the personal utility of the test be evaluated to assist the patient in making an informed decision?
keypoints: Personal utility encompasses multidimensional factors including psychosocial impact, reproductive planning, lifestyle modifications, future decision-making, and the value of information to the patient.

The primary benefits of genetic testing manifest at the personal level, providing patients and their family members with information about disease risk to assist in life planning and end-of-life decisions.

Genetic testing carries risks of psychological burden and potential genetic discrimination; although the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) protects patients from discrimination in health insurance and employment, it does not extend to life insurance or disability coverage.
The balance of risks and benefits varies significantly among individuals, with different patients making testing decisions based on their own values and perceptions of risk.

Respect for patient autonomy is a core principle, requiring healthcare providers to fully understand and support the patient’s wishes, values, and preferences, while avoiding coercion or excessive persuasion.
When clinical utility is limited, the decision hinges on the patient’s subjective evaluation of the test’s personal utility and their acceptance of the information provided.

title: When Patients Seem Overly Optimistic
case:
Dr. Beard was not surprised to see that Mr. Cohen leaned heavily on an ornately carved cane to walk the long corridor to her office. She had just been looking at images of his spine, to which his pancreatic cancer had now metastasized, sprinkling a long stretch of his lumbar spine with ominous grey holes.
Mr. Cohen had previously asked that Dr. Beard be direct with him, so she began as soon a she was settled in the chair in her office. “As you had been guessing from your new back pain, it looks like the cancer has spread to your spine.”
“I’d thought so,” said Mr. Cohen. “I’ve been reading more and more about new treatments, and I really think it’ll work out fine. I’ve just started a new chemotherapy, and I have a big trip planned around the world for next year. Besides, this is a great hospital, and I know you’re the best in the field.”
Dr. Beard hesitated. She had not anticipated this level of optimism. Mr. Cohen had been diagnosed 6 months before. Since then, several chemotherapy protocols had failed to reduce his tumors, and he was increasingly crippled by the metastasis.
“I’m glad you’re thinking so positively,” Dr. Beard said carefully. “But your disease is moving much more quickly than I’d expected. These CT scans show that it is now in your spine.”
“Oh, I know. But the more I read about these new treatments, I really think it’s all going to work out fine,” Mr. Cohen repeated. “Besides, if I don’t hope for the best, well....” His voice trailed off.
Later that day, Dr. Beard received a concerned phone call from Mr. Cohen’s daughter, a nurse in the ICU.
“Dr. Beard, I know what this disease is like, and it’s clearly progressing. My father’s not getting it. You need to make sure that he understands the reality,” she said.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Beard watched as Mr. Cohen made his way down the long hallway to her office, each step supported by an intricately carved cane. Only minutes before, she had been reviewing his most recent scans, which revealed the pancreatic cancer had now metastasized to his lumbar spine, leaving a trail of ominous grey lesions along the vertebrae.

Mr. Cohen had always insisted on candor from Dr. Beard, so as soon as they were both seated, she began, “As you suspected from your increasing back pain, the cancer has unfortunately spread to your spine.”

Mr. Cohen nodded. “I figured as much. But I’ve been reading about all the new treatments coming out, and I really believe things will turn out alright. I just started a new chemotherapy, and I’m planning a trip around the world next year. Plus, I know this hospital is excellent, and you’re the top expert.”

Dr. Beard paused, registering his unexpected optimism. It had been six months since his diagnosis, and in that time, several lines of chemotherapy had failed to halt the tumor’s progression. Now, the metastases were taking a visible toll on his mobility and strength.

“I appreciate your positive outlook,” Dr. Beard replied gently. “But I have to be honest—the disease is advancing more quickly than we hoped. The latest CT scans confirm it’s now in your spine.”

Mr. Cohen smiled, undeterred. “I understand. But with all the new research and treatments, I truly think I’ll be alright,” he said again. “And anyway, if I don’t keep hoping for the best, well…” His voice faded, leaving the sentence unfinished.

Later that afternoon, Dr. Beard’s phone rang. On the line was Mr. Cohen’s daughter, who worked as a nurse in the ICU.

“Dr. Beard, I’m really worried,” she said, her voice tense. “I know what this disease can do, and it’s clearly getting worse. My father isn’t facing what’s happening. I think you need to make sure he really understands what’s going on.”

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances should clinicians consider involving a surrogate decision maker to ensure that the patient receives the best possible care?
keypoints: If a patient is unable to make informed medical decisions due to impaired understanding or cognitive avoidance, clinicians should assess the patient’s decision-making capacity and consider involving a surrogate decision maker when necessary to ensure the quality of care.

Clinicians should respect patient autonomy by engaging in thorough communication to obtain the patient’s consent for involving a surrogate decision maker whenever possible, and proactively communicate with the surrogate if the patient persistently avoids acknowledging a poor prognosis in a manner that may result in harm, thereby ensuring the patient receives optimal treatment.
When medical decision-making is time-sensitive and the patient cannot effectively participate, clinicians should promptly activate a surrogate decision maker to avoid delays in care.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians weigh the risks and benefits of explicit disclosure of prognostic information in order to respect patient autonomy?
keypoints: Physicians should rationally assess the reasons behind a patient’s refusal to accept the prognosis when conveying prognostic information, weigh the risks and benefits of explicit disclosure, and respect the patient’s autonomy to choose not to acknowledge the prognosis.

Reasonable circumstances for allowing patients to maintain unrealistic hopes include a slowly progressing clinical course, emotional fragility of the patient, or a code status that aligns with the patient’s values.

Situations requiring clear and explicit disclosure include rapidly deteriorating clinical status, the presence of significant risks of harm or unresolved issues (such as inadequate family preparedness or guardianship concerns), and a code status that conflicts with the patient’s values.

Clinicians should employ effective communication strategies to enhance the patient’s acceptance of prognostic information and, when necessary, engage surrogate decision makers to facilitate patient-centered shared decision making.
Even if patients ultimately refuse to acknowledge a poor prognosis, clinicians have fulfilled their ethical obligations by respecting patient autonomy and should not consider this a failure of care.

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians assess and address barriers to patient understanding when patients refuse to accept the seriousness of their illness?
keypoints: Physicians should first assess the patient’s level of understanding of their condition and identify any existing barriers, in order to determine what additional information needs to be provided and the most effective method of communication.

Barriers to understanding may arise from cognitive deficits (including undiagnosed neurologic conditions or exacerbation of acute illness), language barriers, emotional disturbances, and the clinician’s communication style (such as the use of medical jargon or euphemisms).

Physicians need to identify and, to the extent possible, remove obstacles that impede the patient’s reception of information, such as emotional overload, language barriers, or the need for interpreter assistance.
If barriers to understanding are insurmountable, physicians should assess the patient’s decision-making capacity and, when necessary, involve a surrogate decision maker or health care proxy.

title: The Use of Informed Assent in Withholding Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in the ICU
case:
Ms. Rose’s family had gathered in the intensive care unit conference room. Her three sons and daughter all looked haggard; their mother’s advancing lung cancer had led to a long stay in the intensive care unit (ICU). This was the second conference since their mother was intubated a week before. After that meeting, she’d done well with treatments, and the breathing tube had just been removed, although she was still drifting in and out of consciousness. However, the last few days had been increasingly difficult, and, although Ms. Rose’s lung function was improved, she was no longer aware of what was going on around her. Her heart had weakened, and her blood pressure had slowly been dropping despite medications.
During the first meeting, it had been easy for the siblings and the ICU attending physician, Dr. Branson, to come to an agreement about a plan. They would put her on the ventilator to see how her lungs responded and would keep her as comfortable as possible, hoping that she could soon recover and get home to enjoy her flower gardens and visits from her many grandchildren.
By 9 AM after their long week, many of the siblings were sipping coffee from styrofoam cups, as they chatted with the chaplain, social worker, and nurse who had also gathered for the meeting. As Dr. Branson entered, the room hushed a little. Despite the long course of Ms. Rose’s worsening pulmonary condition, her family braced for the coming conversation.
“Thanks to all of you for making it in,” Dr. Branson started. “As I’ve discussed with many of you day to day, your mother continues to get sicker. She did well last week after a short amount of time on the ventilator, but the cancer keeps spreading and she’s getting weaker. At this point, I worry that giving her CPR will not improve her chances of ever leaving the hospital and it’ll cause her a lot of discomfort. My understanding from all of you is that what matters to her is being up and busy and taking care of the people in her life. It sounds like she would not want to be resuscitated if it meant that she would likely never leave the ICU, much less the hospital.” He paused and looked around the room. Several of Ms. Rose’s children looked at him and nodded slightly. After allowing a few moments during which no one spoke, Dr. Branson said, “Unless anyone disagrees, I’d like to write in her chart that if her heart stops, she not be resuscitated.”
After answering some questions from the family, he wrapped up the meeting. A few minutes later, the nurse who had been in the family meeting approached him. “You didn’t give the family a chance to choose,” she said angrily. “You just decided for them. What if after CPR she bounces back? It’s happened before.”
case_rewrite:
Ms. Rose’s family gathered once more in the intensive care unit conference room. Her three sons and daughter sat together, their exhaustion etched on their faces after days spent at the hospital as their mother battled advancing lung cancer. This was their second family meeting since Ms. Rose had been intubated the previous week. Following that initial meeting, she had shown some improvement—her breathing tube was recently removed, though she now drifted in and out of consciousness. In the last several days, however, her condition had taken a turn: while her lungs were somewhat better, she seemed unaware of her surroundings. Her heart had grown weaker, and her blood pressure continued to fall despite ongoing medications.

During their first meeting, Dr. Branson, the ICU attending physician, and Ms. Rose’s children had found it easy to agree on the immediate steps. They decided to try her on the ventilator to see if her lungs improved, with the hope that she might recover enough to return home to her beloved flower gardens and the company of her grandchildren. Comfort was a guiding principle.

By 9 AM after this long week, the siblings sat quietly, sipping coffee from styrofoam cups, joined by the chaplain, social worker, and nurse who had come for the meeting. When Dr. Branson entered, the room grew still. The family braced themselves for the discussion ahead, knowing how much Ms. Rose’s condition had deteriorated.

“Thank you all for being here,” Dr. Branson began gently. “As we’ve discussed over the past several days, your mother’s illness is progressing. Last week she did better for a time after being on the ventilator, but now the cancer is spreading and she’s becoming weaker overall. At this point, I’m concerned that trying to resuscitate her if her heart stops would not give her a real chance of leaving the hospital, and would likely cause her more suffering. From what you’ve told me, being active and caring for her family is what matters most to her. It sounds like she would not want to go through resuscitation if it meant she would probably never leave the ICU, or the hospital.” He paused and looked around the table, giving space for the family to process his words. Several of the children exchanged glances and nodded slightly. Dr. Branson waited a few more moments, then continued, “If no one has any concerns, I’d like to note in her chart that if her heart were to stop, we would not attempt resuscitation.”

He then welcomed questions from the family, addressing their concerns and clarifying the situation. Once the conversation had concluded and the family seemed at peace with the plan, Dr. Branson wrapped up the meeting and stepped out. Moments later, the nurse who had been present approached him, her voice tense. “You didn’t let the family make the choice,” she said. “You just made the decision for them. What if she could recover after CPR? It’s happened before.”

ethical_issues.question: In the intensive care unit, how can informed consent or informed assent be obtained without increasing the psychological burden on family members?
keypoints: Informed assent can serve as an ethical alternative to informed consent, thereby avoiding the burden of guilt and psychological distress experienced by family members when refusing non-indicated treatments.

Clinicians should provide comprehensive information regarding the risks, benefits, and medical rationale of the proposed treatments, communicate specific medical recommendations, and explicitly allow room for opposition and discussion to facilitate the family’s rational understanding and acceptance.

The core of high-quality communication lies in assessing and respecting individual family members’ preferences for involvement in decision making, and tailoring the communication style and degree of shared decision making accordingly.

Clinicians’ assumption of responsibility for withholding non-indicated treatments helps alleviate the decision-making burden on family members, enabling them to more comfortably defer to medical judgment.

ethical_issues.question: Do clinicians have the authority to unilaterally refuse to provide a treatment when they determine that it is not indicated?
keypoints: There is currently no unified consensus within the American medical community regarding unilateral physician decision making to withhold treatment based on the principle of medical futility; this remains a subject of intense debate.

Physicians generally do not unilaterally refuse to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR); especially when family members object, a process of mediation should be initiated, family preferences should be respected, and treatment should continue.

For highly resource-intensive and technically complex therapies (such as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, ECMO), if the treatment is clearly not indicated, physicians may unilaterally refuse to provide it.

The American Medical Association recommends that when there are disagreements between clinicians and families regarding treatment decisions, a process of reconciliation should be initiated, and treatment should be continued until consensus is achieved.

Physicians should communicate fully regarding the patient’s condition and prognosis, respect the patient’s values and wishes, and avoid unilateral decision making that could undermine the physician-patient relationship and the foundation of trust.

title: Discounting a Surgical Risk: Data, Understanding, and Gist
case:
Dr. Feng had purposefully scheduled Ms. Reid to come into the office at 4:15 PM on a Friday. Despite the fact that her office staff would be trying to make it home as soon as possible, Dr. Feng had imagined that Ms. Reid might need extra time to discuss her biopsy results: there was a chance that the lump on her neck that she’d felt when tying a scarf might be cancerous.
Ms. Reid had been in the waiting room for an hour already by the time Dr. Feng called her in, trying to keep an eye on her two young sons, who were tipping over towers of cardboard blocks into the aisles between seats.
“Well, Ms. Reid,” Dr Feng started. “I’d hoped that we’d have a clearer answer for you today, but the pathology results from the aspiration of thyroid nodule are unclear. Some of the cells do look concerning for malignancy. We could repeat the aspiration, but I think that we should remove a piece of your thyroid at this point, to be safe.”
“Is this a big surgery? Do I have to stay in the hospital?” Ms. Reid asked. With her job as a teacher and her kids, an inpatient stay would be difficult.
“No, no. It’s a day surgery, and one I do routinely. The complications we might see are mainly bleeding and infection. We can control bleeding by cauterizing blood vessels or tying them off, and if there are signs of infection, for instance, if the wound becomes red or if you begin to have fever, we will start you on an antibiotic. There is always a slight risk of injuring a nerve to your vocal chord, but I’ve done this surgery many times and that’s very rare. What questions do you have for me about the procedure?”
Ms. Reid said, “I’m ready to have this lump gone. Let’s go ahead with the surgery.”
“OK, then, visit with the scheduling nurse out front, and set up a time that works for both of us. You might want to schedule it before one of those occasions when your school has a 3-day weekend, like Easter or Memorial Day. The surgery isn’t urgent.”
Mrs. Reid scheduled the surgery, and it went as planned.
A few days after the surgery, Ms. Reid came in for an emergency appointment with Dr. Feng. It was obvious that she was irate, but her voice could barely be heard above the noise of the clinic.
“I thought you said this was rare,” she said, shaking a printout of a journal article on the subject. “My recurrent laryngeal nerve was injured. I’m a teacher, and I have children! I need my voice. I would have never done the surgery if I knew there was a 4 percent risk that I would lose my voice!” Was Dr. Feng negligent in explaining the risks of surgery to Ms. Reid? Was she required to use precise percentages of risk?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Feng had intentionally scheduled Ms. Reid’s appointment for 4:15 PM on a Friday, anticipating that she might need extra time to discuss her biopsy results. Although the office staff would be eager to leave for the weekend, Dr. Feng felt it was important not to rush—after all, the lump Ms. Reid had discovered on her neck while tying a scarf could potentially be cancerous.

By the time Dr. Feng called her in, Ms. Reid had already spent an hour in the waiting room, doing her best to supervise her two young sons as they toppled cardboard block towers into the aisles between the seats.

“Ms. Reid,” Dr. Feng began, “I was hoping to have a definite answer for you today. Unfortunately, the pathology results from your thyroid nodule aspiration aren’t clear. Some cells do look worrisome for malignancy. While we could repeat the aspiration, I think the safer course is to remove a piece of your thyroid.”

Ms. Reid’s brow furrowed. “Is this a major surgery? Will I have to stay in the hospital? I’m a teacher, and with my boys, an overnight stay would be really hard.”

Dr. Feng shook her head. “No, no—it’s a day surgery, one I do regularly. The most common complications are bleeding and infection. Bleeding is typically controlled by cauterizing or tying off blood vessels, and if you develop redness or a fever suggesting infection, we’d treat you with antibiotics. There’s also a small chance of injuring the nerve to your vocal cord, which can affect your voice, but that’s very rare. I’ve performed this surgery many times, and it seldom happens. Do you have any questions about the procedure?”

Ms. Reid let out a deep breath. “I just want this lump gone. Let’s go ahead with the surgery.”

“Alright,” Dr. Feng replied. “Please see the scheduling nurse out front to find a day that works for both of us. You might want to plan it before a long weekend at your school, like Easter or Memorial Day, since the surgery isn’t urgent.”

Ms. Reid scheduled the operation, which proceeded as planned.

Several days later, Ms. Reid returned for an emergency appointment with Dr. Feng. Her frustration was palpable, even though her voice was barely audible over the din of the clinic.

“I thought you said this was rare,” she said, shaking a printout of a medical journal article at Dr. Feng. “My recurrent laryngeal nerve was injured. I’m a teacher, and I have kids—I need my voice! If I’d known there was a 4 percent chance I could lose it, I never would have agreed to the surgery!” 

Was Dr. Feng negligent in explaining the surgical risks to Ms. Reid? Was she obligated to provide precise numerical risk information?

ethical_issues.question: In discussing surgical risks with patients, should Dr. Feng prioritize providing Ms. Reid with quantitative data rather than qualitative descriptions to ensure informed consent and avoid potential misunderstandings?
keypoints: There are significant variations in patients’ interpretations of terms such as “rare” and “possible,” which has led many experts to recommend providing specific numerical information to enhance the clarity of risk communication.

However, the provision of quantitative risk information can also cause confusion or mislead patients, given the widespread limitations in patients’ understanding of probabilistic concepts (for example, fewer than 50% of adults comprehend complex probabilities), indicating that disclosing exact numbers is not always ethically required.

The central goal of risk disclosure is to assist patients in understanding the complexity and trade-offs involved in the decision-making process, rather than merely conveying precise probability figures.

Therefore, whether clinicians disclose specific numerical risks should depend on whether such information helps patients develop accurate and effective risk perceptions and decision-making gist, rather than on a mechanical obligation to disclose numbers.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where patients have limited numeracy skills, how should physicians effectively communicate risk information to assist patients in making informed decisions?
keypoints: Physicians should assist patients in understanding that they face a difficult decision involving complex and incommensurable tradeoffs, rather than merely disclosing specific probabilities of risk.

Providing exact numerical risk figures is not obligatory; clinicians should assess, based on the patient’s numeracy and comprehension needs, whether quantitative information will help the patient form accurate and effective gist representations of risk.

Physicians ought to employ communication strategies consistent with dual process theory, emphasizing the core meaning of risks (e.g., “important,” “rare”) rather than relying solely on verbatim recall of precise numbers.

Informing patients that a difficult decision must be made does not equate to requiring them to bear decision-making responsibility alone; clinicians should offer support, explanation, and guidance throughout the process to facilitate rational patient decision-making.

title: Special Protections for Mental Health Treatment Notes
case:
Dr. Kessler is a psychiatrist at Parks Medical Associates, a large multispecialty medical practice with more than 60 physicians. Dr. Kessler has had an interest in health information technology since he was an undergraduate majoring in computer science. Over the past year, he has been managing his group’s transition from paper charts to an electronic medical record (EMR) system. He believes that the system will produce more efficient and coordinated patient care by giving clinicians seamless access to patient medical records, thereby leading to better patient health outcomes and overall cost savings for the practice.
Given the sensitive nature of psychiatry visits, Dr. Kessler proposes the use of a firewall as an additional safeguard to ensure the confidentiality of patients’ mental health records. This firewall prevents employees who are not mental health clinicians from accessing psychiatry notes.
When Dr. Kessler presents this proposal at a meeting with senior members of the practice, several physicians raise their concerns. Dr. Liu, an internist, asks, “How will I be able to monitor my patients’ depression or alcohol treatment if I can’t read the psychiatrist’s notes?” Dr. O’Leary, a gynecologist, wonders, “Aren’t we perpetuating the stigma surrounding mental illness by creating special protections?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Kessler, a psychiatrist at Parks Medical Associates—a large multispecialty group with over 60 physicians—has always had a deep passion for health information technology, stemming from his days as a computer science major in college. Over the last year, he has overseen the practice’s shift from traditional paper charts to a comprehensive electronic medical record (EMR) system. Dr. Kessler is convinced that the new system will streamline patient care, enabling clinicians to access medical records efficiently and coordinate care more effectively, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing costs for the practice.

However, Dr. Kessler is acutely aware of the heightened sensitivity surrounding psychiatric records. To better safeguard the confidentiality of his patients, he suggests adding a firewall within the EMR: only mental health clinicians would be able to access psychiatric notes, while non-psychiatric staff would be restricted from viewing them.

At a meeting with the practice’s senior physicians, Dr. Kessler presents his proposal. Almost immediately, some colleagues voice their reservations. Dr. Liu, an internist, asks, “How am I supposed to keep track of my patients’ depression or their progress in alcohol treatment programs if I don’t have access to the psychiatrist’s notes?” Meanwhile, Dr. O’Leary, a gynecologist, adds, “By setting apart mental health records for special protection, aren’t we reinforcing the stigma that mental illnesses are something to be hidden?”

The discussion grows animated, with the group weighing the need to protect patient privacy against the imperative of interdisciplinary communication. Dr. Kessler listens as colleagues debate how to ensure that crucial information—such as psychotropic medication lists or significant risk factors—remains accessible to relevant clinicians, while still honoring patients’ rights to control who sees their sensitive psychiatric information. As the meeting continues, the physicians grapple with how to design an EMR system that allows patients to choose, through a process similar to informed consent, whether and how their mental health records can be shared across specialties, all while supporting coordinated care and minimizing stigma.

ethical_issues.question: How can mental health treatment records be managed to balance patients’ confidentiality needs with the requirements for interdisciplinary communication and care coordination?
keypoints: The confidentiality of psychiatric records must be balanced with the need for interdisciplinary care coordination, as significant risk factors and medication information provide important clinical references for other specialties.
Implementing a patient-informed consent mechanism that allows patients to decide whether to restrict access to their mental health records respects their privacy rights and autonomy.

Permit partial visibility of key information (such as the list of psychotropic medications) to all physicians, while securing the remaining psychiatric record content behind technical access firewalls, thereby balancing confidentiality with clinical coordination.

Electronic medical record systems should support tiered protection of record content and flexible authorization; the documentation management process and access permissions should be openly discussed with patients during the initial visit.

Physicians must exercise caution when drafting psychiatric notes, considering the potential readership to ensure the content is both accurate and comprehensive while adhering to confidentiality and ethical standards.

Healthcare institutions should foster a culture that respects mental health privacy and promotes interdisciplinary collaboration, avoiding protective measures that may inadvertently exacerbate the stigma associated with mental illness.

ethical_issues.question: Should patients be allowed to decide whether to restrict access to their mental health records, similar to an informed consent process?
keypoints: Patients may decide whether to restrict access to their mental health records, analogous to an informed consent process, reflecting a patient-centered approach.
Patient-imposed restrictions on record access may raise concerns among psychiatrists regarding inadequate care coordination, presenting potential risks and ethical tensions.
A balance must be sought between respecting patient autonomy and ensuring patient safety in accordance with the principle of nonmaleficence.
Healthcare institutions should collaboratively develop flexible and acceptable record management strategies with patients to foster trust and cooperation.

title: Treating Bereavement
case:
On the examining table, Mrs. Greene looked much older than her 41 years. There were dark bags under her eyes, and her hair was tied back in a bun. She was seeing her primary care physician, Dr. Samuel, for a routine physical exam.
“Do you have any pain?” Dr. Samuel asked as he pressed on the patient’s belly.
Abruptly, Mrs. Greene sat up. Tears were overflowing her eyes.
“Dr. Samuel, I’m in a lot of pain,” she admitted. “Since my daughter died, I wake up in the middle of the night thinking I hear her calling out my name. Am I going crazy?”
Mrs. Greene’s 8-year-old daughter had died from leukemia about 7 months before, and since then Mrs. Greene had had trouble falling asleep and staying asleep. She had lost 10 pounds. She was on a leave of absence from her job as an accountant because she couldn’t concentrate on her work.
Dr. Samuel handed her a box of tissues. “My heart goes out to you,” he replied. “I can’t imagine what it’s like for you to lose your child. The grief you’re going through must be terrible.”
“It is terrible,” murmured Mrs. Greene. “It’s been going on for months now. Shouldn’t it have stopped by now? Can’t you prescribe me a pill to take away this pain?”
“Would you be interested in grief counseling?” asked Dr. Samuel.
“I went to a group once, but I couldn’t stand it. All those sad people just made me feel worse,” Mrs. Greene explained. “Can’t you just give me something to stop the pain?”
Dr. Samuel recognized that Mrs. Greene had some symptoms of depression, but he was reluctant to diagnose her with major depressive disorder, given that the loss of her daughter was still fairly recent. Furthermore, he was unsure whether medication was warranted at this point. As terrible as it is, grief is a natural human condition, he mused.
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Greene sat quietly on the examining table, her posture slumped, looking far older than her 41 years. Deep shadows ringed her eyes, and her hair was pulled back tightly in a bun, accentuating the lines of exhaustion on her face. She had come in for a routine check-up with her primary care physician, Dr. Samuel.

As Dr. Samuel gently palpated her abdomen, he asked, “Are you experiencing any pain?”

Suddenly, Mrs. Greene pushed herself upright, her face wet with tears that spilled down her cheeks.

“Dr. Samuel, I’m in so much pain,” she managed to say, her voice trembling. “Ever since my daughter died, I wake up at night, convinced I hear her calling for me. Am I losing my mind?”

Seven months earlier, Mrs. Greene’s 8-year-old daughter had died from leukemia. Since that devastating loss, Mrs. Greene had struggled with both falling and staying asleep. She had lost ten pounds and was on a leave of absence from her accounting job, unable to focus or complete her work.

Dr. Samuel offered her a box of tissues. “I’m so sorry for your loss,” he said softly. “I can’t begin to imagine what it’s like to lose a child. The grief you’re feeling must be overwhelming.”

Mrs. Greene nodded, dabbing at her eyes. “It’s unbearable,” she whispered. “I thought it would get better by now, but it hasn’t. Isn’t there something you can give me—a pill or something—to make this pain stop?”

“Have you considered grief counseling?” Dr. Samuel asked gently.

“I tried going to a group once,” Mrs. Greene replied, shaking her head. “But being around so many sad people made me feel even worse. Please, can’t you just give me something to make it go away?”

Dr. Samuel recognized that Mrs. Greene was exhibiting some symptoms associated with depression, yet he hesitated to diagnose her with major depressive disorder so soon after such a profound loss. He carefully weighed whether medication was appropriate at this stage, reflecting that as intense as it is, grief remains a natural human response.

ethical_issues.question: When managing a patient’s grief, should the physician initiate pharmacological treatment immediately to alleviate the patient’s distress?
keypoints: Physicians managing patients experiencing grief should adopt a cautious and comprehensive assessment approach rather than initiating pharmacological treatment immediately.
Given that the loss of the daughter is relatively recent, clinicians should avoid hastily diagnosing major depressive disorder and must differentiate between normal grief and depressive symptoms.
The evaluation process should prioritize the identification of depressive syndromes and suicide risk, including explicitly inquiring whether the patient has suicidal thoughts or plans.
Treatment of depression secondary to grief may require pharmacological intervention, but such decisions must be made cautiously and based on thorough assessment.

When prescribing antidepressants, patients should be warned about the potential increased risk of suicide during the initial phase of medication, and close monitoring of the patient’s condition is essential during this period.

title: Monitoring Blogs: A New Dilemma for Psychiatrists
case:
As Dr. Patel, who specializes in treating mood disorders, walks into the waiting room to greet her new patient Jonas, she notices that he is furiously typing away on his laptop. His brow is furrowed in deep concentration.
Jonas was recently hospitalized for mania and psychosis. He was initially brought to the hospital in police custody after claiming to have a bomb in his backpack and assaulting a police officer. At the hospital, he was started on antipsychotic and mood-stabilizing medications and referred to Dr. Patel for outpatient follow-up care.
Even before they settle into Dr. Patel’s office, Jonas is eager to tell Dr. Patel how much he has improved since his hospitalization. “I am a thousand times better already!” exclaims Jonas. “I’ve realized that I’m on a sacred journey of recovery, and so I started a blog to record all the ups and downs. The blog is going to be huge because I already have a ton of followers on Twitter.”
After Jonas leaves, Dr. Patel begins to wonder if she should take a look at Jonas’s blog. On one hand, she thinks it would allow her get to know Jonas better. On the other hand, she wonders whether she would be crossing patient-doctor boundaries by seeking out the blog. Jonas has not asked her to read it. She thinks to herself,There is no telling what may turn up online.
case_rewrite:
As Dr. Patel, a psychiatrist specializing in mood disorders, enters the waiting area to meet her new patient Jonas, she immediately notices him intensely focused on his laptop, fingers flying over the keyboard and his brow knit in concentration. Jonas, recently discharged after a hospital stay for mania and psychosis, was initially admitted following an incident in which he claimed to have a bomb in his backpack and assaulted a police officer. During his hospitalization, he was started on antipsychotic and mood-stabilizing medications and then referred to Dr. Patel for outpatient follow-up.

Before they even reach Dr. Patel's office, Jonas can hardly contain his enthusiasm. “I am a thousand times better already!” he exclaims, eyes shining. “I’ve realized I’m on a sacred journey of recovery, and I started a blog to document all the ups and downs. The blog is going to be huge—I already have a ton of followers on Twitter.”

After their appointment, as Jonas leaves, Dr. Patel finds herself wondering whether she should look up Jonas’s blog. On one hand, she considers that reading the blog could help her understand Jonas more deeply, especially given his recent history of aggressive behavior and threats. On the other hand, she questions whether seeking out the blog without Jonas’s invitation might overstep important boundaries between doctor and patient. Jonas has not asked her to read it, and she muses to herself, There’s no telling what I might find online.

ethical_issues.question: Should psychiatrists monitor their patients’ blogs to obtain essential clinical information without the patients’ consent?
keypoints: Physicians have justifiable grounds to review a patient’s blog content in order to obtain clinical information when there are recent safety concerns such as aggressive behavior and threats of violence.

If a patient’s blog reveals suicidal, homicidal tendencies, or other serious safety risks, it is necessary for the physician to continuously monitor the blog and intervene clinically in a timely manner.

Physicians should balance the patient’s right to privacy with safety needs, respect the patient’s right to informed consent, and whenever possible, inform the patient about the purpose and scope of blog monitoring to foster trust and collaboration in the therapeutic relationship.

Failure to monitor a patient’s blog may result in severe humanitarian consequences and medicolegal risks, especially in cases involving potentially violent patients; therefore, blog monitoring is a reasonable and necessary clinical measure when clear risks are present.

ethical_issues.question: If a psychiatrist discovers serious safety concerns through monitoring a patient’s blog, is there an obligation to inform the patient post hoc about the monitoring and the findings?
keypoints: When the patient is clinically stable and not at imminent risk of self-harm or harm to others, monitoring the blog can help to promptly identify potential safety concerns and safeguard the patient’s well-being.
The physician should inform the patient that blog monitoring is being conducted, as this facilitates effective communication, enhances trust, and serves the patient’s best interests.
If the patient demonstrates a serious and imminent safety threat, the physician has a duty to warn appropriate third parties to prevent harm.
Relevant discussions and subsequent actions should be thoroughly documented in the medical record to ensure completeness of clinical documentation.

ethical_issues.question: Based on the content of a patient’s blog, when should a psychiatrist initiate involuntary hospitalization or issue a Tarasoff warning to others?
keypoints: Physicians should pay attention to the known blog content of patients, with a particular focus on identifying any indications of suicidal or violent tendencies.

If suicidal or homicidal threats are present in a patient’s blog, the physician should promptly conduct a risk assessment and, if necessary, implement clinical interventions, including involuntary hospitalization or issuing a Tarasoff warning to potential victims.
Failure to adequately monitor a patient’s blog and to take appropriate action upon discovering serious threats may result in legal liability and clinical negligence for the physician.

When monitoring patients’ online content, physicians should respect professional boundaries and patient privacy, avoiding unauthorized or excessive intervention, while ensuring that patient safety remains the primary concern.
