title: Requests for Care from Family Members
case:
Martha was at her cousin’s house for a family dinner when she was approached by her Uncle John. John was one of her favorite uncles—he’d practically raised her for parts of her childhood and had helped her with her student loans during medical school. Since she’d become a doctor, she noticed he always took a certain pride in introducing her to friends as “My niece, the doctor.”
“What’s going on, Uncle John?” she asked.
“Well Martha,” he said, “I was wondering if I could ask you a couple of questions.”
“Sure,” Martha answered. “What’s up?”
“You see, I don’t want to bother you, and I know you must get this all the time, but I’ve just been having this terrible cough these last few weeks, and I don’t know what to do about it.”
“That’s no good,” Martha said. “Have you been to see your doctor yet?”
“No,” said Uncle John. “He was away on vacation, and then I called his office, and they said he wouldn’t be able to fit me in until next month sometime. I’ve just been feeling so sick—I could be dead by then!” He laughed. “That was a joke. I don’t really know if I want to bother my doctor about this. But I have been feeling pretty sick. I’ve had this cough, and a really bad headache. And I’ve been so tired. I just wonder if I’ve got something going on, and I was hoping you’d give me a quick once-over.”
Martha paused, and considered her options. Her Uncle John looked well enough, but he’d been a smoker for most of his life, and had already had one bout with cancer—a small tumor in his colon that’d been caught by routine colonoscopy. “Uncle John,” she said, “have you—” but then she stopped. “You know, Uncle John, I’d love to take a look, but I really shouldn’t. I think you’d do better to go see someone else. Maybe there’s someone else in your doctor’s practice who can see you on short notice? Or the walk-in clinic on Water and Main, if no one at the regular practice can see you and things keep getting worse. I’m sorry, but—do you think that would be alright?”
Uncle John looked hurt. “I suppose so, Martha. This has been going on for a couple of weeks—what’s one more night, right? Anyway,” he said, “I should talk to your cousins. I haven’t seen them in months!” He turned away, and Martha couldn’t help noticing that he avoided her for the rest of the evening.
case_rewrite:
Martha was enjoying a lively family dinner at her cousin’s home when her Uncle John approached her. Uncle John had always held a special place in Martha’s heart—he’d stepped in during tough times when she was growing up and had even helped her cover her medical school loans. Since Martha had become a physician, he seemed to take genuine pride in her accomplishments, often introducing her to others as, “My niece, the doctor.”

As she filled her plate, Uncle John sidled up beside her. “Martha, can I ask you something?” he said quietly.

“Of course, Uncle John. What’s on your mind?” she replied.

He hesitated, glancing around to ensure no one was listening. “I don’t want to trouble you. I’m sure you get this all the time,” he began, “but I’ve had this awful cough for the past few weeks, and I can’t seem to shake it.”

“That sounds rough,” Martha said sympathetically. “Have you had a chance to see your doctor yet?”

Uncle John shook his head. “No, I haven’t. He took some time off, and when I called the office, the earliest they could fit me in is next month. I’ve just been feeling lousy—sometimes I joke that I’ll be dead by then!” He smiled wanly, then continued, “Seriously, though, I’ve been coughing a lot, my head hurts, and I’m always exhausted. I keep thinking something might really be wrong. I was hoping you could give me a quick checkup, just to put my mind at ease.”

Martha hesitated, weighing her response. She knew Uncle John had a long history of smoking and had previously battled a colon tumor, detected early during a routine screening. Still, he didn’t appear acutely ill at the moment. “Uncle John,” she started, then paused. “You know, I really want to help, but it wouldn’t be right for me to examine you here. I think it’s best if you see another doctor. Maybe someone else at your primary care office could see you sooner? Or, if things get worse, there’s always the walk-in clinic over on Water and Main. I’m sorry—I just think that’s the safest way to make sure you get the care you need. Would that work?”

Uncle John’s face fell slightly. “I guess that makes sense, Martha. I’ve waited this long—what’s another day or two?” He managed a small smile, but Martha could tell he was disappointed. After that, Uncle John mingled with other relatives and seemed to avoid Martha for the rest of the evening, leaving her to wonder if she’d done the right thing.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians provide medical care to family members, especially in non-emergency situations?
keypoints: Physicians generally should not provide medical care to themselves or immediate family members to avoid compromising professional objectivity.
Medical professional ethics explicitly warn physicians against treating family members; although not necessarily prohibited by law, medical boards may consider such conduct unprofessional.

Professional medical practice requires adherence to standardized care protocols, including a thorough physical examination and proper medical record documentation; informal “quick assessments” at family gatherings fail to meet these standards and carry the risk of disciplinary action.

Physicians should act as informed guides and facilitators for family members, assisting them in securing appropriate medical appointments or accompanying them to clinical visits, rather than directly diagnosing or treating them.

ethical_issues.question: How can a physician ensure that a family member receives high-quality care and maintain a good relationship when declining to provide medical treatment to that relative?
keypoints: Physicians should clearly define their professional role and avoid providing direct clinical care to family members, instead acting as informed guides and coordinators to facilitate appropriate treatment by other healthcare providers.

Physicians ought to express concern for the family member’s condition by attentive listening and appropriate questioning, thereby encouraging the family member to take their health seriously and ensuring timely and proper medical care.

Physicians may proactively assist family members in coordinating expedited appointments or accompany them to medical visits, thereby avoiding the risks associated with direct treatment while ensuring the family member receives high-quality care and feels supported and cared for.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ensure professional objectivity and avoid providing excessive, insufficient, or inappropriate care when delivering medical services to family members?
keypoints: Physicians generally should not treat themselves or immediate family members, as close personal relationships may compromise professional objectivity and lead to excessive, insufficient, or inappropriate care.
Physicians should objectively assess whether they possess the professional training and competence necessary to meet their relative’s medical needs.

Physicians need to evaluate whether the close relationship poses an emotional barrier to obtaining a complete medical history (such as probing sensitive information) or to engaging in serious communication (such as delivering bad news).
Physicians should consider whether their relatives might be more receptive to medical recommendations provided by an unrelated physician, thereby facilitating effective treatment.
Physicians should carefully consider whether medical involvement could provoke or intensify intrafamilial conflicts.
Physicians should be willing and proactive in referring relatives to other appropriate healthcare professionals to avoid compromised care due to the personal relationship.

Physicians should consciously maintain boundaries between their professional and personal roles, remain attentive to “early warning signs” such as feelings of unease or troubled conscience, and avoid crossing into providing care that exceeds appropriate limits.
Physicians should ask themselves whether they are willing to be accountable to their professional peers and to the public for the care provided in such situations.
Physicians should act as informed guides and facilitators, assisting relatives in obtaining appropriate and objective medical care.

title: Responsibility for Patients after the Handoff
case:
“Is that Mrs. Wilson’s medication list?” Dr. Miller asked the resident, holding up a piece of paper she had found in the chart. It was the first morning of Dr. Miller’s 2 weeks as attending physician on her institution’s hospitalist service. She’d spent some time the night before reviewing the charts of all the patients under her care and gone over their conditions that morning during the handoff from Dr. Jones, the previous attending physician. Now she was meeting them face-to-face. She took a special interest in Mrs. Wilson, an elderly woman with significantly advanced dementia, who’d come to the hospital with pneumonia several weeks before. She’d been treated successfully for the pneumonia, but while she was in hospital, her overall level of functioning had declined.
Where Mrs. Wilson had previously been a kind, if disoriented, woman, she’d become very agitated in the hospital, occasionally acting violently with staff. She’d also developed new pressure ulcers, which were made worse by her agitation: Mrs. Wilson had started rocking herself back and forth in her bed, which made it difficult for the ulcers to heal.
Her agitation made hospital discharge difficult to arrange: Mrs. Wilson would probably need physical therapy at a dedicated rehab facility, but no facility would take her as long as she remained violent and her wounds remained difficult to treat.
In the 2 weeks prior to Dr. Miller’s arrival, Dr. Jones’s hospitalist team had tried to address these problems by instituting a series of measures. First, they’d tried behavioral interventions designed to reduce agitation: letting in light in the morning, encouraging sleep at night, using calendars and clocks to reorient Mrs. Wilson to the current date and time. When these failed, they’d gradually begun to use a combination of antipsychotic and sedative medications, trying several before eventually settling on a combination that seemed to work.
When Dr. Miller began her shift, Mrs. Wilson’s agitation was under good control, and her rocking had subsided. According to her case manager, a rehab facility had agreed to take her sometime in the next several days. But Dr. Miller had just stopped by Mrs. Wilson’s room and didn’t like the looks of her. “She’s snowed. I could barely wake her up,” she told the resident. “And these drugs we’re giving her have been associated with increased mortality in elderly patients. I’m just not comfortable using them without an abundantly clear indication for doing so, and right now I don’t see it. Let’s start decreasing these meds and see how she does.”
Dr. Jones, who was passing by on his way out the door, happened to overhear this conversation, and it made him pause.Should I step in here?he wondered? After all, it’d taken some time to get Mrs. Wilson’s multiple problems under control, and now the medications that’d seemed to be working were going to be discontinued.No, he thought.I’ve signed off. Mrs. Wilson is Dr. Miller’s patient now.
Dr. Miller’s team began to decrease Mrs. Wilson’s sedating medications. Within only a few days, she’d become agitated again and her pressure ulcers had re-opened. Dr. Miller decided they should be brought back up, but by the time they’d taken effect a second time, Mrs. Wilson’s spot at rehab had gone to someone else; she’d now have to wait longer in the hospital for another rehab placement.
case_rewrite:
“Is that Mrs. Wilson’s medication list?” Dr. Miller asked the resident, holding up a sheet she’d just found in the chart. It was the first morning of Dr. Miller’s two-week stint as attending on the hospitalist service at her institution. The night before, she had carefully reviewed charts for all the patients she’d soon be caring for, and that morning she’d discussed their current situations in detail during the handoff with Dr. Jones, the outgoing attending. Now, she was making her first in-person rounds. 

Dr. Miller was especially interested in Mrs. Wilson—a frail, elderly woman with advanced dementia, admitted several weeks earlier for pneumonia. The infection had been treated successfully, but during her hospitalization, Mrs. Wilson’s overall function had declined markedly. Where she’d previously been gentle, if often confused, she had become increasingly agitated, sometimes lashing out at staff. New pressure ulcers had developed, which were exacerbated by her agitation: Mrs. Wilson had started rocking herself vigorously in bed, making it nearly impossible for her wounds to heal.

Her ongoing agitation complicated plans for discharge. Though she would benefit from physical therapy at a rehabilitation facility, no facility was willing to accept her while she remained violent and her wounds so difficult to manage.

In the two weeks before Dr. Miller’s arrival, Dr. Jones’s team had methodically tried a range of interventions. They began with behavioral strategies—opening the blinds in the morning, encouraging nighttime sleep, using clocks and calendars to orient Mrs. Wilson to time and place. When these measures failed, they initiated a cautious trial of antipsychotic and sedative medications, adjusting various combinations until they found a regimen that finally seemed effective.

When Dr. Miller took over the team, she found Mrs. Wilson’s agitation well-controlled and the constant rocking had stopped. The case manager reported that a rehabilitation facility had agreed to accept Mrs. Wilson within the next few days. However, after visiting Mrs. Wilson’s room herself, Dr. Miller was alarmed. “She’s snowed. I could barely rouse her,” she remarked to the resident. “These medications have been linked to higher mortality in elderly patients. Unless there’s a crystal-clear reason to use them, I don’t feel comfortable keeping her on this much. Let’s begin tapering them and watch how she does.”

Just then, Dr. Jones, on his way out, happened to overhear. He paused, conflicted.Should I get involved?he wondered. He remembered how difficult it had been to manage Mrs. Wilson’s agitation and pressure ulcers, and how much effort it had taken to find a medication regimen that worked. If the medications were withdrawn, all their progress could be lost. But,he thought,I’ve signed off. Mrs. Wilson is Dr. Miller’s patient now.

Over the next few days, Dr. Miller’s team tapered Mrs. Wilson’s sedating medications. Predictably, her agitation returned and her pressure ulcers re-opened. Dr. Miller decided to increase the medications again, but by the time they took effect, Mrs. Wilson’s rehabilitation spot had already been given to someone else. She would now have to remain in the hospital and wait for another rehab placement.

ethical_issues.question: During patient handoffs, how can all necessary clinical information be effectively conveyed to ensure that critical aspects of diagnosis and treatment are not overlooked?
keypoints: Utilize SBAR (Situation-Background-Assessment-Recommendation) as a standardized handoff protocol to ensure the transmission of all necessary clinical information.
Provide opportunities for interactive questioning to facilitate clarification and supplementation of critical information between the parties involved in the handoff.

Explicitly emphasize the failure of nonpharmacologic interventions and the ultimate success of the pharmacologic regimen to enable the incoming physician to fully understand the patient’s condition and treatment history.

Encourage the establishment of a supportive hospital culture that permits cross-role and cross-hierarchical inquiry, reinforces physicians’ professional responsibility beyond formal handoffs, prioritizes patient welfare, and promotes information sharing and collaboration.

ethical_issues.question: Does a physician retain a responsibility to intervene in the decisions of the incoming physician after a handoff in order to ensure the patient’s well-being?
keypoints: Although Dr. Jones has completed the handoff and holds no formal clinical responsibility, he retains a professional duty to intervene if he possesses critical information unknown to the new team in order to safeguard the patient’s well-being.
The core of a physician’s professional responsibility is fiduciary duty, which requires prioritizing the patient’s interests above concerns about colleagues’ feelings.
While respecting the clinical decisions of peers, physicians should proactively identify and correct substantive errors in diagnosis or treatment to protect patient safety and welfare.
Open, patient-centered peer communication and scholarly dialogue facilitate the mitigation of communication gaps and help prevent adverse clinical outcomes.

ethical_issues.question: How does hospital culture influence communication between physicians and the implementation of optimal treatment plans for patients?
keypoints: Hospital culture may lead physicians to refrain from commenting on the treatment plans of former patients during handoffs, out of concern for offending the incoming physician, thereby impeding effective communication and the maximization of patient interests.

Dr. Jones’s silence reflects a tendency within hospital culture to prioritize avoidance of colleague conflict over patient welfare; this is an institutional issue that requires reflection and improvement at the cultural level.

Hospital culture reform should promote open communication and inquiry across hierarchies and roles, fostering an environment that supports candid dialogue, thereby reducing medical errors and improving patient outcomes.

title: A University Physician's Duty to Nonpatient Students
case:
It had already been a busy day at the student health center for Dr. Smith when Steve came in. Steve was a 22-year-old senior in the biosciences program at the college where Dr. Smith worked. He had asthma and type 1 diabetes, and had been coming to see Dr. Smith about these problems for as long as he’d been a student. However, Dr. Smith noted as he looked at his schedule, today’s visit was for something else entirely.
“Hi Steve,” Dr. Smith said. “How’s it going?”
“Oh, it’s okay,” Steve replied. “How have you been?”
“I’ve been well, thanks. I haven’t seen you in here lately—your asthma must be behaving itself!”
“It is,” Steve assured him. “And I still have refills on the insulin you gave me at my last visit, so I haven’t had a reason to come in.”
“I’m glad to hear it,” said Dr. Smith. “So why did you come by today?”
“Well,” Steve started, “my grades haven’t been so great lately, and I’m worried that’s going to affect my chances of getting a job after graduation.”
“Alright,” Dr. Smith responded. “Why do you think your grades haven’t been so great lately?”
Steve was vague in his answers—he couldn’t seem to concentrate, wasn’t able to sleep. When Dr. Smith asked what sorts of solutions he had tried, Steve explained that his attempts to drop things from his schedule and get more sleep had failed.
“Hmm,” said Dr. Smith. “How can I help?”
“Honestly,” Steve said, “last week I took some pills from this guy in my dorm—he says truckers sometimes take them to stay awake for long drives—and they worked really well. I was able to stay awake all night and really get a ton of work done. He’s got a bunch, and he says I can just get them from him, but I was wondering if you had anything like that you might prescribe.”
“You’re talking about stimulants, I think. Something like Ritalin?” Dr. Smith asked.
“I guess so,” Steve said. “My friend says he gets them his cousin, and I think his cousin has attention deficit disorder or something like that. I’ve never had a prescription for them before.”
“Hmm,” said Dr. Smith. “Do you know if your friend has told his doctor about these drugs?”
“I don’t know,” Steve replied. “He seems like a pretty healthy guy. I’m not sure he even has a doctor.”
“Well,” Dr. Smith explained, “those drugs can be dangerous, and we don’t like to prescribe them without a diagnosed attention disorder to treat.”
“Oh,” Steve said. “I didn’t know that.”
“So I don’t think I can prescribe you that kind of a drug, and I also want to advise you against taking the ones your friend offers,” Dr. Smith said. “But I also don’t want to leave you without a leg to stand on. Let’s talk about other things you may be able to do to get a handle on all this stress in your life.”
“Okay,” said Steve.
They talked for a while, and Dr. Smith was left with the feeling that he’d helped Steve out. But he felt unsettled about Steve’s friend. It sounded like he was in need of medical attention and might not be getting it. Further, Dr. Smith was concerned that he might be supplying his stimulants to other students besides Steve.
case_rewrite:
It had already been a hectic day at the student health center for Dr. Smith when Steve walked in. Steve, a 22-year-old senior in the biosciences program at the college, had been under Dr. Smith’s care for his asthma and type 1 diabetes since his freshman year. Dr. Smith glanced at his schedule and noticed that today’s appointment was not about either of those chronic conditions.

“Hey Steve,” Dr. Smith greeted him warmly. “How are things?”

“Not bad,” Steve replied. “How about you?”

“I’m doing well, thanks. I haven’t seen you around here for a while—your asthma must be under control!”

“Yeah, it’s been fine,” Steve said. “And I still have plenty of insulin from the last time you prescribed it, so I haven’t needed to come in.”

“That’s good to hear,” Dr. Smith responded. “So, what brings you in today?”

Steve hesitated before answering. “Honestly, my grades have been slipping lately, and I’m worried it’s going to hurt my chances when I start applying for jobs after graduation.”

Dr. Smith nodded. “What do you think has been causing your grades to drop?”

Steve’s answers were vague—he mentioned having trouble focusing and sleeping, and that nothing he’d tried, like cutting back on activities or trying to get more rest, seemed to help.

“I see,” Dr. Smith said. “How do you think I can help?”

Steve looked a bit uneasy. “Well, last week, I tried some pills that a guy in my dorm gave me—he said truck drivers use them to stay awake on long trips. They really helped me stay up all night and get a lot of work done. He has more, and said I could just get them from him, but I thought I’d ask if there’s anything like that you could prescribe.”

“You’re talking about stimulants, like Ritalin or something similar?” Dr. Smith asked.

“I guess so,” Steve replied. “My friend gets them from his cousin, and I think the cousin has some sort of attention disorder. I’ve never had a prescription for them.”

Dr. Smith considered this. “Do you know if your friend has told his doctor about sharing these medications?”

Steve shook his head. “I have no idea. He seems pretty healthy, and I’m not sure he even sees a doctor regularly.”

Dr. Smith took a moment before responding. “Those medications can be risky, and we only prescribe them when there’s a clear diagnosis, like ADHD, that justifies their use.”

“Oh,” Steve said quietly. “I didn’t realize that.”

“So, I can’t prescribe you those kinds of drugs, and I really want to advise you not to take what your friend offers,” Dr. Smith said firmly. “But I don’t want to leave you without support. Let’s talk through some other options for managing your stress and improving your focus.”

“Alright,” Steve agreed.

They spent some time discussing healthy strategies for dealing with academic pressure and sleep difficulties. As the conversation wrapped up, Dr. Smith felt he had given Steve some guidance, but he couldn’t shake concerns about Steve’s friend. It seemed possible that the friend was misusing prescription stimulants and might be distributing them to others, which raised worries about both the friend’s well-being and broader risks on campus.

Despite these concerns, Dr. Smith knew he was bound by his duty of confidentiality to Steve. He reflected on how best to support Steve while respecting his privacy and considered the importance of educating patients about the dangers of stimulant misuse and encouraging those at risk to seek appropriate medical help.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Smith breach his duty of confidentiality to Steve in order to investigate the diversion of prescription medications?
keypoints: Dr. Smith owes Steve a fiduciary duty of confidentiality; as an adult patient, Steve’s right to privacy is strictly protected by privacy regulations.

The principle of medical confidentiality may only be overridden in extremely limited and clearly defined legal or ethical exceptions, such as when there is a credible and serious threat of harm to the patient or others. Steve’s current situation does not meet these stringent statutory exceptions.

The clinician’s obligation to maintain patient confidentiality is a core tenet of professional ethics; without the patient’s explicit consent, information obtained within the therapeutic relationship must not be discussed with university authorities, family members, or any third parties.

At the outset of the physician-patient interaction, the physician should proactively inform the patient of the principles of confidentiality and their exceptions, thereby establishing a transparent and mutually trusting therapeutic relationship.

Although Dr. Smith is concerned about Steve’s friend’s possible substance misuse and the associated public health risks, his professional responsibilities and ethical obligations require that these concerns be addressed without violating Steve’s right to confidentiality. Direct investigation or disclosure of information provided by Steve would constitute a breach of this duty.

Without infringing upon patient privacy, Dr. Smith may address his concerns through indirect and legally compliant means, such as strengthening health education for Steve, clearly explaining the risks of stimulant misuse, and encouraging Steve to guide his friend to seek professional medical help, thereby indirectly addressing potential public health risks.

title: Language Barriers in the Emergency Room
case:
Dr. Willis was chief resident in emergency medicine at an inner city hospital. Late one afternoon a young woman was escorted to the emergency department by her brother. They told the admission clerk that they had come to the U.S. from Brazil to visit family members who lived in the city. With the help of an emergency department aide, they listed the young woman’s name as Bianca, her age as 18, stomachache as the reason for the visit, their relative’s city address, and the number for the cell phone the young man carried. That was all that was on the form.
Bianca was bent over with both hands pressed against her lower belly. Her brother, Elias, who looked to be slightly older than she, said that he would translate for his sister because his English was better than hers. He said that he was very worried because Bianca was usually tough and rarely complained. Today she had pleaded with him to take her to see a doctor.
Dr. Willis started by asking questions about the pain: when had it started; did it seem to be located in one spot; was it a constant pain like a headache, or a sharp intermittent pain; had she ever had pain like this in the same place before? Without asking his sister, Elias answered that the pain had started early that morning. Then he began to translate Dr. Willis’s other questions to his sister in Portuguese. Bianca pointed to the lower right quadrant of her stomach, but Dr. Willis got no answers to his questions. Bianca did not seem to understand what Dr. Willis wanted to know, even though Elias repeated the questions several times, using what sounded to Dr. Willis (who understood no Portuguese) like different words.
Dr. Willis asked whether Bianca had vomited or had diarrhea, and Elias said no. The medical record started by the emergency department nurse noted that Bianca’s temperature and blood pressure were normal. When Dr. Willis asked when Bianca had had her last menstrual period, Elias seemed unable to interpret the question for his sister. “Could she be pregnant?” Dr. Willis asked. “No, she is not,” Elias said.
Dr. Willis asked Elias to translate the questions about Bianca’s menstrual periods and the possibility of pregnancy so that Bianca could reply, but Elias shook his head and said, “She is not pregnant. No.”
Finally, Dr. Willis suggested using the hospital’s telephone interpreting service so that he could get more information about Bianca’s pain and its possible cause, but Elias said that the service was not necessary. He could answer the questions. Dr. Willis responded, “I believe an interpreter would help us take better care of your sister and assist with technical questions.” Dr. Willis explained that he would need Bianca’s consent to the tests he would have to perform to establish the cause of her pain. “First, I want a urine sample and a blood sample that, together, will give me information about pregnancy and infection. While we wait for the interpreter, please explain that to your sister and ask for her consent.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Willis, chief resident in emergency medicine at an inner-city hospital, was nearing the end of his shift one late afternoon when a young woman arrived in the emergency department, accompanied by her brother. At the front desk, they explained they had traveled from Brazil to visit relatives in the city. With the assistance of an emergency department aide, they registered the young woman as Bianca, age 18, with stomach pain as her presenting complaint, listing their relative’s city address and her brother’s cell phone number. No further information was provided on the form.

Bianca entered the exam area, doubled over, clutching her lower abdomen with both hands. Her brother, Elias—who appeared slightly older—offered to translate, explaining his English was better than Bianca’s. He expressed deep concern, noting that his sister was usually resilient and rarely complained, but today she had specifically asked him to bring her to a doctor.

Dr. Willis began by asking Bianca about her pain: when it had started, whether it was localized or diffuse, if it was a steady ache or a sharp, intermittent pain, and whether she had ever experienced similar discomfort before. Instead of translating, Elias answered the first question himself, stating the pain began that morning. For subsequent questions, he switched to Portuguese, repeating Dr. Willis’s inquiries to Bianca. Bianca pointed toward the lower right side of her abdomen, but her responses were minimal; Dr. Willis noticed she didn’t seem to grasp what he was trying to determine, despite Elias’s repeated attempts to explain, using what sounded like varying Portuguese phrases.

When Dr. Willis asked about vomiting or diarrhea, Elias replied negatively. The nurse’s initial assessment recorded normal temperature and blood pressure for Bianca. Dr. Willis then asked when Bianca’s last menstrual period had occurred. At this, Elias hesitated, struggling to relay the question to his sister. “Could she be pregnant?” Dr. Willis pressed. “No, she is not,” Elias stated firmly.

Dr. Willis insisted that Elias translate these questions about menstruation and possible pregnancy so Bianca could answer herself, but Elias simply shook his head, repeating, “She is not pregnant. No.”

Recognizing the communication barrier, Dr. Willis suggested using the hospital’s telephone interpreting service to obtain more precise information regarding Bianca’s pain and potential causes. Elias objected, claiming the service was unnecessary and that he could answer all questions. Dr. Willis responded, “I believe an interpreter would help us take better care of your sister and help with more technical questions.” He explained to Elias that he would need Bianca’s consent before proceeding with any tests to determine the cause of her pain. “First, I’d like a urine and a blood sample, which can help us identify possible pregnancy or infection. While we wait for the interpreter, please explain this to your sister and ask for her consent.”

ethical_issues.question: In emergency situations, how can informed consent be obtained from the patient while ensuring timely medical treatment?
keypoints: In emergency situations, physicians should prioritize responding to the patient’s medical needs by promptly managing acute pain, while rationally assessing the severity of the condition; when necessary, treatment may proceed prior to obtaining informed consent to avoid delaying critical care.

If the patient’s condition is critical or consciousness impaired, the physician may initiate lifesaving interventions in unavoidable emergencies, with informed consent to be supplemented subsequently.

Presentation to the emergency department implies tacit consent for history taking, physical examination, and urgent diagnostic tests; physicians should immediately engage professional interpreting services to ensure accurate communication and avoid reliance on accompanying family members who may have conflicts of interest or communication barriers.

While awaiting professional interpretation, physicians may perform necessary physical examinations and urgent tests; however, non-urgent procedures should be deferred as much as possible to ensure the patient remains an active, voluntary, and informed participant in their care.

Physicians must uphold the primacy of the patient’s interests and endeavor to obtain informed consent within a reasonable clinical framework, thereby embodying the core principles of medical ethics and fulfilling legal obligations.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of language barriers and cultural differences, how can effective communication between healthcare providers and patients be ensured to prevent misdiagnosis or delays in treatment?
keypoints: The physician should immediately engage professional interpreting services to ensure accurate communication between the patient and healthcare providers, thereby preventing misdiagnosis or treatment delays caused by language barriers.

The accompanying family member (brother) should be asked to wait in the waiting area to minimize communication interference and to protect the patient’s autonomy in expressing her wishes; simultaneously, a female chaperone should be arranged to respect the patient’s privacy and cultural background.
While awaiting interpretation, the physician should perform necessary physical examinations and urgent diagnostic tests to safeguard the patient’s safety.

The physician must obtain the patient’s informed consent, ensuring that she is an active, voluntary, and informed participant in her care; non-urgent procedures should be deferred until an interpreter is present to guarantee the patient’s full understanding and involvement in treatment decisions.

title: Fibromyalgia Confounds Allopathic Habits of Mind
case:
Dr. Foote has been seeing Ms. Kirk, now in her forties, for years. She is overweight and depressed, with a history of migraines and irritable bowel syndrome. Dr. Foote is aware that her marriage has been going badly—her husband is unemployed and losing hope, her son is in drug and alcohol rehab. She once saw a psychiatrist who diagnosed her with depression; Dr. Foote has been renewing her SSRI prescription for years, and she reminds Dr. Foote at every visit that she is no better.
For the last few years, she has been particularly bothered by fatigue and constant, persistent joint pain that just won’t let up. She can’t remember the last time she had a good night’s sleep or a day without pain.
Dr. Foote has ordered the usual blood work. The tests have come back negative, and Dr. Foote feels ever more convinced that Ms. Kirk’s symptoms are caused by depression. Perhaps a different SSRI would help.
But Ms. Kirk turns up for another appointment sooner than expected. When Dr. Foote asks her how she’s doing, she pushes a printout of a web page across the table and says, “Read this. I think I have fibromyalgia.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Foote has been caring for Ms. Kirk, a woman now in her forties, for many years. Ms. Kirk struggles with being overweight and has long battled depression; she also has a history of migraines and irritable bowel syndrome. Dr. Foote knows that her personal life has been fraught with difficulties—her marriage is strained, her husband remains unemployed and increasingly despondent, and her son is currently in a rehabilitation program for substance abuse. Years ago, a psychiatrist diagnosed her with depression, and ever since, Dr. Foote has been renewing her SSRI prescription. At every appointment, Ms. Kirk reminds Dr. Foote that the medication has done little to improve her condition.

In recent years, Ms. Kirk has been especially troubled by persistent fatigue and unrelenting joint pain. She cannot recall the last time she enjoyed restful sleep or a single pain-free day. Dr. Foote has ordered the typical panels of blood work, but all results have come back within normal limits. This has reinforced Dr. Foote’s suspicion that Ms. Kirk’s symptoms are rooted in her depression, and she begins to consider whether switching to a different SSRI might be beneficial.

Unexpectedly, Ms. Kirk schedules another appointment sooner than usual. When Dr. Foote greets her and inquires about her well-being, Ms. Kirk slides a printout of a website across the desk and says, “Please read this. I think I have fibromyalgia.”

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians maintain empathy for patients and provide appropriate medical care amid uncertainty when confronted with diseases lacking positive diagnostic markers, such as fibromyalgia?
keypoints: Physicians should patiently listen to patients’ narratives, paying close attention to their subjective experiences and life contexts rather than relying solely on test results, in order to facilitate a more comprehensive diagnosis and understanding.

In the face of diseases lacking positive diagnostic markers, physicians must proactively acquire relevant knowledge and uphold a responsibility to continuously improve patients’ quality of life by providing individualized and holistic medical care.

Physicians should respect and accept patients with negative test results, recognize their suffering and sense of helplessness, and offer ongoing support and empathy to prevent patients from feeling neglected or stigmatized.

The medical profession should engage in systematic reflection to improve the culture and systems of care for patients with test-negative conditions, promoting the establishment of a more inclusive, scientifically grounded, and patient-centered healthcare environment.

title: Family Physicians’ Role in Discussing Organ Donation with Patients and the Public
case:
In a small town in Maine, a school board gathered for its monthly meeting. Dr. Gomez, present at the meeting, had practiced family medicine in this town for more than 25 years and his three children had gone through the local school system.
Weeks before, a serious car crash involved several high school students and resulted in the death of an 18-year-old boy, Keith. Talk of the crash and death consumed the “new business” portion of the evening.
Towards the end of the discussion, a pair of parents slowly rose in the back of the gym.
“Our daughter Stephanie has been lying in a hospital bed for the past 13 weeks. She is there because she is dying of end-stage liver disease; the only thing that will save her now is a liver transplant. We recognize the tragedy of Keith’s death and we are hoping to take this moment to raise awareness about organ donation.” Keith had not listed himself as an organ donor on his license.
“It is never easy when a family or our community confronts such heartbreak as this terrible accident. It would have been possible, however, for good to have come from Keith’s organs. There is a tremendous shortage. Donating your organs is the ultimate gift—the gift of life for desperately ill people.”
This emotional plea sparked a fervent debate among parents. Many left wondering whether conversations like these had a place at school board meetings or in schools themselves. Many in the community turned to Dr. Gomez for his opinion. Did he believe in educating patients about organ donation? He could bring it up at yearly physicals, as he did with advance directives—why didn’t he? Did he think it was an appropriate topic for a public forum?
case_rewrite:
In a quiet Maine town, the school board convened for its usual monthly meeting in the high school gymnasium. Among those present was Dr. Gomez, a family physician who had cared for generations of local families over his 25-year career. His own three children had attended these same schools, and he was a familiar, trusted face in the community.

The meeting’s agenda was overshadowed by a recent tragedy. Just weeks earlier, a devastating car accident had shaken the town, claiming the life of 18-year-old Keith and injuring several other high school students. The loss was still raw, and as the topic came up under “new business,” the pain in the room was palpable.

As the discussion wound down, two parents quietly stood at the back. Their voices trembled as they addressed the gathering. “Our daughter Stephanie has been in the hospital for 13 weeks now. She’s dying of end-stage liver disease. The only hope she has left is a liver transplant.” There was a heavy silence as their words settled over the crowd. “We know how much this community is hurting after losing Keith. We’re not here to diminish that pain, but to try to find something good in the midst of this tragedy—to encourage everyone to think about organ donation.” They explained that Keith had not been registered as an organ donor.

“It’s never easy to face such heartbreak, whether it’s within a family or our whole community,” Stephanie’s parents continued. “But, in tragedy, there’s sometimes a chance for hope. There’s a critical shortage of organs. Donating is the ultimate gift—it means life for people like our daughter, who are running out of time.”

Their heartfelt appeal sparked intense discussion among the parents present. Some wondered whether such emotional and sensitive topics belonged in a school setting or at school board meetings. In the days that followed, many townspeople turned to Dr. Gomez for guidance. They asked whether he believed it was part of a physician’s role to educate patients about organ donation. Could he include this conversation during annual physical exams, as he did with advance directives? Why hadn’t he done so already? And was this kind of topic suitable for a public forum like the school board meeting?

ethical_issues.question: Do family physicians have a moral responsibility to educate patients about organ donation and their options?
keypoints: Family physicians have a moral responsibility to educate patients about organ donation, as this aligns with the principles of promoting public health, alleviating organ shortages, and safeguarding the interests of both patients and society as a whole.
Informing patients about organ donation is consistent with the principles of beneficence, respect for autonomy, and justice, and helps patients make informed and autonomous decisions.

Primary care physicians possess experience in conducting difficult conversations, such as those regarding end-of-life care and advance directives, which facilitates effective discussions about organ donation.

Assisting patients in designating their organ donation status in advance helps to preserve their future autonomy and mitigates the risk that their wishes cannot be expressed in the event of sudden incapacity.

title: Assessing the Motives of Living, Non-Related Donors
case:
Dr. Tan had been a transplant surgeon for 7 years but had never come across a case like this. His patient Victoria had grown tired of waiting for help. She had been diagnosed with end-stage renal disease 3 years prior and was in need of an organ transplant. Due to her illness and the burdens of dialysis she had been unable to keep up with her college classes, and her modeling career, once blossoming, now seemed over. None of her living relatives was a match, and she knew her chances of receiving a deceased-donor organ in Massachusetts, her home state, were low. So she took matters into her own hands and created a profile on matchingdonors.com. She included her compelling narrative and a picture of herself.
It was through this site that Carolyn contacted her. Carolyn had lost her sister to kidney failure and had looked through the profiles to find an individual she considered worthy of receiving one of her kidneys. She read Victoria’s profile and wanted to donate to her. Carolyn flew to Massachusetts from Wyoming to meet with Victoria and the transplant team.
Dr. Tan brought up this case and his hesitation during the transplant center’s organ selection committee meeting. He said, “What is our experience using online portals for living donation? I have to admit I have never come across a donation like this. Radical altruism that involves a life-threatening sacrifice calls for careful scrutiny. It is our job to assess our potential donor, considering all dimensions. Is this type of organ solicitation fair? Does it threaten the view that an organ is not a commodity that can be bought and sold? Is our donor candidate trying to compensate for depression, seeking media attention, or harboring hopes of becoming involved in the recipient’s life? Is operating outside United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) legitimate?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Tan, a transplant surgeon with seven years of experience, found himself facing a situation unlike any he had encountered before. His patient, Victoria, had reached a breaking point after three years of living with end-stage renal disease. The relentless cycle of dialysis had forced her to put her college education on hold and brought her once-promising modeling career to a halt. With none of her family members matching as potential donors, and little hope of securing a deceased-donor kidney in Massachusetts, Victoria decided to act on her own behalf. She registered on matchingdonors.com, sharing her story and a photograph in hopes of finding a living donor.

That was how she connected with Carolyn, a woman from Wyoming who had lost her sister to kidney failure. Driven by her personal loss, Carolyn scrolled through the website’s profiles, eventually choosing Victoria as the recipient she wanted to help. Carolyn reached out, and after exchanging messages, she traveled to Massachusetts to meet Victoria and the transplant team in person.

When Dr. Tan gathered the transplant center’s organ selection committee to discuss the case, he voiced his uncertainty. “What is our experience with online platforms facilitating living donation?” he asked. “I’ve never encountered this type of situation before. Radical altruism that involves risking one’s life warrants careful consideration. Our responsibility is to thoroughly assess the donor from every angle. Is this form of organ solicitation fair? Does it undermine the principle that organs should not be treated as commodities? Could our donor be motivated by a desire to address her own grief or depression, to seek public attention, or to form a relationship with the recipient? And are we justified in proceeding outside the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) framework?”

The committee recognized the need to evaluate Carolyn’s motivations with great care—considering her mental health history, her understanding of the risks and procedures, and her reasons for choosing Victoria as the recipient. They also acknowledged the broader ethical implications, including the possibility of bias or unfairness arising from the use of online platforms, and the need to ensure that the process remained transparent, equitable, and consistent with both ethical and legal standards.

ethical_issues.question: Do the motives of living organ donors involve compensating for depression, seeking media attention, or hoping to become involved in the recipient’s life?
keypoints: The transplant center must conduct a comprehensive assessment of the potential living donor’s motivations to ensure they are grounded in genuine altruism rather than self-serving purposes such as compensating for depression, seeking media attention, or hoping to become involved in the recipient’s life.

The evaluation should thoroughly screen for “high-risk” donor candidates, including their mental health status (e.g., history of psychiatric disorders, substance abuse or dependence), cognitive capacity (understanding of the donation procedure and potential complications), stability of willingness to donate, unrealistic expectations, potential financial or social pressures (such as the risk of extorting the recipient), and the presence or absence of a stable support system during the recovery period.

ethical_issues.question: Does the selection of living organ donors involve selection bias or discrimination based on the recipient’s social worth?
keypoints: Selection bias or discrimination based on the recipient’s social worth may exist in living organ donation, and transplant centers have a responsibility to identify and intervene in such cases.
Soliciting living organ donation through Internet platforms may give rise to ethical concerns, including selection bias, discrimination, and lack of fairness.
The donor’s motivation for selecting a recipient must be carefully evaluated; if based on non-medical criteria such as social worth, the donor may be disqualified.

The transplant team should comprehensively consider medical indications, ethical principles, and legal compliance to ensure that the living donation process is fair, transparent, and consistent with the principle that organs are not commodities.

title: Should a Nonadherent Adolescent Receive a Second Kidney?
case:
Carl is 17-1/2 years old and has familial nephrotic syndrome due to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. His sister also developed renal failure; she underwent hemodialysis and then transplantation. Carl had observed that her quality of life was much better after transplantation.
Carl’s mother died when he was an infant. His father has mental health problems and struggles to cope with those and his two chronically ill children.
The nephrology team was worried about Carl’s ability to comply with a posttransplantation medication regimen, but nevertheless proceeded with a preemptive (i.e., without prior dialysis) transplant when Carl was 14 years old and showed signs of impending renal failure. He had excellent graft function for 9 months, but then experienced acute and, later, chronic rejection due to suspected, but not admitted, nonadherence to medications. He began dialysis the next year. His course on dialysis has been complicated by frequent episodes of fluid overload, hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia. He also has exaggerated fistula pain. He remains short in stature.
Carl does not want to continue on dialysis and has repeatedly asked the nephrology team to list him for another deceased-donor transplant. The health care team has severe reservations about listing him for a second transplant because of the history of presumed medication nonadherence and his ongoing management issues during dialysis. No living-related donor is available.
case_rewrite:
Carl, a 17-and-a-half-year-old, has familial nephrotic syndrome caused by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. His older sister experienced the same illness, progressing to renal failure; she underwent hemodialysis before receiving a kidney transplant. Carl observed firsthand how her quality of life improved significantly following the transplant.

Carl’s mother died during his infancy. His father, who struggles with mental health issues, finds it difficult to cope with both his own challenges and the demands of caring for two chronically ill children.

When Carl was 14 and beginning to show signs of impending renal failure, the nephrology team faced concerns about his ability to consistently follow a posttransplant medication regimen. Despite these worries, they proceeded with a preemptive kidney transplant, hoping to prevent the decline that dialysis often brings. For the first nine months after the transplant, Carl’s new kidney functioned excellently. However, he subsequently developed acute rejection episodes, followed by chronic rejection. Nonadherence to his medication regimen was suspected, though Carl never admitted to missing doses. Eventually, he was forced to return to dialysis the following year.

Carl’s experience on dialysis has been fraught with complications: frequent episodes of fluid overload, persistent hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia. He also suffers from pronounced pain at his fistula site and continues to struggle with short stature.

Now, Carl is adamant that he does not wish to continue dialysis. He has repeatedly asked the nephrology team to list him for another deceased-donor kidney transplant. However, the healthcare team has significant reservations. They question whether a second transplant is appropriate, given Carl’s suspected history of nonadherence following his first transplant and his ongoing difficulties managing dialysis, medications, and dietary restrictions. No living-related donor is available for him.

ethical_issues.question: Should adolescent patients be denied the opportunity for transplantation solely based on their age and potential nonadherence?
keypoints: The opportunity for transplantation should not be denied solely on the basis of adolescent age; decisions must be made based on an individualized assessment.

Posttransplant nonadherence among adolescents is one of the primary causes of graft failure; given the scarcity of organs and patient risk factors, it is essential to evaluate barriers to adherence and feasible interventions to improve compliance.
The patient’s adherence during dialysis can serve as a “trial of therapy” to assess the likelihood of compliance with posttransplant treatment regimens.

If the patient demonstrates consistent adherence to dialysis-related treatment requirements, including medication, dietary and fluid management, and timely clinic attendance, he should be considered eligible for retransplantation.

ethical_issues.question: When assessing whether an adolescent patient is suitable for a second kidney transplant, should an individualized evaluation be conducted to consider barriers to adherence and the potential benefits of interventions that might improve adherence?
keypoints: An individualized assessment should be conducted for adolescent patients, focusing on identifying barriers to adherence and evaluating the potential benefits of interventions aimed at improving adherence.
Kidney transplantation should not be denied solely on the basis of the patient’s age or being deemed at high risk for nonadherence.
The patient’s adherence during dialysis can serve as a “trial of therapy,” providing critical information to assess the likelihood of posttransplant adherence.
Clear expectations regarding treatment should be communicated to the patient, with regular feedback on dialysis adherence and the establishment of a defined endpoint for the “trial of therapy.”

If the patient consistently adheres to medication regimens, dietary and fluid restrictions, and attends dialysis and clinic appointments punctually, they should be considered eligible for a second kidney transplant.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of limited resources, should deceased-donor kidneys be preferentially allocated to patients with high adherence, rather than to those at high risk for nonadherence?
keypoints: Given the extreme scarcity of deceased donor kidneys, the principle of justice requires that organs be allocated preferentially to patients who are most likely to benefit from transplantation.

Patients with a high risk of medication nonadherence and a history of prior graft failure should have a lower priority for retransplantation, in order to avoid resource waste and to maintain fairness in allocation.

Transplantation decisions for adolescent patients require particular caution due to their unique physiological and psychological risks, necessitating a comprehensive assessment of graft survival rates and long-term management capacity.
Resource allocation should take into account patient adherence, anticipated benefit, long-term management ability, and overall risk, to ensure that limited organs achieve maximal utility.
Fair allocation emphasizes not only patient needs and physician judgment, but also the broader interests of society and the rational use of scarce resources.

title: Directive Counseling about Becoming Pregnant
case:
Dr. Brooks picked up the first chart of the day at the free clinic where she had worked for just a few months since finishing her residency. Her first patient was Jessica, a 25-year-old, here for a new patient visit.
“Hi, Jessica. I’m Dr. Brooks, one of the primary care doctors here. What brings you in today?”
Jessica responded, “I just want to make sure that I’m as healthy as I can be before I get pregnant.”
Dr. Brooks began to take Jessica’s medical history. She seemed very healthy, with no major medical problems. Jessica had been pregnant twice and she had delivered two healthy infants without complications. But when Dr. Brooks asked about her kids, Jessica became quiet. As it turned out, Jessica and her boyfriend, the children’s father, had not seen them in over a year, after they were removed from her home by child protective services. “They said we weren’t caring for them properly, not feeding them enough, that sort of thing,” said Jessica. “but I always thought they seemed OK.”
Dr. Brooks was taken aback, but managed to say, “That must be really difficult.”
“Yeah,” agreed Jessica, “and that’s why my boyfriend and I want to have another baby. I miss my babies, and I want to try again. In fact, I wanted to ask you, do you have any advice for me? Is there anything else I should do to help me get pregnant?”
Dr. Brooks paused. Jessica seems not to have known how to care for her first two children, but now she wanted to have another baby? What if this one were neglected and faced years of suffering or worse? Dr. Brooks didn’t want to think about it. As she tried to gather her thoughts, Jessica waited for an answer.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Brooks reached for the first chart of the morning at the free clinic where she had recently begun practicing after completing her residency. Her first patient was Jessica, twenty-five years old, scheduled for a new patient visit.

Entering the exam room, Dr. Brooks smiled and introduced herself. “Hi, Jessica. I’m Dr. Brooks, one of the primary care doctors here. What brings you in today?”

Jessica replied, “I just want to make sure I’m as healthy as possible before I try to get pregnant.”

As Dr. Brooks took a detailed medical history, she noted that Jessica appeared to be in good health, with no chronic illnesses or significant medical concerns. Jessica shared that she had been pregnant twice before and had delivered two healthy babies without complications. When Dr. Brooks gently asked about her children, Jessica’s demeanor changed, becoming subdued. She quietly explained that she and her boyfriend, who is also the father of her children, had not seen them for more than a year. Child protective services had removed the children from their home. “They said we weren’t taking good care of them, not feeding them enough, things like that,” Jessica said. “But I always thought they seemed fine.”

Dr. Brooks was momentarily caught off guard, but managed to respond with empathy. “That must be really hard for you.”

Jessica nodded. “Yeah, it is. That’s why my boyfriend and I want to have another baby. I really miss my kids, and I want to try again. Actually, I wanted to ask you—do you have any advice for me? Is there anything else I should do to help me get pregnant?”

Dr. Brooks hesitated. She was troubled by the knowledge that Jessica had already lost custody of her two children, yet wanted to become pregnant again. She worried about the possibility that another child could face neglect or significant hardship. As Dr. Brooks searched for the right words, Jessica sat quietly, awaiting her guidance.

ethical_issues.question: Does an obstetrician have the authority to decide whether a patient may become pregnant or when she should attempt conception?
keypoints: The decision to become pregnant is a matter of personal autonomy that includes medical considerations; obstetricians do not have the authority to override a patient’s reproductive rights.

Obstetricians have a professional responsibility to provide directive counseling, recommending that the patient postpone pregnancy until relevant health issues are adequately managed; such recommendations are non-coercive and therefore do not violate patient autonomy.

When a patient seeks elective medical services such as assisted reproduction, physicians have greater discretion in deciding whether to provide such services; however, these decisions should be based on expert clinical judgment rather than personal assessments of the patient’s parenting capacity.

ethical_issues.question: Should the physician recommend that the patient postpone pregnancy until she is capable of parenting in order to protect the best interests of the future child?
keypoints: Physicians have an ethical obligation to protect future children from preventable, serious, and irreversible harm, particularly when such risks are clear and highly probable.
Jessica’s prior caregiving history raises concerns that may present biopsychosocial risks to a future child, necessitating a comprehensive assessment of her parenting capacity.
The physician should recommend that Jessica postpone pregnancy until she has demonstrated adequate parenting abilities to promote the best interests of both the future child and herself.

Jessica should be referred for social support services and professional counseling to address the underlying factors contributing to her prior loss of custody and to assist in developing a realistic plan for improvement.

Providing directive counseling grounded in reliable evidence is a professional responsibility of the physician, does not violate patient autonomy, and requires a commitment to fully support the patient in implementing the recommendations.

title: Protecting the Confidentiality of Sexually Active Adolescents
case:
Dr. Nelson was just about to leave the office for the day when her pager went off. She returned the call, and learned that one of her patients, Andrea, was in the emergency room with what looked like pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Dr. Nelson sighed. She had placed an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUD) for Andrea in the office last week, and the PID could be a rare complication of the procedure.
Andrea had come to the appointment last week by herself. She said that she had recently become sexually active with her boyfriend, and she really didn’t want to get pregnant. Although Andrea was only 15, laws in her state allowed her to legally consent to contraceptive services. After reviewing Andrea’s history and doing a physical exam and pregnancy test, Dr. Nelson found no medical contraindications to an IUD. Dr. Nelson counseled Andrea about the risks and benefits of the IUD and alternative methods. Andrea and Dr. Nelson agreed that the IUD was the best option.
When Dr. Nelson arrived in the emergency department, she was dismayed to hear yelling coming from Andrea’s room.
“You’re going to tell me that this isn’t because you were having sex? Well, we’ll see what the doctors have to say about that! You’re my daughter and I’m not going to have you living under my roof if you’re sleeping with that boy!”
Hoping that she could defuse the situation, Dr. Nelson headed into the room. She was met by an angry man who said he was Andrea’s father.
“What’s going on here?” he shouted. “This is because she had sex, right? Well, if she did, she’s out of my house for good!” He stormed out.
After her father left the room, Andrea pleaded with Dr. Nelson not to tell him that she was sexually active. She said that his threat was real—he’d forced her older sister to leave home when she got pregnant at age 18. Andrea said that things at home were fine and that she and her father had always gotten along well, but that he had made it clear that he believed his daughters should wait to have sex until they were married. “Even if you don’t say anything, he’s going to think this is because I’m having sex,” Andrea insisted. “Can’t you just make up another reason why I’m sick?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Nelson was gathering her things to leave the clinic when her pager suddenly buzzed. She quickly returned the call and learned that Andrea, one of her patients, had been admitted to the emergency room with symptoms suggesting pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Dr. Nelson felt a wave of concern; she had inserted an intrauterine device (IUD) for Andrea just last week, and although rare, PID can be a complication following the procedure.

Andrea had come alone to her appointment the previous week. She explained to Dr. Nelson that she had recently become sexually active with her boyfriend and was determined not to become pregnant. At 15, Andrea was legally permitted to consent to contraceptive services under state law. Dr. Nelson carefully reviewed Andrea’s medical history, conducted a physical exam and a pregnancy test, and found no contraindications to placing an IUD. She thoroughly discussed with Andrea the benefits and risks of the IUD, as well as other contraceptive options. After considering everything, both agreed that the IUD was the most suitable choice.

Now, as Dr. Nelson stepped into the emergency department, she could hear raised voices echoing from Andrea’s room. 

“I don’t want to hear any excuses! Don’t tell me this isn’t because you’ve been having sex,” a man’s voice shouted. “Let’s see what the doctors have to say! If you’ve been with that boy, you’re not staying in my house!” 

Realizing the tension, Dr. Nelson approached the room, hoping to help calm the situation. Inside, she found an angry man who introduced himself as Andrea’s father. 

“What’s happening here?” he demanded. “This is because she had sex, right? If she did, she’s out of my house!” He turned and stormed off, slamming the door behind him.

After her father left, Andrea turned anxiously to Dr. Nelson. She begged her not to disclose that she was sexually active, confiding that her father’s threats were genuine—he had forced her older sister to leave home after she became pregnant at eighteen. Andrea explained that, apart from this issue, she and her father generally got along well, but he was firm in his belief that his daughters should abstain from sex until marriage. “Even if you don’t tell him, he’s going to assume it’s because I was having sex,” Andrea said tearfully. “Can’t you just say I’m sick for another reason?”

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician protect a patient’s confidentiality without violating medical ethics when faced with situations that may lead to tension within the patient’s family?
keypoints: Physicians should adhere to the principle of protecting patient confidentiality and must not fabricate false information, thereby ensuring medical integrity.

Physicians should flexibly employ communication skills based on what the patient and family already know, avoiding direct disclosure of the patient’s sensitive information while maintaining the truthfulness and transparency of information.

Physicians should respect the patient’s autonomy and support adolescents in maintaining open communication with their parents under safe circumstances, thereby promoting family support and understanding.

Physicians must comprehensively assess the potential risk of harm to the patient and, when necessary, promptly contact social services or child protective agencies to ensure the patient’s personal safety.

title: Sex Selection for Nonhealth-Related Reasons
case:
Mr. and Mrs. Carter had been married for 6 years when they visited Dr. Jones, a well-known infertility specialist, to ask for help creating their family. Mrs. Carter had given birth to a beautiful, healthy baby girl 3 years earlier. She was the light of their lives, and they loved her dearly. Now that their daughter was in preschool, they had decided it was time for them to complete their family by having another child—a son.
They sat down in the plush chairs in Dr. Jones’s office. Mr. Carter spoke first, “We’ve done a lot of research, Dr. Jones, and we think you can help us. A couple that we are friends with came to you to make sure they had a girl, since they have a disease in their family that runs in boys. We’re here to see if you can help us conceive a son for our family.”
Dr. Jones was confused about what they were asking for, and why. “Have you been having trouble getting pregnant?” he asked Mrs. Carter.
“Oh, no,” she responded. “We haven’t been trying. We wanted to wait to see you, so that we could make sure we had a boy. We love our daughter, and we always thought it would be perfect to have one of each. A balanced family.”
“Hmm,” Dr. Jones said. “We have done sex selection for patients in the past, but only based on medical conditions that occur in certain families, like what we did for your friends—”
“No, it’s nothing like that,” said Mr. Carter. “I just think we should have a boy and a girl. All my life I’ve envisioned having a kid I can take fishing and play ball with.”
“So, what do you think?” Mrs. Carter pressed. “Does this sound like something you can help us with?”
case_rewrite:
Mr. and Mrs. Carter, married for six years, made an appointment with Dr. Jones, a respected infertility specialist, seeking assistance in expanding their family. Three years prior, Mrs. Carter had delivered a healthy baby girl, who quickly became the center of their world. With their daughter now attending preschool, the Carters felt the time was right to try for a second child—a son—to complete what they envisioned as a “balanced family.”

Seated comfortably in Dr. Jones’s office, Mr. Carter began the conversation. “Dr. Jones, we’ve spent a lot of time researching, and we’re confident you’re the right doctor to help us. Some friends of ours came to you because they wanted to ensure they had a girl, since their family has a genetic disease that affects boys. We’re hoping you can help us have a boy.”

Dr. Jones, uncertain about their motivations, asked Mrs. Carter, “Have you been experiencing any difficulties getting pregnant?”

Mrs. Carter shook her head. “Not at all. Actually, we haven’t even started trying. We decided to wait until we could meet with you, so we could be certain we’d have a boy this time. Our daughter means everything to us, and we just always pictured having one of each—a son and a daughter.”

Dr. Jones leaned back thoughtfully. “In the past, we’ve performed sex selection, but typically only in cases where there’s a risk of passing on a genetic disease—like with your friends.”

Mr. Carter interjected, “No, we don’t have any health concerns. It’s just that I’ve always dreamed of having a son—someone I can take fishing, play ball with. I’d really like to have both a son and a daughter.”

Mrs. Carter looked at Dr. Jones expectantly. “So, is this something you can help us with?”

ethical_issues.question: Should assisted reproductive technologies be permitted for sex selection in the absence of medical indications?
keypoints: The use of assisted reproductive technologies for nonmedical purposes, such as sex selection, raises ethical dilemmas, primarily including concerns about potential sex discrimination and societal sex ratio imbalances.
Medical procedures involved in sex selection, such as IVF and PGD, may expose individuals to unnecessary medical risks.
One significant ethical challenge posed by IVF-PGD sex selection is the management of embryos of the undesired sex that are subsequently discarded.

The Ethics Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) does not encourage the use of PGD for nonmedical sex selection but opposes comprehensive legislative prohibitions of such practices.
Physicians should adopt a clear ethical stance of nonintervention regarding nonmedical sex selection in the absence of medical indications.

ethical_issues.question: When performing sex selection for nonmedical reasons, should patients be fully informed of the potential medical risks and ethical controversies involved?
keypoints: Prior to initiating nonmedical sex selection, comprehensive and detailed informed consent must be obtained to ensure that patients fully understand the complexities and potential risks associated with assisted reproductive technologies.

Patients should be explicitly informed of the medical risks associated with IVF, such as ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, as well as the currently unknown or potential risks related to sperm-sorting techniques, including the insufficiently evaluated impact on the health of offspring.
Patients need to be made aware of the ethical dilemmas and psychological burdens related to the possible discarding of embryos of the undesired sex during the IVF-PGD sex selection process.

Before commencing the IVF-PGD cycle, patients should be informed of the small probability of conceiving a child of the undesired sex or producing only embryos of the undesired sex, and there should be thorough discussion regarding their preferences and decision-making plans in these scenarios to avoid rushed decisions on the day of embryo transfer.

ethical_issues.question: Should the discarding of embryos of the undesired sex be permitted, or should alternative options such as donating embryos to infertile couples or for research be offered?
keypoints: The core ethical dilemma of IVF-PGD sex selection lies in the disposal of embryos of the undesired sex; therefore, couples should be informed in advance and offered alternatives, such as donation to infertile couples or use for research purposes.

Given this ethical complexity, thorough communication with the couple regarding their preferences for embryo disposition should occur prior to the initiation of the IVF-PGD cycle, to avoid rushed decisions on the day of embryo transfer.
It should be recognized that some couples opting for IVF-PGD sex selection for nonmedical reasons themselves harbor ethical concerns about their decision.

Despite ongoing controversy, pre-implantation sex selection can be ethically justified as a “lesser of two evils” choice when compared to prenatal diagnosis followed by abortion due to an undesired sex.

title: Writing an Excuse or Educating the Patient
case:
Dr. Sanders is a family physician practicing in a private clinic in Wisconsin. In autumn of 2009, Dr. Sanders was inundated with questions and concerns from patients regarding the H1N1 pandemic, especially since over 2,000 cases had been identified in Wisconsin and neighboring states. In fact, many deaths had been attributed to the virus, mostly in young children, the elderly, and pregnant women. Dr. Sanders and her staff struggled to assuage patients’ concerns by providing up-to-date information on the virus and administering the H1N1 vaccine to all high-risk patients. After several weeks, though, the vaccine supply had run low, and some who wanted the vaccine were unable to get it.
One morning on her walk to work Dr. Sanders met two patients, Mrs. Alcott and her 12-year-old daughter Jessica. Mrs. Alcott expressed anxiety about Jessica’s safety and asked Dr. Sanders if she could give them both the H1N1 vaccine.
“Unfortunately, our supply of the vaccine has been used up,” Dr. Sanders explained, “and we don’t have any more to give to even our high-risk patients. Neither does the hospital’s emergency department. I’m sorry to say it seems like it may be a week or longer before we get more.”
Mrs. Alcott’s eyes widened. “A week? And there are so many unvaccinated people. This is too dangerous. We’re just going to have to stay home until we can get the shots.” She asked Dr. Sanders to write both of them doctor’s notes excusing them from work and school for two weeks.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Sanders, a family physician at a private clinic in Wisconsin, found herself at the center of public anxiety during the autumn of 2009, as the H1N1 pandemic swept through the state. With more than 2,000 cases reported locally and in neighboring states, fears were mounting, particularly since the virus had caused multiple deaths among young children, the elderly, and pregnant women. Dr. Sanders and her staff worked tirelessly to address their patients’ concerns, providing current information about H1N1 and ensuring that those most at risk received the vaccine as soon as it became available. However, after several weeks, the clinic’s vaccine supply dwindled, leaving many patients—some eager but not high-risk—unable to get immunized.

One chilly morning, as Dr. Sanders walked to her clinic, she encountered Mrs. Alcott and her 12-year-old daughter, Jessica, both of whom were her patients. Mrs. Alcott, visibly anxious, approached Dr. Sanders and asked whether she and Jessica could receive the H1N1 vaccine.

Dr. Sanders replied, “I’m sorry, but our vaccine supply has run out. At this point, we don’t have enough to offer even to our highest-risk patients. The hospital’s emergency department is facing the same shortage. Realistically, it could be another week or more before we receive additional doses.”

Mrs. Alcott’s concern deepened. “A week? That’s a long time, especially with so many people still unvaccinated. It just feels too risky to be out in public. We’ll have to stay home until we can get the vaccine.” She then asked Dr. Sanders if she would write notes excusing both her and Jessica from work and school for the next two weeks.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of limited public health resources, how should physicians equitably allocate vaccines to ensure priority immunization for high-risk populations?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize vaccination for high-risk patients to ensure the rational and equitable allocation of limited public health resources.
Low-risk populations should support prioritizing vaccine access for high-risk community members, reflecting sound public health practice and the principle of social justice.

Physicians ought to clearly explain to patients the principles of medical prioritization and risk assessment, assisting them in understanding the scientific rationale and legitimacy behind vaccine distribution.

Physicians should refuse to provide medical certification based on patients’ irrational fears (such as requests for sick leave notes), in order to prevent the reinforcement of unreasonable demands and to uphold professional integrity and fairness in resource allocation.

title: The HPV Vaccine and Parental Consent
case:
As pediatrician Dr. Carson completes her physical exam of Alex, a healthy 15-year-old girl, she senses that Alex has something else on her mind. “Alex, I’m happy to say that you’re in perfect health. Do you have any more questions for me before we bring your mother back into the room?”
