“My boyfriend and I are thinking about having sex,” Alex responds. “I’ve never had sex before.” Dr. Carson asks a few more questions, reviews safe sex practice and provides prophylactic condoms. “You should also know that the CDC recommends the HPV vaccine to girls starting at age 11 to prevent infections that may one day cause cancer.” Dr. Carson continues to describe the vaccine’s efficacy, prevalence, and known side effects. Alex decides she would like to receive the vaccine.
Dr. Carson asks Alex’s mother to re-enter the room and begins to discuss the recommendation for the HPV vaccine. Alex’s mother objects. “The HPV vaccine is mandated here in Virginia for 11-year-old girls. I would have chosen to opt out of the mandate because I don’t want my daughter to act irresponsibly or suffer unknown side effects.”
Alex responds angrily. “I’ll come back to Dr. Carson’s office alone, or get the vaccine at Downtown Family Planning,” she says, referring to a Title-X clinic near where they live in Richmond. Dr. Carson believes that, although physicians can legally provide both reproductive health care and STI diagnosis and treatment to a competent minor, they cannot legally administer the HPV vaccine without parental consent.
case_rewrite:
As Dr. Carson, a pediatrician, wraps up her examination of 15-year-old Alex, she senses there’s something more Alex wants to discuss. “Alex, you’re in excellent health,” Dr. Carson says warmly. “Before I invite your mother back in, do you have any other questions for me?”

Alex hesitates, then confides, “My boyfriend and I are considering having sex. I’ve never done it before.” Dr. Carson listens attentively, asks a few follow-up questions, and reviews safe sex practices with Alex, emphasizing the importance of protection. She also provides Alex with prophylactic condoms. “It’s also important for you to know,” Dr. Carson adds, “that the CDC recommends the HPV vaccine for girls your age, starting at 11, to help prevent infections that could cause cancer later in life.” She explains the vaccine’s effectiveness, how common HPV is, and the known side effects. After this conversation, Alex expresses that she would like to get the HPV vaccine.

Dr. Carson then invites Alex’s mother back into the exam room and discusses the CDC’s recommendation for the HPV vaccine. Alex’s mother is visibly concerned. “Here in Virginia, the HPV vaccine is required for 11-year-old girls, but I would have opted out. I’m worried about possible side effects—and I don’t want my daughter to get the wrong message and start acting irresponsibly.”

Alex’s frustration is immediate. “If you won’t let me get the vaccine here, I’ll just come back to Dr. Carson’s office on my own, or I can get it at Downtown Family Planning,” she says, mentioning the nearby Title-X clinic in Richmond.

Dr. Carson knows that while the law allows her to provide certain reproductive health services and STI care to competent minors, she cannot legally give the HPV vaccine without parental consent.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance confidentiality and parental right to know when a minor requests the HPV vaccination?
keypoints: Physicians should create opportunities for private communication with minors to establish trust, adhering to ethical principles and best practices in adolescent care.

Physicians must be familiar with the laws of their practicing state to clearly understand which reproductive health services may be provided to minors without parental consent or knowledge upon the minor’s request.
Physicians should exercise caution in medical record documentation and insurance claims processes to prevent inadvertent disclosures that could violate the minor’s privacy.
Physicians ought to conduct confidential communications separately with the minor and the parent, followed by a triadic discussion aimed at reaching consensus and fostering trust.
Physicians must explicitly inform both the minor and the parent that HPV vaccination cannot be administered without parental consent.

Physicians may provide educational materials regarding the vaccine, recommend that both parties carefully consider the information, and schedule a follow-up appointment before the patient leaves to facilitate ongoing discussion.

title: Treating Children Whose Parents Refuse to Have Them Vaccinated
case:
Dr. Feyn, a Denver pediatrician, mentions to his colleague Dr. Manning that parents’ refusal of vaccines for their children has become more popular among parents in his patient panel in the last 5 years. “Most of these parents have similar reasons for choosing not to vaccinate their children. They cite alternative vaccination schedules, celebrity campaigns against vaccine side effects, even online forum discussions with other parents.”
Dr. Manning responds, “The CDC has recommended schedules for vaccination, but I know you would like to respect the discretion of patients and parents of patients as much as possible. So what are you going to do?”
“In the past I have documented the vaccine refusal and moved on, but I’m considering changing my approach,” Dr. Feyn responds. “As the number of unvaccinated children in my practice increases, I wonder if I am creating a risky environment for vaccine-preventable infections in my community. We recently witnessed an outbreak of pertussis nearby in Boulder because the percentage of immunized kids at a certain school was below threshold necessary for herd immunity.
“I’m thinking of insisting that my patients receive vaccinations according to the standard schedule, unless, of course, there is a specific health-related reason why an individual child should not be vaccinated. I am also considering not treating children in my practice unless they are vaccinated. What do you think of that?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Feyn, a pediatrician practicing in Denver, confides in his colleague Dr. Manning about a troubling trend he’s noticed in recent years: a growing number of parents in his patient group are refusing vaccines for their children. “Many of these parents give similar reasons for their decision,” Dr. Feyn explains. “They talk about following alternative vaccination schedules, mention concerns fueled by celebrity campaigns warning about vaccine side effects, and reference discussions they’ve had in online parenting forums.”

Dr. Manning listens thoughtfully before replying, “The CDC provides clear recommendations for vaccination schedules, but I know you’ve always tried to honor the preferences of your patients and their families. So how do you plan to handle this?”

“In the past, I’ve just recorded the parents’ refusal in the chart and moved on,” Dr. Feyn admits. “But as the number of unvaccinated children in my practice grows, I’m starting to worry that I might be putting the whole community at risk for vaccine-preventable diseases. Not long ago, there was a pertussis outbreak in Boulder—apparently, the immunization rates at one school dropped below the level needed for herd immunity.”

He continues, “I’m considering a new policy: insisting that my patients follow the recommended vaccination schedule, unless there’s a specific medical reason for an exemption. I’m even thinking about only accepting children into my practice if they’re vaccinated. What’s your take on that?”

ethical_issues.question: How can public health safety and herd immunity be ensured while respecting the autonomous decision-making rights of patients and their parents?
keypoints: Physicians should actively engage in communication with parents who refuse vaccination, fulfilling their roles as patient educators, health advocates, and public health practitioners through patient, evidence-based explanations.
Physicians are the preferred and highly trusted source of vaccine information for parents, and their professional advice significantly influences parental decisions regarding immunization.

Vaccine refusal not only increases health risks for intentionally unvaccinated children but also threatens vulnerable populations who cannot be vaccinated due to age or medical conditions, highlighting the ethical challenge of balancing individual autonomy with public health safety.

tags: Diagnosis/Patient request for a specific diagnosis
title: When Diagnosis is a Double-Edged Sword
case:
Dr. Mitchell, a psychiatrist, specializes in childhood development disorders. One day, a mother and her 5-year-old son came to Dr. Mitchell’s private practice for a first visit.
“Ravi’s been having problems ever since he started school,” his mother explained. “He doesn’t have many friends and is very shy. I’ve been doing research online about Asperger disorder, and I’m worried that Ravi could have it. All the articles mentioned not making eye contact, and I’ve noticed now that Ravi never really looks at me.”
After asking Ravi some questions while she was examining him and observing him while she talked with his mother, Dr. Mitchell agreed that aspects of his behavior correlated with symptoms of Asperger disorder. She believed, in fact, that his was a borderline case. Since Ravi’s problems had not been observed for long, Dr. Mitchell was reluctant to diagnose him with the condition. She worried that the diagnosis would affect how Ravi’s teachers and other adults treated him and that their behavior could affect Ravi’s self-perception. She was also concerned about the label’s accuracy.
Ravi’s mother explained that if her son were diagnosed with Asperger disorder, he would be eligible to receive special services from the school that would help him develop socially. “The sooner he receives these services, the better,” she said. “He is falling farther and farther behind his classmates.”
Dr. Mitchell explained her concerns about a premature diagnosis, but Ravi’s mother insisted that special services would help her son enormously. Dr. Mitchell also believed that Ravi would benefit from such services.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Mitchell, a psychiatrist with expertise in childhood developmental disorders, welcomed a new patient into her private office one afternoon. A mother had brought her 5-year-old son, Ravi, for an initial evaluation. As they settled in, the mother spoke with evident concern. 

“Ever since Ravi began attending school, I’ve noticed he’s been struggling,” she said. “He doesn’t have many friends and is very withdrawn. I’ve been reading about Asperger disorder online, and I’m starting to worry that Ravi might have it. So many articles mention not making eye contact, and I’ve realized lately that Ravi never really looks at me.”

Throughout the session, Dr. Mitchell gently asked Ravi questions during her examination, and observed his interactions while conversing with his mother. She noted several behaviors consistent with symptoms of Asperger disorder, though in her professional judgment, Ravi’s presentation was borderline. Since these issues had only recently become apparent, Dr. Mitchell hesitated to make a formal diagnosis at this stage. She was mindful that assigning such a label could influence how Ravi’s teachers and other adults interacted with him, possibly affecting his self-esteem and the way he saw himself. She also weighed the uncertainty regarding the accuracy of a diagnosis so early in his development.

Ravi’s mother, however, was persistent. She explained that a formal diagnosis of Asperger disorder would allow Ravi to receive specialized support services at school, which she felt were urgently needed to help him improve his social skills. “If he can get these services soon, it could make a big difference,” she urged. “He’s already falling further behind his classmates.”

Dr. Mitchell shared her reservations about making a premature diagnosis, outlining her concerns about the potential consequences and the importance of being certain. Still, Ravi’s mother remained adamant, emphasizing how much her son could benefit from targeted assistance. Dr. Mitchell herself believed that Ravi would likely gain from these services, but felt conflicted about how best to proceed given the borderline nature of his case and the wider implications for Ravi and his family.

ethical_issues.question: When considering the best interests of the child, how should the decision-making capacity of the parent or guardian be assessed, along with the family, economic, and cultural factors that may influence diagnosis and treatment planning?
keypoints: Assess the decision-making capacity of the parents or guardians to ensure they understand the benefits and risks of diagnosis and treatment, and are able to make reasonable decisions based on the child’s best interests.

Take into comprehensive consideration the influence of familial, economic, cultural, and religious background factors on diagnostic and treatment planning, with attention to quality of life and potential impacts on other family members.
Identify and manage potential conflicts of interest among parents, healthcare providers, and educators to safeguard the fairness and effectiveness of the child’s care and educational interventions.

title: Is Physician Self-Disclosure Ever Appropriate?
case:
Dr. Goldberg is a primary care physician in a small rural town. She has been caring for Mrs. Hunter and her grown daughter, Karen, for the past decade. Mrs. Hunter has just been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and she and her daughter have been struggling to cope. Mrs. Hunter lives alone, and Karen is her only child.
Karen comes to Dr. Goldberg one day with severe anxiety and gastrointestinal symptoms. She isn’t sleeping, she has no appetite, and she has been getting frequent colds. In addition to dealing with the emotional burden of her mother’s diagnosis, she has financial worries. She confides in Dr. Goldberg that she is at a complete loss about how to deal with her mother’s illness.
Dr. Goldberg is acutely sympathetic; her own mother passed away from ALS about 5 years prior. She remembers the intense struggle her mother had, as well as her own feelings of powerlessness as a caregiver. She isn’t sure whether it would be appropriate or helpful to share this information with Karen.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Goldberg is a primary care physician in a small rural town. For the past ten years, she has cared for Mrs. Hunter and her adult daughter, Karen. Recently, Mrs. Hunter received a diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and both she and Karen have been struggling to adjust to the news. Mrs. Hunter lives on her own, with Karen as her only child and primary support.

One afternoon, Karen visits Dr. Goldberg’s office, visibly distressed. She reports severe anxiety, ongoing gastrointestinal discomfort, persistent insomnia, lack of appetite, and frequent minor illnesses. As she speaks, it becomes clear that the emotional weight of her mother’s diagnosis is taking a significant toll. Karen also voices worries about her financial situation, and she admits to Dr. Goldberg that she feels completely lost and overwhelmed by her mother’s illness.

Dr. Goldberg listens with empathy. The conversation strikes a personal chord: her own mother died of ALS five years ago. She recalls the overwhelming challenges her mother faced, and the helplessness she herself felt as a caregiver. As Karen sits before her, Dr. Goldberg finds herself considering whether sharing her own experience with ALS in the family might help Karen feel less alone. At the same time, she wonders whether it would be appropriate—or truly helpful—to disclose this personal information. She pauses, reflecting on her motivations and the potential impact her words could have on Karen.

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances should physicians engage in self-disclosure to ensure it benefits the patient rather than serving their own needs?
keypoints: Physicians should always prioritize the needs of the patient above their own and rationally assess whether self-disclosure genuinely serves the patient’s best interests.

Before deciding to engage in self-disclosure, physicians must clarify the specific purpose of the disclosure, comprehensively evaluate potential risks, and weigh alternative approaches to addressing the patient’s needs.

Physicians need to engage in deep self-reflection regarding their motivations, ensuring that self-disclosure is intended to serve the patient rather than fulfill personal emotional needs, and assess whether any related personal trauma has been resolved to avoid impaired professional judgment due to unresolved wounds.
If self-disclosure is deemed appropriate, the content should be concise and focused on the patient’s needs, avoiding excessive elaboration, and promptly returning to the patient’s central concerns.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ensure that self-disclosure remains focused and does not disproportionately address the physician’s own needs rather than those of the patient?
keypoints: Physicians should always prioritize the needs of the patient above their own, ensuring that the purpose of self-disclosure is clear and centered on serving the patient.
Before engaging in self-disclosure, physicians must rationally assess the rationale for disclosure, potential risks and benefits, and weigh alternative approaches to addressing the patient’s needs.
Physicians should engage in self-reflection to confirm that their motivation for disclosure is not to satisfy personal emotional needs or unresolved trauma, but genuinely to benefit the patient.

Through open-ended questioning, physicians should gain a deeper understanding of the patient’s specific feelings and needs, avoiding assumptions about the patient’s situation based on their own experiences.

Physician self-disclosure should be concise and appropriate, consistently focused on the patient’s needs, avoiding deviation from the topic, and promptly returning to the patient’s concerns and issues.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians assess the potential risks and benefits of self-disclosure to patients?
keypoints: Physicians should use open-ended questions to gain a deeper understanding of the patient’s specific needs and emotional responses, and avoid making assumptions based on their own experiences.
Physicians need to examine their own motivations and emotional state to ensure that self-disclosure is intended to support the patient and is not influenced by unresolved personal trauma.
Before deciding to self-disclose, physicians should clearly define the specific rationale for disclosure, assess potential risks, and weigh alternative approaches that might meet the patient’s needs.
Physicians should regard self-disclosure as a deliberate communication tool, to be used only when it is confirmed to be beneficial to the patient and consistent with professional ethical standards.

title: A Virtue Ethics Approach to Framing Troublesome Diagnoses
case:
Dr. Chin has been treating Mr. Bryant for seizures for several years. Although he has tried several different medication regimens, his seizures have been difficult to get under control. Mr. Bryant was recently hospitalized for 3 days due to the frequency and severity of the seizures, and, over the course of the hospitalization, he had three seizures. During the last two, Dr. Chin, a neurologist, used an EEG to record his brain activity.
Reviewing the EEG results, Dr. Chin discovers something unexpected. Mr. Bryant’s brain waves do not show patterns typical of epileptic seizures; they are normal, strongly implying that Mr. Bryant’s seizures have no neurological cause.
Dr. Chin is concerned about the latest EEGs. Since the recent seizures do not have an organic basis, treatment may involve cognitive behavioral therapy or other psychiatric measures. In Dr. Chin’s experience, many patients, upon hearing this diagnosis, deny that it can be correct and seek another physician. Other patients feel trapped and helpless, convinced that no treatment will ever works.
Dr. Chin has witnessed how strongly the seizures have disrupted his patient’s emotional well-being. Mr. Bryant feels helpless, angry, mistrustful of treatments, and resigned that he will never be able to live a normal life. Knowing Mr. Bryant’s personality, Dr. Chin is worried that the news about the nonneurologic nature of the seizures could cause even greater emotional pain and perhaps prompt Mr. Bryant to stop seeing a physician altogether.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Chin has been Mr. Bryant’s neurologist for several years, treating him for a persistent seizure disorder. Despite trying multiple medication regimens, Mr. Bryant’s seizures have remained difficult to control. Recently, Mr. Bryant was admitted to the hospital for three days due to an increase in both the frequency and severity of his seizures. During this hospitalization, he experienced three seizures. For the last two episodes, Dr. Chin used electroencephalography (EEG) to monitor Mr. Bryant’s brain activity as the seizures occurred.

Upon reviewing the EEG results, Dr. Chin notices something unexpected: Mr. Bryant’s brain wave patterns remain normal during the events, lacking the abnormalities typically seen in epileptic seizures. This strongly suggests that Mr. Bryant’s episodes do not have a neurological origin.

Confronted with these findings, Dr. Chin grows concerned. Without evidence of a neurological basis, the diagnosis now points toward functional seizures, meaning treatment may shift from antiepileptic medications to interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy or other psychiatric approaches. Dr. Chin knows from experience that sharing this kind of diagnosis can be very challenging. Some patients, when told their seizures are not due to a neurological disorder, reject the diagnosis outright and seek another physician. Others feel overwhelmed and helpless, believing that no treatment could possibly help.

Dr. Chin has seen firsthand how deeply the seizures have impacted Mr. Bryant’s life. Mr. Bryant feels trapped by his condition, angry and frustrated with previous treatments, and resigned to the idea that he will never regain a sense of normalcy. Given Mr. Bryant’s sensitivity and previous reactions to disappointing news, Dr. Chin worries that explaining the non-neurological nature of the seizures could further damage Mr. Bryant’s emotional well-being and even drive him to abandon medical care entirely.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians avoid using potentially offensive or stigmatizing terminology when disclosing a diagnosis of functional seizures to a patient, in order to respect the patient’s dignity and emotional well-being?
keypoints: Neutral and respectful terminology such as "functional epilepsy" should be chosen, avoiding potentially offensive or stigmatizing labels like "hysterical" or "psychogenic."
Diagnostic language must reflect respect for the patient’s individual dignity and emotional well-being, thereby preventing emotional harm or negative impacts on the patient’s self-perception.
The use of the term "functional" helps to avoid non-diagnostic expressions such as "medically unexplained" and reduces the implicit mind-body dualism often conveyed by other labels.

Communication should be tailored to the patient’s illness beliefs and emotional state, appropriately guiding their understanding of the mind-body interaction to enhance treatment adherence and provide psychological support.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with diagnoses that carry potential emotional impact, how should physicians ethically balance honest communication with the need to avoid causing emotional harm to the patient?
keypoints: Physicians should prudently adjust their communication strategies based on a comprehensive understanding of the patient’s overall character, prior experiences, and emotional responses, thereby demonstrating respect for and care toward the patient’s individual differences.

Communication should be guided by professional virtues such as compassion, respect for the patient’s inherent dignity, honesty, and prudence, avoiding the extremes of blunt disclosure or sugarcoating the truth.
In humane and effective communication, physicians must balance truthful disclosure with emotional support, paying close attention to the patient’s psychological resilience and emotional reactions.

Physicians should endeavor to transform the patient’s frustration and disappointment into positive anticipation for future treatment, assisting the patient in establishing reasonable and achievable therapeutic goals.

Even when faced with challenges such as patient denial, intense emotions, or strained relationships during communication, physicians must uphold their own integrity and professional responsibility as the standard for evaluating the success of the interaction.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians apply humility, virtue, and moral courage in managing a diagnosis of functional seizures to ensure that patients receive appropriate treatment and support without compromising the physician-patient relationship or the truth?
keypoints: Physicians should embody the virtue of humility by recognizing the limitations of both the scientific community and their own clinical capabilities, and by discerning when to seek assistance or modify treatment strategies.

Physicians must possess moral courage to communicate diagnoses honestly and tactfully, employing appropriate terminology such as “functional,” and balancing truth-telling with sensitivity to the patient’s emotional well-being.

Honesty and integrity constitute the foundation of physician-patient communication, requiring avoidance of blunt disclosure or euphemistic distortion, thereby ensuring that information is conveyed truthfully and with humanistic care.

Compassion should permeate the entire communication process, actively addressing the patient’s suffering and frustrations, and facilitating the transformation of therapeutic disillusionment into hope for future treatment.

Prudence, as an integrative virtue, guides physicians in weighing both the content and manner of communication, ensuring that ethical decisions align with the patient’s best interests and uphold professional integrity.

Physicians should measure the success of communication by their own integrity and professional responsibility, maintaining commitment to truthfulness and patient welfare even in the face of patient mistrust or relational breakdown.

title: New Guidelines for Cancer Screening in Older Patients
case:
Mr. Eckler visited his internist, Dr. Gresher, for his annual physical. At 77, Mr. Eckler was in remarkably good health. He reported some pain and stiffness in his fingers and hips, mostly “until I get up and going in the morning,” but he was still active during the day. His blood pressure was normal for his age, and his heart and lungs sounded good. His weight was the same as it had been a year before. Following the exam, Dr. Gresher congratulated Mr. Eckler on his continued good health, asked whether he would be getting the flu vaccine that year, and began to talk about the routine lab work he was ordering.
“And I want to schedule a colonoscopy, Doc,” Mr. Eckler interjected. Dr. Gresher reviewed his patient’s record on the screen in front of him and saw that Mr. Eckler had had colonoscopies at ages 60 and 70, both of which had been clear. He explained to Mr. Eckler that, given his past good reports, no known history of colon cancer in his family, and his age, clinical guidelines did not recommend that he continue to undergo the procedure.
“Yeah, but this guy I meet for coffee every morning, Mike, his 50-year-old nephew just got diagnosed with colon cancer. Mike’s very concerned, and his doctor is ordering a colonoscopy for him.”
An internist with a large percentage of patients on Medicare, Dr. Gresher was well aware of the emphasis on comparative effectiveness research and the practice guidelines that were part of the medical records system the clinic used. He told Mr. Eckler that, for people of his age and with his prior colonoscopy results, the advantages of repeating the procedure did not seem to outweigh the risks.
“I’m more worried about colon cancer than about the test. I’ve had them before. It’s not a big deal,” Mr. Eckler said. “Mike and I agreed we’d drive each other to and from the test, like they advise. His is all set.”
When Dr. Gresher repeated his concern about unnecessary testing of any sort, Mr. Eckler said, “I guess you’re saying that it doesn’t matter if I have colon cancer at my age. Is that what you’re saying, Doc? Mike’s going to have a clean bill of health, and I’m going to go on worrying. Maybe I should ask Mike’s doctor to order me the test.”
case_rewrite:
Mr. Eckler arrived at Dr. Gresher’s office for his annual checkup. Now 77, Mr. Eckler remained impressively healthy for his age. He mentioned some mild discomfort and stiffness in his fingers and hips, mostly upon waking, but said these symptoms eased as he got moving each morning. He continued to stay active throughout the day. His blood pressure was appropriate for someone his age, and Dr. Gresher heard no abnormalities in his heart or lungs. Mr. Eckler’s weight had not changed since his last visit.

After completing the examination, Dr. Gresher praised Mr. Eckler for maintaining his good health. He asked if Mr. Eckler planned to receive the flu shot this year, then moved on to discuss the standard laboratory work he would be ordering.

Before Dr. Gresher could continue, Mr. Eckler spoke up: “And I want to schedule a colonoscopy, Doc.” Dr. Gresher glanced at the electronic record and noted that Mr. Eckler had undergone colonoscopies at ages 60 and 70, both with normal findings. He explained that, considering these results, the absence of a family history of colon cancer, and Mr. Eckler’s current age, clinical guidelines did not recommend further routine colonoscopies.

Mr. Eckler replied, “Well, the thing is, my friend Mike—who I meet every morning for coffee—his nephew, who’s only 50, was just diagnosed with colon cancer. Mike’s really upset. His doctor is ordering a colonoscopy for him, and now Mike’s encouraging me to get one too.”

Dr. Gresher, whose patient panel included many Medicare recipients, was keenly aware of the importance placed on comparative effectiveness research and adherence to the clinic’s evidence-based practice guidelines. He explained to Mr. Eckler that, for someone in his position—with his age and prior clear colonoscopies—the potential benefits of repeating the procedure were generally outweighed by the risks.

Mr. Eckler persisted, “I’m more afraid of colon cancer than of having the test. I’ve done it before, and it wasn’t a big deal. Mike and I already agreed to drive each other to and from the procedure, just like you’re supposed to. Mike’s already scheduled his.”

Dr. Gresher reiterated his concern about unnecessary testing, emphasizing that any procedure carried risks, especially as patients age. At this, Mr. Eckler looked troubled. “So, are you telling me it wouldn’t matter if I had colon cancer at my age? Is that what you’re saying, Doc? Mike’s getting checked and won’t have to worry, but I’m supposed to just hope for the best? Maybe I should ask Mike’s doctor to order the test for me instead.”

ethical_issues.question: In cancer screening for older patients, how can screening decisions be individualized based on the patient’s age, health status, and comorbidities to ensure the principle of justice is upheld?
keypoints: Screening decisions should be based on the patient’s age, overall health status, and comorbidities, with a comprehensive assessment of the risk-benefit ratio of colonoscopy.

Clinical guidelines generally do not recommend routine colorectal cancer screening for adults aged 76 to 85 years, but recommendations should be adapted flexibly according to individual circumstances.
Elderly patients without comorbidities may derive significant life-year benefits from colonoscopy screening, whereas those with multiple comorbidities have limited or no benefit.
The risk of complications from colonoscopy is higher in older patients, necessitating careful consideration of the necessity of screening versus potential harm.

Physicians should engage in thorough shared decision-making with patients, transparently communicating the potential risks and benefits of screening, respecting patient autonomy, and ensuring that screening decisions are just and individualized.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence while respecting patient autonomy when patients request unnecessary tests?
keypoints: The medical profession possesses unique characteristics, and the physician-patient relationship differs fundamentally from typical commercial relationships; the principle that “the customer is always right” does not apply to medical practice.

Physicians must balance respect for patient autonomy with the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence, ensuring that medical decisions are based on the individual circumstances of the patient and the best available evidence.
Physicians should engage in shared decision making with patients, utilizing rational communication and negotiation to develop a personalized care plan that serves the patient’s best interests.

Physicians should clearly explain to patients the risks and benefits of screening procedures, specifically addressing how increasing age affects the risk-benefit ratio of screening (for example, the elevated risk of complications from colonoscopy in older patients).

title: Political Discussions in the Exam Room
case:
Dr. Buccarelli is already behind schedule when he encounters his next patient, Mr. Van Ware. Mr. Van Ware is coming in for a follow-up appointment after a lingering, viral URI that finally resolved. He is politically engaged and has been following the Affordable Care Act legislation closely. His own insurance premiums have risen, and he asks what Dr. Buccarelli thinks of the individual mandate for health insurance.
“You think it’s fair that a young, healthy guy like me should be shouldering the bill for chronic care for the elderly?” Mr. Van Ware asks. Dr. Buccarelli replies in a general way that the current health system has its flaws and he is just happy that legislators are attempting to address the problems. Unsatisfied, Mr. Van Ware repeats his question about young people subsidizing older people’s expensive end-of-life care.
After a couple back-and-forths, in which Dr. Buccarelli politely explains that the ACA is 2,000 pages long and very complicated and that it will be years before the regulations are ironed out, Mr. Van Ware says, “Seriously, Doctor. You must know more about this new act than I do. Do you think the mandate that all of us, healthy or not, have to buy insurance is constitutional? Isn’t it socialism?”
Dr. Buccarelli considers all the answers he can offer Mr. Van Ware (who seems to have forgotten that, young healthy man that he is, he has had a serious URI for several weeks). Dr. Buccarelli feels his clinician’s role conflicting with his educator’s role and, meantime, his waiting room continues to fill.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Buccarelli is running behind schedule as he greets his next patient, Mr. Van Ware. Mr. Van Ware has come for a follow-up after finally recovering from a stubborn viral upper respiratory infection. Known for his political engagement, Mr. Van Ware has been keeping a close eye on developments surrounding the Affordable Care Act. He mentions that his own insurance premiums have gone up, and asks Dr. Buccarelli for his thoughts on the individual mandate for health insurance.

“Do you really think it’s fair that someone young and healthy like me should have to pay for older people’s chronic care?” Mr. Van Ware presses. Dr. Buccarelli responds in a measured, general tone, acknowledging that the current healthcare system is imperfect but expressing some relief that legislators are at least working to address existing problems. Mr. Van Ware, not satisfied with this response, repeats his question, emphasizing his skepticism about younger people subsidizing costly end-of-life care for the elderly.

Their conversation continues in this vein, with Dr. Buccarelli explaining, as diplomatically as possible, that the ACA is an extremely complex, lengthy piece of legislation and that it will take years before all its regulations are worked out. Still, Mr. Van Ware persists. “Come on, Doctor,” he says. “You have to know more about this law than I do. Do you honestly think it’s constitutional to force everyone—healthy or not—to buy insurance? Isn’t that just socialism?”

As Dr. Buccarelli weighs how to reply, he notes that Mr. Van Ware—despite describing himself as a young, healthy man—has just spent weeks battling a serious URI. Dr. Buccarelli finds himself torn between his role as a clinician and the expectation to serve as an educator, all while the waiting room continues to fill with other patients.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians engage in political discussions in the exam room, especially when patients strongly express social or political views, and how can professionalism and the patient-physician relationship be maintained in such situations?
keypoints: Physicians should prepare concise, professionally informed insights to address important public policy issues directly related to medical practice.
Physicians must remain vigilant about the potential impact that discussions involving social and political views in the exam room may have on professionalism and the patient-physician relationship.
Physicians should clearly define their professional role in relation to the patient, avoiding any conflation of the patient-physician relationship with personal friendships.

When patients persist in political debates despite polite cues to the contrary, physicians should take appropriate measures to manage the conversation, such as restating professional boundaries or explicitly terminating the discussion, in order to preserve the integrity of the patient-physician relationship.
Honest, transparent, and clear communication is essential for maintaining a healthy and constructive patient-physician relationship.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient’s political statements may imply bias or discrimination, can the physician continue to provide objective care and maintain the patient-physician relationship?
keypoints: Physicians should uphold professionalism, avoiding the influence of personal political views and emotions on clinical attitudes, and ensure objective and impartial treatment of patients.

When a patient’s remarks may contain bias or discrimination, the physician must clearly delineate the boundaries of the patient-physician relationship to prevent personal emotions from interfering with professional judgment.

Physicians should guide political discussions from a professional standpoint, managing the content of such conversations through tactful cues or explicit communication as appropriate, thereby safeguarding the health of the patient-physician relationship.

Physicians need to engage in self-reflection and proactively regulate their emotions to prevent the patient’s extreme statements from affecting their own psychological state and clinical decision-making.
Maintaining honesty, transparency, and respect in communication not only protects the physician’s professional role but also promotes patient understanding and trust.

title: When Patients Worry about the Doctor
case:
Dr. Weller, a pediatrician in a one-stoplight town, arrives at her practice earlier than usual, avoiding the eye of the office manager, who is sitting at the front desk. No doubt Alex is aware of what much of the town now knows—that Dr. Weller’s 16-year-old son was arrested the night before, after drunkenly driving into a shop front not far from the office Dr. Weller is standing in at the moment.
“Morning, Doc,” Alex calls to Dr. Weller’s retreating back.
“Morning, Alex,” she mutters, busying herself with her coat, bag, and mail. She looks forward to immersing herself in patient visits—any break from the loop of worry, anger, recrimination, and embarrassment that she’s been in since the call came from the county jail.
But work provides little respite. A couple of well-child checkups are canceled; Dr. Weller wonders if there’s a connection. Are her patients doubting her or trying to give her space? Or is it just a coincidence? And a number of patients’ families express condolences and offer parenting advice during their visits, despite her best efforts to redirect conversation to the patients’ condition. Dr. Weller ends the day exasperated and embarrassed.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Weller, the pediatrician in a rural town with just a single stoplight, arrives at her office earlier than usual, hoping to slip inside unnoticed. At the reception desk sits the office manager, Alex, who no doubt has already heard what most of the town now knows—Dr. Weller’s 16-year-old son was arrested the previous night after crashing his car into a nearby storefront while intoxicated.

“Morning, Doc,” Alex calls out as Dr. Weller hurries past.

“Morning, Alex,” Dr. Weller replies in a low voice, preoccupied as she fumbles with her coat, bag, and the morning mail. She eagerly anticipates losing herself in her work with patients, anything to distract from the continual churn of worry, embarrassment, and frustration that’s plagued her since the sheriff’s call from the county jail.

Yet, the day offers little escape. A couple of scheduled well-child visits are canceled, and Dr. Weller can’t help but wonder if the news about her son is the reason. Are families quietly judging her, or are they simply trying to give her space? Or is it all just coincidence? Throughout the day, several patients’ parents express their sympathy and even offer unsolicited advice on parenting, despite Dr. Weller’s attempts to steer the discussion back to her patients’ health concerns. By the end of the day, Dr. Weller feels drained—her embarrassment and frustration only heightened by her inability to keep the focus where it belongs.

ethical_issues.question: In a small community, how can physicians maintain their privacy while establishing good relationships with their patients?
keypoints: Physicians in small communities should accept the well-intentioned concern of community members and skillfully redirect conversations to focus on patients’ health, thereby respecting others while protecting personal privacy.

Actively participating in community activities and maintaining a professional and responsible attitude help to earn the community’s respect and support, thereby promoting a long-term stable physician-patient relationship.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians effectively redirect the conversation back to patients’ health concerns when faced with patients’ attention to their private lives?
keypoints: Physicians should first acknowledge patients’ well-intentioned expressions of sympathy with gratitude, thereby demonstrating respect and understanding.

When patients persist in discussing personal matters, physicians should clearly state their position and redirect the focus back to the patient’s health concerns, emphasizing the primary purpose and objectives of the clinical encounter.

Physicians ought to maintain a professional demeanor, concentrating on clinical care while avoiding in-depth discussion of personal issues, in order to preserve the professionalism and trust inherent in the physician-patient relationship.

title: After the Apology: Coping and Recovery After Errors
case:
It’s nearly the end of his internship year in internal medicine and Jason, who intends to become a rheumatologist, is feeling more and more confident about his abilities as a physician. Just before he signs out after a night on call, he gets a page from the floor nurse about one of his patients, Maude, a 70-year-old woman recovering from pneumonia. She has a headache. Jason goes in to see her and asks her a few questions. “I’m doing okay, doctor,” she tells him. “Just the usual body aches of old age, and now this headache. I can’t wait to get home to my husband, my grandkids, and my television set. When do you think I’ll get out of here?” Jason examines her and, convinced this is a typical tension headache, he reassures her that she’ll be home soon, writes an order for ibuprofen, and heads out.
When he returns a day later for rounds, he learns that Maude has lost vision in both eyes. The night-float resident, Miguel, has started her on glucocorticoid therapy for temporal arteritis but fears this treatment is too late to save her vision. Miguel tells Jason, “When you have an elderly lady with a headache and body pains, you always think temporal arteritis, you do the definitive diagnostic test—temporal artery biopsy—and you start her on steroids. Next time, man. Next time.” Jason goes to see Maude and her family. They are devastated by the news that she may not be able to see again.
Jason feels tremendous guilt and remorse about missing the diagnosis, and his confidence is shaken. The teaching physician, Dr. Joynt, notices that Jason isn’t as sharp as usual. He seems distraught on rounds for several days in a row, so Dr. Joynt asks him if he’s okay. Jason wants to confide in Dr. Joynt, a rheumatologist who has become a mentor to him, but he worries that he will look stupid in front of the man who might write his letter of recommendation for fellowship.
case_rewrite:
As Jason nears the completion of his internship year in internal medicine, his confidence as a physician is steadily growing. Eager to pursue a future in rheumatology, he feels increasingly at ease managing his responsibilities. One morning, just before signing out after a grueling night on call, Jason receives a page from a floor nurse regarding Maude, a 70-year-old patient recovering from pneumonia. The nurse reports that Maude is experiencing a headache. Jason promptly checks on her, asking about her symptoms. Maude responds, “I’m doing okay, doctor. Just the usual body aches that come with age, and now this headache. I’m really looking forward to getting back home to my husband, my grandkids, and my television. When do you think I’ll be discharged?” After a thorough examination, Jason, convinced she is suffering from a simple tension headache, reassures her that she should be able to go home soon. He writes an order for ibuprofen and leaves to finish his shift.

The following day, when Jason returns for rounds, he is stunned to learn that Maude has suffered a sudden loss of vision in both eyes. The night-float resident, Miguel, has already initiated glucocorticoid therapy for temporal arteritis, but he worries that the intervention may have come too late to preserve her sight. Pulling Jason aside, Miguel says, “Whenever you see an elderly woman with a headache and body aches, you have to consider temporal arteritis. You do a temporal artery biopsy and start steroids right away. Remember that for next time.” 

Jason visits Maude and her family, who are reeling from the devastating news that she may never regain her vision. Overwhelmed by guilt and shaken by his oversight, Jason’s self-assurance crumbles. For several days, Dr. Joynt, the teaching physician and a rheumatologist whom Jason deeply admires and hopes will write his fellowship recommendation, notices that Jason is unusually withdrawn and distracted during rounds. Sensing something is wrong, Dr. Joynt gently asks Jason if he’s alright. Jason longs to confide in Dr. Joynt about his mistake and the anguish it has caused, but he hesitates, afraid that admitting his error will make him look incompetent in the eyes of a mentor he deeply respects.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians manage their emotional and professional challenges following a medical error to promote personal recovery and professional growth?
keypoints: Physicians should acknowledge medical errors and proactively communicate with mentors or colleagues to facilitate emotional healing and professional development.

Discussing errors with the attending physician not only provides emotional support but also offers professional guidance, helping clinicians gain a deeper understanding of the causes and nature of the error.

Errors should be disclosed to patients accompanied by an apology; the primary purpose of disclosure is to address the emotional needs of the patient rather than to alleviate the physician’s own burden.
Physicians should prioritize basic self-care and actively manage the emotional and professional stress resulting from medical errors to maintain their mental and physical well-being.
Through reflection, feedback, and mentorship, physicians can identify and avoid cognitive biases and overconfidence, thereby promoting professional maturation and enhancing diagnostic skills.

ethical_issues.question: After a medical error has occurred, how should physicians communicate with the patient and their family to address the patient’s emotional needs and rebuild trust?
keypoints: Physicians should proactively disclose medical errors to patients and their families and offer sincere apologies, focusing on addressing the emotional needs of the patient and rebuilding trust rather than alleviating their own burden.

Physicians must clearly and honestly explain the cause of the error and its potential impact, as well as describe the specific measures taken to prevent similar incidents in the future, thereby meeting patients’ expectations for transparency and accountability.

Trainees involved in medical errors that may lead to serious consequences should promptly report to their supervising attending physician before communicating with the patient, seeking guidance and support to ensure the accuracy and appropriateness of the disclosure.

Supervising physicians should actively participate in the error disclosure process, assisting trainees in conducting open and empathetic communication with patients and their families, helping to alleviate patient distress and facilitate the repair of the physician-patient relationship.

Healthcare teams should prioritize training and practical experience in error disclosure to enhance trainees’ communication skills and psychological resilience, thereby reducing communication barriers and patient mistrust stemming from lack of experience.

title: The Problem with Hand-Offs
case:
Aidan is on the first emergency shift of her third-year surgery rotation. When her resident hands her the file for her first patient, a 60-year-old man with textbook symptoms of appendicitis, she is excited to work on the case. Aidan meets the patient, Ed, takes a thorough history, and does a physical exam that confirms the diagnosis.
She discovers in her history taking that the patient has a diagnosis of Crohn’s disease but has not had symptoms for decades and writes this in her note. She reassures Ed that appendicitis is easily treated with a surgery that gets you home the next day. She presents the case to the resident on call. Two hours later, the resident reports to the attending on-call surgeon, who is busy with a trauma case. Hours pass and personnel change. Aidan spends time with Ed, a pleasant architect with a gentle wit.
The new attending surgeon quickly reads the patient note and orders a CT scan, thinking that the patient might be having a flare-up of Crohn’s disease. The patient waits another hour for a CT scan, which reveals an inflamed appendix. A nurse notices that the patient hasn’t gone to the OR yet and is concerned, but doesn’t feel comfortable bringing this up with the resident or the surgeon. An hour later, when Ed finally gets to the OR, his appendix has ruptured, and the surgeons have to cut out several feet of his small bowel.
When Aidan reports back to the hospital the next day, she sees that Ed hasn’t left. He has developed a surgical site infection. Ed is upset about his long wait in the emergency department and about complications from what he thought was a routine surgery. He ends up staying in the hospital for an extra week to recover.
Aidan wonders whether this outcome is the result of a medical error or errors. She goes to speak about the case with Dr. Sark, who performed Ed’s surgery. He tells her “stuff happens.” He explains that hindsight is 20/20 but that these sorts of events are inevitable in a busy emergency department. When she asks him if someone should disclose or apologize to the patient, he says no.
case_rewrite:
Aidan begins her first emergency shift as a third-year medical student on the surgery rotation, eager to participate in patient care. Her resident hands her the chart of her first patient, Ed, a 60-year-old man presenting with classic symptoms of appendicitis. Aidan meets Ed, who is a gentle, witty architect, and takes a meticulous history. She learns that Ed was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease years ago, but he has had no symptoms for decades—a fact she documents carefully in her note. After a thorough physical exam, which supports her suspicion of appendicitis, Aidan reassures Ed that this is a straightforward condition, usually resolved with a simple surgery and a quick recovery.

Aidan presents Ed’s case to the resident on call. The resident in turn updates the attending surgeon, who is preoccupied with a trauma case elsewhere in the hospital. As the hours tick by, staff shift changes occur. Aidan remains attentive to Ed, who shares stories and jokes to pass the time.

Later, a new attending surgeon assumes responsibility. He quickly skims through Ed’s chart and, noting the mention of Crohn’s disease, suspects a possible Crohn’s flare rather than appendicitis. He orders a CT scan to clarify the diagnosis. Ed waits another hour for the scan, which ultimately confirms an inflamed appendix.

A nurse, noticing that Ed has not yet been taken to the operating room, grows increasingly concerned. Despite her worries, she hesitates to raise the issue with the resident or the attending, feeling uncertain about her authority to intervene.

By the time Ed is finally brought to the operating room, his appendix has ruptured. The surgical team must remove several feet of his small intestine. The next day, Aidan returns to the hospital and is surprised to find Ed still in his bed. He has developed a surgical site infection, requiring a prolonged hospital stay and leaving him frustrated about the extended wait and unexpected complications from what he thought would be a routine procedure.

Reflecting on the case, Aidan wonders if the outcome was the result of medical errors or systemic failures. She discusses her concerns with Dr. Sark, the surgeon who performed Ed’s operation. Dr. Sark dismisses her worries, saying, “Stuff happens.” He tells her that hindsight always makes things look clearer and insists that such events are unavoidable in a busy emergency department. When Aidan asks whether someone should explain to Ed what happened or apologize, Dr. Sark firmly says no.

ethical_issues.question: When a process failure is identified, does Aidan, as a medical student, have an ethical obligation to communicate her concerns to the resident and the attending physician?
keypoints: Nurses have an ethical responsibility to promptly express concerns to the resident and attending physician when they observe that a patient has not been taken to the operating room in a timely manner, in order to ensure patient safety.
The hospital has failed to effectively implement the concept of a “just culture,” resulting in frontline staff, such as nurses, lacking the authority and support to intervene in process failures.

The healthcare team should share collective responsibility for safeguarding patient safety, respecting and accepting nurses’ reasonable interventions and feedback, and promoting the development of a patient-centered culture of care.

ethical_issues.question: Do healthcare institutions have an ethical obligation to disclose to patients the reasons for surgical delays and postoperative infections and to offer an apology?
keypoints: Healthcare institutions have an ethical obligation to honestly disclose to patients and their families the specific reasons for surgical delays and postoperative infections, and to offer an apology on behalf of the institution; this communication responsibility typically rests with the operating surgeon.

Clinicians and healthcare teams bear the responsibility to proactively identify and report systemic errors, advocate for process improvements, and prevent recurrence of similar incidents to ensure patient safety.

ethical_issues.question: Do attending physicians have an ethical responsibility to communicate directly and jointly examine the patient during hand-offs in order to avoid unnecessary investigations and delays?
keypoints: Attending physicians have an ethical responsibility during hand-offs to communicate directly and jointly examine the patient to ensure accurate transmission of clinical information, thereby avoiding unnecessary tests and treatment delays.

The new attending physician, due to lack of direct communication with the predecessor and failure to personally examine the patient, overlooked the critical information in the medical record that the patient’s Crohn’s disease had been asymptomatic for decades, and ordered a CT scan solely based on the history note, resulting in unnecessary testing and delay.

Clinicians should proactively identify and improve systemic errors within clinical workflows, bearing a dual responsibility: to provide patient care and to optimize processes that safeguard patient safety.

When failures in clinical processes cause patient harm, physicians have an ethical obligation to disclose the facts honestly to the patient, offer an apology, and implement measures to prevent recurrence of similar events.

title: Medical Ethics and Retail Clinics
case:
Dr. Bunell was surprised to see Mrs. Scott and her second-to-youngest child when the office assistant showed them into his exam room.
“Long time, no see, Mrs. Scott,” he said. “Everyone’s been well, I take it?”
“Well, I’m worried about this one, “ she said, looking down on her son who sat in her lap. Dr. Bunell figured he must be about 5 years old by now.
“I’ve been taking the boys [she had four] to the SureCare Clinic at the mall for the last 2 years,” Mrs. Scott said. “I can get their immunizations there, get them seen for colds and bouts of poison ivy. My oldest even got his physical to be on a pony league team last spring.” She took a breath. “And it’s so quick and far less expensive than coming here. With a family of six,” she said, “it makes a huge difference in medical bills.”
Before Dr. Bunell could speak, Mrs. Scott started again.
“But, we’ve been treating this one,” she looked down again, and Dr. Bunell wished she’d say the lad’s name because, to tell the truth, he’d forgotten it, “with antibiotics for 3 weeks and he seems to be getting worse, not better. Just look at him.”
Visits like Mrs. Scott’s were becoming familiar to Dr. Bunell. More and more of his patients were showing up after long periods during which he figured they had been well and had had no need for medical care. He found out, instead, that they had been going to retail clinics for the “everyday stuff,” and making appointments with him only when something more serious cropped up. It would be months or years since he had seen them and he’d have no record of what had transpired at the clinics.
A family practice specialist, Dr. Bunell did not know the best and most professional way to manage this situation. Some of his colleagues had told their patients that  they (the physicians) had to manage all the care or none. But Dr. Bunell didn’t know if that was ethical; besides, it was entirely unenforceable. How would one know if a patient had received care elsewhere between visits to the doctor’s office?
On the other hand, Dr. Bunell’s practice depended on routine immunizations, sports physicals, and treatment of everyday infections and injuries. He wasn’t a hospitalist, after all. This was a medical and business problem, as he saw it.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Bunell was caught off guard when Mrs. Scott arrived with her second-to-youngest son, ushered in by the office assistant. 

“It’s been a while, Mrs. Scott,” he greeted her warmly. “I hope everyone’s been keeping healthy?”

She gave a tired smile. “Well, I’m worried about this one,” she replied, glancing down at the boy nestled in her lap. Dr. Bunell estimated the child must be around five years old now.

Mrs. Scott explained, “For the past two years, I’ve been taking the boys to the SureCare Clinic at the mall. They do their immunizations, check them for colds, even handle poison ivy outbreaks. My oldest got his sports physical there last spring to join the pony league.” She paused, then added, “It’s so much quicker and costs a lot less than coming here. With a family of six, saving on medical bills really matters.”

Before Dr. Bunell could respond, Mrs. Scott pressed on. “But we’ve been treating this one”—again she glanced at her son, and Dr. Bunell found himself wishing she’d mention his name, as he couldn’t quite recall it—“with antibiotics for three weeks now, and he’s getting worse, not better. Just look at him.”

This scenario had become increasingly familiar to Dr. Bunell. More of his patients were resurfacing after long gaps, not because they’d been well, but because they’d been seeking care for minor issues at retail clinics. They only reached out to him when something more serious was at stake. Months or even years would pass without a visit, and he’d have no information about what care they’d received elsewhere.

As a family physician, Dr. Bunell found himself uncertain about the best professional course in these situations. Some colleagues had told their patients they needed to provide all of their care or none at all, but Dr. Bunell questioned whether that was ethical—or even realistic. How could he possibly know what care his patients sought between visits?

Yet, the reality was that routine vaccinations, sports physicals, and common illness management formed the backbone of his practice. He wasn’t a hospitalist; his livelihood depended on providing comprehensive, ongoing care to families. As he weighed Mrs. Scott’s concerns, Dr. Bunell recognized that this was both a medical challenge and a matter of sustaining his practice.

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician balance the patient’s health needs with their own livelihood when the patient primarily receives routine care at retail clinics and only visits the family doctor sporadically for acute issues?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize the health of their patients by proactively communicating the importance of continuous and comprehensive care, as well as the potential risks associated with fragmented care—such as that received at retail clinics—particularly for patients with complex or chronic conditions.

Physicians ought to regard patients as whole persons, taking into account their socioeconomic factors including financial status and scheduling constraints, understanding the practical difficulties that lead patients to choose retail clinics, and striving to prevent patients from falling into poverty due to medical expenses.

Physicians and their healthcare teams should actively assist patients in accessing external support systems, such as applying for Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP), and enrolling in local programs for low-income families, to facilitate coordinated and continuous medical care.

Clinical practices should optimize service delivery by employing nurse practitioners or physician assistants to provide affordable and continuous care, while implementing measures to reduce waiting times and costs—such as telephone or email consultations, focus groups, and pre-visit questionnaires—to enhance patient experience and adherence.

Physicians should promote continuity in medical information management by advising patients to maintain portable medical records or establishing information-sharing mechanisms with retail clinics (e.g., faxing visit documentation), thereby ensuring completeness of clinical data and preventing gaps in care.

ethical_issues.question: Does a physician have an ethical obligation to inform patients that retail clinics may lead to fragmented care, which could adversely affect the management of complex or chronic conditions?
keypoints: Physicians have the responsibility to inform patients that fragmented care carries multiple risks, including suboptimal treatment outcomes, potential missed diagnoses of serious conditions, redundant testing or medication, and neglect of the patient’s broader developmental, social, and familial factors. These risks are particularly significant in the management of complex or chronic illnesses; therefore, patients should be advised to maintain a consistent and continuous source of medical care.

Physicians should prioritize the health and life of the patient, adhering to the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence, ensuring that patients are fully informed of the benefits and risks associated with different healthcare options, and respecting their autonomous decision-making rights.

ethical_issues.question: Is it both legally permissible and ethically justifiable for a physician to terminate the physician-patient relationship when faced with a consistently uncooperative patient, such as one who insists on receiving care exclusively at retail clinics?
keypoints: A physician may legally terminate the physician-patient relationship in non-emergent situations, provided that written notice is given and the patient is allowed a reasonable period of time to secure alternative medical care.

Legally justifiable reasons for terminating the relationship include objective circumstances such as missed appointments, unpaid bills, inappropriate behavior, or persistent noncompliance with the treatment plan.

Although termination of the relationship may be lawful, ethically the physician should thoroughly consider the patient’s socioeconomic context and strive to find a balanced approach that accommodates care quality, the physician’s livelihood, and the patient’s health needs.

title: Labeling an Adverse Drug Event “Preventable”
case:
Dr. McKinley walks briskly into her office and consults her computer screen, then her watch. Way behind schedule, and it’s only 2 p.m., she thinks. A typical afternoon in her primary care clinic. She takes a swig of her coffee, peeks into the waiting room where six patients are sitting, and sweeps into exam room 2.
Mr. Chen is a 75-year-old man, recently emigrated from China, who speaks very little English. He has come with his adult son, who is proficient in English, for a follow-up on his high blood pressure. Mr. Chen’s son reports that his father has followed Dr. McKinley’s advice to eat less salt and exercise for 30 minutes a day. Because his in-office blood pressure is still elevated, Dr. McKinley decides to prescribe a low-dose beta-blocker. She carefully explains how to take the drug by halving each pill and asks Mr. Chen if he is taking any other medications, including complementary or alternative medicines. He hesitates, then says no. For a moment, Dr. McKinley wonders if her patient has told her the whole story and asks him again. He says no. She asks if he understands her instructions, and he says yes. Dr. McKinley leaves Mr. Chen and his son to tend to her next patient, who has been waiting for more than an hour with shaking chills and fever.
Mr. Chen goes home and begins taking his beta-blockers at twice the prescribed dose because he does not understand that he must halve the pills. As it turns out, he is also taking a Chinese herbal supplement that he does not believe Dr. McKinley would consider medicine. The double dose of beta-blockers, combined with the herbal supplements, causes acute hypotension, and Mr. Chen falls, breaking his hip.
case_rewrite:
Dr. McKinley strides into her office, glancing quickly between her computer screen and her watch. She lets out a quiet sigh—she’s already running behind, and it’s only mid-afternoon. Six patients wait in the lobby, and the day’s pace feels relentless. Taking a quick sip of her coffee, Dr. McKinley checks the waiting room, then heads straight to exam room 2.

Inside, Mr. Chen, a 75-year-old man who recently emigrated from China, sits quietly. He speaks very limited English and has come today with his adult son, who is fluent in English, for a follow-up visit about his high blood pressure. Mr. Chen’s son explains that his father has been doing his best to follow Dr. McKinley’s earlier recommendations—reducing salt intake and exercising thirty minutes daily. Despite these efforts, Mr. Chen’s blood pressure remains elevated in the office today. After reviewing his chart, Dr. McKinley decides to initiate a low-dose beta-blocker. She carefully goes over the instructions for taking the medication, emphasizing the need to split each pill in half for the correct dose. Turning to Mr. Chen, she asks if he is taking any other medications, including herbal remedies or supplements. Mr. Chen hesitates for a moment before replying no. Sensing some uncertainty, Dr. McKinley gently repeats her question, but Mr. Chen again says no. She then asks if he understands the instructions, and he nods, indicating yes.

Feeling pressed for time, Dr. McKinley leaves the room, moving on to her next patient—a person who has been waiting over an hour and is now febrile and visibly ill.

Later, Mr. Chen returns home. Because he misunderstood Dr. McKinley’s instructions, he begins taking the beta-blocker at twice the prescribed dose, not realizing he was supposed to halve the pills. Furthermore, he continues using a Chinese herbal supplement, which he did not consider to be a “medicine” and thus did not mention to Dr. McKinley. The combination of the excessive beta-blocker dose and the herbal supplement leads to a dangerous drop in his blood pressure. Mr. Chen collapses at home, suffering a hip fracture from the fall.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where a patient has limited English proficiency, does the physician have an ethical obligation to use a professional interpreter to ensure the patient’s understanding of medical instructions and to prevent potential harm?
keypoints: Based on the ethical principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence, and supported by evidence demonstrating that professional interpreters significantly enhance patient safety, physicians have an ethical obligation to utilize professional interpreters whenever possible to ensure patient comprehension of medical instructions and to mitigate potential harm.

When professional interpreters are accessible, physicians should proactively request their services, particularly in situations where patients are reluctant to use family members as interpreters or when the physician questions the ad-hoc interpreter’s ability to facilitate effective communication.

Federal law mandates that healthcare institutions provide professional interpreter services free of charge to patients with limited English proficiency; physicians should collaborate with colleagues and administrators to address systemic barriers impeding access to interpreter services.

Physicians must balance their ethical duties to the patient requiring interpretation with those owed to other patients; if requesting a professional interpreter would substantially compromise the care of other patients, declining to request one may be ethically justifiable.

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician disclose an error following a preventable adverse drug event and take measures to remedy the patient’s harm and restore the integrity of the patient-physician relationship?
keypoints: Physicians should candidly disclose errors to patients, explicitly explaining the cause of the fall—including the interaction between the medication and the herbal supplement as well as the patient’s misunderstanding of the medication regimen—and offer a sincere apology while accepting appropriate responsibility.

Physicians should express sympathy for the injuries sustained by the patient due to the fall and fracture, attend to the patient’s physical and psychological well-being and emotional responses, and actively provide support and follow-up care.

Physicians should report the error to the patient safety committee or a patient safety organization to facilitate institutional monitoring and improvement efforts, thereby preventing recurrence of similar incidents.

Physicians should collaborate with the healthcare team to systematically analyze the root causes of the error (such as language barriers and time constraints) and participate in developing and implementing sustainable improvement strategies to enhance patient safety and the quality of physician-patient communication.

title: Patient Advocacy for Beginners
case:
After finishing another grueling morning of pre-rounding, Rebecca found a moment to grab a cup of coffee with her fellow intern, Samuel. As first-year residents at a competitive internal medicine program in a large county hospital, they were already feeling the much-anticipated burnout just halfway through intern year. “I’m so irritated with some of my patients,” Samuel remarked. “I don’t get how so many of them lack insurance. Most of them don’t even have a PCP!” Not sure what to say, Rebecca pointed to her watch. It was time for rounds with Dr. Myers, the Medicine Team D attending physician for that week.
A couple of hours later, Samuel was about to present the last patient. “So tell me about Mrs. Olson,” instructed Dr. Myers. Samuel began, “She is a 52-year-old female admitted through the ED for community-acquired pneumonia after a 5-day history of productive cough and fever.”
When his presentation was finished, Samuel was surprised by Dr. Myers’ first question. “Why wasn’t she seen by her doctor before the infection got to this point?”
The reason seemed obvious. “She doesn’t have insurance or a PCP.”
Dr. Myers replied, “Well, it looks like you have a job to do. Why don’t you go by her room this afternoon and provide her with some information on insurance options for those with low income? I know she’ll appreciate it. And also, if you wouldn’t mind, go ahead and look up Virchow’s essays on public health for rounds tomorrow. I know we can all learn something.”
Over lunch, Samuel was seething. “I didn’t go to medical school so I could be a social worker. Finding Mrs. Olson health insurance isnotmy job.” Rebecca realized this probably wasn’t the best time to start a debate, but she couldn’t help but frown at her colleague’s tirade.
case_rewrite:
After another exhausting morning of pre-rounding, Rebecca finally managed to slip away for a quick coffee break with her fellow intern, Samuel. Both were first-year residents at a demanding internal medicine program in a sprawling county hospital, and the strain of intern year was already wearing them down. As they sipped their coffee, Samuel vented his frustration. “Some of my patients are really starting to get to me,” he sighed. “I can’t believe how many don’t have insurance. Half of them don’t even have a primary care doctor!” Rebecca glanced at her watch, sensing his mood but unsure how to respond. “We should get going—rounds with Dr. Myers start soon.”

A couple of hours later, they reached the final patient on their list. Dr. Myers, the attending for Medicine Team D that week, turned to Samuel. “Tell us about Mrs. Olson,” she prompted. Samuel launched into his presentation: “Mrs. Olson is a 52-year-old woman admitted from the emergency department with community-acquired pneumonia. She’s had five days of productive cough and fever.”

When he finished, Dr. Myers surprised him with her first question. “Why didn’t she see her physician before her infection escalated like this?” 

Samuel replied, “She doesn’t have insurance or a primary care provider.”

Dr. Myers nodded thoughtfully. “That makes sense. This afternoon, please stop by Mrs. Olson’s room and give her some information on low-income insurance options. I’m sure she’ll appreciate it. And, if you have time, read up on Virchow’s essays on public health for tomorrow’s rounds. There’s a lot we can all learn.”

At lunch, Samuel was visibly agitated. “I didn’t spend all those years in med school just to act as a social worker. It’s not my responsibility to find health insurance for Mrs. Olson.” Rebecca considered arguing but could see her colleague was too upset for a debate, so she simply frowned in response.

ethical_issues.question: Should medical education include political advocacy as a component of professional responsibility?
keypoints: The role of physicians within hospitals and society has garnered significant attention; health is not merely an individual issue but a societal responsibility, and physicians should be attentive to and actively work to alleviate the social injustices faced by their patients.

Some scholars advocate that physicians should actively engage in public discourse and political advocacy, becoming part of the solution to promote social health equity, with advocacy constituting an important component of many physicians’ professional ideals.
Currently, systematic training in political advocacy skills remains markedly insufficient within medical school and residency programs, representing a clear educational gap.

There are also perspectives that political advocacy is inherently political in nature and should be regarded as a civic duty rather than a professional medical responsibility; therefore, it is deemed inappropriate to incorporate it into medical education or residency training.

Given the lack of consensus within the medical community regarding the role of physicians in political advocacy, coupled with the limited capacity of medical curricula, the systematic integration of political advocacy into medical education faces practical challenges and ongoing debate.

title: Balancing Practice Economics with Patient Need
case:
As the medical director for a mid-sized pediatric group practice in a large city, Dr. Sanchez is dismayed to read in the local paper about the state legislature’s recent decision to further slash payment rates for Medicaid. Located on the outskirts of downtown, Dr. Sanchez’s clinic sees patients covered by a mix of insurance plans: 50 percent Medicaid and SCHIP patients predominantly from the low-income areas of the inner city and 50 percent private insurance patients who come from the nearby suburbs. The clinic is barely making ends meet; increasing expenses for staffing and an EMR have been accompanied by decreasing payment rates from private and public insurance programs.
As the young pediatrician finishes reading the disheartening headline, he takes a moment to remember why he decided to pursue a career in medicine. A quick glance at a colorful display board in his office filled with thank-you notes, holiday cards, and photos from patient families helps him recall the sense of pride with which he and his colleagues care for some of the city’s most disadvantaged children. “How are we going to keep our doors open?” he finds himself wondering. “We just can’t take any more cuts to our payment.”
At a staff meeting held later that week, Dr. Sanchez explains the grim financial situation to his colleagues. “We have to do something about this…and I’m not fond of our options. These impending cuts to Medicaid payment will barely allow us to break even.” When he opened the topic to his coworkers, an impassioned discussion ensued. “If we can’t take any more Medicaid patients, then so be it.
