title: Patient Requests for Nonindicated Care
case:
Dr. Michaels was an experienced ER attending physician in a major level 1 trauma center working the night shift. It had been a relatively slow shift so far, so he had spent a lot of time teaching his new intern, Jay. Just after 11 p.m., Jay came to present a 53-year-old patient, Mr. Brower, who was experiencing sudden-onset back pain with numbness and tingling down his leg after having lifted a heavy box. Jay had conducted a thorough history and physical, and Dr. Michaels agreed with his assessment that Mr. Brower had a herniated disc in his lumbosacral spine.
Dr. Michaels asked Mr. Brower to repeat the events surrounding the onset of his back pain, reviewed Mr. Brower’s physical findings, and gave Jay the signal to explain the diagnosis. After explaining the anatomy of the spine and how the herniated disk could cause Mr. Brower’s leg symptoms, Jay recommended 2 days of limited activity and treatment with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug followed by a return to normal activities. He then added that if Mr. Brower’s symptoms did not improve, he could come back for further testing, including an MRI to confirm the diagnosis. Confused, Mr. Brower asked why they did not want to perform an MRI now.
Dr. Michaels stepped in to explain that, given Mr. Brower’s history and physical, there was little doubt that the cause of his discomfort was a herniated disc. “We are confident of the diagnosis, Mr. Brower, having often seen the symptoms you report following an event like you describe—lifting the heavy box. We always recommend conservative management first. If your symptoms improve, which they most likely will, there’s no reason to be concerned. Further imaging and testing is really only necessary when our ‘tried and true’ methods of treatment don’t work. We’ll follow you closely to see how you do.”
“But Doc,” Mr. Brower protested, “why not just do the MRI now? I’m here already and I want to be sure it’s just this disc thing you’re talking about. My insurance will pay for it, so I don’t understand what the big deal is. Is this a cost-cutting thing? I don’t want my health to suffer just to help your hospital’s bottom line!”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Michaels, a seasoned attending in the bustling ER of a level 1 trauma center, was overseeing the night shift, which had been unusually quiet. With the pace slower than usual, he had taken the opportunity to guide his new intern, Jay, through various cases. Just past 11 p.m., Jay approached Dr. Michaels to discuss a new patient: Mr. Brower, a 53-year-old man who had developed sudden back pain accompanied by numbness and tingling radiating down his leg after lifting a heavy box earlier that evening. Jay had completed a meticulous history and physical examination. After reviewing Jay’s findings, Dr. Michaels concurred with his assessment—Mr. Brower likely had a herniated disc in his lower spine.

Dr. Michaels invited Mr. Brower to recount in detail how his pain began, double-checked the physical examination, and then nodded to Jay to share the diagnosis. Jay carefully explained the structure of the spine and how a herniated disc could be responsible for Mr. Brower’s symptoms. He recommended a conservative approach: two days of limited activity along with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication, followed by a gradual return to normal activities. Jay also reassured Mr. Brower that if the symptoms failed to improve, they could pursue further testing, such as an MRI, to confirm the diagnosis.

Mr. Brower looked perplexed. “Why aren’t you doing an MRI right now?” he asked. “I’m already here, and I want to make sure it’s just this disc problem. My insurance covers it, so what’s the issue? Is this about the hospital trying to save money? I don’t want my health to be put at risk just to save costs.”

Dr. Michaels responded thoughtfully. “Mr. Brower, based on your history and our examination, we are very confident your symptoms are from a herniated disc, particularly given how they started after lifting that heavy box. The treatment we’re recommending is based on strong evidence and is what we use for most people in your situation—usually, symptoms improve with rest and medication. We hold off on advanced imaging like an MRI unless the usual treatments don’t help, or if there are warning signs of something more serious. Doing unnecessary tests can sometimes lead to confusion or even interventions that aren’t needed, which can cause harm. Our main focus is your health, not the hospital’s finances, and we want to avoid exposing you to tests you don’t need. If things don’t get better, we’ll absolutely move forward with more testing. In the meantime, we’ll keep a close eye on your progress.”

ethical_issues.question: How can a balance be achieved between respecting patient autonomy and physicians’ clinical judgment while simultaneously upholding the principles of nonmaleficence and distributive justice?
keypoints: Physicians must balance respect for patient autonomy with their own clinical judgment while adhering to the principles of nonmaleficence and distributive justice.
Just allocation of resources should prioritize patients with genuine clinical indications for MRI; scarce medical resources must be allocated rationally to avoid waste caused by nonindicated testing.

Delaying MRI is part of the standard diagnostic pathway designed to prevent potential harms from unnecessary testing (such as over-intervention triggered by false positives), ensuring that patients are exposed to the risks of testing only when it is truly necessary.
Physicians should strive to avoid harm to patients; although patient autonomy is important, it does not obligate physicians to perform tests or treatments beyond established medical indications.

Physician-patient communication should be honest and transparent, clearly emphasizing that clinical decision-making is centered on patient health rather than solely driven by financial considerations or cost-saving measures.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of limited resources, are physicians obligated to fulfill a patient’s request for a nonindicated diagnostic test?
keypoints: Physicians are not ethically obligated to fulfill patient requests for nonindicated tests or treatments; patient autonomy does not compel physicians to perform medical interventions that fall outside the scope of clinical indications.

In the context of limited resources, physicians are ethically justified by the principle of distributive justice in declining requests for nonindicated services, prioritizing the allocation of scarce medical resources to patients who genuinely need them.

title: Rationing Treatments Based on Their Cost per QALY
case:
Dr. Jackson is an orthopedic surgeon with an excellent record for good medical care and patient satisfaction. Over the last 5 years, her hospital’s financial security has declined and administrators have been looking at various options for reducing the cost of care. They have tentatively decided to phase out treatments and services that cost more than a certain amount per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). This will enable them, they feel, to provide the most health for their dollar, so to speak.
Dr. Jackson receives a letter from the hospital stating that she will no longer be able to offer treatments deemed insufficiently cost-effective. This includes the injection of epidural steroids for sciatica, a treatment that has resulted in crucial relief in the short term (about a month) for Dr. Jackson’s patients but, due to the need for repeat injections and the absolute expense of the treatment, has a high cost per QALY.
In disbelief, Dr. Jackson calls her friend Dr. Stein, one of the hospital administrators. She explains to Dr. Stein her view that patient care should not be affected by the cost of the services she uses, especially when the treatments have worked well for her patients; if treatments areclinicallyeffective, they should be offered. Dr. Stein, himself a clinician, agrees personally with this view and knows of Dr. Jackson’s excellent record for patient satisfaction, but he says, “The hospital is going to go under: we simply can’t afford to spend the way we’ve been spending. You know as well as I do that if we close, many of our patients will have nowhere to go. We have to cut back somewhere; what do you suggest?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Jackson, a respected orthopedic surgeon known for her outstanding patient outcomes and high satisfaction rates, has witnessed a downward trend in her hospital’s financial stability over the past five years. In response, hospital administrators have been exploring various strategies to curb spending. Recently, they have leaned toward a policy of discontinuing any treatments or services that exceed a set threshold for cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY), believing this approach will allow them to maximize health benefits within their limited budget.

One afternoon, Dr. Jackson receives official notification from the hospital administration. The letter informs her that, going forward, she is prohibited from providing treatments classified as insufficiently cost-effective according to the new policy. Notably, this restriction includes epidural steroid injections for sciatica—a procedure Dr. Jackson has frequently administered, knowing it brings her patients significant, albeit short-term, relief. However, the necessity for repeated injections and their overall expense have resulted in a high cost per QALY, placing the treatment outside the hospital’s new limits.

Disturbed by this directive, Dr. Jackson calls her longtime friend Dr. Stein, who now serves as one of the hospital administrators. During their conversation, Dr. Jackson voices her deep concern: she argues that financial considerations should not dictate patient care, especially when the treatments in question have demonstrated clear clinical benefits for her patients. In her view, effective medical interventions ought to remain accessible. Dr. Stein, who also has a background in clinical practice, admits that he personally shares Dr. Jackson’s perspective and is well aware of her strong reputation for prioritizing patient well-being. Yet, he responds soberly: “The hospital’s financial situation is dire—if we keep spending at this rate, we won’t survive, and many of our patients will be left without care at all. We have to make cuts somewhere. What would you suggest we do instead?”

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically justifiable to deny treatment based on cost?
keypoints: The fundamental ethical dilemma in medical practice lies in balancing society’s legitimate limitation on the expenditure of scarce healthcare resources with the moral commitment to provide effective treatment to individual patients.
Cost should be considered as an important factor in clinical decision-making but must not serve as the sole or absolute determinant.

Clinical decisions should integrate multiple factors, including prognosis, severity of the condition, and individual patient needs, to ensure the rationality of treatment plans and uphold principles of humanistic care.

In the context of limited resources, healthcare institutions must seek balanced approaches that reconcile overall benefit with individual rights, avoiding the simplistic rejection of effective treatments based solely on cost.

title: Use of Electronic Patient Data in Research
case:
A recent graduate of a large internal medicine residency program, Dr. Smith is beginning her infectious disease fellowship at a top-notch program. As a person who has lived with the HIV virus her entire life, she has a particular interest in infectious diseases—specifically, HIV and HIV transmission. She chooses to focus the research project required for her fellowship on HIV transmission to neonates.
As a physician and a patient, the importance of privacy is not lost upon her, and she chooses to pursue a fellowship in a program that shares her views on privacy and confidentiality. In fact, her program has recently purchased and implemented a new electronic medical record system for patient data.
Dr. Smith is most interested in the soon-to-be mothers and their unborn children. Over the course of her first few months in fellowship, she begins to collect data on HIV-positive mothers and retrieves information regarding the HIV status of their newly born children through her hospital’s electronic health records. While HIV incidence and fetal transmission are well known from a public health standpoint, no specific data exist for her particular community or the hospital’s patients. Although newborn HIV testing is mandatory at her hospital, treatment of an HIV-positive mother is not. Dr. Smith begins to gather data on HIV-positive mothers and transmission to their infants. She wishes to be able to provide more accurate information to her future patients about the incidence of HIV transmission to newborns in her community.
A few months after beginning data collection, Dr. Smith is approached by one of her colleagues, who has become aware of the project and is concerned that it is unethical to collect and compile existing data without obtaining informed consent from the participants.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Smith, a recent graduate from a prominent internal medicine residency, has just embarked on her infectious disease fellowship at a highly respected academic program. Living with HIV since birth, Dr. Smith’s personal experiences have shaped her deep commitment to the study of infectious diseases, especially HIV and its transmission dynamics. For her fellowship’s required research project, she decides to investigate the transmission of HIV from mothers to their newborns.

Dr. Smith is acutely aware of the importance of privacy, both as a physician and as someone living with a chronic illness. She specifically chose a fellowship program that places a strong emphasis on patient confidentiality—a value reflected by the program’s recent investment in a state-of-the-art electronic medical records (EMR) system.

Throughout her early months as a fellow, Dr. Smith turns her attention to expectant mothers with HIV and their infants. She begins to systematically collect data on HIV-positive pregnant women and tracks the HIV status of their newborns using the hospital’s EMR. Although broad statistics on HIV transmission rates are available from public health sources, there is a notable lack of specific data for her hospital’s patient population. While the hospital enforces mandatory HIV testing for all newborns, it does not require HIV-positive mothers to undergo treatment.

Motivated by a desire to give her future patients more precise, community-specific information about the risk of neonatal HIV transmission, Dr. Smith starts compiling data on these mothers and their infants. She hopes her research will fill an important knowledge gap for her local community.

Several months into her data collection, Dr. Smith is approached by a colleague who has learned about her project. The colleague expresses concern, questioning whether it is ethical to collect and use existing patient data for research purposes without first obtaining informed consent from the mothers involved.

ethical_issues.question: Does the collection and compilation of existing patient data without obtaining informed consent from the participants violate ethical principles?
keypoints: Collecting patient data without obtaining informed consent from participants may violate core ethical principles, particularly those of respect for patient autonomy and privacy; scientific objectives alone do not justify exceptions to these requirements.

Smith’s research involves protected health information that could potentially identify individuals, informed consent cannot be routinely waived, highlighting the necessity for strict adherence to ethical, professional, and legal standards.

Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) may grant waivers of informed consent for studies utilizing de-identified or non-identifiable data; however, research involving identifiable patient information requires explicit IRB approval and must comply with established ethical procedures.

Investigators must be thoroughly familiar with, and rigorously comply with, their institution’s IRB policies regarding the use and review of electronic medical record data to ensure that research design and data management practices meet all ethical and legal requirements.

title: Copying and Pasting Patient Treatment Notes
case:
Dr. McGill was the first physician in his family. Success was never easy for him, but his perseverance was legendary in his undergraduate and graduate days; he was known for studying more, arriving earlier, and staying later than anyone. Early in the course of his pediatric residency, however, he began to experience problems with efficiency. As the patient population he was responsible for each day began to grow, he became more and more overwhelmed with his duties. On more than one occasion, he arrived at rounds not having seen all of his patients, written orders, or checked the daily labs.
The breaking point occurred when he arrived for rounds looking disheveled and unkempt and informed his attending that he simply did not go home after his call day, in order to have sufficient time to round on his patients and write their notes. When asked why he was unable to keep up with the demands of his patients and the daily tasks, he explained that the daily progress notes took up the majority of his time, many hours a day.
Only then was he informed that it is common practice for residents to simply copy and paste the previous examination, assessment, and plan to the following day’s notes, only editing if any changes need be made. Because his home institution did not use electronic medical records, he had been unaware that “selective editing” was possible, appropriate, allowed, or even ethical. Now he agreed to selectively edit his daily notes and immediately saw his efficiency of long ago returning.
Unfortunately, a short time later, he transcribed some recommendations on the wrong note. He copied recommendations for one of his pediatric patients with staphylococcal cellulitis to a similarly afflicted patient—who also had renal disease. When the patient with renal failure was written for scheduled vancomycin therapy rather than pulse dose, it caused a rise in creatinine and the patient required a prolonged hospitalization.
case_rewrite:
Dr. McGill was the first in his family to pursue a career in medicine. Throughout his academic journey, he had earned a reputation for his unwavering dedication—he consistently studied longer hours, arrived at the hospital before anyone else, and was always the last to leave. However, as he began his pediatric residency, Dr. McGill found himself struggling with efficiency. The ever-increasing number of patients under his care left him feeling overwhelmed, and he started to fall behind on his responsibilities. More than once, he showed up to morning rounds without having seen all of his patients, written the necessary orders, or reviewed the latest laboratory results.

The situation reached a critical point when Dr. McGill appeared at rounds looking noticeably disheveled. He admitted to his attending that he had not gone home after his overnight call, hoping that the extra hours would finally allow him to catch up on patient rounds and complete his documentation. When questioned about the source of his difficulties, Dr. McGill explained that the daily progress notes consumed the majority of his time, often taking hours each day to complete.

It was only then that Dr. McGill learned from his colleagues that it was standard practice among residents to copy and paste the previous day’s examinations, assessments, and plans into the new day’s notes, making edits only if significant changes had occurred. Because his home institution lacked electronic medical records, Dr. McGill had never realized that “selective editing” was even possible, let alone acceptable or ethical. Reassured by his peers and attendings that this approach was both permissible and efficient, Dr. McGill began to selectively edit his daily notes. Almost immediately, he felt his past efficiency return.

However, not long after adopting this practice, Dr. McGill made a critical error. While updating notes, he inadvertently transferred recommendations intended for one pediatric patient with staphylococcal cellulitis to another patient with a similar condition—overlooking the crucial fact that the second patient also suffered from renal disease. As a result, the patient with renal failure was prescribed a scheduled vancomycin regimen rather than the pulse dosing required for their condition. This oversight led to an increase in the patient’s creatinine levels and necessitated a prolonged hospital stay.

ethical_issues.question: Is copying and pasting patient records in the electronic medical record system consistent with medical ethical standards?
keypoints: Copying and pasting information within electronic medical record (EMR) systems is a common and effective time-saving strategy; however, if performed improperly, it can result in disorganized documentation, missing information, internal inconsistencies, and the propagation of errors, thereby compromising patient safety.

The ethical risks associated with copying and pasting primarily arise from the manner of execution and the selection of content. Appropriately copying static information (such as demographic data, past medical history, and medication lists) with independent verification is acceptable, but this practice must not come at the expense of the quality of patient care or the educational value of documentation.

Healthcare professionals bear primary responsibility for the act of copying and pasting and its consequences, and must ensure the accuracy, completeness, and credibility of medical record information.

Attending physicians or senior staff who encourage, tacitly permit, or overlook the risks of copying and pasting have significant supervisory and instructional responsibilities. They should actively guide and standardize documentation practices to prevent medical errors.

As the provider and administrator of electronic medical record systems, the hospital shares joint responsibility for patient harm resulting from system design flaws or inadequate management, and must work collaboratively to ensure the quality of medical records and the safety of patients.

title: Communicating Results of Community-Based Participatory Research
case:
Drs. Allen, Seymour, and Lesh of Barclay University Hospital had been working in conjunction with the New Hope Church and Grass Blade Youth Community Center to study the link between incarceration and sexually transmitted infection (STI) rates in the Park neighborhood. The findings were striking in the physicians’ minds, revealing that far greater numbers of the community members than expected had histories of incarceration and STIs. The physicians were concerned because they had worked hard to convince the community to allow them into the neighborhood and did not want to alienate residents. Yet they felt the community members had a right to know the facts.
On the day designated to share the findings, the church annex was packed with familiar and unfamiliar faces. Members of the Grass Blade Youth Community Center and eight volunteer members of New Hope Church were present. The church group, headed by Reverend Mason, served as the voice of the community.
The physicians began going through their data, stating that 3 out of 5 males had been incarcerated by the age of 25 and had had an average of 2 STIs by that age. Out of this 60 percent, 25 percent were HIV positive. Reverend Mason was outraged and stood up to leave before the presentation was finished, but not before saying, “We welcome you into our community, and this is the so-called research you do. You paint our community as a sinful, violent place to live. How will this research affect our young people who will think that growing up means going to prison and getting AIDS? What about employers’ decisions when community members are applying for jobs? When our youth are applying for college?”
The physicians tried to explain that the research was done without bias and with the sole purpose of creating interventions.
Other community members started to exclaim, “My children have never been to prison and don’t have any diseases!” Soon, the packed room emptied, save for a few members who were trying to convince people to “hear these doctors out; after all, we do need help.” The research team was disappointed. They believed they had communicated the purpose of the research to the community before they began their work. Obviously more people attended this conclusion meeting than the earlier informational one.
case_rewrite:
Drs. Allen, Seymour, and Lesh from Barclay University Hospital had spent months collaborating with the New Hope Church and Grass Blade Youth Community Center to investigate the relationship between incarceration and sexually transmitted infection (STI) rates in the Park neighborhood. Their research, which depended on the trust and participation of local residents, brought to light findings that startled even the physicians: the prevalence of incarceration and STIs was significantly higher than they had anticipated. The doctors were deeply aware of the effort it had taken to gain the community’s confidence and were concerned about how these results might be received. At the same time, they believed that the community deserved to know the truth about the health challenges it faced.

On the evening set aside to present their findings, the church annex was filled to capacity with both familiar faces and newcomers. In attendance were members of the Grass Blade Youth Community Center, eight volunteers from New Hope Church, and numerous local residents. Reverend Mason, respected leader of the church, presided as the community’s representative.

As the doctors began their presentation, they shared the data: three out of five males in the neighborhood had been incarcerated by age 25, and, on average, had experienced two STIs by that age. Among this 60 percent, a quarter were HIV positive. The mood in the room shifted immediately. Reverend Mason, visibly agitated, stood up before the presentation was over and declared, “You come into our community with promises, and this is the image you present? You make us out to be criminals and diseased. What will our young people think, growing up believing that their future is prison and illness? How will this affect them when they apply for jobs or colleges?”

The doctors attempted to clarify that their research was motivated by a desire to develop interventions and not by any prejudice. They tried to explain that the study had been conducted with care and impartiality. However, their words struggled to calm the rising tension. Several community members voiced their distress: “My children have never been to prison. They’re healthy!” The atmosphere quickly became charged, and people began leaving the hall in frustration and anger, despite the efforts of a few who urged, “Let’s listen to what the doctors have to say—maybe they can help us.”

By the end of the evening, only a small group remained, trying to keep the dialogue open. The research team, left disappointed and discouraged, reflected on where communication had broken down. Although they had previously thought the community understood the purpose of the research, it was clear that many more people had attended the final meeting than the initial informational session. The doctors realized that the way the findings had been presented had not met the community’s expectations, and the experience left both sides questioning how trust and partnership could be preserved moving forward.

ethical_issues.question: In community-based participatory research, how can the dissemination of research results be ensured so that it does not harm the interests of community members or reinforce stereotypes and prejudice?
keypoints: Establish partnerships based on mutual respect and trust to achieve shared authority and prevent misunderstandings and conflicts.
Clarify the responsibilities, rights, and principles and procedures for data dissemination and authorship between academic and community partners through a memorandum of understanding (MOU).
Engage academic and community partners jointly in data interpretation, thoroughly discussing the validity, limitations, and potential social implications of the research findings.
Present research results to the community in a culturally sensitive, accessible, and empowering manner, avoiding labeling and stereotyping.

Researchers must respect the community’s ownership of the data and shall not unilaterally release or publish data without the community’s consent, ensuring shared management of the data by both parties.
Develop dissemination strategies collaboratively with the community prior to communication to ensure that information delivery aligns with community interests and promotes positive interventions.
Maintain ongoing open and transparent communication and negotiation, and when disagreements arise, involve a third party mediator to facilitate consensus building.

ethical_issues.question: In community-based participatory research, how can mutual and respectful trust be established and shared authority be achieved to ensure the integrity of the research process and the stability of the partnership?
keypoints: Establish effective, meaningful, and mutually beneficial partnerships between academic researchers and community members to ensure mutual trust, respect, and shared authority.
Clearly define the responsibilities of academic and community partners in a memorandum of understanding (MOU), including provisions for conflict resolution to prevent dissolution of the partnership.
Anticipate stages in the research process that are likely to generate disagreements and discuss them early to facilitate prompt conflict resolution.

Develop a comprehensive data management plan encompassing data interpretation, dissemination, ownership, and dispute resolution mechanisms, ensuring joint participation and consensus through ongoing dialogue, with the involvement of a third party mediator if necessary.

ethical_issues.question: In community-based participatory research, should academic researchers jointly discuss and interpret research findings with community partners prior to public forums in order to avoid misunderstandings and conflict?
keypoints: Academic researchers should engage in joint discussion and interpretation of research findings with community partners prior to any public forum, ensuring accurate communication of information and preventing misunderstandings and conflict.

Independent interpretation and dissemination of research data by researchers can easily lead to distrust and resistance from the community; therefore, collaborative discussion is necessary to promote mutual understanding and trust.

Establishing prearranged mechanisms for conflict resolution and channels of communication ensures that all parties have the opportunity to express concerns and adjust plans before public dissemination, embodying the core principle of shared authority in community-based participatory research.

Community-based participatory research emphasizes the joint involvement of academic and community partners in data interpretation, integrating scientific analysis with community knowledge to enhance the validity of the data and the comprehensiveness of result interpretation.

Researchers should engage in in-depth discussions with community partners regarding the potential social, cultural, and structural factors underlying the higher-than-expected rates of incarceration and sexually transmitted infections revealed by the research, in order to foster consensus.

The research team and community partners should collaboratively develop strategies for dissemination of findings and reach consensus on the mode of data presentation, thereby avoiding disagreement and misrepresentation in public settings.

title: Setting the Agenda for Community-Based Participatory Research
case:
Dr. Peck, an academic researcher, is looking into the correlation between teen suicides and peer bullying around the country. He goes to Frederick Heights because that community has had two suicides in 3 years, a high occurrence for a small community. His colleague, a psychiatrist, sees several youths from the community, and these patients have reported disturbing patterns of bullying. A Frederick Heights community group has established positive partnerships with other researchers from the local university, and Dr. Peck feels it is best to meet with this group before proceeding with the study. Dr. Peck speaks with the community group’s board of directors to gauge their interest in a study that explores interventions to prevent bullying.
Most of the board members are part of the congregation of a conservative church. In the meeting, members state that the two boys who committed suicide were homosexual and that being gay is wrong. They say the research is neither important nor relevant in their community in spite of the statistical data. The board chairperson attempts to open the members’ minds to the research idea by saying, “I know this is a difficult subject to talk about, but it doesn’t mean those with ‘alternative lifestyles’ who live in our community don’t deserve our protection.”
His words are drowned out by phrases like, “Not here they don’t.” One member says, “I think the board should be focused on bringing research to the community that looks at the positive effects of religion on teen vandalism. Because you know we started a Friday night Bible class for young adults about a year ago, and there has been less graffiti and loitering.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Peck, an academic researcher, is investigating the connection between adolescent suicide and peer bullying across different regions. He turns his attention to Frederick Heights, a small community that has experienced two teen suicides in the past three years—a troublingly high rate for its size. Dr. Peck’s colleague, a local psychiatrist, has seen several young patients from Frederick Heights who have described alarming patterns of bullying. Recognizing the sensitive nature of his research and the importance of community partnership, Dr. Peck decides that before proceeding with his study, he should meet with a community group in Frederick Heights—a group already known for positive collaborations with researchers from the nearby university.

Arranging a meeting with the board of directors of the community group, Dr. Peck hopes to gauge their interest in a study focused on interventions to prevent bullying. Many board members also belong to the congregation of a conservative local church. During the meeting, the board members share their perspectives, asserting that the two boys who died by suicide were homosexual and expressing the belief that being gay is wrong. Despite Dr. Peck’s presentation of relevant statistical data, the board members insist that such research is neither important nor relevant to their community.

As the conversation grows more tense, the board chairperson attempts to broaden the discussion, saying, “I know this is a difficult subject to talk about, but it doesn’t mean those with ‘alternative lifestyles’ who live in our community don’t deserve our protection.” However, his words are quickly drowned out by others: “Not here they don’t.” Another member interjects, “I think the board should be focused on bringing research to the community that looks at the positive effects of religion on teen vandalism. Because you know we started a Friday night Bible class for young adults about a year ago, and there’s been less graffiti and loitering since then.”

Dr. Peck listens intently, aware of the strong and divergent views within the group. The meeting leaves him reflecting on how best to move forward—how to respect the values and autonomy of the Frederick Heights community, foster genuine partnership, and still address the urgent problem of bullying and suicide among its youth.

ethical_issues.question: How can researchers respect the autonomy of the community and establish a genuine partnership in community-based participatory research?
keypoints: Revised Key Points:

Respecting the autonomy of the community is the foundation for establishing a genuine partnership; researchers should collaboratively identify community needs and research priorities at an early stage to ensure that the community’s agenda and interests are fully respected.

Researchers should engage in open and sincere communication with the community board and other key stakeholders to resolve potential conflicts between community autonomy and the goals of health promotion.
Actively seeking common interests and potential allies, such as the board chairperson and other community members, facilitates more constructive research collaboration.

Involving community leaders, individuals personally affected by the suicide incidents, or other representative community members in the research design can enhance the cultural sensitivity and humanistic depth of the study.

ethical_issues.question: In community-based participatory research, how can the research agenda be ensured to both promote the health and well-being of community members and avoid causing harm to the community or the partnership?
keypoints: Respect for community autonomy requires researchers to actively solicit the needs, interests, and values of community members at an early stage of establishing a genuine partnership, ensuring that the research agenda aligns with the community’s actual priorities.

CBPR should adhere to the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence; researchers must ensure that the study genuinely promotes the health and well-being of the community while avoiding harm to the community or the collaborative relationship.

Effective communication and the pursuit of common interests are essential to resolving conflicts between community autonomy and the researcher’s goal of health promotion; researchers should actively listen to and address community concerns.

Incorporating diverse community voices, especially those of individuals personally affected by the suicide incidents and their families, helps deepen the discussion, foster understanding, and facilitate research collaboration.

In situations of conflict, researchers should embody the principles of virtue ethics—such as compassion, courage, honesty, and humility—being transparent about their own limitations, respecting the importance of community assistance, and thereby promoting successful collaboration.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with conflicts between community values and the research agenda, how can researchers balance communitarianism and egalitarianism to advance social justice?
keypoints: The core ethical conflict in this case lies in the tension between communitarianism (community values) and egalitarianism (researcher’s agenda); understanding this tension is fundamental to developing subsequent strategies.

The researcher should thoroughly prepare for the meeting with the board of directors by gaining an in-depth understanding of the community’s background and values, and seek common interests as a starting point to promote collaboration.

The researcher should attempt to persuade the community board by emphasizing that the pursuit of social justice constitutes an ethical obligation of the community, thereby fostering attention to the issues of adolescent suicide and bullying.

The researcher should invite the board chairperson to serve as a principal collaborator in the research design and actively engage potential allies to enhance the community’s recognition and acceptance of the study.

The researcher may incorporate the voices of individuals personally affected by the suicide incidents and other community members to enrich the humanistic depth of the discussion, promoting understanding and empathy.

The researcher can collaborate with public health officials, school boards, parent organizations, and town council members to facilitate the formation of community consensus and the development of practical public health intervention strategies.

title: When the Evidence Isn't There: Seeking Informed Consent for New Procedures
case:
Mr. Roberts had been having difficulty urinating and, because he was 68, figured it was just a normal part of the aging process. Eventually, however, Mr. Roberts noticed that he was starting to have pain with urination as well, and went to his physician to get checked out. A few weeks and a biopsy later, Mr. Roberts was told by his physician that he had prostate cancer. Mr. Roberts was frightened and filled with uncertainty. His physician told him not to worry and recommended an excellent surgeon with whom Mr. Roberts could discuss his treatment options.
That’s how Mr. Roberts ended up at Dr. Klein’s urology clinic. Dr. Klein was a renowned expert in laparoscopic prostatectomy and had built a reputation based on his unusually low rate of complications. Shortly before Mr. Roberts’ visit, Dr. Klein and his colleagues had begun offering robotic-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy to patients like Mr. Roberts. After looking carefully at Mr. Roberts’ lab and biopsy reports, Dr. Klein believed that surgery was the best option for this patient.
Dr. Klein admitted that the robotic procedure was much newer to him than the laparoscopic approach he had been using with success for so many years, but he said that he believed it would soon become the standard protocol for uncomplicated prostatectomy. Nevertheless, Dr. Klein offered Mr. Roberts the choice between robot-assisted prostatectomy or the standard laparoscopic prostatectomy. The robotic surgery, for one thing, was costlier.
Mr. Roberts found himself presented with a decision he did not feel qualified to make. He asked Dr. Klein about the risks and benefits of the two techniques. Dr. Klein was able to give Mr. Roberts an accurate description of the risks of the laparoscopic procedure, both from his personal experience and from hard evidence collected by urologists over many years. When Mr. Roberts asked Dr. Klein to do the same for the robotic procedure, Dr. Klein had to rely upon his limited experience. He was able to tell Mr. Roberts that in the past few months, all of his patients had had a good experience with the robotic procedure, and he thought he was already beginning to see quicker recovery times with those patients. Dr. Klein admitted, however, that more objective data for the robotic procedure was still somewhat sparse, although rapidly accumulating.
Somewhat confused and more than a little frightened by the whole prospect, Mr. Roberts told Dr. Klein that he wanted to have the procedure that Dr. Klein thought was best for him and that he would abide by whatever decision Dr. Klein made.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Roberts, a 68-year-old man, had been experiencing increasing difficulty with urination. Initially, he attributed these symptoms to aging, but when pain began to accompany urination, his concern grew, prompting him to see his physician. After a series of tests and a prostate biopsy, Mr. Roberts received the unsettling news that he had prostate cancer. Overwhelmed by fear and uncertainty, he listened as his physician reassured him and recommended that he consult Dr. Klein, a highly regarded urologist, to discuss possible treatment options.

Dr. Klein was well-known for his expertise in laparoscopic prostatectomy, a procedure he had performed with a notably low complication rate. Recently, however, Dr. Klein and his team had started to offer robotic-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy to suitable patients. Upon reviewing Mr. Roberts’ laboratory and biopsy results, Dr. Klein concluded that surgery would be the most appropriate treatment for him.

During their consultation, Dr. Klein was transparent about his experience. He explained that while he was very experienced with standard laparoscopic prostatectomy, the robotic-assisted technique was relatively new to his practice. He acknowledged that although he believed robotic surgery was likely to become the standard approach for cases like Mr. Roberts’, his own hands-on experience with the equipment was still limited compared to his expertise with traditional laparoscopy. Dr. Klein further noted that the robotic procedure was more expensive and that, although his recent patients had done well, comprehensive, long-term data on outcomes were not yet available.

Mr. Roberts was uneasy about having to choose between the established laparoscopic method and the newer robotic-assisted approach. When he asked about the risks and benefits, Dr. Klein was able to provide detailed, well-supported information about the traditional laparoscopic procedure based on years of personal experience and robust clinical data. For the robotic-assisted option, however, Dr. Klein explained that he could only speak from his limited, recent experience and the still-developing evidence base. He mentioned that early results seemed promising, particularly regarding recovery times, but emphasized that objective data was still emerging.

Feeling confused and frightened, Mr. Roberts admitted to Dr. Klein that he did not feel equipped to make such a decision. He asked Dr. Klein to recommend the option he believed would be best, expressing trust in Dr. Klein’s judgment and stating that he would follow whatever course Dr. Klein advised.

ethical_issues.question: How can a physician ensure that they have acquired the necessary skills and experience before offering a new surgical procedure, and how should they fully disclose their level of experience to the patient during the informed consent process?
keypoints: Physicians must undergo systematic training and practical experience before offering new surgical procedures to ensure they possess the necessary skills and expertise.
Physicians should objectively assess their own experience and the maturity of the technique, confirming that the new procedure is appropriate for the patient and that the risks are manageable.

During the informed consent process, physicians must explicitly disclose to patients the novelty of the procedure, the limited availability of current evidence-based data, and their own level of experience with the technique.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient is unable to make a decision due to confusion and fear, how can a physician provide substantive recommendations to assist the patient in making an informed choice while still respecting patient autonomy?
keypoints: Physicians should, while respecting patient autonomy, proactively offer substantive recommendations based on professional judgment to assist patients in clarifying their options.

Physicians must set aside personal interests and objectively evaluate the risks and potential benefits of both new and established surgical procedures, integrating the patient’s specific circumstances to assess their value.

Physicians should engage in thorough communication with patients regarding the benefits, risks, and uncertainties of the surgery, supporting patients in weighing their choices to ensure decisions align with their best interests and values.

tags: Diagnosis/Patient request for a specific test or procedure
title: Responding to Patient Requests for Nonindicated Care
case:
When Dr. Wainwright entered the room late on a Friday afternoon, the last new patient of his weekly thoracic surgery clinic awaited him anxiously. Mrs. Kitson sat rigidly upright on the edge of the exam table, wringing her hands, as he pulled up the stool.
“Hello, Doctor. We’ve never met before, but I just wanted you to know that I’ve heard wonderful things about you. You performed surgery on my best friend just a few months ago as a matter of fact,” Mrs. Kitson blurted out, giving her friend’s full name.
“Pleasure to meet you, Mrs. Kitson. I remember Mrs. Martin well,” Dr. Wainwright replied. And he did remember Mrs. Martin. She was one of the most difficult lung cancer resections he had done in a long time. An unfortunate story, Mrs. Martin had been diagnosed 4 months before with locally advanced lung cancer, and removing all the cancer proved impossible for Dr. Wainwright and his colleagues.” I haven’t seen her for a couple of months,” he said. “I hope she’s doing well.”
“Very well,” Mrs. Kitson said, rubbing her palms against her thighs.
“Well, what brings you in today?”
Without hesitation, Mrs. Kitson said: “I’d like a CAT scan. As soon as possible. I know my situation isn’t exactly the same as my friend’s, but I just have to know if I have lung cancer. I can’t go through what she went through.”
Over the next few minutes, Dr. Wainwright attempted to understand the reason for Mrs. Kitson’s anxiety. It turned out that she had smoked a pack of cigarettes a day for 5 years a couple of decades earlier. However, she did not have any of the symptoms Dr. Wainwright asked about, such as cough, hemoptysis, or weight loss, and knew of nobody in her family who had had lung cancer. Dr. Wainwright explained to Mrs. Kitson that since she was asymptomatic, there was no evidence that screening for lung cancer would do her any good. In fact, the current position of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force was: “the evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against screening asymptomatic persons for lung cancer with either low-dose computerized tomography, chest x-ray, sputum cytology, or a combination of these tests.” Furthermore, there was the cost to consider, as well as the risks of high-dose radiation exposure and the possibility of invasive work-ups of otherwise benign lesions.
“I know it probably sounds silly to you,” Mrs. Kitson said, “but I have to be sure.”
Although she clearly had no clinical indication for a CT scan, Dr. Wainwright wondered to what extent Mrs. Kitson’s “whole” health, her well-being, might depend on getting the scan. But, then, couldn’t that same reasoning be used for everyone who wanted an unnecessary scan?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Wainwright stepped into the examination room late on a Friday afternoon, finding Mrs. Kitson—the final new patient of his weekly thoracic surgery clinic—waiting with a tense, anxious posture on the edge of the exam table. Her hands twisted nervously in her lap as he pulled up a stool beside her.

“Hello, Doctor. We haven’t met before, but I wanted you to know I’ve heard wonderful things about you. In fact, you operated on my best friend just a few months ago,” Mrs. Kitson blurted out, naming her friend.

Dr. Wainwright nodded warmly. “It’s nice to meet you, Mrs. Kitson. I remember Mrs. Martin very well.” The memory was vivid—Mrs. Martin’s lung cancer surgery had been among the most challenging cases he’d encountered recently. Diagnosed four months earlier with advanced disease, the operation had been fraught, and ultimately, complete removal of her cancer had not been possible. “I haven’t seen her in a while,” he added. “I hope she’s doing alright.”

“She’s doing very well,” Mrs. Kitson replied, rubbing her palms against her thighs.

“What brings you in today?” Dr. Wainwright asked.

Without hesitation, Mrs. Kitson answered, “I’d like a CAT scan. As soon as possible. I know my situation isn’t exactly like my friend’s, but I just have to know if I have lung cancer. I can’t go through what she went through.”

Dr. Wainwright took a few moments to explore the root of her anxiety. He learned that Mrs. Kitson had smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for five years, but that was decades ago. She denied any symptoms—no cough, no coughing up blood, no unintended weight loss. There was no family history of lung cancer either.

He gently explained, “Based on your history and current guidelines, there isn’t evidence that screening you for lung cancer would help. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force currently states that there’s not enough proof to recommend for or against lung cancer screening in people without symptoms—whether using low-dose CT, chest x-ray, or sputum cytology. These tests also carry risks: exposure to radiation, unnecessary costs, and the possibility of follow-up procedures for findings that may turn out to be harmless.”

“I know it probably sounds silly to you,” Mrs. Kitson said quietly, “but I have to be sure.”

Dr. Wainwright paused, reflecting on her distress. Even though there was no clinical justification for a CT scan, he wondered if her sense of well-being depended on getting the test. Still, he questioned whether it would be right to order a scan simply because of her worry—after all, wouldn’t that reasoning apply to anyone with similar fears?

He considered how best to support Mrs. Kitson’s emotional needs while upholding his responsibility to protect her from unnecessary risks, and to ensure his decision was grounded in sound medical judgment rather than mere acquiescence to her request.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians comply with patient requests for tests or treatments that lack medical indication, even when the patient insists strongly?
keypoints: Physicians are not obligated to provide tests or treatments that lack medical indication, even if strongly requested by the patient.
The physician’s duty is to assess the appropriateness of a test or treatment, rather than merely fulfilling the patient’s demands.
Respect for patient autonomy primarily pertains to the patient’s right to refuse tests or treatments; the positive right to demand specific interventions is more limited in medicine.
Physicians have a responsibility to protect patients from unacceptable harm and unnecessary risks, even if this entails refusing the patient’s request.

ethical_issues.question: When refusing a patient’s request for a medically nonindicated test, how can a physician explain the rationale behind the decision without compromising the patient-physician relationship?
keypoints: Physicians should seek to understand the motivations behind patients’ requests for diagnostic testing, paying attention to their emotional and psychological needs in order to provide more comprehensive care.

When declining patient requests for tests lacking medical indication, physicians ought to patiently and sincerely explain the rationale behind their decision to prevent patients from misconstruing it as disregard for their concerns or merely cost-containment.

Physicians need to engage in thorough discussions with patients about their health goals, educating them on the potential risks and benefits of the requested tests, clarifying misunderstandings and misinformation, thereby facilitating informed and rational decision-making.
Through effective communication, physicians should strive to reassure patients while refusing unnecessary testing, thereby preserving and fostering a positive patient-physician relationship.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance respect for patient autonomy with their professional duty to protect patients from unnecessary risks when faced with patient requests for potentially harmful, nonindicated medical interventions?
keypoints: Physicians have the responsibility to determine the appropriateness of diagnostic tests or treatments based on medical evidence and are under no obligation to provide interventions that lack medical indication, even if strongly requested by the patient.

Respect for patient autonomy is primarily manifested in the patient’s right to refuse medical interventions; the positive right of patients to demand specific medical measures is reasonably limited in clinical practice.

Physicians should protect patients from unnecessary risks and potential harm, avoiding fulfillment of nonindicated patient requests that would contravene professional duties and principles of sound medical care.

Physicians should act as advocates for the patient’s health by thoroughly understanding the psychological factors and informational sources underlying patient requests, alleviating anxiety and conflict through clarification of misunderstandings and provision of scientifically grounded explanations.

When declining nonindicated medical requests, physicians should patiently and clearly communicate the rationale behind their decisions, respect the patient’s feelings, and maintain the trust inherent in the patient-physician relationship.

Physicians should comprehensively evaluate patient requests by integrating professional expertise and clinical guidelines to ensure that the medical services provided are consistent with medical indications and the patient’s overall best interests.

title: The Referral-Consultant Relationship
case:
Dr. Nichols, a well-established comprehensive ophthalmologist, refers Mrs. Smith to Dr. Weiman, a specialist at an academic health science center, for a second opinion on the management of her glaucoma. A warm note from Dr. Nichols to Dr. Weiman details Mrs. Smith’s 15-year history of glaucoma, refractory to multiple medical therapies and laser treatments. In his referral letter, Dr. Nichols states that, because conservative measures have failed and Mrs. Smith now has advanced glaucoma, he has offered Mrs. Smith a trabeculectomy, which Mrs. Smith has agreed to have in the coming month. Because Mrs. Smith seemed hesitant about surgery on prior visits and has expressed interest in participating in clinical trials with newer pharmacologic agents, Dr. Nichols is referring her to Dr. Weiman for consultation, specifically for her opinion on any additional conservative therapies that could be attempted before proceeding with the trabeculectomy.
Dr. Weiman greets Mrs. Smith, who professes her satisfaction with Dr. Nichols’ care—she has been his patient for over two decades—and is equally delighted to have Dr. Weiman’s opinion. Dr. Weiman examines Mrs. Smith and notes that both her optic nerves are prominently cupped and she has peripheral visual field defects that fully correspond to the appearance of her optic nerves. Her central vision is threatened by disease progression, and her intraocular pressure is elevated in both eyes despite good compliance with her medications.
Dr. Weiman tells the patient that her examination confirms Dr. Nichols’ findings, and she agrees that a trabeculectomy is indeed the best option for Mrs. Smith. She explains that there are no clinical trials Mrs. Smith would qualify for with her advanced glaucoma without risking further vision loss. Dr. Weiman concludes by wishing her luck with her surgery, but as she is exiting the room, Mrs. Smith says, “Well…I just have one more question.”
“Dr. Weiman,” she begins. “I’m glad you agree with Dr. Nichols. The fact that you’re both a professor and a glaucoma specialist means that you have great expertise with patients like me, and I don’t think I can trust my eyes to anyone but the best. I’ve been very happy with my care from Dr. Nichols, but I would prefer that you perform my surgery.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Nichols, a respected comprehensive ophthalmologist, refers Mrs. Smith to Dr. Weiman, a glaucoma specialist at a leading academic health science center, for a second opinion on her glaucoma management. In a thoughtful letter to Dr. Weiman, Dr. Nichols outlines Mrs. Smith’s 15-year struggle with glaucoma, which has proven unresponsive to multiple medications and laser treatments. Dr. Nichols explains that, with conservative treatments exhausted and Mrs. Smith’s glaucoma now advanced, he has recommended a trabeculectomy, and Mrs. Smith has agreed to proceed with this surgery in the coming month. However, Dr. Nichols notes that Mrs. Smith has previously voiced hesitation about surgery and has shown interest in possible enrollment in clinical trials for novel pharmacologic agents. Therefore, Dr. Nichols requests Dr. Weiman’s expert consultation, specifically to assess whether any other conservative options might still be considered before moving forward with the trabeculectomy.

At her appointment, Mrs. Smith tells Dr. Weiman how pleased she has been with Dr. Nichols, her ophthalmologist for over twenty years, and that she is equally appreciative of Dr. Weiman’s willingness to provide a second opinion. Dr. Weiman conducts a thorough examination, finding pronounced cupping of both optic nerves and peripheral visual field loss that matches the optic nerve damage. Mrs. Smith’s intraocular pressures are elevated in both eyes despite her diligent use of prescribed medications, and her central vision remains at significant risk from ongoing disease progression.

Dr. Weiman reviews the findings with Mrs. Smith, confirming Dr. Nichols’ assessment, and concurs that a trabeculectomy is the most appropriate next step. She carefully explains that, given the advanced stage of Mrs. Smith’s glaucoma, no suitable clinical trials for new medications are available that would not entail an unacceptable risk of further vision loss. Dr. Weiman concludes the visit by wishing Mrs. Smith well with her upcoming surgery.

As Mrs. Smith prepares to leave, she pauses at the door. “Dr. Weiman,” she says, “I truly value Dr. Nichols’ care, and I’ve been his patient for more than twenty years. But knowing that you’re both a professor and a glaucoma specialist, I feel you have exceptional expertise with patients like me. I don’t think I can trust my eyes to anyone but the best. Even though I’ve been happy with Dr. Nichols, I would actually prefer if you could perform my surgery instead.”

ethical_issues.question: Does the referring physician have an obligation to clearly explain to the patient the nature and purpose of the referral prior to the consultation, in order to prevent any misunderstanding regarding who will perform the surgery?
keypoints: The referring physician should clearly explain to the patient the nature and purpose of the referral prior to the consultation, emphasizing that the referral is solely for obtaining a second opinion and does not constitute a formal transfer of care.

The referring physician should inform the patient that if the consulting physician concurs with the necessity of surgery, the procedure will be performed by the original physician as planned, in order to prevent any misunderstanding regarding the surgeon responsible for the operation.
The referring physician has the responsibility to provide the consulting physician with complete and detailed clinical information to ensure the quality of the consultation and continuity of care.

ethical_issues.question: If Mrs. Smith requests that Dr. Weiman assume responsibility for her glaucoma surgery instead of Dr. Nichols, should Dr. Weiman advise Mrs. Smith to discuss her wishes with Dr. Nichols and reconsider the original surgical plan, rather than directly agreeing to take over as the operating surgeon?
keypoints: Dr. Weiman should encourage Mrs. Smith to communicate directly with Dr. Nichols regarding any changes in her treatment preferences or surgical plans, in order to respect the referral relationship and uphold principles of professional courtesy.

Mrs. Smith has a responsibility to inform her primary ophthalmologist, Dr. Nichols, of her decisions regarding her care; Dr. Weiman should not assume responsibility for surgical intervention without appropriate communication and agreement with Dr. Nichols.

As the consulting physician, Dr. Weiman should clearly delineate her consultative role, provide an objective assessment of Mrs. Smith’s condition and available treatment options, and, if no additional conservative therapies are indicated, recommend proceeding with the surgical plan as originally arranged by Dr. Nichols.

ethical_issues.question: After confirming the referring physician’s diagnosis, does the consulting physician have an obligation to communicate the consultation findings and the patient’s additional requests directly to the referring physician in order to prevent the referring physician from passively learning that the patient’s surgery has been taken over?
keypoints: The consulting physician should communicate directly with the referring physician to inform them of the consultation findings and the patient’s request to change the surgeon, thereby demonstrating basic respect for the referring physician and promoting transparency of information.

The consulting physician should not precipitously agree to assume responsibility for the surgery; rather, they should advise the patient to discuss surgical arrangements with the referring physician to avoid overstepping professional boundaries.

The referring physician should remain the central decision-maker in clinical management; the consulting physician must respect the referring physician’s treatment plan and should not unilaterally supplant their role.
