title: Managing Risk in Cataract Surgeries Performed by Resident Ophthalmologists
case:
Dr. Harvey, a first-year resident in ophthalmology, greets Mr. Walter, a retired veteran seeking surgery for a cataract in his right eye. After taking his seat, Mr. Walter states that the vision in his right eye has progressively worsened over the past decade, and now he cannot read, do puzzles with his grandchildren, or drive safely.  Mr. Walter’s best corrected visual acuity is 20/160 in the right eye, and, other than a dense cataract in that eye, the remainder of his examination is unremarkable. An attending physician also examines Mr. Walter; he recommends replacement of the lens that has the cataract and suggests that Dr. Harvey take the case.
Dr. Harvey explains the individual steps of the cataract surgery to Mr. Walter and reviews potential complications, including retinal detachment, need for further surgery, and blindness. She tells him that she is a resident physician and will be performing his surgery under the supervision of an attending physician, but she does not reveal that, although she has performed cataract surgery in animal eyes and using surgical simulators, she has never before performed cataract surgery on a human eye.
Mr. Walter does not inquire about her level of experience, and Dr. Harvey does not disclose the details of her surgery training. When Dr. Harvey asks if he has any further questions, Mr. Walter smiles, shakes her hand, and states that she seems like a kind, wonderful person, and that he trusts her with his vision.
At the conclusion of their interview, Mr. Walter is asked to give informed consent.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Harvey, a first-year ophthalmology resident, welcomes Mr. Walter, a retired veteran, who has come to the clinic seeking surgery for a cataract in his right eye. Settling into the exam room, Mr. Walter shares that his right eye’s vision has steadily declined over the past ten years. Now, he finds himself unable to read, do puzzles with his grandchildren, or drive safely. On examination, Mr. Walter’s best corrected visual acuity in the right eye is 20/160, and apart from a dense cataract, the remainder of the eye exam reveals nothing abnormal. An attending physician subsequently evaluates Mr. Walter and recommends that he undergo lens replacement surgery to address the cataract. The attending suggests that Dr. Harvey be the surgeon for the procedure.

Dr. Harvey carefully outlines each step involved in cataract surgery to Mr. Walter. She reviews possible complications, such as retinal detachment, the need for additional surgery, and even the risk of blindness. Dr. Harvey informs Mr. Walter that she is a resident physician and will perform the surgery under supervision from an attending physician. However, she does not disclose that, while she has conducted cataract surgeries on animal eyes and practiced extensively with surgical simulators, she has never actually performed cataract surgery on a human patient.

Mr. Walter does not ask about Dr. Harvey’s surgical experience, and Dr. Harvey does not volunteer any further specifics regarding her training in human surgery. When she invites questions, Mr. Walter smiles warmly, shakes her hand, and expresses his confidence in her, saying she seems like a kind, wonderful person whom he trusts with his vision.

At the end of the appointment, Mr. Walter is presented with the consent form and asked to provide his informed consent for the procedure.

ethical_issues.question: Should the additional risks associated with the early phase of a resident surgeon’s learning curve be mitigated through concerted efforts by the hospital, supervising faculty, and the resident physician?
keypoints: Patients who seek care in public hospitals due to economic constraints do not thereby grant the medical system or resident physicians the authority to provide higher-risk treatments; the ethical principle of prioritizing patient safety must be upheld.

Hospitals, supervising physicians, and resident doctors have an ethical obligation to minimize the additional risks associated with the early phase of the resident learning curve by appropriately assigning surgical difficulty, enhancing supervision and guidance, and making concerted efforts to protect patient interests.

Teaching institutions should continuously invest in faculty development and advanced equipment, optimize training programs, shorten the resident learning curve, and reduce the risk associated with each surgical case.

Resident physicians must fully acknowledge that their limited experience may increase patient risk and proactively utilize resources such as wet labs, instructional videos, and opportunities to assist in surgeries to accelerate their learning and improve surgical safety.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Clinicians as business owners
title: Contact Lens Prescribing and Dispensing by Ophthalmologists
case:
Dr. Brenner, an ophthalmologist who had been practicing in the same city for over a decade, noticed that an increasing number of patients in his community were simply requesting their contact lens prescription in his clinic and ordering them online instead of through his office, resulting in reduced revenue for his practice.
Over the next couple of years, as more ophthalmologists established themselves in his area and some patients elected to have refractive surgery with other specialists, his practice generated less revenue, and Dr. Brenner was forced to make changes in the way he ran his office. He began working longer hours, participating in more community outreach efforts, and reducing the salaries of his office staff.
To retain patients and revenue, Dr. Brenner began to prescribe mostly varieties of contact lenses that are not easily available over the internet and implemented a policy requiring patients to purchase their first month’s supply of lenses from him. There was no change in the quality of contact lenses provided to patients, and the policy was outlined in paperwork that patients reviewed and approved prior to their office visit.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Brenner, an ophthalmologist with over ten years of experience in the same city, began to notice a shift in his practice. More and more patients were coming to his clinic solely to obtain their contact lens prescriptions, then choosing to purchase their lenses online rather than through his office. This trend led to a noticeable decline in revenue for his practice.

As the years passed, competition in the area intensified. Several new ophthalmologists opened practices nearby, and some of Dr. Brenner’s longstanding patients opted to undergo refractive surgery with other specialists. Faced with these challenges, Dr. Brenner found his income continuing to drop, prompting him to make difficult adjustments to his practice. He extended his working hours, increased his involvement in local community events to maintain visibility, and even made the tough decision to reduce the salaries of his office staff.

In an effort to retain his patient base and bolster the practice’s income, Dr. Brenner adopted new strategies. He began prescribing contact lenses that were less readily available through online retailers. Additionally, he instituted a policy that required patients to purchase their initial month’s supply of lenses directly from his office. The quality of contact lenses provided to patients remained the same, and all details regarding the new policy were explicitly stated in the paperwork patients received and agreed to prior to their appointments.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians separate professional service fees from material and handling fees when providing medical care in order to enhance transparency and fairness?
keypoints: Separating professional service fees from material and handling fees enhances billing transparency, enabling patients to clearly understand the specific components of their charges and reflecting the principle of fairness.
Transparent and segregated billing practices help improve patient satisfaction and trust, strengthen patient loyalty to the practice, and may facilitate referrals of new patients.

Physicians have an ethical obligation to provide patients with accurate and comprehensive information about treatment options, including the risks and benefits of each alternative; transparent billing is a crucial safeguard in fulfilling this responsibility.

Sound ethical practices, such as transparent billing, not only constitute the foundation of medical service but can also serve as a core competitive advantage for the practice in a highly competitive market.

ethical_issues.question: Does the physician exhibit a lack of integrity when selling private-label contact lenses, and even if he does not directly deceive patients, is his conduct ethically appropriate?
keypoints: If the contact lenses sold by the physician differ only in packaging and are priced higher, even without directly deceiving patients, such conduct reflects a lack of integrity.
Physicians have an ethical obligation to provide patients with accurate and comprehensive information about treatment options, including the risks, benefits, and cost differences of each alternative.

If the physician offers a unique, high-quality product that represents the best choice for the patient and is not readily available online, then sales aimed at increasing revenue and the corresponding pricing are ethically justifiable.

title: “Doc, I Need a Smart Pill”: Requests for Neurologic Enhancement
case:
Dr. Warren, the only neurologist in a hardscrabble town of 7,000 residents, looked at his new patient and chewed his lip. They were sitting in a small examining room at Dr. Warren’s clinic. The patient, Mr. Conway, was a soft-spoken 28-year-old unemployed sales clerk who had just explained the reason for his visit: recently laid off, and with no other job prospects in sight, he wanted to attend graduate school. This would require him to take the Graduate Record Examination (GRE), but Mr. Conway said he would have “extreme difficulty” remaining focused for the full 4-hour length of the exam. He wanted Dr. Warren to prescribe something to help him stay focused and think better.
“Just temporarily, Dr. Warren,” the polite Mr. Conway said. “Just so I can do my best on the exam.”
Dr. Warren had listened to his patient’s story with great sympathy. Mr. Conway needed a scholarship to attend graduate school, and a low score on the test would spoil his chances. Based on a growing literature, modafinil might help Mr. Conway focus during the long test. Dr. Warren had explained to Mr. Conway that, because he did not have symptoms of attention deficit disorder (ADD) or other neurological problems, prescribing a cognitive-enhancement drug would be hard to justify.
Dr. Warren asked himself whether helping people without medical impairment perform better academically was an accepted goal of medicine. How strong was the evidence that the medication would improve Mr. Conway’s performance? Supposing it would, couldnotprescribing the drug be considered “harming” Mr. Conway, that is, making him worse off than he was now?
Alternatively, rebuffed by Dr. Warren, Mr. Conway might seek the desired drugs from a local family doctor or other nonneurologist who lacked experience with such medications and would provide him with a lower standard of care. But granting Mr. Conway’s wish could entail serious complications. First, Mr. Conway would receive a powerful psychotropic drug for a nonmedical reason. Mr. Conway predicted having trouble concentrating for the entire test, but that didn’t constitute real cognitive impairment in Dr. Warren’s opinion, given the protracted nature of the exam. Second, if Mr. Conway aced the test and received a scholarship, he might brag about the achievement to his family and friends, earning Dr. Warren a reputation for dispensing “smart drugs” and flooding him with other patients seeking prescriptions for even less legitimate reasons.
Finally, there was matter of Mr. Conway’s long-term goals. Delighted by his performance on the GRE, he might find himself “needing” more cognitive-enhancement drugs to stay sharp during long hours of graduate study. Writing papers, taking exams—it wouldn’t end with the GRE. He wouldn’t want the drug “ just temporarily.” He’d be back.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Warren, the sole neurologist in a rugged town of 7,000 residents, sat quietly across from his newest patient in the cramped exam room of his small clinic. Mr. Conway, a gentle-mannered 28-year-old who had recently lost his job as a sales clerk and faced bleak employment prospects, explained why he had come. With few other options, he hoped to attend graduate school, which meant he needed to take the Graduate Record Examination (GRE). Mr. Conway confessed that he would have “extreme difficulty” staying focused for the exam’s demanding four-hour duration. He asked Dr. Warren if he could prescribe something to help him concentrate and think more clearly.

“Just temporarily, Dr. Warren,” Mr. Conway added politely. “Just so I can do my best on the exam.”

Dr. Warren listened with empathy. He understood that Mr. Conway needed a strong GRE score to secure a scholarship—without it, his hopes for graduate school would collapse. Dr. Warren was aware of a growing body of research suggesting that modafinil might help people stay focused during lengthy tasks like the GRE. Still, he explained to Mr. Conway that, since he had no symptoms of attention deficit disorder (ADD) or any other neurological disorder, writing a prescription for a cognitive-enhancing medication would be difficult to justify medically.

Dr. Warren found himself pondering whether helping someone without a medical impairment perform better academically was truly within the scope of medical practice. Was the evidence strong enough that the medication would actually improve Mr. Conway’s test performance? And if it would, could refusing the prescription be considered as “harming” Mr. Conway by leaving him at a disadvantage?

Dr. Warren also considered what might happen if he said no. Mr. Conway could try to obtain the medication from a local family doctor or another non-specialist who lacked experience with such drugs, potentially exposing him to less careful oversight and a lower standard of care. On the other hand, if Dr. Warren agreed to the request, he would be prescribing a potent psychotropic drug for a nonmedical reason. In Dr. Warren’s assessment, Mr. Conway’s anticipated struggle to concentrate for the whole test did not amount to genuine cognitive impairment, especially given the exam’s length.

There were further risks. If Mr. Conway did exceptionally well on the GRE and secured a scholarship, he might proudly tell friends and relatives about his achievement—and about Dr. Warren’s role. Word could spread, and Dr. Warren feared he might gain a reputation as the neurologist willing to prescribe “smart drugs,” attracting other patients seeking similar prescriptions for even less justifiable reasons.

Finally, Dr. Warren thought about Mr. Conway’s future. If the GRE went well, Mr. Conway might feel compelled to use cognitive-enhancing drugs throughout graduate school—to write papers, take more exams, and meet every academic challenge. The request for medication would not be just “temporary.” Dr. Warren realized that Mr. Conway would likely return, looking for continued prescriptions to maintain his academic edge.

ethical_issues.question: Does enhancing academic performance in individuals without health impairments fall within the goals of medicine?
keypoints: The traditional goals of medicine include the prevention and treatment of disease, alleviation of suffering, patient education, and palliative care; they do not encompass enhancing academic performance in individuals without health impairments.

Assisting individuals without health impairments to improve academic performance falls within the second domain of medical activities, which, although not aligned with traditional medical goals, is socially and ethically permissible because it requires medical knowledge, serves other socially useful purposes, and does not compromise the profession’s core mission.

Prescribing cognitive-enhancement medications is analogous to aesthetic surgery and constitutes an ethically permissible but non-obligatory medical practice; the decision to prescribe should be based on the physician’s professional judgment and the specific circumstances of the patient.

title: Can Parents of a Child with Autism Refuse Treatment for Him?
case:
Dr. Pittman was nearing the end of her shift at a busy community clinic on a Friday afternoon. Her last appointment was with a new patient, Dayton, a 6-year-old boy who, according to his parents, had an earache. Dr. Pittman quickly diagnosed otitis media and talked with Dayton’s parents about treatment.
Dayton’s behavior troubled Dr. Pittman far more than his inflamed eardrum. He did not make eye contact or respond to her questions. He flinched whenever she approached him, cried out in fear when she peered in his ear with an otoscope, and hopped up and down, shaking his hands compulsively, several times during the visit. When Dr. Pittman questioned Dayton’s parents about his behavior, they told her he had been diagnosed with autism at age 4. His development, they said, was delayed.
She asked what treatment Dayton’s parents had sought for him, and the answer shocked her. They were members of the autism self-advocacy movement and believed that Dayton’s condition was simply an example of neurodiversity and was not pathologic. They clearly adored their son, doting on him during the clinic visit and telling Dr. Pittman how they home-schooled him after the public school system failed to meet his social and educational needs. They accepted Dayton as he was and were determined to provide him with lifetime care.
Dr. Pittman viewed Dayton’s situation differently. She knew that with proper therapy and medication his condition could improve considerably—but only if treatment were begun as soon as possible. She worked at a nearby autism clinic, where Dayton could probably qualify for long-term treatment. When she mentioned this to Dayton’s parents, they wanted nothing to do with it. They were adamant in their belief that Dayton’s condition required no medical intervention.
Dr. Pittman had encountered many adult patients with culture-based opinions about their health problems that she found hard to understand, but this was the first time she’d disagreed so fundamentally with parents about a situation that she believed would harm their child by limiting his future opportunities. She fought the urge to reprimand them for what she considered their neglect of his debilitating developmental problem. Did their treatment constitute child endangerment, she wondered? Would she be justified in contacting a child protection agency?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Pittman was wrapping up her hectic Friday shift at the bustling community clinic when her last patient of the day arrived: Dayton, a 6-year-old boy brought in by his parents for an earache. After a brief evaluation, Dr. Pittman quickly diagnosed Dayton with otitis media and began discussing treatment options with his parents.

Yet, it wasn’t Dayton’s ear that most concerned Dr. Pittman. Throughout the appointment, Dayton avoided eye contact and didn’t respond to her questions. Each time Dr. Pittman approached, he recoiled noticeably, and when she examined his ear with the otoscope, he cried out in fear. Periodically, Dayton would hop in place, shaking his hands in a repetitive, compulsive way. Troubled by these behaviors, Dr. Pittman gently inquired about Dayton’s development.

Dayton’s parents explained that he had been diagnosed with autism at the age of four and that his development was delayed. When Dr. Pittman asked what kind of support or therapies they had pursued, the parents’ response surprised her. They explained that they were strong advocates of the autism self-advocacy movement, viewing Dayton’s condition as an expression of neurodiversity rather than a disorder. Throughout the visit, their affection for Dayton was clear; they attended to him with patience and warmth, sharing that they had chosen to homeschool him after finding the public school system unable to accommodate his social and educational needs. They spoke with conviction about accepting Dayton as he was and providing for his needs themselves, both now and in the future.

Dr. Pittman, however, saw things differently. She knew from her experience at a local autism clinic that early intervention—including therapy and, in some cases, medication—could make a significant difference in outcomes for a child like Dayton, especially if begun promptly. She mentioned the clinic to Dayton’s parents, suggesting that he might benefit from long-term treatment services. But the parents firmly rejected the idea, insisting that Dayton did not require medical intervention, and reiterating their commitment to supporting him outside of medical systems.

Dr. Pittman had often encountered adult patients whose cultural perspectives on health differed from her own, but she had never faced such a fundamental disagreement with parents over a course of action that, in her view, could limit a child’s future possibilities. She struggled to suppress her urge to chastise them for what she saw as neglecting a serious developmental issue. Was this parental refusal putting Dayton at risk? Did it cross the line into child endangerment? Dr. Pittman found herself wondering whether she would be justified in contacting child protective services.

ethical_issues.question: Do parents have the right to refuse medical intervention for a child with autism, especially when such refusal may impact the child’s future well-being?
keypoints: Parents are generally regarded as the primary decision-makers for their children because they possess the most comprehensive understanding of the child’s fundamental interests and bear caregiving responsibilities; however, respect for parental choices is not absolute and must be balanced with the child’s interests and developing autonomy.

When parental decisions may expose the child to imminent and serious health risks or irreversible harm, the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence should take precedence over respect for parental autonomy, and physicians have a duty to intervene to protect the child’s welfare.

If a treatment is proven effective with manageable risks and no suitable alternatives exist, physicians have a justified basis to override parental refusal of treatment, provided that the severity and imminence of harm are carefully assessed.

Early intervention for autism heavily depends on active family involvement; coercive treatment approaches may provoke resistance, diminish therapeutic efficacy, and potentially lead to complete disengagement from medical care by the family.

Therefore, establishing a trusting and collaborative therapeutic alliance that respects family values and incrementally promotes the child’s well-being represents a more pragmatic and effective strategy.

ethical_issues.question: How can a balance be achieved between respecting parental autonomy and promoting the well-being of the child, especially in situations where treatment requires active parental involvement?
keypoints: Physicians should understand and respect the parents’ cultural values and perspectives regarding autism, avoid simplistic pathologization, and promote individualized care plans that incorporate diverse viewpoints.

Coercive treatment may exacerbate conflict between the physician and the family, reduce parental willingness to cooperate, and ultimately undermine Dayton’s long-term well-being; therefore, priority should be given to building trust and a therapeutic alliance to foster collaboration.

The therapeutic alliance is grounded in the shared commitment of the physician and parents to serve Dayton’s best interests, and is developed through ongoing communication and negotiation to identify mutually acceptable treatment options.

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances may a physician override parental refusal of treatment in order to ensure that a child is not placed at significant and imminent risk of harm?
keypoints: When parental decisions place the child at significant and imminent risk of serious harm, the physician should intervene immediately.
The refused intervention must be proven effective, low-risk, capable of preventing harm, and its anticipated benefits must clearly outweigh those of the option chosen by the parents.
If refusal of treatment is likely to cause serious and irreversible harm to the child’s current health or future autonomy, the physician is justified in intervening.
When there is no alternative that infringes less on parental autonomy and is more acceptable to the parents, the physician may override the parents’ decision.
State intervention is reasonable in similar circumstances, and such intervention would generally be accepted by most rational parents.

title: The Ethics of Diagnosing Nonepileptic Seizures with Placebo Infusion
case:
Ms. Lamonica was admitted for a neurological evaluation after experiencing 2 severe seizures. At 38, Ms. Lamonica was overweight, but otherwise in good health. All studies including electroencephalograms (EEG) were normal. Because her description of her seizures seemed to exclude epilepsy—she remained fully conscious during the events, for example, and experienced no confusion afterward—her team of neurologists led by Dr. Patel began to suspect that her episodes were nonepileptic seizures (NES). The physicians contemplated using a provocative test to confirm the diagnosis.
The test was controversial because it entailed deceiving the patient. Ms. Lamonica would have EEG electrodes attached to her scalp and an intravenous catheter inserted. Dr. Patel would then tell her he was administering a solution designed to provoke a seizure. In reality, the solution would be simple saline. If Ms. Lamonica had a seizure, Dr. Patel would stop the infusion, tell her the drug was leaving her system, and watch for a concomitant end to the seizure. If no abnormal electrical activity was seen during a seizure, the diagnosis of NES would be confirmed.
An estimated 10 to 20 percent of patients who are hospitalized for seizures or treated at epilepsy clinics are suspected to have NES; some have epilepsy and NES. Nonepileptic seizures are treated with psychiatric rather than neurological interventions. While epilepsy can often be managed with medications, pharmacologic treatment for NES tends to be ineffective. Anticonvulsants are inappropriate. Psychotherapy is useful for some patients, but many remain unimproved long after diagnosis.
The key to distinguishing NES from epilepsy is whether EEG evidence of a true seizure is recorded by EEG during a typical spell. To avoid keeping the patient attached to the EEG machine for hours or days in hopes of witnessing an episode, some physicians choose to employ the so-called provocative saline infusion—the sham test described above—to expedite the diagnosis. Provocative saline infusion is thus a nocebo, a drug the patient perceives as harmful, which in Ms. Lamonica’s case would mean seizure-inducing.
Dr. Patel decided to administer the provocative saline infusion to Ms. Lamonica, and she promptly had a seizure. During the seizure, her EEG remained normal. She was therefore diagnosed with NES.
Afterward, Dr. Patel wrestled with the question of whether to tell Ms. Lamonica that the provocative test had been a ruse. Though the physical risks associated with a saline infusion are minimal and the definitive diagnosis would help her by obviating the need for daily anticonvulsant drug treatment, he regretted the necessity of deceiving the patient, and felt he should reveal the truth.
case_rewrite:
Ms. Lamonica, a 38-year-old woman with a history of being overweight but otherwise in good health, was admitted to the hospital following two severe seizure episodes. Seeking answers, she underwent a comprehensive neurological evaluation, including electroencephalograms (EEGs), all of which yielded normal results. However, her account of the seizures raised questions: during the episodes, Ms. Lamonica never lost consciousness or experienced post-event confusion, features atypical for epilepsy. Dr. Patel, the neurologist leading her care, and his team began to suspect that Ms. Lamonica was experiencing nonepileptic seizures (NES) rather than epileptic ones.

Faced with diagnostic uncertainty, Dr. Patel and his colleagues considered a controversial approach: the provocative saline infusion test. This test involved deceiving the patient. Ms. Lamonica would be fitted with EEG electrodes and an intravenous catheter. Dr. Patel would tell her he was injecting a solution meant to induce a seizure, but this solution would actually be harmless saline. If Ms. Lamonica exhibited a seizure in response, Dr. Patel would halt the infusion, inform her the "drug" was leaving her system, and observe whether the seizure resolved. An absence of abnormal EEG activity during such a seizure would confirm the diagnosis of NES.

NES accounts for an estimated 10 to 20 percent of patients hospitalized for seizures or treated at epilepsy clinics; some individuals may have both epilepsy and NES. Unlike epilepsy, which often responds well to medication, NES is best approached through psychiatric treatment, as anticonvulsants are generally ineffective. Although psychotherapy can benefit some NES patients, many do not achieve significant improvement, even after diagnosis.

The crucial step in differentiating NES from epilepsy is capturing a typical episode on EEG to determine if there is true seizure activity. To avoid the inconvenience of prolonged EEG monitoring in hopes of recording a spontaneous event, some physicians have turned to the provocative saline infusion—a sham test designed to provoke a seizure through suggestion. This method, in Ms. Lamonica’s situation, would involve her believing she is receiving a seizure-inducing drug, when in fact it is only saline.

Dr. Patel proceeded with the provocative saline infusion. Ms. Lamonica promptly experienced a seizure during the test, but her EEG remained normal. The results confirmed a diagnosis of NES.

Afterward, Dr. Patel faced a moral dilemma: should he disclose to Ms. Lamonica that the test was a deception? Though the saline posed negligible physical risk and the diagnosis would spare her from unnecessary anticonvulsant medication, Dr. Patel struggled with the ethical weight of having misled his patient and questioned whether he owed her the full truth about the diagnostic process.

ethical_issues.question: Is the use of a deceptive test necessary for the diagnosis of nonepileptic seizures?
keypoints: The diagnosis of nonepileptic seizures (NES) generally does not require the use of deceptive testing; routine non-deceptive provocative measures—including monitoring of sleep-wake cycles, suggestion therapy, photic stimulation, and hyperventilation—have been demonstrated to be effective and safe.

Studies have shown no significant difference in the detection rates of NES between routine non-deceptive provocative procedures and the deceptive saline infusion test, indicating that the deceptive saline test is neither necessary nor diagnostically superior.
The deceptive saline infusion test carries risks of false-positive and false-negative results, which may lead to misdiagnosis or missed diagnosis, thereby increasing diagnostic uncertainty.

Employing standard diagnostic protocols without deception not only avoids ethical controversies but also preserves the patient-physician trust relationship and reduces psychological burden and potential harm to both patients and physicians.

ethical_issues.question: Should medical practice standards permitting the use of deceptive testing be established?
keypoints: Intentional deception of patients violates the fundamental ethical principles of mutual trust and respect inherent in the patient-physician relationship, potentially undermining the therapeutic value of that relationship and its long-term foundation of trust.

The deceptive saline infusion test is not necessary for the diagnosis of nonepileptic seizures (NES) and carries risks of false positive and false negative results, which may lead to misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment, causing both short-term and long-term medical and psychological harm.

The American Medical Association Council on Ethical and Judicial Affairs explicitly states that the use of placebos without patient informed consent may undermine trust, compromise the patient-physician relationship, and result in medical harm; placebos should only be used for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes with the patient’s full informed consent.

This deceptive test has been prohibited by American medical practice standards and abandoned by the majority of epilepsy centers, reflecting its ethical and clinical unacceptability and indicating that it should not be incorporated into medical practice standards.

ethical_issues.question: After conducting a deceptive test, should the physician disclose the true nature of the test to the patient?
keypoints: Physicians should disclose the true nature of the test to patients, as intentional deception violates the fundamental principles of trust and respect that underlie the patient-physician relationship.
Truth-telling reflects respect for the patient’s dignity and autonomy, and physicians have a fiduciary duty to fulfill this obligation of disclosure.

Deception may lead patients to distrust physicians and medical information, undermining the therapeutic value and long-term foundation of the patient-physician relationship; it may also trigger a broader loss of trust in other physicians, negatively impacting the patient’s overall medical experience and adherence.
Acts of deception damage the physician’s professional ethical image and sense of self-worth, eroding the ethical foundation of integrity within the medical profession.

title: Pediatric Obesity, Statin Use, and the Goals of Medicine
case:
When Jessica was 8 years old, her pediatrician, Dr. Rosen, recommended that she undergo comprehensive nutrition and exercise counseling to reduce her risk of future morbidity and mortality. She was overweight for her age, and there was family history of high blood pressure and coronary artery disease. Jessica’s parents took Dr. Rosen’s warnings seriously; they were both overweight and dealing with high blood pressure and diabetes, and saw their daughter heading down the same path. As a family, they attended classes and made some nutritional and behavioral changes, but with no real clinical success; Jessica’s weight gain was still above the normal curve. Two years later, Jessica and her parents returned to Dr. Rosen’s office. Her parents explained that it was difficult for the family to maintain the diet all the time or to exercise on schedule. Dr. Rosen agreed the task was difficult, but reemphasized its importance. He also told them that Jessica now had high cholesterol.
Worried that, with as little progress as she had made, Jessica would end up just like her parents and grandparents—overweight and struggling with high cholesterol, high blood pressure, diabetes, and coronary artery disease—her parents asked Dr. Rosen if Jessica could start on a medication like prevastatin to try to lower her cholesterol. They had seen advertisements for it that said the medications—known as statins (such as Lipitor)—could now be used in children. They said they also planned to speak to other doctors about aggressive interventions such as bariatric surgery.
case_rewrite:
When Jessica was 8 years old, her pediatrician, Dr. Rosen, advised a comprehensive approach to nutrition and exercise to reduce her risk of serious health problems later in life. Jessica was overweight for her age, and her family history included high blood pressure and coronary artery disease. Jessica’s parents, both of whom struggled with overweight, high blood pressure, and diabetes themselves, took Dr. Rosen’s recommendations to heart. Determined to help their daughter avoid similar health issues, the family enrolled in classes together and made efforts to change their eating habits and routines. Despite their commitment, they found it difficult to sustain these changes, and Jessica’s weight gain continued to outpace normal expectations.

Two years later, Jessica and her parents returned to Dr. Rosen’s office. Her parents candidly explained the challenges they faced: maintaining strict dietary guidelines and regular exercise was harder than they had anticipated, and they found themselves unable to consistently follow through. Dr. Rosen empathized with their struggle but reaffirmed the necessity of these lifestyle modifications. He also informed them that Jessica’s recent lab work showed elevated cholesterol levels.

Concerned that Jessica was already experiencing some of the same health issues that had affected previous generations in the family, her parents voiced their fears that she might develop high cholesterol, high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease, just as they had. They asked Dr. Rosen if Jessica might be a candidate for a medication like prevastatin to help lower her cholesterol, referencing advertisements they had seen describing the use of statins, such as Lipitor, in children. Additionally, they mentioned their intention to consult with other physicians about more aggressive interventions, including the possibility of bariatric surgery.

ethical_issues.question: In light of Jessica’s ongoing difficulty adhering to diet and exercise regimens, how should the physician balance the ethical obligation to recommend effective medical interventions with the duty to ensure that Jessica and her family understand the limitations and potential risks of pharmacologic therapy, in order to determine the most appropriate course of treatment?
keypoints: The physician should acknowledge that, despite optimal efforts at lifestyle modification, Jessica and her family have struggled with adherence and have not achieved the desired clinical outcomes; thus, it is ethically appropriate to consider secondary interventions, such as pharmacologic therapy, to address her elevated cardiovascular risk.

The physician has a duty to balance the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence by recommending evidence-based treatments while ensuring that Jessica and her family are fully informed about the benefits, limitations, and potential risks of statin therapy, thereby supporting shared decision-making in the best interests of the patient.

A combined approach may be ethically justified, wherein continued emphasis is placed on lifestyle interventions alongside the judicious initiation of statin therapy to lower cholesterol and mitigate long-term cardiovascular risk.

The physician must uphold the principle of respect for autonomy by clearly communicating the mechanism of action, potential adverse effects, and limitations of statin medications, thereby preventing misconceptions or overreliance on pharmacologic treatment.

The physician should advocate for a holistic and integrated approach to Jessica’s health management, addressing multiple risk factors and promoting overall well-being, rather than focusing narrowly on the modification of a single clinical parameter.

title: Infective Endocarditis in the Intravenous Drug User
case:
Looking at the chart on the way to visit a new patient in the cardiac intensive care unit, Dr. Collins saw that Mr. Addison had been admitted from the emergency department with a diagnosis of presumed infective endocarditis. When he walked into the room, Dr. Collins recognized Mr. Addison. He had cared for him 5 years earlier, when Mr. Addison had had a mitral valve replacement.
At that time, Mr. Addison had been 40 years old and had a history of intravenous drug use. After the surgery, he had entered a drug rehabilitation program and had remained drug-free (confirmed by urine toxicology screening).
When Dr. Collins began interviewing Mr. Addison, the patient admitted having relapsed into drug use, and, Dr. Collins noted, there were fresh tracks on Mr. Addison’s arms. The echocardiogram from the emergency department showed vegetations on the mitral valve consistent with recurrent infective endocarditis.
The typical clinical management approach would be to examine the patient and recommend that a surgeon be consulted to discuss emergency valve replacement, but Dr. Collins paused. Mr. Addison’s relapse was almost certainly a direct result of his renewed drug use. Dr. Collins could just turf the case to the cardiac surgeon and leave the decision up to him or her, but he wondered whether he had some responsibility to intervene at this point and ask some serious questions about the use of medical resources and money to keep patching up people who abused their bodies, in this instance, unlawfully.
case_rewrite:
As Dr. Collins made his way through the cardiac intensive care unit, he glanced over the chart of his new patient, Mr. Addison, who had just been admitted from the emergency department with a working diagnosis of presumed infective endocarditis. As he entered the patient’s room, Dr. Collins immediately recognized Mr. Addison—five years earlier, he had managed his care during a mitral valve replacement.

Back then, Mr. Addison was a 40-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use. Following his valve surgery, he had entered a drug rehabilitation program and maintained sobriety, a fact verified by regular urine toxicology screens.

Now, as Dr. Collins sat down to speak with him, Mr. Addison confessed that he had relapsed and resumed drug use. Dr. Collins noted the presence of fresh needle marks on Mr. Addison’s arms. An echocardiogram performed in the emergency department revealed vegetations on the mitral valve, consistent with a recurrence of infective endocarditis.

The standard clinical course would be to assess Mr. Addison and recommend evaluation by a cardiac surgeon to discuss the possibility of another emergency valve replacement. However, Dr. Collins hesitated. He realized that Mr. Addison’s return to intravenous drug use had almost certainly contributed to this new infection. Dr. Collins wondered whether he should simply refer the case to the cardiac surgery team and allow them to make the decision, or whether he himself bore responsibility to consider more deeply the implications of repeatedly utilizing significant medical resources for individuals who, in this case, had engaged in unlawful behaviors that harmed their own health.

He paused, reflecting on his obligations—to Mr. Addison as a patient, and to the broader healthcare system—while considering how best to proceed.

ethical_issues.question: In the case of Mr. Addison’s relapse into drug use leading to recurrent infective endocarditis, should the physician continue to provide him with an expensive valve replacement surgery?
keypoints: They should avoid discriminatory treatment based on patient behaviors such as intravenous drug use, recognizing that these behaviors are not fundamentally different from other health-related behaviors, such as smoking or poor dietary choices.

Collins should actively engage in the medical decision-making process and assume appropriate responsibility for Mr. Addison’s care, rather than shifting the burden of decision-making solely to the cardiac surgeon.

Addison’s relapse into intravenous drug use results in recurrent infective endocarditis, physicians remain ethically obligated to offer necessary medical treatment. The concept of medical futility is not absolute, and substance use disorder is a treatable medical condition; emerging pharmacological and psychological interventions can significantly improve long-term abstinence rates.

At present, payers (including insurance companies and society at large) do not ration medical resources based on patient behavior, and physicians do not possess the authority to make allocation decisions on behalf of these entities.

ethical_issues.question: When physicians encounter patients who have relapsed into drug use, should the protection of societal resources take precedence over the patients’ treatment needs?
keypoints: Physicians have an ethical obligation to place the welfare of their patients above their own self-interest and obligations to other groups, steadfastly advocating for patients’ rights.
Physicians do not have the authority to make decisions on behalf of funding entities (such as insurance companies or society) regarding the allocation of medical resources based on patient behavior.

Ethically, refusing treatment to patients who have relapsed into drug use is not substantively different from withholding care from patients with poorly controlled diabetes; physicians have a duty to provide necessary treatment.

title: Cardiac Catheterization and Defensive Medicine
case:
Mr. Damon, a 62-year-old man with known coronary artery disease and a long history of angina, came to see his cardiologist, Dr. Ross, with chest pain—again. Such complaints had been typical during Mr. Damon’s clinic visits over the last two years. Each episode was brought on by physical exertion and, just as predictably, was relieved with rest and a nitroglycerin tablet. Previous stress tests and cardiac catheterizations had shown the presence of stable angina without major blockages or areas of ischemia. Dr. Ross did his usual evaluation of Mr. Damon and concluded that Mr. Damon was having his typical angina, needed no changes to his medications, and did not need invasive cardiovascular testing.
As he was about to send Mr. Damon home, he remembered a fellow cardiologist who, in a similar clinical situation, sent a patient home without a cardiac catheterization. That patient died shortly thereafter of a heart attack, and the patient’s family attempted to sue the physician for malpractice. Dr. Ross’s clinical judgment told him that further testing was unnecessary, but he was concerned that such judgment alone might not hold up in court. While he knew that many of his colleagues would agree with his clinical assessment, he also knew that others would order a catheterization to protect themselves from potential litigation. Dr. Ross was worried about the complication risk of feeding a catheter up through the femoral artery into the heart and injecting dye into the coronary arteries, and he also wondered about the added strain on Mr. Damon’s finances.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Damon, a 62-year-old man with established coronary artery disease and a longstanding history of angina, arrived for another visit with his cardiologist, Dr. Ross, complaining once more of chest discomfort. Over the past two years, these episodes had become a familiar pattern in Mr. Damon’s clinic visits: the pain consistently arose with exertion and reliably subsided after rest and a nitroglycerin tablet. Prior stress tests and cardiac catheterizations had shown findings consistent with stable angina, revealing no significant blockages or evidence of ischemia.

During this appointment, Dr. Ross conducted his standard assessment and determined that Mr. Damon was experiencing his usual stable angina. He concluded that there was no need to adjust Mr. Damon’s medication regimen or to pursue further invasive cardiac testing at this time.

However, as Dr. Ross prepared to send Mr. Damon home, a troubling memory surfaced. He recalled how a colleague of his, faced with a patient presenting in a nearly identical clinical situation, had decided against ordering a cardiac catheterization. Tragically, that patient died soon after from a myocardial infarction, and the family sought to sue the physician for malpractice. Although Dr. Ross’s clinical judgment told him that additional testing for Mr. Damon was unnecessary, he felt uneasy about the prospect of relying solely on his own judgment if a rare adverse outcome were to occur. He recognized that while many of his peers would support his conservative approach, others might recommend a catheterization primarily out of concern for their own legal protection rather than for the patient’s benefit.

Dr. Ross weighed the risks associated with an invasive procedure—threading a catheter through the femoral artery to the heart and injecting contrast dye into the coronary arteries—knowing that such interventions carry complications. He also considered the financial burden an unnecessary procedure might place on Mr. Damon. Torn between the desire to do what was best for his patient and the worry over potential litigation, Dr. Ross found himself confronting a difficult ethical dilemma.

ethical_issues.question: When faced with the possibility of legal litigation, should physicians perform unnecessary invasive procedures to protect themselves rather than prioritize the interests of the patient?
keypoints: Physicians should not perform unnecessary invasive procedures solely to avoid legal litigation, as this constitutes defensive medicine and violates core principles of medical ethics.

The principle of nonmaleficence requires physicians to avoid directly causing harm or imposing risk; any examination or treatment must be necessary, reasonable, and provide substantive benefit to the patient.

The health and welfare of the patient must always take precedence over the physician’s financial, political, or legal concerns; defensive medical practices contravene this fundamental ethical principle.

Physicians should base their decisions on professional judgment and evidence-based medicine, carefully balancing risks and benefits to ensure that medical decisions serve the patient’s best interests rather than merely mitigating legal liability.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians ensure that patients fully understand the potential risks and benefits of a proposed procedure during the informed consent process, thereby safeguarding the patient’s autonomous decision-making?
keypoints: Physicians should ensure that patients fully understand the potential risks, benefits, and uncertainties of the proposed intervention in order to uphold their autonomy in decision-making.
Physicians ought to enhance physician-patient communication, emphasize patient education, and promote meaningful patient involvement in the clinical decision-making process.
Physicians must candidly disclose the risks, benefits, and their own concerns regarding the procedure to facilitate shared decision-making between physician and patient.

In situations of clinical uncertainty or multiple reasonable options, the final management plan should respect the patient’s autonomous choice based on their individual risk assessment and personal values.
The patient’s health and well-being should take precedence over the physician’s financial, legal, or other non-clinical considerations.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Mr. Damon’s case and the prevalence of defensive medicine, how can Dr. Ross ethically perform a risk-benefit analysis under conditions of clinical uncertainty and engage in shared decision-making with his patient?
keypoints: Physicians should proactively seek consultation from colleagues when clinical uncertainty is high, utilizing multidisciplinary expertise to optimize the assessment of risks and benefits.

Physicians must disclose relevant risks, benefits, and their own concerns to patients comprehensively and transparently, facilitating the patient’s full understanding of their condition and treatment options.
Enhancing physician-patient communication is a low-cost and risk-free effective strategy that helps build trust, improve the therapeutic relationship, and reduce disputes.

Respecting patients’ risk tolerance and personal values is essential; physicians should support patients in participating in and ultimately deciding on their treatment plans based on their own judgment, even when it diverges from the clinician’s clinical preference.

Through systematic patient education and meaningful involvement in decision-making, physicians can not only improve the quality of care and patient satisfaction but also strengthen their own legal protection.

title: Conducting Clinical Research during Disasters
case:
On an early summer morning, a 7.8-magnitude earthquake devastated the northwestern United States. Homes and commercial dwellings were rendered uninhabitable, and the local medical infrastructure was overwhelmed with critically ill and injured patients. A large fire originating in a local warehouse spread to numerous surrounding structures, afflicting many workers with smoke exposure as well as acute lung injury (ALI) resulting from smoke inhalation (inhalational lung injury [ILI]).
Dr. Carl, a respected and accomplished critical care physician whose research is federally funded, responded with a non-governmental medical relief group, accompanied by a group of residents and fellows. Dr. Carl was selected to treat patients and direct an ICU erected on-site on the basis of expertise with ALI and previous disaster relief efforts.
Dr. Carl had pioneered a novel but still experimental approach for treating ILI using nebulized N-acetylcysteine and nebulized heparin (NAC-Hep). A major limitation to prior research was the small sample sizes of the studies, owing to the small number of ILI patients in the general population. These prior studies suggested that the NAC-Hep may decrease mortality and duration of mechanical ventilation.
Amidst the controlled chaos of the mobile ICU, Dr. Carl instituted NAC-Hep treatment in addition to standard ILI treatment in some, but not all, ILI patients. The fellows were instructed to keep more detailed records on the ILI patients than on other patients. A fellow with whom Dr. Carl had a good rapport expressed discomfort with participating in research that had not been approved by an investigational review board (IRB) and in which patients and patient surrogates had not given informed consent.
Dr. Carl professed not to know of any laws prohibiting conducting research under such circumstances and asserted that, by shortening ventilation times, their team might be able to treat and save more patients, and, moreover, the results of this project might have far-reaching implications for the treatment of ILI patients, possibly saving many more lives. Despite feeling morally conflicted, the fellow continued to treat patients as directed by Dr. Carl but questioned the ethics of this course of action and feared potential repercussions for involvement in the study.
case_rewrite:
On an early summer morning, a catastrophic 7.8-magnitude earthquake struck the northwestern United States. The disaster left homes and businesses in ruins, and the local healthcare system was immediately inundated with waves of critically ill and injured survivors. As chaos unfolded, a massive fire erupted at a warehouse, spreading rapidly to neighboring buildings and engulfing the area in thick, toxic smoke. Many workers and residents suffered from smoke inhalation, leading to acute lung injury (ALI) and inhalational lung injury (ILI).

Dr. Carl, a widely respected critical care physician with significant federal research funding, joined the disaster response as part of a non-governmental medical relief team. Accompanied by several residents and fellows, Dr. Carl was tasked with treating patients and leading an improvised ICU at the disaster site, selected specifically for his expertise in ALI and his previous experience in disaster medicine.

Dr. Carl had recently developed, but not yet fully validated, a novel treatment protocol for ILI using nebulized N-acetylcysteine and nebulized heparin (NAC-Hep). Previous studies on this regimen had been limited by small patient numbers, but early findings suggested that the combination might reduce both mortality and time on mechanical ventilation.

In the midst of the hectic, makeshift ICU, Dr. Carl implemented the NAC-Hep treatment alongside standard care for some—but not all—of the ILI patients. He instructed his fellows to collect especially detailed records on those receiving the NAC-Hep therapy, compared to other patients. One fellow, who had a good working relationship with Dr. Carl, voiced concern about participating in what felt like unapproved research: there had been no review by an investigational review board (IRB), and neither patients nor their surrogates had provided informed consent to experimental therapy.

Dr. Carl responded that he was unaware of any laws explicitly prohibiting research in such emergency situations. He argued that if their approach shortened ventilation times, it could allow their ICU to treat and potentially save more patients overall. Additionally, Dr. Carl emphasized that the data they could gather might have significant implications, possibly benefiting countless future victims of ILI. Despite these justifications, the fellow remained uneasy about the ethics of the situation and worried about the potential consequences of their involvement in a study lacking appropriate oversight and consent. Nonetheless, the fellow continued to provide care as directed by Dr. Carl, wrestling internally with the moral and professional dilemmas at hand.

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically justifiable to conduct the described research without obtaining informed consent?
keypoints: Informed consent is the cornerstone of human subjects protection and must respect individuals’ bodily autonomy and their right to refuse interventions.

The impracticability waiver requires that the research involve only minimal risk and not adversely affect the rights and welfare of subjects; in this case, the experimental treatment likely exceeds minimal risk.

Even if the research meets criteria for any informed consent waiver, the determination must be made by an independent Institutional Review Board (IRB); researchers are not authorized to make this decision unilaterally.

The emergency research waiver entails multiple stringent conditions, including demonstrating the necessity of the research and the uniqueness of the participant population, community consultation and informing potential subjects, and diligent efforts to obtain consent from subjects or their proxies; none of these conditions are fulfilled in this case.

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically permissible to conduct experimental research on humans during a humanitarian crisis without IRB review?
keypoints: Conducting human subjects research during humanitarian crises must strictly adhere to the ethical principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice, ensuring the fundamental rights and welfare of research participants.

Initiating human subjects research without approval from an Institutional Review Board (IRB) constitutes a serious violation of ethical standards and regulations, is unethical, and may result in legal liability.

Federal regulations explicitly require that all research involving human subjects undergo IRB review; in disaster settings, participants constitute a prototypical vulnerable population, and regulatory protections are even more stringent, making IRB review both urgent and essential.

Although disaster situations may provide valuable opportunities for research on rare diseases and emergency treatments, such research must never come at the expense of participants’ rights and interests, and must be conducted in compliance with ethical and legal standards.

Formal ethical review processes safeguard the rights and interests of research participants through transparent and consistent mechanisms, mitigate potential risks, and maintain public trust in human subjects research, which is foundational to the ongoing conduct and societal acceptance of such research.

Dr. Carl’s failure to comply with regulatory and ethical requirements risks violating participants’ rights to informed consent, exacerbating their vulnerability, and undermining the professional integrity of the medical team, potentially resulting in legal action and a crisis of public trust.

title: The Patient-Physician Relationship in Quarantine
case:
Dr. Lee was a physician in a large urban medical center in New York. He received notification from his institution’s director of disaster preparedness that a transatlantic flight originating in Asia had been diverted over concern of a passenger’s displaying symptoms of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), a highly contagious and potentially life-threatening airborne infection caused by the SARS-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV). Upon landing in New York City, all passengers were transported to Dr. Lee’s medical facility and placed under mandatory quarantine. In accord with Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines, exposed individuals would remain in quarantine for up to 10 days after the most recent patient’s development of symptoms. Following the hospital’s disaster preparedness protocol, Dr. Lee reported for duty to the designated quarantine ward.
Among the 57 passengers under quarantine was a 28-year-old man, Joshua, who was returning from his temporary residence in Hong Kong for the purpose of donating bone marrow for his younger brother with advanced leukemia. Joshua was the only living donor match identified for his brother; he insisted that he must be allowed to leave for that purpose. He was not released and remained under mandatory quarantine. Over the subsequent days, Joshua spent much of his time coordinating a donation schedule to correspond with his expected release from quarantine.
On the morning of the tenth day, an elderly patient with diabetes developed a cough with mild dyspnea. She admitted she had been experiencing myalgias and subjective fever for 2 days, but had not alerted the staff for fear of extending quarantine. The newly symptomatic woman was removed from the general quarantine population, and those quarantined were informed of the new 10-day extension. Joshua pleaded with Dr. Lee to release him so that he could provide a life-saving bone marrow donation to his only brother.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Lee worked as a physician at a major urban hospital in New York City. One afternoon, he received urgent notice from the hospital’s disaster preparedness director: a transatlantic flight originating in Asia had been diverted to New York after reports that a passenger was exhibiting symptoms consistent with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), a highly contagious and potentially fatal airborne illness caused by SARS-CoV. Upon arrival, all passengers from the flight were transported to Dr. Lee’s facility and placed under strict mandatory quarantine. According to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) protocols, these individuals would be quarantined for up to 10 days following the onset of symptoms in the most recent patient. Following standard disaster protocols, Dr. Lee went on shift in the assigned quarantine ward.

Among the 57 individuals quarantined was Joshua, a 28-year-old man who had been living temporarily in Hong Kong. Joshua had flown to New York specifically to donate bone marrow for his younger brother, who was suffering from advanced leukemia. He was the only identified living donor match for his brother. Joshua repeatedly insisted on being allowed to leave so he could proceed with the donation, emphasizing the urgency and gravity of his brother’s condition. However, he was not permitted to exit the quarantine and was required to remain in isolation with the other passengers. Over the following days, Joshua devoted his time to coordinating the bone marrow donation schedule in hopes that it would coincide with his anticipated release date.

On the morning of the tenth day, an elderly woman in the quarantine unit—who had diabetes—developed a cough and mild shortness of breath. She admitted to staff that she had been experiencing muscle aches and subjective fevers for the previous two days, but had hesitated to report her symptoms out of fear that the quarantine would be extended. Once her symptoms were disclosed, she was transferred out of the general quarantine area, and all quarantined individuals were informed that the quarantine period would be extended by 10 more days due to the new potential exposure. Upon receiving this news, Joshua became distraught and pleaded with Dr. Lee for release so he could fulfill his role as his brother’s only bone marrow donor, potentially saving his sibling’s life.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of public health quarantine, does a physician have an ethical responsibility to inform patients of their rights and assist them in exercising those rights?
keypoints: Lee’s primary ethical obligation is to address the predicament of quarantined patients and to safeguard their overall well-being, including physical, psychological, and social aspects.

Lee should ensure that quarantined individuals are fully informed of their rights, such as understanding the quarantine protocols, the appeals process, and the option to request a review by the hospital ethics committee, and should support them in exercising these rights appropriately.

Providing information and assistance to quarantined patients in exercising their rights does not compromise public health or safety; conversely, withholding such information would contravene core principles of medical ethics and the protection of patient autonomy and rights.

ethical_issues.question: During quarantine, should physicians assist patients in seeking alternative solutions to address changes in medical plans caused by the quarantine, such as identifying backup donors?
keypoints: Physicians have a responsibility to attend to the overall well-being of their patients, including changes to medical plans caused by quarantine and the associated psychosocial impacts.

Physicians should assist patients in planning for the possibility of quarantine extension while complying with legal and public health regulations, and coordinate with the patient’s brother’s attending physicians to explore alternative options (such as backup donors).
Physicians ought to actively advocate for patients’ rights by seeking solutions that balance individual interests with public safety, aiming for mutually beneficial outcomes for all parties involved.

title: Mandated Influenza Vaccines and Health Care Workers’ Autonomy
case:
Dr. Ziad, a New York City physician, received a memo from her employer stating that, in accordance with a new hospital policy, she was required to receive both the seasonal influenza and novel H1N1 influenza vaccines. “Failure to comply by the specified deadline may result in disciplinary action,” the memo said, “which could include termination of employment.”
Dr. Ziad was concerned. She had, at times in the past, received the seasonal influenza vaccination, but had not planned to receive the H1N1 vaccine this season. It was her opinion that the H1N1 vaccine had been hastily prepared without appropriate clinical testing. Moreover, it seemed to her that the policy had a certain lack of regard for autonomy that she found very worrisome. She spoke to her departmental chairman to clarify the mandate and to express concern over the ethics and legality of such a policy. Dr. Ziad was informed that the policy stemmed from a September 2009 New York State mandate that all practicing physicians be vaccinated against both seasonal and H1N1 influenza [1]. He explained that the only exemption in this regulation was for cases of true medical contraindication. He emphasized that her failure to comply could result in termination of her hospital privileges or employment.
Dr. Ziad left the meeting dissatisfied and still unconvinced of the ethics of such a mandate. Did her ethical duties as a health care professional override her individual rights to determine her own health care?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Ziad, a physician practicing in New York City, received a memo from her employer outlining a new hospital policy: she was now required to receive both the seasonal influenza vaccine and the novel H1N1 influenza vaccine. The memo made the consequences clear: “Failure to comply by the specified deadline may result in disciplinary action, which could include termination of employment.”

This directive left Dr. Ziad troubled. While she had sometimes opted for the seasonal influenza vaccine in previous years, she had not intended to receive the H1N1 vaccine this season. Dr. Ziad felt that the H1N1 vaccine had been developed too quickly and lacked sufficient clinical testing for her comfort. Beyond her concerns about the vaccine itself, she was unsettled by what she saw as a disregard for her personal autonomy in the new policy. Wanting clarification, Dr. Ziad met with her departmental chairman to discuss the mandate and to voice her ethical and legal concerns about such a requirement.

During their conversation, Dr. Ziad’s chairman informed her that the policy originated from a September 2009 New York State mandate requiring all practicing physicians to be vaccinated against both seasonal and H1N1 influenza. He told her that the only permitted exemption was in cases of genuine medical contraindication. He further stressed that noncompliance could result in the loss of her hospital privileges or even her employment.

Dr. Ziad left the meeting dissatisfied, still questioning the ethical justification for the mandate. She wondered whether her ethical responsibilities as a health care professional should take precedence over her individual right to make her own health care decisions.

ethical_issues.question: In influenza vaccination policies, should an opt-out mechanism be implemented to respect the autonomy of health care workers?
keypoints: Purely voluntary vaccination programs (opt-in) have limited effectiveness and struggle to achieve ideal vaccine coverage rates, prompting exploration of more effective alternatives.

Mandatory vaccination policies may be perceived as coercive infringements on health care workers’ autonomy, especially when linked to severe sanctions such as termination of employment, raising ethical and legal controversies.

Implementing a non-mandatory but default vaccination opt-out mechanism can increase vaccination rates while simultaneously fulfilling the health care system’s duties of beneficence and nonmaleficence, and respecting health care workers’ autonomy.

Opt-out mechanisms have demonstrated effectiveness in other public health domains, such as organ donation programs in certain European countries, and thus hold valuable lessons for influenza vaccination strategies.

There exists a complex ethical balance between health care workers’ professional obligation to protect patients from harm and their individual right to refuse treatment; given individual differences and contextual variability, this balance is difficult to generalize, and opt-out programs offer a more balanced resolution.

ethical_issues.question: Should the professional ethical obligations of health care workers override their individual right to medical autonomy?
keypoints: Health care workers, based on the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence, have an ethical responsibility to protect patient safety and should prioritize receiving influenza vaccination to reduce the risk of nosocomial transmission.

Respect for individual rights and autonomy is a core principle of medical ethics; competent health care workers have the right to make their own decisions regarding medical interventions, including whether or not to receive vaccination.

There exists an ethical tension between the professional obligations of health care workers and their individual autonomy, necessitating a balance between individual rights and the interests of public health.

Implementing a noncompulsory but opt-out vaccination mechanism can help increase vaccination rates while simultaneously respecting health care workers’ autonomy and fulfilling the health care system’s duties of beneficence and nonmaleficence, making it ethically preferable to mandatory vaccination programs.
