title: Homophobic Jokes and Patient Care
case:
Melinda is in the midst of her third-year rotations. She has been following a patient, Debbie, who is on the medicine service recovering from pneumonia and found out during her last admission that she is HIV positive. Melinda noticed that Debbie rarely has visitors, so she has spent most of her downtime visiting with her. Debbie has told Melinda much about her personal life, in particular the difficult time she had revealing her HIV status to her partner of 10 years.
One day while Melinda was writing a progress note, she overheard several residents making fun of Debbie. One resident joked that he couldn’t figure out how Debbie acquired HIV, because “by the looks of it” she had been a lesbian her entire life. Another resident quipped that Debbie’s haircut and clothing were “dead giveaways.” A third said sarcastically, “Hey, whatever floats your boat, right?” and they all laughed. It bothered Melinda to hear the residents talking about Debbie in this way, in part because of the close relationship she had developed with her. But Melinda didn’t know whether to say anything to the residents or not. What if Debbie had heard? What if anyone had heard?
case_rewrite:
Melinda, a third-year medical student, is in the middle of her clinical rotations. She has been closely following a patient named Debbie, who is currently on the medicine service recovering from a bout of pneumonia. During Debbie’s previous hospital admission, she learned that she is HIV positive. Melinda, having noticed that Debbie seldom receives visitors, has taken the time to sit with her during breaks, and over the past several days, Debbie has opened up to Melinda about her personal struggles—especially the challenges she faced disclosing her HIV status to her partner of ten years.

One afternoon, while Melinda is at a workstation updating Debbie’s progress note, she overhears a conversation among several residents nearby. One resident jokes that he can’t figure out how Debbie contracted HIV, because “judging by her appearance,” she must have been a lesbian all her life. Another resident adds that Debbie’s hairstyle and clothing choices are “obvious signs.” A third resident chimes in with a sarcastic, “Hey, whatever floats your boat, right?” The group bursts into laughter.

Melinda feels deeply unsettled by this exchange. Her concern is heightened by the rapport she has developed with Debbie, and she worries about the impact such remarks could have if Debbie or anyone else had overheard. Unsure of how to respond, Melinda is left questioning whether she should address the residents’ comments, and how best to advocate for respect and professionalism in the hospital environment.

ethical_issues.question: In a medical setting, how can respect for patients be ensured and discriminatory remarks based on sexual orientation or gender expression be prevented?
keypoints: Medical practice should be guided by compassion and respect for the patient’s dignity and fundamental rights, with a firm commitment to avoid discriminatory remarks based on sexual orientation or gender expression.
Mocking patients or making disparaging comments is unprofessional and undermines patients’ confidence in their treatment and trust in healthcare providers, thereby compromising the quality of care.

A patient’s sexual orientation is clinically relevant; healthcare professionals should be informed and strictly protect patient privacy, avoiding its use as a subject of jokes or unprofessional discussion.

Residents, as role models for medical students, must lead by example, exercise professional restraint, and actively resist and correct discriminatory language to uphold a positive professional environment.

Healthcare institutions should implement systematic ethics education and training—particularly addressing HIV, homophobia, and the LGBT population—to enhance the professional competence and cultural sensitivity of all healthcare personnel.

When addressing discriminatory remarks, it is advisable to use anonymous or group educational approaches rather than singling out individuals, thereby fostering collective reflection and improvement and promoting an inclusive and respectful clinical environment.

title: Gay Adolescents and Confidentiality
case:
Richard had been seeing Dr. Moore, his pediatrician, since he was a small child. Richard, now 15, came to the office one day with a sore throat. Before Dr. Moore stepped in to see him, Richard’s mother pulled him aside. She expressed concern that Richard had not been “acting like himself” lately and that he had become increasingly withdrawn and uncommunicative over the past few months. “I’ve tried talking to him but he just won’t open up,” she told Dr. Moore. “I know that he trusts you, so if you can find out what’s wrong, it would be so helpful.”
Dr. Moore entered the exam room and began talking with Richard. After some questioning, Richard revealed that he had recently become romantically and sexually involved with another boy at school. He told Dr. Moore that he was afraid he had “caught something” from his current partner. When Dr. Moore mentioned that Richard’s mother was concerned about his low mood, Richard immediately implored Dr. Moore not to reveal what he had confessed. Dr. Moore reassured Richard about confidentiality during doctor visits, noting that most minors are protected or emancipated under state law in situations like this, and, after checking, he knew that Richard’s family’s health insurance bills would not reveal confidential information about the visit.
Richard was still worried. “I don’t want my mom to know about, uh, this relationship. I mean, I don’t even know if I’m gay, I’m just really confused right now. I know that she would just look at me differently if she knew.”
case_rewrite:
Richard had been a patient of Dr. Moore since early childhood. Now fifteen, he arrived at Dr. Moore’s office complaining of a sore throat. Before Dr. Moore entered the exam room, Richard’s mother approached him privately in the hallway. She confided her worries: Richard had become unusually withdrawn and less communicative over the past few months. “I’ve tried to reach out to him, but he keeps shutting me out,” she said. “He trusts you more than anyone; maybe you can find out what’s bothering him.”

Inside the exam room, Dr. Moore greeted Richard and began the consultation. As their conversation deepened, Richard hesitantly opened up. He disclosed that he had recently begun a romantic and sexual relationship with another boy at his school. Richard admitted he was anxious that he might have contracted an illness from his partner. When Dr. Moore brought up his mother’s concern about his low spirits, Richard immediately became anxious and pleaded with Dr. Moore not to share anything about his relationship. Dr. Moore reassured Richard, emphasizing that their conversations were confidential and that state laws protected the privacy of minors in situations like his. Double-checking the family’s insurance protocols, Dr. Moore confirmed that billing statements would not disclose any confidential details about Richard’s visit.

Despite these reassurances, Richard remained uneasy. “Please don’t tell my mom about… all this. I’m not even sure what it means. I don’t know if I’m gay, I’m just confused. If she found out, I think she’d see me differently, and I’m not ready for that.”

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians balance the principle of confidentiality with the promotion of family communication when managing adolescent patients exploring their sexual orientation?
keypoints: Physicians must adhere to the principle of confidentiality and must not disclose the patient’s private information to his mother without the patient’s consent, in order to maintain the trust inherent in the physician-patient relationship and to safeguard the patient’s sense of security.

Physicians should assess the safety of the home environment should the patient choose to disclose his sexual orientation, and, with the patient’s permission, facilitate critical reflection to gradually promote honest communication between the patient and his family.

Physicians must ensure that the patient receives necessary psychological and medical support throughout the process of self-identity formation, provide safe avenues for seeking help, and clearly inform the patient that all information will remain strictly confidential unless there is a risk of harm to self or others.

Physicians should utilize the mother’s observations regarding the patient’s mood changes as an opportunity to encourage the patient to engage in counseling, while simultaneously protecting the patient’s privacy by avoiding direct disclosure of specific sensitive information.

Physicians should recognize that the exploration of sexual orientation in adolescence is a long-term process, respect the patient’s individual pace, support his gradual readiness to disclose to family, and promote both his psychological well-being and the development of a supportive family network.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where adolescent patients may face rejection from their families, how should physicians assess and ensure the patient’s safety and support network?
keypoints: Physicians should conduct a comprehensive assessment of the patient’s family environment and school safety, identifying potential factors of rejection, bullying, or support.

Physicians must ensure that the patient receives necessary support during the process of self-identity development by mobilizing social resources, including psychological counseling and LGBTQ youth support groups, and by facilitating open and honest communication between the patient and their family.

Physicians are obligated to guarantee that the patient has access to safe avenues for seeking help and to clearly communicate the principles of confidentiality at each visit, except in cases where there is a risk of self-harm or harm to others.

ethical_issues.question: When an adolescent patient such as Richard is unwilling to disclose his sexual orientation to his family, how should Dr. Moore balance respect for Richard’s confidentiality and autonomy with the potential benefits of family communication and support?
keypoints: The physician should first assess the family environment to ensure that the patient will have safety and psychological support if their sexual orientation is disclosed.

The physician should assist the patient in identifying and expressing their emotions and feelings through precise questioning, thereby promoting the patient’s understanding of the importance of social support.

The physician should recognize that guiding the patient toward open communication is a long-term process that requires patience and multiple clinical encounters, and should respect the patient’s pace and readiness.

The physician should encourage the patient to gradually disclose relevant information to family members based on adequate preparation and autonomous willingness, and may assist in selecting an appropriate time and manner for disclosure.

Before the patient is ready to disclose, the physician should ensure that the patient has access to safe avenues for seeking help and a trusted support system, thereby safeguarding the patient’s physical and psychological well-being.

title: Justice in Medicine: Conscience Must Not Undermine Patients’ Autonomy and Access to Care
case:
Melanie was a patient at City Fertility Clinic, Inc. She had been trying to conceive for more than a year and had gone through two cycles of in vitro fertilization (IVF) and embryo implantation. Although neither effort had succeeded, Melanie had not given up hope. She had confidence in Dr. Boyles’ professional competence. He had helped her arrange for sperm donation and implantation. Melanie decided to introduce him to her partner, knowing that it might be a surprise to him because, when she started treatment, it was as a single parent. Melanie was now happily in love with Bridget and they lived together. A baby would complete their household, she told Dr. Boyles, and they could share the parenting responsibilities.
A few days after the visit, Melanie received a letter from Dr. Boyles’ office asking that she find another doctor and recommending other clinics. Dr. Boyles wrote that he could not, in conscience, help in bringing a child into a same-sex household and hoped she’d understand that these beliefs were deeply held and grounded in his religious faith. He thought that another physician could act in Melanie’s behalf with greater understanding and enthusiasm than he could.
Shocked at what she read and angry at being abandoned by her physician, Melanie called his office. “I need to speak to Dr. Boyles,” she told the receptionist. “I just got a letter telling me to find another doctor. How can Dr. Boyles dump his patient after more than a year? Just where am I going to find another clinic? You’ve got all my records. It will take weeks to sort this out. You can tell him that I’m reporting him to the state licensing board. This can’t be legal. It’s discrimination.”
case_rewrite:
Melanie had been a patient at City Fertility Clinic, Inc. for over a year, determined to start a family despite several setbacks. After undergoing two cycles of in vitro fertilization (IVF) and embryo implantation without success, she remained hopeful and trusted Dr. Boyles’ expertise. Dr. Boyles had assisted her in arranging for sperm donation and the procedures, supporting her journey from the beginning. When Melanie first sought treatment, she was planning to be a single parent. Now, her life had changed: she was in a loving relationship with Bridget, and the two lived together. Melanie decided it was important for Dr. Boyles to meet Bridget, knowing it might be unexpected since her relationship status had changed since starting treatment. She explained to Dr. Boyles that having a baby would complete her and Bridget’s home, and that they intended to share parenting equally.

Several days after this visit, Melanie was startled to receive a letter from Dr. Boyles’ office. The letter advised her to seek care from another physician and included recommendations for other clinics. Dr. Boyles explained that, due to his deeply held religious convictions, he could not, in good conscience, participate in helping bring a child into a same-sex household. He expressed that his beliefs were sincere and rooted in his faith, and stated that another doctor would likely be able to support Melanie’s goals with greater understanding and enthusiasm than he could.

Melanie was stunned and deeply upset by the letter. She immediately called the clinic. “I need to speak to Dr. Boyles,” she told the receptionist. “I just received a letter telling me to find a new doctor. How can Dr. Boyles abandon me after more than a year of care? Where am I supposed to find another clinic? You have all my records—it’ll take weeks to get things sorted out. You can tell him I’m reporting him to the state licensing board. This can’t be legal. It’s discrimination.”

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically permissible for physicians to refuse to provide nonemergency treatments based on their religious beliefs without compromising patients’ access to care?
keypoints: Physicians may conscientiously refuse to provide non-emergency treatments based on religious beliefs, provided that patients’ reasonable access to care is not compromised.

Physicians have an ethical obligation to promptly and clearly disclose any treatment objections to patients and to refer them to other qualified clinicians willing to provide the requested services, thereby ensuring continuity and timely access to medical care.

Physicians must not refuse treatment based on patients’ identities, sexual orientations, or other personal characteristics; such refusals constitute unethical discrimination and must be firmly opposed.

As professionals entrusted with public health responsibilities, physicians bear a duty to uphold patients’ rights and maintain societal trust; those who impair patients’ reasonable access to care due to personal beliefs may face disciplinary actions or professional restrictions and must accept the corresponding consequences.

ethical_issues.question: Do physicians have an ethical obligation to inform patients of other lawful medical options and provide referrals when they refuse to offer certain medical services?
keypoints: Physicians who refuse to provide certain medical services based on personal beliefs nevertheless bear an ethical obligation to inform patients of other lawful medical options and to make appropriate referrals.

The core ethical conflict lies not in the holding of conscientious beliefs per se, but in physicians’ refusal to fulfill professional duties such as disclosure and referral; it is the failure to uphold these responsibilities that constitutes an ethical breach.
Refusal to inform or refer undermines patients’ right to access care; physicians must ensure that patients’ beliefs and choices receive equal respect.
The establishment of effective referral systems is essential to guarantee that patients can obtain timely medical care when physicians decline to provide services due to conscientious objections.

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically permissible for physicians to refuse treatment based on a patient’s lifestyle or identity without violating their professional ethical obligations?
keypoints: Physicians must not refuse treatment based on a patient’s lifestyle, sexual orientation, or identity, as such conduct constitutes improper discrimination and violates professional ethical obligations.
Physicians have a duty to provide care to all patients in need, including those belonging to socially or morally contested groups.

Since the state grants physicians professional licensure and the authority to provide medical care, they bear a positive obligation to serve the public and must uphold the principles of fairness and equality in healthcare delivery.
Refusing to treat specific patients not only undermines the medical profession’s commitment to justice but also infringes upon patients’ autonomy and fundamental rights to access care.

Tolerating refusals of care based on patient identity erodes trust in the physician-patient relationship and may cause patients to withhold critical information out of fear of abandonment, thereby compromising treatment outcomes.

Healthcare institutions and regulatory bodies should firmly oppose and rectify discriminatory practices based on patient identity to safeguard patient rights and uphold the integrity of medical ethics.

title: Should a Gay Physician in a Small Community Disclose His Sexual Orientation?
case:
Dr. James is a young primary care physician starting out in the rural community of Cedar, where he shares a practice with one other physician; the next nearest outpatient care center is 35 miles away. Dr. James was sorely needed in Cedar. His colleague is minimally trained in obstetrics and gynecology, and Dr. James has a special interest and training in women’s health. He likes the size of the community and believes he makes a difference in the health of his patients. He has become Cedar High School’s sports medicine physician and volunteers at other civic events within the community. Dr. James is gay, and although he was out during medical school and residency, he has not been open about his sexual orientation within the Cedar community for fear of the reception he might receive.
Dr. James sees Mrs. Raymond often. She is a friendly woman having a complication-riddled pregnancy. One day after her exam, Mrs. Raymond and Dr. James were chatting about Cedar High, where Mrs. Raymond’s oldest child was due to start in a couple of months. Mrs. Raymond alluded to a recent controversy in a nearby town over a student’s desire to bring a same-sex date to his senior prom and said, “I’m just worried…how can we be sure kids here aren’t…that way? Dr. James, is there anything you can do to make sure there’s nothing like that going on at Cedar High? You try to keep your kids safe, to protect them, but you never know what bad influences are out there.” Dr. James did not speak, so Mrs. Raymond continued, “I mean, if I ever found out that there was one of them here—especially a teacher or a coach—I don’t know what I’d do.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. James is a young primary care physician who has recently begun practicing in the rural town of Cedar. He shares the clinic with just one other doctor, and the next closest outpatient center is a 35-mile drive away. Cedar had been in dire need of another physician, especially since Dr. James’s colleague has limited training in obstetrics and gynecology, while Dr. James brings specialized training and a keen interest in women’s health to the community. He enjoys the close-knit atmosphere of Cedar and feels his work genuinely makes a difference for his patients. Over time, Dr. James has become the sports medicine physician for Cedar High School and often volunteers at local civic events, further embedding himself in the fabric of the town. 

While Dr. James was open about being gay during his medical school and residency, he has chosen not to disclose his sexual orientation in Cedar, concerned about how the community might react.

One of Dr. James’s regular patients is Mrs. Raymond, a warm and familiar face who is experiencing a pregnancy marked by frequent complications. After a recent exam, as they lingered in conversation, Mrs. Raymond brought up Cedar High—her eldest child would be starting there soon. She referred to a controversy in a neighboring town, where a student wanted to bring a same-sex date to the senior prom. “I’m just worried…how can we be sure kids here aren’t…that way?” she asked, her tone anxious. “Dr. James, is there anything you can do to make sure there’s nothing like that going on at Cedar High? You try to keep your kids safe, to protect them, but you never know what bad influences are out there.” Dr. James remained silent, unsure how to respond. Mrs. Raymond went on, “I mean, if I ever found out there was one of them here—especially a teacher or a coach—I don’t know what I’d do.”

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance their personal privacy with their professional role when encountering patients with homophobic attitudes?
keypoints: Physicians have no obligation to disclose their sexual orientation to patients, as it is unrelated to the provision of medical care and patients have no legitimate medical need to know such personal information.

When encountering homophobic patients, physicians must rationally balance the protection of personal privacy with the demands of their professional role, carefully weighing the potential benefits and risks of disclosing their sexual orientation alongside considerations of personal safety.

Disclosure of sexual orientation may enhance physicians’ authenticity and psychological well-being, thereby fostering trust and inclusivity within the patient-physician relationship; however, in conservative communities, it may also entail professional risks and social pressures.
Concealing one’s sexual orientation can avoid direct conflict but may result in emotional burden, identity fragmentation, and awkwardness or unnaturalness in patient interactions.
Physicians should choose to disclose their sexual orientation appropriately in contexts and at times when they feel safe, avoiding on-the-spot fabrications in order to preserve long-term credibility.

Preparing in advance to address sensitive questions—such as those concerning marital status—can help reduce situational stress and facilitate harmonious integration of professional and personal identities.

title: Applying the Concept of Judicious Dissent in Matters of Conscience
case:
Melanie was a patient at City Fertility Clinic, Inc. She had been trying to conceive for more than a year and had gone through two cycles of in vitro fertilization (IVF) and embryo implantation. Although neither effort had succeeded, Melanie had not given up hope. She had confidence in Dr. Boyles’ professional competence. He had helped her arrange for sperm donation and implantation. Melanie decided to introduce him to her partner, knowing that it might be a surprise to him because, when she started treatment, it was as a single parent. Melanie was now happily in love with Bridget and they lived together. A baby would complete their household, she told Dr. Boyles, and they could share the parenting responsibilities.
A few days after the visit, Melanie received a letter from Dr. Boyles’ office asking that she find another doctor and recommending other clinics. Dr. Boyles wrote that he could not, in conscience, help in bringing a child into a same-sex household and hoped she’d understand that these beliefs were deeply held and grounded in his religious faith. He thought that another physician could act in Melanie’s behalf with greater understanding and enthusiasm than he could.
Shocked at what she read and angry at being abandoned by her physician, Melanie called his office. “I need to speak to Dr. Boyles,” she told the receptionist. “I just got a letter telling me to find another doctor. How can Dr. Boyles dump his patient after more than a year? Just where am I going to find another clinic? You’ve got all my records. It will take weeks to sort this out. You can tell him that I’m reporting him to the state licensing board. This can’t be legal. It’s discrimination.”
case_rewrite:
Melanie had been a patient at City Fertility Clinic, Inc. for over a year, seeking help to have a child. After two unsuccessful cycles of in vitro fertilization (IVF) and embryo implantation, she remained hopeful and trusted Dr. Boyles’ expertise. Dr. Boyles had supported her through the challenges of treatment, arranging for sperm donation and overseeing the procedures. Initially, Melanie began her journey to parenthood as a single woman. However, her life had since changed—she was now in a loving relationship with Bridget, and they lived together. Eager for Dr. Boyles to understand her new circumstances, Melanie introduced Bridget to him at an appointment, explaining that they were partners and intended to raise the child together. It could take weeks to get this sorted out. Tell him I’m reporting him to the state licensing board. This can’t be legal. It’s discrimination.”

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians be required to choose between personal beliefs and professional responsibilities, and how should the tolerability of patient inconvenience resulting from refusal of care be assessed?
keypoints: Physicians have the right to refuse participation in medical interventions they conscientiously deem morally wrong, based on the preservation of moral integrity and religious beliefs, even when patients request such services; this constitutes the core motivation for conscientious objection.

While upholding the right to conscientious objection may cause inconvenience to patients, when balancing the physician’s personal moral integrity against professional responsibilities, the physician’s moral autonomy should generally be prioritized, provided that patient health is not jeopardized.

The reasonableness and tolerability of conscientious objection should be evaluated by considering whether the physician’s beliefs are imposed on the patient, the impact on the patient’s health, scientific integrity, and the potential for discrimination, with refusal being impermissible especially when patient health is at risk.

Pellegrino’s model of “judicious dissent” emphasizes that physicians should adopt a conscientious objection stance only in cases of significant moral conflict, thereby maximizing the autonomy of both physician and patient as well as preserving continuity of care.

ethical_issues.question: Does a physician have the right, on the basis of religious belief, to refuse to provide infertility services to same-sex couples, and does such a refusal constitute discrimination?
keypoints: When a physician refuses to provide medical services on the basis of a patient’s identity (such as sexual orientation), rather than objecting to a specific medical procedure itself, this may constitute discrimination.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) holds that refusal to provide infertility services to lesbian couples violates the ethical principle of justice and constitutes wrongful discrimination, as it exacerbates harm based on sexual orientation.

Organizations such as the Christian Medical and Dental Association (CMDA) maintain that, although refusals based on religious beliefs amount to de facto discrimination, physicians have the right to decline participation in medical practices they consider morally wrong, provided that society’s recognition of family diversity is respected.

The right to conscientious refusal is intended to protect the physician’s moral integrity while also ensuring that patients are free to seek care from other providers; society generally tolerates the inconvenience this may cause, prioritizing respect for the physician’s beliefs.

In balancing patient interests and physician conscience, society tends to avoid compelling physicians to act against their personal convictions, regarding the inconvenience resulting from conscientious refusal as an acceptable trade-off.

ethical_issues.question: How can the physician’s right to conscientious refusal be balanced with the principles of patient autonomy and equitable treatment in medical practice?
keypoints: Pellegrino’s concept of judicious dissent emphasizes that, when exercising the right of conscientious refusal, physicians should respect the patient’s autonomy, avoid moralizing, and clearly articulate the moral basis for their refusal.

The right of conscientious refusal should be limited to situations involving significant moral conflict, thereby safeguarding the physician’s religious and moral integrity while also ensuring that patients are able to seek timely and unimpeded medical care from other providers.

Although the inconvenience experienced by patients as a result of conscientious refusal should not be overlooked, such inconvenience is generally more tolerable and reasonable than compelling physicians to act against their conscience and professional integrity.

In refusing care, physicians should adopt an attitude of judicious dissent, avoiding the imposition of personal beliefs on patients, and upholding the equal status of both parties as moral agents as well as the coexistence of diverse values.

While the judicious dissent model cannot entirely eliminate value conflicts between physicians and patients, by balancing the autonomy of both parties and promoting pluralism and harmony, it can minimize the negative impact of such conflicts to the greatest extent possible.

title: “Please Let Me Hear My Son Cry Once”
case:
Norma had two goals in life: to become a parent and a gynecologist. She achieved the latter and, to boot, married a classmate, George. Her first dream seemed stymied, however, by their long hospital hours, exhaustion, and career demands. When Norma unexpectedly became pregnant at the age of 35, she and George were overjoyed, but also concerned about the risks associated with her relatively advanced age of conception—concern that turned out to be sadly justified when their unborn child was found to have trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. George and Norma discussed options, including aborting the fetus, but decided to move forward with the pregnancy. Norma prayed every night, “Oh God, please let me hear my son cry once…that is all I want…the sound of my own child in this world.”
Norma’s prayers were answered and their son was born. Bob had a severe cleft lip and palate, but Norma and George thought their son was the most beautiful child in the world. Due to their medical competence, they were eventually able to take their child home. Because she spent so much time with her son, Norma quickly became familiar with all of his unique sounds and was quick to notice the onset of short apneic episodes. She could not tell whether Bob was experiencing pain during these attacks, but administered the morphine prescribed by Dr. Moy when she believed he was in pain. The events increased in frequency and duration, and, eventually, Dr. Moy began to advise against using morphine out of concern that this pain relief might result in respiratory failure.
When Bob was 3 months of age, conflict between Norma and Dr. Moy surfaced again when Norma requested that Bob be given his normal childhood vaccinations. Dr. Moy explained that he felt these were unnecessary and might increase morbidity. He expressed his regret at not having been trained for situations like this, and he knew there were many clinical and ethical issues at play.
When Norma called Dr. Moy to report that Bob had developed a fever, Dr. Moy told her to take him to the local emergency room immediately. There, after a taking a history and learning of the trisomy 13 diagnosis, the ED physician told Norma, “Your son is dying. There is little we can do to help him.” Dismayed, Norma pushed him to proceed with a physical examination, upon which the physician, to his surprise, found that Bob had an acute otitis media infection. He asked, “So do you want to treat his infection? Also, does your son have DNR orders?”
case_rewrite:
Norma had always held two dreams close to her heart: becoming a mother and a gynecologist. She fulfilled the latter, and, as an added blessing, married her classmate George. Their shared dedication to medicine left them with little time and energy for starting a family, and for years, Norma’s hope of motherhood seemed out of reach. Then, at age 35, Norma discovered she was unexpectedly pregnant. She and George were overwhelmed with joy, though their happiness was tempered by concern about the risks associated with Norma’s age. Their fears were realized when prenatal testing revealed their unborn son had trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome.

Faced with this diagnosis, Norma and George discussed their options thoroughly, including the possibility of terminating the pregnancy. After much soul-searching, they chose to continue, embracing whatever time they might have with their child. Every night, Norma whispered a prayer: “Oh God, please let me hear my son cry just once… that’s all I ask, to hear my own child’s voice in this world.”

Norma’s wish was granted—her son was born, and his first cry filled the delivery room. Bob, as they named him, had a severe cleft lip and palate, yet to Norma and George, he was the most beautiful child they had ever seen. Drawing on their medical backgrounds, they were able to manage his care at home, adapting to his unique needs. Norma, ever attentive, learned to recognize every nuance in Bob’s sounds and quickly noticed the onset of brief apneic episodes. Though it was hard to tell if Bob was in pain, she administered morphine as prescribed by Dr. Moy when she believed it was needed.

As time passed, Bob’s episodes became more frequent and prolonged. Dr. Moy grew increasingly concerned that the morphine could suppress Bob’s breathing and advised Norma to use it more cautiously. This was the first of several disagreements between Norma and Dr. Moy.

When Bob reached three months, another conflict arose: Norma requested that Bob receive his routine childhood vaccinations. Dr. Moy explained that, given Bob’s condition, he felt the vaccines were unnecessary and could introduce additional risks. He admitted to Norma that he felt unprepared for the complex clinical and ethical questions their situation posed.

One evening, Bob developed a fever. Concerned, Norma phoned Dr. Moy, who urged her to take Bob immediately to the local emergency department. There, the emergency physician took a history and, upon learning of Bob’s diagnosis, told Norma bluntly, “Your son is dying. There is little we can do to help him.” Norma, unsettled by this response, pressed the physician to examine Bob thoroughly. On examination, the physician was surprised to find that Bob had an acute ear infection. He turned to Norma and asked, “Would you like us to treat his infection? And, does your son have do-not-resuscitate orders?”

ethical_issues.question: When the family and the primary physician have reached a consensus on the goals of care, how can coordination across the healthcare system be ensured to avoid unnecessary interventions or erroneous assumptions that no treatment will be provided?
keypoints: Early, thorough communication between the primary physician and the family is essential to clarify and reach mutually agreed-upon goals of care, thereby establishing a foundation for coordinated management.

The primary physician should proactively communicate in advance with the emergency department physician, providing detailed information on the patient’s medical history, care goals, and established care plan to minimize information gaps.

The emergency department physician should actively verify whether the family continues to endorse the predetermined care goals, respect the family’s wishes, and help alleviate anxiety among both family members and healthcare providers.

The integration of hospice and pediatric palliative care teams is recommended to offer ongoing professional support and home visitation services, assist in clarifying care objectives, and reduce unnecessary emergency department visits and interventions.

ethical_issues.question: In managing medical decision-making for children with severe congenital anomalies, how can healthcare providers effectively communicate with families to understand and respect their treatment goals and preferences?
keypoints: Engage in shared decision-making with the parents rather than unilateral decisions, establishing mutually agreed-upon goals of care early to ensure alignment between the healthcare team and the family.

Avoid interrogative communication; instead, inquire about the family’s preferences regarding the extent of medical interventions in an open and respectful manner, rather than directly asking sensitive questions such as the presence of do-not-resuscitate (DNR) orders.

Even when the parents are healthcare professionals, approach them primarily as parents, attending to their emotional and psychological needs, and avoid assuming they possess fully detached and expert clinical judgment.

Recognize that family preferences may evolve in response to changes in the child’s clinical condition and emotional bonding; therefore, treatment decisions require ongoing, dynamic reassessment and communication throughout the disease course.

Assist the family in comprehensively understanding the spectrum of medical options, affirm and support their decisions grounded in their personal values, thereby enhancing their confidence and psychological resilience in decision-making.

Through calm, gentle, and continuous guidance, support the family in navigating this difficult journey, fostering the creation of cherished memories of their child’s life and minimizing trauma associated with conflicts within the healthcare system.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance providing comfort care and prolonging life when caring for a child with trisomy 13 syndrome?
keypoints: Labeling the condition as “lethal” may result in a self-fulfilling prophecy; physicians should recognize the prognostic uncertainty for affected children and avoid unilaterally limiting the scope of treatment.

Physicians should establish an ongoing, dynamic communication process with the child’s parents, explicitly and collaboratively setting goals of care early on, respecting and adapting to evolving family emotions and objectives, and thereby enhancing confidence in providing interventions such as pain management and ensuring a coordinated care plan.

Families may choose to forgo invasive procedures, but the burdens and benefits of such interventions should be carefully weighed, avoiding futile or overly aggressive treatments that impose excessive risk or suffering.
In the absence of disproportionate suffering, prolonging life and improving quality of life are reasonable and acceptable goals of care.
Parents may choose to treat readily curable conditions (such as otitis media) to enhance the child’s comfort and quality of life.
The involvement of palliative care does not preclude hospital readmission for treatable illnesses; care plans should remain flexible to accommodate the actual needs of the child and family.

title: An Overwhelmed Parent
case:
Rosa was overjoyed when she delivered her first son Alan at the hospital. He was going to be their first “true American” child, born and raised in the country she had sacrificed so much to get to. Her husband would soon be moving to the U.S. but was awaiting a work permit. On arrival home from the hospital, Alan’s older sisters were so excited that they fought over who would get to hold him first.
After his first week, however, Rosa noticed that Alan’s cry seemed to be weak and that he had trouble feeding. She reported this information to the pediatrician who quickly reassured her nothing was wrong. Rosa failed to be reassured and 2 weeks later sought consultation with another doctor when Alan’s breathing difficulty increased. The new pediatrician diagnosed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), admitted Alan to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), and had him intubated. Rosa spent 4 nights in the disturbing world of beeps and flashing lights trying to understand the culture of this new environment and what the conversation she overheard meant. She was able to arrange for her daughters to stay at a neighbor’s apartment, fearing that the experience would be too much for them.
This scenario repeated itself several times over the next 3 months, and Alan was rehospitalized after unsuccessful brief stays at home. In her many efforts to understand what was wrong with her child, Rosa felt frustrated with the “doctor speak” she received. During this same time, Alan’s sisters became scared of taking care of their brother, fearing they would do something to worsen his condition. His younger sister began to quietly resent her brother for always absorbing Rosa’s attention. She made this apparent to the family one evening after Rosa refused to allow her to have a sleepover for fear that Alan would get another infection.
Rosa spent countless nights searching the Internet for explanations of what was wrong with her son. This situation came to a head one morning when Alan was in the hospital. An unfamiliar nurse arrived in his room seeking Rosa’s signature on consent forms for a tracheostomy and insertion of a gastric feeding tube. When Rosa questioned the necessity of these interventions, the nurse replied, “Oh, I thought the doctors told you your son has spinal muscular atrophy. They have to do these procedures to save him.” In a state of shock and confusion, Rosa signed the forms and cried.
Soon after the procedures, Alan was sent to a local children’s rehabilitation center on a ventilator. Initially Rosa wanted to take Alan home, but after seeing the “hole in his throat” she thought it would be too difficult for her daughters. Her relationship with the girls had become strained. They refused to talk about Alan or even visit him in the PICU. Rosa struggled to see her son and made excuses when she could not visit.
As the months dragged on, first into a year and then into 2, Rosa stopped visiting Alan. The nursing staff grew quite fond of him and brought him toys and clothing. He even began to communicate through the use of sign language and his smile always brought happiness to the staff. They tried to contact Rosa from time to time, to provide her updates, but she never returned their calls. Many nurses felt that Rosa had abandoned her son and often accused her of being a bad mom and not caring. Even the doctors began to debate whether Rosa should be contacted regarding medical decisions about Alan.
case_rewrite:
Rosa was filled with joy when she welcomed her first son, Alan, at the hospital. This child was especially precious to her—her first to be born and raised in the United States, the country for which she had left so much behind. Her husband remained abroad, waiting on a work permit before he could join the family. When Rosa brought Alan home, his older sisters were thrilled, so eager to meet their new brother that they argued over who could hold him first.

But after Alan’s first week at home, Rosa grew concerned. Alan’s cry was unusually weak, and he struggled to feed. She brought these worries to the pediatrician, who assured her that nothing was wrong. Despite the reassurance, Rosa’s unease lingered, and as Alan’s breathing problems worsened two weeks later, she sought out another doctor. This pediatrician recognized symptoms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), promptly admitted Alan to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), and initiated intubation. For four nights, Rosa remained by Alan’s side, surrounded by the unfamiliar and unsettling world of monitors and alarms, trying to grasp the meaning of hurried conversations among the staff. She arranged for her daughters to stay with a neighbor, not wanting them exposed to the hospital’s intensity.

This ordeal repeated itself several times over the next three months. Alan was hospitalized repeatedly after short, unsuccessful attempts at home care. Rosa’s frustration mounted as she struggled to understand the medical explanations given, finding the doctors’ language confusing and distant. At home, Alan’s sisters grew anxious about caring for him, afraid they might accidentally cause him harm. The younger of the two began to quietly resent Alan, frustrated that Rosa’s attention was always consumed by her brother. One evening, after Rosa refused her request to attend a sleepover out of fear Alan might catch another infection, the girl’s resentment surfaced openly.

Desperate for answers, Rosa spent countless nights scouring the Internet in search of explanations for Alan’s condition. Matters came to a head one morning during another hospital admission. A nurse Rosa had never met entered Alan’s room, asking her to sign consent forms for a tracheostomy and the placement of a gastric feeding tube. When Rosa questioned why these procedures were needed, the nurse replied, “Oh, I thought the doctors told you—your son has spinal muscular atrophy. These procedures are necessary to save him.” Overwhelmed and confused, Rosa signed the forms in tears, scarcely able to process what was happening.

After the procedures, Alan was transferred to a local children’s rehabilitation center, dependent on a ventilator. Though Rosa initially wanted to bring Alan home, the sight of the tracheostomy left her deeply unsettled. She worried that caring for Alan would be too much for her daughters. Her relationship with her girls became strained; they refused to talk about Alan or visit him in the PICU. Rosa herself found it increasingly difficult to see her son and often made excuses to avoid visiting.

As the months passed, eventually stretching into a year and then two, Rosa stopped visiting Alan altogether. Meanwhile, the nursing staff at the center grew deeply fond of him, bringing him toys and clothes and teaching him to communicate with sign language. Alan’s bright smile became a source of happiness for the whole team. The staff tried reaching out to Rosa to provide updates, but she never returned their calls. Many nurses began to feel that Rosa had abandoned her son, questioning her devotion and even labeling her a bad mother. Even the doctors started to discuss whether Rosa should continue to be contacted for important medical decisions about Alan.

ethical_issues.question: When obtaining parental consent for surgery, should healthcare professionals ensure that the parents fully understand the child’s condition and the necessity of the procedure, and actively engage them in shared decision-making?
keypoints: Healthcare professionals must ensure that parents fully understand their child’s medical condition, as well as the purpose and necessity of the proposed surgical intervention, when obtaining parental consent.

Healthcare professionals should proactively assess parents’ level of understanding regarding their child’s illness and communicate information with empathy and clarity to facilitate shared decision making.

In the presence of language barriers or cultural differences, healthcare professionals are obligated to provide professional interpretation and culturally appropriate support to ensure parents accurately comprehend medical information and available options.

Healthcare professionals should provide parents with adequate time and a supportive, safe environment to consider all treatment options, assisting them in making decisions that align with the child’s best interests.

Healthcare professionals must respect parents’ emotional responses and avoid focusing solely on obtaining signatures, ensuring that consent is given with full informed understanding and psychological readiness.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where a pediatric patient requires long-term care, should the medical team provide interdisciplinary palliative care support to assist the family in making optimal decisions regarding care coordination, psychological support, and other related aspects?
keypoints: The medical team should provide interdisciplinary palliative care support at the time of the child’s diagnosis, assisting the family in making optimal decisions regarding care coordination, psychological support, and medical decision-making.

Palliative care is applicable to all life-limiting conditions, including those that are non-progressive but severely impact health, offering comprehensive assistance across multiple domains such as home care, care coordination, and sibling support.
Palliative care encompasses not only symptom management but also psychological, social, and spiritual support, including advance care planning, thereby promoting the overall well-being of the family.

Palliative care should be delivered continuously throughout the entire course of illness, regardless of outcome, with the ultimate goal of creating the best possible quality of life for the patient and family in accordance with their values.

title: Nondisclosure and Emerging Autonomy in a Terminally Ill Teenager
case:
Neil was first diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia at age 3. After induction chemotherapy failed to produce a remission, his family spent the next 6 months traveling around the country trying to find the best doctors and latest chemotherapy options. When they finally decided to seek treatment for Neil at a major children’s hospital hundreds of miles from their rural home, Neil and his mother moved to this city, where he spent the next 3-1/2 years in and out of eventually successful chemotherapy and a bone marrow transplant.
Years later, Neil revealed that most of his early memories involved the staff or patients of the children’s hospital. He certainly remembered good experiences, like the ceremonial head-shaving parties, the local ballet company’s recitals in the hospital, and his close friendships with other patients. But the reality was that Neil had lost many of those friends during his hospital stay, and he had many painful memories, too—the endless nights of nausea and pain, his mother’s constant anxiety about his recovery, and the unexpectedly difficult transition back to “civilian living,” catching up in school and learning to share belongings and his parents’ time with his siblings.
Neil succeeded in putting those painful memories behind him and living the life of an average kid in a small town. He’d developed an enthusiasm for football in long conversations with a football-loving nurse, and he threw himself into playing. However, when he was 14 years old, he began to notice increasing fatigue during practice and games. He didn’t mention it to his mother. During his annual physical, it was noted that he had lost 15 pounds and, when questioned, he revealed his other symptoms. His mother, inconsolable, prepared for another trip to Children’s Hospital.
There, Andrea, a third-year medical student, was assigned to Neil’s case. She, too, shared Neil’s enthusiasm for football, and they developed a rapport. But when Neil began asking Andrea about his diagnosis, she didn’t know how to respond.
Neil’s ALL had, in fact, returned. Because he had relapsed after transplant, only participation in a Phase I trial designed to measure toxicity and maximum dosages of new chemotherapy agents was offered as an option. But his mother had specifically asked the treatment team not to discuss Neil’s diagnosis with him, believing that he couldn’t cope with the news or appreciate its implications.
Meanwhile, Neil confided in Andrea that he would rather die than endure another course of chemotherapy, saying, “It was horrible. I can’t do it again. I just want to go home, but I’m scared my mom and doctors will hate me.”
case_rewrite:
Neil was first diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia when he was just three years old. After his initial course of induction chemotherapy failed to bring about remission, Neil’s family spent the next six months journeying from one hospital to another, determined to find the most advanced treatments and the best doctors. Eventually, they chose to pursue care at a renowned children’s hospital several hundred miles away from their rural community. Neil and his mother moved to the city, and for the next three and a half years, he underwent periods of intensive chemotherapy and a bone marrow transplant, cycling in and out of the hospital until he finally achieved remission.

As Neil grew older, he reflected on those years and realized that most of his earliest memories revolved around the hospital—its staff, fellow patients, and the routines of pediatric oncology care. He remembered the highlights: the camaraderie of head-shaving parties before chemotherapy, the joy of watching ballet performances staged by a visiting dance company, and the deep friendships he formed with other children battling illness. Yet, these bright moments were shadowed by difficult experiences—the loss of many friends to their diseases, countless nights plagued by pain and nausea, his mother’s unrelenting anxiety, and the unexpectedly tough transition back to life outside the hospital. Returning home meant adapting to school again, catching up with his studies, and learning to share his parents’ attention with his siblings after years of being the focus of their worry.

Despite the weight of these memories, Neil worked hard to reclaim a sense of normalcy in his small town. He developed a love for football, sparked by long talks with a nurse who was a passionate fan. Throwing himself into the sport, he finally felt like any other teenager. But at age fourteen, Neil began to notice that he was tiring more easily during practices and games. He kept this to himself, not wanting to trouble his mother. At his annual checkup, his doctor noted he had lost fifteen pounds. When questioned, Neil admitted to other symptoms as well. His mother, devastated by the news, quickly prepared to take him back to the children’s hospital.

At the hospital, Andrea, a third-year medical student, joined Neil’s care team. She and Neil bonded almost immediately over their shared enthusiasm for football, and Andrea quickly became someone Neil trusted. However, when Neil began asking Andrea questions about his diagnosis, she found herself uncertain about how much she could say.

The reality was that Neil’s acute lymphoblastic leukemia had returned. Given that his relapse occurred after a bone marrow transplant, the only remaining treatment option was participation in a Phase I clinical trial—one focused on assessing the toxicity and maximum tolerated dose of new chemotherapy agents, not on achieving a cure. Neil’s mother, however, had made a specific request to the treatment team: she did not want Neil informed about his diagnosis. She believed the news would be too much for him to bear and doubted he could fully comprehend its significance.

Meanwhile, Neil confided in Andrea his dread of further chemotherapy. “It was horrible. I can’t do it again. I just want to go home, but I’m scared my mom and doctors will hate me,” he admitted, voicing his overwhelming fear and desire to avoid more treatment.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Neil’s case, how can clinicians ensure that Neil and his family are able to make an informed decision regarding participation in a Phase I clinical trial, while minimizing the risk of therapeutic misconception?
keypoints: Clearly inform the pediatric patient and their family about the nature of the Phase I clinical trial, emphasizing that the primary objective of the trial is to evaluate drug toxicity and maximum tolerated dose rather than therapeutic efficacy.

Provide a detailed explanation of the low rate of direct benefit from participation in Phase I trials, incorporating historical data (4–6%) and the most recent individual response rates (approximately 2.5%), in order to prevent therapeutic misconception.

Respect and safeguard the informed assent rights of cognitively typical children aged 7 years and older, highlighting their entitlement to participate in research decision-making and to refuse participation.

Recommend initiating a pediatric palliative care referral concurrently with enrollment in a Phase I clinical trial to support the family in making fully informed decisions aligned with comprehensive care goals.

ethical_issues.question: How can pediatric palliative care be effectively integrated into oncology treatment to optimize the overall care experience for patients and their families?
keypoints: Introduce pediatric palliative care (PPC) early as an integrated specialty service accompanying the oncology diagnosis rather than as an optional add-on, thereby alleviating the decision-making burden on families and optimizing the overall care experience for patients and their families.

Timely integrate PPC at critical junctures such as diagnosis, enrollment in Phase I clinical trials, relapse, development of serious complications, and ICU admission or transfer to ensure continuous support and dynamic adjustment of the care plan.

Clearly define the goal of collaborative integration between PPC and the oncology treatment team to avoid framing them as mutually exclusive options, thereby ensuring that patients and families can simultaneously pursue curative treatment and palliative care.

Improve symptom management, sleep, and nutrition through a collaborative care model to enhance treatment tolerance, minimize the negative impact of care team transitions during clinical deterioration, and strengthen the patient’s and family’s sense of security and continuity of care.
Effective integration of PPC not only safeguards the treatment autonomy of patients and families but also promotes overall care quality by providing high-quality, continuous, and equitable services.

tags: Informed consent/Capacity, competency for making decisions
title: Taking No for an Answer: Refusal of Life-Sustaining Treatment
case:
Dr. Sachem, an emergency physician at a regional burns center, had kept the waiting room relatively empty for most of Memorial Day weekend, despite the recent warm weather. At 3:00 AM on Monday, a patch came over the radio. Injured firefighters from a two-alarm house fire were being brought in by ambulance. Five minutes later, the trauma bay was enveloped with the acidic smell of soot and burnt flesh.
A badly burned 41-year-old fireman named Worther complained only of leg pain. “Hey Doc! You gotta fix my leg. We were on the first story trying to get back to the master bedroom when I realized that the fire had started in the cellar. Before I knew it, I was trapped downstairs under a beam.” The medic, who was at the blaze, reported that Mr. Worther was in the flames for 3 minutes before he was extracted. The first responder’s look at Dr. Sachem told her that there was something else that couldn’t be spoken.
The medics had removed much of Mr. Worther’s scorched clothing en route; when the trauma team opened the blankets, skin peeled off with the cloth and much of his body had a white sheen to it. The fireman’s right leg had a compound fracture of the femur and was scorched black. His left hand, shoulders and face were spared, but his mouth and beard were full of soot. Dr. Sachem calculated that full-thickness burns covered 85 percent of Mr. Worther’s body and suspected significant smoke inhalation. She recalled a tragic case in her residency when the ICU team couldn’t keep up with a badly burned patient’s fluid losses and the patient died after 3 weeks on a ventilator. This was what the medic had been saying with his eyes. But recent efforts at her burn center suggested the patient might have a 10 percent chance of survival.
After she told him of the burns’ extent, the firefighter asked earnestly, “Am I going to make it, Doc?” Dr. Sachem responded, “We’re going to put in a central line to give you fluids and will get ready to intubate you because you’ll soon have trouble breathing on your own.” As she set up her equipment, the patient asked his colleagues to leave the room. He looked Dr. Sachem in the eye and clearly told her, “I’ve seen my share of burn deaths and I know where this is heading. Please let me die. Just give me something so I don’t feel anything, but don’t let me live.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Sachem, an emergency physician working the night shift at a regional burns center, had managed to keep the waiting room nearly empty throughout most of Memorial Day weekend, despite the surge in outdoor activities brought on by the warm weather. At 3:00 AM on Monday, a call came in over the radio: several firefighters injured in a two-alarm house fire were en route by ambulance. Within minutes, the trauma bay filled with the acrid odor of soot and burned flesh.

Among the arrivals was a 41-year-old fireman named Worther, whose only complaint was severe pain in his leg. “Doc, you have to fix my leg. We were on the first floor trying to get back to the master bedroom when I realized the fire had started below us in the cellar. Next thing I knew, I was trapped under a beam downstairs,” Worther recounted. The medic, who had pulled Worther from the blaze, reported that he had been exposed to flames for about three minutes before being rescued. The medic exchanged a silent, grave look with Dr. Sachem—something unspoken lingered in the air.

During transport, the medics had cut away most of Worther’s charred clothing. When the trauma team removed the blankets, sheets of skin came away with the fabric, revealing a large swath of his body covered in a pale, waxy sheen. Worther’s right leg showed a compound femur fracture and was blackened by burns. His left hand, shoulders, and face were largely unscathed, but his mouth and beard were packed with soot. Dr. Sachem quickly estimated that full-thickness burns covered 85 percent of Worther’s body, and she suspected significant smoke inhalation. She was reminded of a haunting case from her residency, when a severely burned patient succumbed to fluid losses after weeks on a ventilator, despite intensive care. She recognized the wordless message in the medic’s eyes. Yet, she also knew that recent advances at her burn center suggested Worther’s chance of survival, while slim, was not zero—perhaps 10 percent.

After Dr. Sachem explained the extent of his injuries, Worther looked at her and asked, “Am I going to make it, Doc?” She replied, “We’re going to put in a central line to start fluids and prepare to intubate you, since you’ll probably have trouble breathing soon.” As she readied the equipment, Worther asked his fellow firefighters to step outside. Once alone, he met Dr. Sachem’s gaze and said with unwavering clarity, “I’ve seen what happens to burn victims. I know where this leads. Please, just let me go. Give me something so I don’t feel anything, but don’t keep me alive.”

ethical_issues.question: When a patient refuses life-sustaining emergency treatment, should the physician respect the patient’s autonomy and forgo beneficial intervention?
keypoints: Physicians must assess whether the patient possesses decision-making capacity to refuse treatment, as this is the prerequisite and cornerstone for respecting patient autonomy.

If the patient has decision-making capacity and explicitly refuses life-sustaining emergency treatment, the physician should honor this decision, even if it contradicts the physician’s recommendation.

In the emergency setting, refusal of lifesaving treatment creates an ethical tension between the principle of beneficence and respect for patient autonomy; physicians must carefully balance these considerations and communicate effectively.
Administering lifesaving treatment against the wishes of a patient with decision-making capacity may constitute battery or medical negligence, thereby exposing the physician to legal liability.
Providing a dignified death for certain patients with decision-making capacity may hold ethical value equal to that of preserving life.

ethical_issues.question: In the emergency setting, how should a patient’s decision-making capacity to refuse treatment be assessed?
keypoints: Decision-making capacity is context-specific and requires assessment of the patient’s ability to make a particular medical decision at a specific point in time.

The evaluation of a patient’s capacity to refuse treatment should be a comprehensive clinical judgment based on the patient’s cognitive function, physical condition, and the complexity, risks, and potential consequences of the medical intervention involved.

The patient must be able to understand their medical condition and the consequences of treatment, rationally weigh different options, make a decision consistent with their personal values, clearly communicate this decision, and maintain its consistency over time.

When patients refuse high-risk interventions such as life-sustaining treatment, a “sliding scale” standard should be applied, requiring the patient to demonstrate a higher level of decision-making capacity to ensure the validity of the decision.

Physicians must consider potential impairments to decision-making capacity caused by pathophysiological factors such as acute physical or mental illness, severe pain, medication effects, and emotional stress, but disagreement with the physician’s recommendations alone does not justify a determination of incapacity.

In the emergency setting, assessment of decision-making capacity is constrained by time and resource limitations; physicians must carefully balance respect for patient autonomy with the duty to protect patients from potentially fatal errors, making every effort to conduct a thorough evaluation.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient refuses life-sustaining treatment, should a different standard of decision-making capacity be applied to reflect the risks and consequences associated with that choice?
keypoints: When a patient with decision-making capacity refuses life-sustaining treatment, their decision should be respected; however, it is necessary to assess whether their decision-making capacity meets the higher standard required for high-risk choices.

According to the “sliding scale” model, as the risks and consequences of treatment increase in severity, patients must demonstrate a higher level of decision-making capacity to ensure that their choice is an autonomous decision based on adequate understanding and the maximization of their own interests.

Physicians facing a patient’s refusal of life-sustaining treatment must carefully balance respect for patient autonomy with the prevention of potentially fatal outcomes resulting from a poor decision, ensuring that the decision-making process is both ethically sound and legally compliant.

title: Make It OK That This Life Is Ending
case:
During Dr. Shen’s shift at the cardiac intensive care unit in his regional hospital, airlift brought in an intubated middle-aged woman in respiratory distress from a rural hospital 150 miles away. Ms. Danforth, previously in good health, had had a massive inferior myocardial infarction earlier that day.
“She was fighting the ventilator so much that we needed to sedate her for transport,” the flight nurse reported. “The patient’s daughter and brother left Orchard Hospital about 15 minutes before we did. They wanted to be with Ms. Danforth at all times.” The ED social worker confirmed at the time of the transfer that the patient’s brother had called from his cell phone to say they were on their way but would have spotty reception for an hour or so as they crossed the mountains.
The patient arrived clammy, with cool and mottled extremities. Monitors showed hypoxia and hypotension. Her heart stopped, at which point, Dr. Shen directed CPR and placed a femoral central line to begin pressors. Over the next half hour, the patient coded several times, requiring stretches of CPR every 5 minutes.
At one point when her heartbeat had resumed, Ms. Danforth’s brother called again. “My sister is a single mom and she’s all that Casey has. Save her at all costs, Doc. You need to keep her alive. We’re only a half hour away.”
The patient slipped back into PEA arrest. After 20 minutes of sustained CPR, Dr. Shen asked if anyone else objected to calling the code—just as the social worker burst into the resuscitation bay to say that the family was 10 minutes away.
case_rewrite:
During Dr. Shen’s overnight shift in the cardiac intensive care unit at his regional hospital, an air ambulance delivered a middle-aged woman intubated and in severe respiratory distress. Ms. Danforth, who had previously enjoyed good health, had suffered a massive inferior myocardial infarction earlier that day at a rural facility 150 miles away.

“She kept fighting the ventilator and we had to sedate her for the flight,” the flight nurse explained upon arrival. “Her daughter and brother left Orchard Hospital about 15 minutes before we did. They insisted on being with Ms. Danforth as much as possible.” The emergency department social worker noted that, as the transfer began, the patient’s brother had called in to say he and the daughter were driving over the mountains and would have unreliable cell service for about an hour.

Upon arrival, Ms. Danforth’s skin was cold and clammy, her extremities mottled. Monitors revealed hypoxia and hypotension. Moments later, her heart stopped. Dr. Shen immediately led the team in CPR and quickly placed a femoral central line to initiate pressor support. Over the next thirty minutes, the patient’s heart arrested several times, each event requiring repeated cycles of CPR, sometimes only minutes apart.

During a brief period when circulation was restored, the phone rang again—it was Ms. Danforth’s brother. “My sister is a single mom—she’s all that Casey has left. Please, doctor, you have to save her. Do whatever it takes. We’re about half an hour away.”

Shortly after, Ms. Danforth went into pulseless electrical activity arrest once more. As the team continued with 20 minutes of uninterrupted CPR, Dr. Shen turned to the group and asked if anyone had objections to calling the code. At that moment, the social worker rushed into the resuscitation bay, breathless, to announce that the family was just ten minutes out.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Shen continue cardiopulmonary resuscitation until the family arrives?
keypoints: After prolonged and repeated cardiopulmonary resuscitation, the likelihood of patient survival with preserved neurological function is exceedingly low; continued resuscitation constitutes medically futile treatment.

As the family’s arrival approaches, the goal of resuscitation should shift from “saving life” to “making the dying process more dignified and acceptable,” reflecting the principles of medical humanism.

Continuing CPR until the family arrives, although of limited medical efficacy, provides an opportunity for the family to say goodbye and prepare psychologically, thereby facilitating their coping with the patient’s death.

Physicians should integrate professional medical judgment, ethical principles, and fiduciary responsibility to balance the patient’s best interests, family needs, and allocation of medical resources in making a comprehensive decision regarding the continuation of resuscitation.

ethical_issues.question: In a resource-limited emergency department setting, should aggressive resuscitative efforts be continued for patients with an extremely poor prognosis, especially when doing so may impact the allocation of resources to other patients?
keypoints: Physicians must prioritize the patient’s best interests under conditions of limited information and urgency, while simultaneously considering the allocation of resources and treatment needs for all patients within the emergency department.

Continuous cardiopulmonary resuscitation consumes substantial medical resources; Dr. Shen must weigh the benefits of ongoing resuscitation against the equitable and rational distribution of limited resources among other patients in the emergency department.

After 30 minutes of intermittent CPR followed by 20 minutes of sustained resuscitation, the patient’s likelihood of survival is exceedingly low, with minimal probability of preserved neurologic function; small ICU case series have demonstrated near-zero survival rates for patients undergoing repeated cycles of CPR, indicating an extremely poor prognosis.

Although continued aggressive treatment may shift toward non-medical goals—such as providing comfort to the family—it nonetheless entails ethical considerations requiring a rational assessment of whether the use of scarce medical resources remains justifiable.

The imminent arrival of the family offers a critical temporal window for decision-making; a brief extension of resuscitative efforts can afford the family an opportunity for closure, facilitating their psychological acceptance of the patient’s death.

Physicians should integrate professional medical judgment, the fiduciary responsibility framework, and principles of medical ethics to comprehensively evaluate the patient’s prognosis, resource availability, and family needs, thereby making difficult yet responsible clinical decisions.

ethical_issues.question: In situations where the patient lacks decision-making capacity, how should physicians balance the patient’s best interests with the emotional needs of the family during the process of futility assessment?
keypoints: Physicians must make timely determinations regarding the futility of resuscitation and act accordingly, centering the patient’s best interests, especially when information is limited and the patient lacks decision-making capacity.
The assessment of futility is a dynamic process that should be continually revised in response to the patient’s evolving clinical status and treatment response.
When family members are imminently arriving, the emergency team may appropriately shift the goals of resuscitation from “saving life” to “making the dying process more dignified and acceptable.”
This shift in goals not only modifies clinical actions but also helps reframe the psychological stance of the healthcare team, facilitating the family’s gradual acceptance of the patient’s death.

From the perspectives of resource allocation and practical benefit, briefly prolonging CPR is reasonable, as it provides the family with a crucial opportunity for farewell and supports their emotional and psychological needs.

Physicians should integrate professional judgment, the framework of fiduciary responsibility, and principles of medical ethics to balance the patient’s best interests with the emotional needs of the family, making difficult yet responsible clinical decisions.

title: Outer Ear Construction: Is Advocacy Part of Treatment?
case:
Jonathan was born with unilateral right-sided grade III microtia; his external ear was absent, with a peanut-sized structure in its place and the external ear canal and ear drum also missing. Testing showed that his right inner ear was intact and his hearing was normal on the left side. A CT scan revealed that his right ear canal did exist. Jonathan’s parents were counseled to wait until he turned 8 years old to pursue reconstructive surgery, so his ear would be closer to adult size.
Shortly after his 8th birthday, Jonathan’s parents made an appointment with Dr. Cavanaugh, who had completed both otolaryngology residency and a plastic and reconstructive surgery fellowship. After discussing the risks and benefits of the procedure, Dr. Cavanaugh performed a rib cartilage graft reconstruction procedure on Jonathan. Dr. Cavanaugh had completed the first two stages of her three-stage reconstruction when Jonathan’s insurance company denied preoperative clearance for the third stage, deeming it an elective enhancement procedure not sufficiently related to ear function.
Dr. Cavanaugh helped Jonathan’s parents appeal the insurance company’s decision, but they were rejected twice. Understandably, they were frustrated, and began investigating alternatives. They were informed that other insurance companies also considered the third surgery an elective procedure ineligible for coverage. They decided to seek media publicity to either help raise funds for the final operation or to convince the insurance company to “do the right thing” for the sake of public relations. Jonathan’s parents found a television station that would air their story if they could persuade the doctor to appear on camera or at least comment on the insurance company’s decision.
case_rewrite:
Jonathan was born with a severe congenital ear deformity on his right side—grade III microtia—leaving him without an external ear, just a small, peanut-sized remnant where the ear should be. His external ear canal and eardrum were absent as well. However, hearing tests showed his right inner ear was intact, and his left ear functioned normally. A CT scan revealed that Jonathan did, in fact, have a right ear canal, though it was not open. Jonathan’s parents were told that reconstruction would be best pursued after he turned eight, so that his ear would be closer to its adult size.

Not long after Jonathan turned eight, his parents scheduled a consultation with Dr. Cavanaugh, a surgeon with dual training in otolaryngology and plastic and reconstructive surgery. Dr. Cavanaugh carefully explained the potential benefits and risks of the multi-stage reconstructive ear surgery. With his parents’ consent, she proceeded with the first two stages, which involved a rib cartilage graft to begin rebuilding Jonathan’s ear.

As they prepared for the critical third stage, Jonathan’s insurance company denied preoperative authorization, labeling the final operation an elective enhancement not essential to ear function. Dr. Cavanaugh assisted Jonathan’s parents in appealing the denial, submitting detailed documentation and engaging in extensive communication with the insurer. Despite their efforts, the insurance company rejected the appeal twice. Frustrated, Jonathan’s parents explored other options, only to learn that most insurance providers took a similar stance, classifying the third stage as an elective and therefore not covered.
