In their search for alternatives, Jonathan’s parents decided to seek media attention—hoping either to raise the funds needed for the last stage of surgery or to influence the insurer’s decision by appealing to public sentiment. They found a television station willing to share their story, but the producers wanted Dr. Cavanaugh to participate on camera or, at minimum, provide a professional statement about the insurance company’s decision. Jonathan’s parents approached Dr. Cavanaugh, seeking her support as they considered going public in hopes of securing coverage for their son’s reconstructive surgery.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Cavanaugh advocate publicly for insurance coverage of reconstructive ear surgery for patients like Jonathan, even when certain aspects of the procedure are considered non-therapeutic?
keypoints: Physicians may assist in advocating for insurance coverage at the request of the patient or their parents, but should carefully evaluate the situation and exhaust all conventional appeal and communication channels first.

Physicians should not proactively recommend using media pressure against insurance companies; such actions are a byproduct of an imperfect healthcare system and should be considered a last resort, decided autonomously by the patient or their parents.

If the patient or their parents, fully informed and acting voluntarily, choose to waive medical confidentiality in order to secure funding for treatment, the physician has an ethical and professional obligation to provide the necessary assistance.

ethical_issues.question: Does the physician have an ethical obligation to assist the patient in disclosing medical information publicly in order to pressure the third-party payor to cover the surgical costs?
keypoints: The surgery aims to correct congenital deformities that affect the patient’s physiological function and psychological well-being, rather than serving as a purely cosmetic procedure; this constitutes the fundamental ethical basis for a physician’s assistance in advocating for treatment on behalf of the patient.

Physicians have an ethical responsibility, contingent upon the patient’s informed and voluntary waiver of medical confidentiality, to assist in the disclosure of medical information in order to help the patient secure necessary funding for treatment.

Before assisting the patient in publicizing medical information, the physician should first exhaust conventional avenues, such as direct communication and appeals to the insurance company, to obtain third-party payment support.

Physicians should not proactively recommend that patients resort to media exposure; however, when explicitly requested by the patient, they may provide professional opinions and technical information to support the patient’s reasonable expression of their appeal.

Physicians must engage in thorough communication with the patient and their family to ensure they understand the potential risks and benefits of publicly disclosing medical information, analogous to the informed consent process for treatment.

title: An Argument for Patient Autonomy in Elective Surgery
case:
Florence is a zestful 73-year-old. In addition to spending a lot of time keeping up with her six grandchildren, she exercises most days. She recently won first place in the masters’ division of an Olympic distance triathlon, and is preparing for a 50-mile bike ride for charity. Since her husband passed away last summer, she has thrown herself into exercise, and it shows.
Despite having a very athletic body, particularly for her age, Florence is dissatisfied. Every time she looks in the mirror, instead of seeing toned muscles, she sees sagging breasts, facial wrinkles, drooping eyelids, and crows’ feet. She made an appointment with Dr. Doherty, a plastic and reconstructive surgeon.
Dr. Doherty was surprised at how fit this 73-year-old woman was. After talking about her triathlon success, Dr. Doherty asked, “What can I do for you?” Florence proceeded to explain that, despite all the exercising she does, she feels like “a wrinkled, saggy old prune.” She wants to feel as good on the outside as she does on the inside. She said that, after giving it a lot of thought, she wants a facial makeover—specifically, a rhytidectomy (face-lift) and blepharoplasty (surgery to remove sagging tissue or wrinkles around the eyelids)—and a breast lift. She is even contemplating having very modest breast implants put in. If she is going to have the breast lift surgery anyway, why not go from an A to a B cup?
case_rewrite:
Florence, a spirited 73-year-old, fills her days staying active with her six grandchildren and sticking to a dedicated exercise routine. Just recently, she claimed first place in the masters’ division of an Olympic distance triathlon, and now she’s training for a 50-mile charity bike ride. Since her husband’s passing last summer, Florence has poured her energy into fitness, and the results are evident.

Yet, despite her athletic achievements and toned physique—especially remarkable for her age—Florence remains dissatisfied with her appearance. When she catches her reflection, she doesn’t see her muscular build. Instead, she focuses on sagging breasts, facial wrinkles, drooping eyelids, and crows’ feet. Seeking a change, Florence scheduled a consultation with Dr. Doherty, a plastic and reconstructive surgeon.

Dr. Doherty was struck by Florence’s level of fitness for someone her age. After listening to her recount her recent triathlon victory, Dr. Doherty asked, “What brings you in today?” Florence candidly shared her feelings: despite her efforts, she feels like “a wrinkled, saggy old prune.” She wants her outward appearance to reflect the vitality she feels inside. After careful consideration, she has decided she wants a facial makeover—including a rhytidectomy (face-lift) and blepharoplasty (to address sagging skin and wrinkles around her eyelids). Florence also expresses interest in a breast lift, and she’s even thinking about getting modest breast implants—in her words, “If I’m having the breast lift anyway, why not go from an A to a B cup?”

ethical_issues.question: Is age alone sufficient to refuse the request of a patient who is healthy, competent, informed of the risks and benefits, and has autonomously determined that the surgery will enhance their overall well-being?
keypoints: The ethical justification for surgery is based on the anticipated benefits outweighing the surgical risks; age should be considered as a factor in patient selection, but its relative weight is minor compared to comorbidities and overall health status.
The pursuit of happiness by an individual is ethically legitimate provided it does not infringe upon the rights of others or violate societal moral standards.

Age alone is insufficient grounds to deny the request of a patient who is healthy, competent, informed of the risks and benefits, and who autonomously determines that the surgery will enhance their overall well-being.

title: The “Mommy Makeover” Package
case:
Julie was feeling both happy and sad. She had just tucked her 7-week-old baby girl into her crib, and was overjoyed about being the mother of two adorable, healthy children. However, she caught a glimpse of herself in the mirror as she was changing into her pajamas and was disappointed by what she saw.
Since being discharged from the hospital, Julie had been doing aerobic workouts every day, trying to regain her figure. At 34, she was hoping not merely to return to her prepregnancy weight, but to recapture the body of her 20s, when she had won third place in a statewide beauty pageant.
She was down to 146 pounds, certainly within normal limits for a 5-foot, 8-inch woman (body mass index 22.2), but was not the 123 pounds that she weighed walking down the runway. Julie had struggled to lose weight after giving birth to her first child 6 years before, but it was even more difficult after her second child. She had lost 8 pounds over the last 6 weeks, but seemed to be hitting a plateau.
Inspired by an advertisement she had seen for a “mommy makeover” package, Julie set up an appointment with Dr. Greenwall, a plastic surgeon who had fixed her broken nose after she was hit in the face by a volleyball a few years earlier. Julie told Dr. Greenwall how difficult weight loss had been postpartum, how the extra weight around her belly made her self-conscious, and that she wanted to remain attractive in her husband’s eyes to keep her marriage stable. She requested a tummy tuck (abdominoplasty) and liposuction in hopes of losing some postpregnancy weight and maintaining her marriage, and asked if Dr. Greenwall would give her a discount for having both procedures together, as she had seen in the ad.
case_rewrite:
Julie stood in her softly lit bedroom, feeling a complex mix of emotions. Earlier, she had gently settled her 7-week-old daughter into the crib, her heart full with the joy of motherhood and gratitude for her two healthy, beautiful children. Yet, when she caught her reflection in the mirror while changing into her pajamas, a wave of disappointment washed over her.

Since leaving the hospital, Julie had committed herself to daily aerobic workouts, determined to regain her figure. At 34, she wasn’t just aiming to reach her pre-pregnancy weight; she yearned for the physique she had in her twenties, when she’d proudly taken third place in a statewide beauty pageant. Now at 146 pounds—well within the healthy range for her 5-foot, 8-inch frame (body mass index 22.2)—she couldn’t help but compare that number to the 123 pounds she had been when she walked the runway all those years ago. Losing weight after her first child, six years prior, had been a challenge, but this time, it seemed even more daunting. Over the past six weeks, she had managed to shed eight pounds, but now her progress had stalled.

One afternoon, Julie noticed an advertisement for a “mommy makeover” package. The idea stuck with her. Remembering the care she’d received from Dr. Greenwall—the plastic surgeon who had expertly repaired her nose after a volleyball accident several years before—Julie decided to schedule a consultation. Sitting across from Dr. Greenwall, Julie shared her frustrations: the persistent difficulty of postpartum weight loss, the lingering self-consciousness from the extra belly weight, and her desire to feel attractive for her husband in hopes of keeping their marriage strong. She explained that she was considering both a tummy tuck (abdominoplasty) and liposuction to help lose the post-pregnancy weight and maintain her relationship. Recalling the ad, Julie asked Dr. Greenwall if he would offer her a discount for having both procedures done together, as the package had described.

ethical_issues.question: Does offering discounted package deals to induce patients to undergo non-essential surgeries violate medical ethical standards?
keypoints: Each patient should undergo an individualized assessment to ensure the necessity and appropriateness of the treatment plan, thereby avoiding inducement to undergo unnecessary surgeries due to package discounts.
Package advertisements may mislead patients into believing that multiple procedures are suitable for them; the appropriateness of combining surgeries must be based on individualized medical judgment.
Implying that patients “need” a package may affect their self-perception and exacerbate psychological burden; healthcare professionals should communicate cautiously and respect patient autonomy.
The promotion of surgery packages in itself does not violate ethical standards, but advertisements containing universal claims or scientifically unfounded statements constitute ethical breaches.

title: Weight-Based Stigma and Physician Bias
case:
Mrs. Williams visited her primary care physician, Dr. Smith, for a hospital follow-up (2 days after discharge) and evaluation of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia. She was obese (BMI of 50) and had been hospitalized for acute renal failure due to dehydration, respiratory distress, and poor-healing chronic decubitus ulcers. Her family believed the medical staff was to blame for Mrs. Williams’ current medical problems. They stated that she was receiving “inappropriate care” and that the physicians involved in treatment were “just putting a band-aid on her and trying to discharge her as quickly as possible” during each admission. This hospitalization marked her 10th in the last 5 months for similar symptoms.
During her last hospitalization, the medical team had spoken with Mrs. Williams about her weight’s being the primary confounding factor in treatment of her other medical conditions. Dr. Smith asked, “Mrs. Williams, do you understand how your weight has complicated the care that we are able to provide? We are just treating these acute flare-ups until we can address the fact that each of them will improve with weight loss.” She replied, “I’m tired of you doctors telling me I’m fat. I know that, but I think that you’re using it as an excuse not to try hard enough to address my other issues. I’ve seen how you look at me. I just wish someone would treat me like a human being.”
Mrs. Williams has changed her primary care physician several times over the last few years because of “maltreatment” and “disrespect” by her physicians. She believes that as she has gained weight over the years, she has been treated more poorly by her physicians. She has been on a quest to find a physician who will treat her as he or she would treat a thinner patient, but each physician that she has seen has focused on her morbid obesity as a primary cause of her current diagnoses. While all of them have given her information on dietary changes and physical activity recommendations, she has not heeded their advice, due in part to their abrasive approach.
case_rewrite:
Two days after being discharged from the hospital, Mrs. Williams arrived at Dr. Smith’s clinic for a follow-up appointment. She had a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol. With a BMI of 50, Mrs. Williams struggled with morbid obesity and had just been hospitalized for acute kidney injury caused by dehydration, breathing difficulties, and chronic, slow-healing pressure sores. Mrs. Williams’ family voiced strong frustration, insisting that hospital staff were responsible for her ongoing health issues. They accused the doctors of providing “inappropriate care” and claimed the team was “just putting a band-aid on her and trying to send her home as soon as possible” at every visit. This most recent admission was Mrs. Williams’ tenth hospitalization in five months for similar problems.

During her last hospital stay, the care team had discussed with Mrs. Williams how her weight complicated management of her other health conditions. At this visit, Dr. Smith gently asked, “Mrs. Williams, do you realize how your weight has made it harder for us to treat you? Right now, we’re mainly treating these acute flare-ups, but we know that addressing your weight could help improve each of these conditions.” Mrs. Williams responded with visible frustration: “I’m tired of doctors telling me I’m fat. I already know that. But it feels like you use it as an excuse not to work harder to deal with my other problems. I see the way you look at me. I just wish someone would treat me like a human being.”

Over the past several years, Mrs. Williams had changed primary care physicians multiple times, citing “maltreatment” and “disrespect” from her doctors. She believed that as her weight increased, the quality of her medical care declined. Determined to find a physician who would treat her just as they would a thinner patient, Mrs. Williams repeatedly found that each new doctor focused on her obesity as the main cause of her illnesses. Although every physician gave her advice on diet and exercise, Mrs. Williams had not followed these recommendations—partly because she found their approach abrasive and dismissive.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians avoid weight-related bias and effectively establish a trusting and respectful physician-patient relationship when communicating with patients who are obese?
keypoints: Healthcare professionals should consciously identify and reflect upon weight-related biases and feelings of helplessness in effecting lifestyle changes in patients, uphold the moral obligation to respect patient dignity, and treat all patients equally regardless of their weight or other personal characteristics.

Establish a physician-patient relationship based on mutual trust by candidly acknowledging the limitations of professional knowledge and capabilities, actively listening to and responding to patients’ verbal and nonverbal cues, thereby restoring respect and trust.

Attend to the patient’s lived experience and emotional needs, demonstrate empathy, gently disclose the clinician’s own internal conflicts, and convey confidence in the potential for improvement in the patient’s health status.

Emphasize the patient’s subjective experiences (e.g., increased energy, reduced fatigue, enhanced mobility) as primary motivators, avoiding exclusive reliance on biomedical indicators, to facilitate gradual adoption of healthy behaviors.

Once the physician-patient relationship is strengthened, progressively guide the patient toward acceptance of weight management and related treatment plans, with attention to gradualism and individualization.

ethical_issues.question: How can unconscious physician bias against patients with obesity be identified and overcome in clinical practice to improve treatment outcomes?
keypoints: Cultivating awareness of one’s own unconscious biases is fundamental to improving treatment outcomes for patients with obesity.

Physicians need to reflect on their feelings of helplessness regarding patients’ lifestyle changes and consider their own personal experiences to foster trust and respect in the physician-patient relationship.
Physicians should acknowledge the limitations of their professional knowledge and personal abilities, which facilitates the establishment of mutual trust.
Healthcare professionals have a moral obligation to respect the personhood of patients, independent of the patient’s weight or other personal characteristics.
Actively listening to patients’ life experiences and emotional states, with attention to their feelings of frustration and neglect, helps to rebuild trust in the physician-patient relationship.
Conveying confidence that the patient’s health can improve, regardless of significant weight loss, supports the consolidation of the therapeutic relationship and enhances treatment adherence.
After establishing a solid foundation of trust, implementing gradual, individualized weight management strategies can increase patient engagement and improve clinical outcomes.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians balance respecting patient autonomy with providing effective health guidance when managing obesity and related health issues?
keypoints: Physicians should transcend a narrow interpretation of “respect for autonomy” and fulfill the broader moral obligation of “respect for persons,” affording equal respect to all patients, including those with obesity, thereby avoiding bias or discrimination based on weight.

Physicians need to reflect on their own feelings of helplessness, biases, or personal experiences related to obesity, recognizing how these factors impact the physician-patient relationship as a crucial prerequisite for overcoming barriers to trust.

Physicians should fully acknowledge the patient’s lived experience and bodily awareness, patiently listen to their emotional expressions (including feelings of frustration and neglect), gently disclose their own internal conflicts, and convey confidence in the potential for health improvement, in order to foster the restoration of respect and trust in the therapeutic relationship. Once this relationship is strengthened, gradual, stepwise guidance toward weight management can be reintroduced.

Effective health counseling should embody sensitivity, flexibility, and persistence, emphasizing the patient’s subjective experiences (such as increased energy and enhanced functional capacity) rather than relying solely on biomedical metrics, to enhance intrinsic motivation and engagement.

Establishing realistic initial goals, providing consistent feedback, monitoring adherence, and offering constructive encouragement are essential strategies to promote both short-term and long-term success in weight loss.

Physicians must carefully observe patients’ verbal and nonverbal cues, adapt communication styles and intervention strategies flexibly, respect individual patient differences, and employ ongoing trial and error to identify the most appropriate forms of support for each patient.

title: Does Pediatric Obesity Indicate Child Neglect?
case:
At 9 years old, Tiffany is morbidly obese (above the 150th weight percentile for her age, with a BMI of 35). Tiffany was referred to a pediatric obesity clinic by her pediatrician. Over the years, her weight problem had become more pronounced, leading to impaired fasting glucose and hyperlipidemia. Her pediatrician felt the significant increase in her weight over the last 3 years warranted an intensive approach to her obesity. As the pediatric obesity clinic physician took Tiffany’s history, it became clear that she lived in an environment in which physical activity was not encouraged and fast food was a staple. Tiffany’s mother bragged that she frequented fried chicken and hamburger franchises so much that the managers and salespeople knew her by name. When questioned about whether or not she planned on making changes in her daughter’s diet, Tiffany’s mother emphatically stated, “I do not plan on making any changes to Tiffany’s diet. She’s my kid, and I call the shots about what she eats. Fast food tastes better than the stuff you’re proposing. I know she’s bigger than many of her classmates, but at least she’s happy. All of you doctors are rich anyway, and you think I can afford all that stuff you’re telling me to feed my child.”
Since the mother has been the primary contributor to this patient’s learned behavior (poor dietary choices and sedentary lifestyle), can this be seen as medical maltreatment? Should the physician ask for a child neglect ruling and advise authorities to speak with child protective services for Tiffany?
case_rewrite:
Tiffany, a 9-year-old girl, is morbidly obese, registering above the 150th percentile for weight in her age group and carrying a BMI of 35. Her pediatrician referred her to a pediatric obesity clinic after observing a steady and significant weight increase over the past three years. This escalation in Tiffany’s weight has led to complications including impaired fasting glucose and elevated cholesterol levels. Concerned by the seriousness of her condition, her pediatrician determined that Tiffany needed a more intensive intervention.

At the pediatric obesity clinic, the physician took a thorough history and discovered that Tiffany’s home life offered little encouragement for physical activity. Instead, sedentary behaviors prevailed, and fast food played a central role in the family’s diet. Tiffany’s mother spoke with pride about their frequent visits to local fried chicken and hamburger outlets, even noting that the staff recognized her by name. When the physician broached the topic of dietary changes, Tiffany’s mother responded firmly: “I do not plan on making any changes to Tiffany’s diet. She’s my kid, and I call the shots about what she eats. Fast food tastes better than the stuff you’re proposing. I know she’s bigger than many of her classmates, but at least she’s happy. All of you doctors are rich anyway, and you think I can afford all that stuff you’re telling me to feed my child.”

It became evident that Tiffany’s mother was not only dismissive of medical advice but also played a central role in shaping Tiffany’s unhealthy eating patterns and inactive lifestyle. Given that Tiffany now suffered from serious but potentially reversible health problems due to her obesity, the physician faced a difficult decision: Should this be considered medical neglect? Should the physician seek a child neglect ruling and recommend that child protective services become involved in Tiffany’s case?

ethical_issues.question: Does Pediatric Obesity Constitute Child Neglect, Especially When Caregivers Fail to Seek or Provide Necessary Medical Care?
keypoints: Childhood obesity itself, although it may be severe, typically does not constitute “serious and imminent harm,” and therefore obesity alone is insufficient to establish child neglect.

When childhood obesity results in reversible yet serious comorbid conditions (such as severe obstructive sleep apnea, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, or progressive fatty liver disease), and the caregiver fails to provide or seek necessary medical care, this may constitute medical neglect.

Physicians should report medical neglect only when the following conditions are met: a high likelihood of serious and imminent harm; a reasonable expectation that available interventions will result in effective treatment; and the absence of feasible alternative solutions.

Socioeconomic factors such as poverty, lack of access to healthy foods, and inadequate opportunities for physical activity may exacerbate childhood obesity; however, when a child faces a risk of serious and imminent harm, the state and healthcare professionals retain an obligation to protect the child.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians request a child neglect ruling and recommend involvement of child protective services when pediatric obesity is accompanied by serious comorbid conditions?
keypoints: Physicians should first recommend nutritional, exercise, and behavioral interventions, and refer to specialized professionals to ensure that reporting medical neglect is reserved as a measure of last resort.

Physicians should consider seeking a child neglect ruling and advising child protective services to intervene when pediatric obesity is accompanied by serious comorbidities and there is a high risk of serious and imminent harm.

The criteria for reporting medical neglect include: a high likelihood of serious and imminent harm; a reasonable expectation that available interventions will result in effective treatment; and the absence of alternative options to address the problem.

Both the state and physicians have an obligation to protect children from serious harm, even when factors such as poverty, lack of affordable healthy food, and inadequate space for physical activity contribute to severe pediatric obesity.

ethical_issues.question: In cases of pediatric obesity, should physicians exhaust alternative options, including behavioral modification and involvement of social services, before the condition progresses to the point where mandatory reporting is required?
keypoints: Physicians have an obligation to actively intervene in pediatric obesity, exhaust all alternative options, and take timely action to ensure that comprehensive interventions are implemented before the condition progresses to the threshold requiring mandatory reporting.
The primary step is to establish a trusting relationship with the parent, avoiding excessive lecturing or information overload, in order to facilitate effective communication and cooperation.

The initial goal should be to maintain the current weight, gradually guiding the parent and child to improve dietary patterns and increase physical activity, while proposing practical and feasible strategies tailored to the family’s circumstances.
Multidisciplinary professional resources, such as nutrition counseling and health psychologists, should be utilized to provide individualized support and behavioral modification interventions.

Local social service agencies should be involved as early as possible, leveraging their expertise in comprehensive family assessment and needs identification to complement the work of the medical team and strengthen attention and support for the child’s health status.

Ongoing follow-up and adjustment of intervention plans are necessary to address difficulties in accessing healthy food and limitations in the physical activity environment, thereby promoting improvement in the child’s health status.

Only when all intervention measures have failed and the child faces a risk of serious and imminent health harm should the physician consider reporting medical neglect and initiating child protection procedures.

title: Weight-Related Denial of Insurance for an Infant
case: When Robert’s parents took him to Dr. Cartwright’s office for his 6-month well-baby check, the nurses measured his length, weight, and head circumference to plot on the growth charts. While his length and head circumferences were within normal range (both approximately 50th percentile), Robert’s weight was above the 97th percentile; his weight-for-length was well above the 95th percentile. His parents stated that he had been doing well, tolerating breast milk and vitamin D supplementation, and meeting all developmental milestones. When Dr. Cartwright evaluated the measurements obtained at the 4-month visit, it became apparent that Robert was at the 90th percentile with regard to weight-for-length. The doctor told Robert’s parents, “According to our growth charts, Robert is overweight. We should make some efforts to determine how to reduce the number of calories he consumes on a daily basis.” His mother responded, “Actually, Doctor, we know he’s obese by medical standards. We just sought to add him to our medical insurance, and he was denied coverage after we submitted his weight measurements. I think all of this is a little absurd. He’s just a happy, healthy baby. However, I am concerned that he’s being denied insurance at such an early age with no other health problems. Is there anything that you can do to help?”
case_rewrite:
When Robert’s parents arrived at Dr. Cartwright’s clinic for his routine 6-month well-baby visit, the nurses carefully recorded his length, weight, and head circumference, entering the data onto standardized growth charts. Robert’s length and head circumference each landed close to the 50th percentile, well within the typical range for his age. However, his weight charted above the 97th percentile, and his weight-for-length ratio exceeded the 95th percentile mark. His parents shared that Robert seemed to be thriving—he was exclusively breastfed with added vitamin D, and he was achieving all the expected developmental milestones.

Reviewing the chart from Robert’s 4-month appointment, Dr. Cartwright noted that at that time, Robert’s weight-for-length percentile was at 90. After assessing the current numbers, Dr. Cartwright explained, “Based on these growth charts, Robert’s weight is higher than expected for his length. We should talk about ways to possibly lower the number of calories he’s getting each day.”

Robert’s mother, however, interjected thoughtfully. “Doctor, we’re aware that by medical definitions, Robert is considered obese. When we recently tried to enroll him in our health insurance plan, the company denied his application after we reported his weight. I find this really hard to believe—he’s a happy, healthy baby. Still, I am worried that he’s being denied insurance so early in life, especially when he doesn’t have any health problems. Is there anything you can do to help us?”

ethical_issues.question: Should an infant’s overweight status be considered a legitimate basis for denial of health insurance coverage?
keypoints: Infant overweight status should not be considered a justifiable reason for denial of health insurance coverage, as there is no universally accepted diagnostic criterion for “obesity” in children under 2 years of age, and weight metrics must be evaluated in the context of overall developmental status.

Breastfeeding confers multiple short- and long-term health benefits for infants and young children, including a reduced risk of future obesity; professional organizations uniformly recommend breastfeeding as the optimal mode of nutrition.

When assessing weight-related risk in infants and young children, primary consideration should be given to the weight and health status of the parents, as parental obesity significantly increases the likelihood of persistent overweight in the infant, whereas absence of parental obesity is associated with a greater probability of natural normalization of weight.

Insurance denial based on elevated weight in a 6-month-old breastfed infant lacks scientific justification and may result in erroneous risk assessment, thereby paradoxically increasing the overall risk burden.

Insurance providers should proactively accept infants and young children who meet standards of healthy growth, support their access to equitable medical coverage, and promote investment in health during early life.

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically and socially responsible for an insurance company to deny coverage based on an infant’s weight?
keypoints: Denying insurance coverage for a 6-month-old infant on the basis of “obesity” constitutes a serious oversimplification that disregards the complexity of infant growth and development as well as the health benefits conferred by breastfeeding, lacking both rational justification and ethical foundation.

Breastfed infants generally exhibit better health status and lower medical risks; thus, insurance companies’ refusal of coverage based solely on a single weight metric reflects cognitive bias and poses a risk of misinformation.

Uninsured children are associated with higher medical costs and increased societal burden; ensuring health insurance coverage for children aligns not only with social responsibility but also with clear economic rationale.
Insurance companies should proactively accept healthy infants for coverage, avoiding exacerbation of social inequities and waste of medical resources caused by overly simplistic risk assessments.

ethical_issues.question: Does the physician have an ethical responsibility to advocate and appeal on behalf of the infant who was denied insurance coverage?
keypoints: Infancy is a critical period for preventive health care; timely access to medical services is essential for promoting health and preventing disease. Denial of insurance coverage can severely compromise children’s healthy development and quality of life.

Physicians have an ethical responsibility to advocate for the infant’s right to insurance coverage, as ensuring access to health insurance is directly linked to the patient’s well-being and ongoing access to medical care.

Uninsured children are more likely to experience adverse health outcomes, such as increased reliance on emergency care, higher rates of hospitalization, and elevated morbidity. Ensuring insurance coverage aligns with public health imperatives and societal responsibilities.

Physicians should remain vigilant regarding the negative impact of inappropriate policies on children’s access to health care, actively promote equitable and reasonable insurance policies, and safeguard the rights and interests of children.

tags: Global health/Role of health professions students
title: Caring for Patients in Low-Resource Settings
case:
Jaime, a second-year medical student, has traveled to Zimbabwe for the summer to volunteer at a student- and resident-run health clinic. The clinic is located in a rural area where many people live below the poverty line and lack regular access to health care or basic resources like consistently clean water and electricity.
Shortly after arriving in Zimbabwe, Jaime sees a patient who is visiting the clinic for the first time. Mr. Gazi has come to the clinic after losing some weight over the past two months and recently noticing a reddish-purple nodular growth on his lower right leg. At first, he thought it was a bruise that was taking a long time to heal, but it has been growing and becoming more raised. After talking to Mr. Gazi and examining him, Jaime discusses the patient’s symptoms with Dr. Gordan, the resident who is supervising the medical students in the clinic that day. After hearing about Mr. Gazi’s symptoms, Dr. Gordan immediately suspects that Mr. Gazi has Kaposi’s sarcoma, related to an underlying infection with HIV. Not realizing the clinic’s limitations, Jaime suggests that the next step would be to confirm the diagnosis with laboratory tests to measure CD4 lymphocyte count and HIV viral load. Dr. Gordan explains that in resource-limited settings, where laboratory access is limited, physicians use the WHO Clinical Staging System for HIV/AIDS, which relies on the recognition of clinical findings to direct clinical decision making. He tells Jaime how his own extensive global health experience has helped him strengthen and expand his skills in taking thorough histories and conducting physical exams.
That night, Jaime goes home from his work in the clinic and looks up an article about the WHO Clinical Staging System. He determines that Mr. Gazi must be in Clinical Stage 4 based on his presumed Kaposi’s sarcoma, and that by the WHO criteria, he would be an appropriate candidate for antiretroviral therapy. While he is excited by the idea of relying more on his clinical skills and less on technology, he is concerned about how Mr. Gazi will be able to access the care he will need and what possibly even more dire conditions Mr. Gazi must face in his daily life. Jaime’s thoughts expand to the millions of people worldwide who also lack adequate care, as well as adequate living conditions, and he wonders what he can or should do now and in the course of his career to make a positive impact.
case_rewrite:
Jaime, a second-year medical student, has traveled to Zimbabwe for the summer to volunteer at a health clinic managed by students and residents. The clinic is situated in a rural region where many residents live in poverty and struggle with limited access to basic healthcare, clean water, and reliable electricity.

Soon after his arrival, Jaime meets Mr. Gazi, a new patient visiting the clinic for the first time. Mr. Gazi reports that over the past two months, he has lost some weight and recently noticed a reddish-purple, nodular growth developing on his lower right leg. Initially, he thought it was merely a bruise that was slow to heal, but the lesion has gradually enlarged and become increasingly raised. After taking a careful history and examining Mr. Gazi, Jaime discusses the case with Dr. Gordan, the resident supervising the clinic that day. Upon hearing the details, Dr. Gordan strongly suspects that Mr. Gazi is presenting with Kaposi’s sarcoma, likely associated with underlying HIV infection. Jaime, not yet fully aware of the clinic’s resource limitations, suggests confirming the diagnosis with laboratory tests, such as measuring CD4 lymphocyte count and HIV viral load. Dr. Gordan explains that in settings like theirs, where laboratory testing is often unavailable, clinicians rely on the WHO Clinical Staging System for HIV/AIDS, which uses clinical findings to guide diagnosis and treatment decisions. He shares with Jaime how his experience working in global health settings has helped him develop sharper skills in history-taking and physical examination.

That evening, Jaime returns home and reads an article about the WHO Clinical Staging System. Based on Mr. Gazi’s suspected Kaposi’s sarcoma, Jaime determines that he likely falls into Clinical Stage 4, qualifying him for antiretroviral therapy under WHO guidelines. While Jaime is intrigued by the challenge of practicing medicine with limited technology and greater reliance on clinical judgment, he grows increasingly concerned about how Mr. Gazi will access necessary treatment and the broader hardships he faces daily. Jaime reflects not only on Mr. Gazi’s situation but also on the millions of people around the world who live without adequate healthcare or basic living conditions. He begins to question what meaningful steps he can take, both now and throughout his future career, to make a positive and lasting difference.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the biological, psychological, and social needs of patients when confronted with social circumstances that cannot be resolved?
keypoints: Physicians, when confronted with intractable social challenges, should comprehensively address the biological, psychological, and social needs of patients, striving to provide feasible medical and psychological support within the current context.
Physicians must recognize that achieving health equity is a long-term and complex process, and a single clinical rotation is insufficient to fundamentally alter a patient’s social circumstances.
By listening to patients’ stories and respecting their dignity, physicians can offer crucial psychological support that enhances patients’ sense of trust and security.

Physicians can channel their concern for patients’ hardships into sustained advocacy efforts, leveraging their social influence—for example, by documenting patient experiences and giving voice to marginalized populations—to promote systemic change in resource-limited settings.

ethical_issues.question: When medical students participate in international medical volunteer activities, how can they ensure that their actions do not impose a burden on the host institution but instead provide benefit?
keypoints: Medical students participating in international medical volunteer activities should thoroughly understand the prevalent local diseases, cultural context, and available medical resources.
Solo volunteer efforts should be avoided; priority should be given to programs with established collaborative frameworks to minimize additional burdens on host institutions.
Medical students should proactively seek guidance from international preceptors and mentors at their home institutions to ensure comprehensive preparation before departure.
Sending institutions must ensure that medical students receive adequate preparation and training prior to travel to prevent imposing burdens on host institutions.

tags: Clinical research/Dual roles as clinicians and researchers
title: Technical Skill and Informed Consent
case:
Dr. Crick is participating in a randomized clinical comparison of percutaneous aortic valve replacement therapy with standard medical therapy in a group of patients with aortic valve disease and comorbidities so severe that they cannot undergo open aortic valve replacement. Dr. Crick’s surgical team, part of a multi-institutional investigation, has sought and obtained IRB approval of the study. Each surgeon received didactic training and performed the first two procedures under the supervision of a surgeon experienced in the technique. Mr. Alton, 65, is the 15th patient on whom Dr. Crick will perform the procedure.
Without surgery, the patient has a 50 percent probability of dying in the next 18 months. Two of Dr. Crick’s previous trial patients died following their surgeries, although their deaths may have been due to significant comorbidities. Four other operations resulted in paravalvular leaks that required further surgery. The other surgeons on Dr. Crick’s team have had a lower rate of complications and the study’s Data Safety Monitoring Board has cleared the group to continue the trial. Dr. Crick is confident that Mr. Alton will benefit from this procedure and that the study results will lead to greater benefits for future patients than the current medical standard. In providing information to Mr. Alton during the informed consent process, is Dr. Crick ethically obligated to divulge data about his experience with the procedure beyond what is outlined in the approved IRB consent form?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Crick is involved in a randomized clinical trial comparing percutaneous aortic valve replacement therapy to standard medical management for patients with aortic valve disease who have comorbidities so severe that they are not candidates for open aortic valve replacement. His surgical team is part of a multi-center study, which has already received IRB approval. All participating surgeons, including Dr. Crick, underwent formal instructional training and performed their initial two procedures under the supervision of an experienced surgeon. Mr. Alton, aged 65, is now the fifteenth patient on whom Dr. Crick will perform this procedure.

Without intervention, Mr. Alton faces a 50 percent chance of dying within the next 18 months. Among Dr. Crick’s previous trial patients, two died after their procedures, though these deaths may have been related to their multiple serious comorbidities. Additionally, four of Dr. Crick’s patients developed paravalvular leaks that required secondary surgeries. Other surgeons in the study have experienced fewer complications, but the Data Safety Monitoring Board has reviewed the outcomes and allowed the trial to proceed. Dr. Crick believes that Mr. Alton stands to benefit from the new procedure and is confident that the overall findings from the study will ultimately advance care for future patients beyond current standards. As Dr. Crick prepares to review the informed consent with Mr. Alton, he considers whether he is ethically required to share specifics about his own surgical outcomes and experience that go beyond the details already provided in the IRB-approved consent form.

ethical_issues.question: Does Dr. Crick have an ethical obligation to disclose to Mr. Alton information about his personal surgical experience and outcomes beyond what is specified in the IRB-approved consent form during the informed consent process?
keypoints: Crick’s higher complication rate does not constitute a “significant new finding” under current research ethics guidelines; therefore, there is no ethical obligation to disclose this specific data separately during the informed consent process.
Crick’s surgical competence, indicating that he meets the standard of proficiency required for participation in the clinical trial.

Crick’s complication rate may be attributable to factors such as the procedural learning curve, differences in patient comorbidities, or random variation; moreover, the limited sample size precludes definitive statistical assessment of clinical significance.

Crick’s individual surgical outcome data to Mr. Alton could risk causing misunderstanding or undue anxiety, potentially leading the patient to make decisions based on incomplete or non-generalizable information, which may not be in his best interests.

title: New Devices and Truly Informed Consent
case:
Amy, a medical student, joins her attending physician to obtain informed consent from Mrs. Jones for spinal surgery. The surgeon explains the expected recovery and rehabilitation to Mrs. Jones, who is 70 years old, along with the probable consequences of forgoing surgery. She enthusiastically agrees to the surgery. Her husband walks regularly and she is eager to accompany him in his routine. The attending surgeon schedules Mrs. Jones to have dynamic stabilization system B, a newer class of pedicle screw, implanted into her spine.
Amy is worried that Mrs. Jones is not aware of her option to have a more tried-and-true system implanted instead of System B. System B is FDA-approved, but it is one of many dynamic stabilization devices for spinal fusion whose manufacturers the FDA is requiring to conduct postmarket surveillance of device fusion and adverse events, including failure rates. Recently, Amy read about several national record-keeping systems that similarly track outcomes for other medical device implants. The Swedish hip register, for example, tracks hip implants for 10 years post-surgery. A physician expert in this register estimated that “the risk in the United States that a patient will need a replacement procedure because of a flawed product or technique can be double the risk of countries with databases…and doctors in Sweden are much less likely than American doctors to embrace new devices until registry data show they work.” Is the surgeon ethically obligated to tell Mrs. Jones about the FDA surveillance and to explain the different stabilization systems to her?
case_rewrite:
Amy, a medical student, accompanies her attending physician, Dr. W, as they meet with Mrs. Jones to discuss the details of informed consent for an upcoming spinal surgery. Dr. W outlines the anticipated recovery process, the rehabilitation plan, and the potential consequences should Mrs. Jones decide against the procedure. Mrs. Jones, a 70-year-old woman, listens carefully, her enthusiasm evident as she shares her hope of joining her husband on his daily walks once more. She readily agrees to proceed with the surgery.

Dr. W schedules Mrs. Jones to receive dynamic stabilization system B, a newer pedicle screw device to be implanted in her spine. While System B is FDA-approved, Amy begins to worry that Mrs. Jones might not be fully informed of her option to choose a more traditional, long-established stabilization system instead. System B is among several dynamic stabilization devices for spinal fusion that are currently under FDA-mandated postmarket surveillance—a process requiring ongoing monitoring of device outcomes and adverse events, including failure rates.

Amy recalls her medical coursework, where she learned about national implant registries in other countries, such as the Swedish hip register, which systematically tracks outcomes for at least a decade after surgery. She remembers an expert physician describing how, in the United States, the risk of needing a follow-up procedure due to a problematic device or technique can be twice as high as in countries that maintain such comprehensive databases. In Sweden, physicians are reportedly less likely than their American counterparts to adopt new devices before registry data have confirmed their effectiveness.

As these considerations weigh on Amy’s mind, she also wonders whether Dr. W has any financial relationship with the manufacturer of System B, and if so, whether Mrs. Jones has been informed not only of the existence but also the specific amounts of any such remuneration. Amy is acutely aware that undisclosed financial ties could influence Dr. W’s clinical judgment and the impartiality of information presented to the patient, and she believes that transparency about these relationships is essential to securing truly informed consent.

Amy is further concerned about whether Dr. W has carefully evaluated the quality and reliability of the data supporting System B, and whether this information—such as the device’s regulatory status, the ongoing FDA surveillance, and the distinctions among available stabilization systems—has been clearly conveyed to Mrs. Jones in terms she can easily grasp. Amy questions whether Dr. W is ethically required to disclose all relevant information about the device, alternative options, regulatory oversight, and any financial conflicts of interest, and to communicate this information in a manner that empowers Mrs. Jones to make an autonomous and informed decision regarding her treatment.

ethical_issues.question: Is the physician ethically obligated to disclose financial relationships with the device manufacturer, including specific amounts, to ensure truly informed consent?
keypoints: The physician’s financial relationships with device manufacturers may influence clinical judgment and the objectivity of data; therefore, any form of remuneration and the specific amounts received must be explicitly disclosed.

Detailed disclosure of financial relationships assists patients in identifying potential conflicts of interest, enhances their understanding and critical appraisal of medical recommendations, and safeguards the authenticity and validity of informed consent.

Ensuring the quality of patient care and the impartiality of medical decision-making is the fundamental principle underlying the disclosure of financial relationships; no financial interests should compromise patient autonomy or medical safety.

ethical_issues.question: When evaluating new technologies or drugs, is the physician required to assess the strength of the data quality and communicate with the patient in lay terms to ensure understanding?
keypoints: When evaluating new technologies or medications, physicians should rationally assess the quality of relevant data and the strength of evidence, prioritizing objective and reliable research findings to accurately evaluate the risks and benefits of treatment.

To ensure patients fully understand and to build trust, physicians should use clear and accessible language when obtaining informed consent, creatively employing analogies, examples, and other communication techniques to avoid confusion or alienation caused by technical jargon.

Physicians have an ethical obligation to inform patients about the regulatory status and potential risks of new technologies, including FDA postmarket surveillance requirements and differences among available alternative options, thereby assisting patients in making informed decisions.

ethical_issues.question: Is the physician ethically obligated to inform the patient about the FDA surveillance requirements and to explain the differences between the various stabilization systems?
keypoints: The physician has an ethical obligation to inform the patient, in understandable lay terms, of the reasons for selecting a particular device, as well as the device’s performance and current status, to ensure that the patient is truly giving informed consent.
The physician must disclose to the patient all viable alternative options and explain that the chosen device is relatively new to the market and lacks long-term clinical validation.
The physician should clearly inform the patient that the device is currently under postmarket surveillance, and that there remains uncertainty or controversy regarding its efficacy and safety.

The physician should first explain the differences in risks among the various surgical options, then clarify their own level of familiarity and experience with each procedure, to help the patient fully understand the advantages and disadvantages of each medical choice.
The physician should avoid allowing personal preferences to influence the information provided, thereby safeguarding the patient’s autonomy and ability to make a rational decision.

title: Physicians and Advanced Practice Registered Nurses: The Supervisor-Employer Relationship
case:
Ms. Nolan was a nurse practitioner approved by the board of nursing in her home state as an advanced practice registered nurse (APRN). After 15 years’ experience, she decided to team with another local nurse practitioner and establish an independent practitioner clinic. The law in the state where Ms. Nolan practices requires physician supervision of APRN-run clinics. A written collaborative agreement establishing the supervisory relationship must be registered with the state medical board and must contain a plan for addressing the technical requirements of supervision as set forth by the state, including the duration of the collaborative agreement; the roles, duties, and tasks the nurse practitioner can perform; and the medical treatments and prescriptions he or she can provide. APRNs may expand their scope of practice only as delegated and supervised by a physician. Supervision must be continuous but does not necessarily require the physical presence of the supervising physician every time service is rendered to a patient.
Ms. Nolan and her partner hired a physician, Dr. Roberts, who wished to decrease the level of stress in his life as part of his path to retirement a few years away. He was excited to have an administrative role that would still afford great responsibility but was much less demanding than employment as a partner in a bustling family practice. The collaborative agreement signed by the APRNs and Dr. Roberts outlined their new relationship and settled on a yearly salary for the latter’s involvement with their practice.
About a month into the job, Dr. Roberts began to recognize differences in the way he and Ms. Nolan practiced. While confident in Ms. Nolan’s abilities in matters of routine care, he was concerned about her base of clinical knowledge and diagnostic skills, noting that she often did not consider important possible diagnoses in certain cases. She would ask him to sign off on recommendations for treatment without offering him as much information as he would have liked. When Dr. Roberts voiced this concern, Ms. Nolan responded, “We apparently have differences in our approach to patient care.” Dr. Roberts disagreed, and thought that Ms. Nolan was dangerously unaware of the limits to her medical knowledge. Otherwise happy in his job, Dr. Roberts worried that if he repeatedly questioned some of Ms. Nolan’s recommendations, she would find another supervisor.
Soon after their first discussion of their practice differences, Ms. Nolan approached Dr. Roberts and requested his approval to expand her scope of practice to include the prescription of controlled substances. The idea seriously worried Dr. Roberts.
case_rewrite:
Ms. Nolan, a nurse practitioner with 15 years of experience and board approval as an advanced practice registered nurse (APRN) in her home state, decided to open an independent clinic together with another local nurse practitioner. According to state law, APRN-run clinics require physician supervision. This includes a written collaborative agreement, registered with the state medical board, that clearly outlines the supervisory relationship: specifying the agreement’s duration, detailing the roles, duties, and responsibilities permitted for the nurse practitioners, and listing the types of medical treatments and prescriptions they are authorized to provide. The law also states that APRNs may broaden their scope of practice only with delegation and active supervision by a physician. Supervision must be ongoing, though the physician need not be physically present during every patient encounter.

To satisfy these requirements, Ms. Nolan and her partner hired Dr. Roberts, a physician seeking a less stressful role as he eased into retirement. Dr. Roberts was attracted to the opportunity: an administrative position with meaningful responsibility, but far less demanding than his previous job as a partner in a busy family practice. The collaborative agreement, signed by all parties, set out the terms of their working relationship and stipulated Dr. Roberts’s annual salary for his supervisory duties.

Within the first month, Dr. Roberts began noticing differences in clinical practice between himself and Ms. Nolan. Although he trusted Ms. Nolan’s abilities with routine care, he grew uneasy about her depth of clinical knowledge and diagnostic skill. He observed that she sometimes overlooked significant possible diagnoses and would request his approval for treatment recommendations without providing the level of detail he needed to responsibly sign off. When Dr. Roberts voiced his concerns, Ms. Nolan replied, “It seems we have different approaches to patient care.” Dr. Roberts, however, felt the issue was more serious: he worried that Ms. Nolan did not fully appreciate the limitations of her medical knowledge. Dr. Roberts enjoyed the job otherwise, but he feared that consistently challenging Ms. Nolan’s recommendations might prompt her to seek a different supervisor.

Not long after their initial discussion about their differing clinical approaches, Ms. Nolan approached Dr. Roberts with a request to expand her scope of practice to include prescribing controlled substances. This request made Dr. Roberts deeply uneasy.

ethical_issues.question: In the supervisor-employee relationship, how can physicians ensure that patient welfare is not compromised by conflicts of financial interest?
keypoints: Physicians must always prioritize the welfare of patients, uphold professional ethics, and avoid compromising the quality of care due to conflicts of financial interest.
When there is a potential risk to patient interests, physicians should promptly and clearly express their professional concerns and take necessary measures to ensure patient safety.

Both parties in the supervisory relationship should jointly adhere to professional standards of patient care, establish transparent and effective communication and collaboration mechanisms, and mitigate potential conflicts of financial interest.

If trust and effective collaboration cannot be established between the parties, the physician should acknowledge the limitations of the partnership and consider terminating the agreement to protect patient interests.

ethical_issues.question: When a physician has doubts about the clinical knowledge and diagnostic skills of the supervisee, how should they fulfill their professional self-regulatory obligations to protect the interests of the patient?
keypoints: Physicians must promptly raise concerns regarding any conduct by supervisees that may jeopardize patient interests, thereby fulfilling their professional self-regulatory obligations.

Supervisees are expected to proactively recognize the limitations of their clinical knowledge and diagnostic skills, actively seek support from authoritative resources or refer to specialists; failure to do so constitutes a breach of professional integrity.

Physicians have a duty to supervise and ensure that supervisees fulfill the aforementioned responsibilities; if a supervisee is found to be unaware of their limitations and fails to take remedial actions, the physician must take appropriate measures to safeguard patient safety.
Physicians must not compromise their professional commitments due to financial interests and are required to prioritize the best interests of patients at all times.

If the parties are unable to establish an effective collaborative practice environment, the physician should acknowledge the failure of the collaborative agreement and terminate the professional relationship.

title: Moral Distress and Nurse-Physician Relationships
case:
Gerard was a registered nurse in the intensive care unit (ICU) at a large city hospital. Mrs. Smith was admitted to his unit with chest pain and shortness of breath. At 80, Mrs. Smith had no significant past medical history, apart from mild hypertension and arthritis. Upon admission, she was hypoxic and subsequently received supplemental oxygen. Otherwise her vital signs were stable. On physical exam, Mrs. Smith was noted to have bilateral rales, and the presence of an S3 was noted upon cardiac auscultation. Pertinent laboratory results included cardiac biomarkers (troponin, CK and CK-MB), which were elevated; a portable CXR revealed pulmonary edema; and a 12-Lead ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T wave inversions noted on the anterior precordial leads. Mrs. Smith was admitted for a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, and started on standard medical therapy, which included a heparin drip.
Soon after admission, Mrs. Smith’s hemodynamic status began to deteriorate. She became hypotensive and had evidence of cardiogenic shock and altered mental state. The physician updated Mrs. Smith and her family on her condition, and, considering her cardiogenic shock, recommended taking her to the cath lab. He argued that, despite her advanced age, Mrs. Smith had no significant underlying comorbidities and had been in good health. He believed that opening a closed artery could make her feel better and would give her the best chance at living the longest. Considering Mrs. Smith’s previous health and the promised benefit of catheterization, her three children decided to consent to this invasive procedure.
Shortly after her catheterization, Mrs. Smith went into respiratory distress, and flash pulmonary edema (often a result of acute myocardial infarction) was diagnosed by the attending physician. Mrs. Smith was intubated and sedated, and Gerard became her primary caretaker, making sure her vital signs were good, administering medications, and speaking with her three children about her care.
Mrs. Smith had completed an advance directive several years before, expressing her desire not to be resuscitated or kept alive on a ventilator if she were “in the process of dying.” The attending physician was confident that Mrs. Smith would recover, arguing that the intubation was temporary and that she would be extubated when her lung function improved. Consistent with his prediction, Mrs. Smith improved and was extubated the following morning. Gerard had a talk with Mrs. Smith, in which she stated that she felt terrible, thought it was close to her time, and was at peace with what was to come.
Although stable for a short period during which the conversation occurred, Mrs. Smith soon relapsed, her vital signs destabilized, and she was reintubated. That night, she spiked a fever. Antibiotics were started, and the lab cultures revealedStreptococcus pneumoniaeas the cause of infection. During this time, Mrs. Smith consistently shook her head “no” whenever new drugs were introduced or intravenous lines were inserted. Realizing her discomfort, Gerard asked Mrs. Smith directly if she wanted to continue life-saving measures, and she continued to shake her head “no.” Gerard reported this to the attending physician, who brushed him off, still maintaining her status as a “full code.” The physician was certain she would recover; the antibiotics appeared to be working, he said, and her ejection fraction was steady at 45 percent. The physician believed that Mrs. Smith’s desire to discontinue treatment only reflected her misunderstanding of the situation.
The next day, Mrs. Smith’s children told both Gerard and the attending physician that their mother was clear in her advance directives and that she would not want to be kept alive on a ventilator. Mrs. Smith’s heart measurements were steadily declining, as were her vital signs and consciousness. The physician maintained his hope for her recovery, so the family backed off, trusting his medical judgment.
Gerard was not sure what to do. When a similar situation had occurred the year before, Gerard had called an ethics consult, the result of which ultimately favored the physicians. At that time, the hospital instituted a policy stating that only physicians or family members could call ethics consults. Gerard wanted to voice his concern to the physician again or approach another administrator, but feared getting in trouble with his supervisors for being unprofessional or impeding patient care. He felt that he understood Mrs. Smith’s situation better than anyone, because he had cared for her since her hospitalization and had talked with her during the brief period during which she was off the ventilator. He saw himself as Mrs. Smith’s advocate, and was deeply troubled to see her suffering so greatly and, in his mind, needlessly. Gerard reflected upon how often he ran into situations like this in the ICU, and wondered what he could do about it.
case_rewrite:
Gerard worked as a registered nurse in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a major metropolitan hospital. One evening, Mrs. Smith, an 80-year-old woman, was admitted to his unit with complaints of chest pain and shortness of breath. Other than mild hypertension and arthritis, Mrs. Smith’s medical history was unremarkable. Upon admission, she was found to be hypoxic, prompting the initiation of supplemental oxygen. Her other vital signs remained stable. Physical examination revealed bilateral rales, and an S3 gallop was detected on cardiac auscultation. Laboratory findings included elevated cardiac biomarkers—troponin, CK, and CK-MB. A portable chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema, and her 12-lead ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T wave inversions in the anterior precordial leads. The diagnosis was a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, and Mrs. Smith was started on standard medical therapy, including a heparin infusion.

Shortly after her admission, Mrs. Smith’s condition worsened. She became hypotensive, developed evidence of cardiogenic shock, and her mental status deteriorated. The attending physician updated Mrs. Smith and her family about her critical state, recommending immediate catheterization in the cath lab. He reasoned that, despite Mrs. Smith’s age, her overall health was good and she had no major comorbidities; opening a blocked artery, he argued, would likely improve her condition and offer her the best chance for a longer life. After discussing the options and hearing the physician’s explanation, Mrs. Smith’s three children agreed to proceed with the invasive procedure.

Shortly after the catheterization, however, Mrs. Smith experienced acute respiratory distress. The attending physician diagnosed flash pulmonary edema, a known complication of myocardial infarction. Mrs. Smith was intubated and sedated. Gerard, now her primary nurse, vigilantly monitored her vital signs, administered her medications, and communicated regularly with her three children about her ongoing care.

Several years earlier, Mrs. Smith had completed an advance directive stating that she did not wish to be resuscitated or kept alive on a ventilator if she were “in the process of dying.” The attending physician, however, was optimistic about her prognosis. He believed the intubation would be temporary, expecting to extubate her once her lungs improved. His prediction came true: Mrs. Smith was successfully extubated the following morning. When Gerard spoke privately with her, Mrs. Smith confessed that she felt terrible, sensed that her time was near, and expressed peace with whatever might come.

Although she experienced a brief period of stability, Mrs. Smith’s condition soon declined again. Her vital signs became unstable, necessitating reintubation. That night, she developed a fever. Antibiotics were started, and cultures later identified Streptococcus pneumoniae as the cause of her infection. During this period, Mrs. Smith repeatedly shook her head “no” whenever new medications were offered or intravenous lines were inserted. Noticing her distress, Gerard gently asked if she wanted to continue life-saving interventions, and she continued to shake her head “no.” Gerard reported Mrs. Smith’s apparent wishes to the attending physician, but the physician dismissed his concerns and maintained Mrs. Smith’s status as a “full code.” Confident in her recovery, the physician pointed out that the antibiotics were effective and her ejection fraction remained stable at 45 percent. He attributed Mrs. Smith’s wish to stop treatment to a misunderstanding of her medical situation.

The following day, Mrs. Smith’s children approached both Gerard and the attending physician, emphasizing that their mother had been explicit in her advance directives and would not want to be kept alive on a ventilator. Meanwhile, Mrs. Smith’s heart function and vital signs continued to decline, and her level of consciousness diminished. Despite this, the physician remained hopeful for her recovery, and the family deferred to his judgment.

Gerard found himself in a difficult position. He recalled a similar situation from the previous year, when he had called for an ethics consult, only for the outcome to side with the physicians. Afterward, the hospital implemented a policy that only physicians or family members could request ethics consultations. Although Gerard wanted to raise his concerns again—either to the physician or a hospital administrator—he hesitated, fearing professional repercussions or accusations of interfering with patient care. He felt he had a unique understanding of Mrs. Smith’s situation, having cared for her continuously and spoken with her during her brief period off the ventilator. He saw himself as her advocate and was deeply troubled by the suffering he believed was unnecessary. Gerard reflected on how frequently such ethical dilemmas arose in the ICU and questioned what, if anything, he could do to help patients like Mrs. Smith in the future.

ethical_issues.question: Should healthcare institutions allow nurses to request ethics consultations in order to advocate for the best interests of patients?
keypoints: Healthcare institutions should permit nurses to initiate ethics consultations; restricting this authority lacks justifiable grounds and disregards the important ethical role of nurses as patient advocates.

Nurses have an ethical obligation to take action when patients’ rights or best interests are compromised and should courageously speak up to address moral distress, thereby upholding patient dignity and respecting their wishes.

Healthcare teams should recognize and support nurses’ ethical concerns, fostering interprofessional collaboration and cultivating an ethical decision-making environment that respects the roles of all professional disciplines.

Reforming institutional ethics consultation mechanisms by removing authority restrictions and establishing a pluralistic, open, and transparent ethics support system is essential to effectively address moral distress.

ethical_issues.question: How can the power gradient between physicians and nurses within healthcare teams be addressed to ensure that patient wishes are respected and implemented?
keypoints: Nurses should courageously express patients’ wishes, and members of the healthcare team—especially administrators and physicians—must respect and support nurses’ professional judgment to ensure that patients’ preferences are fully acknowledged and implemented.

Healthcare teams should establish open, transparent, and timely communication mechanisms to ensure that when patients first express clear and decisionally capable wishes, nurses can promptly relay this information to physicians and the team, thereby facilitating multidisciplinary participation in clinical decision-making.

Healthcare institutions should eliminate restrictions that prohibit nurses and direct-care personnel from requesting ethics consultations, guaranteeing that all clinical staff can engage in ethical deliberations and promoting interprofessional collaboration and diverse ethical perspectives.

At the organizational level, institutions must review and reform policies and cultures that give rise to moral distress, establishing policies and procedures that support multidisciplinary teamwork and foster a practice environment in which nurses can fulfill their advocacy roles without being suppressed by hierarchical power dynamics.

Through patient-level, unit-level, and organizational-level interventions, institutions should promote candid discussions and prevent similar ethical conflicts, ensuring the maximization of patient interests and the preservation of moral integrity among healthcare team members.

title: Informing Adolescents of Perinatally Contracted HIV
case:
Dr. Patel was a pediatrics resident on his ambulatory rotation. Picking up the chart of 15-year-old Julio, he read a lengthy discussion between the previous resident, Dr. O’Neill, and Julio’s mother. Dr. O’Neill reported that as she entered the patient’s room, Julio’s mother had pulled him aside to inform him that Julio and she were HIV-positive. Julio had contracted HIV at birth from her but was unaware of her status or his own. His mother had gone on to tell Dr. O’Neill that Julio had never been hospitalized and had never required antiretroviral therapy. She explained that when he was younger, he was always healthy, so she thought there was no reason for him to know that he carried the virus. She then informed Dr. O’Neill that Julio’s previous pediatrician had respected her wishes not to inform him of his status and she expected this behavior to continue at this new clinic.
Dr. O’Neill reported that she had urged Julio’s mother to change her mind. “You need to tell him about his HIV status. He is old enough to understand now, and I would strongly encourage you to sit down with him and have a discussion about it. The longer you wait, the harder it is going to be to tell him you have been hiding something like this from him for so long.”
The mother had replied that Julio was healthy and happy and had lots of friends at school. As long as he was not ill, she felt no reason for him to think he was different from other kids or to worry about getting sick.
From the documentation, Dr. O’Neill and her supervising attending physicians strongly encouraged Julio’s mother to reconsider her decision. Fearing that she would avoid medical care for her son altogether, however, they decided to respect her wishes until a relationship could be built among the patient, his mother, and the clinic members.
Dr. Patel reviewed Julio’s blood work. His CD4 count was suitably high, so he would not require medications. Entering the patient’s room he was relieved to see that Julio’s mother was not with him on this visit. Dr. Patel encountered a healthy-appearing teenage boy who seemed more concerned about whether he should be using Proactive for his facial acne than about why he was at the doctor’s office again and what his blood work had demonstrated. Dr. Patel was relieved that he would not have to deal with all this HIV business on this visit. Wrapping up, he asked Julio if there was anything else he wanted to discuss.
“Um, by the way doc, I didn’t wanna bring this up last time, because the doctor was a girl and all, but uh, you see, me and my girlfriend, we have been dating for almost a year,” Julio said. “We’ve been getting really serious, and we’ve been talking about having sex. I know that we need to use condoms and I know how to use them from that class we took in school. And my girlfriend, she was gonna talk to her doctor about getting birth control pills. We are both virgins, so I’m not worried about STDs. I was wondering if there is anything else that I should know, you know, to keep us both safe?”
Dr. Patel swallowed hard, he said he needed to speak to his attending and then he would come back and address all of Julio’s questions at once. As he left the room, Dr. Patel knew there was definitely something else Julio needed to know.

As Dr. Patel entered the exam room, he noted that Julio’s mother was absent—a small relief. He found a healthy-looking teenage boy more preoccupied with the state of his skin than the blood work Dr. Patel had just reviewed. The appointment seemed routine, and Dr. Patel felt relieved that he wouldn’t have to address the sensitive matter of HIV disclosure that day.

As the visit was wrapping up, Dr. Patel asked, “Anything else you want to talk about?”

Julio hesitated for a moment, then spoke up. “Um, actually, yeah, Doc. I didn’t really want to mention this last time, because the doctor was a woman, but, uh, me and my girlfriend—we’ve been together almost a year.
