Participation is voluntary, and some of our doctors are deeply involved. For instance, Dr. Smith has donated thousands of dollars to various charities over the years, and Dr. Anderson dedicates two weeks of his annual vacation to serve in a clinic in Guatemala. Our physicians are encouraged to use their resources and time in ways that reflect their values.”

That night, Dr. Bryant reflected on Dr. Patel’s points. The appeal of Horizons Clinic was undeniable, but questions about the deeper mission of medicine and the authenticity of each institution’s commitment to social responsibility lingered in his mind. He went to bed still uncertain about which offer would best align with his values and professional purpose.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Dr. Bryant’s decision between City Hospital and Horizons Clinic, how should he ethically evaluate the role of charity care programs within each institution’s organizational culture, and determine whether these programs authentically promote social responsibility or primarily serve as a means of professional penance or medical tourism for high-income physicians?
keypoints: When evaluating the role of charity care programs within the clinic’s culture, attention should be paid to the mechanisms for determining eligibility for assistance on a case-by-case basis and how these processes reflect physicians’ professional commitments to duty, service, compassion, ethics, and responsiveness to patients.

The actual significance and institutional support for charity care within the clinic’s culture should be assessed by examining whether all physicians participate, the voluntariness of participation, and the financial consequences of participation or nonparticipation.
The extent to which the clinic systematically assesses and addresses the health needs of the broader community is a key indicator of whether the charity care program truly creates value.

With respect to international health initiatives, it is important to critically evaluate whether such programs genuinely embody the institution’s core values, with particular attention to the appropriateness of physicians’ time commitments, in order to distinguish between authentic global health contributions and “medical tourism” or acts of professional penance by high-income physicians.

In summary, Dr. Bryant should critically assess whether the charity care program is deeply embedded within the clinic’s culture, avoiding the risk of it becoming a mere formality or an individual burden, and ensuring that it meets the substantive requirements of medical ethics and social responsibility.

title: Are Honorary Authorships Ethical?
case:
After finishing the first 3 years of medical school, Sarah decided to take a year off to spend time in a basic science laboratory. The aspect of the lab that she liked most was the tremendous latitude and independence to devise, develop, and test her own project idea while still receiving the necessary support and guidance from her postdoctoral fellow and her primary investigator, Bill.
As the year-long experience began to draw to a close, Sarah began to spend more nights and weekends in the lab to finish the project before returning to her clinical duties. When she sent the first draft of the manuscript to Bill for review, she was pleased that he believed it to be nearly publication-ready, suggesting only a few minor changes. She was surprised, however, by one of his first comments: “Include Drs. Smith and Jones as coauthors—this is a topic of interest to them.” Drs. Smith and Jones were nationally known, well-regarded senior investigators in the department, but Sarah had never even met either of them.
case_rewrite:
After completing her first three years of medical school, Sarah opted to take a year away from her coursework to immerse herself in a basic science research laboratory. She found herself particularly drawn to the freedom and independence the lab environment offered—she could design, develop, and pursue her own research project while still benefiting from the guidance and support of her postdoctoral mentor and her principal investigator, Bill.

As her year in the lab neared its end, Sarah became increasingly dedicated, often staying late into the night and coming in on weekends to ensure her project would be complete before she returned to her clinical rotations. Once she finished a draft of her manuscript, she eagerly sent it to Bill for his feedback. She was gratified when he responded that the paper was nearly ready for submission, recommending only a handful of minor edits. Yet, one of Bill’s initial remarks caught her off guard: “Add Drs. Smith and Jones as coauthors—this is an area they’re interested in.” Drs. Smith and Jones were prominent, well-respected senior investigators in the department, but Sarah had never interacted with either of them, nor had they contributed to her project.

ethical_issues.question: Are Honorary Authorships Consistent with Medical Ethical Standards?
keypoints: Honorary authorship undermines the principles of academic integrity, accountability, and the accurate attribution of scholarly work, as authorship should reflect only those who have made substantial contributions to the research.

According to the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) guidelines, authorship should be based on significant contributions to the conception or design of the work, acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data, drafting or critically revising the manuscript, and final approval of the version to be published.

Including individuals as coauthors who have not made substantive contributions to the research, such as inappropriately adding names at the suggestion of the primary investigator, violates ICMJE criteria and contravenes the ethical principles of fairness, justice, and transparency.
Sarah should uphold the standards of authorship by resisting honorary authorship practices, thereby maintaining academic integrity and preserving the trustworthiness of the scientific record.

ethical_issues.question: In manuscript authorship, how can it be ensured that listed authors meet the ICMJE criteria for authorship and assume guarantorship responsibility?
keypoints: Authorship qualification should be based on substantial contributions to the conception and design of the study, acquisition or analysis and interpretation of data, as well as participation in drafting the manuscript or critically revising it for important intellectual content and approving the final version.
Each author must publicly commit to taking responsibility for the content of the manuscript, assuming corresponding guarantorship to ensure the quality and integrity of the publication.
Clearly specifying and disclosing each author’s specific contributions facilitates accountability and responsibility, thereby preventing inappropriate authorship or honorary authorship.
Supervising faculty members should proactively coordinate and oversee authorship matters to ensure compliance with ICMJE standards, thereby avoiding authorship disputes and academic misconduct.

title: Suspected Ethical Misconduct in Research
case:
Michael, an MD/PhD student, was working for Dr. Adams, an ambitious, tenure-track associate professor who specialized in several rare genetic diseases. Michael was working on a project of his own, but he heard updates about all of the projects in the research group during a weekly lab meeting.
Michael was rather surprised when, at one of the lab meetings, Dr. Adams announced that the results of a recently concluded clinical trial were positive and had been submitted to a prestigious journal for possible publication. No one else acted surprised or asked Dr. Adams any questions about this report.
After the lab meeting, Michael and his postdoctoral fellow, Lisa, grabbed a cup of coffee before starting their work. Michael said, “It’s kind of surprising that Dr. Adams’ study results were positive. For the last year, everyone has been grumbling about how badly the study was going.”
Lisa, who was also uninvolved in the study, said “Well, that’s why we have peer review. If there are any inconsistencies, they’ll get picked up. So, any big plans this weekend?”
Despite Michael’s marginal involvement with the study, inexperience in the conduct of clinical trials, and lack of training in statistical methodologies, he could not shake the feeling that something was amiss.
In a moment of privacy with Teddy, one of the more junior members of the lab and a listed co-author on the paper, Michael casually mentioned, “Congrats on finishing the paper. That’s pretty exciting. I thought you guys were having trouble recruiting people that fit the inclusion criteria, but it seems like everything has come together.”
Teddy responded, “Thanks, but I can’t take too much credit. In the last few months, Dr. Adams really became more hands-on with this trial. He pretty much took over every aspect of it, which was nice because I have been able to wrap up some loose ends with a few other projects. To tell you the truth, I was pretty surprised when he said it was over and ready to submit for publication.”
case_rewrite:
Michael, an MD/PhD student, was pursuing his research in Dr. Adams’s laboratory. Dr. Adams, an ambitious associate professor on the tenure track, had earned recognition for her contributions to the study of rare genetic diseases. Each week, the team gathered for lab meetings, during which everyone shared updates, keeping the group informed about ongoing projects and developments.

At one such weekly meeting, Michael was caught off guard when Dr. Adams announced that a recently completed clinical trial had yielded positive results and that the findings had already been submitted to a leading journal. No one else in the lab seemed surprised or raised any questions about the announcement, and the meeting quickly moved on to other topics.

Afterward, Michael and Lisa, a postdoctoral fellow who had not been involved in the clinical trial either, went out for coffee before heading back to the lab. As they walked, Michael remarked, “I didn’t expect Dr. Adams’s study to get such good results. For the past year, it sounded like there were a lot of obstacles with that trial.”

Lisa shrugged. “That’s what peer review is for—if there’s anything off, the reviewers are supposed to catch it. But enough about work—do you have any weekend plans?”

Despite his limited involvement with the clinical trial and lack of formal training in clinical trial methodology or advanced statistics, Michael couldn’t shake his sense of unease about the results. Later, he had a private conversation with Teddy, a junior member of the lab who was listed as a co-author on the submitted paper. “Congrats on getting the submission in,” Michael said. “I remember hearing that recruiting enough eligible participants was a big challenge. Did things end up working out in the end?”

Teddy replied, “Thanks, but honestly, Dr. Adams took over pretty much everything those last few months. She managed all the details herself, which gave me time to focus on some other projects I’d fallen behind on. I was actually surprised when she said the trial was finished and ready to submit.”

Michael’s uncertainty lingered. Given that he hadn’t been directly involved in the trial and lacked experience with this kind of research, he wasn’t sure how to proceed with his growing doubts about the integrity of the study’s results.

ethical_issues.question: When Michael suspects that Dr. Adams’ research results may involve ethical misconduct, what steps should he take to verify the accuracy of the information and to gain a comprehensive understanding of Dr. Adams’ work?
keypoints: Accusations of ethical misconduct are a serious matter; before taking any action, Michael should rationally evaluate the information to ensure its accuracy and base it on a thorough understanding of Dr. Adams’ work.
Michael should engage with laboratory colleagues in a nonaccusatory and open manner, sincerely seeking to understand the specifics of the research success and any potential concerns.
If discussions with colleagues do not clarify his doubts, Michael should consider communicating directly with Dr. Adams, providing him the opportunity to explain and clarify the situation.
During such communication, Michael should adopt a respectful and constructive approach, avoiding presumptive suspicion to facilitate an honest and open dialogue.
If doubts persist and cannot be resolved independently, Michael should seek the support of a trusted mentor or the ethics committee to assist with further investigation and management of the matter.

ethical_issues.question: When residents or students suspect that a researcher may be engaging in misconduct, how should they communicate with the researcher in order to avoid confrontation and provide the researcher with an opportunity to clarify or rectify the situation?
keypoints: When a resident or student suspects that a researcher may be engaging in misconduct, they should first communicate directly with the researcher involved, providing an opportunity for clarification or for the researcher to correct any unintentional errors.

Communication should be conducted in a non-confrontational and non-accusatory manner, reflecting a genuine desire to understand the reasons behind the research’s success and avoiding escalation of conflict.

Initiating an institutional review process without first communicating with the researcher may forfeit the opportunity to remedy and correct the issue before it becomes public, potentially hindering the proper resolution of the matter.
Throughout the communication process, the researcher’s professional status and efforts should be respected, maintaining objectivity and rationality to promote constructive dialogue.

title: Avoiding the Appearance of Faculty Favoritism
case:
Jon was a second-year internal medicine resident at a large, academic medical center. Through a series of coincidences, he encountered two patients in clinic whom he believed would benefit from enrollment in a clinical trial getting underway at the center. The trial, about which Jon was particularly knowledgeable, was being conducted by the chairperson of the Department of Medicine, Dr. Anderson. Jon contacted the study coordinator about the patients, and then explained the risks and benefits of participating in the trial to patients.
The following week, at the conclusion of grand rounds, many faculty members, residents, and students were mingling outside the auditorium and grabbing a last cup of coffee before heading back to work. Jon was catching up with a few of his fellow residents when Dr. Anderson stopped to thank him for enrolling the patients in the trial.
“We’ve had a heck of a time getting patients recruited for this study, so I appreciate all the time you spent getting them enrolled,” Dr. Anderson said.
After asking how Jon’s current rotation was going, Dr. Anderson said, “By the way, I have tickets to the game Saturday, and I’ll be out of town, so you’re welcome to them if you can use them. Just let me know.”
case_rewrite:
Jon, a second-year internal medicine resident at a large academic medical center, recently found himself in a unique position. By coincidence, he saw two patients in his clinic whom he believed would benefit from enrolling in a new clinical trial about to launch at the institution. The trial, focusing on an area Jon was well-versed in, was being led by Dr. Anderson, the chairperson of the Department of Medicine. Wanting the best for his patients, Jon reached out to the study coordinator and carefully discussed the risks and benefits of the trial with both individuals.

A week later, following grand rounds, the hallway outside the auditorium buzzed with faculty, residents, and students chatting and gathering their things for the day ahead. Jon was catching up with a few colleagues when Dr. Anderson approached him amid the crowd.

“Jon, thank you for enrolling those patients in the trial,” Dr. Anderson said, his tone appreciative. “Recruitment has been tough, and your efforts have made a real difference.”

After a brief conversation about Jon’s current rotation, Dr. Anderson added, “By the way, I have tickets for the game this Saturday, but I’ll be out of town. If you’re interested, they’re yours—just let me know.”

Dr. Anderson’s words were casual, but the offer of the tickets lingered in Jon’s mind as the conversation shifted and the group prepared to disperse.

ethical_issues.question: Does Jon’s acceptance of a personal gift from Dr. Anderson, the principal investigator, during the recruitment process for a clinical trial constitute a conflict of interest?
keypoints: A resident physician’s acceptance of personal gifts from a trial principal investigator may constitute a conflict of interest, as such gifts have the potential to compromise the physician’s independent judgment and objectivity.

Offering tickets as a personal gift within the same conversation, especially when the giver holds a superior position relative to the recipient, appears preferential and is inappropriate; such conduct should be avoided.
Expressing gratitude openly and publicly is appropriate and sufficient; leaders should recognize that a simple “thank you” is adequate and that additional personal gifts are unnecessary.

Compliant forms of acknowledgment should be documented in writing prior to the initiation of the trial and uniformly applied to all contributors, ensuring transparency, fairness, and equity, thereby distinguishing them from improper personal gifts.

ethical_issues.question: How can fairness and transparency be ensured in the interactions between residents and departmental leadership within an academic medical environment to avoid personal favoritism?
keypoints: In an academic medical setting, it is essential to ensure that interactions between residents and departmental leadership are fair and transparent, guaranteeing that all residents have equal opportunities to establish appropriate and professional relationships with leadership.
Leaders should avoid giving gifts or other personal rewards to individuals privately or publicly in a manner that could create risks of favoritism, conflicts of interest, or undue influence.

Public and measured expressions of gratitude constitute an appropriate means of recognizing residents’ contributions; leaders should understand that verbal thanks alone carry significant value and do not require additional personal rewards.

Any form of reward or compensation must be clearly disclosed in writing in advance and made available to all eligible individuals, thereby ensuring transparency, fairness, and institutional oversight.

Professional boundaries must be established and maintained to prevent personal relationships from influencing clinical trial recruitment or other work-related decisions, thereby safeguarding patient interests and research integrity.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of a clinical trial, how can the contributions of residents be appropriately acknowledged without involving personal rewards or exchanges of favors?
keypoints: Public and succinct acknowledgment of residents’ contributions to patient recruitment for clinical trials is appropriate and necessary, reflecting recognition and respect for their work.

Previous forms of appreciation for faculty or residents who assisted with recruitment (such as books, gift certificates, travel reimbursements, or per-case payments) must be disclosed in writing prior to trial initiation and made available to all relevant personnel to ensure fairness and transparency.

Maintaining fairness and transparency in faculty-trainee and hierarchical interactions is crucial to prevent private or undisclosed exchanges of benefits that could undermine team trust and professional ethics.

The private gift of game tickets by Dr. Anderson constitutes a personal, non-public reward that can be perceived as an exchange of favors, violating principles of fairness and professional ethics, and should be avoided.

Establishing standardized and transparent mechanisms for expressing gratitude helps preserve the professionalism of clinical trial recruitment efforts and the ethical conduct of residents, thereby fostering positive and equitable faculty-trainee relationships.

title: When Patient and Physician Disagree on Patient’s “Best Interest”
case:
Mr. A is making his first visit to Dr. M, an oncologist, because of debilitating bone pain and severe constipation. For the past year, he has been treated for cancer of unknown origin by a state-licensed naturopathic physician whom he has seen extensively over the years for what Mr. A explains were a variety of autoimmune diseases and infections. Despite this therapy, the cancer has progressed to an advanced state with multiple vertebral metastases, including a large tumor in his cervical spine which required emergency surgical decompression 3 weeks prior to his visit to Dr. M. Before the hospitalization for surgery, Mr. A was not under the care of a medical oncologist. Mr. A is aware that he may need additional therapy but is worried about the toxic effects of chemotherapy and radiation.
Mr. A was told to see Dr. M by a close friend who explained that Dr. M “is the kind of doctor who treats the whole person.” In his initial interview with a clinic nurse, he explains that he has suffered all his life from what he believes is heavy metal poisoning. His father was a dentist, and the family was exposed to large amounts of heavy metals which, Mr. A believes, weakened their immune systems and gave them cancer and neurological deficits. Two years earlier he had a large set of silver fillings removed by a dentist who botched the procedure, Mr. A says, exposing him to a high enough dose of silver to precipitate his current disease.
To make matters worse, Mr. A has an adult son who has autism, which Mr. A believes was caused by heavy metal “poisons” that accompanied his childhood vaccinations. His son does not work or help out around the house. Mr. A has received some support from a neighbor but he has been mostly on his own throughout this illness. The nurse listens carefully and makes brief notes about Mr. A’s medical and social history, but Mr. A becomes increasingly frustrated throughout the conversation, as though his view is not being heard.
When Dr. M enters the room he finds an ill man who appears to be in marked discomfort, despite receiving moderate doses of narcotic analgesia. They begin by reviewing Mr. A’s medical chart, including a CT scan of his spine that shows multiple large masses. There is no record of his treatment by the naturopath. Dr. M sits down, faces Mr. A, and begins by addressing his symptoms. He prescribes ethylene glycol as a laxative to relieve Mr. A’s constipation, but the patient refuses the prescription initially, saying he has read that it is toxic. The doctor explains that it is cancer that is killing him, not the drugs. The patient mentions a friend who wasted away while on chemotherapy, and as they talk about what might have caused her death, Mr. A confides his fears to Dr. W and cries.  Dr. M refers Mr. A to a pain specialist and recommends that he begin chemotherapy and radiation the following week, after he has a few more days to gain some strength but before too much time passes. Mr. A tentatively agrees, but Dr. M is afraid that he will not return for follow-up.
case_rewrite:
Mr. A arrives for his first appointment with Dr. M, an oncologist, seeking relief from severe bone pain and persistent constipation. Over the past year, he has been under the care of a state-licensed naturopathic physician, whom he has consulted frequently for what he describes as a range of autoimmune disorders and infections. Despite these extensive naturopathic treatments, Mr. A’s cancer has advanced significantly, now presenting with multiple metastases to his spine. Just three weeks prior, he underwent emergency decompressive surgery to address a sizable tumor compressing his cervical spine, but until that urgent hospitalization, he had not been evaluated by a medical oncologist. While Mr. A understands that further therapy may be necessary, he expresses apprehension about the potential toxicity of chemotherapy and radiation.

It was a close friend who encouraged Mr. A to see Dr. M, assuring him that Dr. M is a physician who “treats the whole person.” During his initial interview with the clinic nurse, Mr. A shares his lifelong conviction that he suffers from heavy metal poisoning. He recounts how his father, a dentist, exposed the family to significant amounts of heavy metals—exposures Mr. A believes weakened their immune systems, causing cancer and neurological problems. Two years ago, he had a large number of silver fillings removed by a dentist, but the procedure was mishandled, and Mr. A believes he received a dangerously high dose of silver, triggering his current illness.

Complicating matters, Mr. A’s adult son has autism. Mr. A is convinced that heavy metal “poisons” in his son’s childhood vaccines caused the condition. His son does not work or contribute to the household, leaving Mr. A largely without support except for occasional help from a neighbor. The nurse listens attentively, making succinct notes about Mr. A’s medical and social background, but Mr. A becomes visibly discouraged during the conversation, feeling as though his perspective is being overlooked.

When Dr. M enters the room, he finds Mr. A appearing acutely unwell, in obvious discomfort despite ongoing narcotic pain management. Together, they review Mr. A’s medical records and examine a recent CT scan, which reveals multiple sizable tumors in his spine. There is, however, no documentation of the naturopathic treatments he has received. Dr. M takes a seat, faces Mr. A, and begins to address his immediate symptoms. He prescribes ethylene glycol as a laxative to help with the constipation, but Mr. A is hesitant, expressing concern after reading that the substance can be toxic. Dr. M responds by gently explaining that it is the cancer that is life-threatening, not the prescribed medication.

As their conversation continues, Mr. A brings up a friend who underwent chemotherapy and, in his words, “wasted away” from the treatment. Discussing this, Mr. A opens up to Dr. M about his fears, becoming emotional and crying. Dr. M listens with empathy, then refers Mr. A to a pain specialist and recommends starting chemotherapy and radiation the following week—allowing a few days for Mr. A to regain some strength, but emphasizing the need to proceed soon. Mr. A gives a tentative agreement but, as the consultation concludes, Dr. M worries that Mr. A may not return for further care.

ethical_issues.question: In the case where Mr. A refuses chemotherapy, does Dr. M have an ethical obligation to attempt to persuade him to accept treatment in order to promote his best interests and improve his quality of life?
keypoints: The physician should assess whether chemotherapy could extend the patient’s life sufficiently to allow him to settle his affairs and arrange appropriate care for his son.
The physician should evaluate whether chemotherapy could significantly alleviate the patient’s pain, enabling him to better enjoy his remaining time with his son.
The physician has a duty to provide comprehensive information based on an assessment of the patient’s best interests and to attempt to persuade the patient to accept treatment.

However, if the patient explicitly refuses treatment based on personal beliefs (such as the view that the therapy constitutes “toxins”), the physician’s obligation to persuade is neither absolute nor unlimited.

In any case, the physician must ultimately respect the patient’s autonomy; if, after fully understanding the risks and benefits of treatment, the patient still refuses, the physician should not coerce the patient but should remain available to provide consultation or further care should the patient change his mind.

tags: Patient-clinician relationship/Patients’ responsibility for their health
title: Low-Tech Solution to a High-Tech Problem
case:
Mr. Jones visited Dr. Green because he had developed an infection on the bottom of his right foot. Before his appointment, Mr. Jones looked up his symptoms on the Internet and found that they could be indicative of type 2 diabetes. After examining Mr. Jones, Dr. Green ordered a fasting glucose test.
The test results showed a glucose level of 250 mg/dL, which indicated that Mr. Jones did indeed have type 2 diabetes. Dr. Green informed Mr. Jones of the results by telephone and asked him to come in to discuss treatment options and lifestyle changes that would help him get control of his diabetes.
“I have read about diet and exercise options for diabetic patients on the Internet, but I don’t think that I can make that sort of change,” Mr. Jones said. “I would prefer to start on medication right away.”
During the next visit, Dr. Green agreed that if Mr. Jones was not willing to make lifestyle changes he should start medication. He wrote a prescription for metformin, a first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes. When Mr. Jones looked at it, he said to Dr. Green, “I have also researched treatments for type 2 diabetes and would prefer to have the newest and best treatment. I can’t remember the name but it is a combination of two drugs.” While Dr. Green knew that this treatment was often an effective option, he was also concerned about using a more potent and expensive treatment before he had seen the effects that metformin had on Mr. Jones’s glucose levels.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Jones arrived at Dr. Green’s office after noticing a troublesome infection on the sole of his right foot. Before making the appointment, Mr. Jones had spent considerable time online, researching his symptoms. He discovered that foot infections like his might be linked to type 2 diabetes, which left him feeling anxious about his health.

During the consultation, Dr. Green conducted a thorough examination and recommended a fasting glucose test to better understand Mr. Jones’s condition. When the lab results came back, they showed a fasting glucose level of 250 mg/dL—clear evidence that Mr. Jones had developed type 2 diabetes. Dr. Green called Mr. Jones to explain the diagnosis and invited him to the office to discuss how best to manage his new condition.

At their next meeting, Dr. Green outlined the importance of lifestyle changes—such as a balanced diet and regular exercise—to help control diabetes. Mr. Jones, however, voiced his doubts. “I’ve read a lot on the Internet about what people with diabetes are supposed to do,” he said frankly. “But I just don’t think I can manage those lifestyle changes. I’d rather start medication right away.”

Listening to Mr. Jones’s concerns, Dr. Green acknowledged his perspective. Since Mr. Jones was reluctant to attempt diet and exercise modifications, Dr. Green agreed to start him on medication. She prescribed metformin, explaining that it is widely recommended as the first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes.

As Dr. Green handed over the prescription, Mr. Jones hesitated. “I’ve also read about other treatments online,” he said. “There’s a newer option—a combination of two drugs. I can’t remember the exact name, but I’d prefer to have the most advanced treatment available.”

Dr. Green recognized the medication Mr. Jones referred to and knew it could be effective for some patients. However, she was wary about immediately resorting to a more potent and costly therapy before seeing how Mr. Jones responded to metformin. She explained her reservations, emphasizing the importance of starting with established treatments and monitoring their effectiveness before considering alternatives. Throughout the conversation, Dr. Green remained attentive to Mr. Jones’s preferences and the information he had gathered online, seeking to balance her medical judgment with his concerns while working together to develop a safe and effective treatment plan.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ensure the safety and efficacy of treatment plans while respecting patient autonomy when patients obtain health information from the Internet?
keypoints: Physicians should understand the patient’s cultural background, lifestyle, health beliefs, and personal preferences in order to collaboratively develop a feasible and individualized treatment plan.

Physicians should explore the underlying beliefs the patient holds regarding medications and treatment options, assess the credibility of the information sources, and identify potential misunderstandings or biases.
Physicians should respond affirmatively to patients’ concerns, clarify shared therapeutic goals, build trust, and seek consensus on the treatment plan.

Physicians should share their professional insights based on evidence-based medicine tailored to the patient’s specific needs, while guiding patients to access authoritative and reliable online resources to promote ongoing education and informed decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of a patient refusing lifestyle modifications and requesting immediate pharmacological treatment, how should the physician balance the patient’s preferences with professional judgment to develop an appropriate treatment plan?
keypoints: Physicians should thoroughly explore the underlying beliefs behind a patient’s refusal to modify lifestyle behaviors, employing open-ended questions to understand the patient’s concerns and motivations, thereby establishing a foundation of trust.

Physicians should share their professional insights based on the patient’s specific concerns, objectively explaining the advantages, disadvantages, and safety considerations of different treatment options to facilitate a comprehensive understanding of available therapies.

Physicians should collaboratively clarify treatment goals with the patient, seeking consensus through effective communication to develop an individualized treatment plan that aligns with the patient’s values and evidence-based clinical practice, thereby enhancing adherence and therapeutic outcomes.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr. Green ethically ensure that Mr. Jones relies on accurate and trustworthy health information sources, and how should she guide him in critically evaluating online medical information to minimize misinformation and potential risks during their clinical communication?
keypoints: Physicians should thoroughly explore the underlying beliefs of patients by inquiring about their views on medications and the sources of their information, thereby gaining a comprehensive understanding of the patients’ perspectives and concerns.

Physicians should employ affirming responses to respect patients’ feelings while balancing respect with professional guidance, clearly explaining the rationale, safety, and potential risks of treatment plans, and avoiding uncritical agreement with patients’ viewpoints.

Physicians ought to be familiar with and proactively recommend authoritative and reliable health information resources, guiding patients in the accurate retrieval and critical appraisal of online health information to minimize misinformation and potential risks.

Physicians should attend to the individual needs and cognitive levels of patients, flexibly adjusting communication strategies to facilitate effective interaction and promote patient engagement in treatment decision-making.
Through effective communication and information guidance, physicians can enhance patients’ understanding and trust in treatment plans, thereby improving adherence and therapeutic outcomes.

title: Youth Violence: Effective Screening and Prevention
case:
Dr. Foster, an emergency room physician in a busy urban hospital, was called in late one Friday night to evaluate Thomas, a teenager who had been involved in a violent altercation. The young man had been brought in by his mother, and refused to divulge anything about what caused his injuries. Once in the examination room, Dr. Foster could see that Thomas wore colors, clothing, and paraphernalia clearly associated with gang members who had been treated in the emergency room. Past interactions with police officers confirmed that the gang was associated with gun and drug violence.
Upon evaluation, Thomas's injuries appeared to be both minor and superficial-he had a variety of bruises, lacerations, cuts, and scrapes-but no evident signs of significant trauma. A neurological exam revealed no focal findings, and all cranial nerves were intact. Thomas had full range of motion in all four extremities. There was no indication of internal organ damage, and, though Thomas sported quite a remarkable black eye, he had no signs of altered consciousness or physical signs consistent with concussion or intracranial hemorrhage.
Dr. Foster presumed that Thomas had most likely been involved in some sort of late-night gang fight, which was consistent with the young man's reticence in answering questions related to the incident itself, though he had been grudgingly cooperative with the physical exam. For the sake of completeness, Dr. Foster ordered a CT scan to rule out any possible head trauma. He also called for blood work and a urine drug screen, to which neither Thomas nor his mother objected.
While Thomas was upstairs for the CT scan, Dr. Foster spoke with his mother who was clearly distraught. She expressed her helplessness in controlling Thomas's behavior and said she was certain that he had been drawn into a group of bad kids. She said he was almost never home, skipped school on a regular basis, and spent all of his time hanging out with friends whom she did not know. This was not the first time that Thomas had been in a fight, she was sure. She begged Dr. Foster to get her son some help.
Dr. Foster was familiar with local gang-intervention and social programs in the area that had been remarkably effective in improving the outlook and welfare of patients. He was also aware of various applicable laws for mandatory physician reporting of criminal activity and child abuse and neglect, although he was not entirely clear on the details. A report of injury from violence triggered involvement of the gang-intervention programs.
Dr. Foster knew the professional principles regarding patient confidentiality and that, in the absence of suspicion of criminal activity or child abuse and neglect, he had a duty to maintain the confidentiality of patient information. The reporting threshold had not yet been met in his estimation. Although intervention would probably be of great benefit to Thomas, the lack of confirmed history prevented formation of a reasonable index of suspicion, and he would, in effect, be "gaming the system," albeit ostensibly in the best interests of his patient, if he reported that Thomas's injuries had resulted from acts of violence.
Once Thomas returned from the CT scan, Dr. Foster spoke to him again, determined to gain the information necessary to confirm a course of action.
"I need you to tell me exactly what happened tonight," he said sternly. "I believe it is likely that you have been the victim of violence, and, if so, I am obligated to report this to the police, who will take appropriate further steps." This was not entirely true, Dr. Foster thought, but it would get Thomas the help he needed.
At this, Thomas seemed to be struggling not to cry. "Please don't say anything to anyone," he begged. "I'm not supposed to talk about what happened."
case_rewrite:
Dr. Foster, an emergency room physician at a bustling city hospital, was called in late on a Friday night to assess Thomas, a teenage boy who had arrived accompanied by his mother after being involved in a violent incident. Thomas, tight-lipped and visibly guarded, refused to reveal any details about how he was injured. Inside the examination room, Dr. Foster noted that Thomas’s clothing and accessories bore unmistakable signs of affiliation with a local gang—a group previously linked by law enforcement to drug and gun-related violence, and whose members Dr. Foster had cared for before.

On examination, Thomas’s injuries appeared to be mostly superficial: he had several bruises, shallow lacerations, and scrapes scattered across his body. His most prominent injury was a swollen black eye, but there were no signs of concussion, intracranial bleeding, or internal trauma. Neurological assessment was reassuring, with intact cranial nerves and full range of motion in all limbs.

Given the context and Thomas’s reluctance to talk, Dr. Foster suspected he had been caught up in a late-night gang altercation. Still, Thomas grudgingly complied with the physical examination. To be thorough, Dr. Foster ordered a CT scan to rule out subtle head injuries, and requested bloodwork and a urine drug screen—neither of which Thomas nor his mother objected to.

While Thomas was away for the scan, Dr. Foster spoke privately with his mother, who was visibly distraught. She confided that she felt powerless to curb Thomas’s behavior, convinced he had fallen in with a dangerous crowd. She described how he was rarely home, often skipped school, and spent his time with friends she didn’t know. This wasn’t the first time Thomas had gotten into trouble, she admitted. Tearfully, she pleaded with Dr. Foster to find a way to help her son.

Dr. Foster was aware of effective gang-intervention and social support programs available in the area, which had helped patients in similar situations. He also knew that laws regarding mandatory reporting of criminal activity and child abuse or neglect could come into play, though he was not entirely confident about every detail of the requirements. He recalled that reporting injuries from violence could trigger intervention by these programs.

At the same time, Dr. Foster understood the ethical imperative to maintain patient confidentiality. Unless there was a reasonable suspicion of criminal activity, child abuse, or neglect, he was obligated to protect Thomas’s privacy. In his own assessment, the threshold for mandatory reporting had not yet been reached. While referring Thomas for intervention might be in his best interest, doing so without clear justification would mean bending the rules—potentially misreporting the nature of the injuries just to secure services for Thomas.

When Thomas returned from his scan, Dr. Foster decided to speak with him again, aiming to clarify what had happened and determine the appropriate course of action. He made sure to talk to Thomas alone, without his mother present, in a private and respectful setting.

“I need you to tell me exactly what happened tonight,” Dr. Foster said, his tone earnest but firm. “If you were the victim of violence, I may be required to report this to the authorities, who would then step in to help.” Dr. Foster knew this wasn’t strictly accurate in every case, but hoped it would encourage Thomas to open up.

At these words, Thomas’s composure faltered. He looked on the verge of tears and pleaded softly, “Please don’t tell anyone. I can’t talk about what happened.”

Dr. Foster found himself weighing his ethical responsibilities: the obligation to protect Thomas’s confidentiality, the legal requirements regarding mandatory reporting, and the genuine need to intervene for Thomas’s wellbeing.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance protecting patient confidentiality with adhering to mandatory reporting laws when treating adolescent patients who may be involved in violence?
keypoints: When protecting patient confidentiality, physicians should conduct inquiries in the absence of parents or visitors and clearly inform the patient that the information disclosed will remain strictly between the patient, the physician, and the medical team, except in cases involving self-harm, harm to others, or the need for protection from harm by others.

Physicians must adhere to the principle of patient confidentiality and have a duty to safeguard patient information from disclosure in the absence of a reasonable suspicion of criminal activity or abuse and neglect.

Physicians should be familiar with and comply with their state’s mandatory reporting laws and guidelines, where the decision to report typically hinges on whether the patient poses an intent to harm themselves or others; in particular, when a patient explicitly expresses intent to harm a specific individual (duty-to-warn), the physician is obligated to promptly notify law enforcement authorities and the potential victim.

ethical_issues.question: In the emergency department setting, how should physicians effectively screen for and identify the risk of violence in adolescent patients while ensuring that the patients feel safe and are willing to share information?
keypoints: The primary objective of screening is to prevent future violent injuries by ensuring that patients receive appropriate counseling, intervention, and referrals, as well as access to effective gang-intervention and social support resources.
Physicians should create a safe and non-threatening communication environment that fosters patient trust and respect.
Inquiry should be conducted in a private setting, avoiding the presence of parents or other visitors, in order to protect patient confidentiality.

Physicians must clearly inform patients that, except in legally mandated exceptions such as self-harm, harm to others, or child protection concerns, all information provided will be kept strictly confidential and shared only with the medical team.
Questions should be posed in a direct, nonjudgmental, and empathetic manner to encourage honest disclosure from the patient.

Structured screening tools and comprehensive social history-taking should be employed to assess the risk of violence and relevant contextual factors, focusing on the identity of the assailant, whether the conflict has ended, any plans to harm others, prior reporting to authorities, as well as academic performance, attendance, past violent behavior, substance use, and illicit weapon possession.

title: What To Do when It Might Be Child Abuse
case:
Dr. Peterson took a deep breath and exhaled thoughtfully as she weighed the possible approaches toward a case that was scheduled for the afternoon. For several years, she had been the primary pediatrician for Adrian, now a rambunctious 7-year-old. During the course of that time, she had developed a constructive, friendly relationship with the boy's parents, who had been fastidious regarding his care and upbringing and seemed like involved, caring parents. Dr. Peterson had enjoyed appointments with this family, trusting that visits would be routine and the boy would be healthy, allowing some time to chat with the parents, who were both executives in a large company headquartered nearby. The boy had always been in good health, and seldom needed to come in for non-routine well-child visits.
Dr. Peterson now questioned her original assumptions. For the past year, Adrian had been in to see her four or five times with a succession of injuries. Dr. Peterson noted numerous bruises and lacerations in different states of healing dispersed on the boy's knees, thighs, and buttocks. Adrian needed a couple of stitches on one occasion. The last time he came in he needed treatment for a broken leg. During all of these visits, his parents had appeared concerned and anxious, attributing the injuries to Adrian's simply being a very active youngster. They told Dr. Peterson that he'd been involved with soccer and martial arts for the past year, and usually had a sports-related explanation for every injury, though they could seldom give specific details. Dr. Peterson was aware that these parents spanked on occasion when the boy misbehaved, but they said that they only swatted lightly, never leaving a mark. Both had been working overtime to handle financial problems, and said that Adrian was often left in the care of a babysitter or aunt.
During recent visits, Dr. Peterson had often noted that Adrian seemed either visibly upset or quiet and withdrawn, behaviors that were completely natural, given his sports-related injuries. Now she had to act on her growing suspicions, but what would that do to her relationship with the family?
case_rewrite:
Dr. Peterson paused by the window of her office, gazing out as she considered the best way to handle an upcoming appointment that weighed heavily on her mind. For years, she had been Adrian’s primary pediatrician, watching him grow from a curious toddler into an energetic 7-year-old. Over time, she had built a positive, friendly rapport with his parents, who were always attentive and meticulous about his health and development. Both worked as executives at a prominent local company, and Dr. Peterson had come to look forward to their visits, confident that Adrian's checkups would be routine and that they might even share a few lighthearted moments together. Adrian had always been a healthy child, rarely needing care outside of his scheduled wellness appointments.

Recently, however, Dr. Peterson found herself questioning her earlier sense of comfort. In the past year alone, Adrian had visited her office four or five times, each time with new injuries. She observed a range of bruises and cuts, all in different stages of healing, scattered across his knees, thighs, and buttocks. Once, Adrian required stitches for a wound. On his most recent visit, he came in with a fractured leg that needed immediate attention. Throughout these visits, Adrian’s parents appeared genuinely distressed and anxious, explaining that their son was simply a high-spirited child who had taken up soccer and martial arts in the past year. They always attributed his injuries to accidents on the playing field or during practice, but when Dr. Peterson pressed for details, they struggled to recall specifics. She also knew that the parents occasionally used spanking as discipline, but they assured her it was only a light swat and never left any marks. Lately, with both parents working long hours to manage financial strains, Adrian had often been cared for by a babysitter or his aunt.

During his recent appointments, Dr. Peterson noticed that Adrian sometimes appeared subdued or visibly upset, a shift from his usual lively demeanor. Given his sports injuries, she reasoned that such reactions might be expected, yet a persistent feeling of unease grew. Now, as she prepared for another visit, Dr. Peterson realized she needed to confront her suspicions, all the while worrying about how this might affect the trust she had built with Adrian’s family.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where child abuse is suspected, how should physicians balance the therapeutic relationship with the family against their responsibility to ensure the child’s safety?
keypoints: The physician’s fundamental responsibility is to ensure the well-being and safety of the minor patient, approaching any suspected diagnosis of child abuse or neglect with rigor, promptly identifying concerns and implementing necessary interventions.

If the information supports suspicion, the physician should communicate openly and respectfully with the caretaker(s), clearly emphasizing that the primary concern is the child’s health and safety, and expressing a willingness to collaborate in safeguarding the child’s welfare.

Avoid immediate accusations or assigning blame, as there may be no clear indication of the perpetrator; instead, stress the importance of assisting in establishing the factual truth to provide the child with optimal protection.

The physician should recognize the long-term and complex nature of the evaluation and intervention process, continuously offering support and medical care to the patient and family; this collaborative approach helps maintain and strengthen the therapeutic relationship.

ethical_issues.question: When faced with a possible case of child abuse, how should a physician determine whether to conduct a thorough investigation and initiate the evaluation process?
keypoints: Physicians should, based on professional training and clinical intuition, establish a broad differential diagnostic framework and comprehensively evaluate the medical history and physical findings to determine whether further investigation is warranted.

Physicians should thoroughly review all available medical history and physical examination information, weighing the possibility of child abuse against alternative reasonable explanations, and consult experienced colleagues or local child abuse specialists when necessary.

Physicians should meet with the family and conduct separate interviews with the caretaker(s) and the child, obtaining detailed information about the injuries to assess their consistency with clinical findings, while also exploring family functioning, stressors, and psychosocial risk factors.

Physicians should perform a comprehensive physical examination of the child, with particular attention to all skin surfaces and injuries in various stages of healing, in order to gather supplementary diagnostic information.

Physicians should, based on the integrated assessment, determine whether the threshold for suspicion of child abuse has been met and subsequently decide whether to initiate the appropriate evaluation and protective procedures.

tags: Disparities in health and health care/Social determinants
title: A Mother and Infant with No Home
case:
Mrs. Patterson delivered her child by cesarean section in a community hospital. She and her child were in good health and ready to be discharged 2 days later. In speaking with Mrs. Patterson, Dr. Blake discovered that she was homeless, a fact that no one else in the hospital knew. When admitted, Mrs. Patterson had given the registrar an old driver's license and did not report that she was currently living in her car and staying with friends occasionally.
When Dr. Blake asked her what she intended to do once she left the hospital, Mrs. Patterson explained that she would not go to a shelter--she was afraid of random violence, substance abuse by fellow tenants, and unsanitary conditions. Friends offered her periodical financial assistance but not a permanent place to stay. Contacting her family or husband, who had been physically abusive, were not options, and she was adamant that social workers not be involved. She planned to live in her car until she could get back on her feet, which she said would only take a few months.
Dr. Blake was conflicted about what to do. On the one hand, she understood why her patient did not want to return home or stay in a shelter. She did not want to put her child in foster care. Even though Mrs. Patterson was mentally sound and competent, a patient could not be discharged without someplace to go. Communities were cracking down on the practice of "patient dumping."
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Patterson gave birth to her baby via cesarean section at a small community hospital. Both mother and child were doing well and were scheduled for discharge two days later. During a routine conversation, Dr. Blake learned something that had not surfaced during admission: Mrs. Patterson was homeless. She had presented an outdated driver’s license at registration and had not mentioned that she was currently living in her car, occasionally staying with friends when possible.

When Dr. Blake gently inquired about Mrs. Patterson’s plans after leaving the hospital, Mrs. Patterson confided that she refused to go to a shelter. She expressed deep concern over the risk of random violence, substance abuse among other residents, and unsanitary conditions she’d witnessed in shelters. While some friends were able to offer her occasional financial help, none could provide her with a stable place to stay. She made it clear that returning to her family or husband—who had been physically abusive in the past—was not an option. Mrs. Patterson also insisted that social workers not be involved. Her plan was to continue living in her car, convinced that this situation was only temporary and that she would be able to secure stable housing within a few months.

Dr. Blake found herself torn about how to proceed. She empathized with Mrs. Patterson’s reasons for avoiding both her previous home and local shelters, and she did not want to risk having the child placed in foster care. Still, hospital policy required that patients not be discharged to the street or to unsafe environments, and recent community efforts had intensified against so-called “patient dumping.” Although Mrs. Patterson was mentally sound and competent, Dr. Blake struggled to find a solution that would respect the mother’s autonomy while ensuring the safety and well-being of the newborn.

ethical_issues.question: How can the mother's autonomy be respected while ensuring the infant's safety and well-being, and how can the needs of both be balanced?
keypoints: The mother’s right to autonomy must be balanced against the infant’s needs for safety and well-being; physicians should respect patient autonomy while remaining vigilant about the influence of their own biases on clinical judgment.
Parents are generally presumed to act in the best interests of their children, but their actual capacity to do so must be assessed; in this context, the infant’s best interests are paramount.

The best interests of the infant are complex, encompassing not only physical safety but also the stability of the mother-infant attachment relationship, which is critical to the infant’s emotional health and early development.
Poverty and homelessness in themselves do not constitute abuse or neglect and should not be the sole grounds for removing a child from parental custody.

Placement of the child into Child Protective Services may disrupt early mother-infant attachment, resulting in multiple changes of caregivers and residences, thereby adversely affecting the infant’s emotional well-being and developmental trajectory.

ethical_issues.question: In the absence of evidence that homelessness constitutes abuse or neglect, should the infant be removed from the homeless mother’s custody and placed under child protective supervision?
keypoints: Poverty and homelessness in themselves do not constitute legal or ethical grounds for removing a child from parental custody; parents are generally presumed to act in the best interests of the child and hold the legal right to consent on their behalf.

Early-life nurturance and stability of attachment are critical to an infant’s emotional health and development; even when the physical environment is unstable, the mother may remain the primary caregiver capable of providing the most stable emotional bond.

Placement of a child into child protective custody may disrupt early mother-infant attachment, resulting in multiple changes of caregivers and living environments, which can adversely affect the child’s emotional and psychological development.

Routinely placing children into foster care solely on the basis of homelessness may produce negative social consequences, discouraging homeless women from delivering in medical facilities and thereby hindering their access to necessary medical and social support.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of homelessness, should the physician notify a social worker to seek assistance even if the patient refuses?
keypoints: As a mandated reporter of child abuse and neglect, the physician should rationally assess the potential risks that homelessness poses to the child's safety, and, if there is reasonable suspicion, notify a social worker even if the patient refuses such involvement.
The physician should prioritize the best interests of the infant, weighing the ethical conflict between safeguarding the child's safety and respecting the patient's autonomy.

Poverty and homelessness alone do not constitute sufficient grounds for the removal of a child; however, the physician may notify a social worker to seek supportive services that promote family stability and child safety.

The physician should actively communicate with the patient to understand the specific reasons for her refusal of social worker involvement, striving to balance respect for patient autonomy with the responsibility to ensure the child's safety.

The physician should be familiar with relevant local laws and community resources, and make reasonable use of multidisciplinary support to provide the patient and child with the safest and most stable discharge arrangement possible.

title: Planning End-of-Life Conversations: Hospitalist and Primary Care Physician Roles
case:
At the end of a busy day in her pediatric clinic, Dr. Smith was going to visit the Johnson family. Even though she and her partners now admitted their patients to the pediatric hospitalist service at the nearby children's hospital, Dr. Smith still visited her patients there whenever her clinic schedule permitted. She had been notified by the emergency department earlier that day that Claire, the Johnsons' third child, had been admitted with a fever and dehydration. Dr. Smith knew the Johnson family well—she had taken care of their older children, both healthy, for the past 7 years, and had gotten to know Mr. and Mrs. Johnson even better during Claire's first year of life.
Claire was born healthy, but stopped making developmental progress at age 6 months. By the time Claire was 1 year old, an extensive workup showed that she had a rare, progressive metabolic disorder. Despite strictly adhering to a special diet and routinely seeing subspecialists, Claire continued to decline. Feeding problems resulted in the need for placement of a gastric tube and Claire's development never progressed beyond that of a 6-month old. Now 4 years of age, Claire had been hospitalized several times for metabolic crises associated with mild infections. Specialists had told the Johnsons that Claire would never walk, talk, or eat by mouth.
While Dr. Smith had never had a discussion specifically about end-of-life issues with the Johnsons, she knew that they wanted Claire to stay out of the hospital as much as possible and hoped she would not have to undergo medical interventions that would cause her to suffer. In light of this admission, Dr. Smith knew the time had come to talk with the Johnsons about goals of care and, specifically, code status for Claire.
Dr. Smith stopped at the nurses' station to review Claire's chart before meeting with the Johnsons. She was surprised to discover that the pediatric hospitalist caring for Claire had already documented a detailed discussion about code status and what medical interventions, if necessary, the Johnsons wanted Claire to have. Dr. Smith recognized the hospitalist, Dr. Adams, sitting at the nurses' station, and decided to approach her. Dr. Adams was surprised that Dr. Smith was interested in this aspect of Claire's care.
“Usually, primary care physicians leave these discussions to us,” said Dr. Adams. “It can be a bit awkward to have conversations about end-of-life issues with someone you've never met before, but we do it so often that it has become second nature with families of patients like Claire. Most primary care physicians don't like to talk about dying during a 20-minute clinic visit.”
case_rewrite:
As dusk settled over her bustling pediatric clinic, Dr. Smith prepared for her final visit of the day: she was heading to see the Johnson family at the nearby children’s hospital. Although she and her colleagues now entrusted inpatient care to the pediatric hospitalist service, Dr. Smith continued to visit her patients there whenever her clinic duties allowed. Earlier that morning, the emergency department had informed her that Claire, the Johnsons’ youngest child, had been admitted due to fever and dehydration. Dr. Smith had cared for the Johnson family for years—she was familiar with their two older, healthy children and had grown especially close to Mr. and Mrs. Johnson over the course of Claire’s first year.

Claire had entered the world healthy, but at six months old, her development plateaued. By her first birthday, after numerous evaluations, Claire was diagnosed with a rare, progressive metabolic disease. The Johnsons rigorously followed a specialized diet for Claire and attended regular appointments with various subspecialists, but despite their efforts, Claire’s condition deteriorated. Persistent feeding difficulties had necessitated a gastrostomy tube, and Claire’s development never advanced beyond that of an infant. Now four years old, she had already endured multiple hospitalizations for metabolic crises triggered by even mild illnesses. Specialist consultations had painted a grim prognosis: Claire would not walk, talk, or ever eat by mouth.

Though Dr. Smith had never explicitly broached the topic of end-of-life care with the Johnsons, she was aware of their hope to minimize Claire’s hospitalizations and their wish to spare her from interventions that might cause suffering. With Claire’s latest admission, Dr. Smith recognized the importance of discussing the family’s goals of care and, specifically, addressing Claire’s code status.

Before entering the Johnsons’ room, Dr. Smith stopped at the nurses’ station to review Claire’s medical record. To her surprise, she discovered that the pediatric hospitalist overseeing Claire’s care had already documented a comprehensive conversation with the Johnsons about code status and the extent of medical interventions they wanted for Claire, should the need arise. Dr. Smith recognized Dr. Adams, the hospitalist, seated nearby at the station and decided to approach her.

Dr. Adams looked up, a bit taken aback by Dr. Smith’s interest in this aspect of Claire’s care. “Usually, primary care physicians let us handle these discussions,” Dr. Adams remarked. “It can feel awkward to talk about end-of-life issues with families you’ve just met, but for us, it’s become almost routine with patients like Claire. Most primary care doctors don’t want to bring up death during a short clinic visit.”

Dr. Smith listened, reflecting on the value of her longstanding relationship with the Johnsons, and the unique insights she could offer about their beliefs and priorities, even as Dr. Adams contributed her expertise in acute care and detailed knowledge of resuscitation protocols. As they spoke, it became clear that both perspectives were essential in supporting the Johnsons through these complex decisions.

ethical_issues.question: How can multidisciplinary collaboration in end-of-life conversations help reduce communication errors and support patients’ families in making decisions that are consistent with their values?
keypoints: Multidisciplinary collaboration, including the palliative care team, nurses, and social workers, can reduce communication errors and ensure that the values of the patient’s family are accurately integrated into treatment goals and end-of-life decision making.

Primary care physicians, by virtue of their long-term relationships with patients and families, are able to gain a deep understanding of their religious, cultural, and personal beliefs, thereby providing ongoing and individualized support throughout the decision-making process.

Hospitalists, due to their routine exposure to families of acutely ill patients, are more familiar with the details of resuscitation, CPR survival rates, and complication statistics, and can provide specialized clinical information to supplement treatment planning.

Although primary care physicians may not possess all up-to-date clinical details, they can offer emotional support and guidance on values during collaboration, thereby enhancing the confidence and reassurance of patients and families in the decision-making process.

ethical_issues.question: Should primary care physicians proactively initiate end-of-life discussions with patients and their families in the outpatient setting, particularly during non-crisis periods?
keypoints: Primary care physicians face practical barriers to initiating end-of-life discussions in the outpatient setting, including lack of time, concerns about causing distress to patients and their families, and insufficient communication skills, all of which affect their proactivity.

Physicians who have established long-term relationships with patients and their families are typically more familiar with their religious, cultural, and personal beliefs, which are key factors in assisting patients and families with end-of-life decision making.

Despite these barriers, it is highly beneficial for primary care physicians to proactively introduce end-of-life discussions during non-crisis periods, as their longitudinal perspective allows them to dynamically assess disease progression and the family’s acceptance of the illness.

Discussing end-of-life preferences in the outpatient setting helps surrogate decision makers gain deeper insight into the patient’s wishes and enables primary care physicians to identify and support families facing complex medical needs early, thereby facilitating better preparation and decision making.

If a primary care physician feels unable to competently conduct end-of-life discussions, timely referral to palliative care services during non-crisis periods is essential to ensure that patients and families receive appropriate professional support.

title: Shared Decision Making: Physicians’ Duties to Patients and Other Physicians
case:
Drs. Johnson and Blake were grabbing a quick bite in the hospital cafeteria. Both were second-year residents in internal medicine, but on different teams. Dr. Johnson's team was headed by a hospitalist (Dr. Norwood), while Dr. Blake's team was headed by rotating attending physicians who came through for 2-week, in-house assignments and then went back to their regular academic and clinic responsibilities. For the current, 2-week block, the general internal medicine attending was Dr. White.
In conversation, Dr. Johnson brought up a patient he had been especially concerned about for several days. “Remember the patient I told you about with cirrhosis? Mr. Hanson? His ascites and edema are out of control. We tapped him just 2 days ago and the fluid's already reaccumulating. When we rounded this morning, Dr. Norwood had us order a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) for him. It's scheduled for tomorrow morning. I sure hope it gives the guy some relief; he's not looking good.”
“Funny you should bring up that case,” his friend said. “Mr. Hanson is one of Dr. White's clinic patients so I asked Dr. White if we had time to stop by Mr. Hanson's room this morning, even though he isn't assigned to our team, because you had mentioned him the other day. We did stop in and, when Dr. White saw the TIPS order, he launched into quite a lecture.”
“Why? What about?” Dr. Johnson asked.
“Oh, Dr. White said that he's sure it's a good decision from the hospital's point of view; the hospital can discharge Mr. Hanson and free up a bed. But then Mr. Hanson goes home, starts getting confused and not taking his meds, and shows up in the clinic. Poor Mr. Hanson has just traded his ascites for encephalopathy.”
“That sounds like a reasonable argument against doing it. What do you think?” Dr. Johnson asked.
“I'm not sure.” Dr. Blake said. “I'd like to hear them discuss it, to be truthful.”
“Right,” said Dr. Johnson. “Like you want to be the one to go to Dr. Norwood and suggest that this is a great ‘teaching moment' and that he and Dr. White should examine this clinical decision together for our edification.”
case_rewrite:
Drs. Johnson and Blake sat across from each other in the bustling hospital cafeteria, trays balanced between them. Both were second-year residents in internal medicine, though assigned to different teams. Dr. Johnson reported to Dr. Norwood, a dedicated hospitalist, while Dr. Blake’s supervising attendings rotated every two weeks; for this block, Dr. White was leading Dr. Blake’s team.

As they started to eat, Dr. Johnson leaned in, concern etched on his face. “You remember Mr. Hanson? The patient I mentioned with cirrhosis? His ascites and edema keep getting worse. We performed a paracentesis just two days ago, but the fluid’s already back. During rounds this morning, Dr. Norwood had us schedule a TIPS procedure for tomorrow. I really hope it helps—Mr. Hanson’s struggling.”

Dr. Blake looked up, surprised. “That’s interesting—you brought him up, because Mr. Hanson is actually one of Dr. White’s clinic patients. I mentioned him to Dr. White after you described his situation, and Dr. White wanted to check in on him, even though he’s not on our service. So, we stopped by Mr. Hanson’s room today. When Dr. White saw the TIPS order, he had a lot to say.”

“About what?” Dr. Johnson asked, curiosity piqued.

“Well, Dr. White said the TIPS might be the right move for the hospital—it can get Mr. Hanson discharged and free up a bed. But then, he said, Mr. Hanson will go home, start getting confused, forget his meds, and end up back in clinic. Basically, he thinks Mr. Hanson might just be trading one problem—his ascites—for another, like hepatic encephalopathy.”

Dr. Johnson nodded thoughtfully. “That’s a good point. Do you agree with Dr. White?”

“I’m honestly not sure,” Dr. Blake admitted. “I’d like to hear both Dr. Norwood and Dr. White talk it through together. There are real risks and benefits either way.”

“Yeah,” Dr. Johnson agreed. “But who’s going to be the one to go up to Dr. Norwood and suggest that this is the perfect ‘teaching moment’—that he and Dr. White should sit down and openly discuss the plan so we can all learn from it?”

ethical_issues.question: When conflicts arise between the interests of the hospital and the best interests of the patient, how should physicians balance these considerations and make decisions that are ethically sound in medical practice?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize recommending treatment plans that are in the best interest of the patient; hospital interests must not be the primary consideration.

Physicians are required to rationally assess the potential risks and benefits of interventions and ensure, through thorough communication, that patients can express their personal preferences based on adequate information.
Physicians should respect patients’ fears and concerns and integrate these into a comprehensive judgment of what constitutes the patient’s best interests.
Involvement of the primary care physician facilitates a comprehensive evaluation of the patient’s capacity for follow-up management and promotes the rationality of medical decision making.

If physicians believe that a proposed treatment plan does not align with the patient’s best interests, they have an obligation to actively advocate for a plan that better serves the patient’s welfare.

ethical_issues.question: When a resident physician discovers critical information that may affect a patient’s clinical course, do they have an ethical obligation to take action and reassess the attending physician’s treatment decisions?
keypoints: Residents have an obligation, based on the principle of maximizing patient benefit, to take proactive action and re-evaluate the attending physician’s treatment decisions upon becoming aware of key information that raises reasonable doubt.

Dr. Johnson should approach Dr. Norwood with relevant data and suggest using this case as a teaching opportunity to facilitate open discussion between Drs. Norwood and White, which would benefit both the residents and the attending physicians in optimizing clinical decision making.

title: Role of Schools in Monitoring Student Health
case:
Sarah is a pleasant, happy-go-lucky 8-year-old at Brookline Elementary School who came home one day with a note from the nurse's office. It warned her parents that their daughter, who weighed 70 pounds and stood 4 feet tall, had a body mass index (BMI) that placed her in the 90th percentile of kids her age. In other words, the note indicated, she was “at risk of becoming overweight.”
Sarah's parents were outraged. Although they considered Sarah to be somewhat pudgy, they weren't worried about her health because they knew that Sarah was an active child who played outdoors, rode her bicycle, and ate healthy meals prepared by her mother, both at home and school.
Sarah herself was deeply disturbed by the letter, convinced that her teachers were rebuking her for eating too much at home or being lazy in school. Her parents then noticed that she began eating less and skipping meals.
After calling the school to complain, Sarah's parents found out that the school had recently instituted a policy under which all children with BMIs above the 85th percentile were referred for a regimen of weight management, behavioral counseling, and other staged interventions under the guidance of a primary care physician to help them achieve certain goals for lifestyle and health consciousness. Even though Sarah's parents were convinced there was nothing wrong with their daughter's health or weight, they made an appointment with Sarah's pediatrician, Dr. James, to discuss the matter.
Having been the family pediatrician for nearly a decade, Dr. James had monitored Sarah's growth and health carefully for most of her life and had always thought of her as a relatively healthy child. When he learned about Sarah's predicament at school, he realized that to comply with the school's expectations of care for children they deemed “overweight” or “obese,” he would have to monitor Sarah's health far differently than he typically did for a child her age. On her regularly scheduled visits, he would have to perform complete work-ups for all obesity-related risk factors; labwork would include blood pressure, lipid profile, fasting glucose, and a variety of other tests. Not only that, he would also have to assess her eating behaviors, including how often her family ate meals away from home, how many sweetened beverages she drank, and how frequently she snacked.
After Dr. James discussed all this with Sarah's family, they found it unjustifiably intrusive into their lives. Sarah was horrified at the idea that she would have to endure so many visits to the doctor and so many questions about her life when she didn't even understand what was wrong.
case_rewrite:
Sarah, an energetic and cheerful eight-year-old attending Brookline Elementary School, came home one afternoon clutching a letter from the school nurse. The note, addressed to her parents, explained that Sarah—who was four feet tall and weighed seventy pounds—had a body mass index (BMI) that placed her in the 90th percentile for her age. The letter stated that this meant Sarah was “at risk of becoming overweight.”

Sarah’s parents were taken aback and upset by the letter. While they acknowledged that Sarah was a bit chubby, they had never been concerned about her health. They knew she spent hours outdoors, rode her bike around the neighborhood, and regularly ate wholesome meals that her mother prepared both at home and packed for school lunches.

The letter, however, deeply unsettled Sarah. She became convinced that her teachers thought she ate too much at home or that she was lazy at school. Soon after, her parents observed that Sarah was eating less at meals and sometimes skipping them altogether.

Disturbed by the changes in their daughter and the tone of the letter, Sarah’s parents called the school to express their concerns. They discovered that Brookline Elementary had recently adopted a policy requiring that all students with BMIs above the 85th percentile be referred for a comprehensive program.
