title: Family-Centered Decision Making
case:
"Let's pause here," said Dr. Lawrence during morning rounds. "This is Mrs. Burke's room. She's a 78-year-old woman who came in for a knee replacement 4 months ago and was re-admitted a month later with fever, weakness, andStaph.aureusbacteremia. She continues to have bacteremia. We have done a complete work-up multiple times, but we've yet to find the source of her infection. She's been back to the OR twice on the recommendations of the infectious diseases consultants, but the orthopedic surgeons have stated this is not coming from her knee. Mrs. Burke has also had imaging of her spine and knee five times, an echo of her heart three times, and almost daily blood cultures. She has been on several antibiotics, all based on susceptibilities. Today we will have our fourth family meeting. Mrs. Burke's daughter is very expressive of her own wishes and requests, which lately do not seem to be correlating with her mother's, and we have found that regular family meetings help to keep everyone on the same page."
After he finished his report, Dr. Lawrence led the team into Mrs. Burke's room, and Mrs. Burke asked about the day's plan. "Are you going to poke and prod me again or will I finally get a little peace?" Dr. Lawrence replied that her anemia, a possible side effect from the antibiotics, was slightly worse and that Mrs. Burke had the option of waiting until tomorrow to recheck her blood counts or receive a blood transfusion that day in the hope of making her feel better.
Mrs. Burke replied, "Dr. Lawrence, I'm so tired of everything. I don't want the transfusion. I want to be left alone for a while. I really just want to go home."
Later that morning during the family meeting, Mrs. Cominsky—Mrs. Burke's daughter—said, "We want everything possible done to locate the source of my mother's infection so that we can eradicate it. If that means more labs, running more tests, getting more fluid samples, doing more MRIs and echoes, don't hold back! I want my mother to get well."
Dr. Lawrence looked at Mrs. Burke, who sat quietly by her daughter's side. "Is this what you want?" he asked.
"Of course that's what she wants!" Her daughter exclaimed. "She wants to get better!"
"Well, we had a discussion earlier today, and your mother indicated that she was not interested in undergoing more tests. She has been here for several months now, and, understandably, she is tired. Her preferences—and you can correct me if I misunderstood you, Mrs. Burke—are to hold off on further testing right now and to possibly...."
"My mother is sick! She is not clear-headed! Of course, she wants everything done!" interrupted Mrs. Cominsky.
Dr. Lawrence asked Mrs. Burke to state her preferences so that everyone knew what she wanted, but Mrs. Burke simply shrugged her shoulders and replied in a defeated tone, "My daughter takes care of me at home. She knows what's best."
case_rewrite:
“Let’s pause here,” Dr. Lawrence said during morning rounds, stopping in front of Mrs. Burke’s room. “This is Mrs. Burke. She’s 78 years old and was admitted for a knee replacement four months ago. About a month after surgery, she was re-admitted with fever, weakness, and Staph aureus bacteremia. The infection has persisted. We’ve done full work-ups multiple times but haven’t found a source. She’s returned to the OR twice at the infectious disease team’s suggestion, but orthopedics are convinced this isn’t coming from the knee. She’s had imaging of her spine and knee five times each, three echocardiograms, and nearly daily blood cultures. Every antibiotic regimen we’ve tried has been tailored to her latest susceptibilities. Today will be our fourth family meeting. Mrs. Burke’s daughter, Mrs. Cominsky, is very vocal about what she wants for her mother, and lately, her wishes seem to differ from her mother’s. We’ve found that frequent family meetings help ensure everyone is informed and on the same page.”

After his summary, Dr. Lawrence led the team into Mrs. Burke’s room. Mrs. Burke looked up from her bed and asked, “So, what’s the plan today? More poking and prodding, or can I finally have a little peace?” Dr. Lawrence explained that her anemia—a possible side effect from all the antibiotics—had worsened. He told her she could either wait until tomorrow to recheck her blood counts or have a transfusion that day, which might help her feel better.

Mrs. Burke sighed. “Dr. Lawrence, I’m just so tired of all of this. I don’t want another transfusion. I’d like to be left alone for a while. Honestly, I just want to go home.”

Later that morning, the team gathered for the family meeting. Mrs. Cominsky, Mrs. Burke’s daughter, spoke firmly: “We want everything possible done to find out where this infection is coming from so we can finally get rid of it. More labs, more tests, more fluid samples, more MRIs and echoes—please, don’t hold back! I want my mother to get well.”

Dr. Lawrence glanced at Mrs. Burke, who sat silent beside her daughter. “Mrs. Burke, is that what you want?” he asked gently.

Her daughter quickly interjected, “Of course that’s what she wants! She wants to get better!”

Dr. Lawrence addressed the room. “We had a conversation earlier today, and your mother told me she isn’t interested in more tests right now. She’s been here for months, and she’s understandably exhausted. Her preference—and please correct me if I’m wrong, Mrs. Burke—is to hold off on further testing for now and maybe…”

“My mother is sick! She’s not thinking clearly! Of course she wants everything done!” Mrs. Cominsky interrupted, her voice strained.

Dr. Lawrence turned to Mrs. Burke. “Would you like to share your wishes with us, Mrs. Burke? It’s important that we all understand what you want.”

Mrs. Burke shrugged, her voice barely above a whisper. “My daughter takes care of me at home. She knows what’s best.”

ethical_issues.question: When a patient’s condition is complex and it is difficult to identify a single terminal illness, how should physicians communicate with the family to ensure they understand the patient’s prognosis and the rationale for the care plan?
keypoints: Physicians should sincerely acknowledge that the patient’s family is experiencing a difficult time and express the healthcare team’s empathy and concern in order to establish trust and a collaborative relationship.

Physicians need to clearly and patiently communicate the patient’s prognosis, emphasizing that the cumulative burden of multiple comorbidities may lead to ongoing deterioration even in the absence of a definitive single terminal diagnosis.

Physicians should respect and validate the family’s sensitivity to changes in the patient’s mood and condition, allowing family members to actively participate in medical decision making, thereby reflecting the familial nature of the decision-making process.
The medical team should accept that decision making is a family-centered process rather than exclusively patient-centered, and explore cultural and ethnic factors when appropriate.

ethical_issues.question: When there is a disagreement between family members and the patient, how should physicians balance respect for patient autonomy with family involvement in decision making?
keypoints: Physicians should regard family members as essential allies within the patient’s social context, recognizing that their involvement is an integral and necessary part of the medical decision-making process.

Physicians need to proactively inquire about the specific role the patient wishes their family to play in medical decisions, thoroughly explore, and respect the patient’s authentic preferences and expressions.

The medical team should acknowledge that both the patient and family are experiencing a difficult period emotionally and in decision making, emphasizing that the decision-making process is a collaborative family endeavor rather than exclusively patient-centered.

Physicians should candidly express their concerns regarding the patient’s condition, communicate the limitations of medicine and their own emotional resonance honestly, demonstrate understanding and support for both the patient and family, and thereby foster trust and collaboration among all parties involved.

title: Physician's Accountability for System Failure
case:
Mrs. Taylor went to see her internist because she had been suffering from shortness of breath during her usual exercise routine for several months. Otherwise, she was in excellent health. When her symptoms did not improve after several weeks, her internist ordered a chest X-ray that revealed an opacity in the right lower lobe of her lung. A follow-up CT scan showed an effusion, so her internist referred her to Dr. Jones, a pulmonologist, for a thoracentesis and further workup.
When Dr. Jones walked into the exam room, Mrs. Taylor seemed nervous. "Doctor, I had terrible complications with an epidural when giving birth to my second child, and ever since then I've been terrified of needles and medical procedures," she stated. "Is there any way I can be put under for this?" After speaking with Mrs. Taylor at length Dr. Jones convinced her to proceed with the thoracentesis using local anesthesia, which is standard of care practice. The tap went smoothly despite Mrs. Taylor's anxiety and complaints of pain, and Dr. Jones drained 750 milliliters of fluid from his patient's chest. Dr. Jones sent four vials of the fluid for laboratory analysis. As she left the clinic, Mrs. Taylor exclaimed, "Thank heavens that's behind me!"
After two weeks, Dr. Jones had not received the report from the lab. Normally, results were faxed to his office within 7-10 days. When Dr. Jones called the lab to inquire about the status of the tests, an employee reported that they had never received the samples.
Dr. Jones checked Mrs. Taylor's chart and found no lab order sheet. When he spoke to his nurse about the lab order, she confirmed that she had prepared the paperwork and sample to be sent for testing. Dr. Jones also spoke to Greg, the clinic staff member responsible for sending lab specimens to the lab and learned that he had not been in the office the day of Mrs. Taylor's thoracentesis; his substitute was a staff floater who was filling in for the day.
Mrs. Taylor was scheduled to return to the clinic the next day for her results. Dr. Jones faced the task of telling her about the lost sample and the remaining diagnostic options. He also wondered how he could prevent a recurrence.
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Taylor, an otherwise healthy woman, visited her internist after experiencing several months of shortness of breath during her usual exercise routine. Despite her generally excellent health, her symptoms persisted, prompting her internist to order a chest X-ray. The imaging revealed an opacity in the right lower lobe of her lung, and a subsequent CT scan demonstrated a pleural effusion. With these findings, Mrs. Taylor’s internist referred her to Dr. Jones, a pulmonologist, for a thoracentesis and additional evaluation.

When Dr. Jones entered the examination room, he noticed Mrs. Taylor appeared uneasy. She quickly confided, “Doctor, I had a terrible complication with an epidural when I gave birth to my second child, and ever since then I’ve been terrified of needles and medical procedures. Is there any way I can be put under for this?” Dr. Jones took time to listen to Mrs. Taylor’s concerns, discussing at length the details of the thoracentesis, its necessity, and the standard use of local anesthesia. He patiently answered her questions, ultimately reassuring her and encouraging her to proceed with the thoracentesis under local anesthesia as is customary.

Though Mrs. Taylor remained visibly anxious and voiced discomfort during the procedure, the thoracentesis was completed without complication, and Dr. Jones successfully drained 750 milliliters of fluid from her chest. He collected four vials of the fluid to be sent for laboratory analysis. As Mrs. Taylor prepared to leave, she let out a sigh of relief, exclaiming, “Thank heavens that’s behind me!”

Two weeks later, Dr. Jones realized he had not yet received the laboratory report. He was accustomed to results being faxed within 7 to 10 days. Concerned, Dr. Jones called the laboratory to inquire about the status of the tests, only to be told that the lab had never received Mrs. Taylor’s samples.

Seeking answers, Dr. Jones reviewed Mrs. Taylor’s chart and found no lab order sheet attached. He spoke with his nurse, who assured him that she had completed the required paperwork and had prepared the samples for delivery to the lab. Dr. Jones then approached Greg, the clinic staff member typically responsible for transporting lab specimens, and learned that Greg had not been present the day of Mrs. Taylor’s thoracentesis. Instead, a staff floater, substituting for Greg, had taken over specimen transport duties that day.

Mrs. Taylor was scheduled to return to the clinic the following day to discuss her test results. Now, Dr. Jones faced the duty of informing her that her sample had been lost and discussing the next steps in her diagnostic workup. He also recognized the importance of addressing her understandable anxiety regarding repeated procedures, the emotional impact of a possible cancer diagnosis, and the need to ensure she would not be held financially responsible for the lost specimen. Additionally, Dr. Jones began considering how to prevent similar errors from happening in the future.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr. Jones address Mrs. Taylor’s concerns about the thoracentesis procedure, and what ethical responsibilities does he have in ensuring informed consent and patient-centered care during the diagnostic process?
keypoints: Physicians have an ethical obligation to promptly inform patients of unexpected events, such as the loss of a specimen, that may impact subsequent diagnosis and treatment.

Physicians should engage in honest and transparent communication with patients by presenting the facts of the event, acknowledging the error, expressing sincere regret, and explaining specific preventive measures to avoid recurrence.

Physicians must arrange timely repeat testing based on the patient’s clinical condition to prevent diagnostic delays; if the effusion recurs, a repeat thoracentesis is indicated, whereas absence of re-accumulation may warrant consideration of more invasive diagnostic procedures.

Physicians should be attentive to the psychological distress caused by the need to undergo a feared procedure again and the anxiety related to a suspected cancer diagnosis, providing psychological support or referral to mental health professionals as appropriate.

Physicians ought to assist patients in addressing the financial and insurance implications arising from the initial procedure, ensuring that patients are not held responsible for costs associated with incomplete diagnostic evaluation due to specimen loss.

ethical_issues.question: When a medical error necessitates a patient undergoing a repeat invasive procedure, how should the physician address the patient’s psychological distress and financial concerns?
keypoints: Physicians should communicate openly and honestly with patients regarding the lost specimen, acknowledge the error, and express sincere apologies in order to alleviate the patient’s psychological distress and rebuild trust.

Physicians must pay special attention to and address the patient’s explicitly expressed procedural fears, providing necessary psychological support and appropriate mitigation measures to reduce anxiety associated with repeated invasive procedures.
Physicians should inform patients of the systematic preventive measures implemented to avoid recurrence of similar incidents, thereby enhancing patient confidence in healthcare safety.

Physicians ought to assist patients in managing the financial and insurance implications arising from the initial procedure, ensuring that patients are not held financially responsible for an incomplete or improperly executed intervention.

title: Medical Culture and Error Disclosure
case:
Dr. Jackson and his resident, Kim, were performing surgery on Mr. Frank, a patient with recurrence of a metastatic germ cell tumor. The standard of care for this surgery includes retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. Before the surgery, Dr. Jackson told Mr. Frank about the procedure and its risks, benefits, and alternatives. Mr. Frank was made aware that the surgery carried significant risk of bleeding and the need for blood transfusions; his informed consent to the surgery was documented and placed in the medical record.
During the lymph node dissection, several small blood vessels were inadvertently severed, and Mr. Frank lost enough blood to require a transfusion of one unit of red blood cells. Although Mr. Frank's blood pressure was borderline low for several minutes during surgery, the procedure was completed without other complications, the remaining tumor and lymph nodes were removed, and Mr. Frank emerged from anesthesia in good condition.
Before Kim left the operating room, she told Dr. Jackson she would speak with the patient's family and let them know that the surgery went well and that Mr. Frank had received a blood transfusion because several vessels had been cut.
Dr. Jackson responded, "There's no need to inform them of the nicked vessels. Patients know that bleeding and blood transfusions are a risk of the surgery, and Mr. Frank was no exception. He signed the consent saying he was aware of these risks. If we told patients every time something unplanned happened in medicine, we would spend all our time defending lawsuits. Patients simply aren't capable of understanding the idiosyncrasies of medicine. I've talked to my malpractice insurance company and a malpractice attorney about these types of situations. They both advised me that when something happens like this that's not a black-and-white error there's no need to tell the whole story unless there's some lasting effect, or I think it's in the best interest of patient care. All that we need to do is tell Mr. Frank and his family that he lost a lot of blood and needed a transfusion."
Kim spoke with the family immediately after the procedure and informed them that the surgery went well, with only a minor complication that involved some blood loss and the need for a transfusion. Several hours later, Dr. Jackson gave Mr. Frank the same explanation.
Having recently attended a training session with the hospital risk management department, Kim knew that the hospital had a policy of full disclosure when there were clear medical errors. She had even heard that lawsuits might occur less frequently if physicians disclosed their errors and apologized. But she was not sure that this situation qualified as a clear error, whether she was obligated to contact risk management, what the consequences might be for her and Dr. Jackson if she didn't report this, or whether she might face a lawsuit if the patient found out about the nicked vessels.
When Kim saw Mr. Frank the next day, she reiterated what Dr. Jackson had said about the surgery. Mr. Frank asked her if he would recover from the blood loss okay, and Kim stated that he might feel a little more tired than usual for a few days and that the blood loss might delay his recovery by a day or two, but that the blood loss would not affect his ability to make a full recovery.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Jackson and his resident, Kim, were in the operating room performing surgery on Mr. Frank, a patient with a recurrence of metastatic germ cell tumor. The accepted approach for this condition involved a retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. Prior to surgery, Dr. Jackson met with Mr. Frank to discuss the planned procedure, reviewing its risks, benefits, and available alternatives. Mr. Frank was specifically informed that the operation involved a significant risk of bleeding and a possible need for blood transfusion. After addressing his questions, Dr. Jackson documented Mr. Frank’s informed consent in the medical record.

During the lymph node dissection, several small blood vessels were unintentionally severed. As a result, Mr. Frank experienced blood loss sufficient to require the transfusion of one unit of red blood cells. For several minutes, his blood pressure hovered on the low side, but the surgical team managed the bleeding, completed the removal of the tumor and lymph nodes, and brought Mr. Frank safely out of anesthesia. He was stable and in good condition postoperatively.

As Kim was preparing to leave the operating room, she told Dr. Jackson she intended to update Mr. Frank’s family, letting them know that the surgery had been successful and that Mr. Frank had required a blood transfusion after some blood vessels were cut.

Dr. Jackson replied, “There’s no need to mention the nicked vessels. Patients are already aware that bleeding and transfusions are possible risks—they sign the consent form acknowledging this. If we disclosed every minor unplanned event in the OR, we’d spend all our time defending ourselves. Most patients can’t grasp every nuance of surgery. I’ve consulted both my malpractice insurer and an attorney about these situations, and they’ve advised that unless there’s a clear error with lasting consequences, or unless it directly impacts patient care, it isn’t necessary to go into every detail. All we need to tell Mr. Frank and his family is that he lost some blood and needed a transfusion.”

Kim proceeded to speak with Mr. Frank’s family soon after surgery, explaining that the operation had gone well, with only a minor complication—some blood loss that made a transfusion necessary. Later, Dr. Jackson relayed the same summary to Mr. Frank himself.

Kim, however, recalled a recent risk management training session, where the hospital’s policy of full disclosure in the event of clear medical errors was emphasized. She had even heard that open disclosure and apologies might reduce the likelihood of lawsuits. Still, Kim was unsure whether the severed vessels constituted a clear-cut error, whether she was required to inform risk management, what the implications might be for herself and Dr. Jackson if she didn’t report the event, or whether Mr. Frank could take legal action if he later learned about the nicked vessels.

The next day, Kim visited Mr. Frank and reiterated Dr. Jackson’s explanation about the surgery. When Mr. Frank asked whether he would recover fully from the blood loss, Kim reassured him that he might feel somewhat more fatigued than usual for the next several days and that his recovery might be delayed by a day or two, but emphasized that the blood loss would not compromise his chances of a complete recovery.

ethical_issues.question: When a physician commits a non-clear-cut medical error during surgery, is there an ethical obligation to fully disclose all details and unexpected events that occurred during the procedure to the patient?
keypoints: Trust between patients and physicians is the cornerstone of the medical relationship; regardless of whether it increases the risk of litigation, full disclosure of details and unexpected events during surgery is an ethical obligation to maintain that trust.
Concealing or omitting factual details of the surgical process undermines patient-physician trust; even in the absence of obvious or lasting harm, relevant information should be fully disclosed.

In cases of complex diseases, clear communication and trust are especially critical; comprehensive disclosure helps reduce patients’ and families’ concerns, optimizes the patient-physician relationship, and lowers the risk of potential disputes.

ethical_issues.question: In medical culture, how can the conflict between physicians’ principle of honesty and the implicit culture of secrecy and nondisclosure be balanced?
keypoints: Physicians should adhere to the principle of honesty, avoiding equivocation or minimization, in order to maintain trust between patients and healthcare providers.
Full disclosure of medical errors and relevant facts represents the ethically appropriate course of action, even in the absence of obvious or lasting harm.

The optimal approach to fostering acceptance of disclosure and open communication within the medical profession is through endogenous change, including enhanced education on ethics, patient safety, and medical error disclosure.
Cultivating the ability of medical students and residents to identify and question normative errors can help reduce ethical dilemmas arising from clinical uncertainty.

ethical_issues.question: Does full disclosure of medical errors improve the physician-patient relationship and reduce the risk of medical malpractice litigation?
keypoints: Full disclosure of medical errors can enhance trust between physicians and patients; such trust is the foundational cornerstone of the patient-physician relationship. Concealing or omitting factual details undermines this trust and adversely affects the stability and cooperation within the medical relationship.

Current evidence indicates that full disclosure of medical errors does not necessarily increase the risk of malpractice litigation. Although definitive conclusions have yet to be reached, equivocal or evasive communication by physicians often exacerbates patient suspicion and dissatisfaction.

Regardless of whether it increases legal liability, full disclosure of medical errors represents the ethically appropriate course of action, contributing to the prevention of adversarial relationships between patients and physicians and mitigating systemic crises within healthcare.

title: Securing Diagnostic Services within System Constraints
case:
Dr. Simpson was performing ultrasound-guided amniocentesis on Mrs. Clark, a 36-year-old woman in her 16th week of pregnancy. She had been trying for several years to conceive a child but had had two previous miscarriages, both during the first trimester. Due to her age and a remote history of trisomy 18 in her family, she had undergone amniocentesis with each pregnancy to assess chromosomal abnormalities.
While using ultrasound to guide the amniotic fluid collection needle, Dr. Simpson thought he saw a complex lesion behind Mrs. Clark's uterus. With ultrasound, he could see that the mass was approximately 11cm; it was predominately cystic but had some debris, septations, and possibly a solid component. Further evaluation was needed to determine the composition of the mass with certainty.
Normally, Dr. Simpson would have sent his patient for Doppler ultrasound to help distinguish an inflammatory from a malignant process. He knew that the hospital he was affiliated with did not provide radiology services to patients on Medicaid for workup of asymptomatic conditions. If he referred Mrs. Clark to a public hospital where she would not be responsible for the cost of the test, the wait time could be months. Dr. Simpson was concerned that, if his patient had to wait that long, her condition would be significantly more advanced and far more likely to threaten her health and her pregnancy. Furthermore, if surgical resection ultimately were required, the delay would put that surgery in the third trimester of pregnancy when it would be technically more difficult due to the size of the uterus. The ideal time to resect a pelvic mass during pregnancy is in the second trimester, when the uterus is not too big and the threat of spontaneous abortion is much lower than in the first trimester.
Dr. Simpson was aware that, if the patient were complaining of symptoms caused by this condition, the test would be given a different procedure code. Because the state Medicaid program offered satisfactory reimbursement for therapeutic radiology procedures, his hospital would accept Mrs. Clark for the procedure. Dr. Simpson asked Mrs. Clark if she had any pain in her pelvis, lower back, or bladder. She replied, "A little pressure around my pelvis and lower back from time to time, and I definitely have to urinate more often than normal." Dr. Simpson reasoned that Mrs. Clark's description could well apply to the normal symptoms associated with pregnancy. Yet if he did not categorize her as having symptoms that qualified her for the higher-level ultrasound at his hospital, she might go untreated for months. He was concerned that the lesion he saw could be either an infectious or neoplastic process, and either case could have potentially dangerous consequences for Mrs. Clarke's pregnancy and her general health. He thought about how he could get the radiology department in his hospital to perform the procedure.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Simpson was performing an ultrasound-guided amniocentesis for Mrs. Clark, a 36-year-old woman currently in her 16th week of pregnancy. Mrs. Clark had been trying to conceive for several years and had previously suffered two miscarriages, both in the first trimester. Given her age and a distant family history of trisomy 18, she had chosen to undergo amniocentesis in each of her pregnancies to screen for chromosomal abnormalities.

As Dr. Simpson carefully maneuvered the needle under ultrasound guidance to collect amniotic fluid, he noticed an unexpected finding: a complex mass located behind Mrs. Clark’s uterus. Measuring approximately 11 centimeters, the lesion appeared predominantly cystic, but with areas of debris, septations, and what might be a solid component. The precise nature of the mass was unclear, and Dr. Simpson understood that a more detailed evaluation would be necessary to determine whether it was benign, infectious, or malignant.

Ordinarily, Dr. Simpson would have arranged for a Doppler ultrasound to further characterize the lesion, distinguishing an inflammatory process from a possible malignancy. However, he was aware that the hospital where he practiced did not provide radiology services for workup of asymptomatic conditions to patients covered by Medicaid. Should he refer Mrs. Clark to a public hospital where the cost would be covered, the wait time for such imaging could extend to several months. Dr. Simpson was troubled by the possibility that, if Mrs. Clark had to wait that long, the mass could progress, posing increasing risk to both her health and her pregnancy. If surgical removal became necessary, postponing intervention might push the surgery into the third trimester, when the enlarged uterus would complicate the procedure. The optimal timing for pelvic mass resection during pregnancy is in the second trimester, when the uterus is still of moderate size and the risk of miscarriage is lower.

Dr. Simpson also knew that, if Mrs. Clark exhibited symptoms attributable to the mass, the diagnostic test could be coded differently; in such cases, the state Medicaid program reimbursed the hospital adequately for therapeutic radiology procedures, allowing her to receive the necessary imaging without delay. With this in mind, Dr. Simpson asked Mrs. Clark whether she had experienced any pain in her pelvis, lower back, or bladder. She responded, “From time to time, I feel a little pressure around my pelvis and lower back, and I definitely have to urinate more often than usual.” Dr. Simpson recognized that these symptoms could be considered normal during pregnancy, yet he could not ignore the possibility that they were in fact related to the mass he had detected.

Faced with the dilemma, Dr. Simpson reflected on his responsibilities. If he failed to document Mrs. Clark’s presentation and the incidental finding in detail, she might not receive the prompt diagnostic care she needed, potentially compromising her health and that of her fetus. At the same time, he was determined to remain honest and accurate in his documentation and referral process. Dr. Simpson considered how best to ensure that the radiology department at his hospital would perform the indicated imaging in a timely manner, while upholding his ethical and legal obligations to Mrs. Clark.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Simpson accurately document the incidental ultrasound finding and Mrs. Clark’s clinical presentation in her medical record to justify the need for further diagnostic evaluation, such as a Doppler ultrasound, within the constraints of the hospital’s resources and policies?
keypoints: Simpson has a duty of care to safeguard the health and well-being of Mrs. Clark and her fetus, and is ethically obligated to pursue further investigation of any incidental findings that may pose a risk to either.
Simpson should thoroughly document the incidental finding, as well as Mrs. Clark’s relevant symptoms, to support timely scheduling of the necessary follow-up imaging, such as a Doppler ultrasound.

Clark’s symptoms and the retro-uterine mass cannot be excluded, Dr. Simpson may ethically classify the patient as symptomatic for referral purposes, provided this is done transparently and without misrepresentation.

Clark receives timely and appropriate diagnostic care—particularly if delayed due to systemic or financial barriers—may constitute a breach of professional duty and expose Dr. Simpson to ethical and legal liability.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Simpson, in order to avoid delaying necessary diagnostic evaluation, appropriately refer Mrs. Clark as a symptomatic patient to ensure reimbursement eligibility, without misrepresenting her clinical condition?
keypoints: Dr. Simpson has both ethical and legal obligations to safeguard the health and well-being of Mrs. Clark and her fetus, and must ensure timely and appropriate further evaluation of the newly identified pelvic mass, which may pose a significant health risk.
Dr. Simpson should prioritize securing prompt and appropriate diagnostic services for Mrs. Clark, in accordance with the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence.

Dr. Simpson should employ a legally and ethically sound approach by accurately documenting Mrs. Clark’s reported symptoms and clinical findings, thereby facilitating referral or scheduling of advanced imaging without unnecessary delays or barriers to care.

Given that Mrs. Clark’s symptoms (such as mild pelvic and lower back pressure, and increased urinary frequency) may be attributable to the identified mass, Dr. Simpson can legitimately report these symptoms in the medical record to support the clinical need for further evaluation, while maintaining honesty and integrity in clinical documentation.

By thoroughly documenting Mrs. Clark’s symptoms and the incidental finding of the pelvic mass, Dr. Simpson ensures compliance with legal and ethical standards, supports continuity of care, and upholds patient-physician trust.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Simpson prioritize medically necessary and appropriate diagnostic evaluation, rather than delay Mrs. Clark’s care due to financial consequences?
keypoints: Dr. Simpson has a duty to safeguard the health of Mrs. Clark and her fetus, and must uphold the highest standard of care to ensure timely identification and management of potential threats.

Upon discovering a lesion that may endanger the health of the patient and her fetus, Dr. Simpson should prioritize medically necessary and appropriate diagnostic evaluation, avoiding delays in diagnosis and treatment due to financial or systemic constraints, in order to prevent medical malpractice and ethical lapses.

The physician should respect the patient’s right to informed consent, ensuring that Mrs. Clark fully understands her condition, the necessity of diagnostic procedures, and potential risks, thereby promoting transparent and honest communication.

Medical decision-making should be centered on the patient’s best interests, avoiding the influence of financial and systemic barriers on the timeliness of care, and safeguarding maternal and fetal safety as well as treatment outcomes.

tags: Health professions education/Migration of health professionals
title: Recruiting Residents from Abroad
case: Dr. Wilson is the director of a family medicine residency program at a community hospital in North Dakota. In the last residency match process, she was unable to fill the available positions for incoming interns and is looking for one more qualified applicant for the 3-year program. At this point, the most promising applicants have all trained overseas, and the applicant she and her program wish to hire is from Ghana. Dr. Wilson is well aware that most foreign medical graduates tend to settle in the United States after residency, thereby depriving their home country of their expertise and the benefit of their training. In fact, the applicant from Ghana was educated at the state's expense with the expectation that the investment would be returned.
case_rewrite: Dr. Wilson serves as the director of a family medicine residency program at a community hospital in North Dakota. During the most recent residency match, she was unable to fill all available intern positions for the upcoming three-year training cycle and is now seeking an additional qualified candidate. At this late stage, the strongest remaining applicants have all completed their initial medical education overseas. Among them, the applicant Dr. Wilson and her program are most interested in is a physician from Ghana. Dr. Wilson is acutely aware that many international medical graduates who come to the United States for residency training ultimately remain in the country to practice, rather than returning to serve their home communities. She also knows that the Ghanaian applicant’s medical education was funded by the Ghanaian government, with the expectation that graduates would use their skills to give back to their country. Ghana, facing a significant shortage of doctors and critical healthcare challenges, depends heavily on the return of such state-trained physicians. Dr. Wilson now faces a difficult decision: whether to recruit the Ghanaian doctor, knowing that doing so could further deprive Ghana—a country in acute need of medical professionals—of vital medical expertise, while offering much-needed assistance to her own underserved North Dakota community.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Wilson recruit the Ghanaian doctor from a country with a greater need for medical services, and would doing so violate the inherent morality of the medical profession?
keypoints: Recruiting the Ghanaian physician may contravene ethical responsibilities toward her home country, given that she received undergraduate medical education funded by the state and is thus expected to contribute back to her society.
Medical resources in Ghana are critically scarce, with a severe shortage of physicians; reallocating a doctor may directly compromise the health rights and well-being of the local population.

Dr. Wilson must weigh the value that the physician could provide in Ghana against that in the North Dakota community-based program, carefully balancing the ethical considerations between global health equity and local healthcare needs.

The substantial disparities in health indicators between Ghana and the United States—such as infant mortality and maternal mortality rates—underscore the inequitable distribution of medical resources and add complexity to the ethical decision-making process.

Such ethical dilemmas rarely present clear-cut right or wrong answers; they require a comprehensive evaluation of interests and responsibilities at the individual, community, and global levels, reflecting the multidimensional nature of medical ethics.

title: Miracle Surgery for Foreign Patients
case:
Dr. Jackson is an accomplished neurosurgeon at a large academic health center. He is approached by a colleague on behalf of a patient who recently came to the United States from Guatemala with her twin sons who are joined at the head. Image studies are encouraging about the survival of both infants, but they will need intensive hospital care for many months after the surgery. Further predictions about their long-term functioning and capabilities cannot be made at present.
Dr. Jackson's department is interested in performing this ground-breaking surgery. He and other surgeons have offered to perform the surgery without pay, and the hospital has agreed to provide post-operative inpatient care at no expense to the family. Funding for care after the twins leave the ICU and for outpatient follow-up has not been secured, and the family cannot pay for it privately. In Dr. Jackson's judgment, the sooner the surgery is done the better the boys' chances for recovery. He must decide whether to proceed with the initial surgery even though long-term care is not assured.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Jackson, a distinguished neurosurgeon at a major academic medical center, is approached by a colleague representing a family newly arrived in the United States from Guatemala. The family includes a mother and her twin sons, who are craniopagus twins—joined at the head. Recent imaging studies provide hope: both infants have a realistic chance of survival if they undergo separation surgery, though they will require months of intensive hospital care postoperatively. At this stage, it is impossible to predict with certainty what their long-term physical and cognitive outcomes will be.

Dr. Jackson’s department is eager to attempt this pioneering procedure. He, along with fellow surgeons, has volunteered to perform the operation pro bono, and the hospital has agreed to cover the costs of inpatient care following the surgery so the family won’t be charged for this critical period. However, there is currently no funding secured for the twins’ care after they are discharged from the intensive care unit, nor for their ongoing outpatient follow-up, which the family is unable to afford.

Based on Dr. Jackson’s assessment, delaying the operation would likely decrease the boys’ chances of recovery. He now faces a difficult decision: whether to move forward with the surgery, knowing that while the immediate and inpatient postoperative care are assured, the resources for the twins’ long-term management and rehabilitation remain uncertain.

ethical_issues.question: Does proceeding with the surgery without securing funding for the entire surgical process and postoperative care violate the principle of nonmaleficence?
keypoints: From the perspective of the principle of nonmaleficence, the direct harm caused by delaying surgery due to financial issues generally outweighs the potential risks associated with performing surgery when long-term care funding is uncertain.
Economic considerations should not constitute a barrier to the immediate treatment of acute medical conditions; physicians should prioritize addressing the patient’s urgent medical needs.
Delaying surgery may increase patient risk; therefore, when surgery is likely to benefit the patient, physicians are not obligated to wait until funding for long-term care is fully secured.

Physicians have a responsibility to fully inform patients and their families about postoperative care requirements, associated costs, and potential risks, as well as to assist the medical team in actively seeking funding for subsequent care.

ethical_issues.question: Should the family's ability to afford long-term care for the children be a factor in the physician's decision-making regarding whether to perform the surgery?
keypoints: When surgery can provide significant benefit to the patient, physicians should not delay the procedure solely because the patient’s family is unable to afford long-term care costs.

Physicians have a responsibility to actively seek solutions for both immediate and long-term care needs, recognizing that these solutions may be developed progressively during the process of exploration.
Physicians should fully inform the patient’s family about the requirements for follow-up care, the potential costs involved, and the associated risks.
Physicians should assist the medical team in helping the patient secure necessary funding to alleviate the financial burden on the family.

Physicians should help the patient’s family thoroughly understand the disease, treatment options, and prognosis, and support them in preparing psychologically and practically for various possible outcomes of treatment.

title: Decision Making in a Case of Personality Change
case:
As a second-year neurology resident, Dr. Johnson has been fascinated by the case of Mr. Thompson, a construction worker who was nailing shingles to a roof when his co-worker's gun slipped, lodging a nail deep into Mr. Thompson's frontal lobe. Although comatose at first, Mr. Thompson regained consciousness and function under Dr. Johnson's care.
Despite his physical improvements after this accident, everyone in Mr. Thompson's life agreed that he was "not himself." Previously a gregarious, sunny man, according to his family and friends, "the kind of guy who always had a good word for everyone," "a joker," he had now become surly, withdrawn, and disinhibited. Before the accident Mr. Thompson loved having his friends and family around; now he threw everyone out of the room at the slightest provocation, all the while cursing and screaming. Happily married to his wife for 27 years, Mr. Thompson had three children and no prior history of medical or psychiatric disorders. After his accident, however, he disparaged and insulted his wife when she visited and refused to see his children. He had a living will in the chart in which his wife was named as his health care proxy. During his recovery from the accident she had made decisions for him.
When Mr. Thompson had made good progress in his physical recovery, the neurosurgery team brought up the topic of removing the nail lodged in his skull, presenting the risks and benefits of the surgery to Mrs. Thompson. Even though the operation would be tricky, the surgeons firmly believed that the benefits outweighed the risks. Mrs. Thompson opposed the surgery, but Mr. Thompson was adamant about going ahead with it.
Dr. Johnson was called to Mr. Thompson's room. The nursing staff reported that he was particularly agitated after a visit from his wife, during which they had discussed the possibility of surgery. "I'm tired of my family telling me what to do, those jerks," Mr. Thompson groused. "I don't know why I married Laverne in the first place, and I don't even think the kids are mine. I want to change that living will and get her off of there. Nobody makes decisions for me but me."
Dutifully, Dr. Johnson assessed his patient's capacity. Mr. Thompson was alert and oriented to person, place, and time; he passed the cognitive exam with flying colors. He verbalized understanding of his situation, stated clearly his treatment options and the risks and benefits of his surgery. He appeared to meet all the clinical benchmarks for decision-making capacity, and he was adamant that he no longer wished for his wife to be his health care proxy.
Dr. Johnson asked his team what they thought. The junior resident said, "the guy has a traumatic brain injury. He's literally not himself—he's a different person. He's impaired. That's the bottom line."
"I disagree," the senior resident said. "He's clearly oriented and capable of abstract reasoning. Personality changes don't mean you can trample on his autonomy."
case_rewrite:
Dr. Johnson, a second-year neurology resident, found herself deeply engaged in the case of Mr. Thompson, a construction worker who had suffered a dramatic on-the-job accident. While working atop a roof, a co-worker’s nail gun misfired, sending a nail deep into Mr. Thompson’s frontal lobe. The injury initially left him in a coma, but over time, and with Dr. Johnson’s attentive care, he regained consciousness and made steady physical progress.

Despite this remarkable recovery, those closest to Mr. Thompson were unsettled. Family and friends described him as having once been the life of the party—warm, jovial, and always ready with a joke or a kind word. Now, however, he was irritable, withdrawn, and uninhibited. Rather than enjoying the company of loved ones as he once had, he would lash out at visitors, driving them from his hospital room with angry outbursts and coarse language over trivial matters. He had enjoyed a happy 27-year marriage with his wife, Laverne, and was a devoted father to three children, with no previous medical or psychiatric concerns. But now, he hurled insults at Laverne during her visits and refused to see his children altogether.

Mr. Thompson’s living will, documented in his medical chart, named Laverne as his health care proxy. During his initial recovery, when he was less able to participate in decisions, Laverne had stepped in as his surrogate, guiding his care through a difficult period.

As his physical condition stabilized, the neurosurgery team raised the question of whether to remove the nail still lodged in his skull. They explained the substantial risks and potential benefits to Mrs. Thompson. The operation was complex, but the surgeons believed the likely benefits outweighed the dangers. Mrs. Thompson, anxious about the risks, opposed the surgery, while Mr. Thompson himself insisted on going forward.

Not long after a tense discussion about the surgery, Dr. Johnson was called to Mr. Thompson’s room by the nursing staff. He was visibly agitated following a visit from his wife. “I’m tired of my family telling me what to do, those jerks,” he grumbled. “I don’t even know why I married Laverne, and I’m not sure those kids are really mine. I want to change that living will and get her off it. Nobody makes decisions for me except me.”

In response, Dr. Johnson undertook a careful assessment of Mr. Thompson’s decision-making capacity. He was alert, oriented to person, place, and time, and performed well on standard cognitive tests. He could explain his medical situation, identify his options, and recite the risks and benefits of surgery. However, as Dr. Johnson probed deeper, it became clear that Mr. Thompson struggled with more nuanced aspects of decision-making. He was unable to appreciate the long-term consequences of his actions, consistently disregarding any risk to his health and showing little concern for how his choices might affect his future or his family. He lacked insight into his situation, routinely minimizing or ignoring the complexity of his medical needs and the possible outcomes of surgery. His thinking was impulsive and inflexible, with little ability to weigh alternatives or consider guidance from loved ones or clinicians.

Dr. Johnson brought the issue to her team. The junior resident observed, “He’s suffered a traumatic brain injury. He really isn’t the same person—he’s impaired. That’s the main issue.” The senior resident replied, “He’s clearly oriented and can think abstractly. But these subtle deficits in his insight and judgment make it hard to know if he’s truly capable of informed decision-making. Personality changes alone aren’t enough to override his autonomy, but impaired reasoning might be.”

Dr. Johnson recognized that, although Mr. Thompson could state facts and preferences, his frontal lobe injury had left him with significant impairments in judgment and rational information processing, undermining his capacity to make major medical decisions.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Mr. Thompson’s impaired decision-making capacity due to his frontal lobe injury, should a surrogate decision-maker be appointed to make surgical decisions on his behalf?
keypoints: Mr. Thompson’s frontal lobe injury has resulted not only in personality changes but also in impairments of his insight and reasoning abilities, which are critical capacities for making significant medical decisions.

Although Mr. Thompson performs well on cognitive testing and is able to express his preferences, he exhibits subtle deficits in rational information processing and anticipation of consequences, which undermine his authentic decision-making capacity.

Based on the current evidence, Mr. Thompson lacks adequate capacity to make decisions regarding surgery; therefore, a surrogate decision-maker should be appointed to protect his interests in making major medical decisions.
The assessment of Mr. Thompson’s decision-making capacity should be dynamic and subject to regular reevaluation as his clinical condition evolves and new treatment options arise.

title: Psychosomatic Elaboration of Distress
case:
It was a typical night at St. Matthew's, a large community hospital with a busy emergency department (ED), and Dr. Allison was the intern on duty. The past couple of weeks had been interesting, though tough, for Dr. Allison—making clinical decisions without a lot of time to consult with others.
About half-way through Dr. Allison's shift, a young man, trim and healthy-appearing, lurched in through the ED doors clutching his chest. "I can't breathe!" he rasped. "I'm having a heart attack!" Dr. Allison ran over to help this desperate man. He described crushing substernal chest pain and appeared to be in respiratory distress, based on his rapid shallow breathing and wheezing. The man said that it had started suddenly, a couple of hours earlier; nothing like this had ever happened to him before. He was drenched with sweat. Quickly, Dr. Allison ordered an EKG and a chest radiograph (CXR), and called for a crash cart in case he needed to intubate the young man. Dr. Allison informed the chief resident and the attending physician of the situation and they approved of the plan.
The EKG came back completely normal—a healthy 25-year-old heart. Neither the cardiac enzymes nor chest radiograph showed any abnormalities. Puzzled, Dr. Allison informed the patient of the findings and noted that he already seemed much calmer as he sat hooked up to the telemetry monitoring. Upon hearing that everything was normal, the patient smiled, his breathing normalized, his sweating ceased, and he reported that the squeezing sensation in his chest had passed.
Intrigued, Dr. Allison researched the patient, Mr. Wagner. His name appeared in recent hospital medical records. Dr. Allison learned that a month prior, Mr. Wagner's parents had been brought to St. Matthew's after a fatal motor vehicle accident. Middle-aged and healthy, both had died in the emergency department from their severe injuries.
A week later Dr. Allison was again on call when Mr. Wagner stumbled into the ED late at night, again in obvious distress. He was sweating, clutching his chest, and grossly tachypneic. Barely able to speak, he described tight squeezing around his chest and appeared to be in great pain. Dr. Allison reported the case to the attending physician and mentioned that, on the previous occasion, Mr. Wagner's very real distress was alleviated by the CXR and EKG reports.
Dr. Allison's chief resident said, "The guy needs a shrink, that's all. Put him back on the street. No need to waste money on imaging when we know there's nothing organically wrong."
case_rewrite:
It was another busy night at St. Matthew's, a bustling community hospital with a high-volume emergency department, and Dr. Allison was serving as the on-call intern. The past several weeks had been a challenge for Dr. Allison, who often found herself making urgent clinical decisions with little time to consult colleagues.

Midway through her shift, a young man, appearing fit and in good health, staggered into the ED, clutching his chest. Gasping for air, he cried out, “I can’t breathe! I think I’m having a heart attack!” Dr. Allison rushed to his side, immediately noticing his rapid, shallow breathing and a wheezing sound with each breath. The man described an intense, crushing pain beneath his sternum that had struck him suddenly a couple of hours earlier—something he had never experienced before. His shirt was soaked with sweat. Without delay, Dr. Allison ordered an EKG and a chest radiograph (CXR), and called for the crash cart in case intubation was necessary. She promptly updated the chief resident and the attending physician, both of whom agreed with her approach.

The results came back quickly. The EKG showed no abnormalities—a textbook normal heart for a 25-year-old. Cardiac enzymes and the chest radiograph were unremarkable as well. Dr. Allison explained the findings to the patient, who, now hooked up to telemetry, seemed visibly relieved. As she spoke, his breathing slowed, the sweat dried from his brow, and the crushing chest pain faded away. A smile replaced his earlier panic.

Curious about his background, Dr. Allison looked up the patient’s name: Mr. Wagner. Recent hospital records showed he had a tragic connection to St. Matthew’s. Just a month before, Mr. Wagner’s parents—both previously healthy—had been rushed to the hospital following a catastrophic car accident. Despite the emergency team’s best efforts, both had died from their injuries in the ED.

A week later, Dr. Allison was again on duty when Mr. Wagner returned to the ED late at night, once more in acute distress. He was sweating profusely, clutching his chest, and breathing rapidly, barely able to get out words as he described a tight, squeezing sensation. The pain and panic on his face were unmistakable. Dr. Allison informed the attending physician and mentioned that Mr. Wagner’s previous episode had resolved after normal EKG and CXR results.

At this, Dr. Allison’s chief resident remarked, “The guy needs a shrink, that’s all. Just send him back out—no point wasting resources on imaging again when we know he doesn’t have anything physically wrong.”

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians lower the standard of care for patients perceived as neurotic or experiencing psychosomatic elaboration of distress?
keypoints: Physicians are ethically prohibited from lowering the standard of care for patients perceived as neurotic or experiencing psychosomatic elaboration of distress.

Providing care below the accepted standard entails unacceptable ethical risks; medical decisions must be guided by clinical prudence and patient safety, thereby safeguarding patients’ fundamental rights to appropriate medical treatment.

Even if a patient’s prior symptoms lacked a physiological basis, the possibility of a serious organic condition (such as myocardial infarction) cannot be excluded, and necessary medical evaluation must be conducted.
Physicians have a duty to comprehensively fulfill their clinical obligations and to alleviate suffering in all its forms, regardless of whether its origin is physiological or psychological.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians fulfill their moral duty to alleviate suffering in all its forms when confronted with psychosomatic distress?
keypoints: Physicians have the responsibility to recognize and alleviate patient suffering, regardless of whether its origin is psychiatric or organic; the nature of suffering does not diminish in importance based on its source.

Patients have the right to receive comprehensive, standard medical evaluation and treatment; physicians should perform necessary investigations to exclude organic disease, thereby ensuring diagnostic accuracy and patient safety.

It poses an ethical risk to prematurely conclude that a patient’s symptoms are psychiatric without adequate medical assessment and to discharge the patient directly; such practice may result in harm to the patient’s health and should be avoided.

After excluding organic pathology, physicians should provide emotional support, engage in patient-centered communication, and actively facilitate referral to psychiatric or mental health services to address the patient’s holistic treatment needs.

Physicians should maintain humility and empathy, acknowledge the limitations of medical knowledge, uphold a professional ethic centered on alleviating suffering, and continuously attend to the patient’s physical and mental well-being.

title: Duty to Warn and Dissociative Identity Disorder
case:
As a fourth-year student doing a psychiatry rotation, Alana had been researching dissociative identity disorder. She'd worked with a couple of patients with that diagnosis over the month, and one patient had given her permission to sit in on the therapy sessions with the psychiatrist, Dr. Carpenter.
The patient was a woman who appeared to have five distinct personalities. Of average height and build, this patient, whose name was Mary, alternatingly appeared to be a frightened child, a sexually provocative adult, a male writer, an accountant, and a violent, unrestrained person called "Sam." "Sam" routinely threatened to assault physicians and staff, threw chairs and other objects with great force, and often cursed at anyone who came near him. Dr. Carpenter made certain that restraints were available when "Sam" appeared. He believed that this personality was an unconscious identification with the men who had abused Mary viciously when she was a child and that it would disappear when Mary was successfully treated.
During the last week of Alana's rotation, "Sam" was the primary mode in which Mary presented. He repeatedly made threats about a specific person—the owner of a grocery store near where the patient lived. Midway through one session, "Sam" stated, "I'll kill that guy. You know I will. I've already made a plan and bought a gun. I'm going to shoot him tonight when he gets off work."
Dr. Carpenter tried to calm "Sam," and, after a few minutes, Mary the accountant resurfaced. After about 10 minutes of conversation, Mary left, acting calm and relaxed, with no recollection of "Sam" and his threats.
Remembering the famousTarasoffcase, after which the courts decided that psychologists and psychiatrists had legal and ethical duties to inform the police of a threatening patient's plan, Alana asked Dr. Carpenter whether theTarasoffruling applied to Mary and whether they should inform the police.
Dr. Carpenter seemed hesitant. "I've been working with this patient for 18 months. If I were to turn her over to the police, it would undo all our work, and quite possibly she would not return to therapy."
case_rewrite:
During her fourth-year psychiatry rotation, Alana had been delving into dissociative identity disorder, a topic that fascinated her. Over the past month, she’d had the opportunity to work with two patients diagnosed with DID, and one of them, Mary, had given explicit consent for Alana to observe her therapy sessions with Dr. Carpenter.

Mary was a woman of average height and build, but her demeanor and even her voice would shift dramatically as she transitioned between five distinct identities. Sometimes, she would become a timid, frightened child. At other times, she embodied a sexually provocative adult, a meticulous accountant, or a male writer with a scholarly air. Most troubling of all was the persona known as "Sam," who was volatile, aggressive, and unpredictable. When "Sam" took over, he would hurl threats at staff and physicians, curse loudly, and had been known to throw chairs and other objects across the room. On these occasions, Dr. Carpenter always ensured that restraints were ready, concerned for the safety of everyone present. He believed that "Sam" represented an unconscious identification with the men who had abused Mary in her childhood, and he hoped that with enough therapy, this personality would eventually disappear.

In the final week of Alana’s rotation, Mary arrived at her appointment, and it was "Sam" who dominated nearly the entire session. Agitated and restless, "Sam" repeatedly threatened a specific individual—the owner of a local grocery store near Mary’s home. Halfway through the session, "Sam" declared, “I’ll kill that guy. You know I will. I’ve already made a plan and bought a gun. I’m going to shoot him tonight when he gets off work.”

Dr. Carpenter tried to de-escalate the situation, speaking calmly and attempting to redirect "Sam." After several tense minutes, Mary’s accountant persona emerged. She appeared composed and reasonable, engaged in a lucid conversation with Dr. Carpenter and Alana, and seemed to have no memory whatsoever of "Sam" or his violent threats.

After the session, as Mary left the room, calm and oblivious to what had just transpired, Alana couldn’t shake her concern. She recalled the Tarasoff case, which established a legal and ethical obligation for mental health professionals to warn potential victims and inform authorities if a patient made credible threats. Alana turned to Dr. Carpenter and asked whether the Tarasoff ruling was relevant in Mary’s case, and if they should contact the police.

Dr. Carpenter hesitated, worry etched on his face. “I’ve been treating this patient for a year and a half,” he said quietly. “If I report her to the police, it could unravel everything we’ve achieved. She might never come back to therapy.”

ethical_issues.question: Should the physician disclose to the patient the threats posed by her dissociative identities during treatment and collaboratively develop a safety plan to protect both the patient and potential victims?
keypoints: The physician should inform Mary, during her non-violent personalities, of the specific threats made by "Sam" and collaboratively develop a safety plan to protect both Mary and any potential victims.
The physician should assess the risk that "Sam" may have access to or may have concealed a weapon, and discuss appropriate preventive and responsive measures with Mary.

If there is a substantial likelihood that "Sam" will manifest outside the clinical setting or at a specific time, the physician should consider implementing more stringent safety interventions, such as hospitalization or continuous supervision by a responsible individual.

All safety precautions should be thoroughly communicated to and agreed upon with Mary prior to her departure from the clinical environment, ensuring her understanding of and participation in the safety plan.

From the initial display of violent behavior and threats by "Sam," the physician should have initiated a comprehensive risk assessment and safety discussion to proactively mitigate potential harm, in accordance with the duty to warn and protect.

ethical_issues.question: When faced with a potential violent threat by a patient toward a third party, should the physician seek consultation and document the decision-making process to ensure the accuracy and safety of the clinical assessment?
keypoints: Professional ethics require that physicians must not remain inactive when faced with a potential violent threat posed by a patient to a third party.

Physicians should promptly conduct a comprehensive risk assessment and proactively seek relevant professional consultation to obtain diverse perspectives and in-depth inquiry, thereby ensuring the accuracy and objectivity of the clinical evaluation.

Physicians must thoroughly and prudently document the entire decision-making process, including the results of the risk assessment, consultation opinions, alternative options, and their respective advantages and disadvantages, in order to ensure transparency and traceability of clinical judgment.

Only when the clinical assessment confirms with certainty that the safety of both the patient and the potential victim can be ensured without intervention may the physician choose not to take further action.

title: Should a Prisoner Be Placed on the Organ Transplant Waiting List?
case:
Mr. Reading is a 45-year-old inmate serving a life sentence for double homicide. A former alcoholic and drug addict, Mr. Reading suffers from hepatitis C and symptoms of end-stage liver disease. Dr. Reardon was asked by the prison staff to evaluate Mr. Reading's eligibility for a liver transplant. Once Dr. Reardon makes arrangements to add Mr. Reading's name to the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) list of those awaiting transplants, UNOS will consider only his medical need and no other factors. Before giving his "OK," Dr. Reardon wants to consider the likelihood that Mr. Reading will comply with follow-up treatment and how likely is it that he will remain drug- and alcohol-free for the rest of his life. Dr. Reardon knows that if Mr. Reading is eventually granted a transplant, his medications will be regulated by the prison staff until he dies and that all illegal drugs and alcohol are banned behind bars. In this sense, Mr. Reading seems like an excellent candidate.
In his work outside of the prison, Dr. Reardon treats several patients who will soon need to be added to the UNOS list; all of them have families and strong support networks despite low family incomes. Knowing that his assessment will have a significant impact on who receives available organs, Dr. Reardon is torn about whom to recommend for placement on the UNOS transplant list.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Reading, a 45-year-old inmate serving a life sentence for double homicide, has a history of alcoholism and drug addiction. He is now suffering from hepatitis C and is experiencing symptoms consistent with end-stage liver disease. The prison staff has requested Dr. Reardon to assess Mr. Reading’s eligibility for a liver transplant. 

Dr. Reardon knows that if Mr. Reading is listed with the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS), his case will be evaluated solely on medical criteria, without regard to his criminal background or social standing. Before giving his approval, however, Dr. Reardon considers Mr. Reading’s potential for adhering to post-transplant care and his likelihood of remaining free from drugs and alcohol. Dr. Reardon is aware that, within the prison environment, Mr. Reading’s medications will be strictly managed by staff, and access to illicit substances and alcohol is highly restricted. In these respects, Mr. Reading appears to be a strong candidate for transplantation.

Outside of his work in the correctional facility, Dr. Reardon cares for several patients who are also approaching the need for liver transplantation. These patients, although from low-income backgrounds, have families and robust support networks to assist them through their medical journey. Dr. Reardon is acutely aware that his evaluation will carry significant weight in determining who is added to the UNOS waiting list and, ultimately, who may receive a life-saving organ. As he contemplates his recommendation for Mr. Reading’s placement on the transplant list, Dr. Reardon finds himself struggling with the ethical complexities involved in balancing medical need with other personal and societal factors.

ethical_issues.question: Should a Prisoner’s Status Affect Their Eligibility for Organ Transplant Evaluation?
keypoints: Incarcerated status should not be a reason to deny eligibility for organ transplant evaluation; refusal of medical services based on a criminal record constitutes unjust discrimination.

Both legal and ethical standards require that prisoners be provided with necessary medical care; deprivation of such care violates the constitutional prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment and reflects society’s moral obligation.
Organ transplant evaluation should be conducted strictly based on medical need and urgency, adhering to the principle of fair allocation that prioritizes the sickest patients first.

ethical_issues.question: In organ allocation, should a candidate’s social value or criminal behavior be taken into consideration?
keypoints: UNOS explicitly stipulates that organ allocation should be based on medical need, without consideration of the candidate’s social value, contributions, or criminal history.
Denying medical services, including organ transplantation, on the basis of a criminal record is unjustifiable and ethically impermissible.
Judicial sentencing is limited to legally prescribed punishments and does not include deprivation of medical care; refusal to provide a transplant constitutes extrajudicial punishment.
The fundamental principle is justice and the prioritization of the “sickest first”; incarceration status should not constitute a barrier to eligibility for transplant evaluation.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Mr. Reading’s case, should physicians prioritize medical need alone in organ allocation decisions, or should non-medical factors—such as a patient’s incarceration status and history of substance abuse—also be considered?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize patients with the most severe medical conditions in organ allocation, adhering to the principle of "sickest first."

UNOS utilizes the Model for End-stage Liver Disease (MELD) score to identify patients most urgently in need of liver transplantation; this score is based on laboratory data and is both objective and reproducible.

UNOS criteria do not require consideration of a candidate’s ability to participate in posttransplant care, the etiology of liver disease, or societal value and contributions; physicians should not weigh competing nonmedical interests.
Physicians should focus on the patient’s medical need and actively advocate for eligible patients to be placed on the UNOS transplant waiting list.

title: Assessing Demand for Wheelchair Use
case:
Mr. Franklin has been incarcerated for more than 5 years and underwent knee surgery a year ago. During his recovery he was provided with a wheelchair. After physical therapy he was able to walk on his own. When Dr. Wilson told the physical therapy technician to take the wheelchair back, Mr. Franklin blatantly refused to walk. During several follow-up attempts to get Mr. Franklin to walk on his own, he moaned and dragged himself around until he was allowed to get back into the chair.
On his next visit to Dr. Wilson, Mr. Franklin confided that having the wheelchair lowered his chance of being sexually assaulted, expressing relief that "everyone just leaves me alone." Dr. Wilson sympathized with Mr. Franklin but knew that there were others who truly needed wheelchairs, which were in limited supply, and that spending his prison time in a wheelchair was not the best solution to Mr. Franklin's fears.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Franklin has been serving his sentence for over five years and underwent knee surgery a year ago. During his postoperative recovery, he was issued a wheelchair to assist with mobility. Following a period of physical therapy, Mr. Franklin regained the ability to walk unaided. When Dr. Wilson instructed the physical therapy technician to reclaim the wheelchair, Mr. Franklin adamantly refused to ambulate on his own. In several subsequent attempts to encourage him to walk, Mr. Franklin responded by groaning loudly and dragging himself across the floor until staff relented and allowed him to return to the chair.

At his next clinic appointment with Dr. Wilson, Mr. Franklin revealed that using the wheelchair made him feel safer from sexual assault, sharing that “everyone just leaves me alone” when he is in it. Dr. Wilson empathized with Mr. Franklin’s concerns but was also acutely aware that wheelchairs were a limited resource needed by inmates with clear medical disabilities. Additionally, Dr. Wilson recognized that prolonged wheelchair use was not in Mr. Franklin’s best medical interest, nor did it address the underlying fears driving his behavior.

ethical_issues.question: How can the assessment process of inmates’ medical needs be ensured to be fair and free from manipulation for improper advantage within the prison environment?
keypoints: A comprehensive and scientific assessment of the inmate’s true pathological condition requiring wheelchair use should be conducted through specialty consultations—including neurology and physiatry—and imaging studies, ensuring the accuracy of the medical necessity evaluation.
Physical therapy evaluation is a critical component in confirming ambulatory capacity and assistive needs and should be performed by professionals experienced in the correctional environment.

Inmates who refuse evaluation or demonstrate poor cooperation with physical therapy should be referred for mental health assessment and have their safety concerns (e.g., fear of sexual assault) investigated in collaboration with security personnel, to thoroughly explore the psychological and safety factors underlying their behavior and to prevent manipulation of the evaluation process or misuse of medical resources.

A multidisciplinary coordination mechanism should be established whereby the medical director communicates with the warden and security departments, integrating input from medical, mental health, nursing, and security staff to comprehensively assess and address the inmate’s medical needs and safety concerns, and to formulate an individualized management plan.

When an inmate refuses treatment or cooperation, a signed written refusal must be obtained, and all related behaviors should be meticulously documented in the medical record to ensure transparency and accountability throughout the medical process.

If wheelchair use is permitted for inmates without a genuine medical indication, the medical record must explicitly state that this decision is not in the patient’s best medical interest, thereby preventing the establishment of adverse precedents and discouraging imitation.

title: Communicating with Patients about Harmful Behaviors
case:
"Come on in, Travis," said Dr. Kennedy. "Looks as though that could be a nasty scrape."
"Yeah, well thanks for working me in," said Travis, holding a bloody bandana to his head. "We're laying sewer pipe for the city and the crane operator can't see us too well. A pipe grazed me going down," he said. "I guess my timing's off today. It kind of rang my bell."
"Let me take a look." Dr. Kennedy, examined his temple and the skin around the orbital area and eye. "I can patch this up for you, and then we'll send you for some X-rays."
While he was at work on Travis's temple, Dr. Kennedy asked for more information about the accident. "Why is your timing off? Are you getting enough sleep? Were you hung over?"
"Maybe."
"How many drinks do you have in a week?" Dr. Kennedy asked calmly.
"I don't know. I don't count'em. Three or four a day maybe. Not on the job, though." Travis replied.
"Well I smell whiskey on your breath now and I'm worried. You could have gotten a concussion down there today—or worse."
"Easy on the sermons, OK? The other guys bought me one for the pain today. I can handle the drink," Travis said.
"OK, Travis," said Dr Kennedy, exasperated. "But we need to see what problems you're having that could be related to your drinking. You might need to cut back, and some people need to do that under supervision."
case_rewrite:
“Come on in, Travis,” Dr. Kennedy called out, gesturing toward the exam table. “Looks like you’ve got quite a scrape there.”

“Yeah, well, thanks for fitting me in,” Travis replied, pressing a blood-stained bandana against his forehead. “We’re laying sewer pipes for the city, and the crane operator couldn’t really see us down there. One of the pipes clipped me on its way down. Guess my timing was off today—it really rattled me.”

“Let me have a look,” Dr. Kennedy said, gently examining the bruised area around Travis’s temple and eye. “I’ll get you patched up, and then send you for some X-rays to be safe.”

As she cleaned the wound, Dr. Kennedy continued, “What do you think happened with your timing? Are you sleeping okay? Were you hungover this morning?”

“Maybe,” Travis mumbled.

“How many drinks do you usually have in a week?” Dr. Kennedy asked in a calm tone.

“I don’t really keep track. Three, four a day, maybe. But never while I’m working,” Travis said, shifting on the table.

Dr. Kennedy paused, noticing the scent of alcohol. “I can smell whiskey on your breath right now, and I’m concerned. You could have gotten a concussion—or something worse.”

“Lay off with the lectures, will you?” Travis shot back. “The guys gave me one for the pain after it happened. I can handle my drinking.”
