Dr. Kennedy sighed. “Alright, Travis. But we need to talk about whether your drinking might be causing you problems—even if you don’t think so right now. Cutting back can be tough, and sometimes people need support to do it safely.”

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically permissible to mandate treatment when a patient lacks the willingness to change?
keypoints: Coercive treatment is unlikely to be effective when the patient lacks readiness to change, as the patient is not yet prepared to engage in therapy.
Physicians who recommend treatment without adequately eliciting the patient’s consent risk bypassing the patient’s stage of readiness, thereby undermining the therapeutic relationship.
When the patient does not associate alcohol use with the injury nor perceive increased future risk from drinking, mandatory recommendations are unlikely to facilitate behavioral change.

Physicians should adopt a non-confrontational approach that helps patients identify intrinsic motivations, thereby enhancing their willingness and confidence to change autonomously rather than imposing directives.

title: Why Must Pain Patients Be Found Deserving of Treatment?
case:
Dr. Maier entered the small curtained room in the emergency department and introduced himself to the patient, Mrs. Winter. Then he asked whether the fourth-year medical student with him, Miss Malloy, could be present for the encounter.
"I suppose so," Mrs. Winter said. "But I can't promise that I won't be cranky. I'm in considerable pain."
"Tell me about it." Dr. Maier said.
Mrs. Winter explained that her doctor, Dr. Caruso, had diagnosed fibromyalgia about a year ago. She was generally tired, had low energy, and almost always had some pain in her shoulders, neck and head. But the pain flared up from time to time. Right now, her neck was so sore that she couldn't move it; it even hurt when she walked. When this happened, she said, she just had to give in and spend a few days on the sofa "knocked out" until whatever had caused the painful episode resolved. She used the word "resolved." Mrs. Winter gestured with her hands as she spoke, letting her manicured finger tips hover over the areas she mentioned as she described the pain. Her several gold bracelets lent a jingling flourish to the account.
When Dr. Maier asked Mrs. Winter to rate the pain from 1 to 10, compared to the worst she had experienced, she said, "8.7. Of course I've had worse or I wouldn't have been able to get here. But I certainly couldn't wait until Monday to see Dr. Caruso."
Dr. Maier asked Mrs. Winter a few more questions about the nature of the pain, then examined her to determine whether some injury or inflammatory condition unrelated to her diagnosis could be the cause of her current pain.
Dr. Maier said he had found nothing to indicate that Mrs. Winter was experiencing anything different from the flare-ups she described having had in the past. "What does Dr. Caruso usually prescribe?" he asked.
"He usually gives me Tramadol," she said. "Twenty-four will get me through the duration of the bout."
"Well, this is Saturday," Dr. Maier said. "Suppose I give you a prescription for 10 to get you through Sunday night, and you can call Dr. Caruso on Monday, if you are still in pain. Shall I ask our desk attendant to call this in for you?"
"No. That's ok. I'll just stop at the drug store on my way home. I was hoping to avoid making another trip to the doctor on Monday," Mrs. Winter said. "But if that's all you can prescribe, I guess I'll see how I feel by then." Mrs. Winter winced again as she stepped carefully from the table.
Dr. Maier shook her hand; Miss Malloy said, "Thank you for allowing me to observe. I hope you feel better."
As Dr. Maier finished his notes and carried the chart to the center desk, Miss Malloy ventured quietly, "Mrs. Winter didn't get the third degree like Mr. Washington did this morning."
"What do you mean?"
"You remember Mr. Washington—with the toothache? You asked him what pharmacy he used, and did he always use the same one, and why didn't he call his dentist for the medication, and had he tried Tylenol. Then you told him to get ibuprofen at the drug store."
"You mean the gent that looked as though he'd slept in his clothes?"
case_rewrite:
Dr. Maier stepped into the small curtained alcove in the emergency department and introduced himself to Mrs. Winter. At his side stood Miss Malloy, a fourth-year medical student. “Would it be all right if Miss Malloy joins us for your visit today?” he asked.

“I suppose that’s fine,” Mrs. Winter replied, her voice tinged with fatigue. “But forgive me if I’m cranky—I’m in a lot of pain right now.”

“I understand,” Dr. Maier said gently. “Tell me what’s going on.”

Mrs. Winter began to describe her history: about a year ago, her physician, Dr. Caruso, had diagnosed her with fibromyalgia. She often felt exhausted, had little energy, and suffered from persistent pain in her shoulders, neck, and head. Occasionally, the pain would intensify dramatically, as it had now: her neck hurt so badly she couldn’t turn it, and even walking sent jolts through her body. When these episodes struck, she explained, she typically surrendered to several days on the sofa, “knocked out” until the pain—she used the word “resolved”—finally eased. As she spoke, Mrs. Winter gestured with her manicured fingertips, hovering them over her neck and shoulders, and her stack of gold bracelets chimed softly with her movements.

Dr. Maier asked her to rate her pain on a scale from one to ten, compared to the worst she’d ever felt. “About an 8.7,” Mrs. Winter answered. “If it were any worse, I wouldn’t have made it here. But there was no way I could wait until Monday to see Dr. Caruso.”

He continued with a few more questions, probing for signs of any new injury or inflammatory process unrelated to her fibromyalgia. After a careful exam, he concluded that nothing suggested a problem different from her usual flare-ups. “What does Dr. Caruso usually prescribe for you?” Dr. Maier inquired.

“Tramadol,” Mrs. Winter replied. “A prescription for twenty-four tablets usually gets me through these bouts.”

Dr. Maier glanced at the clock. “Since it’s Saturday,” he said, “I can give you a prescription for ten tablets to get you through Sunday night. If you’re still in pain on Monday, you can call Dr. Caruso for further management. Would you like our desk attendant to call the prescription in for you?”

Mrs. Winter shook her head. “No, that’s all right. I’ll stop at the pharmacy on my way home. I was hoping to avoid another doctor’s visit on Monday, but if ten is all you can do, I’ll see how it goes.” She winced, easing herself down from the exam table.

Dr. Maier shook her hand in farewell. Miss Malloy smiled and said, “Thank you for letting me observe. I hope you feel better soon.”

Afterward, as Dr. Maier completed his charting at the central desk, Miss Malloy quietly remarked, “Mrs. Winter’s visit was handled very differently than Mr. Washington’s this morning.”

Dr. Maier looked up. “What do you mean?”

“Remember Mr. Washington? He came in with a toothache. You asked him which pharmacy he used, whether he always used the same one, why he hadn’t called his dentist for medication, if he’d taken Tylenol. Then you told him to try ibuprofen from the drug store.”

“You mean the gentleman who looked as though he’d slept in his clothes?” Dr. Maier replied.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with the potential risks of drug misuse or addiction, how should physicians ethically balance the responsibility to prescribe opioids appropriately with the obligation to prevent drug abuse?
keypoints: Physicians must validate patients’ pain experiences through respectful listening to their narratives, recognizing that this process itself holds significant therapeutic value.

It is essential to rationally distinguish between the motives for medication use and addiction risks in pain patients versus those with substance abuse, acknowledging that appropriately prescribed opioids rarely lead to addiction in patients without a history of misuse.

Undertreatment of pain may constitute a serious breach of medical ethics; clinicians bear the responsibility to balance the judicious prescription of opioids with the prevention of misuse, avoiding inadequate treatment driven by fears of addiction.

Physicians should critically reflect on how their own emotions and biases influence clinical interactions and decision-making, ensuring that patients are treated with compassion and respect to foster trust and effective communication.

ethical_issues.question: How can emergency department physicians ensure equitable pain management for all patients in a tense and uncertain environment, without being influenced by patients’ appearance, socioeconomic background, or other biases?
keypoints: Physicians should first engage in self-reflection and remain vigilant about how their own emotions, biases, and social stereotypes influence patient interactions and clinical decision-making, ensuring equitable treatment for every patient.
Physicians need to understand the subjective nature of pain from the patient’s perspective and respond to the patient’s narrative with empathy and trust to foster a positive therapeutic relationship.
Physicians must acknowledge and validate the patient’s experience of pain as a fundamental prerequisite for effective pain management.
In the context of a tense and uncertain environment, physicians should treat each individual patient with compassion and respect, transcending diagnostic labels to realize truly humane care.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ensure that they give adequate attention and respect to patients’ experiences of pain during assessment, rather than allowing personal emotions and biases to influence their judgment?
keypoints: Physicians must acknowledge and validate the patient’s experience of pain in order to ensure effective treatment and uphold the patient’s dignity.
Physicians should respond to patients with empathy and trust, striving to understand their subjective experience of pain from the patient’s perspective.
Physicians should avoid stereotyping and focus on the specific individual patient and their unique experience of illness and pain.
Physicians need to reflect on and remain vigilant about how their personal emotions, biases, and preconceived notions may influence interactions with patients and clinical decision-making.
Respecting and listening to the patient’s narrative is itself of significant therapeutic value, helping to establish trust and promote recovery.

title: Smoking and Medicaid Benefits
case:
Dr. Smith's spirits fell as soon as he noticed Jack fidgeting uncomfortably in the waiting area of his small private practice office. Jack usually dreaded even the thought of seeing a doctor.
Upon his first visit to Dr. Smith's office several years ago, Jack was diagnosed with diabetes and high blood pressure. As a result, Dr. Smith placed him on four different medications, one of which was insulin.
Whenever Jack came in for a checkup, Dr. Smith would repeat his pleas that Jack quit smoking and adopt healthier lifestyle choices. Jack's usual response to the former: "Why the hell should I stop smoking when I've done it for 20 years now?" His response to the latter: "Doc, I eat what I like and what I can afford. That's it. I'm not going to waste money on stuff I won't eat."
On this visit, Dr. Smith hoped things would be different. He reminded Jack, who received Medicaid benefits, that he had signed a contract with the state of West Virginia entitling him to additional health benefits—such as weight-loss and anti-smoking programs, mental health services, diabetes management classes, and cardiac rehabilitation—if he kept his medical appointments, took his medications, and followed health improvement plans. If he reneged on these obligations—and so far, Jack had—Dr. Smith would be forced to report this noncompliance to the state. Jack would still get basic Medicaid services but would only get four free drug prescriptions per month, among other limitations.
"So this is what happens when there's a crunch for taxpayer money," Dr. Smith thought to himself. "You end up doling out service based on compliance." What really worried Dr. Smith was that if Jack ever got sick with an infection, for example, one that required antibiotic treatment, and the prescription exceeded the dollar limit, there would be no telling what would happen to Jack or his kids.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Smith’s mood sank as he spotted Jack shifting restlessly in the waiting room of his modest private practice. Jack, never one for doctor visits, looked more uneasy than usual.

Years ago, during Jack’s first appointment, Dr. Smith had diagnosed him with diabetes and high blood pressure. Since then, Jack had been prescribed four medications, including insulin. At every follow-up, Dr. Smith would urge Jack to quit smoking and work on healthier habits. Jack’s answers were always the same: “Why should I quit after twenty years?” he would grumble about smoking. As for diet, Jack would shrug and say, “Doc, I eat what I like and what I can afford. I’m not spending money on stuff I won’t eat.”

Today, Dr. Smith hoped for a change. He reminded Jack, who was covered by Medicaid, of the contract he’d signed with the state of West Virginia. This agreement granted Jack access to extra health benefits—weight-loss and anti-smoking programs, mental health counseling, diabetes classes, even cardiac rehab—so long as he kept appointments, took his medications, and followed recommended health plans. If Jack failed to meet these terms—and so far, he had—Dr. Smith would be obligated to report his noncompliance to the state. Jack would still receive basic Medicaid, but with new restrictions: only four free prescriptions per month and other cutbacks.

“So this is what it comes to when public funds are tight,” Dr. Smith thought, troubled. “Care gets rationed according to compliance.” What truly unsettled him was the risk Jack faced if he developed an illness like an infection needing antibiotics. If Jack’s prescriptions exceeded the Medicaid limit, there was no telling what would happen to him—or to his children.

ethical_issues.question: Does the West Virginia Medicaid reform serve the best interests of patients, or does it threaten patient interests?
keypoints: The West Virginia Medicaid reform aims to promote improvement in unhealthy lifestyles and enhance health outcomes while reducing healthcare costs by strengthening personal health responsibility and establishing incentive mechanisms.
Proponents argue that the program motivates patients to engage in self-management and adhere to treatment plans, thereby improving health outcomes and conserving public healthcare resources.

Opponents contend that the program may undermine physician-patient trust, increase ethical conflicts for physicians between legal obligations and the duty to act in the patient’s best interests, and disrupt traditional models of the physician-patient relationship.

Physicians must distinguish between achievable and ideal patient behaviors, avoiding the simplistic classification of patients as noncompliant when goals are not fully met, and should adjust treatment and management plans through physician-patient communication.

The program may result in service limitations for economically disadvantaged patients, exacerbating health inequities; particular attention must be paid to the economic and health risks faced by patients and their families.

Only through fair pilot implementation, ongoing monitoring, and multi-stakeholder feedback can the reform be comprehensively evaluated to determine whether it truly serves the best interests of patients and safeguards their rights.

title: Communicable Disease and Immigration Fears
case:
Joseph had been feeling sick for a few weeks, with a severe cough and poor appetite. He even started losing weight. Despite his condition, Joseph did not seek medical care because if he called in sick at the construction company where he worked (either to visit the doctor or to stay home after being diagnosed) his paycheck would be docked. Joseph had a family of five to support: himself, his wife, and three small boys. A few years earlier with the help of some distant relatives, the family had managed to cross the border from Mexico—where Joseph had worked as a farmer and earned a few dollars a day—to California.
In America Joseph was earning nearly 10 times the amount of money he made in Mexico. Still, he couldn't afford a loss in his daily pay. One morning, Joseph woke up coughing violently and eventually spit up blood. He decided to go to work anyway. When he arrived at work, his condition drew the attention of his boss, who sent him to the community health clinic where he saw Dr. Monroe. After hearing how long Joseph had had the cough, Dr. Monroe ordered a chest X-ray which showed that Joseph had active tuberculosis (TB).
When Dr. Monroe talked to Joseph about the test results, he cautioned him that his tuberculosis was highly infectious, imposing special restrictions on his life. He would have to isolate himself to limit the exposure of others. The public health department would also have to be notified, an idea which terrified Joseph. He pleaded with the doctor not to take this step, citing fears that he would be arrested and sent back to Mexico. Dr. Monroe assured Joseph that deportation would be a highly unlikely outcome, although he was unable to guarantee it would not happen. Dr. Monroe added that the health care system in the United States operated outside of immigration law enforcement. Still, Joseph was not reassured. He tried to bargain with Dr. Monroe, repeatedly promising to isolate himself voluntarily so long as neither he nor anyone else alerted the authorities.
case_rewrite:
For several weeks, Joseph had been battling a persistent cough, a dwindling appetite, and noticeable weight loss. Despite his worsening symptoms, he avoided seeking medical attention. Joseph worked long hours at a construction company in California, and missing a day—either for a doctor’s visit or to recover—meant a cut in his much-needed wages. He was the sole provider for his wife and three young sons. Years earlier, with assistance from distant relatives, Joseph and his family had crossed the border from Mexico, where he had toiled as a farm laborer for only a few dollars a day. Life in America brought better pay—almost ten times what he earned back home—but his family’s expenses left little room for any loss in income.

One morning, Joseph awoke to a violent coughing fit and was alarmed to find blood in his sputum. Nevertheless, he forced himself to work, fearing the consequences of absence. At the construction site, his boss quickly noticed his poor condition and insisted he go to the local community health clinic. There, Joseph was evaluated by Dr. Monroe. After listening to Joseph’s account of his prolonged cough, Dr. Monroe ordered a chest X-ray. The results revealed that Joseph had active tuberculosis.

When Dr. Monroe met with Joseph to discuss the diagnosis, he explained that tuberculosis was highly contagious and would require Joseph to take strict precautions, including isolating himself to prevent spreading the infection. Dr. Monroe also informed him that the case would need to be reported to the public health department, as mandated by law. This news left Joseph visibly shaken. He begged Dr. Monroe not to notify the authorities, voicing his deep fear that he might be arrested and deported back to Mexico. Dr. Monroe tried to reassure him, explaining that deportation was highly unlikely and that the healthcare system functioned separately from immigration enforcement. Still, he could not make any absolute promises. Dr. Monroe emphasized that patient information would remain confidential throughout the process, and that the purpose of notifying public health authorities was solely to protect the community and ensure Joseph received appropriate care.

Despite these assurances, Joseph remained anxious and pleaded with Dr. Monroe, repeatedly offering to isolate himself if only the authorities were not contacted. Dr. Monroe listened empathetically but was clear about his responsibilities. He explained the importance of collaboration with the public health department—not only to track and control the spread of tuberculosis but also to connect Joseph with resources such as treatment support and social services. Dr. Monroe stressed that Joseph’s cooperation was vital, both for his own recovery and for the safety of his family and the wider community.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance the responsibility between protecting patient privacy and ensuring public health safety when managing patients with communicable diseases?
keypoints: Physicians are legally obligated to report notifiable communicable diseases to the local health department to safeguard public health.
Patients have a right to privacy, and physicians must ensure that patient information is strictly confidential throughout the reporting and follow-up processes to prevent unauthorized disclosure.

Physicians should engage in thorough communication with patients to build trust, explain the impact of the disease and the treatment plan, and encourage patient adherence to therapy and isolation measures to minimize the risk of treatment interruption.
Physicians must clearly articulate their public health responsibilities and emphasize the importance of patient cooperation in protecting community health.

Physicians should collaborate closely with public health authorities to coordinate patient treatment, contact tracing, and social support services, balancing the protection of patient rights with community safety.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where the patient fears deportation, should the physician report the communicable disease to the public health department?
keypoints: Physicians are legally obligated to report cases of tuberculosis to the public health department, as tuberculosis is a reportable communicable disease in all jurisdictions within the United States, and the diagnosing or treating physician has a duty to notify the authorities.

Physicians have the responsibility to thoroughly inform patients about the infectious nature of the disease, the treatment regimen, and isolation requirements, emphasizing the public health implications of tuberculosis and the physician’s social responsibility.

In response to patients’ fears of deportation, it must be clearly communicated that the public health system operates independently from immigration enforcement agencies, and that strict confidentiality protections are in place; reporting the disease will not directly result in deportation.

Public health personnel must adhere to stringent confidentiality obligations, and municipal services are prohibited from inquiring about or reporting patients’ immigration status, thereby ensuring that patients receive evaluation and treatment without immigration status verification.

To prevent disease transmission due to patients’ fear-driven avoidance of care, healthcare providers and public health departments should collaborate to develop comprehensive management plans that balance public health safety with the protection of patients’ rights, ensuring that individuals with tuberculosis receive thorough and confidential treatment.

title: Suspected Child Abuse
case:
Jimmy, a 2-year-old toddler, was taken by his mother to his pediatrician, Dr. Wagner, because he had been holding his wrist and crying that it "hurt real bad." Dr. Wagner had been the family's pediatrician for the past year and was just getting to know them. Jimmy's father sat on the board of directors for the hospital, so Dr. Wagner always went the "extra mile" to provide the best care and tried to portray the Department of Pediatrics in the best light.
When Dr. Lawrence, the pediatric radiologist at the same hospital, analyzed Jimmy's X-ray, she noticed signs of two healed fractures in addition to the new fracture. The child's bones otherwise appeared normal.
Dr. Lawrence called Dr. Wagner to discuss what she had found and mentioned abuse as a possible cause for the fractures. Dr. Wagner made light of the situation, saying that it would not be appropriate to make such an accusation of a member of the hospital's board of directors.
Dr. Lawrence was frustrated. If the pediatrician wasn't going to follow up on suspected abuse, what steps should she take?
case_rewrite:
Two-year-old Jimmy was brought to his pediatrician, Dr. Wagner, by his mother after he began clutching his wrist and complaining that it "hurt real bad." Dr. Wagner had been caring for Jimmy and his family for about a year and was still building rapport with them. Notably, Jimmy’s father held a seat on the hospital’s board of directors, a fact that often motivated Dr. Wagner to go above and beyond in providing care and to ensure the Department of Pediatrics was held in high regard.

After examining Jimmy, Dr. Wagner ordered an X-ray, which was interpreted by Dr. Lawrence, the hospital’s pediatric radiologist. As Dr. Lawrence reviewed the images, she identified not only a fresh fracture but also evidence of two older, healed fractures in Jimmy’s wrist. The remainder of Jimmy’s bones appeared normal and healthy.

Concerned by these findings, Dr. Lawrence phoned Dr. Wagner to discuss her suspicion that the pattern of injuries might point to possible abuse. Dr. Wagner, however, played down her concerns, remarking that it would be inappropriate to raise such an accusation involving the child of a hospital board member.

Dr. Lawrence was left feeling troubled and uncertain. With the pediatrician dismissing the possibility of abuse and offering no alternative explanation for the injuries, Dr. Lawrence now faced a difficult decision about what action she should take next.

ethical_issues.question: Should the radiologist, upon suspecting child abuse, bypass the primary care physician and report directly to the child protective services agency?
keypoints: As a licensed healthcare provider, the radiologist has a legal obligation to report suspected child abuse as a mandatory reporter.

When the primary physician disagrees and fails to provide sufficient evidence to dispel reasonable suspicion, the radiologist should bypass the primary physician and report directly to the child protective services agency.

Physicians have a duty to protect their patients, especially children who lack the capacity for self-care; safeguarding vulnerable victims is a fundamental ethical responsibility of the medical profession, even if it entails potential professional risks.

ethical_issues.question: When the referring physician disagrees but does not provide compelling evidence to dispel the radiologist’s concerns, does the radiologist have an obligation to inform the patient or the patient’s guardian directly?
keypoints: The radiologist has a responsibility to the patient that goes beyond issuing an imaging report and must reasonably ensure that the patient or their legal guardian is informed of any adverse findings.

When the referring physician disagrees but fails to provide compelling evidence to dispel the radiologist’s concerns, and there is a risk of conflict of interest, the radiologist should actively promote further evaluation and communication, and, if necessary, directly inform the patient or their guardian to prevent any obstruction in the transmission of critical information.

Due to the practical challenge of information asymmetry, as the radiologist may not have access to the patient’s complete medical record, suspected child abuse cases should be handled with caution, taking into account the clinical context and relevant legal requirements.

The law clearly stipulates that physicians have a mandatory duty to report suspected child abuse; the radiologist must act in accordance with legal requirements, prioritizing the safety and best interests of the patient.

ethical_issues.question: How can a radiologist fulfill their duty to inform when identifying a potentially life-threatening condition, without compromising their relationship with the referring physician?
keypoints: The radiologist’s responsibilities extend beyond merely issuing imaging reports; she must reasonably ensure that critical abnormal findings are effectively communicated to the referring physician as well as to the patient or the minor’s guardian.

When the referring physician cannot reasonably be informed of key diagnostic information, or there is evidence of negligence or significant misjudgment, the radiologist has a duty to directly inform the patient or their guardian to ensure patient safety.

The radiologist should adhere to professional communication guidelines, thoughtfully assess communication strategies, and balance the responsibility of maintaining the physician-patient relationship with the obligation to protect the patient’s best interests.

Protecting defenseless victims is the physician’s foremost duty; doctors should place the patient’s welfare at the center of their actions and have the courage to face potential professional risks and interpersonal pressures.

title: Outsourcing: A Limited View of Radiology's Role
case:
As part of a private practice radiology group in a small town, Dr. Adams had been reading the imaging studies from a local community hospital, Holmes Medical Center, for 15 years. A native of the town, Dr. Adams grew up learning about his community and embraced its culture. He lived in the same neighborhood as many of his patients and often saw them at the local coffee shop and diner. Through these informal interactions, Dr. Adams was able to observe the changing health of his patients over a period of years. He has also been an active member of the local medical community, meeting face-to-face with the referring physicians from the medical center weekly.
At a meeting with Holmes' administrators Dr. Adams heard for the first time about a proposed cost-cutting initiative. The hospital was considering whether to send imaging studies to specialists at a large academic medical center in a different state. The larger center had more radiologists and performed the services for less than Dr. Adams's group charged. After Dr. Adams described the disadvantages of the proposed initiative, a hospital administrator said, "Without the large source of images from us, your small group probably won't be able to support a practice anymore. I think your arguments are motivated primarily by concerns about your financial well-being."
case_rewrite:
For the past fifteen years, Dr. Adams had served as a radiologist in a private practice group, reading imaging studies for Holmes Medical Center, the local hospital in his small hometown. Having grown up in the area, Dr. Adams was intimately familiar with the community's people and customs. He lived just blocks away from the hospital, sharing the same neighborhood as many of his patients, and it was not uncommon for him to greet them at the local coffee shop or while dining downtown. Over time, these regular encounters gave Dr. Adams a unique window into the evolving health concerns of his neighbors and fostered a sense of continuity and trust. He was also deeply involved in the local medical scene, meeting in person every week with the referring physicians on staff at Holmes Medical Center to discuss cases and collaborate on patient care.

During a recent meeting with the hospital’s administrators, Dr. Adams was introduced to a new proposal aimed at reducing operational costs. Holmes Medical Center was considering outsourcing its imaging studies to a team of specialists at a prominent academic medical center in another state. This larger institution boasted a greater number of radiologists and could offer their interpretation services at a lower rate than Dr. Adams’s local group. Dr. Adams voiced his concerns about the potential drawbacks of this plan, emphasizing the importance of local expertise and personal relationships in patient care. One of the hospital administrators responded pointedly, “If Holmes stops sending you our imaging work, your group probably won’t be able to keep your practice going. Isn’t it true that your objections are mainly about protecting your own financial interests?”

ethical_issues.question: Does the low-cost service provided by the out-of-state academic institution truly encompass all the essential responsibilities of radiologists, including on-site operations and relationship-building within the community?
keypoints: It is essential to clarify whether the out-of-state academic institution provides comprehensive services, including fluoroscopic examinations that require the on-site presence of a radiologist, rather than limiting its scope to image interpretation of CT and MRI studies that do not necessitate a radiologist’s physical presence.

The responsibilities of radiologists extend beyond image interpretation to include establishing and maintaining ongoing trust and communication with patients, referring physicians, and the community; this community linkage represents a core value that remote outsourcing services are inherently unable to replace.

The frequency and depth of the out-of-state radiology team’s participation in hospital grand rounds, professional committees, and multidisciplinary collaboration should be evaluated to assess their actual contribution to clinical decision-making and team integration within the hospital.

The extent of the out-of-state physicians’ volunteer service and engagement in local community, religious, educational, and public health organizations should be examined, as physicians’ sense of community responsibility and involvement directly impact the overall quality of medical services and patient satisfaction.

A comprehensive assessment should balance the potential cost savings of outsourcing against the possible adverse effects on the operational stability of the local medical team, continuity of community healthcare services, and the trust relationships with patients, thereby ensuring that decisions consider both economic efficiency and medical ethical obligations.

title: Disclosure and the Retrospectoscope
case:
Mrs. Lee is a busy, working mother. She has raised three children, all of whom are successful attorneys, and was looking forward to retirement when she was diagnosed with breast cancer in her left breast. Her tests following surgery showed no cancer, and six months later Mrs. Lee went to a breast imaging center for a follow-up visit.
Dr. Harris reviewed old imaging studies in preparation for her meeting with Mrs. Lee. She looked at the mammogram that had been interpreted as normal by another radiologist, 18 months before Mrs. Lee was diagnosed with breast cancer. After careful examination, Dr. Harris noted a small, ill-defined density in the left breast. It was in the location where the cancer was diagnosed on the subsequent mammogram and, in retrospect, it most likely represented the cancer in an earlier stage. In her own mind, Dr. Harris believed that many radiologists, possibly even she herself, would have interpreted the mammogram as normal. She wondered whether to tell Mrs. Lee what she had seen.
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Lee is a dedicated working mother who has successfully raised three children, each of whom has become an accomplished attorney. She had been eagerly anticipating her retirement when she was diagnosed with cancer in her left breast. Following surgical treatment, subsequent tests showed no evidence of disease, and six months later, Mrs. Lee attended a follow-up appointment at a breast imaging center.

Dr. Harris, the radiologist preparing for Mrs. Lee’s visit, reviewed her previous imaging studies. Among them was a mammogram from 18 months before Mrs. Lee’s cancer diagnosis, which had been interpreted as normal by a different radiologist. On close examination, Dr. Harris detected a small, indistinct density in the left breast—precisely in the area where Mrs. Lee’s cancer was later discovered. In hindsight, Dr. Harris thought this shadow likely represented the earliest stage of Mrs. Lee’s cancer. However, she also recognized that the finding was subtle; many radiologists, perhaps even herself, might have reasonably read the mammogram as normal at the time.

Dr. Harris now faced a dilemma: Should she inform Mrs. Lee about her retrospective observation, or was it better not to mention a finding that might not clearly represent an error? The uncertainty lingered in Dr. Harris’s mind as she considered the implications of disclosure—for Mrs. Lee, for the radiologist who originally read the scan, and for the trust within the medical team.

ethical_issues.question: When a physician discovers a possible medical error made by another doctor, do they have an ethical obligation to proactively disclose this information to the patient?
keypoints: When a physician identifies a potential medical error committed by another physician, they should first utilize protected peer review mechanisms to objectively assess whether a harmful error occurred and evaluate its actual impact on the patient.
When the ethical rationale is strong and the error is likely to cause serious future harm, physicians have a positive obligation to proactively disclose the relevant information to the patient.

If there is reasonable doubt as to whether the prior interpretation constitutes a clear error, and no substantive harm has been caused to the patient, mandatory disclosure is not advisable in order to avoid unnecessary patient anxiety and medico-legal disputes.

Healthcare institutions and the medical profession should establish explicit ethical and legal standards to regulate the procedures and scope of disclosing another physician’s medical error, thereby protecting patient rights while maintaining trust and collaboration within the healthcare team.

ethical_issues.question: In the absence of explicit guidance, how should physicians approach the disclosure of potential medical errors involving another physician?
keypoints: Physicians should utilize protected peer review mechanisms or independent third parties to objectively evaluate prior imaging interpretations in order to determine whether a harmful error occurred and to assess its impact on the patient.
If a harmful error is clearly identified and disclosure is necessary to prevent serious future harm, physicians have a positive obligation to proactively disclose relevant information to the patient.

When the nature of the error is uncertain, disclosure should be approached with caution to avoid misleading the patient, while ensuring that the information provided is complete, truthful, and not misleading.

If a potential error involves another physician, the current physician should contact the original physician to discuss whether he or she will communicate directly with the patient, thereby demonstrating respect and professional collaboration.

Physicians have a positive duty to ensure that patients receive truthful, accurate, and comprehensive information, and should take the initiative to disclose when a clearly harmful error has occurred.

title: Physicians' Duties in Treating Wartime Detainees
case: Dr. Thompson is a military reservist deployed with a mobile medical field unit in Iraq. Several weeks into a grueling tour during which a number of American soldiers sustained serious injuries, a young Iraqi man who had been detained for questioning was brought to Dr. Thompson by the military police (MP). The MP said that the man had been found at a military checkpoint with what appeared to be a broken ankle and asked Dr. Thompson to assess the extent of the injury so that the man could be returned to the detention unit. During his examination, Dr. Thompson found that the young man had a grossly swollen orbit and bright red welts and lacerations covering his back, in addition to a fractured left ankle. Dr. Thompson strongly suspected that his patient had been beaten by a member of the unit and knew that he should notify the unit commander. Although he was well aware of international law governing prisoners of war and detainees, and although he had received comprehensive ethics training from the military regarding his duty to report signs of abuse, Dr. Thompson found himself hesitating to make a report.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Thompson, a military reservist, is serving with a mobile medical field unit stationed in Iraq. After several exhausting weeks marked by the treatment of multiple American soldiers suffering from serious combat injuries, Dr. Thompson is approached by military police (MP) with a new patient. The MPs bring in a young Iraqi man who has been detained for questioning. They inform Dr. Thompson that the man was discovered at a checkpoint appearing to have a broken ankle and request that Dr. Thompson assess his condition so that he can be returned to the detention unit.

During his examination, Dr. Thompson immediately observes signs that raise deep concern. The young man not only has a fractured left ankle, but also presents with a grossly swollen eye socket and vivid, fresh red welts and lacerations crisscrossing his back. The injuries are consistent with recent blunt force trauma, and Dr. Thompson strongly suspects that the detainee has been physically assaulted, likely by someone within the unit. Aware of both international standards regarding the treatment of detainees and the comprehensive ethics training he received as a military physician—including his duty to report suspected abuse—Dr. Thompson recognizes that he must notify the unit commander.

Yet, as he stands beside the injured man, Dr. Thompson hesitates. He is acutely aware of the possible implications of reporting: the risks to the safety of the detainee, to his own position within the unit, and to the trust and functioning of the team. Despite knowing his ethical and legal responsibilities, and the protocols for documentation and reporting, Dr. Thompson struggles with uncertainty about the best course of action to ensure the well-being of his patient and to uphold his professional obligations in this challenging environment.

ethical_issues.question: How should Dr. Thompson determine the appropriate reporting mechanism to ensure the safety of the detained Iraqi man and uphold his own professional ethical obligations?
keypoints: Dr. Thompson’s primary ethical obligation is to ensure that the detainee receives timely, appropriate, and impartial medical care, and to take all reasonable measures to prevent further harm.

Dr. Thompson should meticulously document all findings, including the nature and extent of the detainee’s injuries and any evidence suggestive of abuse, ensuring that the medical record is thorough, objective, and accurate.

Dr. Thompson has a duty to report suspected abuse or mistreatment to a senior military medical officer or to personnel with designated ethical oversight responsibilities within the unit (such as a military chaplain or ethics committee), in order to seek guidance and facilitate appropriate internal review.

If there are concerns regarding the impartiality or effectiveness of the immediate chain of command in addressing the suspected abuse, Dr. Thompson should consider escalating the report through alternative trusted military channels or, if necessary, to independent international organizations with mandates to protect human rights (such as the International Committee of the Red Cross).

Dr. Thompson must carefully assess the potential risks associated with reporting, including possible repercussions for the detainee and for himself, and should select the reporting pathway that best upholds professional ethical obligations while maximizing the safety and rights of the patient.

Dr. Thompson should seek support and advice from trusted medical colleagues within and, where feasible, outside the military, and advocate for collective action to strengthen the effectiveness and security of the reporting process.

tags: Patient-clinician relationship/Patients’ responsibility for their health
title: Pregnant Women Who Smoke: A Challenge to the Patient-Physician Relationship
case:
Ms. Davis had many attributes that suggested she would become a successful parent. She was pleased with her current career position, had a strong support network of friends and family, and enjoyed a healthy relationship with her partner. She began prenatal care early in her pregnancy and was now at 20 weeks. The pregnancy had a single complication.
"I know what you are going to ask me," she began defensively as Dr. Golden stepped into the room. "Yes, I am still smoking. You have told me the risks at each of my visits: low birth weight, preterm birth, placental abnormalities, sudden infant death syndrome," she listed. "I just cannot seem to quit. Each time I think I have gathered enough willpower, all it takes is the sight of another smoker before I start having these terrible cravings again. All of my friends smoke. The baby's father smokes. Idocare about the health of my baby, but this addiction is very strong. I almost think that going through the physical and emotional upheaval of quitting now would be worse for my baby. I can't help but also feel that this is ultimately my body and my choice. Wouldn't you agree, Dr. Golden?"
case_rewrite:
Ms. Davis appeared to embody many qualities of a future devoted parent. She was content with her current job, relied on a solid network of family and friends, and enjoyed a supportive relationship with her partner. From early in her pregnancy, she attended regular prenatal appointments and now, at 20 weeks, her pregnancy had proceeded smoothly except for a single ongoing concern.

As Dr. Golden entered the exam room, Ms. Davis spoke up with a hint of defensiveness, “I know what you’re about to ask,” she said. “Yes, I’m still smoking.” She recited the risks that Dr. Golden had discussed at each visit: “You’ve told me about low birth weight, preterm labor, placental problems, SIDS… I know all of it.” She sighed, her frustration evident. “But I just can’t seem to stop. Every time I think I’ve finally summoned enough willpower, I’m around someone else who lights up, and the cravings hit so hard. Most of my friends smoke. The baby’s father smokes, too. I really do care about my baby’s health, but this addiction is just so strong. Sometimes I honestly wonder if the stress of quitting now would be worse for my baby than if I just keep smoking.” She paused, her voice softening. “And I have to admit, I still feel that it’s my body and my decision at the end of the day. Don’t you think so, Dr. Golden?”

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance providing recommendations with respecting patient autonomy when addressing the issue of smoking in pregnant women?
keypoints: Physicians’ actions should be grounded in the two fundamental ethical principles of nonmaleficence and beneficence, serving as the theoretical foundation for providing advice and balancing decision-making.
Physicians must respect the pregnant woman’s autonomy, even when her choices may conflict with the fetus’s best interests, thereby upholding the patient’s dignity and right to self-determination.

Providing counseling and recommendations is the physician’s responsibility, but it requires a deep understanding of the patient’s addiction origins and persistence mechanisms, employing empathetic and supportive communication strategies.
Inviting the baby’s father to participate in prenatal visits and joint counseling sessions may strengthen familial support and motivate a shared commitment to smoking cessation.

Physicians should strive to establish a strong patient-physician relationship and form a therapeutic alliance to promote the pregnant woman’s active engagement and facilitate positive health behavior changes.

While advocating for the health of the child, it is imperative to protect the rights of the pregnant woman; this balance represents a central challenge faced by both physicians and members of society.

ethical_issues.question: Within the two-patient model, how should physicians ethically manage the conflict between a pregnant woman’s informed refusal and the well-being of the fetus?
keypoints: Physicians should respect the autonomy of pregnant women, even when their choices may conflict with the best interests of the fetus.
The patient-physician relationship founded on respect for patient dignity is central to an effective therapeutic alliance.
Physicians have the responsibility to provide comprehensive counseling, information, and advice, but must refrain from coercive or police-like interventions.
Upholding fetal health is premised on protecting the rights of the pregnant woman; these are complementary and require seeking a unified benefit rather than opposition.

title: Pregnant Women and Cervical Cancer: Balancing Best Interest of Mother and Fetus
case:
Mrs. Smith arrived at the clinic nearly 30 minutes late. Patty, the nurse at the front desk, watched her enter. Mrs. Smith's 10-year-old daughter was whining and grasping at her sides while her adolescent son ineffectually instructed the little girl to "stop it or else." When Mrs. Smith came into full view, it was obvious that she was pregnant.
Dr. Daniels quickly glanced over Mrs. Smith's chart before entering the exam room and saw that her last recorded visit was a routine postpartum care appointment nearly one decade prior.
Dr. Daniels greeted Mrs. Smith with a warm smile that had come to be one of her trademarks. "What brings you to clinic today?" she began.
"Well, now, isn't that pretty clear?" Mrs. Smith said jovially while patting her belly. A large smile spread across her face. "I'm probably almost five months along!"
Throughout the course of the interview, it became clear to Dr. Daniels that this pregnancy meant a great deal to Mrs. Smith. She had recently remarried and was carrying the child of her new husband, who was also extremely excited about the recent developments. When Dr. Daniels probed to find if Mrs. Smith had been receiving any form of health care since her last clinic visit, Mrs. Smith disclosed sheepishly that she had been battling unemployment intermittently and had only recently regained her health insurance.
Dr. Daniels then finished the interview. "Today we'll draw blood, do a urinalysis, and perform a Pap smear along with your exam. Then we'll schedule an ultrasound to confirm your dates and ensure that the pregnancy is proceeding normally. Do you have any questions or concerns for me?"
Mrs. Smith did not.
They proceeded with the physical exam. Dr. Daniels was alarmed to find several suspicious lesions involving the cervix, so she told Mrs. Smith that in addition to the Pap smear she would likely need to biopsy these sites.
A week later, Mrs. Smith found herself again in the obstetrician's office-this time alone. Dr. Daniels began to explain that the Pap smear and biopsies showed clear evidence of abnormal cells.
"What do you mean, 'abnormal cells?' Are you saying that I have cancer?" interrupted Mrs. Smith. "How will that affect my baby?"
"Well," began Dr. Daniels, "if a pregnant woman is found to have very early stage disease, most physicians are comfortable delaying interventions until after delivery regardless of how far along in the pregnancy you are. For late stage cancers, we generally recommend that treatment-which might include hysterectomy-begin immediately, again, regardless of the stage of pregnancy. I'd like to do a few more tests today, and we'll go from there."
One week later Dr. Daniels had to deliver the news to Mrs. Smith that she had stage II cancer and discuss with Mrs. Smith her treatment options and their affect on her pregnancy.
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Smith hurried into the clinic, nearly thirty minutes behind schedule. Patty, the nurse stationed at the front desk, watched as Mrs. Smith entered, accompanied by her two children. Her ten-year-old daughter clung to her sides, whining in discomfort, while the adolescent son tried unsuccessfully to quiet his younger sister with warnings to “stop it or else.” As Mrs. Smith came into clearer view, it was apparent that she was pregnant.

Dr. Daniels, preparing for her next patient, quickly skimmed Mrs. Smith’s chart before stepping into the exam room. She noted that Mrs. Smith’s last documented visit had been almost ten years ago, for a routine postpartum check-up. Entering the room with her trademark warmth, Dr. Daniels greeted her. “What brings you to the clinic today?”

Mrs. Smith grinned broadly, patting her pregnant belly. “Well, isn’t it obvious?” she replied with a laugh. “I’m probably just about five months along!”

As the visit progressed, Dr. Daniels learned that this pregnancy carried special significance for Mrs. Smith. She had remarried recently, and her new husband was overjoyed about the baby. When Dr. Daniels gently inquired about Mrs. Smith’s medical care since her last visit, Mrs. Smith admitted, somewhat embarrassed, that intermittent periods of unemployment had left her without health insurance until quite recently.

Concluding the interview, Dr. Daniels explained, “Today we’ll take some blood, do a urinalysis, and perform a Pap smear as part of your exam. We’ll also schedule an ultrasound to confirm your dates and make sure everything’s going smoothly. Do you have any questions or concerns?”

Mrs. Smith shook her head, indicating she was ready to proceed.

During the physical exam, Dr. Daniels grew concerned upon discovering several suspicious lesions on Mrs. Smith’s cervix. She explained to Mrs. Smith that, in addition to the Pap smear, a biopsy of these areas would be needed.

A week later, Mrs. Smith returned to the obstetrician’s office, this time by herself. Dr. Daniels sat down with her and began to review the results. “Your Pap smear and biopsies indicate the presence of abnormal cells,” she began.

Mrs. Smith interrupted anxiously, “What do you mean, ‘abnormal cells’? Are you saying I have cancer? What does this mean for my baby?”

Dr. Daniels answered carefully, “If a pregnant woman is found to have very early-stage disease, most doctors feel comfortable waiting until after delivery to begin treatment, no matter how far along the pregnancy is. For more advanced cases, we generally recommend starting treatment immediately—including procedures like a hysterectomy—even if that means acting before the pregnancy is viable. I’d like to run a few more tests today, and we’ll talk more once we have those results.”

A week later, Dr. Daniels met with Mrs. Smith again to deliver the diagnosis: stage II cervical cancer. She discussed with Mrs. Smith her treatment options, explaining how each choice could affect both her own health and the pregnancy.

ethical_issues.question: How can the patient’s autonomy be respected while ensuring that she makes a fully informed decision regarding the delay or immediate initiation of treatment for cervical cancer?
keypoints: Respect for patient autonomy requires ensuring that the patient makes decisions independently based on full disclosure and nondirective counseling. Physicians must provide objective and comprehensive information about all known and unknown factors, including the risks, benefits, and prognostic uncertainties associated with different treatment options.

Clearly inform the patient about the medical uncertainties regarding the prognosis of stage II cervical cancer when treatment is delayed until fetal viability, assisting the patient in understanding the potential risks and possible consequences.

Present a dual perspective on the treatment of stage II cervical cancer during pregnancy: describe the standard practice of immediate treatment and its role in optimizing maternal prognosis, while also explaining the option of delaying treatment along with its potential risks and benefits.

Introduce chemotherapy during pregnancy as an option to prevent metastatic spread of the cancer, emphasizing that this approach is still emerging and not yet considered standard of care, necessitating careful weighing of risks and benefits and disclosure of related uncertainties.

ethical_issues.question: May physicians conscientiously object to terminating the pregnancy before fetal viability, and how should the patient’s referral needs be managed in such circumstances?
keypoints: Healthcare professionals may conscientiously object to terminating a pregnancy before fetal viability; however, they must clearly disclose their positions on the sanctity of life and induced abortion to the patient prior to the initiation of care.

When healthcare providers refuse to carry out a patient’s decision to terminate a pregnancy on grounds of conscience, they are ethically obligated to facilitate timely referral to ensure that the patient’s access to necessary medical services and autonomous decision-making rights are upheld.

title: Assisted Reproduction andPrimum Non Nocere
case:
Mr. and Mrs. Jones were in many ways not unlike the other couples that had come to the infertility clinic. They were pleasant-appearing, affectionate towards one another and eager to become parents. They were extremely organized and had brought copies of their relevant medical records. Nevertheless, they managed to capture the attention of the entire waiting room: they both had the characteristic body size and features of achondroplasia.
Mrs. Jones began to rattle off facts in the examining room before Dr. West could even introduce himself. "We understand achondroplasiaverywell. It has autosomal-dominant genetics. When inherited homozygously, it is lethal, but."
"Well, you certainly have done your homework very well," chuckled Dr. West. "I'm Dr. West. How exactly is it that I can help you?"
"We have been trying to become pregnant for years now," chimed in Mr. Jones. "We have been to numerous doctors and had every test performed. They finally figured out that I have a slight blockage in the passage of sperm. We were referred to you for in vitro fertilization. Your colleagues say that you're one of the best."
Dr. West went on with a mixture of modesty and pride to describe the clinic's excellent success rates for in vitro fertilization.
Mr. Jones then lowered his voice slightly as he elaborated to Dr. West his fears regarding the psychological repercussions on his wife should she conceive a homozygous child who was essentially born only to die. The couple also expressed their strong opposition to abortion. They were simply unwilling to accept a 25 percent chance that their baby would be homozygous for achondroplasia.
"Given what you have just told me," Dr. West asserted, "in conjunction with the complexities of your genetic background, we would consider preimplantation genetic diagnosis to be appropriate in avoiding this outcome and increasing the probability that you would have a child of normal stature."
Mr. and Mrs. Jones looked shocked. "Well, actually, we were hoping that you might assist us in having a childwithachondroplasia. How would we care for or understand a child who was not like us?"
Realizing his false assumption, Dr. West thought carefully about his next words. He had never been asked to perform preimplantation genetic diagnosis and specifically choose embryos that would become what many would consider "impaired" children. While medically it may be safe, something didn't sit right with Dr. West.
case_rewrite:
Mr. and Mrs. Jones, like many couples who visited the infertility clinic, presented themselves as warm, affectionate partners, eager to start a family. They arrived well-prepared, carrying neatly organized copies of all pertinent medical records. Yet, they drew glances throughout the waiting room, as both displayed the unmistakable physical features of achondroplasia.

Once in the examination room, Mrs. Jones launched into a detailed explanation before Dr. West even had a chance to introduce himself. "We’re very knowledgeable about achondroplasia. It’s an autosomal-dominant condition. If inherited in a homozygous state, it’s lethal, but—"

Dr. West interrupted her with a friendly smile. "You two have certainly done your research. I’m Dr. West. How can I help you today?"

Mr. Jones quickly added, "We’ve been trying to have a child for several years. We’ve seen many specialists and undergone every possible test. It turns out I have a minor blockage affecting sperm transport, and that’s why we were sent to you. Your colleagues said you’re among the best for in vitro fertilization."

With a mix of humility and pride, Dr. West outlined the clinic’s impressive IVF success rates.

Then, Mr. Jones spoke more quietly, his voice tinged with concern. He confided his anxiety about the emotional impact on his wife if she were to carry a homozygous fetus—one that would not survive. The couple also made it clear they were strongly opposed to abortion, and could not accept the 25 percent risk of having a baby who would be homozygous for achondroplasia.

"Given everything you’ve told me," Dr. West replied, "and considering the specific genetic circumstances, I would recommend preimplantation genetic diagnosis to help avoid that outcome and increase the chance of having a child without achondroplasia."

At this, Mr. and Mrs. Jones looked genuinely surprised. "Actually," Mrs. Jones said, "we were hoping you could help us have a child with achondroplasia. We wouldn’t know how to raise or understand a child who wasn’t like us."

Dr. West paused, realizing he had made an assumption. He had never been asked to use preimplantation genetic diagnosis to specifically select embryos that would develop into children whom many might view as "impaired." While the procedure itself was safe, Dr. West felt unsettled by the request, unsure how to proceed.

ethical_issues.question: In the application of reproductive technologies, does the physician have an obligation to avoid or prevent the implantation of embryos that may result in disability, thereby adhering to the principle of nonmaleficence?
keypoints: Physicians should respect and uphold the principles of reproductive autonomy and equity when utilizing reproductive technologies, and should not refuse to assist couples in their reproductive choices solely because the embryo carries a genetic disability.

The principle of nonmaleficence requires physicians to avoid causing direct harm; however, selecting an embryo carrying the FGFR3 gene mutation for achondroplasia does not constitute a direct harmful act by the physician.

A strict adherence to harm prevention may result in excessive restrictions on reproductive autonomy and therefore should not serve as a sufficient justification to refuse the implantation of an affected embryo.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians use preimplantation genetic diagnosis to select embryos carrying the gene mutation for achondroplasia in order to fulfill the reproductive wishes of the couple?
keypoints: The main arguments against selecting embryos with achondroplasia through reproductive technology are based on the principles of reproductive nonmaleficence and procreative beneficence; however, the restrictions these principles impose on reproductive freedom are insufficient to justify refusing to fulfill the couple’s wishes.

The physician’s selection and implantation of an embryo carrying the FGFR3 gene mutation for achondroplasia does not constitute a direct act of harm by the physician; any harm experienced by the future individual arises from the abnormal gene itself, not from the physician’s actions.
The principle of procreative beneficence is insufficient to restrict the physician from respecting the couple’s reproductive wishes in this case.

In order to respect reproductive autonomy and equity, individuals with genetic disabilities should have the same reproductive choices as others, and physicians should not refuse to assist couples in achieving their reproductive choices solely because the embryo carries a genetic disorder.

title: Susto: Acknowledging Patients' Beliefs about Illness
case:
Junior is admitted for treatment for presumed Guillain-Barre syndrome. On discussing the history of the 15-year-old boy's illness with the doctor, his mother volunteers her opinion that the illness resulted from a "susto"—a common folkloric concept among some Latino communities, where illness is thought to be provoked by psychological trauma. When asked what the inciting episode may have been, Junior's mother replies, "We don't want to talk about it."
"Is that right, Junior?" asks the physician.
"Yeah, it's fine."
The physician, Dr. Bernard, has to finish rounds but makes a note to herself to revisit the issue with Junior.
Dr. Bernard finds Junior alone the next day during her afternoon rounds and talks to him some more. They establish rapport, and he tells her that he is interested in science and wants to be a physician himself one day. Dr. Bernard decides now is a good time to ask the patient once more what might have caused the "susto."
"It was just something my father said."
"What did he say?"
"I don't want to talk about it."
Dr. Bernard, trained to search for underlying problems, is concerned that the boy may have been a victim of emotional abuse. At the same time, she has witnessed the interaction between the boy and his father, and also between both parents, and does not otherwise have any other reason to suspect abuse. Junior then asks, "Do you think he could have made me sick like my mom says?"
case_rewrite:
Junior, a 15-year-old boy, is admitted for treatment of presumed Guillain-Barre syndrome. During the initial conversation about his illness, Junior’s mother shares her belief that his condition was brought on by a “susto”—a concept rooted in some Latino communities where illness is thought to result from a significant psychological shock or fright. Dr. Bernard, the attending physician, gently asks what specific incident might have caused the “susto.” Junior’s mother quietly responds, “We don’t want to talk about it.”

Dr. Bernard then turns to Junior. “Is that right, Junior?”

Junior nods, “Yeah, it’s fine.”

Although Dr. Bernard is required to continue her rounds, she makes a mental note to revisit this topic with Junior later.

The following afternoon, Dr. Bernard finds Junior alone during her rounds. Seizing the opportunity for a more private conversation, she sits down with him and they chat. As they talk, Junior opens up about his interests, mentioning that he likes science and dreams of becoming a doctor someday. Sensing a rapport, Dr. Bernard decides it may be a good moment to gently approach the topic again.

She asks, “Do you have any idea what might have caused the ‘susto’ your mom mentioned?”

Junior looks away. “It was just something my father said.”

Dr. Bernard probes carefully, “What did he say?”

Junior hesitates, then says, “I don’t want to talk about it.”

Dr. Bernard, alert to the possibility of underlying problems, becomes concerned about potential emotional abuse. Still, she recalls having observed interactions between Junior and his father, as well as between both parents, and has not noticed any overt signs of abuse or distress beyond what has already been disclosed.

Junior then looks up and asks, “Do you think he could have made me sick, like my mom says?”

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians effectively communicate and negotiate with patients and their families regarding cultural beliefs they do not personally endorse, in order to optimize clinical interactions?
keypoints: Understanding and acknowledging the profound impact of culture on patients’ health beliefs, practices, and behaviors is fundamental to effective communication with patients and families from diverse cultural backgrounds.

Developing cultural awareness involves proactively learning about the commonly held beliefs, practices, and values of the population served, in order to more accurately comprehend the cultural context of the patient and their family.

Assessing whether the patient’s family subscribes to a particular cultural belief system and clarifying the specific circumstances under which these beliefs apply facilitates targeted and meaningful communication.

During negotiation, physicians are not obligated to endorse the patient family’s belief system but should seek compromise solutions—such as inquiring about the family’s treatment preferences—to minimize cultural conflicts that may adversely affect the child, thereby promoting constructive dialogue and optimizing the clinical encounter.

ethical_issues.question: In a multicultural context, how can physicians identify and address potential emotional abuse while respecting the cultural beliefs and values of the patient’s family?
keypoints: Physicians should understand and respect the profound impact of culture on patients’ health beliefs, practices, and behaviors.
Physicians should assess whether the patient’s family adheres to a particular cultural belief system and verify this within the specific clinical context.

Physicians should create opportunities for private conversations, especially with adolescent patients, to gain deeper insight into their relationships with parents, particularly with family members who may be involved in problematic dynamics.
After excluding cultural factors, if concerns about potential abuse persist, physicians should address these issues directly with the patient and their family.

Physicians should seek compromise through negotiation to facilitate constructive dialogue and optimize the clinical encounter, particularly when cultural conflicts may have significant implications for the child’s health.

ethical_issues.question: In a cross-cultural medical setting, how can physicians balance direct communication with cultural sensitivity within limited consultation time to prevent patients and their families from feeling alienated or withholding critical information?
keypoints: Physicians should understand and respect the profound influence of culture on patients’ and their families’ health beliefs, behaviors, and communication preferences, emphasizing the establishment of personalized relationships to enhance trust and facilitate effective communication within cross-cultural clinical settings.

Employing the "awareness-assessment-negotiation" model of cultural competence assists physicians in balancing direct communication with cultural sensitivity within limited consultation time, thereby preventing patient and family alienation or the withholding of critical information.

During the assessment phase, physicians should proactively inquire about and confirm the specific cultural beliefs held by the patient’s family and the contexts in which these beliefs apply, avoiding stereotyping and ensuring communication that is both targeted and respectful.

In the negotiation phase, although physicians are not obligated to endorse the cultural beliefs of patients and their families, they should seek compromise solutions that acknowledge the impact of cultural factors on patient health and treatment adherence, thereby promoting effective clinical care.

title: Western Medicine's Diagnostic Labels Are Not Universal
case:
Mr. Phal had a history of intermittent sharp neck pains and dizziness and was seeing his internist, Dr. Lang, for persistent abdominal pain. After a thorough work-up, including several visits, extensive laboratory analyses, and a negative abdominal CT, no explanation for the pain could be found. Dr. Lang therefore referred Mr. Phal to a psychiatrist in her group to screen him for somatization disorder, depression, or other psychiatric illness that might underlie his symptoms. Mr. Phal was Cambodian and 55 years old. He was resistant to seeing a psychiatrist because he believed that taking pills to feel better was an American practice. But because the work-up had revealed nothing so far, he decided he would try this too.
The psychiatrist, Dr. Hanson, greeted Mr. Phal and learned that he was employed as a store manager and that he enjoyed his work. Mr. Phal was widowed and had two grown children. He did not seem depressed to the psychiatrist. He stated that he did occasionally have bad dreams, but they were not frequent. When asked the question, "Have you ever had a panic attack, when you suddenly felt frightened or anxious or suddenly developed a lot of physical symptoms?" Mr. Phal replied, "No." Nonetheless, Dr. Hanson was worried because he was familiar with this patient population and realized that most adult Cambodians residing in the U.S. had suffered some form of trauma during the period of upheaval and genocide of the 1970s. He probed further and learned that the neck pains reminded Mr. Phal of pains he had had while he was in a labor camp. On the basis of this interview and other assessment tools, Dr. Hanson diagnosed Mr. Phal with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and explained to Dr. Lang in a letter that Mr. Phal's somatic complaints were most likely a manifestation of this diagnosis. Dr. Hanson recommended cognitive behavioral therapy in addition to treatment with an antidepressant (an SSRI, or selective seratonin reuptake inhibitor) for management of Mr. Phal's symptoms.
Dr. Lang was conflicted. She had thought the referral would result in a diagnosis of "somatization disorder," which she would use mainly for documentation purposes. She was not sure she agreed with Dr. Hanson's diagnosis, particularly given the lack of classic symptoms and therefore did not fully agree with the psychiatrist's management plan. At the same time, she had no alternatives and so she was willing to transfer management to the psychiatrist. Nevertheless she thought that Mr. Phal would probably resist medication for a psychiatric condition and did not think that talking would do him much good. The internist wondered how she might best care for Mr. Phal.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Phal, a 55-year-old Cambodian man, had been experiencing intermittent sharp neck pains and persistent abdominal discomfort that brought him repeatedly to his internist, Dr. Lang. Despite multiple appointments, comprehensive laboratory work, and a normal abdominal CT scan, Dr. Lang could not identify a physical cause for his symptoms. With no clear explanation after extensive evaluation, Dr. Lang decided to refer Mr. Phal to a psychiatrist within her practice group to assess for somatization disorder, depression, or another psychiatric condition that might account for his complaints.

Mr. Phal was initially hesitant about this referral. He explained to Dr. Lang that, in his view, taking medication to feel better was a distinctly American approach, not one that resonated with him culturally. Still, with no answers from his medical work-up, he reluctantly agreed to try the psychiatric consultation.

When Mr. Phal met with Dr. Hanson, the psychiatrist, Dr. Hanson welcomed him and asked about his life. Mr. Phal shared that he worked as a store manager, a role he found satisfying. He mentioned that he was widowed and had two adult children. During their conversation, Dr. Hanson did not observe signs of depression. Mr. Phal admitted to occasional bad dreams, but he did not consider them significant. When Dr. Hanson asked, “Have you ever had a panic attack—suddenly felt frightened, anxious, or experienced sudden physical symptoms?” Mr. Phal replied, “No.”

However, Dr. Hanson, familiar with the experiences of Cambodian immigrants in the United States, was aware that many had endured profound trauma during the upheaval and genocide of the 1970s. Sensing that there might be more beneath the surface, Dr. Hanson gently probed further. He discovered that Mr. Phal’s neck pain reminded him of similar pain he had suffered while in a labor camp years ago. With this context and the support of other assessment tools, Dr. Hanson diagnosed Mr. Phal with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). He wrote to Dr. Lang, explaining that Mr. Phal’s physical symptoms likely stemmed from this trauma. Dr. Hanson recommended a combination of cognitive behavioral therapy and an antidepressant, specifically a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), to help address Mr. Phal’s symptoms.

Dr. Lang found herself conflicted. She had expected the referral to confirm a somatization disorder, which she primarily saw as helpful for documentation. She was uncertain about Dr. Hanson’s PTSD diagnosis, especially given the absence of classic symptoms, and was not fully convinced by the proposed management plan. At the same time, lacking other options, she was prepared to let the psychiatrist take over Mr. Phal’s care. Still, Dr. Lang doubted that Mr. Phal would be open to psychiatric medication and wondered if talk therapy would truly benefit him. She questioned how she could best support Mr. Phal going forward.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians effectively communicate and understand patients' conditions and treatment preferences in a cross-cultural context?
keypoints: Physicians should engage in mindful practice by attending to their own physical and mental processes in a nonjudgmental manner, focusing attentively on patients’ distress, recognizing their own biases and errors, continuously refining their professional skills, integrating evidence-based medicine into clinical decision-making, and clarifying how their personal values influence diagnosis and treatment.

Physicians should adopt a stance of cultural humility by relinquishing the role of “expert on the patient” and instead becoming the “student of the patient,” respecting the patient’s cultural background and individual experiences, and establishing an equitable and trusting therapeutic alliance.

Physicians should provide patient-centered care that respects and responds to the individual patient’s preferences, needs, and values, ensuring that these values guide all clinical decisions; this can be achieved by eliciting the patient’s perspectives on diagnosis and treatment, and by involving significant family members in communication and decision-making processes.

tags: Decision making/Patient and family centered care
title: Who Decides, Patient or Family?
case:
Mrs. Odundo was admitted to a Los Angeles medical center after several weeks of dysphagia. She was accompanied by her husband who provided the history of her illness. Originally from East Africa, Mrs. Odundo spoke no English, and no speakers of her particular dialect were available at the hospital.
"For the last few weeks, she hasn't been able to swallow anything," her husband said. "First, it was solid food, now liquids too." The treating physician, Dr. Martinez, was concerned about esophageal cancer, and, indeed, an endoscopy performed the following day revealed a mass which was probably an advanced carcinoma. Treatment options were limited, and surgery was unlikely to be curative.
While awaiting further characterization of the mass, Mr. Odundo told Dr. Martinez, "We've talked about this, and she wants everything possible to be done. She's 55; that's too young to let her go."
"You both understand that there's only a small chance we can actually remove the entire mass and offer anything close to a cure."
"We understand that."
Mrs. Odundo's husband repeated the statement—on many occasions, to many doctors —that his wife would want to exhaust all treatment options, including surgery, even if there were only a minimal chance for improvement or cure.
Several days after Mrs. Odundo's hospitalization, her children spent some time alone with their mother, after which they spoke with Dr. Martinez.
