"Our mother is telling us that she doesn't want any surgery." They also stated their fear that she was acquiescing to her husband's wishes. Dr. Martinez realized at this point that he had never heard directly from the patient what she would like to have done, nor was he certain about the extent of her understanding of her own disease, so he arranged to have an interpreter called in. Through the interpreter, Mrs. Odundo stated that she did not wish to have this discussion alone but wanted her husband and children to be present. During the discussion, she stated that she understood that surgery was unlikely to be curative but that she wished to proceed regardless. The children objected that these were her husband's wishes and not her own—saying that this was not what she had told them—but Mrs. Odundo insisted that she wished to have the surgery.
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Odundo was admitted to a Los Angeles medical center after experiencing several weeks of difficulty swallowing. Her husband accompanied her, providing the history of her illness. Originally from East Africa, Mrs. Odundo did not speak any English, and the hospital did not have access to anyone fluent in her specific dialect.

“For the past few weeks, she hasn’t been able to swallow anything,” her husband explained. “It started with solid foods, and now she can’t even manage liquids.” Dr. Martinez, the attending physician, became concerned about the possibility of esophageal cancer. An endoscopy performed the next day revealed a mass highly suggestive of advanced carcinoma. The available treatment options were limited, and surgery was unlikely to offer a cure.

While awaiting further diagnostic information, Mr. Odundo spoke with Dr. Martinez. “We have discussed this, and she wants everything possible to be done. She’s only 55; it’s too soon to give up on her.”

“You both understand there’s only a small chance we could actually remove the whole mass and achieve anything close to a cure?” Dr. Martinez clarified.

“Yes, we understand,” Mr. Odundo replied.

Over subsequent days, Mr. Odundo reiterated to multiple doctors that his wife wished to pursue every possible treatment, including surgery, regardless of how slim the chances of improvement or cure might be.

A few days into Mrs. Odundo’s hospitalization, her children spent some time alone with her. Afterwards, they approached Dr. Martinez, expressing concern: “Our mother is telling us she doesn’t want any surgery.” They added that they feared she might simply be complying with their father’s wishes. Dr. Martinez realized that he had yet to hear directly from Mrs. Odundo regarding her own preferences, nor was he certain how much she understood about her condition. He arranged for a professional interpreter to be brought in.

With the interpreter present, Mrs. Odundo requested that her husband and children join her for the discussion. During this conversation, she confirmed that she understood surgery was unlikely to cure her, but expressed her desire to proceed nonetheless. Her children objected, insisting that these were actually their father’s wishes, not her own, and that she had told them something different in private. Despite their objections, Mrs. Odundo maintained that she wanted to have the surgery.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of language barriers, how can it be ensured that the patient fully understands the diagnosis and treatment options and provides valid informed consent?
keypoints: In the context of language barriers, ensuring patient comprehension of diagnosis and treatment plans requires the provision of professional interpreter services, particularly at critical points in care such as disclosure of diagnosis, discussion of treatment options, and prognosis communication.

Physicians should use short sentences and pause frequently to facilitate accurate interpretation, while also employing techniques such as restating the patient’s statements, clarifying contradictory information, and attending carefully to nonverbal cues to ensure effective communication and accurate understanding.

Healthcare providers must deliver complete and truthful information to patients, including diagnostic results, prognosis, and the risks and benefits of treatment options, in order to meet legal requirements and obtain valid informed consent.

Physicians should anticipate and negotiate cultural differences, recognizing that in certain cultural contexts, patients may exercise autonomy by deferring decision-making to family members rather than adhering strictly to the Western model of individual autonomy.

When language and cultural barriers exist, medical staff should actively facilitate the joint participation of patients and their families, respect the patient’s authentic wishes, and avoid reliance solely on family members’ accounts that may lead to misunderstandings or neglect of the patient’s rights.

ethical_issues.question: In situations where cultural differences influence decision-making, how should physicians reconcile conflicts between patient autonomy and collective family decision-making?
keypoints: Physicians must recognize that while American medical practice places a high value on patient autonomy, it is equally important to respect the significance of family-centered decision making in different cultures, avoiding the imposition of Western values as the sole standard for interpreting patients’ expressions of their wishes.

When there are conflicting accounts from family members regarding the patient’s wishes, physicians should communicate directly with the patient to ensure full understanding of the illness and treatment options, prioritizing the patient’s authentic preferences.

Physicians should arrange for professional interpreters to facilitate discussions involving both the patient and family members, and may consider privately consulting the children about East African cultural norms and the nature of their parents’ relationship to gain deeper insight into the cultural and emotional factors underlying the decision-making process.

It should be understood that a patient’s “deference to family wishes” may represent an exercise of autonomy; in the absence of indications of abuse, coercion, or undue influence, and where such delegation aligns with the patient’s cultural practices or relational dynamics, their choice ought to be respected.

If concerns or potential risks arise, major treatment decisions should be deferred until the patient’s wishes are clearly established and it is confirmed that the decision-making process has not been compromised by improper influence.

title: Competing for the Physician's Attention after Hours
case:
Dr. Leigh wanted to go home. He exited the elevator and walked toward the parking garage. It was 6:00 p.m., and Dr. Leigh, an internist, had just finished making his afternoon rounds at a community teaching hospital. It had taken longer than expected. Two of his patients had had family members in the room when he entered, and had each asked several questions. Dr. Leigh had told his wife that he would be home by 5:30, and he was worried that she would be angry with him because she was frustrated the last time this happened—yesterday. He was fishing for his car keys when his pager went off.
The message said that Mr. Thompson, the husband of a patient Dr. Leigh had seen that afternoon had just arrived at the hospital. Dr. Leigh called the charge nurse, who reported that Mr. Thompson was sorry that he had not been present when Dr. Leigh rounded—he had gone to the cafeteria to pick up dinner. Now he "anxiously" wanted an update on his wife's status and the plan for her care.
Just before he left for the day Dr. Leigh had checked out his patients to the doctor on night float, a second-year resident whom he trusted. He knew that the resident was capable of managing any acute events, but he could not deny that, as the primary physician, he was the person who could best explain Mrs. Thompson's status and treatment plan to her husband. He also knew that, were he in Mr. Thompson's position, he would want to hear about his wife's condition from her doctor.
Nevertheless, Dr. Leigh was frustrated by the request to return to the floor. His contract stated that on non-call weeks, his clinical responsibilities ended when the night float resident arrived at 5:00 p.m. Moreover, these extra calls seemed to be happening more frequently—twice this month he had missed dinner because of them.
As he considered whether or not to return to talk to Mr. Thompson, his cell phone rang. He recognized his home number and was sure that his wife or one of his children wanted to know when he would be home.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Leigh was eager to get home. He stepped out of the elevator and made his way toward the parking garage, the evening sun casting long shadows across the hospital lot. It was already 6:00 p.m.—later than he’d promised. As an internist at the community teaching hospital, his afternoon rounds had run over. Two of his patients had family in the room, each with a string of questions that kept him longer than he’d planned. He’d told his wife he’d be home by 5:30, and he couldn’t help but worry that she’d be upset—especially since he’d been late just the night before. As he fished for his car keys, his pager buzzed insistently at his hip.

The message was about Mr. Thompson, the husband of one of the patients he’d seen earlier that day. Dr. Leigh called the charge nurse, who explained that Mr. Thompson had missed Dr. Leigh during rounds because he’d gone to the cafeteria to pick up dinner. Now, he was back on the floor, “anxiously” requesting an update on his wife’s condition and the plan for her care.

Dr. Leigh had just finished handing off his patients to the night float resident, a capable second-year whom he trusted to manage any urgent issues. Technically, his clinical duties ended at 5:00 p.m. on non-call weeks, per his contract. He knew the resident could handle immediate medical needs, but Dr. Leigh also recognized that, as Mrs. Thompson’s primary physician, he was best positioned to explain her situation and treatment plan to her husband. He thought about how, if he were in Mr. Thompson’s shoes, he’d want clear answers directly from the doctor in charge.

Still, Dr. Leigh felt exasperated at the prospect of returning to the ward. Lately, these after-hours requests seemed to be coming more often—twice this month, he’d missed dinner at home for similar reasons. As he weighed whether to go back upstairs to speak with Mr. Thompson, his cell phone rang. The display showed his home number—almost certainly his wife or one of their children, probably checking when he’d be home. The decision pressed in on him: professional obligations on one side, family responsibilities on the other, both demanding his time and presence.

ethical_issues.question: When Dr. Leigh faces the conflict between contractual obligations and patient needs, should he prioritize the patient’s care requirements over the terms of his contract?
keypoints: The central objective of medical care is to ensure that the patient receives appropriate and adequate care, rather than merely fulfilling contractual obligations.
Contractual provisions define only the minimum standards of economic and legal conduct; a physician’s professional responsibilities extend far beyond what is stipulated in the contract.
Refusal to communicate with a patient’s family members cannot be justified by citing contractual terms, as such reasoning is unpersuasive to the patient, their family, and the healthcare team.
Physicians should base their actions on trust and empathy, reflecting on how they would want a colleague to treat their own relatives in a similar situation.
The fiduciary duties of the physician—rooted in trust and empathy—supersede any contractual excuse for disengagement.

ethical_issues.question: When Dr. Leigh must choose between his familial responsibilities and professional duties, how can he balance these conflicting demands to ensure that the patient and her family receive appropriate and adequate care?
keypoints: Dr. Leigh should prioritize ensuring that the patient receives appropriate care, upholding trust and empathy, and considering how he would wish to be treated if he were in the family member’s position.

Dr. Leigh may adopt various short-term contingency measures: communicate with his wife to explain the situation and negotiate dinner timing; contact Mr. Thompson by phone to explain the current status, address urgent questions, and arrange a follow-up discussion; and request that the trusted night float resident visit the patient’s room that evening to provide an update, thereby meeting the family’s needs and fostering the resident’s professional development.

Dr. Leigh should take a long-term perspective to review and optimize his practice arrangements, exploring systemic solutions such as coordinating meeting times with patients’ families and reasonably allocating work responsibilities to reduce the frequency of extra calls and conflicts.

Dr. Leigh needs to balance his professional and familial responsibilities, recognizing his dual roles as both physician and individual, and strive to achieve a harmonious integration of work and personal life that promotes both mental and physical well-being as well as sustainable professional development.

title: Avoiding Disincentives to Treat in Designing Pay-for-Performance Measures
case:
Mr. Hill arrived in the emergency department (ED) dehydrated and disoriented. He had a history of type II diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and poorly controlled hypertension, and when he came to the ED his blood glucose measured 750. After receiving normal saline and insulin intravenously, Mr. Hill was admitted to the internal medicine floor where he was stabilized and kept overnight for monitoring. The next day, the internist who admitted Mr. Hill requested a consultation from the hospital's endocrinologist, Dr. Vernon.
Dr. Vernon learned from Mr. Hill's chart that his primary care physician had prescribed a reasonable medication regimen, although a few of the medicines were outdated and considered second-line. He also learned that Mr. Hill had a history of noncompliance, frequently missed appointments, and had come to the ED with hyperglycemia three times that year. His HbA1c was elevated at 9.5 percent. As he read the chart, Dr. Vernon could not help but think that Mr. Hill would be a difficult patient to manage and that, based on past behavior, he was not likely to do what was necessary to bring his glucose, cholesterol, and blood pressure under control. Dr. Vernon also knew that, under the hospital's new pay-for-performance system, he was expected to have two-thirds of his diabetic patients at or below an HbA1c of 8 percent and that he could be penalized if he did not meet this goal.
Dr. Vernon explained to Mr. Hill that he was going to prescribe different medications to control his diabetes and that he would write a letter to his primary care physician explaining the reasoning behind the changes. "If you have any problems in the future, you can call or have your doctor call, and I'll be happy to see you in the clinic," Dr. Vernon said.
Four months later Mr. Hill went to the ED again with severe hyperglycemia and was again admitted to the medicine floor, where Dr. Vernon was again asked to see him. When Dr. Vernon reached the floor, the internist was hostile. "This is the fifth time he's come in this year. His primary doctor clearly doesn't know how to handle this problem. You are anendocrinologist. Why didn't you schedule an appointment to see him in clinic?"
case_rewrite:
Mr. Hill presented to the emergency department (ED) in a state of dehydration and confusion. His medical history included type II diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and poorly controlled hypertension. On arrival, his blood glucose level was found to be 750. After receiving intravenous normal saline and insulin, Mr. Hill was admitted to the internal medicine floor, where his condition stabilized, and he was kept overnight for observation. The following day, the internist overseeing Mr. Hill’s care requested an endocrinology consult from Dr. Vernon.

Reviewing Mr. Hill's medical chart, Dr. Vernon noted that the patient’s primary care physician had prescribed a generally reasonable medication regimen, though some prescriptions were outdated and considered second-line by current standards. Dr. Vernon also observed that Mr. Hill had a documented history of nonadherence to his treatment plan, missed appointments frequently, and had already been treated in the ED for hyperglycemia three times earlier that year. His HbA1c was markedly elevated at 9.5 percent. As Dr. Vernon absorbed these details, he couldn’t help but anticipate significant challenges in managing Mr. Hill’s care, given his history. Complicating matters, the hospital’s recently adopted pay-for-performance system now required Dr. Vernon to have at least two-thirds of his diabetic patients at or below an HbA1c of 8 percent, with penalties imposed for failing to meet this benchmark.

In his discussion with Mr. Hill, Dr. Vernon explained that he would be prescribing new medications to improve diabetes control and that he would send a detailed letter to Mr. Hill’s primary care physician outlining the rationale for these changes. “If you have any issues in the future, you or your doctor can reach out to me, and I’ll be happy to see you in my clinic,” Dr. Vernon assured him.

Four months later, Mr. Hill returned to the ED with another episode of severe hyperglycemia and was again admitted to the internal medicine floor. Dr. Vernon was once again consulted. When Dr. Vernon arrived, he was met by the internist, who was visibly frustrated. “This is the fifth time he’s been admitted this year. His primary care doctor obviously isn’t managing his diabetes effectively. You’re the endocrinologist—why didn’t you schedule him for a clinic follow-up?”

ethical_issues.question: Does the pay-for-performance system lead physicians to avoid treating severely ill and non-adherent patients, thereby affecting the quality of care?
keypoints: Pay-for-performance systems may incentivize physicians to avoid treating severely ill and non-adherent patients because these programs focus on outcome measures without adequately accounting for individual patient differences, making it difficult for clinicians to meet targets with challenging cases.

Such systems can lead to a range of unintended negative consequences, including excessive focus on target metrics, up-coding of patient severity, and suppression of intrinsic motivation, all of which may adversely affect the quality of care.

Although pay-for-performance programs have notable adverse effects, their overall value should not be dismissed. Payers must carefully weigh the benefits and drawbacks, establish appropriate targets, and incorporate risk adjustment mechanisms to ensure fairness and effectively mitigate risks such as patient dumping.

ethical_issues.question: Can pay-for-performance systems ensure a net benefit to patients while minimizing physicians’ incentives to avoid difficult cases?
keypoints: The impact of pay-for-performance systems on patients’ net benefit remains uncertain and may lead physicians to focus excessively on meeting performance targets while neglecting individual patient differences and personalized treatment needs.

Pay-for-performance incentives may provoke physician behaviors that involve avoiding difficult-to-treat patients, thereby exacerbating inequities in healthcare resource allocation and increasing the complexity of patient management.

Optimizing incentive design should incorporate continuous reward functions or link payments to improvements relative to patients’ baseline indicators, in order to reduce physicians’ motivation to avoid challenging cases and to promote overall enhancement of treatment outcomes.

The specific design and implementation details of pay-for-performance programs determine their positive and negative effects; payers must carefully plan, dynamically adjust, and continuously monitor these programs to maximize patient benefit and minimize adverse consequences.

title: Sex Selection for Nonmedical Reasons
case:
Dr. Harris has been helping couples have children with the use of assisted reproductive technology (ART) for over 20 years. A reproductive endocrinologist, he got involved in the practice when it was new and extremely controversial and has had a rewarding career helping infertile couples. ART includes in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer, gamete intrafallopian transfer, zygote intrafallopian transfer, tubal embryo transfer, and frozen embryo transfer. These procedures help couples when less complex and less expensive methods of treatment have failed. Recently, Dr. Harris has been disturbed by trends at fertility clinics, including the one at which he works, to provide reproductive services based on patient demands and ability to pay rather than on medical need.
Recently, for example, Mr. and Mrs. Taylor, a couple in their late 20s, came to see Dr. Harris. Neither husband nor wife had any suspected fertility problems but they had decided they wanted only one child, and both really wanted a girl. Initially interested in preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) followed by selective implantation (of female embryos), the Taylors had read a newspaper article about sperm sorting and sought more information about this technique. Although sperm sorting was not available at the clinic, Dr. Harris was conflicted—not only regarding how to counsel this couple, but about whether or not he could in good conscience continue to provide ART to couples for reasons he viewed as nonmedical.
case_rewrite:
For more than two decades, Dr. Harris has devoted his career to helping couples conceive through assisted reproductive technology (ART). As a reproductive endocrinologist, he entered the field when ART was still new and its use widely debated. Over the years, he has found deep fulfillment in aiding couples who struggled with infertility, offering techniques such as in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer, gamete intrafallopian transfer, zygote intrafallopian transfer, tubal embryo transfer, and frozen embryo transfer—procedures typically reserved for those who have exhausted simpler and less costly options.

Lately, however, Dr. Harris has grown uneasy about the direction fertility clinics—including his own—seem to be heading. Increasingly, reproductive services are being offered based on a patient’s preferences and ability to pay, rather than strict medical necessity. This trend troubles Dr. Harris, who feels it challenges the professional values at the heart of his practice.

A recent case has brought these concerns into sharp focus. Mr. and Mrs. Taylor, a married couple in their late twenties, scheduled a consultation with Dr. Harris. Unlike most of his patients, the Taylors did not present any signs of infertility. Instead, they had made a personal decision to have just one child, and both were determined that the child should be a girl. Initially, they expressed interest in preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD), hoping to select and implant only female embryos. After reading a newspaper article about sperm sorting as another method to influence a baby’s sex, they asked Dr. Harris for more details about this technique.

Dr. Harris explained that sperm sorting was not offered at his clinic, but he found himself deeply conflicted—not only about how to counsel the Taylors, but about his own role in providing ART for reasons that were not medically indicated. He questioned whether it was ethical to fulfill such requests, especially given the lack of medical justification and the potential broader consequences. Dr. Harris also felt a responsibility to clarify for couples like the Taylors that there is currently no conclusive evidence about the safety of sex selection technologies, nor about their long-term psychosocial impact on children or families.

As he considered how to respond, Dr. Harris grappled with the tension between patient autonomy and the preservation of professional integrity, wondering whether he could, in good conscience, continue to provide ART services when they were requested solely on the basis of patient preference rather than genuine medical need.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians provide assisted reproductive technology services for sex selection for nonmedical reasons?
keypoints: Major medical ethics organizations, such as ACOG, ASRM, FIGO, and HFEA, generally oppose sex selection for nonmedical reasons due to concerns that it may promote gender discrimination and reinforce societal devaluation of women.

Physicians’ professional integrity requires avoiding disproportionate risks of harm unless balanced by corresponding medical benefits; since sex selection technologies carry potential medical risks without legitimate medical indications, their justification is problematic.

The core of medical ethics lies in preserving professional integrity and must not be reduced to the ethics of marketplace transactions; physicians should avoid transforming medical services into purely consumer-driven practices.
Physicians have the professional right to reasonably refuse to provide sex selection services for nonmedical reasons based on considerations of professional integrity.

Physicians should clearly inform patients that there is currently a lack of controlled trials evaluating the safety of sex selection technologies and that no studies have confirmed the long-term psychosocial effects of sex selection on children and their families.

title: Cosmetic Surgery: When Fifty Doesn't Feel Fabulous
case:
Ms. Wagner has been a patient of Dr. Holmes, a general practitioner, for over 15 years. Ms. Wagner is 51 years old and recently became a partner at a prominent law firm. She is in generally good health but takes prescription medication for mild hypertension and seasonal allergies, so she comes in every few months. Approximately five years ago, after the death of Ms. Wagner's mother, Dr. Holmes prescribed antidepressants and recommended counseling because she was having some difficulties at work.
During a recent visit to renew a prescription for her blood pressure medication and request a prescription for a sleeping aid, Ms. Wagner told Dr. Holmes that she had been considering cosmetic surgery. She wanted to "make some improvements" on her eyes, chin and forehead—hoping to appear younger. Due to her recent promotion, Ms. Wagner had more face-to-face contact with clients. She seemed very happy about this promotion and talked about how much she loved her job. She admitted that her new responsibilities had increased the pressure she felt to look good at work. She mentioned that her appearance was discussed during her promotion review but did not elaborate. Ms. Wagner also mentioned that she was becoming increasingly self-conscious about her age. She had taught high school for 15 years and had not entered law school until she was in her late 30s. Due to this somewhat late start on her legal career, she was a bit older than the other lawyers who had recently made partner at her firm. Ms. Wagner, who had always maintained a stable, normal healthy weight, had lost almost 15 pounds since her last visit six months before. When Dr. Holmes asked about dieting methods, Ms. Wagner laughed and said, "I guess I've been so swamped at work, I've been forgetting to eat."
Dr. Holmes asked Ms. Wagner how much research she had done on cosmetic surgery. Ms. Wagner said she had not done any research but had made up her mind about undergoing the procedures. She asked Dr. Holmes to recommend a reputable local cosmetic surgeon. Money was not a problem for her, and she said, "The potential impact a new face will have on my career is worth some temporary pain and swelling." Dr. Holmes personally believed that unnecessary surgery for aesthetic reasons was not worth the medical risks but wanted to give appropriate medical advice.
case_rewrite:
Ms. Wagner has been under the care of Dr. Holmes, a general practitioner, for over 15 years. Now 51, Ms. Wagner recently achieved partnership at a well-known law firm. Her overall health is good, though she takes prescribed medications for mild hypertension and seasonal allergies, requiring regular follow-up visits every few months. About five years earlier, following her mother’s death, Dr. Holmes had prescribed her antidepressants and suggested counseling to help with work-related difficulties.

At a recent appointment to renew her blood pressure medication and to request a prescription for a sleep aid, Ms. Wagner confided to Dr. Holmes that she was thinking about having cosmetic surgery. She explained her wish to "make some improvements" to her eyes, chin, and forehead in hopes of appearing younger. With her recent promotion, Ms. Wagner was now meeting more clients face-to-face and appeared genuinely pleased with her new position, often mentioning how much she enjoyed her work. She acknowledged, however, that the new responsibilities increased the pressure to look her best. Ms. Wagner noted that her appearance had come up during her promotion review, though she didn’t provide further details. She also admitted to feeling more self-conscious about her age lately. Having spent 15 years teaching high school before attending law school in her late 30s, Ms. Wagner was somewhat older than most new partners at her firm.

Dr. Holmes noticed that Ms. Wagner, who had always maintained a healthy and stable weight, had lost almost 15 pounds since her last visit six months prior. When he inquired about her eating habits, Ms. Wagner chuckled and replied, “I guess I’ve been so busy at work, I just forget to eat.”

Dr. Holmes asked how much research Ms. Wagner had done regarding cosmetic surgery. She admitted that she had not researched the procedures, but stated that her mind was made up. She then asked Dr. Holmes to recommend a reputable local cosmetic surgeon. Money, she said, was not a concern; she believed, “The potential impact a new face will have on my career is worth some temporary pain and swelling.” Dr. Holmes, personally skeptical about undergoing surgery solely for aesthetic reasons due to the associated medical risks, nonetheless wanted to ensure Ms. Wagner received appropriate and unbiased medical advice.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient requests cosmetic surgery, should the physician recommend a plastic surgeon and provide information about the risks and benefits of the procedure?
keypoints: Physicians should comprehensively disclose the risks, benefits, and alternative options of cosmetic surgery during the informed consent process to ensure that patients receive sufficient information for autonomous decision-making.
Physicians ought to transcend personal value judgments and objectively present all medical options, thereby upholding professional integrity and prioritizing patient interests.

When recommending board-certified plastic surgeons, physicians should explicitly clarify the differences in qualifications and potential risks, assisting patients in distinguishing between legitimate professional services and non-specialized cosmetic providers, thus preventing medical safety hazards arising from inadequate information.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians allow their personal beliefs to influence their professional judgment and refuse to provide certain treatment information or prescribe medications when offering medical advice?
keypoints: A physician’s personal beliefs should not influence professional judgment; the needs of the patient must be placed above those of the physician.
Physicians have an obligation to present a comprehensive range of options during the informed consent process, including treatment plans they may personally disagree with.
Physicians should, based on their professional expertise, candidly communicate the risks and benefits of all available options to ensure the patient’s autonomous decision-making.

While physicians may express their personal opinions when providing a list of board-certified plastic surgeons, they must not refuse to supply relevant information or to issue appropriate prescriptions.

title: Negotiating Parental Requests for Medication
case:
Mr. and Mrs. Green took their 11-year-old son, to see Dr. Frank, a pediatrician. This was the first time Dr. Frank had seen the boy, who was in the sixth grade and had played piano since he was five. He loved music and showed exceptional promise. Within the preceding month, however, he had been struggling with piano lessons and practice. The boy told Dr. Frank that piano was very important to him and that he really wanted to be accepted into a special school for the performing arts. His audition for the school was to take place in six months. But he had been having trouble concentrating and therefore had been practicing less. His parents said that "until now," the boy had never exhibited any behavioral or emotional problems at home or at school. Mr. and Mrs. Green wondered whether he had attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and whether medication could help their son with his concentration, at least until after his audition.
Dr. Frank asked the Greens if their son had been evaluated by a school psychologist. They replied that he attended a small private school with no psychologist on staff. To determine whether he met the criteria for a diagnosis of ADHD, Dr. Frank asked the Greens about symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity. The Greens said that, in addition to trouble with piano practice, his math teacher had contacted them regarding his forgetfulness, distractibility and daydreaming in class. Their son had always done well in math, but now he was struggling to keep a C. They stressed several times that their son's piano teacher was especially concerned about his recent distractibility.
Dr. Frank asked the Greens about the boy's mood, and they admitted that he had become somewhat withdrawn. Every day he sat down at the piano after finishing his after-school snack. Mrs. Green had noticed that he played for a few minutes and then stopped, and she would find him staring off into space, still sitting at the piano, 15 or 20 minutes later. He exhibited no signs of hyperactivity. The Greens said that there had been no major changes at home and no incidents at school that they were aware of, such as fights with friends or teachers.
During most of the appointment, the boy sat quietly in a chair with his head down. When questioned by Dr. Frank about his mood and concentration, he responded mostly with "yes" and "no" answers, and a few times he said, "I've just been having trouble concentrating." Dr. Frank did not believe that the boy met the criteria for a diagnosis of ADHD and, because the changes had only occurred in the last month, Dr. Frank was not yet concerned. He recommended some dietary changes, told Mr. and Mrs. Green to monitor their son's sleeping and activity habits, and said that he would like to schedule another appointment in six weeks to see whether the dietary changes had had any effect. Mr. Green got very angry and said, "This is ridiculous! There's clearly something wrong with the kid. Why can't we just get a prescription to try for a few months?"
case_rewrite:
Mr. and Mrs. Green brought their 11-year-old son to see Dr. Frank, a pediatrician, for the first time. Their son, a sixth grader, had a deep passion for music and had played piano since the age of five, demonstrating remarkable talent. However, over the past month, he had begun to struggle with his piano lessons and practice sessions. The boy confided in Dr. Frank that music was extremely important to him and that he aspired to be accepted into a prestigious performing arts school, with an audition scheduled in six months. Recently, though, he found it increasingly difficult to concentrate, leading to less time spent practicing.

The Greens explained that, up until this point, their son had never shown any behavioral or emotional issues either at home or at school. They were concerned that he might have developed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and wondered whether medication could help improve his focus, at least until the audition had passed.

Dr. Frank inquired whether the boy had been assessed by a school psychologist, to which the Greens replied that his small private school did not have one on staff. To evaluate the possibility of ADHD, Dr. Frank asked the Greens about symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. The parents mentioned that, besides his difficulties with piano, his math teacher had reached out to them, noting his increased forgetfulness, distractibility, and tendency to daydream during class. Although their son had always excelled in math, he was now struggling to maintain a C. They repeatedly emphasized that his piano teacher was particularly troubled by his newfound distractibility.

When Dr. Frank asked about his mood, the Greens admitted that their son had become somewhat withdrawn. Each afternoon, after his after-school snack, he would sit at the piano, but after playing for only a few minutes, he would stop, and Mrs. Green would often find him staring blankly into space, still seated at the piano 15 or 20 minutes later. There were no signs of hyperactivity. The Greens stated that there had been no significant changes at home and no incidents at school, such as conflicts with friends or teachers, that they were aware of.

Throughout much of the appointment, the boy sat quietly with his head lowered. When Dr. Frank questioned him about his mood and ability to concentrate, he responded mostly with short "yes" or "no" answers and occasionally said, "I've just been having trouble concentrating." Based on the information gathered, Dr. Frank did not feel the boy met the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis. Since these difficulties had only arisen in the past month, Dr. Frank was not immediately alarmed. He suggested making some dietary adjustments, advised the Greens to monitor their son's sleep and daily activities, and recommended scheduling a follow-up visit in six weeks to assess any changes.

At this, Mr. Green grew visibly frustrated. He exclaimed, "This is ridiculous! There's clearly something wrong with the kid. Why can't we just get a prescription to try for a few months?"

ethical_issues.question: How should a physician make clinical decisions when faced with parental requests for medication?
keypoints: Physicians should base their decisions on a thorough assessment, rationally weighing the potential risks of prescribing stimulants against the possible consequences of inaction.
In the absence of clear diagnostic evidence for ADHD, prescribing stimulants may cause physical and psychological harm to the child due to unnecessary medication exposure.

Premature reliance on pharmacological treatment may obscure or delay a comprehensive evaluation of the child’s actual problems and hinder the implementation of multifaceted, non-pharmacological interventions.
Excessive or inappropriate prescribing of stimulants not only poses risks to individual health but may also contribute to medication misuse and broader public health concerns at the societal level.

Physicians should adhere to the principle of nonmaleficence by engaging patiently with parents, explaining the diagnostic rationale and treatment options, thereby fostering reasonable expectations and shared decision-making.

ethical_issues.question: How can a physician effectively conduct an initial consultation under time constraints to fulfill the principle of beneficence?
keypoints: Physicians should recognize that the requests of patients and their families may carry multiple underlying meanings; through patient communication and educational guidance, they should broaden the family’s understanding of the nature of the condition and the range of possible treatments.

Within the time constraints of an initial consultation, physicians should focus on initiating care in an effective and appropriate manner, including thorough history-taking, obtaining collateral information from teachers or other third parties, engaging in private dialogue with the child, and formulating a plan for follow-up assessment and monitoring.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians broaden parents’ understanding of the nature of the condition and the range of possible treatments when addressing parents’ narrow demands, in order to prevent potential harm?
keypoints: Physicians should be sensitive to the underlying distress signals behind parental requests, recognizing their anxiety and expectations regarding the child’s condition, and, guided by the principle of beneficence, actively investigate the problem and seek appropriate solutions.

Physicians should provide parents with a comprehensive explanation of the differential diagnosis for the symptoms, including attention deficit disorders, depression, generalized anxiety disorder, organic causes such as malnutrition or iron deficiency, as well as the potential impact of social stressors (e.g., pressure related to the piano audition) on the child’s presentation.

Physicians should avoid prescribing medication as the sole or primary intervention, in order to prevent premature pharmacological treatment from overshadowing other potential etiologies and non-pharmacological interventions, thereby ensuring a comprehensive and evidence-based approach to diagnosis and management.

Upon recognizing the parental distress, physicians have a duty to educate and guide the family, assisting them in broadening their understanding of the nature of the condition and the possibilities for multifaceted treatment, reframing the clinical encounter to alleviate the child’s actual suffering and to avoid a narrowly focused therapeutic approach.

title: The Hard Case of Palliative Sedation
case:
Mr. Johnson had been battling cancer for as long as he could remember. At 65 years old, he still remembered the day when he was first told that he had prostate cancer at the age of 45. The past 20 years had been one struggle after another, each with its own twist. Most recently, Mr. Johnson had been diagnosed with metastatic cancer in his lungs, spine and brain. Years of illness had made his body fragile and frail. Even the smallest everyday tasks seemed nearly impossible. Pain seemed not to radiate from any single point but rather to encompass his entire body. The mere act of breathing now seemed an insurmountable task, one that caused excruciating pain and increased his hunger for oxygen. He had tried every analgesic that had been offered and seen palliative specialists from across the country. None had been able to offer him any real relief from his pain. Recently Mr. Johnson confided to Dr. Jackson that he was considering suicide as a way out of his pain, but Mr. Johnson was a religious man and was afraid of the consequences he might face in the afterlife.
Dr. Jackson, an anesthesiologist at St. Luke's, believed he might be able to help. "Mr. Johnson, none of the medications we have tried in the past has been able to alleviate your pain. What I suggest may be quite extreme, but it is most likely the only means that will give you any relief and put your conscience at ease. I believe that by placing you in a chemically induced state of unconsciousness, similar to that of a comatose individual, you will be free from your pain." Mr. Johnson was in so much pain that he was willing to try anything. After much deliberation and reflection, he agreed to the procedure. In Dr. Jackson's judgment, the patient possessed decision-making capacity sufficient to provide informed consent. Prior to undergoing the induction, Dr. Jackson broached the subject of what other care and life-sustaining measures Mr. Johnson wanted taken while he was sedated.
"Several options exist for your care while you are in this state," Dr. Jackson explained. "One of these is the means by which we may provide nutrition and hydration. Since you will be unable to eat normally, we can feed you through a surgically inserted tube. Would that be something that you would want?"
Mr. Johnson thought carefully about this offer. "Am I right in presuming that the last few weeks I have to live will be spent in this unconscious state and that I will not awaken?" Dr. Jackson replied affirmatively. "Then I don't see the point in prolonging the inevitable by having the artificial nutrition and hydration. I'm not going to feel anything, right? Let me go when the time comes."
The next day Mr. Johnson was sedated into unconsciousness. Several days passed, and Mr. Johnson's medical condition began to deteriorate due to dehydration. Eventually Mr. Johnson's body went into multi-organ failure. It was at this point that another member of the staff, concerned with the course of events, informed not only the hospital administration but also the local bishop, claiming that this act was directly contrary to the Catholic mission of St. Luke's Hospital. The local bishop responded promptly to the hospital administration, clearly stating his deep disapproval of recent events and demanding reconsideration of Mr. Johnson's care. The alternative, he claimed, was to institute a review process that could revoke St. Luke's Catholic identity and its ability to claim a religious affiliation. This seemed to the bishop to be a case of assisted suicide, if not out-and-out euthanasia.
Dr. Jackson had become dismayed at these turns of events. Suddenly, many serious thoughts began to bear down on him: the patient's proper care in a situation of true intractable pain, the patient's stated wishes, Dr. Jackson's own faith, the divided sentiment of the staff, and the identity and mission of St. Luke's Hospital. Knowing that events were only going to become more tense tomorrow, Dr. Jackson slept little that night as he considered his options.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Johnson had been living with cancer for as long as he could recall. Now 65, he still remembered the day, two decades ago, when he first learned he had prostate cancer at age 45. Since then, his life had been marked by endless battles—each one bringing new challenges. Most recently, the cancer had spread to his lungs, spine, and brain. Years of relentless illness had left his body weak and wasted; even the simplest activities seemed nearly impossible. The pain he felt was not confined to one area—it seemed to envelop his entire being. Breathing itself was a torment, each breath coming with searing agony and an ever-present struggle for air. He had tried every pain medication available and had consulted palliative care specialists from across the country, but nothing had brought him lasting relief. 

Not long ago, Mr. Johnson confided in Dr. Jackson, his anesthesiologist at St. Luke’s Hospital, that he was contemplating suicide to escape his suffering. Yet Mr. Johnson's strong religious beliefs left him fearful of the spiritual consequences such an act might bring after death.

Dr. Jackson, wanting to help, offered an alternative. “Mr. Johnson, none of the medications we’ve tried have managed to ease your pain. What I’m about to suggest is quite drastic, but it may be your only path to relief and peace of conscience. I can place you into a medically induced unconsciousness, similar to a coma. In that state, you would no longer feel pain.”

Desperate for respite, Mr. Johnson was open to the idea. After thoughtful deliberation and deep reflection, he agreed to the proposed sedation. Dr. Jackson carefully assessed Mr. Johnson’s decision-making capacity and was satisfied that his patient was able to give informed consent.

Before proceeding, Dr. Jackson discussed with Mr. Johnson the details of his care while sedated, including options for sustaining life. “We have several choices for your care while you are unconscious,” he explained. “One important consideration is whether you want us to provide nutrition and hydration through a feeding tube, since you won’t be able to eat or drink on your own. Is this something you would want?”

Mr. Johnson listened and took time to consider. “If I understand correctly, I’ll spend my remaining weeks in this unconscious state and won’t wake up again?” Dr. Jackson confirmed this was so. Mr. Johnson replied, “Then I don’t see any reason to prolong things by using artificial nutrition and hydration. If I won’t be aware of anything, let me go when it’s my time.”

The following day, Dr. Jackson initiated deep sedation, rendering Mr. Johnson unconscious. In the days that followed, Mr. Johnson’s condition worsened, primarily due to dehydration. Eventually, his body succumbed to multi-organ failure.

It was at this point that another staff member raised concerns about the situation, alerting both hospital administration and the local bishop. The staff member argued that what had transpired directly contradicted the Catholic mission of St. Luke’s Hospital. The bishop responded swiftly, expressing his strong disapproval to the administration and demanding a reassessment of Mr. Johnson’s care. He warned that, failing this, the hospital’s Catholic identity could be reevaluated, with the possibility of losing its religious affiliation. To the bishop, this appeared to be a clear case of assisted suicide, if not outright euthanasia.

Dr. Jackson was deeply troubled by these developments. He now found himself weighed down by many heavy considerations: the right way to care for a patient in true, unrelenting pain, honoring the patient’s explicit wishes, his own religious faith, the divided opinions among staff, and the very identity and mission of St. Luke’s Hospital. With tensions rising and difficult decisions looming, Dr. Jackson spent a sleepless night reflecting on the choices ahead.

ethical_issues.question: In religious healthcare institutions, how can controversial practices such as terminal sedation be managed without violating religious beliefs?
keypoints: The principle of double effect is a crucial ethical tool for religious healthcare institutions in addressing controversial practices such as terminal sedation, emphasizing the central role of the agent’s intent in morally evaluating actions.

According to the principle of double effect, it is impermissible to achieve a good outcome by means of causing harm; however, harm that is foreseen but not intended as a side effect of pursuing a good end may be ethically permissible under certain conditions.

Within religious healthcare institutions, if the primary purpose of sedation is to relieve intractable pain, the accompanying potential side effect of hastening death can be ethically acceptable; conversely, sedation aimed at removing the burden of consciousness or intentionally hastening death is not permissible.

Catholic healthcare institutions typically manage sensitive services such as abortion, contraception, and assisted reproduction through structural separation or referral partnerships; however, decisions regarding sedation and withdrawal of artificial nutrition and hydration in palliative care are more ethically and operationally complex due to their close integration with acute medical care.

Clearly delineating the scope of responsibilities for personnel in religious healthcare institutions involved in end-of-life care—balancing patient autonomy, professional judgment, intra-team disagreements, and religious beliefs—remains a significant ongoing challenge for Catholic hospitals.

title: The Question of Uterine Isolation in Catholic Health Care Ethics
case:
"I guess it's about that time again, Mrs. Northern. We should probably head over to pre-op and get this C-section started," Dr. Jones said. "Before we go there are a few things I want to discuss with you. Given the fact that this will be your fifth C-section, during the operation I will be evaluating your uterus for stress and damage. It's common that after repeat C-sections, scarring and potential weaknesses occur and can pose serious risks for future pregnancies. If we did identify any abnormalities, we would have a few options." Dr. Jones and Mrs. Northern spoke at length regarding the alternatives. Given the potential risk for rupture and the danger it would pose for both the mother and fetus if another pregnancy were to occur, Mrs. Northern needed to consider her options carefully.
"So basically if everything is OK through this pregnancy," she said, "I can choose to do nothing, take my chances with having another pregnancy, use some sort of birth control, or not have sex at all. The only other option would be for you to tie my tubes?"
Before Dr. Jones could answer, Mrs. Northern continued, "Honestly, Dr. Jones, I'm not sure what to do. I don't know how I feel about taking hormones for the next 20 years, and condoms and the rhythm method can fail. As a Catholic, I don't believe in abortion, so if I were to get pregnant, I would feel obligated to have the baby. Frankly, my husband and I have been having enough difficulties lately, and I'm not sure how he's going to respond to all of this, especially with the possibility that we would need to abstain from sex."
After much deliberation and discussion with Dr. Jones, Mrs. Northern decided that the only viable option would be to go ahead with the uterine isolation by means of tubal ligation if that were medically indicated. Dr. Jones felt as if he had been placed in a difficult situation, given that the delivery was taking place in a Catholic hospital. According to the ethical and religious directives that governed the hospital's practices, Dr. Jones would not be allowed to perform uterine isolation because it would be a form of direct sterilization. On the other hand, Dr. Jones faced the prospect that, if Mrs. Northern got pregnant again, her uterus could rupture and pose a serious risk to her and her fetus if he did not perform the procedure. Then there were the difficulties that the Northerns would face if nothing was done and they had to restrict their sexual relationship. Dr. Jones hoped for the best as the surgery began, fearing the dilemmas that might ensue should his patient's uterus appear to be less than healthy.
As the surgery progressed and the newborn was delivered successfully, it became clear that Mrs. Northern's uterus had sustained significant stress and another pregnancy would put her at high risk. "Dr. Jones, are you ready to close?" asked the scrub nurse.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Jones glanced at the clock and smiled gently at his patient. “It looks like it’s that time again, Mrs. Northern. Let’s get you over to pre-op so we can begin your C-section,” he said. Before they left, Dr. Jones paused, his tone turning serious. “There’s something important I want to discuss with you first. Since this is your fifth C-section, I’ll be closely evaluating your uterus during the operation for any signs of stress or damage. With multiple C-sections, it’s common for scarring and areas of weakness to develop, which can create significant risks if you were to become pregnant again. If I do notice anything abnormal, there are a few potential courses of action.”

The two spoke at length, exploring the possibilities. Dr. Jones explained the risk of uterine rupture, emphasizing how dangerous another pregnancy could be for both Mrs. Northern and a future baby. He wanted her to understand the gravity of the situation and the options available.

Mrs. Northern listened carefully before responding. “So, if everything looks alright this time,” she summarized, “I could just do nothing and risk another pregnancy, or I could use birth control, or abstain from sex altogether. The only other possibility would be for you to tie my tubes, right?”

Before Dr. Jones could reply, Mrs. Northern continued, her voice tinged with worry. “Honestly, Dr. Jones, I’m not sure what to do. I don’t like the idea of being on hormones for the next couple of decades, and I know condoms and natural methods sometimes fail. As a Catholic, I don’t believe in abortion, so if I were to become pregnant again, I’d feel obligated to carry the baby. To be honest, things have already been hard enough between my husband and me, and I don’t know how he’ll react, especially if we have to consider abstaining from sex.”

After much discussion and reflection, Mrs. Northern concluded that, should her uterus show signs of significant risk during surgery, the only realistic option would be to proceed with tubal ligation for her safety. Dr. Jones, however, found himself in a challenging position: the hospital where Mrs. Northern was delivering was Catholic, and its ethical directives strictly prohibited direct sterilization, including tubal ligation, regardless of medical risk. Dr. Jones was troubled—on one hand, he worried about the life-threatening consequences for Mrs. Northern if she were to become pregnant again; on the other, he was bound by institutional rules that forbade the very intervention that could protect her. He was also mindful of the strain and limitations the Northerns would face in their marriage if no permanent solution was possible.

As the surgery commenced and Dr. Jones successfully delivered Mrs. Northern’s newborn, it became apparent that her uterus had endured considerable damage, and another pregnancy would put her at grave risk. The scrub nurse looked up and asked, “Dr. Jones, are you ready to close?” The weight of the ethical dilemma pressed on him as he considered his next step.

ethical_issues.question: In the case of Mrs. Northern at a Catholic hospital, is it ethically permissible for Dr. Jones to perform a tubal ligation during her C-section to prevent future pregnancy-related health risks, without contravening Catholic health care ethical directives?
keypoints: Catholic moral teaching explicitly forbids direct and intentional sterilization procedures, even when a future pregnancy may pose a life-threatening risk to the patient.

The principle of double effect constitutes the central point of contention in Catholic ethics regarding such procedures: some scholars argue that the primary intention of tubal ligation is to protect the mother’s health, with sterilization as a permissible secondary effect; however, the 1993 document issued by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith unequivocally rejects this view, stating that the direct intention of the procedure remains sterilization and is therefore unacceptable.

The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith’s document emphasizes that the clarity of the agent’s intention is critical in determining ethical legitimacy; since the primary goal of tubal ligation is to prevent pregnancy through direct and intentional sterilization, the procedure is expressly prohibited in Catholic hospitals.

ethical_issues.question: How can the principle of double effect be applied to medical interventions that may result in infertility in order to comply with Catholic ethical standards?
keypoints: The principle of double effect permits medical actions to result in unintended and unavoidable adverse side effects, provided that the agent does not intend these effects and there exists a proportionately justifiable reason.

Catholic doctrine prohibits direct, intentional sterilization, but permits medical interventions that result in infertility as an unintended side effect when such treatment is necessary to preserve life or health (such as oophorectomy, hysterectomy, or chemotherapy and radiation therapy).

The primary intention of tubal ligation is the direct interruption of fertility, constituting an act of direct sterilization, and therefore does not meet the criteria for application of the principle of double effect.

Consequently, within the context of a Catholic hospital, tubal ligation as a form of direct sterilization is explicitly prohibited by ethical and religious directives, even when its purpose is to isolate a damaged uterus in order to protect the patient’s health.

Physicians must balance respect for patient autonomy with adherence to institutional ethical norms, clarify the intention behind their actions, avoid performing direct sterilization, and seek alternative options that are both consistent with Catholic teaching and medically feasible.

title: Is Artificial Nutrition and Hydration Extraordinary Care?
case:
Mrs. Henderson's eyes darted to the side of the bed as her nurse attempted to obtain an arterial blood gas. This response slightly startled John and made him consider whether or not he was causing her discomfort. John had often found it unsettling that she appeared awake, her eyes open, spontaneously moving her arm or leg, but it was a thought he repeatedly tried to dismiss.
Mrs. Henderson had been a resident in the ICU at Sacred Heart Hospital for seven months after a serious motor vehicle crash that claimed the lives of two of the four passengers. Her husband had been driving and had sustained only minor injuries. Mrs. Henderson, however, had suffered severe damage to her brain as a result of hypoxia secondary to cardiopulmonary arrest at the scene that ultimately caused her to lapse into a coma.
Her physician, Dr. Bernard, had informed Mr. Henderson after several months that, given his wife's MRI and physical exam, she most likely was no longer in a coma but in a persistent vegetative state (PVS). Dr. Bernard asked Mr. Henderson to consider goals for his wife's care.
"What do you mean…goals?" Mr. Henderson asked, slightly annoyed.
"I know this must be very difficult, Mr. Henderson. But now may be the time to consider what your wife would have wanted should she be in a position such as this. Did she ever discuss any of her wishes with you? Was your wife religious?"
Mr. Henderson said, "Yes, my wife was very explicit about a situation like this. She had even written out a living will that specified that she never would want to be kept alive artificially with food and water. I will bring you the living will tomorrow when I come in."
Then Mr. Henderson remembered something about a speech that the pope had made not long ago, in which he seemed to say that artificial nutrition and hydration were mandatory for Catholic patients in PVS. Upon realizing this, Mr. Henderson turned to Dr. Bernard and said, "Doctor, my wife was a devout Catholic, and because the pope seemed to require all Catholics to be given artificial food and water, I think my wife would now want these measures given to her."
Dr. Bernard was now perplexed. It appeared to him that a patient's signed living will to forgo artificial nutrition and hydration would supersede the claim by Mrs. Henderson's husband that she would want these measures given to her. He was aware that the local bishop of the diocese had recently come out with a strong statement in support of the pope's speech, but Sacred Heart Hospital had not as yet officially reacted to the bishop. What was Dr. Bernard to do? Was he to follow the living will and discount the pope's and bishop's statements, or was he to follow Mr. Henderson's interpretation of what his wife would want in light of the recent ecclesial documents? Dr. Bernard wanted to accommodate his patient's request even if this might go against church and hospital policy. He decided to give himself a day to think about all the complexities of this case.
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Henderson’s gaze flickered toward the edge of the bed as her nurse prepared to draw an arterial blood gas. The subtle movement caught John off guard, making him wonder if he was inadvertently causing her distress. The uncertainty gnawed at him—he found it unsettling that she could appear awake, her eyes open, occasionally moving an arm or leg on her own. Yet, he tried to set aside the thought.

For seven months, Mrs. Henderson had remained in the ICU at Sacred Heart Hospital, following a devastating car accident that claimed the lives of two other passengers. Her husband, who had been driving, escaped with minor injuries. Mrs. Henderson, however, suffered severe brain damage due to hypoxia after experiencing cardiopulmonary arrest at the scene, which led to her falling into a coma.

Several months into her hospitalization, Dr. Bernard, her attending physician, explained to Mr. Henderson that, based on her MRI and physical findings, Mrs. Henderson was no longer in a coma but had entered a persistent vegetative state (PVS). Dr. Bernard encouraged Mr. Henderson to reflect on what his wife would have wanted in this situation.

“What are you asking me to do—think about goals for her care?” Mr. Henderson responded, his tone tinged with irritation.

“I understand how difficult this must be, Mr. Henderson,” Dr. Bernard replied gently. “But it may be time to consider your wife’s wishes if she were able to speak for herself. Did she ever share her preferences about situations like this? Was she a religious person?”

Mr. Henderson nodded. “Yes, my wife was very clear about this. She even wrote a living will stating she wouldn’t want to be kept alive with artificial food and water. I’ll bring it in tomorrow.”

A moment later, a memory surfaced for Mr. Henderson—he recalled a recent speech by the pope that seemed to declare artificial nutrition and hydration mandatory for Catholics in a persistent vegetative state. This realization gave him pause. Turning back to Dr. Bernard, he said, “Doctor, my wife was a devout Catholic. If the pope says all Catholics should receive artificial food and water, I think she would want that now.”

Dr. Bernard found himself at a crossroads. On the one hand, Mrs. Henderson’s signed living will unambiguously stated her wish to forego artificial nutrition and hydration. On the other, her husband now felt—based on recent statements from the pope and a strong endorsement from the local bishop—that providing such measures aligned with her faith. Meanwhile, Sacred Heart Hospital had not formally responded to the bishop’s position.

Dr. Bernard was uncertain: Should he honor the living will and set aside the recent church directives, or should he follow Mr. Henderson’s interpretation of his wife’s wishes in light of new ecclesiastical guidance? Dr. Bernard wanted to respect his patient’s autonomy and values, even if this conflicted with church or hospital policy. He resolved to take a day to carefully consider the complexities before making a decision.

ethical_issues.question: Is it ethically permissible to consider artificial nutrition and hydration as disproportionate means of life support and, therefore, to discontinue feeding in patients in a persistent vegetative state?
keypoints: Patients have the right to refuse life-sustaining treatments that they judge to be disproportionate, meaning those that do not offer a reasonable hope of benefit or impose an excessive burden.

The living will clearly articulates the patient’s position regarding artificial nutrition and hydration while competent, indicating that she regarded artificial nutrition and hydration as disproportionate means of life support.

The ethics consultant determines that the patient’s advance directive and her surrogate decision maker indicate that artificial nutrition and hydration constitute disproportionate means; therefore, withdrawal of artificial nutrition and hydration is an ethically acceptable option of care, provided it is permitted by law.

title: Self-Interest versus Friendship in Medical School
case:
Joe and Mary were friends and classmates on their third-year clerkship in obstetrics-gynecology. Mary had known for a while that she wanted to go into ob-gyn, and she hoped to make a good impression during her brief time in the clerkship. Joe liked ob-gyn too, but was still undecided about what field he wanted to pursue. Throughout the clerkship, Mary made a point of scrubbing in for surgery at every chance—which sometimes meant that Joe could not. Several of the procedures she observed were particularly instructive, including an emergency tubal resection following a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
Joe scrubbed in on half as many surgeries as Mary. He was relegated to following the more routine cases and had to do a disproportionate amount of "scut" work on the floors. The residents and attending physicians were too busy to notice the discrepancy. Joe learned a lot on his rotation, but he felt somewhat shortchanged and thought that Mary acted inappropriately. At the end of the rotation, Joe and Mary sat down to exchange feedback on their experience working together as part of the clerkship's professionalism evaluation. Joe was ambivalent about whether to confront his friend, thinking perhaps it was his fault for not being assertive enough. Even if it was her fault, Joe thought to himself, "I don't want to jeopardize our friendship and make a big deal of this." He decided simply to praise Mary for her enthusiasm and wish her good luck with her plans to apply for an ob-gyn residency.
case_rewrite:
Joe and Mary were friends and classmates undertaking their third-year clerkship in obstetrics-gynecology. Mary had long aspired to a career in ob-gyn and was eager to make a strong impression during her rotation. Joe, although interested in ob-gyn, remained uncertain about his ultimate career path. Throughout the clerkship, Mary consistently seized every opportunity to scrub in for surgeries—even when it meant Joe would have to step aside. As a result, Mary observed several significant procedures, such as a critical emergency tubal resection after a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, that Joe did not witness.

While Mary accumulated valuable surgical experience, Joe found himself participating in only half as many surgeries. He was left to handle more routine cases and shouldered a greater share of the "scut" work on the wards. The residents and attending physicians, preoccupied with their busy schedules, were unaware of this imbalance. Though Joe gained knowledge during the rotation, he couldn’t help but feel slighted and questioned whether Mary’s actions were fair. When the rotation concluded, Joe and Mary met for the professionalism evaluation, a session set aside to exchange feedback about their teamwork during the clerkship. Joe was conflicted about whether to raise the issue with Mary, wondering if he was to blame for not asserting himself more. Even if responsibility lay with Mary, Joe hesitated, worried that speaking up might harm their friendship and create unnecessary conflict. Ultimately, he chose not to address the matter, instead commending Mary on her enthusiasm and wishing her success as she prepared to apply for an ob-gyn residency.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical students effectively provide feedback when confronted with a peer’s selfish behavior in order to promote mutual professional growth?
keypoints: Medical students should, early in the rotation, identify specific instances of peer misconduct that affect collaboration and learning opportunities, and offer practical and feasible suggestions for improvement.
Timely, private, and concrete correction of inappropriate behavior when it occurs, along with modeling and encouraging desirable behaviors, facilitates effective behavioral modification.

Successful implementation of peer feedback requires confidence, courage, and communication skills; the mandatory feedback session at the end of the clerkship provides a safe environment to practice delivering and receiving constructive criticism.

Failure to provide honest feedback regarding selfish behavior deprives both parties of growth opportunities; students should seize this altruistic opportunity to support their peers’ development and better prepare both for future professional challenges.

title: Fudging an Answer during Clinical Rounds
case:
Leah is a third-year medical student doing her internal medicine rotation. She is a diligent student who has quickly learned her role and responsibilities. She enjoys taking care of patients and does her best to know all of their current medical needs and treatment plans. She is also aware that achieving a high grade in this clerkship is important, since she plans to pursue a career in internal medicine.
Every morning Leah dutifully pre-rounds on her patients so that later, on team rounds, she is able to share the patients' overnight events, vital signs for the past 24 hours and results of that morning's lab work with the other medical students, interns, residents and the attending physician. Leah has done such exemplary work that the interns covering her patients save rounding on her patients for last in the morning and occasionally, if they are particularly frantic, do not see them at all before the work day starts.
One day the full team was rounding with the attending physician, who joined the team one morning each week. He had a somewhat gruff demeanor and liked everything to be presented in a specific manner, with no straying from the typical format. In fact, he tended to be so rigid that medical students often did not present their own patients to him, lest he be annoyed at the student and the team. He was also responsible for 50 percent of the student's grade. Leah was presenting that day, as was required at least once during her clerkship. Her patient was Mrs. Lang, a 72-year-old woman with coronary artery disease, systolic heart failure secondary to ischemic cardiomyopathy, type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic renal insufficiency who had been admitted for cellulitis.
Leah gave a seamless presentation and had started to summarize the most recent labs when she realized that she had logged off the computer without writing down the basic metabolic panel (BMP) for Mrs. Lang in order to be on time to rounds. After a moment of hesitation she said that the BMP was unchanged from previous readings for this patient—whose baseline renal insufficiency had been constant throughout her visit. The intern and resident both jotted down on their route sheets that the BMP was unchanged, planning to check the values themselves when they had the time.
Two hours later, after their lengthy rounds, Leah finally had a chance to sit down at a computer and check Mrs. Lang's labs. Just as she saw that Mrs. Lang's potassium, BUN and creatinine were elevated, Mrs. Lang's intern was paged by the pharmacist, who was inquiring about the appropriate antibiotic dosing, given that the new lab results indicated acute renal failure.
case_rewrite:
Leah, a third-year medical student, was in the midst of her internal medicine rotation. Known for her diligence and careful attention to detail, she quickly adapted to her responsibilities and took pride in knowing every detail about her patients’ conditions and treatment plans. She was motivated not only by her desire to provide excellent care but also by the knowledge that her performance in this clerkship would be crucial for her goal of pursuing a career in internal medicine.

Each morning, Leah made it a point to pre-round on her assigned patients well before the rest of the team gathered. This allowed her to report on overnight events, 24-hour vital signs, and early morning laboratory results during team rounds with her fellow students, interns, residents, and the attending physician. Leah’s thoroughness became well-known; the interns, confident in her work, often left her patients for last on their own rounds and, in especially hectic moments, sometimes skipped seeing them before rounds altogether.

One morning, the entire team was rounding with the attending physician, who only joined them once a week. The attending was known for his stern demeanor and strict expectations regarding case presentations—he insisted on a rigid format and had little patience for deviations. Most medical students, wary of his temperament and the fact that he determined half of their final grade, avoided presenting in front of him when possible. Still, Leah was scheduled to present that day, as every student was required to do at least once during the clerkship.

Leah’s patient was Mrs. Lang, a 72-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, systolic heart failure due to ischemic cardiomyopathy, type 2 diabetes, and chronic renal insufficiency, who had been admitted to the hospital for cellulitis. Leah began her presentation smoothly, summarizing Mrs. Lang’s overnight status and recent clinical progress. As she started to review the most current laboratory data, she suddenly realized she had signed off the computer that morning before writing down the latest basic metabolic panel (BMP). She had rushed in order to be on time for rounds and now did not have the precise laboratory values at hand.

Pausing briefly, Leah hesitated. Then, recalling that Mrs. Lang’s renal function had been stable throughout her admission, she stated that the BMP was unchanged from previous results. Both the intern and the resident, trusting Leah’s report, wrote on their rounding sheets that the BMP remained stable, intending to confirm the values themselves later when they had more time.

Rounds continued for another two hours before Leah was able to sit down at a computer and finally review Mrs. Lang’s laboratory results. To her dismay, she saw that Mrs. Lang’s potassium, BUN, and creatinine were all elevated, indicating acute renal failure. At that moment, the intern was paged by the pharmacist, who wanted to clarify the appropriate antibiotic dosing in light of the new lab findings.

ethical_issues.question: During clinical clerkships, when thorough preparation conflicts with honest reporting, which should medical students prioritize?
keypoints: Medical students in clinical clerkships should prioritize honest reporting, especially when it involves medical data related to patient health or safety; making unfounded assumptions violates professional ethics and is unacceptable.
Maintaining honesty in the face of pressure or potential adverse consequences is central to professionalism and helps medical students develop and reinforce long-term ethical conduct.

Clinical teams and attending physicians should foster an environment that supports truthful reporting, valuing honesty as a vital attribute and encouraging medical students to candidly communicate the facts during presentations.

title: Diagnostic Testing for Diseases in the News
case:
Dr. Carpenter entered the exam room to see her next patient, Andrew, and his mother. Andrew was an 8-year-old-boy who was athletic and active. His mother was a bit of a worrier and frequently brought him to Dr. Carpenter for (generally) minor reasons.
During this visit, Andrew's mother pointed out a small rash on his right calf that had appeared the day before. She was extremely concerned about the rash because of news reports of a flesh-eating bacteria spreading throughout the community. She believed the report mentioned that someone in Andrew's soccer league had come down with the infection.
Dr. Carpenter began her examination by asking Andrew about the rash. He said it was a little itchy, but not painful. He said he had not felt sick, and his mother reported that Andrew had not had a fever. During her examination, Dr. Carpenter noted no swelling, bleeding, pus or visibly dead tissue. She then explained to Andrew's mother that he had no symptoms consistent with the flesh-eating bacteria. But she did not seem convinced, and she repeatedly emphasized that her son might have been exposed to the infection during soccer. She wanted more elaborate tests done, not satisfied with watching and waiting.
Realizing that this mother's anxiety could not be allayed, Dr. Carpenter debated about how to proceed. A proper diagnostic test for necrotizing fasciitis would require a biopsy, gram stain and culture.
