title: Dispensing Cosmeceuticals from the Office
case:
Mrs. Schweppe had just finished seeing her dermatologist, Dr. Fletcher, and was in the process of making an appointment to follow up about her eczema treatments when her eye caught three non-descript bottles with gold writing displayed on a short platform.
"Angie," Mrs. Schweppe asked Dr. Fletcher's secretary, "what are these bottles?"
"These are our special sunscreens and moisturizers," Angie answered. "Are you currently using any special sunscreen on your face?"
"Well, no," Mrs. Schweppe answered. "I mean, I always use an SPF 15—or 30 if I'm in the garden—but I usually buy whatever is on sale at the pharmacy."
"Perhaps you should talk to Dr. Fletcher about the product before he meets with his next patient. Most of the doctors in the practice recommend this sunscreen to all of their patients, but if Dr. Fletcher hadn't mentioned it, maybe it's because it would interact badly with your eczema medication." While Angie went to find Dr. Fletcher, Mrs. Schweppe read the short pamphlet that showed before and after pictures and offered testimonials about the benefits of the lotions.
"So, Marie," Dr. Fletcher warmly greeted her, "Angie tells me that you're interested in some of our products."
"Well," Mrs. Schweppe began, "they just caught my eye and I wondered if it was something new that I should be using."
"I can tell you that the sunscreen here offers you the protection of SPF 30, moisturizes very well and never leaves your face feeling dry or oily like some of the mass-marketed products can. It's much gentler on the skin." Dr. Fletcher picked up the "tester" bottle and allowed Mrs. Schweppe to feel and smell the lotion.
"Do you think that this is something I need? How much is it?" she asked, clearly impressed by what she had seen so far.
"It's kind of expensive, which is why I hadn't mentioned it to you before. I think that it's great and that it can only help your skin, but what you use now probably gives you the minimum protection that you need."
"Well, if it's so expensive here, maybe I can find it cheaper at a discount store or pharmacy." Mrs. Schweppe offered.
"Unfortunately, you can't get it anywhere else in the state—we have an exclusive contract with the manufacturer. We're currently trying to expand their distribution but that could take months. The good news is that you don't need a prescription. It's about $35 a bottle and each bottle, if you use it everyday, will last about a month. I can assure you, however, that your face will be well protected when you're in the garden if you use this lotion. Also, we can offer you a better deal if you buy several months' worth today."
"I suppose I should get it then," Mrs. Schweppe said with a hint of reluctance in her voice. "It's almost impossible to cover my face completely when I'm in the sun and with the increase of skin cancer that you hear about on the news, you can never be too careful."
"That sounds great. How many months' worth can Angie get for you?"
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Schweppe had just wrapped up her appointment with Dr. Fletcher regarding her persistent eczema and was standing at the reception desk, arranging her next follow-up. As she waited, her gaze fell on a small stand nearby, where three elegant bottles adorned with gold lettering were neatly displayed.

“These bottles look interesting,” Mrs. Schweppe remarked to Angie, the receptionist.

Angie offered a polite smile. “Those are skincare products our practice makes available to patients. If you’d like more information, Dr. Fletcher can discuss them with you in our consultation area.”

A moment later, Dr. Fletcher approached. “Marie, I heard you noticed our skincare products. Would you like to learn a bit more about them?”

“I was curious,” Mrs. Schweppe replied. “Is this something I should be using now?”

Dr. Fletcher gestured for her to follow to a consultation area adjacent to the reception desk, where the products were displayed. The small space was clearly set apart from the main clinical rooms. “These are specialty sunscreens and moisturizers offered to patients here. I want to make it absolutely clear: there is no requirement for you to purchase anything, and your decision will never impact your care or our relationship. The sunscreen you’re currently using—SPF 15 or 30 from the pharmacy—still provides the essential protection you need.”

Mrs. Schweppe considered this. “Is there anything special about these?”

Dr. Fletcher picked up a tester bottle and handed it to her. “This sunscreen is SPF 30 and designed specifically for sensitive, eczema-prone skin. It’s formulated to moisturize well and isn’t greasy like some over-the-counter brands. You’re welcome to try a tester—we want patients to make informed choices based on what works best for them.”

She examined the lotion and took in the scent. “How much does it cost?”

“It’s $35 per bottle, which usually lasts about a month with daily application,” Dr. Fletcher explained. “This particular product is available only through our practice due to an exclusive contract with the manufacturer. That means you won’t find it elsewhere or be able to compare prices directly, which I realize may be a limitation. We do offer a discount if you purchase several months at a time. However, there are many other high-quality sunscreens at various price points at local pharmacies. If you’d like, I can recommend alternative brands that are suitable for eczema. You’re under no obligation to buy anything here.”

Mrs. Schweppe hesitated. “It’s good to know there are options. I’ve been worried about skin cancer, but I’m also not sure about spending that much.”

“That’s completely understandable,” Dr. Fletcher replied gently. “Please take a complimentary sample home and see how it feels for you. If you decide later you’d like to purchase it, just let us know—there’s absolutely no pressure. If the price is a concern or if you ever have financial difficulties, we can also look into additional support or guidance. Remember, you are welcome to stick with your current sunscreen or choose another brand entirely—whatever you decide will not affect your care with us.”

“Thank you, Dr. Fletcher. I’ll try the sample and think about it.”

“Of course. If you have any questions or need recommendations for other sunscreens, just ask. Angie can help you schedule your next visit whenever you’re ready.”

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians participate in the exclusive distribution of cosmeceutical products?
keypoints: Physicians should not engage in exclusive distributorships of cosmeceutical products, as such arrangements may give rise to conflicts of interest, suspicions of coercive sales practices, and patient deception, thereby violating principles of medical ethics.

Physicians ought to clearly inform patients whether the recommended skincare products are private-label items, in order to prevent patients from mistakenly believing that the products possess unique therapeutic efficacy or exclusive authorization.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians avoid exerting purchasing pressure on patients when selling skincare products in the clinical setting?
keypoints: Physicians should ensure that patients feel no pressure when purchasing products and explicitly inform them that their decision to buy or not will not affect their subsequent medical care, thereby avoiding any sense of coercion.

The sale of products should be managed by a medical spa or designated area adjacent to but separate from the clinical treatment space, so as to prevent interference with the clinical environment and the physician-patient relationship.

Product explanations and recommendations must be conducted by professionally qualified medical personnel or skin care specialists; receptionists and other untrained staff are not permitted to explain or sell products.

A range of products at various price points, as well as tester samples, should be made available to facilitate patients’ autonomous decision-making based on their individual needs and financial circumstances.
For patients experiencing financial hardship or uncertainty, product samples or other forms of support should be provided to alleviate purchasing pressure and safeguard patient interests.

title: Can There Be Healing without Trust?
case:
Dr. Burton is an internist at a student health center. Julie, a freshman at the college, made an appointment for an initial medical evaluation. It was flu season and Dr. Burton was running 30 minutes late. He apologized for the delay immediately after introducing himself to his new patient. He asked Julie routine medical questions, thinking to himself that she was rather disengaged. Julie reported a recent onset of gastrointestinal cramping, bloating and constipation which caused her to miss classes. Midway through the medical history, she matter-of-factly told Dr. Burton, “I’m just here for a sick note.” Dr. Burton patiently explained to Julie that he needed to collect further medical information to complete the evaluation. Julie reluctantly acquiesced, and Dr. Burton discovered that her father had died in a motor vehicle accident two years before, and this had led to some significant financial stress.
Following the interview and physical exam Dr. Burton diagnosed Julie with irritable bowel syndrome. He educated her about the condition and made some treatment recommendations including a prescription drug. Julie stated she had been surfing the Web, figured that was her diagnosis and ordered a month’s supply of several herbal supplements for approximately $50 because she knew she could not afford the copay for Dr. Burton’s prescriptions.
Later, when Dr. Burton discussed this case with the clinic nurse he learned that Julie’s father had actually been in a relatively minor car accident in which he had sustained a fractured femur. His death, Dr. Burton discovered, had been the result of preventable medical complications during surgery. The surgeon in this case was known in the medical community for his brusque interpersonal manner and his cavalier approach to patient care. According to the clinic nurse, the outcome of the case was widely known to have been avoidable, but no one on the treatment team had discussed the situation forthrightly with Julie’s mother. The family suspected that someone was to blame and had been very upset by the apparent cover-up. Dr. Burton was sure his patient’s previous experiences with the medical profession had affected her ability to trust him as her internist.
One month later Dr. Burton notices Julie’s name on his afternoon clinic schedule and wonders how he should address what he has learned.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Burton, an internist at the university’s student health center, was moving quickly between exam rooms during a busy flu season. Running half an hour behind schedule, he greeted his next patient, Julie, a freshman, with an apology for the delay. As he began her intake, Dr. Burton noticed Julie seemed distant and somewhat uninterested. She described recent symptoms: abdominal cramps, bloating, and constipation significant enough to have kept her from attending classes. About halfway through the medical history, Julie said plainly, “I’m just here for a sick note.” Dr. Burton, maintaining a patient demeanor, explained that it was important for him to gather more information to complete a proper evaluation. Julie agreed, though not without hesitation. As their conversation continued, Dr. Burton learned that Julie’s father had died two years prior in a car accident, which had left her family facing substantial financial hardship.

After finishing the interview and physical examination, Dr. Burton diagnosed Julie with irritable bowel syndrome. He took time to explain the condition and discussed several treatment options, including a prescription medication. Julie replied that she had researched her symptoms online, suspected IBS herself, and had already ordered a month’s supply of various herbal supplements online for around $50, as she believed she could not afford the copay for the medication Dr. Burton recommended.

Later that day, Dr. Burton spoke with the clinic nurse about Julie’s situation. The nurse shared that Julie’s father’s accident had not initially been life-threatening; he had suffered a fractured femur. His death, the nurse revealed, had actually resulted from preventable medical complications during surgery. The surgeon involved had a reputation in the medical community for brusque, dismissive behavior and a lack of thoroughness in patient care. According to the nurse, the circumstances surrounding the case were widely regarded as avoidable, but no one on the hospital team had openly discussed what happened with Julie’s mother. The family, suspecting wrongdoing, had been deeply troubled by what felt like a cover-up. Dr. Burton realized that these experiences likely influenced Julie’s skepticism toward doctors and her reluctance to trust him as her physician.

A month later, Dr. Burton noticed Julie’s name listed for an upcoming afternoon appointment. He found himself reflecting on what he had learned and considering how best to approach her care during their next encounter.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Burton address Julie’s refusal of the prescribed medication for irritable bowel syndrome and explore the underlying reasons for her skepticism toward medicine during her second clinic visit?
keypoints: Dr. Burton should not proactively disclose the sensitive information about Julie’s family medical history that he learned from the nurse, so as to avoid compromising patient trust and confidentiality.

Dr. Burton should engage Julie in a discussion about her overall experience during the initial visit, inviting her to express any concerns or topics she wishes to address, including her views on prescription medications and herbal supplements.

Through open, respectful, and nonjudgmental communication, Dr. Burton can encourage Julie to voluntarily share her negative experiences with the medical profession and her resulting skepticism toward physicians when she feels ready.

Establishing a trusting relationship is essential to facilitating Julie’s acceptance of medical recommendations and achieving effective treatment, thereby preventing the reduction of the physician’s role to merely issuing “sick notes.”

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians, in the context of a breakdown of trust between patients and the medical profession, engage patients through a caring approach to strengthen the patient-physician relationship and improve the quality of care?
keypoints: Physicians should enhance patient trust by eliciting and validating patients’ concerns, inquiring about their expectations, and responding to their emotional distress with empathic language.

Physicians may proactively inquire about patients’ views on the use of prescription medications and herbal supplements, thereby creating a safe space that encourages patients to share negative experiences related to their family and the healthcare system.

If patients are willing to discuss their feelings toward physicians, doctors should listen patiently and respond with a caring attitude, helping patients overcome distrust, which enables more effective application of professional skills in treating illness and ultimately improves the quality of care.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Burton discuss Julie’s first clinic visit with her and inquire about her views on the use of prescription medications and herbal supplements, in order to help her voluntarily raise her family’s negative experiences with the medical profession?
keypoints: Dr. Burton should take the initiative to discuss Julie’s first clinic visit with her, in order to understand her feelings and perspectives regarding the experience.
Dr. Burton should inquire about Julie’s views on the use of prescription medications and herbal supplements, thereby encouraging her to express her attitudes and concerns about the treatment plan.
Through Dr. Burton’s proactive discussion and inquiry, Julie may gradually overcome the distrust stemming from her family and prior medical experiences.

Establishing a trusting relationship is essential for Dr. Burton to provide effective medical care and support for Julie’s physical and mental well-being, and to avoid being reduced to the role of merely issuing sick notes.

title: "Can We Just Drop the Copay?"
case:
Once every 6 months for the past 15 years, Mr. Delmand has been taking a morning off from his job as construction foreman to visit Dr. Robiel’s office. Over the years, Dr. Robiel has diagnosed Mr. Delmund’s high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and type 2 diabetes and helped him manage these conditions.
As the patient enters the examination room, Dr. Robiel glances at his chart. Although he has written all the entries himself, he likes to remind himself what Mr. Delmand’s 3 children are doing these days and what concerns he had at the last visit. He also notes that Mr. Delmand had an HbA1C drawn last week; the levels had bounced up to 8 percent, despite 3 oral hypoglycemic medications.
As they chat, Dr. Robiel learns that Mr. Delmand, now 53, is taking his medications daily but that he was recently seen in the ER for an infected foot blister that he “just hadn’t noticed.” He has been checking his blood glucose twice a day but doesn’t write down the numbers. Dr. Robiel mentions to Mr. Delmand that their control of his diabetes had slipped a little; they had been quite successful for the past 8 years, but they might need to add insulin to his regimen if the current treatments were not working.
“Actually Doc,” Mr. Delmand interjects, “I feel like my diabetes is not the only thing I’m losing control over. The company is making changes in our health insurance; they want me to switch to a doctor on their preferred list. If I stick with you, they’re going to charge me 20 percent of your bill. With 2 of the girls in college, that 20 percent carries a noticeable punch for us. You understand...isn’t your oldest boy in college now?”
Dr. Robiel nods. “I would hate to have you leave my practice, Mr. Delmand.” He sincerely enjoys visits with Mr. Delmand, and he feels that his dedication to this patient’s health has made a genuine difference. They have worked well as a team to avoid complications of Mr. Delmand’s hypertension and his diabetes. Dr. Robiel appreciates how college tuition bills stress a family’s budget—he recently added an extra weekly evening session to his practice to ease the burden on his savings. “I understand your dilemma, but I’d love to convince you to stay.”
“Well Doc,” Mr. Delmand continued, “maybe we could find a balance that suits us both. You’re my doctor. I’m not anxious to switch to someone who doesn’t know me or my conditions. We’ve worked together for a long time. Would you consider forgiving the extra 20 percent reimbursement—and just accepting what my insurance pays you—if I do stick with you?”

As Mr. Delmand steps into the exam room, Dr. Robiel reviews his chart—a ritual that helps him recall both medical details and personal touches, like updates about Mr. Delmand’s three children and concerns mentioned at prior appointments. Dr. Robiel gently notes that their previously well-controlled diabetes has recently slipped, suggesting that insulin might be necessary if current strategies are falling short.

“Actually, Doc,” Mr. Delmand interrupts, “it feels like I’m losing control of more than just my diabetes. My company’s changing our health insurance—they want me to pick a doctor from their approved list. If I keep seeing you, I’ll have to pay 20 percent of your bill out-of-pocket. With two daughters in college, that extra cost hits us pretty hard. You get it… isn’t your oldest in college too?”

Dr. Robiel nods, sharing the sentiment. He truly values his professional and personal connection with Mr. Delmand, believing their teamwork has played a crucial role in preventing complications from his chronic conditions. Having recently added an extra weekly evening clinic to help cover his own son’s tuition, Dr. Robiel empathizes with the financial strain. “I understand what you’re facing, and I’d really hate to see you leave my care, Mr. Delmand. Mr. Delmand leans forward, his voice earnest. “Maybe there’s a way to make this work for both of us. You’re my doctor—I trust you, and I’m not eager to start over with someone unfamiliar. Would you consider waiving that extra 20 percent and just take what my insurance pays if I stay with you?”

ethical_issues.question: When patients face financial difficulties, should physicians modify their clinical care approach to support the patients’ medical needs?
keypoints: Healthcare costs may affect the accessibility and continuity of care; physicians should rationally assess patients’ financial difficulties and appropriately adjust care delivery models to ensure patients receive necessary medical services.

Trust within the patient-physician relationship forms the foundation for effective communication and shared decision-making, providing physicians with opportunities to address patients’ financial concerns and helping to maintain a long-term, stable therapeutic relationship.

Physicians should adopt an open mindset and innovative thinking to develop cost-saving alternatives that achieve a win-win outcome for patient well-being and both parties’ interests, thereby promoting patient health and the sustained development of the patient-physician relationship.

ethical_issues.question: Should the physician waive the patient’s copayment to help alleviate his financial burden?
keypoints: Dr. Robiel may refuse to waive the copayment, as doing so could impact his income and the operation of his practice, and may be unfair to other patients; he must balance professional ethics with economic sustainability.

Dr. Robiel should emphasize the importance of continuity of care to prevent deterioration in Mr. Delmand’s diabetes management due to a change in providers, thereby maintaining his overall health stability.

Dr. Robiel needs to carefully weigh the pros and cons of waiving the copayment, taking into account the maintenance of a long-term patient-doctor relationship, the patient’s well-being, and his own professional ethical responsibilities.

Dr. Robiel should actively explore flexible, cost-saving alternatives—such as telephone consultations, adjusting the frequency of follow-up visits, or optimizing the treatment plan—to alleviate the patient’s financial burden while ensuring the quality of care.

Addressing financial barriers requires the physician to maintain an open mindset and innovative thinking, balancing patient welfare, the patient-doctor relationship, and the sustainability of his own professional practice.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians proactively discuss and seek solutions with patients when patients raise financial difficulties, in order to maintain the patient-physician relationship and promote patient health?
keypoints: Physicians should proactively and transparently communicate with patients about health care costs, attend to patients’ financial difficulties, and thereby maintain the patient-doctor relationship and safeguard patient health.
A strong patient-doctor relationship and mutual trust are essential foundations for encouraging patients to openly discuss financial pressures and collaboratively seek solutions.

Physicians should adopt a patient-centered psychosocial communication style and, by adjusting care plans as appropriate, demonstrate sensitivity to patients’ financial circumstances in order to reasonably address financial barriers to care.

title: Unnecessary Antibiotics
case:
Dr. Waterman had a 12-year-old general pediatrics practice in a rapidly growing suburban community. Although well liked by his patients and their families, he found it increasingly difficult to thrive as a solo practitioner under a managed care system. After careful consideration, he decided to merge his practice with a fairly new pediatrics group in the same community.
During merger negotiations with his three new partners, Dr. Waterman agreed to a compensation formula based largely on the number of patients seen. His new partners, led by the ambitious Dr. Connolly, have also made no secret of their desire to increase the "market share" of the practice and the importance of securing a strong foothold in the community before more competition “moves in.”
In the winter, a few months after the merger, the office was flooded with anxious parents and their sneezy, sniffling and coughing youngsters. Ever since a medical school buddy told him about a case of community-acquired MRSA (methicillin-resistantStaphlococcus aureus) he had encountered, Dr. Waterman has been particularly sensitive to the threat of antibiotic resistance. He has therefore adjusted his prescribing pattern over the last few years to minimize antibiotic use. Although it requires more clinic time, Dr. Waterman is careful to explain to each parent why antibiotics might not be indicated for his or her child and what can be done to manage cough and cold symptoms at home.
The clinic was characteristically overbooked one Saturday in January, and Dr. Waterman was called in to see patients even though it was his day off. Assisted by Joan, the clinic nurse, he examined one of Dr. Connolly’s regular patients, a 4-year-old boy named Colby. Dr. Waterman told Colby’s mother that he suspected his symptoms were due to a respiratory virus and would not therefore prescribe antibiotics. She listened attentively to what he said and then became somewhat agitated, arguing that Dr. Connolly always gave Colby an antibiotic “just to be safe.” In fact, as she told him, she had spoken with Dr. Connolly that morning and he had specifically told her to bring Colby in for an antibiotic prescription. “Now, after listening to what you told me, I am just confused.” As the clinic nurse slipped out of the room, Dr. Waterman tried yet again to alleviate her anxiety and explain his reasoning.
Suddenly, Dr. Connolly opened the door and burst into the examining room with Joan at his side and gave Colby and his mother a big smile. “Everything going all right?” he asked. “I have your prescription right here. Sorry about the delay.” Later on, Dr. Connolly sympathetically told Dr. Waterman that making parents you haven’t met before “happy” isn’t always easy and that he was glad he could “help out” with Colby’s case.
That evening, after everyone had left the clinic, Dr. Waterman looked through every one of the past week’s charts. He noticed that Dr. Connolly and the other two pediatricians regularly prescribed antibiotics inappropriately. He also observed that they each managed to see about 20 percent more patients than he did.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Waterman had dedicated twelve years to building his general pediatrics practice in a rapidly expanding suburb. Well respected by his young patients and their families, he nonetheless found himself struggling to keep his solo practice afloat under the mounting pressures of managed care. After much deliberation, Dr. Waterman decided to merge his practice with a relatively new pediatric group operating in the same community.

During discussions about the merger, Dr. Waterman and his three soon-to-be partners agreed on a compensation model that heavily rewarded the number of patients seen. The group, led by the enterprising Dr. Connolly, made it clear that growing the practice’s "market share" was a top priority, especially with more competitors poised to enter the area.

Over recent years, he had intentionally reduced his antibiotic prescribing, taking extra time during appointments to explain to parents why antibiotics were often unnecessary, and how to manage cold symptoms at home.

On a typically hectic Saturday in January, the clinic was overbooked, and Dr. Waterman was asked to come in, even though it was supposed to be his day off. With help from Joan, the clinic nurse, he saw one of Dr. Connolly’s regular patients—a four-year-old boy named Colby. After examining Colby, Dr. Waterman explained to his mother that her son likely had a viral respiratory infection and that antibiotics would not help. Colby’s mother listened, but soon became upset, insisting that Dr. Connolly always prescribed antibiotics for Colby “just to be safe.” She explained that she had spoken with Dr. Connolly earlier that day, and he had instructed her to bring Colby in specifically for an antibiotic prescription. “Now I don’t know what to think,” she said, clearly frustrated. As Joan quietly left the room, Dr. Waterman patiently tried once more to reassure her and clarify his reasoning.

At that moment, Dr. Connolly swept into the exam room with Joan beside him, greeting Colby and his mother with a warm smile. “Is everything going well?” he asked cheerfully. “Here’s your prescription—sorry for the wait.” Later, Dr. Connolly told Dr. Waterman, with a sympathetic tone, that making new parents feel reassured wasn't always simple, and expressed relief that he could “help out” with Colby’s case.

That evening, after the clinic had emptied, Dr. Waterman reviewed the previous week’s patient charts. He noted that Dr. Connolly and the other two pediatricians routinely prescribed antibiotics in situations where they were not indicated. He also realized that each of his colleagues managed to see about 20 percent more patients than he did.

ethical_issues.question: How can a physician maintain professional integrity when practicing within a team that has differing clinical approaches or values?
keypoints: Physicians should proactively address differences in clinical philosophy and practice within their teams through optimized communication and interpersonal negotiation.
The team should reach consensus on key clinical areas, advocating for and implementing evidence-based medicine to prevent patient confusion arising from varying treatment approaches among physicians.
Physicians need to rationally assess their compatibility with the quality of care and values upheld by the team, engaging in necessary self-reflection and professional positioning.

Physicians must recognize the cumulative and far-reaching impact of individual clinical decisions on public health (such as antibiotic resistance) and on their own professional integrity, thereby assuming corresponding ethical responsibilities.

title: The Gift-Giving Influence
case:
It’s late Friday afternoon in the residents’ lounge of the Department of Surgery at Metro Academic Medical Center. A few on-call interns are napping on the tattered couches. Others who have just finished their shifts are making plans for later that evening. Someone from the chair’s office is stuffing mailboxes with an invitation to a summer picnic. Along one wall, a pharmaceutical sales representative sets up a long table with the city’s best pizza and a large supply of bright purple penlights, pins, logo-emblazoned pens, notebooks and stuffed toys. Three third-year medical students—Michael, Carly and Holly—are the first to grab a few hot slices and a pen or two and to greet the smiling sales rep, who tells them about a new addition to the hospital’s formulary.
Friday afternoon pizza is part of what they jokingly call their regular “food rounds.” Only two months into their third year, they have quickly learned when and where free food might be found in the hospital. Tuesdays there is free lunch during the department of internal medicine grand rounds. Wednesdays there are bagels and juice during the department of pediatrics morning report for residents and students. And cookies, brownies and coffee regularly appear on the psychiatry and neurology floors. They never mind talking to the sales reps at these things, although they tend to stuff the glossy literature into their bags and forget about it.
Michael has even become friendly with one of the sales reps who encouraged him to apply for a grant sponsored by the pharmaceutical company. With the money he was awarded, Michael was able to attend a pediatrics conference in Miami.
A few weeks later, the three friends attend a required meeting of all third- and fourth-year medical students where they are lectured about various pharmaceutical sales techniques, including how gift relationships can create a sense of obligation. Michael, Carly and Holly meet up in the hall afterwards to discuss the presentation. They all scoff at the idea that their future prescribing habits will be influenced by a slice of pizza and a pen. “How naïve do they think we are?” asks Carly. “We’re scientists, not gullible spectators,” protests Michael. The dean of students, Dr. Markovsky, overhears their conversation and wonders if it is time to start seriously considering banning all pharmaceutical industry-promoted activities to prevent prescribing bias.
case_rewrite:
It’s late on a Friday afternoon in the residents’ lounge at Metro Academic Medical Center’s Department of Surgery. A handful of on-call interns are dozing on worn-out couches, while others who have just completed their shifts gather in the corner, chatting about their plans for the evening. Someone from the department chair’s office moves through the room, tucking invitations to the upcoming summer picnic into mailboxes. Against one wall, a pharmaceutical sales representative is arranging an impressive spread: boxes of the city’s most popular pizza, stacks of brightly colored penlights, pins, pens with company logos, notebooks, and even a few plush toys.

Three third-year medical students—Michael, Carly, and Holly—are the first to approach, helping themselves to slices of hot pizza and picking up a pen or two. The sales rep greets them warmly and begins explaining the benefits of a new medication recently added to the hospital’s formulary. Friday afternoon pizza has become something of a tradition for the trio, who jokingly refer to these moments as their “food rounds.” Only two months into their third year, they have already mastered the art of tracking down complimentary food around the hospital: lunch on Tuesdays during internal medicine grand rounds, bagels and juice on Wednesdays at the pediatrics morning report, and an endless supply of cookies, brownies, and coffee on the psychiatry and neurology floors. The students don’t mind chatting with the sales reps at these events, though they usually toss the glossy promotional material into their bags and promptly forget about it.

Michael, in particular, has struck up a friendly rapport with one of the sales reps. Encouraged by the rep, he recently applied for—and received—a grant from the pharmaceutical company, which allowed him to attend a pediatrics conference in Miami.

A few weeks later, the trio attends a mandatory meeting for all third- and fourth-year medical students. The session focuses on the various techniques pharmaceutical companies use to influence prescribing, with an emphasis on how even small gifts can foster a sense of obligation, subtly shaping professional decisions. After the presentation, Michael, Carly, and Holly regroup in the hallway to discuss what they’ve just heard. All three are skeptical about the idea that their future clinical choices could be swayed by something as minor as a slice of pizza or a free pen. “How gullible do they think we are?” Carly asks, rolling her eyes. “We’re scientists, not easy marks,” Michael adds with a laugh. Their conversation is overheard by Dr. Markovsky, the dean of students, who pauses thoughtfully, considering whether it might be time to propose a serious discussion about banning all pharmaceutical promotional activities on campus to address the potential for prescribing bias.

ethical_issues.question: Should medical schools implement a complete ban on pharmaceutical industry promotional activities to prevent prescribing bias?
keypoints: Revised key points:

Pharmaceutical industry promotional activities may lead medical students and physicians to deviate from evidence-based prescribing guidelines, increasing the risk of irrational prescribing, as well as prescribing of more expensive and non-generic drugs.

The influence of small gifts can sometimes exceed that of large gifts, because any gift creates a sense of indebtedness that compels the recipient to reciprocate, and this feeling of obligation is independent of the gift’s monetary value.

An increasing number of physicians and organizations advocate for a complete ban on physicians’ acceptance of gifts from the pharmaceutical industry, as existing partial restrictions are often ambiguous, difficult to enforce, and underestimate the potential impact of small gifts.

Restricting medical students’ and residents’ contact with pharmaceutical representatives can reduce susceptibility to influence; however, merely establishing policies is insufficient to change behavior, as effectiveness depends not only on students’ awareness of the policies but is also easily undermined by contradictory behaviors exhibited by physician role models.
Formal education for medical students is unlikely to meaningfully change their attitudes and behaviors if it conflicts with the hidden curriculum, such as observing mentors accepting gifts.

Implementation of stringent restrictions may face strong opposition from influential faculty members and organizations with industry ties; therefore, comprehensive bans may require public oversight and demonstration to be realized.

There is currently no consensus on which educational, political, or regulatory interventions are most effective, but there are emerging positive signs of progressively strengthening the boundary between the pharmaceutical industry and the medical profession.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical students and physicians be effectively educated to reduce the influence of pharmaceutical industry marketing activities on their professional judgment?
keypoints: Systematically implement education on the relationships between pharmaceutical companies and physicians, covering the characteristics of the pharmaceutical industry, drug development and market approval processes, industry influence on scientific literature, pharmaceutical marketing strategies, and their potential biases, in order to enhance the critical awareness of medical students and physicians.

Develop and rigorously enforce policies restricting contact between medical students, residents, and pharmaceutical sales representatives, ensuring that the policy content is thoroughly communicated and understood to effectively reduce the potential impact of marketing activities on professional judgment.

Medical schools and hospitals should promote and implement comprehensive prohibitions on physicians’ acceptance of gifts from the pharmaceutical industry through role-modeling, thereby preventing covert influences and prescribing biases.

Incorporate pharmaceutical marketing-related knowledge into the mandatory curriculum and include it in national medical licensing examinations to ensure that medical students’ understanding of marketing influences and their coping abilities are systematically assessed and continuously reinforced.

ethical_issues.question: Are medical students and physicians able to recognize and resist the potential influence of gifts from pharmaceutical sales representatives on their prescribing behavior?
keypoints: Medical students and physicians commonly overestimate their ability to resist the influence of pharmaceutical sales representatives’ marketing, reflecting a universal self-serving bias in which individuals overrate their own self-control and rationality.

The principle of reciprocity induces an unconscious sense of indebtedness in recipients of gifts, prompting them to adjust their prescribing behavior to reciprocate the favor; this sense of obligation is independent of the gift’s value.

Medical students’ attitudes and behaviors are profoundly shaped by physician role models, especially when they witness mentors accepting gifts; such “hidden curriculum” effects can undermine the impact of formal ethics education.

Medical students often have difficulty recognizing bias in pharmaceutical representatives’ messaging, and are more likely to lower their guard and become susceptible to marketing influence when enjoying free food and a congenial atmosphere.

title: Prescribing Placebos
case:
Dr. Gibson, a second-year family medicine resident, spends two afternoons a week working in a busy urban clinic. His attending physician, Dr. Marshall, asks him to see a patient named Ms. Wood. “She’s a challenging patient, but not in the medical sense,” she winks at him. “Just try not to spend too much time in there,” she further cautions. “A regular frequent flyer,” says one of the medical assistants handing Dr. Gibson the chart. He glances through the 3-inch thick file quickly as he walks down the hall to the examining room.
Ms. Wood has had a surprising number of medical workups for a person of 39 who is, on the whole, pretty healthy, though overweight. Two weeks before she had undergone a complete cardiac workup, including a stress test. With the exception of a finding of chronic hypertension, all of her extensive diagnostic testing has been normal. Her current medication list includes an antihypertensive and a variety of vitamin supplements. Today she says she is terribly fatigued and has some “pretty bad stomach gas” pain at night. “I just can’t seem to get out of bed these days, Doctor,” she tells him. “You’ve got to give me something to boost my energy!” Dr. Gibson performs a careful physical examination, including a complete abdominal exam, the results of which are unremarkable. He suspects, based on further discussion, that her gas pains are due to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and tells her that he will prescribe an antireflux medication. He also spends some time explaining measures she can take to minimize her reflux symptoms. “But what about my fatigue?” she complains. “You haven’t given me anything for that and it’s worse than the stomach thing!”
Dr. Gibson sympathetically agrees with her and tells her he needs to step out for a few minutes to discuss the fatigue with her regular physician, Dr. Marshall. He is firmly convinced that Ms. Wood would benefit from a psychiatric evaluation and treatment for anxiety or depression, but he has not seen any mention of either in her chart. Her blood work from two weeks ago rules out thyroid problems and anemia as possible causes for the fatigue.
“I am sure that you must have considered a psychiatric condition at some point?” queries Dr. Gibson. “Of course,” says Dr. Marshall, “but she absolutely refuses to meet with a psychiatrist and she will not take any psychiatric medications for insurance reasons. She is afraid that she will lose her life insurance if she has a documented history of being treated for depression or anxiety.
“I’ve just been giving her some herbal and vitamin therapy and occasional shots of vitamin B-12, which seem to help her energy levels," reveals Dr. Marshall, “and I’m encouraging her to exercise, of course. A B-12 shot should do the trick for a few more weeks at least,” he tells Dr. Gibson. “Go ahead and have the nurse draw it up.”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Gibson, a second-year resident in family medicine, spends two afternoons each week at a bustling urban clinic. One day, his supervising physician, Dr. Marshall, asks him to see a patient named Ms. Wood. “She’s a bit of a handful, though not because of any medical complexity,” Dr. Marshall says with a wink. “Try not to get bogged down in there,” she adds. As Dr. Gibson takes the chart, a medical assistant comments, “She’s one of our regular frequent flyers.” Glancing at the hefty three-inch file as he walks to the exam room, Dr. Gibson notes that Ms. Wood has undergone an extraordinary number of medical evaluations for someone her age—39 years old—who, apart from being overweight, appears generally healthy. Just two weeks earlier, she’d completed a comprehensive cardiac workup, including a stress test. Other than a longstanding diagnosis of chronic hypertension, all her extensive tests have returned normal results. Her medication list includes an antihypertensive and several vitamin supplements.

Today, Ms. Wood complains of severe fatigue and describes experiencing “pretty bad stomach gas” pain at night. “I just can’t get out of bed lately, Doctor,” she laments. “You have to give me something to boost my energy!” Dr. Gibson conducts a thorough physical, including a complete abdominal examination, but finds no notable abnormalities. Based on their conversation, he suspects her nighttime pain is likely due to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and tells her he’ll prescribe an antireflux medication. He takes time to explain lifestyle changes that might help alleviate her reflux. Still, Ms. Wood protests, “But what about my fatigue? You haven’t given me anything for that, and it’s worse than the stomach stuff!”

Dr. Gibson listens sympathetically and excuses himself, saying he’d like to discuss her fatigue with Dr. Marshall. He strongly suspects that Ms. Wood could benefit from psychiatric evaluation and possible treatment for anxiety or depression, but notes there’s no mention of either in her chart. Her recent lab work rules out thyroid dysfunction and anemia.

Approaching Dr. Marshall, Dr. Gibson asks, “Have you considered a psychiatric cause for her symptoms?” Dr. Marshall responds, “Absolutely, but she refuses to see a psychiatrist or take any psychiatric medications. She’s worried that having a documented history of depression or anxiety will jeopardize her life insurance coverage.”

Dr. Marshall continues, “I’ve just been giving her some herbal and vitamin therapies, and now and then a B-12 shot. They seem to perk her up a bit, and I encourage her to stay active, of course. I think another B-12 injection should keep her going for a few weeks,” she concludes. “You can have the nurse get it ready.”

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians use nonspecific treatments, such as vitamin B12 injections, to alleviate patient symptoms when no clear etiology has been identified?
keypoints: When physicians employ nonspecific treatments such as vitamin B12 injections in the absence of a definitive etiology, they must rationally weigh the anticipated benefits against potential risks to ensure the promotion of the patient’s overall well-being.

Although evidence supporting the efficacy of vitamin B12 for nonspecific fatigue is limited, its relatively high safety profile means that, given thorough assessment and when benefits outweigh burdens, such treatment does not necessarily constitute inappropriate medical practice.

The central ethical issue in this case lies in the physicians’ failure to engage in honest communication with the patient, resorting instead to deceptive practices that violate patient autonomy and undermine the trust inherent in the patient-physician relationship—concerns that are more consequential than the use of nonspecific treatment per se.

Upholding patient autonomy and preserving trust in the patient-physician relationship require that physicians openly and honestly discuss the risks, benefits, and alternatives of treatment options, obtain informed consent, and share responsibility for healthcare decisions with the patient.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians disclose the use of placebos to patients and obtain their informed consent in order to uphold patient autonomy?
keypoints: Physicians have an obligation to obtain patients’ informed consent for the use of placebos through open and honest discussions of risks, benefits, and alternative options, thereby respecting patient autonomy.
Deceiving patients by administering placebos undermines trust in the patient-physician relationship, erodes that relationship, and may potentially result in medical harm.
Fully informing patients about the possible therapeutic effects and potential adverse reactions of placebos is an ethically necessary practice.
The ethical “safe harbor” principle does not apply when patients are intentionally misled; physicians should avoid such conduct.
The attending physician’s failure to model a positive patient-physician relationship and shared responsibility in medical decision-making to the resident reflects a deficiency in professional ethics.

ethical_issues.question: Does the use of placebos in clinical practice undermine the patient-physician relationship and pose potential medical harm to the patient?
keypoints: The deceptive use of placebos undermines patient trust and erodes the foundation of the patient-physician relationship.
The breakdown of the patient-physician relationship not only affects current treatment but may also lead to long-term distrust of the healthcare system and decreased patient adherence.
Substituting placebos for effective treatments carries potential medical risks and may give rise to ethical and legal liabilities.
Physicians should respect patients’ right to informed consent and avoid resorting to deception when addressing complex challenges in patient communication.

title: Stigmatized Patients' Right to Equal Treatment
case:
Mr. Jones had always been healthy, a high school athlete and active in outdoor landscaping before becoming owner of the business. When he began to work full-time in the office, however, the long hours and decrease in physical activity began to take a toll. At 50, Mr. Jones weighed 284 pounds. For years, his physician, Dr. Kowey, had urged Mr. Jones to exercise more and change his diet in order to avoid many of the health complications associated with severe obesity. When Mr. Jones’s lipid profiles began to change for the worse, Dr. Kowey had a serious heart-to-heart with him. Mr. Jones acknowledged his need to lose weight and be more concerned about his health, but admitted that he often couldn’t force himself to refuse good food. “Hell, doc,” he said, “who wants to live to be 100 on a diet of shredded wheat and trail mix? If I can’t have a decent burger and a few beers from time to time, what’s the use of living?”
Dr. Kowey noted Mr. Jones’s lack of commitment to losing weight in his medical record and became increasingly frustrated. At one annual physical, Mr. Jones’s PSA had increased to 4.5. Dr. Kowey performed a digital rectal exam, and, when that indicated no change in the prostate, he suggested that they continue to monitor Mr. Jones’s PSA carefully.
Two years after the first elevated serum level, Mr. Jones’s PSA level was 7.5—high enough to warrant a needle biopsy. When the pathology report came back, Dr. Kowey called Mr. Jones in to inform him that he had a moderately differentiated prostate cancer with a Gleason score 4.
Dr. Kowey explained to Mr. Jones that, along with increased cardiovascular risks, obesity was also a risk factor for a variety of cancers, including prostate cancer. “Since you are at such high risk for a variety of different dangerous diseases, I’m going to suggest we watch and wait. In the meantime, I want you to commit yourself to losing weight. Then we’ll discuss surgery and other options.”
Shaken by the news of his diagnosis, Mr. Jones set up a diet based on what Dr. Kowey had been urging him to do for so long and even established a mild exercise regimen. He also researched prostate cancer on the Internet and was concerned to see that, at age 52, he was more likely to have an aggressive form of prostate cancer. Though he found a “watchful waiting” approach mentioned in several places, he got the impression that such therapy was reserved for older patients with less aggressive cancers.
During his next visit, Mr. Jones told Dr. Kowey about his diet and exercise and then brought up the research findings he had discovered on the Internet. Dr. Kowey was surprised and pleased. “Well,” he said. “The news seems to have jolted you into taking some responsibility for your own health.”
case_rewrite:
Mr. Jones had always enjoyed robust health. In high school, he was an athlete and later worked for years outdoors in landscaping before eventually owning the business. However, once he transitioned to full-time office work, the long hours and reduced physical activity began to affect his well-being. By age 50, Mr. Jones’s weight had climbed to 284 pounds. For several years, his physician, Dr. Kowey, had encouraged him to adopt healthier eating habits and exercise more, warning about the many health risks associated with severe obesity. When Mr. Jones’s cholesterol and lipid profiles began to deteriorate, Dr. Kowey sat down with him for a candid conversation. Mr. Jones acknowledged that he needed to lose weight and take better care of his health but confessed that resisting tempting foods was a struggle for him. “Honestly, doc,” he said, “who wants to live to be 100 if it means eating nothing but shredded wheat and trail mix? If I can’t have a good burger and a couple of beers now and then, what’s the point?”

Dr. Kowey documented Mr. Jones’s ongoing ambivalence about weight loss in his medical notes, feeling mounting frustration as time went on. At Mr. Jones’s next annual physical, his PSA level had risen to 4.5. Dr. Kowey performed a digital rectal exam, finding no changes in the prostate, and recommended that they continue monitoring the PSA closely.

Two years later, Mr. Jones’s PSA had increased further, reaching 7.5—enough to justify a needle biopsy. The pathology report revealed a moderately differentiated prostate cancer with a Gleason score of 4. Dr. Kowey called Mr. Jones into the office to deliver the diagnosis.

During their conversation, Dr. Kowey explained that, in addition to higher cardiovascular risks, obesity is also associated with increased risks for several cancers, including prostate cancer. “Given that you’re at especially high risk for a range of serious diseases, my recommendation is that we take a watch-and-wait approach for now. In the meantime, I’d like you to make a real commitment to losing weight. Once you’ve done that, we can revisit surgery and other treatment options.”

The news of his cancer diagnosis deeply unsettled Mr. Jones. Motivated, he started following a diet similar to what Dr. Kowey had been urging for years and incorporated some light exercise into his daily routine. He also spent time researching prostate cancer online and was troubled to learn that, at 52, he was at greater risk for having a more aggressive form of the disease. While he found references to “watchful waiting,” he noticed that this approach was often reserved for older patients with less aggressive cancers.

At his next appointment, Mr. Jones reported his changes in diet and activity level to Dr. Kowey and shared some of the information he had found in his research. Dr. Kowey was both surprised and pleased at Mr. Jones’s new resolve. “It looks like this news has finally given you the push to start taking responsibility for your health,” he remarked.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians require patients to lose weight as a precondition for receiving medical treatment?
keypoints: Physicians should not make weight loss a prerequisite for patients to receive treatment, as this attributes health problems to personal failings and may lead to a lack of empathy and unjust medical discrimination against obese individuals.

Linking medical services to weight loss lacks sufficient medical justification and overlooks the low success rates of weight loss interventions as well as the complex socioeconomic factors underlying obesity; this is analogous to requiring impoverished individuals to become wealthy before accessing care.

Clinical practice should avoid imposing separate and stringent treatment thresholds on obese patients, as such practices constitute weight bias and are inconsistent with the standards applied to other common risk factors such as smoking, alcohol abuse, and physical inactivity.

The fundamental goal of modern medicine is to provide equitable and non-discriminatory care to all patients in need; medical decisions should be based on scientific evidence and the patient’s overall health status rather than on non-medically relevant personal characteristics.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians minimize the impact of weight bias while emphasizing the importance of healthy behavior change when treating obese patients?
keypoints: Physicians should cultivate self-awareness of potential weight bias that may unintentionally influence clinical decision-making, and avoid making assumptions about patients’ character, health status, or lifestyle based solely on body weight.

Physicians should acknowledge the difficulty of achieving sustainable and significant weight loss, and understand the multifactorial complexity of obesity, including physiological, psychological, and social-environmental factors.

Physicians should approach patients with empathy, recognizing that patients may have previously experienced weight bias in healthcare settings, and should respect individual differences and patients’ efforts.

Physicians should emphasize healthy behavior change and comprehensive health management, rather than focusing solely on weight loss metrics, and should recognize the significant health benefits that can result from modest weight loss and lifestyle modifications.

Physicians should conduct a comprehensive assessment of patients’ health status, exploring all relevant etiologies beyond body weight, to ensure that treatment plans are individualized and multidimensional.

title: Disagreement over Resuscitation
case:
After trying for 4 years to have a child, Jane and her husband, George, were thrilled when Jane became pregnant. The couple considered Jasmine a “miracle baby.” Just after her first birthday, Jasmine fell down the stairs of the family’s third-floor apartment and suffered serious head trauma. The injury, coupled with prolonged hypoxemia following the fall, left Jasmine with severe mental and physical handicaps—she was unable to walk or speak coherently, suffered from seizures, and lost her vision. Jane and George coped with this sudden, devastating situation as best they could, but caring for Jasmine was a hardship. George, a bank teller, began to work extra shifts to help pay for the medical bills. Jane left gainful employment so she could provide 24-hour care for Jasmine.
A year after Jasmine’s accident, Jane found that she was pregnant again. This time the pregnancy was not a uniformly joyous event; both Jane and George worried about how they would manage, financially and emotionally, having another child. With the help of George’s health insurance coverage, Jane was able to have routine visits with her obstetrician-gynecologist, Dr. Hearth. Dr. Hearth, who had overseen Jane’s first pregnancy and had become quite close to her family, understood Jane’s concerns and had been thorough in monitoring this pregnancy.
Twenty-four weeks into her pregnancy, Jane felt a dull, aching pain in her stomach and lower back that quickly progressed to contractions. She called George at work and together they went by ambulance to the hospital. Terbutaline therapy was started immediately in an attempt to stop the contractions, but Jane soon developed severe hypotension, and therapy was discontinued. When Dr. Hearth arrived at the hospital she had a chance to speak with the couple. She stated that, since Jane’s membranes had ruptured, it would be dangerous to continue trying to stall labor. She spoke at length with the Jane and her husband about the prognosis for children born at 24 weeks; many of the possible outcomes reminded them of the limitations that Jasmine faced on a daily basis. The couple told Dr. Hearth that unless the baby was born “alive and vigorous,” they did not want him to be resuscitated.
Jane was given oxytocin to induce labor, and Dr. Hearth oversaw the birth of a 652-gram, cyanotic boy with a weak, slow heartbeat and an extremely slow respiratory rate. His Apgar score at 1 minute was 4. Dr. Hearth was mindful of the parents’ wishes, but, as she stood there over the infant, she believed that it would be morally wrong to let him die. She quickly intubated the baby and sent him to NICU, while informing George about the baby’s status. He became both distraught and enraged. Half-crying, he demanded to know why the child had been resuscitated and requested that the breathing tube be removed immediately. When Dr. Hearth went to check on the baby, his Apgar scores had improved to a 6. Though he had moderately diminished reflexes, he seemed to Dr. Hearth to be doing as well as other infants she had delivered at 24 weeks.
case_rewrite:
After four years of hoping to start a family, Jane and her husband, George, were overjoyed when Jane finally became pregnant. To them, their daughter Jasmine was a “miracle baby.” But tragedy struck just after Jasmine’s first birthday: she tumbled down the stairs of their third-floor apartment, suffering a severe head injury. The trauma, combined with a prolonged period of low oxygen, left Jasmine profoundly disabled—she lost her vision, was unable to walk or speak coherently, suffered frequent seizures, and required constant care. Jane and George did their best to cope with their new reality, but Jasmine’s needs were overwhelming. George, who worked as a bank teller, began taking extra shifts to keep up with mounting medical bills. Jane left her job to care for Jasmine around the clock.

A year after Jasmine’s accident, Jane discovered she was pregnant again. This time, the news brought more anxiety than joy. Both Jane and George worried about how they would manage another child—financially and emotionally—given their experience with Jasmine’s needs. With George’s health insurance, Jane was able to attend regular appointments with her obstetrician-gynecologist, Dr. Hearth, who had been with them through Jane’s first pregnancy and had grown close to the family. Dr. Hearth was attentive to Jane’s worries, carefully monitoring her throughout the pregnancy.

At twenty-four weeks, Jane developed a dull, persistent pain in her abdomen and lower back, which quickly escalated to contractions. She called George at work, and together they rode by ambulance to the hospital. Doctors started terbutaline to stop the labor, but Jane soon developed severe hypotension, forcing them to discontinue the therapy. When Dr. Hearth arrived, she spoke at length with Jane and George. She explained that Jane’s membranes had ruptured, making it dangerous to try to delay labor any longer. Dr. Hearth outlined the likely prognosis for babies born at 24 weeks, describing outcomes that painfully echoed Jasmine’s daily struggles. After a long conversation, Jane and George told Dr. Hearth that if their baby was not “alive and vigorous” at birth, they did not want any resuscitation efforts made.

Labor was induced with oxytocin, and Dr. Hearth delivered a 652-gram baby boy. He was cyanotic, with a weak and slow heartbeat and barely perceptible breaths. His Apgar score at one minute was 4. Standing over the tiny, struggling infant, Dr. Hearth considered the parents’ wishes, but felt deeply that to let him die would be morally wrong. She rapidly intubated him and transferred him to the NICU, then updated George on the situation. George, already distraught, became inconsolable and angry, demanding to know why his son had been resuscitated and insisting that the breathing tube be removed immediately. Later, when Dr. Hearth checked on the baby, she found that his Apgar scores had improved to 6. Although his reflexes were somewhat diminished, he seemed, in Dr. Hearth’s experience, to be doing as well as other 24-week infants she had cared for.

ethical_issues.question: Why did the physician and Jasmine’s parents arrive at fundamentally different conclusions regarding her resuscitation, despite both engaging in rational decision-making and acting in accordance with their ethical convictions?
keypoints: This case presents a moral dilemma arising from conflicts among core ethical principles—such as beneficence, nonmaleficence, autonomy, and justice—that cannot all be fully satisfied; decision-makers must choose a course of action that best aligns with the principles they prioritize most highly.

The healthcare team may believe that withholding resuscitation is not in the best interests of the newborn, emphasizing the ethical principle of beneficence and advocating for the infant’s welfare, potentially holding different views from the parents regarding what constitutes an acceptable quality of life.

Clinicians may also consider that parents, due to the emotional and informational challenges of the prenatal period, may not be able to make a fully informed decision about resuscitation, and that decisions should be guided by the infant’s actual condition at birth.

In applying the best interest standard, Jane and George incorporate not only the potential future quality of life for their newborn son but also the overall impact on their family, drawing on their lived experience caring for their severely disabled daughter to make a realistic and holistic assessment of their son’s prospective quality of life.
