title: Autonomy and Public Health: When the Patient Is a Physician
case:
Twenty-four hours after his visit to the internal medicine clinic, Luc was not surprised to discover a raised swelling on the inside of his forearm where the PPD test for tuberculosis had been administered. During his childhood in France he had received the Bacillus Calmette-Guerin TB vaccine. Then midway through the first year of his emergency medicine residency he was diagnosed with a case of active pulmonary TB, most likely acquired from patient exposure. Following his diagnosis, Luc took a leave of absence until chest x-rays confirmed his response to drug therapy. Now returning to finish his intern year, he was still required by hospital policy to receive an annual tuberculin skin test despite his past medical history and the likelihood of a false positive result.
“I’ve had positive skin tests before so I’m not worried,” Luc said later that day over lunch, after he and 2 friends, also residents, claimed a table in the back corner of the cafeteria. “I just wish I could shake this cold—I haven’t been able to run much lately. But anyway,” he continued, “my last x-ray 6 months ago was fine and I don’t want to alarm anyone at the clinic by telling them the skin test was positive. I mean isn’t that what you’d expect?”
“Wait a minute Luc,” Sriranjani, a third-year emergency resident, interrupted. “You really need to have another x-ray just to make sure. Are you saying you’re not going to follow through with that?”
“Well, I don’t really want to,” Luc replied, pausing for a moment to cough. “Sorry about that,” he continued. “I’m already behind because I took time off. Besides, I really don’t want to start taking meds again. The side effects are not something I want to go through a second time, especially when I really think medication isn’t needed. I mean come on,” he said, pausing to cough again deeply. “I had TB but it’s fine now—I don’t want to be taking isoniazid at 6-month intervals for the next 4 years just because some doctor at the clinic gets nervous.”
“Luc,” Sriranjani started cautiously, “how long have you been coughing?”
“Sri, please!” Luc exclaimed. “Don’t start with that. I just have a bit of a cold. I’m fine!”
“Any pleuritic chest pain? Night sweats?” asked Dr. Theophilus, the third member of the group, and a second-year resident.
“Will you 2 stop trying to diagnose me?” Luc asked, tossing a wadded-up napkin onto his half-empty plate in exasperation. “So I’m coughing and it’s a little tight when I breathe. I have a cold! You know, those things called viruses? If I go in and make a big deal about this,” he said, gesturing to his arm, “they might start me on meds again and I don’t want that. I’m fine, trust me, and I’d really appreciate it if you both just stay quiet about this. I had an x-ray 6 months ago and I don’t have time to get another one right now so I’m just not going to mention the PPD [purified protein derivative skin test] results. Once this cold goes away,” he paused, coughing again, “I’ll be fine!”
case_rewrite:
A day after his appointment at the internal medicine clinic, Luc noticed a raised bump on his inner forearm where the PPD test for tuberculosis had been placed. This didn’t surprise him; as a child in France, he had received the Bacillus Calmette-Guerin TB vaccine. During the first year of his emergency medicine residency, Luc had been diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis, most likely contracted through patient exposure. After his diagnosis, he had taken a leave of absence until chest x-rays confirmed that his treatment was effective. Now, as he resumed his intern year, hospital policy still required him to undergo an annual tuberculin skin test, despite his history and the high likelihood of a false positive.

Over lunch later that day, Luc sat with two friends, also residents, at a quiet table in the back of the cafeteria. “I’ve had positive skin tests before so I’m not worried,” Luc said, pushing his tray aside. “I just wish I could shake this cold—I haven’t been able to run much lately. Anyway, my last x-ray six months ago was clear, and I don’t want to make a fuss at the clinic by mentioning a positive skin test. Isn’t that what you’d expect?”

Sriranjani, a third-year emergency resident, cut in. “Luc, you really should get another x-ray just to be sure. Are you saying you’re not going to follow up?”

Luc hesitated, then shrugged. “Honestly, I don’t want to. I’m already behind from taking time off. Plus, I really don’t want to go back on meds. The side effects were rough last time, and I don’t think I need them again. Seriously,” he said, pausing to cough, “I had TB but it’s resolved. I don’t want to keep taking isoniazid every six months for the next several years just because someone in the clinic is anxious.”

Sriranjani eyed him carefully. “Luc, how long have you been coughing?”

“Sri, please,” Luc replied, exasperated. “Don’t start. It’s just a cold. I’m fine.”

Dr. Theophilus, the third member of their group and a second-year resident, spoke up: “Any pleuritic chest pain? Night sweats?”

Luc tossed a crumpled napkin onto his plate, frustration clear in his expression. “Can you two stop trying to diagnose me? Yeah, I’m coughing and my chest feels a bit tight when I breathe, but that’s what happens with a cold. Look, if I go in and make a big deal out of this”—he motioned to his arm—“they might put me back on meds, and I really don’t want that. I’m fine, really, and I’d appreciate it if you both kept this to yourselves. My last x-ray was only six months ago, and I don’t have time right now for more tests. I’m not going to mention the PPD result. Once this cold passes”—he broke off, coughing again—“I’ll be back to normal.”

ethical_issues.question: Do Luc’s colleagues have a responsibility to report his symptoms to the hospital’s occupational health department if he refuses to do so himself?
keypoints: Colleagues should first respect Luc’s wishes, providing him with the opportunity to voluntarily report his symptoms and cooperate with medical evaluation, while engaging in thorough communication and counseling.

Physicians have a responsibility to attend to patient health and public safety; especially when facing potentially communicable diseases, they must carefully balance personal privacy with the interests of the public.
Pulmonary tuberculosis is a serious and highly infectious disease; physicians are obligated to promptly report and follow up on symptoms that may endanger the health of patients and the public.

If Luc refuses to voluntarily report his symptoms or cooperate, his colleagues should clearly inform him that they will report his symptoms to the hospital’s occupational health department in order to safeguard patient and workplace safety.

Reporting and following up on Luc’s symptoms are necessary measures to prevent the spread of infectious diseases and to protect the safety of emergency department patients and colleagues, reflecting the professional responsibilities of medicine.

Professional medical responsibility requires physicians to prioritize the health and safety of patients and the public, to assume corresponding ethical and legal obligations, and to ensure the safety and trustworthiness of the clinical environment.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with a colleague who may pose a threat to patient health, do physicians have an obligation to prioritize patient safety over the wishes of their colleague?
keypoints: The professional responsibilities of physicians require that they always place the health and safety of patients as the highest priority, even when this may conflict with the personal wishes of their colleagues.

Given the highly contagious nature and severe life-threatening risk of tuberculosis, physicians have a duty to promptly report and follow up on any possible symptoms in order to prevent harm to patients and public health.

When suspecting that a colleague may have a communicable disease, it is appropriate first to offer them the opportunity to self-report and cooperate with medical evaluation, respecting their privacy and autonomy.

If the colleague refuses to cooperate, it should be made clear that their symptoms will be reported to the hospital’s occupational health department or relevant authorities to ensure the safety of patients and the public.

The purpose of reporting is to protect patient and public health, not to punish the colleague; such actions should be grounded in respect, empathy, and professional ethics, emphasizing that this is a necessary safeguard for medical safety.

Healthcare professionals should balance the individual rights of colleagues with patient safety, ensuring that while protecting patient health, they also strive to maintain the dignity and trust of their colleagues.

title: Changing the Rules in Times of Crisis: Do Desperate Times Allow Desperate Measures?
case:
Dr. Green hadn’t slept in 38 hours. An as-yet-unidentified respiratory virus had overloaded the medicine service at the hospital where she was on staff, and, if the news reports were any indication, there was no end in sight. Preliminary reports suggested the infection could be related to severe acute respiratory syndrome, or SARS, but global medical communication had so far failed to establish anything beyond the fact that the virus was highly contagious, with devastating mortality and morbidity statistics. Roughly 10 percent of those who acquired it would die while another 10 percent would suffer brain damage as a consequence of the raging fevers the disease induced. Neither statistic seemed to be affected by supportive measures, but at the moment nothing else could be done.
Bleary-eyed, the doctor almost didn’t see the man waiting for her outside the room of one of her patients. “Dr. Green, Dr. Green,” he said, a note of panic in his voice as he moved away from the wall against which he had been leaning. “Dr. Green, I know everyone is doing all they can, but my wife is getting worse. She’s delirious now, with that fever you were telling us about.”
“I’m so sorry, Mr. Patterson,” she said as she moved to open the door. “I need to examine her again and work on getting that fever down. We’re doing everything we can to stabilize her condition.”
“That’s just it,” Mr. Patterson replied as he followed her into the room. “I know how hard you’re working, but this is my wife! She’s never been sick like this ever. And we have 3 children at home—she just has to get better. I’ve been doing some reading and something called interferon seemed to help with SARS. Everyone keeps telling me this is like SARS, and even if it’s not, interferon is a powerful antiviral medication, isn’t it? It could work, couldn’t it?”
The doctor stopped and turned back toward the door as she pulled on the gown and gloves of respiratory isolation. “Mr. Patterson, I know you want your wife to get better,” she said, “but we can’t just start treating her with every antiviral in the pharmacy. Interferon is a powerful drug with many potential side effects. No one knows what it might do in a case like this or how it might react with the other medications your wife needs to keep her fever down. We can’t start experimenting on patients to find out.”
“But why not?” Mr. Patterson asked. “Right now she’s dying—you warned us about what a fever that high could mean. She’s a fighter, my wife, and I know if she could talk to you she would want to try anything, even if it might not work. I know I want you to. If it gives her even a chance it’s worth the risk—it can’t be worse than dying, can it?”
“But Mr. Patterson,” she started to say.
“Please, won’t you try?” he interrupted. “She’s dying! Can’t you make an exception when someone is dying?”
case_rewrite:
Dr. Green hadn’t slept in 38 hours. The medicine service at her hospital was overwhelmed by an unidentified respiratory virus, and news outlets offered little hope that things would improve soon. Preliminary findings hinted at a possible link to severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), but worldwide medical experts had yet to pinpoint the origin or nature of the illness. What was clear was the virus’s terrifying virulence: it spread easily, and the toll was grim—one in ten infected patients died, and another ten percent developed brain damage from relentless, high fevers. For now, supportive care was all anyone could provide, though it seemed to make little difference.

Exhausted, Dr. Green nearly missed the figure standing outside the room of one of her patients. “Dr. Green, Dr. Green,” the man called, his voice edged with panic as he stepped away from the wall. “Dr. Green, I know everyone’s working hard, but my wife is getting worse. She’s delirious now with that fever you warned us about.”

“I’m so sorry, Mr. Patterson,” Dr. Green said, moving toward the door. “I need to check on her and try again to bring her fever down. We’re doing everything we can to keep her stable.”

“That’s just it,” Mr. Patterson replied, trailing closely behind her as she entered the room. “I know you’re trying, but this is my wife. She’s never been this sick before, and we have three children at home—she has to pull through. I’ve been reading, and it sounds like interferon helped people with SARS. Everyone keeps saying this virus is similar, and even if it isn’t exactly the same, interferon is supposed to be a strong antiviral, right? Couldn’t it help her?”

Pausing to don a gown and gloves for respiratory isolation, Dr. Green turned to him. “Mr. Patterson, I understand how much you want your wife to recover,” she said gently, “but we can’t just give her any antiviral medication we have. Interferon is a powerful drug with serious potential side effects. We don’t know what it would do in this situation, or how it might interact with the medications we’re using to control her fever. We can’t simply try untested treatments on patients.”

“But why not?” Mr. Patterson pressed, desperation rising in his voice. “She’s dying—you said yourself how dangerous these fevers are. My wife is a fighter, and I know if she could speak, she’d tell you to try anything, even if it’s risky. I want you to try. If there’s even a small chance, isn’t it worth it? It can’t be worse than dying, can it?”

“But Mr. Patterson—” Dr. Green began.

“Please,” he interrupted, his voice breaking. “She’s dying! Can’t you make an exception for her now?”

ethical_issues.question: In emergency situations, is it ethically permissible to temporarily override the principle of informed consent in order to pursue experimental treatment based on the principle of beneficence?
keypoints: In emergency and life-threatening situations, the principle of beneficence may temporarily supersede informed consent to a certain extent, but this must be balanced with the principle of nonmaleficence and ethical prudence.
Experimental treatments should be conducted within a scientific research framework, as the outcomes of using investigational drugs in single cases have limited value for both the patient and society.

Prior to implementing experimental therapy, potential risks and possible benefits must be carefully weighed to ensure that decisions are grounded in ethical principles, scientific evidence, and the patient’s best interests.

ethical_issues.question: Should randomized controlled trials be promoted during infectious disease outbreaks or in the context of rare, fatal diseases to validate the efficacy of experimental treatments?
keypoints: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) represent the gold standard for evaluating drug efficacy and should be actively promoted and conducted even during outbreak situations or in the context of rare, life-threatening diseases.

Experimental treatments must be implemented within a scientifically rigorous research framework, avoiding ad hoc clinical attempts, to ensure the acquisition of reliable data, safeguard patient safety, and render the results meaningful for both the patient population and society at large.

Globally, mechanisms and preparedness should be established and enhanced to enable the rapid initiation of large-scale randomized controlled trials during epidemics, thereby addressing the public health challenges posed by emerging or re-emerging infectious diseases.

title: To Scan or Not To Scan?
case:
As a fourth-year medical student planning a residency in internal medicine, Rose enjoyed her rotation in the emergency room and saw it as a chance to learn practical points about patient management. She purposely chose Percy Hospital because of its diverse patient population.
One evening Rose was working with Dr. Charles, a respected attending who had been at Percy for almost 10 years. Dr. Charles handed her a chart. “Twenty-two-year-old male with abdominal pain, Rose. See him in Room 15 and then present him to me.”
Fifteen minutes later, Rose returned with her note and a radiology order form in hand. “Twenty-two-year-old male, no previous medical history, presents with abdominal pain that started this morning as crampy and diffuse and localized to the right lower quadrant over the past 2 hours,” she reported to Dr. Charles. “He’s febrile to 102, slightly tachycardic, with rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. His white blood cell count is 16 000 with a left shift. Sounds exactly like the patient with a possible appendicitis that we sent to CT this afternoon; want to sign this order form so I can send him too?”
Dr. Charles hesitated. “What does this gentleman do for work?” he inquired. Rose replied that he worked as a cashier in his family’s grocery store. “Does he have insurance?” Now it was Rose’s turn to hesitate: “He mentioned that he didn’t, but I reassured him that we would make sure that he gets the medical care he needs.”
“I’ll take a look at him to confirm your findings. Then, why don’t we call the surgeons and tell them that this patient needs to go to the operating room?” offered Dr. Charles. He looked up from another patient’s chart to meet Rose’s confused stare. “CT can be helpful for the diagnosis of appendicitis, but it’s not the standard of care. This kid’s family would have to swallow the cost; $1500 is a lot of night shifts at the grocery—or an uncompensated loss for the hospital. We can save the family the trouble—and save ourselves a potentially inconclusive scan—by trusting our clinical intuition and calling the surgeons now.”
case_rewrite:
Rose, a fourth-year medical student with plans to pursue a residency in internal medicine, thoroughly enjoyed her emergency room rotation and valued the opportunity to gain hands-on experience in patient management. She had specifically chosen Percy Hospital for her rotation, drawn by its reputation for serving a diverse community.

One evening, Rose was paired with Dr. Charles, a well-regarded attending physician who had spent nearly a decade working at Percy. Dr. Charles handed her a patient chart and said, “Rose, we have a twenty-two-year-old male with abdominal pain in Room 15. Please see him and present your findings to me afterward.”

After spending fifteen minutes with the patient, Rose returned, bringing her written note and a radiology order form. She reported, “This is a twenty-two-year-old man with no significant past medical history, presenting with abdominal pain that began this morning as crampy and diffuse, and has shifted to the right lower quadrant in the past two hours. He’s running a fever of 102 degrees, has a slight tachycardia, and there’s rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. His white blood cell count is 16,000 with a left shift. It’s very similar to the earlier case of possible appendicitis that we sent to CT today. Would you like to sign this order so I can send him as well?”

Dr. Charles paused before responding. “What does he do for work?” he asked. Rose replied, “He works as a cashier in his family’s grocery store.” Dr. Charles continued, “Does he have insurance?” Rose hesitated, then answered, “He told me he doesn’t, but I reassured him that we’ll make sure he gets the medical care he needs.”

Dr. Charles nodded. “Let me examine him myself to confirm your findings. After that, let’s call the surgeons and let them know this patient needs to go to the operating room.” He glanced up from another chart to catch Rose’s uncertain expression. “CT scans can help diagnose appendicitis, but they aren’t always necessary. In this case, the clinical picture is straightforward. If we order the scan, his family could be stuck with a $1500 bill—that’s a lot of extra shifts at the grocery store, or a financial loss the hospital might have to absorb. We can spare them that expense—and avoid a potentially inconclusive result—by relying on our clinical judgment and getting the surgeons involved now.”

ethical_issues.question: When caring for uninsured patients, should physicians adjust diagnostic and treatment plans based on the patient’s financial situation to avoid costly investigations?
keypoints: It is ethically acceptable and necessary to reasonably adjust diagnostic and treatment plans based on the patient’s financial situation in order to avoid unnecessary and costly investigations.
Developing a streamlined care plan for uninsured patients when clinical presentation is classic and clinical suspicion is high is a rational and resource-efficient strategy.
The physician’s attention to the patient’s financial burden reflects respect for and concern about the patient’s social context and overall health status.
Clinical decision-making should balance medical evidence, patient interests, and societal resources, avoiding overutilization while ensuring patients receive necessary care.

title: The Pitfalls of Drug Company Sample Use
case:
Dr. Sentzer takes pride in keeping her office free of pharmaceutical advertisements. She refuses pens and paper plastered with drug company logos. She does not attend dinners sponsored by pharmaceutical companies, even when they are at her favorite French bistro. And she does not see company representatives—nor accept their free medication samples.
In preparation for her afternoon appointments, Dr. Sentzer reviews the chart for the first patient—Martha Lodge, a 72-year-old woman whom Dr. Sentzer sees regularly. Martha takes several medications but manages them meticulously. She does not welcome changes to this regimen, as it complicates her daily routine and her monthly budget. But she tends to follow Dr. Sentzer’s advice faithfully.
Dr. Sentzer enters the exam room and is greeted by a relieved and grateful smile from Martha. “Thank you for squeezing me in, doctor,” she dives in immediately. “I hate to bother you when I’m doing well, but I really need your help. Do you remember how we changed my blood pressure medicines at my last visit? Because I was—well, you remember—not making it to the bathroom in time? I’m afraid the change didn’t help at all.”
“I’m sorry to hear that, Martha,” replied Dr. Sentzer.
Martha continued: “The exercises are no help either, doctor. I can’t go out with my husband for dinner or with my friends to a movie because if I laugh too hard…. Even at home, sometimes I suddenly need to go, but I can’t always get to the bathroom in time. Can you help me?”
Dr. Sentzer does have a solution, but she knows it is not what Martha wants to hear. “There are medications I could prescribe—to calm down your bladder. They might give you more control. But it would add another medication to your pillbox. And the once-daily pill only comes as a brand name, so it wouldn’t be a cheap addition.”
“Dr. Sentzer,” said Martha, crestfallen, “there really isn’t room in our budget for another brand name drug. Between my husband’s pension and our Social Security, we barely cover our medicines already. Some of my friends say that their doctors give them free samples to cut down their costs. Could I at least start with some samples to see if it works for me?”
The frustration on Martha’s face wins Dr. Sentzer’s sympathy. She does recall turning away a salesman for one of these medicines just last week; he managed to leave his business card, but she refused to accept the free samples that he wanted to leave with her.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Sentzer has always taken a firm stance against the influence of pharmaceutical marketing in her medical practice. She keeps her office clear of branded notepads and pens, declines invitations to industry-sponsored dinners—even when they’re hosted at the charming French bistro she loves—and steadfastly refuses to meet with drug representatives or accept their complimentary medication samples.

On this particular afternoon, Dr. Sentzer sits at her desk preparing for her next appointment by reviewing the chart of Martha Lodge, a 72-year-old patient who visits her regularly. Martha is diligent with her medication regimen, managing several prescriptions with care. Any changes to her routine unsettle her, both because of the complexity and the strain on her fixed monthly budget. Nevertheless, she has always trusted and followed Dr. Sentzer’s guidance.

When Dr. Sentzer enters the exam room, Martha greets her with a look of relief and gratitude. “Thank you for fitting me in, doctor,” Martha says, quickly getting to the point. “I hate to bother you when things are mostly okay, but I need your help. Remember when we changed my blood pressure meds last time because I was having… well, accidents before I could get to the bathroom? I’m afraid the switch didn’t help at all.”

“I’m sorry to hear that, Martha,” Dr. Sentzer replies gently.

Martha sighs. “The exercises you suggested haven’t made a difference either. I can’t risk going out with my husband for dinner, or to the movies with friends, because if I laugh too hard… Even at home, I sometimes just can’t make it in time. Is there anything else you can do?”

Dr. Sentzer considers her options. There are medications available that could relax Martha’s bladder and help her regain some control. But she knows these drugs come only as brand-name prescriptions, and the once-daily pill would add another item to Martha’s already crowded pillbox—not to mention a significant cost.

“Martha,” Dr. Sentzer says carefully, “there is a medication that might help you. But it would mean taking another pill every day, and unfortunately, it’s only available as a brand-name drug, so it’s expensive.”

Martha’s face falls. “Doctor, we just can’t afford another brand-name prescription. My husband’s pension and our Social Security barely cover what we’re already paying for my medicines. Some of my friends say their doctors give them free samples when they can’t pay for a new drug. Could you give me a few samples so I can at least see if it works?”

Dr. Sentzer feels a pang of sympathy as she sees Martha’s frustration and embarrassment. She remembers just last week when she refused to accept free samples from a pharmaceutical representative who had stopped by to promote this exact medication—leaving only his business card behind as Dr. Sentzer declined the samples he offered.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians accept free medication samples from pharmaceutical companies to assist patients who cannot afford their prescriptions?
keypoints: Drug samples are essentially promotional tools employed by pharmaceutical companies, typically consisting of expensive, brand-name medications that may lead patients to long-term use of unaffordable prescriptions rather than providing genuine financial assistance.

The direct distribution of samples by physicians lacks the medication safety checks and counseling routinely performed by pharmacists during dispensing, thereby posing potential risks to medication safety.
Pharmaceutical assistance programs offer eligible patients formal and sustainable avenues for medication access, representing a more economical and long-term effective solution compared to samples.
The availability of low-cost generic drugs provides patients with effective and affordable alternatives that should be prioritized.

Compared to physicians’ direct sample distribution, assistance methods such as pharmacy vouchers that dispense medications in appropriate quantities are more standardized and cost-effective, contributing to improved medication safety and reduced financial burden for patients.

ethical_issues.question: Do pharmaceutical company drug samples inadvertently influence physicians’ prescribing decisions, resulting in patients using unnecessary or unaffordable medications?
keypoints: Drug samples are often expensive, newly marketed medications, which may lead physicians to subsequently prescribe the same drugs, thereby imposing unnecessary or unaffordable medication costs on patients.
Drug samples are misused as a stopgap measure to patch deficiencies in the healthcare system, when in reality they serve as an effective promotional tool for pharmaceutical companies.
Direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical advertising may exacerbate the influence of samples on physicians’ prescribing decisions and patients’ medication choices.

The purported dilemma of “samples or no medication” faced by physicians is a false dichotomy; if pharmaceutical companies were genuinely concerned about patients’ medication needs, they would provide pharmacy vouchers for medications in appropriate quantities rather than promotional free samples.

title: Ethics Expertise and Cultural Competence
case:
Mrs. Ramsarathan was brought to the hospital by her son-in-law. She had arrived in America 2 days earlier from her remote village in India in anticipation of the birth of her first grandchild. Soon after arriving, Mrs. Ramsarathan's family noticed that she was unable to keep down much, if any, food. Though they had avoided the American medical system in the time they had been in this country, the family was frightened at her continued vomiting and took her to the hospital.
With the help of a translator, the primary team at the hospital was able to gather Mrs. Ramsarathan's story. She had rarely seen a doctor during her lifetime. She spoke no English and had never learned to read. She said she had begun developing difficulty eating certain foods 6 months earlier, and the problem seemed to get progressively worse.
A gastroenterologist, Dr. Ellamjeet, was consulted. Before emigrating to the US to complete his training, Dr. Ellamjeet had gone to medical school in India and was fluent in the same dialect as Mrs. Ramsarathan, which was a great comfort to her. She was still visibly unsettled by her surroundings. While a translator was intermittently available for the primary team, it soon became clear that Mrs. Ramsarathan and especially her family wished for Dr. Ellamjeet to be her primary doctor.
Mrs. Ramsarathan's son-in-law, who emerged as the spokesperson for the family, was concerned that the tests would reveal a serious diagnosis and asked Dr. Ellamjeet not to tell his mother-in-law directly, but to allow him and the other decision makers in the family to decide when, and how, and to what extent to communicate the diagnosis to Mrs. Ramsarathan. A limited work-up revealed, as suspected, a mass highly suspicious for advanced carcinoma. Mrs. Ramsarathan's son-in-law believed, and Dr. Ellamjeet concurred, that frankly revealing a dire diagnosis in these surroundings would not be in her best interest.
Dr. Ellamjeet explained this to the primary team. "This kind of information is not something that is forced upon the patient in this culture. It would be doubly cruel to her. Not only would she find out that she is dying, but she would find out in a way that is completely foreign to her, deprived of traditional, subtle ways and cues of expressing and accepting death. It would be to foist the entire burden of this knowledge on her and not let her family carry the burden for her in the way they are accustomed. The humane thing is to do what the family wants—let them care for her as they would if she were back home."
Members of Mrs. Ramsarathan's care team wanted a better sense of her prognosis and what treatment options she would be forgoing if they accepted Dr. Ellamjeet's suggestion. They consulted Dr. Cameron Michaels of the surgical oncology team. Dr. Michaels expressed his conviction that Mrs. Ramsarathan ought to be told her likely diagnosis and said that he would not treat her unless she knew what her diagnosis and treatment options were. Furthermore, he would not treat her if she wholly deferred medical decision making to her son-in-law. "While the overall benefits of the treatments I can offer her in terms of longevity and pain relief might outweigh the harms, to inflict those known harms on her (eg, the probable side effects of chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation) without her knowing why it was being done would be inhumane. There is a world of difference, at least as I see it, between enduring the costs of a treatment as a necessary evil in view of some greater good and suffering through that evil for no known reason. I refuse to walk into her room after putting her through one of these therapies and have her look up at me with eyes that say, Why are you doing this to me?'"
Facing an impasse, the primary team discussed calling for an ethics consult. They approached Dr. Ellamjeet who responded, "If you need to get an ethics consult for legal reasons to protect the hospital and physicians or to ensure that there is no misunderstanding, I understand. But simply from the perspective of the best interest of this patient, Mrs. Ramsarathan, no ethics consult is going to be informative. I don't consider myself an ethicist, but, having been down this road with patients from this part of India many times, I can confidently say that I have a better grasp of Mrs. Ramsarathan's interests than would a Western-educated ethicist, no matter how well-intentioned, with only a cursory understanding of her culture, family dynamics, and traditions of living and dying. But do as you wish."
Now, unsure whether an ethics consult will be helpful, the primary team tries to regroup. The intern on the team thinks aloud, "Is there such a thing as cultural expertise and, if so, how would it fit into clinical bioethics?"
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Ramsarathan arrived in the United States just two days ago, having traveled from her small village in India to await the birth of her first grandchild. Shortly after her arrival, her family became alarmed by her inability to eat or keep down food. Despite their initial reluctance to engage with the American healthcare system, the family’s concern grew as her vomiting persisted, and they decided to bring her to the hospital, accompanied by her son-in-law.

With assistance from a hospital translator, the primary care team began piecing together Mrs. Ramsarathan’s history. She had rarely sought medical care throughout her life, could not speak English, and was illiterate. She recounted, through translation, that eating had become difficult about six months ago, and her symptoms had slowly worsened since then.

Dr. Ellamjeet, a gastroenterologist, was brought in for consultation. Having completed medical school in India before coming to the US for further training, Dr. Ellamjeet spoke the same dialect as Mrs. Ramsarathan, which immediately put her somewhat at ease in the unfamiliar hospital environment. Although a translator was sporadically available to the primary team, it quickly became clear that both Mrs. Ramsarathan and her family preferred Dr. Ellamjeet to act as her primary physician.

Her son-in-law, assuming the role of family spokesperson, voiced his apprehension about the results of medical tests and specifically requested that Dr. Ellamjeet not disclose any diagnosis directly to Mrs. Ramsarathan. Instead, he asked that the family be allowed to determine if, when, and how she should be told, in keeping with their cultural traditions. Initial investigations confirmed a mass highly suggestive of advanced carcinoma. The son-in-law, with Dr. Ellamjeet’s agreement, believed that bluntly delivering such grave news in this unfamiliar setting would not serve Mrs. Ramsarathan’s best interests.

Dr. Ellamjeet relayed this perspective to the primary care team. “Sharing information like this is not customary in her culture,” he explained. “It would be doubly cruel—not only would she learn she is gravely ill, but she would have to do so in a setting that feels alien, stripped of the gentle, traditional ways her family would provide support and comfort. By insisting she bear this burden alone, we deny her the collective strength her family would offer at home. The compassionate approach is to let her family guide her care, as they would in India.”

Some members of the care team, however, were uneasy about what this would mean for Mrs. Ramsarathan’s prognosis and treatment. They consulted Dr. Cameron Michaels from surgical oncology, who strongly believed Mrs. Ramsarathan should be told of her diagnosis and that he could not ethically treat her without her informed consent. Dr. Michaels asserted, “Even if the treatments I can provide might improve her life or relieve her pain, it would be unethical to subject her to the considerable risks and side effects of chemotherapy, surgery, or radiation without her understanding why these interventions are being done. Suffering these hardships makes sense only when the patient knows what is at stake. I cannot in good conscience treat her without her knowledge or if she delegates all decisions to her son-in-law. I refuse to look into her eyes after a difficult therapy and see confusion or betrayal, wondering why she is being put through this.”

With the care team at an impasse, the idea of seeking an ethics consultation was raised. When approached, Dr. Ellamjeet replied, “If you feel an ethics consult is necessary for legal protection or to avoid misunderstandings, I understand. But if you want to do what is truly best for Mrs. Ramsarathan, I doubt an ethics consult will clarify matters. I’m not an ethicist, but I have cared for many patients from her part of India. I understand her cultural context and family dynamics better than any well-meaning Western-educated ethicist with only superficial cultural knowledge. But you must do what you think is right.”

Now uncertain about whether an ethics consultation would be useful, the primary team regrouped. The intern wondered aloud, “Does cultural expertise have a role here, and if so, how does it fit with clinical ethics?”

ethical_issues.question: Should Mrs. Ramsarathan be informed of her diagnosis in accordance with principles of patient autonomy and informed consent?
keypoints: Disclosing the diagnosis to the patient reflects the core American cultural values of truthfulness and personal autonomy.

Respecting the patient’s family and cultural background by allowing decision making through the family embodies the values of filial piety and collective decision making characteristic of Far Eastern cultures.
Ethics consultation should focus on the legitimacy of withholding the diagnosis under cultural considerations, clarifying the balance between patient decisional authority and cultural sensitivity.

Through an independent and professional translator, the patient should be asked early whether she wishes to be informed of her diagnosis directly and whether she wants to participate in medical decision making.

Clarifying the patient’s preferences helps determine the locus of medical decision making, accommodating both personal autonomy and familial cultural needs, thereby promoting individualized and culturally respectful clinical practice.

ethical_issues.question: Should an ethics consultation be requested despite objections from members of the primary medical team?
keypoints: The primary care team should request an ethics consultation, as ethics consultants possess cultural sensitivity and can provide valuable support in complex cross-cultural contexts.

Ethics consultants bring traditions of ethical reasoning, multidisciplinary knowledge, and extensive practical experience, enabling them to offer a rigorous and generalizable decision-making framework.

When the values of patients or their families seriously conflict with the physician’s core professional convictions, priority should be given to consulting an ethics consultant with cultural expertise to facilitate clinical management.
Cultural expertise and ethics expertise are complementary; their synergistic application helps resolve the most challenging ethical and cultural conflicts encountered in clinical practice.

title: Ethics Consultation and Clinical Expertise
case:
Mrs. Curtin, a patient well-known to the university hospital and its house staff, was admitted 2 weeks ago with chest pains. She has had many admissions and discharges in the last year related to her severe peripheral vascular disease. She's also struggling with diabetes, kidney disease, and coronary artery disease and returns to the hospital because of nonhealing wounds of her lower extremities. During the last year, what started as simple blisters on the heels of her feet progressed to amputations of her feet and then of her right lower leg, when at each stage her wounds failed to heal and subsequently became infected. She often required antibiotics and increasingly developed more antibiotic-resistant infections.
On this admission, the attending was a physician Mrs. Curtin had not encountered before. Her own internist, Dr. Wagner, was informed of her admission and visited her a couple of times during her first week in the hospital. Test results from that week revealed that Mrs. Curtin had advanced coronary disease. Fortunately, Dr. Wagner's annual month-long assignment as attending on the medicine unit at the university hospital began during Mrs. Curtin's second week there, and he was able to take over as head of her health care team for the remainder of her stay. Dr. Wagner had been Mrs. Curtin's physician for 7 years and had coordinated her care with the many other specialists who had treated her for specific emergent conditions.
At 49, Mrs. Curtin is uncharacteristically young for the development of such severe complications of poor circulation. She has a loving husband and 2 teenage children who have been involved in her care. Dr. Wagner has good communication with both Mrs. Curtin and her husband. He has always been honest with them in his judgment about Mrs. Curtin's diagnoses, treatment options, and prognoses, and he believes that they share their important questions, values, and worries with him.
Mrs. Curtin and her husband have pressed aggressively for treatment, a position that has at times endeared them to, and at other times exhausted, her medical team. During this current hospitalization, though, when the consulting vascular surgeon brought up the option of coronary surgery for Mrs. Curtin's heart disease, she vacillated between wanting and not wanting the operation. She told the attending who cared for her before Dr. Wagner's arrival on the unit that she was tired of being so sick, of disrupting her family's life with her many costly hospitalizations, and of being unable to lead a normal life. She said that if she thought her family could stand the idea, she would just stop the constant stream of hospitalizations and operations. The house and nursing staffs have heard the same sorts of feelings from Mrs. Curtin, and, when Dr. Wagner talks with them about the proposed coronary surgery, the staff says that they think an ethics consult should be called.
Dr. Wagner resists the idea. He believes that, for the present, Mrs. Curtin's other problems might finally be under control (eg, her kidney function is stable and she has no evidence of systemic infection). Based on noninvasive studies, he believes that it is likely she has a high-grade stenosis of her left anterior descending artery. He thinks an interventional cardiologist could confirm the diagnosis and place a stent. If that doesn't work, Dr. Wagner thinks that she might benefit from minimally invasive bypass surgery, using an internal mammary artery. In either case, he believes the result may improve her cardiac function and thereby also improve her peripheral circulation, helping her to heal better in the future. The nursing and house staffs fail to share his optimism. They argue that she has a lot of microvascular disease from her diabetes and that it would be safest to manage her coronary disease medically. They assert that major surgery at this time would put Mrs. Curtin at unnecessary risk. They reiterate their desire for an ethics consultation.
Dr. Wagner replies that a nonclinician ethicist who just happens to be "on call" for such a conference will not be able to appreciate Mrs. Curtin's current medical conditions as well as he and her other physicians. Moreover, Dr. Wagner argues, his professional relationship with the patient and her husband is one of long standing, whereas the ethicist would be a stranger to them both. He asks the house staff, "What could such a person add to the intimate value-based discussion about Mrs. Curtin's life and quality of life?" Without being specific, Dr. Wagner worries that the presence of this "ethics stranger" could actually be harmful rather than beneficial.
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Curtin, a familiar face to the university hospital and its house staff, was admitted two weeks ago with chest pain. Over the past year, she has been admitted and discharged multiple times due to her severe peripheral vascular disease. Her complicated medical history includes diabetes, kidney disease, and coronary artery disease, and she frequently returns to the hospital for nonhealing wounds on her lower legs. What began as simple blisters on her heels a year ago advanced to multiple amputations—first her feet, then her right lower leg—each time because her wounds failed to heal and became infected. She has repeatedly required antibiotics and has developed increasingly resistant infections over time.

For this admission, Mrs. Curtin was initially cared for by an attending she had not met before. Her long-term internist, Dr. Wagner, was notified of her hospitalization and visited her a couple of times during her first week as a patient. During that week, test results revealed that Mrs. Curtin’s coronary disease had progressed significantly. Fortunately, Dr. Wagner’s annual month-long rotation as attending on the medicine unit commenced in Mrs. Curtin’s second week, enabling him to assume leadership of her care team for the rest of her stay. Dr. Wagner has been Mrs. Curtin’s physician for seven years, coordinating her complex care with numerous specialists for her acute medical crises.

At just 49, Mrs. Curtin is unusually young to suffer such grave complications from poor circulation. She has a devoted husband and two teenage children, both of whom have played an active role in her care. Dr. Wagner maintains a strong, communicative relationship with both Mrs. Curtin and her husband, always providing honest assessments regarding diagnoses, treatment options, and likely outcomes. He feels that Mrs. Curtin and her husband are forthcoming with their questions, values, and concerns.

Throughout her illness, Mrs. Curtin and her husband have persistently advocated for aggressive treatment—an approach that has sometimes won the admiration of her medical team, but has also, at times, left them feeling drained. During her current hospitalization, when the consulting vascular surgeon raised the possibility of coronary surgery to address her heart disease, Mrs. Curtin wavered between wanting and not wanting the procedure. She confided in the attending physician who cared for her prior to Dr. Wagner’s arrival that she was weary of her illness, tired of repeatedly disrupting her family’s lives with frequent and costly hospitalizations, and frustrated by her inability to live normally. She admitted that, were it not for her concern about how her family would cope, she might choose to forgo further hospitalizations and operations altogether. The house staff and nursing staff have also heard Mrs. Curtin express similar feelings, and when Dr. Wagner consulted them about the proposed coronary surgery, several staff members suggested that an ethics consultation should be arranged.

Dr. Wagner disagreed with this suggestion. He believed that Mrs. Curtin’s other medical issues were, for the moment, reasonably well managed—her kidney function was stable, and there were no signs of systemic infection. Based on noninvasive tests, Dr. Wagner suspected a significant stenosis in her left anterior descending artery. He felt that an interventional cardiologist could confirm the diagnosis and place a stent if appropriate. Should that approach fail, Dr. Wagner thought Mrs. Curtin might benefit from a minimally invasive bypass using an internal mammary artery. He believed either intervention could improve her cardiac function and, as a result, her peripheral circulation, possibly enhancing her ability to heal in the future.

The nursing and house staff, however, did not share Dr. Wagner’s optimism. They pointed out that Mrs. Curtin’s diabetes had caused extensive microvascular disease and argued that it would be safer to manage her coronary artery disease medically at this stage. They raised concerns that major surgery would pose unnecessary risks and reiterated their call for an ethics consultation.

In response, Dr. Wagner questioned the value of involving a nonclinician ethicist who happened to be “on call” for such cases, suggesting that no outsider could fully grasp the nuances of Mrs. Curtin’s current medical situation as well as he and her other physicians. He also noted his long-standing professional relationship with Mrs. Curtin and her husband, emphasizing that an ethicist would be a stranger to them. “What could such a person contribute to the deeply personal, value-laden discussions about Mrs. Curtin’s life and quality of life?” he asked the house staff. Dr. Wagner, though unspecific, expressed concern that bringing in this “ethics stranger” could prove more harmful than helpful.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient experiences ambivalence about continuing treatment, how should the healthcare team coordinate to ensure the patient receives optimal care?
keypoints: The medical team should fully recognize that different members may interpret the patient’s ambivalence from multiple perspectives, and through effective communication, reach a consensus on treatment goals to ensure the patient receives optimal care.

The team must thoroughly explore the underlying causes of the patient’s ambivalent attitude, understanding her individual values, psychological state, and social context, and use this as a foundation to optimize medical decision-making while respecting the patient’s wishes.

The experienced attending physician should assume a leadership and coordinating role, fostering open communication and collaboration among team members, jointly clarifying the medical issues, and reviewing the best available evidence to promote the development of a unified treatment plan that aligns with the patient’s best interests.

ethical_issues.question: How can ethics consultation facilitate consensus among members of the health care team when there is disagreement about the optimal treatment plan?
keypoints: The medical team should first clarify the clinical questions and collaboratively evaluate treatment options based on evidence-based medicine, thereby establishing a solid factual foundation for ethical deliberation.

Ethics consultation facilitates the team’s understanding of how differing professional roles and value systems influence perspectives on treatment options, promoting mutual understanding, respect, and effective communication among members.

The ethics consultant can situate the patient’s medical decision-making within a framework of professional and societal values, assisting the team in comprehensively understanding the patient’s values, life goals, and expectations.

Ethics consultation can be conducted behind the scenes, providing communication tools and coordination strategies to enhance internal team collaboration and consensus-building, while avoiding direct intervention with the patient and family.

The senior attending physician should exercise leadership and a teaching role, encouraging open communication and collective learning among team members, in order to establish unified treatment goals and coordinated action plans.

title: Evidence-Based Medicine and Clinical Expertise
case:
Ms. Moran was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis 3 years ago. She has been followed in the neurology residency clinic of a university hospital since. Soon after her diagnosis, she was started on a first-line medication for a relapsing-remitting form of multiple sclerosis (MS). Since starting the medication, she has had fewer "MS flares" (she estimates a reduction of about a third) and is satisfied with the therapy. About 2 years ago Ms. Moran began developing signs of depression and was referred to a psychiatrist.
Ms. Moran, who is 34 years old, has not had any new MS symptoms since her last visit, but comes to the clinic complaining that her depression is getting worse. She recounts that her psychiatrist has tried a "half dozen different medications and combinations" without any improvement. In fact, she feels like her mood is worse than ever. She recently lost her job as a social worker and her husband filed for divorce. Her social circle has become smaller, and she has found it increasingly difficult to leave her apartment, let alone look for a new job. She feels like she is losing hope.
Dr. Logan, the new attending physician staffing the resident clinic, is concerned that her multiple sclerosis medication may be causing or worsening Ms. Moran's depression. Dr. Logan has a background in psychiatry, having completed a combined residency in neurology and psychiatry after med school. She works almost exclusively with multiple sclerosis patients and, given her psychiatry background, has attracted a large referral base for patients with concomitant psychiatric illness. After interviewing her, Dr. Logan is confident that Ms. Moran's MS medication should be stopped.
Dr. Alderman, the resident caring for Ms. Moran, is uncomfortable with this decision. What studies there are on patients with MS and depression seem to suggest that the medication Ms. Moran is taking does not cause depression. And, given her reduction in MS flares, Dr. Alderman is reluctant to take Ms. Moran off her current medication.
Acknowledging Dr. Alderman's concern, Dr. Logan explains that in her experience the particular class of medication that Ms. Moran is taking for her multiple sclerosis does increase the occurrence of clinical depression. Dr. Alderman counters that "the evidence" says differently. Besides pointing out limitations of the studies Dr. Alderman cites, Dr. Logan explains that the particularities of this patient make it hard to apply the studies to her case. She points out Ms. Moran's family history of depression (ie, her mother suffers from depression, and her brother has attempted suicide), her current stressors, and her failure on a multitude of antidepressants. These factors, as well as others, she argues, are important in deciding on the best therapy for Ms. Moran, but they are "too particular" to get taken into account in any systematic study. "Yes," she argues, "there is evidence, but it is often too general in character to be useful for the individual patient. Ms. Moran deserves to have therapy that is tailored to her, don't you agree?"
Frustrated and a little perplexed, Dr. Alderman wonders to herself, "How do I mediate the conflict between clinical expertise and evidence-based medicine, and what do I tell Ms. Moran?"
case_rewrite:
Ms. Moran, a 34-year-old woman, was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis three years ago and has since been a regular patient at the neurology residency clinic of a university hospital. Not long after her diagnosis, she began taking a first-line therapy suited for relapsing-remitting MS. Since starting this medication, she has noticed roughly a one-third reduction in her MS flares and feels generally satisfied with her current treatment.

However, about two years ago, Ms. Moran started to exhibit symptoms of depression. She was referred to a psychiatrist, but despite trying a "half dozen different medications and combinations," she reports no improvement—if anything, she feels her mood has only worsened. Recently, she lost her job as a social worker, and her husband has filed for divorce. Her social connections have dwindled, and she finds herself increasingly isolated, often unable to leave her apartment or contemplate searching for new employment. Ms. Moran admits she is struggling to maintain hope.

At her latest clinic visit, Ms. Moran reports no new neurological symptoms but expresses concern about her deepening depression. Dr. Logan, the newly appointed attending physician supervising the resident clinic, listens carefully. Dr. Logan brings a unique background, having completed a combined residency in neurology and psychiatry, and now devotes her practice almost exclusively to MS patients, many of whom have concurrent psychiatric conditions. Drawing on her psychiatric expertise, Dr. Logan grows concerned that Ms. Moran’s MS medication could be contributing to, or worsening, her depressive symptoms. After a thorough evaluation, Dr. Logan concludes that discontinuing the MS medication would be in Ms. Moran’s best interest.

Dr. Alderman, the neurology resident responsible for Ms. Moran’s care, is uneasy about this recommendation. The available research on MS medications and depression does not, in Dr. Alderman’s view, support a link between the therapy and depressive symptoms. Moreover, considering the clear reduction in Ms. Moran’s MS relapses, Dr. Alderman is hesitant to risk a flare-up by stopping the current medication.

Dr. Logan acknowledges Dr. Alderman’s concerns, but counters by highlighting her own clinical experience: in her practice, she has frequently observed that the class of medication Ms. Moran is taking appears to increase the risk of depression. Dr. Alderman insists that “the evidence” does not support this assertion, but Dr. Logan points out the limitations of the studies Dr. Alderman cites, noting that published research often cannot account for the complexities of individual cases. She draws attention to Ms. Moran’s family history—her mother’s depression and her brother’s suicide attempt—as well as Ms. Moran’s recent personal losses and her lack of response to several antidepressants. These, Dr. Logan argues, are crucial factors that studies rarely capture, and they must be considered when tailoring treatment to the individual.

“Yes, there is evidence,” Dr. Logan explains, “but it is often too general to apply to the situation of a specific patient. Ms. Moran deserves a therapy plan that addresses her unique needs and values. Don’t you agree?” Dr. Logan emphasizes that understanding Ms. Moran’s own priorities—whether she feels the burden of depression outweighs her concern about MS flares—should guide their next steps.

Feeling both frustrated and uncertain, Dr. Alderman reflects: “How do I reconcile Dr. Logan’s clinical expertise with the best available evidence, and, most importantly, how do I communicate these complex issues and options in a way that centers Ms. Moran’s preferences and goals?”

ethical_issues.question: In clinical decision-making, how can the evidence from evidence-based medicine be balanced with the application of clinical expertise to ensure that the individualized treatment needs of the patient are met?
keypoints: Although evidence derived from clinical research holds significant value, its generalizable nature often fails to meet the demands of individualized patient care.

Clinical experts develop specialized insights through the accumulation of extensive experience managing a particular disease; expert opinion thus represents the highest form of evidence-based clinical experience.
The establishment of clinical goals must be grounded in an understanding of the individual patient’s values, with ultimate decision-making hinging upon those patient values.

Optimizing individualized care requires not only mastery of relevant literature evidence but also the integration of physiological and experiential medical knowledge, clarification of patient goals, and the achievement of multidimensional balance within a complex healthcare system.

ethical_issues.question: How can clinicians integrate patients’ values and individual preferences into clinical practice to ensure that medical decisions align with the patient’s best interests and quality of life?
keypoints: Clinical judgment should integrate all relevant forms of medical knowledge, combined with the patient’s goals, values, and preferences, in order to formulate the optimal medical decision for the patient at hand.

The establishment of clinical goals must be grounded in a thorough understanding of the individual patient’s values and quality of life, especially when the patient perceives their quality of life to be below an acceptable threshold, such that prolongation of survival or disease control may not represent the ideal outcome.

The crux of the ultimate decision lies in understanding the patient’s individual values—for example, whether the patient considers the impact of depressive symptoms on their quality of life to outweigh that of multiple sclerosis itself—which will directly influence the choice of therapeutic strategy.

Healthcare professionals should focus on eliciting and understanding the patient’s personal concerns and values, engaging proactively in dialogue about their expectations and worries, rather than becoming preoccupied solely with how to inform the patient, thereby ensuring that medical decisions genuinely align with the patient’s best interests and quality of life.

ethical_issues.question: In the absence of clear clinical evidence, how should clinical expert opinion be evaluated and incorporated to address potential adverse drug reactions or other individualized health risks?
keypoints: Clinical judgment should integrate all relevant forms of medical knowledge, combined with the patient’s goals, values, and preferences, to formulate the optimal decision for the patient at hand.

Expert opinion, grounded in extensive clinical experience and informed by professional literature, provides a crucial reference for assessing the potential association between medication and depressive symptoms.

When evaluating expert opinion, one should critically examine the depth of clinical experience and the degree of conviction held by the expert, while also considering the applicability and limitations of the published evidence, thereby rationally weighing the different sources of warrant.

The ultimate decision should center on the patient’s values, involving thorough communication regarding the trade-offs between depressive symptoms and MS disease control, respecting the patient’s wishes, and developing an individualized treatment plan.

title: Patient-Requested, Non-Recommended Screening
case:
Mrs. Ackerman went to visit Dr. Noell for an annual gynecological exam that included a Pap smear. She sees Dr. Noell regularly for check-ups and the recommended screening tests for women in her risk and age groups. So far, she has been remarkably healthy—she exercises regularly, does not smoke, and is a vegetarian—and no screening test has ever shown cause for concern.
Following the exam, Mrs. Ackerman told Dr. Noell that she had seen an ad in a newspaper for a whole body CT scan for $600. "I'd like to have this done to make sure there's not a treatable problem in there," Mrs. Ackerman said, pointing to her stomach. "The problem, Dr. Noell, is that it's a pretty expensive test. But imagine how muchmoreexpensive it would be if they didn't find something until it was too late." Dr. Noell gently told Mrs. Ackerman that there was no reason to think that there was a disease "lurking" inside her and that, after having a scan, many patients believed that it was a "waste of time and money" as it did not show anything that wasn't already known. As a compromise, Mrs. Ackerman suggested ordering a CT scan of only the abdomen and pelvis "just to check."
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Ackerman arrived at Dr. Noell’s office for her annual gynecological examination, which included the routine Pap smear. Over the years, Mrs. Ackerman has been a consistent patient of Dr. Noell, always diligent about her regular check-ups and the recommended screenings for women of her age and risk profile. Her overall health has been excellent—she maintains an active lifestyle, refrains from smoking, and follows a vegetarian diet. None of her previous screening tests have ever raised any concerns.

After concluding the exam, Mrs. Ackerman brought up something she had come across recently. She mentioned to Dr. Noell that she’d seen a newspaper advertisement promoting a whole-body CT scan for $600. “I think I’d like to get this done, just to make sure there isn’t something treatable going on inside me,” she explained, pressing her hand over her abdomen. “The thing is, it’s a pretty costly test. But if something serious was missed now and only caught later, that could turn out to be far more expensive.”

Dr. Noell responded gently, assuring Mrs. Ackerman that there was no medical reason to suspect any hidden disease. She explained that in her experience, many patients who underwent such scans later felt it had been a “waste of time and money,” since the scans rarely revealed anything not already known, and sometimes led to unnecessary worry or additional, more invasive tests. 

Hoping to find a middle ground, Mrs. Ackerman then proposed an alternative: “What if we just did a CT scan of my abdomen and pelvis? Maybe that would be enough to check, just in case.”

ethical_issues.question: Should a physician comply with a patient’s request for an expensive whole-body CT scan in the absence of clear medical indications?
keypoints: As a teacher rather than a servant to the patient, the physician is under no obligation to order tests lacking medical indication solely at the patient’s request; respecting patient autonomy does not equate to acquiescing to personal preferences.

Existing medical evidence does not support the anticipated benefits of whole body CT scanning and may lead to invasive follow-up procedures for indeterminate abnormalities, thereby increasing physical risks and financial burdens for the patient.
Guided by the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence, the physician should rationally counsel the patient to avoid unnecessary testing in order to safeguard the patient’s best interests.

Physicians should be mindful of social justice by responsibly managing healthcare resources, refraining from fabricating indications to obtain insurance coverage, and thereby promoting equitable access to medical care for all.

ethical_issues.question: How can a physician ensure that a patient’s decision is based on fully informed consent rather than fear or undue influence, while simultaneously respecting the patient’s autonomy?
keypoints: Dr. Noell should clearly define her role as an educator and counselor, guiding Mrs. Ackerman to critically assess the necessity and appropriateness of the requested whole-body CT scan rather than simply acquiescing to the patient’s request.

Dr. Noell should thoroughly explore Mrs. Ackerman’s motivations for seeking the whole-body CT scan, with particular attention to underlying fears, misconceptions, or informational gaps, in order to clarify her genuine health concerns.

Dr. Noell should implement a robust informed consent process, fully disclosing to Mrs. Ackerman the potential risks, benefits, and scientific evidence regarding whole-body CT screening, and emphasizing the test’s applicability and limitations given her current health status.

Dr. Noell should respect Mrs. Ackerman’s autonomy, ensuring that any decision regarding the CT scan is made voluntarily, free from coercion, and based on a rational understanding of the information provided.

Dr. Noell should attend to Mrs. Ackerman’s emotional state, addressing and alleviating any fears or anxieties to prevent emotional distress from unduly influencing her medical decisions, thereby upholding the ethic of care.

ethical_issues.question: Should a physician provide false information on an insurance application in order to obtain coverage for a patient-requested, non-indicated screening test?
keypoints: Physicians should provide honest disclosure and arrange examinations strictly based on medical necessity and clinical indications, thereby upholding the trust and contractual obligations among patients, physicians, and insurance providers.

Physicians have a responsibility to rationally manage healthcare resources and should avoid ordering unnecessary tests and procedures, thereby promoting the fairness and accessibility of medical services.

Unnecessary additional testing not only increases the financial burden on patients but may also raise overall societal healthcare costs, leading to higher insurance premiums and strained medical resources, ultimately undermining public health interests.

title: Presymptomatic Genetic Testing for ALS
case:
Mr. Smith is a fit 35-year-old without any major health complaints. He recently moved, and, during his first visit with his new physician, Dr. Sanders, he revealed that his older brother had died of amytrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also called Lou Gehrig's disease at age 47. Dr. Sanders acknowledged that this must have been a staggering loss for Mr. Smith, who disclosed that what his brother went through was terrible and quite traumatic. He told Dr. Sanders that he could not imagine going through that disease course and doesn't know how his brother coped.
Dr. Sanders remembered having read that about 10-15 percent of ALS cases are familial. She inquired whether any other family members had developed the disease, and Mr. Smith said that a great-uncle had died of an unknown disease at a young age, but no one ever thought it might have been ALS. Other than that, there was no reason to think ALS ran in his family.
Dr. Sanders thought about offering genetic screening to Mr. Smith but wanted to consider further the risks and benefits to her patient. She wondered whether telling Mr. Smith that he had the genetic markers for this deadly disease before he became symptomatic would only distress him and not yield an offsetting benefit, since the age of onset was unpredictable.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Smith, a healthy 35-year-old, had no significant medical complaints when he arrived for his first appointment with his new physician, Dr. Sanders, after recently relocating. During their conversation, Mr. Smith shared that his older brother had passed away from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease, at the age of 47. Dr. Sanders expressed her sympathy, realizing the profound impact such a loss must have had on him. Mr. Smith confided that witnessing his brother’s decline was a harrowing experience, and he struggled to fathom how his brother endured the disease.

Recalling from her training that approximately 10-15% of ALS cases are familial, Dr. Sanders gently asked whether any other relatives had developed similar conditions. Mr. Smith replied that a great-uncle had died young from an unspecified illness, though no one in the family had ever suspected ALS. Aside from that, he said, there was no known history of ALS in his family.

As Dr. Sanders considered Mr. Smith’s history, she weighed the possibility of offering genetic screening for ALS. She paused to reflect on the potential psychological ramifications: Would learning about the presence of genetic markers for this fatal disease, especially before any symptoms appeared, only cause Mr. Smith unnecessary distress? At the same time, she recognized that knowledge of such genetic risks could influence important decisions regarding insurance, family planning, and future health surveillance. Dr. Sanders found herself deliberating how best to balance these risks and benefits before proceeding further with her patient.

ethical_issues.question: Does informing a patient of the presence of genetic markers for a fatal disease prior to symptom onset increase psychological burden without providing substantive benefit?
keypoints: Disclosing to a patient the presence of genetic markers for a fatal disease prior to symptom onset may increase psychological burden; however, the right to be informed enables the patient to optimize insurance choices, family planning, and future testing decisions.
Although discussions related to genetic testing may provoke anxiety and psychological stress, the likelihood of severe depression or suicidal ideation is low.
Even if the patient opts not to undergo testing, gaining knowledge about the genetics of ALS and the availability of testing allows for more rational preparation for future life decisions.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. Sanders discuss the hereditary nature of ALS and the option of presymptomatic genetic testing with Mr. Smith, even without knowing how he might respond to information about the potential risks and benefits of such testing?
keypoints: Dr. Sanders may find it challenging to accurately anticipate Mr. Smith’s response to discussions about the hereditary nature of ALS and the risks and benefits of presymptomatic genetic testing; therefore, relevant information should not be withheld without first assessing Mr. Smith’s attitudes, values, and psychological resilience.

Unless there is compelling evidence that disclosure of information regarding genetic testing would cause Mr. Smith significant and irreversible psychological harm, withholding such information risks undermining patient autonomy and eroding the trust fundamental to the physician-patient relationship.

Discussing the genetics of ALS and the availability of presymptomatic genetic testing provides Mr. Smith with essential information to support informed decision-making regarding insurance, family planning, and future health management.

While conversations about genetic testing may elicit psychological distress or anxiety, the likelihood of precipitating severe psychological crises such as depression or suicidal ideation is generally low; thus, Dr. Sanders has an ethical obligation to initiate this discussion in a sensitive and supportive manner.

Given the complexity and specialized nature of genetic counseling, it is advisable for Dr. Sanders to refer Mr. Smith to a genetic counselor or a neurologist with expertise in ALS genetics to ensure comprehensive and professional counseling.

With adequate information and support, Mr. Smith can exercise his autonomy in deciding whether to pursue genetic testing, thereby enabling him to make informed choices about his future in light of potential ALS risk.

title: Controlling Diabetes
case:
Sharon Smith was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age 11. Under the watchful eye of her parents, Sharon was an active teenager, participating in high school sports and extracurricular activities. In college, she continued with soccer and diligently controlled her blood sugar, following the same insulin regimen she had begun in her mid-teens.
After college, Sharon moved across the country to pursue graduate studies. To help pay her living expenses, she began working 4 days a week as a waitress. One night as her shift was ending she noticed that her hands were shaking as she was replacing glassware, and she later passed out. The restaurant staff, unaware that she was diabetic, called 911 for assistance.
Sharon was admitted to the hospital, and Dr. Stone—an endocrinologist—was called. Dr. Stone had seen Sharon quite a few times since her move to the city about 6 years earlier, usually after emergency episodes. When he first met Sharon, she was moderately overweight and had elevated cholesterol levels. Examining Sharon's medical records at that time, Dr. Stone noted that these developments were recent.
Since their initial clinical encounter, Dr. Stone had encouraged Sharon to lose weight and had explained the possible complications for someone who had had type 1 diabetes for more than 5 years. Sharon claimed that she had tried to lose weight, but found it impossible to balance glycemic control with weight loss. Adding to her frustration were a bum ankle, intense graduate coursework, and her waitressing job, all of which prevented her from exercising as regularly as she had in college.
Dr. Stone has attempted—numerous times—to modify Sharon's insulin regimen and provide her with a clearly laid-out dietary plan to help her lose weight and control her blood sugar. He believes some of Sharon's noncompliance might be due to depression or other psychological factors and referred her to a counselor who had worked successfully with many of his patients with diabetes. Sharon saw the counselor once but refused to continue, stating that she had neither the time nor the money to attend regular sessions. Despite Dr. Stone's continued efforts, Sharon has been admitted to the hospital a number of times with recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis.
Sharon repeatedly tells Dr. Stone that she understands the consequences of ignoring his advice, and she constantly expresses her annoyance with this disease, especially in relation to her living situation. Dr. Stone is sympathetic to Sharon's plight—she is young, busy, and burdened with a disease that will be with her for the rest of her life. But he is frustrated by her lack of responsibility; she doesn't adhere to the diet, she sometimes cancels appointments at the last minute, and, he suspects, she has begun drinking alcohol. When he confronted Sharon about her behavior during her latest hospital stay, she shrugged and responded, "C'mon, Dr. Stone. It's not that bad. You always pull me through."
case_rewrite:
Sharon Smith received her diagnosis of type 1 diabetes when she was 11 years old. Throughout her teenage years, with her parents closely monitoring her condition, Sharon led an active lifestyle, taking part in high school athletics and various extracurriculars. When she transitioned to college, she remained committed to soccer and carefully managed her blood sugar, sticking to the insulin routine she had established in her later teens.

After graduating, Sharon relocated across the country to begin graduate school. To cover her living costs, she started working four days a week as a waitress. One evening, as her shift was winding down, Sharon noticed her hands trembling as she arranged glassware; soon after, she lost consciousness. None of her coworkers knew she was diabetic, so the restaurant staff called 911 for emergency help.

Sharon was admitted to the hospital, where Dr. Stone, an endocrinologist, was called in to evaluate her. Dr. Stone had become familiar with Sharon over the six years since she’d moved to the city, often seeing her after similar emergencies. When he first met her, Sharon had gained some weight and her cholesterol was elevated—both changes that stood out as recent developments in her medical history.

Since that initial consultation, Dr. Stone had consistently encouraged Sharon to lose weight, explaining the serious complications someone with more than five years of type 1 diabetes might face. Sharon explained that while she wanted to lose weight, it felt impossible to do so without compromising her blood sugar control.
