Her frustration was compounded by a troublesome ankle, the demands of graduate school, and her waitressing shifts, all of which left her little time or energy for exercise compared to her college years.

Dr. Stone had tried several times to adjust Sharon’s insulin regimen and had provided her with a detailed dietary plan aimed at helping her both lose weight and regulate her glucose levels. Suspecting that psychological factors such as depression might be influencing Sharon’s difficulties with adherence, Dr. Stone referred her to a counselor who had helped many of his other diabetic patients. Sharon attended only one session, insisting that regular appointments were too costly and that she simply didn’t have the time. Despite Dr. Stone’s persistent efforts, Sharon was repeatedly hospitalized for episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis.

Sharon often assured Dr. Stone that she understood the risks of not following his guidance, but she also made no secret of her irritation with her illness, particularly in the context of her busy, independent life. Dr. Stone empathized with Sharon—she was young, overextended, and challenged daily by a lifelong disease. Yet he couldn’t help feeling frustrated by her apparent disregard for her own care: she frequently ignored dietary advice, occasionally canceled appointments on short notice, and, he suspected, had started drinking alcohol. When he questioned Sharon about her choices during her most recent hospitalization, she simply shrugged and said, “Come on, Dr. Stone. It’s not that bad. You always get me through.”

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians modify a treatment plan to better accommodate a patient’s lifestyle when the patient does not adhere to medical recommendations?
keypoints: Physicians should prioritize assisting patients in developing practical and sustainable diabetes management plans that are tailored to their individual lifestyles and real-world circumstances, ensuring that treatment regimens are both feasible and actionable.

Physicians should adopt a communication approach that respects patient autonomy, minimizes paternalism, and empowers patients to make informed choices and assume responsibility for their care by providing the best available evidence-based medical advice.

Physicians should attend to patients’ psychosocial factors, understanding their life stressors and barriers, and, when necessary, coordinate or provide psychological support and social resources to promote comprehensive health management.

Physicians should maintain empathy, avoid blame and emotional reactions, and strive to build a trust-based, collaborative physician-patient relationship that enhances patient adherence and motivation for treatment.

Physicians should regularly assess the feasibility of the treatment plan and the patient’s adherence, and flexibly adjust therapeutic strategies to accommodate the patient’s evolving life circumstances and needs.

tags: Health professions education/Humanities in health professions education
Health professions education/Learner roles and responsibilities
title: Responding to Insensitive Remarks about a Patient: Resident to Patient's Family and Attending Physician
case:
An attending physician uses disrespectful nicknames and makes remarks that you, the resident, find inappropriate. You are uncomfortable because he often refers to the HIV/AIDS clinic as death row, the nurses as little helpers, the pharmacists as Rex, and transfer to palliative care as the long walk. In the most recent incident, he made a derogatory remark about a comatose patient ("deadhead") that the patient's family heard.
When you tell the attending that the family overheard the insensitive comments, he suggests dismissively that you can discuss it with the family "if that will make you feel better."
case_rewrite:
Dr. W, an attending physician, has developed a reputation for using disparaging nicknames and making inappropriate remarks in the hospital setting. As a resident on his team, you have grown increasingly uncomfortable with his language. Dr. W frequently refers to the HIV/AIDS clinic as “death row,” calls the nurses “little helpers,” labels the pharmacists “Rex,” and describes transfer to palliative care as “the long walk.” During a recent patient round, Dr. W referred to a comatose patient as a “deadhead”—a comment that was overheard by the patient’s family, who appeared visibly distressed.

After the encounter, you approach Dr. W and inform him that the patient’s family heard his insensitive remark. Dr. W responds dismissively, suggesting, “You can talk to the family if that will make you feel better,” and shows little interest in addressing the situation further.

ethical_issues.question: When confronted with an attending physician’s use of derogatory language, should the resident communicate with the attending and provide feedback to promote behavioral change?
keypoints: The resident physician should communicate with the attending physician within the context of a trusting and professional relationship, providing direct and constructive feedback to promote behavioral change.
Constructive feedback should be timely, specific, and delivered in a private setting to minimize the attending physician’s defensive response.

When giving feedback, the resident should identify the specific problematic behavior, express their own feelings, and clarify why the behavior is problematic, avoiding accusatory language to reduce defensiveness.

Such mature, sensitive, and professional dialogue by the resident can prompt the attending physician to reflect on the impact of their language on both patients and healthcare providers, potentially leading to positive change.

ethical_issues.question: How can a resident physician effectively communicate with a patient’s family to rebuild trust and address the emotional harm caused by the attending physician’s inappropriate remarks?
keypoints: The resident physician should proactively arrange a meeting with the patient’s family to engage in necessary and therapeutic communication, directly addressing the emotional harm caused by the attending physician’s inappropriate remarks.

Employing an empathic communication framework, the resident should recognize and validate the family’s intense emotions, pause to listen attentively and appreciate their feelings, explicitly convey understanding and acknowledgment of these emotions, respect the family’s efforts to cope with the situation, and offer support and partnership.

Initiate the conversation with open-ended questions to encourage the family to express their feelings; the resident should patiently listen and paraphrase the family’s statements to create an empathic feedback loop that demonstrates understanding and care.

Avoid making excuses for the attending physician or engaging in superficial damage control; the resident should focus on the family’s feelings, sincerely express understanding and respect, and uphold the trust fundamental to the physician-patient relationship.

At the conclusion of the dialogue, the resident should thank the family for their candid sharing, affirm the medical team’s ongoing commitment to providing respectful and compassionate care, and thereby facilitate the restoration of trust and healing.

ethical_issues.question: How can medical students and residents maintain professionalism and avoid being negatively influenced by poor role modeling when an attending physician uses inappropriate language?
keypoints: Professionalism requires treating patients with dignity, warmth, and empathy, as well as engaging in effective communication.

The core dilemma faced by the resident physician is that remaining silent may be the easier option, but proactive communication represents the more professional approach and can have a positive impact.
The resident can address the attending physician’s inappropriate language by rebuilding trust with the patient’s family and providing feedback to the attending.
When communicating with the attending physician, an empathic, non-accusatory approach that focuses on one’s own feelings should be employed to facilitate constructive dialogue.

title: Following the Golden Rule toward Respectful Relationships: Physician-to-Nurse Communication.
case: An ICU nurse consistently informs, you, the junior resident, that he would have handled a particular problem or conversation with a patient differently, often explaining what he would have done instead. This morning, he started to correct you in front of a patient but was interrupted by the entrance of the patient's primary care physician.
case_rewrite: During your rotation in the ICU, you, a junior resident, have noticed that one of the nurses is particularly vocal about how he would approach certain situations with patients. After patient rounds, he often approaches you to explain how he would have managed a specific issue differently, detailing his own preferred methods or communication strategies. This morning, while you were speaking with a patient about her treatment plan, the nurse began to interject, attempting to correct your explanation in front of the patient. Before he could finish, the patient's primary care physician entered the room, interrupting the exchange.

ethical_issues.question: Is it appropriate for healthcare professionals to correct each other’s behavior in front of a patient, and how can disagreements be avoided in the presence of patients?
keypoints: Healthcare professionals should never correct each other or engage in clinical disagreements in front of the patient, in order to preserve the patient’s trust and maintain a professional image.
Both residents and nurses should avoid pointing out each other’s errors in the presence of the patient, upholding mutual respect and fostering teamwork.
The clinical interaction with the patient should be completed first, and only afterward should the parties engage in a calm and collegial manner for private discussion to resolve any disagreements.

An effective signaling mechanism should be established to enable healthcare providers to promptly prevent potential errors and then transition to a private setting to collaboratively determine the best course of action.

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians proactively seek nurses’ input and feedback to promote communication and collaboration?
keypoints: Physicians should proactively seek input and feedback from nurses to enhance communication and collaboration, thereby improving the overall quality of team-based patient care.
Physicians must recognize that they are not omniscient; soliciting nurses’ opinions does not undermine their authority but rather demonstrates professionalism and a willingness to collaborate.
Attentively listening to the insights of experienced nurses within the care team is an important indicator of a physician’s professional maturity.
Both physicians and nurses are highly trained professionals who require mutual respect and close cooperation to jointly provide high-quality patient care.
Treating clinical colleagues as one would wish to be treated fosters mutual trust, earns respect, and facilitates effective collaboration.

title: Hoping for the Best, Preparing for the Worst: Physician to Patient in Clinical Trial
case: A patient of yours with prostate cancer has been given a prognosis of 4-6 months and has enrolled in a Phase II clinical trial. In discussing the research protocol with him, you have repeatedly emphasized there is no guarantee of therapeutic benefit. The patient, however, discusses the potential for long-term plans, now that he's "part of the study." How should you, as his clinician, communicate that the study may not change the prognosis?
case_rewrite:
Dr. W has been caring for SB, a patient diagnosed with advanced prostate cancer. After careful evaluation, Dr. W informed SB that his prognosis is approximately 4 to 6 months. Despite this, SB recently enrolled in a Phase II clinical trial, hoping it might offer new possibilities. Throughout several discussions about the research protocol, Dr. W has repeatedly underscored that participation in the trial cannot guarantee any therapeutic benefit or significantly alter the expected course of illness.

However, during a follow-up clinic visit, SB seems buoyed by new optimism. He begins talking about making long-term plans, remarking, “Now that I’m part of the study, maybe I’ll have more time than we thought.” His wife, who has accompanied him to the appointment at his request, listens intently as SB shares his hopes for the future.

Dr. W, recognizing the importance of honesty and compassion, prepares himself for a difficult but necessary conversation. He ensures they are in a quiet, private consultation room and lets SB know that he is available for as much time as needed. Dr. W also checks with SB to confirm that he wants his wife present for the discussion. Sensing SB’s optimism, Dr. W listens carefully, maintaining gentle eye contact and an open posture.

Before addressing SB’s expectations directly, Dr. W offers a gentle warning: “SB, I want to talk with you about something important regarding the study, and some of it might be difficult to hear.” He acknowledges SB’s hope, saying, “It’s completely natural to want to believe in a breakthrough, and I admire your strength.” Dr. W then asks SB to describe what he hopes the trial will achieve for him, encouraging SB to elaborate on his thoughts and feelings.

As SB shares his dreams of a much longer future, Dr. W uses the “ask-tell-ask” approach, first asking what SB understands about the study, then carefully explaining again that while there is always room for hope, the trial is primarily designed to test safety and efficacy, not to guarantee a cure or even an extension of life. He invites SB and his wife to reflect back what they have heard, clarifying any misunderstandings with patience and empathy.

Understanding that such news can take time to process, Dr. W assures SB and his wife that these conversations can continue over future visits. He stresses that, regardless of the study’s outcome, he and the care team will remain by SB’s side, providing support and guidance every step of the way. Dr. W emphasizes, “We will hope for the best, but also prepare together for whatever may come. You are not alone in this.”

ethical_issues.question: How should clinicians communicate to patients in clinical trials the reality that the study may not alter their prognosis?
keypoints: Prior to communicating with the patient, the physician should engage in self-reflection to ensure emotional stability and adequately prepare for the possibility of the patient expressing strong emotions.
Select a quiet and private setting for the conversation, inquire whether the patient wishes to have family members or support persons present, and create a safe and comfortable atmosphere.
Use a preparatory warning signal to help the patient psychologically brace for unfavorable information; maintain appropriate eye contact during communication to convey care and respect.

Initially respond to the patient’s expressions of hope with empathic acknowledgment, then gently guide the patient to elaborate on their specific expectations, advocating a realistic strategy of “hoping for the best while preparing for the worst.”
Employ the “ask-tell-ask” communication model to deliver information in segments, encourage the patient to restate their understanding, and promptly clarify any misunderstandings.
Recognize that conveying bad news is a dynamic and iterative process that requires multiple conversations to deepen the patient’s comprehension and acceptance.
Provide the patient with truthful and achievable reassurances, emphasizing ongoing follow-up and continuous presence, thereby reflecting trust and support within the physician-patient relationship.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians respond to patients who hold unrealistic expectations regarding the benefits of experimental treatments?
keypoints: Physicians should first engage in self-reflection, manage their own emotions, and prepare psychologically for difficult communications.

Physicians should employ empathic acknowledgment of the patient’s hopes and proactively inquire about the patient’s specific expectations for the future in order to gain a deeper understanding of the patient’s mindset and needs.

Physicians may recommend that patients adopt a strategy of “hoping for the best while preparing for the worst,” thereby helping patients maintain a positive outlook while realistically preparing for potential disease progression.

Physicians should utilize the “communication sandwich” approach (Ask-Tell-Ask) to convey information incrementally, ensuring that both the patient and accompanying persons comprehend the actual effects of the clinical trial and the possible course of the illness.

Physicians should provide a commitment of ongoing presence and support, emphasizing that they will not abandon the patient even if the disease progresses, thereby enhancing the patient’s sense of security and trust.

ethical_issues.question: When conveying bad news, how can physicians ensure that patients both understand the information and feel empathy and support?
keypoints: Physicians should undertake thorough self-preparation before delivering bad news, including gathering comprehensive information, managing their own emotions, and anticipating possible patient reactions along with appropriate response strategies.

Select a quiet and private setting, ensure sufficient uninterrupted time for communication, and inquire whether the patient wishes to have someone accompany them, thereby creating a safe and supportive environment.

Use a “warning shot” to alert the patient that important information is forthcoming; maintain a seated posture, eye contact, and appropriate physical touch during communication to convey care and empathy.

Begin by assessing the patient’s existing knowledge and concerns, patiently listen and observe their emotions and values, and express understanding through reflective feedback to enhance the patient’s sense of being heard.

Employ the “ask-tell-ask” approach to deliver information in segments, repeatedly confirming the patient’s and any companion’s comprehension, and when necessary, request the patient to restate key points for clarification.
Recognize that conveying bad news is an ongoing process requiring multiple conversations to assist the patient in gradually processing and accepting the information.

Clearly assure the patient of continued follow-up and comprehensive support, emphasizing that they will not be abandoned even if the disease progresses, thereby providing a sense of security and reassurance.

tags: Conflicts of interest/Clinician relations with industry
title: Finding the (Right) Time: Physician-to-Drug Rep Communication
case: A pharmaceutical company representative drops off samples at Dr. Mann's office about every 2 weeks. Dr. Mann uses the samples and wants to keep receiving them. The rep always asks to talk with Dr. Mann in person and lingers in the office until Dr. Mann makes time between patients to shake hands and chat for a few minutes. Dr. Mann wants the drug company rep to know that he does not want to talk with him each time he visits; the rep's lingering presence in the office is, at best, distracting and, at worst, annoying to the staff and reduces the time Dr. Mann has to spend with patients.
case_rewrite: Every couple of weeks, a pharmaceutical representative visits Dr. Mann’s clinic to deliver free drug samples. Dr. Mann values these samples and wants to continue receiving them for his patients. However, the representative consistently requests to speak with Dr. Mann face-to-face during each visit, often waiting in the office until Dr. Mann can spare a few moments between patient appointments. These encounters typically involve a handshake and brief conversation, but Dr. Mann finds the rep’s persistent presence increasingly disruptive. The lingering visits not only distract Dr. Mann and his staff but also cut into the limited time he has to care for his patients. Dr. Mann wishes to convey to the representative that, while he appreciates the samples, he does not want to have a conversation during every visit. The situation is becoming a source of annoyance for the office staff and is beginning to interfere with the smooth flow of the clinic. Dr. Mann is considering how best to communicate his concerns to the representative in a way that is both professional and respectful.

ethical_issues.question: How can Dr. Mann appropriately communicate his concerns about the pharmaceutical representative’s persistent presence in his office while maintaining professionalism and upholding ethical standards in their interactions?
keypoints: Physicians should thoroughly prepare before communicating with pharmaceutical representatives, clearly articulating their concerns and objectives while ensuring emotional stability and appropriate language use.
Communication should employ “I” statements to express personal feelings and perspectives, avoiding accusatory or blame-oriented language.

The opening statement should clearly identify the representative’s problematic behavior, its consequences, and the physician’s feelings, while also demonstrating understanding and empathy toward the representative’s viewpoint.
Avoid initiating discussions when emotionally agitated or under significant stress; maintain emotional control and actively work to alleviate the other party’s negative emotions.
If the conversation becomes unmanageable, promptly acknowledge this and suggest adjusting the communication approach to keep the discussion constructive.
Focus on shared goals and seek mutually acceptable solutions rather than becoming entangled in assigning blame or responsibility.

title: Disclosing Error to a Patient: Physician-to-Patient Communication
case:
You are halfway through a busy clinic afternoon and seeing Mr. Osler, a middle-aged man with hypertension. His blood pressure diary indicates that he is above your therapeutic target, and you decide to add a new antihypertensive drug to his regimen. You write a prescription, the nurse faxes it to the pharmacy, and you move on to the next patient.
Two days later you are called by the emergency room about Mr. Osler, who became dizzy while getting his morning paper. He fell on his porch, sustaining a forehead laceration. A careful evaluation showed only postural hypotension, and his laceration was closed. You arrive to say hello to him and see his medication bottles at the bedside. You are shocked to find that the hospital pharmacy dispensed the new drug at 10 times the dose you intended. You step out of the room to collect yourself and decide what to do.
case_rewrite:
It’s a hectic afternoon in clinic when you see Mr. Osler, a man in his fifties with a long-standing history of hypertension. Reviewing his blood pressure diary, you note that his readings remain consistently above target, so you decide to prescribe an additional antihypertensive medication. After discussing the change with Mr. Osler, you write the prescription and hand it to the nurse, who faxes it to the pharmacy. Feeling satisfied with the plan, you move on to your next patient.

Two days later, you receive a call from the emergency department. Mr. Osler was brought in after becoming lightheaded while retrieving his morning newspaper and falling on his porch, resulting in a laceration on his forehead. In the ER, he is found to have postural hypotension, but fortunately, no other injuries. His wound is cleaned and sutured. When you go to check on him, you notice his medication bottles by the bedside. Looking closely, you are alarmed to see that the new antihypertensive medication was dispensed at ten times the dose you had intended.

Feeling shaken, you step out of the room to gather yourself and consider how best to proceed.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians effectively communicate with patients following a medical error to prevent loss of trust and mitigate potential litigation risks?
keypoints: Ensure the patient is stable and provide optimal care while gathering the basic facts available at the time.
Before communication, assess your own emotional state; if feeling anxious, angry, or defensive, seek assistance or accompaniment from a colleague to ensure the quality of the communication.

When communicating with the patient and their family, objectively state the facts without assigning blame or conjecture, clearly explaining the sequence of events, consequences, corrective treatment plan, and treatment outcomes.
Express empathy by explaining that the event was neither expected nor intentional, that the patient’s emotional response is understandable, and offer timely regret and a personal apology.

Inform the patient that the primary goal is to ensure they receive the best possible care, and explain that efforts are underway to identify the cause of the error and implement measures to prevent recurrence.
Clearly express the desire to continue providing care, aiming to earn the trust and cooperation of the patient and their family.

ethical_issues.question: How should healthcare institutions manage and document medical errors to ensure patient safety and prevent the occurrence of similar incidents in the future?
keypoints: Addressing medical errors requires abandoning a "blame culture" and establishing an open and transparent communication system, with the core objective of repairing patient safety system vulnerabilities to prevent harm to future patients.
Following the occurrence of a medical error, the patient’s stability must be ensured first, along with the provision of optimal care.
Errors should be promptly reported to the quality management department, typically through an incident report, with critical event review or root cause analysis initiated as necessary.

The medical record should comprehensively document the event details, patient impact, treatment measures, and outcomes, while avoiding speculation about causes or assigning blame to others; disclosure of involved individuals’ identities, disciplinary actions, review findings, or legal consultations is prohibited.

The fundamental goal of error disclosure and reporting is to safeguard patient safety and prevent recurrence of similar incidents, which constitutes a vital ethical responsibility in medical practice.

title: Frame Feedback to Improve Professional Performance: Colleague-to-Colleague Communication.
case: You are a radiologist in a hospital-based group practice. While one of your partners is on vacation, an internist calls you because your partner read a head MRI for one of his patients a short while ago. The internist is concerned because his patient's headaches are becoming worse, and she is now developing visual field deficits. Before considering a second MRI, the internist would like you to review the first one. When you get off the phone, you pull the patient's (Mrs. Kirk's) MRI; there is a suspicious "spot" in the pituitary gland that you think called for further evaluation. This difference of opinion has happened twice before with radiographic studies that were originally read by your partner and reviewed by you over the last 6 months. You think he is making some obvious omissions in his readings, and you recognize that something must be done. Patient safety could be at risk. You decide that the best course of action is to talk to your partner as soon as he returns from vacation. What do you say to him and how do you say it?
case_rewrite:
You are a radiologist working in a hospital-based group practice. While your colleague Dr. W is on vacation, you receive a call from SB, an internist, regarding a mutual patient. SB explains that his patient, Mrs. Kirk, has been experiencing worsening headaches and has now developed visual field deficits. SB mentions that Dr. W recently read Mrs. Kirk’s head MRI, but before ordering another scan, he asks if you could review the initial images.

After finishing the call, you retrieve Mrs. Kirk’s MRI and examine it closely. You notice a suspicious area in the pituitary gland that you believe deserved further evaluation—something you do not see mentioned in Dr. W’s original report. This is not the first occurrence: over the past six months, you have twice before disagreed with Dr. W’s interpretations after reviewing studies he initially read. In both previous cases, you felt that Dr. W overlooked findings that seemed apparent and important to you.

These repeated discrepancies raise serious concerns for you about Dr. W’s pattern of omissions in his radiology readings. Recognizing that patient safety might be at risk, you feel an ethical obligation to address the issue. After careful consideration, you resolve that the most appropriate course is to speak directly with Dr. W as soon as he returns from vacation.

You plan to arrange a private, undisturbed meeting with Dr. W. In this conversation, you intend to present your concerns using clear, factual examples, focusing specifically on the differences you have observed in the readings, including Mrs. Kirk’s case and the two earlier incidents. Your goal is to express your worries for both patient safety and Dr. W’s professional development, and to approach the issue collaboratively, inviting Dr. W to share his perspective and participate in identifying the underlying causes. You hope to work together in finding constructive solutions and ensuring that future patient care is not compromised.

ethical_issues.question: How can critical feedback be provided to a colleague in a constructive manner while ensuring patient safety?
keypoints: When recognizing that a pattern of potential errors has emerged and may jeopardize patient safety, physicians have an ethical obligation to take timely action to ensure the quality of diagnosis and treatment as well as patient safety.
Choose an undisturbed and private setting for delivering feedback to avoid triggering defensiveness and to foster an open and respectful communication environment.
Provide feedback using descriptive, specific, and fact-based data, focusing on key issues while avoiding vague or evaluative language.

Clearly articulate dual concerns for both patient safety and the professional development of the colleague, thereby promoting constructive collaboration and a shared willingness to resolve the problem.

Allow the colleague ample opportunity to respond, encouraging their engagement in problem analysis and the formulation of improvement plans; feedback should focus on remediable behaviors and directions for improvement.

ethical_issues.question: How can one communicate effectively about a colleague’s clinical errors without triggering a defensive response?
keypoints: Frame the communication as a collaborative problem-solving process between allies, emphasizing cooperation rather than blame.
Choose an undisturbed, private setting and arrange a planned face-to-face meeting, avoiding surprise or impromptu interactions.
Use descriptive, specific data and facts, focusing on key points for improvement while avoiding vague or evaluative language.
Clearly express dual concerns for patient safety and the colleague’s professional development to foster mutual understanding and support.
Provide the colleague with ample opportunity to respond, encouraging their active participation in problem analysis and solution formulation.
Ensure feedback targets remediable behaviors and decisions, aiming to optimize clinical outcomes and professional performance.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of a colleague’s ongoing clinical errors, how should one balance ethical responsibilities with professional relationships and take appropriate actions to prevent further risk to patients?
keypoints: Physicians have an ethical obligation to ensure the accuracy of diagnosis and treatment, and must take timely action to safeguard patient safety upon identifying clinical errors made by colleagues.
Communication with colleagues should be conducted in a constructive and collaborative manner, avoiding the provocation of defensiveness and thereby promoting professional improvement.
Feedback should be delivered in a private, undisturbed setting, employing specific, descriptive language grounded in factual data, and focusing on key issues.

It is essential to thoroughly understand the underlying causes of errors, paying attention to potential factors such as incompetence, mental health concerns, or other influences, and to recommend that colleagues seek professional support when necessary.
Colleagues should be given ample opportunity to respond, encouraging their active participation in problem analysis and resolution; feedback should concentrate on specific, remediable behaviors.
If clinical errors persist despite communication efforts, reporting to a quality assurance committee should be considered, but this measure ought to be reserved as a last resort.

title: Doctor and Friend
case:
Dr. Cleveland has been treating Mr. Neezer for 20 years, and they've been fishing buddies for at least 15. Two years ago Mr. Neezer began consistently complaining about lower back pain. Initially Dr. Cleveland tried to treat it with muscle relaxants and referred Mr. Neezer to a physical therapist. Mr. Neezer went the first time, but failed to show up for the second appointment. When Dr. Cleveland asked him about it, Mr. Neezer just said he wasn't into "that physical therapy thing."
"And besides," he said, "Medicare won't cover all of it."
As the back pain continued, Dr. Cleveland noticed that Mr. Neezer moved more stiffly and had particular trouble getting onto and off the exam table. He began including a prescription analgesic along with the muscle relaxants. For the last several months, Mr. Neezer has been making appointments every 6-8 weeks. He consistently asks Dr. Cleveland "What're we going to do about this pain?" and requests stronger pain control, while refusing to schedule the surgery consult that Dr. Cleveland has recommended.
"Look, Doug, with you as my doctor I don't need to go see some surgeon, you're doing a great job taking care of me."
case_rewrite:
Dr. Cleveland has cared for Mr. Neezer for two decades, and over the last fifteen years, their friendship has grown through shared fishing trips. Two years ago, Mr. Neezer began to complain regularly about persistent lower back pain. At first, Dr. Cleveland managed the symptoms with muscle relaxants and referred Mr. Neezer to a physical therapist. While Mr. Neezer attended the initial session, he didn't return for follow-up appointments. When Dr. Cleveland asked about this, Mr. Neezer shrugged it off, saying physical therapy just wasn't for him.

"Besides," Mr. Neezer added, "Medicare doesn't cover the whole thing, anyway."

As time passed and the pain continued, Dr. Cleveland noticed Mr. Neezer moving with increasing stiffness and struggling to get on and off the exam table. In response, Dr. Cleveland prescribed an analgesic in addition to the muscle relaxants. For the past several months, Mr. Neezer has been coming in every six to eight weeks, each time asking, "So, what're we going to do about this pain?" He consistently requests stronger pain relief but refuses to schedule the surgical consultation Dr. Cleveland has recommended.

"Come on, Doug," Mr. Neezer insists, "as long as you're my doctor, I don't need to see any surgeon. You're taking good care of me."

ethical_issues.question: How should a patient’s refusal of recommended treatment affect the physician’s clinical decision-making and provision of care?
keypoints: Competent patients have the right to refuse any medical treatment, but they do not have the right to compel physicians to provide any therapy that lacks medical indication.

Physicians should incorporate the patient’s refusal of treatment into the informed consent process, thoroughly informing the patient of the potential health risks and consequences associated with declining the recommended care.

Physicians must clearly communicate their own boundaries during discussions with the patient (for example, that adjustments to pain medication will only be considered if the patient agrees to a surgical consultation) and be prepared with contingency plans should these conditions not be met, including referral to another provider or modification of the treatment approach.

ethical_issues.question: If a dual relationship poses a risk to the patient’s best interests, how should the physician proceed, and how should the physician appropriately inform the patient about referral options and the potential impact on their friendship?
keypoints: When it is clear that a dual relationship poses a significant risk and may jeopardize the patient’s best interests, the physician should proactively initiate a referral to another provider, fully explaining the reasons and necessity for this action.

The physician should disclose any potential conflicts of interest to the patient and specifically employ Fisher and Ury’s negotiation technique of “separating the people from the problem,” engaging in a joint discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of the dual relationship for medical care, and assisting the patient in rationally weighing the option of referral.

Based on the shared goal of optimizing patient health outcomes and maintaining both interpersonal and professional relationships, the physician should reasonably articulate concerns regarding the dual relationship and provide a sound medical rationale for recommending a surgical consultation.
The physician should respect the patient’s emotional responses, avoid personalizing the issue, and be prepared to accept the potential loss of friendship if necessary for the patient’s well-being.

The physician should arrange the referral process appropriately to ensure the patient’s continuity of care, clearly communicate to help the patient understand the referral options and their possible impact on the friendship, and remain attentive to the patient’s emotions and needs throughout the process.

ethical_issues.question: How should dual relationships be managed when a physician and patient share a non-medical relationship, in order to prevent harm?
keypoints: Identify and clarify the existence of a dual relationship and its core risks, namely that emotions or external factors may compromise the objectivity of the physician’s professional judgment.
The physician should always prioritize the patient’s best interests and adhere to the principle of “do no harm,” preventing the dual relationship from adversely affecting the quality of care.

When a dual relationship may result in significant risk or a conflict of interest, the physician should proactively disclose the situation to the patient, fully explain the reasons, and, depending on the level of risk, weigh or decide on referral to another physician.

The physician should engage in a rational discussion with the patient regarding the advantages and disadvantages of continuing the physician-patient relationship versus referral, weighing the potential impact on the patient’s health.

If it is decided to continue treatment, clear boundaries and rules should be established to regulate the overlap between friendship and the professional relationship, and a mutually agreed-upon treatment plan should be negotiated.
If consensus cannot be reached through negotiation, the physician should prioritize the patient’s best interests and opt for referral to avoid potential harm.

title: Familial Genetic Risk
case:
Dr. Twitchell, a family physician, is scheduled to meet with 18-year-old Andrew this afternoon. "Drew" is an only child and has always looked up to Dr. Twitchell as a mentor. Whenever he comes to the office, he asks Dr. Twitchell's advice about something, sometimes medical, sometimes not. Dr. Twitchell has consistently gotten the impression that Andrew does not know that his parents are carriers of sickle cell anemia, and Andrew has never been tested. Despite his urgings, Andrew's parents have never committed to tell him about their status.
As Dr. Twitchell enters the exam room, he begins, "How are you doing today, Drew?"
Andrew blurts out, "Well, I'm getting married."
"That's exciting news, I bet your parents are excited."
Andrew responds quietly, "Well, they don't exactly know yet. We're planning to elope in Vegas. Neither of us has ever been to Vegas before, and Vanessa doesn't want to make a big deal out of it anyway."
"Don't you think your parents would like to know about your wedding, Drew?" Dr. Twitchell asks.
Andrew shifts uncomfortably.
"Well, Drew, let's leave it at that. Just remember that I think you should let your parents know."
As Dr. Twitchell continues the examination, he wonders how to get Drew the information about his parents' carrier status without telling his parents he plans to elope.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Twitchell, a family physician, is preparing for his afternoon appointment with 18-year-old Andrew. Known to everyone as "Drew," he is an only child who has long regarded Dr. Twitchell as a trusted mentor. Over the years, Drew has often sought Dr. Twitchell’s advice—sometimes on medical matters, other times about life in general. Through their conversations, Dr. Twitchell has become convinced that Andrew is unaware that both his parents are carriers of sickle cell anemia, and Andrew himself has never undergone testing. Despite Dr. Twitchell’s encouragement, Andrew’s parents have never agreed to discuss their carrier status with him.

When Dr. Twitchell enters the exam room, he greets Drew warmly. "How are you doing today, Drew?"

Without hesitation, Andrew announces, "Well, I’m getting married."

“That’s exciting news! I bet your parents are thrilled," Dr. Twitchell replies.

Andrew’s expression grows guarded. "Well, they don’t exactly know yet. We’re actually planning to elope in Vegas. Neither of us has ever been, and Vanessa wants to keep things low-key."

Dr. Twitchell raises an eyebrow. "Don’t you think your parents would want to know about the wedding, Drew?"

Andrew shifts uneasily in his seat.

Sensing his discomfort, Dr. Twitchell says gently, "Alright, let’s leave it at that for now. Just remember, I think your parents would appreciate being included."

As Dr. Twitchell proceeds with the physical examination, he finds himself reflecting on how best to ensure Drew receives important information about his family’s genetic background—particularly his parents’ sickle cell carrier status—without revealing Drew’s confidential plans or breaching the trust of his parents.

ethical_issues.question: Should the physician, without breaching patient confidentiality, facilitate a discussion between the patient and his parents regarding genetic risk information?
keypoints: Physicians should respect the duty of patient confidentiality and, without breaching this principle, facilitate discussions between the patient and his parents regarding genetic risk information.
Physicians may recommend convening a family meeting, provided that all participants voluntarily consent to engage.

Physicians should inform Andrew’s parents that, based on principles of fidelity and moral obligation, they ought to disclose the genetic risk to Andrew and encourage joint deliberation on this matter.
Physicians may advise Andrew to consider discussing with his parents the potential implications and consequences of sharing genetic information.

If the parents refuse to disclose the information directly, physicians should explore the reasons for their refusal and assist in alleviating their concerns (such as stigma or insurance discrimination).
Should the parents find it difficult to communicate this information, physicians may, with their permission, act as intermediaries to facilitate disclosure.
If the parents persist in withholding the information, physicians must respect their decision and refrain from forcibly disclosing genetic information.

Given that this genetic risk does not constitute an immediate and serious health threat to Andrew or his fiancée, nor does it pose a clear and preventable harm to any identifiable third party, physicians lack the authority to override confidentiality and disclose the information unilaterally.

Without revealing the parents’ carrier status, physicians may inquire whether Andrew is aware of any family history of genetic disease to assess his level of knowledge and inform subsequent health management needs.

tags: Patient-clinician relationship/Patients’ responsibility for their health
title: When Depression Affects Treatment Decisions
case:
Mr. Li moved to the area about a year ago, and this is his second visit to Dr. Rodale's office. Dr. Rodale reviews her notes from the last appointment. At that time, Mr. Li's blood pressure was elevated (143/88) and his total cholesterol was 235 mg/dL, with LDL at 163 mg/dL, HDL at 44 mg/dL, and triglycerides at 427 mg/dL.
Dr. Rodale remembers informing Mr. Li of the findings and saying "Mr. Li, although making certain lifestyle changes like more exercise and healthy eating may help with your blood pressure, I think you should get a prescription to help with your high cholesterol numbers."
Mr. Li simply shook his head. "I think you're overestimating the risk and I'm not sure it matters anyway."
"Have you taken a prescription for high blood pressure or high cholesterol before?" Dr. Rodale inquired.
"Nope."
"Well, I've got a few samples here in the office. Perhaps you could see if you're able to keep up with the regimen and, if so, I can call in a full prescription later on."
Mr. Li began gathering his things without responding.
"Mr. Li, although your risks are not dangerously high yet, if you don't do something about your blood pressure and cholesterol, they will be."
"It doesn't really make a difference, doc."
"I'm not sure what you mean, Mr. Li. In terms of your future health and risk of cardiovascular problems, it very much does make a difference." Dr. Rodale responds.
"Thanks for seeing me, Doc." Mr. Li mumbles as he walks out the door.
Two weeks later, as Dr. Rodale enters the room for Mr. Li's next appointment, she notices in the chart that his blood pressure is even higher. Mr. Li is staring absently at the corner of the ceiling.
"How are you doing today, Mr. Li?" Dr. Rodale asks.
Mr. Li informs Dr. Rodale he has a fever, which she thinks is viral. After Dr. Rodale informs him that he should drink plenty of fluids, she asks for his permission to retest his cholesterol. As during the last appointment, Mr. Li is despondent, and nothing that Dr. Rodale tells him seems to have an effect.
Dr. Rodale informs Mr. Li that he should make a follow-up appointment for a couple of weeks later to check on his viral infection and discuss the results of the cholesterol test.
Mr. Li fails to make an appointment as he leaves and does not return any phone calls during the next week about his cholesterol test. Dr. Rodale is concerned that he is depressed.
case_rewrite:
Mr. Li relocated to the neighborhood about a year ago, and today marks his second visit to Dr. Rodale’s office. As Dr. Rodale sits down, she reviews her notes from their previous encounter. At that first appointment, Mr. Li’s blood pressure registered at 143/88. His cholesterol panel was concerning: total cholesterol was 235 mg/dL, LDL 163 mg/dL, HDL 44 mg/dL, and triglycerides 427 mg/dL.

Dr. Rodale recalls clearly discussing these findings with Mr. Li. “Mr. Li, while adopting healthier eating habits and increasing your physical activity could help your blood pressure, your cholesterol levels are high enough that I recommend you start medication,” she had explained.

Mr. Li had simply shaken his head. “I think you’re making too much of this. I’m not convinced it matters.”

“Have you ever taken medication for high blood pressure or cholesterol before?” Dr. Rodale had asked gently.

“No, never.”

“Well, I have a few sample medications here you could try. This would let you see if you can manage the routine, and if it works out, I can write you a full prescription later on.”

Instead of responding, Mr. Li started to gather his belongings.

“Mr. Li, while your numbers aren’t at a crisis point yet, if you don’t address your blood pressure and cholesterol, they’re likely to get worse,” Dr. Rodale cautioned.

“It doesn’t really make a difference, doc.”

Unsure, Dr. Rodale pressed, “What do you mean, Mr. Li? These numbers definitely matter for your future health and risk of heart disease.”

“Thanks for your time, Doc,” Mr. Li muttered, making his way to the door.

Two weeks later, Dr. Rodale enters the exam room to see Mr. Li again. She notes that his blood pressure has risen further. Mr. Li sits slouched in the chair, his gaze fixed on a distant corner of the ceiling.

“How are you feeling today, Mr. Li?” Dr. Rodale asks.

Mr. Li mentions he has a fever. Dr. Rodale suspects a viral illness and advises him to drink plenty of fluids. She then asks if he would allow her to retest his cholesterol. Throughout the visit, Mr. Li remains withdrawn and unresponsive, his demeanor subdued no matter what Dr. Rodale says.

Before he leaves, Dr. Rodale reminds Mr. Li to schedule a follow-up appointment in a couple of weeks to recheck his viral symptoms and review his cholesterol results.

However, Mr. Li does not make a follow-up appointment as he leaves, nor does he respond to any phone calls from the office regarding his cholesterol test over the next week. Dr. Rodale begins to worry that Mr. Li may be experiencing depression.

ethical_issues.question: In cases where a patient may be suffering from depression and refuses treatment, should the physician breach medical confidentiality to protect the patient’s safety?
keypoints: The principle of medical confidentiality is a cornerstone of Western healthcare systems; however, when a patient presents an imminent risk of self-harm or harm to others, physicians are permitted to breach confidentiality to protect the patient’s safety.
Physicians have the responsibility to promptly breach confidentiality and implement necessary interventions upon determining the presence of danger, in order to prevent self-harm or harm to others.
In this case, Mr. Li’s depressive symptoms and risk of self-harm remain unclear; therefore, the physician should first gather additional information to avoid precipitous action.

If breaching confidentiality becomes necessary, the least harmful approach should be employed, such as conducting a welfare check through law enforcement or contacting the patient’s family members, to ensure that interventions are appropriate and justified.

ethical_issues.question: When a patient refuses treatment and their capacity for autonomous decision-making may be impaired by depression, how should a physician balance respect for patient autonomy with the principle of beneficence?
keypoints: Physicians should recognize that a patient’s refusal of treatment constitutes an ethical dilemma requiring a balance between respecting patient autonomy and the principle of beneficence.
Physicians should assess the patient’s depressive status, as depression may impair decision-making capacity and value judgment.

If depression is diagnosed, active treatment should be initiated to help restore the patient’s decision-making ability, with long-term health issues to be reconsidered following remission of depressive symptoms.

If the patient refuses treatment and there is no immediate threat to life, the physician does not have the authority to impose treatment but should maintain ongoing monitoring of the patient’s health status.
Physicians should periodically revisit the topic of treatment, respecting the dynamic nature of patient decisions and allowing for adjustments based on changes in the patient’s condition and values.

ethical_issues.question: If the decision is made to breach patient confidentiality, what actions should the physician take to minimize harm and negative consequences to the patient?
keypoints: Physicians should conduct a rational assessment of the patient’s condition and gather additional relevant information before breaching medical confidentiality, ensuring that any action taken is prudent and necessary.

With the patient’s prior consent, physicians may contact the patient’s family members to request that the patient return a call or schedule a follow-up appointment, while avoiding disclosure of sensitive information such as the patient’s depression, so as to minimize harm and negative impact on the patient.

When the patient’s condition may pose a risk to their own safety or that of others, physicians may consider requesting a “welfare check” by law enforcement, thereby involving an authoritative agency to mitigate adverse consequences.
In extreme and necessary circumstances, physicians may seek court-ordered psychiatric admission through legal procedures to ensure the patient’s safety and protect the public interest.

title: Physicians' Dual Loyalties
case:
Mr. and Mrs. Samir have both been patients of Dr. Lachman for 4 years. They live a 30-minute drive from his office, so they regularly schedule their appointments on the same day. As usual he sees Mrs. Samir first.
During the examination, Mrs. Samir asks if she should see an obstetrician—she and Mr. Samir have stopped using birth control (a barrier method) because they are trying to get pregnant. She's a little worried because she's had some lower abdominal pain and post-coital bleeding.
"Well, have you taken a pregnancy test? Some abdominal pain and light bleeding are not uncommon in pregnant women."
"No, we just started trying a few weeks ago."
"Perhaps we should go ahead and do a pregnancy test now," Dr. Lachman suggests. "Would you like me to get Mr. Samir in here for the results."
Mrs. Samir fidgets for a moment. "Perhaps we better not," she finally says, "I just don't feel very pregnant and that would get his hopes up."
Dr. Lachman continues the physical examination and tries to isolate the cause of Mrs. Samir's abdominal pain, but he's unable to identify more than just general tenderness.
"Mrs. Samir, I'd like to run a couple of tests to rule out infection. Is that okay with you?" Dr. Lachman suspects that Mrs. Samir has contracted some kind of STD, perhaps from Mr. Samir, but he doesn't want to upset her by saying so. She agrees to undergo a few tests.
Just as Dr. Lachman guessed, Mrs. Samir tests positive for Chlamydia. He informs Mrs. Samir, and tells her that she needs to start a course of antibiotics and that he needs to test Mr. Samir.
Mrs. Samir demands that Dr. Lachman not disclose what he has discovered to Mr. Samir—test him if he agrees to it, but do not tell him about her condition.
case_rewrite:
Mr. and Mrs. Samir have both been under Dr. Lachman’s care for the past four years. Since their home is about a thirty-minute drive from his clinic, they usually coordinate their visits to see him on the same day. On this occasion, Dr. Lachman sees Mrs. Samir first, as is their custom.

During the examination, Mrs. Samir brings up a concern. She asks Dr. Lachman whether she should schedule an appointment with an obstetrician, explaining that she and Mr. Samir have recently stopped using their usual barrier contraception and are actively trying to conceive. She confides that she’s a bit anxious because she has experienced some lower abdominal discomfort and post-coital spotting.

Dr. Lachman responds, “Have you taken a pregnancy test yet? Mild abdominal pain and light bleeding can sometimes occur early in pregnancy.”

Mrs. Samir shakes her head. “No, we only just started trying a few weeks ago.”

“In that case,” Dr. Lachman suggests, “perhaps we should do a pregnancy test now. Would you like me to bring Mr. Samir in when we get the results?”

Mrs. Samir hesitates, shifting in her seat. “Maybe it’s better if we don’t,” she says quietly. “I don’t really feel pregnant, and I’d hate to get his hopes up for nothing.”

Dr. Lachman continues with the physical exam, attempting to pinpoint the source of her abdominal pain, but finds only vague tenderness without any clear cause.

“Mrs. Samir, I’d like to run a few tests to rule out infection. Would that be alright with you?” he asks. Based on her symptoms, Dr. Lachman suspects a possible sexually transmitted infection, perhaps contracted from Mr. Samir, but he avoids mentioning this directly to avoid causing distress. Mrs. Samir consents to the tests.

The results confirm Dr. Lachman’s suspicion: Mrs. Samir tests positive for Chlamydia. He informs her of the diagnosis, explains the need to begin antibiotic treatment, and tells her that Mr. Samir should also be tested.

At this, Mrs. Samir becomes anxious and insists, “Dr. Lachman, please don’t tell my husband about this. You can test him if he agrees, but do not reveal anything about my condition to him.”

ethical_issues.question: Under what circumstances may physicians breach patient confidentiality in order to protect the health and safety of third parties?
keypoints: The physician’s duty of confidentiality is relative rather than absolute and requires balancing the protection of patient privacy with safeguarding the health and safety of identifiable third parties.
Physicians may consider breaching confidentiality when the patient poses a risk of serious harm to identifiable third parties.
If the likelihood of harm is high and constitutes a real threat, physicians may breach confidentiality to prevent such risk.
When no less invasive alternative means of warning or protecting those at risk are available, physicians may disclose necessary information.
Physicians may breach confidentiality if disclosing information enables third parties to take effective preventive measures to avoid harm.
The harm resulting from the breach of confidentiality should be controllable and ethically acceptable, ensuring that risks are minimized.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians manage diagnostic information requested to be kept confidential by a patient, especially when such information may impact the health of another patient?
keypoints: Physicians should respect patients' right to privacy; the duty of confidentiality is a fundamental principle of medical ethics, but this duty is relative rather than absolute.

Breaching confidentiality is justified only as a last resort when efforts to persuade the patient to inform their partner have failed and no less intrusive alternatives are available; it requires careful assessment of the potential risks, necessity, and proportionality of the disclosure.

Physicians should actively encourage patients to disclose information to their partners themselves or to authorize the physician to do so on their behalf, while providing necessary psychological support, joint consultations with the couple, and referral to couples therapy as appropriate.

Physicians should inform patients that failure to notify their partners may result in the partner developing symptoms, raising questions about the route of infection, as well as placing the patient at risk of reinfection and related complications, thereby assisting patients in rationally weighing the benefits and harms of disclosure.

Physicians have a moral obligation to protect identifiable third parties from foreseeable and serious harm, and the strength of this obligation does not vary depending on whether the third party is also their patient.

tags: Health professions education/Learner roles and responsibilities
title: "Trust Me. I'm a Doctor."
case: You are a third-year medical student on the last day of a clinical rotation. You have seen a total of 2 lumbar punctures. Just before you enter a patient's room and leaving you no time to respond, your attending physician says, "I'm going to introduce you as 'doctor.' It makes it easier for the patient and you need to do a spinal tap before you finish your rotation." As you enter the room, the attending physician tells the patient, "This is Dr. [Smith], who will be doing your lumbar puncture." The attending physician and the patient both look at you expectantly. What do you do? What are the ethical and professional considerations that would guide your response?
case_rewrite:
It is your final day as a third-year medical student on your clinical rotation. Throughout this rotation, you have watched two lumbar punctures being performed but have yet to carry out the procedure yourself. As you gather your notes and prepare to see your next patient, your attending physician, Dr. W, intercepts you in the hallway. Without pausing for your response, Dr. W says, “I’m going to introduce you as ‘doctor.’ It makes things simpler for the patient, and you need to do a spinal tap before you finish your rotation.”

Before you have a chance to object or ask questions, Dr. W ushers you into the patient’s room. Inside, Dr. W turns to the patient, SB, who is sitting upright in bed, and announces, “This is Dr. Smith, who will be performing your lumbar puncture today.” SB looks at you expectantly, appearing comforted by the introduction and expressing no sign of concern. Dr. W then looks to you, making it clear that you are expected to proceed with the procedure.

At that moment, you realize both SB and Dr. W expect you to move forward. However, SB has not been told that you are a medical student rather than a physician, nor has SB been informed about your limited experience with lumbar punctures. You are faced with an immediate decision: whether to clarify your actual role and experience to SB or to let the misunderstanding stand. You must weigh your ethical and professional responsibilities, particularly regarding the patient’s right to informed consent, respect for patient autonomy, and the importance of honesty and trust in the physician-patient relationship.

ethical_issues.question: Should Dr. [Smith], a third-year medical student, correct the patient's misunderstanding of their professional status after being falsely introduced as a doctor by the attending physician? What ethical principles and professional responsibilities should guide Dr. [Smith]'s response in this situation?
keypoints: To safeguard the patient’s right to informed consent, medical students have the responsibility to disclose their true status as trainees, especially prior to performing procedures that carry significant risk.

Medical students should communicate privately with the attending physician to express their desire to learn and their concerns, seeking a mutually agreeable approach to uphold patient trust while avoiding direct confrontation in front of the patient.

Ultimately, medical students bear the responsibility to clarify their trainee status to the patient, the attending physician, and themselves, as this represents the least risky course of action and is essential to ensuring valid informed consent.

ethical_issues.question: In medical education, how can a balance be achieved between respecting patient autonomy and ensuring that medical students acquire the necessary procedural experience?
keypoints: Upholding the principle of informed consent is central to balancing patient autonomy with medical students’ procedural experience.
Medical students should fully disclose their trainee status and level of experience, as this is a prerequisite for ensuring patients’ rights to informed consent and autonomous decision-making.
Many patients are willing to allow medical students to participate in certain aspects of their care and may even permit students to perform lumbar punctures.
Appropriate patient education and communication help correct misconceptions and increase patient acceptance of medical student involvement in higher-risk procedures.

Waivers of informed consent and concealment of a medical student’s true status should only be considered in rare and well-justified circumstances, as such deception generally lacks ethical justification.

title: An Adolescent with an Eating Disorder
case:
Carli recently made an appointment for her yearly physical with Dr. Goldstein. Dr. Goldstein always enjoyed seeing Carli, a motivated and responsible teenager who, at 17, seemed to have direction and plans for her future. In accordance with Dr. Goldstein's office protocol, Carli's mother remained in the waiting room during the visit.
During the interview, Carli was bubbly and vivacious. She enjoyed school and was looking forward to college. She had lots of friends, but no steady boyfriend. She played tennis and soccer. She explained that she had recently developed an interest in baking and had won a prize in a school contest for a cherry pie. When asked if she had any concerns, she explained that she was trying to "take off a little weight" that she gained after the soccer season. She also stated that she had occasional headaches, but she attributed them to stress about taking the SATs. Otherwise, she had no health concerns.
Dr. Goldstein noted that Carli had lost about 7 pounds since her last visit 6 months ago, but she did not appear grossly underweight. During the HEENT exam, Dr. Goldstein saw some dental enamel erosion on the posterior surfaces of her teeth. He also detected mild enlargement of her parotid glands bilaterally. Her cardiovascular and pulmonary exams were normal. On abdominal exam, Carli complained of mild nausea with deep palpation, but no masses or painful areas were found. Her neurologic, musculoskeletal, and genitourinary exams were normal. She had mild facial acne. Dr. Goldstein also noted a callus on her right middle finger. Carli explained that she has developed that callus "from all the writing that I have to do in my English class. We write long essays!"
After completing the physical, Dr. Goldstein explained to Carli that he was concerned about bulimia. At first, Carli flatly denied any binge-purge behavior. Dr. Goldstein suggested that Carli go down the hall to the lab and give a blood sample so he could get some screening labs. Carli seemed worried. "Do you think something's wrong with me?" she asked. Dr. Goldstein said he just wanted to make sure nothingwaswrong, and Carli agreed to the test.
Not long afterward, Dr. Goldstein's nurse called Carli back in from the waiting room where she had been working on school assignments. Her screening blood work showed mild hypokalemia, increased serum amylase, and a normal CBC. Dr. Goldstein showed these results to Carli and explained that they were highly suggestive of bulimia. Sighing, she admitted to bingeing and purging during the past 5 months. She explained that she would get the urge to eat and then feel as though she couldn't stop eating. Afterwards, she felt guilty and purged by vomiting. She had tried diuretics a few times but felt they were "less effective than vomiting." Carli told Dr. Goldstein that she thought she was getting better. A few months ago she was bingeing and purging almost daily and she now only did it a few times a week. She begged him not to tell her mother. "My mom is under a lot of stress right now since her sister was diagnosed with cancer, and I don't want her stressed out with my problems," she explained. She promised to work with Dr. Goldstein to stop her behavior as long as he did not tell her mother. Carli promised to come in for weekly weight checks and exams or do "whatever," so long as Dr. Goldstein kept her secret.
Dr. Goldstein was concerned about Carli. He knew that her physical manifestations and lab values showed that she was probably sicker than she realized. However, she was 17 and had been a reliable patient in the past.
case_rewrite:
Carli had scheduled her annual physical with Dr. Goldstein, a visit both looked forward to each year. At seventeen, Carli was industrious and mature for her age, with clear goals and a positive outlook. As was standard practice in Dr. Goldstein’s office, Carli’s mother waited outside in the reception area during the appointment.

During their conversation, Carli was upbeat and energetic. She talked about her enjoyment of school, her excitement about college applications, and her busy social life, though she mentioned she wasn’t dating anyone steadily. She played on the school’s tennis and soccer teams and recently discovered a passion for baking, even winning a prize for a cherry pie in a school competition. When Dr. Goldstein asked if she had any health concerns, Carli admitted she was hoping to lose a bit of weight she’d gained after soccer season, and that she occasionally got headaches, which she attributed to SAT stress. Otherwise, she reported feeling well.

Dr. Goldstein reviewed her chart and noted a seven-pound weight loss since her last visit six months prior, though Carli’s weight was not alarmingly low. During the head and neck exam, he observed some erosion of the enamel on the back surfaces of her teeth and slight swelling of both parotid glands. Her heart and lungs sounded normal. On abdominal exam, Carli mentioned mild nausea with deep palpation, but there were no abnormal findings. Her neurological, musculoskeletal, and genitourinary exams were unremarkable. She had mild facial acne. Dr. Goldstein also noticed a callus on Carli’s right middle finger, which she explained was from extensive essay writing in English class.

Once the physical was complete, Dr. Goldstein gently shared with Carli his concern about possible bulimia. At first, Carli firmly denied any episodes of bingeing or purging. Dr. Goldstein suggested that she have some routine blood work done, just to be thorough. Carli seemed anxious and asked if he thought something was wrong. Dr. Goldstein reassured her that he simply wanted to make sure everything was alright, and Carli agreed to the lab tests.

Shortly after, Dr. Goldstein’s nurse asked Carli, who was now in the waiting room working on homework, to return for a follow-up discussion. The lab results indicated mild hypokalemia and elevated serum amylase, while her complete blood count was normal. Dr. Goldstein reviewed the results with Carli and explained that these findings were highly suggestive of bulimia. With a sigh, Carli admitted that she had been bingeing and purging for the past five months. She described feeling unable to stop eating during urges to binge, followed by guilt that led her to induce vomiting. She acknowledged trying diuretics a few times, but found them less effective than vomiting. Carli insisted she was improving, explaining that while she used to binge and purge almost daily, it was now only a few times each week.

Carli pleaded with Dr. Goldstein not to tell her mother. “My mom has enough to deal with right now—her sister was just diagnosed with cancer—I don’t want her to have more to worry about because of me,” she said. Carli promised to work with Dr. Goldstein to stop the behavior as long as he kept her secret. She agreed to weekly weigh-ins and checkups, or “whatever you think I need,” so long as her mother wasn’t told.

Dr. Goldstein was deeply concerned for Carli. Her exam and lab results suggested her condition was more serious than she realized. Nevertheless, at seventeen, Carli was nearly an adult and had always been a dependable patient.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance respecting the autonomy of adolescent patients with eating disorders and the ethical responsibility to inform parents in order to secure necessary treatment resources?
keypoints: The physician must balance respecting the adolescent patient's autonomy with the duty to disclose imposed by the severity of the eating disorder, ensuring that the patient receives necessary medical support and safety assurances.

On the basis of respecting the patient's privacy and trust, the physician should gradually guide the patient to understand the necessity of disclosing the condition to her parents, thereby promoting the patient’s active participation in treatment and the establishment of family support.

Taking advantage of the patient’s agreement to return for follow-up visits, the physician should collaboratively explore with the patient the timing and manner of disclosure to her parents, striving to achieve a dynamic balance between maintaining patient autonomy and ensuring therapeutic efficacy.

ethical_issues.question: In the medical care of adolescents, how should physicians handle patients’ requests for confidentiality, especially when serious health issues are involved?
keypoints: Physicians should respect the privacy and autonomy of adolescent patients, but must balance the patient’s interests with their duty of protection when serious health issues are involved.

Eating disorders carry potentially life-threatening risks, and physicians have a responsibility to facilitate disclosure of the condition to ensure the patient receives necessary treatment and support.

Physicians should gradually guide patients to recognize the necessity of disclosing their illness, using follow-up visits to discuss the optimal manner of disclosure and to assist the family in facing the condition and working toward recovery.

ethical_issues.question: In the face of denial commonly observed in adolescent patients, how should physicians facilitate patient disclosure of their condition to enable effective treatment while maintaining a trusting doctor-patient relationship?
keypoints: Respect Carli’s autonomy as an emerging adult by ensuring her participation and informed consent in treatment decisions.

Recognize that the denial phase is a common psychological defense mechanism in patients with eating disorders; clinicians should patiently and gradually guide the patient toward understanding the necessity of disclosing the illness.

Within the framework of maintaining the patient-physician trust relationship, the physician should collaboratively discuss with the patient the timing and manner of informing family members, respecting the patient’s wishes while progressively facilitating family support.
Utilize the patient’s agreement to return for follow-up visits to continuously build trust and create conditions conducive to subsequent treatment and family communication.
The physician’s responsibility extends beyond facilitating patient disclosure to assisting both the patient and her family in confronting the illness together and promoting the recovery process.

title: Transition of Care
case:
Heather was born with cystic fibrosis (CF) and has been under the care of the pediatric CF team since her diagnosis. As a child, Heather was quite healthy and had few hospitalizations. At age 3 her parents divorced, and her mother remarried shortly thereafter. Heather's father has maintained limited contact with her since that time. Heather moved into an apartment with her mother and stepfather, a smoker, and it was at about that time that she began to need more hospitalizations for CF exacerbations. She has been in charge of her own medications and chest physical therapy since she was 16, when her mother felt she was "old enough to do all that herself. " Heather spent so much time in the hospital during 11th grade that she failed her exams and had to repeat the year.
Heather's pediatric CF team consists of Dr. Smith, as team leader, and a group of physicians, nurses, nurse practitioners, social workers, respiratory therapists, and nutritionists who closely monitor her care from multiple angles. At each clinic visit she sees several team members who provide information, support, and reinforcement of positive medical treatments.
At 19, Heather has just finished high school and is working part-time as a cashier, while living with her mother and stepfather. On her last visit to the University Pediatric CF unit, Heather talked with her pediatrician, Dr. Smith, about her ambition, saying that she would like to become a veterinary assistant in the future, but that she has not yet applied to any colleges or vocational programs. Heather says that she began smoking about 2 years ago and, when Dr. Smith asked about alcohol use, she said that she drinks alcohol 2 or 3 times a week. She said she does not use any other drugs and would like to quit smoking. She says she takes her prescribed medications according to directions, but her frequent hospitalizations suggest that she may be slipping in this regard. She has kept approximately half of her scheduled appointments in the CF clinic, often showing up late.
The hospital administration has put pressure on the pediatric CF team and Dr. Smith to transfer Heather to the adult team—a transition that usually occurs when the patient is about 18. The hospital has received complaints from parents of patients on the pediatric unit that Heather is too old to be there. Several parents have also expressed concern about the way Heather dresses and the friends that visit her while she is on the unit. One parent claimed to smell cigarette smoke coming from Heather's room.
The pediatric CF team is concerned about Heather: her smoking and suspected noncompliance with her medication worries doctors that she could "slip through the cracks" with the less intensive monitoring that goes along with adult patient care but Dr. Smith understands that Heather is no longer a child and must accept the consequences of adult decision making. When Dr. Smith asked Heather how she felt about the transition, Heather said, "whatever you guys decide is fine with me."
case_rewrite:
Heather was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis (CF) early in childhood and has been cared for by the pediatric CF team ever since. In her younger years, Heather generally enjoyed good health and required only occasional hospital visits. When she was three, her parents divorced, and her mother soon remarried. Since then, Heather's father has kept only minimal contact with her. After the divorce, Heather moved in with her mother and stepfather, who is a smoker. Around this time, Heather's health declined, and she began needing more frequent hospitalizations for CF flare-ups.

By age sixteen, Heather’s mother decided she was mature enough to manage her own medications and chest physiotherapy. Heather took on this responsibility herself from then on. The strain of her illness grew during her high school years; in eleventh grade, her hospital stays became so frequent that she failed her exams and had to repeat the year.

Heather’s pediatric CF team is led by Dr. Smith and includes physicians, nurses, nurse practitioners, social workers, respiratory therapists, and nutritionists. At each clinic appointment, Heather meets with several team members who provide her with guidance, encouragement, and practical support to help her stay on track with her treatment.

Now nineteen, Heather has just completed high school. She works part-time as a cashier and lives with her mother and stepfather. At her latest appointment in the University Pediatric CF unit, Heather confided in Dr. Smith about her aspirations to become a veterinary assistant, though she has yet to apply to any college or vocational program. She also revealed that she started smoking cigarettes about two years ago. When Dr. Smith inquired about alcohol use, Heather responded that she drinks two or three times a week but does not use any other substances. She expressed a desire to quit smoking. She insisted she takes her medications as prescribed, yet her frequent hospital admissions suggest she may not be fully adherent. Heather has only attended about half of her scheduled CF clinic appointments, and she often arrives late.

Pressure is mounting from the hospital administration for Dr. Smith and the pediatric CF team to transition Heather to the adult CF team, as is customary around age eighteen. Some parents of other pediatric patients have complained that Heather is too old to remain in the unit.
