title: Drugs for the Shy?
case:
Jonathan Parker was brought to Dr. Reiser, a psychiatrist, by his mother. Mrs. Parker said that Jonathan, aged 22, lived at home with her and his father and seldom left the house alone. He would socialize with his siblings and cousins, occasionally go to the movies with one of them or with his mother, and went to family gatherings and church. But, as Mrs. Parker told it, Jonathan never brought a friend to the house and, since completing his BS in computer science, had not been going out daily for school or work or anything else. He was pretty unhappy and had agreed to his mother's plea that he "get some help."
Jonathan had done well in school, had applied for a dozen or so jobs, and had been called in for several interviews. But he always returned home dejected, saying, "They're not going to call back." So far, he had been right.
Dr. Reiser accepted Jonathan as a patient and began seeing him once weekly. After 3 visits, he asked Jonathan whether he would agree to try one of a class of drugs known as SSRIs. Dr. Reiser wasn't certain it would help, but it had produced some good results in certain sociophobic patients. Jonathan agreed. Jonathan was bright, and, as he became more comfortable with Dr. Reiser, the psychiatrist could see Jonathan's mind at work, trying to understand the responses and feelings he had when he was alone with a stranger or in a social situation without his family members beside him.
After 3 months, Jonathan told Dr. Reiser that he felt ready to leave therapy. He had had a callback following an interview, and a job offer seemed likely. The drug was really working, Jonathan said. He and his family had talked about it and everyone was pleased. Jonathan said he wanted to continue on the prescription and stop therapy. Dr. Reiser opposed the idea, explaining that Jonathan's shyness had causes that would go undiscovered and unmanaged if he masked the symptoms with drugs. The psychiatrist preferred to continue the drug and "talk" therapies in tandem, so that they could get to the bottom of the shyness problem and eventually wean Jonathan from the drug. Jonathan said all he cared about was getting rid of the symptoms. Why did it matter what had caused the shyness if it had disappeared? Jonathan began to get angry. Once he had a job, he said, he wouldn't be able to take time off for the appointments. If Dr. Reiser wouldn't agree to prescribe the drug, Jonathan said, he'd find another doctor who would.
case_rewrite:
Jonathan Parker, a 22-year-old recent computer science graduate, was brought to see Dr. Reiser, a psychiatrist, by his mother. Mrs. Parker explained that Jonathan still lived at home with his parents and rarely ventured out alone. While he did interact with his siblings and cousins, occasionally joined his mother for a movie, and attended family gatherings and church events, he never invited friends over or pursued any social activities independently. Since finishing his degree, Jonathan had not established a daily routine involving work, school, or outside hobbies, and he seemed increasingly unhappy. At his mother's urging, Jonathan reluctantly agreed to seek professional help.

Jonathan had a strong academic record and had applied to numerous jobs. Although he was called in for several interviews, he always returned from them discouraged, convinced that he would not be hired. So far, his pessimism had been correct.

Dr. Reiser began seeing Jonathan once a week. After three sessions, Dr. Reiser asked Jonathan if he would consider trying a medication from the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class. He explained that while he couldn't guarantee results, some patients with social anxiety had experienced significant improvement. Jonathan consented to the trial. As therapy progressed and Jonathan grew more comfortable, Dr. Reiser observed Jonathan’s keen intellect as he tried to make sense of his emotional reactions, especially when alone with strangers or in unfamiliar social situations without the support of his family.

After three months of combined therapy and medication, Jonathan announced that he felt ready to stop therapy. He had received a callback after a job interview, was optimistic about a forthcoming offer, and credited the medication with his progress. He and his family had discussed the matter and were pleased with the changes. Jonathan expressed a strong desire to continue the medication but discontinue therapy. Dr. Reiser disagreed, explaining that while the medication alleviated symptoms, underlying causes of Jonathan’s shyness could remain unaddressed if therapy was abandoned. He recommended continuing both medication and psychotherapy to fully address the problem and, in time, potentially taper off the drug.

Jonathan was unconvinced. He insisted that resolving the symptoms was all that mattered to him, questioning why he should focus on the root causes if the problem was effectively managed. As the discussion continued, Jonathan grew frustrated. He pointed out that once employed, he would not have the flexibility to attend regular therapy appointments. He told Dr. Reiser that if he could not get the prescription from him, he would seek another physician who would provide the medication without the requirement for ongoing therapy.

ethical_issues.question: How can appropriate informed consent be ensured during the course of treatment, including informing the patient about the research, benefits, and potential side effects of the medication?
keypoints: Dr. Reiser should inform Jonathan Parker about the relevant research on the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for treating social anxiety disorder, including the expected benefits and potential side effects.

Dr. Reiser should explain the type of psychotherapy recommended, its utility in Jonathan’s specific circumstances, and the rationale for combining it with pharmacotherapy to more comprehensively address both the symptoms and their underlying causes.

Dr. Reiser should clearly communicate to Jonathan, early in the course of treatment, the anticipated duration of both medication and psychotherapy, as well as the possibility of adjustments to the treatment plan.

Dr. Reiser should appropriately tailor the level of detail in the informed consent process based on the development of the patient-physician relationship, ensuring that Jonathan fully understands the treatment options and actively participates in decision-making.
Dr. Reiser and Jonathan should engage in thorough communication regarding informed consent issues early in the evaluation to establish trust and facilitate collaborative treatment.

ethical_issues.question: How can a balance be achieved between patient autonomy and physician beneficence, especially when the patient chooses medication-only treatment while the physician recommends continuing psychotherapy?
keypoints: Physicians should sensitively and clearly communicate their best medical recommendations to the patient, respect the patient’s choices, and keep open the possibility for future psychotherapy.

When the patient opts for medication-only treatment, the physician should continue to provide prescriptions and monitor the patient’s response through appropriately scheduled follow-up visits to ensure symptom stability and absence of deterioration.
Physicians should maintain a good patient-physician relationship, respect patient autonomy, and fulfill their professional obligations to promote the patient’s overall well-being.

title: Managed Care and Physician Burnout
case:
Dr. Richard Kent walked into the office and pulled up his schedule for the day on the computer. Another full one. Four patients had been scheduled for every hour. Contractually, he was allowed 20 minutes per visit, but Hippocrates Health Care, the organization for which he worked, operated on the assumption that 1 out of every 4 patients doesn't show for his or her appointment. Great; suppose all of his "assumed" no-shows for the day showed up. Suppose 4 didn't, but they were all scheduled for 4 pm. His day would be hectic. He found himself hoping that all the assumed no shows would indeed fail to keep their appointments. In truth, he hoped evenmorethan that wouldn't show.
Hippocrates Health Care had been moving into the area and signing up increasing numbers of company health benefits contracts over the last 5 years. Now, few physicians in the region were not part of the system. When more and more of Dr. Kent's patients had told him they'd have to leave him and find a physician on the Hippocrates list, he and his partners signed on as Hippocrates employees. They immediately enjoyed some perks, full patient load on days when they worked, no more filing paperwork for reimbursement from 10 or even 12 separate insurance plans, no more uncollectible accounts.
But the numbing sameness of his days was getting to him. Patient records were automated, and there were computers in each examining room. On initial visits, Dr. Kent would sit at the computer and ask each patient 30 or so questions beyond what the nurse or PA had already asked and click in the proper field on the answer given by the patients. Then he would leave while the patient undressed, go ask patient 2 the same 30 questions, and return to examine the patient 1.
Physicians under contract to Hippocrates were required to practice within the boundaries of what was "customary and standard" throughout Hippocrates' nationwide service area. Dr. Kent had to document deviations from those standards of care, get approval before rendering the service, or apply retroactively for reimbursement for an extra day in the hospital or for a particular brand of drug.
What compromised Dr. Kent's sense of professional integrity more than anything was having to explain Hippocrates' business-based decisions to his patients. When Hippocrates suddenly dropped a brand name drug from its formulary, Dr. Kent would have to tell patients, some of whom had been successfully dose-calibrated and maintained on that drug for years, that they would have to change. He had to be truthful in telling them why he was changing their prescriptions; he couldn't say medical judgment was behind the decision, because it wasn't. The same was true in limitations or delays placed on diagnostic tests that, based on his own medical judgment, Dr. Kent would have ordered without delay. He worried that explaining the reasons for such bottom-line-oriented decisions was eroding his patients' trust in medicine and in him.
What a rut, Dr. Kent thought. Imagine hoping that patients don't show up. This doesn't feel like the noble profession of medicine.
case_rewrite:
Dr. Richard Kent entered his office and, settling into his chair, opened his schedule for the day on his computer. The sight was all too familiar: another fully packed day. Four appointments were squeezed into every hour. According to his contract, he was supposed to have 20 minutes with each patient, but at Hippocrates Health Care—the organization that now employed him—scheduling was based on the assumption that one out of every four patients would miss their appointment. Dr. Kent couldn’t help but wonder: what if every “no-show” on his schedule actually turned up today? Or if they all missed the same late afternoon slot? The thought made him uneasy; secretly, he caught himself hoping that more than the expected number of patients would simply not come.

Hippocrates Health Care had rapidly expanded in the region over the last five years, signing contracts with more and more employer health plans. Now, it was rare to find a physician in the area who wasn’t affiliated. When an increasing number of Dr. Kent’s patients told him they’d have to leave his practice to stay within their insurance networks, he and his partners decided to join Hippocrates as employees. Initially, the change brought certain conveniences: a consistently full schedule on workdays, no more hassling with reimbursement from numerous insurance companies, and no more worries about unpaid bills.

Yet, the monotony of his days had begun to wear on Dr. Kent. Patient records were now fully digital, with computers stationed in every exam room. For every new patient, Dr. Kent would sit at the screen, asking about 30 standardized questions—many already covered by the nurse or physician assistant—and click in each response. Then, as the patient changed for the exam, he’d move on to the next room, repeat the same set of questions for the next patient, and circle back as needed.

As a contract physician for Hippocrates, Dr. Kent was required to practice strictly within the boundaries of what was considered “customary and standard” across the company’s vast national network. Any deviation from these care standards had to be meticulously documented, pre-approved before proceeding, or justified retroactively for reimbursement—whether it was an extra day in the hospital or a specific brand of medication.

What gnawed most at Dr. Kent’s sense of professional integrity was having to relay Hippocrates’ business-driven decisions to his patients. When the company abruptly removed a brand-name drug from its formulary, Dr. Kent was tasked with informing patients—some of whom had been stabilized on that very medication for years—that they would need to switch. He insisted on being honest, telling them the change was not medically motivated, because it wasn’t. The same uncomfortable truth applied when diagnostic tests were delayed or limited by the system, even when his medical judgment called for immediate action. He worried that explaining such cost-driven choices was gradually eroding his patients’ trust in him and, by extension, in the institution of medicine itself.

What a rut, Dr. Kent thought to himself. Imagine wishing your patients didn’t show up. This hardly felt like the noble calling that drew him to medicine in the first place.

ethical_issues.question: How can physicians ethically balance the conflict between commercial interests and the optimal treatment plans for patients within a managed care system?
keypoints: One ethical conflict faced by physicians within managed care systems is the necessity to explain business-driven decisions to patients, which may undermine patients’ trust in their physicians and the medical profession, as well as compromise professional dignity.

Physicians can mitigate physician-patient conflicts and enhance patient trust and treatment adherence by understanding patients’ concerns, demonstrating empathy, and encouraging patients to participate in clinical decision-making, such as collaboratively negotiating alternative medication regimens.

To address patients’ feelings of loss of control caused by managed care restrictions, physicians may employ both behavioral and cognitive strategies to regulate their emotional responses, while focusing on the positive aspects of the doctor-patient interaction to alleviate distress arising from adverse external factors.

Physicians and their practice teams should actively advocate for healthcare system reforms to eliminate management practices that impair quality of care, such as establishing dynamically updated databases of insurance formularies, thereby reducing frustration caused by administrative limitations.

Although there is a gap between the ideal and the reality of medical practice, physicians should uphold the core values of medicine and strive to provide the best possible care within institutional constraints, thereby preserving professional integrity and maintaining a sound foundation for the physician-patient relationship.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of managed care limiting physicians’ clinical autonomy, how should physicians uphold their professional dignity and maintain patient trust?
keypoints: Physicians should first confront the core issue, namely the crisis of trust between doctor and patient caused by the necessity to explain business-driven decisions to patients; recognizing this dilemma is fundamental for subsequent coping strategies.

Physicians should enhance their communication skills by understanding patients’ concerns, demonstrating empathy, and encouraging patient participation in clinical decision-making, thereby reducing conflicts and strengthening trust.

Physicians may negotiate adjustments to their work schedules, such as reducing patient load or shortening working hours, while collaborating with practice partners to advocate for reforms in the healthcare system to achieve a more reasonable practice environment.

Physicians should adjust their expectations to align with the realities of practice, focusing on the positive aspects of the doctor-patient interaction to alleviate distress caused by adverse external factors.

Physicians need to recognize that feelings of frustration related to limitations on professional autonomy are a normal response and should balance occupational stress through spending time with family and friends, regular relaxation, and self-care to maintain physical and mental well-being.

title: Obesity as Medical Neglect: Should Doctors Report?
case:
MD is a 15-year-old Hispanic boy with a medical history of chronic renal failure (CRF) and morbid obesity. As an infant, MD was taken from a migrant worker camp into the custody of the Department of Social Services because his biological mother failed to provide adequate nutrition and care. He was later adopted by a family that attended more closely to his needs and care. At age 2 he was diagnosed with renal failure secondary to focal segmental glomerular sclerosis (FSGS) and required peritoneal dialysis until age 3, when he received a cadaveric kidney transplant.
Over time MD's linear growth decelerated, crossing from about the 25th percentile at age 6 to less than the 5th percentile by age 8. At 11, he had an acute rejection event, and he has remained in chronic renal failure. MD has experienced other problems related to his renal failure such as hypertension and renal osteodystrophy.
MD suffers from excessive weight gain; at his current height of 134 cm (5th percentile) and weight of 130 kg (>95th percentile) his body mass index is 72 kg/m2, which greatly exceeds the 95th percentile for his age and sex. He suffers from many of the morbidities associated with obesity, including obstructive sleep apnea, and requires continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) while sleeping. He has dyspnea on exertion and severe exercise intolerance resulting in both his inability and unwillingness even to take walks around the neighborhood. MD does not attend high school because he cannot tolerate moving from class to class. The hypertension associated with CRF is exacerbated by his obesity, and he has developed left ventricular hypertrophy. His excessive weight stresses his musculoskeletal system, and in concert with renal osteodystrophy, has resulted in genu valgum (deformity of the legs that produces "knock knees") requiring surgical repair. He has poor self-esteem and periods of depression and has developed ADD secondary to sleep apnea (no longer requiring medication because of CPAP treatment). MD's elevated insulin levels (fasting c-peptide level of 7.4, normal range 0.4-2.2) suggest that he has developed insulin resistance that will likely progress to type II diabetes. MD needs treatment for the chronic renal failure but his obesity makes him a very poor candidate for either dialysis or a repeat transplant. His obesity is, therefore, exacerbating the morbidity and mortality risks associated with his underlying renal disease, may prevent him from getting the definitive life-preserving treatment he needs (a kidney transplant), and is causing morbidity and mortality risks independent of his renal disease.
MD and his family have been told about the risks associated with his obesity, have received extensive dietary counseling, and have worked with mental health services. Social workers, occupational therapists, and exercise counselors have all visited the family's home. On 2 different occasions, when MD was 12 and again at 13, he was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation facilities to increase his exercise tolerance and weight loss. On both occasions MD lost weight, but his family withdrew him because they felt that he was being "starved" and treated cruelly. He was also enrolled in a hospital-based outpatient wellness/fitness program, from which his parents also withdrew him. MD rarely brings his food diary to appointments with his dietician, and his parents also refused a proffered liquid diet because they felt it would be cruel to him. The patient and his family acknowledge that he is excessively overweight, but blame his medications, including steroids (currently 10 mg prednisone per day), and wish "there was a magic bullet" to solve this problem. With respect to all other aspects of his health care, MD and his family are extremely reliable, and he is apparently compliant with his medications.
case_rewrite:
MD is a 15-year-old Hispanic boy who has struggled with chronic renal failure (CRF) and severe obesity throughout his life. As an infant, MD was removed from a migrant worker camp by the Department of Social Services because his biological mother did not provide adequate nutrition or care. He was eventually adopted by a family who has since been attentive to his needs. At age 2, he was diagnosed with renal failure due to focal segmental glomerular sclerosis (FSGS), requiring peritoneal dialysis until he received a cadaveric kidney transplant at age 3.

MD’s linear growth slowed over the years—dropping from the 25th percentile at age 6 to below the 5th percentile by age 8. When he was 11, he experienced an acute rejection episode and has remained in a state of chronic renal failure since then. In addition to his renal issues, MD has developed hypertension and renal osteodystrophy.

MD’s excessive weight gain has further complicated his health. He is currently 134 cm tall (5th percentile) and weighs 130 kg (well above the 95th percentile), giving him a BMI of 72 kg/m²—an extreme value for his age. He suffers from numerous obesity-related complications, including obstructive sleep apnea, for which he uses CPAP each night. He experiences shortness of breath with exertion and has such poor exercise tolerance that he is unable and unwilling to walk around his neighborhood. MD does not attend high school because he cannot manage the physical demands of moving between classes. His obesity has worsened his CRF-associated hypertension and led to left ventricular hypertrophy. The stress on his bones, combined with renal osteodystrophy, has caused genu valgum (“knock knees”) requiring surgical intervention. Emotionally, MD battles low self-esteem and periods of depression; he also developed attention deficit disorder (ADD) as a result of his sleep apnea, which improved after starting CPAP. MD’s fasting c-peptide level is 7.4 (normal range 0.4-2.2), indicating insulin resistance and a high risk for developing type II diabetes. His obesity now makes him a poor candidate for both dialysis and a repeat kidney transplant—treatments essential for his survival. Thus, MD’s weight problem not only exacerbates his existing health issues but also poses independent risks to his morbidity and mortality.

MD and his adoptive family have been counseled extensively about the dangers of his obesity. They have received dietary guidance and mental health support, and their home has been visited by social workers, occupational therapists, and exercise counselors. Twice, at ages 12 and 13, MD was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation centers to help with weight loss and exercise tolerance; each time, he succeeded in losing weight, but his family withdrew him, feeling the staff were “starving” him and treating him harshly. MD was subsequently enrolled in a hospital-based outpatient wellness program, but his parents withdrew him from that as well. He rarely brings his food diary to dietician appointments, and his parents declined a suggested liquid diet, considering it too harsh. Both MD and his family recognize his severe overweight, but attribute it mainly to his medications—including his current daily dose of 10 mg prednisone—and express a wish for a “magic bullet” to resolve his weight. Despite these challenges, MD and his family are otherwise highly reliable with his medical care and strictly compliant with his medication regimen.

ethical_issues.question: When reporting child neglect, how should the ethical considerations between the child’s best medical interests and the patient’s confidentiality rights as well as family autonomy be balanced?
keypoints: Determining the best medical interests of the child is the core principle of medical decision-making and should serve as the starting point for all actions.

Healthcare professionals have a legal and ethical obligation to report suspected child neglect to child protective services; however, this duty must be balanced against ethical conflicts involving respect for patient confidentiality and family autonomy.

The failure of MD’s parents to effectively implement critical medical recommendations may constitute medical neglect, providing a significant basis for the reporting obligation, but the complexity of the situation requires avoidance of absolutist judgments.

As an adolescent, MD’s autonomy and capacity for self-determination are progressively increasing, limiting parental responsibility for his behavioral choices; his rights to participate in medical decision-making should be respected.

The decision to report should be based on a comprehensive assessment of the child’s best interests, ensuring that reporting will genuinely contribute to improving his health status while avoiding unnecessary disruption of the therapeutic alliance.

Maintaining the therapeutic alliance with the patient and family is essential for long-term management and improved medical outcomes; the healthcare team should seek a balance between reporting obligations and supporting the family to foster cooperation and trust.

title: Cultural Differences at the End of Life
case:
When Dr. Lim entered the room, Mrs. Drake's son and daughter-in-law were there. Her daughter-in-law's chair was pulled up to the bedside and she sat there holding Mrs. Drake's hand, rubbing it gently. Dr. Lim greeted them and then examined his patient.
Mrs. Drake had suffered a moderate stroke 3 years ago. At that time she had difficulty swallowing and was unable to move her right side. She could no longer verbalize sentences and could only communicate by pointing. A feeding tube was placed. Recently she developed a pneumonia secondary to aspiration. After suffering a cardiopulmonary arrest she required continued mechanical ventilation for the past 3 weeks. She was minimally responsive, but did open her eyes to command and was able to squeeze with her left hand.
Mrs. Drake's daughter arrived and, as soon as the 3 visitors had greeted one another, they asked to speak with Dr. Lim outside the room. There, Mrs. Drake's son and daughter said that they thought that continued treatment of their mother was causing her to suffer and asked whether or not the ventilator could be removed. They did not want to give up on her and asked his advice.
Dr. Lim could not help but disagree. He himself was the eldest of 6 siblings. His own mother had had a stroke 8 years prior. He and his siblings had taken care of her throughout the years. She was bed-bound and contracted, nonverbal but awake. His siblings followed his directions regarding the care of his mother. He was the doctor and the eldest. He knew the quality of her life was poor but he could not reconcile her loss.
But the Drakes thought differently. Dr. Lim suggested that Mrs. Drake's son and daughter might feel regret or even guilt if they allowed their mother to die. "We each get only one mother," he said to them. The Drake children had discussed this very point at length among themselves. They had agreed that what their mother was currently experiencing was not life and certainly not life as she had enjoyed it. She had been, until 3 years ago, a vibrant woman, active in the town's Cultural Arts Council and in her church and oftentimes winner of the Yard of the Month in recognition of her imaginative and tireless gardening activities. No, that was not "Mom" in the bed, and it had not been since the first of her strokes. Now she was just a body, lying there with no hope of getting off the ventilator. They felt conflicted. They thought she would be furious at the thought of living like that. However, they did not want her life to end. Of course, their decision was not an easy one. They had been hoping for confirmation or assurance from the professional in charge of their mother's care. Instead, Dr. Lim said, in parting, "Well, there's time. Why don't you think about it. If you stop her feedings, she will starve. If you take her off the ventilator, she will die. What do you want me to do?"
case_rewrite:
When Dr. Lim walked into the hospital room, he found Mrs. Drake's son and daughter-in-law sitting quietly at her bedside. The daughter-in-law had pulled her chair close and was gently holding Mrs. Drake’s hand, softly rubbing her fingers. Dr. Lim greeted them, then proceeded to examine Mrs. Drake.

Three years earlier, Mrs. Drake had suffered a moderate stroke. Since then, she struggled to swallow, had lost movement on her right side, and could no longer speak in sentences. She communicated mostly by pointing. A feeding tube was placed after her stroke. Recently, she developed pneumonia from aspiration. Following a cardiopulmonary arrest, she had been dependent on mechanical ventilation for the past three weeks. She was now minimally responsive—she could open her eyes when prompted and squeeze Dr. Lim’s hand with her left.

Soon Mrs. Drake’s daughter arrived. After a brief reunion by the bedside, the three family members asked to speak with Dr. Lim in the hallway. There, Mrs. Drake’s son and daughter expressed their concern: they felt that continuing intensive treatment was only prolonging their mother’s suffering. They wondered if it would be possible to discontinue the ventilator, though they admitted they were struggling with the idea of “giving up” on her, and asked Dr. Lim for his advice.

Dr. Lim found himself internally conflicted. He was the eldest of six siblings, and his own mother had suffered a stroke eight years before. For years, he and his siblings had cared for her—bed-bound, contracted, nonverbal, but awake. As the family’s doctor and oldest child, his siblings had looked to him for guidance. He had always known his mother’s quality of life was very poor, but emotionally, he could never fully accept the loss.

But the Drakes approached it differently. Dr. Lim suggested to Mrs. Drake’s son and daughter that they might later experience regret or guilt if they chose to let their mother die. “We each get only one mother,” he reminded them. The siblings explained they had discussed this together many times. They agreed that what their mother was now enduring was not life—certainly not the life she had once loved. Until her first stroke, Mrs. Drake had been lively and vital, a leader in the town’s Cultural Arts Council, active in her church, and a frequent winner of the Yard of the Month for her creative gardening. The woman lying in the hospital bed now seemed nothing like the mother they remembered. There was no hope she would recover or live off the ventilator. Still, they felt torn. They imagined she would be angry at the idea of living in such a state, but could not bring themselves to wish for her death. The decision weighed on them heavily, and they hoped Dr. Lim would give them guidance or reassurance.

Instead, as the conversation ended, Dr. Lim said, “There’s time. Why don’t you think it over? If you stop her feedings, she will starve. If you remove the ventilator, she will die. What would you like me to do?”

ethical_issues.question: In end-of-life decision-making consultations, how can clinicians guide family members to focus on what burdens the patient is willing to endure to prolong life, rather than on the family members’ own wishes?
keypoints: Guide the family to focus on the burdens the patient can endure in the continuation of life, avoiding making the family’s own emotions and wishes the central basis for decision-making.
Physicians should clearly, empathetically, and respectfully explain why aggressive treatment is no longer reasonable when it only results in a painful prolongation of life without clear benefit.

Use communication that conveys the professional recommendations of the medical team (e.g., “We recommend not to perform resuscitation/long-term artificial feeding/mechanical ventilation”) instead of directly asking “Do you want this treatment?” to alleviate the family’s decisional burden and feelings of guilt.

Enhance the family’s understanding and engagement in medical decision-making by thoroughly explaining the medical rationale behind the recommendations, the patient’s prognosis, and quality of life, thereby promoting the formation of a rational consensus.

title: Gynecological Care for Adolescents
case:
Mrs. Johnson brought her daughter, Mandy, to see Dr. Jones for her first gynecological visit when Mandy was 13 ½ years old and had just begun to menstruate. Dr. Jones performed a regular physical, but not a vaginal exam, and talked to Mandy about the changes that were leading her to sexual maturity.
Dr. Jones did not see Mandy again until 15 or 16 months later when Mandy made an appointment and showed up on her own worried about vaginal irritation and itchiness. Dr. Jones examined Mandy and, by microscope confirmed his suspicion that Mandy had contracted trichomoniasis. He told Mandy what the infection was and that the person from whom she got it needed to be told so that he could get treatment. Mandy was vague and non-communicative about the topic. Dr. Jones could understand her embarrassment, but Mandy was not able to agree that she would tell her partner. Her main concern was whether Dr. Jones was going to tell her mother.
Mandy was in otherwise good health, upon general examination. Dr. Jones prescribed metronidazol and, because he wanted to talk to her again, asked to see her in 3 weeks. He spoke to her about safe sex and the possible long-term consequences of certain STDs. He assured her that he would not call her mother, but said that the diagnosis would go into Mandy's own personal and private medical record. Mandy kept the appointment 3 weeks later and was clear of infection.
Four months later, however, Mandy was back, again with symptoms of an STD. Dr. Jones is concerned, not only about Mandy's recurrent infection, but also about what appears to be casual sexual activity; she's not yet 16 years old.
case_rewrite:
Mrs. Johnson accompanied her 13-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Mandy, to Dr. Jones for Mandy’s first gynecological appointment. Mandy had recently begun menstruating, and during the visit, Dr. Jones conducted a standard physical examination—excluding a vaginal exam—and discussed with Mandy the physical and emotional changes signaling her entry into sexual maturity. 

After this initial visit, Dr. Jones did not see Mandy again until about 15 or 16 months later, when Mandy independently scheduled an appointment. She arrived alone, expressing concern about vaginal irritation and itching. Following an examination and microscopic analysis, Dr. Jones diagnosed Mandy with trichomoniasis. He explained the nature of the infection and emphasized that her partner also needed to be informed and treated. Mandy, however, was reticent and avoided specifics about her sexual activity. Dr. Jones noticed her discomfort and embarrassment, and Mandy’s primary worry was whether Dr. Jones would disclose her diagnosis to her mother.

Dr. Jones found Mandy to be in good overall health otherwise. He prescribed metronidazole and, wanting to ensure follow-up, asked her to return in three weeks. During this visit, he discussed safe sex practices and the potential long-term effects of sexually transmitted infections. He reassured Mandy that he would not contact her mother but clarified that the diagnosis would be included in her personal and confidential medical record. Mandy returned for the follow-up appointment as scheduled, and her infection had resolved.

However, four months later, Mandy returned once again, presenting with symptoms of another sexually transmitted infection. Dr. Jones grew increasingly concerned—not only about the recurrence of infection but also about what seemed to be ongoing sexual activity, given that Mandy was still under 16 years old.

ethical_issues.question: How can adolescents’ autonomy be respected and confidentiality ensured during sexual health counseling?
keypoints: Physicians should see adolescent patients alone and explain to both the adolescent and their parent the routine practice of private consultation, thereby respecting the adolescent’s autonomy.

Physicians must clearly inform adolescent patients about the confidentiality of medical information and its legal exceptions (such as mandatory reporting of self-harm, harm to others, or physical/sexual abuse), ensuring the patient understands the principles of privacy protection and the foundation of trust.

Physicians should commit to not proactively contacting the adolescent’s parents but inform the patient that the diagnosis will be recorded in their personal confidential medical record, thereby safeguarding patient privacy and continuity of care.

During consultations, physicians should seek the adolescent’s input to demonstrate respect, encourage autonomous expression of their knowledge, and, when necessary, obtain permission before providing corrective information to facilitate effective communication.

Physicians should emphasize the adolescent’s autonomy by clarifying that any recommendations are advisory only, that behavior change is ultimately the patient’s decision, and express this sincerely to reduce resistance and promote constructive collaboration.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians ethically balance informing the patient’s mother with respecting the adolescent patient’s privacy when managing sexually transmitted infections in adolescent patients?
keypoints: Physicians should establish a confidential and trusting clinical environment to ensure that adolescent patients feel safe, respected, and willing to communicate openly.

Physicians need to clearly explain to both the patient and her guardian the routine practice of seeing adolescents alone during part of the visit, as well as the principles of medical information confidentiality.

Physicians should thoroughly clarify the scope of privacy protection, specifying which information is protected and which circumstances (such as self-harm, suicidal ideation, or abuse) legally require mandatory reporting.

Physicians must respect the patient’s right to privacy by reasonably committing not to proactively disclose specific diagnoses to guardians, while documenting relevant information in the patient’s confidential personal medical record to safeguard patient rights and clinical safety.

ethical_issues.question: In the context of Mandy, an adolescent patient presenting with a sexually transmitted infection, how should Dr. Jones ethically assess and address Mandy’s sexual behavior patterns while maintaining a nonjudgmental approach?
keypoints: When encountering adolescent patients with recurrent sexually transmitted infections, physicians should rationally assess the causes of infection and avoid making value judgments about “casual sexual activity” based solely on reinfection; priority should be given to considering reinfection from untreated partners, maintaining an objective and neutral stance.

Physicians should respect patient autonomy by clearly informing patients that behavior change is entirely their own decision, emphasizing that the physician provides advice but does not coerce, with the aim of reducing patient resistance and promoting open communication.

Communication should avoid binary value-laden language such as “good/bad” and instead use neutral terms like “benefits” and “less favorable aspects” to prevent patients from feeling labeled or manipulated.

Before expressing health concerns and offering recommendations, physicians should first obtain the patient’s permission by asking if they are willing to hear the concerns and prevention strategies, thereby demonstrating respect and fostering collaboration.

With patient consent, physicians should concisely explain health risks and recommendations, and provide at least three to four alternative behavioral options to assist the patient in autonomously selecting the most suitable preventive measures, avoiding presenting a single option that may provoke rebuttal.

Physicians should assess the patient’s readiness for behavior change and adjust communication strategies according to the patient’s willingness, recognizing that education alone is often insufficient to effect behavior change and that attention to patient receptivity and engagement is essential.

tags: Patient-clinician relationship/Patients’ responsibility for their health
title: Never Symptom-Free
case:
When Dr. Alverdo saw Richard Edmunds' name on the index card of appointments that the secretary handed him, he thought, "What can I possibly say or do that will make a difference?" Mr. Edmunds, a high school English teacher, was 46 and has a history seasonal allergies. Nevertheless, Mr. Edmunds was in the office, on average, every 6 weeks. His symptoms varied but were always difficult to verify or quantify—pain, discomfort, "just not feeling right."
Three months ago, Mr. Edmunds presented with complaints of headaches. He described the pain as generalized and worse in the afternoon than in the morning. The headache was not accompanied with nausea or visual changes. They never woke him from sleep and were not associated with any particular activity or food. Non-narcotic analgesics were ineffective. Based on the history and physical, which included a normal neurological exam, Dr. Alverdo concluded that the headaches were most likely caused by muscle tension and prescribed a course of anti-inflammatory medications, muscle relaxant, and physical therapy exercises. Mr. Edmunds made 3 visits to the therapist but said the exercises were not helping. He kept asking, "How do you know I don't have a tumor or an aneurysm about to blow, Doc?" Finally, Dr. Alverdo ordered a CT scan, which, he had to admit, he believed was a "shot in the dark." The scan was negative. After that report, Mr. Edmunds complained less about the headaches. Dr. Alverdo hadn't heard about headaches for a couple of months now.
Lately, Mr. Edmunds was having chest pains. Faithful about his annual physical exam, Mr. Edmunds had no previous history of exertional angina or shortness of breath. There was no known heart disease in Mr. Edmunds' immediate family. Dr. Alverdo had ordered an EKG and cardiac stress test, both of which Mr. Edmunds passed with flying colors. Then, thinking the persistent pain might be digestion-related, Dr. Alverdo ordered a barium swallow and upper GI series. Negative.
Looking at the name on the card, Dr. Alverdo thought, what's Edmunds going to want today? At the last visit, Mr. Edmunds reported that he could not sleep because of the crushing pain. The only remaining diagnostics for chest pain were highly invasive. Dr. Alverdo resolved that he would not be talked into ordering an angiogram or anything else that would put Mr. Edmunds at risk. There simply was no indication for it. He imagined how the conversation would go. Mr. Edmunds would dispute everything Dr. Alverdo said. This generally went on for 25 or 30 minutes. "Doctor," Edmunds would say. "Do you want me to be one of those cases you read about in the paper where it says, "he kept telling the doctor he was sick, but no one believed him?"
case_rewrite:
When Dr. Alverdo glanced at the day’s schedule and saw Richard Edmunds’ name among his appointments, a familiar sense of resignation crept in. “What can I possibly say or do that will make a difference?” he wondered. Richard Edmunds, a 46-year-old high school English teacher with a background of seasonal allergies, had become a regular fixture in Dr. Alverdo’s office, showing up roughly every six weeks. The complaints changed from visit to visit but shared a common thread: vague and difficult-to-verify symptoms—pain, discomfort, or simply, as Mr. Edmunds often put it, “just not feeling right.”

Three months earlier, Mr. Edmunds had come in troubled by headaches. He described them as a generalized ache, worse in the afternoons, with no nausea or vision changes. The headaches didn’t wake him from sleep, nor did they seem tied to any activity or particular food. Over-the-counter painkillers hadn’t helped. After a thorough history and a normal neurological exam, Dr. Alverdo concluded the headaches were likely due to muscle tension. He prescribed anti-inflammatory medication, a muscle relaxant, and recommended physical therapy exercises. Mr. Edmunds attended three sessions with the therapist, but reported no relief. “How do you know I don’t have a tumor or an aneurysm about to blow, Doc?” he pressed at each visit. Eventually, Dr. Alverdo ordered a CT scan, privately acknowledging it was “a shot in the dark.” The scan results came back normal. After that, the headaches seemed to fade from Mr. Edmunds’ list of complaints, and Dr. Alverdo hadn’t heard him mention them for a couple of months.

More recently, Mr. Edmunds had begun to focus on chest pains. He was conscientious about his annual physicals and had never before reported exertional chest pain or shortness of breath. He had no known family history of heart disease. Dr. Alverdo ordered an EKG and a cardiac stress test—both of which Mr. Edmunds completed without any trouble. Suspecting the pain might be gastrointestinal, Dr. Alverdo next arranged for a barium swallow and an upper GI series. The results, once again, were negative.

Now, as Dr. Alverdo prepared for today’s appointment, he couldn’t help but wonder what new concern Mr. Edmunds would present. At their last meeting, Mr. Edmunds had described sleepless nights due to “crushing” chest pain. The remaining diagnostic options for chest pain were highly invasive, and Dr. Alverdo firmly decided he would not be pressured into ordering an angiogram or other risky procedures, given the lack of any clinical indication. He could already picture how the conversation might unfold: Mr. Edmunds would challenge each of his explanations, as he often did, prolonging their discussion for half an hour or more. “Doctor,” Mr. Edmunds would inevitably say, “do you want me to be one of those cases you read about in the paper where it says, ‘he kept telling the doctor he was sick, but no one believed him?’”

ethical_issues.question: Should physicians perform high-risk and non-indicated diagnostic tests solely to reassure patients?
keypoints: The physician’s primary obligation is to safeguard the patient’s well-being and should not perform high-risk diagnostic tests without clear indications solely to reassure the patient, as the anticipated benefit of reassurance does not justify the potential risks involved.
Patient autonomy is important, but it does not obligate physicians to provide medical interventions that may be dangerous or non-beneficial.

Physicians should make diagnostic and therapeutic decisions based on clinical probabilities and principles of evidence-based medicine; in this case, the probability of a cardiac etiology is very low and does not support the use of high-risk testing.
Ordering high-risk tests without indication may exacerbate tension and maladaptive dynamics in the physician-patient relationship, creating a vicious cycle that undermines effective care.

Physicians should attend to the patient’s psychological and emotional needs by helping them understand and accept medical uncertainty, thereby preventing excessive testing driven by vulnerability and anxiety, as well as avoiding unnecessary consumption of healthcare resources.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance patient autonomy and the principle of nonmaleficence when confronted with excessive patient activism?
keypoints: Physicians should not yield to patients’ demands for dangerous or non-beneficial interventions, in order to uphold the principle of nonmaleficence and safeguard patient safety and well-being.

Physicians ought to employ effective communication to help patients understand the risks of excessive testing and the inherent uncertainties in medicine, thereby facilitating acceptance of reality and interrupting the vicious cycle of anxiety driven by compulsive reassurance-seeking.
If candid communication fails to alleviate the patient’s medical anxiety, physicians should consider referral to psychiatry for more specialized support.

title: When Disability Is in Question
case:
Dr. Lowe, a family practice physician, has been following Mrs. Darrell for many years—since her kids, now grown and married (one divorced) were in their teens. She is 56 years old, has diabetes, for which she takes glyburide, and is overweight, but active. She raised the 4 children on her own and is now serving in the role of "mother" to one of her granddaughters.
Mrs. Darrell works from 10 to 4 each day as a certified nurse's aide. She was employed by an agency that supplied home care personnel for the chronically ill, those convalescing, and, increasingly, for elderly individuals who wanted to stay in their own homes. Through the agency, Mrs. Darrell was assigned to a particular client, a woman in her 80s who wanted daily help. Mrs. Darrell cemented a relationship with the client and, after a few months, left the agency and made a private arrangement with her client.
Mrs. Darrell was involved in a traffic accident about 3 months ago. Standing at a rural railroad crossing, about third in line, Mrs. Darrell was hit from behind. The car was not traveling fast, and Mrs. Darrell did not hit the car in front of her. She came to Dr. Lowe the next day with neck pain. Her neurological exam was nonfocal and consistent with muscle strain. He prescribed some non-steroidals and told her to wear a cervical collar. He told her to come back if her neck did not feel better in 7 to 10 days. When Mrs. Darrell returned in 3 days, the pain was worse, not better. Her shoulder hurt now, also, and she said that she felt weaker in her left arm; she had trouble supporting her client, who weighed 128 lbs, when helping her in and out of her wheel chair or while bathing her.
On exam, it was difficult to assess whether there was asymmetric strength in her upper extremities, but given the trauma history, Dr. Lowe ordered an urgent cervical MRI. The results of the MRI were negative for nerve compression or bony abnormalities. In addition to the non-steroidals, Dr. Lowe prescribed a muscle relaxant and physical therapy.
A week later, Mrs. Darrell returned with complaints that the pain was not getting better. She was unable to work and asked whether Dr. Lowe could help her get disability status form the Social Security Commission. Dr. Lowe asked whether she might not get some workman's compensation for a while to see whether the neck and shoulder pain resolved. This is when Mrs. Darrell told him that she had left the agency and was working directly for 1 client. Dr. Lowe had assisted in the disability process before and knew it was important to be precise and get the facts straight. In further questioning Mrs. Darrell about her work, he discovered that Mrs. Darrell had an "off-the-books" arrangement with her client. The elderly woman was not withholding income tax from Mrs. Darrell, was not paying employer's social security benefits, and was paying Mrs. Darrell in cash each week. In other words, Dr. Lowe conjectured, Mrs. Darrell could easily continue this arrangement while receiving disability payments, and no one would be the wiser.
Dr. Lowe likes Mrs. Darrell—she's a survivor. She raised those kids on her own without complaint or bitterness and enjoys having a young one to take care of now. He imagines that she's a welcome companion and more-than-competent caregiver to her client, but he seriously doubts that she has an injury that warrants permanent disability status.

He likes Mrs. Darrell, recognizing her strength and resilience—she raised her family single-handedly and now cares for her granddaughter. He also suspects she is a capable and devoted caregiver to her elderly client. However, Dr. Lowe seriously doubts that her injury justifies permanent disability status.

ethical_issues.question: In the doctor-patient relationship, how should physicians address the issue of trust regarding the veracity of a patient’s statements, particularly in the absence of clear evidence?
keypoints: Physicians should reasonably and respectfully believe the patient’s account in the absence of clear and convincing evidence to the contrary, especially regarding subjective symptoms such as pain.

Physicians ought to candidly communicate their professional assessment of the patient’s injury and functional status, clearly indicating whether the criteria for disability are met, while maintaining an open and respectful dialogue.

Physicians should collaborate with patients to develop a treatment plan focused on functional recovery and pain relief, including interventions such as physical therapy, to promote the patient’s overall well-being.

The fundamental goal of the physician-patient relationship is to enhance the patient’s health and functional restoration rather than solely to secure financial compensation; physicians should uphold this principle in guiding clinical care and communication.

ethical_issues.question: How should physicians balance patient welfare with the potential for financial compensation when providing medical evidence of disability?
keypoints: Physicians should base their assessments on professional judgment and rational evaluation of the patient’s reported symptoms, extending trust especially in the absence of clear contradictory evidence.
Physicians should maintain ongoing communication with the patient to dynamically assess their capacity to return to work and functional status.

Physicians should assist patients in formulating and implementing rehabilitation plans, including physical therapy, to promote pain relief and functional recovery, prioritizing the patient’s well-being.

Medical evidence provided by physicians regarding disability should adhere to principles of objectivity and truthfulness, avoiding the influence of financial compensation considerations, thereby preserving the professionalism and integrity of the doctor-patient relationship.

title: When a Nonadherent Patient Needs Your Care
case:
Dr. Jefferson, an OB/GYN in private practice, first took care of Ms Carr when her mother brought the 15 year-old girl in for a pregnancy evaluation. The test was positive, and Ms Carr's mother accompanied her daughter on every prenatal visit. After a successful delivery, Dr. Jefferson brought up the topic of birth control. Ms Carr, partly on the insistence of her mother, wanted to take birth control pills because she had heard that they improved one's complexion and didn't cause much weight gain. Concerned about the 15-year-old's ability to stick with a contraceptive that required daily vigilance, Dr. Jefferson suggested taking a longer acting contraceptive, but Ms Carr insisted that birth control pills were the only kind of contraceptive she wanted.
Over the next 3 years, Dr. Jefferson saw Ms Carr for routine care, including renewing her prescription for birth control pills, always accompanied by her mother. One day, she came in without her mother; and Dr. Jefferson learned that the 2 had had a falling out and Ms Carr had moved in with her boyfriend.
Ms Carr missed a scheduled appointment, and when Dr. Jefferson saw her again, she was several weeks pregnant. When asked why she had missed her appointments, Ms Carr replied that she couldn't make it at the scheduled time and didn't think that missing an appointment was such a big deal–she wanted to get pregnant. During the visit, Dr. Jefferson stressed the importance of prenatal care for the health of both Ms Carr and her baby and the need for Ms Carr to come to all her scheduled appointments.
Ms Carr made her next appointment before she left the office but she failed to keep it. She did not respond to several calls prompted by Dr. Jefferson's tickler file for women receiving prenatal care. Four months into her pregnancy, Ms Carr appeared without an appointment. When asked about the missed appointment, Ms Carr apologized. "I know I should have come, but I have a job and another child to take care of and now that I live with my boyfriend, your office is much farther away than when I lived with my mother. I can't take off work without being docked and I can't leave the 3-year-old after I get home. I knew you needed to see me." Dr. Jefferson was worried about how Ms Carr looked; she had gained too much weight. Dr. Jefferson went ahead and saw her at the unscheduled time. She did an exam and got blood work. She sent Ms Carr away with a printed diet that called for less salt, decreased carbohydrates, and fewer calories in general.
The lab work showed that Ms Carr's blood sugar was elevated, so Dr. Jefferson had the office secretary call to schedule an urgent appointment because of concerns about gestational diabetes and its potential negative impact on the fetus.
Despite repeated attempts to contact her, Ms Carr didn't return to the doctor's office until 4 weeks later, now 5 months pregnant. She had gained more weight and had some swelling in her ankles. Dr. Jefferson informed her of the importance of closely monitoring and treating her diabetes, and that it might be better if Ms Carr found a physician closer to home or work whom she could get to more regularly. Dr. Jefferson said that Ms Carr's last trimester should be monitored carefully and that she, Dr. Jefferson, would help Ms Carr find another physician. Two weeks later, Dr. Jefferson was happy to receive a request from a colleague for Ms Carr's medical records.
One month later, Dr. Jefferson received a call from labor and delivery at a hospital where she attends. A nurse's aide said that Ms Carr had showed up at the ER in premature labor and had been admitted. When asked who her doctor was, Ms Carr promptly gave Dr. Jefferson's name.
